He traveled in North Africa in search of exotic subject matter rather than relying on classical Greek and Roman models.
His Romanticism is characterized as individualist, avoiding sentimentality and bombast.
Together with Ingres, Delacroix is considered one of the last old masters of painting; he was also one of the few old masters ever photographed.

overview.text: Boston is the capital and most populous city of Massachusetts. It is a cultural and financial center of New England, the northeastern U.S. region. English Puritan settlers founded it on the Shawmut Peninsula in 1630 and named it after Boston, Lincolnshire, England.

Boston became a major port, manufacturing center, and education and culture center after American independence. It is closely associated with major American Revolution events, including the Boston Massacre, Boston Tea Party, Battle of Bunker Hill, and Siege of Boston.

key_facts.text: Boston Common, established in 1634, is identified as the nation’s first public park.
Boston Latin School, founded in 1635, is identified as the nation’s first public school.
The Tremont Street subway, opened in 1897, is identified as the first subway system.
Boston is a major center for higher education and research and has become a large biotechnology hub.

overview.text: Jack London (born John Griffith Chaney; 1876–1916) was an American novelist, journalist, and activist. He helped pioneer commercial fiction in American magazines and became an international celebrity. His most famous works include The Call of the Wild and White Fang, both set in Alaska and the Yukon during the Klondike Gold Rush. His short stories include “To Build a Fire,” and his writing also addressed animal welfare, workers’ rights, and socialism.

key_facts.text: London belonged to “The Crowd,” a radical literary group in San Francisco.
The Iron Heel is a dystopian novel, while The People of the Abyss is a nonfiction exposé.
Other short stories include “An Odyssey of the North” and “Love of Life.”
He wrote about the South Pacific in stories such as “The Pearls of Parlay” and “The Heathen.”

overview.text: Ohio is a state in the Midwestern United States. It borders Lake Erie and Ontario to the north and five states: Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky, Indiana, and Michigan. Its landscape includes broad rolling glaciated plains, rugged southeastern hills, and a Lake Erie shoreline. Columbus is the capital and most populous city; Cleveland, Cincinnati, Dayton, Akron, and Toledo are other major metropolitan centers.

The region, once called the Ohio Country, was inhabited by Algonquian and Iroquoian nations and contested by Native American tribes, Britain, and France. After American independence, it became part of the Northwest Territory and achieved statehood in 1803. Ohio’s economic identity includes manufacturing and agriculture, while attractions range from Cuyahoga Valley National Park to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

key_facts.text: Ohio’s name comes from the Ohio River, whose name derives from a Seneca term interpreted as “good river,” “great river,” or “large creek.”
The nickname “Buckeye State” refers to Ohio buckeye trees.
The Wright brothers designed and built the world’s first successful airplane in Ohio; its first flight took place in North Carolina.
Other major Ohio attractions include Cedar Point and the National Museum of the United States Air Force.

overview.text: The domestic pigeon is a domesticated bird derived from the rock dove, Columba livia. Although it is often called a subspecies, it is not an accepted zoological subspecies; the domestic pigeon instead represents a collection of more than 350 breeds. Its long relationship with humans connects it to animal domestication, cultural symbolism, urban ecology, and communication through its homing ability.

key_facts.text: Evidence from Mesopotamian cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs places pigeon domestication more than 5,000 years ago.
People have kept pigeons as food, pets, symbolic animals, and messengers.
Homing ability enabled pigeons to carry messages, including as war pigeons during both world wars.
Urban pigeons are generally feral rather than domesticated individuals and are often regarded as pests because of their droppings and a reputation for spreading disease.

overview.text: French (français) is a Romance language in the Indo-European family. It descended from Vulgar Latin, with influence from Celtic languages of northern Roman Gaul and the Germanic language of the Franks. French largely supplanted most regional Romance varieties across France, Belgium, and Switzerland; its closest relatives include the langues d’oïl historically spoken in northern France and southern Belgium.

French spread through French and Belgian colonialism to parts of the Americas, Africa, and Asia, where French-based creoles such as Haitian Creole developed. It has a long history as an international language of literature, diplomacy, and science, and is used by many international organizations. A French-speaking person or nation may be called Francophone.

key_facts.text: French is spoken as a first language in places including France, Quebec, Wallonia and Brussels, western Switzerland, Luxembourg, and Monaco.
In Francophone Africa, French is often used as a second language or lingua franca, though it is native in some urban areas.
French is an official language in 26 countries, and the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie has 54 member states that share its use or teaching.
French is used by international institutions including the United Nations, European Union, NATO, and the International Olympic Committee.

overview.text: Leonardo da Vinci’s The Last Supper is a High Renaissance mural in the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, painted around 1495–1498. It shows Jesus with the Twelve Apostles just after announcing that one of them will betray him, a scene drawn from the Gospel of John. Its carefully organized space, use of perspective, sense of movement, and varied human emotion have made it one of Leonardo’s most recognizable and celebrated works.

key_facts.text: The work is also known by the Italian titles Il Cenacolo and L’Ultima Cena.
It was commissioned during renovations to the church and convent by Leonardo’s patron, Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan.
Leonardo used tempera on gesso, pitch, and mastic, materials that permitted repeated alterations.
Environmental conditions and intentional damage severely affected the mural; little of the original remains despite repeated restorations, the last completed in 1999.
It is Leonardo’s largest work apart from the Sala delle Asse.

overview.text: The Birth of Venus (Nascita di Venere) is Sandro Botticelli’s Renaissance painting of Venus arriving at the shore after emerging fully grown from the sea. Probably made in the mid-1480s, it is held in Florence’s Uffizi Gallery. Its subject is a traditional scene from classical Greek mythology.

The painting is closely discussed with Botticelli’s Primavera, another large mythological work in the Uffizi, although the two are not a pair. Its direct, sensory appeal has helped make it an enduringly popular work of Italian Renaissance art.

key_facts.text: Its large scale and prominent nude female figure were highly unusual in Western art after classical antiquity.
The image of Venus emerging from the sea fully grown is known as Venus Anadyomene.
Art historians commonly connect the painting with the imitation of ancient painters and with wedding celebrations; a Neoplatonic interpretation remains debated.
The identity of the commissioner is unresolved, and the older idea that it and Primavera shared a Medici patron is now uncertain.

overview.text: Olympus Mons is a shield volcano on Mars associated with the Tharsis Montes region. It rises 21.287 kilometers and is Mars’s tallest volcano and tallest planetary mountain. It is approximately tied with Rheasilvia on Vesta for the tallest mountain currently discovered in the Solar System.

The volcano formed during Mars’s Hesperian Period, with eruptions continuing into the Amazonian Period. Astronomers recognized it in the late 19th century as the albedo feature Nix Olympica, and its mountainous nature was suspected before space probes confirmed it.

key_facts.text: Olympus Mons is the youngest of Mars’s large volcanoes.
Its last eruption occurred about 25 million years ago.
Two provisionally named impact craters on it are suspected source areas for shergottites, the most abundant class of Martian meteorites.

overview.text: Sicily (Sicilia) is an island in the central Mediterranean and one of Italy’s twenty regions. It lies south of the Italian Peninsula and is both the largest and most populous island in the Mediterranean. Sicily is one of Italy’s five autonomous regions and is considered part of southern Italy. The Strait of Messina separates it from Calabria. Its prominent natural landmark is Mount Etna, the tallest active volcano in Europe.

key_facts.text: The island’s name comes from the Sicels, an Iron Age people who lived in eastern Sicily.
Phoenician and Greek colonies developed along Sicily’s coasts; the island became a center of Magna Graecia.
After Giuseppe Garibaldi’s Expedition of the Thousand and a plebiscite, Sicily became part of unified Italy in 1860.
Sicily received special status as an autonomous administrative division in 1946.

overview.text: Roald Dahl’s 1964 children’s novel follows young Charlie Bucket during his adventures inside the chocolate factory run by Willy Wonka, an eccentric chocolatier. The factory is the story’s central setting, making chocolate-making, unusual inventions, and Wonka’s secrecy central associations with the book.

Dahl drew inspiration from chocolate companies that gave schoolchildren new products to test and from industrial secrecy between major English chocolate makers. These influences help explain the story’s recipe-protecting spies and its elaborate factory machinery.

key_facts.text: The novel was first published in the United States in 1964 and in the United Kingdom 11 months later.
Its sequel, Charlie and the Great Glass Elevator, appeared in 1972; Dahl planned a third installment but never completed it.
Two major film adaptations are Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory (1971) and Charlie and the Chocolate Factory (2005).
A separate 2023 film, Wonka, explores Willy Wonka’s origins.
In 2012, Royal Mail issued a first-class stamp depicting Charlie Bucket with a Golden Ticket.

overview.text: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a colorless, normally odorless gas made of carbon and oxygen. It is central to the carbon cycle: plants, algae, and cyanobacteria use it in photosynthesis, while aerobic organisms release it during respiration. Dissolved CO₂ participates in water chemistry associated with ocean acidification. In the atmosphere, it absorbs infrared radiation and acts as a greenhouse gas. The rise in CO₂ from fossil-fuel burning is a primary cause of climate change; land and ocean sinks absorb some excess, but that storage can be temporary.

key_facts.text: Its chemical formula is CO₂: each molecule has one carbon atom covalently double-bonded to two oxygen atoms.
When CO₂ dissolves in water, it forms carbonate and mainly bicarbonate; increasing atmospheric CO₂ contributes to ocean acidification.
Carbon can eventually be stored long-term in rocks and organic deposits such as coal, petroleum, and natural gas.
Commercial uses include fertilizer production, enhanced oil recovery, food and beverage production, cooling, fire suppression, and greenhouse plant growth.

overview.text: Joan of Arc (Jeanne d’Arc, c. 1412–1431) was a French military leader during the Hundred Years’ War. She claimed divine guidance and became associated with the French cause as a defender of the nation. In 1429, her arrival at Orléans helped inspire French forces, and the English abandoned their siege nine days later. Her victories helped open the route to Reims, where Charles VII was crowned with Joan beside him.

Joan was later captured by Burgundian forces, transferred to the English, tried for heresy, and burned at the stake in 1431. A 1456 investigation overturned the verdict, finding serious procedural problems. She became a national symbol of France and was canonized by Pope Benedict XV in 1920.

key_facts.text: Joan came from a propertied peasant family in Domrémy, in northeastern France.
In testimony, Joan said visions from the archangel Michael, Saint Margaret, and Saint Catherine guided her mission.
Her capture occurred in 1430 while she was organizing volunteers to relieve Compiègne, which was besieged by Burgundian allies of the English.
In 1922, she was declared one of France’s patron saints, two years after her canonization.

overview.text: In number theory, a perfect number is a positive integer whose proper positive divisors—its divisors other than itself—add up to the number. The smallest examples are 6 and 28: 1+2+3=6, while 1+2+4+7+14=28.

Perfect numbers connect an elementary divisor-sum test with a long history in number theory. The idea appears in Euclid’s Elements, and later work produced the Euclid–Euler theorem about the form of even perfect numbers. Important questions remain open: no odd perfect number is known, and it is unknown whether infinitely many perfect numbers exist.

key_facts.text: The sum of a number’s proper divisors is called its aliquot sum; a perfect number equals its aliquot sum.
Euclid’s formation rule involves what is now called a Mersenne prime; Euler later proved that every even perfect number has this form.
Beyond 6 and 28, the sequence includes 496 and 8128.

overview.text: Frank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959) was an American architect, designer, writer, and educator who played a key role in twentieth-century architecture. He called his approach “organic architecture,” which aimed to design in harmony with people and the environment. Fallingwater exemplified this philosophy.

Wright pioneered the Prairie School movement and developed the concept of the Usonian home within Broadacre City, his vision for American urban planning. His work included churches, schools, skyscrapers, hotels, museums, and commercial buildings, with elements such as windows, furniture, and floors integrated into the structures.

key_facts.text: Wright opened his own Chicago practice in 1893 and established a studio at his Oak Park, Illinois, home in 1898.
Wright mentored hundreds of apprentices in his Taliesin Fellowship.
In 2019, a selection of Wright’s work became a World Heritage Site under the name “The 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright.”

overview.text: Albert Einstein was a German-born theoretical physicist whose work linked relativity, gravitation, quantum theory, and cosmology. His special theory of relativity yielded mass–energy equivalence, expressed as E = mc². His general theory of relativity extended his mechanics to incorporate gravitation and informed models of the universe’s structure and evolution. Einstein also studied the photoelectric effect and argued that light consists of particles later called photons, connecting his work to quantum physics.

key_facts.text: Einstein’s 1905 “annus mirabilis,” or miracle year, included papers on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity, and mass–energy equivalence.
He proposed general relativity in 1915; a later paper introduced the cosmological constant and helped establish modern theoretical cosmology.
He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his services to theoretical physics, especially his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.
His work on stimulated emission supplied the core mechanism behind lasers and masers.
With Satyendra Nath Bose, Einstein laid the groundwork for Bose–Einstein statistics.

overview.text: Georgia is a U.S. state in the Southeast, South Atlantic, and Deep South. It borders Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, Alabama, and Florida, with the Atlantic Ocean along its eastern edge. Atlanta is both the state capital and its largest city.

The Province of Georgia was established in 1732, with Savannah founded in 1733. As a British royal colony, Georgia was the last and southernmost of the original Thirteen Colonies. It ratified the Constitution in 1788, seceded in 1861, and was the last state readmitted to the Union after the Civil War.

key_facts.text: Georgia includes the Blue Ridge Mountains, part of the Appalachian range, and the Piedmont plateau. Most of the state has a humid subtropical climate.
Among the 50 states, Georgia ranks 24th in area and eighth in population.
After Reconstruction, Henry W. Grady promoted the “New South” idea, emphasizing reconciliation and industrialization.
Martin Luther King Jr. was among notable Georgians who became key leaders in the mid-20th-century civil rights movement.

overview.text: One Hundred Years of Solitude is a 1967 novel by Colombian author Gabriel García Márquez. It tells the multigenerational story of the Buendía family, whose patriarch, José Arcadio Buendía, founded the fictitious town of Macondo. Its magical-realist style and themes connect it to the Latin American Boom, a literary movement of the 1960s and 1970s.

The novel is widely acclaimed and recognized as a significant work in both the Hispanic literary canon and world literature. Its central recognition associations are García Márquez, the Buendías, Macondo, magical realism, and the Latin American Boom.

key_facts.text: Its original Spanish title is Cien años de soledad.
The novel was first published in Buenos Aires in May 1967 by Editorial Sudamericana.
It has been translated into 46 languages and has sold more than 50 million copies.

overview.text: Sparta was a prominent ancient Greek polis in Laconia, in the southeastern Peloponnese. In classical antiquity, Lacedaemon named the state, while Sparta referred to its capital. It became the Greek world’s leading land military power during the 7th century BC and retained that position until its defeat at Leuctra in 371 BC.

Sparta founded the Peloponnesian League and later led it against Athens in the Peloponnesian War, emerging victorious in 404 BC. Its society was unusually militarized: Spartiate citizens focused on military training, including the agoge, while helots—state-owned enslaved locals—formed most of the population.

key_facts.text: During the second Persian invasion of Greece, Spartan forces played major roles at Thermopylae under Leonidas and Plataea under Pausanias.
After the Peloponnesian War, Spartan armies under Agesilaus II campaigned in western Anatolian satrapies of the Achaemenid Empire to protect Ionian cities.
Epaminondas defeated Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC; this victory began Theban hegemony and coincided with the freeing of Messenia from Spartan rule.
Spartan society included full-citizen Spartiates, free non-citizens such as perioikoi and mothakes, and helots; social mobility was nearly nonexistent.
Admiration for Sparta in later Western culture is known as Laconophilia.

overview.text: The Phillips curve is a macroeconomic representation of the relationship between unemployment and inflation. Its central idea is a short-run tradeoff: lower unemployment can coincide with higher inflation, making price stability and very low unemployment competing goals in the model.

Later economic analysis argued that this tradeoff does not persist in the long run: inflationary policies would not permanently reduce unemployment. The curve remains relevant because central banks use it to help understand and forecast inflation, although its predictive usefulness has been debated.

key_facts.text: Economist Bill Phillips identified the relationship; Paul Samuelson and Robert Solow later explicitly connected employment and inflation, while Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps developed theoretical arguments about it.
In 1967 and 1968, Friedman and Phelps argued that the Phillips curve applies only in the short run.
Friedman correctly predicted the stagflation of the 1970s.
The curve’s slope appeared to decline in the 2010s; a 2022 study found it was small even during the early 1980s.

overview.text: Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, Op. 27 No. 2, is marked “Quasi una fantasia.” He completed it in 1801 and dedicated it the following year to his pupil, Countess Julie “Giulietta” Guicciardi.

The work is widely called the Moonlight Sonata, though Beethoven did not give it that name. The nickname grew from imagery later proposed by poet Ludwig Rellstab; the sonata was already popular during Beethoven’s lifetime and remains among his most famous piano compositions.

key_facts.text: The sonata was written when Beethoven was around 30 years old.
Its familiar Moonlight title is a later nickname, not Beethoven’s original title.
Beethoven wrote it after completing some commissioned work, but there is no evidence that this sonata itself was commissioned.

overview.text: Munich (München) is the capital and most populous city of Bavaria, Germany. It lies on the Isar River north of the Alps and is the seat of the Upper Bavarian administrative region. The city is a major center for science, technology, finance, business, tourism, and culture.

Munich combines an important role in Bavarian and German history with a modern economy based on high technology, automobiles, engineering, and services. Its recognizable cultural profile includes historic architecture, cultural venues, sports events, exhibitions, and the annual Oktoberfest.

key_facts.text: Munich’s first recorded mention dates to 1158; it became the capital of the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806.
The city remained a Catholic stronghold during the Reformation and became a center of political movements, including the rise of the Nazi Party, in the 1920s.
Munich was heavily bombed during World War II, but much of its historic architecture was later restored. It hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics and the 1974 FIFA World Cup final.
BMW, Siemens, Allianz SE, and Munich Re are among the multinational companies headquartered in Munich; the city also has two research universities.
Oktoberfest is held annually in Munich and is described as the world’s largest Volksfest, or large popular festival.

overview.text: In the biblical account in 1 Samuel, Goliath is a giant Philistine warrior who challenges the Israelites to single combat. David, described as a young shepherd, accepts the challenge, knocks Goliath down with a stone from a sling, and then uses Goliath’s sword to behead him. The episode also presents King Saul’s failure to face Goliath as evidence of Saul’s unfitness to rule.

The name “David and Goliath” has become a common expression for an underdog contest between a smaller, weaker opponent and a much stronger one. Some modern scholars have proposed that an earlier version of the story credited Goliath’s death to Elhanan rather than David, though the familiar biblical account names David.

key_facts.text: Goliath issues a challenge for one-on-one combat instead of asking the armies to fight him together.
David’s weapon is a sling, and the stone fells Goliath before the beheading.
The story connects Saul’s refusal to accept Goliath’s challenge with the king’s unfitness to rule.
“David and Goliath” is widely used as a metaphor for an underdog facing a much stronger adversary.
Second Samuel contains a passage in which Elhanan is said to kill Goliath the Gittite, leading some scholars to argue that the tradition was later associated with David.

overview.text: George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950) was an Irish playwright, critic, polemicist, and political activist born in Dublin. He wrote more than sixty plays, including Man and Superman, Pygmalion, and Saint Joan. His work combined contemporary satire with historical allegory, and his influence extended across Western theatre, culture, and politics. He received the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature.
Influenced by Henrik Ibsen, Shaw sought to bring new realism to English-language drama. He also used plays to present political, social, and religious ideas.

key_facts.text: Arms and the Man was Shaw’s first public success, in 1894.
After joining the Fabian Society, a gradualist political group, Shaw became its most prominent pamphleteer.
Shaw wrote the screenplay for a 1938 filmed version of Pygmalion and received an Academy Award for it.
The term “Shavian” refers to Shaw’s ideas and his characteristic way of expressing them.

overview.text: Electronegativity (χ) describes how strongly an atom attracts shared electrons in a chemical bond. It helps estimate bond polarity and bond energy, and describes bonds along a continuum from covalent to ionic. Nuclear charge, electron shielding, and the distance of valence electrons from the nucleus affect this attraction.

Electronegativity is calculated rather than directly measured. The commonly used Pauling scale is dimensionless; different calculation methods may produce slightly different values but preserve the same periodic trends. On that scale, fluorine is highest at 3.98 and caesium lowest at 0.79.

key_facts.text: Linus Pauling proposed his electronegativity scale in 1932, basing it on bond energies and valence bond theory.
Hydrogen has a Pauling electronegativity value of 2.20.
Electronegativity is usually treated as a property of an atom within a molecule, so its value can vary somewhat with chemical environment.
Electropositivity is the contrasting tendency to donate valence electrons.

overview.text: Real numbers describe continuous one-dimensional quantities such as length, duration, and temperature. They can be pictured as points on the real number line, where integers are equally spaced; each real number can be represented, almost uniquely, by an infinite decimal expansion.

The real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers. They are fundamental to calculus, especially its ideas of limits, continuity, and derivatives, and to real analysis, the study of real functions and real-valued sequences.

key_facts.text: The set of real numbers is commonly written using a bold or blackboard-bold R.
√2 is an algebraic irrational real number, while π is a transcendental real number—that is, it is not a root of a polynomial with rational coefficients.
The term “real” distinguishes these numbers from imaginary numbers, such as square roots of negative numbers.
A rigorous modern definition treats the reals as a Dedekind-complete ordered field; equivalent constructions use Cauchy sequences or Dedekind cuts.

overview.text: A ribosome is a molecular machine made of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins. Found in all cells, it produces proteins by translating the genetic information in messenger RNA (mRNA). During this process, the ribosome reads mRNA codons and works with transfer RNA (tRNA) to connect amino acids into a polypeptide chain. Each ribosome consists of a small subunit and a large subunit, both containing rRNA and ribosomal proteins.

key_facts.text: Ribosome biogenesis—the production of functional ribosomes—involves making and processing rRNA and assembling ribosomal proteins into subunits.
Ribosomes vary among bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes, but share a core structure reflecting a common evolutionary origin.
Eukaryotic mitochondria, and the chloroplasts of plants and algae, contain distinct ribosomes.
George Emil Palade first observed ribosomes in 1955.
Ribosome discovery was recognized by the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; research determining ribosome structure and mechanism received the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

overview.text: Temperature is a quantitative measure of how energy is distributed among the microscopic particles in a system. In classical thermodynamics and kinetic theory, it reflects the particles’ average kinetic energy. A thermometer measures temperature, which is commonly expressed in Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F), or kelvins (K).

The kelvin is used especially in science and is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units. Temperature matters across natural sciences—including physics, chemistry, Earth science, astronomy, and biology—as well as in everyday life.

key_facts.text: Absolute zero is 0 K, equal to −273.15 °C or −459.67 °F. It can be approached experimentally but not reached.
Temperature scales are calibrated using reference points and thermometric substances.
Negative absolute temperatures can exist; thermodynamically, they are hotter than any positive temperature.

overview.text: Anna Karenina is a Russian novel by Leo Tolstoy, first published in book form in 1878 after appearing serially. It is often regarded as a major work of world literature. The novel centers on Anna’s extramarital affair with cavalry officer Count Alexei Kirillovich Vronsky, which scandalizes Saint Petersburg society.

Alongside betrayal and desire, the novel explores faith, family, marriage, Imperial Russian society, and the contrast between rural and urban life. Trains and railway stations recur as an important motif, while the story unfolds amid reforms under Alexander II and rapid social change.

key_facts.text: Tolstoy called Anna Karenina his first true novel.
Anna and Vronsky flee to Italy in pursuit of happiness before returning to Russia, where their lives continue to unravel.
The novel has been adapted for theater, opera, film, television, ballet, figure skating, and radio drama.

overview.text: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (1818) is an English Gothic novel by Mary Shelley. Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist, discovers how to create life and assembles a large humanoid creature from human body parts. Horrified by the result, Victor abandons it, beginning the novel’s central conflict.

The creature learns language, writing, and reading while observing a family, but humans repeatedly reject or attack it. It confronts Victor, whose experiment is followed by murders, pursuit, and an Arctic conclusion. The novel combines Gothic and Romantic elements and has influenced later literature and popular culture. The name Frankenstein is also often used to refer to the creature.

key_facts.text: The first edition was published anonymously in London on 1 January 1818; a revised edition appeared under Shelley’s name in 1831.
While observing a family, the creature learns to speak, write, and read; its reading includes Paradise Lost.
Victor studies at the University of Ingolstadt and later marries Elizabeth Lavenza, his childhood friend.
Shelley’s idea emerged during a 1816 ghost-story-writing challenge involving Lord Byron, Percy Shelley, and John Polidori.
Captain Robert Walton rescues Victor after he nearly dies from exhaustion and hypothermia in the Arctic; Walton hears Victor’s account before his crew turns back.

overview.text: Tibet is a region in western East Asia covering much of the Tibetan Plateau, the homeland of the Tibetans. It lies within the Himalayas and is described as Earth’s highest region by average elevation; Mount Everest is its highest point and the world’s highest peak.

Tibetan Buddhism is the region’s dominant religion and strongly shapes its art, music, and festivals; Bön is another indigenous tradition. Tibet also has a major historical association with Tibetan political rule: the Yarlung dynasty expanded in the seventh century, and the Tibetan Empire became a large regional power by the ninth.

key_facts.text: The modern Chinese state governs most of the historical region through the Tibet Autonomous Region and autonomous prefectures in several provinces.
The Tibetan Empire once extended from the Tarim Basin and Pamirs to Yunnan and Bengal, ruling over several non-Tibetan peoples.
After the empire dissolved, Tibet was divided among principalities and tribal groups; central and peripheral areas sometimes came under Chinese or Mongol patronage.
Tibetan cuisine prominently includes roasted barley, yak meat, and butter tea.

overview.text: Beijing, also known as Peking, is China’s capital in Northern China. It is governed as a provincial-level municipality with 16 municipal districts, is mostly surrounded by Hebei Province, and borders Tianjin to the southeast.

The city combines modern development with a long imperial and cultural history. Its recorded history spans more than three millennia, while landmarks include the Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, Summer Palace, sections of the Great Wall, and traditional hutong alleys between siheyuan courtyard homes.

key_facts.text: Beijing is one of China’s Four Great Ancient Capitals and was the country’s political center for most of the past eight centuries.
In 2022, Beijing became the first city to host both the Summer and Winter Olympics, as well as both sets of Paralympic Games.
Beijing is a major international center for diplomacy, politics, finance, education, research, culture, and technology.
Tsinghua University and Peking University are among the city’s prominent universities, while Zhongguancun is a center of scientific and technological innovation.

overview.text: Peru is a country in western South America with a Pacific coast. Its landscape includes arid coastal plains, the Andes Mountains, and tropical Amazon basin rainforest, giving it major geographic variety. Lima is the capital and largest city. Peru also has a long history of civilization, including the Caral-Supe, Nazca, Moche, Wari, Cusco, and Inca cultures.

key_facts.text: Peru borders Ecuador and Colombia to the north, Brazil to the east, Bolivia to the southeast, and Chile to the south; the Pacific Ocean lies to its south and west.
The Andes extend through Peru from the north toward the southeast, while tropical Amazon basin rainforest is located in the east.
The Caral-Supe civilization, located in ancient Peru, is described as the earliest civilization in the Americas.
The Inca Empire, which developed in the region, was the largest known state in the pre-Columbian Americas.
Spanish is the main spoken language; Quechuan languages, Aymara, and other Indigenous languages are also spoken.

overview.text: The United States Constitution is the supreme law of the United States. It replaced the Articles of Confederation in 1789 and established the basic structure of the federal government. Its first three articles divide federal power among a bicameral Congress, a president-led executive branch, and a judiciary headed by the Supreme Court. Later articles address relations between the states and federal government, constitutional amendments, and ratification.

The Constitution has been amended 27 times. The first ten amendments, called the Bill of Rights, protect individual liberty and limit government power; later amendments expanded civil-rights protections and changed government procedures. The document remains central to U.S. law and has influenced constitutions in other countries.

key_facts.text: The Constitutional Convention met at Independence Hall in Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787.
Its design drew on English common law and Enlightenment thinkers including John Locke and Montesquieu.
The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments are collectively known as the Reconstruction Amendments.
Constitutional amendments are appended to the document rather than inserted into its original text.

overview.text: Sappho was an ancient Greek poet from Lesbos, active around 630–570 BC. She wrote lyric poetry—poems intended to be sung with musical accompaniment. Most of her work is lost or survives only in fragments; the Ode to Aphrodite is the only poem considered certainly complete.

Her surviving poetry is associated with love, family, religion, and intensely personal emotion. It is known for clear language, vivid images, and immediacy. Sappho was admired in antiquity, included among the Nine Lyric Poets honored by Hellenistic Alexandrian scholars, and continues to influence writers. She also became a symbol of love and desire between women.

key_facts.text: Ancient admirers gave Sappho titles such as the “Tenth Muse” and “The Poetess.”
Her poems may have been composed for both solo and choral performance; many of the best-preserved fragments were probably intended for solo performance.
The English words sapphic and lesbian derive from Sappho’s name and the name of her home island, Lesbos, respectively.
Little is certain about her life: even her birthplace is given as either Eresos or Mytilene, both on Lesbos.

overview.text: A galaxy is a gravitationally bound system of stars, planetary systems, stellar remnants, substellar objects, interstellar gas, dust, and dark matter. Stars orbit the galaxy’s center of mass; the Milky Way is the galaxy containing the Solar System.

Galaxies are classified by visual forms such as elliptical, spiral, and irregular. They may also be recognized by unusual properties, including interactions, unusually rapid star formation, or active galactic nuclei, and they occur in larger groups and clusters.

key_facts.text: Most of the mass in a typical galaxy is dark matter; only a small fraction is visible in stars and nebulae.
Supermassive black holes are a common feature at the centers of galaxies.
The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy in the Local Group, which includes Andromeda; the Local Group is part of the Virgo Supercluster.
Galaxy formation is less well understood than star formation and operates on a billion-year timescale.
Galaxies occasionally collide during their lifetimes.

overview.text: One Thousand and One Nights, also called The Arabian Nights, is a collection of Middle Eastern folktales assembled in Arabic during the Islamic Golden Age. It developed over many centuries through the work of authors, translators, and scholars, drawing on Arabic, Persian, Mesopotamian, and Indian-related traditions.

Its central frame story features Scheherazade telling tales to the ruler Shahryar, with one story leading into another across successive nights. Some tales contain additional stories, while others stand alone; surviving editions differ in their selection and arrangement.

key_facts.text: There is no surviving single canonical version with every tale in a fixed order; editions may contain several hundred nights or 1,001 or more.
Aladdin and Ali Baba were added to the collection by French translator Antoine Galland after he heard them from Syrian writer Hanna Diyab; they were not in the original Arabic versions.
Sinbad’s voyages existed independently before appearing in later manuscripts and translations of the collection.
The work is primarily prose, but it also includes verse used for songs, riddles, and heightened emotion.

overview.text: A centaur is a creature from Greek mythology with a human upper body and the lower body and legs of a horse. Myths associate centaurs especially with mountainous Thessaly, making them a distinctive hybrid figure in Greek myth.

Centaurs are often portrayed as wild, like untamed horses. The figure later appeared in Roman mythology, medieval bestiaries, and modern fantastic literature, giving this mythological creature a long cultural afterlife.

key_facts.text: One mythic version says centaurs were named after Centaurus and were related to the Lapiths through his brother Lapithes.
Their supposed habitats included Magnesia and Mount Pelion in Thessaly, the Foloi oak forest in Elis, and the Malean peninsula in southern Laconia.
Centaur is also associated with the terms hippocentaur and the Ancient Greek kéntauros; the group was collectively called the Centaurs or Ixionidae.

overview.text: Kurt Vonnegut (1922–2007) was an American author known for satirical and darkly humorous novels. Over more than fifty years, he also published short-story collections, plays, and nonfiction.

Vonnegut served in World War II, was captured during the Battle of the Bulge, and survived the Allied bombing of Dresden while imprisoned there. His breakthrough novel, Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), gained attention for its anti-war sentiment during the Vietnam War. Vonnegut was also praised for his darkly humorous commentary on American society.

key_facts.text: Player Piano (1952) was Vonnegut’s first novel; it received favorable reviews but sold poorly.
The Sirens of Titan (1959) and Cat’s Cradle (1963) were nominated for the Hugo Award for best science-fiction novel.
Welcome to the Monkey House, a collection of short stories, appeared in 1968.
Later works included Fates Worse Than Death (1991) and A Man Without a Country (2005).

overview.text: The Brothers Karamazov, also translated as The Karamazov Brothers, is Fyodor Dostoevsky’s sixteenth and final novel. Published in serial form from 1879 to 1880, it is set in nineteenth-century Russia. Its plot centers on patricide, while its philosophical and theological concerns include God, free will, morality, faith, doubt, and reason. The novel connects these questions to a society undergoing modernization.

key_facts.text: The Russian title is Братья Карамазовы, romanized as Brat'ya Karamazovy.
Dostoevsky spent nearly two years writing the novel.
It appeared serially in The Russian Messenger from January 1879 through November 1880.
Dostoevsky died less than four months after the novel’s publication.
Much of the novel was composed in Staraya Russa, which inspired its main setting.

overview.text: Tennessee Williams, the pen name of Thomas Lanier Williams III, was an American playwright and screenwriter. His work gained broad recognition with the success of The Glass Menagerie in 1944. He is associated with 20th-century American drama alongside Eugene O’Neill and Arthur Miller.

His major plays include A Streetcar Named Desire, Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, Sweet Bird of Youth, and The Night of the Iguana. Williams’s work was often adapted for film, and he also wrote short stories, poetry, essays, and memoirs.

key_facts.text: Williams wrote his first play in 1930, but his work did not gain much traction until The Glass Menagerie became successful in 1944.
A Streetcar Named Desire (1947) is often included on short lists of the finest American plays of the 20th century.
Cat on a Hot Tin Roof dates to 1955, Sweet Bird of Youth to 1959, and The Night of the Iguana to 1961.
Williams was inducted into the American Theater Hall of Fame in 1979, four years before his death.

overview.text: X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than ultraviolet rays but longer than gamma rays. Their ability to penetrate many solid materials and living tissue makes X-ray radiography useful for medical diagnosis, including checking for broken bones.

X-rays are also useful in materials science, where they can help identify some chemical elements and reveal weak points in construction materials. Because X-rays are ionizing radiation, excessive exposure can damage DNA and harm health, so their production and use are controlled.

key_facts.text: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and called them “X-radiation” to indicate that they were then unknown.
Their approximate wavelength range is 10 nanometers to 10 picometers.
X-ray exposure can cause DNA damage and cancer; very high intensities can also cause burns and radiation sickness.
X-ray radiography is used beyond medicine, including in materials science and the examination of construction materials.

overview.text: Las Meninas is a 1656 oil painting by Diego Velázquez, now in the Museo del Prado in Madrid. It shows a moment in the Spanish court of King Philip IV, with the five-year-old Infanta Margaret Theresa among her entourage. The work belongs to Spain’s Golden Age of painting.

Its complex arrangement makes viewers question what lies inside and outside the painted space. Figures look toward the viewer, while a background mirror reflects the king and queen. This uncertainty has made Las Meninas a major subject in debates about reality, illusion, representation, and the social status of the artist.

key_facts.text: The Spanish title means “The Ladies-in-waiting.”
Velázquez appears inside the scene, working at a large canvas and looking beyond the pictured space toward the viewer.
The entourage includes maids of honour, a chaperone, a bodyguard, two dwarfs, and a dog.
The room is believed to be in Madrid’s Royal Alcázar, the royal residence during Philip IV’s reign.

overview.text: Confucius (c. 551–479 BCE), born Kong Qiu, was a Chinese philosopher of the Spring and Autumn period. His teachings, later called Confucianism, connected personal and governmental morality with harmonious relationships, righteousness, kindness, sincerity, and rulers’ responsibility to lead by virtue. He promoted filial piety—family loyalty, respect for elders, and ancestor veneration—and viewed a strong family as the basis of ideal government.

The Analects compiles sayings about his teachings, although it was assembled years after his death, and scholars caution that not every text or idea associated with him can be confidently attributed to him. Confucianism later received official support under Han Emperor Wu and became deeply integrated into Chinese cultural life.

key_facts.text: Confucius’s “Silver Rule” advises people not to do to others what they would not want done to themselves.
He presented himself as a transmitter of earlier values rather than simply an originator of new ones.
Under Emperor Wu of Han, Confucian ideas gained official sanction, and related works became required reading for paths into government service.
Confucianism developed into Neo-Confucianism during the Tang and Song dynasties and inspired New Confucianism in the twentieth century.

overview.text: The Netherlands is a country in northwestern Europe and the largest of the four constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. It is also informally called Holland and has territories in the Caribbean. European Netherlands borders Germany and Belgium and has a North Sea coastline. Dutch is the official language, with West Frisian also official in Friesland. [p1]

A defining geographic feature is its low, flat landscape: many areas below sea level are polders, created through land reclamation. Historically, the Dutch Republic underwent major political, economic, and cultural development during the Dutch Golden Age, while Dutch trading companies established colonies and trading posts. The country was invaded and occupied by Nazi Germany from 1940 to 1945. [p2]

key_facts.text: About 26% of the Netherlands lies below sea level; land reclamation for polders began in the 14th century. [p2]
Amsterdam is the nominal capital and most populous city, while The Hague contains the main national political institutions. [p3]
The Netherlands has been a parliamentary constitutional monarchy with a unitary structure since 1848. [p4]
Although neutral in World War I, the Netherlands was invaded and occupied by Nazi Germany during World War II. [p2]

overview.text: Chromosomes are DNA-based structures that package part or all of an organism’s genetic material. In eukaryotic cells, histones and other packaging proteins bind and condense the long DNA molecule, helping preserve its integrity. Their three-dimensional organization also plays a role in regulating transcription.

Chromosomes are most readily observed when highly condensed during metaphase, after duplication has produced two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. Recombination involving chromosomes during meiosis and sexual reproduction contributes to genetic diversity.

key_facts.text: Depending on the centromere’s position, a duplicated chromosome may appear X-shaped or as a structure with two arms.
During metaphase, chromosomes align at the cell’s center; in animal cells, they reach their greatest compaction during anaphase.
The term “chromosome” can broadly mean an individualized portion of chromatin, or narrowly mean the condensed, microscope-visible form seen during cell division.
Chromosomal instability and translocation can lead to mitotic catastrophe, usually prompting apoptosis; mutations can sometimes allow cancer to progress instead.

overview.text: Amino acids are organic compounds containing both amino and carboxylic acid functional groups. They are prominent in biology because amino-acid residues are incorporated into proteins and form a major component of muscles and other tissues. The broader amino-acid family can be classified by structural position and by properties such as polarity, ionization, and side-chain type.

key_facts.text: More than 500 amino acids occur in nature, but 22 α-amino acids are identified as the main amino acids incorporated into proteins.
Amino acids may be categorized as α-, β-, or γ-amino acids according to the location of their core functional groups.
Beyond their role in proteins, amino acids participate in processes including neurotransmitter transport and biosynthesis.

overview.text: An enzyme is a biological macromolecule—usually a protein—that acts as a catalyst, speeding chemical reactions without being consumed. The substances it acts on are substrates, which become products. Enzyme-catalyzed steps are central to metabolic pathways, allowing many cellular reactions to proceed at biologically useful rates.

Enzymes work by lowering activation energy while leaving a reaction’s overall equilibrium unchanged. Their three-dimensional shapes give them high specificity, while temperature, pH, activators, and inhibitors can alter their activity. This combination of speed and selectivity makes enzymes useful in cells and in products such as biological washing powders and meat tenderizers.

key_facts.text: The study of enzymes is called enzymology.
Catalytic RNA molecules are called ribozymes and are sometimes classified as enzymes even though they are made of RNA rather than protein.
Inhibitors reduce enzyme activity; some are used as drugs, while others can act as poisons.
If an enzyme loses its structure through denaturation, it can lose its function.
Laundry enzymes break down protein, starch, and fat stains, while papain and related enzymes help tenderize meat by breaking down proteins.

overview.text: Iran, officially the Islamic Republic of Iran and historically known as Persia, is a country in West Asia. It has land borders with several countries and sea frontages on the Caspian Sea to the north and the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman to the south. Its strategically significant location and large fossil-fuel reserves contribute to its regional importance.
Tehran is Iran’s capital and largest city and serves as its primary economic center. The country is divided into five regions and 31 provinces, and it is also a major center of Shia Islam.

key_facts.text: Iran’s land neighbors are Iraq, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan.
The territory of present-day Iran was home to one of the world’s oldest continuous major civilizations and was once a center of Zoroastrianism.
The Safavid dynasty reunited Iran as a state in the 16th century and made Twelver Shia Islam its official religion.
The 1979 Iranian Revolution overthrew the monarchy and established the Islamic Republic of Iran.

overview.text: Iran, historically called Persia, is centered on the Iranian plateau and has one of the world’s oldest continuous civilizations. Its history connects developments in the Middle East and Central Asia with those of Greece, Rome, India, China, and Egypt. Major ancient eras included the Achaemenid, Parthian, and Sasanian Empires; after Alexander’s conquest and Seleucid rule, Iranian states again became major regional powers.

The seventh-century Muslim conquest ended the Sasanian Empire and began Iran’s Islamization. The Safavid dynasty reunited the country in 1501 and converted it to Shia Islam. In modern history, a U.S.- and U.K.-aided 1953 coup removed an elected prime minister, while the Shah’s autocratic monarchy lasted until the 1979 Iranian Revolution, which established an Islamic republic.

key_facts.text: Around 550 BC, Cyrus the Great displaced the Medes and established the Achaemenid Empire, which expanded across much of West and Central Asia.
Alexander the Great’s Macedonian conquest ended Achaemenid rule; the Seleucid Empire was later replaced by the Parthian and Sasanian Empires.
Zoroastrianism, once Iran’s majority religion, declined after the Muslim conquest, while Iranian achievements contributed to the Islamic Golden Age.
In the 19th century, Iran fought the Russian Empire in the Russo-Persian Wars; Russia annexed the South Caucasus by the end of those conflicts.

After 1979, Iran’s political system was restructured as an Islamic republic; later foreign-policy issues included the Iran–Iraq War, tensions with the United States and Israel, and the nuclear program.

overview.text: The Achaemenid Empire was an ancient Iranian empire founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC. Rising from Persis on the Iranian plateau, it defeated Media, Lydia, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, establishing a major imperial power in the ancient Near East.

The empire is associated with centralized bureaucracy, organized administration, infrastructure such as the Royal Road and postal system, and the use of Persian and Aramaic as official languages. Its policies toward different peoples included religious tolerance, especially under Cyrus.

key_facts.text: At its height, the empire extended from the Balkans and Cyrenaica to the Indus Valley, including Anatolia, Mesopotamia, and the Levant.
Achaemenid expansion was checked in Scythia and in several campaigns against Greece, including those of 492–490 BC and 480–479 BC.
Alexander the Great conquered the empire in 330 BC and incorporated it into his Macedonian Empire.

overview.text: Ethiopia’s history reaches back thousands of years and includes diverse communities across highlands, lowlands, and eastern regions. Ancient kingdoms connected the area to Red Sea power and trade, while Muslim groups formed the Ifat and Adal sultanates in the east. Ethiopia is therefore a useful World History subject for studying African kingdoms, Christianity, Islam, and regional expansion.

The Aksumite Kingdom rose in the first century CE, and Christianity became its state religion under Ezana in the early fourth century. After Aksum declined, the Zagwe dynasty established a capital at Lalibela. The Solomonic dynasty replaced it in the thirteenth century and expanded Ethiopia’s military and imperial reach in the Horn of Africa.

key_facts.text: Damot was an early kingdom whose capital was at Yeha.
Aksum had its capital at Aksum and became a major power on the Red Sea, extending influence into South Arabia and Meroe.
The rise of Islam in the Arabian Peninsula gradually redirected trade away from Christian Aksum, contributing to its isolation and decline.
The Ifat and Adal sultanates were associated with Muslim communities including the Argobba, Afar, Harari/Harla, and Somalis.

overview.text: The Magic Flute, or Die Zauberflöte, is a two-act opera by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart with a German libretto by Emanuel Schikaneder. It is a Singspiel, a form combining singing with spoken dialogue. The opera premiered in Vienna on September 30, 1791, was Mozart’s final opera, and remains a staple of the repertory.

The plot follows Prince Tamino, who sets out to rescue Pamina but comes to admire the ideals of the community led by the high priest Sarastro. Tamino’s companion is the earthy Papageno, whose story becomes connected with Tamino and Pamina’s initiation trials.

key_facts.text: The opera’s catalog number is K. 620.
The Queen of the Night persuades Tamino to rescue her daughter Pamina from Sarastro’s captivity.
Tamino and Pamina undergo difficult initiation trials, separately and then together.
Papageno fails the trials but is rewarded with his ideal companion, Papagena.

overview.text: Distillation is a physical separation process in which a liquid mixture is selectively boiled and its vapors are condensed in a still. It separates components by exploiting differences in their relative volatility.
The process can handle diverse chemicals continuously and at high flow rates, but its required phase changes consume substantial energy and contribute to a large environmental footprint.

key_facts.text: Fractional distillation in oil refineries produces fuels and chemical raw materials.
Distilling fermented products produces alcoholic beverages with high ethyl-alcohol content.
Distillation can desalinate water for drinking and medical-industrial uses.
Cryogenic air separation uses distillation to obtain oxygen, nitrogen, and argon as industrial gases.

overview.text: Latin is a classical language in the Italic branch of the Indo-European family. It began among the Latins in Latium, the region around Rome, then spread across Italy and the Roman Empire as Rome expanded. Latin also contributed many words to English and remains visible in technical vocabulary for theology, science, medicine, and law.

Latin developed several forms, including Classical Latin, colloquial Vulgar Latin, Medieval Latin, Renaissance Latin, and Neo-Latin. Although often called a “dead language,” changing regional forms of Latin developed into the Romance languages. Latin also remained a major language of scholarship and international communication in Europe for centuries after the Western Roman Empire.

key_facts.text: Ecclesiastical Latin remains the official language of the Holy See and the Roman Rite of the Catholic Church.
Contemporary Latin is generally studied for reading rather than speaking; spoken skills began to decline in the late seventeenth century.
Latin has highly inflected grammar: word forms can mark features such as case, number, gender, tense, mood, voice, and aspect.
The Latin alphabet developed directly from the Etruscan and Greek alphabets.

overview.text: Gibbs free energy is a thermodynamic potential used to analyze closed systems at constant temperature and pressure. Under those conditions, it helps assess chemical reactions and describes the equilibrium state: Gibbs energy is minimized when a system reaches chemical equilibrium, provided no applied electrolytic voltage drives it.
It also sets a limit on useful work. A closed system can yield a maximum amount of work other than pressure–volume work, but that maximum is attainable only through a completely reversible process.

key_facts.text: For a change, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
When reactants and products are in their standard states, the relation is written ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.

At equilibrium, the derivative of Gibbs energy with respect to the reaction coordinate is zero; a decrease in Gibbs energy is necessary for a reaction to be spontaneous under constant-temperature, constant-pressure conditions.
Josiah Willard Gibbs developed the concept in the 1870s, originally calling it “available energy.”

overview.text: The Old Man and the Sea is a 1952 novella by American author Ernest Hemingway. It follows Santiago, an aging fisherman, through a long struggle to catch a giant marlin. It was the last major fictional work Hemingway published during his lifetime.

The novella has drawn critical attention for its Christian imagery, symbolism, and connections to themes in Hemingway’s other works. It won the 1953 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and was the only work explicitly mentioned when Hemingway received the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature.

key_facts.text: Hemingway began writing the novella in Cuba and completed its manuscript in six weeks.
Life published the full novella on September 1, 1952; Scribner’s released its first edition one week later.
Early reviews were strongly positive, but later critics debated whether the work was inferior or equal to Hemingway’s other writing.
The story began as an addendum to a planned sea trilogy before Hemingway decided it could stand alone as a novella.

source.title: The Old Man and the Sea

overview.text: Titan is Saturn’s largest moon and the Solar System’s second-largest, after Jupiter’s Ganymede. It is the only known moon with a dense atmosphere, and the only known Solar System object besides Earth with clear evidence of stable surface liquids. These unusual characteristics give Titan a distinctly planet-like character.

Titan’s atmosphere is mainly nitrogen and methane, while its climate includes wind and rain and creates dunes, rivers, lakes, seas, and deltas. The seas are probably made of liquid methane and ethane. Titan’s methane cycle nearly resembles Earth’s water cycle, but at a temperature of about 94 K (−179 °C); the Cassini–Huygens mission discovered its polar hydrocarbon lakes.

key_facts.text: Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan in 1655; it was the first known moon of Saturn.
The Cassini–Huygens mission in 2004 provided major information about Titan’s surface and atmosphere, including the discovery of liquid hydrocarbon lakes.
Titan is composed mainly of ice and rocky material, with a rocky core, multiple ice layers, and a subsurface layer of ammonia-rich liquid water.
Its geologically young, generally smooth surface has few impact craters, but includes mountains and several possible cryovolcanoes.
Titan is larger in diameter than Mercury but has only about 40% of Mercury’s mass because Titan is mostly lower-density ice, whereas Mercury is mainly iron and rock.

overview.text: The Great Northern War (1700–1721) was a struggle over Sweden’s supremacy in Northern, Central, and Eastern Europe. Russia, Denmark-Norway, and Saxony-Poland-Lithuania initially formed the anti-Swedish coalition. Sweden’s Charles XII won early victories at Travendal and Narva, but Russia recovered, gained ground in Sweden’s Baltic provinces, and founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 to secure access to the Baltic Sea.

Charles XII’s campaign into Russia ended with the destruction of Sweden’s main army at Poltava in 1709. The coalition then revived, and the war concluded through treaties from 1719 to 1721. Sweden ceded the Baltic provinces and southern Swedish Pomerania; Russia emerged as the dominant Baltic power and a major force in European politics.

key_facts.text: The first anti-Swedish coalition was led by Peter I of Russia, Frederick IV of Denmark-Norway, and Augustus II the Strong of Saxony-Poland-Lithuania.
After Poltava, Charles XII went into exile in the Ottoman town of Bender; the Ottoman Empire had temporarily hosted him and intervened against Russia.
Charles XII was killed in 1718 during Sweden’s campaign against Norway. The campaign’s failure effectively ended Sweden’s offensive war.
The formal peace included the Treaties of Stockholm (1719), Frederiksborg (1720), and Nystad (1721).

overview.text: Amaterasu Ōmikami, usually shortened to Amaterasu, is the sun goddess of Japanese mythology and is often treated as the chief kami, or deity, of Shinto. Japan’s earliest literary texts, the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, portray her as a ruler of Takamagahara, the heavenly realm.

In these traditions, Amaterasu is the mythical ancestress of Japan’s Imperial House through her grandson Ninigi, linking her to the traditional origin story of the imperial line. Her principal place of worship is the Grand Shrine of Ise, one of Shinto’s holiest sites and a major pilgrimage center.

key_facts.text: Amaterasu is also known as Amateru Kami and Ōhirume no Muchi.
She is one of the Three Precious Children, alongside the moon deity Tsukuyomi and the storm god Susanoo; all three are offspring of Izanagi.
The Kojiki dates to about 712 CE, while the Nihon Shoki dates to 720 CE.
The Grand Shrine of Ise is located in Ise, Mie Prefecture, and Amaterasu is also enshrined at other Shinto shrines throughout Japan.

overview.text: Whales are diverse, fully aquatic marine mammals. In common usage, the term usually refers to larger cetaceans rather than dolphins and porpoises. Whales include two major groups: baleen whales, which filter krill and plankton through fringed plates, and toothed whales, which use teeth to catch fish or squid; some toothed whales make deep dives.

Whales evolved from land mammals but live at sea, surfacing through blowholes to breathe. Streamlined bodies, flippers, blubber, sensitive hearing, and vocalizations help them survive in marine environments. Whales were once heavily hunted, and they still face threats from accidental capture and marine pollution.

key_facts.text: The blue whale is the largest known animal ever to have lived; the sperm whale is the largest toothed predator on Earth.
Humpback whales are known for extended songs, and some whales can travel thousands of miles without feeding.
Sperm whales can remain underwater for up to 90 minutes while pursuing deep-water prey such as squid.
Whales feature in literature and film, including the great white whale in Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick.

overview.text: Halogens are the chemically related elements of periodic-table group 17: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine, and tennessine. Some authors exclude tennessine because its chemistry is unknown. The name means “salt former,” reflecting the salts produced when halogens react with metals, including sodium chloride (table salt), calcium fluoride, silver bromide, and potassium iodide.

Halogens are the only periodic-table group represented in all three main states of matter at standard temperature and pressure. They form acids when bonded to hydrogen, while elemental halogens can be dangerous and toxic.

key_facts.text: Chlorine, bromine, and iodine are often used as disinfectants.
Organobromides are the most important class of flame retardants.
Most halogens are typically produced from minerals or salts.

overview.text: The Nemean Lion is a mythical lion in Greek mythology that lived at Nemea. Its story centers on Heracles (Hercules), who killed it as one of the mythical beasts in his twelve labors. The lion’s golden fur made it impossible to kill with mortal weapons, while its claws could cut through strong armor. Afterward, its pelt became a visual symbol of Heracles and his strength, helping artists signal the myth and connect Heracles’ heroism with other figures.

key_facts.text: The lion lived at Nemea.
Its claws were sharper than mortal swords and could cut through strong armor.
Heracles is also called Hercules.
Artists used the pelt to recognize the myth and connect Heracles’ heroism with other figures.

overview.text: Their Eyes Were Watching God is a 1937 novel by American writer Zora Neale Hurston. It follows Janie Crawford’s development from a voiceless teenager into a woman who directs her own life, making personal growth a central association of the novel.

Set in central and southern Florida in the early twentieth century, the novel is associated with the Harlem Renaissance and has come to be regarded as influential in both African-American literature and women’s literature.

key_facts.text: Hurston wrote the novel in Haiti in seven weeks.
The novel initially received a poor reception within the African-American community.
Interest in Hurston’s work revived after Alice Walker’s 1975 article and Robert Hemenway’s 1980 biography.

overview.text: Haitian Vodou is an African diasporic religion that developed in Haiti from the 16th through 19th centuries by blending West and Central African traditions with Catholicism. It centers on Bondye, a transcendent creator, and the lwa, spirits approached through offerings, divination, and ceremonies involving drumming, singing, dancing, and temporary possession. Vodou has no central authority, so practices vary among communities.

Louisiana Voodoo was a related but distinct African diasporic religion practiced in Louisiana and the Mississippi River valley from the 18th to the early 20th centuries. It combined African traditions with Catholicism and, through migrants fleeing the Haitian Revolution, Haitian Vodou. Organized through independent groups, it later declined, although some practices survived through hoodoo.

key_facts.text: Haitian Vodou may be practiced in an ounfò, or temple, led by an oungan (priest) or manbo (priestess); other practice occurs in families or secret societies.
Vodou developed among Afro-Haitian communities during the Atlantic slave trade, and many Vodouists participated in the Haitian Revolution.
Historical records on Louisiana Voodoo are incomplete, but they describe altars, animal sacrifices, spirits of the dead, Catholic saints, and gris-gris charms used for healing or cursing.

Louisiana Voodoo practitioners faced restrictions, arrests, and prosecutions, especially as authorities limited when and where Black people could gather; the religion died out in the early 20th century.
A Louisiana Voodoo revival beginning in the 1990s drew heavily on other African diasporic religions, including Haitian Vodou and Cuban Santería.

overview.text: The liver is a major metabolic organ in vertebrates. In humans, it lies in the upper-right abdomen below the diaphragm and is partly protected by the rib cage. It is the largest internal organ in vertebrates and is mostly divided into right and left lobes.

The liver supports digestion by producing bile, which emulsifies dietary fat. It also detoxifies substances, stores and converts nutrients, helps process carbohydrates, produces some proteins and hormones, and breaks down red blood cells. Most of its specialized cells are called hepatocytes.

key_facts.text: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile made by the liver before releasing it into the duodenum.
The prefix hepat- comes from the Greek word for liver and appears in terms such as hepatology and hepatitis.
Long-term artificial replacement of liver function has not been developed; as of 2018, transplantation was the only option for complete liver failure.

overview.text: Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer and mathematician who became a major figure in the 17th-century Scientific Revolution. He is chiefly associated with his laws of planetary motion, which helped develop modern astronomy.

Kepler treated astronomy as part of a broader mathematical study of nature, calling his approach “celestial physics.” He also made important contributions to optics, including an improved refracting telescope whose design became a foundation of modern refracting telescopes.

key_facts.text: Kepler worked as an assistant to the astronomer Tycho Brahe in Prague.
His major books include Astronomia nova, Harmonice Mundi, and Epitome Astronomiae Copernicanae.
The improved refracting telescope associated with Kepler is called the Keplerian telescope.
Kepler’s work helped provide a foundation for Isaac Newton’s theory of universal gravitation.

overview.text: Neptune is the eighth and farthest known planet from the Sun. It is an ice giant: its interior is mainly ices and rock, while the planet as a whole lacks a sharply defined solid surface. Hydrogen and helium dominate its atmosphere; traces of methane help give it a faint blue appearance. Neptune is more massive than Uranus but slightly smaller and denser, and it takes 164.8 years to orbit the Sun.

Neptune’s discovery links astronomy with mathematical prediction: irregularities in Uranus’s orbit led John Couch Adams and Urbain Le Verrier to calculate its position, and Johann Gottfried Galle observed it in 1846. Neptune has active weather, including dark spots and exceptionally strong winds; its largest moon is Triton. Voyager 2’s 1989 flyby was the only spacecraft visit, and the planet also has faint, fragmented rings.

key_facts.text: Triton was discovered shortly after Neptune; the planet’s other moons were not found telescopically until the 20th century.
Neptune’s winds can reach about 2,100 km/h, the strongest sustained planetary winds described in the source.
Temperatures near the cloud tops approach 55 K (−218 °C).
Its faint ring system consists of fragmented arcs, discovered in 1984 and confirmed by Voyager 2.
The planet’s name comes from the Roman god of the sea, and its astronomical symbol represents Neptune’s trident.

overview.text: J. D. Salinger, whose full name was Jerome David Salinger, was an American writer best known for The Catcher in the Rye (1951). The novel became an immediate popular success and was influential for its depiction of adolescent alienation and loss of innocence. It was also widely read and controversial, bringing Salinger public attention and scrutiny.

Salinger also wrote short fiction. “A Perfect Day for Bananafish” appeared in The New Yorker in 1948, and later books included Nine Stories, Franny and Zooey, and Raise High the Roof Beam, Carpenters and Seymour: An Introduction, a volume containing two novellas. After Catcher’s success, he became reclusive and published less frequently.

key_facts.text: Salinger lived from 1919 to 2010.
He published short stories in Story magazine in 1940 before serving in World War II.
His last published work was the novella Hapworth 16, 1924, which appeared in The New Yorker in 1965.

overview.text: The chicken is a domesticated bird first domesticated around 8,000 years ago and now one of the world's most widespread domesticated animals. It is mainly raised for meat and eggs, though some chickens are kept as pets.

Chickens are social animals with complex vocalizations and behaviors, and they appear in folklore, religion, and literature across many societies. Their economic importance makes them a central part of global animal husbandry.

key_facts.text: Scientific name: Gallus gallus domesticus.
The chicken’s wild source species is the red junglefowl, originally native to Southeast Asia.
A hen bred for laying can produce more than 300 eggs per year.
Broilers are specialized for meat production, while laying hens are specialized for egg production.

overview.text: Pegasus is a winged horse of Greek mythology, usually imagined as a white stallion. In mythic genealogy, Poseidon fathers him in his horse-god aspect, while Medusa gives birth to him and Chrysaor from her blood after Perseus decapitates her.

Pegasus appears in stories of heroic quests and journeys toward Olympus. Greco-Roman poets also described his ascent to heaven and service to Zeus, who directed him to bring lightning and thunder from Olympus.

key_facts.text: Bellerophon captured Pegasus near the Peirene fountain with help from Athena and Poseidon, then rode him against the Chimera.
Pegasus is credited with creating Hippocrene, a fountain on Mount Helicon.
Accounts differ about Olympus: some say Zeus brought Pegasus there to carry thunderbolts, while others say Zeus killed Pegasus and Bellerophon for attempting the ascent.
Pegasus is also the name of a constellation and appears in ancient Greek pottery and Renaissance paintings and sculptures.

overview.text: Dizzy Gillespie was an American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, composer, educator, and singer. As a virtuoso improviser, he expanded on Roy Eldridge’s trumpet style with unusually complex harmonies and rhythms. His musicianship, showmanship, and humor helped popularize early bebop.

Gillespie became a major figure in the development of bebop and modern jazz during the 1940s, working alongside Charlie Parker. His distinctive bent horn, puffed cheeks, beret, and horn-rimmed spectacles became recognizable parts of his public image, while his teaching influenced later musicians.

key_facts.text: Gillespie’s musical approach combined virtuosic trumpet playing with complex harmonic and rhythmic ideas.
He taught and influenced musicians including Miles Davis, Fats Navarro, Clifford Brown, Arturo Sandoval, and Lee Morgan.
He won several Grammy Awards.
His nickname was “Dizzy”; his full name was John Birks Gillespie.

overview.text: Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus was Roman emperor from 54 to 68 CE and the last ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty. Adopted by Emperor Claudius as his heir, he became emperor after Claudius died, initially backed by the Praetorian Guard and the Senate.

His reign combined imperial government and military conflict with strong interest in culture. Nero sponsored entertainment and appeared publicly as a performer, but rebellion eventually forced him from power. He committed suicide in 68 CE, beginning the civil conflict called the Year of the Four Emperors.

key_facts.text: Nero’s mother, Agrippina the Younger, and other advisers helped guide his early reign; later, Nero orchestrated Agrippina’s murder.
During Nero’s reign, Roman forces made peace with Parthia, suppressed Boudica’s revolt in Britain, and began the First Jewish–Roman War.
Nero performed as an actor, poet, musician, and charioteer—roles that scandalized many aristocrats but helped make him popular with some lower-class Romans.

Ancient sources claimed that Nero blamed Christians for the Great Fire of Rome and punished them, while modern historians question some ancient accounts of his tyranny. Claims that Nero deliberately started the fire remain reports or allegations, not established fact.

overview.text: Aristotle (384–322 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath whose writings ranged across the natural sciences, philosophy, linguistics, economics, politics, psychology, and the arts. He founded the Peripatetic philosophical school at the Lyceum in Athens, beginning a tradition that influenced later thought and helped lay groundwork for modern science.

He studied at Plato’s Academy, later tutored Alexander the Great at Philip II’s request, and built a library at the Lyceum. Although only about a third of his original writings survives, his methods and teachings had wide influence. His work shaped Judeo-Islamic philosophy, Christian theology, medieval scholarship, logic, and later interest in virtue ethics.

key_facts.text: Aristotle was born in Stagira in northern Greece and joined Plato’s Academy at about age eighteen, remaining there until roughly age thirty-seven.
His writings include the earliest known systematic study of logic.
Medieval Muslim scholars called him “The First Teacher”; medieval Christians such as Thomas Aquinas called him “The Philosopher.”
His physical science influenced scholarship from late antiquity through the Renaissance, before later theories such as classical mechanics displaced it systematically during the Enlightenment.

overview.text: Inflation is an increase in the average prices of goods and services. As the general price level rises, each unit of currency buys less, reducing money’s purchasing power. Economists measure it with price indexes, often including the consumer price index (CPI).

Inflation may reflect changes in the money supply, demand, available supplies, major cuts in central-bank interest rates, or expectations about future prices. Its effects vary: rapid inflation can encourage hoarding, while uncertainty can discourage saving and investment. Central banks generally seek low, stable inflation through monetary policy.

key_facts.text: The inflation rate is the annualized percentage change in a general price index.
Deflation is a decrease in the general price level—the opposite direction from inflation.
Central banks use tools such as setting interest rates and conducting open-market operations in efforts to keep inflation low and stable.

overview.text: Cosmic inflation—also called cosmological inflation or simply inflation—is a theory that space underwent exponential expansion in the very early universe. This enormous expansion supercooled the universe; it ended when energy in the field driving inflation condensed into hot, dense particles, a process called reheating. Expansion then continued more slowly.

Inflationary theory addresses features of the cosmos on large scales. Quantum fluctuations in the tiny inflationary region could have been magnified to cosmic dimensions, supplying seeds for cosmic structure. Many physicists also believe inflation explains the universe’s apparent uniformity in all directions and the even distribution of cosmic microwave background radiation.
