The chorus “Va, pensiero” from Nabucco was associated with those ideals, although Verdi himself was intensely private. After Aida, his later output included the Requiem, Otello, and Falstaff; his operas remain among the most popular in the repertoire.

key_facts.text: Verdi was born near Busseto, in the modern province of Parma, and received musical education with help from local patron Antonio Barezzi.
Macbeth (1847) has been called Verdi’s first masterpiece.
His “middle period” included Rigoletto (1851), Il trovatore (1853), and La traviata (1853).
After Aida (1871), Verdi produced the Requiem (1874) and the operas Otello (1887) and Falstaff (1893).

overview.text: The Rite of Spring (French: Le Sacre du printemps) is a ballet and orchestral concert work by Russian composer Igor Stravinsky. Written for Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes, it premiered at Paris’s Théâtre des Champs-Élysées on 29 May 1913. Vaslav Nijinsky created the original choreography, while Nicholas Roerich designed the stage settings and costumes.

Its scenario portrays rituals celebrating spring and the selection of a young girl as a sacrificial victim. The score experiments with rhythm, meter, tonality, stress, and dissonance; it is considered an early modernist work, influenced many leading 20th-century composers, and became at least as recognized as a concert piece as a stage ballet.

key_facts.text: The premiere caused a sensation, but the familiar “riot” or “near-riot” description became a later label associated with 1924 reviews.
The work was Stravinsky’s third major Ballets Russes project, following The Firebird (1910) and Petrushka (1911).
A 1920s revival used choreography by Léonide Massine instead of Nijinsky’s original version.
In the 1980s, the Joffrey Ballet reconstructed Nijinsky’s original choreography, which had long been thought lost.

overview.text: Gamal Abdel Nasser was an Egyptian military officer and revolutionary who led the 1952 Egyptian Revolution. He introduced major land reforms, became Egypt’s executive leader after placing President Mohamed Naguib under house arrest, and served as president from 1954 until his death in 1970.

Nasser’s nationalization of the Suez Canal made him highly popular in Egypt and across the Arab world after the Suez Crisis. He promoted pan-Arab unity, including the United Arab Republic with Syria from 1958 to 1961, while also pursuing socialist reforms, modernization, and projects such as the Aswan Dam.

key_facts.text: After a 1954 assassination attempt by a Muslim Brotherhood member, Nasser cracked down on the organization and placed Mohamed Naguib under house arrest.
After Egypt’s defeat by Israel in the 1967 Six-Day War, Nasser resigned; he later returned to office following demonstrations calling for his reinstatement.
After returning to office, Nasser launched the War of Attrition in an effort to regain the Israeli-occupied Sinai Peninsula.

Nasser is associated with social justice, Arab unity, modernization, and opposition to imperialism, while critics emphasize his authoritarian rule, human-rights violations, and the military’s dominance over civil institutions.

overview.text: Moment of inertia, also called rotational inertia or mass moment of inertia, measures how difficult it is to change a rigid body’s rotation rate about a chosen axis. It plays the same role in rotational motion that mass plays in linear motion. Its value depends on both the object’s mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis; increasing either mass or distance from the axis increases the moment of inertia.

Moment of inertia is also linked to torque and angular acceleration: it is the ratio between the applied torque and the resulting angular acceleration. This makes it a central quantity for describing how objects respond when their rotation is changed.

key_facts.text: For a point mass, moment of inertia equals mass multiplied by the square of its perpendicular distance from the rotation axis: I = mr².
For a rigid object made of multiple parts, the total moment of inertia is the sum of the moments of its parts, calculated about the same axis.
When an object rotates in a plane, the relevant moment of inertia is a single scalar value for the axis perpendicular to that plane.

overview.text: Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister and civil-rights activist who became a prominent movement leader from 1955 until his assassination in 1968. He promoted nonviolent resistance and civil disobedience against Jim Crow laws and other legalized discrimination.

King led or participated in the Montgomery bus boycott, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, protests in Birmingham, and voting-rights marches from Selma to Montgomery. The civil-rights movement achieved pivotal legislative gains through the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

key_facts.text: King delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech at the 1963 March on Washington.
He won the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize for combating racial inequality through nonviolent resistance.
In his final years, King expanded his work to include opposition to poverty and the Vietnam War.
King was assassinated in Memphis on April 4, 1968, while planning the Poor People’s Campaign; James Earl Ray was convicted of the assassination.
The federal Martin Luther King Jr. holiday was first observed in 1986.

overview.text: Rome is Italy’s capital, situated in Lazio along the Tiber Valley. Its history spans 28 centuries, and it successively served as the capital of the Roman Kingdom, Roman Republic, and Roman Empire. These roles connect the modern city with the major political stages of ancient Roman history.

After the western Roman Empire fell, Rome came under papal political control and became the capital of the Papal States in the eighth century. Renaissance popes sponsored major architectural and urban projects, making Rome a major artistic and cultural center. Rome became capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871 and of the Italian Republic in 1946.

key_facts.text: Rome is known as the “City of Seven Hills” and the “Eternal City.” The latter name was used by the poet Tibullus in the first century BC and later by Ovid, Virgil, and Livy.
Vatican City, headquarters of the worldwide Catholic Church under the Holy See, is an independent country within Rome’s municipal boundaries.
Rome’s site has been inhabited for more than three millennia; early inhabitants included Latins, Etruscans, and Sabines.
Rome’s historic center is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

overview.text: Rome is Italy’s capital and largest city, located in Lazio on the central-western Italian Peninsula along the Tiber Valley. Vatican City, an independent country and the headquarters of the Catholic Church, lies within Rome’s municipal boundaries—making Rome the setting of a rare country-within-a-city geographic relationship.

Rome’s history includes successive roles as capital of the Roman Kingdom, Republic, and Empire. After the Western Empire fell, the papacy shaped the city politically and architecturally. Renaissance building programs helped establish Rome as a major artistic center and a birthplace of Baroque and Neoclassical styles.

key_facts.text: Rome is associated with the names “City of Seven Hills” and “Eternal City.”
Rome became the capital of the Kingdom of Italy in 1871; Italy became a republic in 1946.
Rome’s historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Rome hosted the 1960 Summer Olympics.

overview.text: A laser is a device that produces light through optical amplification based on stimulated emission of electromagnetic radiation. Its name comes from “light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.” Laser light is coherent, meaning its waves maintain a consistent relationship; this allows beams to be focused tightly and remain narrow over long distances.
These properties support uses in optical communication, lidar, pointers, manufacturing, medicine, scanning, and other technologies.

key_facts.text: The first laser was built in 1960 by Theodore Maiman at Hughes Research Laboratories, drawing on work by Charles H. Townes, Arthur Leonard Schawlow, and Gordon Gould.
Laser light can have a very narrow frequency spectrum, and lasers can produce extremely short pulses of light.
Lasers are used in fiber-optic communication, optical-disc drives, laser printers, barcode scanners, and semiconductor chip manufacturing.
Other applications include surgery and skin treatments, cutting and welding materials, and devices that mark targets or measure range and speed.

overview.text: An electric guitar needs external electrical amplification for normal performance volume. Its pickups turn vibrating strings into electrical signals, which speakers reproduce as sound. Players can alter its tone with amplifier or guitar controls and effects including reverb, distortion, and overdrive.

Invented in 1932, the electric guitar was adopted by jazz guitarists who wanted single-note solos audible in large big-band settings. By the 1950s and 1960s, it had become a major instrument in popular music, supporting styles from rock, electric blues, and heavy metal to pop, country, folk, and jazz.

key_facts.text: The six-string model is the most common and is usually tuned E–A–D–G–B–E, from lowest to highest strings.
In rock, rhythm guitar handles chord progressions and riffs, while lead guitar provides melodies, fills, and solos. One guitarist may perform both roles in a small group.
Electric guitars include hollow-body semi-acoustic and later solid-body designs; their bodies, necks, bridges, and pickup arrangements vary.
A spring-loaded bridge can help players bend pitch and create vibrato. Other techniques include tapping, hammering-on, feedback, and slide playing.

overview.text: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, better known as Vladimir Lenin, was a Russian revolutionary, politician, and Marxist political theorist. He developed Leninism and became the first and founding head of government of Soviet Russia from 1917 to 1924 and of the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1924. His name is closely associated with the Bolsheviks and the formation of the early Soviet state.

After the February Revolution removed the tsar and created a Provisional Government, Lenin returned to Russia and played a leading role in the Bolsheviks’ October overthrow of that regime. His government withdrew Russia from World War I, centralized political power, and fought a civil war; its rule also included state repression. Lenin remains divisive: supporters identify him with socialism and the working class, while critics connect his rule to dictatorship, mass killings, and repression.

key_facts.text: In 1903, Lenin played a key role in the split of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party and led its Bolshevik faction.
The Bolshevik government signed a treaty with the Central Powers to leave World War I, accepting territorial concessions.
The Bolshevik government had centralized power in the Communist Party by 1918; it also redistributed land among peasants and nationalized banks and large-scale industry.
In response to wartime devastation, famine, and uprisings, Lenin backed the New Economic Policy in 1921 to encourage economic growth.
Lenin died in 1924; Joseph Stalin then became the pre-eminent figure in the Soviet government.

overview.text: HyperText Markup Language (HTML) is a markup language for documents displayed in web browsers. It defines the content and structure of web material, letting authors organize headings, paragraphs, lists, links, quotations, and other items. Browsers interpret HTML rather than displaying its tags directly.

HTML elements use tags written in angle brackets and can include images, forms, and other objects. Browsers receive HTML from servers or local storage and render it as multimedia web pages. CSS commonly controls appearance and layout, while scripting languages such as JavaScript can change a page’s behavior and content.

key_facts.text: An HTML page can embed images, interactive forms, and other objects.
HTML tags can surround text, as with a paragraph element and its closing tag, or directly introduce content, as with image and input elements.
The World Wide Web Consortium has encouraged using CSS for presentation instead of explicit presentational HTML since 1997.

overview.text: The Nutcracker, Op. 71, is a two-act classical ballet by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky dating to 1892. Set on Christmas Eve in a child’s imagination, it features a Nutcracker doll and combines music, dance, and fantasy.

The ballet adapts Alexandre Dumas’s 1844 tale, itself based on E. T. A. Hoffmann’s 1816 story The Nutcracker and the Mouse King. Marius Petipa was its first choreographer, assisted by Lev Ivanov. Although the complete staged work was initially less successful than the shorter Nutcracker Suite, it became popular later and has been performed by many companies, especially in North America.

key_facts.text: The score is noted for its use of the celesta, an instrument Tchaikovsky had also used in his 1891 symphonic ballad The Voyevoda.
The 20-minute Nutcracker Suite premiered nine months before the complete staged ballet.
Shchelkunchik is the ballet’s Russian title.

overview.text: The brainstem is the posterior, stalk-like part of the brain that connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord. In humans, it consists of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. Despite its small size, it helps regulate heart and breathing rates, supports the body’s sleep cycle, and carries motor and sensory information between the brain and body.

The brainstem also provides the main motor and sensory nerve supply to the face and neck through cranial nerves. Together, these roles make it a key link between the brain and the rest of the nervous system.

key_facts.text: The brainstem makes up around 2.6 percent of the brain’s total weight.
Ten pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brainstem.

Major pathways through it include the corticospinal tract for motor function, the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway for fine touch and vibration, and the spinothalamic tract for pain and temperature.

overview.text: Langston Hughes (James Mercer Langston Hughes) was an American poet and a leader of the Harlem Renaissance. He also worked as a social activist, novelist, playwright, and columnist, and was an early innovator of jazz poetry. His writing included poetry, fiction, drama, and nonfiction.
Hughes moved to New York City as a young man and made his career there. He gained notice from The Crisis magazine and book publishers, becoming known in Harlem’s creative community.

key_facts.text: Hughes lived from 1901 to 1967.
The Weary Blues was his first poetry collection and appeared in 1926.
He studied at Columbia University, left without graduating, and later graduated from Lincoln University.
From 1942 to 1962, Hughes wrote a weekly opinion column for The Chicago Defender.

overview.text: A vowel is a speech sound produced with minimal to no narrowing in the vocal tract. Vowels form one of the two principal classes of speech sounds, alongside consonants. They are usually voiced and commonly serve as the center, or nucleus, of a syllable.
In English, “vowel” can refer both to the sound and to the written symbols used to represent it, especially a, e, i, o, and u; y and w can sometimes also function this way.

key_facts.text: Vowels can vary in quality, loudness, and length.
Vowels are closely involved in tone, intonation, and stress, which are features of speech rhythm and melody.
Although a vowel typically forms a syllable’s nucleus, some syllables do not have a vowel as their nucleus.
The term “vowel” comes from the Latin word vocalis, meaning “vocal” or related to the voice.

overview.text: Barack Hussein Obama II was a Democratic politician who served as the 44th president of the United States from 2009 to 2017. He was the first African American president. Before becoming president, he worked as a community organizer and constitutional-law professor, served in the Illinois legislature, and represented Illinois in the U.S. Senate.

Obama’s presidency included responses to the Great Recession, health-care reform, and new financial regulations. In foreign and domestic policy, his administration oversaw the end of the Iraq War, authorized the raid that killed al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden, addressed climate change, negotiated a nuclear agreement with Iran, and expanded recognition of LGBTQ rights.

key_facts.text: In the 2008 presidential election, Obama defeated Republican nominee John McCain; Joe Biden was his running mate.
Obama received the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts in international diplomacy; the decision drew both praise and criticism.
He appointed Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan to the Supreme Court; Sotomayor became the first Hispanic American on the Court.
Obama won reelection in 2012 by defeating Republican nominee Mitt Romney.
He became the first sitting U.S. president to publicly support same-sex marriage.

overview.text: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens, an American writer, humorist, and essayist. His novels include The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), the latter often called the “Great American Novel.” He also wrote A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court and Pudd’nhead Wilson. William Faulkner called Twain “the father of American literature.”

Twain’s wit and satire—humorous criticism—earned praise from critics and peers, and he became a sought-after speaker. He was raised in Hannibal, Missouri, which later became the setting for Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn. His experience as a Mississippi River pilot provided material for Life on the Mississippi.

key_facts.text: His first major writing success was “The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County” (1865), which brought him international attention.
Twain co-wrote The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today with Charles Dudley Warner.
From 1901 until his death, he served as vice president of the American Anti-Imperialist League and opposed American colonialism.
After investments caused severe financial losses and bankruptcy, Twain eventually paid all his creditors in full.

overview.text: Florence (Italian: Firenze) is the capital and most populous city of Tuscany, Italy. It was a wealthy medieval center of trade and finance and is often identified by scholars as a birthplace of the Renaissance. Its influence extended across artistic, cultural, commercial, political, and economic life.

Located northwest of Rome, Florence is associated with Renaissance art and architecture, the Medici family, and landmarks such as the Uffizi Gallery and Palazzo Pitti. Its historic center is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

key_facts.text: The Medici family ruled Florence during periods of turbulent political history that also included religious and republican revolutions.
Florence served as the capital of the Kingdom of Italy from 1865 to 1871.
The Florentine dialect helped form the basis of standard Italian and became a language of culture across Italy.
UNESCO designated the Historic Centre of Florence a World Heritage Site in 1982.
The Uffizi Gallery and Palazzo Pitti are among Florence’s museums and art galleries.

overview.text: William Wordsworth was an English Romantic poet who, with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, helped launch the Romantic Age in English literature. Their joint collection, Lyrical Ballads (1798), links Wordsworth to both Coleridge and the rise of English Romanticism.
Wordsworth’s major work, The Prelude, is a semi-autobiographical poem about his early years. He revised and expanded it repeatedly; his wife titled and published it posthumously.

key_facts.text: Before its publication as The Prelude, the poem was generally known as “The Poem to Coleridge.”
Wordsworth served as Poet Laureate from 1843 until his death.
He died of pleurisy in 1850.

overview.text: Achilles, also called Achilleus, is a Greek mythological hero and the central character of Homer’s Iliad. He is the son of the Nereid Thetis and Peleus, king of Phthia, and is presented as the greatest of the Greek warriors in the Trojan War. His most notable feat is killing the Trojan prince Hector outside Troy.

The Iliad does not narrate Achilles’ death. Later sources say Paris killed him with an arrow, while later legends describe him as invulnerable except at the heel after Thetis dipped him in the Styx while holding that spot. This tradition produced “Achilles’ heel,” meaning a weakness that can bring down an otherwise strong person or thing.

key_facts.text: Achilles was raised in Phthia, educated by Chiron the centaur, and grew up with Patroclus as his childhood companion.
In the Iliad, Achilles commands the Myrmidons, a mythical tribe.
The heel vulnerability belongs to later legends rather than the account of Achilles’ death in the Iliad.
The Achilles tendon receives its name through the same heel legend.

overview.text: A photon is an elementary particle and a quantum—discrete unit—of the electromagnetic field. It includes electromagnetic radiation such as visible light and radio waves and serves as the force carrier of the electromagnetic force. Photons are massless bosons and move at the speed of light in a vacuum.

Quantum mechanics describes photons as showing wave–particle duality: experiments reveal both wave-like and particle-like behavior. The modern photon concept developed through Planck’s work and Einstein’s explanation of the photoelectric effect; Gilbert N. Lewis popularized the term “photon” in 1926.

key_facts.text: Planck proposed that energy could occur in discrete equal-sized units; Einstein extended this idea to light to explain the photoelectric effect.
Photon research contributed to developments including lasers, quantum field theory, and Bose–Einstein condensation.
Photon-based applications include photochemistry, high-resolution microscopy, optical imaging, and optical communication.
Photons have been studied for quantum computing and quantum cryptography.

overview.text: A quark is an elementary particle and a building block of matter. Quarks combine into composite particles called hadrons, including baryons such as protons and neutrons and mesons. Protons and neutrons form atomic nuclei. Quarks are not observed alone: color confinement keeps them inside hadrons or in quark–gluon plasma.

Quarks come in six flavors. Up and down quarks are the lightest and generally stable, while heavier flavors decay into them and are produced in high-energy collisions. Quarks also have a distinctive property: their electric charges are not whole-number multiples of the elementary charge.

key_facts.text: The six flavors are up, down, charm, strange, top, and bottom.
Each quark flavor has a corresponding antiquark, with some properties—such as electric charge—reversed in sign.
Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig independently proposed the quark model in 1964; deep-inelastic-scattering experiments at SLAC provided evidence in 1968.
The top quark was first observed at Fermilab in 1995 and was the last of the six flavors to be discovered.

overview.text: Anton Pavlovich Chekhov (1860–1904) was a Russian playwright and short-story writer who worked as a physician. His dramatic work includes The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard. These plays are associated with the development of early modernism in theater.

In these four plays, Chekhov replaces conventional action with a “theatre of mood” and a “submerged life in the text.” His short stories used formal innovations that influenced the development of the modern short story.

key_facts.text: After The Seagull’s 1896 reception, Konstantin Stanislavski’s Moscow Art Theatre revived it to acclaim in 1898.
The Moscow Art Theatre later produced Uncle Vanya and premiered Three Sisters and The Cherry Orchard.
Chekhov wrote that a writer’s duty is to state problems correctly rather than solve them.
He described medicine as his “lawful wife” and literature as his “mistress.”

overview.text: Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 6 in B minor, Op. 74, is his final completed symphony, written between February and August 1893. It is commonly called the Pathétique Symphony. Tchaikovsky’s original Russian title meant “passionate” or “emotional,” while the French form pathétique carries “solemn” or “emotive” associations.

Its performance history is closely tied to the end of Tchaikovsky’s life. He conducted the premiere in Saint Petersburg on 28 October 1893, nine days before his death. The work was also the last of his compositions to be premiered during his lifetime, giving its premiere an important biographical context.

key_facts.text: The symphony is in B minor and bears the opus number 74.
Eduard Nápravník conducted the second performance at a memorial concert 21 days after the premiere.
Tchaikovsky made minor corrections after the premiere; the second performance was the first in the form now recognized.
The first Moscow performance took place on 16 December 1893 under Vasily Safonov.

overview.text: Anubis is an ancient Egyptian god connected with funerary rites, the protection of graves, and guidance to the underworld. He was usually shown either as a canine or as a human with a canine head, making his animal form a major recognition clue.

Anubis was also associated with embalming and with guiding souls into the afterlife. During the Weighing of the Heart, he attended the scale used to decide whether a soul could enter the realm of the dead. In the Middle Kingdom, Osiris replaced him as lord of the underworld, but Anubis retained other funerary roles.

key_facts.text: Ancient Egyptian names for Anubis include Inpu, Inpw, Jnpw, and Anpu.
Anubis was depicted as a protector of graves as early as the First Dynasty, conventionally dated to about 3100–2890 BCE.
His black depiction symbolized regeneration, life, the soil of the Nile, and the discoloration of a corpse after embalming.

overview.text: Dwight D. “Ike” Eisenhower (1890–1969) was the 34th president of the United States, serving from 1953 to 1961. Before entering the White House, he became a five-star general and commanded Allied forces in World War II, including the D-Day invasion. He later became NATO’s first supreme commander.

Eisenhower’s presidency combined Cold War strategy with major domestic initiatives. He pursued containment and nuclear deterrence, supported federal enforcement of school integration, and oversaw development of the Interstate Highway System. After Sputnik, his administration helped create NASA and strengthen science education. In his farewell address, he warned about the “military-industrial complex.”

key_facts.text: Eisenhower won the 1952 and 1956 presidential elections, defeating Adlai Stevenson II both times.
His “New Look” defense policy emphasized nuclear weapons while reducing funding for expensive Army divisions.
During the 1956 Suez Crisis, Eisenhower opposed the Israeli, British, and French invasion of Egypt and forced the invaders to withdraw.
He sent Army troops to Little Rock, Arkansas, to enforce federal court orders integrating schools.
Before becoming president, Eisenhower served as military governor of occupied Germany, Army Chief of Staff, and president of Columbia University.

overview.text: The Golden Horde—also called the Ulus of Jochi and Kipchak Khanate—was a Mongol khanate that emerged from the northwestern Mongol Empire in the 13th century. After the empire’s 1259 division, it became functionally independent and was later Turkicized.

At its height, it extended from Siberia and Central Asia across Eastern Europe, reaching from the Urals to the Danube and from the Black Sea to the Caspian Sea. Political instability and Timur’s 1396 invasion led to fragmentation. Moscow’s Great Stand on the Ugra River in 1480 traditionally marks the end of Mongol rule over Russia.

key_facts.text: Its original lands were those assigned to Jochi, while the polity grew greatly under Batu Khan.
The Horde’s military power peaked under Özbeg Khan (1312–1341), who adopted Islam.
The Great Troubles (1359–1381) were followed by a brief reunification under Tokhtamysh (1381–1395).
By the early 15th century, the Horde was breaking apart, and numerous predominantly Turkic khanates emerged within its former territories.
The Crimean Khanate and Kazakh Khanate, described as its last remnants, survived until Russian conquest in 1783 and 1847, respectively.

overview.text: Mímir (also Mim) is a Norse mythological figure renowned for knowledge and wisdom. After being beheaded during the Æsir–Vanir War, his head is carried by Odin; it recites secret knowledge and counsels him. This makes Mímir especially associated with wisdom that remains available to Odin even after Mímir’s death.

Mímir appears in the Poetic Edda and Prose Edda, two 13th-century works connected with earlier Norse traditions. His name also appears in Mímisbrunnr and in Mímameiðr and Hoddmímis holt, names that scholars generally identify with Yggdrasil.

key_facts.text: Mímir is beheaded during the Æsir–Vanir War.
Odin carries Mímir’s severed head, which gives him counsel and recites secret knowledge.
Mímir is attested in both the Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda.
The name Mímir is connected with Mímisbrunnr and with names generally understood by scholars as referring to Yggdrasil.

overview.text: Maya Angelou, born Marguerite Annie Johnson, was an American memoirist, essayist, poet, and civil-rights activist. Her seven autobiographies focus on childhood and early adulthood; the first, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969), recounts her life through age 17 and brought her international recognition.

Her works center on racism, identity, family, and travel, and have been considered a defense of African-American culture. Angelou also challenged conventional autobiography by reshaping its structure. In 1993, she recited “On the Pulse of Morning” at Bill Clinton’s first inauguration.

key_facts.text: Angelou was active in the Civil Rights Movement and worked with Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X.
She was named Wake Forest University’s first Reynolds Professor of American Studies in 1982.
Critics have debated whether her celebrated works should be labeled autobiographical fiction or autobiography; Angelou intentionally challenged the genre’s usual form.
Her books have been widely used in schools and universities, while some U.S. libraries have faced attempts to ban them.

overview.text: Bigfoot, or Sasquatch, is a large, hairy humanoid of North American folklore, especially associated with forests of the Pacific Northwest. Since the mid-20th century, it has become a cultural icon in American and Canadian popular culture and developed a distinct subculture.

Folklorists connect the figure to European wild-man traditions, folk tales, and Indigenous cultures. Although enthusiasts have circulated sightings and alleged physical or recorded evidence, scientists reject Bigfoot as a real living animal; the claimed evidence has been attributed to folklore, mistaken identification, or hoaxes.

key_facts.text: Sasquatch is an alternate name for Bigfoot.
Some Bigfoot enthusiasts are associated with the pseudoscience of cryptozoology and have offered alleged evidence such as photographs, recordings, hair samples, and casts of large footprints.
Comparable hairy humanoid figures in folklore include the skunk ape of the southeastern United States, the Almas and Yeren of Asia, the Yeti, and the Australian Yowie.

overview.text: Kim Jong Un has been North Korea’s supreme leader since 2011, after the death of his father, Kim Jong Il. He is the third ruler from the Kim family, following his grandfather Kim Il Sung and his father, and represents North Korea’s hereditary leadership system.

Under Kim, North Korea maintained a repressive dictatorship and a Kim family personality cult while promoting nuclear-weapons and missile programs. These programs heightened tensions with South Korea, the United States, and China. Kim’s 2018–19 summits with leaders from those countries briefly eased relations, but negotiations ended without progress on nuclear disarmament or Korean reunification.

key_facts.text: Kim holds the top offices of the Workers’ Party of Korea and the State Affairs Commission, as well as senior military positions.

His Byungjin policy promoted developing North Korea’s nuclear program and economy in parallel, while departing from his father’s military-first Songun policy in favor of a stated “people-first” approach.

The 2018–19 diplomacy included meetings with Chinese president Xi Jinping, South Korean president Moon Jae-in, and U.S. president Donald Trump; the meetings with a U.S. president were unprecedented between the two countries’ heads of state.
Kim’s half-brother Kim Jong-nam was assassinated in Malaysia in 2017; claims that Kim ordered the killing are presented as allegations.

overview.text: An ode is a form of lyric poetry that originated in ancient Greece. It is an elaborately structured poem that praises or glorifies an event or individual; it may also describe nature through both intellectual and emotional responses. Its formal design and elevated expression give it a recognizable literary character.

Greek odes began as performances with musical accompaniment, especially using the aulos or lyre. Over time, the term also covered personal lyrics that were sung or recited. The main traditional categories are Pindaric, Horatian, and irregular, while a classic ode has three sections: the strophe, antistrophe, and epode.

key_facts.text: Pindaric odes follow the form and style associated with Pindar.
Horatian odes follow Horace’s conventions and imitate earlier Greek lyric poets such as Alcaeus and Anacreon.
Irregular odes use rhyme without the Pindaric three-part structure or the Horatian stanza patterns.
The aulos and lyre were important instruments in ancient Greek ode performances; the lyre was especially revered.

overview.text: Nematoda is the phylum of nematodes, also called roundworms or eelworms. Its members live in marine and fresh water, soil, and nearly every terrestrial region. Most species are free-living and feed on microorganisms, while many others are parasites. Some parasitic nematodes cause diseases in their hosts.

Nematodes are ecologically prominent: they are often more numerous than other animals in their environments, occur at several trophic levels, and have varied life cycles. These traits point to important roles in many ecosystems.

key_facts.text: Unlike flatworms, nematodes have a tubular digestive system with openings at both ends.
Nematodes belong to Ecdysozoa, the animal clade that includes arthropods and tardigrades.
Nematode species are difficult to distinguish, so estimates of total diversity vary widely, from at least 40,000 to figures near one million.
Parasitic nematodes include pathogens of plants and animals; about 35 species are human parasites.
Nematodes are especially abundant in soil, with their highest densities observed in tundra and boreal forests.

overview.text: Seattle is Washington’s most populous city and a major city of the Pacific Northwest. It lies on an isthmus between Puget Sound—an inlet of the Pacific Ocean—and Lake Washington, about 100 miles south of the Canadian border.

The settlement was named for Chief Seattle after the Denny Party arrived in 1851 and moved to the eastern shore of Elliott Bay in 1852. Seattle developed from a logging center into a commercial and shipbuilding hub, an aircraft-manufacturing center associated with Boeing, and a technology center linked to Microsoft.

key_facts.text: The Port of Seattle serves as a trade gateway to the Asia-Pacific region.
The Seattle area had Native American communities, including the Duwamish, for at least 4,000 years before permanent European settlement.
Seattle’s Jackson Street jazz scene helped launch the careers of Ernestine Anderson, Ray Charles, and Quincy Jones.
Seattle is strongly associated with grunge and bands such as Alice in Chains, Nirvana, Pearl Jam, and Soundgarden; Jimi Hendrix and Heart are also linked to the city’s music history.

overview.text: The Qing dynasty, officially the Great Qing, was a Manchu-led imperial dynasty and the last imperial dynasty in Chinese history. It followed the Ming and was succeeded by the Republic of China. Qing forces seized Beijing and North China in 1644, conventionally marking the beginning of Qing rule; the dynasty ended when the Xuantong Emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912 after the 1911 Xinhai Revolution.

The Qing created a multiethnic empire that at its height stretched across much of East Asia. In the nineteenth century, internal rebellions and foreign pressure challenged the state, while reform efforts attempted to modernize it. Defeat in the Opium Wars brought unequal treaties, foreign trading privileges, extraterritoriality, and treaty ports under foreign control.

key_facts.text: Nurhaci, founder of the Later Jin dynasty and leader of the Aisin Gioro house, established the Eight Banners military system. His son Hong Taiji proclaimed the Great Qing in 1636.
The Qing adapted the traditional tributary system in relations with neighboring states such as Joseon Korea and the Lê dynasty in Vietnam, while extending control into Inner Asia.
The Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864) and Dungan Revolt (1862–1877) were major Qing-era upheavals; together, they led to more than 20 million deaths from famine, disease, and war.
The Tongzhi Restoration and Self-Strengthening Movement of the 1860s introduced foreign military technology and other reforms.
After the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895), the Qing lost suzerainty over Korea and ceded Taiwan to Japan.

overview.text: Human skin is a soft, flexible outer tissue that interfaces with the environment. As mammalian skin, it is part of the integumentary system and helps guard underlying muscles, bones, ligaments, and internal organs.

Its central roles include protection, regulation, and sensation: skin helps limit pathogen entry and excessive water loss, contributes to insulation and temperature regulation, and may form scar tissue when severely damaged.

key_facts.text: Human skin varies in thickness by location; skin around the eyes is described as thinnest, while skin on the palms and soles is thickest.
All mammals have some hair on their skin, including marine mammals that may appear hairless.
The term “cutaneous” means “of the skin,” and cutis is the Latin word for skin.
Skin also contributes to the production of vitamin D folates.

overview.text: The Aztec Empire, also called the Triple Alliance, was a political alliance of three Nahua city-states: Mexico-Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco, and Tlacopan. It ruled in and around the Valley of Mexico from 1428 until combined forces of Spanish conquistadors and Indigenous allies under Hernán Cortés defeated it in 1521. Although founded as a partnership, Tenochtitlan became the dominant city and the alliance was effectively governed from there by 1519.

The alliance expanded across most of central Mexico and some more distant Mesoamerican territories. Its indirect imperial system often left conquered rulers in place while requiring tribute and military support, allowing local communities significant autonomy within an integrated political and economic network.

key_facts.text: The alliance formed from victorious factions in a civil war involving Azcapotzalco and its former tributary provinces.
The Mexica patron god Huitzilopochtli was central to the imperial cult; conquered peoples could keep their own religious traditions if they added him to their local pantheons.
“Triple Alliance” is another name for the political entity; its people and civil society are also described historiographically as Aztecs or Culhua-Mexica.

overview.text: The Aztecs were a broad group of Mesoamerican peoples—especially Nahuatl speakers—whose civilization flourished in central Mexico from about 1300 to 1521. “Aztecs” can refer narrowly to the Mexica of Tenochtitlan or more broadly to Nahua peoples and states of central Mexico.

The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on islands in Lake Texcoco and became the leading power in the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan. The resulting empire expanded through conquest and trade while relying on client city-states rather than uniform direct rule. After Hernán Cortés allied with opponents of the Mexica, Tenochtitlan fell in 1521, and Mexico City was built on its ruins.

key_facts.text: The Triple Alliance began in 1427 as an alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan against Azcapotzalco.
Imperial control included installing friendly rulers and arranging marriages between ruling dynasties; client city-states paid taxes to the imperial center.
Central Mexican culture included maize farming, a division between nobles and commoners, a pantheon, and a calendric system.
Knowledge of Aztec history comes from archaeology, Indigenous writings, Spanish eyewitness accounts, and the bilingual Spanish-Nahuatl Florentine Codex.

overview.text: In Franz Kafka’s short story “A Hunger Artist,” first published in 1922, fasting becomes a public performance and artistic vocation. The protagonist sits in a cage while spectators and rotating watchers observe him. His promoter limits each fast to forty days, but the artist regards that limit as arbitrary and wants to continue longer.

As public interest fades, the artist joins a circus but is neglected near the animal cages and eventually found near death. He explains that he fasted because he could not find food he liked. A panther replaces him and attracts crowds, creating a contrast between the artist’s self-denial and the animal’s apparent vitality.

key_facts.text: The story’s German title is “Ein Hungerkünstler,” and it became the title piece of the collection A Hunger Artist, the last book Kafka prepared for publication.

Critical interpretations differ: some see the hunger artist as a saint-like or Christ-like ascetic, others as a misunderstood artist, and others as a figure in Kafka’s ironic critique of artistic pretensions.
In several interpretations, the panther is the hunger artist’s antithesis: it is satisfied with food and expresses a worldly vitality that the artist lacks.

overview.text: “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening” is a Robert Frost poem written in 1922 and published in 1923 in his volume New Hampshire. Its notable literary features include imagery, personification—giving human qualities to nonhuman things—and repetition, making those strong recognition associations for Frost’s work.

key_facts.text: Author: Robert Frost.
It was written in 1922.
It was published in 1923 in New Hampshire.
Frost described it in a letter to Louis Untermeyer as “my best bid for remembrance.”

source.title: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening

overview.text: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair, an English novelist, poet, essayist, journalist, and critic. His writing is associated with clear prose, social criticism, opposition to totalitarianism—including authoritarian communism and fascism—and support for democratic socialism.

Orwell wrote fiction, literary criticism, poetry, and polemical journalism, as well as nonfiction about working-class life and the Spanish Civil War. His work remains influential in popular and political culture, and “Orwellian” describes totalitarian or authoritarian social practices.

key_facts.text: Animal Farm (1945) is an allegorical novella.
Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) is a dystopian novel.
The Road to Wigan Pier (1937) documents Orwell’s experience of working-class life in industrial Northern England.
Homage to Catalonia (1938) recounts Orwell’s experiences as a soldier for the Republican faction in the Spanish Civil War.
Terms associated with Orwell include “Big Brother,” “Thought Police,” “Newspeak,” and “doublethink.”

overview.text: Plato (c. 428–347 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher of Classical Athens and the founder of the Academy, a philosophical school in Athens. He helped develop philosophical dialogue and dialectic—reasoning through questions and responses—and his work addressed both theoretical questions about reality and practical questions about how people should live.

A major Platonic idea is the Theory of Forms, or Ideas, which seeks to address the problem of universals: how general concepts relate to particular things. Plato was the teacher of Aristotle and the student of Socrates, and his surviving works remained influential through later centuries. Platonism and its outgrowth Neoplatonism also influenced Christian, Jewish, and Islamic philosophy.

key_facts.text: Plato’s writings are chiefly associated with literary dialogues and dialectic, rather than only straightforward exposition.
His philosophical influences included Pythagoras, Heraclitus, and Parmenides; much later knowledge of those thinkers comes through Plato’s writings.
Plato’s complete works are believed to have survived, unlike those of nearly all his contemporaries.

overview.text: Marie Curie was a Polish and naturalized-French physicist and chemist who pioneered research on radioactivity, a term she coined. With Pierre Curie, she shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics. Her 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognized her discovery of radium and polonium and her study of radium.

Curie’s work also had medical applications. During the First World War, she developed mobile radiography units that brought X-ray services to field hospitals, and she later founded medical research institutes in Paris and Warsaw.

key_facts.text: Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, the first person to win two, and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different scientific fields.
She named polonium after Poland, her native country, while retaining a strong Polish identity after becoming a French citizen.
She founded the Curie Institute in Paris in 1920 and another in Warsaw in 1932; both became major medical research centers.
The synthetic element curium was named in Marie Curie’s honor.

overview.text: Charles-Pierre Baudelaire (1821–1867) was a French poet, essayist, translator, and art critic. His poetry combines controlled rhythm and rhyme with an exoticism inherited from Romantic poetry and observations of real life. His best-known work, Les Fleurs du mal (The Flowers of Evil), is a collection of lyric poetry.

Les Fleurs du mal expresses changing ideas of beauty amid the rapid industrialization and rebuilding of nineteenth-century Paris. Baudelaire also used the term modernité for the fleeting experience of urban life and art’s responsibility to capture it. His prose-poetry style influenced later poets including Paul Verlaine, Arthur Rimbaud, and Stéphane Mallarmé.

key_facts.text: Baudelaire’s full name was Charles-Pierre Baudelaire; he lived from 1821 to 1867.
He worked in several literary and artistic roles: poet, essayist, translator, and art critic.
Les Fleurs du mal responds to Paris’s transformation during Haussmann’s mid-nineteenth-century renovations.
Marshall Berman credited Baudelaire as the first Modernist.

overview.text: Haiku is a short-form poetic form that originated in Japan. Traditional Japanese haiku consist of three phrases totaling 17 morae (units called on in Japanese), arranged in a 5–7–5 pattern. They include a kigo, or seasonal reference, and a kireji, or “cutting word.” Classical poets such as Matsuo Bashō sometimes departed from the 17-on pattern or omitted a kireji.

Haiku grew from the opening stanza of renga, a larger Japanese poetry genre. These stanzas were called hokku and eventually became stand-alone poems; Masaoka Shiki gave haiku its current name in the late nineteenth century. Japanese haiku are traditionally printed on one line, while English versions often use three. Writers worldwide adapt the form, varying in how closely they follow traditional elements.

key_facts.text: Similar poems that do not follow traditional haiku rules are generally classified as senryū.
A haijin is a master or practitioner of haiku.
Tanka is another Japanese poetry form related to haiku; haibun and haiga are art forms that incorporate haiku.

overview.text: Kazakhstan is a landlocked country primarily in Central Asia, with part of its territory in Eastern Europe. It borders Russia, China, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. Its combination of Central Asian location and huge area gives it a distinctive geographic profile: it is the world’s largest landlocked country and the ninth-largest country by land area.

Its terrain includes extensive hilly plateaus and plains, while lowlands cover another large portion; mountains form its southern and eastern frontiers. This combination of vast low-lying regions and bordering mountains is a central feature of Kazakhstan’s physical geography.

key_facts.text: Although it is landlocked, Kazakhstan has a coastline along the Caspian Sea.
Astana is the capital. Almaty is the largest city and served as the capital until 1997.
Kazakhstan was the last constituent republic of the Soviet Union to declare independence, doing so in 1991.

overview.text: Enthalpy is a thermodynamic state function equal to a system’s internal energy plus the product of its pressure and volume. The pressure–volume term represents work involved in making room for the system against external pressure, so enthalpy is especially useful for measurements at constant pressure.

Because enthalpy depends only on a system’s initial and final states, not the path between them, scientists usually measure changes in enthalpy rather than absolute enthalpy. Under constant pressure, with matter and non-pressure work excluded, that change equals energy transferred as heat.

key_facts.text: The SI unit of enthalpy is the joule; calories and British thermal units are also used historically.
A standard enthalpy of reaction describes the change from reactants in their standard states to products in their standard states, commonly using 1 bar and 298 K.
For an endothermic process, ΔH is positive; for an exothermic process, ΔH is negative.
For an ideal gas, enthalpy depends on temperature rather than pressure or volume.

overview.text: Canada is a North American country extending from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific and northward into the Arctic Ocean. Its territory includes ten provinces and three territories, with varied weather and geological regions ranging from densely settled urban areas to vast sparsely populated spaces.
Canada is the world’s second-largest country by total area and has the longest coastline of any country. Its boundary with the United States is the longest international land border.

key_facts.text: Ottawa is the capital; Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver are the three largest metropolitan areas.
Indigenous peoples have continuously inhabited what is now Canada for thousands of years.
Canada was formed in 1867 when three British North American colonies joined in Confederation as a federal dominion of four provinces.
English and French are the country’s official languages in the federal jurisdiction.

overview.text: Philip George Zimbardo (1933–2024) was an American psychologist and Stanford professor whose work covered topics including time perspective, cognitive dissonance, persuasion, cults, deindividuation, shyness, and heroism.

He became especially associated with the 1971 Stanford prison experiment, which attracted major attention but was later criticized because its methods allowed Zimbardo and possible researcher biases to influence the results. His notable books include Shyness, The Lucifer Effect, and The Time Paradox.

key_facts.text: Zimbardo founded and led the Heroic Imagination Project, which promotes everyday heroism and resistance to bullying, bystander behavior, and negative conformity.
In the 1970s, he pioneered the Stanford Shyness Clinic and offered an early comprehensive treatment program for shyness.
He served as president of the American Psychological Association in 2002 and led the Western Psychological Association in 1983 and 2001.

overview.text: An acid is a chemical species that either donates a proton (H⁺), under the Brønsted–Lowry definition, or accepts an electron pair, under the Lewis definition. In water, proton-donating acids produce hydronium ions and are called Arrhenius acids.

An aqueous acid solution has a pH below 7; a lower pH indicates greater acidity and a higher hydrogen-cation concentration. Acids can turn blue litmus red and react with bases or some metals to form salts.

key_facts.text: Common examples include hydrochloric acid in gastric acid, acetic acid in vinegar, sulfuric acid in car batteries, and citric acid in citrus fruits.
Strictly, “acid” refers to the solute, while everyday usage may call the entire aqueous solution an acid.
Boron trifluoride (BF₃) is a Lewis acid: its boron atom accepts an electron pair from ammonia’s nitrogen atom to form a covalent bond.

overview.text: Time is used to order events, compare durations and intervals, and measure rates of change. It is often called the fourth, or temporal, dimension alongside the three spatial dimensions.

Modern physics joins time and space in spacetime. Under extreme conditions involving very high velocity or strong gravity, time can pass at different rates for an outside observer. Clocks and calendars provide everyday measurements, while time has also been important in navigation, astronomy, philosophy, and science.

key_facts.text: Everyday timekeeping uses clocks and calendars, with familiar cycles based on a 24-hour day and a 365-day year linked to Earth’s astronomical motion.
Scientific time scales range from Planck time to spans of billions of years.
Time dilation—the passing of time at different rates for an outside observer—matters especially at relativistic speeds or near black holes.
Time has been studied as a major subject in religion, philosophy, and science.

overview.text: The Hundred Years’ War was an intermittent series of conflicts between England and France during the late Middle Ages. It grew from feudal disputes over the Duchy of Aquitaine and Edward III of England’s claim to the French throne. Although commonly dated from 1337 to 1453, the conflict was repeatedly interrupted by truces, the Black Death, and other events.

The struggle expanded into a wider military, economic, and political contest involving factions across Western Europe. Five generations of rival dynasties fought over France, and the conflict helped reshape European warfare and strengthen national identities and centralized government in both kingdoms.

key_facts.text: The war is commonly divided into the Edwardian War, the Caroline War, and the Lancastrian War, separated by truces.
English forces initially prevailed, but the French House of Valois ultimately retained control of France.
Professional standing armies and artillery emerged among the military developments that changed European warfare.
Chivalry reached a high point during the conflict and then declined afterward.

overview.text: Israel, officially the State of Israel, is a country in the Southern Levant of West Asia. It borders Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, and Egypt; its western coast is on the Mediterranean Sea, and its southern tip reaches the Red Sea. The Dead Sea region includes the lowest point on Earth. Jerusalem is the government seat and proclaimed capital, while Tel Aviv is the country’s largest urban area and economic center. Israel’s location near major continental crossroads has given the region long historical importance. The modern state declared independence on 14 May 1948 after the British Mandate and a proposed UN partition, and its establishment was followed by war and a continuing Israeli–Palestinian conflict.

key_facts.text: The region has also been called Palestine or the Holy Land and was associated with ancient Canaanite, Israelite, Judahite, and Hasmonean polities.
The Zionist movement advocated a Jewish homeland in Palestine; Britain expressed support for that goal in the 1917 Balfour Declaration.
After the 1949 armistice, Gaza came under Egyptian control and the West Bank under Jordanian rule; no independent Palestinian Arab state was established then.
Israel’s political system includes the Knesset, a proportionally elected parliament; the prime minister leads the government, while the president is largely ceremonial.
Hebrew is Israel’s revived official language, and the country’s culture combines Jewish traditions with Arab influences.

overview.text: The Waste Land is T. S. Eliot’s 1922 poem and a central work of modernist poetry. Rather than following one continuous story, it moves among changing voices, narrators, locations, times, and styles. Its subject matter includes disillusionment and despair, presented through a fragmented and culturally wide-ranging design.

The poem’s five-part structure combines satire, prophecy, philosophical meditation, character vignettes, and a desert journey. It draws on literary and mythic sources including Ovid, Dante, Chaucer, and the Fisher King legend. Although its initial reception was mixed, it later became an established and influential work of modernism.

key_facts.text: The five sections are “The Burial of the Dead,” “A Game of Chess,” “The Fire Sermon,” “Death by Water,” and “What the Thunder Said.”
“The Burial of the Dead” introduces disillusionment and despair, while “A Game of Chess” presents alternating narrations and vignettes of empty lives.
“What the Thunder Said,” the final section, develops the poem’s earlier themes through a description of a desert journey.
Famous phrases include “April is the cruellest month,” “I will show you fear in a handful of dust,” and “These fragments I have shored against my ruins.”
The poem’s allusions range from Ovid’s Metamorphoses and Dante’s Divine Comedy to Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales and the Fisher King legend.

overview.text: The Pomp and Circumstance Marches are Edward Elgar’s series of orchestral marches: five original works composed from 1901 to 1930, followed by a sixth march assembled from Elgar’s sketches. The series is associated with England’s Last Night of the Proms and with graduation ceremonies in the United States and elsewhere, giving it a recognizable place in ceremonial performance.

key_facts.text: The five original marches were dedicated to Elgar’s friends, including conductor Alfred E. Rodewald, composer Granville Bantock, and several organists.
The sixth march was created in 2006 by Anthony Payne from sketches left by Elgar.
The first march is an established annual feature of England’s Last Night of the Proms.
The first march’s slow middle section is traditionally played as processional music at high-school and college graduation ceremonies in the United States and elsewhere.

overview.text: Calcium (Ca), atomic number 20, is a reactive alkaline earth metal. Calcium carbonate occurs in limestone and fossils of early sea life; gypsum, anhydrite, fluorite, and apatite are other calcium sources. These associations make calcium a useful recognition link between chemical elements and minerals.

Calcium matters in both technology and biology. Its compounds are used in foods and pharmaceuticals, cement, paper, electrical insulators, and soaps. In organisms, calcium ions help control cell signaling, neurotransmitter release, muscle contraction, enzyme activity, fertilization, membrane electrical differences, and bone formation.

key_facts.text: Humphry Davy isolated pure calcium in 1808 by electrolyzing one of its compounds.
Calcium is the fifth-most abundant element in Earth’s crust and the third-most abundant metal there, after iron and aluminum.
The name calcium comes from the Latin word calx, meaning “lime.”
Pure calcium has few applications because it is highly reactive; small amounts are used in steel alloys, and calcium–lead alloys are sometimes used in automotive batteries.

overview.text: Hinduism is an umbrella term for diverse Indian religious and spiritual traditions connected by dharma, a cosmic order maintained through ritual and righteous living. Scholars describe it as a synthesis with varied roots and no specific founder, developing after the Vedic period. Hinduism is practiced mainly in South Asia but also has communities across many other regions.

Its major scriptures include the Vedas, Upanishads, Puranas, Ramayana, Mahabharata—including the Bhagavad Gita—and the Agamas. Key ideas include karma, samsara (rebirth), and moksha (liberation). Devotion, worship, sacrifice, meditation, and Yoga are important practices; Hinduism has no central doctrinal authority.

key_facts.text: Sanātana Dharma means “eternal dharma” and is a name used for Hinduism since the 19th century.
Scholars commonly recognize four major denominations: Vaishnavism, Shaivism, Shaktism, and Smartism.
The six Āstika schools of Hindu philosophy are Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, and Vedanta.
Hindus live chiefly in India, Nepal, Mauritius, and Bali, Indonesia, with additional communities throughout South Asia and around the world.

overview.text: Louis Daniel Armstrong (1901–1971), nicknamed Satchmo, Satch, and Pops, was an American jazz and blues trumpeter and vocalist from New Orleans. He rose to prominence in the 1920s as an inventive trumpet and cornet player and helped shift jazz from collective improvisation toward solo performance.

Armstrong also became an influential singer: his gravelly voice, improvisation, and scat singing connected jazz with popular music. Recognized recordings include “What a Wonderful World,” “Hello, Dolly!,” and “When the Saints Go Marching In.” By the 1950s, he was an international musical icon appearing in broadcasts and films.

key_facts.text: Around 1922, Armstrong followed his mentor Joe “King” Oliver to Chicago to play in Oliver’s Creole Jazz Band; he later became a featured soloist and recording artist in New York.
With Ella Fitzgerald, he made Ella and Louis (1956), Ella and Louis Again (1957), and Porgy and Bess (1959).
Armstrong won a Grammy for Best Male Vocal Performance for “Hello, Dolly!” in 1965 and received a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 1972.
He took a well-publicized stand for desegregation during the Little Rock Crisis.
His recording of “Melancholy Blues” was included on the Voyager Golden Record, a collection of Earth’s sights and sounds sent into space.

overview.text: The Importance of Being Earnest: A Trivial Comedy for Serious People is Oscar Wilde’s farcical comedy, first performed in London in 1895. Two young men lead double lives to escape unwanted social obligations, both assuming the name Ernest while courting two young women. Through these tangled relationships, the play gently satirizes late Victorian manners.

The play is known for its wit and repartee, its parody of contemporary dramatic conventions, and comic figures such as Lady Bracknell, Miss Prism, and Canon Chasuble. It has remained a frequently revived work, with adaptations for radio, television, film, opera, and musical theater.

key_facts.text: It was the last of Wilde’s four drawing-room plays.
The opening performance took place on 14 February 1895 at London’s St James’s Theatre.
Reviews in Britain and overseas praised the play’s humor, though some critics questioned its lack of social messages.
The original production closed in May 1895 after 86 performances, as a result of the disgrace surrounding Wilde.

overview.text: Arabic is a Central Semitic language in the Afroasiatic family, spoken primarily across the Arab world. Its standard form, Modern Standard Arabic, derives from Classical Arabic; Western linguists often distinguish these forms, while Arabic speakers commonly group them under al-fuṣḥā, meaning “the eloquent Arabic.”

Arabic is one of the six official languages of the United Nations and the liturgical language of Islam. During the Middle Ages, it served as a major language of culture and learning, especially in science, mathematics, and philosophy.

key_facts.text: Arabic is written from right to left using the Arabic alphabet, an abjad script.
Arabic vocabulary has influenced many languages, notably Spanish and, to a lesser extent, Portuguese, Catalan, and Sicilian.
Maltese developed from an Arabic dialect but is written with the Latin alphabet.
Classical and Modern Standard Arabic preserve important grammatical and consonantal features of older Semitic languages, making them useful for reconstructing Proto-Semitic.

overview.text: Jane Eyre is a novel by English writer Charlotte Brontë about its title heroine’s growth to adulthood and her love for Mr. Rochester, the master of Thornfield Hall. A bildungsroman, or coming-of-age novel, it uses intimate first-person narration to present Jane’s experiences with psychological intensity.

Alongside its romance, the novel offers social criticism and a strong Christian moral framework. Jane’s individualistic character helps the work examine class, sexuality, religion, and feminism, while its focus on a protagonist’s inner life became an important part of its literary reputation.

key_facts.text: Brontë published the novel under the pen name Currer Bell on 19 October 1847.
Its original title was Jane Eyre: An Autobiography.
Critic Daniel S. Burt linked Brontë’s attention to private consciousness with later writers such as Marcel Proust and James Joyce.

overview.text: Claude Monet (Oscar-Claude Monet) was a French painter and a founder of Impressionism. He often painted outdoors, or “plein air,” trying to capture how nature appeared to him. His approach made him an important precursor to modernism.

Monet often painted the same subject repeatedly to show changing light and seasons. This method shaped his haystack and Rouen Cathedral series, while his garden at Giverny provided the setting for his long-running water-lily paintings.

key_facts.text: The movement’s name came from Monet’s painting Impression, Sunrise, exhibited in 1874.
Artist Eugène Boudin introduced Monet to plein-air painting.
Monet lived at Giverny from 1883 and developed a landscaped property that included a water-lily pond.
His haystack paintings date mainly to 1890–1891, and his Rouen Cathedral paintings to 1892–1894.

overview.text: Special relativity is a scientific theory about the relationship between space and time. Associated with Albert Einstein, it was presented in his 1905 paper “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies.” Its central principles state that the laws of physics are the same in all nonaccelerating reference frames and that all observers measure the same speed for light in a vacuum, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.

key_facts.text: An inertial reference frame is a frame of reference with no acceleration.
The shared-laws principle is called the principle of relativity.
The constant vacuum speed of light is called light-speed invariance, or the principle of light constancy.
The first postulate of the theory was first formulated by Galileo Galilei.

overview.text: Gregor Samsa is the central character in Franz Kafka’s novella The Metamorphosis. He is a salesman who wakes to discover that he has inexplicably become a huge insect, and the story follows both his struggle and his family’s attempt to adjust to the change.

The novella is one of Kafka’s best-known works and has prompted varied literary interpretations. Kafka’s wording describes Gregor generally as a huge insect or monstrous vermin, while adaptations and popular culture commonly portray him as a cockroach.

key_facts.text: The German title is Die Verwandlung, also translated as The Transformation.
Kafka published The Metamorphosis in 1915.
It first appeared in the October 1915 issue of Die weißen Blätter; a book edition followed in December.
At about 70 printed pages, it is the longest story Kafka considered complete and published during his lifetime.

overview.text: Mount Everest is the highest mountain on Earth when measured above sea level. It belongs to the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas, and its summit marks part of the China–Nepal border. A joint Nepalese-Chinese survey in 2020 measured it at 8,848.86 meters (29,031 feet).

Everest attracts many climbers and has main routes approaching from Nepal to the southeast and China to the north. The mountain presents hazards including altitude sickness, severe weather and wind, avalanches, and the Khumbu Icefall.

key_facts.text: The mountain has several regional names: Sagarmāthā in Nepali, Chamolangma in Sherpa, and Jomolangma or Čhomolangma in Tibetan.
Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary made the first documented ascent in 1953, using the Southeast Ridge route.
George Mallory and Andrew Irvine disappeared during a 1924 summit attempt; whether they reached the top remains debated.
A Chinese team made the first reported ascent from the North Ridge on May 25, 1960.

overview.text: Fungi are a kingdom of eukaryotic organisms that includes yeasts, molds, and mushrooms. Unlike plants, fungi do not photosynthesize; they obtain nutrients by absorbing dissolved organic molecules, often after releasing digestive enzymes. Their cell walls contain chitin, and they are major decomposers of organic matter.

Fungi occupy many ecological roles, including decomposers, parasites, and partners in symbioses with plants and animals. They matter to people as foods and fermentation organisms, as sources of antibiotics and industrial enzymes, and as causes of disease, toxins, crop losses, and food spoilage.

key_facts.text: Mycology is the branch of biology that studies fungi.
More than 90% of plants are described as dependent on mycorrhizal symbiosis, an association between plants and fungi.
Fungi are used in bread making and in fermenting products such as wine, beer, and soy sauce; they have also been used to produce antibiotics since the 1940s.
Some fungi produce mycotoxins, while fungal diseases such as rice blast can damage crops and food supplies.

overview.text: Jesus, also called Jesus Christ and Jesus of Nazareth, was a first-century Jewish preacher and religious leader in Roman Judaea. He is the central figure of Christianity, and the four canonical Gospels of the New Testament provide its principal accounts of his life. Modern scholars of antiquity broadly agree that he existed historically.

In Christian tradition, Jesus was arrested and crucified under Pontius Pilate, followed by the Resurrection, a foundational belief of the early Christian Church. Islam recognizes Jesus—Isa—as a messiah and prophet born to the virgin Mary, but not as divine; most Muslims believe that God raised him to Heaven rather than that he was crucified.

key_facts.text: Jesus taught through parables, debated the Pharisees and Sadducees about Jewish law, performed healings, and appointed twelve apostles.
Many Christian branches identify Jesus as the incarnation of God the Son; Christian theology also connects his death with atonement and expects his return.
Christmas, Good Friday, and Easter commemorate Jesus’s birth, crucifixion, and resurrection, respectively.
Mainstream Judaism rejects Jesus as the awaited messiah, while Islam regards him as both messiah and prophet.

overview.text: Utah is a landlocked state in the Mountain West and one of the Four Corners states. Most of its western half lies in the Great Basin, while urban development is concentrated largely along the Wasatch Front in the north-central part of the state, including the capital, Salt Lake City.

key_facts.text: Utah borders Arizona, Colorado, and New Mexico at the Four Corners; it also borders Wyoming, Idaho, and Nevada.
The Wasatch Front is home to roughly two-thirds of Utah’s population.
After becoming U.S. territory in 1848, Utah was admitted as the 45th state in 1896 after agreeing to outlaw polygamy.
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has its world headquarters in Salt Lake City and strongly influences Utah’s culture, politics, and daily life.
Utah has long been inhabited by Indigenous peoples including the ancient Puebloans, Navajo, and Ute.

overview.text: The clarinet is a single-reed woodwind instrument with a nearly cylindrical bore (inner air passage) and a flared bell. The name usually refers to the B-flat soprano clarinet, the most common member of a broader family of differently sized and pitched instruments.

The clarinet is a standard part of orchestras and concert bands. It is also used in classical music, military bands, klezmer, jazz, and other styles, giving it a broad role across concert and popular traditions.

key_facts.text: The clarinet family ranges from the A-flat piccolo clarinet to the B-flat contrabass clarinet.
Johann Christoph Denner is generally credited with developing the clarinet around 1700.
Denner’s instrument developed from the chalumeau, an earlier single-reed instrument, by adding a register key.
Later additions of keywork and airtight pads improved the instrument’s tone and playability.

overview.text: The Scarlet Letter: A Romance is Nathaniel Hawthorne’s 1850 historical novel, set in the Puritan Massachusetts Bay Colony between 1642 and 1649. It follows Hester Prynne, who has a daughter with a man she is not married to and is punished by being required to wear a scarlet “A” for “adultery.” Her attempt to create a new life of repentance and dignity gives the novel a framework for exploring legalism, sin, and guilt, alongside religious and historical allusions.

key_facts.text: The book was one of the first mass-produced books in the United States.
It was popular when first published and is considered a classic of American literature.
The novel has inspired adaptations for film, television, and the stage.

overview.text: The Handmaid’s Tale is Margaret Atwood’s 1985 dystopian novel. In near-future New England, the Republic of Gilead—a patriarchal, totalitarian religious state that has overthrown the United States—assigns women called Handmaids to bear children for high-status men. Its protagonist, Offred, lives under this system.

The novel examines women’s powerlessness, the suppression of reproductive rights, and the ways people resist while trying to preserve individuality and independence. Its title echoes Geoffrey Chaucer’s The Canterbury Tales and the tradition of fairy tales in which a central character tells her story.

key_facts.text: The novel won the 1985 Governor General’s Award and the first Arthur C. Clarke Award in 1987.
It was also nominated for the Nebula Award, Booker Prize, and Prometheus Award.
Adaptations include a 1990 film, a 2000 opera, and a 2017 television series.
Atwood published a sequel, The Testaments, in 2019.

overview.text: The Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS) is the highest court in the federal judiciary. It has ultimate appellate jurisdiction over federal cases and over state cases involving U.S. constitutional or federal law. It also has limited original jurisdiction, including certain cases involving states or diplomats. In 1803, it asserted judicial review, the power to invalidate a law that conflicts with the Constitution; it may likewise reject presidential directives that violate constitutional or statutory law.

Article III provides the Court’s constitutional foundation, while the First Congress established its initial composition and procedures through the Judiciary Act of 1789. The Court has nine justices—a chief justice and eight associate justices—who meet in Washington, D.C. Justices have lifetime tenure unless they die, retire, resign, or are impeached and removed.

key_facts.text: When a vacancy occurs, the president appoints a justice with the advice and consent of the Senate.
Each justice casts one vote in a case.
A justice may write a concurring or dissenting opinion, and other justices may join it.
If the chief justice is in the majority, the chief justice assigns the Court’s opinion; otherwise, the most senior justice in the majority assigns it.

source.title: Supreme Court of the United States

overview.text: The Doppler effect, also called Doppler shift, is a change in a wave’s observed frequency—or equivalently, its period—when the observer and source move relative to one another. Its familiar sound example is a passing siren: the pitch is higher during approach, unchanged at the instant of passing, and lower during recession.

The effect comes from changes in the spacing and timing of successive wave cycles reaching the observer. For waves traveling through a medium, such as sound, motion of the source, observer, medium, or any combination can contribute; for waves traveling through a vacuum, only source-observer relative motion matters.

key_facts.text: The effect is named for physicist Christian Doppler, who described it in 1842.
A source moving toward an observer emits successive cycles from progressively closer positions, shortening the observed period and increasing frequency.
A source moving away has the opposite effect: the observed period increases and frequency decreases.
Sound illustrates medium-dependent Doppler behavior, while electromagnetic or gravitational waves in a vacuum depend only on relative source-observer velocity.

overview.text: Washington Crossing the Delaware is the shared title of three 1851 oil-on-canvas paintings by German-American artist Emanuel Leutze. They portray General George Washington crossing the Delaware River with the Continental Army on the night of December 25–26, 1776, during the American Revolutionary War. The covert crossing led to a surprise attack and victory over Hessian forces at the Battle of Trenton, New Jersey, on December 26. The subject connects Washington’s image with this specific Revolutionary War episode.

key_facts.text: The original painting belonged to the Kunsthalle in Bremen, Germany, and was destroyed in a British bombing raid in 1942 during World War II.
One surviving version is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City.
Another version was formerly displayed in the White House and was purchased in March 2015 for display at the Minnesota Marine Art Museum in Winona, Minnesota.

overview.text: Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750) was a German composer and musician of the late Baroque period. His wide-ranging output includes the Brandenburg Concertos, Goldberg Variations, The Well-Tempered Clavier, organ music, and the Sonatas and Partitas for Solo Violin. His music is strongly associated with counterpoint and forms such as the canon and fugue.

Bach’s posthumous history includes nineteenth-century biographies and the printing of his known music. Felix Mendelssohn’s 1829 performance of the St. Matthew Passion helped precipitate the Bach Revival.

key_facts.text: From 1723, Bach served as Thomaskantor in Leipzig, directing music for four Lutheran city churches and the St. Thomas School.
He wrote hundreds of sacred and secular cantatas, as well as Passions, oratorios, motets, and Latin church music.
Bach adapted musical rhythms, forms, and textures associated especially with Italy and France into established German styles.
Four of Bach’s sons—Wilhelm Friedemann, Carl Philipp Emanuel, Johann Christoph Friedrich, and Johann Christian—became composers.

overview.text: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca citadel in southern Peru’s Eastern Cordillera. It stands on a mountain ridge at 2,430 meters, above the Sacred Valley and along the Urubamba River, which forms a deep canyon in the region.

Built around 1450, Machu Picchu may have served as an estate for Inca emperor Pachacuti, although no contemporary written records confirm that role. Abandoned roughly a century later, it remains an iconic symbol of Inca civilization and a major archaeological site.
