overview.text: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is an extensive, membrane-bound network of connected tubes and flattened sacs inside eukaryotic cells; its membrane is continuous with the nuclear envelope, and its interior forms a compartment separate from the cytosol. Its two regions are named for their appearance: rough ER has ribosomes attached, while smooth ER lacks them. Ribosomes on rough ER make proteins destined for membranes, secretion, or certain organelles; the ER helps process these proteins before they travel in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus. Smooth ER makes lipids, including phospholipids, and can store calcium and help detoxify some chemicals. Together, the ER’s production and transport roles help supply cell membranes and route proteins.

key_facts.text: The ER’s membrane network is continuous with the nuclear envelope, while the ER interior remains separate from the cytosol.
Ribosomes attached to rough ER give it a dotted or granular appearance; smooth ER has few or no attached ribosomes.
Rough ER makes and processes proteins for cell membranes, export from the cell, and destinations such as lysosomes.
Smooth ER produces lipids, including phospholipids; some cells also use it to store calcium or detoxify certain chemicals.
Some ER-made proteins travel in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus for further processing.

overview.text: Inertia is matter’s tendency to resist a change in its motion: an object at rest stays at rest, while one already moving continues in a straight line at constant speed unless a net external force acts. This principle is stated in Newton’s first law, also called the law of inertia, and explains why motion can continue without a continuing push. Everyday objects often slow because friction or drag supplies an external force, not because inertia makes them stop. More massive objects have greater inertia, so their motion is harder to change; mass measures inertia and, unlike weight, does not depend on location or gravity.

key_facts.text: With no net external force, an object at rest remains at rest.
An object in motion keeps a constant velocity—a straight path at constant speed—unless a net external force acts.
Friction and drag can slow moving objects; inertia itself is not what makes them stop.
Greater mass means greater inertia, making an object’s motion harder to change.
Newton’s laws describe how inertia behaves, but do not explain its underlying nature.

overview.text: Influenza viruses, commonly called flu viruses, are contagious respiratory viruses that infect the nose, throat, and lungs. They belong to the Orthomyxoviridae family and carry their genetic information as segmented, single-stranded RNA. Four types—A, B, C, and D—are recognized; types A and B cause seasonal epidemics in people, while influenza A is the only type known to cause flu pandemics. Influenza A is notable for its changing surface proteins: hemagglutinin (H) helps the virus attach to cells, and neuraminidase (N) helps newly formed viruses leave infected cells. A subtype name such as H1N1 identifies the virus’s H and N versions. Flu spreads mainly in respiratory droplets.

key_facts.text: Influenza A and B cause seasonal epidemics in people; influenza A is the only type known to cause flu pandemics.
Influenza A subtypes are named by combining their hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) types, as in H1N1; 18 H and 11 N subtypes are recognized.
Influenza A and B viruses have genomes made of eight separate RNA segments.
Hemagglutinin binds to a cell receptor, while neuraminidase helps new viruses release from an infected cell.
Flu spreads mainly through droplets produced when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks; spread from contaminated surfaces is less common.

overview.text: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or NASA, is a U.S. government agency responsible for research and exploration in both air and space. President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the law creating NASA on July 29, 1958; the agency began operating on October 1 that year, following the Soviet Union’s Sputnik launch and drawing on the earlier National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics. NASA is distinctive because its work spans aviation research, Earth and space science, and both human and robotic spaceflight. Its missions range from studying Earth and the solar system to exploring the universe, while its aeronautics research seeks to improve aircraft and aviation. This combination makes NASA a major organizer of U.S. scientific exploration and flight research.

key_facts.text: The National Aeronautics and Space Act was signed on July 29, 1958, and NASA opened for business on October 1, 1958.
NASA took over much of the work of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA), connecting its space program to an existing U.S. aeronautics research tradition.
NASA’s work includes human spaceflight, robotic spacecraft, science missions, and aeronautics research—not space travel alone.
NASA’s early programs included Mercury and Apollo human spaceflight, robotic missions to other worlds, and research intended to improve air transport.
NASA science missions study Earth and destinations across the solar system, as well as objects and questions beyond it.

overview.text: Red is a family of hues perceived when light stimulates vision in a way associated with the long-wavelength edge of the visible spectrum; NASA places that edge near 700 nanometers, beyond which lies invisible infrared. It is not one single wavelength or one fixed pigment: hue varies continuously, and red paints and dyes can be made from different materials. Red’s role as a “primary” depends on the mixing system: it is primary for combining emitted light (RGB), but printing inks use cyan, magenta, and yellow. Its meanings also depend on culture; for example, Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art describes red in China as linked with celebration, prosperity, power, and good fortune.

key_facts.text: NASA gives the typical visible-light range as about 380–700 nanometers; red is near its long-wavelength edge, and infrared is beyond what people can see.
On screens and in other additive-light systems, red is one of the red-green-blue primaries; red plus green light appears yellow.
In subtractive color mixing used for printing, cyan, magenta, and yellow are the primaries; combining magenta and yellow can produce red.
Red is not one fixed material: the museum describes vermilion as a red pigment made from cinnabar or produced synthetically, and notes that artworks use varied red pigments and dyes.

In the Chinese contexts described by the National Museum of Asian Art, red has been associated with celebration, prosperity, power, and good fortune; these are cultural meanings, not universal definitions.

overview.text: Natural gas is a fossil fuel found in underground rock formations, formed over geologic time from buried organic remains transformed by heat and pressure. It is a mixture, but methane (CH4) is usually its largest component; raw gas may also contain other hydrocarbons, water vapor, and nonhydrocarbon gases. In its untreated form it is colorless and odorless, so gas companies add mercaptan—a sulfur-containing odorant with a strong smell—to many supplies to help people notice leaks. People burn natural gas for electricity and building heat, and industry also uses it for heat, power, and as a feedstock for products and chemicals.

key_facts.text: Methane (CH4) is natural gas’s largest component, but the fuel also contains smaller amounts of other substances.
Heat and pressure acting on buried remains of plants and animals formed natural gas over millions to hundreds of millions of years.
Mercaptan, a sulfur-containing odorant, is added to natural gas in distribution pipelines to help people detect leaks; the gas itself is odorless.
Natural gas is used to generate electricity and heat buildings, and industry uses it for energy and as a raw material in products.

overview.text: The thyroid is a small, butterfly-shaped endocrine gland at the front of the neck. It releases thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), hormones that regulate how the body uses energy and affect nearly every organ. The pituitary gland helps control thyroid hormone production by releasing TSH, which signals the thyroid how much T3 and T4 to make. The thyroid’s C cells also produce calcitonin, which helps lower blood calcium and counteracts parathyroid hormone. Together, these functions make the thyroid important to energy use and a contributor to calcium balance. Too much or too little thyroid hormone is associated with hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism.

key_facts.text: The thyroid sits at the front of the neck and is commonly described as butterfly-shaped.
T4 is thyroxine; T3 is triiodothyronine. The hormones help regulate the body’s use of energy.
TSH is made by the pituitary gland and signals the thyroid how much T3 and T4 to produce.
Thyroid C cells make calcitonin, which helps lower blood calcium and opposes parathyroid hormone’s action.
Hyperthyroidism means the thyroid makes more hormone than the body needs; hypothyroidism means it does not make enough.

overview.text: In programming, a variable is a named way for a program to refer to data used in calculations and instructions. In languages such as C#, a declaration associates a name and type with a storage location; assignment places a value there, and a later assignment can replace it. Variables make programs adaptable: code can reuse and update information, such as a running score, instead of repeating fixed values. A variable’s scope determines where its name can be used. The details vary by language: JavaScript `let` variables can be reassigned, but `const` variables cannot; Java also distinguishes local variables, fields, and parameters. Thus, a variable is more than an algebra symbol: it is a programming-language construct governed by rules for naming, values, and access.

key_facts.text: In C#, a declaration associates a variable’s name and type with a storage location; assignment stores a value there.
An assignment evaluates the expression on its right, then stores its result in the variable on the left; a later assignment can replace the earlier value.
A variable’s scope sets where its name can be accessed; JavaScript `let` and `const` are block-scoped.
In Java, variables include local variables, fields, and parameters; local variables are visible within the methods where they are declared.
In JavaScript, `let` can be reassigned, while `const` must be initialized when declared and cannot be reassigned.

overview.text: Syphilis is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Treponema pallidum; it matters because, although curable, untreated infection can persist and cause serious damage. It usually spreads through direct contact with infectious sores during vaginal, anal, or oral sex, and can pass from a pregnant person to a fetus. The illness is described in primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary stages: an often painless sore called a chancre may appear first, followed by a sometimes faint rash, often on the palms or soles. Symptoms can disappear during latent infection. Years later, some untreated cases affect the heart, brain, or nervous system. Testing is important because signs may go unnoticed; antibiotics can cure the infection, though not always reverse damage.

key_facts.text: The bacterium Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, a sexually transmitted infection.
Syphilis can spread through direct contact with sores during vaginal, anal, or oral sex, and from a pregnant person to a fetus.
Its stages are primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary. The first may feature a painless chancre; secondary syphilis may cause a rash, including on the palms or soles.
Latent syphilis may have no visible signs; some untreated infections later damage the heart, brain, or nervous system.
Syphilis is curable with appropriate antibiotics, but treatment may not undo damage already caused by the infection.

overview.text: Betelgeuse, also designated Alpha Orionis, is an orange-red red supergiant marking Orion the Hunter’s shoulder. Its size, brightness, and relative closeness make it one of the few stars whose surface astronomers have resolved and monitored directly. It is a semiregular variable: its brightness rises and falls, with occasional irregular changes. During the Great Dimming of late 2019 and early 2020, it faded dramatically; observations showed that cooled ejected gas formed dust that temporarily obscured it, rather than the dimming signaling an imminent supernova. As a massive, evolved star, Betelgeuse is expected eventually to explode as a supernova, but the event is not predicted soon.

key_facts.text: Betelgeuse marks Orion’s shoulder and is also called Alpha Orionis.
Its brightness varies semiregularly, with both recurring cycles and occasional irregular changes.
In late 2019 and early 2020, a cloud of dust formed from ejected gas temporarily dimmed the star; the event was not evidence of an imminent supernova.
Astronomers have directly imaged Betelgeuse’s surface, making it unusually useful for studying changes in a red supergiant.
Betelgeuse is expected eventually to become a supernova, but that does not mean an explosion is imminent.

overview.text: Redshift is the shift of light’s spectral features toward longer wavelengths, toward the red end of the visible spectrum. Astronomers identify familiar emission or absorption lines and compare their observed positions with laboratory wavelengths; the displacement reveals a redshift, often written z. For a source moving away relative to an observer, the Doppler effect stretches observed light, while approaching sources are blueshifted. For distant galaxies, the major redshift is generally cosmological: expansion of space stretches light as it travels, rather than the simple motion-through-space Doppler shift. Measuring redshift helps astronomers study galaxy motion and cosmic expansion, and investigate light from the distant, earlier universe.

key_facts.text: Redshift means a shift toward longer wavelengths; the opposite shift, toward shorter wavelengths, is called blueshift.
Astronomers measure redshift by comparing recognizable spectral lines with their known wavelengths in laboratory spectra.
Redshift can have different causes: source motion (Doppler), the stretching of space (cosmological), or light escaping a gravitational field (gravitational).
For distant galaxies, cosmological redshift occurs as the universe’s expansion stretches light on its journey to us; it is not simply ordinary motion through space.
Redshift measurements help astronomers investigate galaxy recession and cosmic expansion; greater cosmological redshift can also reveal light from farther back in the universe’s history.

overview.text: Mechanical stress describes the intensity of forces carried inside a material when external loads push, pull, or shear it. In a simple uniform case, stress equals force divided by the area over which it acts (σ = F/A), so its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), or newton per square metre. Strain, by contrast, measures deformation—such as the fractional change in a rod’s length—and has no units. Stress may be tensile (pulling), compressive (squeezing), or shear (sliding layers). In the elastic, approximately linear range, stress is proportional to strain; the slope is an elastic modulus, such as Young’s modulus for stretching or compression. This relationship helps engineers estimate material deformation under load, while excessive stress can cause permanent deformation or failure.

key_facts.text: For tensile or compressive stress, the force acts perpendicular to a cross-section; in the simple uniform case, stress is that force divided by the area.
Shear stress comes from forces parallel to a surface and tends to make neighboring parts of a solid slide past one another.
A rod’s tensile strain is its change in length divided by its original length, making strain a unitless measure of deformation.
Young’s modulus is the stress-to-strain ratio for tensile or compressive deformation in the linear elastic range; shear deformation has its own shear modulus.
Loads that vary or repeat, and flaws in a material, can increase the risk of stress-related damage or failure.

overview.text: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a method for working out molecular structure by reading signals from magnetically responsive atomic nuclei. In a strong magnetic field, nuclei such as hydrogen-1 and carbon-13 occupy different energy states; radiofrequency energy can prompt transitions, and the resulting resonance frequencies depend on each nucleus’s local chemical surroundings. A spectrum displays these differences as chemical shifts, usually in parts per million relative to a reference such as tetramethylsilane (TMS), allowing chemists to distinguish kinds of atomic environments. Because patterns and couplings among signals reveal how atoms connect, NMR is important for identifying molecules and studying their structure and motion, including proteins and other biological molecules.

key_facts.text: Common NMR-active nuclei include hydrogen-1 and carbon-13; nitrogen-15 and phosphorus-31 can also be studied.
A chemical shift reflects a nucleus’s electronic and chemical environment; distinct environments can produce distinct signals.
Chemical shifts are conventionally reported in parts per million (ppm); in proton NMR, TMS is defined as zero on the shift scale.
Spin-spin coupling can provide clues about connections between atoms through the bonds in a molecule.
NMR helps determine molecular structures and study biomolecules, including protein structure and molecular motion.

overview.text: Binary is a base-two number system: it writes numbers using only 0 and 1, with each position representing a power of two. A digit, or bit, tells whether that place value contributes to the number; for example, 1011₂ represents 8 + 2 + 1, or eleven. Binary is important in computing because digital devices can represent information using two distinguishable states, and patterns of bits can encode numbers, text, images, and other data. Binary logic also uses two values—true and false—and operations such as AND, OR, and NOT. The ideas are related but distinct: binary numerals represent quantities, while Boolean values express whether logical statements are true or false.

key_facts.text: Base two uses only the digits 0 and 1; after 1, counting continues as 10₂.
Binary place values grow by powers of two from right to left: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.
A bit is a binary digit. With n bits, there are 2ⁿ possible patterns; for unsigned numbers, those patterns represent values from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
Boolean logic works with true and false values. AND, OR, and NOT combine or change those values according to rules shown in truth tables.
Computers often use 1 and 0 to encode true and false, but that convention does not make a binary numeral the same thing as a logical truth value.

overview.text: Evolutionary theory explains how populations change across generations and how life’s diversity arose through branching descent from shared ancestors. In biology, evolution involves changes in inherited genetic material in a population; individuals do not evolve during their own lives. Natural selection is one major mechanism: when heritable differences affect survival or reproduction, associated traits can become more common over time. Mutation and sexual reproduction contribute genetic variation. Fossils, DNA, anatomy, and embryological patterns provide evidence for evolutionary relationships. In science, a theory is a well-tested explanation supported by evidence, not a casual guess. Research continues to refine details of evolutionary history and the processes involved.

key_facts.text: Evolution is change in inherited genetic material in populations over time; it does not change an individual organism during its lifetime.
Natural selection occurs when inherited differences affect survival and reproduction, changing how common traits are in a population.
Mutation and sexual reproduction contribute to heritable genetic variation; competition and differences in reproductive success can influence which traits spread.
Evidence for common ancestry includes similarities in DNA, anatomy, and embryological development; fossils also document changes in life through time.
A scientific theory is a tested explanation supported by evidence, rather than an untested opinion; evolutionary science continues to investigate its details.

overview.text: Mosquitoes are slender, winged insects in the family Culicidae, with thousands of species; the name comes from Spanish for “little fly.” Their life cycle has four stages—egg, aquatic larva, aquatic pupa, and flying adult. In species that take blood meals, females feed on people or other animals because blood supplies protein for making eggs; males do not bite. Mosquitoes matter because some species carry pathogens between hosts, but the risk is species- and pathogen-specific. Malaria, for example, is transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, and only a minority of Anopheles species can transmit it.

key_facts.text: Mosquitoes belong to the family Culicidae; the word “mosquito” comes from Spanish for “little fly.”
Mosquitoes develop through four stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult; the first three stages are aquatic.
In blood-feeding mosquito species, females use blood to obtain protein for egg production; males do not bite.
Only female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit human malaria, and only a minority of Anopheles species transmit it in nature.

overview.text: Sodium (Na), element 11, is a soft, silvery metal in Group 1, the alkali metals. Its metallic form reacts vigorously with water and air, so sodium is not found as a free metal in nature. A useful clue to its identity is the intense yellow-orange light associated with sodium in flame tests; its characteristic spectral line is near 589 nanometres. Sodium is more commonly encountered in compounds: sodium chloride is table salt, sodium carbonate is soda ash, sodium bicarbonate is baking soda, and sodium hydroxide is caustic soda. Humphry Davy first isolated the metal in 1807 by using electricity to decompose sodium hydroxide.

key_facts.text: Sodium’s symbol is Na, its atomic number is 11, and it belongs to Group 1; its outer-electron configuration is [Ne]3s¹.
Pure sodium is a soft, silvery metal that reacts vigorously with water and is not found as a free metal in nature.
Sodium gives a distinctive yellow-orange flame-test glow; its prominent solar-spectrum line is near 589 nm.
Familiar sodium compounds include table salt (NaCl), soda ash (Na₂CO₃), baking soda (NaHCO₃), and caustic soda (NaOH).
Humphry Davy isolated sodium in 1807 by electrolysis of caustic soda, or sodium hydroxide.

overview.text: The Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram is a graph astronomers use to compare stars by intrinsic brightness—usually luminosity or absolute magnitude—and surface temperature, often represented by spectral type or color. In the customary layout, hotter stars appear to the left and brighter stars higher up. Stars form recognizable groups rather than appearing randomly: the main sequence is a diagonal band running from hot, bright stars at the upper left to cool, faint stars at the lower right. Giants occupy a bright region above it, while white dwarfs are hot but faint and appear at the lower left. These patterns help astronomers study stars and their evolution.

key_facts.text: Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell independently developed the diagram through studies in the early 1900s.
The horizontal axis can show surface temperature or spectral class; the vertical axis shows luminosity. Observational versions may instead use color and absolute magnitude.
The main sequence runs diagonally from hot, luminous stars to cool, faint stars; stars on it generate energy by fusing hydrogen into helium.
Giants are bright despite relatively cool surfaces and therefore appear above the main sequence; white dwarfs are hot but faint and appear at the lower left.
A star’s position reflects its properties and can help astronomers investigate its stage of evolution.

overview.text: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium is a population-genetics model describing how allele and genotype frequencies behave when evolutionary forces are absent. For a gene with two alleles, frequencies p and q produce expected genotype frequencies p², 2pq, and q²; the heterozygote frequency is 2pq. The model assumes random mating, a very large population, and no selection, mutation, or migration. Under these ideal conditions, allele frequencies stay constant across generations, providing a baseline for studying genetic change. Real populations do not perfectly meet these assumptions, so differences from the model’s predictions can help researchers investigate possible evolutionary influences.

key_facts.text: For two alleles, p + q = 1, and the expected genotype frequencies are p² (one homozygote), 2pq (heterozygote), and q² (the other homozygote).
The model assumes random mating, a very large population, and no natural selection, mutation, or migration at the gene being studied.
Hardy and Weinberg independently described the relationship between genotype and allele frequencies in 1908.
The model is a baseline for population genetics: deviations from its expected frequencies can prompt investigation, but matching the model does not by itself prove that every assumption holds.

overview.text: In signal processing and statistics, noise is variation or interference in recorded data that is not the information a measurement is meant to capture; it can mask or be mistaken for the signal. Often random, noise is not always random, and its meaning depends on the question: radio static can obscure a broadcast, while chance variation among observations can obscure a pattern in data. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compares useful signal strength with noise, so a higher ratio generally means the signal is easier to distinguish. There is no single formula for every field: one statistical definition compares a sample mean with its standard deviation, while signal measurements may compare signal amplitude with noise's standard deviation. Repeated measurements or filtering can sometimes improve SNR.

key_facts.text: Noise does not have to be sound: radio static and random fluctuations in measurements are examples.
Noise is often random, but it can also be nonrandom; whether something counts as noise depends on what information you are trying to detect.
A higher signal-to-noise ratio generally means the useful signal is stronger relative to interference and easier to distinguish.
There are different SNR definitions. NIST describes one statistical version as sample mean divided by sample standard deviation, for suitable ratio-scale data.
When the underlying signal repeats consistently and the noise is random, averaging repeated measurements can make the signal clearer.

overview.text: Retroviruses are RNA-genome viruses distinguished by copying their genetic information into DNA after entering a cell, then inserting that DNA into the host’s genetic material. The enzyme reverse transcriptase makes the DNA copy; viral integrase helps insert it. Once integrated, the viral DNA can be used by the cell to make viral proteins and new virus particles. HIV is a well-known example and belongs to the lentiviruses, a subgroup of retroviruses. This replication strategy matters medically: some retroviruses are associated with serious diseases, including AIDS and some cancers.

key_facts.text: Reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy from the virus’s RNA; this RNA-to-DNA step is called reverse transcription.
Integration is a separate step: the viral enzyme integrase helps insert viral DNA into the host cell’s DNA.
After integration, HIV uses parts of its host CD4 cell to make viral proteins and new virus particles.
HIV belongs to the lentiviruses, a subgroup of retroviruses.
Retroviruses are associated with illnesses that include AIDS and some cancers.

overview.text: The Boltzmann constant, written k or k_B, is a conversion factor linking thermodynamic temperature in kelvins to energy in joules. It lets physicists describe thermal behavior at the scale of individual particles rather than per mole: k = R/N_A, where R is the molar gas constant and N_A is Avogadro’s constant. Its SI value is exactly 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ joules per kelvin, and fixing this value defines the kelvin. For a monatomic ideal gas, the average translational kinetic energy per particle is 3/2 k_B T—not simply k_B T—while in statistical physics the constant also appears in the entropy relation S = k ln Ω.

key_facts.text: The SI fixes k at exactly 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J/K; its numerical value has no uncertainty in the SI.
The kelvin is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant’s numerical value, connecting the unit of temperature to energy.
For a monatomic ideal gas, a particle’s average translational kinetic energy is 3/2 k_B T; k_B T alone is not that average.
Statistical physics uses the relation S = k ln Ω, linking entropy S with the number Ω of accessible states.

overview.text: Gravitational waves are traveling disturbances in spacetime itself, not ordinary light waves or ripples moving through air. Predicted by Einstein’s general theory of relativity, they are produced by changing motions of mass; the strongest detectable signals come from extreme events such as black holes or neutron stars spiraling together. As a wave passes, it changes distances between objects, but the effect is extraordinarily small. LIGO’s first direct detection, in 2015, came from two merging black holes. Gravitational waves carry information from cosmic events and give scientists a new way to study the universe, complementing observations made with light.

key_facts.text: Einstein’s general theory of relativity predicts gravitational waves; direct detection later provided strong evidence for the theory.
When black holes or neutron stars orbit closer together, their system can emit waves that carry away energy.
A passing gravitational wave changes distances between objects; the resulting length changes are extremely small.
LIGO directly detected waves from merging black holes in 2015; the discovery was announced in 2016.
Gravitational-wave observations can be combined with observations of light to study cosmic events in a complementary way.

overview.text: A double bond is a covalent bond in which two atoms share two pairs of electrons—four electrons altogether. In the usual bonding model, it consists of one sigma (σ) bond and one pi (π) bond. A Lewis structure represents it with two lines, as in C=C, but the two parts differ: the sigma bond forms through head-on orbital overlap, while the pi bond forms through sideways overlap of p orbitals, creating electron density above and below the line between the nuclei. In ethene (C₂H₄), this arrangement helps keep the molecule planar; twisting the atoms would disrupt the pi-bond overlap. A triple bond, by comparison, contains one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

key_facts.text: In a double bond, the shared four electrons occupy one sigma bond and one pi bond.
The sigma bond forms through head-on orbital overlap; the pi bond forms through sideways overlap of p orbitals.
In ethene, the pi bond’s electron density lies above and below the plane of the sigma-bond framework.
Ethene is planar; rotating around its carbon–carbon double bond would disrupt the pi-orbital overlap.
A triple bond has one sigma bond and two pi bonds, distinguishing it from a double bond.

overview.text: A Wheatstone bridge is a four-resistor circuit used to find an unknown resistance by comparing it with known resistors. Its name honors Charles Wheatstone, who publicized it in 1843; Samuel Hunter Christie had described the arrangement in 1833, though accounts differ on whether Christie intended it specifically for resistance measurement. The resistors form two branches, with a detector joining their midpoints. When the bridge is balanced, the detector shows no current; the ratios of the resistances then determine the unknown. This “null” method makes the comparison useful without directly measuring the unknown’s current or voltage. Bridge circuits also help sensors detect resistance changes caused by properties such as temperature or stress.

key_facts.text: At balance, no current flows through the detector between the two branches’ midpoints, and the resistance ratios are equal.
With one resistor unknown, its value can be calculated from the other three; for the Open University’s labeling, R4 = R2 × R3 ÷ R1.
In a classroom setup, an adjustable resistor and a galvanometer can be used to find the balance point and determine the unknown resistance.
Bridge circuits can detect changes in sensor resistance caused by temperature or stress, helping measure physical properties.
Christie described the arrangement in 1833; Wheatstone brought it wider attention in 1843. Historical accounts differ on whether Christie originally intended it for resistance measurement.

overview.text: Biological evolution is change in the inherited genetic makeup and characteristics of populations across generations, not a transformation of an individual during its lifetime. Mutations and other genetic variation supply differences that can be inherited. Natural selection can make traits that improve survival and reproduction more common, but it is only one mechanism: random genetic drift and gene flow also change populations. Across many generations, these changes help explain adaptation, life’s diversity, and the divergence of populations into distinct species. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace jointly presented their theory of evolution by natural selection in 1858; Darwin’s influential On the Origin of Species followed in 1859.

key_facts.text: Evolution occurs in populations across generations; inherited variation, including variation from mutations and genetic recombination, provides differences that may be passed on.
Natural selection is one mechanism of evolution: heritable variants linked to greater reproductive success can become more common in a population.
Evolution is not limited to natural selection; genetic drift changes variant frequencies by chance, and gene flow can also contribute to evolutionary change.
Accumulated population changes can lead to divergence and, sometimes, the formation of a distinct species.
Alfred Russel Wallace shared credit with Charles Darwin for the theory of evolution by natural selection; they jointly presented it in 1858, and Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.

overview.text: Binary search is an algorithm for finding a target in an ordered collection. In a sorted array, it checks the middle item, then uses the comparison to discard the half where the target cannot be; it repeats on the remaining interval until the target is found or no candidates remain. This makes the worst-case search time logarithmic, or O(log n), rather than linear in the number of items, provided the array is already sorted. A related method searches a binary search tree: values smaller than a node lie in its left subtree, and larger values in its right. Tree searches take time proportional to tree height—O(log n) when balanced, but potentially O(n) when skewed.

key_facts.text: Array-based binary search requires the values to be sorted; each comparison narrows the candidate interval to one side of its midpoint.
If the target is not in the array, the search ends when the remaining interval is empty.
For a sorted array, binary search has worst-case logarithmic time, O(log n), because each step discards about half the remaining candidates.
In a binary search tree, keys smaller than a node’s key are in its left subtree and larger keys are in its right subtree; a search follows only the relevant branch.
Tree-search time depends on height: it is O(log n) for a balanced tree, but can reach O(n) if the tree is shaped like a linked list.

overview.text: Ivan Petrovich Pavlov (1849–1936) was a Russian physiologist whose experiments linked digestion with the nervous system. After beginning religious studies, he turned to science and investigated how digestive secretions worked. While studying dogs, Pavlov observed that salivation could begin before food arrived; he tested how a signal repeatedly paired with food could later trigger salivation on its own. He called this acquired response a “conditioned reflex,” distinguishing it from an unlearned reflex. This work helped make learned responses experimentally measurable and influenced the study of behavior. Pavlov received the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his research on digestion, not for the conditioning experiments.

key_facts.text: Pavlov was born in Ryazan in 1849, studied for the priesthood before pursuing science, and died in 1936.
His 1904 Nobel Prize recognized his research on the physiology of digestion.
His digestive research included methods for collecting secretions from different glands to study how they worked.
Pavlov called a learned response to a signal associated with food a “conditioned reflex”; he distinguished it from an unconditioned reflex.
His work helped establish experimental ways to investigate learned behavior and the relationship between behavior and bodily processes.

overview.text: Octane rating, also called octane number, describes how well a spark-ignition fuel resists auto-ignition as it is compressed. If fuel-air mixture ignites too early, it can cause engine knock, a pinging combustion event that may damage an engine. The rating compares a fuel’s knock behavior with reference fuels: iso-octane is assigned 100 and n-heptane 0. Standardized engine tests measure this resistance. In the United States, pump labels commonly show the average of research and motor octane numbers, which are measured under different operating conditions. A higher number indicates greater knock resistance, but does not mean every engine needs the highest grade.

key_facts.text: Knock occurs when unburned fuel-air mixture auto-ignites under high temperature and pressure before the advancing flame reaches it.
The reference value 100 is assigned to iso-octane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane); n-heptane is assigned 0.
In the United States, the pump label’s (R+M)/2 value is the average of research octane number (RON) and motor octane number (MON).
RON and MON tests use different operating conditions; MON testing uses higher air temperature and engine speed than RON testing.
An international standard describes determining MON with a standardized, variable-compression test engine.

overview.text: An atomic orbital is a quantum-mechanical description of an electron’s state in an atom, commonly visualized as a three-dimensional region where the chance of finding the electron is high—not a fixed track around the nucleus. It comes from solutions to the Schrödinger equation; the squared magnitude of its wavefunction gives the probability distribution. Quantum numbers describe orbitals: the principal number n relates to shell, general size, and energy, while the angular-momentum number ℓ identifies subshell type and shape. The familiar s, p, d, and f labels correspond to ℓ = 0, 1, 2, and 3. S orbitals are spherical, p orbitals often appear two-lobed, and d and f shapes are more complex. These patterns help chemists understand how atoms bond.

key_facts.text: An orbital is not a classical path: it describes the electron’s probability distribution in space.
The squared magnitude of the wavefunction, |ψ|², gives the probability distribution for finding an electron.
The principal quantum number n relates to an orbital’s shell and general size and energy; the angular-momentum quantum number ℓ determines its subshell type and shape.
The s, p, d, and f labels correspond to ℓ values 0, 1, 2, and 3. A subshell contains 1, 3, 5, or 7 orbitals, respectively.
S orbitals have spherical probability distributions; p orbitals are often shown as two-lobed and oriented in space. D and f orbital shapes are more complex.
Orbital directionality matters to chemists studying how atoms bond and form molecules.

overview.text: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes over time: over an interval, average acceleration equals the change in velocity divided by elapsed time. Because velocity includes both speed and direction, acceleration occurs when an object speeds up, slows down, or turns—even if its speed stays constant. Acceleration is a vector, so it has direction, and its SI unit is meters per second squared (m/s²). Newton’s second law connects acceleration to the net external force: F_net = ma. For a given mass, a larger net force produces greater acceleration; balanced forces mean zero net force and therefore zero acceleration. This relationship helps explain how forces change motion.

key_facts.text: Average acceleration is change in velocity divided by the time interval: a_avg = Δv/Δt.
Its SI unit is meters per second squared (m/s²), meaning velocity changes by a number of meters per second each second.
An object moving at constant speed still accelerates if its direction changes, as when it turns.
Acceleration can point opposite an object’s velocity, as when it slows down; a negative acceleration component indicates direction along the chosen axis, not automatically slowing.
Newton’s second law relates acceleration to net external force and mass: a = F_net/m. With zero net force, acceleration is zero.

overview.text: Sputnik 1 was the Soviet Union’s first artificial satellite and the first human-made satellite to orbit Earth. Launched on October 4, 1957, as part of the International Geophysical Year, it was a 58-centimeter-wide sphere weighing about 83.6 kilograms. Its transmitters sent repeating radio pulses that operators could detect, and the satellite circled Earth in roughly an hour and a half. Though modest in design, Sputnik demonstrated that a satellite could be placed in orbit and became a symbol of Soviet technological achievement. Its launch surprised many in the United States, heightened Cold War anxieties, and helped ignite the U.S.–Soviet Space Race—so it is widely treated as the beginning of the Space Age.

key_facts.text: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, during the International Geophysical Year.
It was a 58-centimeter-diameter sphere weighing about 83.6 kilograms (184 pounds).
Its radio transmitters sent repeating signals that could be monitored by radio operators; Sputnik itself carried no scientific instruments.
Its batteries ran out on October 26, 1957, and it reentered Earth’s atmosphere on January 4, 1958.
The launch began the Space Race and intensified Cold War concerns about Soviet technological and military capabilities.

overview.text: Bernoulli’s principle describes how pressure, speed, and height trade off in moving fluids through conservation of mechanical energy. In the familiar level-flow case, when height is unchanged, faster-moving fluid has lower static pressure; the broader Bernoulli equation includes gravitational height as well. The idealized relation is used for incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline, so it is not a rule that can be applied without checking conditions. Named for Swiss mathematician and physicist Daniel Bernoulli, it appeared in his 1738 work Hydrodynamica. It helps explain devices such as pitot tubes, which infer fluid speed from pressure differences, but it should not be treated as a complete, stand-alone explanation of how airplane wings produce lift.

key_facts.text: Bernoulli’s equation expresses conservation of mechanical energy in a fluid: pressure energy, kinetic energy, and gravitational potential energy per unit volume sum to a constant along a streamline under the stated ideal conditions.
For flow at constant height, the equation simplifies: if fluid speed increases, static pressure decreases, assuming the other conditions of the model hold.
The familiar form applies to incompressible, frictionless flow along a streamline; real flows may require accounting for effects the idealized relation leaves out.
The principle is named after Daniel Bernoulli; OpenStax notes that he published studies of fluid motion in Hydrodynamica in 1738.
A pitot tube uses pressure differences to measure fluid speed; aircraft commonly use this type of device for air-speed indication.

Bernoulli’s equation can relate airflow speed to pressure around a wing, but NASA cautions that the “equal transit time” explanation of lift misapplies it; wing lift involves the overall flow and pressure around the body.

overview.text: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide: a long, unbranched chain of glucose molecules joined by β(1→4) bonds. Those bonds make the chains extended; neighboring chains hydrogen-bond together into bundles called microfibrils. In plants, cellulose is a principal material of cell walls, which lie outside the cell membrane and help protect cells, give them shape, and provide support. The bundled fibers resist pulling forces, helping the wall withstand mechanical stress. Cellulose is also abundant in wood and is a major component of paper.

key_facts.text: Cellulose is made of glucose units linked by β(1→4) bonds.
Its chains are linear and extended; in each chain, every other glucose unit is flipped over.
Hydrogen bonds help neighboring cellulose chains assemble into strong bundles called microfibrils.
Plant cell walls are outside the cell membrane; cellulose is a major wall material that contributes structural support and shape.
Cellulose is a major component of wood and paper.

overview.text: Free radicals are atoms, molecules, or ions with at least one unpaired electron. Many are highly reactive, although some can be unusually stable. They matter because they act as intermediates in chemical reactions, including chain reactions and polymer production. In homolytic bond cleavage, a shared pair splits evenly, with one electron going to each product and producing two radicals. Their unpaired electrons give them magnetic properties that allow detection by electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy. EPR uses a magnetic field and microwave energy to detect such species, and its signals can reveal information about the molecular surroundings of unpaired electrons.

key_facts.text: A radical may be an atom, molecule, or ion; a dot beside its formula can mark the unpaired electron.
In homolysis, a bond splits so each product receives one of the bond’s electrons, forming two radicals.
Radicals can take part in addition reactions, and radical coupling can join two radicals to form a bond.
EPR detects species with unpaired electrons; it can help researchers learn about the molecular environment near an unpaired electron.
In 1900, Moses Gomberg reported the triphenylmethyl radical, challenging the then-common belief that carbon could form only four bonds.

overview.text: Ethanol, also called ethyl alcohol or EtOH, is a two-carbon organic alcohol with molecular formula C₂H₆O (structural formula CH₃CH₂OH); its terminal hydroxyl (–OH) group identifies it as an alcohol. It is the intoxicating alcohol in beer, wine, and spirits, but also an important industrial chemical used as a solvent and fuel. Yeast can produce it by fermenting sugars from plant material, while distillation separates it from the fermentation mixture. A notable feature is that ethanol and water form an azeotrope, so ordinary distillation cannot produce completely pure ethanol. Ethanol is also used in some hand sanitizers, though alcohol sanitizers do not eliminate every kind of germ.

key_facts.text: Ethanol’s molecular formula is C₂H₆O; its structural formula, CH₃CH₂OH, shows the hydroxyl group characteristic of alcohols.
Yeast fermentation can produce ethanol from sugars; industrial fuel production may use starch- or sugar-based crops, or cellulosic plant material.
Ethanol is used in beverages, as an industrial and laboratory solvent, and as a fuel.
Because ethanol and water form an azeotrope, ordinary distillation cannot separate them into completely pure ethanol; the source gives a maximum of about 95.6% ethanol by volume.
Some hand sanitizers use ethanol, but alcohol-based sanitizers do not eliminate every kind of germ.

overview.text: A website is an organized set of linked web pages and related resources, usually grouped under one domain name. It is different from a single web page, which is a browser-displayable document, and from a web server, the computer that hosts websites. Pages have web addresses called URLs, and links let people move between resources. A browser requests those resources from servers and displays the returned content, which may include text, images, styles, or scripts. Websites are one way people use the World Wide Web’s system of identified, connected resources. The Web was proposed at CERN in 1989 to help scientists share information; CERN’s public release of the software in 1993 helped it spread.

key_facts.text: A web page is a browser-displayable document; a website groups linked pages and associated resources, usually under a shared domain.
A URL is a web address used to locate a resource; hyperlinks connect resources and let users navigate between them.
A browser retrieves and displays web resources; a web server hosts them. A search engine helps users find pages but is not the browser.
Some websites are single-page apps: they update content within one page, and the address may not change as users navigate.
The Web was conceived at CERN to support information-sharing among scientists. CERN put its software in the public domain on April 30, 1993.

overview.text: An electric circuit is an interconnected path of conductors and components through which electric charge can move. When the path is complete, a source such as a battery provides electrical potential that drives current. A simple circuit might include wires, a switch and a lamp or resistor; more complex circuits combine many components. Opening a switch breaks the path and stops current from flowing through that route. Circuit diagrams use standard symbols to show components and their connections. Circuits are essential to electrical devices, from household lights to computers and phones, whose circuitry can be extraordinarily small.

key_facts.text: Current can flow when there is a complete path; opening a switch interrupts the path and stops current in that circuit.
Circuit diagrams use standard symbols for components and lines for connecting wires.
Conventional current is drawn from a battery’s positive terminal toward its negative terminal. In metal wires, electrons move in the opposite direction.
In a series circuit, components are connected one after another in the same branch; in the simple series circuit described by OpenStax, current is the same throughout.
A capacitor can store electric charge, a property used in many circuits.

overview.text: Richard P. Feynman (1918–1988) was a theoretical physicist whose work helped shape quantum electrodynamics (QED), the theory describing how charged particles interact with light. Born in New York City, he earned his doctorate at Princeton and later taught at Caltech. With Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga, he shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics for fundamental work on QED. Feynman diagrams gave physicists a visual shorthand for calculating how quantum particles behave in electromagnetic fields. An influential teacher, he also served on the commission investigating the 1986 Challenger disaster. In his own report, he challenged NASA reliability estimates and highlighted the gap between management’s and engineers’ assessments.

key_facts.text: Feynman was born in New York City in 1918 and earned his physics Ph.D. from Princeton in 1942.
He shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics with Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga for fundamental work on quantum electrodynamics.
Feynman diagrams are visual tools physicists use in calculations involving particle interactions.
He served on the Rogers Commission, which investigated the 1986 Challenger accident.
In his commission report, Feynman criticized the handling of reliability estimates and warned that O-ring erosion was evidence of a problem, not proof of safety.

overview.text: Ecological carrying capacity is the largest population of a particular species that an environment can sustain under its available conditions; ecologists often represent it as K in the logistic growth model. As a population grows, individuals share limited supplies—such as food, water, nutrients, and space—so competition can increase and population growth slows. In the simplified logistic model, growth levels near K, but real populations may overshoot and fluctuate around it. Carrying capacity is not a permanent number: seasons, climate, habitat changes, and disturbances can alter resources and shelter. Understanding this limit helps explain population change and informs wildlife and habitat management.

key_facts.text: In the logistic growth model, K represents carrying capacity; when population size reaches K, the model predicts zero net growth.
Resources that can limit a population include food, water, nutrients, energy, living space, and shelter.
When resources become scarce, birth rates may fall, death rates may rise, or both; real populations can fluctuate around or temporarily exceed carrying capacity.
Carrying capacity can change with seasons and weather, and natural events such as fires can alter habitat conditions and available resources.
The National Park Service’s Florida panther lesson illustrates that shrinking habitat and reduced food, water, or shelter can lower the number of panthers an area can support.

overview.text: Geothermal energy is heat from within Earth, accessed from hot rocks, underground water or steam, and—in heating and cooling systems—the relatively steady temperature of shallow ground. Its significance is its versatility: deep geothermal fluids can be brought up through wells and used to turn turbines and generate electricity, while direct-use systems supply heat to buildings or industrial processes. Geothermal heat pumps work differently: they exchange heat with the ground, drawing it into buildings in winter and transferring indoor heat into the ground in summer. Electricity plants include dry-steam, flash-steam, and binary-cycle designs. Earth’s interior heat is continually replenished by the natural decay of radioactive elements.

key_facts.text: “Geothermal” means heat from Earth; geothermal resources include hot rocks and underground water or steam.
In geothermal power plants, underground heat reaches the surface through wells and is used to drive turbines that generate electricity.
Dry-steam, flash-steam, and binary-cycle plants use different methods to turn geothermal heat into turbine power.
Geothermal heat pumps use the ground’s relatively steady temperature: they bring heat indoors in winter and move indoor heat into the ground in summer.
Geothermal heat can also be used directly for building heat and industrial processes, without first generating electricity.

overview.text: A capacitor is an electrical component that stores separated charge: its conducting parts hold equal amounts of positive and negative charge, usually with an insulating material between them. This arrangement creates an electric field, and the capacitor’s energy is stored in that field. Capacitance describes how much charge is stored for a given voltage, so it is calculated as charge divided by voltage. Its SI unit is the farad, equal to one coulomb per volt. Capacitors are useful in circuits for tasks such as filtering static from radio reception and storing energy for heart defibrillators.

key_facts.text: A typical capacitor has two nearby conductors that do not touch; an insulator, called a dielectric, often separates them.
Charging a capacitor separates equal positive and negative charges onto its conductors, while the capacitor as a whole remains neutral.
Capacitance is charge divided by voltage: C = Q/V. A larger capacitance means more charge stored for the same voltage.
The farad (F) is the SI unit of capacitance; one farad equals one coulomb per volt.
A charged capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its conductors; its energy can be calculated as U = ½CV².

overview.text: Frequency describes how often a repeating event occurs: it is the number of cycles or oscillations completed—or waves passing a fixed point—per unit time. It is a core way to characterize periodic motion and waves, alongside period, amplitude, and (for waves) wavelength. If one cycle takes period T, frequency f = 1/T, so a faster repetition has a shorter period. Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), with 1 Hz equal to one cycle per second. For a traveling wave, speed v equals frequency times wavelength (v = fλ); when wave speed in a medium is fixed, higher frequency corresponds to shorter wavelength. In sound, higher frequency is heard as higher pitch.

key_facts.text: For repeating motion, the period is the time taken for one complete oscillation; frequency counts oscillations per unit time.
Frequency and period are reciprocals: f = 1/T. A shorter period means a higher frequency.
The hertz (Hz) is the SI unit of frequency; 1 Hz equals one cycle per second.
For a traveling wave, v = fλ; at a fixed wave speed, increasing frequency means decreasing wavelength.
For sound, higher frequency corresponds to higher pitch.

overview.text: Kinetic energy is the energy associated with motion: a moving ball, flowing water, or spinning wheel can possess it. For an object moving as a whole in translational motion, its kinetic energy is KE = ½mv², where m is mass and v is speed; the unit is the joule. Because speed is squared, doubling speed gives four times as much translational kinetic energy, while doubling mass at the same speed doubles it. A rotating rigid object also has rotational kinetic energy, KE = ½Iω², where I reflects how its mass is distributed around the axis and ω is angular speed. As an object falls, gravitational potential energy can change into kinetic energy.

key_facts.text: Translational kinetic energy is KE = ½mv²; m is mass and v is speed. Its SI unit is the joule.
At the same mass, doubling an object's speed makes its translational kinetic energy four times greater.
For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, rotational kinetic energy is KE = ½Iω²; I is moment of inertia and ω is angular speed.
Moment of inertia depends on how much mass lies at different distances from the rotation axis; mass farther from the axis contributes more.
A rolling object can have both translational and rotational kinetic energy; as it rolls downhill, gravitational potential energy can become both forms.

overview.text: Diffraction is a wave behavior: waves spread and bend around obstacles or after passing through openings. It occurs with water, sound, and light, but is easiest to notice when the opening or obstacle is about the same size as the wavelength; sound, for example, can spread around a doorway, while light usually does not. Huygens’s principle helps model the effect by treating points on a wavefront as sources of smaller wavelets. These waves can overlap and form patterns of stronger and weaker signals. In X-ray crystallography, scientists study those patterns to work out how atoms are arranged in repeating crystal structures.

key_facts.text: Diffraction is the spreading or bending of waves at an opening or obstacle; it occurs with different kinds of waves, not only light.
Diffraction is more noticeable when an opening or obstacle is similar in size to the wave’s wavelength.
Huygens’s principle models wavefronts as producing secondary wavelets, which together form a new wavefront.
Diffraction patterns can be evidence of wave behavior; light spreading through slits is one example.
X-ray crystallography uses the patterns made when X-rays scatter from crystals to determine the arrangement of atoms.

overview.text: A polar covalent bond forms when two atoms share bonding electrons, but one attracts the shared electron cloud more strongly because it has higher electronegativity. The sharing remains covalent rather than involving complete electron transfer, yet the unequal distribution gives the atoms partial charges: δ− on the electron-richer atom and δ+ on the other. In methanol’s C–O bond, for example, oxygen pulls electron density away from carbon. Hydrogen chloride also has a polar covalent bond; its measurable dipole reflects charge separation, not a full electron transferred. Bond polarity helps describe the continuum between covalent and ionic bonding, and generally increases as the electronegativity difference grows.

key_facts.text: Electronegativity describes an atom’s ability to attract shared bonding electrons; a difference between bonded atoms causes unequal sharing.
The more electron-attracting atom is labeled δ−, and the other atom δ+; these are partial charges, not full ionic charges.
A C–O bond in methanol is polar: oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than carbon.
A bond dipole describes charge separation; in HCl, the electron distribution favors chlorine, while hydrogen is partially positive.
A molecule’s dipole is the vector sum of its bond dipoles, so bond polarity and whole-molecule polarity are related but distinct ideas.

overview.text: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1632–1723) was a Dutch microscopist from Delft whose careful observations helped reveal a previously unseen living world and made microscopy a powerful tool for studying nature. He made his own lenses and used compact, single-lens handheld instruments, which could magnify up to about 250 times. Through them, he described tiny organisms in water—now identified as bacteria and protozoa—and observed red blood cells. Rather than presenting a single organized scientific book, he shared observations over decades in letters, including an extensive correspondence with the Royal Society. His work helped establish the study of microscopic life.

key_facts.text: He was born in Delft in 1632 and died there in 1723.
He made his own lenses and used small, handheld, single-lens microscopes; a Royal Society collection page says they could magnify up to 250 times.
He described microscopic organisms living in water, now known as bacteria and protozoa.
The Royal Society credits him with being the first to see and describe red blood cells and bacteria.
He communicated observations in letters for about fifty years; a scholarly review describes hundreds of letters written between 1673 and 1723.

overview.text: A phosphate group is a phosphorus-and-oxygen functional group: a phosphorus atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and in a molecule one oxygen connects the group to the rest of that molecule. Cells can attach phosphate groups through phosphorylation, usually with help from enzymes called kinases; this modification can change a protein’s activity, and phosphatases can remove the group again. Phosphates also have a structural role in genetic material: they link sugars into the outer backbone of DNA and RNA strands, while the bases extend from the sugars. These chemical and biological roles make phosphate groups important both as molecular attachments and as links in essential cellular structures.

key_facts.text: A phosphate functional group has one phosphorus atom bonded to four oxygen atoms; one oxygen bonds to another atom in the molecule.
Phosphorylation is the addition of a phosphate group to a molecule; kinases catalyze the transfer.
Adding or removing phosphate groups can activate or deactivate proteins and other signaling molecules.
In DNA and RNA, alternating sugar and phosphate groups form the strand’s backbone; in DNA, the bases are attached to the sugars.

overview.text: Astronomical distance describes how far a celestial object is from an observer and is fundamental to mapping the universe and determining objects’ intrinsic properties. Astronomers use the light-year—the distance light travels in a year—and the parsec, about 3.26 light-years. For nearby stars, parallax measures their apparent shift against background stars as Earth moves around the Sun: smaller shifts indicate greater distances. Beyond the reach of direct parallax, a calibrated “distance ladder” uses standard candles—objects whose known intrinsic brightness can be compared with how bright they appear. On cosmic scales, galaxy redshift interpreted through Hubble’s law also helps estimate distance, linking spectral shifts to the universe’s expansion.

key_facts.text: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year; one parsec equals about 3.26 light-years and corresponds to a parallax angle of one arcsecond.
As Earth orbits the Sun, nearby stars appear to shift against the distant background; the smaller the parallax, the farther the star.
A standard candle’s known intrinsic brightness can be compared with its apparent brightness to estimate its distance.
Cepheid variable stars are useful standard candles because their pulsation period is related to their luminosity.
Galaxy redshift measures shifts in spectral lines; interpreted with Hubble’s law, it can help estimate distance while reflecting the universe’s expansion.

overview.text: Soil is the natural material at Earth’s surface where rooted plants can grow. Unlike bare, unaltered rock, it contains mineral particles, organic matter, water and air, and it often has distinct layers called horizons. Its ingredients and properties vary from place to place: particle sizes such as sand, silt and clay influence texture, while climate, organisms, landscape and time help shape the soil. Living things in soil—including fungi, bacteria and animals—break down organic remains and cycle nutrients. Soil matters because it supports plant life and also helps regulate water flow, filter pollutants and provide habitat.

key_facts.text: Soil includes solid minerals and organic matter, plus liquid water and gases such as air.
Sand, silt and clay are mineral particle sizes that contribute to soil texture.
Soil forms through interactions among parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time; these influences can produce distinct horizons.
Soil organisms, including fungi, bacteria, nematodes and earthworms, contribute to decomposition and nutrient cycling.
Soil helps sustain plants and animals, regulate water flow, and filter or buffer pollutants.

overview.text: Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium commonly found in the lower intestine of warm-blooded animals. Most strains do not cause illness, but certain strains have traits that let them cause disease, including diarrhea; Shiga toxin-producing strains can sometimes lead to serious kidney complications. E. coli is also important in science and biotechnology: researchers can manipulate it readily, grow it quickly and inexpensively, and use its well-studied genetics and available laboratory tools to produce recombinant proteins. Its distinguishing significance is this contrast: the same bacterial species includes ordinary gut inhabitants, disease-causing strains, and laboratory strains useful for research and production.

key_facts.text: E. coli is a Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium.
It commonly lives in the gastrointestinal tract, and most strains do not cause illness.
Disease-causing strains differ in their virulence traits; Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, particularly some O157 strains, can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome, which can damage the kidneys.
Certain extraintestinal pathogenic strains cause urinary tract infections; CDC reports that E. coli causes 80–90% of UTIs.
E. coli is widely used to produce recombinant proteins because it is relatively easy to manipulate and grow, and researchers have many compatible laboratory tools and strains.

overview.text: Crystals are solids distinguished by an ordered microscopic arrangement of particles that repeats in space; unlike amorphous solids such as glass, their internal structure has long-range order. A crystal’s pattern can be described by a tiny repeating building block called a unit cell, and the cell’s dimensions and symmetry help classify crystal systems. Their structure matters because it helps determine recognizable forms and properties, aiding mineral study and identification. For example, salt commonly forms cube-shaped crystals, while quartz and topaz have distinct crystal systems. A mineral’s color may change with small amounts of other elements without changing its characteristic crystal structure.

key_facts.text: A unit cell’s side lengths and angles describe the repeating pattern that builds a crystal lattice.
The USGS describes minerals as having an orderly internal structure and characteristic composition; rocks are aggregates of minerals or mineral matter.
Crystals contain imperfections: vacancies can help atoms diffuse, while line defects can affect mechanical strength.
Salt commonly forms cube-shaped crystals; the museum also shows diamond, muscovite, quartz, and topaz with different crystal systems.
Small amounts of other elements can change a mineral’s color, even when its characteristic crystal structure remains the same.

overview.text: The Pauli exclusion principle, named for physicist Wolfgang Pauli, is a rule of quantum mechanics first proposed in 1925 while scientists were working to understand atomic shells and the periodic table. It says that identical fermions—particles with half-integer spin, including electrons—cannot occupy the same complete quantum state. For electrons in atoms, a state is specified by four quantum numbers, including a spin value. As a result, an orbital can hold at most two electrons, and they must differ in spin. By limiting how electrons fill atomic shells and subshells, the principle helps explain the structure of atoms and the chemical patterns of the elements.

key_facts.text: Pauli proposed the principle in 1925 in the context of atomic shell completion and the periodic system.
The rule applies to identical fermions, which have half-integer spin; electrons and protons are examples.
For an electron in an atom, four quantum numbers specify its state; two electrons in the same orbital can differ in their spin projections.
The principle limits a subshell with orbital quantum number l to 2(2l + 1) electrons; for an s subshell, that means two.
The principle helps explain electron configurations and the resulting physical and chemical patterns among elements.

overview.text: Search algorithms are procedures that look through data or a possible solution space to find a target, decide it is absent, or identify a best option. For a list, linear (sequential) search checks entries one by one and works even when they are unsorted, but may inspect every entry. Binary search is faster on sorted data: it checks the middle and repeatedly discards the half that cannot contain the target, taking logarithmic rather than linear growth in the worst case. Searching also applies to graphs: pathfinding algorithms explore connections between places, and Dijkstra’s algorithm finds lowest-total-weight routes when edge weights are nonnegative. These methods matter because the chosen procedure affects how much work a computer needs to solve a search task.

key_facts.text: Linear search checks a list from the beginning; if the target is absent, it must inspect all n entries.
Binary search requires sorted data. Each middle-value comparison lets it discard half of the remaining possibilities, so its worst-case work grows logarithmically with list size.
Dijkstra’s algorithm finds lowest-total-weight paths in a directed graph whose edge weights are nonnegative; “shortest” refers to the sum of weights, not necessarily the fewest edges.
Search procedures can report whether an item is present or absent, and the algorithm’s steps can be written as pseudocode before being implemented as code.

overview.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a research field within computer science concerned with building systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence, such as learning from experience, solving problems, recognizing patterns, planning, or working with language. It is not one particular kind of machine: AI includes approaches ranging from programs that use explicit logic and rules to machine-learning systems that improve through data. Machine learning is therefore a branch of AI, not a synonym for the whole field. The term was coined by computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955; a 1956 Dartmouth workshop helped establish the emerging field, though participants disagreed about how to create intelligent machines. AI can imitate selected abilities without necessarily thinking as people do.

key_facts.text: Computer scientist John McCarthy coined the term “AI” in 1955.
At a 1956 Dartmouth workshop, researchers named the emerging field artificial intelligence, but disagreed about how to build intelligent machines.
Machine learning is one part of AI: it studies how systems can improve their perception, decisions, or actions using experience or data.
Symbolic AI uses logic and rules to work with symbols; neural networks are a different approach, loosely inspired by brain structures.
Narrow AI focuses on particular tasks, while artificial general intelligence describes the aim of broadly capable, context-aware machines.

overview.text: Graphene is a form of carbon consisting of a single atomic layer in a repeating hexagonal, honeycomb-like arrangement. It is the basic building sheet of graphite: stacked layers make the material used in pencil cores. Unlike ordinary graphite, an isolated graphene sheet is only one atom thick, yet it is flexible and conducts heat and electricity exceptionally well. Isolating and studying individual sheets helped establish research into two-dimensional materials. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolated graphene at the University of Manchester in 2004 by peeling layers from graphite with adhesive tape; their experiments on graphene received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

key_facts.text: Graphene is one layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb lattice.
It is a building block of graphite, the material used in pencil cores.
Geim and Novoselov isolated graphene at Manchester in 2004 using adhesive tape to peel layers from graphite.
Graphene is flexible and conducts heat and electricity exceptionally well despite being one atom thick.
The researchers’ graphene experiments were recognized with the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

overview.text: Lanthanides are a family of metals conventionally comprising the 15 elements from lanthanum (La, atomic number 57) through lutetium (Lu, 71), usually shown in a detached row beneath the periodic table’s main body. IUPAC prefers “lanthanoids” as the collective name, while recognizing the common inclusion of lanthanum. The 14 elements from cerium through lutetium are associated with progressive filling of the 4f sublevel; this distinction helps explain why descriptions of the series and the f-block boundary can differ. Lanthanides matter in technology: members are used in optical devices and alloys, and rare-earth elements are used in electronics and magnets.

key_facts.text: The commonly defined 15-element series spans atomic numbers 57–71, from lanthanum to lutetium.
The 4f sublevel is progressively filled across cerium–lutetium; lanthanum is included in the broader named series by common usage.
The series is commonly displayed as a separate row at the bottom of the periodic table.
Lanthanides are metals; examples of their uses include alloys, petroleum refining, and optical devices.
The EPA notes that rare-earth elements, including the lanthanides, are used in modern electronics and magnets.

overview.text: Protein folding is the process in which a newly made chain of amino acids takes on a particular three-dimensional shape. The chain’s amino-acid sequence influences that shape, while interactions among parts of the chain help it become compact and organized. Folding can begin while the chain is still being made and continue afterward. The resulting shape is important because it helps determine what the protein can do. Some proteins fold without assistance; others are helped by cellular proteins called chaperones, which can reduce incorrect folding or clumping. Folding is not simply a random search through every possible shape: proteins reach their structures through pathways shaped by their chemistry.

key_facts.text: A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; folding may start during translation and continue afterward.
The amino-acid sequence helps specify a protein’s three-dimensional shape, though the chemical environment also matters.
In many proteins, water-avoiding (hydrophobic) amino-acid side chains tend to cluster inside, helping the chain become compact.
Some proteins fold spontaneously, while chaperones help others fold and can prevent them from aggregating.
A protein’s folded shape is important to its function; abnormal temperature or pH can interfere with correct folding.

overview.text: A submarine is a self-propelled watercraft designed to travel and operate underwater for extended periods. Its ballast tanks take in water to help it dive; compressed air expels that water to help it rise, while ballast adjustments and diving planes control depth and trim. Because its hull is windowless, a periscope can give the crew a limited view of the surface, though sonar and electronic sensors are also vital. Submarines have mattered as naval vessels and as vehicles for exploring the undersea world. They should not be confused with many small research submersibles, which make short excursions from a support ship.

key_facts.text: Flooding ballast tanks adds water and helps a submarine submerge; blowing water out with compressed air helps it surface.
Ballast adjustments and diving planes help control a submarine’s depth and trim while it is underwater.
A periscope provides a limited view outside the otherwise windowless hull; modern submarines also use sonar and electronic sensors.
Sonar lets a submarine detect sounds or echoes underwater, without needing to rise to periscope depth.
Submarines have served naval purposes and helped people explore underwater; many small research submersibles instead make short excursions from a support ship.
