Visitors may consult materials on site, borrow them, or access digital collections and services. Library buildings can also be important works of architecture. Geisel Library at the University of California, San Diego, was designed by William Pereira and opened in 1970. Its stacked concrete levels project outward, or cantilever, giving it a distinctive shape. It is a well-known example of Brutalism, an architectural style that often uses bold geometric forms and exposed concrete. Whether a library is a striking landmark or a small neighborhood building, its main purpose is to make knowledge available to its community.

Frank Gehry is a Canadian-American architect born in Toronto who later based his career in Los Angeles. He is known for sculptural buildings with sweeping curves and reflective metal exteriors. His Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, opened in Spain in 1997, uses titanium panels that suggest fish scales or a ship’s sails, linking the museum to its port-city setting. The building became a major attraction and helped revive Bilbao’s waterfront. In downtown Los Angeles, Gehry designed the Walt Disney Concert Hall, whose curving stainless-steel exterior also resembles sails. Opened in 2003, the concert hall is home to the Los Angeles Philharmonic. Other Gehry projects include the Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Chicago’s Millennium Park, where a large metal trellis helps support the sound system.

Dissonance is the effect created when two or more musical tones sound tense, unstable, or harsh together. Composers often use it to create suspense or a feeling that the music needs to move somewhere else. Its opposite is consonance: tones that sound smoother, more stable, and settled. A passage may move from dissonance to consonance, giving listeners a sense of release and a point of rest after tension. Dissonance is not necessarily a mistake or “bad” sound; it can make music more expressive. For example, the last of Mozart’s six string quartets dedicated to Joseph Haydn is nicknamed the “Dissonance” quartet because of the strikingly tense harmonies in its opening.

A domestic dog is an animal people have bred for companionship and work, and artists often use dogs to suggest loyalty. In Jan van Eyck’s Renaissance painting The Arnolfini Portrait, also called The Arnolfini Wedding, a small dog stands at the feet of an Italian merchant and his wife. It is commonly interpreted as a symbol of fidelity, or faithfulness. Behind the couple, a convex mirror curves outward and reflects the room and its figures in miniature. Its frame is decorated with ten tiny scenes from Christ’s Passion, the events leading to his death. Dogs appear in later European art too: Diego Velázquez included a large mastiff in his painting Las Meninas.

The Pulitzer Prize for Music is an annual American award recognizing a distinguished musical composition. It is one of the Pulitzer Prizes, which also honor achievements in journalism and the arts. For many years, the music prize mostly went to classical works, but its winners now reflect a wider range of styles. In 1997, trumpeter and composer Wynton Marsalis won for Blood on the Fields, a jazz oratorio—a large work that tells a story through music and voices. He was the first jazz musician to receive the award. Marsalis comes from a New Orleans jazz family and is the artistic director of Jazz at Lincoln Center. In 2018, rapper Kendrick Lamar won the Pulitzer Prize for Music for his album DAMN.

The Opening of the Fifth Seal is a painting by El Greco, a Greek-born artist who worked in Spain and is known for dramatic scenes and elongated figures. It depicts a vision from the biblical Book of Revelation: Saint John stands on the left, raising his arms toward heaven, while angels give white robes to figures in the background. The painting is also called The Vision of Saint John. Centuries later, Pablo Picasso studied it while developing Les Demoiselles d’Avignon. El Greco’s other works include The Disrobing of Christ and View of Toledo, which shows a storm gathering over the Spanish city. Remember the raised Saint John and white robes to identify the painting, and El Greco as its artist.

Luigi Boccherini was an Italian cellist and composer born in Lucca in 1743. He became known for chamber music, especially works for small groups of string instruments. After moving to Spain, he served at the court of Infante Luis, where he wrote music inspired by his surroundings. His celebrated Minuet comes from a String Quintet in E major and is often played on its own, including at weddings. A minuet is a dance in triple meter, with three beats in each measure. Another of Boccherini’s string quintets, Op. 30, No. 6, depicts nighttime street life in Madrid. It includes a passage imitating a military retreat and is commonly known by its Italian title, Musica notturna delle strade di Madrid, meaning “Night Music of the Streets of Madrid.”

The Goldberg Variations is a keyboard work by Johann Sebastian Bach, a German composer of the Baroque era. It begins with an aria, a gentle opening piece, followed by thirty variations that transform its musical material in different ways. The work ends with the aria played again, letting listeners hear the original music after all those changes. It was written for a keyboard instrument called the harpsichord, though pianists often perform it today. A traditional story says Bach composed the variations for Count Keyserlingk to help him through sleepless nights, but historians are unsure whether that story is true. Bach also wrote The Well-Tempered Clavier, a collection of preludes and fugues in every major and minor key, and the Brandenburg Concertos.

The tarantella is a fast, lively folk dance from southern Italy, often accompanied by a quick musical rhythm. It plays an important part in Henrik Ibsen’s play A Doll’s House. Nora Helmer has secretly borrowed money to pay for a trip to Italy that helped her husband, Torvald, recover from illness. To get the loan, she forged her father’s signature, and the lender, Krogstad, later threatens to expose her. When Krogstad sends Torvald a letter revealing the secret, Nora tries to stop Torvald from reading it by practicing the tarantella. She dances with increasing wildness, prompting Torvald to tell her, “Not so violent.” Her frantic performance shows how desperate she is to delay his discovery.

Islamic calligraphy is the art of turning writing into visual design. Artists often use a qalam, a cut reed pen, to draw carefully shaped letters in ink. Arabic scripts such as Kufic, known for its angular forms and even strokes, can decorate pages, buildings, and everyday objects. In Iran, artists also formed Kufic letters with patterned bricks or tiles. Calligraphy appears in books as well: during the Ilkhanid period, artists combined elegant writing with illustrated scenes from the Shahnameh, a Persian epic poem. These handwritten books are called illuminated manuscripts when their pages are richly decorated with images, ornamental designs in the margins, and sometimes gold. The writing and decoration work together to make the text both readable and beautiful.

Tempo is the speed at which music is performed: it tells musicians how quickly or slowly the beats should pass. A score may give a number in beats per minute (BPM), such as 120 BPM, or use an Italian word. Allegro means a brisk, lively tempo and often suggests roughly 120 beats per minute, though the exact speed can vary. Other directions describe changes in tempo. Accelerando tells performers to become progressively faster, while ritardando tells them to slow down gradually. This is different from starting a passage at one steady, fast speed. Performers may also use rubato, gently stretching some beats and shortening others for expression rather than keeping every beat perfectly even. A conductor can guide these tempo choices during a live performance.

The Son of Man is a 1964 painting by Belgian artist René Magritte, who was part of the Surrealist movement. Surrealist artists often combined ordinary things in strange, dreamlike ways to make viewers question what they see. In this painting, a man in a dark suit and bowler hat stands in front of a low wall, with a cloudy seascape behind him. A green apple floats directly in front of his face, hiding much of it. The man’s clothes and surroundings look realistic, but the hovering fruit makes the scene mysterious. Magritte often explored the difference between what is visible and what remains hidden, and the apple turns a familiar portrait into a puzzle about the person beneath the hat.

Art Blakey was an American jazz drummer and bandleader who helped shape hard bop, a lively style that combined bebop’s fast improvisation with blues and gospel influences. In the 1950s, he co-founded the Jazz Messengers with pianist Horace Silver, then led the group for decades. Blakey played drums, driving the music with powerful rhythms and energetic solos. He led the band on Moanin’, one of its best-known albums. The Jazz Messengers became famous not only for their music but also for giving talented younger musicians a place to develop. Its members over the years included trumpeter Lee Morgan and saxophonist Wayne Shorter, as well as Silver. If a question mentions the drummer who led Moanin’ or the long-running hard-bop group he led, the answers are Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers.

The Problem We All Live With is a 1964 painting by American artist Norman Rockwell. It shows six-year-old Ruby Bridges walking to William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans, Louisiana, escorted by federal marshals. In 1960, Ruby became one of the first Black children to attend a formerly all-white school in the city after courts ordered schools to desegregate. Some people protested her enrollment, and the painting hints at their hostility without showing the crowd: a tomato has splattered against the wall behind Ruby, and a racial slur is written on it. Ruby’s white dress stands out against the marked wall and the marshals’ dark suits. Rockwell’s painting asks viewers to consider the courage it took for a child to claim her right to an equal education.

Pale Blue Dot is a photograph of Earth taken in 1990 by NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft as it traveled through the outer Solar System. At the urging of astronomer and science writer Carl Sagan, NASA turned Voyager’s camera back toward the planets before switching it off. From that great distance, Earth appears as a tiny point smaller than a single pixel, caught in a faint band of scattered sunlight. The image shows how small our planet looks from far away, even though it holds everyone we know. Sagan made the photograph central to his 1994 book Pale Blue Dot, which explores humanity’s place in the cosmos. Like Earthrise and The Blue Marble, it has become a famous image of Earth, but its distant viewpoint makes it especially striking.

Jelly Roll Morton was an American pianist, composer, and bandleader who helped shape early jazz. He blended the steady, syncopated rhythms of ragtime with blues and improvisation, and his band, the Red Hot Peppers, made influential recordings in the 1920s. Morton wrote tunes including “King Porter Stomp” and “Dead Man’s Blues.” In recorded conversations with folklorist Alan Lomax for the Library of Congress, he famously claimed to have invented jazz, though jazz developed through the work of many musicians. Morton also argued about scat singing—the use of improvised, wordless syllables—with New Orleans trumpeter Louis Armstrong. Armstrong discussed his recording of “Heebie Jeebies,” led the Hot Five, and later became widely known for singing “What a Wonderful World” in his gravelly voice.

Die Brücke, meaning “The Bridge,” was a German Expressionist art movement founded in Dresden in 1905 by four young artists: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Fritz Bleyl, Erich Heckel, and Karl Schmidt-Rottluff. They wanted to move beyond traditional academic art and create work that expressed intense feelings through bold colors, simplified shapes, and energetic lines. Emil Nolde later became associated with the group. One of its founders, Kirchner, painted Self-Portrait as a Soldier in 1915 during World War I. In the painting, he wears a military uniform and depicts himself with a severed hand, even though his hand had not actually been amputated. The image expresses his fear that war could destroy his ability to make art.

Musical inversion means changing the order of notes in an interval or chord. An interval is the perceived distance between two notes; for example, C to E is a major third. To invert an interval, move one of its notes above or below the other: moving the lower C above E turns that major third into a minor sixth. In a chord, inversion changes which note is lowest, or “in the bass,” while keeping the same chord tones. A C-major triad contains C, E, and G. With C in the bass, it is in root position. With E in the bass and C and G above it, it is in first inversion; with G in the bass, it is in second inversion.

Bluegrass is an American roots-music genre that grew from the folk traditions of Appalachia, a mountainous region in the eastern United States. Its bands commonly feature banjo, fiddle, mandolin, acoustic guitar, and upright bass, with musicians taking turns playing fast, lively solos. Singer and mandolin player Bill Monroe helped shape and popularize the style with his band, the Blue Grass Boys. In 1945, North Carolina-born banjo player Earl Scruggs joined the band. His rapid three-finger picking style became one of bluegrass music’s defining sounds. Scruggs later teamed up with guitarist Lester Flatt to form the Foggy Mountain Boys. Although bluegrass draws on older Appalachian songs and instruments, its driving rhythms and close vocal harmonies give it a distinctive sound.

Bridges appear again and again in Claude Monet’s paintings. At his home in Giverny, France, he repeatedly painted the Japanese-style bridge crossing his water-lily pond, often showing it surrounded by flowers and reflected in the water. In London, he painted bridges spanning the River Thames. One series, made around 1900 from rooms at the Savoy Hotel, shows Waterloo Bridge beneath changing fog and light. Monet was an Impressionist: rather than recording every detail of a bridge, he focused on how it looked at a particular moment. By returning to the same subject in different conditions, he could explore how sunlight, mist, colour and reflections changed what he saw.

Water Music is a set of orchestral suites by George Frideric Handel, a German-born composer of the Baroque era who spent much of his career in Britain. It is closely associated with a royal barge journey along the River Thames in London in 1717, when musicians played for King George I and his guests. The music includes dances and other short movements, with instruments such as strings, oboes, horns, and trumpets creating a festive sound suited to an outdoor celebration. One of its best-known movements is the lively “Alla Hornpipe” in D major. Handel also wrote the oratorio Messiah, which includes the famous “Hallelujah” chorus, and the coronation anthem Zadok the Priest.

Edward Burne-Jones was an English painter and designer associated with the Pre-Raphaelite movement, whose artists drew inspiration from medieval stories, religion, and detailed early Renaissance art. While studying at Oxford, he met Dante Gabriel Rossetti and joined the Pre-Raphaelite circle. Burne-Jones later created designs for Morris & Co., a company known for decorative arts. His paintings include The Golden Stairs and The Beguiling of Merlin, but he also helped revive the medieval craft of stained glass. In this art form, pieces of colored glass are assembled to make images that glow when light shines through them, often in church windows. One of Burne-Jones’s stained-glass designs depicts St Cecilia, the patron saint of music, playing a small handheld organ.

Jules Massenet was a French composer of the Romantic era, a time when musicians often used expressive melodies to convey strong emotions. He is best known for his operas, including Manon, Werther, and Thaïs. An opera tells a story through singing, acting, and orchestral music. In Thaïs, Massenet wrote a short instrumental passage called the Méditation, or “Meditation.” It features a prominent solo violin accompanied by an orchestra and is often performed on its own at concerts or by violin students. The piece’s lyrical, reflective sound has made it one of Massenet’s most familiar works, even to people who have never seen the opera. If a question names those three operas, the composer is Massenet; if it asks for the famous violin passage from Thaïs, the answer is the Méditation.

An oratorio is a large-scale musical work that tells a dramatic story through singing and instrumental music. It typically brings together solo singers, a chorus, and an orchestra, often using a religious or biblical subject. Unlike an opera, an oratorio is generally performed as a concert, without costumes, scenery, or actors staging the action. Oratorios were especially popular during the Baroque period. A famous example is Messiah by George Frideric Handel, first performed in Dublin in 1742. Its best-known section is the “Hallelujah” chorus. Another Baroque composer, Antonio Vivaldi, wrote the oratorio Juditha Triumphans. If a question describes a dramatic work for soloists, chorus, and orchestra without theatrical staging, the answer is likely oratorio; if it asks who composed Messiah, the answer is Handel.

The double bass, also called the upright bass, is the largest and lowest-pitched standard bowed string instrument in a symphony orchestra. Its four strings are typically tuned E1–A1–D2–G2, and its notes sound an octave lower than they are written in a score. A player can draw a bow across the strings for sustained orchestral lines or pluck them with a finger. This plucking technique is called pizzicato: the player pulls a string and releases it to make a short, distinct note. In jazz, the double bass joins the piano and drums in the rhythm section. Bassists often play a “walking” bass line, a steady series of low notes that helps connect one chord to the next.

W. C. Handy (1873–1958) was an Alabama-born American composer, bandleader, and music publisher often called the “Father of the Blues.” He did not invent the blues, a form of African American music that developed before his career, but he helped bring it to a wider audience by writing down, publishing, and performing blues-inspired songs. Among his best-known works are “Beale Street Blues,” named for a famous Memphis street, and “St. Louis Blues,” published in 1914. “St. Louis Blues” became one of his most enduring standards: it pairs a verse built on the familiar twelve-bar blues pattern with a contrasting section influenced by the habanera, a dance rhythm associated with Cuba. Handy’s compositions helped establish the blues as a major part of American popular music.

Jenny Lind was a Swedish operatic soprano whose voice made her an international star in the nineteenth century. Nicknamed the “Swedish Nightingale,” she became especially famous in the United States during an 1850 tour promoted by showman P. T. Barnum. Her nickname also links her to Hans Christian Andersen, the Danish author of the fairy tale “The Nightingale.” Andersen admired Lind, and people have often connected her with the bird in his story, though the tale was not simply a portrait of her. Andersen also wrote “The Snow Queen,” “The Emperor’s New Clothes,” and “The Little Mermaid.” Remembering Lind’s nickname and Barnum’s tour helps identify the singer, while “The Nightingale” and Andersen’s other fairy tales help identify the author.

Francis Bacon was a British painter born in Dublin, Ireland, in 1909. He became famous for paintings of human figures that look twisted, isolated, and deeply distressed. Rather than painting people realistically, Bacon used distortion to convey fear, pain, and other powerful emotions. One of his best-known early works is the 1944 triptych Three Studies for Figures at the Base of a Crucifixion. A triptych is a work made of three panels; Bacon’s shows three anguished, biomorphic figures against a vivid orange background. “Biomorphic” means that the shapes suggest living things without looking like ordinary bodies. The painting helped establish Bacon’s reputation as a major modern artist. He later made a series of paintings inspired by a portrait of Pope Innocent X, turning the pope’s face into a terrifying scream.

Different Trains is a 1988 composition by American minimalist composer Steve Reich, written for the San Francisco-based Kronos Quartet. Violinist David Harrington founded the four-member ensemble in 1973. In the piece, a string quartet plays alongside recordings of spoken memories and train sounds. Reich shaped some of the string melodies to echo the rhythms and pitches of the recorded voices. The work has three sections: “America—Before the War,” “Europe—During the War,” and “After the War.” Reich drew on his childhood train trips across the United States and contrasted their safety with the train journeys that carried Jews to Nazi concentration camps during World War II. By placing these experiences side by side, Different Trains shows how the same kind of journey can have profoundly different meanings.

Diego Rivera was a Mexican artist famous for large murals that brought history and politics into public spaces. His Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in Alameda Park gathers figures from different periods of Mexican history in one crowded scene, including leaders Porfirio Díaz and Francisco Madero. Rivera also painted scenes of Indigenous cultures and the lives of workers. In the 1930s, he was commissioned to paint a fresco for the lobby of 30 Rockefeller Plaza in New York City. The mural, called Man at the Crossroads, showed people facing different possible futures. Rivera included a portrait of the communist leader Vladimir Lenin, which caused a dispute with the building’s owners. Nelson Rockefeller ordered the unfinished mural destroyed, making it one of Rivera’s most famous controversies.

Vocalists are performers who use their voices as musical instruments. They may sing lyrics, follow a melody, or make other musical sounds, and in popular music performances they often use handheld microphones so audiences can hear them clearly. Vocalists work in many styles, including pop, classical music, and jazz. Jazz singer Ella Fitzgerald was especially famous for scat singing, an improvisational technique in which a vocalist sings made-up syllables instead of words. A scat singer might use sounds such as “doo” or “bop,” changing the notes and rhythm while performing. Scat singing lets vocalists explore a melody and express musical ideas without relying on lyrics.

Maria Tallchief was an Osage-American dancer who became the first major American prima ballerina of American Indian descent. Born Elizabeth Marie Tallchief in Oklahoma, she built an international career at a time when few American dancers held leading roles in ballet. She was especially celebrated for performing works choreographed by George Balanchine, a major figure in American ballet. Her breakthrough came when she danced the title role in Balanchine’s 1949 staging of The Firebird, portraying a magical bird. The ballet’s score was written by Russian-born composer Igor Stravinsky and was first performed in Paris in 1910. Tallchief later danced the Sugar Plum Fairy in Balanchine’s production of The Nutcracker. The Osage Nation honored her as a princess and called her “Woman of Two Worlds,” recognizing her achievements in ballet and her Osage heritage.

Praxiteles was a Greek sculptor of the fourth century BCE whose figures helped make classical sculpture look more natural and relaxed. Instead of stiff poses, he favored gentle curves and expressions that made gods seem approachable and human. One work associated with him shows Hermes carrying the infant Dionysus; its damaged remains no longer show the bunch of grapes Hermes is thought to have held out to the child. Praxiteles also created the Aphrodite of Knidos, a famous statue of the goddess shown nude, an unusual choice for a major Greek sculpture of a woman at the time. According to ancient accounts, Phryne may have modeled for it. The statue became a celebrated attraction at a sanctuary in Knidos, an ancient Carian port city on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor.

A ballet class usually begins at the barre, a horizontal handrail fixed to a studio wall or mounted on stands. Dancers hold it lightly for balance while they warm up and practice controlled movements before moving to the center of the room. Barre exercises include tendus, in which a foot stretches along the floor, and ronds de jambe, in which a leg traces a circular path. Dancers also practice the five basic positions of the feet. In fifth position, the last of these, both feet turn outward, with one foot crossed closely in front of the other. From fifth position, a dancer can bend the knees in a demi-plié, then spring up into a relevé on the balls of the feet. This movement is called a sous-sus.

Buddy Rich was an American jazz drummer and bandleader famous for his extraordinary speed, precise technique, and long, energetic solos. Born in Brooklyn in 1917, he began performing as a child and was billed as “Traps the Drum Wonder.” He later led a celebrated big band and became one of jazz’s best-known drummers. His main instrument was the drum kit, a set of percussion instruments that typically includes a snare drum, a bass drum played with a foot pedal, and cymbals. Drummers strike the kit with sticks, using either a traditional grip, in which the hands hold the sticks differently, or a matched grip, in which both hands hold them in the same way. Rich used the kit to create rhythms and dazzling solos that made him stand out.

The Rokeby Venus is a painting by the Spanish Baroque artist Diego Velázquez. It shows Venus, the Roman goddess of love, lying nude with her back to the viewer while her son Cupid holds up a mirror toward her face. The painting is also called The Toilet of Venus or The Venus at Her Mirror; “Rokeby” comes from an English estate where it was once kept. In 1914, while it was on display at London’s National Gallery, British suffragette Mary Richardson struck the canvas repeatedly with a meat cleaver. She carried out the attack as a protest connected to the campaign for women’s voting rights. The damaged painting was later repaired and remains one of Velázquez’s best-known works.

A hymn is a religious song of praise or devotion, often sung by a congregation during worship. Christian hymns usually have verses and a melody that a group can sing together, and some close with the word “amen.” They grew out of older traditions of church singing, including Gregorian chant, but hymns are generally more familiar as songs with words and tunes shared by a whole congregation. One famous example is “Amazing Grace,” whose lyrics were written by John Newton, an Anglican clergyman who had formerly been a slave trader. The words first appeared in the 1779 collection Olney Hymns. Today, “Amazing Grace” is commonly sung to a melody called “New Britain.”

The Two Fridas is a 1939 double self-portrait by Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, painted shortly after her divorce from Diego Rivera. It shows two seated versions of Kahlo holding hands, with their exposed hearts connected by an artery. One Frida wears a white European-style dress, while the other wears traditional Mexican clothing, suggesting different sides of her identity. Blood on the white dress adds to the painting’s sense of pain and heartbreak. Kahlo often used self-portraits to explore her experiences, including physical suffering and difficult relationships. Rivera, her former husband, was a Mexican muralist known for large public artworks, including the Detroit Industry fresco cycle. Remember that the painting is called The Two Fridas and that Kahlo divorced Diego Rivera in 1939.

Billie Holiday was an influential American jazz singer born Eleanora Fagan in Philadelphia in 1915. Saxophonist Lester Young gave her the nickname “Lady Day.” She was admired for her expressive phrasing: the way she shaped the timing and feeling of a song made its words especially powerful. Before becoming a solo star, she sang with Count Basie’s band, led by the pianist. Her recordings include “God Bless the Child” and “Strange Fruit.” Holiday’s 1939 recording of “Strange Fruit” became a landmark protest against lynching, the racist killing of Black people. The song describes bodies hanging from a poplar tree and contrasts the scent of magnolia with the smell of burning flesh. Its disturbing images helped listeners confront the violence of racism.

Luciano Pavarotti was an Italian operatic tenor born in Modena in 1935. He became one of opera’s most recognizable performers, admired for his warm voice and ringing high Cs, especially in the demanding opera La Fille du Régiment. His performances and recordings helped introduce opera to people who might not otherwise have heard it. One of his best-known arias was “Nessun dorma,” from Giacomo Puccini’s opera Turandot. Pavarotti sang it at his final public performance, during the opening ceremony of the 2006 Winter Olympics. He also performed with fellow tenors Plácido Domingo and José Carreras in a celebrated trio called the Three Tenors. Their concerts reached huge audiences around the world and made operatic singing more familiar to the public.

Relief sculpture is a technique in which figures remain attached to a background, such as a stone wall or panel, rather than standing freely like a statue. In low relief, also called bas-relief, the figures project only slightly above the surface. In sunken relief, the artist cuts the outlines and forms into the surface, leaving them below the surrounding stone. This method was especially important in ancient Egyptian art: strong daylight could cast shadows along the recessed edges, making the images easier to see on temple walls. Sunken relief became particularly prominent during the Amarna period, when artists depicted figures such as Nefertiti and her family. When identifying a relief, look at whether its forms rise from the background or are carved into it.

Ritual dance is movement performed as part of worship, rites, or important community ceremonies rather than primarily for entertainment. It can express beliefs, tell stories, honor ancestors, or bring people together. Polynesian cultures have several dance traditions connected to ceremony. Hawaiian hula uses gestures and movement to tell stories and is also performed at celebrations such as luaus. Another example is the haka, a Māori group performance from Aotearoa, or New Zealand. A haka can include chanting, rhythmic foot stamping, and emphatic gestures. It may be performed to welcome guests, mark significant occasions, or express a group’s strength and unity. New Zealand’s national rugby team, the All Blacks, is especially well known for performing a haka before matches.

Edward Elgar’s Enigma Variations, also called Variations on an Original Theme, is an orchestral work built from one theme followed by fourteen contrasting variations. Elgar associated the variations with people close to him, calling them his “friends pictured within”; some are labeled with initials, such as “C.A.E.” for his wife, Caroline Alice Elgar. The best-known variation is the ninth, “Nimrod,” which honors Augustus J. Jaeger, a friend who worked for a music publisher and encouraged Elgar when he doubted himself. Its slow, expressive music has made it especially famous. The title “Enigma” refers to a musical mystery Elgar left unexplained: he suggested that another, unheard melody fits with the theme. Listeners have proposed possible answers, including “Rule, Britannia,” but none is certain.

The Last Judgment is a monumental fresco by the Italian Renaissance artist Michelangelo on the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel in Vatican City. Painted in the 1530s and 1540s, it shows the Second Coming of Christ, when the dead rise and their souls are judged. Christ appears near the center, surrounded by saints and angels. Some figures ascend toward heaven, while others are pulled down toward damnation. Among the saints is St. Bartholomew, who holds the flayed skin associated with his martyrdom. Michelangelo painted his own face on that skin, making it an unusual self-portrait. The fresco’s crowded figures and dramatic movement help convey the fear and hope of judgment.

Beauty is an aesthetic concept: a quality in art, nature, or everyday life that can inspire admiration or pleasure. People may disagree about what is beautiful, but artists and writers often use the idea to explore how we respond to the world. In her poem “Renascence,” Edna St. Vincent Millay praises beauty as “multi-colored, multiform,” suggesting that it can appear in many shapes and experiences. Beauty is also central to “Ode on a Grecian Urn” by the English Romantic poet John Keats. The poem ends with the famous words “Beauty is truth, truth beauty,” linking beauty to truth. If asked for the aesthetic concept associated with admiration and pleasure, the answer is beauty; if asked who wrote that line, the answer is John Keats.

The tabla is an Indian percussion instrument made of two tuned hand drums played together. The smaller drum, called the dayan, produces higher-pitched treble sounds and is usually played with the right hand. The larger drum, called the bayan, produces lower-pitched bass sounds and is usually played with the left hand. A player strikes the drumheads with fingers and hands to create rhythms and can change the bayan’s pitch by pressing the heel of the hand against its drumhead. Tabla players combine sounds from both drums to make a wide range of rhythmic patterns. Like snare drums and bass drums, tablas belong to the drum family, but their two-drum design and pitch-changing techniques give them a distinctive sound.

The AIDS Memorial Quilt is a vast collaborative textile artwork that honors people who died of AIDS-related causes during the AIDS epidemic. It is made up of individual fabric panels, often created by family members and friends to remember a particular person through names, pictures, and meaningful objects. The project was conceived by San Francisco activist Cleve Jones after a 1985 march where he saw placards bearing the names of people who had died of AIDS. He imagined joining such tributes together into a quilt that would make the scale of the loss visible while celebrating individual lives. The quilt was first displayed on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., in 1987. As more people contributed panels, it grew into a powerful work of art and public remembrance.

The Parthenon is a classical Greek temple on the Acropolis, the hilltop overlooking Athens. Commissioned by the Athenian leader Pericles in the fifth century BCE and designed by Ictinus and Callicrates, it was dedicated to Athena, the city’s patron goddess. Inside stood a huge statue of Athena made by the sculptor Phidias from gold and ivory. The building was also decorated with carved panels called metopes, figures on its triangular ends, and a sculpted frieze. In the early 1800s, many of these sculptures were taken to Britain under the direction of Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire. They are commonly called the Elgin Marbles, or Parthenon Marbles.

4′33″ (“four minutes, thirty-three seconds”) is a 1952 composition by American composer John Cage. It has three movements, but the performer plays no notes. At its premiere in Woodstock, New York, pianist David Tudor marked each movement by opening and closing the piano lid. The audience instead heard sounds from the room and surroundings, such as movement, breathing, and outdoor noise. Cage wanted listeners to notice that sound is always present, even when musicians are silent, and to reconsider what can count as music. He explored unusual sounds in other works too: in Sonatas and Interludes, he placed objects between piano strings to change their sound. Cage also used chance procedures inspired by the I Ching and collaborated for many years with choreographer Merce Cunningham.

Scat singing is a jazz vocal technique in which a singer improvises a melody using made-up syllables instead of conventional lyrics. Sounds such as “doo,” “bop,” and “ba” let the voice act like an instrument, following the music’s rhythm while creating new patterns. A singer may change the notes and syllables from one performance to the next, making each solo different. Ella Fitzgerald was one of the most celebrated scat singers. Born in Newport News, Virginia, she became famous for her vocal skill and improvisation. She also recorded several albums with jazz musician Louis Armstrong, including the 1959 album Porgy and Bess, featuring music by George Gershwin.

B-flat is a musical pitch halfway between A and B natural: it is one semitone above A and one semitone below B natural on the chromatic scale. The flat sign lowers B natural by one semitone. B-flat is also the tonal center, or “home” note, of B-flat major. This major key has exactly two flats in its key signature: B-flat and E-flat. Flats are added to key signatures in a standard order, so B-flat comes first and E-flat comes second. The tenor saxophone and clarinet are commonly called B-flat instruments because a written C on either instrument sounds as a B-flat. By contrast, the alto saxophone is an E-flat instrument.

The Swing is a Rococo oil painting by the French artist Jean-Honoré Fragonard. It shows a young woman swinging through a lush garden while a hidden admirer watches from the bushes. As she rises, one of her shoes flies through the air toward him. A small sculpted cherub, called a putto, holds a finger to its lips, as if urging everyone to keep the playful scene secret. Another man pulls the swing’s ropes, unaware of the admirer nearby. The painting’s soft colors, elaborate garden setting, and lighthearted sense of romance are typical of Rococo art, a style popular in eighteenth-century France. It is also known by the longer title The Happy Accidents of the Swing.

A typeface is a designed set of letterforms used to make written words readable and visually distinctive. Typefaces may have serifs, the small strokes at the ends of letters, or be sans-serif, meaning they lack those strokes. Designers choose typefaces for books, signs, posters, and screens because the shapes of letters affect both how easily text can be read and the impression it creates. At the Bauhaus school in Germany, artists favored simple, practical designs built from basic shapes. In 1925, Bauhaus artist Herbert Bayer designed a geometric, lowercase-only typeface called Universal. It was part of his proposal for an alphabet that could be used across languages, reflecting the Bauhaus interest in clear, efficient communication.

Illuminated manuscripts are books copied and decorated by hand, especially before printed books became widespread. Scribes wrote the text, while artists might add elaborate initial letters, small painted scenes called miniatures, and figures or patterns in the margins, known as marginalia. Gold leaf or other metallic foil could make the pages gleam, giving “illumination” its name. These books appeared in many cultures and served religious, literary, and other purposes; examples include Books of Hours and illustrated copies of the Persian Shahnameh. One famous example is the Book of Kells, an Insular Gospel book made around the late eighth or early ninth century. Preserved at Trinity College Dublin, it is especially admired for its intricate Chi-Rho page, which decorates the opening letters of Christ’s name.

Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 29 in B-flat major, Op. 106 is commonly called the Hammerklavier Sonata. “Hammerklavier” is a German word for piano, and the nickname suits this enormous, technically demanding work. Written during Beethoven’s late period, the sonata has four expansive movements. It opens with bold, energetic music, then moves through a lively scherzo and a long, searching Adagio sostenuto before ending with a famously difficult fugue, in which several musical lines weave together. Beethoven dedicated the sonata to Archduke Rudolph of Austria, a Habsburg royal who was his pupil and longtime patron. Rudolph was also the dedicatee of Beethoven’s Op. 97 piano trio, known as the Archduke Trio.

The Corinthian order is one of the three main styles, or “orders,” of ancient Greek architecture, alongside the Doric and Ionic orders. It is named after the Greek city of Corinth and is best recognized by its column capitals—the decorative tops of columns. Corinthian capitals are more elaborate than those of the other two orders, with carved acanthus leaves curling around them. The Roman writer Vitruvius told a story about how the design began: the Greek sculptor Callimachus saw a basket placed on a young woman’s grave, with acanthus plants growing around it, and used the sight as inspiration for a capital. Although this is a legend rather than a proven history, it helps explain the order’s distinctive leafy appearance.

Winterreise, meaning “Winter Journey,” is a cycle of 24 songs by the Austrian composer Franz Schubert. It belongs to the Romantic tradition of the lied, a German art song for voice and piano. Schubert set a sequence of poems by the German writer Wilhelm Müller, whose poetry he also used for another song cycle, Die schöne Müllerin. In Winterreise, a young man leaves his beloved and travels alone through a winter landscape, reflecting on heartbreak, loneliness, and despair. The piano does more than accompany the singer: its sounds help suggest the traveler’s surroundings and changing emotions. The cycle begins with “Gute Nacht” (“Good Night”), in which he says farewell, and ends with “Der Leiermann” (“The Hurdy-Gurdy Man”), an unsettling encounter with a street musician.

The Black Paintings are a series of fourteen unsettling works that Spanish artist Francisco Goya painted directly onto the walls of his home, the Quinta del Sordo, in the early 1820s. Their dark colors and disturbing scenes gave the series its name. In Saturn Devouring His Son, a mythological figure eats one of his children; Witches’ Sabbath shows Satan as a goat, and Fight with Cudgels shows two men battling while stuck in the ground. Goya had lost much of his hearing, and these private paintings reflect a darker side of his art. He also created The Disasters of War, a series of prints about the violence of war, and The Third of May 1808, a painting of Spanish civilians facing execution.

Ludwig van Beethoven’s Symphony No. 6 in F major, Op. 68, is also called the Pastoral Symphony. Completed in 1808, it uses music to suggest the feelings and sounds of a visit to the countryside. Unlike most of Beethoven’s symphonies, it has five movements rather than four, each with a descriptive title. The second movement, “Scene by the brook,” evokes flowing water; near its close, woodwind instruments imitate the calls of a nightingale, quail, and cuckoo. Other movements portray a cheerful gathering of country folk, a sudden thunderstorm, and a peaceful song of thanks afterward. Beethoven wanted listeners to experience the joy and calm of nature, not just imagine a series of literal sound effects.

Nefertiti was a queen of ancient Egypt during the Amarna Period, a time when royal art and religion changed dramatically. Her husband, the pharaoh Akhenaten, shifted Egypt’s religious focus toward Aten, represented as a sun disk, and founded a new capital called Akhetaten. In artworks, Nefertiti often appears beside Akhenaten and their children, sometimes beneath Aten’s rays. Amarna artists portrayed the royal family in unusually intimate scenes and with distinctive features, such as elongated heads. Nefertiti is especially famous for a painted limestone bust showing her wearing a tall blue crown. The bust is displayed at the Neues Museum in Berlin. These images make her one of the most recognizable figures from ancient Egypt.

A bagatelle is a brief instrumental piece, usually light in character and often written for solo piano. Its name suggests a “trifle,” but a bagatelle can still contain striking melodies and inventive musical ideas. Beethoven’s Für Elise is a well-known example. Bagatelles are not limited to piano: composers can write or arrange them for other instruments and ensembles. The 20th-century Hungarian composer György Ligeti, for instance, wrote a piano cycle called Musica Ricercata. He later selected six of its movements and rearranged them for wind quintet, a group of flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon, and horn. The resulting work is called Six Bagatelles for Wind Quintet.

Beijing National Stadium is an 80,000-seat sports venue in Beijing, China, widely nicknamed the “Bird’s Nest” because its exposed steel beams crisscross like woven twigs. Its design was led by Herzog & de Meuron, a Swiss architecture firm based in Basel, working with Chinese collaborators. The firm is also known for converting a former power station into London’s Tate Modern art museum. The stadium was the principal venue for the 2008 Summer Olympics, hosting major athletics events and the opening and closing ceremonies. When Beijing hosted the 2022 Winter Olympics, the stadium again hosted the opening and closing ceremonies. Its role in both Games made the Bird’s Nest a symbol of Beijing’s Olympic history as well as a landmark of modern architecture.

Book from the Sky is an installation by Chinese contemporary artist Xu Bing, created in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It fills a gallery with hanging scrolls and bound books that look as though they contain traditional Chinese writing. To make them, Xu Bing invented and carved thousands of characters that resemble Chinese characters but have no meanings. He then used them to print hundreds of pages. Visitors are surrounded by what appears to be an enormous collection of written knowledge, yet no one can read it. This contrast between familiar-looking writing and meaningless text encourages viewers to think about how language conveys meaning and why printed words can seem authoritative.

The tuba is the largest and lowest-pitched instrument in a typical orchestra’s brass section. A player buzzes their lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece, then presses valves to change the length of air flowing through its broad, coiled tubing and produce different notes. Its deep sound provides a foundation for orchestras and concert bands and is also heard in military and marching bands. A marching-band version of the tuba is the sousaphone, named for the American bandmaster John Philip Sousa, who helped develop its design. Rather than being held in front of the player like a concert tuba, a sousaphone wraps around the player’s body and rests on the shoulders. Its large, forward-facing bell projects sound toward the audience while the player marches.

Georges Bizet was a French composer of the Romantic period, best known for his operas Carmen and The Pearl Fishers, both sung in French. Carmen is based on a novella by Prosper Mérimée and follows a fiercely independent woman and a soldier named Don José. Carmen sings the famous “Habanera,” but their troubled relationship ends when Don José kills her. The Pearl Fishers is set on Ceylon, now called Sri Lanka. Its story follows two pearl divers, Nadir and Zurga, who have both fallen in love with Leïla, a priestess. The men sing the celebrated duet “Au fond du temple saint,” remembering when they first saw her. Bizet’s memorable melodies and dramatic stories have made his operas popular long after his death.

Christoph Willibald Gluck was a German composer and a leading figure in 18th-century opera reform. He wanted music to serve the story and express characters’ emotions directly, rather than interrupt the drama with elaborate vocal displays designed mainly to show off singers’ skills. His opera Orfeo ed Euridice, first performed in Vienna in 1762, shows this approach in its retelling of the Greek myth of Orpheus, who travels to the underworld to bring back his wife, Eurydice. One of the opera’s best-known passages is the Dance of the Blessed Spirits. Led by a gentle solo flute, this serene ballet music accompanies Orpheus as he moves through the Elysian Fields, the peaceful realm of the blessed dead.

Pieter Bruegel the Elder was a 16th-century Netherlandish painter who made ordinary people and their surroundings central to his art. His busy village scenes show peasants at work and play, while his landscapes capture details of the seasons. In Netherlandish Proverbs, originally called The Blue Cloak, villagers act out dozens of familiar sayings. Hunters in the Snow shows hunters and their dogs returning through a wintry landscape, with people skating on frozen water below. Bruegel also used everyday scenes to explore human behavior. In his 1568 painting The Blind Leading the Blind, six men with impaired sight walk along a country path; their leader falls into a ditch, and the others follow him. That painting is now held at the Capodimonte Museum in Naples.

Aaron Copland’s Clarinet Concerto is a work for solo clarinet and orchestra that he completed in 1948. It was commissioned by and dedicated to Benny Goodman, a famous swing-era bandleader and clarinetist whose big band popularized the 1937 recording of “Sing, Sing, Sing.” The concerto begins with a slow, lyrical movement that lets the clarinet sing over the orchestra. A solo cadenza—a passage played by the clarinet without the orchestra—then leads into a lively, jazz-influenced finale, reflecting Goodman’s musical background. Goodman gave the work’s premiere in 1950 with the NBC Symphony Orchestra conducted by Fritz Reiner. The concerto brings together Copland’s classical style and sounds associated with jazz, making it a notable example of American orchestral music.

The Suicide of Dorothy Hale is a 1939 painting by Mexican artist Frida Kahlo. It shows the death of Dorothy Hale, an American socialite, in three stages: standing at the top of a New York skyscraper, falling through the air, and lying on the ground below. Clare Boothe Luce commissioned the painting after Hale’s death, but she was horrified by Kahlo’s direct depiction of the tragedy. Rather than making a conventional memorial portrait, Kahlo told the story of what happened in one unsettling image. Kahlo is also known for expressive self-portraits, including one in which she wears a thorn necklace with a hummingbird hanging from it. She was married to the Mexican muralist Diego Rivera.

Voguing is a dance style that grew out of Harlem’s ballroom scene in New York City, where Black and Latino LGBTQ+ communities held balls with performances and competitions. Dancers turn poses inspired by fashion photography and runway modeling into a performance, using angular lines, expressive hand movements, and dramatic changes of position. They may face off in battles, showing creativity and control while responding to the music. Different approaches include Old Way, which emphasizes graceful lines and fluid movement, and New Way, which features sharper angles and intricate arm movements. Madonna brought wider attention to the style with her song “Vogue,” whose lyrics urge listeners to “strike a pose.” Harlem is also home to the Apollo Theater, a landmark venue for Black performers.

Mingus Ah Um is a 1959 jazz album by bassist, composer, and bandleader Charles Mingus, who led a changing group of musicians called the Jazz Workshop. The album brings together blues, gospel, and lively group improvisation, showing how Mingus could honor jazz history while making music that sounded new. “Better Git It in Your Soul” draws on the energy of gospel music, while “Jelly Roll” pays tribute to early jazz pianist Jelly Roll Morton. “Open Letter to Duke” honors Duke Ellington, a major influence on Mingus. The album’s quieter “Goodbye Pork Pie Hat” is an elegy for Lester Young, a tenor saxophonist known for his relaxed phrasing and his work with Count Basie’s orchestra. Its title refers to the distinctive hat Young often wore.

Kabuki is a form of Japanese theater that began in the early 17th century. It combines dramatic acting, dance, and music in highly stylized performances. Actors wear elaborate costumes and striking makeup, and they may hold a dramatic pose at an important moment to emphasize a character’s emotion or action. Kabuki was influenced by bunraku, another Japanese theatrical tradition. In bunraku, large painted puppets act out stories while a narrator tells the story in a style called joruri, accompanied by music played on a shamisen, a three-stringed instrument. Each puppet is operated by a team of three people, who control different parts of its body. The key distinction is that kabuki features actors onstage, while bunraku centers on puppets.

French classical music includes works for solo instruments, small groups, and orchestras. Around the turn of the 20th century, three French composers helped give this concert tradition a distinctive sound. Erik Satie wrote the Gymnopédies and Gnossiennes, short piano pieces known for their simplicity and unusual harmonies. Maurice Ravel composed Boléro, an orchestral work built around a repeating rhythm and a gradual increase in volume. Claude Debussy explored the colors and textures of sound in works such as the piano piece “Clair de Lune” and the orchestral triptych La Mer. Inspired by the sea, La Mer premiered in Paris in 1905. Its three movements are titled “From Dawn to Noon on the Sea,” “Play of the Waves,” and “Dialogue of the Wind and the Sea.”

Joseph Haydn’s Symphony No. 94 in G major is nicknamed the “Surprise” Symphony. Haydn composed it for his first visit to London, where audiences heard it in 1792; it is the second of his twelve London symphonies. The surprise comes in the second movement, marked Andante, an Italian tempo word meaning “at a walking pace.” This movement begins with a quiet theme that is repeated softly, then suddenly interrupted by a very loud chord played by the orchestra. The unexpected burst of sound gave the symphony its nickname. Like many Classical-period symphonies, it has four movements with contrasting speeds and moods, but it is the dramatic moment in the Andante that has made Symphony No. 94 especially memorable.

Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star is a traditional English-language children’s song about a shining star, described in its best-known line as “like a diamond in the sky.” Its familiar words come from “The Star,” a poem by the English poet Jane Taylor, published in 1806 in the collection Rhymes for the Nursery. The song uses the melody of the French tune “Ah! vous dirai-je, maman,” which is also the melody of the alphabet song. Although Mozart wrote twelve variations on that tune, he did not write the words to Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star. The melody has appeared in other classical music too, including violin exercises in Shinichi Suzuki’s teaching method. To identify the song, remember its star and shared alphabet-song tune; to identify the poet, remember Jane Taylor.

Erlkönig is a dramatic song, or lied, composed by the Austrian musician Franz Schubert. He set a ballad by the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, first published in 1782. Goethe also wrote Faust and The Sorrows of Young Werther. In the story, a father rides through the night carrying his sick child, who sees and hears a supernatural figure called the Erlking. The father tries to reassure him, but the child grows more terrified. A single singer performs all four roles—the narrator, father, child, and Erlking—changing vocal color and range to distinguish them. Meanwhile, a relentless pattern of three quick notes in the piano suggests the horse’s galloping hooves. When the father finally reaches home, the child is dead in his arms.

Castles were fortified residences built for rulers and nobles, especially in medieval Europe. They provided a place to live while helping defend against attack. A castle might have a keep, the strong central tower; curtain walls around its grounds; a portcullis, or heavy gate that slid vertically across an entrance; and a moat, a ditch that made the walls harder to reach. Early motte-and-bailey castles placed a tower on an artificial mound called a motte beside an enclosed courtyard called a bailey. Castles could also have garderobes, small rooms used as toilets. In France’s Loire Valley, later castles became grand royal residences. Château de Chambord, built during the Renaissance, is famous for a double-helix staircase whose two winding routes let people go up and down without crossing paths.

A bagpipe drone is a pipe that sounds continuously at an unchanging pitch while the bagpipe is played. The player blows air into a bag, or uses bellows on some types of bagpipes, then squeezes the bag to keep air flowing steadily through the pipes. The drone provides a sustained note beneath the tune, creating a steady accompaniment. Some bagpipes have more than one drone, and their notes can be tuned before playing, but they do not change as the melody moves. The changing notes come from a separate pipe called the chanter. The player covers and uncovers holes on the chanter with their fingers to play the melody. This contrast between the steady drone and the moving tune is a distinctive part of bagpipe music.

A flower is the reproductive structure of a flowering plant. Its parts often include colorful petals, protective sepals, pollen-producing stamens, and carpels, which contain the structures that can develop into seeds. Flowers are also a popular subject in botanical art, where artists may paint them close up to show these details. American painter Georgia O’Keeffe made flowers the focus of many large, striking paintings, including Black Iris III and Oriental Poppies. By enlarging and simplifying their shapes, she encouraged viewers to notice forms they might overlook in a small flower. O’Keeffe was married to photographer Alfred Stieglitz, who interpreted some of her flower paintings as resembling parts of the human body, though she rejected that interpretation.

Tuning is the practice of adjusting an instrument so its notes match a chosen reference pitch or tuning system. Before playing, a musician might turn pegs to tighten or loosen strings, changing their pitch, or adjust another sound-producing part of the instrument. To check a note, musicians can compare it with a tuning fork, a small metal device with two prongs. When struck, the fork vibrates and produces a steady pitch; a common one sounds A4, the A above middle C, at 440 hertz. Musicians then listen for differences and adjust their instruments until the pitches agree. Tuning helps players sound in harmony with one another, especially in an ensemble where everyone needs to use the same pitch reference.

Tombs are structures or sites where people are buried or remembered after death. They range from simple graves to elaborate mausoleums, sepulchres, and royal burial complexes. Many tombs combine architecture with sculpture, such as a carved burial effigy showing the person who died. During the Renaissance, the Italian sculptor Donatello helped create monumental tombs for Cardinal Rainaldo Brancacci and Antipope John XXIII. He worked with the architect and sculptor Michelozzo on John XXIII’s tomb, which stands inside the Baptistery of San Giovanni in Florence. This historic octagonal building faces Florence Cathedral and has long been used for Christian baptism, a ceremony of initiation into the faith. The monument shows how a tomb can honor a person while also becoming part of a larger religious building.

Stride piano is a lively jazz piano style that grew in popularity in Harlem, New York, in the early 1900s. Its name comes from the way the pianist’s left hand seems to “stride” across the keyboard: it plays a low bass note, then leaps up to play a chord, repeating this pattern to create a steady rhythm. Meanwhile, the right hand plays the melody, adds flourishes, and improvises. James P. Johnson, often called the “Father of Stride,” helped develop and popularize the style. His demanding solo “Carolina Shout” became a piece that other pianists studied and learned to play. Fats Waller and Art Tatum were other celebrated stride pianists.

Mannerism was a style of European art that developed after the High Renaissance in the 1500s. While High Renaissance artists often aimed for balanced, lifelike scenes, Mannerist artists favored dramatic effects: elongated figures, artificial poses, intricate compositions, and unusually arranged space. Parmigianino’s Madonna with the Long Neck is a well-known example. Tintoretto, a Venetian painter associated with Mannerism, used this dramatic approach in The Origin of the Milky Way. The painting shows the infant Heracles nursing at the breast of the goddess Hera; milk scattering from her breast becomes stars in the sky. Tintoretto also painted a crowded version of The Last Supper, arranging the table diagonally rather than placing it straight across the scene as Leonardo da Vinci did.

A stencil is a reusable template with shapes or letters cut out of it. When an artist places it against a surface and applies paint, the template masks some areas while paint passes through the openings, creating a planned image or sign. The same stencil can reproduce a design on many surfaces, from paper and fabric to walls. Stencils are useful for crisp edges, repeated patterns, and images that can be made quickly, so they are common in signs and street art. In Paris during the 1980s, the French street artist Blek le Rat used stencils to create images of rats and life-size human figures in public places. His stencil work is often cited as an influence on the street artist Banksy.

A musical interval is the perceived distance in pitch between two notes. The notes can sound at the same time, creating harmony, or one after the other, forming part of a melody. Intervals are named by counting the letter names from the first note to the second, including both notes: C to E is a third (C, D, E), while C to G is a fifth. Words such as “major” and “perfect” identify the interval more precisely. An octave spans eight diatonic scale steps: from C4 up to C5, count C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C. The higher C has twice the frequency of the lower C, so the notes sound closely related even though one is higher.

Ballet jumps are movements in which a dancer pushes off the floor and, for a moment, both feet are in the air. Dancers use strength and timing to rise, shape their legs while airborne, and land with control. One example is the pas de chat, meaning “cat’s step,” in which the dancer lifts one knee and then the other while jumping. Another is the grand jeté, a large traveling leap: the dancer takes off from one foot, stretches the legs into a wide split in the air, and lands on the other foot. These jumps can make a ballet look light and effortless, but they require practice to perform safely and gracefully.

Saint Basil’s Cathedral is a Russian Orthodox church on Red Square in Moscow, famous for its brightly colored, patterned onion domes. Ivan IV commissioned it to celebrate his army’s capture of Kazan in 1552, a major victory that expanded Russian territory. The cathedral was built in the 1550s and 1560s and became one of Moscow’s most recognizable landmarks. Its popular name honors Saint Basil the Blessed, a religious figure who was buried there. Ivan IV had been crowned Russia’s first tsar in 1547. He is also known as Ivan the Terrible, a name associated with the harsh and often violent way he ruled. Remembering the link between the cathedral, the conquest of Kazan, and Ivan IV helps identify both the building and the ruler who commissioned it.

A pencil is a drawing tool with a core of graphite and clay, usually enclosed in wood. Although the core is often called “lead,” it contains no metal lead. Changing the proportions of graphite and clay makes pencils softer or harder: softer pencils generally leave darker, broader marks, while harder ones make lighter, finer lines. A common medium grade is the #2 pencil. Artists use pencils not just for outlines but also to show shading, texture, and depth. In cross-hatching, overlapping lines create darker areas where the lines are closer together. Stippling works differently: the artist makes separate dots instead of overlapping lines. Dots packed closely together make an area appear darker, while dots spaced farther apart make it appear lighter.

Charlie “Bird” Parker was a Kansas City-born American alto saxophonist and composer who helped create bebop, a fast, inventive style that transformed jazz in the 1940s. His playing featured rapid melodies, surprising rhythms, and complex harmonies, giving later musicians new ways to improvise. Parker recorded influential pieces such as “Ko-Ko” and “Ornithology” and often worked with trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, another central figure in bebop. Gillespie was recognizable for his puffed cheeks when he played and for his trumpet’s sharply upward-bent bell. He co-wrote “A Night in Tunisia” and helped bring Afro-Cuban jazz to wider audiences through music such as “Manteca.” Together, Parker and Gillespie helped shape the sound of modern jazz.

A skyscraper is a very tall building with many floors, often used for offices, homes, hotels, or a mix of these. Its height is possible because a strong steel or reinforced-concrete frame supports the building, rather than relying on thick outer walls to carry its weight. William Le Baron Jenney’s Home Insurance Building, completed in Chicago in 1885, is often cited as an early skyscraper because its metal frame supported its exterior walls. As engineers developed stronger structural systems, skyscrapers grew taller and became landmarks in major cities. One example is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, designed by Adrian Smith. Opened in 2010, it reaches 828 meters including its spire and is the world’s tallest building.

A column is a vertical architectural support that helps hold up a building. In classical architecture, it typically has a base at the bottom, a long shaft, and a capital at the top. The capital supports the entablature, the horizontal structure above the columns. The three major classical orders—Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian—give columns different proportions and decorations. Doric capitals are relatively plain, Ionic capitals have scrolls, and Corinthian capitals are decorated with carved acanthus leaves. Columns can also be monuments rather than building supports. Trajan’s Column in Rome is a famous freestanding example: a spiral relief winds around its shaft, telling the story of Emperor Trajan’s victories in two campaigns against the Dacians in the early second century CE.

The bass is a low-pitched string instrument that anchors the bottom of a band’s harmony and helps establish its rhythm. An electric bass, or bass guitar, usually has a solid body and is played through an amplifier; the much larger upright bass, also called the double bass, has a hollow acoustic body. In jazz, bassists often play a “walking” bass line: a steady sequence of notes that outlines the chords and keeps the music moving. Charles Mingus was a celebrated upright bassist and composer whose album Mingus Ah Um includes “Goodbye Pork Pie Hat.” Jaco Pastorius was an American electric-bass virtuoso who joined the jazz-fusion group Weather Report in 1976. His composition “Portrait of Tracy,” on his self-titled debut album, showcases his fretless bass playing.

The Gross Clinic is an 1875 painting by American artist Thomas Eakins. It shows the surgeon Samuel D. Gross leading an operation while medical students watch from the seats of an amphitheater at Jefferson Medical College in Philadelphia. Gross stands at the center with bloodstained hands, pausing to explain the procedure. In the foreground, a distressed woman, often identified as the patient’s mother, turns away and covers her face. Eakins painted the scene with striking realism rather than making surgery look neat or heroic. Gross was an influential Philadelphia physician who also wrote A System of Surgery. The painting’s title refers to him: “clinic” here means a teaching session in which students learn by observing a doctor at work.

“Drunken Sailor” is a traditional sea shanty, a work song sailors used to help coordinate tasks such as hoisting sails and scrubbing decks. Its brisk call-and-response pattern lets a leader sing a line and the crew answer together, keeping everyone moving in time. The song repeatedly asks, “What shall we do with a drunken sailor?” and each verse offers a different, sometimes humorous, response. One well-known suggestion is to “put him in a longboat till he’s sober.” A longboat was a smaller boat carried by a larger ship, so this verse means leaving the intoxicated sailor in the ship’s auxiliary craft until he recovers. The repeated question and changing answers make the shanty easy for a crew to learn and sing together.

I Vow to Thee, My Country is a British patriotic hymn that brings together words by diplomat Cecil Spring Rice and music by composer Gustav Holst. Spring Rice drafted the poem in 1908 under the title “Urbs Dei, or The Two Fatherlands.” During World War I, he served as Britain’s ambassador to the United States. The poem speaks of devotion to one’s country and to a second, spiritual homeland. The hymn’s melody, known as “Thaxted,” was adapted from the central theme of “Jupiter,” the fourth movement of Holst’s seven-part orchestral suite The Planets. Other movements in the suite include “Mars, the Bringer of War” and “Venus, the Bringer of Peace.” Although the words and tune were written separately, together they became one of Britain’s best-known patriotic hymns.

Swans Reflecting Elephants is a 1937 painting by Salvador Dalí, a Spanish artist associated with Surrealism. In the scene, three white swans float on a lake beside thin, spindly trees. Look at their reflections, though, and the birds seem to become elephants: the swans’ necks form long trunks, while their bodies and the trees help create the animals’ huge shapes. This double image makes viewers question what they see, a common feature of Surrealist art, which often draws on dreams and unexpected connections. Dalí also painted The Persistence of Memory, famous for its melting clocks, and spent much of his later life in Portlligat, a village on the coast of Spain.

Fanfare for the Common Man is a short, powerful piece by American composer Aaron Copland, written for brass instruments and percussion. Conductor Eugene Goossens commissioned it for the Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra’s 1942 season, during World War II. Copland was inspired by a speech that year in which U.S. vice president Henry A. Wallace called for a “Century of the Common Man,” a future shaped by the efforts and rights of ordinary people. Rather than honoring a king or a military leader, the fanfare celebrates everyday people. It begins with striking percussion sounds, followed by a bold trumpet melody whose opening notes rise from F to B-flat to F. Its grand sound has made it a popular choice for ceremonies and public celebrations.

The triangle is a small percussion instrument made by bending a metal rod into an open, three-sided shape. It is usually struck with a metal beater, producing a bright, ringing sound that can be heard even when an orchestra is playing. A player can strike it once or make a rapid series of strokes called a roll. Triangles appear in orchestral and popular music; for example, a triangle roll opens “Anitra’s Dance” in Edvard Grieg’s Peer Gynt Suite No. 1. The instrument also has a memorable connection to composer Franz Liszt. Critic Eduard Hanslick mocked Liszt’s first piano concerto as a “triangle concerto” because of the triangle’s conspicuous part. Liszt also wrote an 1853 piano sonata in B minor that is associated with double-function form.

Ikebana is the Japanese art of arranging flowers, branches, leaves, and other plant materials. Rather than simply gathering colorful blooms into a bouquet, an ikebana artist places each element deliberately, paying attention to line, balance, shape, and the empty spaces between plants. A tall branch might draw the eye upward, while a lower stem or flower helps balance the composition. Traditional ikebana also gives the arrangement a symbolic meaning: its parts can represent three realms of the cosmos—heaven, humanity, and earth—and bring them into harmony. This focus on both natural materials and thoughtful design makes ikebana more than a flower display. It is a way of expressing a relationship between people, the natural world, and the heavens.

A triumphal arch is a freestanding monumental gateway built to celebrate a military victory or another major event. Unlike an arch that supports a wall, its main purpose is to honor people or events, often through carved reliefs and inscriptions. The tradition began in ancient Rome and inspired later monuments, including the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. It stands at the center of Place Charles de Gaulle, historically called Place de l’Étoile, where twelve avenues meet. One of those avenues is the Champs-Élysées, famous for its shops and the annual Bastille Day parade. Beneath the Arc de Triomphe is France’s Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, honoring those who died in World War I without being identified. An eternal flame beside the tomb is rekindled each evening.

Joe Hisaishi is a Japanese composer and pianist born Mamoru Fujisawa. He became internationally known through his long creative partnership with director Hayao Miyazaki, writing music for many Studio Ghibli films, including My Neighbor Totoro, Princess Mononoke, Spirited Away, and Howl’s Moving Castle. His scores help bring the films’ imaginary worlds and characters’ emotions to life. In the 2001 film Spirited Away, a girl named Chihiro enters a mysterious spirit world after her parents eat food there and are transformed into pigs. To survive and find a way to save them, she works at a bathhouse for spirits. Spirited Away won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, helping introduce Hisaishi’s music and Miyazaki’s storytelling to an even wider audience.

Opera houses are theaters designed for opera, a form of drama in which performers sing their roles, usually accompanied by an orchestra. Their auditoriums and stages are built to help audiences see and hear the performance, but many opera houses are also famous for their architecture. The Oslo Opera House in Norway has a broad, sloping roof that people are invited to walk across, turning part of the building into a public space. Another landmark is the Sydney Opera House at Bennelong Point in Sydney, Australia. Designed by Jørn Utzon, it is recognized by its white, sail-like concrete shells; engineer Ove Arup helped develop the ribs that support them. These buildings show how an opera house can be both a place for music and a striking feature of a city.

G is one of the seven letter-named notes in Western music. Moving upward from C through C, D, E, F, and G places G a perfect fifth above C. When G is the tonic, or home note, of a major scale, the key is G major. Its scale is G, A, B, C, D, E, F-sharp, and back to G, so its key signature has one sharp: F-sharp. E minor is the relative minor of G major because both keys use those same notes and share that one-sharp key signature, even though E minor has E as its tonic. E is a major third above C. G can also be the tonic of G minor, a different key whose signature has two flats.

The British Museum in London holds objects from many world civilizations, including a clay tablet recording one of the oldest known written complaints. Around 1750 BCE, a man named Nanni complained that a merchant called Ea-Nasir had supplied poor-quality copper ingots. The message was written in cuneiform, an ancient writing system used in Mesopotamia, a region that included Babylon and lay between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. To write cuneiform, people pressed a cut reed into soft clay, making wedge-shaped marks. The museum also holds the Parthenon sculptures, sometimes called the Elgin Marbles. Their presence in London has prompted debate about cultural repatriation: whether objects should be returned to the places they came from.

A gargoyle is a carved waterspout that projects from the roof or upper wall of a building. Rainwater flows through its hollow body and often pours out of its mouth, landing away from the walls. This helps protect the masonry from water damage. Gargoyles are especially associated with medieval Gothic churches and cathedrals, including Notre-Dame de Paris, and often look like strange animals, monsters, or demonic figures. Their frightening appearance makes them memorable, but their practical job is to drain rainwater. Other grotesque carvings may look similar; if they do not carry water away from the building, they are not functioning as gargoyles.

Ansel Adams was an American photographer celebrated for sharply detailed black-and-white landscapes of the American West. He helped make photography widely recognized as an art form and was a member of Group f/64, whose photographers favored crisp focus and rich detail. With photographer Fred Archer, Adams developed the Zone System, a way to plan exposure and development by dividing tones from black to white into numbered zones. This helped photographers control how light and shadow appeared in a finished image. In the 1940s, the federal government commissioned Adams to photograph protected scenic lands for a mural project. He photographed national parks, including Yosemite National Park, where he captured famous landmarks such as Half Dome and El Capitan.

Come from Away is a musical by Irene Sankoff and David Hein based on what happened in Gander, Newfoundland, after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. When U.S. airspace closed, 38 planes carrying thousands of passengers were diverted to this town in eastern Canada. The travelers could not continue their journeys, so Gander residents welcomed them into their homes and community buildings, offering food, shelter, and support. The musical tells the stories of both the stranded passengers and the local people who helped them; one character is based on real-life pilot Beverley Bass. Its song “38 Planes” refers to the unexpected arrivals. Come from Away shows how a small community responded with kindness during a frightening time.

Kind of Blue is a landmark jazz album recorded in 1959 for Columbia Records under trumpeter Miles Davis’s leadership. Rather than relying mainly on fast-changing chords, much of its music uses modal jazz, giving musicians room to explore melodies built around particular scales. Its tracks include “So What” and “Flamenco Sketches.” The group included pianist Bill Evans and tenor saxophonist John Coltrane, whose solo can be heard on “So What.” Coltrane later became a major bandleader in his own right. He wrote “Giant Steps,” a composition known for its rapidly changing chords, and led the quartet that recorded A Love Supreme. Kind of Blue remains one of jazz’s best-selling and most influential albums, admired for its relaxed sound and inventive improvisation.

Romeo and Juliet is a three-act ballet composed by Sergei Prokofiev from William Shakespeare’s tragedy. Set in Verona, Italy, it tells the story of two young lovers whose families, the Montagues and the Capulets, are bitter enemies.
