Prokofiev’s music helps show the contrast between the lovers’ tenderness and the hostility around them. One of the ballet’s best-known numbers is Dance of the Knights, a weighty, march-like piece heard during a formal gathering of Verona’s aristocracy. Its strong rhythm and imposing sound suit the proud, powerful families. Dance of the Knights is also called Montagues and Capulets, after the two rival houses whose feud drives the story toward its tragic ending.

Giuseppe Tartini was an Italian Baroque composer and virtuoso violinist who spent much of his career performing and teaching in Padua. He is best known for the “Devil’s Trill Sonata,” a piece famous for its difficult, rapid trills, in which a player alternates quickly between two notes. The sonata is written for violin, a bowed instrument with four strings tuned G, D, A, and E from lowest to highest. The violin is the highest-pitched standard member of the orchestral string family, above the viola, cello, and double bass. Tartini’s music shows how the violin can play both expressive melodies and dazzling passages that demand great skill from the performer.

The Lincoln Memorial stands at the western end of the National Mall in Washington, D.C., and honors Abraham Lincoln, the U.S. president who led the country through the Civil War. Designed to resemble an ancient Greek temple, it has 36 Doric columns, representing the 36 states in the Union when Lincoln died in 1865. Inside is a monumental seated marble statue of Lincoln, designed by American sculptor Daniel Chester French. French also created The Minute Man, a statue in Concord, Massachusetts, commemorating a soldier of the American Revolution. The Lincoln Memorial faces toward the Washington Monument, the tall white obelisk on the Mall. Its architecture and sculpture make it both a tribute to Lincoln and a place where Americans gather to reflect on freedom and equality.

Katajjaq is a traditional Inuit vocal performance in which two people face each other and use their voices to make short, rhythmic sounds. Rather than playing conventional instruments, the performers create sounds with their mouths and throats, often alternating breaths, syllables, and other vocal effects. Their patterns fit together in an interlocking exchange, so each person responds closely to the other. Rhythm and coordination are more important than singing a melody with a fixed pitch. Katajjaq is often performed as a friendly game: the performers try to keep the shared pattern going, and the exchange may end when one person laughs or loses the rhythm. The name of this performance form is katajjaq, and its sound-producing medium is the human voice.

Tosca is an opera by Italian composer Giacomo Puccini, set in Rome in June 1800. Its title character, Floria Tosca, is a celebrated singer whose lover, Mario Cavaradossi, is a painter. Cavaradossi helps a political prisoner escape, bringing him into conflict with the corrupt police chief Baron Scarpia. Scarpia orders Cavaradossi’s execution and tries to use his power over Tosca to force her to submit to him. In an attempt to save her lover, Tosca kills Scarpia, but she later discovers that Cavaradossi’s execution was real. While awaiting the firing squad at Castel Sant’Angelo, Cavaradossi sings the aria “E lucevan le stelle,” remembering happier moments with Tosca.

Bunraku puppets are large, painted figures used to tell stories in traditional Japanese puppet theater. Each puppet is operated in view of the audience by a coordinated team of three performers. The lead operator, called the omozukai, controls the puppet’s head and right hand; the hidarizukai moves its left hand, and the ashizukai moves its legs. The operators often wear black clothing so viewers can focus on the puppet’s actions. A narrator speaks the characters’ lines and tells the story, accompanied by music played on a shamisen, a three-stringed instrument. This combination of storytelling and music is known as joruri. Bunraku’s dramatic stories and performance techniques later influenced kabuki theater.

The Lion King is a stage musical adapted from Disney’s 1994 animated film. It follows Simba, a young lion prince who must face his past and reclaim his place as king of the Pride Lands. Its songs include “Circle of Life,” which introduces the interconnected lives of the animals; “Hakuna Matata,” a “problem-free philosophy” taught to Simba by Timon the meerkat and Pumbaa the warthog; and “Be Prepared,” sung by Simba’s scheming uncle Scar. The Broadway production is famous for showing the human performers alongside the animal characters they portray, using elaborate masks, puppets, and costumes. Director and designer Julie Taymor shaped this distinctive look and became the first woman to win the Tony Award for Best Direction of a Musical for her work on The Lion King.

The Beginning of the World is a polished, egg-like sculpture by Constantin Brâncuși, a Romanian-born artist who helped shape modern sculpture. Rather than carving a detailed figure, Brâncuși used a smooth, simple form to suggest an egg—the source of new life. Its rounded shape and reflective surface express his search for perfect beauty and evoke the primordial origins of the world. This approach is an example of abstraction: an artist simplifies a subject to communicate an idea instead of copying its appearance exactly. Brâncuși also created a sculptural ensemble at Târgu Jiu in Romania. It includes the towering Endless Column, a monument honoring soldiers who died in World War I.

Watercolor is a painting medium in which pigments are mixed with water and usually applied to paper. As the water dries, it leaves color behind, often in transparent layers called washes. These washes let the paper or earlier colors show through, so artists can build up color while keeping a sense of light. Unlike opaque paints that cover a surface, watercolor often depends on the brightness of the paper beneath it. In the 20th century, artist Helen Frankenthaler adapted a related idea in her soak-stain technique. She poured or brushed heavily diluted paint onto large, unprimed canvases, allowing color to soak into and spread through the fabric rather than sit on top as a conventional paint layer. Her approach helped shape Color Field painting.

A porch is a roofed platform or gallery attached to a building’s entrance or exterior wall. It provides a sheltered place to sit and a transition between indoors and outdoors. In the late 1800s, many people believed fresh air could help treat tuberculosis, a lung disease then often called consumption. This belief encouraged builders to add porches and more windows to homes and other buildings so patients could spend time in the open air. Porches also gave their name to a famous political strategy. During the 1896 U.S. presidential campaign, Ohio Republican William McKinley stayed mainly at his home in Canton, Ohio, instead of touring the country. Delegations came to visit him, and he addressed them from his home’s porch in what became known as a “front porch campaign.”

Musical meter is the pattern that organizes beats into recurring groups called bars or measures. A time signature shows how beats are arranged: in 3/4, for example, each bar has three quarter-note beats. Musicians use meter as a rhythmic framework for playing, singing, and dancing together. To identify a meter, listen for the main beats and notice how each one divides into smaller parts. “Duple” means there are two main beats in a bar, while “compound” means each main beat divides into three equal parts. Music written in 6/8 often has compound duple meter: its six eighth notes are felt as two groups of three, not as six separate main beats.

A paper crane, or orizuru, is a folded-paper model of a crane made in origami, the Japanese art of paper folding. It has a long neck and tail, a pointed beak, and broad wings. In Japan, people traditionally fold one thousand paper cranes, called senbazuru, while making a wish for health, hope, or good fortune. Paper cranes also became a symbol of peace through the story of Sadako Sasaki. She survived the 1945 atomic bombing of Hiroshima but later developed leukemia. While ill, Sadako folded cranes, hoping to recover. Her story spread around the world, and folded paper cranes are now often made to remember victims of war and express hope for peace.

Edward Steichen was a Luxembourg-born American artist who grew up in the United States and worked as both a painter and a photographer. He became a leading figure in Photo-Secession, a movement that argued photography could be a form of fine art. With Alfred Stieglitz, he helped establish the influential 291 gallery in New York. One of Steichen’s best-known works is The Pond—Moonlight, an early color photograph made near Mamaroneck, New York, in 1904. He created its blue-green appearance by applying successive layers of light-sensitive gum by hand. Steichen also supported other modern artists, including the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși. Later, he directed the photography department at the Museum of Modern Art, where he organized the 1955 exhibition The Family of Man, which explored shared human experiences through photographs.

Walt Disney Concert Hall is a performing-arts venue in downtown Los Angeles and the home of the Los Angeles Philharmonic. It opened in 2003 and is especially famous for its sweeping, sculptural exterior, made of curved stainless-steel panels that catch and reflect the light. The hall was designed by Frank Gehry, a Canadian-American architect known for creating buildings with unusual, flowing shapes. His other major works include the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in Spain and the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris. Although the concert hall’s exterior looks like a work of sculpture, it surrounds a space built for live music. Its distinctive appearance has made it one of Los Angeles’s best-known architectural landmarks.

Peter and the Wolf is a narrated symphonic fairy tale written by Sergei Prokofiev in 1936 for the Moscow Central Children’s Theatre. It tells the story of Peter, a brave boy who ventures outside despite his grandfather’s warning about a wolf. Prokofiev gives each character a musical theme played by a particular instrument or group of instruments, helping listeners follow the action and recognize who is in the story. The string instruments represent Peter, and the bassoon’s low voice represents his grandfather. Among the animals, a flute plays the bird’s quick, lively theme, an oboe represents the duck, and a clarinet represents the cat. The wolf’s threatening theme is played by French horns. When the wolf appears, Peter works with the bird to catch it, turning the music into part of the adventure.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart completed Symphony No. 40 in G minor in 1788. It is the second of his three final symphonies, written between Symphony No. 39 and Symphony No. 41, nicknamed the “Jupiter” Symphony. Its Köchel catalogue number is K. 550; the Köchel catalogue is a system used to identify Mozart’s works. Symphony No. 40 is also called the “Great G Minor Symphony” to distinguish it from his earlier “Little G Minor Symphony,” No. 25. The restless opening melody and dramatic contrasts help make No. 40 one of Mozart’s most recognizable works. It is written in G minor, a key with two flats, B-flat and E-flat, and follows the four-movement pattern common in Classical-period symphonies.

A synthesizer is an electronic musical instrument that generates sounds from waveforms and shapes them using components such as filters and envelopes. An oscillator produces a repeating waveform; a filter can change its tone, while an envelope controls how the sound develops over time, such as how quickly it starts and fades. Many synthesizers have keyboards, but they can also be controlled in other ways. Musicians use them to create new sounds or imitate instruments such as violins. Wendy Carlos helped popularize synthesizers through recordings including Switched-On Bach. One important feature of any musical sound is pitch, which is how high or low it seems. Pitch is related to frequency: raising an oscillator’s frequency raises the pitch, while lowering the frequency makes the pitch lower.

Clapping is the sound made by striking the hands together. In music, performers can use it as percussion, creating a beat without an instrument. Audiences also clap to show appreciation after a performance; sustained applause may lead performers to give an encore. American minimalist composer Steve Reich explored clapping as music in his 1972 piece Clapping Music. It is performed by two people using only their hands. Both begin with the same repeating rhythm, but one performer keeps that pattern steady while the other gradually shifts it, changing how the two rhythms fit together. This technique, called phasing, lets listeners hear new patterns emerge even though the performers use no instruments.

The Wedding Feast at Cana is a monumental painting by the Italian artist Paolo Veronese. It shows a story from the Gospel of John: at a wedding banquet in Cana, Jesus performs his first miracle by turning water into wine. Veronese painted the biblical event as a grand, crowded feast, mixing figures from Jesus’s time with guests dressed like people of his own era. The canvas is about ten meters wide and was originally made for the refectory, or dining hall, of a Benedictine monastery on the island of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice. French troops removed it from Venice in 1797 and took it to Paris. Today, this enormous work of Renaissance art is displayed in the Louvre Museum.

The string section is the group of orchestral musicians who play violins, violas, cellos, and double basses. Unlike brass, woodwind, and percussion instruments, these instruments make sound when their strings vibrate, usually after a player draws a bow across them, though players can also pluck them. Violins generally play the highest notes, followed by violas and then cellos. The double bass plays the lowest notes and is larger than a cello; its player usually stands or sits on a tall stool to play it upright. Together, the strings can carry a melody, add harmony, or provide a deep foundation for the orchestra. In Sergei Prokofiev’s Peter and the Wolf, the string section represents Peter.

The bass clef is a symbol at the beginning of a five-line musical staff that tells musicians how to read low-pitched notes. It assigns the fourth line, counted from the bottom, to the F below middle C. The clef’s two dots sit on either side of that line, pointing out the F, which is why the bass clef is also called the F clef. It is commonly used for low-register instruments such as cello and trombone, as well as for the left-hand staff in piano music. Once the fourth line is identified as F, musicians can work out the pitches on the other lines and spaces by moving up or down the musical alphabet.

Spring, or La Primavera in Italian, is the first of Antonio Vivaldi’s four violin concertos known as The Four Seasons. Published in 1725 as part of his Op. 8 collection, The Contest Between Harmony and Invention, the concertos use music to suggest the sights and sounds of each season. Spring is in E major and opens with a lively Allegro movement. A sonnet associated with the concerto describes birds celebrating spring’s return, and the violins imitate their calls. In a slower movement, a viola figure played “always forte,” or loudly, represents a barking dog. These details help listeners recognize which season Vivaldi is portraying and show how instruments can tell a story without words.

The Space Needle is a futuristic observation tower in Seattle, the largest city in Washington state. It was built as the signature landmark for the city’s 1962 world’s fair, officially called the Century 21 Exposition. The fair showcased ideas about science, technology, and life in the future, and the tower’s design matched that theme. Three splayed legs support its tall, narrow structure, while a broad, saucer-shaped top makes it look like something from a science-fiction story. Visitors can go up to an observation deck for views of Seattle and nearby Puget Sound. The top also includes a rotating restaurant. More than sixty years after the fair, the Space Needle remains one of Seattle’s most recognizable landmarks.

Ai Weiwei is a Chinese contemporary artist whose sculptures, installations, photographs, and performances often question political power and explore human rights and memory. He served as an artistic consultant on Beijing’s National Stadium, nicknamed the Bird’s Nest, for the 2008 Olympics. In one photographed performance, he dropped and shattered a Han-dynasty ceramic urn, challenging viewers to think about the value of cultural objects. He also created a vast installation of 100 million handmade porcelain sunflower seeds. After the 2008 Sichuan earthquake, Ai investigated the deaths of schoolchildren whose buildings collapsed. To commemorate them, he covered the façade of Munich’s Haus der Kunst with thousands of brightly colored school backpacks. The backpacks spelled out words quoted from a bereaved mother. This installation is titled Remembering.

The Vienna Secession was a group of Austrian artists who broke away from Vienna’s conservative Künstlerhaus art establishment in 1897. Led by Gustav Klimt, they wanted more freedom to create and exhibit modern art, including painting, design, and architecture. Their exhibition pavilion, designed by Joseph Maria Olbrich, bears the motto “To every age its art, to art its freedom,” expressing their belief that artists should be able to explore new ideas. From 1898 to 1903, the group published an illustrated official magazine called Ver Sacrum, a Latin title meaning roughly “Sacred Spring.” It featured work by Klimt, Koloman Moser, and other artists, helping the Secession share its ideas beyond its exhibitions.

De Stijl was a Dutch modernist art movement that began in the early 20th century. Its artists wanted to create a clear, orderly kind of abstract art by reducing images to simple geometric forms. Their works often feature horizontal and vertical lines, squares and rectangles, and a limited palette of red, blue, and yellow—the primary colors—alongside black and white. Piet Mondrian is one of the artists most closely associated with De Stijl. In many paintings titled Composition, he arranged black grid lines around blocks of primary color and white space. His later painting Broadway Boogie Woogie uses a lively grid of colored lines and squares inspired by the energy of New York City, while still reflecting De Stijl’s emphasis on horizontal and vertical structure.

Fountain is a 1917 artwork by Marcel Duchamp, a French artist associated with Dada, a movement that challenged traditional ideas about art. Duchamp took a mass-produced urinal, turned it on its side, signed it “R. Mutt,” and submitted it to an exhibition of the Society of Independent Artists. The work caused controversy because Duchamp had not made the object by hand; he had chosen an ordinary item and presented it as art. This kind of work is called a “readymade.” Fountain asks whether an artist’s choice and the setting in which an object is displayed can make it art. Duchamp also created L.H.O.O.Q., a work in which he added a mustache and goatee to a reproduction of the Mona Lisa.

An equestrian statue is a sculpture showing a person riding a horse. These monuments often honor rulers, military leaders, or civic founders and are usually placed in public spaces where many people can see them. One famous example is the Bronze Horseman in St. Petersburg, Russia. Designed by Étienne Maurice Falconet, it portrays Peter the Great, the city’s founder, on a rearing horse. The statue stands on the Thunder Stone, an enormous granite boulder moved to the site to serve as its base. Another well-known equestrian statue is Donatello’s Gattamelata, which depicts the military leader Erasmo da Narni. Although the rider is often the person being honored, the horse is an essential part of an equestrian statue.

Girl with Balloon is one of the best-known works by Banksy, a British street artist whose identity remains unknown. The stencil image shows a small, dark silhouette of a girl in a dress reaching toward a red, heart-shaped balloon that appears to be floating away. Its simple design has led people to interpret it in different ways, including as an image of hope or loss. In 2018, a framed version of the work sold at a Sotheby’s auction. Moments after the sale, a shredder hidden inside the frame switched on, cutting the image into strips as it passed through. The shredding stopped partway through, leaving the artwork only partially destroyed. Banksy gave the altered work a new title: Love is in the Bin.

Stippling is a drawing technique that uses many small dots to create texture, shading, and a sense of depth. An artist places dots close together to make an area look darker and spreads them farther apart to make it look lighter. Stippling often uses just one color, such as black ink, and relies on the spacing of the dots rather than overlapping lines, as cross-hatching does. It is easy to confuse stippling with pointillism because both use dots. Pointillism, however, is a late-19th-century painting technique that uses separate dots of different colors. Seen from a distance, those colors blend in the viewer’s eye to form an image. Georges Seurat used pointillism in A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte.

Pitch is the quality of a sound that makes a note seem high or low. It depends mainly on frequency: faster sound-wave vibrations produce higher pitches, while slower vibrations produce lower pitches. Pitch is different from loudness, so a note can be played softly or loudly without changing how high or low it sounds. Musicians use changes in pitch to create melodies, and instruments such as violins and synthesizers can produce many different pitches. A violinist can also make a sustained note gently waver by moving a finger back and forth, causing small, repeated changes in pitch. This expressive effect is called vibrato. On a synthesizer, a low-frequency oscillator can create vibrato by repeatedly shifting the pitch slightly above and below the note being held.

The Gateway Arch is a 630-foot-tall stainless-steel monument beside the Mississippi River in St. Louis, Missouri. Designed by architect Eero Saarinen and completed in 1965, it symbolizes St. Louis’s historic role as a gateway to the American West. The arch is the centerpiece of Gateway Arch National Park, established in 2018 from the former Jefferson National Expansion Memorial. Its outline is not part of a circle: it follows an inverted catenary curve. A catenary is the shape a uniform chain makes when it hangs freely between two fixed points. Turn that shape upside down, and it forms the arch’s graceful profile.

La Cenerentola is an 1817 comic opera by the Italian composer Gioachino Rossini. Its title means “Cinderella” in Italian, and its heroine, Angelina, is Rossini’s version of Cinderella. She lives with her vain stepsisters, Clorinda and Tisbe, and their father, Don Magnifico, who treats her like a servant. Prince Ramiro visits the family while searching for a bride, but he wants to learn what people are really like before revealing who he is. He exchanges clothes with his valet, Dandini: Ramiro pretends to be a servant, while Dandini poses as the prince. This disguise lets Ramiro observe Angelina and her family. Unlike many Cinderella stories, the opera has no fairy godmother or glass slipper; its happy ending emphasizes Angelina’s kindness and forgiveness.

The Hebrides is a concert overture by the German Romantic composer Felix Mendelssohn. He was inspired to write it after visiting Fingal’s Cave, a sea cave on the Scottish island of Staffa, during his travels. The piece is also called Fingal’s Cave, but its main title refers to the Hebrides, the group of Scottish islands that includes Staffa. Mendelssohn used the orchestra to suggest the cave and the sea around it: flowing notes evoke rolling waves, while the timpani, a percussion instrument, add a low rumble. Although an overture can introduce an opera, this one is a stand-alone concert piece and an early example of music that paints a scene. Travel also inspired Mendelssohn’s Symphony No. 4, known as the Italian Symphony.

The Philadelphia Orchestra is one of the “Big Five” major American symphony orchestras. It became famous for the rich, blended “Philadelphia Sound” developed under conductor Leopold Stokowski, who led the orchestra from 1912 to 1938 and conducted much of the music in Disney’s 1940 film Fantasia. Eugene Ormandy succeeded Stokowski as the orchestra’s leading conductor in 1936 and remained in that role until 1980, helping make its distinctive sound known around the world through concerts and recordings. The orchestra performs regularly at the Kimmel Center in Philadelphia. Its concert hall was called Verizon Hall when the quiz question was written and is now named Marian Anderson Hall. Today, the orchestra is also closely associated with conductor Yannick Nézet-Séguin.

The can-can is a lively French dance that became popular in nineteenth-century Parisian music halls. It is often performed by a line of dancers who repeatedly kick their legs high in time with fast, energetic music. One of the most famous pieces associated with the dance is the “Infernal Galop” from the comic opera Orpheus in the Underworld. The opera was written by Jacques Offenbach, a French composer known for his humorous stage works. His rapid, bouncy music helped make the can-can instantly recognizable, even to people who have never seen it performed. Offenbach also composed The Tales of Hoffmann. If you hear a question about high-kicking French chorus lines or the composer of the “Infernal Galop,” think of the can-can and Offenbach.

Yinka Shonibare is a British-Nigerian contemporary artist whose sculptures and installations explore colonialism, cultural identity, and hybridity—the mixing of cultures. He often dresses headless figures in brightly patterned Dutch wax-print fabric. Although the cloth is closely associated with Africa, its history connects Europe, Asia, and Africa, making it a way to question simple ideas about where a culture belongs. Shonibare also recreates scenes from European art, changing them to make viewers think about who is represented and who has power. One installation, titled The Swing (after Fragonard), reimagines the French Rococo painter Jean-Honoré Fragonard’s painting The Swing. In the original, a young woman in a shepherdess hat kicks off a shoe while a hidden admirer watches from the bushes and a putto, or small winged figure, signals for silence.

Rococo was an eighteenth-century European art style that developed after the dramatic Baroque style and is sometimes considered its later phase. It became especially popular in France, where artists favored playful scenes of aristocratic leisure over grand displays of power. Rococo paintings often use delicate pastel colors, graceful figures, and a lighthearted mood, while Rococo interiors feature elaborate, curving ornament inspired by shells and plants. The French painter Jean-Antoine Watteau helped establish the fête galante, a type of painting showing elegantly dressed couples socializing in gardens or parkland. His best-known works include The Embarkation for Cythera, which shows couples gathering for a journey associated with love. Watteau’s work captures Rococo’s interest in elegance, romance, and pleasure.

Tango is a dramatic partner dance and musical style that emerged in the late 1800s around the Río de la Plata, the estuary between Argentina and Uruguay. It grew in the dance halls of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, where dancers developed close embraces, walking steps, sharp turns, and expressive pauses. Tango music is especially associated with the bandoneón, a bellows-driven free-reed instrument related to the accordion. Players push and pull its bellows while pressing buttons on both sides, producing a plaintive, sometimes mournful sound; unlike many accordions, it does not have a piano-style keyboard. The composer and bandoneón player Astor Piazzolla later brought jazz and classical influences into tango. Its theatrical movements, including dips in which one partner leans toward the floor, also influenced other partner dances.

A piano concerto is a classical work in which a solo pianist plays with an orchestra. The two parts often seem to have a musical conversation: the piano may introduce a melody, and the orchestra may answer, support it, or play it in a different way. Concertos also give the soloist chances to show technical skill and expression. The composer Sergei Rachmaninoff wrote four piano concertos. His Second Piano Concerto is in C minor, a key whose relative major is E-flat major. Relative major and minor keys share the same key signature but have different tonic notes, or “home” notes. In C minor, that home note is C.

Bunraku is a traditional Japanese form of theater in which large, elaborately made puppets act out stories. Each puppet is usually operated by three people: one controls the head and right hand, another the left hand, and a third the feet. The operators may wear black clothing so the audience can focus on the puppet. Instead of the puppets speaking, a narrator delivers the dialogue and describes the action, often voicing many different characters. A musician accompanies the performance on the shamisen, a plucked, three-stringed Japanese lute. Its music helps set the mood and pace of the drama. Together, the puppeteers, narrator, and shamisen player bring the story to life.

Netherlandish Proverbs is a 1559 painting by the sixteenth-century Flemish artist Pieter Bruegel the Elder. In its crowded village scene, more than a hundred figures act out Dutch and Flemish sayings, turning familiar expressions into funny, strange, and sometimes foolish actions. One person bangs his head against a wall, while a woman places a blue cloak on her husband, an image linked to deception in marriage. The painting was once called The Blue Cloak, but its commonly used English title is Netherlandish Proverbs. Bruegel was known for detailed scenes of everyday life and also painted The Hunters in the Snow and The Peasant Wedding. His sons became painters too, continuing the Bruegel artistic dynasty.

Belly dance is a dance tradition associated especially with Egypt and the Middle East. Performers use controlled movements of the hips and torso, including quick, repeated motions called shimmies or shivers. They often match these movements to percussion, and some play small finger cymbals called zils to add their own rhythmic accents. One common Egyptian rhythm used in belly dance is maqsoum, a four-beat pattern whose Arabic-derived name means “divided.” Drummers create its pattern with deep, low “dum” strokes and sharper “tek” accents. These sounds give dancers a steady foundation for timing their hip movements, while leaving room to vary how they move with the music.

The Athenaeum Portrait is an unfinished painting of George Washington, the first U.S. president, made by American artist Gilbert Stuart in 1796. It shows only Washington’s head and neck against a plain background; Stuart never completed the rest of the portrait. Even so, it became one of the most widely reproduced images of Washington. You may recognize his face from the U.S. one-dollar bill, which uses an image based on this portrait. Stuart painted Washington several times, including in the Lansdowne portrait, which shows him standing in a formal setting. The Athenaeum Portrait is named after the Boston Athenaeum, an institution that once owned it.

Fifth position is the last of the five basic foot placements in classical ballet. The dancer places one foot directly in front of the other, with the feet turned outward and the heel of each foot near the toes of the other. This creates a tight, crossed position in which the heels are aligned. Dancers often practise fifth position at the barre, the handrail that provides support during warm-ups and exercises. One movement that begins in fifth position is a sous-sus: the dancer bends the knees in a demi-plié, then springs up into a relevé, rising onto the balls of the feet or, for an advanced dancer wearing pointe shoes, onto the tips of the toes.

Automat is a 1927 painting by American artist Edward Hopper. It shows a woman in a yellow hat sitting alone at a small table, holding a mug. Behind her, the dark window reflects two rows of ceiling lights, but reveals little of the world outside. An automat was a self-service restaurant where customers could buy food from coin-operated compartments. Hopper’s quiet scene suggests that a person can feel isolated even in a public place. He explored a similar mood in Nighthawks, painted in 1942. That painting shows four people in a brightly lit city diner at night, viewed through a broad window with no visible entrance. Both works use light, windows, and spaces between people to create a sense of distance and mystery.

A musical scale is a set of notes arranged in pitch order, from low to high or high to low. Musicians often practice scales in both directions to develop coordination and become familiar with the notes used in a piece of music. Major and minor scales have different patterns of steps between notes, giving them different sounds. A chromatic scale moves in the smallest steps commonly used in Western music, called semitones or half steps. It includes all twelve pitch classes within an octave before returning to a higher or lower version of the starting note. On a piano, playing a chromatic scale means using both white and black keys as you move up or down.

Robert Schumann was a German Romantic composer and music critic whose work often explored moods, imagination, and personal feelings. In his piano piece Carnaval, he portrayed different characters, including Florestan and Eusebius, fictional alter egos he also used in his music criticism. His orchestral works include the symphonies nicknamed “Spring” and “Rhenish.” Schumann married Clara Wieck in 1840; she was a pianist and composer who performed and promoted his music. The couple also supported a younger German composer, Johannes Brahms. In an 1853 essay, Robert Schumann praised Brahms and predicted that he would open new paths in music. Brahms later became famous for works including A German Requiem, the Hungarian Dances, and a well-known lullaby.

Time Out is a 1959 album by the Dave Brubeck Quartet that made unusual time signatures sound exciting and accessible. Most popular music is grouped into beats of two, three, or four, but this album experiments with less familiar patterns. Its opening track, “Blue Rondo à la Turk,” begins in 9/8, grouping nine quick beats in a distinctive rhythm. The album’s most famous piece, “Take Five,” stays in 5/4, with five beats in each measure. Alto saxophonist Paul Desmond composed “Take Five” and played the alto saxophone parts on the album, while Brubeck played piano. “Take Five” became one of jazz’s best-known recordings, helping Time Out show that challenging rhythms could also be catchy and enjoyable.

In the Hall of the Mountain King is a dramatic orchestral movement by Edvard Grieg, a leading Norwegian composer of the Romantic era who also wrote the Holberg Suite. Grieg composed it as incidental music for Henrik Ibsen’s play Peer Gynt, and it later appeared in a Peer Gynt Suite. The piece begins with a quiet, repeating tune played in a low register. As the tune returns, the music grows steadily faster and louder, creating a sense of mounting danger. This change suggests Peer’s frantic escape as he is pursued by trolls in the mountain king’s hall. Trolls are creatures from Scandinavian folklore, sometimes described as humanoid beings with tails that can turn to stone in sunlight.

Stained glass is a decorative art that uses pieces of colored glass to make images or patterns, especially in windows. Artists often fit the pieces into strips of lead called cames, which hold the design together. Stained-glass windows can fill buildings with colored light; famous examples include the rose windows of Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris. The artist Edward Burne-Jones helped revive the art in the 19th century, while Louis Comfort Tiffany used colored glass to create elaborate lampshades as well as windows. In the 20th century, Marc Chagall created a predominantly blue stained-glass work called America Windows. It commemorates the United States’ bicentennial and is displayed at the Art Institute of Chicago.

Peter is the brave young boy at the center of Peter and the Wolf, a 1936 symphonic fairy tale by Russian composer Sergei Prokofiev. Prokofiev wrote it to introduce children to the sounds of orchestral instruments: each character has a distinctive musical theme played by a particular instrument or group. Peter’s theme is played by the strings. Although his grandfather warns him to stay inside because a wolf is nearby, Peter ventures into the meadow. There, the wolf threatens Peter’s animal friends, including a bird, a duck, and a cat. Peter asks the bird to distract the wolf while he lowers a rope from a tree and loops it around the wolf’s tail. When hunters arrive, they help capture the wolf.

Horses have carried people in travel, farming, warfare, and sport, so artists have often shown them with riders in equestrian sculptures. These statues can honor leaders or soldiers while suggesting movement and power. In Saint Petersburg, Russia, Étienne Falconet designed a monument showing Peter the Great, the city’s founder, riding a horse. The statue stands on the Thunder Stone, an enormous boulder moved to the site for the project, and is known as the Bronze Horseman. Another famous equestrian sculpture is Donatello’s Gattamelata, which honors the Italian military leader Erasmo da Narni. Its horse has one front hoof resting on a cannonball, a detail that helps support the bronze statue.

A staircase is an architectural structure made of a succession of steps that lets people travel between floors or other levels. Staircases can be practical features of buildings, but artists can also use them to explore movement and perspective. In the 1960 lithograph Ascending and Descending, Dutch artist M. C. Escher pictured robed figures walking on a staircase atop a rooftop structure. The stairs appear to form a continuous loop: the figures seem to climb or descend forever without reaching a different level. This impossible, self-returning staircase is an example of the visual paradoxes for which Escher is famous. Staircases also appear in other art, including Marcel Duchamp’s painting Nude Descending a Staircase.

Francis Poulenc was a French composer whose music ranged from witty, lively pieces to deeply serious works. He belonged to Les Six, a group of six early 20th-century French composers who sought fresh approaches to music. Poulenc wrote the opera Dialogue of the Carmelites, which tells the story of nuns facing danger during the French Revolution. He also composed Concert champêtre for the Polish musician Wanda Landowska, a leading performer on the harpsichord. A harpsichord is a keyboard instrument that came before the modern piano. Pressing a key plucks a string inside it, whereas a piano key causes a hammer to strike a string. Poulenc made this older instrument the soloist in Concert champêtre, combining its distinctive sound with a modern orchestra.

Georg Philipp Telemann was a prolific German composer of the Baroque period, which lasted from about 1600 to 1750. He wrote music for churches, orchestras, and individual instruments. One of his best-known publications, Tafelmusik, was a collection of pieces intended for entertainment at meals and gatherings. Subscribers helped pay for its publication, and fellow composer George Frideric Handel was among them. Telemann also wrote 12 Fantasias for Viola da Gamba Solo, pieces for a bowed string instrument that were thought lost until their rediscovery in 2015. In addition, he composed 12 solo fantasias for flute. The flute is a woodwind instrument played by blowing across an opening; its smaller, higher-pitched relative is the piccolo. Frederick the Great of Prussia was a keen flute player.

The Carnival of the Animals is a humorous suite by French composer Camille Saint-Saëns. Its short movements form a musical portrait gallery: a proud lion marches, tortoises move to a deliberately slow dance, and “Fossils” rattles with sounds that suggest old bones. One of its best-known movements, “The Swan,” portrays a graceful bird through a smooth, lyrical melody played by a solo cello over rippling piano notes. The cello is a bowed string instrument with a rich, low sound; its pitch lies below the viola and above the double bass. “The Swan” is often performed on its own, but it is not actually the suite’s finale: a lively movement called “Finale” comes after it.

The Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C., honors U.S. service members who died or remain missing from the Vietnam War, a conflict in Southeast Asia that lasted from 1955 to 1975. Its best-known feature is an installation of two polished black granite walls that meet in a V shape. The walls are inscribed with the service members’ names, and their reflective surfaces let visitors see themselves alongside the names as they remember those who served. The design was selected in a national competition that drew more than 1,400 entries. Its creator, Maya Lin, was a 21-year-old architecture student at Yale University when she won. The memorial stands on the National Mall near the Three Soldiers statue.

Mambo is a Cuban music-and-dance genre that grew out of danzón, a slower style of dance music. Musicians made its rhythms faster and added influences from American swing, creating energetic music that suited lively partner dancing. Mambo became an international craze in the 1940s and 1950s, especially in American ballrooms, before the cha-cha became more popular there. One of mambo’s best-known figures was Cuban bandleader and pianist Pérez Prado, whose recordings helped bring the style to a wide audience. His 1955 hit version of “Cherry Pink and Apple Blossom White” is a famous example, and he also recorded “Mambo No. 5.”

A fugue is a form of contrapuntal music, meaning that two or more independent melodic lines, called voices, sound together. It usually begins with one voice stating the main theme, or subject. Other voices then enter one after another, repeating the subject at different pitches. As the piece continues, the voices weave together and the theme may be imitated, varied, or transformed. Fugues were especially important in Baroque music, and J. S. Bach was one of their great composers. His collection The Musical Offering includes two fugue-like pieces called ricercars: one for three voices and one for six. Both develop a “royal theme” given to Bach by Frederick II of Prussia. The collection also includes canons and a trio sonata featuring a transverse flute.

En pointe is a classical ballet technique in which a dancer balances and moves with their body weight supported on the tips of their toes. It requires specially constructed pointe shoes, not ordinary ballet slippers. At the front of each shoe, a stiffened compartment called the toe box surrounds and supports the toes, helping distribute the dancer’s weight. Dancers also need strength, balance, and careful training to work en pointe safely. The technique can make their movements appear light and effortless, even though it is physically demanding. In the nineteenth century, ballets such as La Sylphide used en pointe dancing to give characters an airy, otherworldly appearance.

A lullaby is a gentle song or musical piece traditionally sung to a baby or young child to comfort them and help them fall asleep. Lullabies often have slow tempos, soft sounds, and simple, repetitive melodies that are easy for a child to recognize. Families around the world have their own lullabies, passed down through generations, but composers have written them too. One famous example is Wiegenlied, Op. 49, No. 4, by the 19th-century German composer Johannes Brahms. The German title means “cradle song.” Brahms dedicated the piece to Bertha Faber in connection with the birth of her son. He also composed A German Requiem and the Hungarian Dances.

Trajan’s Column is a marble monument completed in 113 CE in Rome to celebrate Emperor Trajan’s victories in the Dacian Wars. About 30 meters tall, it is wrapped in a continuous spiral relief that winds up its shaft like a picture story. The carvings show Roman soldiers marching, building forts, and fighting in Trajan’s two campaigns against Dacia, a kingdom north of the Danube River. Rome defeated and annexed Dacia in 106 CE. Like other columns, the monument has a tall shaft, but it was built to honor a victory rather than to support a building. Its detailed carvings provide a valuable record of how Romans wanted these wars and their emperor to be remembered.

A mural is a large painting made directly on a wall, ceiling, or other permanent architectural surface, often as part of a public building. When an artist paints onto wet plaster so the colors become part of the surface as it dries, the technique is called fresco. Raphael’s The School of Athens is a famous fresco showing ancient thinkers, including Plato and Aristotle, walking together. Centuries later, Mexican artist Diego Rivera created the Detroit Industry mural cycle for the Garden Court of the Detroit Institute of Arts. Its scenes of factory work and manufacturing celebrate the people and machines involved in industry. Murals can tell stories, express ideas, or show what a community values, and their large size lets many people experience the artwork in the space around them.

Duke Ellington, born Edward Kennedy Ellington, was an American jazz pianist, composer, and bandleader whose orchestra helped define big-band jazz. He led the group for decades, shaping its sound around the distinctive styles of its musicians. The orchestra performed regularly at New York’s Cotton Club and became known for pieces such as “Mood Indigo.” Ellington also wrote ambitious longer works, including Black, Brown, and Beige, a suite inspired by African American history. In 1939, composer and arranger Billy Strayhorn joined Ellington’s orchestra and became his longtime creative partner. Strayhorn wrote the melody for “Take the A Train,” a song about taking the subway to Harlem that became the orchestra’s signature tune. Together, Ellington and Strayhorn expanded what a jazz orchestra could play.

Jean-Antoine Houdon’s marble statue of George Washington stands in the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond. To make an accurate portrait, the French sculptor traveled to America in 1785 and modeled Washington from life. The statue shows Washington standing with one hand on a cane and the other resting on a bundle of fasces, rods that symbolize unity and civic authority. His calm pose presents him as both a military commander and a leader of a republic. Washington appears in many other artworks: John Trumbull painted him with his horse Blueskin, and Emanuel Leutze showed him standing in a boat crossing the icy Delaware River. Washington was the first U.S. president, and his portrait also appears on the one-dollar bill.

The Sound of Music is a stage musical by Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein II. Set in Austria, it follows Maria, a novice nun who becomes governess to the seven children of Captain von Trapp, a widowed naval officer. Maria brings music into the household, and she and the captain fall in love. As Nazi rule reaches Austria, the family escapes across the Alps. The musical includes the song “My Favorite Things,” in which Maria lists things that comfort her when she feels afraid or sad. Jazz saxophonist John Coltrane recorded an extended modal jazz interpretation of the song on his 1961 album My Favorite Things. Coltrane is also known for albums such as Giant Steps and A Love Supreme.

Buckingham Fountain is a monumental water feature in Chicago’s Grant Park, near the Lake Michigan shoreline. Opened in 1927, it was donated by Kate Sturges Buckingham in memory of her brother Clarence Buckingham. Its wide, tiered design was inspired by the Latona Basin in the gardens of the Palace of Versailles in France. That basin illustrates a story from Greek mythology: after peasants refuse water to the goddess Latona and her children, the peasants are transformed into frogs. Buckingham Fountain is much larger than its model and includes sculpted seahorses, powerful water jets, and evening light displays. It has become one of Chicago’s best-known landmarks and a centerpiece of the city’s lakefront parkland.

The Reformation Symphony is an orchestral work by Felix Mendelssohn, an early Romantic German composer who also wrote the Italian and Scottish symphonies. He composed it in 1830 to mark 300 years since the presentation of the Augsburg Confession, an important statement of Protestant beliefs during the Reformation. Its fourth and final movement incorporates Martin Luther’s hymn “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God,” linking the music to that history. Although Mendelssohn wrote the symphony early in his career, it was not published until 1868, more than 20 years after his death. By then, his other symphonies had already been numbered, so this earlier work became known as Symphony No. 5. Its more descriptive name, the Reformation Symphony, was chosen by his sister Fanny.

Scheherazade, Op. 35, is an 1888 symphonic suite by Russian composer Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, inspired by stories from One Thousand and One Nights. In those tales, Scheherazade tells stories to a sultan night after night to save her life. The suite has four movements, including “The Sea and Sinbad’s Ship” and a final movement featuring a festival at Baghdad. A recurring solo violin melody represents Scheherazade as the storyteller. The violin is accompanied by a harp, a plucked-string instrument whose pedals change the pitches its strings can play. Rimsky-Korsakov was celebrated for his orchestration—the way he chose and combined instruments to create vivid sounds. Those colorful sounds help suggest the suite’s characters, scenes, and adventures.

Linear perspective is a drawing system that helps artists make a flat surface look three-dimensional. In a scene such as a street, parallel edges of buildings or paving stones appear to move closer together as they recede, meeting at a point called the vanishing point. Artists also make distant objects look smaller, creating an illusion of depth. During the Renaissance, the Florentine artist and architect Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective using a mirror to compare a painted view with the real scene. Earlier, he had lost a competition to Lorenzo Ghiberti to design doors for the Florence Baptistery. Brunelleschi later designed the great octagonal brick dome of Florence Cathedral. His work helped make the convincing depiction of space a central part of Renaissance art.

Vampire is a late-19th-century painting by the Norwegian artist Edvard Munch. It shows a red-haired woman bending over a seated man and pressing her face to his neck while he hides his face in his arms. Her hair spreads across him, making the embrace look mysterious or threatening to some viewers. That appearance led people to call the painting Vampire, although Munch said he had painted a woman kissing a man on the neck, not a supernatural attack. The work is also known as Love and Pain, a title that suggests a more human interpretation of the scene. Munch explored powerful emotions in many paintings, including several versions of The Scream, with its distressed figure beneath a swirling sky.

The Palace of Versailles is a grand royal residence near Paris, France. Louis XIV transformed it from a hunting lodge into a vast palace that displayed the wealth and power of the French monarchy. Its formal gardens are famous for their carefully planned paths, fountains, and sculptures, while the Hall of Mirrors is a long gallery lined with mirrors and windows. Versailles is closely linked to the arts of Louis XIV’s reign, but later artists portrayed a changing world. Jean-Antoine Watteau painted a scene in which a portrait of Louis XIV is being packed away. Watteau worked in the Rococo style, which is sometimes considered a later phase of Baroque art and is known for its graceful, playful scenes.

Lyric Pieces is a collection of 66 short piano works arranged in ten books by the Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg. Written over several decades, the pieces often capture a mood, scene, or moment in a compact musical form. The first piece, “Arietta,” and the last, “Remembrances,” share a melody, linking the beginning and end of the collection. Another well-known piece, “Wedding Day at Troldhaugen,” celebrates an occasion at Grieg’s home near Bergen, Norway. Grieg also wrote music for Henrik Ibsen’s play Peer Gynt. Two of its best-known pieces are “Morning Mood,” which suggests a peaceful sunrise, and “In the Hall of the Mountain King,” which builds in speed and intensity as Peer Gynt is pursued by trolls.

The Marriage of Figaro is a comic opera by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, first performed in Vienna in 1786. Its Italian libretto—the words sung by the characters—was written by the poet Lorenzo Da Ponte. The opera follows Figaro, a former barber from Seville who now serves Count Almaviva, and Susanna, his fiancée. As they prepare to marry, the Count tries to interfere, but the couple use clever plans to outmaneuver him. Figaro and the Count are characters introduced in Beaumarchais’s play The Barber of Seville. Mozart and Da Ponte also worked together on Don Giovanni and Così fan tutte, making The Marriage of Figaro one of their three famous operatic collaborations.

João Gilberto was a Brazilian singer and guitarist whose quiet, precise playing helped establish bossa nova in the late 1950s. Developed in Rio de Janeiro from samba, bossa nova has a gentle, swaying rhythm. Gilberto’s softly syncopated guitar style placed accents in unexpected spots, while his restrained singing gave the music an intimate sound. In 1964, he teamed up with American tenor saxophonist Stan Getz on the landmark album Getz/Gilberto. It included “The Girl from Ipanema,” a song written by Brazilian composer Antônio Carlos Jobim with lyricist Vinicius de Moraes. Gilberto’s wife at the time, Astrud Gilberto, sang its English-language verse. The recording became an international hit and helped introduce bossa nova to listeners around the world.

The Cardsharps is an early genre painting by the Italian artist Caravaggio. A genre painting shows a scene from everyday life, and this one captures a card game in which a young, unsuspecting player is being cheated. An older accomplice peers over the player’s shoulder at his cards and signals to the other cheat through a hole in his glove. That cheat, wearing a feathered hat, secretly pulls a six of clubs from his belt to use in the game. Caravaggio made the deception feel immediate through lifelike figures and expressive gestures. He is also famous for his dramatic use of light and shadow, called chiaroscuro. In another of his paintings, The Calling of St. Matthew, a shaft of light falls across the title tax collector.

Bass is the lowest standard voice part in a traditional chorus, below tenor, alto, and soprano. Bass singers provide deep notes that often support the harmony, though they can also introduce a melody. One example is the Kyrie movement of the Requiem in D minor, a “mass for the dead” by the Austrian composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. Its double fugue begins with the bass part; in a fugue, a musical idea is introduced by one voice and then taken up by others. Mozart, a former child prodigy who also wrote Eine kleine Nachtmusik, died before finishing the Requiem. Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it after Mozart’s death.

Annie is a 1977 Broadway musical about a spirited orphan living in New York City during the Great Depression. Its book was written by Thomas Meehan, with music by Charles Strouse and lyrics by Martin Charnin. The opening number introduces Annie and the other children at the orphanage run by the harsh Miss Hannigan. Annie’s life changes when billionaire Oliver Warbucks invites her to stay at his home. Although times are difficult, she remains hopeful, singing that “the sun will come out tomorrow” in the musical’s best-known song, “Tomorrow.” The show also depicts people living in a shantytown who sarcastically thank former president Herbert Hoover for their hardships. Later, Annie visits the White House and meets President Franklin D. Roosevelt, who took office in 1933 and introduced the New Deal.

The Smithsonian Institution is a major U.S. museum and research complex created by Congress in 1846. It was funded by a gift from James Smithson, a British scientist who had never visited the United States. Today, the Smithsonian operates dozens of museums and research centers. In Washington, D.C., these include the National Air and Space Museum, devoted to flight and space exploration, and the National Museum of African Art, which studies and displays art from Africa. The African art museum’s home on the National Mall opened in 1987 and is especially known for works from societies south of the Sahara. Its collection includes royal objects from Benin, such as carved ivory works. In 2022, the Smithsonian announced plans to return its Benin Bronzes to the Benin people.

A minaret is a tall tower associated with a mosque. Traditionally, a muezzin used its elevated position to give the call to prayer so people nearby could hear it. One famous example is the Qutb Minar in Delhi, India. This five-storey minaret stands in the Qutb complex, a historic site that includes an early mosque. Qutb al-Din Aibak, the first ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, began building it around 1199, and his successor Iltutmish later extended it. Minarets are also part of the history of Hagia Sophia in Istanbul. Originally built as a Christian church, Hagia Sophia became a mosque after the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople, and minarets were added to it.

Yayoi Kusama is a Japanese contemporary artist whose work includes paintings, sculptures, installations, and performances. She is especially known for covering artworks and spaces with repeated polka dots. Her Infinity Mirror Rooms use mirrors, lights, and repeating shapes to make a small space seem to stretch on endlessly. Kusama has also used her own body and clothing in her art. In the 1960s, she painted polka dots on nude participants in New York City performances. In a 1966 work called Walking Piece, she walked through New York City wearing a brightly colored kimono, and the action was recorded in photographs. Across these different forms, repetition helps turn ordinary sights and spaces into striking experiences.

Ravi Shankar was an Indian musician and composer famous for his mastery of the sitar, a plucked string instrument used in Indian classical music. This music often develops a melody within a raga and follows a rhythmic pattern called a tala. Shankar helped introduce these traditions to audiences around the world through performances, recordings, and collaborations. He taught George Harrison, the Beatles’ guitarist, about the sitar, and the two became friends and musical collaborators. Harrison’s interest helped draw many rock fans toward Indian music; the Beatles’ song Norwegian Wood features a sitar. In 1971, Harrison helped organize the Concert for Bangladesh, a major benefit concert in which Shankar performed. Shankar’s career made him one of the best-known ambassadors for the music of India.

Cave paintings are prehistoric images made directly on the walls and ceilings of natural caves, often using mineral pigments or charcoal. Many show animals, people, handprints, or symbols, giving us clues about how ancient people saw and represented their world. One famous site is Lascaux Cave in southwestern France, near the town of Montignac. Discovered in 1940, this Paleolithic cave complex includes a chamber known for its large painted bulls and other animals. Important cave art has also been found in Maros Regency on the Indonesian island of South Sulawesi. Because these paintings were made long before written records, they are valuable evidence of early human creativity, although the exact meanings of many images remain uncertain.

Tristan und Isolde is a 19th-century opera by the German composer Richard Wagner. It tells the story of Tristan and Isolde, whose forbidden love ends in tragedy. The opera’s prelude begins with an unusual chord made from the notes F, B, D-sharp, and G-sharp. Often called the “Tristan chord,” its harmony does not resolve in the expected way, creating a feeling of longing that runs through the music. In the final scene, Isolde sings the “Liebestod,” or “love-death,” over Tristan’s body. Wagner also composed the Ring cycle, a series of four operas based on Germanic myths. One of them, The Valkyrie, contains the famous orchestral passage “Ride of the Valkyries.”

Steam trains became a subject for nineteenth-century painters as railways changed how people travelled and how landscapes and cities looked. In 1844, the British artist J. M. W. Turner painted Rain, Steam and Speed – The Great Western Railway. It shows a locomotive rushing across the Maidenhead Railway Bridge over the River Thames, with a small hare running ahead of the engine. Turner blurred the rain, smoke and scenery to suggest the train’s speed. Later in the century, the French Impressionist Claude Monet painted several views of trains arriving at Paris’s Gare Saint-Lazare station. He focused on clouds of steam and changing light around the platforms. Together, these works show how artists used trains to explore movement, modern technology and the atmosphere of a rapidly changing world.

Gregorian chant is a collection of religious songs used in worship by the Western Christian Church. It is traditionally named after Pope Gregory I, although it developed over many years rather than being written by one person. Most chants were sung in Latin, without instruments, and in a single melodic line: this is called monophonic music. In the Middle Ages, chant melodies became a foundation for polyphonic music, in which two or more different melodic lines sound together. Chant is also associated with church modes, patterns of notes that give melodies different sounds. One of these is the Dorian mode, which has a minor third and a natural sixth; played on a piano’s white keys, its standard form runs from D to the next D. Modes such as Dorian and Mixolydian later influenced jazz musicians.

Auld Lang Syne is a traditional Scottish song widely sung at midnight on New Year’s Eve as people say goodbye to the old year and welcome the new one. Its opening question, “Should auld acquaintance be forgot,” asks whether we should forget people we have known. The song answers by celebrating friendship and shared memories; its title roughly means “old times” or “days gone by.” The words come from a poem associated with Robert Burns, a Scottish poet who collected and adapted traditional songs as well as writing his own poetry. Burns is also known for “To a Mouse” and “Tam o’ Shanter.” Although the verses use Scots words that may be unfamiliar, the song’s message of remembering friends helps explain why it has become a New Year’s tradition.

City gates are fortified entrances through a city’s defensive walls. They let people, carts, and goods pass in and out, while allowing guards to control access by closing the gates when needed. In ancient Rome, gates were also connected to religious ideas about entrances and transitions. Janus, a Roman god often shown with two faces looking in opposite directions, was believed to watch over gates, doorways, beginnings, and endings. The doors of a shrine named for Janus had a special meaning: they were traditionally shut when Rome was at peace and opened during war. This made a doorway a symbol of whether the city was at peace or involved in conflict.

String instruments make sound when stretched strings vibrate. A player can set the strings moving by bowing, plucking, or striking them, and changes in string length or tension help produce different pitches. This broad family includes Western orchestral instruments such as the violin and cello, as well as traditional Chinese instruments such as the erhu and pipa. The pipa is plucked, while the erhu is a two-string fiddle played with a bow. The erhu has a small resonator traditionally covered with snakeskin, which helps amplify its sound. In the solo piece Sai Ma, an erhu player uses sliding pitches and rapid bowing to imitate a horse’s neighing and galloping.

Mycenaean pottery is the ceramic art of the Mycenaeans, a Late Bronze Age civilization in Greece associated with palace centers such as Mycenae, Tiryns, and Pylos. Potters made vessels for storing, serving, and mixing food and drink, including jars, urns, and large bowls called kraters. Many were painted with floral patterns, sea creatures, or figures from stories and daily life. One famous example is the Warrior Vase, a krater decorated with a row of helmeted warriors marching with spears and shields while a woman gestures toward them. Its painted scene offers a glimpse of how the Mycenaeans represented soldiers. Mycenaean civilization declined during the Bronze Age Collapse, but its pottery remains an important source of evidence about its art and culture.

In 3/4 time, each measure has three beats, with the first beat usually receiving the strongest accent. Musicians often count it “ONE, two, three,” creating a repeating pattern that suits turning dance steps. This pattern is also called triple meter and appears in minuets, many scherzos, and especially waltzes. A minuet is an older, graceful dance, while a scherzo is usually a lively piece of music. The waltz is a partnered ballroom dance whose name comes from a German word meaning “to turn.” Dancers rotate together as they move across the floor. Waltzes became a defining feature of 19th-century Viennese balls, and their music is conventionally written in 3/4 time.

Antonín Dvořák’s String Quartet No. 12 in F major, Op. 96, nicknamed the “American” Quartet, is a four-movement chamber work for two violins, viola, and cello. He composed it in the summer of 1893 while staying in Spillville, Iowa, a Czech-speaking town founded by immigrants from his homeland. Dvořák was then working in the United States, and the quartet reflects his interest in the music he encountered there. Its melodies often use the pentatonic scale, a five-note pattern that gives them a direct, memorable sound, while its rhythms can feel folk-like and energetic. The opening features a rising viola melody over softly trembling violins. These qualities helped make the “American” Quartet one of Dvořák’s best-known chamber pieces.

The Washington Monument is a tall, Egyptian-style stone obelisk on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. It honors George Washington, the first president of the United States. In 1836, a design by American architect Robert Mills was selected for the memorial. His original plan included not only the obelisk but also a circular colonnade and a statue of Washington. Only the obelisk was built. Construction began in 1848 but stopped for decades because of funding problems and the Civil War. When work resumed, builders used marble from a different source, creating a visible change in color partway up the shaft. Today, the monument is one of Washington, D.C.’s most recognizable landmarks.

Minoan pottery is the tradition of ceramic vessels and decorative objects made by the Minoan civilization, which flourished on the island of Crete during the Bronze Age. Minoan potters shaped clay into cups, jars, and other containers, then decorated many of them with painted patterns or images inspired by nature. Their work shows both practical skill and artistic imagination. One especially celebrated style is Kamares ware, named after a cave on Mount Ida where examples were found. Kamares vessels are often finely made and feature vivid, multicolored designs painted against a dark background. These flowing designs help distinguish Minoan pottery from other ancient ceramic traditions.

Charles Mingus was an American jazz bassist, composer, and bandleader whose music mixed the energy of blues and gospel with adventurous jazz. He played the double bass, a low-pitched string instrument that often provides a steady “walking” line in a jazz rhythm section. Mingus wrote “Pithecanthropus Erectus,” a piece imagining humanity’s development from its early ancestors, and led a group that recorded “Fables of Faubus,” a protest against racial segregation. His 1959 Columbia album Mingus Ah Um opens with “Better Git It in Your Soul” and includes “Goodbye Pork Pie Hat,” a moving tribute to saxophonist Lester Young. Mingus is remembered for music that was both emotionally powerful and willing to challenge social injustice.

A raga is a melodic framework in Indian classical music. It gives musicians a set of characteristic pitches, recurring motifs, and ways to move between notes, creating a particular musical mood. A raga is more than a scale: performers use its patterns as a guide while developing and improvising a melody. Rhythm has its own organizing framework, called a tala. A tala is a repeating cycle of beats, often divided into smaller groups, that helps musicians keep time as the music unfolds. In a performance, the melody may explore a raga while the rhythm follows a tala. These ideas are central to Indian classical music, including music played on the sitar by musicians such as Ravi Shankar.

Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 8 is an unusually large work in E-flat major that combines a full orchestra with vocal soloists and several choruses. Its enormous performing forces led to the nickname “Symphony of a Thousand,” although it does not always require exactly a thousand musicians. Unlike most symphonies, which are mainly instrumental, this one uses singing throughout. Part I sets Veni Creator Spiritus, a Latin hymn traditionally sung at Pentecost that calls on the Holy Spirit. Part II sets the closing scene of Faust, a play by the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. By placing these very different texts together, Mahler explores ideas of inspiration, love, and spiritual redemption on a grand musical scale.

Eugène Viollet-le-Duc was a 19th-century French architect and architectural theorist famous for restoring medieval buildings. He worked in the Gothic Revival style, which drew inspiration from medieval Gothic architecture. One of his best-known projects was the restoration of Notre-Dame de Paris, a Catholic cathedral on the Île de la Cité, an island in the River Seine. Its name means “Our Lady of Paris.” During the restoration, Viollet-le-Duc designed a new spire, which collapsed in the cathedral’s 2019 fire. Notre-Dame is also known for its flying buttresses and large rose windows. Until 1793, statues representing 28 kings of Judah stood along its west façade. These details help identify both the architect and the cathedral.

Mount Rushmore National Memorial is a giant granite sculpture carved into a mountainside in the Black Hills of South Dakota. It shows the faces of four U.S. presidents: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln. The carving was created between 1927 and 1941 and has become one of the best-known landmarks in the United States. Also in the Black Hills is the unfinished Crazy Horse Memorial, which has been under construction since 1948. It honors Crazy Horse, a Lakota leader who fought at the Battle of the Little Bighorn. The two memorials honor different figures from American history, and Mount Rushmore’s location in the Black Hills is important to many Indigenous people.

Dance of the Knights is a dramatic orchestral movement from the ballet Romeo and Juliet by Russian composer Sergei Prokofiev, who also wrote the children’s orchestral tale Peter and the Wolf. Based on Shakespeare’s tragedy, the ballet tells the story of two young people whose families are enemies. This movement accompanies the entrance and formal dance of the male guests at the Capulets’ ball, where Romeo and Juliet first meet. It begins with an ominous, pulsing beat in the low brass, followed by a broad melody in the strings. The heavy rhythm and powerful sound make the dance feel grand and threatening, hinting at the conflict that will shape the lovers’ story. The movement is also known as Montagues and Capulets.

Man Ray was the professional name of Emmanuel Radnitzky, an American modernist artist who worked as a photographer, painter, and filmmaker. He was associated with Dadaism, which challenged traditional ideas about art, and Surrealism, which explored dreams and unexpected combinations of images. After moving to Paris, Man Ray became known for inventive photographs of artists and performers. He photographed fellow Dada artist Marcel Duchamp dressed as his alter ego, Rose Sélavy. In Man Ray’s 1926 photograph Noire et Blanche, Kiki de Montparnasse rests her head on a table beside an African mask. The two heads are positioned as contrasting forms, making the viewer notice their shapes and the differences between them. These photographs show how Man Ray used the camera not just to record people, but to create striking works of art.

The Lansdowne Portrait is a full-length painting of George Washington made in 1796 by Gilbert Stuart, an artist who painted several portraits of the first U.S. president. Washington stands beside a table with an ornate gold-colored leg, extending one hand in a formal gesture while holding a sword in the other. The sword suggests his military leadership, while the classical architectural details help present him as a dignified leader of the new republic. The painting is named for the Marquess of Lansdowne, a British nobleman. Stuart also painted the unfinished Athenaeum Portrait of Washington, whose image later became familiar from the one-dollar bill.

An arpeggio is a chord whose notes are played one at a time instead of all at once. Because the chord is spread out, it is sometimes called a “broken chord.” For example, a pianist might play the notes C, E, and G in succession rather than pressing all three keys together. An ascending arpeggio starts on the chord’s lowest pitch and moves upward to its highest; a descending arpeggio starts at the highest pitch and moves downward. Musicians practice arpeggios to build coordination and to recognize the sound of chords in melodies and accompaniments. Unlike a scale, which follows a sequence of pitches such as a major or minor scale, an arpeggio uses the notes of a particular chord.

Roy Lichtenstein was an American artist and a leading figure in Pop Art, a movement that brought images from popular culture, such as comics and advertisements, into fine art. He enlarged comic-book panels into paintings with bold black outlines, flat colors, and Ben-Day dots—small printed dots that create shading and color effects. His 1963 diptych Whaam! shows an action-packed aerial battle. Another 1963 painting, Drowning Girl, was based on a panel from a DC romance comic. It shows a woman in the water beneath a large curling wave, with a thought balloon referring to a man named Brad. By turning familiar comic imagery into large paintings, Lichtenstein invited viewers to look at everyday mass-produced images in a new way.

The Guggenheim Museum Bilbao is a contemporary art museum in Bilbao, a city in Spain’s Basque Country. Designed by Canadian-born American architect Frank Gehry, it opened in 1997 beside the Nervión River and became a landmark of the city’s waterfront redevelopment. Its sweeping, curved exterior is covered in thin titanium panels that catch and reflect the light. The building’s forms are often compared to a ship, a nod to Bilbao’s history as a port city, while its shimmering surface can also suggest fish scales. The museum helped draw international attention to Bilbao and showed how a striking cultural building could help transform a city’s image. Gehry also designed the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles and the Dancing House in Prague.

The Band’s Visit is a musical about the Alexandria Police Orchestra, a group of Egyptian musicians traveling to Israel to perform. A ticketing misunderstanding sends them to Bet Hatikva, a fictional small Israeli town, instead of their intended destination. With no way to continue their journey until the next day, the musicians spend an unexpected night with local residents. As they share meals, music, and conversations, people who at first seem very different find moments of friendship and understanding. The musical is adapted from a 2007 Israeli film of the same name and won the 2018 Tony Award for Best Musical.

Richard Serra was an American sculptor known for enormous works made from steel. His sculptures often change how people move through and experience a space, rather than simply giving them something to look at. Critics have linked him to process art, which values the materials and methods used to make a work as well as the finished result. One of Serra’s steel works is Equal-Parallel. Another, Tilted Arc, was a long, curving steel wall designed specifically for Federal Plaza in New York City. Because it cut across the plaza, some people felt it got in their way or made the space less welcoming. After a public hearing and years of controversy, Tilted Arc was dismantled in 1989.

Berthe Morisot was a French painter and a leading member of the Impressionist movement. Impressionists often used loose, visible brushstrokes to capture light and everyday life rather than painting every detail precisely. Morisot exhibited with the Impressionists and painted scenes of family life, women and children, as well as outdoor views. She was the sister-in-law of fellow painter Édouard Manet, whose brother Eugène she married. In Harbor at Lorient, Morisot portrayed a woman with a parasol sitting on a stone wall by the water. Another of her best-known paintings, The Cradle, shows a woman watching over her sleeping daughter. Its quiet domestic subject is a good example of Morisot’s ability to give ordinary moments a sense of tenderness and importance.

Ancient Egyptian pyramids were monumental tombs built for pharaohs and other elites. Egyptians believed that preserving the dead and providing for them helped them reach the afterlife, so burial chambers were placed within or beneath these structures. Some of the most famous pyramids stand on the Giza plateau, near the Great Sphinx. An earlier example is Djoser’s Step Pyramid at Saqqara. Instead of having smooth sides, it rises in tiers that resemble mastabas, the flat-roofed tombs used before pyramids. Imhotep, an architect and high official, is traditionally credited with designing Djoser’s pyramid. Later builders experimented with different shapes, including the Bent Pyramid built for Pharaoh Sneferu, before creating the smooth-sided pyramids seen at Giza.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s Luncheon of the Boating Party shows a cheerful group of friends sharing a meal on a balcony overlooking the Seine River in France.
