Painted in the early 1880s, it captures the relaxed atmosphere of a boating-party lunch, with people talking, eating, and enjoying one another’s company beneath a pink-striped awning. Renoir used bright colors and lively brushwork to suggest the sunlight and movement of the scene, making it a well-known Impressionist painting. Near the front, two people in straw hats lean against a diagonal railing. The woman seated in the foreground plays with a small dog: she is Aline Charigot, a seamstress who later became Renoir’s wife.

Anton Webern was an Austrian composer whose brief, carefully structured pieces had a major influence on modern classical music. He was a member of the Second Viennese School, a group of composers centered in Vienna, Austria’s capital. The group also included Arnold Schoenberg, Webern’s teacher, who developed twelve-tone technique, a way of composing that uses all twelve notes of the chromatic scale in an organized pattern. Webern explored this approach in music known for its clarity and economy: even a short piece could make every note feel important. His works include the 1908 Passacaglia for Orchestra and the 1934 Concerto for Nine Instruments. He also wrote two late cantatas based on poems by Hildegard Jone. Webern died in 1945 after being accidentally shot by an American soldier.

The King and I is a musical by composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist Oscar Hammerstein II. It follows Anna Leonowens, a Welsh-born British schoolteacher hired to teach the children of King Mongkut of Siam, the country now known as Thailand. At the royal court, Anna introduces the children to new ideas while learning about their customs. She and the king often disagree, but they gradually come to respect each other. The musical includes “Getting to Know You,” which Anna sings as she becomes familiar with her pupils, and “Shall We Dance?,” a scene in which Anna and the king dance together. A performance based on Uncle Tom’s Cabin also appears in the show.

Ivory is a hard, dense material found mainly in elephant tusks. For centuries, artists have carved it into sculptures, ceremonial objects, jewelry, and other decorative works. In the Kingdom of Benin, in present-day Nigeria, skilled carvers made ivory objects for the royal court and ancestral shrines. One famous example is an ivory pendant mask depicting Queen Idia, remembered as Benin’s first Iyoba, or Queen Mother. Her son Esigie became an Oba, or king, in the 16th century. Ivory was prized because its smooth surface could be carved into fine details, but demand for it has also contributed to the killing of elephants. Many countries now restrict the ivory trade to help protect them.

Artemisia Gentileschi was an Italian Baroque painter celebrated for dramatic scenes from the Bible and history, especially stories featuring courageous women. She painted Judith killing the enemy general Holofernes and Jael killing Sisera, using strong contrasts of light and shadow to heighten the action. Gentileschi learned to paint in her father’s studio in Rome and later worked in Florence, Naples, and London. Florence was especially important to her career: she received support from the powerful Medici family and became the first woman admitted to the city’s Accademia delle Arti del Disegno, an artists’ academy. One of her best-known paintings, Judith Slaying Holofernes, is displayed in Florence’s Uffizi Gallery.

Comedian is a 2019 conceptual artwork by the Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan. First shown at Art Basel Miami Beach, it consists of a fresh banana attached to a gallery wall with a strip of duct tape. The work attracted attention because it used an ordinary, replaceable fruit instead of a traditional material such as marble or paint. Two editions sold for $120,000 each, prompting debate about what collectors were paying for: the banana itself or Cattelan’s idea and the right to display it. The banana can be replaced as it ripens, so the artwork’s identity does not depend on one particular piece of fruit. Its surprising simplicity and high price made Comedian a widely discussed example of contemporary conceptual art.

The lyre is a string instrument from ancient Greece, usually pictured with a curved body, two arms, and strings stretched up to a crossbar. Players plucked its strings to accompany songs and poetry. In Greek myth, the god Hermes made the first lyre from a hollow tortoise shell. After stealing a herd of Apollo’s cattle, Hermes gave Apollo the lyre in exchange for them. Apollo later played it in a musical contest against the satyr Marsyas. Another famous lyre player was Orpheus, whose music was said to charm animals and even the rulers of the Underworld. When his wife Eurydice died, Orpheus played so beautifully that Hades and Persephone allowed him to lead her back to the living world. He lost her again by looking back before they reached the surface.

Harold in Italy is an 1834 symphony by the French Romantic composer Hector Berlioz. It was inspired by Lord Byron’s poem Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, whose central figure is a traveler journeying through Europe. Berlioz gives the orchestra vivid scenes of Italian life, while a solo viola plays a recurring melody associated with Harold, as though he is observing the events around him. The work ends with a lively “orgy of bandits.” The viola is a four-string instrument pitched between the violin and the cello. Its strings are tuned C–G–D–A, from lowest to highest, and its music is commonly written in alto clef. Although the viola has a prominent part, Harold in Italy is a symphony rather than a conventional concerto.

The Ardabil Carpet is a celebrated Persian rug woven in 1539–40 for the shrine of Shaykh Safi al-Din in Ardabil, northwestern Iran. Its richly patterned surface features a large central medallion, floral designs, and two lamps that seem to hang from the medallion. An inscription names its maker, Maqsud Kashani. Carpets like this were valued both as practical floor coverings and as works of art requiring great skill to weave. Two related Ardabil carpets survive, though they are now in different collections. Since 1893, the larger one has belonged to the Victoria and Albert Museum in South Kensington, London, an institution founded to promote excellence in design and manufacturing.

Jackson Pollock was an American painter and a leading figure in abstract expressionism, a movement that grew in New York after World War II and emphasized emotion, movement, and gesture. Instead of working at an easel, Pollock often spread large canvases on the floor so he could move around them. He poured, dripped, and flicked paint onto the canvas, creating dense webs of lines and splashes. This energetic approach made him famous as “the Dripper” and is associated with action painting, a style within abstract expressionism. One of his best-known works is the monumental 1950 painting Autumn Rhythm, made with enamel paint on canvas. It is also cataloged as Number 30 and is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City.

Gamelan is a traditional Indonesian musical ensemble and the music it plays, especially associated with the islands of Java and Bali. Its sound comes mainly from percussion instruments, including tuned metallophones, which have metal bars struck with mallets, and gongs of different sizes. Musicians often play interlocking parts: one instrument fills the spaces between notes played by another, creating a flowing, intricate pattern. A key instrument is the kendang, a hand-played, double-headed drum. The kendang player helps guide the tempo and signals changes or transitions so the ensemble stays together. Gamelan can accompany dance and theater as well as be performed on its own. Although ensembles vary by region, the combination of layered metal tones, gongs, and guiding drums is a hallmark of this musical tradition.

La mer, meaning “The Sea,” is a set of three orchestral sketches by the French composer Claude Debussy. He completed it in 1905, using the orchestra to suggest the sea’s changing light, movement, and moods rather than telling a story. One section, “Jeux de vagues” (“Play of the Waves”), evokes rippling, shifting water. Debussy creates these effects with changing harmonies, passages based on the whole-tone scale, and a wide range of instrumental colors, including two harps. The music can feel calm one moment and powerful the next, like the sea itself. If a question mentions three orchestral sketches about the sea or “Jeux de vagues,” the work is La mer. Debussy also wrote Clair de lune and Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun.

Watson and the Shark is a dramatic late-18th-century painting by John Singleton Copley, an American artist born in Boston in 1738 who later became a leading portrait painter in London. It shows sailors in a small boat trying to pull a boy from Havana harbor while a shark lunges beneath him. The scene is based on a real attack on Brook Watson, who survived but lost part of a leg, leaving him with a lifelong injury. Copley uses the sailors’ urgent movements and the shark’s looming shape to make the rescue feel tense and immediate. He also painted The Death of Major Peirson.

Philip Glass is an American composer and a major figure in musical minimalism. His music often uses short, repeating patterns that change gradually, creating a sense of movement even when the basic idea stays familiar. He has written operas, film scores, and other works; two of his best-known operas are Einstein on the Beach and Satyagraha. Glass’s music has also influenced artists outside classical music, including the alternative rock band Muse. Another classical composer connected to Muse is Frédéric Chopin, a Polish composer famous for piano pieces such as the Minute Waltz, Fantaisie-Impromptu, and many nocturnes. Muse’s song “United States of Eurasia” quotes music by Chopin.

Dogs Playing Poker is the commonly used name for a series of humorous paintings by American artist Cassius Marcellus Coolidge. The paintings show dogs acting like people: they sit around card tables, play poker, and sometimes hold drinks or cigars. One of the best-known paintings in the series is A Friend in Need. In it, a dog secretly passes a playing card beneath the table to another dog while the other players focus on the game. That hidden exchange adds a joke to a scene that otherwise looks like a serious poker match. If you are asked to name the series, the answer is Dogs Playing Poker; if you are asked which painting shows the secret card pass, it is A Friend in Need.

Antoni Gaudí was a Catalan architect whose imaginative buildings helped shape the look of Barcelona, Spain. His designs often drew on forms found in nature, such as curves that suggest waves, bones, plants, and animals. He also used colorful ceramic mosaics to decorate surfaces. At Park Güell, visitors can see a famous mosaic salamander; at Casa Milà, nicknamed “The Stone Quarry,” the stone façade seems to ripple. Gaudí spent the later decades of his life working on the Sagrada Família, a monumental church with towers and richly detailed façades. Another of his best-known works is Casa Batlló, a remodeled residence on Passeig de Gràcia. Its mask-like balconies and roof covered in vivid ceramic tiles make the roof look like a dragon’s back.

The Alhambra is a palace-fortress complex on a hill overlooking Granada, Spain. It was built primarily during the Nasrid dynasty, the last Muslim dynasty to rule the region in the Middle Ages. Its buildings combine defensive walls and towers with royal rooms, gardens, and courtyards. The Alhambra is celebrated for Islamic architecture that uses intricate geometric patterns, carved plaster, colorful tiles, and water to create spaces that feel cool and peaceful. One of its best-known courtyards is the Court of the Myrtles in the Comares Palace. A long reflecting pool runs through its center, bordered by neatly clipped evergreen myrtle hedges. The pool reflects the surrounding arches and walls, making water an important part of the courtyard’s design.

The marimba is a keyboard percussion instrument made of tuned wooden bars arranged much like piano keys. Players strike the bars with mallets, and resonators beneath them help produce its warm, ringing sound. The instrument is especially associated with the folk music of Guatemala and southern Mexico, where marimba ensembles have long performed at celebrations and community events. In the United States, virtuoso Clair Omar Musser helped bring the marimba to wider attention by leading a traveling, all-female orchestra with more than 100 performers. Today, its sound is heard in music around the world. Many people also recognize the name “Marimba” from a classic iPhone ringtone.

The Barber of Seville is a comic opera by the Italian composer Gioachino Rossini, first performed in Rome in 1816. Its resourceful barber, Figaro, helps Count Almaviva court Rosina, who is kept under the watchful eye of her guardian, Dr. Bartolo. Bartolo hopes to marry Rosina himself, so Almaviva uses disguises and Figaro’s schemes to reach her. After a series of comic mix-ups and deceptions, Almaviva and Rosina marry with Figaro’s help. Figaro’s energetic entrance aria, “Largo al factotum,” is one of the opera’s best-known pieces; in it, he repeatedly calls out his own name. Rossini also composed William Tell, whose overture includes the famous galloping “March of the Swiss Soldiers.”

Vaslav Nijinsky was a celebrated Russian ballet dancer and choreographer and a leading male star of Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes. Audiences admired his powerful jumps and expressive performances, but his choreography could challenge their expectations. In 1912, he choreographed and performed the title role in L’Après-midi d’un faune (Afternoon of a Faun). His portrayal of the Faun scandalized some Paris spectators. The following year, Nijinsky created the choreography for The Rite of Spring, a ballet with music by Igor Stravinsky. Its 1913 premiere at Paris’s Théâtre des Champs-Élysées became notorious for an uproar in the audience. The ballet’s unfamiliar music and striking movements both contributed to the reaction. Nijinsky’s work helped change ideas about what ballet could look like.

Der Schwanendreher is a concerto for viola and orchestra written in 1935 by the German composer Paul Hindemith, who also wrote the opera Cardillac and the orchestral work Mathis der Maler. Hindemith was a skilled viola player, and the concerto gives the instrument a leading role rather than leaving it in the background of the orchestra. Its music draws on old German folk songs, using their melodies as starting points for new musical ideas. The work has three movements, including sections named “Between Mountain and Deep Valley” and “Now, Little Linden Tree, Grow Leaves!” The viola is a string instrument pitched between the violin and the cello, with a deeper, warmer sound than the violin.

Rain, Steam, and Speed – The Great Western Railway is an 1844 oil painting by the British Romantic artist J. M. W. Turner. It shows a steam locomotive hurtling across Brunel’s Maidenhead Bridge as rain, steam, and mist blur the train and surrounding landscape. Rather than painting every detail sharply, Turner used light and color to convey the speed and energy of the new railways. The painting captures both the excitement of technological progress and the changing relationship between machines and nature. Turner was famous for this atmospheric treatment of light. Two of his other well-known paintings are The Fighting Temeraire, which also reflects on a changing age, and The Slave Ship, which uses a turbulent sea and sky to heighten its dramatic subject.

St. Paul’s Cathedral is a major Anglican church in London and one of the city’s most recognizable landmarks. An earlier cathedral on the site was destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666. The English architect Sir Christopher Wren oversaw its rebuilding, creating the cathedral that stands today. Its enormous dome became a defining feature of the London skyline and is one of the building’s most famous features. Wren served as Surveyor of the King’s Works and helped reshape London after the fire by designing many other buildings. He also designed the Royal Hospital Chelsea. If a question asks for the London church rebuilt after the Great Fire and famous for its dome, the answer is St. Paul’s Cathedral; if it asks who oversaw that rebuilding, the answer is Sir Christopher Wren.

Perspective is an artistic technique that makes a flat drawing or painting appear to show depth and three-dimensional space. In linear perspective, artists draw lines that represent parallel edges, such as the sides of a road, so they seem to move closer together as they recede into the distance. If extended, these lines would meet at a vanishing point, usually on the horizon line. The vanishing point helps establish the direction of depth in the picture. Perspective also includes other ways to suggest distance: nearby objects may look larger or overlap farther ones, while distant objects may appear less detailed, less clear, or paler in color. Artists can use these effects to create convincing scenes or surprising optical illusions.

Così fan tutte is a comic opera by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart that premiered in 1790. Its Italian title is often translated as “Thus do all women” or “All women are like that.” In the story, two young men, Ferrando and Guglielmo, make a bet about whether their fiancées, Dorabella and Fiordiligi, will remain faithful. Pretending to leave for military service, the men return in disguise and each tries to win over the other’s fiancée. The plot explores love, trust, and deception, although its claim about women reflects a sexist view that audiences may question today. The opera’s words, called a libretto, were written by the Italian poet Lorenzo Da Ponte. He also worked with Mozart on The Marriage of Figaro and Don Giovanni.

A Roman triumphal arch is a monumental freestanding gateway built to celebrate a military victory and honor the victorious emperor or general. Unlike an ordinary doorway, it often stood along a public route where people could see it and remember the achievement. Its stone surfaces could carry inscriptions and carved reliefs showing events from the campaign. One surviving example is the Arch of Titus on the Via Sacra, an ancient road in Rome. It commemorates the Roman victory in Judea, and one of its reliefs shows soldiers carrying spoils from Jerusalem, including the Temple menorah. The Arch of Titus shows how Roman rulers used architecture and art together to present military success to the public.

Disco is a dance-oriented style of popular music that became a defining sound of clubs in the 1970s. Its steady “four-on-the-floor” beat puts a bass drum hit on every beat, while bass lines, rhythms, and often strings or horns create a groove that keeps people dancing. Disco culture is also associated with DJs, crowded dance floors, and mirrored disco balls that scatter light around a club. Decades later, artists still draw on its energy. Beyoncé’s 2022 album Renaissance takes inspiration from disco and other dance music. Its lead single, “BREAK MY SOUL,” opens with a sample from Big Freedia’s song “Explode,” including a voice repeating “yaka.”

Robert Johnson (1911–1938) was an American singer and guitarist who played Delta blues, a form of blues music that developed in the Mississippi Delta. His expressive singing and guitar playing influenced generations of blues and rock musicians. Johnson recorded only a small number of songs, but they include “Hellhound on My Trail” and “Love in Vain.” In “Love in Vain,” recorded in 1937, the narrator watches a train leave with the person he loves aboard. The Rolling Stones later covered the song on their 1969 album Let It Bleed. Johnson’s fame also grew because of a legend that he met the devil at a crossroads and traded his soul for extraordinary musical skill. That story is folklore, not an established fact.

Flight of the Bumblebee is a famous orchestral interlude by the Russian composer Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. It comes from his opera The Tale of Tsar Saltan, in which Prince Gvidon is transformed into a bumblebee so he can fly to visit his father, Tsar Saltan. The music brings that journey to life through rapid chromatic runs: notes that move quickly by small steps, creating the impression of a bee’s restless buzzing and darting flight. Players often perform the passage at dazzling speed, and it has become a popular showpiece for many instruments. Although it is frequently heard on its own, it was originally written as part of the opera’s story.

A metronome helps musicians keep a steady tempo by producing regular clicks, flashes, or other signals. Musicians set its speed in beats per minute: at 60 beats per minute, for example, it marks one beat each second. Traditional mechanical metronomes use an adjustable pendulum, while electronic versions can offer different sounds and visual pulses. Musicians often practice with a metronome to play evenly, then change its setting to build speed or work on difficult passages. The Hungarian composer György Ligeti used metronomes in an unusual way in his 1962 conceptual composition Poème Symphonique. It calls for 100 metronomes to be wound and started together. Their overlapping clicks create a changing pattern that gradually thins out and falls silent as each metronome runs down.

A concert is a live musical performance presented to an audience. Unlike a recording, it happens in real time, with musicians and listeners sharing the same space, whether that is a small hall or a large arena. A concert might feature one performer or several acts; a music festival usually brings together many performers over a longer period. Some gatherings become important cultural landmarks as well as musical events. In August 1969, a farm near Bethel, New York, hosted Woodstock, a three-day festival billed as “3 Days of Peace & Music.” Its large crowds and connection to the youth counterculture made it one of the most famous music events of the era. Altamont, a concert held in California later that year, is another event often discussed in accounts of that period.

Joaquín Rodrigo was a Spanish composer who lost his sight after contracting diphtheria at age three. He went on to become one of Spain’s best-known composers, writing music for orchestra, piano, and classical guitar. His most famous work is Concierto de Aranjuez, a concerto for classical guitar and orchestra named after a Spanish town. Its lyrical second movement, called the Adagio, became especially famous for its expressive guitar melody. Rodrigo drew on sounds associated with Spanish music, helping bring the classical guitar to a wider concert audience. The Adagio also reached jazz listeners when trumpeter Miles Davis adapted it for his 1960 album Sketches of Spain. If you hear about a blind Spanish composer whose guitar concerto inspired Davis, the composer is Rodrigo and the concerto is Concierto de Aranjuez.

The Well-Tempered Clavier is a collection of keyboard music by Johann Sebastian Bach, a German composer of the Baroque period. It has two books, each containing a prelude and a fugue in every one of the 24 major and minor keys. Bach completed the first book in 1722. A prelude introduces musical ideas freely, while a fugue develops a main melody by passing it between different musical voices. By writing in every key, Bach showed how a well-tempered keyboard tuning system could make all of them usable. The collection became a landmark for keyboard players and composers. Bach also wrote the Brandenburg Concertos and the Goldberg Variations.

Carl Czerny was an Austrian pianist, composer, and influential piano teacher born in Vienna in 1791. He studied piano with Ludwig van Beethoven, then devoted much of his career to teaching and writing music that helped students develop their technique. His many piano exercises and études include The School of Velocity, a collection designed to build speed and control. In the 1820s, Czerny taught the Hungarian-born child prodigy Franz Liszt in Vienna. Liszt became one of the Romantic era’s most celebrated virtuoso pianists and composed demanding works such as the Hungarian Rhapsodies and the Transcendental Études. Liszt later dedicated the Transcendental Études to Czerny, showing the lasting importance of his teacher’s guidance.

Wicked is a Broadway musical that retells the world of The Wizard of Oz from a different point of view. Its story begins before Dorothy arrives in Oz and focuses on the unlikely friendship between two young women: popular Glinda, who becomes known as the Good Witch, and green-skinned Elphaba, who comes to be called the Wicked Witch of the West. As they face prejudice, difficult choices, and political conflict, the show asks whether Elphaba is truly wicked or simply misunderstood. One of its best-known songs is “Defying Gravity,” sung by Elphaba as she decides to follow her own path. The musical is adapted from Gregory Maguire’s 1995 novel Wicked: The Life and Times of the Wicked Witch of the West.

Keith Haring was an American artist who became famous in 1980s New York for energetic drawings in public spaces. He first gained attention by making chalk drawings on unused black advertising panels in subway stations. His style is easy to recognize: thick outlines, bright colors, simplified human figures, and short lines that suggest movement or excitement. Haring wanted art to be accessible to everyone, not just people who visited museums, so he created murals that could be seen on city streets. In 1986, he painted a vivid anti-drug mural on a handball-court wall in East Harlem. Widely called Crack is Wack, it warned about the dangers of crack cocaine, a drug causing serious harm in New York at the time.

A pentatonic scale is a musical scale with five distinct notes in each octave, rather than the seven notes of a major scale. The five black keys on a piano provide a familiar example: play them in order, and you hear a pentatonic pattern. Pentatonic scales appear in many musical traditions, including East Asian music. One example is the Japanese yona-nuki scale, used in many enka melodies. It is formed by taking a major scale and leaving out its fourth and seventh degrees. For instance, removing F and B from the C major scale leaves C, D, E, G, and A. Because those are five distinct notes, the yona-nuki scale is a type of pentatonic scale.

The Eiffel Tower is a wrought-iron lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris. It was built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, a world’s fair that celebrated new ideas in industry and engineering. Its open framework made it tall and strong without requiring solid walls. The tower takes its name from Gustave Eiffel, the French civil engineer whose company designed and built it. Eiffel’s company also worked on bridges and railway structures, including Budapest’s Nyugati Station. After the engineer originally responsible for the Statue of Liberty’s internal metal framework died, sculptor Auguste Bartholdi asked Eiffel to complete that work. Although the Paris tower was originally intended as a temporary attraction, it became one of the world’s most recognizable landmarks.

Bebop, also called bop, is a jazz style that developed in the 1940s. Instead of focusing on the dance-band arrangements popular in earlier jazz, bebop musicians often played in small groups and emphasized listening and improvisation. Their music featured fast tempos, intricate chord progressions, and solos that demanded great skill. Alto saxophonist Charlie Parker, nicknamed “Bird,” was one of bebop’s pioneers. His recordings include “Ko-Ko” and “Ornithology,” and he worked closely with trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, another leading figure in the style. Bebop influenced later jazz musicians and reached beyond jazz: in A Tribe Called Quest’s hip-hop track “Excursions,” Q-Tip describes his father hearing a connection between hip-hop and bebop.

A musical chord is a group of notes that sound at the same time. Chords often contain three or more pitches and help create harmony beneath a melody, such as when a guitarist or pianist accompanies a singer. Common types include major, minor, diminished, and augmented chords, each with a different sound. In tonal music, chords also have jobs within a key: the chord built on the fifth scale degree, labeled V, often leads to the chord built on the first scale degree, labeled I. A more specialized example is the Neapolitan chord. It is built on the lowered second scale degree and usually appears in first inversion, written ♭II6. It acts as a predominant, preparing the music to move toward the dominant chord.

Neuschwanstein Castle is a 19th-century Romantic Revival palace perched on a hill above Hohenschwangau in the Bavarian Alps of southern Germany. It was commissioned by King Ludwig II of Bavaria, who loved stories of medieval knights and wanted a grand retreat that looked like a castle from a fairy tale. Its towers, decorated rooms, and dramatic mountain setting make it one of Germany’s best-known landmarks and helped inspire the design of the palace in Disney’s Sleeping Beauty. Ludwig II also built Linderhof Palace and Herrenchiemsee, two other elaborate residences in Bavaria. His love of imaginative architecture earned him the nickname the “Fairytale King.”

Evita is a stage musical by composer Andrew Lloyd Webber and lyricist Tim Rice about the life of Eva Perón. It follows Eva’s rise from an aspiring performer to the wife of Juan Perón, who becomes Argentina’s president. As Argentina’s first lady, Eva gains fame and political influence, especially through her connection with ordinary people. One of the musical’s most important scenes takes place at the Casa Rosada, Argentina’s presidential palace. From its balcony, Eva addresses the crowds below by singing “Don’t Cry for Me Argentina.” The song became Evita’s best-known number. Although the musical draws on real people and events, it dramatizes Eva’s life rather than telling it as a documentary.

José Clemente Orozco was a Mexican artist best known for murals: large paintings made directly on walls. Along with Diego Rivera, he helped make mural painting an important part of Mexican art in the 20th century. Orozco’s murals often explored history and conflict, encouraging viewers to think about how societies change. One of his major works is The Epic of American Civilization, a cycle of murals painted for Baker Library at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. The cycle portrays Indigenous cultures, including the Aztecs, as well as European colonization and later developments in the Americas. If you are asked who painted The Epic of American Civilization, the answer is José Clemente Orozco; if you are asked where to see it, the answer is Dartmouth College.

Pythagoras of Samos was an ancient Greek philosopher and mathematician who connected music with numbers. He is traditionally associated with the idea that consonant intervals—combinations of notes that sound pleasing together—can be explained by simple ratios. Using a monochord, an instrument with one string, you can hear how changing the string’s sounding length changes its pitch. If the length is shortened to half, the note sounds one octave higher: it has a higher pitch but keeps the same note name. Other simple ratios produce intervals such as the perfect fifth. A later story says Pythagoras began investigating pitch after hearing a blacksmith’s hammers, though the story may not be historically accurate. His ideas helped shape later thinking about musical harmony and tuning.

Orchestration is the art of deciding which instruments play each part of a piece of music. A composer or arranger considers how instruments’ sounds blend or contrast, then assigns melodies, harmonies, and rhythms to create a particular effect. The word can also describe adapting music originally written for a solo performer or small group so that an orchestra can play it. Russian composer Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov was especially skilled at orchestration. In his symphonic suite Scheherazade, a solo violin plays a recurring theme representing the title character. A harp accompanies the violin, adding a delicate, shimmering sound. The harp is a plucked-string instrument; a concert harp typically has 47 strings and pedals that change their pitches.

The Musée d’Orsay is an art museum in Paris on the Left Bank of the Seine, across the river from the Louvre. Its building was originally the Gare d’Orsay, a monumental Beaux-Arts railway station that opened for the 1900 Exposition Universelle, a world’s fair. French architect Victor Laloux designed the station; he also designed the Hôtel de Ville, or city hall, in Tours. Today, the museum’s spacious central hall and enormous clock recall its railway past. The Musée d’Orsay is especially famous for its Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings, including works by artists such as Claude Monet and Vincent van Gogh. Do not confuse the former Gare d’Orsay with Gare Saint-Lazare, another Paris station that Monet painted.

Johann Gottlieb Goldberg was a German harpsichordist and composer who studied with Johann Sebastian Bach and served Count Hermann Karl von Keyserlingk in Dresden. Goldberg’s name became attached to Bach’s Goldberg Variations, a keyboard work built from an opening aria, 30 variations, and a return to the aria. Every third variation is a canon, a piece in which one musical line follows and imitates another. According to a well-known story, Keyserlingk commissioned the work to help soothe his sleepless nights, and Goldberg played it for him. Historians debate that story and Goldberg’s role in the work’s first performance. Bach and Goldberg lived during the Baroque era, a period of music lasting roughly from 1600 to 1750.

Eco-brutalism combines the bold, blocky forms of Brutalist architecture with abundant greenery and environmentally conscious design. Brutalism emerged in the 1950s and is known for large concrete structures, geometric shapes, and an emphasis on function. Eco-brutalism keeps that monumental look but softens it with plants growing on terraces, walls, and facades. The greenery can provide shade and help cool the building, while creating space for nature in a city. Architects may also cover a building’s roof—its uppermost horizontal surface—with plants. This feature is called a green roof. Besides adding greenery, a green roof can absorb rainwater, helping manage stormwater, and reduce how much heat the building absorbs.

Brutalism is an architectural style that emerged in the 1950s and became less popular in the 1970s. It emphasizes function and often uses large, bold geometric forms, exposed concrete, and steel rather than decorative details. Brutalist buildings can look heavy or monumental, with their structural materials left visible instead of hidden behind a polished exterior. A famous example is Habitat 67, a residential complex in Montreal designed by Moshe Safdie for Expo 67, the 1967 world’s fair. It is made from 354 identical prefabricated concrete modules arranged in varied configurations. By stacking and connecting these boxlike units, Safdie created homes with an unusual, striking shape while exploring new ways to build urban housing.

Edgar Degas was a French artist associated with Impressionism, a movement that explored modern life and changing light. He became especially known for scenes of dancers, bathers, and city life. Many of his paintings show ballet performers practicing at the barre, waiting backstage, or rehearsing in tutus rather than appearing in a finished performance. Degas was interested in how people moved, so he often captured unusual poses and everyday moments. He also made portraits of bathers, including After the Bath. In The Absinthe Drinker, he pictured people sitting in a Paris café, showing a quieter side of urban life. If you see a question about an Impressionist who painted ballet dancers and The Absinthe Drinker, the artist is Edgar Degas.

Fine Wind, Clear Morning is a Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock print by Katsushika Hokusai, an artist of the Edo period. It is the second print in his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, following The Great Wave of Kanagawa. Unlike the dramatic wave and boats in that famous print, Fine Wind, Clear Morning focuses on the mountain itself. Mount Fuji appears deep red beneath a band of clouds, while much of its foreground slopes remain in shadow. The striking color has given the print its nickname, Red Fuji. Hokusai made Mount Fuji the subject of the series, showing how one familiar landmark could look different in changing weather and light.

Bronze is a copper-based alloy traditionally made mainly from copper and tin. Because it is strong and can be melted and poured into molds, people have used it for tools, weapons, and cast sculptures. Artists can use casting to create detailed figures and raised designs. The “Benin Bronzes” are a group of plaques and sculptures made by artists in the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria; despite the nickname, not every object in the group is made of bronze. Many were taken during a British attack in 1897 and later entered museums abroad. In March 2022, the Smithsonian Institution announced plans to return its collection of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria. The Smithsonian is a U.S. museum-and-research organization that operates the National Museum of African Art and the National Air and Space Museum.

Woodwind instruments are a family of instruments played by blowing air into or across a tube. Players change the pitch by covering holes with their fingers or pressing keys. The family includes flutes, clarinets, oboes, bassoons, and saxophones, even though some of these instruments are made of metal rather than wood. Woodwinds make sound in different ways: a flute splits the player’s airstream at an edge, a clarinet or saxophone uses one vibrating reed, and an oboe or bassoon uses two reeds. The clarinet can play across several octaves and is common in orchestras and concert bands. It has a famous moment at the start of George Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue, where it slides upward through the notes in a rising glissando.

Robert Indiana was an American Pop artist who turned familiar letters, numbers, and short words into bold works of art. His best-known design spells LOVE in four block capitals arranged in a square: L and a tilted O sit above V and E. He first developed the image in the 1960s, and it later appeared in prints, stamps, and monumental sculptures. Many LOVE sculptures use bright red letters, making the word stand out in public spaces. Indiana’s simple shapes and strong colors make his work easy to recognize, but they also invite viewers to think about how a familiar word can become a powerful visual symbol.

The Hallelujah Chorus is one of the best-known pieces of Baroque choral music. It concludes Part II of Messiah, a three-part English-language oratorio by George Frideric Handel that was first performed in Dublin in 1742. An oratorio is a large work for singers and orchestra that tells a religious story without costumes or acting. Handel drew the words of Messiah from the Bible, including the King James Bible. In the Hallelujah Chorus, the choir repeatedly sings “Hallelujah” and praises the “King of Kings” and “Lord of Lords,” celebrating God’s reign. The chorus is often performed on its own, but it is only one part of Handel’s larger work, Messiah.

The Ambassadors is a 1533 double portrait by Hans Holbein the Younger, a German-born artist who later became court painter to England’s Henry VIII. It shows two French diplomats standing beside a table crowded with a globe, books, and scientific instruments. These objects suggest their learning and interest in a changing world, while a red carpet on the table signals their high status. Across the foreground stretches a strange, distorted shape: viewed from the right angle, it becomes a skull, a reminder that everyone eventually dies. Holbein used this optical trick, called anamorphosis, alongside his remarkably detailed painting of fabrics and objects. He was also known for portraits of figures at Henry VIII’s court, including Jane Seymour, and painted Christina of Denmark.

Akira Yoshizawa was a Japanese artist who helped transform origami, the art of folding paper, into a way to create expressive sculptures. He pioneered wet-folding, a technique in which paper is lightly dampened before it is folded. The moisture makes the paper easier to shape into smooth curves and rounded forms; as it dries, the paper holds its new shape. Yoshizawa also helped make origami easier to teach and share. With Samuel Randlett, he developed the Yoshizawa–Randlett system, a widely adopted way of diagramming folding instructions. Its symbols and arrows show where to fold and how to move the paper, so people can follow the steps even when they do not share a language.

The French horn is a brass instrument made from a long tube of metal coiled into a circular shape and ending in a wide, flared bell. Players blow into a mouthpiece and often place one hand inside the bell to support the instrument and help shape its sound. French horns can sound warm and gentle or bold and threatening, which makes them useful for telling stories through music. In Sergei Prokofiev’s narrated orchestral tale Peter and the Wolf, different instruments and sections represent different characters. The French horn section plays the recurring theme for the wolf, the dangerous animal that threatens Peter and is eventually captured. Peter’s own theme is played by the string section, including violins, violas, and cellos.

Grisaille is a painting technique that uses varying shades of gray instead of a full range of colors. By placing light and dark grays next to each other, an artist can model a figure so it looks three-dimensional, almost like a sculpture. A painting made entirely this way is monochromatic, meaning it uses variations of one color. Artists used grisaille during the Renaissance, and contemporary painters still use it. American painter Amy Sherald often paints her subjects’ skin tones in gray while using bright colors elsewhere. In her portrait of Breonna Taylor, Sherald placed Taylor against an aqua background. Taylor was fatally shot in her Louisville apartment in 2020, and her death sparked protests across the United States.

Fazlur Rahman Khan was a Bangladeshi-American structural engineer born in Dhaka in 1929. He helped change how skyscrapers are built by finding ways to make very tall buildings strong without using as much steel. At the architecture and engineering firm Skidmore, Owings, and Merrill, Khan was a key structural engineer on Chicago’s John Hancock Center and Sears Tower, now called Willis Tower. For the Sears Tower, he devised the bundled-tube system: several linked vertical tube-like sections work together as one load-bearing structure. This arrangement helps a skyscraper support its weight and resist strong winds. Khan’s ideas made tall buildings more efficient to design and influenced skyscraper construction around the world.

Drag is a performance art in which people use costumes, makeup, movement, music, and theatricality to present stylized versions of gender. A drag queen often performs femininity, while other drag performers may explore masculinity or mix gender styles. Performances can include lip-syncing, dancing, comedy, and competitions. Voguing battles are sometimes part of drag and ballroom events. In voguing, dancers strike poses inspired by fashion photography, as if someone were taking their picture; Madonna brought the style to a wider audience with her song “Vogue.” Voguing developed in the ballroom scene of Harlem, a New York City neighborhood with a rich history of Black performance. Harlem is also home to the Apollo Theater, where performers such as tap dancer Bill “Bojangles” Robinson appeared.

Caspar David Friedrich (1774–1840) was a German Romantic painter born in Greifswald. He is known for atmospheric landscapes in which a solitary person faces away from the viewer and looks out over nature. Rather than simply showing a place, these paintings invite viewers to think about the person’s feelings and their place in a much larger world. In Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, a figure stands on a rocky height overlooking mist-covered mountains. Another important work, The Monk by the Sea, was exhibited in Berlin in 1810. It shows a tiny monk standing alone on a shore beneath a vast, nearly empty sky. The contrast between the small figure and the open landscape gives the painting its powerful sense of solitude.

The Habanera is a famous aria from Georges Bizet’s opera Carmen, sung by the title character, a mezzo-soprano, as she flirts with a crowd of men. Its French words begin “L’amour est un oiseau rebelle,” meaning “Love is a rebellious bird.” Carmen suggests that love cannot be controlled or made to follow rules. The melody descends in small, chromatic steps over a repeating musical pattern called an ostinato, while the chorus warns, “Prends garde à toi,” or “Watch out.” Soon afterward, Carmen throws a flower to the soldier Don José, drawing him into the opera’s story. Another well-known number from Carmen is the “Toreador Song,” sung by the bullfighter Escamillo.

The Seattle Central Library is the main downtown branch of Seattle’s public library system in Washington state. Opened in 2004, it was designed by Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas and his firm, OMA (Office for Metropolitan Architecture). Koolhaas received the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 2000, one of architecture’s most important honors. The library stands out because its exterior is an irregular, faceted structure wrapped in diamond-patterned glass, rather than a traditional rectangular building. Inside, bright yellow escalators connect floors, and the fourth-floor corridor is known as the Red Hall for its intense red color. These bold features make the library a landmark as well as a place to read, study, and find information. Its full name is Seattle Central Library.

Henri Cartier-Bresson was a French photographer who helped pioneer candid street photography: taking pictures of everyday life as it unfolded rather than asking people to pose. He believed a photograph could capture the “decisive moment,” the brief instant when a scene’s action and composition come together to tell a story. His book The Decisive Moment helped make that idea famous. In 1947, Cartier-Bresson co-founded Magnum Photos with Robert Capa, David Seymour, George Rodger, and William Vandivert. Magnum was a photographer-owned cooperative agency that gave its members more control over how their pictures and stories were used. It became an important international home for documentary photographers, whose images record real people, places, and events.

The Curse of the Ninth is a superstition in classical music: after completing a ninth symphony, a composer will die before finishing another major symphonic work. The idea is often linked to Ludwig van Beethoven, who completed nine symphonies; his Ninth, famous for its choral finale, was his last. Stories about composers such as Franz Schubert and Anton Bruckner helped keep the belief alive, though it is not a real rule. The Austrian composer Gustav Mahler knew the superstition and feared it. He avoided calling his large orchestral song cycle Das Lied von der Erde a numbered symphony, even though he considered it symphonic. Mahler then completed a work he called his Ninth Symphony, but died before he could finish his Tenth.

Pointe shoes are specialized ballet footwear that lets trained dancers perform en pointe, or balance on the tips of their toes. Unlike soft ballet slippers, they have a stiff toe box that supports the foot and a small, flat platform at the front to stand on. Dancers usually build strength and technique first, often practicing at a barre, the handrail used for support in ballet class. Pointe work requires careful training because the shoes alone cannot hold a dancer up safely. It became a celebrated part of Romantic-era ballet in the 1800s. Marie Taglioni’s performance in the 1832 ballet La Sylphide is often cited as an early landmark: her dancing en pointe helped create the light, floating appearance associated with that style.

A Lied is a German-language art song that sets a poem to music, usually for one singer accompanied by piano. Its plural is lieder. Lieder became especially important during the Romantic period, when composers used melody and piano accompaniment to bring out a poem’s emotions, characters, and story. Franz Schubert wrote hundreds of them, including Die Forelle (“The Trout”) and songs based on poems by Goethe. One of his best-known Goethe settings is Erlkönig. It tells of a father riding through the night with his sick son. The child hears the Erlking, a supernatural figure, calling to him, but his father tries to explain what the child senses as ordinary sounds and sights.

The daguerreotype was one of the earliest ways to make a photograph. It is named after Louis Daguerre, a French artist and physicist who publicly introduced the process in France in 1839. To make one, a photographer polished a silver-coated copper plate, made it sensitive to light with iodine vapor, and placed it in a camera. After a long exposure, mercury vapor brought out the image on the plate. The result was a remarkably detailed, one-of-a-kind picture: unlike a film negative, the plate could not be used to print multiple copies. Daguerreotypes helped make photography popular, although their long exposure times meant people being photographed had to hold still.

The Tale of Tsar Saltan is a 1900 opera by Russian composer Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, based on a poem by Alexander Pushkin. Its story follows Prince Gvidon, the son of Tsar Saltan. After Gvidon and his mother are sent away in a barrel, they reach the island of Buyan, where Gvidon eventually becomes its ruler. He helps a magical Swan-Bird, who later transforms him into a bumblebee so he can visit his father without being recognized. The opera’s best-known orchestral interlude, Flight of the Bumblebee, portrays that journey. Its rapid, winding notes suggest the insect’s restless buzzing and frantic movement. Knowing the opera’s title and Gvidon’s role in the story helps connect the famous music to the larger tale.

Hark! The Herald Angels Sing is a Christmas carol that celebrates the birth of Jesus. Its words are based on a hymn by Charles Wesley, first published in 1739, but the familiar tune came later. German composer Felix Mendelssohn wrote the melody for the second section of Festgesang, a festival cantata composed in 1840 to mark the 400th anniversary of Gutenberg’s invention of the printing press. The melody was later adapted for Wesley’s words, creating the version of Hark! The Herald Angels Sing commonly heard today. The carol is often performed by choirs at Christmas, with its strong, bright tune helping to express the joy announced in its opening line.

A Gothic window is a glazed opening associated with Gothic architecture, which became prominent in medieval European churches and cathedrals. It often has a pointed arch, allowing builders to create tall openings that fill interiors with light. Many Gothic windows contain stained glass: pieces of colored glass arranged to show religious stories, figures, or patterns. Stone tracery, the framework that divides and supports the glass, can form elaborate designs. One special type is the rose window, a large circular window with tracery radiating outward like the spokes of a wheel. Rose windows are often placed above a cathedral’s main entrance. Gothic-style windows also appear in later buildings; one is visible behind the figures in Grant Wood’s painting American Gothic.

Crack Is Wack is a 1986 mural by New York artist Keith Haring on a handball court wall in East Harlem. It warns about crack cocaine, a smokable form of cocaine that was causing serious harm in many communities at the time. Haring painted the mural in a public place so people passing by could see its anti-drug message. Its bold black outlines, vivid colors, and energetic, cartoonlike figures are hallmarks of his style. The words “Crack Is Wack” make the warning direct and memorable. The mural has since been restored to preserve both Haring’s artwork and its original message.

The Shard is a 310-metre skyscraper beside London Bridge in London. Completed in 2012, it became the tallest building in the United Kingdom. Its name comes from its shape: the tower tapers to a point, and its angled glass surfaces make it look like a shard of glass rising above the city. The building was designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, who also co-designed the Centre Pompidou in Paris with Richard Rogers. The Shard contains offices, restaurants, a hotel and a public viewing platform with wide views across London. If you are asked to identify the tall London tower beside London Bridge, the answer is The Shard; if you are asked who designed it, the answer is Renzo Piano.

The Night Watch is a monumental group portrait painted in 1642 by the Dutch artist Rembrandt van Rijn. It shows an Amsterdam civic militia company led by Captain Frans Banning Cocq preparing to move into action. Instead of arranging the members in a still, orderly row, Rembrandt made the scene feel busy and alive, using dramatic contrasts of light and shadow to draw attention to key figures. Although the title suggests darkness, the painting depicts a daytime scene; its darkened appearance helped give it the nickname The Night Watch. Rembrandt was born in Leiden in 1606 and became known for expressive portraits and many self-portraits. He also painted The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp, which shows a doctor demonstrating a dissection to a group of observers.

A first inversion chord is a triad arranged so that its third, rather than its root, is the lowest note, or bass note. For example, a C major triad contains C, E, and G. In first inversion, E is in the bass, while G and C appear above it. The root, C, is a sixth above the bass note, E. In figured bass, a system of numerals written with a bass line to show which notes to play above it, first inversion is commonly marked with the numeral 6. This is shorthand for the chord’s fuller interval pattern, 6/3. Figured bass was widely used during the Baroque era, especially to guide musicians accompanying a melody.

Die Forelle, meaning “The Trout,” is a German art song by the Austrian composer Franz Schubert. It sets a poem by Christian Friedrich Daniel Schubart, a different person from the composer. Like many German art songs, or lieder, it was written for a solo singer with piano accompaniment. The song describes a trout swimming in a stream while a fisherman tries to catch it. When the fisherman muddies the water and succeeds, the music shifts from major to minor, darkening the mood. Schubert later used the song’s melody as the basis for variations in the fourth movement of his Piano Quintet in A major, commonly called the Trout Quintet. Schubert is also known for his Eighth Symphony, nicknamed the Unfinished Symphony because he completed only two movements.

Sketches of Spain is a 1960 album by jazz trumpeter Miles Davis that blends jazz with music associated with Spain. Rather than focusing on small-group improvisation, Davis plays alongside an orchestra whose parts were arranged and conducted by his longtime collaborator Gil Evans. The album includes a version of the slow second movement of Concierto de Aranjuez, a work by Spanish composer Joaquín Rodrigo, as well as “Will o’ the Wisp.” Evans’s arrangements draw on the sounds and moods of Spanish classical music and flamenco, a tradition known for expressive singing, guitar playing, and dance. The result is an atmospheric album in which Davis’s trumpet often sounds like a solo voice against the orchestra. Its title is Sketches of Spain, and Evans was central to shaping its distinctive sound.

Bird in Space is a series of abstract sculptures by Romanian artist Constantin Brâncuși. Rather than carving a recognizable bird with wings, feathers, and a beak, Brâncuși used a smooth, elongated, highly polished form that rises to a narrow tip. He wanted to suggest the feeling of a bird in flight, not copy its appearance. When one version arrived in the United States in 1926, customs officials classified it as a manufactured object instead of a work of art and charged an import duty. Brâncuși challenged the decision in a case called Brâncuși v. United States. In 1928, the court ruled in his favor, recognizing that a sculpture could be art even if it did not look like the thing it represented.

The Hunters in the Snow is a winter landscape painted in 1565 by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, a Flemish Renaissance artist also known for The Tower of Babel and The Peasant Wedding. In the foreground, a party of hunters carrying spears returns with its dogs toward a village. Below them, people skate and play on frozen ponds, while snow-covered mountains rise in the distance. Bruegel included many small details of everyday life, so the painting shows more than a hunting trip: it gives a broad view of how people lived and enjoyed themselves in winter. The Hunters in the Snow belongs to his celebrated series of landscapes depicting different seasons of the year.

Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun is an orchestral work by the French composer Claude Debussy. It begins with a prominent solo flute melody that moves down and up through chromatic notes—notes close together on the musical scale. Debussy drew inspiration from L’Après-midi d’un faune, a poem by the French Symbolist poet Stéphane Mallarmé. The poem imagines a faun, a mythical creature that is part human and part goat, reflecting on a dreamlike afternoon. Rather than telling the poem’s story step by step, Debussy’s music suggests its hazy atmosphere through shifting harmonies and orchestral colors. The piece is often associated with musical Impressionism, a style that emphasizes mood and sensory impressions. Its English title is Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun, and the poet behind it is Stéphane Mallarmé.

Anish Kapoor is a British-Indian sculptor known for large public artworks that change how viewers see the space around them. One of his best-known works stands in Chicago’s Millennium Park. Officially titled Cloud Gate, it is popularly nicknamed “the Bean” because of its rounded shape. The monumental sculpture is made of mirror-polished stainless steel, and its curved surface reflects and distorts Chicago’s skyline, the sky, and visitors walking around it. Kapoor has also drawn controversy for securing exclusive commercial rights to use Vantablack, an ultra-black material that absorbs nearly all visible light. Some other artists objected because they felt such a striking material should not be reserved for one artist.

The Emperor Quartet is Franz Joseph Haydn’s String Quartet in C major, Op. 76 No. 3. It is one of six quartets Haydn dedicated to Count Erdődy. Like other string quartets, it is written for two violins, a viola, and a cello. Its nickname comes from the melody in its slow second movement: Haydn had written the tune to honor the Austrian emperor, and it was later adopted as the melody of Germany’s national anthem. Haydn, an Austrian composer who worked for the Esterházy family for much of his career, helped make the string quartet a major form of chamber music. He is often called the “father of the string quartet.”

A crescendo is a musical direction telling performers to get gradually louder over a passage, rather than suddenly changing volume. The word comes from Italian and means “growing.” In a score, a crescendo may be written as “cresc.” or shown by a hairpin symbol that opens outward from left to right beneath the notes. Performers build the sound across the marked span, often to create excitement or lead toward a dramatic moment. Crescendos can be played by a soloist, such as a pianist, or by a whole orchestra. The Italian composer Gioachino Rossini used swelling orchestral crescendos so memorably that he was nicknamed “Signor Crescendo.” He also wrote the comic opera The Barber of Seville and the opera William Tell.

Soprano is the highest of the four standard voice parts in an SATB choir, whose sections are soprano, alto, tenor, and bass. It is above alto and is also a common operatic voice type for women. Some soprano roles feature coloratura: elaborate passages with quick notes, wide leaps, and trills. A soubrette is one kind of soprano, often cast in lively, youthful roles. One celebrated soprano was Montserrat Caballé, who was born in Barcelona, Spain. She became an international sensation in 1965 when she stepped in for Marilyn Horne at Carnegie Hall to sing the title role in Donizetti’s opera Lucrezia Borgia. Her career shows how a soprano can become famous not only for reaching high notes but also for musical skill and expression.

The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa is a marble sculpture by the Italian Baroque artist Gian Lorenzo Bernini in the Cornaro Chapel in Rome. It shows Teresa of Ávila, a Carmelite nun and mystic, reclining as an angel prepares to pierce her heart with a spear. Teresa described this experience as a powerful encounter with divine love, and Bernini made it feel like a scene unfolding on a stage. Golden rays behind the figures suggest heavenly light, while sculpted members of the Cornaro family watch from boxes along the chapel walls. Bernini used the setting, light, and expressive figures to draw viewers into the moment. He also created the Fountain of the Four Rivers in Rome’s Piazza Navona and designed the bronze Baldacchino over the main altar of St. Peter’s Basilica.

A handscroll is a long horizontal painting or illustrated manuscript, usually made on paper or silk and mounted so it can be rolled up. Instead of seeing the whole work at once, a viewer unrolls it section by section, following a story or landscape as it unfolds. Handscrolls were an important art form in China and Japan, where Japanese illustrated examples are called emakimono. A famous Chinese example is Zhang Zeduan’s Northern Song painting Along the River During the Qingming Festival. It portrays springtime life in Kaifeng, from quieter areas outside the city to busy streets and waterways. Near the center, a crowded bridge crosses the river. By revealing only part of the panorama at a time, the handscroll makes viewing feel like a journey through the scene.

A national anthem is a patriotic song officially recognized by a country as a symbol of its collective identity. Anthems are often performed at public ceremonies, sporting events, and other occasions when people come together to represent or honor their country. India’s national anthem is “Jana Gana Mana.” Its lyrics were written by Rabindranath Tagore, a Bengali poet born in Kolkata who is also known for his poetry collection Gitanjali. Tagore wrote in Bengali, a language spoken in India and neighboring Bangladesh. Other examples of national anthems include France’s “La Marseillaise” and the United Kingdom’s “God Save the King” (or “God Save the Queen” when the monarch is a queen). Although their words and music differ, national anthems serve a similar purpose: expressing a country’s shared identity.

Swing is a style of jazz that became hugely popular as dance music during the big-band era of the 1930s and 1940s. Its defining feature is a lively rhythmic feel: instead of playing paired eighth notes evenly, musicians often play the first note longer and the second shorter. Big bands used sections of trumpets, trombones, and saxophones alongside a rhythm section to create an energetic sound. Clarinetist and bandleader Benny Goodman was one of swing’s best-known figures. His band’s 1938 concert at Carnegie Hall helped bring swing from dance halls into a prestigious concert venue. Goodman also made small-group recordings with pianist Teddy Wilson and drummer Gene Krupa, who played on the band’s 1937 hit “Sing, Sing, Sing.”

Trans-Fixed is a 1974 performance artwork by American artist Chris Burden. Burden lay shirtless with his arms extended across the rear of a Volkswagen Beetle while nails were driven through his palms, briefly holding him to the car. The pose evoked the crucifixion of Jesus, and photographs documented the event. Burden used his own body to make viewers think about pain, risk, and the meaning of an image that resembles a familiar religious scene. He had explored physical danger in an earlier performance, Shoot (1971), in which an assistant fired a rifle and struck him in the arm. In Trans-Fixed, the ordinary automobile became part of a startling artwork rather than simply a means of transportation.

Blue is one of the three primary colors of light, along with red and green. When all three are combined at full strength, they make white light. In art, blue can come from many dyes and pigments. Woad is a plant that supplied blue dye for textiles, including the Unicorn Tapestries. Ultramarine was traditionally made by grinding lapis lazuli, a stone mined in Afghanistan; because it was costly, medieval artists often reserved it for images of the Virgin Mary. Prussian blue is a synthetic pigment also associated with the blue of technical drawings called blueprints. Johannes Vermeer used costly ultramarine for the blue fabric in Girl with a Pearl Earring, a 17th-century Dutch painting of a young woman in a blue-and-yellow turban turning toward the viewer against a dark background.

A convex mirror curves outward, like the outside of a ball. Because of its shape, it reflects a wider area than a flat mirror, though the people and objects in its reflection appear smaller. Jan van Eyck painted a detailed convex mirror on the back wall of The Arnolfini Portrait, also called The Arnolfini Wedding. It shows a broad view of the room, including details beyond what is directly visible from the viewer’s position. Ten small scenes from the Passion of Christ, the events surrounding Jesus’s suffering and death, decorate its frame. In front of the mirror stand an Italian merchant in a large black hat and his wife in a green dress. Above them hangs a chandelier with a single candle, and a small dog stands at their feet.

The Musical Offering is a collection of Baroque instrumental music that Johann Sebastian Bach created after visiting Frederick the Great, the king of Prussia. Frederick gave Bach a melody known as the “royal theme,” which Bach used as the basis for the collection. Its pieces include ten canons, two ricercars and a trio sonata. Canons and ricercars use counterpoint, in which separate melodies fit together; a ricercar is a fugue-like piece whose musical lines repeat and transform a theme. The trio sonata features a transverse flute, a woodwind instrument held sideways when played. It is larger than a piccolo and was an instrument Frederick played himself. By developing the king’s theme in several different ways, Bach showed how much musical variety could grow from one melody.

The tenor saxophone is a single-reed woodwind instrument widely used in jazz combos and concert bands. Its sound comes from a reed vibrating against a mouthpiece, even though the instrument’s body is usually made of brass. Among common saxophone sizes, the tenor is larger and lower-pitched than the E-flat alto saxophone but smaller and higher-pitched than the baritone saxophone. It is a B-flat instrument: when a player reads and plays a written C, the note heard is B-flat. Jazz saxophonist John Coltrane made the tenor saxophone central to his music. On “Psalm,” the final movement of his 1965 album A Love Supreme, he played a saxophone line that he described as a musical recitation of a poem.

Suite bergamasque is a four-movement work for solo piano by the French composer Claude Debussy. He began writing it as a young man, revised it later, and published it in 1905. Its movements are “Prélude,” “Menuet,” “Clair de lune,” and “Passepied.” The third movement, “Clair de lune,” is especially famous and is often performed on its own. Its title means “moonlight,” and its gentle, flowing sound helps explain its lasting popularity. Debussy is often associated with musical impressionism, which uses color and atmosphere to suggest a mood rather than tell a precise story. He also wrote the piano suite Children’s Corner, dedicated to his daughter Claude-Emma, and the orchestral work Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune (Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun).

Twelve Variations in C Major on “Ah vous dirai-je, Maman,” K. 265 is a solo keyboard work by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, a Classical-era composer born in Salzburg who was famous as a child prodigy. The piece begins with the simple French song melody “Ah vous dirai-je, Maman,” then presents it in twelve contrasting variations. In each variation, Mozart keeps the tune recognizable while changing features such as its rhythm, ornamentation, accompaniment, or mood. The same melody later became familiar to English-speaking children through “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star,” whose best-known words come from a poem by Jane Taylor. It is also the tune of the alphabet song. Mozart’s work shows how a composer can build a lively, inventive piece from a melody that listeners may already know.

Broadway is New York City’s best-known theater district, centered around the streets near Times Square in Manhattan. The name also refers to the city’s professional commercial theater industry, especially its musicals, though Broadway stages plays as well. One famous example is Neil Simon’s comedy The Odd Couple, which opened on Broadway in 1965. After his wife leaves him, the tidy, anxious Felix Ungar moves in with his friend Oscar Madison, who is messy and easygoing. Their opposite habits turn everyday life in their shared apartment into a series of arguments and jokes. Broadway productions like this one are performed for paying audiences by professional actors and theater crews, helping make the district an internationally recognized center for live theater.

“So What” is the opening track of Miles Davis’s 1959 album Kind of Blue, one of the most influential jazz recordings. It begins quietly, with a spare piano-and-bass introduction, before the rest of the group joins in and Davis enters on trumpet. Davis was both the bandleader and a celebrated trumpeter; the recording also features saxophonists John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley. “So What” is an example of modal jazz, in which musicians improvise using musical scales, or modes, rather than following a fast-changing sequence of chords. This gives the players room to explore melodies and rhythms at a relaxed pace. On Kind of Blue, the next track after “So What” is “Freddie Freeloader.”

The Art Institute of Chicago is a major art museum on Michigan Avenue in Chicago, Illinois. Its collection includes two famous American paintings: Grant Wood’s American Gothic and Edward Hopper’s Nighthawks, which shows people in a late-night diner. American Gothic depicts a stern-looking man holding a pitchfork beside a woman. The house behind them was modeled on a real house in Eldon, Iowa, and the painting’s title refers to the Gothic-style window near the top of that house. Wood entered American Gothic in a competition held by the Art Institute of Chicago, where it placed third and won a $300 prize. The painting is now part of the museum’s collection.

The chromatic scale includes all twelve different pitches used in most Western music before the starting note repeats at the next octave. It moves in the smallest standard steps of twelve-tone equal temperament: each neighboring pair of notes is separated by a semitone, also called a half step. A semitone is half of a whole tone. On a piano, you can play a chromatic scale by starting on any key and playing every adjacent black or white key in order until you reach the same note an octave higher. Composers use chromatic notes to add color, tension, or a sense of movement to a melody. For example, Claude Debussy’s flute solo in Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun uses chromatic movement.

Henri Matisse was a French painter and a leading figure in Fauvism, an early twentieth-century art movement known for bold colors that do not have to match real life. Rather than painting a scene exactly as it appeared, Matisse used strong color and simplified shapes to express energy and feeling. His painting The Joy of Life shows people relaxing and dancing in a brightly colored landscape. In his monumental 1910 painting The Dance, five vivid red figures hold hands and move in a circle against a simple blue and green background. The figures’ movement and the striking contrast of colors make The Dance one of his best-known works. Matisse’s approach helped expand what modern painting could do.

Adagio is an Italian musical term that tells performers to play at a slow, expressive pace. It is generally faster than largo or lento but slower than andante, giving the music a broad, unhurried feeling. In Tchaikovsky’s ballet The Sleeping Beauty, the Rose Adagio is a famous scene in which Princess Aurora dances with four suitors. Another well-known example is Samuel Barber’s Adagio for Strings. Barber first wrote this music as the slow movement of his 1936 String Quartet, Op. 11, scored for two violins, a viola, and a cello. He later arranged the movement for a string orchestra, and that version became widely performed.

Domenico Scarlatti was an Italian Baroque composer famous for his 555 keyboard sonatas: short pieces that explore a wide range of sounds and playing techniques. Many were associated with Infanta Maria Barbara, whom he taught and who later became queen of Spain. Scarlatti wrote much of this music for the harpsichord, a keyboard instrument that came before the modern piano. Pressing a harpsichord key moves a jack that plucks a string; in a piano, a hammer strikes a string instead. Scarlatti used the harpsichord’s bright sound in lively pieces full of quick notes, hand crossings, and rhythms influenced by music he heard in Spain. His collection called the 30 Essercizi is one early group of these sonatas.

Treemonisha is a 1911 opera in English by Scott Joplin, the composer famous for piano rags such as “Maple Leaf Rag” and “The Entertainer.” Joplin wrote both its music and its libretto, the words sung by the performers. Often called a “ragtime opera,” it brings elements of his lively ragtime style into a longer stage work. The story centers on Treemonisha, an educated young woman in a Black community who challenges conjurers such as Zodzetrick. They exploit people’s fears and superstitions for their own benefit. After Treemonisha is rescued from danger, the community chooses her as its leader. She encourages her neighbors to value education, reason, and cooperation instead of letting the conjurers mislead them.

Marc Chagall was a Belarusian-French modernist painter born in Vitebsk, a city in present-day Belarus. Memories of Jewish folklore and village life shaped his colorful, dreamlike paintings, in which people, animals, and buildings often appear in surprising arrangements. His 1911 painting I and the Village brings together a large green-faced man and a white-faced farm animal, along with a small red figure and angular houses. These images suggest his memories of rural life while showing his interest in modern ways of organizing a picture. Chagall also made unusual self-portraits, including Self-Portrait with Seven Fingers, whose title points to an extra-fingered image of the artist. Together, these works show how he combined familiar stories and places with imaginative forms.

Optical illusions occur when what we see seems different from an image’s or object’s physical properties. Artists can create them with patterns, contrasts, shapes, and carefully arranged lines. In optical art, or Op Art, Victor Vasarely’s Zebra and Bridget Riley’s Movement in Squares use patterns that may seem to ripple, shift, or move even though the artworks are completely still. Other illusions make a flat picture appear three-dimensional. One way to suggest depth is linear perspective: an artist draws parallel lines, such as the edges of a road, so they seem to get closer together as they recede and eventually meet at a vanishing point. Artists can also play with our expectations of space, as M. C. Escher did in pictures of staircases that appear possible at first but could not exist in reality.

Pastel is a dry art medium made by mixing colored pigment with a binder and shaping the mixture into sticks. Artists draw with these sticks directly on paper or another textured surface, building up color with strokes that can be blended or layered. Pastels can create both soft, hazy effects and strong, vivid colors. Unlike paint, they do not need to be mixed with water or another liquid before use. Edvard Munch used pastel for two versions of his famous composition The Scream. It shows a lone, distressed figure on a bridge, pressing its hands to its head beneath a turbulent red-orange sky. Remembering both the pigment-and-binder sticks and this striking image helps connect the medium, pastel, with the artwork, The Scream.

Gustave Caillebotte was a French painter associated with Impressionism, a movement that often captured everyday life and the changing effects of light. His 1875 painting The Floor Scrapers shows three laborers kneeling to scrape a parquet floor. The official Salon rejected it, but Caillebotte later displayed it at an Impressionist exhibition in Paris. His best-known work, Paris Street; Rainy Day, was painted in 1877. It shows sharply dressed pedestrians carrying umbrellas across a broad Paris intersection near Place de Dublin. The wet cobblestones reflect the light, while the wide streets and buildings show how modern Paris looked at the time. Caillebotte’s careful perspective and attention to ordinary scenes make his paintings distinctive.

Assassins is a musical with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim and a book by John Weidman. Instead of telling one continuous story, it uses a dark, episodic structure to bring together people from different periods who assassinated or tried to assassinate U.S. presidents. Its characters include Charles Guiteau, who killed President James Garfield, and Lee Harvey Oswald, who killed President John F. Kennedy. Another character is John Wilkes Booth, the actor who assassinated President Abraham Lincoln. In “The Gun Song,” Booth sings, “Move your little finger and you can change the world,” expressing the dangerous idea that an act of violence can make someone important. Through songs and scenes that mix history with fiction, Assassins examines political violence and the desire to be noticed.

Yo-Yo Ma is a cellist born in Paris to Chinese parents and raised in the United States. He became famous for his expressive playing and extensive recordings of classical music, including works for solo cello. His instrument, the cello, is a large bowed string instrument with a deep, warm sound. Ma’s playing is also heard in films, including Ang Lee’s Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon. In 2000, he founded the Silk Road Ensemble, an international group of musicians from many traditions. Its name refers to the historic Silk Road trade routes that linked Asia and Europe. By bringing different instruments and musical styles together, the ensemble explores how cultures can exchange ideas and create something new.
