Italian Renaissance palaces, or palazzi, were large residences and civic buildings that expressed the wealth and public importance of their owners. Their façades often drew on ancient Roman architecture, using orderly rows of windows, pilasters, and carefully balanced proportions. In Florence, Leon Battista Alberti designed the façade of Palazzo Rucellai for a wealthy merchant family. Its three stories are divided by pilasters, and its stonework appears stronger and more rugged on the lower level, then smoother and more refined above. Another Florentine example is Palazzo Vecchio, the city’s historic government seat, which shows that a palazzo could be a public building as well as a family home. Today, some former palaces, including Palazzo Pitti, serve as art museums.

An octave is a musical interval, or the perceived distance between two notes. It spans eight scale degrees when both ends are counted: C, D, E, F, G, A, B, and the next C form one octave. The two C notes have the same note name, but the higher C vibrates twice as fast as the lower C. Their frequencies therefore have a 2:1 ratio: if the lower note vibrates 200 times per second, the upper one vibrates 400 times per second. Because notes an octave apart sound closely related, the octave is considered one of the least dissonant intervals. You can hear octaves in melodies, where a tune leaps from a low note to a higher version of the same note.

Misty Copeland is an American ballet dancer who made history in 2015 when she became the first Black principal dancer at American Ballet Theatre, one of the country’s leading ballet companies. A principal dancer performs major roles and is among the company’s highest-ranking artists. Copeland’s achievement brought wider attention to the barriers Black dancers have faced in ballet, though she was not the first Black principal dancer at any major ballet company; Debra Austin had reached that rank earlier. Like many ballet dancers, Copeland performs en pointe, a technique in which a dancer balances and moves on the tips of the toes. Pointe shoes have reinforced toe boxes that help support the dancer’s feet, but performing en pointe still requires years of training, strength, and careful technique.

The Luncheon on the Grass is an 1863 painting by French artist Édouard Manet. It shows two fully clothed men sitting with a nude woman in a wooded setting, while another woman bathes in the background. The scene resembles an ordinary outdoor lunch, or picnic, but the contrast between modern clothing and nudity shocked many viewers. Manet drew on earlier art, including Titian’s Pastoral Concert, yet his direct presentation of the nude woman challenged traditional ways of painting such subjects. The official Paris Salon rejected the work, so Manet exhibited it at the Salon des Refusés, a show for rejected artworks. Today, The Luncheon on the Grass is considered an important work in the development of modern art.

The Human Condition is an oil painting by Belgian artist René Magritte. An easel stands in front of a window, and the landscape painted on its canvas lines up with the scenery outside. At first glance, the canvas seems to be part of the view, but it may be hiding what is actually beyond the window. Magritte also made a second work with the same title that uses a seascape instead of a landscape. He was a Surrealist, part of a 20th-century art movement that often explored dreams and unexpected combinations of familiar things. Here, Magritte uses an ordinary room, window, and painting to raise a question: are we seeing the world itself, or only an image of it?

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart completed his Clarinet Concerto in A major, K. 622 in 1791, near the end of his life. He wrote it for Anton Stadler, an Austrian clarinet virtuoso working in Vienna and a friend of the composer. Stadler played a basset clarinet, a version of the instrument with an extended lower range, and Mozart used those extra-deep notes in the solo part. In a concerto, one musician plays a featured part while an orchestra provides accompaniment and joins in the musical conversation. This concerto has three movements: a lively opening, a slow and expressive middle movement, and a closing rondo. A rondo brings back a main theme between contrasting sections; here, that recurring theme gives the finale a buoyant feel.

Heitor Villa-Lobos was a Brazilian composer who became a central figure in 20th-century art music by bringing together European classical techniques and the sounds of Brazil. He drew inspiration from folk traditions and urban street music, using their rhythms, melodies, and instrumental styles in works for concert audiences. His Chôros cycle takes its name from a Brazilian style of popular instrumental music and explores its lively, varied character. Between 1930 and 1945, Villa-Lobos also wrote nine compositions called Bachianas Brasileiras. In this cycle, he combined Brazilian musical idioms with techniques associated with the European composer J. S. Bach, including counterpoint, in which independent melodies sound together. These works show how Villa-Lobos made Brazilian traditions a distinctive part of modern classical music.

The Battle Hymn of the Republic is a patriotic American song written by Julia Ward Howe during the Civil War. Howe used the melody of “John Brown’s Body,” a marching song popular with Union soldiers about the abolitionist John Brown, whose “soul is marching on.” She gave the tune new lyrics that connect the Union cause with religious ideas about justice. The song begins “Mine eyes have seen the glory” and declares that “God’s truth is marching on.” Its chorus repeats the four-word refrain “Glory, glory, hallelujah.” Because it was easy to sing and carried a powerful message, the Battle Hymn of the Republic became one of the best-known songs associated with the Civil War.

Guerrillero Heroico is a famous photograph of Argentine revolutionary Che Guevara taken by Cuban photographer Alberto Korda in Havana on March 5, 1960. Korda was covering a memorial service for victims of the La Coubre explosion when he captured Guevara wearing a beret with a star and gazing beyond the camera. The title means “Heroic Guerrilla.” Guevara had helped Fidel Castro’s revolution in Cuba, and the portrait came to symbolize revolutionary politics far beyond the country. Years later, Korda allowed Italian publisher Giangiacomo Feltrinelli to reproduce the photograph without charge. It spread around the world on posters, clothing, and other objects, becoming one of the most widely reproduced political images in history.

Strange Fruit is a 1939 protest song made famous by jazz singer Billie Holiday, who was nicknamed “Lady Day.” Its haunting lyrics describe “strange fruit” hanging from Southern trees: the bodies of Black people murdered by lynching. By contrasting the scent of magnolia with the smell of burning flesh, the song turns familiar images of the Southern landscape into an indictment of racist violence. It began as a poem by Abel Meeropol, a New York City schoolteacher and songwriter, after he saw a photograph of a lynching in Indiana. Meeropol published the poem under the pseudonym Lewis Allan and later set it to music. Holiday’s recording brought the song to a wide audience, and it remains a powerful example of music used to confront injustice.

In Tchaikovsky’s ballet The Sleeping Beauty, Princess Aurora celebrates her sixteenth birthday at a royal party. Four suitors come to meet her, and she dances with them in the famous Rose Adagio. But the celebration turns dangerous when the wicked fairy Carabosse’s curse takes effect: Aurora pricks her finger and falls asleep. The kind Lilac Fairy softens the curse so that Aurora will sleep for a hundred years rather than die. After a century has passed, the visiting nobleman Prince Florimund finds Aurora and awakens her with a kiss. The ballet ends with their wedding. Aurora’s story is told through music and dance, and her birthday scene and awakening are two of its most important moments.

Hungarian bridges connect places and tell stories about the country’s landscape and history. In Hortobágy National Park, on Hungary’s Great Plain, the stone Nine-Arched Bridge crosses a waterway used by people traveling through the region. Farther west, in the capital, Budapest, the Széchenyi Chain Bridge spans the Danube River between Buda and Pest. Named for the Hungarian reformer István Széchenyi, it opened in 1849 as the first permanent bridge across the Danube in Budapest. Its design uses heavy chains to support the roadway, making it a famous 19th-century suspension bridge. The bridge was destroyed during World War II but later rebuilt. Together, the Nine-Arched Bridge and the Széchenyi Chain Bridge are two well-known examples of Hungarian bridges.

Johannes Vermeer was a 17th-century painter from the Netherlands, active during the Dutch Golden Age. He lived in Delft and often painted quiet moments of everyday life, especially people in rooms lit by daylight. In The Milkmaid, a woman carefully pours milk into a bowl beside a table holding bread. Although she is doing an ordinary task, Vermeer’s use of light and detail gives the scene a sense of calm importance. Another famous work, Girl with a Pearl Earring, shows a young woman turning toward the viewer while wearing a large pearl earring. Vermeer also painted his hometown in the celebrated cityscape View of Delft. Together, these works show his skill at capturing light, familiar places, and small moments.

Woman and Child on the Balcony is a painting by Berthe Morisot, one of the few prominent women in the French Impressionist movement. It shows a woman and a young girl standing beside a balcony railing and looking out over Paris. The balcony gives them a view of the city while placing the figures in an everyday, personal moment. Impressionist painters were interested in how light and atmosphere could make a scene feel immediate. They often painted outdoors and used loose, sketch-like brushstrokes rather than carefully outlining every detail. Morisot brought this approach to scenes of modern life, including women and children. If you are asked to name the painting with the woman and girl overlooking Paris, it is Woman and Child on the Balcony; its artist is Berthe Morisot.

Figaro is a quick-witted barber and servant who appears in two famous comic operas. In Gioachino Rossini’s The Barber of Seville, he helps Count Almaviva win the love of Rosina by arranging meetings and clever disguises. Figaro makes his entrance with the lively aria “Largo al factotum,” in which he boasts that everyone in Seville needs his help; its rapid refrain repeats his name several times. Figaro returns in Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro, where he is preparing to marry Susanna while navigating trouble caused by the Count. In that opera, he also teases the young page Cherubino about leaving his carefree life for the military in the aria “Non più andrai.”

The Lady and the Unicorn is a celebrated cycle of six French tapestries made in the late 15th century. Each hanging shows a richly dressed woman with a unicorn, a fantastical creature with one long horn. The tapestries use a millefleur background, meaning that their fields are filled with many small flowers. Five panels are commonly interpreted as allegories of the senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. The sixth is more mysterious. It shows the woman beside a jewel casket beneath a tent bearing the French motto “À mon seul désir,” often translated as “To my sole desire.” Scholars still debate whether this scene represents desire, love, or a choice to set aside worldly pleasures.

Mary Cassatt was an American painter and printmaker born in 1844 in Allegheny City, Pennsylvania. She moved to Paris and became associated with Impressionism, a 19th-century art movement that often showed everyday life through loose brushwork and close attention to light and color. Edgar Degas invited Cassatt to exhibit with the Impressionists in 1877. Cassatt is especially known for intimate scenes of women and children, including moments of care at home. In her 1893 painting The Child’s Bath, a seated woman supports a young child while washing the child’s feet in a basin. Viewed from above, the scene draws attention to their closeness and the woman’s careful movements. The painting is in the collection of the Art Institute of Chicago.

Vitruvian Man is a late-15th-century drawing by the Italian Renaissance artist Leonardo da Vinci. It shows a nude man with overlapping arms and legs in two positions, arranged to fit inside both a circle and a square. Leonardo used the drawing to explore ideal human proportions: how the lengths and positions of different body parts relate to one another. The ideas came from Vitruvius, an ancient Roman architect who described human proportions in his book De architectura. By turning those written principles into an image, Leonardo connected art with mathematics, anatomy, and architecture. The drawing reflects a Renaissance interest in studying the human body and using observation and measurement to understand the world.

Thelonious Monk was an American jazz pianist and composer born in Rocky Mount, North Carolina, in 1917. His playing sounded unlike anyone else’s: he used angular melodies, unexpected silences, and dissonant harmonies—combinations of notes that can sound tense or surprising. Monk helped shape modern jazz and wrote pieces that became standards, meaning other musicians continued to learn and perform them. One of his best-known compositions is “Round Midnight,” a slow, chromatic jazz ballad written in the 1940s. Chromatic melodies use notes that move in small steps, adding to the piece’s expressive mood. Early recordings by trumpeter Cootie Williams and later performances by Miles Davis helped make it widely known. Monk also composed the lively jazz standard “Straight, No Chaser.”

Ships are a recurring subject in nautical painting, which depicts the sea and life on the water. Artists have painted many kinds of ships, from sail-powered vessels to steamships and warships, sometimes using them to tell stories about travel, danger, or changes in technology. In J.M.W. Turner’s The Fighting Temeraire, an aging naval ship is towed to its final berth by a steam-powered tugboat. Another maritime painting, Winslow Homer’s 1899 The Gulf Stream, focuses on a Black fisherman bracing himself in a small boat amid rough, shark-infested water. A larger vessel appears on the distant horizon. Together, these paintings show that ships can be the main subject of a work or a small but meaningful part of a wider scene.

Wynton Marsalis is an American jazz trumpeter, composer, and educator from New Orleans, a city famous for its jazz history. He grew up in a musical family: his father, Ellis Marsalis Jr., was a jazz pianist and teacher, and his brother Branford is a saxophonist. Wynton has performed and recorded both jazz and classical music, and his jazz albums include Black Codes (From the Underground). As artistic director of Jazz at Lincoln Center in New York City, he helps bring jazz performances and education to audiences. He also composed Blood on the Fields, a large-scale jazz work about slavery and the struggle for freedom. In 1997, it became the first jazz composition to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music.

Conga is a lively Cuban dance and musical style associated with carnival celebrations. In the dance, people form a conga line, moving one behind another to a strong rhythm, often with their hands on the shoulders or waist of the person in front. The word “conga” can refer to the music, the dance, or the line of dancers itself. Conga lines became popular in American entertainment partly through Cuban musician and actor Desi Arnaz. He starred with his real-life wife, comedian Lucille Ball, in the 1950s television sitcom I Love Lucy. Ball’s character, Lucy Ricardo, memorably struggled to keep up with a chocolate-factory conveyor belt and appeared in an advertisement for a tonic called Vitameatavegamin.

The Light of the World is a religious painting by the English artist William Holman Hunt, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood. It shows Christ standing outside a closed door overgrown with ivy and weeds, holding a lantern and knocking. The door has no handle on the outside: it represents a person’s heart, which must be opened from within to welcome Christ. The lantern’s light suggests spiritual guidance in darkness, giving the painting its title. Hunt and other Pre-Raphaelite artists used vivid colors and carefully observed details while drawing inspiration from art made before the painter Raphael. Hunt also painted The Scapegoat and The Finding of the Saviour in the Temple, both of which explore religious subjects.

Antoine-Jean Gros was a French painter trained in the studio of Jacques-Louis David. He became known for dramatic paintings of Napoleon’s military campaigns that combined carefully observed details with strong emotion. In Bonaparte Visiting the Plague Victims of Jaffa (1804), Gros shows Napoleon tending a plague-stricken soldier during a campaign in the Middle East. The painting reflects the growing French interest in Orientalism, or European depictions of places and cultures seen as Eastern, following Napoleon’s invasion of Egypt. Gros’s monumental 1808 painting Napoleon on the Battlefield of Eylau shows the emperor on horseback amid wounded soldiers on a snowy battlefield. It commemorates the French victory over Russian and Prussian forces at the Battle of Eylau in 1807, while also showing the human cost of war.

Pale Blue Dot is a 1990 photograph of Earth taken by NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft from the outer Solar System. At that great distance, Earth appears as a tiny speck caught in a ray of sunlight rather than as the detailed world we know. Astronomer and science communicator Carl Sagan helped persuade NASA to turn Voyager’s camera back toward Earth before the spacecraft continued its journey. He later popularized the image in his 1994 book Pale Blue Dot, which reflects on humanity’s place in the cosmos. Sagan urged readers to look again at the dot: “That’s home. That’s us.” Like the earlier Earthrise and The Blue Marble photographs, Pale Blue Dot gives viewers a new perspective on our planet, but from much farther away.

Borobudur is a monumental Buddhist temple in Central Java, Indonesia, built around the ninth century. It is the world’s largest Buddhist temple and rises like a stepped pyramid, with stacked terraces that visitors can climb. Its walls are covered with carved relief panels depicting Buddhist teachings and scenes of daily life, while numerous seated Buddha statues appear throughout the complex. The temple’s design represents a journey toward enlightenment: as visitors move upward, they pass through levels that symbolize stages of Buddhist understanding. Borobudur stands on the island of Java, one of the major islands of Indonesia, a Southeast Asian country whose capital is Jakarta.

A tritone is a musical interval spanning three whole tones, or six semitones. In equal-tempered music, it divides the octave exactly in half. Depending on how its notes are written, it can be called an augmented fourth, such as C to F♯, or a diminished fifth, such as C to G♭. Tritones often sound tense, making them useful in dominant seventh chords. For example, C–E–G–B♭ is a C dominant seventh chord, usually written C7: it has a C major triad plus the lowered seventh, B♭. Its notes E and B♭ form a tritone that typically resolves to F and A when C7 moves to an F major chord. Jazz musicians can also replace a dominant chord with another dominant chord a tritone away, a technique called tritone substitution.

Gothic architecture developed in 12th-century France after the Romanesque style and was later succeeded by Renaissance architecture. Its pointed arches, rib vaults, and flying buttresses helped builders create taller churches with thinner walls and larger windows. Rib vaults supported the ceilings, while flying buttresses carried some of the roof’s weight outward, making room for stained glass that filled interiors with colored light. An important early example is the rebuilt choir of the Basilica of Saint-Denis near Paris. Begun around 1140 under the sponsorship of Abbot Suger, it used an ambulatory, or walkway around the choir, and radiating chapels to admit more light. Notre-Dame de Paris is another famous Gothic cathedral, known for its rose windows and flying buttresses.

The London symphonies are Joseph Haydn’s final group of twelve symphonies, numbered 93 through 104. He composed them for his visits to England in the 1790s, where they were performed for enthusiastic London audiences. A symphony is a large-scale orchestral work, usually divided into several movements, or sections. These works show Haydn’s skill at combining clear Classical-period forms with lively rhythms, memorable melodies, and surprises. One of the best-known is Symphony No. 100, nicknamed the “Military” symphony. In its second movement, sudden loud passages introduce a triangle, cymbals, and bass drum. Their striking sounds create a Turkish-style effect that listeners of Haydn’s time associated with military music.

The Beethoven Frieze is a monumental artwork created by Austrian artist Gustav Klimt for the 1902 Vienna Secession exhibition honoring composer Ludwig van Beethoven. Painted across three walls, it tells a symbolic story of humanity’s search for happiness and its struggle against threatening forces. In its central section, three Gorgons—figures from Greek mythology—stand beside Typhoeus, a hairy brown monster. The artwork ends with an image of joy and love, suggesting that art can help people overcome suffering. Klimt co-founded the Vienna Secession, a movement that sought new ways to make and exhibit art. He is also known for The Kiss, which shows an embracing couple, and for his portraits of Adele Bloch-Bauer.

The Pietà is a scene in Christian art showing the Virgin Mary holding the body of her son, Jesus Christ, across her lap after his Crucifixion. The name comes from an Italian word meaning “pity” or “compassion,” and the scene invites viewers to reflect on Mary’s grief and Jesus’s death. Artists have depicted the Pietà in paintings and sculptures, but one of the most famous examples is a marble sculpture completed in 1499 by the Renaissance artist Michelangelo. It is displayed in St. Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City. Michelangelo also carved the colossal marble David, which stands in Florence. Remembering these two works can help you connect the name of the scene, Pietà, with its celebrated sculptor, Michelangelo.

Ludwig van Beethoven wrote 32 piano sonatas, a landmark collection of solo-keyboard music that shows how his style changed from the Classical period into a more dramatic and experimental one. His early “Pathétique” Sonata has a lyrical slow movement marked Adagio cantabile, while the much later “Hammerklavier” Sonata ends with a massive fugue, in which musical lines enter and weave together. Another famous sonata, the “Moonlight,” begins with an unusually slow, quiet movement. Beethoven also wrote the “Appassionata” Sonata, dedicated to Count Franz von Brunswick. Its second movement presents a tranquil theme and variations in D-flat major, then leads directly, without a pause, into a stormy finale in F minor. Beethoven was also the composer of the Eroica Symphony.

Sergei Prokofiev was a Russian and Soviet composer, pianist, and conductor known for music that could be bold, playful, and dramatic. He left Russia in 1918, spent years working abroad, and returned to the Soviet Union in 1936. His works include the ballet Romeo and Juliet and Peter and the Wolf, a 1936 “symphonic fairy tale” for narrator and orchestra. In this story, each character has a distinctive musical sound: a flute represents the bird, an oboe the duck, and strings represent Peter. A narrator tells how Peter, despite his grandfather’s warning about a dangerous wolf, works with the bird to catch it. The changing instruments help listeners follow the action and recognize the characters, making Peter and the Wolf a popular introduction to orchestral music.

Louis Comfort Tiffany (1848–1933) was an American artist and designer best known for colorful stained-glass windows and richly patterned lamps. He was the son of Charles Lewis Tiffany, the founder of the jewelry company Tiffany & Co., but built his own reputation in the decorative arts. Tiffany’s studio developed an iridescent, handmade glass that he trademarked as Favrile glass. Its shimmering colors were part of the glass itself, rather than simply painted onto the surface. Artists at his studio shaped Favrile glass into decorative vases and other vessels and used it to create lamp shades. Inspired by flowers, plants, and other natural forms, Tiffany’s designs helped make glass both a useful material and an expressive art form.

Opera is a staged musical work that tells a dramatic story through singing, instrumental music, and theatrical action. Performers play characters, act out events, and sing with accompaniment from an orchestra. Operas often move between recitatives and arias. A recitative is a speech-like style of singing that follows the rhythms of spoken language; it commonly carries dialogue and moves the plot forward. An aria is a more melodic song in which a character may express feelings or reflect on events. Operas can be serious or comic. Two famous comic operas are Gioachino Rossini’s The Barber of Seville and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro, both featuring the character Figaro.

Piet Mondrian was a Dutch painter who helped found De Stijl with artist Theo van Doesburg. This avant-garde movement aimed to make art from simple geometric forms rather than realistic images. Mondrian became famous for abstract compositions of straight black horizontal and vertical lines, white spaces, and blocks of the primary colors: red, yellow, and blue. He believed that reducing paintings to these basic elements could create a sense of balance and order. His late painting Broadway Boogie-Woogie was inspired by New York City: its grid suggests Manhattan’s streets, while its lively pattern evokes the rhythm of jazz. Small yellow squares in the painting can be seen as taxis moving through the city.

Jean-Honoré Fragonard was a leading French Rococo painter known for lively, playful scenes of romance and leisure. He trained in Paris under the painter François Boucher, won the Prix de Rome in 1752, and later studied in Italy. His most famous painting, The Swing, is set in a lush garden. A young woman in a pink dress swings through the air while an older man pulls the ropes from behind. As she swings toward a concealed admirer, one of her slippers flies off. Nearby, a putto—a small, childlike figure in the artwork—holds a finger to his lips, as if asking viewers to keep the flirtation secret. The painting’s soft colors, movement, and playful mood are characteristic of Rococo art.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir was a French Impressionist painter who captured everyday pleasure, especially people talking, dancing, and spending time with friends. Like other Impressionists, he used visible brushstrokes and lively effects of light to give his paintings a sense of the moment. In his celebrated 1876 painting Bal du moulin de la Galette, dancers and other visitors mingle at an outdoor dance hall in the Montmartre neighborhood of Paris. Another famous work, Luncheon of the Boating Party, shows friends sharing a meal on a balcony at the Maison Fournaise, a restaurant overlooking the Seine River. A small dog sits near the diners in the foreground. Both paintings show Renoir’s interest in social gatherings and sunlit figures.

Aram Khachaturian was an Armenian-Soviet composer who brought the rhythms and melodies of Armenian folk music into orchestral works and ballets. His best-known ballets include Spartacus and Gayane. Gayane is set on an Armenian collective farm and follows a young woman whose wedding celebrations are disrupted by a rival’s attack. Its most famous episode, the fast and energetic “Sabre Dance,” is often performed on its own and has appeared in films and popular culture. Khachaturian worked in the Soviet Union, where the government sometimes praised composers but also criticized music it considered unsuitable. Remembering the link between Khachaturian, Gayane, and the “Sabre Dance” helps identify both the composer and the ballet.

Along the River During the Qingming Festival is a celebrated Chinese handscroll painted by Zhang Zeduan during the Northern Song dynasty. A handscroll is viewed by unrolling it section by section, so the scene unfolds as the viewer moves along it. This long painting shows a springtime panorama of life in and around Kaifeng, the Northern Song capital. Boats travel along the river, while merchants, travelers, and residents fill the busy streets. One of its most recognizable features is the arched Rainbow Bridge, crowded with people above the water. Rather than focusing on a single event, the painting brings together many small scenes to show the energy and variety of daily life in a thriving city.

The Tony Awards are annual honors for outstanding work in Broadway theater, including acting, directing, writing, and stage design. Their full name is the Antoinette Perry Awards for Excellence in Broadway Theatre. Antoinette Perry was an actress, director, and producer who helped found the American Theatre Wing and served as its president. After her death, the awards were named in her honor; “Tony” comes from her first name. Winning a Tony is one of Broadway’s highest achievements. The award is also the “T” in EGOT, a term for someone who has won an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony. Liza Minnelli is one performer who has achieved an EGOT.

The exposition is the opening main section of a movement written in sonata form. It introduces the principal musical themes, usually beginning in the tonic, or home key, before moving toward a contrasting key. The development section follows, exploring and transforming those themes. After the development comes the recapitulation, which brings the principal themes back, generally placing them in the tonic key. Some composers direct performers to repeat the exposition, giving listeners another chance to hear its themes before the development begins. A famous example is the long first movement of Ludwig van Beethoven’s Eroica Symphony, also known as Symphony No. 3: repeating its exposition makes the movement even longer.

Ralph Vaughan Williams was an English composer whose music often drew on folk songs, older English music, poetry, and literature. His Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis takes its melody from a 16th-century English composer, while his Fantasia on “Greensleeves” uses a traditional tune. Vaughan Williams also wrote music for voices and orchestra. His Serenade to Music sets words by William Shakespeare and was written for 16 solo voices and string orchestra. His first symphony, A Sea Symphony, was also his first large-scale work for choir and orchestra. Premiered in 1910, it sets poems from Walt Whitman’s Leaves of Grass and opens with the choir singing “Behold, the sea itself.”

The Sugar Plum Fairy is the ruler of the Land of Sweets in Act II of The Nutcracker, a ballet about a girl’s magical Christmas Eve journey. She welcomes the girl and her companion to her kingdom, where a celebration of dances takes place. Her best-known dance is a delicate solo often called the “Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy.” Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote the ballet’s score, including the solo’s distinctive, bell-like music. The Nutcracker premiered in St. Petersburg, Russia, in 1892 and has since become a Christmas tradition in many countries. In George Balanchine’s influential 1954 staging, American ballerina Maria Tallchief performed the role of the Sugar Plum Fairy.

La Marseillaise is France’s national anthem. Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle wrote it in Strasbourg in 1792 as a call to arms for the Army of the Rhine during the French Revolution. Its forceful melody later became a symbol of France. The Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky used that melody to represent Napoleon’s advancing French army in his 1812 Overture. Written in 1880, the orchestral work commemorates Russia’s victory over Napoleon’s invasion in 1812. It begins with the hymn “O Lord, Save Thy People,” also includes the folk song “At the Gate,” and uses “God Save the Tsar” to signal the French army’s defeat. Performances of its dramatic climax often include cannon fire.

The Wilton Diptych is a small, two-panel English devotional altarpiece made in the late fourteenth century. A diptych has two hinged panels that can be opened for prayer or folded shut. On the left, King Richard II kneels wearing his white-hart badge, a symbol associated with him. Three saints—John the Baptist, Edward the Confessor, and Edmund the Martyr—present him to the Virgin Mary and the Christ Child on the right. Mary and the angels around her wear blue, a color often used for Mary in medieval art. The painting connects Richard’s kingship with Christian faith: he appears not as a ruler giving orders, but as a worshipper seeking Mary’s blessing.

C418 is the stage name of Daniel Rosenfeld, a German electronic musician and composer best known for music he created for Minecraft. Minecraft is a sandbox video game in which players gather resources, explore a world made of cubic blocks, and build structures. C418’s gentle, atmospheric tracks often play while players explore or work on their creations, giving the game a calm feeling even when danger is nearby. His Minecraft music includes “Subwoofer Lullaby” and “Stal”; players can also find some of his songs on music discs within the game. One familiar danger is the creeper, a hostile creature that can explode and damage what players have built. C418’s music has become closely associated with the experience of playing Minecraft.

The Burghers of Calais is a sculptural group by the French artist Auguste Rodin. It shows six prominent citizens of Calais, a French port city besieged by English forces during the Hundred Years’ War. In 1347, after a long siege, the men offered themselves as hostages to help save their city. Rodin portrayed them standing together but expressing fear, sorrow, and determination in different ways, rather than presenting them as triumphant heroes. Their gestures and faces draw attention to the human cost of war and the courage involved in their decision. To remember the work, connect its title to the people it depicts: “burghers” means townspeople, and Calais is the city they sought to protect.

The Blue Marble is a famous color photograph of Earth taken by the Apollo 17 crew in December 1972 as they traveled toward the Moon. It shows the fully illuminated planet against the darkness of space, with Africa and Antarctica visible. The photograph’s name comes from Earth’s round shape and its blue oceans, which make it resemble a marble. Apollo 17’s crew included Eugene Cernan, Ronald Evans, and Harrison Schmitt, and it was the final mission to land astronauts on the Moon. The Blue Marble is one of several well-known photographs that show Earth from space. Earthrise shows Earth above the Moon’s surface, while Pale Blue Dot shows our planet as a tiny speck of light.

Girl with a Pearl Earring is a celebrated 17th-century painting by Johannes Vermeer, a Dutch Golden Age artist born in Delft. It shows a young woman turning toward the viewer against a nearly black background. She wears a blue-and-yellow head covering and a large pearl earring that catches the light. Vermeer used ultramarine, an expensive blue pigment made from lapis lazuli, in her headscarf. The painting is often called a tronie: a study of a face, expression, or costume rather than a formal portrait of a named person. The young woman’s identity is unknown. Today, Girl with a Pearl Earring is held by the Mauritshuis museum in The Hague. Vermeer’s other well-known works include The Milkmaid and View of Delft.

Knight, Death, and the Devil is a 1513 engraving by the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer. It shows an armored rider moving steadily through a rugged landscape while two threatening figures accompany him: Death, shown as a rotting corpse holding an hourglass, and the Devil, a goat-headed figure carrying a halberd, or long-handled weapon. The hourglass suggests that life is short, while the Devil represents temptation and danger. Dürer used fine engraved lines to create detailed textures and strong contrasts of light and shadow. He also made the 1514 engraving Melencolia I, which shows a seated winged figure surrounded by geometric objects and carpentry tools. Both prints are celebrated for their intricate detail and mysterious symbolism.

Merce Cunningham was an American modern dancer and choreographer who changed how people thought about dance. He studied at the Cornish School in Seattle, danced with Martha Graham’s company, and founded his own dance company in 1953. Cunningham believed that movement did not have to tell a story or closely follow music. He often used chance procedures, such as random choices, to decide the order of steps or other parts of a performance. His longtime collaborator, the American composer John Cage, also used chance in his work, sometimes drawing on the I Ching, an ancient Chinese text. Cage composed 4’33”, a piece in which performers make no intentional sounds for four minutes and thirty-three seconds, inviting audiences to notice the sounds around them.

D minor is a key in Western music built around the note D. Its key signature has one flat, B-flat, and its natural minor scale is D, E, F, G, A, B-flat, C, and back to D. Johann Sebastian Bach wrote many works for the organ, a keyboard instrument that sends air through pipes to make sound. One famous organ piece associated with him is Toccata and Fugue in D minor, catalogued as BWV 565. It begins with a dramatic flourish, followed by a descending passage and a sustained chord. The earliest known source of this work is a manuscript copied by Johannes Ringk. The title names both the key, D minor, and the work’s two sections: a free-flowing toccata and a fugue built from a recurring musical idea.

La Damnation de Faust (The Damnation of Faust) is a dramatic legend by the French Romantic composer Hector Berlioz. Inspired by Goethe’s Faust, it tells of a scholar who is tempted by Mephistopheles, a devilish figure, and makes a bargain that leads toward disaster. Berlioz wrote the work for singers, chorus, and orchestra, combining storytelling with vivid musical scenes rather than presenting it as a conventional opera. It opens with the Rákóczi March, a stirring melody associated with a Hungarian national hero. Berlioz was famous for using orchestral instruments to create striking sounds and dramatic effects. Another of his best-known works is Symphonie fantastique. Remember the pairing: La Damnation de Faust is the work, and Hector Berlioz is its composer.

Gustave Eiffel was a French civil engineer whose innovative metal structures helped shape modern architecture. His best-known project is the Eiffel Tower, a roughly 300-meter-tall iron lattice tower built on the Champ de Mars in Paris for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, or World’s Fair. Although some people initially disliked its unusual appearance, it became one of the world’s most recognizable landmarks. Eiffel also worked on railway structures, including Budapest’s Nyugati Station. Another important contribution is less visible: after the original engineer died, sculptor Auguste Bartholdi asked Eiffel to design the iron framework inside the Statue of Liberty. That framework supports the monument’s copper exterior while allowing it to withstand wind. The statue was a gift from France to the United States.

Pop Art emerged in the mid-20th century and turned images from everyday popular culture into fine art. Instead of focusing only on traditional subjects, Pop artists borrowed from advertising, comic strips, product packaging, movies, and celebrity photographs. They often used bright colors, bold outlines, repeated images, and techniques that made their work look mass-produced. Andy Warhol, for example, made silkscreen prints of celebrities and consumer products, while Roy Lichtenstein imitated comic-book printing with Ben-Day dots. Lichtenstein’s 1963 painting Whaam! is a diptych, meaning it has two panels. Adapted from a war comic, it shows a fighter jet firing a rocket at another plane, which bursts into an explosion accompanied by the large comic-book sound effect “WHAAM!” Pop Art asks viewers to reconsider the images they encounter every day.

Elektra is a one-act opera with music by the German composer Richard Strauss and a libretto, or text, by Hugo von Hofmannsthal. Based on an ancient Greek story, it follows Elektra, the daughter of Agamemnon, as she becomes consumed by the need to avenge her father’s murder. Her brother Orestes returns and kills those responsible, and Elektra celebrates so intensely that she dances herself to death. Strauss’s forceful, highly dissonant music uses clashing sounds to express her anger and obsession. Strauss and von Hofmannsthal also worked together on the comic opera Der Rosenkavalier, in which Octavian presents Sophie with a silver rose. Another well-known work by Richard Strauss is the tone poem Also sprach Zarathustra.

Jean Sibelius was a Finnish composer whose music helped give Finland a distinct musical voice. He wrote seven symphonies and the tone poem Finlandia, which became closely associated with Finnish national identity. Many of his works draw on the Kalevala, Finland’s national epic. Elias Lönnrot assembled this collection of traditional stories and poems from oral poetry, and it was first published in 1835. Sibelius used its characters and legends in Kullervo, the Lemminkäinen Suite, and Tapiola. One movement of the Lemminkäinen Suite, The Swan of Tuonela, features a haunting English horn solo representing a swan in the underworld. Sibelius’s music often evokes the landscapes and myths of his homeland.

Erik Satie was a French modernist composer who challenged traditional ideas about classical music. He is best known for his short piano collections Gymnopédies and Gnossiennes, which use spare textures, gentle melodies, and unusual harmonies to create a distinctive mood. Satie also worked with artists in other fields. In 1917, he composed the score for Parade, a ballet created for Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes. Writer Jean Cocteau devised its scenario, and Pablo Picasso designed its sets and costumes. The ballet’s music included unexpected sounds, and its Paris premiere caused a notorious disturbance among the audience. Satie’s willingness to experiment made him an important influence on later composers.

Moai are monumental human statues carved by the Rapa Nui people on Easter Island, also known as Rapa Nui. They are often called “stone heads,” but many have torsos, and some once stood on stone platforms facing inland toward the communities they represented. Most moai were carved from volcanic tuff, a relatively soft rock, at Rano Raraku, the island’s principal quarry. Unfinished figures still remain in and around the crater, offering clues about how the statues were made. The Rapa Nui created the moai to honor important ancestors and express the strength of their communities. In 2022, a wildfire damaged a number of moai near Rano Raraku, drawing attention to the need to protect these sculptures.

Maurizio Cattelan is an Italian contemporary artist known for using humor and surprise to make people question what counts as art. His 2019 work Comedian, shown at Art Basel Miami Beach, consisted of a banana duct-taped to a gallery wall. The simple-looking piece drew worldwide attention, especially when artist David Datuna removed and ate the banana in an intervention he called a performance. Cattelan also created America, a functioning toilet made of 18-karat gold. Both works turn familiar objects into art: a piece of fruit becomes the center of a debate, while a luxurious toilet raises questions about wealth and value. Cattelan’s sculptures and installations are often satirical, meaning they use wit to challenge expectations about art and society.

A window is an opening in a building’s wall or roof that lets daylight in and usually provides a view. Most windows have glass panes, and some can be opened to bring in fresh air. Architects choose their size, shape, and placement to affect how a room looks and feels. Churches, for example, often use stained-glass windows, which turn sunlight into patterns of color. A bay window is a group of windows that projects outward from an exterior wall. It often has a large central pane with smaller side panes set at angles. This arrangement creates a small alcove inside the room and offers views in several directions.

Claude Monet painted Impression, Sunrise in 1872, showing the harbor of Le Havre, a French port city in Normandy, at dawn. Monet had spent much of his early life in Le Havre after his family moved there from Paris. In the painting, small boats appear as dark shapes on misty water, while an orange sun rises and casts a reflection across the harbor. Rather than carefully outlining every object, Monet used loose brushstrokes to capture the changing light and the feeling of a particular moment. Some critics mocked this unfinished-looking style; one compared the painting to “wallpaper in its embryonic state.” The word “Impression” in its title helped give Impressionism, the art movement most closely associated with Monet, its name.

Damien Hirst is a British contemporary artist and a leading figure in the Young British Artists movement. He is known for provocative sculptures and installations that explore death, medicine, and how people respond to both. One of his most famous works, The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living, displays a tiger shark preserved in formaldehyde inside a glass tank. Hirst also uses images associated with medicine, such as pills and surgical equipment, to make viewers think about health and mortality. His work reaches beyond galleries: he designed the cover of Canadian rapper Drake’s 2021 album Certified Lover Boy. The cover shows rows of pregnant-woman emojis, and the album includes the songs “Way 2 Sexy” and “Knife Talk.”

Odette is the enchanted princess at the center of Swan Lake, a ballet by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky that premiered at Moscow’s Bolshoi Theatre in 1877. The evil sorcerer Rothbart casts a spell that turns her into a white swan. Prince Siegfried meets Odette by a lake and hopes to break the spell, but Rothbart tries to deceive him with Odile, the black-swan character who resembles her. The same ballerina traditionally dances both Odette and Odile, showing their contrast through movement and expression. If a question asks for the princess transformed into a white swan, her name is Odette; if it asks for the Tchaikovsky ballet in which she appears, the answer is Swan Lake.

A musical mode is a way of organizing pitches around a central note, called a final or tonic. Like a scale, each mode has a particular pattern of intervals that gives it a distinctive sound. Modes were important in Gregorian chant, the monophonic religious music of the medieval church, and musicians still use them today, especially in jazz improvisation. Two examples are the Dorian and Mixolydian modes. Dorian sounds similar to a natural minor scale, but its sixth degree is raised by a half step. For example, D Dorian uses only the white keys of a piano, from D up to the next D: D, E, F, G, A, B, C, D. That B natural is its raised sixth, distinguishing it from D natural minor.

Rrose Sélavy was a feminine alter ego and pseudonym created by the French artist Marcel Duchamp. He used the name in his art, including the title of the readymade sculpture Why Not Sneeze, Rrose Sélavy? Duchamp also posed as Rrose Sélavy in feminine clothing for a series of portraits taken by Man Ray, an American artist and photographer associated with Dada and Surrealism. A readymade is an ordinary manufactured object that an artist presents as art, often to challenge ideas about what art can be. By inventing Rrose Sélavy, Duchamp similarly played with identity and authorship: a work could appear under a name other than his own.

Kinkaku-ji, commonly called the Golden Pavilion, is a three-story Zen Buddhist temple pavilion in Kyoto, Japan. It stands beside Mirror Pond in the Rokuon-ji temple complex, and gold leaf covers its upper two stories, giving the pavilion its famous appearance. The building also has a place in Japanese literature: it inspired Yukio Mishima’s novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion. The novel follows Mizoguchi, a young novice monk whose obsession with the pavilion ends when he sets it on fire. Mishima was a major Japanese writer who also wrote Confessions of a Mask. He died by seppuku, a form of ritual suicide, after a failed attempt to inspire a military coup.

Cross-hatching is a drawing technique that builds tone, or the appearance of light and dark, by laying one set of strokes over another so the lines intersect. Lines that are close together and cross frequently make an area look darker; lines spaced farther apart make it look lighter. Artists use cross-hatching in pencil illustrations and printmaking to suggest shadows, texture, and depth without filling an area with solid color. A related technique, hatching, also shades with lines, but its strokes run parallel in one direction and do not cross a second set. In hatching, artists adjust the spacing or density of those parallel strokes to create lighter or darker areas. The key difference is whether the sets of lines intersect.

Walking is a way sculptors suggest movement in a still object. Archaic Greek kouroi, statues of young men, often stand with one leg placed ahead of the other. This stiff pose echoes earlier Egyptian statues and suggests that the figure is about to take a step, even though it remains balanced and motionless. Centuries later, the Swiss sculptor Alberto Giacometti explored walking in a very different style. His figures are tall, thin, and rough-surfaced, with long limbs that seem to stride forward. His famous 1960 bronze Walking Man I shows a solitary man in mid-stride. In both the ancient kouros and Giacometti’s modern figure, the position of the legs helps viewers imagine the human action of walking.

Daniel Burnham was an American architect and urban planner who helped shape Chicago, the largest city in Illinois, on Lake Michigan. He worked with architect John Wellborn Root in a Chicago-based firm and served as a leading organizer of the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition, a world’s fair held in the city. Burnham later joined urban planner Edward H. Bennett to prepare a 1909 proposal called the Plan of Chicago. It imagined a more orderly, attractive city with radial boulevards, more parks, and an improved lakefront that people could enjoy. The plan was not built exactly as proposed, but it influenced Chicago’s growth and became an important example of city planning in the United States.

Marche slave, also called Slavic March, is a patriotic orchestral work written in 1876 by the Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. He composed it to show support for the Serbian people during their conflict with the Ottoman Empire. The music draws on two Serbian folk melodies and later quotes “God Save the Tsar,” the anthem of imperial Russia. Its changing moods suggest the drama of a battle and a hopeful victory, but despite its title, it does not keep the steady rhythm of a military marching tune. Marche slave is often performed alongside Tchaikovsky’s 1812 Overture, another patriotic orchestral piece. Tchaikovsky also wrote the ballet The Nutcracker and his Sixth Symphony, commonly called the Pathétique.

Degenerate Art was the English name for a Nazi campaign against modern art in Germany and for an exhibition that opened in Munich in July 1937. The Nazi regime confiscated works from German museums and displayed them in crowded, deliberately mocking arrangements, with insulting labels meant to make the art seem corrupt or worthless. The campaign targeted styles that did not fit Nazi ideas about what art should look like, including Expressionism and other experimental approaches. One artist whose work was condemned was Otto Dix, a German veteran of World War I. His antiwar triptych The War portrayed the suffering and destruction of combat, while his 1926 portrait Sylvia von Harden showed a modern woman in an unconventional style. Today, the exhibition is remembered as an example of political censorship of art.

Melencolia I is a 1514 engraving by the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Dürer. At its center, a winged figure sits in thought, surrounded by carpentry tools, a sphere, a large truncated polyhedron, and a magic square whose rows and columns add up to the same number. Although the figure has tools for making and measuring things, it seems unable to begin working. This contrast has led many viewers to see the print as an image of intellectual frustration: the desire to understand or create something, paired with the feeling of being stuck. Dürer was celebrated for prints full of fine detail and layered meaning. Another of his famous prints is Knight, Death, and the Devil.

A is the second note of the G major scale, which begins G, A, B. It is also an important reference pitch for tuning: an oboe traditionally sounds A so the rest of the orchestra can match it. Under standard concert pitch, this reference is A4, the A in the octave immediately above middle C, vibrating at 440 hertz (440 times per second). Some musicians have used other tuning standards, including “Verdi pitch,” which sets A4 at 432 hertz. The key of A minor has no sharps or flats because it is the relative minor of C major, while A major has three sharps. A major is also the dominant key of D major, making it a common key for the development section of a sonata-form piece in D major.

Billy Strayhorn was an American jazz pianist, composer, and arranger who worked for decades with bandleader Duke Ellington. Strayhorn wrote “Take the A Train,” which became the theme song of Ellington’s orchestra. Its title refers to the A subway train, a quick way to reach Harlem, the New York neighborhood central to much of Ellington’s music. Ellington’s orchestra was associated with Harlem’s Cotton Club, where it performed regularly. In 1956, Ellington’s career gained new attention at the Newport Jazz Festival when saxophonist Paul Gonsalves played an exciting extended solo during “Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue.” Strayhorn’s compositions and arrangements were an important part of the orchestra’s sound, making his long collaboration with Duke Ellington one of jazz’s most significant musical partnerships.

Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio was an Italian Baroque painter known for making scenes look vivid and immediate. He often used chiaroscuro, a strong contrast between light and shadow, to draw attention to important figures and actions. His people look natural rather than idealized, even in religious paintings. In The Calling of St. Matthew, Christ gestures toward Matthew, a bearded tax collector seated at a table, while a beam of light cuts through the dim room and falls on him. The light helps show the moment Matthew is called to follow Christ. Caravaggio also painted The Cardsharps, a scene of young men playing cards in which one player is being secretly cheated. Together, these works show his interest in dramatic lighting and believable human behavior.

How High the Moon is a jazz standard first introduced in the 1940 Broadway revue Two for the Show. Morgan Lewis composed the music, and Nancy Hamilton wrote the lyrics. A revue is a stage show made up of songs, sketches, and other short performances rather than one continuous story. After its Broadway debut, How High the Moon became popular with jazz musicians, who used its melody and chord changes as a starting point for their own interpretations and improvisations. Guitarist Les Paul and singer Mary Ford later recorded a hit version. If you are asked who wrote the song, remember the two different roles: Hamilton supplied the words, while Lewis supplied the music.

Phidias was a leading sculptor in ancient Greece during the fifth century BCE, when the statesman Pericles supported major building projects in Athens. He was renowned for monumental cult statues: large images of gods made for religious sites. His statue of Athena Parthenos stood inside the Parthenon and was chryselephantine, meaning it was made with gold and ivory. It showed Athena holding a small figure of Nike, the goddess of victory. Phidias also supervised major sculptures for the Parthenon, a temple dedicated to Athena on the Acropolis in Athens. Architects Ictinus and Callicrates designed the temple. Some of its sculptures later became known as the Elgin Marbles. In 1687, an explosion of ammunition stored inside the Parthenon badly damaged the building.

Cole Porter was an American composer and lyricist who wrote both the music and words for many Broadway songs. His 1934 musical Anything Goes is set aboard an ocean liner and features “You’re the Top” and “I Get a Kick Out of You.” Porter also wrote “Night and Day,” another of his best-known songs. For the 1935 Broadway musical Jubilee, he wrote “Begin the Beguine.” A beguine is a dance rhythm, and bandleader Artie Shaw’s 1938 big-band recording helped turn the song into a hit. Porter’s witty lyrics and memorable melodies remained popular beyond the stage: singer Ella Fitzgerald, nicknamed the “First Lady of Song,” recorded many of his works, including “I Get a Kick Out of You,” for her first songbook album.

The Sleeping Beauty is a ballet that premiered in St. Petersburg, Russia, in 1890. Its music was written by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, a Russian Romantic composer who also wrote the scores for Swan Lake and The Nutcracker. Marius Petipa choreographed the ballet, creating the dances that bring its fairy-tale story to life. At Princess Aurora’s christening, the evil fairy Carabosse curses her to prick her finger on a spindle and die. The Lilac Fairy, who has not yet given her gift, weakens the curse: instead of dying, Aurora will fall into a long sleep until a prince awakens her. The ballet is known for its graceful classical dancing and Tchaikovsky’s expressive music, which help tell the story alongside the dancers’ movements.

Gustav Mahler was an Austrian composer of the late Romantic era, famous for large, emotionally intense symphonies and songs for voice and orchestra. His song cycle Kindertotenlieder, meaning Songs on the Death of Children, sets poems by Friedrich Rückert about grief. Another major work, Das Lied von der Erde, or The Song of the Earth, combines features of a symphony and a song cycle. Its six movements draw on poetry and explore nature, loneliness, and the passing of life. One movement is called “The Solitary One in Autumn,” while the scherzo-like third movement makes extensive use of the pentatonic scale, a set of five notes common in many musical traditions. Mahler avoided calling this work his Ninth Symphony because he feared a supposed “curse of the ninth.”

Drumsticks are handheld percussion tools used to strike drumheads, cymbals, and other instruments. Drummers usually play with one in each hand, creating rhythms by changing how hard and where they strike. A typical drumstick is tapered: it becomes narrower toward the tip, which is the part that usually hits the instrument. Drumsticks are commonly made from hardwoods such as hickory or maple, though they come in different sizes and weights to suit different playing styles. Many have wooden tips, while others have molded nylon tips. Nylon tips are durable and often produce a brighter, more consistent sound when played on cymbals. Related striking tools include mallets and clappers, which are used with other percussion instruments.

A Japanese rock garden, also called a Zen garden or dry landscape garden, uses carefully placed stones, raked gravel, and sometimes a little moss instead of ponds and dense planting. The gravel’s patterns can suggest rippling water, while the stones may evoke mountains or islands. These gardens often use asymmetry and invite quiet observation. The best-known example is at Ryōan-ji, a Zen temple in Kyoto whose name is often translated as “Temple of the Peaceful Dragon.” There, visitors look from a veranda across white gravel at fifteen stones arranged in five groups. The restrained design shows how a garden can suggest a larger natural landscape with just a few elements.

The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood was an English artists’ movement founded in 1848 by John Everett Millais, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, and William Holman Hunt. Its members admired the vivid colors, careful observation of nature, and detailed compositions of early Italian painting before the artist Raphael, which gave the group its name. They often painted scenes from literature, religion, and history, filling them with realistic plants, flowers, and other details. One of the movement’s best-known paintings is Millais’s Ophelia. It shows the young woman from Shakespeare’s Hamlet floating in a stream after drowning, surrounded by colorful flowers. Hunt’s The Light of the World, which depicts Christ holding a lantern and knocking on an overgrown door, is another famous Pre-Raphaelite work.

The Buddhas of Bamiyan were two enormous standing Buddha figures carved into niches in a cliff in the Bamiyan Valley of central Afghanistan, in the Hindu Kush region. Created in the sixth century, they showed how Buddhism had spread along trade routes linking different parts of Asia. The larger statue stood about 55 meters tall, and the smaller one about 38 meters tall. Both were important examples of ancient Buddhist sculpture. In 2001, the Taliban, which controlled much of Afghanistan at the time, destroyed the statues with explosives. Their empty niches remain visible in the cliff and have become reminders of the loss of cultural heritage during conflict. The sculptures are collectively called the Buddhas of Bamiyan, and the landlocked country where they stood is Afghanistan, whose capital is Kabul.

Samuel Barber was an American composer born in West Chester, Pennsylvania, in 1910. He wrote expressive music for orchestras, singers, and the stage. His best-known work, Adagio for Strings, began as the slow movement of his String Quartet, Op. 11. Barber arranged it for string orchestra, and conductor Arturo Toscanini premiered it with the NBC Symphony Orchestra in 1938. Its solemn, emotional sound has made it a frequent choice for memorial services. Barber also wrote Knoxville: Summer of 1915, a work for voice and orchestra based on a text by James Agee. His opera Vanessa premiered at the Metropolitan Opera in 1958 and won him the Pulitzer Prize for Music.

Waltzing Matilda is an Australian folk song written in 1895 by poet Banjo Paterson while he was visiting an outback station. Often called Australia’s unofficial national anthem, it tells the story of a jolly swagman, an itinerant bush worker who travels with his belongings rolled in a bundle, or swag. He camps beside a billabong, a waterhole left behind by a changing river, and steals a jumbuck, an Australian word for sheep. When the sheep’s owner and the police arrive, the swagman leaps into the water rather than be caught. The title uses bush slang: “waltzing” means travelling on foot, and “Matilda” refers to the swag carried over the shoulder. Its memorable story and chorus have made the song a lasting symbol of Australian culture.

Taliesin is the Wisconsin home and studio of American architect Frank Lloyd Wright. He built it in the countryside near Spring Green, where its low rooflines and connection to the surrounding landscape reflected ideas behind his Prairie-style architecture. Fires damaged Taliesin more than once, and Wright rebuilt it several times, changing the estate as his work developed. It remained an important place for him to live, design buildings, and teach young architects, including during the period when he developed affordable Usonian houses. Wright also designed Fallingwater, a Pennsylvania house with terraces that extend over a waterfall. Later, he established Taliesin West, a winter home and studio in the Arizona desert. The name Taliesin usually refers to his Wisconsin estate, while Taliesin West is the Arizona site.

Charles Ives’s The Unanswered Question, composed in 1908, uses three groups of musicians to create a conversation without words. The strings play slow, sustained music that forms a calm, contemplative background. Against it, a solo trumpet repeatedly states a short phrase, as if asking a question. Four flutes reply with music that grows faster, louder, and more discordant, but they never settle on an answer. The contrast lets listeners hear the peaceful strings, the questioning trumpet, and the agitated flutes as separate layers. The flute is a high-pitched woodwind instrument; it also represents the bird in Prokofiev’s Peter and the Wolf. The title points to the piece’s central idea: some questions remain unresolved.

Gold is a rich yellow color named after the precious metal. Its warm, gleaming appearance can suggest light, wealth, or importance, so artists may use it to draw attention to a figure in a painting. One artist who did this was Artemisia Gentileschi, an Italian painter of the Baroque period, when art often featured dramatic scenes and rich colors and textures. She used gold-colored dresses to emphasize the female protagonists in paintings such as Judith Beheading Holofernes and Salome with the Head of John the Baptist. Gentileschi also painted Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting. Remember that gold is the color with a metallic-looking yellow hue, while Artemisia Gentileschi is the artist associated with these works.

The Baroque was a European artistic period that followed the Renaissance and preceded Rococo. It began around 1600 and was especially influential during the seventeenth century. Baroque artists used dramatic compositions, ornate details, strong contrasts of light and shadow, and rich textures to make scenes feel vivid and emotionally powerful. Their work often showed religious stories, historical events, or moments of intense action. One important Baroque painter was the Italian artist Artemisia Gentileschi. In her painting Judith Beheading Holofernes, she depicted Judith and her maidservant killing the general Holofernes in a forceful, dramatic scene. Gentileschi also painted Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting, showing herself as a personification of the art of painting.

The Pirates of Penzance is a comic opera by W. S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan that uses lively songs and wordplay to tell the story of Frederic, a young man apprenticed to a band of pirates. His nursemaid, Ruth, was supposed to apprentice him to a pilot, someone who guides ships, but misheard the word as “pirate.” Frederic plans to leave the pirates when he turns 21 and do his duty by helping to capture them. Then he learns that his apprenticeship lasts until his 21st birthday, not until he has lived 21 years. Because he was born on February 29, a date that occurs only in leap years, he will not have his 21st birthday until he is 84 years old.

Gaspard de la nuit is a three-movement solo piano suite by the French composer Maurice Ravel, inspired by prose poems by Aloysius Bertrand. Each movement creates a different eerie scene: “Ondine” portrays a water spirit, “Le Gibet” evokes a body hanging from a gallows, and “Scarbo” depicts a mischievous, goblin-like sprite. Ravel used the piano to suggest these images through shimmering sounds, repeated notes, and sudden changes in mood. The finale, “Scarbo,” is especially famous for its extreme technical difficulty, which demands speed and precision from the pianist. Ravel intended it to be even harder to play than “Islamey,” a famously challenging piano piece by Mily Balakirev.

Andy Warhol’s Cars is a body of artwork centered on automobiles, especially Mercedes-Benz models. Warhol, a leading Pop artist, used familiar images from advertising and popular culture in his work; here, cars became subjects for art rather than simply machines for travel. His Mercedes-Benz paintings explored different vehicles and their designs, and he was also commissioned to paint cars made by BMW and Daimler. In 1979, Warhol painted a BMW M1 Group 4 racing coupe. It became the fourth vehicle in BMW’s Art Car project, in which artists transformed racing cars into works of art. Remember the series title, Andy Warhol’s Cars, and the model of his BMW Art Car, the BMW M1.

The Surrender of Breda is a history painting by the Spanish artist Diego Velázquez. It shows the aftermath of the Dutch city of Breda’s capitulation to Spanish forces in 1625. At the center, the defeated governor, Justin of Nassau, hands the city’s keys to the victorious commander, Ambrosio Spinola, a Genoese-born general who led the Spanish army. Spinola reaches toward Justin in a gesture often interpreted as generous and respectful rather than humiliating. Behind them stand ranks of soldiers and a dense forest of upright pikes. By focusing on the meeting between the two commanders instead of the fighting, Velázquez presents the surrender as a moment of dignity for both sides.

Ludwig Mies van der Rohe was a German-American architect whose simple, modern buildings helped shape the International Style. He favored open spaces, clean lines, and materials such as glass and steel; his approach is often summed up by the phrase “less is more.” In Germany, he became the final director of the Bauhaus, a school of art, design, and architecture founded by Walter Gropius in 1919. The Bauhaus aimed to bring together artistic ideas and practical design, but it closed in 1933. Mies later moved to the United States, where he became an important figure in Chicago architecture. His Lake Shore Drive Apartments in Chicago use glass-and-steel exteriors that show his belief that a building’s structure and design could be both functional and elegant.

The Alexander Mosaic is a large ancient floor artwork discovered in the House of the Faun, a wealthy Roman house in Pompeii. It is made from thousands of tiny pieces of colored stone called tesserae, fitted together to create a detailed image. The scene shows Alexander the Great, king of Macedon, charging toward the Persian ruler Darius III, who turns to flee in his chariot. It portrays the Battle of Issus, fought in 333 BCE near the Gulf of İskenderun in what is now Turkey. Alexander’s Macedonian forces won the battle despite facing a much larger Persian army. The mosaic’s dramatic faces, crowded soldiers, and sense of movement make it one of the best-known surviving images of Alexander from the ancient world.

The guitar is a fretted string instrument played by plucking or strumming its strings. Players press the strings against the frets on its neck to change their pitch, allowing the guitar to play melodies, chords, and rhythms. It is central to Spanish flamenco music and appears in many Mexican musical traditions. The vihuela used in mariachi is a small guitar-like instrument, while the bajo sexto is a larger regional form heard in norteño music from northern Mexico. A bajo sexto typically has 12 strings arranged in six pairs. Often played alongside an accordion, it provides low notes and rhythmic accompaniment. These different forms show how musicians adapt the guitar to suit the sounds of their traditions.

Der Rosenkavalier, or The Knight of the Rose, is a comic opera by composer Richard Strauss and librettist Hugo von Hofmannsthal. Its story centers on the Marschallin, a married noblewoman, the young Octavian, and Sophie, whom Octavian falls in love with. Octavian presents Sophie with a silver rose as part of a marriage ceremony, but the meeting sparks a romance between them. Octavian is a “breeches role”: although the character is a young man, he is usually played by a woman with a mezzo-soprano voice. Strauss and Hofmannsthal also created Elektra, a much darker opera named for a princess from Greek myth. Elektra seeks vengeance for the murder of her father, Agamemnon, and her brother Orestes helps carry it out.

Gelt is a Yiddish word for money. During Hanukkah, it traditionally refers to coins or money given to children, and today it often takes the form of foil-wrapped chocolate coins. Children may use gelt when playing dreidel, a game with a four-sided spinning top. Players put coins or other tokens into a shared pot, then spin the dreidel to find out whether they add to the pot, take from it, or do nothing. Each side of the dreidel bears a Hebrew letter. In many versions used outside Israel, the letters stand for a phrase meaning “A great miracle happened there,” referring to the Hanukkah story of a small supply of oil lasting eight days. Gelt connects gift-giving, play, and the holiday’s history.

An orphan is a child whose parents have died or are permanently absent, leaving the child without parental care from either parent. Orphans may be cared for by relatives, guardians, foster families, or other members of their community. In fiction, becoming an orphan can change a character’s life and set a story in motion. In Lemony Snicket’s darkly comic novel series A Series of Unfortunate Events, the Baudelaire siblings—Violet, Klaus, and Sunny—become orphans after a fire destroys their home and kills their parents. The children must then navigate a series of dangers, including the schemes of Count Olaf, who wants their fortune. The series begins with The Bad Beginning and also includes The Reptile Room.

Tea is a drink made by steeping processed leaves of the Camellia sinensis plant in hot water. How the leaves are processed helps create different kinds of tea, including green and black tea. Tea was known in China before the Song dynasty, but its cultivation and consumption became deeply established in Chinese culture during the Song period, which lasted from 960 to 1279. People enjoyed tea in daily life and at social gatherings, and it also played a part in art and ceremony. The Song dynasty is also associated with the reformer Wang Anshi, who implemented the baojia system of local law enforcement. The dynasty was eventually defeated by Kublai Khan and replaced by the Yuan dynasty.

Ancient Greek prostitution was a form of paid sex work in city-states such as Athens, where people used the drachma and celebrated festivals like the Panathenaia. It took several forms, from work in brothels to arrangements made independently. Some women known as hetairai provided paid companionship and were often valued for conversation, music, or other social skills as well as sexual relationships. Hetairai could work independently or in brothels, though their circumstances varied widely. They were not the only people involved in prostitution, and the freedom to choose their work differed from person to person; some sex workers were enslaved. Studying this part of everyday life helps historians understand social class, gender, and the limited choices available to many people in ancient Greece.

Medieval European coinage was the metal money used across Europe during the Middle Ages. Rulers and their mints issued coins in different denominations for everyday purchases and for paying rents, taxes, and other obligations. Coins varied by place and period: many were made of silver, while some inexpensive small-denomination coins were made of reddish copper. Coins also appear in a famous dispute over indulgences, payments associated with the Catholic Church’s promise to reduce punishment for sins. A saying about fundraising claimed that “as soon as the coin in the coffer rings,” a soul is released from purgatory. Martin Luther criticized this idea because he believed money could not secure forgiveness or free a soul. His objections helped launch the Protestant Reformation.

Kindergarten is an early-childhood class that usually comes before first grade, often for children around five years old. Its name comes from a German phrase meaning “children’s garden.” In 1840, the German educator Friedrich Froebel coined the name because he believed young children should be cared for and given room to grow, much like plants in a garden. He promoted learning through play, songs, games, and hands-on activities rather than relying only on formal lessons. Today, kindergarten helps children build early reading, language, and number skills while also learning to share, work with others, and follow classroom routines. Approaches differ between schools, but the idea that young children learn by exploring and doing remains an important part of kindergarten.

Flappers were young women in the 1920s Jazz Age who challenged older expectations about how women should dress and behave. They were known for shorter skirts, loose or revealing dresses, bobbed hair, and a more androgynous look. Flappers also came to symbolize greater social freedom, including dancing to jazz and enjoying nightlife. Film star Clara Bow, known as the “It Girl,” helped popularize the flapper image. Hairstyles were an important part of that image: some women wore carefully shaped Marcel waves, while performer Josephine Baker helped popularize the Eton crop, a very short, close-cropped haircut. Not every young woman dressed or lived like a flapper, but the style became a lasting symbol of cultural change in the 1920s.

Milk is a dairy beverage made mostly of water, with fat globules, proteins, and other substances spread throughout it. It is a colloid: a mixture in which tiny particles remain dispersed in a liquid instead of quickly settling out. Fresh milk can separate as larger fat globules rise and form a cream layer on top. To help prevent this, producers use homogenization, a treatment that forces milk through tiny openings under high pressure. This breaks large fat globules into smaller ones, making the fat more evenly dispersed and slowing the formation of a cream layer. Homogenization changes how the fat is distributed; it does not remove the fat. Milk is also often pasteurized, but that is a different process that uses heat to reduce harmful microbes.

Butter is a dairy fat made by churning cream until its fat gathers into a solid. People spread it on bread, melt it over vegetables, and use it to cook or bake many foods. In classic sauce-making, cooks combine butter with flour in roughly equal proportions to make a roux. They heat and stir the mixture so the flour cooks evenly, then add liquid to make a thickened sauce, soup, or stew. A roux can be pale, blond, or dark depending on how long it cooks; a darker roux adds a deeper, nuttier flavor. The combination of butter and flour is a useful kitchen technique, and butter itself is a familiar ingredient in everyday meals as well as French cooking.

The United States dime is a coin worth ten cents, or one-tenth of a dollar. Since 1946, its obverse (front) has shown President Franklin D. Roosevelt. The reverse (back), designed by John R. Sinnock, shows a torch flanked by an olive branch and an oak branch, symbols of liberty, peace, and strength. Roosevelt was chosen partly because of his connection to the March of Dimes, a campaign that raised money to fight polio, a disease he had lived with.
