Before 1946, the dime showed a figure representing Liberty wearing a winged cap. Many people mistook the figure for Mercury, the winged messenger god of Roman mythology, so the earlier coin became known as the Mercury dime.

Pinto beans are a variety of common bean with tan seeds covered in reddish-brown speckles. Their name comes from the Spanish word for “painted,” and the speckles often fade when the beans are cooked. Widely eaten in Mexico, pinto beans provide protein and fiber and appear in many everyday meals. They are often used to make refried beans: cooks simmer the beans until tender, then mash and season them, often cooking them again with a little oil or fat. Despite the name, refried beans are not necessarily fried twice. They can be served as a side dish or used as a filling for tacos, burritos, and other foods. Beans are also one of the “three sisters” crops, traditionally grown alongside corn and squash.

Papa John’s is an American pizza restaurant chain founded by John Schnatter in Jeffersonville, Indiana. Its slogan, “Better Ingredients. Better Pizza,” reflects the company’s claim that the ingredients it uses make its pizzas better. Like its competitor Domino’s, Papa John’s sells pizzas for delivery or pickup, making it a familiar choice for parties and game nights. From 2010 through 2018, Papa John’s was the official pizza of the National Football League, or NFL. The NFL is the major U.S. professional league for American football, and its teams compete each season to reach the Super Bowl. The winning team receives the Lombardi Trophy. So if a question connects “Better Ingredients. Better Pizza” to a restaurant, the answer is Papa John’s; if it asks which league the chain partnered with, the answer is the NFL.

Whitewashing a fence means brushing whitewash, a mixture traditionally made from lime and water, onto wood to give it a bright, chalky coating. In Mark Twain’s novel The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Aunt Polly assigns Tom the chore of whitewashing the household fence as a punishment. Tom would rather enjoy his free time, so he pretends that painting the fence is a rare privilege that takes special skill. Other boys become eager to try it and offer him small treasures in exchange for a turn. Ben Rogers, who had been planning to go swimming, even offers Tom an apple. By making the work seem desirable, Tom gets the fence whitewashed without doing most of it himself.

Left-hand traffic is a road-traffic convention in which vehicles travel on the left side of a two-way road and usually overtake on the right. It is used in Britain and many former British colonies, while the United States uses right-hand traffic. Cars designed for left-hand traffic generally have the steering wheel on the right, placing the driver closer to the center of the road and making it easier to judge oncoming traffic. In 2009, the Pacific island nation of Samoa switched from driving on the right to driving on the left. One reason was to make it easier for residents to use cars imported from nearby Australia and New Zealand, where people also drive on the left. When traveling abroad, drivers and pedestrians need to check which side of the road local traffic uses.

Pink Sauce is a brightly colored bottled condiment created by chef Carly Pii. It attracted attention online in 2022, partly because early bottles were shipped without refrigeration even though the sauce contained dairy, which raised concerns about whether it would stay safe to eat. Its vivid pink color comes from dragon fruit, a tropical cactus fruit, blended into a recipe that also includes honey. Dragon fruit can have white or magenta flesh dotted with tiny black seeds, and the magenta variety gives foods a striking color. Although the name Pink Sauce sounds simple, knowing its creator, the concern about unrefrigerated shipping, and the dragon fruit behind its color helps explain why it became so widely discussed.

E is the fifth letter of the English alphabet and the letter used most often in English writing. Its absence makes Georges Perec’s novel A Void especially remarkable: Perec wrote the entire book without using the letter e. The novel was first published in French in 1969 as La Disparition. Writing that deliberately avoids a particular letter is called a lipogram, and Perec belonged to Oulipo, a group of writers who explored creative rules and constraints. E also appears in other subjects. In music, E major is a key with four sharps. In mathematics, lowercase e is a number, about 2.718, that forms the base of natural logarithms; a backward capital E is a symbol meaning “there exists.”

A Christmas tree is an evergreen tree, often a fir or spruce, that people display and decorate during the Christmas season. Families may hang lights, colorful ornaments, and tinsel on its branches, then place a star or angel at the top. Presents are often set beneath it. The tree is also important in The Nutcracker, a ballet by Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. During the first act, a Christmas celebration takes a magical turn at midnight: mice fill the room, and the Christmas tree grows to an enormous size. That scene helps show the story shifting from an ordinary holiday gathering into a fantasy adventure.

Video rental is a service that lets customers use movies, television programs, or video games for a limited time instead of buying them. Customers traditionally visited stores such as Blockbuster, paid a rental fee, and returned a VHS tape or DVD by a due date. Later, Redbox offered DVD rentals through automated kiosks in places such as grocery stores and pharmacies. Netflix challenged Blockbuster with a different approach: customers chose DVDs online, received them by mail in distinctive red envelopes, and mailed them back after watching. As internet connections improved, Netflix shifted toward streaming, which lets viewers watch instantly without handling a disc. It is now known for series such as Stranger Things and The Witcher. These changes show how the same desire to watch entertainment at home led to different ways of providing it.

A credit card lets shoppers buy goods or services by borrowing from a credit account rather than paying immediately from a bank account. The card issuer records the charges on a statement, and the cardholder must repay them; unpaid balances may incur interest. Familiar plastic credit cards often have a magnetic stripe that can be swiped and an EMV chip that can be read by a payment terminal. They also carry a card number and a separate three-digit security value called the CVV. On Visa cards, the CVV is printed in the signature panel on the back and is often requested for online or phone purchases, when the card is not physically present. It is not the card number or the PIN. Criminals may use “skimmers” or “shimmers” to steal card information, while EMV chips help reduce some types of fraud.

Chile peppers are fruits of plants in the genus Capsicum, used in cuisines around the world to add flavor and heat. Their spiciness comes mainly from capsaicin, and different varieties range from mild to extremely hot. Serrano and jalapeño chiles are common in Mexican cooking, while the larger, milder poblano is often stuffed to make chile relleno. Thai bird’s eye chiles and African piri piri chiles bring heat to dishes and sauces elsewhere. The Carolina Reaper is famous for its extreme heat. In New Mexico, Hatch chiles are named for the village of Hatch, which holds an annual chile harvest festival. In late summer, vendors often roast freshly harvested Hatch chiles at roadside stands, giving them a smoky flavor.

A hotel is a business that provides rooms for travelers to stay in, often along with services such as meals, housekeeping, and meeting space. Motels are a related type of lodging, traditionally designed for motorists. Hotels and motels have also been settings for important events in U.S. history. Robert F. Kennedy was shot at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles in 1968, and Martin Luther King Jr. was killed at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis the same year. The Washington Hilton is another example of a hotel. In the 1964 case Heart of Atlanta Motel, Inc. v. United States, the Supreme Court ruled that Congress could use its Commerce Clause power to enforce the Civil Rights Act against a Georgia motel that served interstate travelers but refused rooms to Black guests.

A refrigerator keeps food cold by moving heat out of an insulated storage compartment and releasing it into the surrounding room. Its cooling loop works like a heat pump in reverse: a fluid called a refrigerant circulates through coils, changing between liquid and gas as it moves. Inside the refrigerator, the refrigerant evaporates in the evaporator coil, the cold-side heat exchanger. Evaporation absorbs heat from the air and food in the compartment, lowering their temperature. A compressor then raises the refrigerant’s pressure and temperature. In the warm-side condenser coil, often at the back or underneath the appliance, the refrigerant releases heat into the room and becomes liquid again. The cycle repeats to keep the compartment cold.

Candles are portable lights made from wax or another fuel surrounding a wick. When the wick is lit, the fuel burns and produces a steady flame. People use candles during power outages and in celebrations and religious observances, where lighting one can carry a special meaning. During Kwanzaa, a celebration of African-American culture held from December 26 to January 1, seven candles stand for its seven principles. They are arranged in a holder called a kinara, with one black candle in the center, three red candles on one side, and three green candles on the other. Candles are also important during the Jewish holiday of Hanukkah: its special menorah holds nine candles, including one used to light the others.

Public restrooms, also called bathrooms or toilets, are shared facilities found in schools, parks, libraries, and other public places. Rules about who may use them have become an important issue in transgender rights. In 2014, Maine’s highest court ruled that a school district violated state law when it barred a transgender girl from using the girls’ restroom, which matched her gender identity. It was the first state high court ruling to establish that right. In Virginia, transgender student Gavin Grimm sued the Gloucester County school board after it barred him from using the boys’ bathrooms at school. His case drew national attention and reached the U.S. Supreme Court in 2017. Both cases concerned whether transgender students could use school restrooms that matched their gender identity.

Hunting is the pursuit of wild animals as game, practiced for recreation, food, or as a profession. Hunters may track animals on foot, use trained dogs, or wait in places where their prey is likely to appear. The activity also plays a major role in fiction. In Saki’s short story “The Interlopers,” two rival hunters meet in a forest where each claims the right to hunt. Richard Connell’s “The Most Dangerous Game” gives hunting a deadly twist: a professional hunter named Rainsford is stranded on Ship-Trap Island, where his aristocratic host hunts humans instead of animals. These stories use hunting not only as an outdoor activity but also to explore rivalry, danger, and what happens when people become prey.

Clothing includes items such as shirts, trousers, dresses, and coats that people wear to cover, protect, or adorn their bodies. What people wear can reflect the weather, local customs, personal style, or religious beliefs. In Jainism, a religion that originated in India, some male ascetics renounce clothing as part of their commitment to giving up possessions. They belong to the Digambara sect, whose name means “sky-clad.” For these ascetics, going without clothes expresses detachment from material things; it is a religious practice, not an everyday rule for all Jains. Jainism’s other major sect is Svetambara, a name meaning “white-clad.” Thus, the everyday items the Digambara ascetics renounce are clothes, and the sect associated with the “sky-clad” practice is Digambara.

Pie is a dish with a crust that holds a filling. Dessert pies are usually baked and served in wedges. Their fillings can be made from fruit, nuts, or custard, and the crust may cover the top as well as the bottom. In the United States, pumpkin pie and pecan pie are especially popular at Thanksgiving. Key lime pie is another well-known variety, associated with the Florida Keys. Its tart filling combines juice from small, aromatic Key limes with sweetened condensed milk, and it is commonly set in a graham-cracker crust rather than a traditional pastry crust. Key lime pie is often topped with whipped cream or meringue. Although pies are often sweet, savory pies filled with ingredients such as meat or vegetables are also eaten around the world.

Newspapers are publications issued regularly, often daily or weekly, that report current events. They contain news stories about local and world events, as well as features, opinions, and advertisements. The Daily Mail and The New York Times are well-known examples. Newspapers also appear in literature and drama: in Harold Pinter’s absurdist play The Dumb Waiter, one of the characters reads a newspaper report about a car accident. The play follows two hitmen, Ben and Gus, who wait in a basement for instructions while unexpected food orders arrive through a service hatch. The newspaper is an ordinary object in their strange situation, showing how everyday routines can continue even when events around the characters seem confusing or unsettling.

Julia Child was an American cook, author, and television host who helped make French cooking approachable for home cooks in the United States. She studied at Le Cordon Bleu in Paris and, with Simone Beck and Louisette Bertholle, coauthored the 1961 cookbook Mastering the Art of French Cooking. Its detailed instructions helped readers try techniques and dishes that might otherwise have seemed intimidating. Beginning in 1963, Child hosted The French Chef, a cooking series produced by Boston station WGBH and broadcast on public television. Her lively demonstrations showed viewers that mistakes were part of learning to cook. Child also filmed cooking programs with her friend Jacques Pépin in her Cambridge, Massachusetts, home kitchen. That kitchen is now preserved at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.

A shepherd is a person who looks after sheep, guiding a flock to places where it can graze and helping keep the animals safe. Shepherds have long been part of rural life, and literature often portrays them in peaceful countryside settings called pastoral scenes. At the start of Paulo Coelho’s novel The Alchemist, Santiago works as a shepherd in Spain. He repeatedly dreams of treasure near the Egyptian pyramids and decides to leave his familiar life to search for it. Along the way, people encourage him to follow what the novel calls his Personal Legend: the unique destiny or purpose he is meant to fulfill. Santiago’s journey connects his everyday work as a shepherd with the larger question of whether he will pursue his dream.

Gambling is the practice of risking money or something else valuable on an uncertain outcome, hoping to win a prize or more money. It includes buying lottery tickets, betting on sports, playing card games for money, and playing games in casinos. Las Vegas, Macau, and Singapore are well-known casino destinations, and some Native American reservations operate casinos that support their local economies. One casino game is roulette: players place bets on a felt layout marked with numbers and other choices. A casino employee called a croupier spins a numbered wheel and sends a small ball around its rim. The ball eventually lands in a pocket, and that pocket determines which bets win. Because outcomes are uncertain, gambling can also lead to losing money.

A watch is a portable device for telling time, usually worn on the wrist or carried in a pocket. In O. Henry’s short story “The Gift of the Magi,” James Dillingham Young, known as Jim, owns a valuable gold watch. He sells it to buy a set of beautiful hair combs for his wife, Della, as a Christmas gift. At the same time, Della sells her long hair to buy a chain for Jim’s watch. Because of their sacrifices, neither can use the gift they receive right away. Their choices show how much they care for each other: each gives up a prized possession to make the other happy.

A firefighter is a trained emergency responder who puts out fires, rescues people in danger, and helps during other emergencies. Firefighters use equipment such as hoses, protective clothing, breathing masks, and ladders to control flames and protect people from smoke and heat. They also teach communities how to prevent fires. Literature sometimes gives this familiar job an unexpected twist. In Ray Bradbury’s dystopian novel Fahrenheit 451, firefighters do not extinguish fires: they burn books, which their society has banned. The main character, firefighter Guy Montag, begins to question his work after meeting a curious young woman named Clarisse McClellan. His story contrasts the real purpose of firefighting—protecting lives and communities—with a fictional society that uses fire to destroy knowledge.

Pink is often associated with gentleness and calmness, in contrast to red, which is sometimes linked with energy and aggressiveness. One particular shade, called Baker-Miller pink, became famous for a proposed calming effect. In the 1970s, researcher Alexander Schauss advocated testing whether exposure to this shade could reduce aggressive behavior in correctional facilities. Some facilities painted holding cells pink, hoping to lower violence among people detained there. Early reports suggested that the color might help, but later studies produced mixed results, so it is not proven that pink walls reliably prevent aggression. Still, Baker-Miller pink remains a well-known example of how people have tried to use color to influence mood and behavior.

The New York Times is an American daily newspaper founded in 1851 by Henry Jarvis Raymond and George Jones. Known for its national and international reporting, it publishes news, investigations, opinion pieces, and other features in print and online. Its slogan is “All the News That’s Fit to Print.” Journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones and other Times journalists developed the 1619 Project, which examines the history and lasting effects of slavery in the United States. The newspaper also offers games: its crossword puzzle debuted in 1942, and Wordle joined its Games portfolio in 2022. In Wordle, players have six attempts to guess a five-letter word. After each guess, colored tiles show whether letters are in the correct position, elsewhere in the word, or not in the word.

Pride parades are public marches and celebrations of LGBTQ+ identity, community, and progress. The first were held in June 1970 in cities including New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago. They commemorated the Stonewall uprising, which began a year earlier, after police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in New York City’s Greenwich Village, on June 28, 1969. People resisted the raid, and the protests that followed helped energize the modern LGBTQ+ rights movement. Pride parades began as both a remembrance of Stonewall and a call for equal rights. Today, they often include rainbow flags, music, and people marching together to show support for LGBTQ+ communities.

Gauchos were traditional rural horsemen who worked with cattle and roamed the plains of Argentina and Uruguay, especially during the 18th and 19th centuries. Skilled riders, they became an enduring symbol of independence and life on the open range. Gauchos sometimes hunted with bolas, weights attached to leather cords that they threw to entangle an animal’s legs. Many also carried a long knife called a facón for work and self-defense. Their culture included payadas, improvised ballads sung in verse, which influenced José Hernández’s epic poem Martín Fierro. In Argentina, gauchos lived not only in the grassy Pampas but also in Patagonia, the vast southern region stretching from the Colorado River to Tierra del Fuego. Patagonia is also associated with the Indigenous Tehuelche people.

Starbucks began in Seattle in 1971 as a shop selling coffee beans and brewing equipment. It later grew into an international coffeehouse chain known for drinks such as lattes and Frappuccinos. In recent years, some Starbucks workers have tried to form unions, which let employees act together to seek changes in pay, schedules, and working conditions. These efforts have drawn attention from the Jorts social-media account, an orange-cat persona that often supports workers’ rights. Former Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz accused the National Labor Relations Board, or NLRB, of improperly influencing union votes at the company. Established under the Wagner Act, the NLRB is a federal agency that oversees union representation elections and handles disputes about workers’ rights to organize.

A taco is a Mexican dish made by placing a filling on a tortilla, then folding the tortilla so it can be eaten by hand. A tortilla is a thin, round flatbread, commonly made from corn or wheat flour. It is often warmed before the filling is added, making it easier to fold. Tacos are usually smaller than burritos, which are typically wrapped around their fillings. Taco fillings vary widely and can include meat, fish, beans, or vegetables. Popular toppings include salsa, chopped onion, cilantro, and a squeeze of lime. Different regions of Mexico have their own styles of tacos, using local ingredients and cooking methods. Together, the tortilla, filling, and optional toppings make tacos a flexible and popular meal.

IKEA is a Swedish furniture retailer known for affordable home products that customers often assemble themselves. It was founded in 1943 by Swedish entrepreneur Ingvar Kamprad in Älmhult, Sweden. At first, his small mail-order business sold everyday items such as pens and wallets, but it later expanded into furniture and grew into a global chain. Many IKEA tables, shelves, and chairs are sold in flat packs: boxes of separate parts that are easier to transport and store, with instructions for assembling them at home. IKEA stores also sell household goods and often have food areas serving Swedish-style meatballs. These features have made IKEA familiar to shoppers around the world.

Umami is the savory taste found in foods such as meat, mushrooms, tomatoes, and broth. It is one of the five basic tastes, alongside sweet, sour, salty, and bitter. Umami is closely associated with glutamate, a substance that occurs naturally in many foods and can also be added to foods such as meat substitutes to give them a more savory flavor. In 1908, Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda investigated why broth made from kombu, a type of seaweed, tasted so satisfying. He linked its savory flavor to glutamate and named the taste umami. His research helped establish umami as a distinct basic taste rather than just a combination of the other four.

Beer is an alcoholic drink made by brewing grains, usually malted barley or wheat. During brewing, yeast ferments sugars from the grains, producing alcohol and bubbles of carbon dioxide. Hops are often added to give beer bitterness and aroma. Beer comes in many styles: Guinness, associated with Dublin in Ireland, is a dry stout known for its dark color. Beer is also part of festivals and local traditions around the world. One famous example is Oktoberfest, held in Munich, a city in southeastern Germany and the capital of the state of Bavaria. More than seven million liters of beer are served at the festival each year. In many places, drinking beer is restricted to adults because it contains alcohol.

The McDonald’s Happy Meal is a children’s combo meal that usually includes a main food item, such as Chicken McNuggets, a side, a drink, and a toy or other prize. Its toys have often been linked to movies and popular collectibles. In 1992, a Happy Meal promotion tied to Tim Burton’s superhero film Batman Returns was cancelled because the movie was considered too graphic for young children. In 1997, demand for Teenie Beanies offered with Happy Meals became so intense that it caused crowd-control problems, including arrests and hospitalizations. Happy Meal toys have also raised questions about marketing food to children. In 2010, San Francisco passed an ordinance restricting free toys in children’s meals that did not meet specified nutrition standards.

An aviator is a person who pilots an aircraft, such as an airplane. Aviators learn to control their aircraft, navigate, understand weather, and follow safety procedures. Some fly passengers or cargo, while others explore new routes or attempt aviation records. In 1927, American aviator Charles Lindbergh became famous for making the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic, flying from New York to Paris. His custom-built Ryan monoplane was named the Spirit of St. Louis, and the flight won him the Orteig Prize. Amelia Earhart also became famous for record-setting flights; she disappeared near Howland Island in 1937 while attempting to fly around the world with navigator Fred Noonan. Bessie Coleman was the first Black woman to earn a pilot’s license in the United States.

Cotton is a natural fiber that grows around the seeds of plants in the botanical genus Gossypium. After the fluffy fibers are harvested, they are cleaned, spun into yarn, and woven or knitted into fabric for clothing, towels, sheets, and other everyday items. Cotton is a major textile crop grown in many parts of the world. Upland cotton supplies most of the world’s cotton, while another cultivated species produces the extra-long fibers, or “staples,” prized for fine fabrics such as Egyptian cotton. Cotton has also played an important role in history: enslaved people produced it in the Southern United States before the Civil War, and irrigation for cotton farming in Uzbekistan helped cause the Aral Sea to shrink.

Italics are a style of type in which letters usually lean to the right instead of standing upright. Writers use italics to emphasize a word or phrase, mark titles of books and films, or show that a word comes from another language. In handwriting, people may underline words when they cannot easily write in italics. The style became widely known through the Aldine Press, a printing house founded in Venice by Aldus Manutius in the late 1400s. Its printers used slanted letters in compact books that were easier to carry than many earlier printed volumes. So, if a question asks for the right-leaning style, the answer is italics; if it asks for the name of Manutius’s Venetian workshop, the answer is the Aldine Press.

A taxi horn is a sound-making device mounted on a taxi, a car that carries passengers for a fare. Like the horn on another automobile, it gives an audible warning to nearby drivers or pedestrians. Honking can alert someone to a vehicle’s presence, but it also contributes to the familiar noise of busy streets. The American composer George Gershwin brought that everyday sound into his orchestral work An American in Paris. He included four taxi horns to evoke the traffic he heard on Paris streets. Gershwin also wrote Rhapsody in Blue and Cuban Overture. Although taxi horns are normally used for road safety rather than music, their distinctive blasts helped Gershwin create a vivid impression of city life.

Walgreens began as a single drugstore in Chicago in 1901 and grew into a nationwide pharmacy and retail chain. Its stores sell everyday goods and have pharmacy counters where customers can fill prescriptions. In the 2010s, Walgreens partnered with Theranos, a Silicon Valley health-technology startup founded by Elizabeth Holmes, to offer blood-testing services in some stores. Theranos promoted its Edison analyzer as a device that could run many medical tests using only a tiny sample of blood from a finger prick. Walgreens planned to expand the service, but serious problems emerged: Theranos’s technology did not perform as promised. The partnership ended, and Walgreens sued Theranos. The case shows why claims about new medical technology need careful testing before people rely on them for health decisions.

Carpets are woven textiles used to cover and decorate floors, often combining practical warmth with intricate art. Persian carpets may show flowers, geometric patterns, or Arabic calligraphy, and some are made with the asymmetrical Senneh knot. One famous example is the Ardabil Carpet, named after a town in northwestern Iran. Woven in the 16th century for the shrine of Shaykh Safi al-Din, it has a large central medallion and two hanging-lamp motifs. Carpets also appear in European paintings: Hans Holbein placed a red one on a table in The Ambassadors, where it helped suggest the figures’ wealth and status. Smaller rugs are used by Muslims as clean surfaces for prayer.

Nestlé is a Swiss multinational company that makes and sells foods and beverages, from chocolate and packaged foods to bottled water sold under brands such as Arrowhead. It has faced criticism over the environmental impact of plastic bottles, its use of water resources, and labor conditions in its cocoa supply chain, including child labor. Critics sometimes describe a company’s environmental marketing as greenwashing when its claims create a greener image than its actions support. The term was coined by Jay Westerveld in a 1986 essay about hotels asking guests to reuse towels to “save the environment” while doing little else to reduce their environmental impact. Understanding the difference between an environmental claim and a company’s actual practices helps consumers judge such marketing.

New Year’s Day is the holiday on January 1 that marks the start of a new year in the Gregorian calendar, which is used in many countries. People often welcome it at midnight with countdowns, fireworks, parties, or gatherings with family and friends. A common tradition is to make a New Year’s resolution: a personal goal or promise to work on during the coming year, such as exercising more, saving money, or learning a new skill. Not all cultures begin their year on January 1. Lunar New Year is celebrated on a changing date and is associated with giving children red envelopes containing money. Jewish New Year, called Rosh Hashanah, begins the High Holy Days, while the Bahá’í New Year, Nowruz, follows the Nineteen Day Fast.

Smoking means drawing smoke from a burning tobacco product, such as a cigarette, or aerosol from an electronic cigarette into the lungs. Both can damage the cells lining the lungs and contribute to respiratory disease. Vaping is sometimes described as safer than smoking cigarettes, but its aerosol can still contain harmful substances. In 2020, investigators examined an outbreak of EVALI, short for e-cigarette or vaping use-associated lung injury. Many cases were linked to THC vaping products containing vitamin E acetate, an additive that can harm the lungs when inhaled. Vitamin E itself is a fat-soluble antioxidant found in foods such as plant oils, and its most common form is called alpha-tocopherol. The concern in EVALI was inhaling vitamin E acetate, not eating foods that contain vitamin E.

A zoo is a public facility that keeps living animals in managed habitats where visitors can observe them. Zoos help people learn about wildlife and may support scientific research and conservation, including efforts to protect endangered species. Good zoos also provide food, shelter, and veterinary care suited to the animals’ needs. The zoo in Guadalajara, Mexico, is a large example with an extensive exhibit called a nocturnario. This Spanish word names an area devoted to nocturnal animals—creatures that are most active at night. A nocturnario may use carefully controlled lighting so visitors can watch these animals during their active hours while the animals keep a suitable day-and-night routine.

Perfume is a scented preparation worn on the body to make a person smell pleasant. Perfumers blend aromatic materials into layers called top or head notes, heart notes, and base notes: the first are noticed immediately, while the others emerge and last longer. The overall blend, or accord, helps place a perfume in a fragrance family, such as chypre or fougère. Perfumes are also classified by how much aromatic oil they contain. Eau de toilette is generally lighter than eau de parfum, while extrait, also called parfum, is more concentrated. One famous example is Chanel No. 5, created by Ernest Beaux in 1921. Its floral scent makes prominent use of aldehydes, and its simple rectangular bottle helped make it an icon of fashion history.

A fighter pilot is a military aviator trained to fly fast combat aircraft, especially jets designed to intercept and engage enemy aircraft. Fighter pilots practice maneuvers called dogfighting and work with other pilots and ground crews to help their military control the air during a conflict. Some also attack targets on the ground. In the 2022 film Top Gun: Maverick, Tom Cruise plays a veteran U.S. Navy fighter pilot whose call sign is Maverick. He returns to an elite flying school to train younger aviators for a dangerous mission. Fighter pilots also appear in animated stories: Studio Ghibli’s Porco Rosso follows a former fighter pilot who has been cursed to look like a pig and now works as a bounty hunter.

Cannibalism means eating human flesh. In Greek mythology, it often appears as a shocking act that breaks the bonds of family and hospitality. In one story, Tereus harms his wife Procne’s sister, Philomela. To take revenge, Procne kills her and Tereus’s son Itys and serves Tereus a meal made from the boy. Another myth tells of King Tantalus, who kills his son Pelops and serves him to the gods at a feast. The gods recognize what he has done and punish him in the underworld. Tantalus must stand in water that recedes whenever he tries to drink, beneath fruit that moves out of reach whenever he tries to eat. His punishment reflects both his crime and his endless hunger.

Kimchi is a traditional Korean dish made by fermenting salted vegetables, most famously napa cabbage or radish. The vegetables are mixed with seasonings such as garlic, ginger, and red chili, then left to ferment. This process preserves them and gives kimchi its tangy flavor. There are many kinds of kimchi, which can be eaten as a side dish or added to meals such as rice and soups. In late autumn, families and communities often prepare large batches to last through winter. This shared tradition is called kimjang. In the past, people commonly stored the kimchi in large earthenware jars called onggi, sometimes buried in the ground to help keep the contents cool.

A café is a public place where people gather to drink coffee or other beverages, talk, and sometimes eat light meals. Cafés have also inspired artists who wanted to show everyday social life. In Vincent van Gogh’s 1888 painting The Night Café, the café’s interior in Arles, France, is shown after dark in vivid colors, with a billiard table at its center. The table is a useful clue for recognizing the painting, while its title tells you what kind of place it depicts. French painter Gustave Caillebotte also painted a café interior in 1880, showing a large mirror and a man with his hands in his pockets. These paintings capture cafés as places where people might spend time outside their homes, whether alone or with others.

A beet, also called beetroot, is a taproot vegetable with a sweet, earthy flavor. The familiar red beet gets its deep crimson color from pigments that can stain hands and cutting boards when it is peeled or chopped. Beets can be roasted to bring out their sweetness, pickled for a tangy taste, or grated raw into salads. They are also a key ingredient in many versions of borscht, a soup associated especially with Ukrainian and other Eastern European cuisines. Beets give the soup its vivid red color, although recipes vary and may include vegetables such as cabbage, potatoes, and carrots. Borscht can be served hot or cold and is often topped with sour cream and dill.

Soylent is a food company that makes meal replacements: products designed to provide nutrients people would normally get from a meal. Its offerings have included powdered mixes that users prepare themselves, ready-to-drink bottles, and bars. The company was founded by software engineer and entrepreneur Rob Rhinehart. In a 2013 essay titled “How I Stopped Eating Food,” Rhinehart described his experiments with replacing conventional meals with a carefully formulated mixture. Soylent grew from that idea, offering a convenient option for people who want a quick meal without shopping for ingredients or cooking. Although its products are designed to supply a range of nutrients, they are meal replacements rather than a requirement to stop eating ordinary food.

A flag is a piece of cloth with distinctive colors, patterns, or emblems that represents a nation, group, institution, or cause. People display flags to show identity, pride, or support, and artists sometimes use them to show what a crowd is fighting for. In Eugène Delacroix’s painting Liberty Leading the People, the central figure raises the French tricolour above the barricades. This national flag has three vertical bands of blue, white, and red. The painting shows the July Revolution of 1830 in France, when protesters challenged the king. The raised flag helps viewers recognize the country and understand that the people in the painting are acting together for political change.

Rice is an edible cereal grain and a staple food for billions of people around the world. Different varieties behave differently when cooked: long-grain rice tends to stay separate and fluffy, while aromatic basmati rice is often used in South Asian and Middle Eastern cooking. Rice is the foundation of Saudi Arabian kabsa, a spiced rice dish often served with meat, and of pilaf-style dishes called pulao, polo, or plov in different regions. In parts of Brazil, it also accompanies a chicken dish called galinhada. Biryani is a South Asian rice dish associated with Mughal culinary traditions. It combines rice with meat and aromatic spices and is often assembled in layers before cooking, making it distinct from a simpler pilaf.

A picnic is an informal meal or social gathering held outdoors, often in a park, garden, or the countryside. People usually bring food from home in a basket or cooler and eat it on a blanket or at a picnic table. Sandwiches, fruit, and other easy-to-carry foods are common choices. Because picnics take place outside, people may need to watch out for insects, especially ants. Ants are small social insects whose workers search for food. When one finds crumbs or a sugary spill, it can leave a chemical scent trail that other workers follow between the food and their nest. Cleaning up spills and taking leftover food home helps keep a picnic area pleasant for everyone.

The Rainier cherry is a sweet cherry variety developed at Washington State University in 1952 by crossing two other cherry varieties, Bing and Van. Its skin is mostly yellow with a red blush, making it easy to recognize among darker red cherries. It is named after Mount Rainier, a mountain in Washington State near Seattle. Like other cherries, it grows on a tree in the genus Prunus and is a stone fruit, or drupe: its soft flesh surrounds a hard pit containing a seed. Plums, peaches, nectarines, and apricots are related stone fruits. Some cherries, including Rainier cherries, can be preserved in sweet syrup to make maraschino cherries, which are often used to garnish drinks.

Wool is a natural animal fiber obtained mainly by shearing sheep. Its fibers can trap pockets of air, making wool clothing warm even in cold weather. People use it to make sweaters, coats, blankets, tweed, and other textiles. Before wool is spun into yarn, it is washed in a process called scouring to remove dirt, sweat, and a waxy substance called lanolin. Lanolin comes from glands in a sheep’s skin and helps protect its fleece; after removal, it can be used in cosmetics and skin-care products. Wool has also been an important trade good for centuries, supporting cloth-making industries and merchants across Europe.

Weaving is the craft of making cloth by interlacing two sets of threads: lengthwise threads called the warp and crosswise threads called the weft. People weave by hand or on looms, creating fabrics that may be plain or richly patterned. In Ghana, kente is a vividly patterned ceremonial cloth associated especially with Akan and Ewe communities. Weavers make narrow strips of fabric, which are then sewn together into larger pieces. Weaving also appears in Greek mythology. After Tereus cut out Philomela’s tongue, she wove a cloth telling the story of his crime so her sister Procne could learn what had happened. Penelope used weaving to delay choosing a new husband: she worked on a shroud for Laertes by day, then secretly undid her work each night.

A Ferris wheel is a large amusement ride with passenger cabins attached around the edge of a tall, rotating wheel. As the wheel turns, the cabins travel in a circle, lifting riders high above the ground before bringing them back down. Unlike a roller coaster, a Ferris wheel usually moves slowly, giving passengers time to enjoy views of a fair, a city, or the surrounding landscape. One famous example is the London Eye in London, the capital of the United Kingdom. It stands on the South Bank of the River Thames, opposite the Houses of Parliament, and opened to the public in 2000 as part of celebrations marking the new millennium. Its height and location make it a popular place to see London from above.

A post office is a public-service building where people send letters and parcels, buy stamps, and collect mail. Some post offices are also important historic landmarks. Dublin’s General Post Office, often called the GPO, stands on O’Connell Street in Ireland’s capital. During the 1916 Easter Rising, Irish insurgents occupied the building and used it as their headquarters in a rebellion against British rule. Its façade still bears marks from the fighting. New York City also has monumental post-office buildings; one is engraved with a famous motto beginning “Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night.” These examples show how buildings used for everyday mail services can become symbols of a city’s history and identity.

Pilaf is a family of rice dishes found in many parts of the world. Cooks often start by briefly toasting the rice with aromatics such as onion, garlic, or spices. They then simmer it in seasoned broth, a savory liquid made from meat or vegetables, until the rice absorbs the liquid and becomes tender. The broth gives the rice moisture and flavor, while the cooking method helps keep the grains separate rather than sticky. Meat, vegetables, nuts, or dried fruit may also be added. Related dishes have names such as pulao, polo, and plov in different cuisines. Although the ingredients and seasonings vary from place to place, rice—often a long-grain variety such as basmati—remains the foundation of pilaf.

Ivory is a hard, dense material found mainly in elephant tusks. Because it can be shaped and polished, craftspeople have used it for detailed carvings, including Chinese puzzle balls made from several nested, movable layers. Ivory was also used for ceremonial and court objects in parts of Africa. In the Kingdom of Benin, located in what is now Nigeria, artists carved ivory heads and made objects for the royal court. Benin’s rulers were called obas, and their images appear on cast-brass plaques and sculptures commonly known as the Benin Bronzes. During a British punitive expedition in 1897, troops took thousands of artworks from Benin, including carved ivory objects. Today, the trade in elephant ivory is restricted in many places to help protect elephants from poaching.

Wood is a strong, natural material that comes mainly from the stems and branches of trees and other woody plants. It helps support a tree as it grows and is widely used to build houses, make furniture, and produce paper. Wood contains cellulose and lignin, two substances that help give it strength. Cellulose is a polymer made of many glucose molecules joined together and is also found in plant cell walls. Lignin helps stiffen the wood. After a tree dies, decomposers help recycle its materials: some fungi can break down lignin, while soft-rot fungi secrete enzymes that break down cellulose. Termites can also feed on wood. These organisms return nutrients from dead wood to the environment.

Sugar is a sweet ingredient made chiefly of sucrose. It can be extracted from sugarcane, a tall tropical plant, and refined into the crystals used in foods and drinks. During the colonial era, Caribbean plantations in places such as Haiti and Barbados grew cane and processed it into sugar and molasses; molasses could then be fermented to make rum. This work relied heavily on enslaved Africans brought across the Atlantic, making sugar a major part of the Atlantic slave trade. Some opponents of slavery tried to change this system through their shopping choices. In 1791, the English abolitionist William Fox published a widely read pamphlet urging people to stop buying West Indian sugar produced by enslaved labor. His appeal made an everyday purchase a form of antislavery protest.

Beanie Babies are small collectible plush toys introduced by Ty Inc. in 1993. Instead of being filled entirely with ordinary fiber stuffing, they contain plastic pellets that give them a floppy, distinctive feel. Their heart-shaped swing tags became important to collectors, who often kept the tags attached to preserve the toys’ value. In the 1990s, demand grew as shoppers searched for particular characters and treated the toys as collectibles. In 1997, McDonald’s, the fast-food chain known for its Golden Arches, offered miniature versions called Teenie Beanies with Happy Meals. A Happy Meal is a children’s meal that typically combines food, a drink, and a toy. The Teenie Beanies promotion drew enormous crowds and helped make the Beanie Babies craze even more visible.

“Let them eat cake” is a famous four-word quotation traditionally attributed to Marie Antoinette, the Austrian-born queen consort of France and wife of King Louis XVI. According to the story, she said it after being told that poor French people had no bread. The remark suggests that she did not understand their hunger or how difficult it was for them to afford food, so it became a lasting symbol of aristocratic indifference. Historians doubt that Marie Antoinette actually said it; the story is probably apocryphal, meaning it is widely repeated but likely untrue. In the French version, the food is brioche, a rich bread, rather than cake. Marie Antoinette was guillotined during the French Revolution in 1793, during the Reign of Terror.

An egg is a reproductive structure that protects a developing embryo and contains nutrients to help it grow. Bird eggs have a hard shell, and chicken eggs are also a familiar food. In cooking and baking, eggs can bind ingredients together and help cakes rise. Eggs also play a part in Jonathan Swift’s novel Gulliver’s Travels. When Gulliver visits Lilliput, he finds that its tiny people are divided over which end of an egg to crack first. The emperor orders his subjects to crack eggs at the smaller end. People who follow this rule are called Little-Endians, while those who favor the larger end are called Big-Endians. Swift uses this dispute to make fun of how fiercely people can argue over small differences.

A party is a social gathering where people come together to celebrate an occasion or enjoy one another’s company. Guests may share food and drinks, talk, play games, listen to music, or watch entertainment. Birthdays are a common reason for a party, but people also hold parties for holidays, achievements, or no special reason at all. Parties appear in plays too: Czech writer Václav Havel wrote The Garden Party, while British playwright Harold Pinter wrote The Birthday Party. In Pinter’s absurdist drama, Stanley Webber is a quiet lodger at a seaside boarding house. When two visitors, Goldberg and McCann, arrive, what seems to be a birthday celebration becomes a frightening ordeal. The contrast between an ordinary party and the play’s disturbing events helps make its title memorable.

Personal names are words used to identify individuals in introductions, conversations, and official records. Many cultures use a given name, chosen for a person, and a family name or surname, shared by relatives and often passed from one generation to the next. Wang is one of the most common family names in China. Names and titles can also describe a person’s role, such as parent, teacher, or ruler. The ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius argued that a well-ordered society depends on people behaving as their roles require: for example, a parent should care for a child, and a ruler should govern responsibly. This idea is called the “rectification of names.” Confucius’s teachings are recorded in a collection called the Analects.

Fishing is the practice of catching fish and other aquatic animals for food, income, or recreation. People have long competed over access to valuable fishing grounds. Wealthy Basque merchants once dominated fishing for cod on Newfoundland’s Grand Banks, while England’s Magna Carta restricted the use of weirs—barriers placed in waterways to trap fish. In the late 20th century, Iceland and the United Kingdom fought a series of disputes called the Cod Wars over fishing rights. Such conflicts involve not just boats and fish, but also rules about who may use the sea’s resources. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), an Exclusive Economic Zone extends up to 200 nautical miles from a coastal state’s baselines. Within that zone, the state has rights to natural resources, including fish.

Midsummer is the period around the summer solstice, the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, usually in late June. In many Northern European traditions, people celebrate the long daylight hours with bonfires, dancing around maypoles, and wearing flower crowns. Customs vary by country, but they often bring communities together outdoors and mark the changing seasons. Midsummer also appears in literature. William Shakespeare’s comedy A Midsummer Night’s Dream follows four Athenian lovers and a troupe of amateur actors into a forest, where the fairy king Oberon, fairy queen Titania, and mischievous Puck cause confusion with magic. The title evokes a season traditionally associated with celebration, imagination, and enchantment.

Lumberjacks are workers who cut down trees and haul timber from forests. Before modern logging machines, they often spent long periods in remote North American logging camps, where storytelling helped pass the time. Their tall tales featured “fearsome critters,” strange imaginary animals supposedly hiding in the woods, such as the Axehandle Hound. The most famous legendary lumberjack is Paul Bunyan, a giant woodsman whose enormous size explains his impossible feats. He is often pictured with Babe, his giant blue ox, who helps him with his work. In one version of the story, Paul carved the Grand Canyon by dragging his huge axe across the ground. These stories are folklore, not historical accounts, and they turn the hard work of lumberjacks into larger-than-life adventures.

De Beers is a diamond mining and trading company founded in Kimberley, South Africa, in 1888. Cecil Rhodes built the company from the region’s diamond mines, and it became a dominant force in the worldwide diamond trade. Diamonds are gemstones made of carbon that are often cut and polished for jewelry. De Beers also shaped how people buy them: in 1947, copywriter Frances Gerety wrote its four-word advertising slogan, “A Diamond Is Forever.” The campaign helped make an expensive diamond ring a customary symbol of engagement by linking the stone’s durability with lasting love. The diamond industry has also faced criticism over “blood diamonds,” stones mined and sold to fund armed groups and conflicts. De Beers shows how a company’s control of a product and its advertising can influence consumer traditions.

Thrift stores sell secondhand items, especially donated clothing, shoes, books, and household goods. Buying something used gives it a second life, often at a lower price than buying it new. It can also reduce waste and offer an alternative to fast fashion, a business model that rapidly produces and sells new clothing styles. Many thrift stores are run by charities that use sales to fund community programs. One major example is Goodwill Industries, often called Goodwill. Founded in Boston in 1902 by Reverend Edgar J. Helms, Goodwill operates a large network of local thrift stores across the United States. Money from its donated goods helps support services such as job training and employment assistance.

A pen is a handheld writing tool that leaves marks on paper by depositing liquid or gel ink. Different pens deliver ink in different ways: a ballpoint pen uses a tiny rotating ball, a rollerball uses a similar ball with more fluid ink, and a fountain pen feeds ink to a pointed metal nib. One especially familiar mass-produced pen is the BIC Cristal, known for its clear, hexagonal plastic barrel that lets you see the ink tube inside. Its cap has a small hole that allows air to pass through if the cap is accidentally swallowed. Other designs include the space pen, which uses pressurized ink so it can write in unusual conditions. Whether inexpensive or luxurious, pens serve the same basic purpose: making lasting written marks.

The Gullah people, also called Geechee, are an African American ethnic group with longstanding communities in the Sea Islands and coastal Lowcountry of South Carolina and Georgia. In South Carolina, Gullah communities have lived around Charleston, along the Santee River, and on islands such as Hilton Head and Saint Helena. Their ancestors included enslaved Africans who worked on coastal rice plantations. Because some plantations were on relatively isolated islands, their descendants were able to preserve and develop distinctive traditions. These include food, storytelling, music, crafts, and Gullah, an English-based creole language shaped by African languages such as Mende and Fulani. Gullah culture remains an important part of the region today.

The flag of Mozambique is a national symbol that brings together ideas about the country’s history and hopes for the future. It has a red triangle on the hoist side, the edge nearest the flagpole. Inside the triangle, a yellow star sits behind an open book, with a hoe and an AK-47 assault rifle crossed above the book. The book represents education, the hoe represents farming, and the rifle recalls the struggle for independence and the defense of the country. Across the rest of the flag are green, black, and yellow horizontal bands separated by narrow white stripes. The AK-47 makes Mozambique’s flag unusual among national flags. In 2005, a proposal to remove the rifle from the design was rejected.

The toga was a distinctive formal garment worn by male citizens in ancient Rome, including senators. Usually made of white wool, it was a large piece of cloth draped over one shoulder and wrapped around the body rather than sewn into a fitted shape. Wearing one showed a man’s status as a Roman citizen, but togas could be awkward to move in, so people generally chose simpler clothes for everyday work. Different styles also signaled a wearer’s role or age. The toga praetexta had a purple border and was worn by Roman magistrates, who held public office, and by freeborn boys before they came of age. Thus, both the garment itself and its decoration could communicate a person’s place in Roman society.

Purple is a color often made by mixing red and blue paint. In ancient times, purple cloth was especially prized because its dye was difficult and expensive to produce. The famous dye known as Tyrian purple was made from the secretions of marine snails in the genus Murex. It became closely associated with Tyre, a Phoenician city on the Mediterranean coast, whose traders helped spread the dye. Producing a small amount required many snails and considerable work, so purple clothing could signal wealth or high status. Purple also appears outside textiles: solutions of potassium permanganate are purple and can stain skin, while iodine vapor is violet. If a question mentions red and blue paint or ancient snail dye, the color is purple; if it asks which snails supplied Tyrian purple, the answer is Murex.

Used cars are automobiles that have had at least one previous owner and are offered for resale by dealerships, other vehicle retailers, or private sellers. Because their condition, mileage, and history vary, shoppers often compare listings and inspect a car before deciding whether its price is fair. The way prices are presented can also affect their judgment. In behavioral economics, which studies how psychology influences decisions, anchoring bias occurs when people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they receive. For example, a used-car dealer might set a high initial asking price. Even after learning more about the car or negotiating a discount, a buyer may continue to judge its value in relation to that first price rather than the prices of similar cars.

A house is a building where people live. When a house is for sale, buyers can find its listing on real-estate websites such as Zillow or Redfin. They often compare houses by square footage, which measures the amount of floor space, and by the number of bedrooms and bathrooms. Because a house can be expensive, many buyers use a mortgage: a loan they repay over time, usually with interest. During the sale, the buyer and seller must meet agreed conditions, such as completing inspections and providing payment. An arrangement called escrow helps protect both sides: a neutral third party holds money and important documents until those conditions are met. Once the sale is complete, the funds are released and ownership transfers to the buyer.

The Impossible Burger is a plant-based burger designed to look, cook, and taste like a beef burger while using no meat. It was developed by Impossible Foods, a company founded in 2011 by Stanford biochemist Patrick Brown. One ingredient that helps give the patty its beef-like flavor and color is soy-derived heme, a form of a molecule also found in animal meat. The burger also uses plant proteins, including soy protein, to give it a meat-like texture. Impossible Foods sells its products to restaurants and shoppers as alternatives to conventional meat. Burger King brought the patty to a wider audience by using it in the Impossible Whopper, a meat-free version of its famous Whopper sandwich.

A librarian is a professional who cares for a library’s collection and helps people find and use its books and other resources. Librarians also organize and preserve materials so others can access them. In Umberto Eco’s novel The Name of the Rose, a medieval monastery has a jealously guarded library. The monk Malachi holds the office of librarian, overseeing its books, and Bernard serves as his assistant. Both men die after encountering a poisoned manuscript, leaving dark stains on the fingers of their right hands. Adso of Melk and William of Baskerville investigate the deaths. The story shows how valuable and closely controlled books could be in a monastery, while Malachi’s role illustrates a librarian’s responsibility for a collection.

Public markets are places where shoppers buy food and other goods from producers and independent vendors, often at stalls in a market hall or district. Unlike a conventional grocery store, a public market brings many sellers together, so shoppers can browse fresh produce, meat, fish, baked goods, and crafts in one place. Farmers’ markets are a related type, usually focused on goods sold directly by farmers. Famous public markets include Philadelphia’s Reading Terminal Market and Seattle’s Pike Place Market. Pike Place Market opened in 1907 above Elliott Bay and is especially known for its fishmongers, who toss customers’ fish orders across the counter. Public markets can also serve as community gathering places and showcase foods grown or made in the surrounding region.

La Tomatina is an annual festival in Buñol, a town in Spain’s Valencia province about 40 kilometers west of the city of Valencia. Each August, crowds gather in the streets for a huge food fight, throwing ripe tomatoes at one another until the streets are covered in red pulp. The event began in the mid-20th century and has grown into a well-known celebration that attracts visitors from around the world. Although it looks chaotic, the tomato fight has rules designed to help keep participants safe, such as squashing tomatoes before throwing them. If asked to name the festival, the answer is La Tomatina; if asked where it takes place, the answer is Buñol, Spain.

Cheese is a dairy food made by coagulating milk: the milk separates into solid curds and liquid whey, and the curds are used to make cheese. Many varieties use an enzyme called rennet to form the curds, but different methods produce cheeses with different textures and flavors. Cheddar and Swiss are generally firm cheeses, while French cheeses such as Brie and Camembert have soft, ripened interiors. Paneer, a fresh cheese common in Indian cooking, is made differently. An acid such as lemon juice curdles the milk instead of rennet, and the curds are pressed into a firm block. Because paneer holds its shape when heated, it is often cooked in curries. An unusual cheese from the Italian island of Sardinia, Casu Marzu, contains live insect larvae.

A tent is a portable shelter made from a flexible covering stretched over a frame. Poles usually support it, and stakes or ropes can hold it in place. Campers use tents to sleep outdoors because they can be taken down, packed up, and carried to another location. Tents range from small shelters for one person to much larger structures. For nomadic families, who move from place to place, a portable shelter can serve as a home rather than just a place to spend the night. In Mongolia and other parts of Central Asia, a traditional round dwelling called a yurt has a collapsible wooden lattice frame covered with felt. A yurt is more substantial than an ordinary camping tent, but it too can be dismantled and moved.

Planned Parenthood is a nonprofit organization that provides reproductive health care, including birth control, pregnancy testing, and information about sexual health. Its history traces back to the American Birth Control League, founded by birth-control advocate Margaret Sanger in 1921. Before that, Sanger and her sister Ethel Byrne opened the first birth-control clinic in the United States in Brooklyn, New York, in 1916. At a time when information about contraception was often restricted, Sanger argued that people should be able to learn about and control their reproductive health. She also wrote What Every Girl Should Know, a series of articles about health and sexuality. The American Birth Control League later developed into Planned Parenthood, connecting Sanger’s early advocacy with an organization that still provides reproductive health services today.

Puppets are figures that performers animate to tell stories, often by moving them with their hands, strings, or rods. They can be made from materials such as cloth, paper, or wood, and performers may give them voices and personalities. Puppets appear in plays, festivals, and other performances around the world. In Igor Stravinsky’s ballet Petrushka, a magician brings three puppets to life at a Russian fair. Another famous puppet is Pinocchio, a wooden boy carved by the woodcarver Geppetto. In his story, Pinocchio’s nose grows whenever he lies, and he longs to become a real child. Whether they are simple hand puppets or elaborate figures controlled by several people, puppets let storytellers make imagined characters seem alive.

A piggy bank is a small household container for saving coins and other small amounts of money. It is traditionally shaped like a pig, with a narrow slot on top for dropping coins inside. Some piggy banks have a plug or opening underneath, while others must be broken to get the money out. That is why “breaking the piggy bank” can also mean using money you have saved. Pig-shaped money boxes have a long history in different cultures. On the Indonesian island of Java, terracotta artworks that served as piggy banks were called cèlèngan. Terracotta is clay that has been shaped and fired until hard. Whether made from clay, ceramic, or another material, a piggy bank offers a simple way to set money aside for later.

Poaching is the illegal hunting or capture of wild animals without permission. Poachers may kill elephants for their ivory tusks or rhinos for their horns, even where laws protect these animals. Poaching can reduce wildlife populations and put species at risk of extinction. One region affected by poaching is the Serengeti, a vast grassland in East Africa. Its name is shared by Serengeti National Park in Tanzania, and the wider Serengeti ecosystem extends into Kenya’s Maasai Mara. Black rhinos in this region have been severely threatened by poaching. The Serengeti is also known for the seasonal migration of wildebeests and zebras, which travel across the grasslands in search of fresh grass.

Chanel No. 5 is an iconic perfume launched in 1921 by the French fashion house Chanel. It was created by Ernest Beaux, a Russian-born perfumer who had served at the Russian imperial court before moving to France. Beaux combined floral scents with a prominent use of aldehydes, ingredients that give the perfume a bright, distinctive quality. Like other perfumes, Chanel No. 5 has layers of scent that change as it is worn: the first impression comes from its top notes, followed by heart notes and longer-lasting base notes. Its name came from the fifth sample Beaux presented to Coco Chanel, the fashion house’s founder. The fragrance became one of the world’s most recognizable perfumes and remains a famous example of how a scent can become part of a brand’s identity.

Motorcycles are two-wheeled vehicles powered by engines, used for everyday travel as well as long-distance journeys. They play an important role in two well-known books about life on the road. In 1952, Che Guevara and his friend Alberto Granado set out across South America on a Norton 500 motorcycle. Guevara’s account of their travels was published after his death as The Motorcycle Diaries, which was adapted into a 2004 film starring Gael García Bernal. In his 1974 book Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, Robert Pirsig also uses a motorcycle trip, but combines the journey with reflections on philosophy and how people understand the world. In both works, traveling by motorcycle gives the writers a way to explore places and ideas.

The potato is a starchy tuber, or underground plant stem, first domesticated in the Andes of South America. After transatlantic contact in the 1500s, people carried potatoes to Europe, where they eventually became an important staple food because they could provide plenty of food from a small area of land. Potatoes also contain vitamin C, although the amount depends on how they are stored and cooked. Vitamin C helps the body make collagen, a protein needed for healthy gums, skin, and wound healing. A severe lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, which can lead to bleeding gums and wounds that heal poorly. Scurvy was once a major problem on long sea voyages. As potatoes became more widely eaten in Europe, they helped reduce scurvy among people on land.

A vacuum cleaner is a powered household appliance that picks up dust, crumbs, and other debris from floors, carpets, and furniture. Its motor drives a fan that lowers the air pressure inside the cleaner. Because the surrounding air is at higher pressure, air rushes through the nozzle, carrying dirt with it. A bag or canister collects the debris, while a filter helps keep fine dust from blowing back into the room. Despite its name, a vacuum cleaner does not create a perfect vacuum, or a space with no air. An important early inventor was James Murray Spangler, an Ohio department-store janitor. In 1907, he built an electric suction sweeper using parts that included a fan, a soap box, and a pillowcase.

A detergent is a cleaning substance found in products such as laundry powder and dish liquid. It helps water remove oily dirt and grease that water alone cannot easily wash away. Detergents contain surfactants: molecules with a water-attracting head and a water-repelling tail that is drawn to oil and fat. During washing, the tails attach to oily soil while the heads remain in the water. Groups of surfactant molecules can surround a small droplet of oil, with their tails pointing inward and their heads pointing outward. This roughly spherical cluster is called a micelle. By trapping grease in micelles, detergent disperses it through the wash water so it can be rinsed off clothes, dishes, and other surfaces.

A shirt is an upper-body garment worn in everyday life and in more formal settings. Shirts come in many styles, from T-shirts to button-front dress shirts, and can be made from fabrics such as cotton or linen. A conventional button-front shirt has a collar near the neck, cuffs at the ends of its sleeves, and a placket: the narrow, finished strip down the center front that carries the buttons and buttonholes so the shirt can close. Shirts also appear in memorable scenes in literature. In Haruki Murakami’s The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, Toru Okada calms himself by ironing shirts in a strict 12-step order. In F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby, Daisy becomes emotional when Gatsby shows her his collection of beautiful shirts.

Volkswagen, often shortened to VW, is a German automaker founded in 1937. It became famous worldwide for the Volkswagen Type 1, better known as the Beetle, whose rounded shape made it one of the most recognizable cars in history. In 2015, Volkswagen admitted that many of its diesel cars contained software designed to cheat emissions tests. The software recognized when a car was being tested in a laboratory and changed how the engine ran so it appeared to meet pollution limits. During ordinary driving, the cars released far more pollutants. Regulators call this kind of test-detecting system a defeat device because it defeats the purpose of emissions rules. The scandal also showed how a company’s environmental marketing can conflict with its actual practices.

The Flag of Chicago is the city’s municipal banner. It has a white background, two horizontal blue stripes, and four red six-pointed stars in the space between the stripes. Each star commemorates an important event in Chicago’s history. One honors the World’s Columbian Exposition, an international fair held in Chicago in 1893 to mark the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’s arrival in the Americas. Like other world’s fairs, it brought together exhibits from different places to showcase art, culture, and new technologies. The fair helped establish Chicago’s reputation as a major city. If you see a question about Chicago’s white-and-blue flag with four red stars, remember that the banner is the Flag of Chicago and that its 1893 fair was formally called the World’s Columbian Exposition.

A strawberry is a sweet, usually red fruit eaten fresh, in desserts, or with cream. Although people call it a berry, botanists do not consider it a true berry: its juicy red part is an enlarged flower receptacle, and the tiny specks on its surface are separate fruits called achenes. Strawberries and cream are a longstanding tradition at the Wimbledon Championships, the annual grass-court tennis tournament held at the All England Club in southwest London. Strawberries also appear in popular culture: Strawberry Fields Forever is a Beatles song named after Strawberry Field, a children’s home in Liverpool. The fruit lends its name to Ingmar Bergman’s film Wild Strawberries and to a strawberry-patterned dress designed by Lirika Matoshi.

Infant formula, also called baby formula, is a manufactured food designed to meet a baby’s nutritional needs when breast milk is unavailable or not used. It contains a carefully balanced mix of nutrients and is sold as powder, liquid concentrate, or ready-to-feed liquid. In 2022, the United States experienced a severe infant formula shortage after Abbott Nutrition, a major producer, recalled some products over concerns about bacterial contamination and shut down a factory. Because only a few companies make most of the formula sold in the country, the disruption had a widespread effect. To help bring in supplies, the federal government arranged for military aircraft to fly formula from overseas to the United States. This emergency import effort was called Operation Fly Formula.

A bowler hat is a stiff hat with a rounded crown and a short, narrow brim. It became popular in the nineteenth century and is often associated with formal clothing, especially men’s suits. In Milan Kundera’s novel The Unbearable Lightness of Being, however, the artist Sabina wears a bowler hat in an unexpected way: it becomes a distinctive prop in photographs of her posing nude. The person behind the camera is Tereza, a photographer and the wife of Tomas, who is also involved with Sabina. The contrast between the formal hat and Sabina’s nudity makes it memorable. If asked to identify the hat, the answer is a bowler hat; if asked who takes the photographs, the answer is Tereza.

A cuckoo clock is a traditional wall-mounted clock that announces the hour with a bird call. On many models, a small door opens and a carved cuckoo bird pops out while the clock makes a “cuckoo” sound, often once for each hour. The word “cuckoo” imitates the bird’s call, making it an example of onomatopoeia. Traditional cuckoo clocks are strongly associated with the Black Forest, a mountainous, heavily wooded region in southwestern Germany. Villages there became known for making clocks, and many cuckoo clocks feature carved wooden designs inspired by forests and village life. Although modern versions may use electronic sounds, traditional ones use mechanical parts to keep time and produce the bird’s call.

Sailors are people who work aboard ships, carrying out jobs such as scrubbing decks, handling ropes, and hoisting sails. Before powered equipment became common, many of these tasks required crews to pull or push together at the same moment. Sailors sometimes sang sea shanties, rhythmic work songs led by one singer with the rest of the crew responding, to help coordinate their movements. Some shanties tell stories about life at sea. “Wellerman” describes sailors in the whaling trade waiting for supplies from merchants known as Wellermen. Whalers hunted whales partly for their blubber, which could be made into oil for lamps before kerosene became widely used. Scottish singer Nathan Evans’s 2021 performance brought “Wellerman” to broad public attention again.

The Joy of Cooking is a classic American cookbook first published in 1931 by Irma S. Rombauer, an author from St. Louis, Missouri. It became a favorite in many home kitchens because its friendly, conversational voice made cooking feel less intimidating. It was also known for its “action method” of writing recipes: instead of putting every ingredient in a separate list at the start, Rombauer introduced ingredients in the directions as the cook needed them. Her daughter helped prepare later editions, allowing the book to grow and change over time. The Joy of Cooking taught many Americans practical kitchen skills, including Julia Child, who later became famous for introducing French cooking to a wide audience in the United States.

A flower is the reproductive structure of an angiosperm, or flowering plant. Its parts often include colorful petals, protective sepals, pollen-producing stamens, and carpels that can develop seeds. Many flowers attract insects, birds, or other pollinators, helping the plant reproduce. Flowers also play an important role in celebrations and traditions. During Onam, a harvest festival in Kerala, India, people arrange colorful flower petals into elaborate patterns, often at the entrance to a home. This traditional decoration is called a pookalam. Elsewhere, people give bouquets to express affection, wear corsages or boutonnieres at weddings, and practice ikebana, the Japanese art of flower arrangement. Flowers such as roses, daffodils, and carnations can therefore be valued both for their role in nature and for their cultural meaning.

Tires are rubber coverings mounted around the wheels of cars, bicycles, and other vehicles. They help vehicles grip the road, making it easier to steer, brake, and accelerate, while also cushioning bumps. The patterned grooves on a tire’s surface are called treads; they help move water away from the wheel, but gradually wear down with use. Worn tires have less traction and may need replacing. On snowy or icy roads, drivers can fit removable metal-link devices called tire chains around their tires to improve grip. The chains are taken off when road conditions no longer require them. Some cars also carry a small temporary spare tire, nicknamed a “donut,” for emergencies. It is less durable than a regular tire and is meant for limited use.

Fried chicken is chicken coated in seasoned flour, breading, or batter and cooked in hot oil until its outside is crisp and its meat is fully cooked. It is strongly associated with Southern American cuisine, though people around the world make many different versions. Restaurants may serve it as bone-in pieces, strips, or sandwiches. Nashville hot chicken is a spicy variation. Fried chicken is also a major fast-food dish: Chick-fil-A is known for chicken sandwiches, while KFC stands for Kentucky Fried Chicken. KFC became famous for a recipe advertised as containing eleven herbs and spices. Its founder, Harland Sanders, is widely known as Colonel Sanders. His white suit and portrait remain familiar symbols of the chain.

A safari is an expedition, traditionally in Africa, to observe or hunt wild animals. Today, many safaris focus on watching and photographing wildlife in places such as national parks. Ernest Hemingway’s short story “The Snows of Kilimanjaro” features a big-game safari, reflecting the older association between safaris and hunting. The South African writer Nadine Gordimer uses the word very differently in her short story “The Ultimate Safari.” It follows a Mozambican girl and her family as they flee civil war through South Africa’s Kruger National Park. Their journey is dangerous and forced, not a holiday spent looking for animals, so the title is ironic. Gordimer, who also wrote the novel July’s People, received the 1991 Nobel Prize in Literature.

A dictionary is a reference work that lists words and explains what they mean. It can also show how to spell and pronounce them, give examples of how they are used, or provide translations into another language.
