People consult dictionaries when they meet an unfamiliar word or want to check that they are using one correctly. Some dictionaries serve a special purpose, such as listing terms used in law. Scrabble, a word-building board game, has its own dictionary of words that players are allowed to use. In Scrabble, players take turns placing lettered tiles on a 15-by-15 grid to form words. They score points for their letters, with extra points available for high-value letters such as Q and Z or for landing on premium squares.

Chewing gum is a confectionery product made to be chewed for its flavor and texture rather than swallowed. It usually contains a chewy gum base, flavorings, and a sweetener. Bubble gum is a type designed to stretch so you can blow bubbles; it is often pink, though gum comes in many colors and flavors. Popular brands include Orbit, Extra, and Big Red. Many sugar-free gums use xylitol, a sugar alcohol that tastes sweet but does not feed the bacteria that cause tooth decay in the same way sugar does. Chewing xylitol gum may therefore help reduce the risk of cavities. If you accidentally swallow a piece of gum, it cannot be digested like ordinary food, but it normally passes through your digestive system rather than staying there indefinitely.

Black is the darkest achromatic color, meaning it has no hue like red or blue. Paired with white, it describes the monochrome images common in early cinema: movies were often called “black and white.” Black also appears in familiar titles and names, including Black Panther, the Black Eyed Peas, and the Netflix prison drama Orange Is the New Black. That series was adapted from Piper Kerman’s memoir about her time in prison. Its main characters are held in a fictional federal women’s prison called Litchfield Penitentiary. Outside entertainment, black can suggest formality, as in a little black dress, or be used to create strong contrast with lighter colors.

New Year is the observance that marks the end of one calendar year and the beginning of the next. In the Gregorian calendar, widely used around the world, people commonly celebrate it at midnight on January 1. Other calendars place New Year on different dates. Nowruz, the Persian New Year, begins at the spring equinox, around March 20 or 21, and starts a new year in the Solar Hijri calendar used in Iran. A Nowruz tradition is the Haft-Sin table, which holds seven symbolic items whose Persian names begin with the letter sin. The Bahá’í faith also celebrates a spring New Year called Naw-Rúz, following a nineteen-day fast. The Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, falls in autumn and includes customs such as eating apples dipped in honey.

A red chili pepper is the ripe, red fruit of a Capsicum plant. Its pungent heat comes from a substance called capsaicin, and cooks use fresh, dried, or ground red chilis to add spice and color to food. Red chili peppers are ingredients in hot sauces such as Tabasco and Sriracha. They are also used in Korean cooking. Gochujang is a thick, fermented Korean chili paste made with red chili powder, rice, fermented soybeans, and salt. It adds a spicy, savory flavor to sauces and dishes such as bibimbap, a rice dish topped with vegetables and other ingredients. Korean kimchi, a fermented vegetable dish often made with cabbage or radish, may also be seasoned with red chili pepper.

Garbage is unwanted material that people throw away, such as food scraps, packaging, and broken household items. Municipal collection services pick up garbage from homes so it can be recycled, composted, or taken to a landfill. When waste is not disposed of properly, it can enter rivers and oceans. In the North Pacific, currents concentrate floating debris in a broad region between Hawaii and California called the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. It is not a solid island of trash; it contains scattered larger objects as well as many tiny plastic fragments. These fragments are called microplastics when they are smaller than five millimeters. They often form as sunlight and waves break larger plastic items into smaller pieces, and marine animals may mistake them for food.

Jewelry is the broad name for decorative items people wear, including necklaces, bracelets, rings, and earrings. It can be made from precious metals such as gold and silver, gemstones such as diamonds, or less expensive materials. People wear jewelry to express their style, celebrate important events, or show a connection to a person or tradition. Because diamonds can be valuable, the jewelry trade also has rules about where they come from. The Kimberley Process Certification Scheme, launched in 2003, requires participating countries to verify shipments of rough, or uncut, diamonds. Its aim is to keep “conflict diamonds”—diamonds sold to help fund armed violence—out of legitimate trade.

Libraries collect, organize, and preserve books and other recorded materials so people can find and use them. Today, many libraries offer places to read and study, help from librarians, and books people can borrow. Earlier libraries held clay tablets, manuscripts, and papyrus scrolls as well as other writings. One of the ancient world’s best-known libraries was the Great Library of Alexandria in Egypt. Established during the Ptolemaic era and associated with the Mouseion, a center of scholarship, it was famous for its ambitious effort to gather writings from across the known world. Although that library no longer exists, libraries continue its important work: making knowledge available to readers now while helping preserve it for future generations.

Embalming is the treatment of a dead body to preserve its tissues and slow decomposition, often so family and friends can view the person before burial or cremation. A trained professional may inject preservative fluid into blood vessels and treat other tissues. Traditional embalming fluid often contains formaldehyde, a chemical that “fixes” tissues by helping their proteins hold their structure. This also makes it harder for microorganisms to break down the body. Formaldehyde is produced industrially by oxidizing methanol, the simplest alcohol, whose chemical formula is CH3OH. When formaldehyde is dissolved in water, the solution is commonly called formalin. Embalming delays decomposition but does not prevent it forever, and customs and requirements surrounding it vary among cultures and religions.

A message in a bottle is a written note sealed inside a bottle or another watertight container and set adrift in a sea, river, or lake. The sender may not know who will find it, or whether anyone will find it at all. The message travels wherever the water carries it, making its delivery a matter of chance rather than a direct exchange like a letter or text. People have used messages in bottles to share news, ask for help, or leave a record of an experience. In Edgar Allan Poe’s 1833 story “MS. Found in a Bottle,” a shipwreck survivor boards a mysterious vessel and casts his written account into the ocean. The story won a contest held by the Baltimore Saturday Visiter.

Forever 21 is an American fast-fashion retailer founded in Los Angeles in 1984 by Do Won Chang and Jin Sook Chang. Fast fashion means producing inexpensive clothing based on current trends and moving new styles into stores quickly. Forever 21 became popular with shoppers who wanted fashionable clothes at low prices, and its bright yellow shopping bags became a recognizable part of the brand. On the bottom of those bags was the biblical citation John 3:16, a verse commonly recognized by its opening words, “For God so loved the world.” Like other fast-fashion companies, Forever 21 has faced criticism over the waste created when clothes are bought and discarded quickly. Several designers have also accused the retailer of copying their designs.

A shield is a defensive object held in the hand or worn on the arm to block weapons such as swords, spears, and arrows. Shields have been made from materials including wood, leather, and metal, and many are round, though they come in other shapes too. Warriors often carried a shield alongside a sword or spear, using it for protection while they fought. Shields also appear in mythology. In Homer’s Iliad, the god Hephaestus makes an elaborate shield for the hero Achilles, decorating it with heavenly bodies, flourishing cities, and scenes of everyday life. In Greek mythology, a divine protective object associated with Athena and Zeus is called the Aegis; it is often described or shown as bearing the head of Medusa.

The Running of the Bulls is an annual event in Pamplona, Spain, during the San Fermín festival in July. The festival honors Saint Fermín, and each morning of the bull runs, participants race ahead of a herd of bulls through the narrow streets of Pamplona’s old quarter. The route ends at the city’s bullring, or arena. Pamplona is the capital of Navarre, a region in northern Spain. The run is a famous local tradition, but it is dangerous: both runners and animals can be injured. Knowing the festival’s name, San Fermín, and its host city, Pamplona, helps distinguish this event from other Spanish celebrations.

Kintsugi is a Japanese technique for repairing broken ceramics, such as bowls, cups, and plates. Instead of hiding the cracks, it makes them part of the object’s appearance. The broken pieces are joined with urushi lacquer, a traditional Japanese adhesive made from the sap of the tree Toxicodendron vernicifluum. The repaired seams are then mixed with or highlighted by metallic powder, often gold, silver, or platinum, so they stand out against the ceramic surface. A kintsugi repair can turn a break into a distinctive pattern rather than trying to make the object look untouched. The technique shows that an object can remain useful and beautiful after it has been damaged and repaired.

Biryani is a South Asian dish built around rice, often long-grain basmati, combined with aromatic spices and meat such as chicken or lamb. Cooks commonly layer spiced meat with partially cooked rice, then cover the pot and finish cooking everything together over low heat. This helps the rice absorb the flavors while keeping its grains separate. Biryani is closely linked to the courtly cooking traditions of the Mughal Empire, which ruled much of the Indian subcontinent from the 16th to the 19th centuries. Over time, different regions developed their own versions. Hyderabadi biryani is known for its bold spices, while Lucknowi biryani is often more delicately seasoned. Although recipes vary, the combination of rice, spices, and layered cooking makes biryani distinctive.

A blacksmith is a craftsperson who makes and repairs objects from iron or steel. In a traditional workshop, the blacksmith heats metal in a forge until it is soft enough to shape, then strikes it with a hammer to make tools, hardware such as hinges, or horseshoes. The metal rests on an anvil, a heavy block that provides a hard surface for hammering. Its flat face supports straight work, while its projecting horn helps the blacksmith form curves and bends. Blacksmiths once played an important role in village life because people relied on them to make and mend everyday items. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem “The Village Blacksmith” describes one working beneath a spreading chestnut tree.

An Afro is a rounded, voluminous hairstyle created when tightly curled hair grows outward from the head, often with its shape maintained using a comb or pick. Although people can wear Afros simply because they like the look, the style has also been an important expression of Black pride, natural beauty, and the freedom to choose how to wear one’s hair. In Lorraine Hansberry’s play A Raisin in the Sun, Beneatha Younger is an aspiring doctor who questions expectations about her identity and future. After straightening her hair, she decides to wear it naturally in an Afro. Joseph Asagai, one of her suitors, encourages her to value her African heritage, making her hairstyle part of the play’s exploration of identity and self-expression.

Automobiles, commonly called cars, are self-propelled vehicles used to travel on roads. They take people to school, work, shops, and other places, and companies such as Volkswagen manufacture them. Cars can also appear in art and popular culture. In the performance piece Trans-Fixed, artist Chris Burden was attached to an automobile. In Nebraska, Jim Reinders arranged old cars to resemble the ancient stone monument Stonehenge. His roadside attraction is called Carhenge. Diego Rivera depicted workers making automobiles in a series of murals, while the Futurist Manifesto praised the speed and beauty of a racing car. In the 1960s, some hippies drove brightly painted Volkswagen minibuses decorated with peace signs. These examples show how automobiles can be more than transportation: they can also express ideas and inspire art.

Lyft is a San Francisco-based technology company co-founded in 2012 by Logan Green and John Zimmer. It is best known for its ridesharing app, which lets passengers request trips from nearby drivers, usually in the drivers’ own vehicles. A passenger enters a pickup location and destination in the app, then checks details such as the driver’s name and license plate to find the right car. Lyft and Uber are two major companies offering this kind of service. Lyft has also expanded into other ways of getting around. In 2018, it acquired Motivate, the company that operated Citi Bike, New York City’s blue, station-based bicycle-rental service. Citi Bike users can pick up a bike at one station and return it to another.

A funeral is a ceremony or set of customs held after someone dies. It gives family and friends a chance to honor the person, mourn their death, and say goodbye. Funerals may include prayers, music, stories, or a gathering, depending on a community’s cultural or religious traditions. They may also involve handling the person’s remains through burial or cremation. Grief at a funeral can feel overwhelming, as the poet W. H. Auden shows in “Funeral Blues.” In the poem, the speaker calls for clocks to be stopped and telephones to be silenced, then imagines even the stars being extinguished. These impossible requests express how deeply a loved one’s death can affect someone, while funeral customs give people a way to share and acknowledge that loss.

Fashion is the design and creation of clothing and other wearable styles. Designers choose shapes, fabrics, colors, and patterns to make clothes that are useful, expressive, or both. Fashion can also draw inspiration from other art forms. In 1965, French fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent created A-line dresses inspired by the work of Dutch painter Piet Mondrian. Mondrian made abstract art: instead of showing realistic scenes, he arranged geometric shapes to express ideas. His compositions often used thick black lines, white spaces, and rectangles of the primary colors red, yellow, and blue. Saint Laurent turned this bold visual style into clothing, showing how a painting’s design could become something people wear.

Soft drinks are nonalcoholic beverages that are usually sweetened and often carbonated, meaning they contain bubbles. Examples include colas, fruit-flavored sodas, and other fizzy drinks. Vita Cola is a cola developed in East Germany, where it became a familiar product of everyday life. Today, some people remember it fondly as part of “Ostalgie,” or nostalgia for life in the former East Germany. Another soft drink with a German history is Fanta. During World War II, Coca-Cola’s German operation could no longer obtain the syrup needed to make Coca-Cola because of wartime trade restrictions. It created a new drink using ingredients it could get locally. That drink was Fanta, which later became known worldwide as an orange-flavored soda.

Ford Motor Company is an American automaker founded by Henry Ford in 1903. It became famous for the Model T, a rugged, relatively low-priced car introduced in 1908 and nicknamed “Tin Lizzie.” The Model T helped make car ownership possible for many Americans rather than only the wealthy. Ford also transformed manufacturing by using a moving assembly line to produce cars quickly and in large numbers, helping lower their cost. Near Detroit, Michigan, the company built the enormous River Rouge manufacturing complex, named for the nearby Rouge River. There, many stages of production took place on one site, from processing raw materials to assembling vehicles. Ford remains one of the best-known companies in the American automotive industry.

Cherries are small, fleshy fruits that grow on trees in the genus Prunus, making them relatives of plums, peaches, nectarines, and apricots. Each cherry has a hard pit in the center, so it is classified as a drupe, or stone fruit. Cherries can be eaten fresh or used in desserts, and some are preserved in sugar syrup and colored to make maraschino cherries, the bright garnishes often served in drinks. One sweet variety sometimes used for maraschino cherries is the Rainier cherry. It was developed in Washington state and named after Mount Rainier, a mountain near Seattle. Another variety used for maraschino cherries is the Royal Anne, which is also known as the Napoleon cherry.

A knife is a tool with a sharpened blade used for cutting, preparing food, and other everyday tasks. Knives come in many shapes and sizes: some have fixed blades, while others fold into a handle for safe carrying. A Swiss Army knife is a folding pocketknife that combines a blade with useful tools such as a screwdriver and a can opener. In the 18th and 19th centuries, gauchos—the cowboys of Argentina and Uruguay—often carried a long knife called a facón. They used it for practical work on the plains, but it could also serve as a weapon in a fight. The facón shows how a knife’s design can reflect the needs and traditions of the people who use it.

LEGO is a Danish toy brand known for small plastic bricks that can be joined to build models, vehicles, buildings, and almost anything you can imagine. Studs on top of each brick fit into tubes underneath another brick, holding the pieces together while allowing builders to take them apart and create something new. The LEGO company was founded by Ole Kirk Christiansen, and its name comes from the Danish words “leg godt,” meaning “play well.” In 1978, LEGO introduced the minifigure, a small character with a cylindrical head and movable arms and legs. Minifigures can wear different hats, hold tools, and swap accessories or other parts. LEGO creations also appear in movies and theme parks, including LEGOLAND in Carlsbad, California.

Murano glass is a centuries-old glassmaking tradition from Murano, an island in the lagoon north of Venice, Italy. In 1291, Venice ordered glassmakers to move their furnaces there because the hot furnaces posed a fire risk in the crowded city. Murano’s artisans became famous for making both useful objects, such as drinking glasses and household vessels, and decorative pieces with intricate shapes and colors. Their skills helped make the island a major center of glassmaking. In the 15th century, master glassmaker Angelo Barovier was credited with developing cristallo, an especially clear, colorless type of glass designed to resemble rock crystal. Today, “Murano glass” refers to glass made on the island using its long-established craft traditions.

Pins are small metal fasteners with a sharp point at one end and a head at the other. In The Wealth of Nations, economist Adam Smith used a pin-making workshop to explain the division of labor: instead of each worker making a whole pin, different workers carried out separate steps, such as drawing out the wire, cutting it, sharpening the point, and attaching the head. By repeating a specialized task, workers could become faster and more skilled, so the workshop could produce many more pins than if everyone worked alone. “Labor” means the human work needed to make a product, and dividing that labor into tasks can make production more efficient.

A hatchet is a small axe with a short handle that can be swung with one hand. Its blade is set across the end of the handle, making it useful for chopping small pieces of wood and splitting kindling for a fire. Hatchets are often carried on camping trips because they are more compact than full-sized axes. The tool also has an unusual place in American history. Around 1900, Carrie Nation, an activist in the temperance movement, entered saloons in Kansas and used a hatchet to smash liquor containers and furnishings. Temperance supporters wanted to reduce or ban the drinking of alcohol, and Nation’s dramatic raids made her nationally famous. The movement later helped bring about Prohibition, a nationwide ban on alcoholic beverages.

School dances are social events organized by schools where students gather to listen to music, dance, and spend time with friends. They often take place in a school gym or hall and may have decorations, a theme, and refreshments. Some are casual evenings, while others are milestones: homecoming often celebrates a school’s community and sports traditions, and prom is usually a more formal event for older students. School dances also appear in movies and television. In Back to the Future, Marty McFly attends Hill Valley High’s 1955 Enchantment Under the Sea Dance. There, he performs “Johnny B. Goode” while his future parents reconnect. Whether formal or informal, these events give students a chance to celebrate together outside the classroom.

Alcohol is the broad name for beverages containing ethanol, including beer, wine, and distilled spirits such as whiskey. In the United States, the 18th Amendment and the Volstead Act began a period called Prohibition in 1920. These laws banned the manufacture and sale of alcoholic drinks, though drinking alcohol itself was not banned nationwide. People who illegally made or sold alcohol were known as bootleggers, and the illegal trade helped some criminal gangs grow. One weapon associated with Prohibition-era gang violence was the Thompson submachine gun, nicknamed the “Tommy gun.” It could fire rapidly and was reportedly carried in violin cases. Bootleggers and law enforcement both used it, and it became especially associated with the 1929 St. Valentine’s Day Massacre in Chicago. Prohibition ended in 1933.

Ridesharing is a transportation service that lets passengers request rides through a phone app or similar platform. Instead of driving vehicles from a company fleet, participating drivers usually use their own cars to pick up passengers and take them to their destinations. A passenger enters a pickup location and destination in the app, then checks details such as the driver’s name, car, and license plate to find the right vehicle. Uber and Lyft are well-known ridesharing companies. Uber began in San Francisco in 2009 and offers ride options such as Black, for a higher-end trip, and XL, for larger groups. It also operates a food-delivery service called Uber Eats.

The coconut is the large fruit of the coconut palm, a tree that grows throughout tropical Polynesia. Inside its fibrous outer husk is a hard shell containing edible white flesh and drinkable coconut water. People eat the flesh fresh or use it to make coconut milk, while fibers from the husk can be made into rope and other useful objects. Coconuts are therefore important in both everyday life and culture. In one Polynesian origin story, the trickster demigod Maui kills and buries an eel, and the first coconut tree grows from its grave. Maui also appears in a Hawaiian story in which he uses a magic fishhook to pull the Hawaiian Islands from the sea.

The taxi industry carries passengers for a fare in licensed cabs, usually for individual trips rather than along fixed bus routes. Cities often regulate taxis by setting safety rules and limiting who can operate them. In New York City, a yellow cab traditionally needed a taxi medallion: a limited, transferable authorization that could be bought and sold. Because the number of medallions was restricted, they became very valuable, but their prices fell after ride-hailing services such as Uber and Lyft expanded in the mid-2010s. The industry can also involve fierce competition over routes and passengers. Near Cape Town, South Africa, conflict between taxi operators in 2021 led to more than 80 deaths. These examples show how rules, competition, and new technology can shape the taxi industry.

A ghost kitchen is a food business that prepares meals for delivery or pickup but has no customer-facing dining room. Customers usually order through a website or app, and the food may be cooked in a shared kitchen or in the back of an existing restaurant. A ghost kitchen can use a separate “virtual” brand name, so customers might not realize where their meal was made. These businesses grew rapidly during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many people ordered food instead of eating at restaurants. For example, It’s Just Wings has prepared orders in Chili’s kitchens. Another delivery-first brand is MrBeast Burger, developed by the YouTube creator MrBeast, whose legal name is Jimmy Donaldson.

The Gregorian calendar is the dating system used for most civil purposes around the world today. Pope Gregory XIII introduced it in 1582 to replace the Julian calendar, whose year was slightly too long. Over centuries, that small error had caused calendar dates to drift away from the seasons, affecting the timing of Christian celebrations such as Easter. The reform adjusted the leap-year rule: years divisible by 100 are not leap years unless they are also divisible by 400. Gregory XIII formally announced the reform in a papal bull dated 24 February 1582. Its Latin title was Inter gravissimas. Some countries adopted the new calendar quickly, while others took centuries to switch. During the French Revolution, revolutionaries introduced a different calendar partly to reduce the Catholic Church’s influence, but it did not replace the Gregorian calendar permanently.

Sake is a Japanese alcoholic drink made from rice. To produce it, brewers use koji, a mold that helps turn rice starch into sugar; yeast then ferments the sugar into alcohol. Sake is brewed, not distilled, so calling it a “rice wine” does not fully explain how it is made. It has an important place in Japanese celebrations and religious customs. At some traditional weddings, the couple drinks sake in a ritual called san-san-kudo, taking three sips from each of three cups; their families may also share sake to symbolize a new bond. Sake is also offered at shrines in Shinto, Japan’s indigenous religion. In Shinto, sacred spirits or deities are called kami, and sake offerings can express respect and gratitude to them.

A substitute teacher temporarily takes over a class when its regular teacher is absent, for example because of illness or training. The substitute follows the lesson plans left behind, takes attendance, supervises students, and helps keep learning on track. This everyday school role is the focus of a famous sketch from the comedy show Key & Peele. Comedian Keegan-Michael Key plays a stern substitute teacher taking roll call, while his comedy partner Jordan Peele plays one of the students. The humor comes from the substitute mispronouncing familiar names and refusing to believe the students when they correct him. His frustrated line to a student named Aaron, “You done messed up, A-A-ron,” became especially well known.

An emoji is a small picture or symbol used in digital messages to communicate an emotion, object, action, or idea. You might add a tears-of-joy face to show that something is funny or a thumbs-up to show approval. Emojis can make a short message clearer or more expressive, though their meaning can depend on context. They also appear in popular culture: the cover of Canadian rapper Drake’s 2021 album Certified Lover Boy arranges twelve pregnant-woman emojis in a grid. The album includes the songs “Knife Talk” and “Way 2 Sexy.” If you see those songs mentioned alongside a cover made of pregnant-woman pictograms, the album is Certified Lover Boy, and the pictograms are emojis.

Mole is a family of rich Mexican sauces, not a single recipe. Cooks make it by combining and grinding ingredients such as dried chiles, spices, nuts or seeds, then simmering the mixture into a thick sauce. Recipes vary by region and family, so moles can differ in color, flavor, and heat. One famous variety is mole poblano, associated with Puebla. Some mole recipes also include cacao beans, the bitter, unsweetened seeds that can be processed into chocolate. Toasted or ground with chiles and spices, cacao adds depth to the sauce rather than making it taste like a chocolate dessert. Mole is often served over chicken or other meats, and preparing it for a celebration can be a lengthy process.

Dal, also spelled dhal, is a South Asian staple made by simmering dried pulses such as lentils, split peas, or beans until they soften into a thick dish or stew. Cooks often season it with spices, onion, garlic, or ginger, and serve it with rice or flatbread. The word “dal” can refer both to the split pulses and to the cooked dish. Dal is also common in Guyana, a Caribbean country on the northern coast of South America whose cuisine reflects its many cultural influences, including South Asian traditions. Another well-known Guyanese dish is pepperpot, a slow-cooked stew flavored with cassareep, a dark sauce made from cassava. So if a question mentions split pulses cooked into a seasoned stew, think dal; if it links dal with cassareep pepperpot, think Guyana.

Bananas are tropical fruits that grow in bunches on large plants. They are eaten fresh and used in foods such as smoothies and banana bread. During the twentieth century, the United Fruit Company grew and sold bananas on a huge scale in Central America; its operations later continued under the Chiquita name. The company owned large areas of land and had great political influence. This helps explain the term “banana republic,” used for a country whose economy and government are heavily influenced by foreign fruit companies. In Guatemala, President Jacobo Árbenz proposed land reforms that threatened United Fruit’s interests. The company opposed his plans and lobbied the U.S. government. In 1954, a CIA-backed operation called PBSUCCESS helped overthrow Árbenz in Guatemala.

Fast fashion is a retail business model that makes large quantities of inexpensive, trend-driven clothing and brings new styles into stores quickly. Retailers such as Zara and H&M are well-known examples. Low prices and frequent new arrivals can encourage shoppers to buy more clothes and replace them sooner, creating textile waste when unwanted items are thrown away. One alternative is to buy secondhand clothing from thrift stores, also called thrift shops or charity shops. These stores sell donated items, often at low prices, giving clothes another chance to be worn instead of discarded. Goodwill and the Salvation Army operate well-known thrift stores, and money from their sales often supports charitable programs.

Babysitters are people trusted to look after children for a short time while their parents or guardians are away. They may play with the children, prepare snacks or meals, help with bedtime, and make sure everyone stays safe. Babysitters appear in many stories about family life. In The Baby-Sitters Club, Kristy Thomas starts a club that helps families find babysitters; Stacey and Claudia are among its members. In Pixar’s short film Jack-Jack Attack, Kari McKeen babysits Jack-Jack, the youngest child in the Parr family. After she realizes that the villain Syndrome tricked her, her memory of the experience is erased. These examples show how babysitting can be an ordinary job in real life and a source of adventure in fiction.

The exclamation mark (!) has two common uses. In English writing, it can end a sentence that expresses strong emotion, such as “What a surprise!”, or a forceful command, such as “Stop!” It is also called an exclamation point. In mathematics, an exclamation mark placed after a nonnegative integer means “factorial.” To find a factorial, multiply the integer by every positive whole number below it, down to 1. For example, 5! (read “five factorial”) equals 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, or 120. Factorials appear in formulas for counting arrangements and selections, including permutations, where order matters, and combinations, where it does not. The symbol’s meaning depends on its context: sentence-ending punctuation in writing, but an operation in mathematics.

Fireworks are devices that use pyrotechnic materials—substances that burn rapidly—to produce colored light, sparks, loud bangs, and other effects. They are often launched into the sky during public celebrations. In the United States, fireworks are especially associated with Independence Day on July 4. Although they can be exciting to watch, fireworks contain explosive materials and can cause serious harm if they are made, stored, or handled unsafely. In May 2000, a fireworks factory exploded in Enschede, a city in the Netherlands. The blast destroyed about 400 homes, showing why fireworks require careful storage and strict safety rules.

Toyota Motor Corporation is a Japanese automaker known for models such as the Corolla, Camry, and Prius, a hybrid car that uses both a gasoline engine and an electric motor. The company grew from a business associated with automatic looms, and that background helped shape how it builds cars. Its influential factory method is called the Toyota Production System. It emphasizes just-in-time manufacturing: making or delivering parts only when they are needed, rather than storing large amounts. Workers and machines are also expected to stop production when they find a defect so the problem can be fixed. By continually improving processes and reducing wasted time, materials, and effort, Toyota made its methods influential in factories around the world.

Tobacco is a plant grown for its leaves, which are dried and processed for products such as cigarettes. In the early 1600s, tobacco became a major export from the English colony of Virginia. John Rolfe arrived at Jamestown with the Third Supply and cultivated a strain of tobacco that buyers in England wanted, helping the colony earn money through trade. Rolfe later married Pocahontas, a Powhatan woman. Tobacco was packed into large barrels called hogsheads for shipment across the Atlantic. Although it brought wealth to some colonists, tobacco farming depended heavily on the labor of enslaved people. Smoking and other tobacco use can cause addiction and serious illnesses, so tobacco’s importance in history should not be confused with being safe to use.

The beef industry is the part of agriculture that raises cattle and turns their meat into beef for people to eat. Cattle may begin on ranches, move to feedlots where they are fed before sale, and then go to slaughterhouses and meatpacking plants. Businesses process, package, and distribute the beef to stores and restaurants. A small number of large meat processors handle much of this work in the United States; they are often called the industry’s “Big Four.” One of them is JBS, a company founded in Brazil that expanded its U.S. operations by acquiring Swift & Company in 2007. The industry also includes smaller processors and ranchers, whose costs and access to processing can affect the price of beef, including steaks.

Slapping means striking someone or something with an open hand, usually with the palm, rather than with a closed fist as in a punch. A slap can express anger or disrespect, but it can also refer to a way of striking guitar strings with the knuckles. Because slapping a person can cause pain and humiliation, it is often treated as a serious act. One well-known example involved U.S. Army General George S. Patton during the 1943 Sicily Campaign of World War II. Patton slapped two hospitalized soldiers whose conditions he believed were not serious. The soldiers were suffering from psychological effects of combat, then commonly called “shell shock.” News of the incidents caused a major controversy, and Patton was ordered to apologize.

Pajamas are clothes designed mainly for sleeping or relaxing at home. A typical pair has two loose-fitting pieces: a top and matching trousers. They are often made from comfortable fabrics such as cotton or flannel, and people may call them PJs or jammies. Not all pajamas come in two pieces, though. A onesie is a one-piece style that covers the torso and legs in a single garment, often with a zipper or buttons down the front. Onesies are common as infant sleepwear, but older children and adults can wear them too. Pajamas are part of the broader category of nightwear, which also includes garments such as nightgowns.

Maple syrup is a sweet, amber-colored topping made by boiling down sap tapped from maple trees. In late winter and early spring, producers collect the watery xylem sap as it flows through the trees, then heat it until much of the water evaporates and the sugars become concentrated. Sugar maples and other maples grow in eastern North America, where their leaves turn vivid red and gold in autumn. Québec, in Canada, produces most of the world’s maple syrup. People often pour it over pancakes and waffles, but it is also used in baking and other foods. During syrup season in Québec, visitors can go to a sugar shack, a rustic place where producers boil sap and serve treats such as maple taffy made by pouring hot syrup onto snow.

The Falkland Islands are an archipelago in the South Atlantic Ocean, east of Argentina. They consist of two main islands, East Falkland and West Falkland, along with many smaller islands. The United Kingdom administers the islands, but Argentina also claims sovereignty over them and calls them the Islas Malvinas. In 1982, Argentina invaded the islands, leading to a war with the United Kingdom. British forces regained control, and the islands remain British-administered. Their capital and largest settlement is Stanley, on East Falkland beside a sheltered harbor. Stanley is the islands’ principal port and administrative center. Fishing and sheep farming are important to the islands’ economy, and their location has made them a focus of a long-running dispute between Britain and Argentina.

Ibiza is a Spanish island in the western Mediterranean Sea and part of the Balearic Islands, an archipelago that also includes Mallorca, Menorca, and Formentera. It is the second most populous island in the group, after Mallorca, which is also known as Majorca. Ibiza attracts visitors from around the world to its beaches and resorts, but it is especially famous for its nightlife. Its clubs and festivals have made it an internationally prominent destination for electronic dance music, often called EDM. Although many people associate Ibiza with summer parties, it also has quieter villages and historic sites. If a question asks for the Balearic island known for resorts and EDM, the answer is Ibiza; if it asks which archipelago Ibiza belongs to, the answer is the Balearic Islands.

Copenhagen is the capital and largest city of Denmark, a country in northern Europe. It lies mainly on Zealand, Denmark’s largest island, which is also home to the historic city of Roskilde. Across the Øresund strait to the east is Sweden. Since 2000, the Øresund Bridge and its connecting tunnel have provided a fixed route between Copenhagen and the Swedish city of Malmö. Copenhagen’s waterfront is home to the Little Mermaid statue, inspired by a fairy tale written by Danish author Hans Christian Andersen. Other landmarks include Amalienborg, the royal palace complex, and Tivoli Gardens, a famous amusement park. If you are asked to identify the city from the bridge or the Little Mermaid, the answer is Copenhagen; if asked for its island, the answer is Zealand.

Denali is the highest mountain in North America, rising about 20,310 feet (6,190 meters) above sea level in the Alaska Range. It stands in Alaska, the largest U.S. state by area. Alaska lies in the far northwest of North America and is separated from Russia by the Bering Strait. For many years, the mountain was officially called Mount McKinley, after a former U.S. president. In 2015, the U.S. government restored its official name to Denali, a name of Athabaskan origin meaning “the High One.” Indigenous people in Alaska had used the name Denali long before the mountain was called Mount McKinley.

An airport is a place where aircraft take off, land, and receive services such as refueling and maintenance. It usually has runways for takeoffs and landings, taxiways that connect them to other areas, and terminals where passengers check in, board flights, and collect luggage. Quito, Ecuador, once had a Mariscal Sucre airport in the city center; it closed in 2013, and the site became a public park. Chicago, the largest city in Illinois, has two operating airports called O’Hare and Midway. Chicago Midway International Airport lies southwest of the city center and is a major base for Southwest Airlines. Its name honors the Battle of Midway, a decisive U.S. naval victory in the Pacific during World War II in 1942.

Tamil Nadu is a state in southeastern India that occupies much of the Coromandel Coast along the Bay of Bengal. Its capital, Chennai, was formerly called Madras and was an important center of British colonial power in southern India. Fort St. George, built by the British, and the long Marina Beach are well-known Chennai landmarks. The city is also a center of Tamil-language filmmaking, an industry nicknamed “Kollywood.” Across the state, the Tamil language and longstanding Dravidian traditions shape its literature, arts, and architecture. Tamil Nadu is especially known for its elaborate Hindu temples, including Brihadisvara Temple and Ranganathaswamy Temple. The experimental township of Auroville is located mostly in Tamil Nadu’s Viluppuram district.

The Aral Sea is an inland lake in Central Asia, east of the Caspian Sea, between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. It was once one of the world’s largest lakes, fed mainly by the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers. During the Soviet era, water from those rivers was diverted to irrigate farmland, especially fields growing cotton, a fiber crop that became a major Uzbek export. Cotton was also harvested by enslaved laborers in the American South before the Civil War. With far less river water reaching the Aral Sea, it shrank dramatically and broke into separate bodies of water. The retreating water exposed salty lakebed, harming fishing communities and creating dust storms that can carry salt and pollutants across the region.

The South Pole is Earth’s southernmost point, at 90° south latitude on the Antarctic ice sheet, near the center of Antarctica. Unlike the North Pole, which lies on sea ice over an ocean, the South Pole sits on ice covering a continent. In 1911, two expeditions raced to reach it: Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen arrived first, in December, while British explorer Robert Falcon Scott arrived several weeks later. Scott and his companions died on the return journey. Today, scientists work at the U.S. Amundsen–Scott South Pole Station, named for both explorers. Its modern elevated complex was completed in 2008. Researchers there study topics including climate, the atmosphere, and space, despite extreme cold and months of winter darkness.

The Tigris–Euphrates river system is a paired drainage network in southwestern Asia. Its two major rivers rise in eastern Turkey and flow southeast, eventually crossing Iraq. Near the Iraqi town of Al-Qurnah, the Tigris and Euphrates meet to form the Shatt al-Arab, a waterway that carries their combined flow toward the Persian Gulf. The land between the two rivers is called Mesopotamia, a name meaning “between the rivers.” Their water and fertile floodplains supported farming and some of the world’s earliest civilizations, including Sumer, whose city-states included Ur and whose people developed cuneiform writing. The rivers remain important sources of water for communities and agriculture in the region.

Dhaka is the capital and largest city of Bangladesh, a South Asian country mostly surrounded by India. It lies near the Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, where major rivers spread across low-lying land before reaching the Bay of Bengal. Dhaka’s historic center developed on the northern bank of the Buriganga River, which flows along the city’s southern edge. The river was an important waterway for trade when the city was part of the Mughal Empire; during Mughal rule, Dhaka was also called Jahangirnagar. Today, Dhaka is a crowded center of government, business, and culture. It faces challenges including traffic, pollution, and the arrival of people displaced by flooding and other effects of climate change elsewhere in Bangladesh.

Eilat is Israel’s southernmost city, located at the northern end of the Gulf of Aqaba. It is a port and resort known for its warm weather, beaches, and access to the sea. Eilat also serves as a gateway to the Southern Negev, a desert region where visitors can explore landscapes such as the sandstone cliffs of nearby Timna Park. The Gulf of Aqaba is a narrow northern extension of the Red Sea. The Red Sea lies between northeastern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula and borders countries including Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, and Yemen. Eilat’s position on this gulf gives Israel access to the Red Sea and helps explain the city’s importance for travel and trade.

Verona is a city in northern Italy on the Adige River. Its best-known ancient landmark is the Arena di Verona, a first-century Roman amphitheater in Piazza Bra. Built for public spectacles nearly 2,000 years ago, the arena is still used for performances and hosts a celebrated summer opera festival. Verona is also the principal setting of William Shakespeare’s tragedy Romeo and Juliet. In the play, the Montagues and Capulets are two families whose long-running feud divides the city. Romeo Montague and Juliet Capulet fall in love despite that conflict, and their story ends tragically. These connections to Roman history, live performance, and Shakespeare make Verona an important cultural destination.

Bulgaria is a country in southeastern Europe with Sofia as its capital and a coastline on the Black Sea. Much of its northern border with Romania follows the Danube River, which flows east and empties into the Black Sea through a large delta. Bulgaria has a long history shaped by its position between Europe and Asia. During the Middle Ages, the Bulgarian Empire was a major power in the region. It fought the Magyars, who settled in the Carpathian Basin and later founded the Kingdom of Hungary, as well as the Byzantine Empire to the south. In 1014, Byzantine emperor Basil II defeated Bulgarian forces at the Battle of Kleidion. Today, Bulgaria is bordered by Romania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece, and Turkey.

Port Royal was a harbor settlement on the Palisadoes spit, a narrow strip of land at the entrance to Kingston Harbour in Jamaica. In the 1600s, its position on Caribbean shipping routes helped it become a busy English trading center and a haven for pirates. Some pirates later became legal English privateers, who attacked enemy ships with government permission; Henry Morgan was one of the best known. In June 1692, a powerful earthquake struck Jamaica and devastated Port Royal. Severe shaking caused liquefaction, in which waterlogged ground lost its firmness, and much of the settlement slipped beneath the sea. A tsunami added to the destruction. This disaster is commonly called the 1692 Jamaica earthquake, and it ended Port Royal’s days as a major Caribbean port.

Libya is a North African country with a long Mediterranean coastline between Tunisia and Egypt. Much of its interior is desert, and it borders Chad to the south. Muammar Gaddafi ruled Libya for more than four decades before he was overthrown during the 2011 Arab Spring. Along the Libya–Chad border lies the Aouzou Strip, a sparsely populated desert territory that both countries claimed, partly because of its possible mineral resources. Their dispute helped fuel fighting, including the 1980s Toyota War, in which Chadian troops used pickup trucks fitted with weapons against Libyan forces. In 1994, the International Court of Justice ruled that the Aouzou Strip belonged to Chad, settling the border dispute.

Orogeny is the geological process that builds mountain belts over millions of years as tectonic plates move. When plates collide, compression can squeeze layers of rock into folds, break them along faults, and push them upward. Orogeny can occur where two continents converge or where an oceanic plate meets the edge of a continent. One major example is the Himalayan orogeny: the Indian Plate has moved northward and collided with the Eurasian Plate, raising the Himalayas along the southern edge of the Tibetan Plateau. This collision continues today, so the range, which includes Mount Everest, is still being uplifted. Mountains formed by orogeny can also affect climate by forcing moist air upward, producing rain on one side and a drier “rain shadow” on the other.

British Columbia is Canada’s westernmost province, on the Pacific coast. It shares part of its southern border with the U.S. state of Washington. Its landscapes include coastal islands, forests, and mountain ranges such as the Rockies. Vancouver Island lies off the province’s mainland coast, and near its southern end is Victoria, British Columbia’s capital. The provincial legislature meets in Victoria, where elected representatives debate and make provincial laws. Although Vancouver is the province’s largest city, it is on the mainland and is not the capital. Remember the distinction: British Columbia is the province, Vancouver Island is an island within it, and Victoria is the capital city on that island.

Asia is the world’s largest continent. It stretches from the Middle East across central and southern Asia to the Pacific Ocean and includes countries such as China, Japan, and India. The Italian composer Giacomo Puccini set two of his operas there: Turandot takes place in China, while Madama Butterfly is set in Japan. In Turandot, Puccini used traditional Chinese melodies, including “Mò Li Hūa,” to evoke the setting’s musical traditions. Asia also includes much of Russia, the world’s largest country by land area. Russia stretches across two continents: its western part lies in eastern Europe, while its vast eastern part extends through northern Asia to the Pacific.

Sierra Leone is a country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa. It borders Guinea to the north and east and Liberia to the southeast. Its capital, Freetown, is a port city on one of the world’s largest natural harbors. Freetown was founded in 1792 as a settlement for Black Loyalists, formerly enslaved people who had supported Britain during the American Revolutionary War and later relocated from Nova Scotia. Sierra Leone is also known for its diamond mines. During a civil war from 1991 to 2002, rebel groups sold diamonds to help pay for weapons and fighting. Diamonds used to fund violence in this way are called “blood diamonds.”

Bangkok is the capital and largest city of Thailand, a country in Southeast Asia that was officially called Siam until 1939. The city grew along the Chao Phraya River, a major waterway that flows through central Thailand and empties into the Gulf of Thailand south of Bangkok. The river helped make the city a center of travel, trade, and settlement. During the 1800s, Bangkok developed into a major industrial center under Kings Mongkut and Chulalongkorn, also known as Rama IV and Rama V. Today, it remains Thailand’s main center of government and business. If asked to name Thailand’s capital and largest city, the answer is Bangkok; if asked which river it grew along, the answer is the Chao Phraya River.

The Las Vegas Strip is a famous stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard lined with large hotels, casinos, theaters, and restaurants. It is part of Nevada’s largest metropolitan area, but most of the Strip is not within the city limits of Las Vegas: it lies in the neighboring unincorporated community of Paradise. Despite its name, the Strip is an area along a road, not a separate city. One of its best-known hotels is the Bellagio. Outside the Bellagio, an artificial lake holds fountains that send water into the air in shows choreographed to music. Inside the hotel is Fiori di Como, a colorful glass installation by artist Dale Chihuly. These attractions help make the Strip a major destination for visitors.

The Avenue des Champs-Élysées is a grand east–west thoroughfare in Paris, France. It stretches from the Arc de Triomphe at Place Charles de Gaulle, formerly called Place de l’Étoile, to Place de la Concorde near the Jardin des Tuileries. The Arc de Triomphe is a monumental arch, and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier lies beneath it. At the avenue’s other end, Place de la Concorde is easy to recognize by the ancient Egyptian Luxor Obelisk at its center. The avenue’s name refers to the Elysian Fields, a paradise in ancient Greek mythology. Famous for its luxury shops and cafés, the Champs-Élysées is also the route of France’s annual Bastille Day military parade on July 14.

Manchester is a populous city in northwestern England whose historic center developed beside the River Irwell. The river also flows through neighboring Salford before joining the River Mersey near Irlam. Manchester grew rapidly during the Industrial Revolution, when its cotton mills and textile trade made it one of the world’s leading manufacturing cities. Canals and railways helped bring in raw cotton and carry finished cloth to markets. Today, Manchester is known for its universities, music, and football clubs, including Manchester City and Manchester United. Do not confuse it with Manchester in New Hampshire, a U.S. city on the Merrimack River. If a question mentions cotton manufacturing in industrial England or the River Irwell, the city it is pointing to is Manchester.

The Mojave Desert is an arid region that covers much of southeastern California and extends into parts of Nevada, Arizona, and Utah. Its boundaries are often associated with the range of the Joshua tree, a distinctive desert plant that gives Joshua Tree National Park its name. The Mojave has broad valleys, rugged mountains, and very little rainfall. It also includes Death Valley National Park, one of the hottest and driest places in North America. Within that park, Badwater Basin lies about 282 feet below sea level, making it the lowest point in North America. These landmarks help identify the Mojave Desert and show how varied its landscape can be.

Sapporo is the capital and largest city of Hokkaido, Japan’s northernmost main island. Known for its snowy winters, it became the first Asian city to host the Winter Olympics in 1972. Decades later, Sapporo also played a role in a Summer Olympics: the 2020 Summer Olympics, officially hosted by Tokyo. Those Games were postponed for one year because of the COVID-19 pandemic and took place in 2021, but they kept “2020” in their name. Organizers moved the marathon and race-walking events from Tokyo to Sapporo because they were concerned that Tokyo’s high summer temperatures could endanger athletes. These events were therefore held on Hokkaido, even though the Games were known as the Tokyo Olympics.

The Aswan High Dam is a major dam across the Nile River in southern Egypt. Built during the rule of President Gamal Abdel Nasser and completed in 1970, it holds back the river to form Lake Nasser, one of the world’s largest artificial reservoirs. Before the dam, the Nile flooded farmland each year; the dam made it possible to regulate that flooding, store water for dry periods, and generate hydroelectric power. Creating Lake Nasser also submerged a large area, putting ancient monuments at risk. Among them were the Abu Simbel temples, famous for four colossal seated statues carved into a mountainside. To save the temples, workers dismantled them and rebuilt them on higher ground above the new reservoir.

The Pearl River is a major river system in southern China. As it approaches the South China Sea, it spreads into a broad delta with many channels. This Pearl River Delta includes Guangzhou, the capital of Guangdong province. Guangzhou was historically called Canton in English, which is why the Pearl River has also been called the Canton River. The delta lies between Hong Kong to the east and Macau to the west, two cities on opposite sides of its waters. The river’s English name is linked to round, pale shells once found near Guangzhou. Today, the delta is one of China’s most densely populated and economically important regions, with busy ports and cities connected by waterways.

Palestine is a historic region of the Levant on the eastern Mediterranean. After World War I, Britain administered much of this area as Mandatory Palestine, until its mandate ended in 1948 and Israel was established. Today, the name Palestine is also used for the Palestinian territories, chiefly the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, whose borders and political status remain part of an ongoing conflict with Israel. The West Bank lies inland, west of the Jordan River. The Gaza Strip is a densely populated coastal enclave along the Mediterranean Sea, about 40 kilometers long. It borders Egypt to the southwest and Israel to the east and north. Understanding the difference between historic Palestine and the modern Palestinian territories helps explain why the name appears in both historical and current maps.

Mauna Kea is a dormant shield volcano on Hawaiʻi Island, also called the Big Island. Rising about 4,207 meters (13,803 feet) above sea level, it is the tallest mountain in the state of Hawaiʻi. Its summit is sacred in Native Hawaiian culture, making the mountain important for reasons beyond its height. The high elevation, dry air, and often clear skies also make the summit area an excellent place to study space. Several major research facilities there, including the Keck telescopes and the Subaru Telescope, are collectively known as the Mauna Kea Observatories. Plans to build another facility, the Thirty Meter Telescope, have drawn major protests from Native Hawaiians concerned about the mountain’s cultural and spiritual significance.

Kharkiv Oblast is an administrative region in northeastern Ukraine. It borders Russia to the north and Donetsk Oblast to the southeast. Its administrative center, Kharkiv, is Ukraine’s second-largest city and an important center of education and industry. Kharkiv Oblast became a major area of fighting after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In September of that year, Ukrainian forces launched a rapid advance that retook towns and cities that had been under Russian occupation, including Balakliia and Izium. Izium lies on the Siverskyi Donets River and is a strategic transport hub, with routes linking different parts of eastern Ukraine. Knowing the oblast’s location, its main city, and Izium’s role helps explain why control of the region mattered during the war.

Burundi is a small, landlocked country in East Africa. It borders Rwanda to the north, Tanzania to the east and south, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the west. Part of its western edge follows the shore of Lake Tanganyika, a long, deep African Great Lake shared by four countries. The lake’s northern end is near Bujumbura, Burundi’s largest city and former capital. In 2018, Burundi began moving its political capital from Bujumbura to Gitega, a city closer to the center of the country. Bujumbura remains an important economic center. If a question describes a country moving its capital from Bujumbura to Gitega, the answer is Burundi; if it asks for the lake beside Bujumbura, the answer is Lake Tanganyika.

The Bellagio is a luxury hotel and casino on the Las Vegas Strip in Nevada. It opened in 1998 and takes its name and design inspiration from Bellagio, a lakeside town on Lake Como in northern Italy. Outside the resort is a large artificial lake where the Fountains of Bellagio perform: jets of water rise and move in patterns choreographed to music and lights. Inside the hotel’s lobby, visitors can look up to see Fiori di Como, a colorful ceiling installation by glass artist Dale Chihuly. Made from thousands of hand-blown glass flowers, its name means “Flowers of Como” in Italian, connecting the artwork to the lake that inspired the resort.

The Peloponnese is a large peninsula in southern Greece, extending into the Mediterranean Sea. It was historically joined to the rest of mainland Greece by the narrow Isthmus of Corinth, a strip of land at its northeastern end. In 1893, the Corinth Canal opened through this isthmus, creating a navigable passage that cuts the Peloponnese off from the mainland by water. The canal is about 6.3 kilometres long and links the Saronic Gulf on the east with the Gulf of Corinth on the west. Although the canal makes the Peloponnese look like an island on a map, it is still commonly called a peninsula because of its natural connection to mainland Greece.

Transylvania is a historical region in central Romania, surrounded on three sides by the arc of the Carpathian Mountains. It has a long and varied history: for centuries it was associated with the Kingdom of Hungary, and it later existed as the Principality of Transylvania. Today it is part of Romania, with a mix of Romanian, Hungarian, and German cultural influences visible in its languages, architecture, and traditions. The region’s largest city is Cluj-Napoca, an important center of education and culture. It is home to Babeș-Bolyai University, one of Romania’s major universities. In the city’s central Union Square stands the Gothic Church of St. Michael, a landmark that reflects Transylvania’s medieval past.

Quebec is Canada’s largest province by area and its only province where most people speak French as their first language. Its distinct language and culture have shaped its history and politics. During the 1960s, Quebec underwent the Quiet Revolution, a period of rapid social change rather than armed conflict. The provincial government expanded its role in education, health care, and the economy, while the Catholic Church’s influence declined. These changes strengthened a sense of Quebec identity and helped fuel a sovereignty movement whose supporters want Quebec to become an independent country. Debates over independence continued for decades, including province-wide votes in 1980 and 1995.

Nevada is a western U.S. state that contains much of the Great Basin, a dry region of deserts and mountain ranges. Its best-known cities include Las Vegas and Reno, where casinos and tourism are important to the economy. Reno calls itself “The Biggest Little City in the World.” Along Nevada’s western border with California lies Lake Tahoe, a deep, clear alpine lake in the Sierra Nevada mountains. Water leaves Lake Tahoe through the Truckee River, which flows through Reno. Farther south, the Colorado River forms part of Nevada’s border with Arizona, where the Hoover Dam was built. Nevada is also the site of Yucca Mountain, which has been proposed as a storage facility for nuclear waste.

Arlington National Cemetery is a major U.S. military cemetery in Arlington, Virginia, across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. It was established in 1864, during the Civil War, on the former estate of Confederate general Robert E. Lee. Thousands of service members and other people honored for their national service are buried there. The estate’s mansion, now called Arlington House, stands within the cemetery. Designed in the Greek Revival style by George Hadfield, it was completed in 1818 for George Washington Parke Custis, the adopted grandson of George Washington. Lee later lived in the house after marrying Custis’s daughter, Mary Anna. Today, Arlington House helps visitors understand the estate’s history before it became a national cemetery.

The Iberian Peninsula is a large landform in southwestern Europe that contains modern Spain and Portugal. The Pyrenees Mountains separate it from the rest of Europe, while the Atlantic Ocean lies to its west and the Mediterranean Sea to its east. Its location made it a meeting place for different peoples and cultures. In the early eighth century, Muslim armies conquered much of the peninsula, and Muslim states ruled parts of it for centuries. Christian kingdoms in the north gradually expanded southward in a long campaign known as the Reconquista, meaning “reconquest.” The campaign ended in 1492, when Christian forces captured Granada, the last Muslim-ruled kingdom on the peninsula.

Maryland is a Mid-Atlantic state on the eastern coast of the United States. Chesapeake Bay reaches deep into the state and has shaped its ports, fishing communities, and history. Maryland borders Washington, D.C., and is the “M” in the regional name DMV, which stands for D.C., Maryland, and Virginia. Baltimore, Maryland’s largest city, lies near the bay and is known for its Inner Harbor and the Orioles’ baseball park at Camden Yards. Baltimore is not the state capital: that is Annapolis. Located on the Severn River near Chesapeake Bay, Annapolis is also home to the U.S. Naval Academy, where future Navy and Marine Corps officers are trained.

Lockerbie is a town in Dumfries and Galloway in southern Scotland. It is best known internationally for the Lockerbie bombing on 21 December 1988, when a bomb destroyed Pan Am Flight 103 while the passenger aircraft was flying over the town. The plane was travelling from Frankfurt to Detroit, with stops in London and New York. Wreckage fell across Lockerbie and the surrounding countryside, killing all 259 people aboard and 11 people on the ground. The disaster gave the bombing its name and made Lockerbie a focus of international investigations into terrorism. Libya later accepted responsibility for the actions of its officials in connection with the attack. Today, memorials in and around Lockerbie remember those who died.

A monsoon is a seasonal shift in prevailing winds that changes how much rain a region receives. In South Asia, the land heats up faster than the ocean in summer, drawing moisture-laden air inland from the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal. As this air rises and cools, its water vapor condenses, producing the heavy rains of the summer monsoon. Mountains can make the contrast between wet and dry places even stronger. The Western Ghats, a mountain range that parallels India’s western coast beside the Arabian Sea, force moist winds upward. This brings heavy rain to the slopes facing the sea. By the time the air crosses the mountains, it has lost much of its moisture, leaving the inland Deccan Plateau comparatively dry in a rain shadow.

The Galápagos Islands are an Ecuadorian archipelago in the eastern Pacific Ocean that lies astride the equator. Its volcanic islands include Isabela, Santa Cruz, and Española. Because the islands are isolated from mainland South America, many species evolved there that are found nowhere else, including giant tortoises and marine iguanas. Their unusual wildlife helped make the Galápagos a natural laboratory for studying evolution and influenced Charles Darwin’s ideas about how species change over time. Established in 1959, Galápagos National Park protects nearly all the islands’ land area, while a separate marine reserve protects the surrounding waters. Together, these protected areas help conserve the islands’ distinctive ecosystems.

Trafalgar Square is a major public gathering place in central London, England. It was named for the Battle of Trafalgar, a British naval victory in 1805. At the square’s center stands Nelson’s Column, a monument honoring Admiral Horatio Nelson, who led the British fleet in that battle. Four large bronze lions rest at the base of the column. They were designed by Edwin Landseer, a 19th-century British painter and sculptor famous for depicting animals; his paintings include The Monarch of the Glen. The square also has a feature called the Fourth Plinth. Unlike the other plinths, which hold permanent statues, it is used for a changing program of contemporary-art commissions. Trafalgar Square is therefore both a historic landmark and a place where visitors can see new art.

Alexandria is a major port city on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast. Alexander the Great founded it in 331 BCE, and after his generals fought for control of his empire in the wars of the Diadochi, it became the capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom. Alexandria grew into a center of trade and Hellenistic scholarship, especially through its famous Great Library, where scholars collected and studied texts from across the ancient world. Its busy harbor was marked by an enormous beacon on the nearby island of Pharos. Known as the Lighthouse of Alexandria, it guided ships toward the city and was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. A series of earthquakes eventually damaged and destroyed the lighthouse.

Edmonton is the capital and largest city of Alberta, a province in western Canada. The city lies on the North Saskatchewan River and is part of a busy corridor of communities that stretches south to Calgary, with Red Deer roughly halfway between them. Edmonton is especially known for West Edmonton Mall, a huge shopping and entertainment complex often described as North America’s largest mall. Among its attractions is a large indoor lake. Alberta is also known for an unusual pest-control achievement: an extensive program along its borders has kept the province free of established rat populations since the 1950s. If a question asks for the city on the river with the famous mall, the answer is Edmonton; if it asks for the rat-free province Edmonton governs, the answer is Alberta.

The Western Wall is an ancient stone wall in Jerusalem’s Old City. It is the best-known surviving section of the retaining wall that supported the elevated complex of the Second Temple, an ancient Jewish sanctuary destroyed by the Romans in 70 CE. The wall is not a surviving wall of the Temple building itself, but its closeness to the Temple’s former site makes it one of Judaism’s most important accessible places of prayer. Visitors often tuck written prayers or requests into gaps between its stones. The sacred precinct above the wall is commonly called the Temple Mount in Jewish usage. Today, that compound contains two important Islamic landmarks, the Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa Mosque. The Western Wall is also known as the Kotel or the Wailing Wall.

Thebes, known to the ancient Egyptians as Waset, was a major city on the Nile in southern Egypt, near modern Luxor. It became an important political capital and religious center during the New Kingdom. After the pharaoh Akhenaten moved the royal court to his new city of Amarna, his son Tutankhamun abandoned Amarna and restored Thebes as Egypt’s capital. The city was especially important to the worship of Amun, one of Egypt’s chief gods. At Thebes, successive pharaohs expanded the vast Karnak Temple Complex, a religious precinct centered on Amun’s temples. Thebes also had temples and royal burial grounds nearby, including the Valley of the Kings, where Tutankhamun was buried. It is not the same city as Thebes in Greece.

Baku is the capital and largest city of Azerbaijan, a country in the South Caucasus region. It stands on the Absheron Peninsula, which extends into the western side of the Caspian Sea. Baku’s coastal location has made it an important port and a center for the oil and gas industry. Despite its name, the Caspian Sea is often described as the world’s largest lake because it is enclosed by land and has no natural outlet to the ocean. A body of water with no such outlet is called endorheic. Several rivers flow into the Caspian Sea, including the Volga, Europe’s longest river. To remember the key connection: Baku is Azerbaijan’s capital, and it sits beside the Caspian Sea.

Dearborn is a city in Wayne County, Michigan, just west of Detroit. It is closely linked to Henry Ford, who was born there and transformed carmaking by using assembly-line production to build Model T cars. Ford Motor Company’s world headquarters and its large Rouge manufacturing complex are in Dearborn. The city is also known for its substantial Arab American and Muslim communities, which have helped shape its culture, businesses, and public life. Opened in Dearborn in 2005, the Arab American National Museum is affiliated with ACCESS, a community organization. The museum explores Arab American history and culture, including the experiences of a diaspora with roots in 22 countries across the Middle East and North Africa.

Belize is a small Central American country on the Caribbean Sea. It borders Mexico to the north and Guatemala to the west and south. Its Caribbean coast is home to a significant Garifuna community, especially in the town of Dangriga. The Garifuna are a people with African and Indigenous Caribbean ancestry who also live in other parts of Central America. Offshore, Belize has many islands known locally as cayes. The largest is Ambergris Caye, which lies off the country’s northeastern coast near the Belize Barrier Reef, a long chain of coral reefs rich in marine life. San Pedro is the principal town on Ambergris Caye. These clues—Dangriga, the Caribbean coastline, and Ambergris Caye—help identify Belize on a map.

Canadian national parks are a system of federally administered protected areas that preserve examples of Canada’s natural landscapes and ecosystems, from mountains and forests to coastlines and tundra. They help protect wildlife and natural features while giving people places to learn about and enjoy nature. Banff National Park, in Alberta’s Rocky Mountains, is the oldest park in the system. The area was first set aside in 1885 and was later known as Rocky Mountains Park before receiving its current name. Another Alberta national park is Jasper, which lies north of Banff. Together, parks such as Banff and Jasper protect important mountain environments for future generations.

A desert is a region or biome defined by very low precipitation, not simply by high temperatures. Deserts can be hot, like much of the Sahara in North Africa, or cold, like the Gobi, which stretches across parts of Mongolia and China. Because water is scarce, vegetation is usually sparse, although plants and animals can survive there through adaptations that help them conserve water. Some deserts have vast fields of sand dunes, while others are mostly gravel or rock; an oasis is a place where water supports more life. China’s largest desert located entirely within its borders is the Taklamakan Desert. It covers much of the Tarim Basin in Xinjiang, west of Lop Nur, between the Tian Shan Mountains to the north and the Kunlun Mountains to the south.

Siena is a historic city in Tuscany, a region of central Italy. During the Middle Ages and Renaissance, it was a major center of art and gave its name to the Sienese School of painting. Artists associated with the city include Duccio, Simone Martini, and Ambrogio Lorenzetti. In Siena’s civic palace, the Palazzo Pubblico, Lorenzetti painted the Allegory of Good and Bad Government, a fresco cycle showing how a city and its people are affected by wise or poor leadership. Siena was also a powerful medieval rival of Florence, another Tuscan city. Florence later became the center of rule by the Medici family and is home to the Uffizi Gallery, which holds many important works of Italian art.

Chinatowns are urban neighborhoods where Chinese immigrants and their descendants have established businesses, community institutions, and cultural traditions. As ethnic enclaves, they often offer familiar languages, foods, places of worship, and services that help newcomers settle while sharing Chinese culture with the wider city. Chinatowns exist in many countries, though each has its own history and character. The Manila district of Binondo, established under Spanish rule in 1594, is widely regarded as the world’s oldest Chinatown. In New York City, one Chinatown is in Manhattan near Columbus Park, in an area that has absorbed much of the former Little Italy. Another is in Flushing, a neighborhood in the borough of Queens.

The Snake River is the largest tributary of the Columbia River, which means it is the biggest river that flows into it. Beginning in Wyoming, the Snake winds through the American West, including Idaho, before joining the Columbia in Washington. Along part of the Idaho–Oregon border, it cuts through Hells Canyon, a steep, rugged gorge with high walls enclosing the river. Hells Canyon is often described as North America’s deepest river gorge. Several dams on the Snake River generate hydroelectric power, but they are also controversial. Salmon must travel upstream to reproduce, and dams can block or delay their migration. This has led to efforts to balance electricity production with protecting salmon and the river environment.

Burlington is Vermont’s most populous city, located on the eastern shore of Lake Champlain. This long, narrow freshwater lake forms much of Vermont’s western boundary with New York and extends north into Quebec, Canada. Burlington’s waterfront looks out across the lake toward the Adirondack Mountains. Although Burlington is Vermont’s largest city, it is not the state capital; that is Montpelier, one of the smallest state capitals in the United States. Burlington is a center for education, shopping, and cultural life in Vermont, and Bernie Sanders was elected its mayor in 1981. If a question asks for Vermont’s most populous city on Lake Champlain, the answer is Burlington. If it asks which lake Burlington faces, the answer is Lake Champlain.

Grand Teton National Park is in northwestern Wyoming, immediately south of Yellowstone National Park. It protects the rugged Teton Range and part of Jackson Hole, a broad valley between the Tetons and the Gros Ventre Range. The park takes its name from Grand Teton, the highest peak in the Teton Range, which rises steeply above the valley. Visitors can see mountain lakes, forests, rivers, and wildlife such as elk and moose. Yellowstone is famous for geysers and hot springs, but Grand Teton is especially known for its dramatic mountain scenery. If a question describes the Wyoming park just south of Yellowstone, the answer is Grand Teton National Park; if it asks for the valley within the park, the answer is Jackson Hole.

Mammoth Cave is a vast network of underground passages in Kentucky and the longest known cave system in the world. Explorers have surveyed more than 400 miles of passages, and parts of the system may still be undiscovered. The caves formed over millions of years as water dissolved layers of limestone. Mammoth Cave National Park protects the cave system and the landscape above it. The Green River flows through the park before joining the Ohio River; it has also helped shape the area’s caves. Despite the name, Mammoth Cave is not named for mammoth fossils found inside it—none have been found there. Instead, “mammoth” describes the enormous size of its passages.

French Guiana lies on the northeastern coast of South America, between Suriname and Brazil. Although it is on a different continent from mainland France, it is an overseas department and region of France, not an independent country.
