Its capital is Cayenne, and its official language is French. West of Cayenne is the coastal town of Kourou, home to the Guiana Space Centre, also known as Europe’s Spaceport. The European Space Agency launches rockets from there. French Guiana’s location near the equator helps rockets gain speed from Earth’s rotation, making launches more efficient. Most of the region is covered by tropical rainforest, while its main towns are near the Atlantic coast.

The Navajo Nation is the largest federally recognized tribal nation in the United States. Its reservation stretches across parts of Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah, making it much larger than many U.S. states. The Navajo people, who also call themselves Diné, have their own government, which makes decisions about many matters within the nation. Its capital is Window Rock, a community in northeastern Arizona near the New Mexico border. Window Rock takes its name from a nearby sandstone formation with a large, window-like opening. Knowing both the nation’s name and the location of its capital helps identify the Navajo Nation on a map of the American Southwest.

Milan is a major city in northern Italy and the capital of Lombardy. In Roman times it was called Mediolanum and grew substantially under Emperor Maximian, who made it an important imperial center. Later, St. Ambrose served as bishop of Milan. He famously excommunicated Emperor Theodosius I after the Massacre of Thessalonica. The city also gives its name to the Edict of Milan, a proclamation issued in 313 by the emperors Constantine I and Licinius. It established religious toleration in the Roman Empire, allowing Christians to worship openly. Constantine had defeated his rival Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge the year before, in 312. Milan’s Roman and Christian history helps explain why the city appears in questions about both ancient geography and religion.

Saint Petersburg is a major Russian city at the eastern end of the Gulf of Finland, where the Neva River reaches the Baltic Sea. Tsar Peter the Great, also known as Peter I, founded it in 1703 as part of his effort to modernize Russia and strengthen its connections with Western Europe. During his Grand Embassy to Western Europe, Peter studied shipbuilding in the Netherlands, knowledge that helped him develop Russia’s navy. Saint Petersburg later served as the capital of the Russian Empire. Its famous Bronze Horseman statue shows Peter on horseback and commemorates his role in founding the city. In the 20th century, the city was renamed Petrograd and then Leningrad before its historic name, Saint Petersburg, was restored.

Guatemala is Central America’s most populous country. It borders Mexico to the north and west, Belize to the northeast, and Honduras and El Salvador to the east and southeast. Guatemala has a long Pacific Ocean coastline and a shorter coastline on the Caribbean Sea. Its longest international land border is with Mexico, where the Mexican states of Chiapas and Tabasco meet Guatemala. The country is also known for its Maya heritage and for writer Miguel Ángel Asturias, whose novel El Señor Presidente portrays life under a dictator. Guatemala’s civil war lasted from 1960 to 1996 and devastated many Indigenous communities. Rigoberta Menchú, an Indigenous Guatemalan activist, described their experiences in her autobiography, I, Rigoberta Menchú.

The Azores are a group of nine volcanic islands belonging to Portugal in the North Atlantic Ocean, far west of mainland Europe. They lie near a triple junction, where the Eurasian, North American, and African tectonic plates meet. Movement of these plates helps create volcanoes and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a long underwater mountain range formed as the seafloor spreads apart. Most of the ridge is hidden beneath the ocean, but parts of it rise above the surface in the Azores. On the island of Pico, Mount Pico reaches about 2,351 meters (7,713 feet) above sea level. This volcanic summit is the highest point in Portugal.

The United States Capitol is the domed building on Capitol Hill, a rise east of the National Mall in Washington, D.C. It houses both chambers of Congress: the Senate and the House of Representatives. On September 11, 2001, terrorists hijacked four airplanes in attacks on the United States. One of them, United Airlines Flight 93, was reportedly headed for the Capitol. After passengers and crew resisted the hijackers and tried to regain control, the plane crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, instead of reaching Washington. Everyone aboard died. The Flight 93 National Memorial, near the crash site, honors the passengers and crew and tells the story of their actions.

Panama is a Central American country on the narrow strip of land connecting North and South America. It lies between Costa Rica to the west and Colombia to the east, with the Caribbean Sea along its northern coast and the Pacific Ocean along its southern coast. The Panama Canal crosses the country, allowing ships to travel between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans without sailing around South America. An important part of the canal is Lake Gatún, an artificial lake formed by damming the Chagres River. The lake serves as a major reservoir and is part of the canal’s high-level route. In eastern Panama, the Darién Gap is a region of thick rainforest with no road crossing into Colombia, interrupting the route for drivers traveling between the two continents.

Virginia is a U.S. state on the Atlantic coast, with Richmond as its capital. It borders Kentucky to the west and has a long colonial history: Jamestown, founded in 1607, was the first permanent English settlement in North America, and Virginia’s colonial assembly became known as the House of Burgesses. Much of Virginia’s eastern shoreline faces Chesapeake Bay, a large estuary where river water mixes with ocean water. The bay’s mouth lies between Cape Charles and Cape Henry, and its watershed—the land whose water drains into it—extends across six states. Virginia is also part of more recent U.S. history: in 2020, it passed the Virginia Values Act, which expanded legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Wuhan is a major city in central China and the capital of Hubei Province. It stands where the Han River flows into the Yangtze River, one of the world’s longest rivers. From Wuhan, the Yangtze continues east across China toward Shanghai and the East China Sea. The modern city encompasses three historic urban centers: Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang. Its position at the meeting of two rivers has long made it an important center for trade and transportation. Wuhan also became known worldwide in late 2019, when the first recognized outbreak of COVID-19 was reported there. Its river location, three historic districts, and role as Hubei’s capital are useful clues for identifying Wuhan on a map or in a geography quiz.

Kangchenjunga is the world’s third-highest mountain, rising to about 8,586 metres in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and the Indian state of Sikkim. Its name is traditionally associated with “five treasures of snow,” a reference to its five prominent peaks. Some climbers stop just short of its highest point out of respect for local beliefs about the summit. The Himalayas are a vast South Asian mountain range formed as the Indian tectonic plate pushed into the Eurasian plate, lifting the land upward. They contain many of the world’s highest mountains, including Mount Everest, the tallest peak on Earth. So Kangchenjunga is the peak on the Nepal–India border, and the Himalayas are the range it belongs to.

Mongolia is a landlocked country in East Asia, bordered by Russia to the north and China to the south. Its landscapes include wide grasslands and the Gobi Desert, which it shares with China. Herding livestock has long been central to Mongolian life, and some families still move with their animals between seasonal pastures. These nomadic families traditionally live in portable round tents called yurts, or gers, and horses remain important for travel and herding. Each year, Mongolia hosts Naadam, a festival celebrating traditional sports. Its main competitions are wrestling, archery, and horse racing, often called the “three manly games.” Naadam is an important celebration of Mongolian culture and history.

Medina is a city in western Saudi Arabia, about 300 miles (480 kilometers) north of Mecca. In 622 CE, the Prophet Muhammad and his followers migrated there from Mecca in an event known as the Hijra. Medina became an important center of the early Muslim community and was the first capital of the Rashidun Caliphate. It is considered Islam’s second-holiest city, after Mecca, and Muhammad is buried there in the Prophet’s Mosque. Mecca, to the south, is Islam’s holiest city. It contains the Kaaba, the sacred structure toward which Muslims face when they pray, within the Masjid al-Haram, also called the Grand Mosque.

An island is a landmass surrounded by water. Islands range from small rocky outcrops to vast regions with mountains, rivers, and cities. A group or chain of islands is called an archipelago. Japan is an archipelago made up of thousands of islands, including Honshu, where Tokyo is located, and Hokkaido, its northernmost major island. Islands can form in several ways, such as through volcanic eruptions, the buildup of coral, or rising sea levels that separate land from a continent. The world’s largest island by area is Greenland, which lies between the Arctic and North Atlantic oceans. Although Greenland is geographically part of North America, it is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Australia is larger, but it is generally classified as a continent rather than an island.

The Cascade Range, or Cascades, is a mountain chain that stretches from British Columbia in Canada through Washington and Oregon into northern California. Many of its peaks are volcanoes, formed as one of Earth’s tectonic plates sinks beneath another along the Pacific coast. Famous Cascade volcanoes include Mount Rainier in Washington and Mount Hood in Oregon. Crater Lake, in southern Oregon, fills the remains of an ancient volcano. Another Cascade volcano, Mount St. Helens in Washington, erupted catastrophically on May 18, 1980. An earthquake triggered a huge landslide on the mountain’s north side, followed by a powerful sideways explosion called a lateral blast. The eruption dramatically reshaped the mountain and spread ash across a large area.

The Outer Banks are a long chain of narrow barrier islands off the coast of North Carolina. They separate the Atlantic Ocean from sheltered waters such as Pamlico Sound. Barrier islands are made largely of sand and can shift over time as waves, storms, and currents reshape them. The islands include beach towns such as Buxton, Avon, and Kitty Hawk, and parts are protected by Cape Hatteras National Seashore. Dangerous waters and many shipwrecks earned the area the nickname “Graveyard of the Atlantic.” Kitty Hawk, a town in Dare County, is often named as the site of the Wright brothers’ first powered flight in 1903. Their flights actually took place several miles south, near Kill Devil Hills.

Costa Rica is a Central American country on the narrow isthmus between Nicaragua to the north and Panama to the southeast. It is known for its rich biodiversity, including the Monteverde Cloud Forest, which is home to thousands of plant species. The phrase “Pura Vida,” meaning “pure life,” is widely used in Costa Rica as a greeting and an expression of its relaxed outlook. The country abolished its military in 1948 and has since directed more resources toward public services such as education and health care. Part of Costa Rica’s northern boundary with Nicaragua follows the San Juan River. The 1858 Cañas–Jerez Treaty established this border, but the two countries have continued to disagree over how parts of the treaty should be interpreted.

St. Louis is a major city in Missouri on the western bank of the Mississippi River. The Mississippi forms much of Missouri’s eastern border, and the Missouri River joins it just north of the city. St. Louis is known for its Missouri Botanical Garden, which contains the Climatron, an enclosed geodesic dome inspired by architect Buckminster Fuller’s ideas. Its framework of triangles helps spread stress, or force, across the structure. Another landmark is the Wainwright Building, an early skyscraper designed by Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan. Its terracotta exterior makes it distinctive. Together, the garden and the Wainwright Building highlight St. Louis’s place in the history of architecture, while the nearby meeting of two great rivers helps explain the city’s importance as a transportation center.

The National Mall is a broad civic park and monumental area in Washington, D.C., the capital of the United States. It stretches from the U.S. Capitol toward the Lincoln Memorial, with lawns, paths, museums, and memorials along the way. Many Smithsonian museums border the Mall, making it a place to explore American history, art, and science. Near its center stands the Washington Monument, a tall stone obelisk honoring George Washington, the first U.S. president. At the Mall’s western end, the temple-like Lincoln Memorial honors Abraham Lincoln, the 16th president. Inside is a monumental seated statue of Lincoln, and inscriptions of his speeches appear on the walls. The nearby Vietnam Veterans Memorial and Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial commemorate other important parts of U.S. history.

The Benguela Current is a cold ocean current that flows northward through the South Atlantic Ocean along the coasts of western South Africa, Namibia, and southwestern Angola. Winds push surface water away from the shore, allowing cold, nutrient-rich water to rise from deeper in the ocean. This process, called upwelling, supports abundant plankton and exceptionally productive fisheries. The cold water also cools the air above it, helping create thick fog along Namibia’s Skeleton Coast. The current affects the coast of the Namib Desert, an arid region stretching across Namibia and into southwestern Angola. Although the desert receives very little rain, coastal fog can provide moisture for some plants and animals. The Namib is also known for its huge sand dunes around Sossusvlei.

Lubbock is a city on the Llano Estacado, a broad, flat region of Northwest Texas. It is a major regional center for education, business, and transportation, with Interstate 27 running north from Lubbock to Amarillo. The city is the birthplace of Buddy Holly, an influential early rock-and-roll musician, and is home to the National College Baseball Hall of Fame. Lubbock is also home to the main campus of Texas Tech University. Texas Tech’s athletic teams compete in the Big 12 Conference, and its live mascot, the Masked Rider, rides a horse at university events. The university operates the National Ranching Heritage Center, which preserves and teaches visitors about the history of ranching in the American West.

Ghana is a country in West Africa with a coastline on the Gulf of Guinea, part of the Atlantic Ocean. It borders Côte d’Ivoire to the west, Burkina Faso to the north, and Togo to the east. Its capital, Accra, lies on the coast and is Ghana’s largest urban center. Accra is the seat of the national government and an important center for business and culture. Ghana became independent from British rule in 1957, making it one of the first countries in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence during the twentieth century. Kwame Nkrumah, a leader of the independence movement, later became Ghana’s president. Remembering Ghana’s three neighbors, its Gulf of Guinea coastline, and the coastal capital of Accra will help you identify it on a map.

Byblos is an ancient port city on Lebanon’s Mediterranean coast and one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities. It was an important center of trade for the Phoenicians, a seafaring people who connected places around the Mediterranean. Byblos was especially known for trading papyrus from Egypt, which people used to make writing material. Its Greek name became linked with Greek words for books, including ta biblia, meaning “the books.” That phrase is the source of the familiar English name Bible, used for the Christian scriptures. So if a question asks for the ancient Phoenician city in Lebanon whose name is connected to books, the answer is Byblos; if it asks for the name of the Christian scriptures that reflects this connection, the answer is Bible.

The Tower of London is a historic fortress and royal complex beside the River Thames in England’s capital. William the Conqueror began building it after the Norman Conquest of 1066, and it later served as a royal residence, prison, and place of execution. It is linked to the mystery of the “Princes in the Tower”: Edward V and his younger brother Richard of Shrewsbury disappeared there in 1483. The fortress also has a connection to the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, an attempt by English Catholic conspirators to blow up the Houses of Parliament and kill King James I. Guy Fawkes was discovered guarding barrels of gunpowder beneath Parliament. After his arrest, he was taken to the Tower and interrogated; an exhibit there marks the place where he confessed.

The Everglades is a vast wetland in South Florida, often called the “river of grass.” Unlike a typical river, its shallow water moves slowly south across a broad, nearly flat landscape rather than through a single channel. Historically, much of that water flowed from Lake Okeechobee, a broad, shallow lake just north of the Everglades and the largest lake entirely within Florida. The wetland includes wide sawgrass marshes, where tall, grasslike plants grow in freshwater, as well as coastal mangrove forests. Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees that can grow where fresh and salt water mix. Together, these habitats support many kinds of wildlife, making the Everglades an important and unusual natural landscape.

Glasgow is Scotland’s largest city, although Edinburgh is the country’s capital. It grew along the River Clyde, whose access to the sea helped Glasgow become a major center of trade and shipbuilding. During the Industrial Revolution, its docks and factories supported a rapidly growing population, and ships built on the Clyde became famous around the world. Today, Glasgow is also known for its universities, museums, music, and sport. Two of Scotland’s best-known football clubs, Celtic and Rangers, are based in the city. Their long-running rivalry is called the Old Firm derby, and matches between them attract enormous attention from supporters. Glasgow’s history shows how a riverside trading settlement developed into a major industrial city and cultural center.

Mar-a-Lago is a historic oceanfront estate in Palm Beach, Florida. Cereal heiress Marjorie Merriweather Post commissioned it, and it was completed in 1927. The name means “sea to lake,” reflecting the property’s location between the Atlantic Ocean and Lake Worth Lagoon. Donald Trump bought the estate in 1985 and later turned part of it into a private club while using it as a residence. In August 2022, FBI agents searched Mar-a-Lago under a federal warrant as part of an investigation into government records taken from the White House. An inventory filed after the search listed records with classification markings. The FBI search of Mar-a-Lago became a major national news story and led to legal disputes over the materials found there.

Congo is a geographic name shared by two neighboring Central African countries: the Republic of the Congo and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It also names the Congo River and its vast basin, which stretches across much of the region. The Republic of the Congo’s capital is Brazzaville. Directly across the Congo River, on the opposite shore of a wide stretch called Pool Malebo, is Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The name also appears in the region’s history. The Kingdom of Kongo existed near the Atlantic coast, while the Congo Free State was controlled by Belgium’s King Leopold II in the late 1800s. Keeping the two modern capitals straight—Brazzaville for the Republic and Kinshasa for the Democratic Republic—helps distinguish the countries.

The Great Salt Lake is a large, shallow lake in northern Utah. It has no outlet to the ocean: rivers bring water and dissolved minerals into the lake, but water leaves mainly through evaporation. Because the minerals stay behind, the lake is much saltier than most freshwater lakes. Its shoreline can shift as water levels rise and fall. On the lake’s northeastern shore, artist Robert Smithson created Spiral Jetty in 1970. This work of land art is a huge coil made from basalt rock and earth that extends into the water. Depending on the lake’s level, the spiral may be submerged or clearly visible, and salt crystals can form on its rocks.

The Maghreb is a region of northwestern Africa commonly defined to include Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya. Its name comes from an Arabic word meaning “the west,” reflecting its position at the western edge of the Arab world. The region has a long history shaped by its Indigenous Amazigh (Berber) peoples, Arab cultures, and connections across the Mediterranean Sea and the Sahara Desert. One of its major physical features is the Atlas Mountains, a highland chain that stretches through Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia. The range’s highest peak, Toubkal, is in Morocco. Landscapes across the Maghreb vary widely: the Atlas Mountains and Mediterranean coast contrast with the vast Sahara to the south.

St. Augustine is a city on the Atlantic coast of northeastern Florida. It was founded by Spain in 1565, when an expedition led by Spanish admiral Pedro Menéndez de Avilés established a settlement there. Menéndez de Avilés became the first governor of Spanish Florida. Because people have lived in St. Augustine continuously since its founding, it is commonly regarded as the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the continental United States. Its location made it an important base for Spain as it tried to control Florida and nearby lands, including territory that is now Georgia. The city’s long history helps explain why its Spanish colonial buildings and fortifications remain important landmarks today.

Las Vegas is the largest city in Nevada and a major center for tourism and conventions. It is known internationally for its resort hotels, casinos, live entertainment, and large trade shows. Many famous attractions are along the Las Vegas Strip, a stretch of road lined with hotels and entertainment venues. Although people often associate the Strip with Las Vegas, much of it lies just outside the city limits in the town of Paradise. One of its best-known hotel-casinos is the Bellagio. In front of the Bellagio, giant fountains send jets of water into the air in shows set to music, on an artificial lake said to be inspired by Italy’s Lake Como. Inside the hotel is Fiori di Como, the largest glass sculpture by artist Dale Chihuly.

The Eurasian Steppe is a vast belt of temperate grassland stretching from northeastern China and Mongolia westward to Eastern Europe. A steppe is generally a broad, mostly flat inland plain that receives too little rain for forests to grow but enough to support grasses rather than desert. These open landscapes made it easier for people to travel long distances, helping horse riding and wheeled transport spread between regions. In the western part of the Eurasian Steppe, the Ural Mountains form a long range commonly used to mark the boundary between Europe and Asia. The Urals extend southward into Kazakhstan, a large landlocked country whose northern areas include dry steppe.

Perth is the capital and largest city of Western Australia, a state on Australia’s west coast. It stands on the banks of the Swan River, which flows through the city and reaches the Indian Ocean near the port of Fremantle. This location helped Perth develop as a center for trade and transport. The city is known for its sunny climate, nearby beaches, and Kings Park, a large green space overlooking the city and river. Kings Park includes the Western Australian Botanic Garden on Mount Eliza, where visitors can see many plants native to the state. If a question asks for Western Australia’s capital or largest city, the answer is Perth; if it asks for the river running through Perth, the answer is the Swan River.

The Atlantic Ocean is the world’s second-largest ocean. It lies between the Americas to the west and Europe and Africa to the east, stretching from the Arctic toward Antarctica. Its eastern shores include Angola and South Africa: Luanda, Angola’s capital, and Cape Town, South Africa, both face the Atlantic. Farther north along Africa’s coast, the cold Benguela Current helps create the dense fog of Namibia’s Skeleton Coast. Beneath the ocean, a vast mountain chain called the Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs roughly down its middle. There, tectonic plates slowly move apart, allowing molten rock to rise and harden into new seafloor. Most of the ridge is underwater, but parts of it rise above sea level, including Iceland.

Baffin Island is Canada’s largest island and part of Nunavut in the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. It lies east of the mainland’s Melville Peninsula, west of Greenland, and between the Arctic Ocean and the North Atlantic. Its coastline has deep inlets, while glaciers and rugged mountains shape much of the landscape. The Baffin Mountains stretch along the island’s eastern side, and many of their peaks are named after Norse deities. Their highest summit is Mount Odin, which rises about 2,147 metres on the Cumberland Peninsula. Despite its vast size, Baffin Island has a small population, living mainly in coastal communities such as Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. Inuit people have lived in the region for thousands of years and continue to shape its culture.

A mappamundi is a medieval or early modern world map that shows how people understood the world, not just where places were. It may combine geographic information with religious symbolism, biblical history, and stories about distant lands. For example, Jerusalem might appear at the center because of its importance to Christianity, even though a modern map would place it differently. One of the largest surviving medieval examples is the Hereford Mappa Mundi, made around 1300 and displayed in Hereford Cathedral in England. An inscription associates it with Richard of Haldingham and Lafford. Like other mappamundi, it is a culturally meaningful picture of the world rather than a strictly measured survey.

Montpelier is the capital of Vermont, a northeastern U.S. state nicknamed the Green Mountain State. Vermont lies between New York to the west and New Hampshire to the east. Montpelier has fewer than 10,000 residents, making it the least populous state capital in the United States. Although it is the seat of state government, it is not Vermont’s largest city. That distinction belongs to Burlington, which is located on Lake Champlain. Vermont’s nickname refers to its forested mountains, which are part of the Appalachian Mountains. To remember the key facts, connect the small capital, Montpelier, with Vermont, the Green Mountain State: Montpelier is the capital with the smallest population, while Vermont is the state between New York and New Hampshire.

The Baltic states are three countries in northern Europe: Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. They lie along the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea, which gives the region its name. From north to south, the countries are Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. Estonia is the northernmost Baltic state, and its capital is Tallinn. It has land borders with Latvia to the south and Russia to the east. Latvia lies between Estonia and Lithuania, while Lithuania is the southernmost of the three. Although they are grouped together because of their location and shared history, each is an independent country with its own language and culture. When a question asks for the collective name of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, the answer is the Baltic states.

New Hampshire is a state in New England, in the northeastern United States. It borders Vermont to the west, Maine to the east, Massachusetts to the south, and the Canadian province of Quebec to the north. Its capital is Concord, which lies on the Merrimack River. Farther south on the same river is Manchester, New Hampshire’s largest city. In the northern part of the state, the White Mountains are a highland region known for forests, hiking, and skiing. They contain the Presidential Range, whose peaks are named after U.S. presidents and other prominent Americans. Its best-known peak, Mount Washington, is the highest mountain in the northeastern United States and is famous for severe weather, including powerful winds and sudden changes in temperature.

The Bronx is one of New York City’s five boroughs. It lies north of Manhattan and is the only borough located primarily on the mainland of the United States; the others are mainly on islands. Along the Bronx’s western edge, the Harlem River separates it from Manhattan. Despite its name, the Harlem River is a tidal waterway that connects the Hudson River to the East River. The Bronx is also a setting for stories about New York life: John Patrick Shanley’s play Doubt: A Parable takes place there, and books such as Don DeLillo’s Underworld and E. L. Doctorow’s Billy Bathgate feature people growing up in the borough.

Kunming Lake is a large artificial lake in the Summer Palace, an imperial garden in Beijing, China. It was created as the centerpiece of a landscape designed for the imperial court, with water, islands, hills, and buildings arranged to create scenic views. Its design drew on Chinese garden traditions, including the use of a lake paired with three hills. One of the lake’s best-known landmarks is the Seventeen-Arch Bridge, an ornate stone bridge that connects the eastern shore to Nanhu Island. Despite its name, the bridge is not simply a way to cross the water: its graceful arches and carved stone lions make it an important part of the garden’s appearance. Kunming Lake is also home to a marble boat built under Empress Dowager Cixi.

Mount Parnassus rises in central Greece above the ancient sanctuary of Delphi, which lies on its southern slopes. In Greek mythology, the mountain was linked to Apollo, the god of music and archery, and to the Muses, who inspired poetry and the arts. It was also said to be where Deucalion and Pyrrha came ashore after surviving a great flood. Delphi was famous for its oracle: a priestess called the Pythia delivered prophecies associated with Apollo. Visitors could wash at the nearby Castalian Spring before seeking her advice. The sanctuary also held an omphalos, a stone believed to mark the center of the world. According to myth, Zeus found that center by releasing two eagles that flew around the world and met at Delphi.

Milwaukee is a major city in southeastern Wisconsin, on the western shore of Lake Michigan. In the early 1900s, it became known for “sewer socialism,” a practical approach to Socialist politics that emphasized clean, efficient city services, including sewers. The phrase was originally used to mock Milwaukee Socialists for boasting about their sewer system, but it also captured their focus on everyday improvements. In 1910, Milwaukee voters elected Emil Seidel, making him the first Socialist mayor of a major American city. After losing his bid for reelection in 1912, Seidel became the vice-presidential candidate on a Socialist ticket led by Eugene V. Debs. These events made Milwaukee an important center of the Socialist movement in the United States.

Galveston is a city on a barrier island along the Texas Gulf Coast, near Houston. In the nineteenth century, its busy harbor made it one of Texas’s most important ports and commercial centers. In 1900, a powerful hurricane struck the island, killing thousands of people in what remains the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history. The storm destroyed much of Galveston and weakened its position as a trading center. Nearby Houston grew into the state’s leading port, aided by the Houston Ship Channel, which connects the city to the Gulf of Mexico. Houston is now Texas’s most populous city. Galveston remains an important coastal city, but its history shows how a natural disaster can change where people and businesses choose to build and trade.

Lake Powell is a large artificial lake, or reservoir, on the Colorado River. It stretches through Glen Canyon across the Utah–Arizona border, near Rainbow Bridge, a natural sandstone arch. The reservoir formed when Glen Canyon Dam was built near Page, Arizona. Completed in 1966, the dam is a concrete arch-gravity structure: its curved shape and great weight help it hold back the river’s water. Lake Powell stores water used by communities and farms in the American Southwest and is also popular for boating and other recreation. It is different from Lake Mead, another Colorado River reservoir farther downstream, which is held back by Hoover Dam.

Marco Polo Bridge, also called Lugou Bridge, is a historic stone bridge on the southwestern outskirts of Beijing. It crosses the Yongding River, which was once called the Wuding River and received its present name during the Qing dynasty. The bridge is especially famous for the many carved stone lions that decorate its railings; their different poses have made them a memorable feature of the landmark. Its English name comes from the traveler Marco Polo, who wrote about the bridge after visiting China. The bridge was also the site of an important 1937 clash between Chinese and Japanese forces, often called the Marco Polo Bridge Incident. Remember its two key identifiers: stone lions line the Marco Polo Bridge, and the river beneath it is the Yongding.

The Ring of Brodgar is a large Neolithic circle of standing stones on Mainland, the largest island in Scotland’s Orkney archipelago. It stands between the Loch of Stenness and the Loch of Harray and was built thousands of years ago, when communities across Orkney were creating stone monuments and settlements. The stones surround a broad open space; although the circle’s exact purpose is unknown, it may have been used for gatherings or ceremonies, perhaps connected to the changing seasons. The Ring of Brodgar is part of the Heart of Neolithic Orkney, a UNESCO World Heritage property that also includes the nearby Stones of Stenness, the chambered tomb of Maeshowe, and the remarkably preserved village of Skara Brae. Together, these sites reveal how people lived and built in prehistoric Orkney.

Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland, a country that is part of the United Kingdom and lies north of England. The city is famous for its medieval Old Town, with narrow streets and historic buildings, and its Georgian New Town, planned in the 18th century with broad streets and elegant squares. Edinburgh Castle stands on Castle Rock, a volcanic hill overlooking the city centre. Each August, Edinburgh hosts major arts festivals, including the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, which brings performers and visitors from around the world. Although Edinburgh is Scotland’s capital, it is not the country’s largest city. That is Glasgow, which lies on the River Clyde. Glasgow is home to the football clubs Celtic and Rangers, whose long-standing rivalry is called the Old Firm derby.

Sand dunes are hills or ridges of loose sand built by wind. When wind slows near an obstacle, it drops some of the sand it carries. Over time, the sand piles up, and dunes may change shape or move as prevailing winds shift. Dunes form in deserts, but they also occur near lakes and oceans. Indiana Dunes National Park protects dunes along the southern shore of Lake Michigan. In Colorado, Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve has dunes rising against the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. Its Star Dune reaches about 750 feet from its base, making it the tallest dune in North America. These two parks show that wind-built sand landforms can appear in very different landscapes.

Beirut is the capital and largest city of Lebanon, a country in the Middle East. It lies on Lebanon’s western coastline beside the Mediterranean Sea. Its position made Beirut an important seaport and a center for trade, travel, and culture for centuries. The city’s port was also the site of a catastrophic explosion in August 2020, when a large quantity of improperly stored ammonium nitrate detonated. The blast destroyed nearby buildings, killed more than 200 people, and left hundreds of thousands temporarily homeless. Despite this disaster, Beirut remains Lebanon’s main urban center. If you are asked to identify Lebanon’s coastal capital or the sea beside Beirut, the answers are Beirut and the Mediterranean Sea.

Manila is the capital of the Philippines, an island country in Southeast Asia. It lies on the island of Luzon at the mouth of the Pasig River, where the river meets Manila Bay. During Spanish colonial rule, Manila became an important center of government and trade. Its historic heart is Intramuros, a walled district whose name means “within the walls.” Intramuros contains Fort Santiago, once a defensive fortress, as well as stone walls and colonial-era churches. Quezon City served as the national capital for several decades before Manila regained that status in 1976, during the rule of Ferdinand Marcos. Today, the City of Manila is part of Metro Manila, a much larger urban area that also includes Quezon City.

Angel Falls is a waterfall in southeastern Venezuela’s Canaima National Park. It plunges from Auyán-tepui, a flat-topped mountain called a tepui, and has a total height of about 979 meters (3,212 feet). Its longest uninterrupted drop is about 807 meters (2,648 feet), making it the world’s tallest uninterrupted waterfall. Angel Falls is a single towering waterfall, unlike Iguazu Falls, a vast system of waterfalls on the border of Argentina and Brazil. The waterfall’s English name honors Jimmie Angel, an American aviator whose 1933 flight over the Venezuelan tepui region helped bring it to wider attention. It is also known by its Indigenous Pemon name, Kerepakupai Meru.

Jingdezhen is a city in northeastern Jiangxi Province, China, known as China’s porcelain capital. For centuries, its workshops have made pottery and other ceramics, especially porcelain. Porcelain is made from clay materials that include kaolin and is fired at very high temperatures. This makes it dense and hard; it often has a white body that can be slightly translucent, meaning light can pass through it. Jingdezhen became particularly famous for blue-and-white porcelain. To create its designs, makers painted patterns using cobalt pigment before firing the wares, producing a distinctive blue against the white surface. Bowls, plates, and vases from Jingdezhen were valued in China and traded abroad, helping the city build a lasting reputation for skilled ceramic production.

The Baltic Sea is a large sea in Northern Europe bordered by Poland, Estonia, Latvia, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Germany, Lithuania, and Russia. Its waters reach the North Sea through a series of straits between Denmark and Sweden, including the Øresund. Ships can also travel between the two seas using the Kiel Canal, an artificial waterway across northern Germany. Opened in 1895, the canal runs from Brunsbüttel on the North Sea side to the Baltic coast near Kiel. It gives ships a shorter route and lets them avoid sailing around Jutland, the peninsula that makes up most of Denmark. Because many countries border the Baltic, it is an important route for trade and travel in Northern Europe.

Northern Ireland is a constituent country of the United Kingdom in the northeastern part of the island of Ireland. The North Channel separates the island from Great Britain, and Northern Ireland shares a land border with the independent Republic of Ireland to the south and west. It consists of six traditional counties, and its capital is Belfast. West of Belfast lies Lough Neagh, the largest lake in the British Isles by surface area. Its shores touch five of Northern Ireland’s counties: Antrim, Down, Armagh, Tyrone, and Londonderry. Northern Ireland was also the main setting of the Troubles, a decades-long conflict involving disputes over whether it should remain in the United Kingdom or join the Republic of Ireland. The 1998 Good Friday Agreement helped bring that conflict to an end.

The Iguazu River is a major tributary of the Paraná River in South America. It flows through southern Brazil and along the border with northeastern Argentina before joining the Paraná. Near the border, the river plunges over a wide series of cliffs to form Iguazu Falls, one of the world’s largest waterfall systems. The falls stretch between Argentina’s Misiones Province and the state of Paraná in Brazil. On the Brazilian side, the nearby city of Foz do Iguaçu is a common starting point for visitors. One of the most dramatic parts of the falls is Devil’s Throat, a semicircular gorge into which roughly half the river’s water flows. The river and the falls share the name Iguazu, also spelled Iguaçu in Brazil.

The Guarani Aquifer is one of the world’s largest underground freshwater reserves. An aquifer is a layer of rock or sediment that holds water in its spaces and cracks, allowing people to draw it through wells. This aquifer stretches beneath parts of four South American countries: Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and Argentina. Because it crosses national borders, it is called a transboundary groundwater reservoir, and the countries share an interest in protecting its water from overuse and pollution. Its name comes from the Guarani, an Indigenous people of the region. One of the countries above the aquifer is Paraguay, a landlocked country with its capital at Asunción. Paraguay also shares the Itaipu Dam with Brazil on the Paraná River.

Guadalajara is a major city in western Mexico and the capital of Jalisco state. Often described as Mexico’s second most populous city, it is an important center of culture, business, and education. In its historic center stands Guadalajara Cathedral, one of the city’s most recognizable landmarks. The cathedral is a large Christian church, and its twin spires are prominent features of the skyline. Its design reflects several architectural traditions, including Gothic influences, visible in the tall spires, and Baroque influences in its decorative details. If a question asks for the Jalisco capital famous for this cathedral, the answer is Guadalajara. If it asks for the religious landmark with the twin spires in Guadalajara’s historic center, the answer is Guadalajara Cathedral.

Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It lies in a valley along the Miljacka River, surrounded by the Dinaric Alps. In 1914, Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary there, an event that helped trigger World War I. Decades later, Sarajevo became a major focus of the Bosnian War. From 1992 to 1996, the city endured a nearly four-year siege in which civilians faced shelling and sniper fire. One especially dangerous route was an exposed stretch of Ulica Zmaja od Bosne and Meša Selimović Boulevard. People crossing it could be shot by hidden gunmen, so it became known as “Sniper Alley.” These two events make Sarajevo an important city in the history of both the early and late twentieth century.

The Adriatic Sea is a long, narrow arm of the Mediterranean Sea between Italy and the Balkan Peninsula. Italy forms most of its western shore, while its eastern shore includes Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Albania. At its southeastern end, the Strait of Otranto connects the Adriatic to the Ionian Sea. Croatia’s coast is known for its many islands and historic ports, including Split and Dubrovnik. Dubrovnik, in southern Croatia, is especially famous for the medieval walls surrounding its Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The sea has long been an important route for trade and travel between Italy and southeastern Europe.

An impact crater is a depression formed when an asteroid, meteorite, or other object from space strikes a planet’s surface at high speed. The collision blasts out rock and soil, often leaving a circular hollow with a raised rim. Barringer Crater in Arizona is a well-preserved example. Some impact craters are difficult to see because erosion, sediment, or later geological activity has hidden them. The Chicxulub impact crater lies beneath the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, the landform that includes the cities of Cancún and Mérida. The asteroid strike that formed it is linked to the end-Cretaceous extinction about 66 million years ago, when the non-avian dinosaurs and many other species died out.

Shanghai is a major city and municipality in China, near the East China Sea where the Huangpu River meets the Yangtze River estuary. Its river access and coastal location helped it grow into an important port. In the 1800s, Shanghai became a “treaty port,” open to foreign trade under agreements imposed on China, and it developed into a major financial center. The city’s name is also linked to “shanghaiing,” a practice from the age of sail. Unscrupulous recruiters would trick or incapacitate men and put them aboard departing ships, where they were forced to work as sailors. The term reflects Shanghai’s association with long-distance shipping, although the practice was not limited to ships bound for that city.

Silicon Valley is a technology and business region centered in Santa Clara County, California, near the southern end of San Francisco Bay. Its name comes from silicon, a material used to make computer chips, but the region is now known for many kinds of technology, including software and internet services. Companies such as Apple and Google helped make it a global center of the American tech industry. The region’s largest city by population is San Jose, which is also California’s third-largest city and home to the SAP Center arena. Silicon Valley has attracted entrepreneurs and investors from around the world, though its rapid growth has also contributed to high housing costs, and its companies have faced criticism for discrimination against women and minorities.

Bucharest is the capital and largest city of Romania, a country in southeastern Europe with a coastline on the Black Sea. The Danube River reaches the sea through the Danube Delta in eastern Romania. Bucharest is the country’s center of government and was a major center of the Romanian Revolution in 1989. During that uprising, a large rally in the city turned against Communist leader Nicolae Ceaușescu. He and his wife, Elena, fled the Communist Party headquarters by helicopter, but were later captured. Their trial and execution on December 25 marked the end of Ceaușescu’s rule. Bucharest remains Romania’s political, economic, and cultural center today.

The Skeleton Coast is a remote stretch of Namibia’s western shoreline in southwestern Africa. It runs roughly from the Kunene River near the border with Angola south to the Swakop River. The coast faces the Atlantic Ocean, which also borders Angola and South Africa. Offshore, the cold Benguela Current cools moist air and helps create thick fog, even though the land beside the sea is very dry. This fog, together with strong waves and difficult conditions for sailors, has contributed to the many shipwrecks that gave the Skeleton Coast its name. If a question describes Namibia’s fog-bound, shipwreck-strewn coast, the place is the Skeleton Coast; if it asks which ocean borders it, the answer is the Atlantic Ocean.

Gombe Stream National Park is a protected area on the shoreline of Lake Tanganyika in western Tanzania. It is famous for a long-term study of wild chimpanzees begun in 1960 by British primatologist Jane Goodall. By patiently observing the chimps, Goodall learned about their social relationships, conflicts, and ways of finding food. One of her most important discoveries was that chimpanzees use tools: she watched them insert grass stems into termite mounds and pull them out covered with termites to eat, a behavior often called “termite fishing.” Her findings challenged the belief that only humans make and use tools. Decades of research at Gombe have helped scientists understand chimpanzee behavior and the similarities between humans and other primates.

Kitty Hawk is a town in Dare County on North Carolina’s Outer Banks, a chain of barrier islands along the Atlantic coast. It is widely associated with Orville and Wilbur Wright’s first successful powered airplane flight in December 1903. The brothers worked in the area, and news of their achievement was sent from Kitty Hawk, helping its name become famous. The flights themselves, however, took place several miles south of Kitty Hawk, at a sandy site in what is now the town of Kill Devil Hills. That site is preserved as part of Wright Brothers National Memorial. If asked for the town commonly credited with the first flight, the answer is Kitty Hawk; if asked where the flight site is located, the answer is Kill Devil Hills.

Kowloon is a peninsula that forms much of Hong Kong’s urban mainland, across Victoria Harbour from Hong Kong Island. Its name means “Nine Dragons,” and today it is a busy area of neighborhoods, shops, and transport links. Kowloon is also known for the Kowloon Walled City, a small enclave within the peninsula. During British rule of Hong Kong, the Walled City remained legally under Chinese jurisdiction even though British-controlled territory surrounded it. Over time, buildings were packed so tightly together that it became one of the world’s most densely populated places. The Walled City was demolished in the early 1990s, and its site is now Kowloon Walled City Park. Hong Kong was transferred from Britain to China in 1997.

Chichén Itzá is a major ancient Maya city and archaeological site on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, the landmass between the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea. It was an important center of religion, trade, and political power. Its most famous structure is El Castillo, a stepped pyramid also called the Temple of Kukulcán, named for a feathered-serpent deity. Another landmark is the Great Ball Court, one of the largest ceremonial ball courts in Mesoamerica. Its long, parallel walls are decorated with carvings of the Maya ballgame, including a scene showing a decapitated player. The game had religious and political importance, although historians do not know exactly how often its players were sacrificed. Together, these structures show the scale and complexity of Maya civilization.

Juneau is the capital of Alaska, the U.S. state separated from the other 48 contiguous states by Canada. It lies in the Alaska Panhandle on the mainland shore of Gastineau Channel, a waterway that separates Juneau from Douglas Island. The Coast Mountains rise behind the city, while the channel runs along its waterfront. Unlike most U.S. state capitals, Juneau has no road connection to the rest of its state or to the outside road network. People and supplies therefore reach it mainly by plane or boat, including ferries on the Alaska Marine Highway. Its coastal setting helps explain both the importance of water travel and why reaching the capital can be different from traveling to other American cities.

Cahokia was a major Native American city built by people of the Mississippian culture centuries before Europeans arrived. Located in present-day Illinois, across the Mississippi River from St. Louis and near its meeting with the Missouri River, it was one of the largest cities north of Mexico. Cahokia had neighborhoods, open plazas, and many earthen mounds built for important public and ceremonial purposes. At its center stands Monks Mound, a massive, flat-topped structure about 100 feet high that covers roughly 14 acres. It is the largest pre-Columbian earthwork in North America. Today, Cahokia is a historic site that preserves evidence of the engineering, organization, and culture of the people who lived there.

A river delta is a landform that develops at a river’s mouth, where the river flows into a standing body of water such as a lake or sea. As the river slows, it drops sediment it has carried downstream. Over time, the sediment builds a low plain that is often triangular or fan-shaped. The river may split into smaller channels called distributaries, which carry water and sediment across the delta. Deltas do not form at every river mouth: strong tides or currents can sweep sediment away before it builds up. One famous example is the Nile Delta at the northern edge of Egypt, where the Nile flows into the Mediterranean Sea. Its major distributary outlets have historically been associated with Rosetta and Damietta.

Texas is a state in the southern United States and the second-largest U.S. state by area, after Alaska. Its capital is Austin, while its largest city by population is Houston. Houston lies near the Gulf of Mexico and is home to the Rothko Chapel, an octagonal building whose interior contains fourteen dark-toned paintings by the artist Mark Rothko. Another major Texas city is Dallas, in the northern part of the state. Texas has a varied landscape, from Gulf Coast plains to dry areas in the west, and its economy includes energy, technology, farming, and trade. Remember that Austin is the capital, Houston is the most populous city and the site of the Rothko Chapel, and Dallas is another major city.

Bohemia is the largest of Czechia’s three historic lands, alongside Moravia and Czech Silesia. It occupies the western part of the country, and mountain ranges form much of its borders with Germany and Austria. Its capital, Prague, is also the capital of Czechia. The Vltava River flows through Prague beneath the famous Charles Bridge, then continues north to join the Elbe River at Mělník. For centuries, English speakers often used “Bohemia” as a name for the wider Czech lands. The word also gave rise to “bohemian,” which can describe artists and writers who live in unconventional ways or reject traditional social rules. Although Prague is sometimes confused with other Central European capitals, it stands on the Vltava, not the Danube.

Itaipu Dam is a huge hydroelectric dam on the Paraná River, where the river forms part of the border between Brazil and Paraguay. The two countries operate it together and share the electricity it produces. Hydroelectric dams generate power by holding back water and directing its flow through turbines, which spin generators. Itaipu is one of the world’s largest power-generating facilities and supplies an important share of Paraguay’s electricity. Paraguay is a landlocked South American country, meaning it has no coastline. It lies north of Argentina, and its capital is Asunción. If a question asks for the jointly operated dam on the Paraná River, the answer is Itaipu Dam; if it asks which country shares the dam with Brazil, the answer is Paraguay.

Siberia is a vast region of northern Asia that makes up much of Russia east of the Ural Mountains. The Urals are a north–south mountain chain commonly used to mark the divide between Europe and Asia, as well as Siberia’s western boundary. Siberia stretches east toward the Pacific Ocean and north to the Arctic Ocean. It is known for long, cold winters, broad forests called taiga, and areas of treeless tundra in the far north, though its southern areas can be much warmer in summer. In Fyodor Dostoevsky’s novel Crime and Punishment, the student Raskolnikov is convicted of murder and sentenced to penal servitude in Siberia. Russia used this remote region as a place of exile and punishment.

The Bay of Fundy lies on Canada’s Atlantic coast between the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, northeast of Maine. It is famous for some of the world’s highest tides: the water can rise and fall by more than 15 metres in parts of the bay. At low tide, large areas of seafloor are exposed, but they flood again as the tide comes in, so visitors must pay attention to tide times. One of the bay’s best-known attractions is the Hopewell Rocks on the New Brunswick shore. Waves and tides have eroded the soft rock into tall sea stacks with narrower bases and wider tops, giving them a “flowerpot” shape. Visitors can walk around their bases at low tide and see them surrounded by water at high tide.

Mount Tambora is a stratovolcano on Sumbawa Island in Indonesia. In April 1815, it produced one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in recorded history. The eruption blasted out ash and gases and caused the volcano’s summit to collapse, forming a huge bowl-shaped depression called a caldera. Fine particles and sulfur aerosols spread high through the atmosphere, where they reflected some sunlight away from Earth. This helped cool the planet, especially across the Northern Hemisphere. In 1816, unusually cold weather, frosts, and heavy rain damaged crops and contributed to food shortages in many places. Because summer weather was so cold and disrupted, 1816 became known as the Year Without a Summer.

Tripoli is Lebanon’s second-largest city and a major port on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, about 85 kilometers north of the capital, Beirut. Its name can be confusing because Tripoli is also the name of Libya’s capital, another Mediterranean city. Lebanon’s Tripoli has a historic center with busy souks, or traditional markets, dating from the Mamluk period. A hilltop citadel overlooking the city is associated with Raymond de Saint-Gilles, a leader of the First Crusade. Just offshore lies Palm Islands Nature Reserve, a protected area established in 1992. It includes three small islands and the surrounding waters, providing nesting habitat for loggerhead sea turtles and a place for migratory birds to rest during their journeys.

Sleepy Hollow is an incorporated village on the Hudson River in Westchester County, New York, just north of Tarrytown. It was called North Tarrytown until 1996, when it adopted a name made famous by “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.” In that short story, schoolteacher Ichabod Crane hears tales of the Headless Horseman, a ghostly soldier searching for his missing head. The story was written by the 19th-century American author Washington Irving, who also wrote “Rip Van Winkle.” Both stories appeared in Irving’s collection The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon. Irving’s fiction helped make the village’s name familiar to readers, and the village’s later name change strengthened its connection to the tale.

Liberia is a country in West Africa with an Atlantic coastline. It borders Sierra Leone to the west, Guinea to the north, and Côte d’Ivoire to the east. Its flag has red-and-white stripes and a blue canton in the upper left with one white star, making it look similar to the flag of the United States. Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, is a major Atlantic port at the mouth of the Mesurado River. The city was named in honor of James Monroe, who was president of the United States during the early settlement of Liberia by formerly enslaved and free Black people from America. Liberia is divided into 15 counties, each with its own flag; the flag of Maryland County shows a lighthouse at Cape Palmas.

Lake Tana is Ethiopia’s largest lake. It lies in the highlands of northwestern Ethiopia and is an important source of the Blue Nile. The river flows out of the lake and, a short distance downstream, plunges over a waterfall called Tis Abay, also spelled Tis Abbai. The Blue Nile then travels toward Sudan, where it meets the White Nile at Khartoum. Together, their waters form the Nile, which flows north through Egypt to the Mediterranean Sea. Lake Tana therefore connects a lake in Ethiopia to one of the world’s best-known river systems. To remember the key names, think of Lake Tana as the lake that feeds the Blue Nile and Tis Abay as the waterfall the river passes after leaving it.

El Salvador is the smallest sovereign country in mainland Central America and one of the three countries of the Northern Triangle, along with Guatemala and Honduras. Its capital is San Salvador. It borders Guatemala to the west and Honduras to the north and east. Unlike its neighbors, El Salvador has a Pacific coastline but no Caribbean shore. On its southeastern coast lies the Gulf of Fonseca, a Pacific inlet shared by El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua. The Salvadoran port city of La Unión sits on the gulf, which also contains islands such as Meanguera. El Salvador’s landscape includes volcanoes, whose heat can be used to generate geothermal power. In 2021, the country also made Bitcoin legal tender.

The Ganges, also called the Ganga, is a major river of South Asia. It rises in the Himalayas, flows across northern India and enters Bangladesh, where its main channel is called the Padma. There, its waters join the Brahmaputra river system and help form the vast, low-lying delta on which much of Bangladesh lies. The Ganges is sacred in Hinduism and is revered as the goddess Ganga. One of the most important cities on its banks is Varanasi, in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. Historically also known as Benares, Varanasi is famous for its riverside ghats—steps leading down to the water—and its temples. Many Hindu pilgrims visit the city to pray and bathe in the river.

Maine is a New England state in the northeasternmost corner of the contiguous United States and is nicknamed the Pine Tree State. It borders Canada and has a rugged Atlantic coast with many islands. Aroostook County, in northern Maine, was the site of a bloodless border dispute with Canada known as the Aroostook War. Off the coast, Mount Desert Island is home to much of Acadia National Park, the only national park in New England. Acadia protects rocky shorelines, forests, lakes, and Cadillac Mountain, the highest point on an island along the Atlantic coast of the United States. The park also has a network of scenic carriage roads financed by John D. Rockefeller Jr.

Parícutin is a volcano in the Mexican state of Michoacán, near the city of Uruapan. It began erupting in 1943 when a crack opened in a farmer’s cornfield. Ash and fragments of rock piled up around the opening, forming a new cinder cone that grew rapidly. Scientists were able to observe much of Parícutin’s formation, making it a famous example of how a volcano can appear and change the landscape. Lava from the eruption eventually overwhelmed the nearby settlement of San Juan Parangaricutiro. Most of the town was buried, but the spires of its church, dedicated to St. John, remained visible above the hardened lava. Parícutin’s eruption continued for about nine years, ending in 1952.

Savannah is a historic coastal city in Georgia and a major port on the Atlantic Ocean. It played a role in two American wars. During the Revolutionary War, British forces held Savannah, and American and French troops tried to retake it in the 1779 Siege of Savannah. Casimir Pulaski, a Polish-born officer in the Continental Army, was mortally wounded while leading a cavalry charge during that attack. Decades later, in the Civil War, Union general William Tecumseh Sherman led his “March to the Sea” across Georgia, destroying railroads and other resources that supported the Confederacy. The march ended when his forces captured Savannah in December 1864. These events make Savannah an important place to remember in both Revolutionary War and Civil War history.

Pikes Peak is a 14,115-foot mountain in Colorado’s Front Range, part of the Rocky Mountains. It rises just west of Colorado Springs and is the tallest summit in the southern Front Range. During the Colorado Gold Rush, some prospectors used the slogan “Pikes Peak or bust,” even though no gold was found near the mountain. Colorado Springs, the city at its base, is also home to Garden of the Gods, a park famous for striking sandstone formations called the Kissing Camels and Cathedral Spires. If a question asks for the mountain west of Colorado Springs, the answer is Pikes Peak; if it asks for the city east of Pikes Peak with Garden of the Gods, the answer is Colorado Springs.

The Atacama Desert stretches across northern Chile, west of the Andes Mountains. It is widely regarded as the driest nonpolar desert on Earth, with some areas receiving almost no measurable rain for years. The Andes help create these conditions by blocking moisture from the east, leaving the desert in a rain shadow. Along the coast, the cold Humboldt Current cools moist air, producing a fog called camanchaca. A temperature inversion traps the fog near the ground, where its moisture helps some native plants survive despite the lack of rainfall. The Atacama is also rich in minerals: copper and saltpeter mining have long supported the economies of nearby cities, including Iquique and Antofagasta.

Delphi was an ancient Greek sanctuary and settlement in Phocis, near Mount Parnassus in central Greece. It was famous throughout the Greek world as the home of Apollo’s oracle. People traveled there to ask questions about important decisions, including wars, journeys, and the founding of new cities. The priestess who delivered Apollo’s prophecies was called the Pythia. She traditionally sat on a tripod in Apollo’s temple and gave responses that priests helped visitors interpret. Delphi was also a place of religious festivals and athletic contests. According to Greek myth, Apollo claimed the site after defeating a serpent called Python, a story connected to the Pythia’s name. Today, the ruins of Delphi are an important archaeological site and a reminder of the sanctuary’s influence in ancient Greece.

Chennai is the capital of Tamil Nadu, a state on India’s southeastern Coromandel Coast. Formerly called Madras, the city is a major port on the Bay of Bengal and a center of Tamil language and culture. Its Tamil-language film industry is nicknamed “Kollywood.” Chennai also played an important role in British colonial history. In 1644, the English East India Company established Fort St. George there, creating an early base for British power and trade along the coast. Today, the fort houses a museum and the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. Other well-known Chennai landmarks include Marina Beach and buildings that reflect the region’s Dravidian architectural traditions.

Karst is a type of landscape that forms when groundwater slowly dissolves soluble bedrock, especially limestone. Limestone is a sedimentary rock made mostly of calcium carbonate, often in the form of the mineral calcite. As water moves through cracks in the rock, it widens them over time, creating underground passages and caves. If the ground above an empty space collapses, a sinkhole can form. Water may also flow through underground rivers instead of staying in streams on the surface. Inside karst caves, dripping mineral-rich water can build stalactites on the ceiling and stalagmites on the floor. The rock most closely associated with karst is limestone; when heat and pressure change limestone through metamorphism, it can become marble.

Missouri is a Midwestern U.S. state with Jefferson City as its capital. It entered the Union in 1821 as a slave state under the Missouri Compromise of 1820, which also admitted Maine as a free state. The agreement was an attempt to preserve the balance between free and slave states in Congress. Two major rivers shape Missouri’s geography: the Missouri River crosses the state, while the Mississippi River forms much of its eastern border. Near where the Missouri River joins the Mississippi sits St. Louis, a major city known for the Gateway Arch, a monument to westward expansion. Missouri’s history also includes the 1838 Mormon War, a conflict between Mormon settlers and other residents.

Tokyo is Japan’s national capital and largest metropolitan center. It lies on the island of Honshu in the Kanto region, near Tokyo Bay. Its busy districts include Shinjuku, known for its major railway station and skyscrapers, and Shibuya, famous for its crowded pedestrian crossing. The wider Tokyo metropolitan area extends beyond the city to places such as Yokohama and Chiba, and Narita International Airport serves the region. Tokyo is also an important center for anime, with many animation studios based there. One of its best-known landmarks is Tokyo Skytree, a 634-meter broadcasting and observation tower that opened in 2012. It is the tallest structure in Japan and offers views across the city.

Manhattan Island is a long, narrow island that forms the central borough of New York City. The Hudson River runs along its west side, while the East River separates it from Brooklyn and Queens to the east. Manhattan is densely built and contains famous landmarks and neighborhoods, including Central Park, Washington Heights, the Upper East Side, and Harlem. Bridges connect it to other parts of the city; the Williamsburg Bridge, for example, links Manhattan with Brooklyn. Harlem, in northern Manhattan, became a major center of African American art, music, and writing during the 1920s, a period known as the Harlem Renaissance. One of its best-known landmarks is the Apollo Theater on 125th Street, an important venue for generations of performers.

A mid-ocean ridge is a long underwater mountain system formed where oceanic tectonic plates move apart at a divergent boundary. As the plates separate, molten rock rises from below, cools, and becomes new ocean crust. This process, called seafloor spreading, gradually widens the ocean floor. Mid-ocean ridges extend for thousands of kilometres through ocean basins and may have a central rift valley where the plates are pulling apart. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is one example; although most of it is underwater, parts rise above sea level in places such as the Azores. Another example is the Gakkel Ridge, a slow-spreading section beneath the Arctic Ocean. Together, these ridges form a connected mountain system across the world’s oceans.

Jeju Island is a volcanic island and province of South Korea, located south of the Korean Peninsula. It was once the center of the Tamna kingdom and still has a distinctive local culture, including the Jeju language, sometimes called Jeju-mal. Near the center of the island rises Mount Hallasan, a dormant shield volcano formed by many flows of lava. At about 1,947 meters, Hallasan is the highest mountain in South Korea. Its summit contains a crater lake called Baengnokdam. Jeju’s volcanic origins have also shaped its wider landscape, leaving lava tubes and other unusual rock formations. Together, the island’s history, culture, and volcanic scenery make it one of South Korea’s best-known places.

The Mojave River is an intermittent river in Southern California’s Mojave Desert. It begins in the San Bernardino Mountains near Cajon Pass, then flows northeast past Victorville and Barstow toward an inland basin. Unlike many rivers, it has no outlet to the ocean. Its sandy channel is often dry at the surface because much of the water seeps underground, though rain and snowmelt can produce visible flows and floods. The river ends at Soda Lake, a dry lake bed, or playa, near Baker. Floodwater that reaches Soda Lake may collect there briefly before evaporating. Remembering the river’s route and its dry-lake endpoint helps distinguish the Mojave River from other rivers of the American West.

North Korea, officially the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, occupies the northern part of the Korean Peninsula in East Asia. Its capital is Pyongyang, and it shares land borders with China and Russia. To the south, the Korean Demilitarized Zone separates it from South Korea, running roughly along the 38th parallel. Much of North Korea’s northwestern border with China follows the Yalu River, which flows into Korea Bay near Sinuiju in North Korea and Dandong in China. North Korea has been ruled by the Kim family since its founding in 1948. Its first leader, Kim Il-sung, promoted the ideology of Juche, which emphasizes self-reliance; his grandson Kim Jong-un became leader in 2011.

Longitude is a geographic coordinate that tells how far a place lies east or west of the Prime Meridian, the line designated as 0 degrees longitude that passes through Greenwich, England. Lines of longitude run from the North Pole to the South Pole. Together with latitude, which measures distance north or south of the equator, longitude helps identify a location on Earth. Longitude is also connected to time: as Earth rotates, different places face the Sun at different times. Earth makes one full 360-degree rotation in roughly 24 hours, so dividing 360 by 24 shows that a one-hour difference in local solar time corresponds to 15 degrees of longitude. Accurate clocks, such as John Harrison’s marine chronometer, helped sailors calculate longitude while at sea.

The Caucasus Mountains are a rugged mountain system between the Black Sea to the west and the Caspian Sea to the east. They form part of the traditional boundary between Europe and Asia, southwest of the Ural Mountains. The Greater Caucasus range runs roughly west to east through the region of Georgia and Azerbaijan, with Russia to its north. Its peaks include Mount Elbrus, which is often considered the highest mountain in Europe. The Caspian Sea, at the eastern end of the range, is the world’s largest inland body of water, and Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan, stands on its shore. These landmarks help locate the Caucasus on a map: mountains between two seas, with Elbrus among their peaks.

Réunion is a volcanic island in the Indian Ocean, about 400 miles (650 kilometers) east of Madagascar. It belongs to the Mascarene Islands and is a French overseas department, meaning it is part of France rather than an independent country. Its capital is Saint-Denis. Réunion drew international attention in 2015 when a flaperon, part of an airplane wing, washed ashore and was identified as coming from the missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. About 200 kilometers northeast of Réunion lies Mauritius, another Mascarene island. Unlike Réunion, Mauritius is a sovereign country. Its capital is Port Louis, and the dodo, an extinct flightless bird that once lived there, has become one of its national symbols.

The Danube is Europe’s second-longest river, after the Volga. It forms in Germany’s Black Forest where the Brigach and Breg rivers meet, then flows east across Central and Southeastern Europe before reaching the Black Sea. Along its route, it passes through or beside four capital cities: Vienna in Austria, Bratislava in Slovakia, Budapest in Hungary, and Belgrade in Serbia. The river and its tributaries drain a large area called a drainage basin, linking many countries and providing routes for transport and trade. Near the Black Sea, the Danube divides into many channels, creating the Danube Delta. This vast wetland lies mostly in Romania and extends into Ukraine. Its lakes and reed beds support abundant wildlife, including pelicans, and the delta is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Krakatoa is a volcanic island in Indonesia’s Sunda Strait, the waterway separating the islands of Java and Sumatra and connecting the Java Sea with the Indian Ocean. In 1883, Krakatoa erupted with enormous explosions heard thousands of kilometers away. The eruption destroyed much of the island and sent powerful tsunamis crashing into nearby coasts, killing tens of thousands of people. Ash and gases rose high into the atmosphere and spread around the world, producing unusually colorful sunsets for months afterward. The event showed that a volcanic eruption can have effects far beyond the volcano itself: it can reshape islands, threaten coastal communities, and even change the appearance of skies on the other side of the world.

The Palm Islands are a group of artificial archipelagos built and planned off the coast of Dubai, the most populous city in the United Arab Emirates. Seen from above, each island group resembles a palm tree, with a broad central trunk and curved rows of fronds. Land for the islands was created in the Persian Gulf, and the projects were designed to make more space for homes, hotels, and beaches. The best-known island, Palm Jumeirah, was developed, but plans for other parts of the group were delayed or changed after the 2008 financial crisis. Dubai is also home to the Burj Khalifa, the world’s tallest building. The islands and skyscraper are examples of the city’s ambitious construction projects.

The Mozambique Channel is a stretch of the Indian Ocean between the island country of Madagascar and the southeastern African mainland, especially Mozambique. It separates Madagascar from the rest of Africa, helping explain why animals such as lemurs evolved there and are found naturally nowhere else. The channel also receives water from the Zambezi River, one of southern Africa’s major rivers. The Zambezi flows through Zambia and plunges over Victoria Falls on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. Farther downstream, it crosses Mozambique and spreads into a large delta before entering the Mozambique Channel. So, if a question asks for the water between Madagascar and southeastern Africa, the answer is the Mozambique Channel; if it asks for the river that reaches it after passing Victoria Falls, the answer is the Zambezi River.

Myanmar, also called Burma, is a country in Southeast Asia. Its largest city, Yangon, served as the national capital until the government moved the capital to Naypyidaw in 2005. Naypyidaw is a purpose-built inland city in a specially designated union territory near the center of the country. Myanmar also contains Mandalay, a major city farther north. The Irrawaddy River, one of the country’s most important waterways, flows south through Myanmar toward the Andaman Sea. These landmarks help identify the country: if a question mentions Mandalay and the Irrawaddy alongside a capital change in 2005, the answer is Myanmar. If it asks which city replaced Yangon as Myanmar’s capital, the answer is Naypyidaw.

The Equator is an imaginary line that circles Earth at zero degrees latitude, dividing it into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. It is a great circle, meaning its plane passes through Earth’s center. Because Earth bulges slightly around the Equator, places along it are farther from Earth’s center than places near the poles. On the March and September equinoxes, the Sun is directly overhead at noon for locations on the Equator. Trade winds from both hemispheres meet near it in a region called the intertropical convergence zone, where rising air often brings clouds and rain. The Equator crosses several countries, including Ecuador in South America. Ecuador’s capital is Quito, its largest city is Guayaquil, and its territory includes the Galápagos Islands.

North Dakota is a Great Plains state in the north-central United States, bordering Canada and South Dakota. It entered the Union in 1889, alongside South Dakota. President Benjamin Harrison reportedly shuffled the two statehood papers before signing them, so it is unclear which Dakota became the 39th state and which became the 40th. The two states also share the Standing Rock Indian Reservation. One of North Dakota’s most important waterways is the Missouri River, the longest river in the United States. Garrison Dam holds back the Missouri in North Dakota to form Lake Sakakawea, a large reservoir. The river also flows through South Dakota before eventually joining the Mississippi River near St. Louis, Missouri.
