Delos is a small island in the Cyclades, a group of Greek islands in the Aegean Sea. In Greek mythology, it was the birthplace of the twin gods Apollo and Artemis, making it an important sacred site. Delos also played a role in Greek history after the Persian Wars. Athens led an alliance of Greek city-states that continued fighting Persia, and the allies initially kept their shared treasury on Delos. Because of this connection, the alliance was called the Delian League. Delos later became a busy trading port, including for enslaved people, before attacks and changing trade routes reduced its importance. Its archaeological remains still show how an island could be both a religious center and a meeting place for a powerful alliance.

Great Smoky Mountains National Park straddles the border between North Carolina and Tennessee in the southern Appalachian Mountains. Its forested ridges are famous for a bluish haze: plants release natural compounds into the air that help create the misty appearance that gave the mountains their name. The park protects a wide range of wildlife and habitats, from valleys to high mountain peaks. Its highest summit is Kuwohi, which is also the highest point in Tennessee. Formerly known as Clingmans Dome, Kuwohi has a steep, paved trail leading to an observation tower near the top. The park’s highest point should not be confused with Mount Mitchell in North Carolina, which lies outside the park and is the highest point in the United States east of the Mississippi River.

The Drakensberg is a mountain range along the eastern side of South Africa, extending into the kingdom of Lesotho. It forms the highest section of the Great Escarpment, a steep boundary between South Africa’s high interior plateau and lower land toward the coast. Near Lesotho, the range has dramatic cliffs and basalt highlands formed from ancient volcanic rock. Its highest summit is Thabana Ntlenyana, which rises to about 3,482 metres in Lesotho and is the highest point in southern Africa. The Drakensberg is important for its mountain scenery and as a source of rivers that supply water to surrounding areas. Its name means “Dragon Mountains” in Afrikaans, a reference to its rugged peaks.

The North Sea is a shallow arm of the northeastern Atlantic Ocean between Great Britain to the west and Norway, Denmark, Germany, and the Low Countries to the east. Its southern end connects to the English Channel, while its northern waters extend toward the Atlantic near the Shetland Islands. The sea is known for busy shipping routes, fishing, rough weather, and oil and natural gas beneath its seabed. One of its largest offshore oil developments is the Statfjord field, east of the Shetland Islands in the Norwegian sector. Statfjord began producing oil in 1979 and has three major concrete platforms named Statfjord A, B, and C. North Sea petroleum has helped Norway build its large sovereign wealth fund.

Lighthouses are tall structures with powerful lights that help ships navigate near land, especially at night or in poor visibility. They mark harbor entrances and warn sailors about dangerous coastlines, rocks, and shallow water. Many have distinctive shapes or contrasting stripes, such as red and white, so crews can recognize them during the day; their lights may flash in patterns that help sailors identify their location after dark. One historic example is the Cape Palmas Lighthouse in Maryland County, Liberia. It stands near Cape Palmas and guided vessels into the port of Harper. The lighthouse also appears on the flag of Maryland County, showing its importance as a local landmark and aid to navigation.

Nazareth is a city in Lower Galilee in northern Israel, just north of the Jezreel Valley. In Christian accounts, it is the town where Jesus grew up after Mary and Joseph returned from Egypt, so it is often called his childhood hometown. Nazareth is also closely linked to the Annunciation: the moment when the angel Gabriel told Mary that she would bear Jesus. The city’s Basilica of the Annunciation is a major Roman Catholic pilgrimage church built above a grotto traditionally identified as the site of that event. Its present monumental building was consecrated in 1969. A Greek Orthodox church in Nazareth marks another traditional location for the Annunciation, showing that different Christian communities preserve different traditions about where it happened.

The New Jersey Pine Barrens are a heavily forested region of the coastal plain in southern New Jersey, the state whose capital is Trenton. Despite the name, the area is not barren: it has pine and oak forests, streams, and extensive wetlands. Its sandy, acidic, nutrient-poor soils make farming difficult but support plants adapted to those conditions. Much of the region is protected within the Pinelands National Reserve. The Pine Barrens are also famous for the legend of the Jersey Devil, a creature often described as winged and hoofed. According to a traditional story, Deborah Leeds gave birth to the creature at Leeds Point in 1735. The legend is folklore, not evidence that such an animal exists, but it remains a well-known part of New Jersey culture.

The Hudson River is a major waterway in eastern New York. It rises in the Adirondack Mountains, flows mainly south past Albany and New York City, and empties into New York Harbor. For centuries, people used the river to travel and move goods between inland communities and the coast. In 1807, a steamboat developed and promoted by American engineer and entrepreneur Robert Fulton made a landmark commercial voyage from New York City to Albany. That trip showed that steam-powered boats could carry passengers upstream more reliably than boats that depended on wind. The Hudson soon became a busy steamboat route, helping connect Albany with the growing port of New York City. Later, entrepreneurs such as Cornelius Vanderbilt competed for business on its waters.

Uganda is a landlocked country in East Africa bordered by South Sudan, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It has a long northern shoreline on Lake Victoria, Africa’s largest lake, and its capital is Kampala. Nearby, on the lake’s northern shore, is Entebbe International Airport. In 1976, hijackers forced Air France Flight 139 to fly to Entebbe, where they held its passengers hostage with the support of Uganda’s ruler, Idi Amin. Israeli forces carried out a daring rescue mission there, known as Operation Entebbe, and freed more than 100 hostages. The raid made the airport internationally famous and remains a well-known event in Uganda’s history.

Alberta is a province in western Canada known for its Rocky Mountain landscapes, prairie farmland, and energy industry. Its capital, Edmonton, lies on the North Saskatchewan River. Edmonton and Calgary are connected by a busy urban corridor, with Red Deer roughly halfway between them. Edmonton is home to West Edmonton Mall, a huge shopping and entertainment complex with an indoor lake and water park. Alberta also contains famous national parks, including Banff and Jasper, which attract visitors to the Rocky Mountains. One unusual fact about the province is that an aggressive control program has kept it free of established rat populations since the 1950s. If a question asks for the province whose capital is Edmonton, the answer is Alberta; if it asks for Alberta’s capital, the answer is Edmonton.

A lake is a natural body of standing water that fills a basin and is surrounded by land. Rivers or streams may flow into or out of it, but unlike a river, the water in a lake does not generally flow from one end to the other. Lakes vary greatly in size, from small mountain pools to the Great Lakes of North America, which include Erie and Superior. Some lakes form when glaciers carve hollows in the landscape. A glacier can erode a bowl-shaped basin called a cirque high in the mountains. When the glacier melts and the cirque fills with water, the small lake left behind is called a tarn.

Jakarta is Indonesia’s largest city and its capital, located on the northwestern coast of Java, one of the country’s main islands. The city faces the Java Sea, which lies north of Java and south of Borneo and connects westward to the South China Sea. Jakarta is a major center of government, business, and culture, but its coastal location also makes it vulnerable to flooding. Much of the city is low-lying, and some areas are sinking because groundwater has been pumped out from beneath them. This land subsidence, combined with rising sea levels and heavy rains, increases the risk of severe floods. Sea walls and other defenses can help, but protecting Jakarta remains a major challenge.

The Nazca Lines are a group of enormous ancient designs, called geoglyphs, on a dry plateau in southern Peru. People associated with the Nazca culture made them by removing dark surface stones to reveal the lighter ground beneath. The designs include long straight lines, geometric shapes, and figures of animals such as a hummingbird, spider, and monkey. Many are so large that they are easiest to recognize from above. The desert’s dry climate has helped preserve them for centuries, although their original purpose remains uncertain. Maria Reiche, a German-born mathematician and archaeologist, spent decades measuring, studying, and helping protect the Nazca Lines. Her dedication earned her the nickname “Lady of the Lines.”

Sinkholes are depressions or holes in the ground that often form in karst landscapes, where groundwater slowly dissolves soluble rock such as limestone or dolomite. As the rock wears away, it can leave an underground cavity. If the ground above that cavity collapses, a sinkhole opens at the surface. Groundwater can also dissolve passages through the rock, creating caves, also called caverns. Unlike sinkholes, which are openings or depressions visible at the surface, caves are underground spaces that people can enter and explore. People who explore caves are called spelunkers. Inside some caves, dripping water deposits minerals over long periods, forming stalactites that hang from the ceiling and stalagmites that rise from the floor.

The South China Sea is a marginal sea of the western Pacific Ocean, lying east of Vietnam and west of the Philippines. It is an important route for international shipping and contains fishing grounds and possible oil and gas resources. Several countries have overlapping claims to its islands and waters. Near the center of these disputes are the Spratly Islands, an archipelago of more than 100 islands, reefs, and shoals claimed in whole or in part by China, the Philippines, Vietnam, and others. China’s nine-dash line marks a broad claim across much of the sea. The Philippines and Vietnam dispute that claim where it overlaps waters in which they assert exclusive economic rights, including rights to resources.

Mariupol is a major port city in Donetsk Oblast in southeastern Ukraine. It stands on the northern shore of the Sea of Azov, an inland sea connected to the Black Sea by the Kerch Strait. Its coastal location made Mariupol one of Ukraine’s key seaports and an important centre for industry and trade. During Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian forces besieged the city for months. Fighting and bombardment destroyed much of Mariupol, killed many residents, and forced many others to flee. The siege made the city a symbol of the war’s destruction and the suffering of civilians. If asked to name the devastated port city, the answer is Mariupol; if asked which sea borders it, the answer is the Sea of Azov.

Lisbon is the capital and largest city of Portugal, the smaller of the two countries on the Iberian Peninsula. It stands beside the estuary of the Tagus River, which flows west across the peninsula and reaches the Atlantic Ocean near the city. Lisbon’s position made it an important port, connecting Portugal with trade routes across the sea. In 1755, a devastating earthquake and tsunami destroyed much of the city. Its central Baixa district was rebuilt with a planned grid of streets and buildings in a style known as Pombaline architecture, named after the Marquis of Pombal, who directed the rebuilding. Lisbon is also the westernmost capital in mainland Europe, and its Vasco da Gama Bridge crosses the Tagus.

Memphis is a city in southwestern Tennessee, on a bluff overlooking the Mississippi River. It is famous for Beale Street, a center of blues music, and for its important place in the history of American civil rights. In the late 1800s, journalist Ida B. Wells owned and wrote for a Memphis newspaper called the Free Speech and Headlight. She used it to report on racial violence and challenge lynching, the murder of people by mobs. Her reporting made her a leading voice against that injustice. Decades later, during a strike by Memphis sanitation workers, Martin Luther King Jr. gave his “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” speech in the city on April 3, 1968, the day before he was assassinated there.

K2 is a mountain in the Karakoram range, on the border between Pakistan and China. At 8,611 meters (28,251 feet) above sea level, it is the world’s second-highest mountain, surpassed only by Mount Everest. K2’s southern side is in Gilgit-Baltistan, a region administered by Pakistan; Pakistan’s capital is Islamabad, and its national language is Urdu. The mountain is nicknamed the “Savage Mountain” because its steep slopes, severe weather, and dangerous climbing routes make it especially difficult to climb. In 1954, Italian climbers Lino Lacedelli and Achille Compagnoni became the first people to reach its summit. Everest, by contrast, is in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and China.

Donbas is a coal-rich historical region in eastern Ukraine, mainly covering Donetsk Oblast and Luhansk Oblast, two provinces named after their major cities. Its name comes from “Donets Basin,” and it is also commonly spelled Donbass in English. Coal mining and heavy industry have long shaped the region. Donbas became a major focus of the Russo-Ukrainian War after fighting began there in 2014. In 2022, shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia recognized claims of independence by separatist groups in the Donetsk and Luhansk areas. Luhansk Oblast is also important to remember by its former name: during two periods of Soviet rule, including from 1970 until 1990, it was officially called Voroshilovgrad Oblast.

The Cape of Good Hope is a rocky headland on South Africa’s Cape Peninsula. It became an important landmark for sailors seeking a sea route from the Atlantic Ocean around Africa to the Indian Ocean. In 1488, the Portuguese navigator Bartholomeu Dias reached southern Africa and passed the cape during his return voyage. He called it the Cape of Storms, reflecting the dangerous weather and rough seas there. Portugal’s King John II later renamed it the Cape of Good Hope because the voyage suggested that ships could reach India by sailing around Africa. Dias wanted to continue, but his crew voted to turn back. A later Portuguese explorer, Vasco da Gama, completed the sea voyage to India.

Alcatraz Island is a small island in San Francisco Bay, near San Francisco, California. It is famous for its former federal penitentiary, which held prisoners from 1934 to 1963. In 1969, Native American activists from a group called Indians of All Tribes began an occupation of the island that lasted about 19 months, until 1971. They claimed Alcatraz under the Treaty of Fort Laramie and proposed building a cultural center where people could study Native American history. Activist LaNada War Jack helped lead the occupation. The protest drew attention to Native American rights and the need for Native people to have a stronger voice in decisions about their land and culture. Today, visitors can learn about both the prison and the occupation on the island.

The Indian Ocean is the world’s third-largest ocean. It lies between East Africa to the west, southern Asia to the north, and Australia to the east. Tanzania has a long coastline on this ocean, part of the East African region known as the Swahili Coast. Along the ocean’s northern edge are two major bodies of water: the Arabian Sea, west of India, and the Bay of Bengal, east of India. The Bay of Bengal is a broad inlet bordered by India and Bangladesh to the west and north and Myanmar to the east. The Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems flow into the bay, carrying water and sediment from a vast area of South Asia.

Seoul is the capital and largest urban center of South Korea, a country in East Asia. The city grew along the Han River, which is formed where the Bukhan and Namhan rivers meet. From Seoul, the river flows westward toward the Yellow Sea. Its banks have long provided space for travel, trade, and settlement, helping Seoul develop into a major city. Today, the wider Seoul metropolitan area is the country’s center of government, business, culture, and transportation. It includes Gangnam, a well-known district associated with shopping, offices, and entertainment. Seoul combines historic palaces and neighborhoods with modern skyscrapers and extensive subway lines. To identify the city, remember that South Korea’s capital is Seoul, and the river running through it is the Han River.

Delft is a city in South Holland, in the Netherlands, between The Hague and Rotterdam. It gave its name to Delftware, a tradition of blue-and-white tin-glazed pottery that became famous in the 17th century. Delft is also closely linked to two Dutch Golden Age painters. Johannes Vermeer was born there in 1632 and spent most of his career in the city. His paintings include Girl with a Pearl Earring, The Milkmaid, The Little Street, and the cityscape View of Delft. Carel Fabritius also worked in Delft; his painting The Goldfinch survived a 1654 explosion at a gunpowder store that killed him and damaged much of the city. These connections make Delft important in both Dutch art and craft history.

An Exclusive Economic Zone, or EEZ, is a maritime area that can extend up to 200 nautical miles from a coastal country’s baselines, the lines used to measure its maritime zones. Within its EEZ, a country has special rights to explore, exploit, conserve, and manage natural resources in the water and seabed, such as fish, oil, and gas. An EEZ is not the same as territorial waters: it gives the coastal country resource rights, not complete control over all activities at sea. EEZs are governed by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a treaty adopted in 1982 in Montego Bay, Jamaica, and brought into force in 1994. Overlapping claims to EEZs can cause disputes between countries.

Puget Sound is a branching tidal inlet in northwestern Washington State. Its many channels, islands, and bays border the Seattle–Tacoma area, where its sheltered waters support busy ports. The Sound connects to the Pacific Ocean through the Strait of Juan de Fuca, a passage along Washington’s northwestern edge near the border with Canada. Puget Sound also forms much of the eastern edge of the Olympic Peninsula, a large landform that extends westward to the Pacific coast. The peninsula’s mountainous interior includes Olympic National Park. On a map, you can find Puget Sound between the Seattle–Tacoma area and the Olympic Peninsula, then trace its waters northwest to the strait and the ocean.

The Great Smoky Mountains, often called the Smokies, are a rugged subrange of the southern Appalachian Mountains along the border between Tennessee and North Carolina. Their name comes from the bluish mist that often hangs over their forested ridgelines. Much of the range lies within Great Smoky Mountains National Park, where visitors hike through diverse forests and see waterfalls, wildlife, and mountain views. The Appalachian Trail passes through the park. The range’s best-known summit is Kuwohi, which rises 6,643 feet (2,025 meters) and is the highest point in Tennessee. A circular observation tower at the top offers wide views on clear days. Kuwohi is a Cherokee name; the summit was formerly called Clingmans Dome.

Babylon was an ancient city on the Euphrates River in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. It became the capital of Babylonia and flourished under rulers including Hammurabi, whose famous law code included the principle “an eye for an eye.” Centuries later, King Nebuchadnezzar II expanded the city and commissioned the Ishtar Gate, a monumental entrance covered in blue-glazed bricks and decorated with images of bulls and dragons. The gate was dedicated to Ishtar, a goddess of love and war. Nebuchadnezzar also rebuilt the great temple tower called Etemenanki. Babylon is associated with the legendary Hanging Gardens, although historians debate whether they existed there. After Nebuchadnezzar’s forces destroyed Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem, many Jews were taken to Babylon in an event known as the Babylonian captivity.

Martha’s Vineyard is an island off the southern coast of Cape Cod in Massachusetts, a northeastern U.S. state whose capital is Boston. The island is part of Dukes County and can be reached by ferry from Woods Hole on the Massachusetts mainland. Its towns include Edgartown, known for its historic buildings and harbor, and Oak Bluffs, known for its colorful cottages. Martha’s Vineyard is a popular summer resort, drawing visitors to its beaches, villages, and coastline. It has also been a vacation destination for U.S. presidents; Barack Obama bought a waterfront home there. Despite its name, Martha’s Vineyard is an island rather than a vineyard. If you are asked which island lies south of Cape Cod, the answer is Martha’s Vineyard; the state it belongs to is Massachusetts.

Polynesia is a vast cultural and geographic region of the Pacific Ocean and, in the traditional division of Pacific islands into Polynesia, Micronesia, and Melanesia, is the largest of the three. It is often pictured as a triangle with Hawaiʻi at its northern corner, New Zealand at its southwestern corner, and Rapa Nui at its eastern corner. Rapa Nui is commonly called Easter Island in English. It is under Chilean control and is famous for its moai, monumental stone figures carved by its Indigenous people. Polynesia also includes islands such as Samoa, Tonga, and Tahiti. Although its islands are separated by great distances, Polynesian peoples share related languages and cultural traditions shaped in part by the long ocean voyages of their ancestors.

The Continental Divide of the Americas, also called the Great Divide, is a long watershed boundary that separates land draining toward the Pacific Ocean from land draining toward the Atlantic Ocean. It follows high ground through western Canada and the United States, including the Rocky Mountains, and continues south along the Andes. Rain or melting snow that falls on opposite sides of the divide can end up in different oceans, even if it lands only a short distance apart. In Glacier National Park, Montana, the Continental Divide meets another watershed boundary called the Northern Divide at Triple Divide Peak. From this summit, water can drain in three directions: toward the Pacific, the Atlantic, or the Arctic Ocean via the Hudson Bay region.

Port Arthur is a historic site on the Tasman Peninsula in Tasmania, the Australian island once called Van Diemen’s Land. In the nineteenth century, it was a British penal settlement where convicts transported to Australia were imprisoned. Its prison complex was designed to punish prisoners and change their behaviour. Today, visitors can see its preserved buildings and ruins, which are part of the Australian Convict Sites UNESCO World Heritage property. Port Arthur is also remembered for a tragedy in 1996: gunman Martin Bryant killed 35 people there in one of the deadliest mass shootings in modern Australian history. The attack led Australia to introduce stricter gun laws.

Rwanda is a small, landlocked country in the African Great Lakes region of east-central Africa. Its capital is Kigali, and it borders Uganda to the north, Tanzania to the east, Burundi to the south, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the west. Along that western border lies Lake Kivu, a deep freshwater lake shared by Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Methane dissolved in its waters is extracted to produce energy. Rwanda is home to Hutu, Tutsi, and Batwa communities. In 1994, extremist Hutu leaders organized a genocide against the Tutsi, killing hundreds of thousands of people; many Hutu who opposed the violence were also murdered. This history remains important to understanding Rwanda today.

Roads are constructed routes that let motor vehicles travel between places. They range from local streets to highways, freeways, and interstates built for faster, longer-distance travel. State departments of transportation help regulate and maintain many roads, while interchanges allow traffic to move between major routes without stopping at ordinary intersections. Some roads charge drivers tolls to pay for construction or upkeep. A famous example is the Pennsylvania Turnpike, a toll road that opened in 1940. It crosses the Allegheny Mountains and was one of the first long-distance, limited-access highways in the United States, helping inspire the later Interstate Highway System. That nationwide system was authorized by a 1956 law signed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower and uses numbered routes to connect regions across the country.

Corinth was a powerful ancient Greek city-state, or polis, on the Isthmus of Corinth, the narrow land bridge joining the Peloponnese to mainland Greece. Its position let it control an important overland route and benefit from trade between two nearby seas. According to Greek legend, Sisyphus founded the city, though its real origins go back to prehistoric settlement. Corinth was also associated with the Corinthian style of architecture, known for its ornate column capitals. Near the city, at a sanctuary dedicated to Poseidon on the isthmus, Greeks from many city-states gathered for a major athletic festival called the Isthmian Games. Like the Olympic Games, these were Panhellenic games, meaning they brought together participants from across the Greek world.

National flags are official symbols that represent sovereign countries. Their colors, shapes, and images often reflect a country’s history, values, or identity. The United States flag, nicknamed the Stars and Stripes, has stars and alternating red and white stripes. France’s flag is a tricolor made of three vertical bands of blue, white, and red, while Japan’s shows a red sun on a white background. Most national flags are rectangular, but Nepal’s is unusual because it is made of two stacked triangular shapes. Mozambique’s flag is especially distinctive: it shows an AK-47 crossed with a hoe above an open book, beside a red triangle. A proposal in 2005 to remove the AK-47 was rejected, so it remains on the flag.

Kent is a county in the southeastern corner of England, often called the “Garden of England” because of its orchards and farmland. Its northern coastline borders the Thames Estuary, while its southern and eastern shores face the English Channel. Kent is one of the Home Counties, the counties surrounding London. Canterbury, in Kent, is home to Canterbury Cathedral, an important site in English Christianity. Kent also shares its name with one of the early Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, which was the first of those kingdoms to convert to Christianity. On the Channel coast, the port town of Dover faces Calais, France, across the narrowest part of the English Channel. Dover is famous for its white chalk cliffs and its castle overlooking the harbor.

The Rhône River begins in the Swiss Alps and flows through Lake Geneva before crossing southeastern France. At Lyon, it meets the Saône River, then continues south past Avignon and Arles. Near Arles, the Rhône splits into two branches, the Great Rhône and the Little Rhône. These branches form a delta before the river empties into the Mediterranean Sea. The delta lies in the Camargue, a protected wetland region known for its lagoons, salt flats, and flamingos. The river’s waters and fertile valley have shaped the places along its course, supporting farming, travel, and towns. If a question describes a river flowing from the Swiss Alps through Lake Geneva to the Mediterranean, it is the Rhône; if it asks for the wetland at its mouth, the answer is the Camargue.

The Missouri River is often described as the longest river in the United States. It begins in the Rocky Mountains of Montana, crosses the Great Plains, and eventually joins the Mississippi River near St. Louis, Missouri. The river flows through both North Dakota and South Dakota, passing their capitals, Bismarck and Pierre. In South Dakota, people often use the Missouri to distinguish the state’s “West River” and “East River” regions. Dams along the river store water and create reservoirs. In western North Dakota, Garrison Dam forms Lake Sakakawea, a large reservoir named for Sakakawea, the Shoshone woman who helped the Lewis and Clark expedition as an interpreter. Together, the Missouri and Mississippi form one of North America’s great river systems.

Detroit is Michigan’s largest city and a major port in the Great Lakes region. It stands on the Detroit River, which connects Lake St. Clair to Lake Erie and forms part of the border between the United States and Canada. Across the river is Windsor, a city in the Canadian province of Ontario; the Ambassador Bridge links Windsor and Detroit. Ontario is also home to Toronto, Canada’s most populous city, and Ottawa, Canada’s capital. Detroit is especially known as a center of the American automotive industry. Companies such as Ford Motor Company and General Motors helped make it famous for car manufacturing, earning it the nickname “Motor City.”

Santiago is the capital and largest city of Chile, a long, narrow country in South America. It lies in Chile’s Central Valley, between the Andes Mountains to the east and the Coastal Range to the west. Founded by Spanish explorer Pedro de Valdivia in 1541, Santiago grew into the country’s political and economic center. One of its best-known landmarks is Cerro San Cristóbal, a hill that forms part of a major urban park and offers views over the city. At its summit is a sanctuary crowned by a statue of the Immaculate Conception, a representation of the Virgin Mary. Visitors can reach the top of Cerro San Cristóbal by funicular railway or cable car.

Abu Dhabi is the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and the capital of the emirate that shares its name. The city lies on an island just off the Arabian Peninsula’s coast and is the seat of the UAE’s federal government. Etihad Airways is based there, while Dubai, another UAE city, is the country’s largest city. One of Abu Dhabi’s best-known landmarks is the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, a vast Islamic place of worship clad in white marble. It has 82 domes and four minarets, the towers associated with a mosque, as well as a huge hand-knotted carpet in its main prayer hall. The mosque is named after Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the UAE’s founding president.

The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean on Earth. It stretches from Asia and Australia in the west to North and South America in the east and covers about one-third of Earth’s surface. It contains thousands of islands, including those in Polynesia, a major region of the central and southern Pacific. The name Polynesia means “many islands,” and its island groups include Samoa, Tonga, and the Society Islands. Hawaii and New Zealand are also part of the wider Polynesian region. Polynesian peoples developed skilled ocean navigation, using stars, winds, and waves to travel between islands. Their traditions include stories about Maui, a hero who is said in Hawaiian mythology to have helped create the Hawaiian Islands.

The Okavango River rises in the highlands of Angola and flows southeast through Namibia before entering Botswana. Unlike most major rivers, it does not reach the sea. Instead, its waters spread across the flat Kalahari region to form the Okavango Delta, a vast inland network of channels, wetlands, and islands. Much of the water eventually evaporates or soaks into the ground. Thousands of years ago, the river helped feed a much larger lake called Lake Makgadikgadi. Today, the delta supports wildlife and communities, including San peoples such as the Bugakwe and Xanekwe. The country containing the delta is Botswana, a landlocked nation whose capital is Gaborone and whose neighbors include Namibia, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and South Africa.

Jacksonville is Florida’s most populous city and a major center of northeast Florida. It lies in Duval County, where the St. Johns River flows through downtown. Unlike many rivers, the St. Johns runs northward across the state before reaching the Atlantic Ocean near Mayport, just east of Jacksonville. The river has long helped make the city an important port and transportation center. Jacksonville is also the eastern terminus of Interstate 10, a major highway that stretches west across the southern United States. If a question describes a large Florida city in Duval County at the east end of I-10, the answer is Jacksonville. If it asks which river flows through the city, the answer is the St. Johns River.

Death Valley is a long desert trough in eastern California, near the Nevada border, and much of it lies within Death Valley National Park. Surrounded by mountains, the valley is famous for its extreme summer heat and dry climate. Its lowest area is Badwater Basin, a broad, salt-crusted flat about 282 feet below sea level—the lowest point in North America. Water that reaches the basin usually evaporates, leaving salt behind on the ground. Death Valley also has sand dunes, colorful rock formations, and Racetrack Playa, where some stones have moved across the dry lakebed when thin sheets of ice were pushed by wind. Despite its harsh conditions, the park supports plants and animals adapted to desert life.

Stalactites are icicle-shaped mineral deposits that hang from cave ceilings and grow downward over time. They often form in caves within limestone, a rock that slowly dissolves as slightly acidic rainwater seeps through it. The water carries dissolved calcium carbonate into the cave. When it drips from the ceiling, some of that material is left behind and builds up layer by layer. The most common mineral in these deposits is calcite, a crystalline form of calcium carbonate also found in limestone. Stalagmites form in a similar way, but they grow upward from the cave floor where drops land. A useful way to remember the difference is that stalactites cling to the ceiling, while stalagmites rise from the ground.

Lawrence is a city in eastern Kansas founded in 1854 by antislavery settlers organized by the New England Emigrant Aid Company. It became a major Free-State stronghold during “Bleeding Kansas,” a period of violent conflict over whether the Kansas Territory would allow slavery before the Civil War. On May 21, 1856, a pro-slavery posse led by Sheriff Samuel J. Jones entered Lawrence, destroyed the printing presses of two antislavery newspapers, and burned the Free State Hotel. This attack is known as the Sacking of Lawrence. Three nights later, abolitionist John Brown and his followers killed five pro-slavery men in the Pottawatomie Massacre. Violence returned to Lawrence during the Civil War: in 1863, Confederate guerrillas led by William Quantrill raided the city and killed many residents.

Île de la Cité is an island in the River Seine at the historic heart of Paris, France. Several bridges connect it to both banks of the river. The island was an important center of the city for centuries and is home to two major Gothic landmarks. Sainte-Chapelle is a royal chapel commissioned by King Louis IX in the 1200s and is celebrated for its tall stained-glass windows. Nearby stands Notre-Dame de Paris, a Catholic cathedral whose name means “Our Lady of Paris.” It is recognizable by its twin square towers, flying buttresses, and large rose windows. A fire in 2019 destroyed Notre-Dame’s spire and damaged the building; after extensive restoration, the cathedral reopened in 2024.

The Taklamakan Desert is a vast sandy desert in China’s Xinjiang region. It occupies much of the Tarim Basin, an immense lowland bordered by the Tian Shan mountains to the north and the Kunlun Mountains to the south. The basin has no outlet to the sea, so its rivers drain inward and their water eventually evaporates or collects in inland lakes. Because the desert’s shifting dunes and scarce water made crossing its center dangerous, travelers on the historic Silk Road followed routes around its margins, stopping at oasis towns such as Kashgar. Remember the distinction: the Taklamakan is the desert, while the Tarim Basin is the larger lowland that contains it.

Germania was the name Roman writers used for a broad region of central and northern Europe inhabited by many Germanic peoples. Much of it lay east of the Rhine River and beyond the Danube, outside the Roman Empire’s direct rule. Germania was not a single country: it was home to groups such as the Ingaevones, whom the Roman historian Tacitus described in a first-century account. It was also the setting of a major Roman defeat in 9 CE. Arminius, a leader of the Cherusci who had served Rome, turned against the Romans and led an ambush in which three legions commanded by Publius Quinctilius Varus were destroyed. This clash is known as the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, and Emperor Augustus was said to have mourned the lost legions.

Colorado Springs is a city near the southern end of Colorado’s Front Range, a mountain range east of the Rocky Mountains. It is known for Garden of the Gods, a public park where towering red sandstone formations include the Kissing Camels and the Cathedral Spires. The city is also an important center for U.S. sports: it has a major Olympic training facility and is home to the headquarters of the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee. Just west of Colorado Springs stands Pikes Peak, the highest summit in the southern Front Range. During the Colorado Gold Rush, prospectors used the slogan “Pikes Peak or Bust” as they traveled west hoping to strike it rich, even though little gold was found near the mountain itself.

Venice is a city in northeastern Italy built on islands in a lagoon at the northern end of the Adriatic Sea. Instead of relying only on streets, it has a historic transport network called the Canals of Venice. These waterways run between buildings and islands, carrying gondolas, water buses, and other boats that move people and goods around the city. The largest and best-known waterway is the Grand Canal. It curves in an S-shape through Venice’s historic center, dividing the city into two principal sides. Several bridges cross it, including the famous Rialto Bridge. Together, the canals and bridges have shaped how Venetians travel and how the city looks, making its waterways an essential part of everyday life and a major reason Venice is famous.

NEOM is a planned development region in northwestern Saudi Arabia, near the borders with Jordan and Egypt and the coast of the Red Sea. It is part of Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 plan, which aims to expand the country’s economy beyond oil by attracting businesses, residents and tourists. One proposed part of NEOM is The Line, a 170-kilometer-long linear city designed to concentrate homes and services along a narrow route. Another is Trojena, a planned high-altitude mountain destination intended to offer recreation and tourism, including skiing. NEOM is a plan rather than a completed city: its projects are being developed, and their final size and design may differ from the original proposals.

Saint Vincent is a mountainous Windward Island in the eastern Caribbean and the main island of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, an independent country since 1979. The Grenadines are a chain of smaller islands stretching south from Saint Vincent. The island is historically associated with the Garifuna people and their language. Many Garifuna descendants now live along the Caribbean coasts of Central American countries, including Honduras and Belize. At the northern end of Saint Vincent stands La Soufrière, an active stratovolcano. A stratovolcano is a steep-sided volcano built up by layers of lava and ash. La Soufrière erupted explosively in 1902, causing widespread destruction. After renewed activity began in 2020, another explosive eruption occurred in April 2021, prompting evacuations of nearby communities.

The Empire State Building is a 102-story Art Deco skyscraper in Manhattan, a borough of New York City. Completed in 1931, it was the world’s tallest building until 1970. Its stepped shape and decorative details are features of Art Deco, a style popular when the building was designed. Manhattan is the island borough bordered by the Hudson River to the west and the East River to the east; it is also home to Times Square and Central Park. The Empire State Building is an important New York landmark, with observation decks that give visitors wide views of the city. Its height also makes it a frequent target for lightning: it is struck about twenty-five times a year.

The Canal of the Pharaohs was an ancient waterway that linked the Nile River to the Red Sea through the Wadi Tumilat, a valley in northeastern Egypt. Unlike today’s Suez Canal, which runs directly between the Mediterranean and Red Seas, this route used the Nile as part of the connection. It helped boats carry people and goods between Egypt and lands around the Red Sea. The canal was built and repaired at different times, so its history involves more than one ruler. During the Achaemenid period, when the Persian Empire controlled Egypt, the canal was reopened. Inscriptions name the Persian king Darius I, also called Darius the Great, in connection with a water route from the Nile to the Red Sea. The Canal of the Pharaohs is regarded as a predecessor of the Suez Canal.

A fjord is a long, narrow coastal inlet with steep sides, formed when the sea floods a valley carved by a glacier. Glaciers are massive bodies of ice that move slowly across land. As a glacier flows through a valley, it grinds away rock and can deepen and widen the valley, leaving steep walls. If the glacier retreats and seawater enters, the valley becomes a fjord. Fjords are especially common in Norway and other parts of Scandinavia, and the word “fjord” comes from Old Norse. Glaciers can show alternating light and dark bands called ogives. They also lose ice through ablation, such as melting, and through calving, when chunks break off into water and become icebergs.

The Congo River is a major waterway in Central Africa. It drains Africa’s largest river basin, carries more water than any other river on the continent, and is Africa’s second-longest river after the Nile. Much of its course runs through the Democratic Republic of the Congo before it flows west into the Atlantic Ocean. The river gives its name to both the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the neighboring Republic of the Congo. Near the two countries’ capitals, it separates Kinshasa, on the south bank, from Brazzaville, on the north bank. Kinshasa is the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and one of Africa’s largest urban centers. The river also forms a natural barrier between habitats of bonobos to its south and chimpanzees farther north.

The Faroe Islands are a group of islands in the North Atlantic Ocean, north of Scotland and between Iceland and Norway. They are self-governing but remain part of the Kingdom of Denmark. The islands have their own parliament, called the Løgting, which meets in their capital, Tórshavn. Tórshavn is on Streymoy, the largest of the Faroe Islands. This means that both the islands’ government and their capital are located on Streymoy. The Faroe Islands were once linked to Norway, but after the Napoleonic Wars they remained with Denmark. During World War II, British forces occupied the islands while Denmark was under German occupation. If a question asks for the archipelago with the Løgting, the answer is the Faroe Islands; if it asks for the capital on Streymoy, the answer is Tórshavn.

Kinshasa is the capital and largest urban center of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a country in Central Africa. It stands on the southern bank of the Congo River, directly across from Brazzaville, the capital of the neighboring Republic of the Congo. The two capitals face each other across the water, but they belong to different countries: Kinshasa to the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Brazzaville to the Republic of the Congo. The Congo River is one of Africa’s longest rivers and eventually flows into the Atlantic Ocean. Its position helps make Kinshasa an important center for government, trade, and culture. Remembering the two capitals as neighbors on opposite banks of the river makes it easier to tell them apart.

Hurricane Harvey was an Atlantic storm that made landfall on the Texas coast in August 2017. Instead of moving away quickly, it lingered near Houston and dropped enormous amounts of rain. Streets and waterways overflowed, including Buffalo Bayou, which runs through downtown Houston. The resulting floods covered neighborhoods, damaged homes and businesses, and forced many people to evacuate. Houston is the largest city in Texas, and its low-lying, flood-prone landscape made the extreme rainfall especially dangerous. Harvey became one of the costliest tropical cyclones in U.S. history. Remember the connection: the 2017 storm was Hurricane Harvey, and the Texas city it flooded was Houston.

Maine and New Hampshire are neighboring states in New England, in the northeastern United States. Part of their border follows the Piscataqua River, which flows into the Atlantic Ocean near Portsmouth, New Hampshire. In the river is Seavey’s Island, home to Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, a facility where the U.S. Navy builds and repairs submarines. Although the shipyard has “Portsmouth” in its name, the island is in Maine. The two states disagreed about where their boundary ran in the river around the island. Because the dispute was between states, it went to the U.S. Supreme Court, which resolved the disagreement in 2002. The key places to remember are the two states, Maine and New Hampshire, and the island, Seavey’s Island.

Ottawa is the capital of Canada and the seat of its federal government. It lies in the province of Ontario on the Ottawa River, close to the border with Quebec. Parliament Hill, where Canada’s Parliament meets, is one of the city’s best-known landmarks. Ottawa was also the intended destination of a major protest during the Great Depression. In 1935, unemployed men left government relief camps and began traveling east to demand better conditions and work. Their protest became known as the On-to-Ottawa Trek, but they never reached the capital: police stopped the marchers in Regina, Saskatchewan. The trek shows why Ottawa matters not only as a place on a map, but also as the city where people seek to make their concerns heard by Canada’s national leaders.

Bolivia is a landlocked country in central South America. The Andes rise in its west, while lower plains stretch toward its eastern border. Bolivia includes the southeastern shore of Lake Titicaca, which it shares with Peru. It borders five countries: Peru and Chile to the west, Argentina and Paraguay to the south, and Brazil to the north and east. Brazil, the largest country in South America by area, shares Bolivia’s longest international boundary. Bolivia has two important capital cities: Sucre is its constitutional capital, while La Paz is the seat of government. The country is home to many Indigenous peoples, including the Aymara, who live mainly in the Andean highlands, and Guaraní communities in its eastern and southern regions.

Long Island is New York State’s largest island. It stretches east from New York City into the Atlantic Ocean, with Long Island Sound along its northern shore. The western part of the island contains two New York City boroughs: Brooklyn and Queens. Farther east are Nassau and Suffolk counties, including the Hamptons, a group of seaside communities known for beaches and summer vacations. Queens is home to both LaGuardia Airport and John F. Kennedy International Airport, two major gateways to New York City. It also contains Flushing Meadows–Corona Park, which hosted the 1939–40 and 1964–65 World’s Fairs. Manhattan and Staten Island are separate islands, so they are not part of Long Island.

Skara Brae is a remarkably well-preserved Neolithic village on Mainland, the largest of Scotland’s Orkney Islands. Its stone-built houses stand beside the Bay of Skaill and are associated with the Grooved Ware culture, whose pottery was decorated with grooves. People lived there roughly 5,000 years ago, long before written records in Britain. The houses contain stone furniture, including beds, dressers, and hearths, offering clues about everyday life. Sand covered the abandoned village for centuries, helping protect it. In 1850, a powerful storm stripped away some of that sand and exposed the remains beside the bay. Today, Skara Brae is part of the Heart of Neolithic Orkney World Heritage Site and helps archaeologists understand how prehistoric communities lived.

Sacramento is the capital of California, located in the state’s Central Valley where the American River joins the Sacramento River near Discovery Park. The American River flows west from the Sierra Nevada, and Folsom Dam holds back its water to form Folsom Lake. Sacramento was also the site of an attempted assassination of President Gerald Ford in 1975. After Ford spoke at a Host Breakfast and met with California Governor Jerry Brown, Lynette “Squeaky” Fromme, a member of the Manson Family, approached him with a gun. She was stopped before she could fire. These facts connect Sacramento to both a major event in U.S. history and the rivers that shape its geography.

Yorkshire is a historic county in northern England and was by far the largest of England’s historic counties by area. Today, its territory is divided among several administrative counties, including North Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, West Yorkshire and the East Riding of Yorkshire. Coal mining was once a major industry in parts of Yorkshire, especially South Yorkshire, where many communities depended on local pits for jobs. In 1984, the National Union of Mineworkers opposed plans by the National Coal Board to close pits. The resulting nationwide confrontation, known as the 1984–85 miners’ strike, lasted about a year and was particularly strong in Yorkshire. Understanding Yorkshire’s size, its modern divisions and its coal-mining history helps explain why the county features in accounts of this major British industrial dispute.

Prince Edward Island, often called PEI, is Canada’s smallest province by area. It lies in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, off the east coast of Canada, and its capital is Charlottetown. Although it is an island, PEI is connected to the mainland province of New Brunswick by the Confederation Bridge. This 12.9-kilometre fixed crossing opened in 1997 and carries the Trans-Canada Highway across the Northumberland Strait. Before the bridge was built, travellers relied on ferries to make the crossing. PEI is also known for its red-sand beaches, farmland, and the novel Anne of Green Gables, which is set on the island. If a question mentions Canada’s smallest province, Charlottetown, or the Confederation Bridge, the province is Prince Edward Island.

Mount Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece, rising to 2,918 meters at its tallest summit, Mytikas. It stands in northern Greece and has steep slopes and several peaks. For the ancient Greeks, Olympus was more than a landmark: mythology placed the home of the Olympian gods on the mountain, high above the human world. Zeus, the ruler of the gods, presided over their divine court there and was commonly shown holding or throwing a thunderbolt. Other Olympian gods included Hera, Athena, and Apollo. Stories about their lives on Olympus helped ancient Greeks explain the world around them and explore human behavior. Although it is a real mountain that people can climb today, its place in mythology has made it famous far beyond Greece.

Iguazu Falls is a vast waterfall system on the border between Argentina and Brazil, close to Paraguay. It consists of hundreds of cascades spread across the Iguazu River, rather than a single drop. One of its most dramatic features is the Devil’s Throat, a deep, U-shaped chasm where water plunges with tremendous force. The Iguazu River forms part of the boundary between Argentina and Brazil and flows into the larger Paraná River near the Triple Frontier, the area where Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay meet. The falls are protected by national parks on both sides of the border and are surrounded by subtropical rainforest. Their scale, powerful flow, and wildlife make them one of South America’s best-known natural landmarks.

Bavaria is a state in southeastern Germany, and its capital is Munich. Bavaria has a strong regional identity, reflected in traditions such as lederhosen, leather shorts often worn at festivals. It is also famous for its beer: in 1516, a Bavarian duke issued the Reinheitsgebot, a law regulating which ingredients could be used to make it. Munich hosts the world’s largest Oktoberfest celebration, where Bavarian food, music, clothing, and beer are part of the festivities. The city is also home to the headquarters of the car company BMW. Another well-known Bavarian landmark is Neuschwanstein Castle, commissioned in the 19th century by King Ludwig II of Bavaria. Together, these places and traditions make Bavaria one of Germany’s most recognizable regions.

Cape Cod is a hook-shaped peninsula that extends from southeastern Massachusetts into the Atlantic Ocean. Although it is part of the mainland, the man-made Cape Cod Canal cuts across its base, separating it from the rest of Massachusetts by water and giving ships a shorter route between Cape Cod Bay and Buzzards Bay. Nantucket Sound borders much of the cape’s southern shore, and its beaches, harbors, and villages make it a popular vacation area. Near the cape’s northern tip is Provincetown, a town close to Race Point. Provincetown Harbor was one of the Pilgrims’ first stops in North America in 1620. The town’s 252-foot granite Pilgrim Monument commemorates their arrival.

Croatia is a country in southeastern Europe that occupies much of the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea. The Adriatic is an arm of the Mediterranean Sea between the Balkan Peninsula and the Italian Peninsula, with the Italian city of Venice near its northern end. Croatia’s long coastline includes Dalmatia, a historic region known for its coastal towns and islands. More than a thousand islands and islets lie off Croatia’s coast, though only some are inhabited. The city of Dubrovnik, on the Dalmatian coast, was once the center of the Republic of Ragusa, an independent maritime republic. Croatia also extends inland, where its capital, Zagreb, is located.

Fort Worth is a city in North Texas and the western anchor of the Dallas–Fort Worth metropolitan area, with Dallas to its east. Together, the two cities are part of the largest metro area in Texas. Fort Worth is home to Texas Christian University, often called TCU. Waterways also help shape the city: near downtown, the Clear Fork and West Fork meet to form the main channel of the Trinity River. The river then flows east through the Dallas area. Fort Worth is known for its cattle-trading history, reflected in the historic Stockyards, but today it is also a major center for education, business, and culture.

Mount Chimborazo is a volcano in Ecuador and the country’s highest mountain. Its summit is about 6,263 meters above sea level, much lower than Mount Everest’s summit. Yet Chimborazo holds a different record: its summit is the point on Earth’s surface farthest from the planet’s center. This is possible because Earth is not a perfect sphere. Its rotation makes the planet slightly wider around the equator than from pole to pole, a shape known as the equatorial bulge. Chimborazo is close to the equator, so it starts farther from Earth’s center than Everest does. Adding the mountain’s height puts its summit farther from the center, even though Everest rises higher above sea level.

Ngorongoro Crater is a roughly 20-kilometer-wide volcanic basin in northern Tanzania, just east of Serengeti National Park. It formed when a huge volcano erupted and then collapsed inward, leaving one of the world’s largest intact calderas. A caldera is a large hollow created by the collapse of a volcano, even though Ngorongoro is commonly called a crater. Its grasslands, forests, and lakes support animals such as zebras, wildebeests, and lions. The crater lies within the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that protects both wildlife and places important to human history. In the broader area, Olduvai Gorge is a steep-sided ravine famous for hominin fossils and stone tools that have helped researchers investigate human origins.

The Republic of Cyprus is an island country in the eastern Mediterranean, south of Turkey, with its capital in Nicosia. It is internationally recognized as the government of the whole island, but it does not administer the Turkish-controlled north. Cyprus gained independence from Britain in 1960. Some Greek Cypriots supported enosis, or union with Greece, and a 1974 coup backed by supporters of enosis overthrew the country’s first president. Turkey then invaded, saying it wanted to prevent Cyprus from joining Greece. The island remains divided: the Republic’s government controls the south, while a separate Turkish Cypriot administration controls the north. Between them lies the Green Line, a United Nations-patrolled buffer zone that also runs through Nicosia, making it a divided capital.

Laramie is a city in southeastern Wyoming, between the Laramie Range and the Medicine Bow Mountains. It is Wyoming’s third-largest city by population, after Cheyenne and Casper, and is home to the University of Wyoming, the state’s flagship university. The remains of Fort Sanders, a nineteenth-century military post, are nearby. Wyoming’s capital is Cheyenne, while Yellowstone National Park lies in the state’s northwestern corner. Laramie is also known for the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard, a gay university student. The crime and its impact on the community inspired the play The Laramie Project.

Tulsa is a city in northeastern Oklahoma on the Arkansas River. It is home to Oral Roberts University and the historic Greenwood District. In the early 1900s, Greenwood became a thriving center of Black-owned businesses and earned the nickname “Black Wall Street.” Much of the district was destroyed in the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, but its history remains an important part of the city’s identity. The Arkansas River rises in Colorado, flows east across Kansas into Oklahoma, and then continues through Arkansas. It joins the Mississippi River, which eventually empties into the Gulf of Mexico. Remembering Tulsa’s university and Greenwood District can help you identify the city; remembering the river’s route can help you name the Arkansas River.

Sequoia National Park protects part of the southern Sierra Nevada mountains in California, immediately south of Kings Canyon National Park. Its western slopes contain the Giant Forest, a grove of giant sequoias. One of these trees, General Sherman, is the largest tree in the world by volume, meaning the amount of wood in its trunk is greater than that of any other known tree. The park also reaches into rugged high country, where Mount Whitney rises to 14,505 feet. Mount Whitney is the highest summit in the contiguous United States—the 48 states connected to one another, excluding Alaska and Hawaii. Sequoia National Park is known both for its enormous trees and for the mountain scenery around this exceptionally high peak.

The taiga, also called the boreal forest, is a vast subarctic biome that forms a broad belt across northern North America, Europe, and Asia. It lies between the treeless tundra to the north and temperate deciduous forests farther south. Long, cold winters and short growing seasons favor evergreen conifers such as spruce, pine, and fir, whose needlelike leaves help them withstand harsh conditions. In many parts of the taiga, the thin surface layer of soil thaws during summer; this is called the active layer. Beneath it, ground that remains frozen for years is called permafrost. Permafrost can limit how deeply tree roots grow and prevent water from draining away, creating wet or boggy areas. Animals of the taiga include caribou, pine martens, and woodpeckers.

The New River Gorge Bridge is a steel arch bridge that carries U.S. Route 19 across the New River Gorge near Fayetteville, West Virginia, in the Appalachian Mountains. It is 3,030 feet long and was once the longest single-span steel arch bridge in the world. Before it opened in 1977, crossing the gorge meant taking a much longer, winding route down to the river and back up. Today, the bridge is a landmark as well as an important transportation link. Each October, Bridge Day draws visitors to watch permitted BASE jumping from the bridge. The river far below is also known for whitewater rafting: people ride inflatable rafts through its rapids, which are rated from Class I, the easiest, to Class VI, the most dangerous.

Castro Street runs from Market Street to 19th Street in San Francisco, California, and gives its name to the surrounding Castro neighborhood. The area became one of the best-known centers of LGBTQ+ life and activism in the United States, with businesses and community groups that helped residents organize and find support. Harvey Milk owned a camera shop on Castro Street and became a leading neighborhood organizer, earning the nickname “mayor of Castro Street.” In 1977, he won election to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, becoming one of the first openly gay people elected to public office in the United States. In 1978, former supervisor Dan White assassinated Milk and San Francisco mayor George Moscone. Today, Castro Street remains closely associated with Milk’s work and the broader fight for LGBTQ+ rights.

Central Park Zoo is a small zoo in the southeastern corner of Central Park, the 843-acre green space in Manhattan, New York City. It sits near Fifth Avenue and East 64th Street and has exhibits called the Tropic Zone, Temperate Territory, and Polar Circle, which introduce visitors to animals from different habitats. The zoo is operated by the Wildlife Conservation Society, an organization that also runs the Bronx Zoo and the New York Aquarium. Central Park Zoo is also connected to literature: in J.D. Salinger’s novel The Catcher in the Rye, Holden Caulfield takes his younger sister Phoebe to ride the carousel near the zoo.

Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. It stands on the banks of the Vistula River, Poland’s longest river, which flows north toward the Gulf of Gdańsk and the Baltic Sea. Warsaw has a long and often difficult history. During World War II, Nazi Germany established the Warsaw Ghetto, where Jewish residents were confined; in 1943, they fought back in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Much of the city was destroyed during the war, but its historic center was later carefully rebuilt. In 1955, the Soviet Union and several Eastern European countries formed a military alliance called the Warsaw Pact, named for the city where it was signed. Today, Warsaw is Poland’s political, economic, and cultural center.

South Carolina is a southeastern U.S. state on the Atlantic Ocean, with its capital in Columbia. Its coastal Lowcountry includes marshes, rice-growing areas, and the Sea Islands. Many Gullah Geechee people, descendants of enslaved West Africans, have preserved a distinctive culture and a creole language that developed on Lowcountry rice plantations. Their communities include places around the Santee River, Charleston, Hilton Head Island, and Saint Helena Island. Saint Helena Island is known for its Gullah Geechee heritage; it shares its name with the South Atlantic island where Napoleon spent his final years in exile. South Carolina also played a major role in U.S. history: it challenged federal authority during the Nullification Crisis, and the Civil War began when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor in 1861.

Saint Helena Island is a Sea Island in Beaufort County, South Carolina, near Hilton Head Island. It is a historic center of Gullah culture. The Gullah people, also called Geechee, are descendants of Africans who were enslaved on rice plantations in the coastal Lowcountry. Their communities preserved distinctive traditions, including food, music, storytelling, and a creole language shaped by English and West African languages, with words from Fulani and Mende. Saint Helena Island is also associated with the inspiration for Gullah Gullah Island, a children’s television series that portrayed life and culture in the Sea Islands. Despite its name, this South Carolina island is different from the remote Saint Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean, where Napoleon was imprisoned and died.

Michigan is a U.S. state in the Great Lakes region with two main parts: the larger Lower Peninsula and the smaller Upper Peninsula. The Straits of Mackinac separate them, and the Mackinac Bridge connects them. Michigan borders four of the five Great Lakes: Superior, Michigan, Huron, and Erie. Its Upper Peninsula forms much of the southern shore of Lake Superior, the largest Great Lake by surface area. Water from Lake Superior flows toward Lake Huron through the St. Marys River. Michigan’s cities include Detroit, Grand Rapids, and Saginaw. Its location among the lakes has shaped its transportation, industries, and outdoor recreation.

Lake Titicaca is a large, high-altitude lake in the Andes Mountains on the border between Peru and Bolivia. It was important to the Inca, whose traditions connected the lake to the beginnings of their empire. In one origin story, Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo emerged from Lake Titicaca. Manco Capac was a legendary founder of the Inca and was credited with founding Cusco, the empire’s capital in what is now Peru. Some versions of the story describe him as a son of Inti, the Inca sun god. These traditions make Lake Titicaca more than a landmark on a map: they also make it a place tied to Inca beliefs about where their people and rulers came from.

The Great Barrier Reef is the world’s largest interconnected coral reef ecosystem. It stretches about 2,300 kilometers along the coast of Queensland in northeastern Australia, in the Coral Sea. This southwestern Pacific sea lies between eastern Australia and island groups including Vanuatu and New Caledonia. Despite its name, the reef is not one continuous wall: it is a vast network of individual reefs and islands. Reefs are built over many years by tiny animals called coral polyps, which create hard skeletons that provide shelter for fish and other marine life. The Great Barrier Reef is famous for its biodiversity, but its corals are threatened by warming seas, which can cause coral bleaching, as well as pollution and other environmental pressures.

Acadia National Park protects mountains, forests, and rocky coastline on Maine’s Mount Desert Island and nearby islands. Its best-known peak, Cadillac Mountain, is one of the first places in the United States to see the sunrise during parts of the year. Visitors can hike the steep Beehive Loop, which has iron rungs fixed into the rock, or the even steeper Precipice Trail. The nearby town of Bar Harbor is a popular starting point for exploring the park. Acadia and Bar Harbor lie southwest of the Bay of Fundy, a bay between the Canadian provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The Bay of Fundy is famous for its exceptionally high tides, and the city of Saint John, New Brunswick, sits on its shore.

Lake Tahoe is a large freshwater lake high in the Sierra Nevada mountains, straddling the border between California and Nevada. Its surface is about 6,225 feet (1,897 meters) above sea level, and it is the second-deepest lake in the United States, after Crater Lake in Oregon. The lake is known for its clear water and is fed by streams, rain, and snowmelt from the surrounding mountains. Its only natural surface outlet is the Truckee River, which leaves the lake near Tahoe City, California. The river flows northeast into Nevada, passes through Reno and Sparks, and eventually empties into Pyramid Lake. Because Pyramid Lake has no outlet to the ocean, this water remains within an inland drainage basin.

The Balkans are a region of southeastern Europe centered on a peninsula bordered by the Adriatic Sea to the west, the Aegean Sea to the south, and the Black Sea to the east. Much of the region was ruled for centuries by the Ottoman Empire. As Ottoman power weakened, nationalist movements and rivalries over territory helped spark wars and made the Balkans a focus of European tensions before World War I. This instability earned the region the nickname “Europe’s powder keg.” One Balkan country, Bosnia and Herzegovina, has its capital in Sarajevo. Although most of the country is inland, it has a short stretch of Adriatic coastline around the town of Neum, which separates two stretches of Croatia’s coast.

The Black Sea is a large inland sea between southeastern Europe and western Asia. Ukraine lies to its north, Bulgaria to its west, and Turkey to its south; Russia, Georgia, and Romania also have Black Sea coastlines. Water from the Black Sea flows through the Bosphorus, a narrow strait that passes through Istanbul and separates the city’s European and Asian sides. From there, ships enter the Sea of Marmara and then pass through the Dardanelles to reach the Aegean Sea and the wider Mediterranean. The Crimean Peninsula extends into the Black Sea from the north, and the port city of Sevastopol stands on its coast. Some researchers have proposed that a rapid rise in the Black Sea’s water level long ago helped inspire ancient flood stories, though this idea is debated.

Wall Street is an east–west street in Lower Manhattan that runs from Broadway toward the East River. Its name recalls a defensive wall built by Dutch colonists in the 1600s, when New York was called New Amsterdam. The street gave its name to the surrounding financial district and became a symbol of U.S. stock markets and finance. The New York Stock Exchange is located there, and the nearby Charging Bull sculpture represents a strong or rising market. Wall Street also has an important place in U.S. political history. At 26 Wall Street stands Federal Hall, a Greek Revival building marking the site where George Washington took the presidential oath in 1789, when New York City was the nation’s capital.

Tasmania is an island state of Australia that lies south of the mainland. Bass Strait, the stretch of sea between Tasmania and the state of Victoria, separates the island from mainland Australia. People crossed this region and settled Tasmania thousands of years before Europeans arrived. British colonists later called the island Van Diemen’s Land and used it as a destination for convicts transported from Britain. In the 1820s and early 1830s, British settlers and authorities fought Aboriginal Tasmanians in a violent colonial conflict known as the Black War. Today, Tasmania is known for its rugged landscapes and wildlife, but its history also includes the lasting effects of colonization on its Indigenous peoples.

Zimbabwe is a landlocked country in southeastern Africa. It was formerly called Rhodesia, a name linked to Cecil Rhodes, who founded the De Beers diamond company. Zimbabwe became independent in 1980. The country shares its name with Great Zimbabwe, a medieval stone city built by ancestors of the Shona people. Its surviving walls and ruins show the skill and wealth of a kingdom that flourished there centuries ago. Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia is defined largely by the Zambezi River. The river flows over Victoria Falls, one of the world’s largest waterfalls, before continuing east toward Mozambique. Robert Mugabe led Zimbabwe for decades after independence; he died in 2019.

Osaka is a major city in western Japan, on the island of Honshu. In 1583, Toyotomi Hideyoshi began building the enormous Osaka Castle there as a symbol of his growing power. Hideyoshi had risen to prominence after the death of Oda Nobunaga and became known as one of Japan’s great unifiers. He also launched two invasions of Korea in the 1590s. After Hideyoshi’s death, his son Hideyori remained at Osaka Castle as the Toyotomi family struggled for power against Tokugawa Ieyasu. The castle became the center of the Osaka campaigns of 1614–1615, which ended in the Toyotomi clan’s defeat. Thus, Osaka is linked both to Hideyoshi’s rise and to the fall of his family’s rule.

Louisville is Kentucky’s most populous city and the seat of Jefferson County. It lies on the Ohio River across from southern Indiana and was named for King Louis XVI of France. Louisville is best known for the Kentucky Derby, an annual horse race held at Churchill Downs, a thoroughbred racetrack that has hosted the event since 1875. The track’s twin spires are a recognizable city landmark. Louisville is also associated with baseball: the Louisville Slugger Museum & Factory on Museum Row offers tours showing how its famous wooden bats are made. Nearby on Museum Row is the Muhammad Ali Center, honoring the boxer who was born in the city. These landmarks help make Louisville an important center of sports and culture in Kentucky.

Zanzibar is an archipelago in the Indian Ocean off the coast of East Africa and is part of Tanzania. Its two main islands are Unguja and Pemba. Unguja is the largest island and lies south of Pemba; it is home to Zanzibar City, whose historic Stone Town sits on the island’s western coast. Stone Town grew as a center of Indian Ocean trade, especially in spices, and its buildings and streets reflect both Swahili culture and centuries of Omani influence. Omani sultans once ruled Zanzibar and parts of the nearby mainland coast, leaving landmarks such as the House of Wonders. Although people often use “Zanzibar” to mean its largest island, the island’s Swahili name is Unguja, while Zanzibar names the wider archipelago.

The Korean Demilitarized Zone, or DMZ, is a roughly 250-kilometer-long strip of land that separates North Korea from South Korea. It was established by the 1953 armistice that halted fighting in the Korean War, and it follows a boundary near the 38th parallel. Although “demilitarized” means free of military forces, the areas around the DMZ are among the world’s most heavily fortified frontiers. Within the DMZ at Panmunjom is the Joint Security Area, where blue conference buildings straddle the military boundary between the two countries. This area has hosted important talks, including an April 2018 meeting between North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and South Korean president Moon Jae-in.

Nunavut is Canada’s largest and northernmost territory. Created in 1999 from the eastern part of the Northwest Territories, it stretches across Arctic islands and mainland areas. Its capital, Iqaluit, is so cold that the Airbus A380 passenger plane was tested there in winter conditions. Most of Nunavut’s residents are Inuit, and Inuktut, which includes Inuktitut, is widely spoken. Some Inuit communities continue to hunt whales, including bowhead whales, as part of their traditional way of life. Nunavut’s northern coastline borders the Arctic Ocean, the world’s northernmost ocean. The North Pole lies in this ocean, much of which is covered by sea ice throughout the year.

Surtsey is a volcanic island in the North Atlantic Ocean, off the southern coast of Iceland near the Vestmannaeyjar archipelago. It began forming in November 1963 when an underwater volcano erupted and sent ash and lava above the sea. The eruption continued until 1967, leaving behind a new island. Scientists protected Surtsey from most human interference so they could study ecological succession: how plants, animals, and other living things gradually colonize bare land. Iceland, the island nation to which Surtsey belongs, has its capital at Reykjavík. Its largest airport is at Keflavík, on the site of a former U.S. naval air station. Iceland is also known for its geysers and active volcanoes, including Eyjafjallajökull, whose 2010 eruption disrupted air travel across Europe.

Honolulu is the capital and largest urban center of Hawaiʻi, the most recent state to join the United States. It lies on the southeastern shore of Oʻahu, one of the state’s main islands. Honolulu is a center of government, business, and travel, and it is served by Daniel K. Inouye International Airport, the state’s principal international airport. Within Honolulu is Waikiki, a coastal district famous for its beaches, resort hotels, and long surfing tradition. Visitors to Waikiki can also see Diamond Head, a volcanic landmark near the shore. If a question asks for Hawaiʻi’s capital city, the answer is Honolulu; if it asks for Honolulu’s well-known resort and surfing district, the answer is Waikiki.

The Basque Country is a cultural region that crosses the border between northern Spain and southwestern France. It lies near the western Pyrenees and has a northern coastline on the Bay of Biscay, a large gulf of the Atlantic Ocean called the Golfe de Gascogne in French. Basque people share a distinct identity, traditions, and a language called Euskara, which is unrelated to Spanish, French, or other Romance languages spoken nearby. Much of the Spanish part forms the Basque Autonomous Community, which has its own regional government; Basque communities also live in neighboring Navarre and across the border in France. Basque pride can be seen in local festivals, food, and sports. For example, the soccer club Athletic Bilbao is known for its policy of recruiting players connected to the Basque region.

Slovakia is a landlocked country in Central Europe, meaning it has no coastline. Its capital, Bratislava, lies near the country’s borders with Austria and Hungary, just east of Vienna, Austria’s capital. Slovakia became independent in 1993, when Czechoslovakia peacefully divided into two countries: Slovakia and the Czech Republic. This separation is known as the Velvet Divorce. The Danube River flows through Bratislava and links it with several other European capitals. Following the river downstream, it passes through Vienna before Bratislava, then continues through Budapest, Hungary, and Belgrade, Serbia. The Danube begins in Germany’s Black Forest and eventually empties into the Black Sea.

Harpers Ferry is a historic town in present-day West Virginia where the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers meet, beside a gap in the Blue Ridge Mountains. In 1859, abolitionist John Brown led an armed raid on the town’s federal arsenal, hoping to seize weapons and spark an uprising against slavery. Harriet Tubman, famous for guiding enslaved people to freedom along the Underground Railroad, helped recruit supporters for Brown’s plan but did not take part in the raid. The raid failed, and Brown was captured, tried for treason against the state of Virginia, and hanged.
