At the time, Harpers Ferry was part of Virginia; West Virginia did not become a separate state until 1863. Brown’s raid intensified national arguments over slavery in the years before the Civil War.

Appalachia is a mountainous cultural region that follows the Appalachian Mountains through much of the eastern United States, from southern New York toward northern Alabama and Mississippi. Its communities have varied histories, but many share traditions of storytelling, crafts, and music played on instruments such as the fiddle, banjo, and Appalachian dulcimer. Coal mining has also shaped parts of the region, including its labor struggles and protest songs. Appalachian old-time music helped inspire bluegrass, a fast-paced string-band genre played mainly on acoustic instruments. Mandolinist Bill Monroe helped popularize bluegrass, while banjo player Earl Scruggs became famous for the three-finger picking style that helped define its sound.

Atlanta is the capital and largest city of the U.S. state of Georgia. During the American Civil War, Union forces captured the city in 1864 during General William Tecumseh Sherman’s Atlanta Campaign, and much of it was burned. Atlanta later grew into a major transportation and business center and played an important role in the civil-rights movement. It hosted the 1996 Summer Olympics and is served by Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, one of the world’s busiest airports. The Chattahoochee River runs along the western side of the Atlanta metropolitan area. It begins in Georgia’s Blue Ridge Mountains and flows through Lake Lanier, a reservoir that supplies water to the region. Farther south, the Chattahoochee joins the Flint River to form the Apalachicola River.

Troy was an ancient city in northwestern Anatolia, in what is now Turkey. It is famous as the setting of the Trojan War in Greek legend, when a Greek army led by Agamemnon fought the Trojans. King Priam ruled Troy, and his daughter Cassandra was said to foresee the city’s fall, though a curse meant no one believed her warnings. Troy was also known as Ilium or Ilion. Archaeologists generally identify its remains with Hisarlik, a mound near the Dardanelles strait in northwestern Turkey. Excavations there have uncovered layers of settlements built over many centuries. These finds show that a city existed at the site, although they do not prove that the legendary war happened exactly as the stories describe.

Guantánamo Bay is an inlet on the southeastern coast of Cuba, near the city of Guantánamo. The United States established a naval base there in 1903 and continues to operate it under a long-term lease, despite the Cuban government’s opposition to the U.S. presence. The base is separate from the rest of Cuba, and the United States controls access to it. In 2002, the U.S. opened a prison at the base to hold foreign terrorism suspects captured during the War on Terror. It is commonly called the Guantánamo Bay detention camp, or simply “Gitmo.” The camp has drawn international criticism over the treatment of prisoners, including allegations of torture and detention without trial. Thus, Guantánamo Bay refers both to a coastal location and to a U.S. military site associated with the detention camp.

The White Mountains are a mountain range in northern New Hampshire, a New England state whose capital is Concord and whose western border meets Vermont. Part of the Appalachian Mountains, the White Mountains include the Presidential Range, whose peaks are named after U.S. presidents. Its best-known summit is Mount Washington, the highest peak in the northeastern United States. The range is notorious for severe, rapidly changing weather: a sunny hike can turn cold, windy, or stormy, especially above the tree line. Its high elevations and exposed slopes make careful planning important for hikers. The White Mountains also draw visitors for their forests, mountain trails, and broad views.

Pike Place Market is a historic public market in Seattle, Washington, overlooking Elliott Bay on Puget Sound. It opened in 1907 so local farmers could sell directly to shoppers rather than going through middlemen. Today, the multilevel market is known for stalls selling fresh produce, seafood, crafts, and prepared food. Its fishmongers have become famous for tossing customers’ fish orders across the counter, a lively tradition that draws visitors. Near the main arcade stands Rachel, a large bronze piggy bank that serves as the market’s beloved mascot. Visitors can put coins and bills into Rachel to support the Pike Place Market Foundation, a nonprofit that helps people in the market community.

Ocean currents are large-scale flows of seawater that move water around the planet. The Kuroshio Current near East Asia and the Canary Current off northwest Africa are two examples. Scientists measure the volume of water a current carries in sverdrups; one sverdrup equals one million cubic metres of water per second. Winds drive many surface currents, while deep currents are driven by differences in water density caused by temperature and salinity, or salt content. Earth’s rotation also affects the paths of moving water. This is called the Coriolis effect: it deflects currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The same effect helps explain why large storms rotate in opposite directions in the two hemispheres.

Pittsburgh is a city in southwestern Pennsylvania, built around the meeting of three rivers. The Allegheny River flows in from the north and the Monongahela River from the south; where they meet in Pittsburgh, they form the Ohio River. The Ohio flows west from the city, then turns south and eventually joins the Mississippi River. Pittsburgh is also important in American theater. Playwright August Wilson set many works in its Hill District, a neighborhood central to the city’s Black history. His Pittsburgh Cycle explores African American life across the 20th century and includes The Piano Lesson and Fences. In The Piano Lesson, characters speak of the “Ghosts of the Yellow Dog”; in Fences, the main character, Troy Maxson, has an affair with Alberta.

Lapland is Finland’s northernmost region, known for long, snowy winters, Sámi culture, and views of the aurora borealis, or Northern Lights. The Sámi are Indigenous people whose homeland extends across northern Finland and parts of neighboring countries. Lapland’s administrative capital is Rovaniemi, a city promoted as the official hometown of Santa Claus. Nearby Santa Claus Village has a marked line showing where the Arctic Circle passes, making it a popular place for visitors to cross into the Arctic. Tourists also visit Lapland for winter activities and to watch the aurora; some accommodations have glass roofs so guests can look for the lights from bed. The region’s mix of Arctic scenery and cultural traditions makes it a distinctive part of Finland.

Gerardus Mercator was a 16th-century Flemish cartographer, or mapmaker, who published a world map in 1569. The map introduced the Mercator projection, a method of showing Earth’s curved surface on a flat map. It was especially useful to sailors because a route that follows a constant compass direction appears as a straight line, making it easier to plot a course. The projection has a major drawback, though: it stretches places more and more as they get closer to the poles. As a result, Greenland looks nearly as large as Africa on a Mercator map, even though Africa is far larger in reality. Mercator’s work is an important example of how a map’s design can make one task easier while distorting other information.

The Rio Grande is a major North American river that begins in Colorado’s San Juan Mountains. It flows south through New Mexico, then turns southeast and forms much of the border between Texas and Mexico for more than 800 miles. In Mexico, it is called the Río Bravo del Norte. The river passes through dry regions where its water is important for farms, cities, and wildlife. Near the neighboring cities of Brownsville, Texas, and Matamoros, Mexico, the Rio Grande empties into the Gulf of Mexico. The Gulf is a large body of water bordered by the southern United States, Cuba, and Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula. Remembering the river’s route from Colorado to the Gulf can help you identify it on a map.

Benghazi is a major city in eastern Libya, on the Mediterranean coast. It has long been an important center of trade and education and was a key location during Libya’s 2011 uprising against Muammar Gaddafi. The city became internationally known again after an attack on U.S. facilities there on September 11, 2012. Armed militants attacked a U.S. diplomatic compound and a nearby site, killing four Americans, including Chris Stevens, the U.S. ambassador to Libya. At the time, Hillary Clinton was the U.S. secretary of state, the official responsible for American diplomacy. The attack led to investigations and debate in the United States about security at diplomatic posts. If a question asks for the eastern Libyan city where Ambassador Stevens was killed, the answer is Benghazi.

Rio de Janeiro is a major city in southeastern Brazil, on the Atlantic coast beside Guanabara Bay. The city spreads along the bay’s western shore, with beaches such as Copacabana facing the open ocean. High above Rio, the Christ the Redeemer statue stands on Mount Corcovado in Tijuca National Park. Portuguese explorers reached the area on January 1, 1502, and mistook the bay’s entrance for the mouth of a river. They called the place Rio de Janeiro, meaning “January River”; the inlet itself is known as Guanabara Bay. Rio was Brazil’s capital for nearly 200 years, until the planned inland city of Brasília became the capital in 1960. Today, Rio remains one of Brazil’s best-known cities.

Buenos Aires is the capital and largest city of Argentina. It stands on the western shore of the Río de la Plata, a broad estuary that opens into the Atlantic Ocean, and is the country’s main political and cultural center. At its heart is the Plaza de Mayo, where the Casa Rosada, Argentina’s pink presidential palace, faces a public square known for political demonstrations. During and after the Dirty War, mothers gathered there to demand answers about children who had disappeared under military rule. Argentina also claims the Falkland Islands, a South Atlantic archipelago known in Argentina as the Islas Malvinas. In 1982, Argentina invaded the islands, leading to a short war with the United Kingdom, which regained control.

Queens is the easternmost of New York City’s five boroughs. It lies on the western end of Long Island, alongside Brooklyn, and includes neighborhoods such as Astoria and Flushing. Flushing has a large Chinatown and is close to Flushing Meadows–Corona Park, one of Queens’s best-known green spaces. The park contains the Unisphere, a giant globe built for the 1964–65 World’s Fair, and it hosted both that fair and the 1939–40 World’s Fair. Today, the park is also home to the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, where the U.S. Open tennis tournament is played, and Citi Field, the home stadium of the New York Mets.

Bangladesh is a South Asian country that occupies much of the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta, where major rivers spread across a low-lying plain before reaching the Bay of Bengal. India borders it on most sides, while Myanmar lies to the southeast. After the 1971 Liberation War, Bangladesh became independent from Pakistan. Its capital and largest city is Dhaka, which lies on the Buriganga River and is the country’s center of government. The delta’s fertile land supports a large population, but its low elevation also makes many areas vulnerable to flooding and cyclones. These environmental pressures have led some people to move from rural areas to cities such as Dhaka.

Tirana is the capital and largest city of Albania, a Balkan country in southern Europe. Much of the city’s center is organized around Skanderbeg Square, named for Albania’s national hero, who resisted Ottoman rule in the 1400s. On the square stands the Et’hem Bey Mosque, an Ottoman-era place of worship completed in the early 1800s. Its painted frescoes are unusual for a mosque because they show landscapes, including trees, waterfalls, and bridges. Tirana also has Bunk’Art, a museum inside a former Cold War bunker that helps visitors learn about life under Albania’s communist government. These landmarks show different parts of the city’s history: its Ottoman past, its years under communism, and its role as the center of modern Albania.

The Boston Mountains are a rugged upland in the southern United States. They form the highest and easternmost subdivision of the Ozark Mountains, also called the Ozarks, and lie chiefly in northern Arkansas, extending into southern Missouri. Despite their name, they are not near Boston, Massachusetts: the two places simply share a name. The landscape includes steep hills, deep valleys, forests, and streams. Large areas of the Boston Mountains in Arkansas are protected within the Ozark National Forest, a federally managed forest named for the broader Ozark region. If a question asks for the highest subdivision of the Ozarks, the answer is the Boston Mountains; if it asks for the national forest protecting much of this upland, the answer is Ozark National Forest.

San Antonio is a major city in south-central Texas known for its history and its sports teams. It is home to the San Antonio Spurs of the NBA, where Becky Hammon worked as an assistant coach under Gregg Popovich. The city also once had a WNBA team, the San Antonio Stars, which moved to Las Vegas in 2017 and became the Las Vegas Aces. In downtown San Antonio stands the Alamo, a former Spanish mission that later served as a fortress. During the Texas Revolution, a small group of defenders held the Alamo through a 13-day siege in 1836 before Mexican forces captured it. The battle made the Alamo one of the best-known historic sites in Texas.

Sacred rivers are natural waterways that hold religious importance for the people who live near or travel to them. In Yoruba religion, worshippers may leave offerings beside a river to honor Oshun, an orisha associated with love and fresh water. In Hindu traditions, pilgrims bathe in sacred rivers as an act of purification and gather there for festivals. One of the largest such pilgrimages is the Kumbh Mela. At Prayagraj in India, it takes place where the Ganges and Yamuna rivers meet. The Ganges is especially sacred to many Hindus and draws millions of visitors. Because rivers also supply water to large populations and cities, pollution can threaten both their ecosystems and the people who rely on them.

Gare Saint-Lazare is a major railway terminus in Paris, France, where trains arrive and depart beneath a large iron-and-glass roof. It became a subject for artists interested in the changing city and the effects of steam, light, and movement. In 1877, the Impressionist Claude Monet painted several views of the station, including trains surrounded by clouds of steam under its roof. Another painter, Édouard Manet, set his painting The Railway near Gare Saint-Lazare: a young girl looks through an iron railing toward the tracks while steam rises behind her. Manet also painted Olympia and The Luncheon on the Grass. Decades later, photographer Henri Cartier-Bresson captured a man leaping over a puddle in his famous photograph Behind the Gare Saint-Lazare.

Timbuktu is a historic city in present-day Mali, near the southern edge of the Sahara Desert. During the Middle Ages, it flourished as a major stop on trans-Saharan trade routes, where merchants exchanged goods such as salt, gold, and books. It was an important city in the Mali Empire, whose rulers included Mansa Musa. Timbuktu also became a renowned center of Islamic scholarship. Its University of Sankore, associated with the Sankore Mosque, attracted scholars and students who studied subjects including religion, law, and mathematics. The city’s libraries and manuscripts helped preserve knowledge and spread ideas across West Africa and beyond. In the 19th century, Timbuktu gained a reputation in Europe as a mysterious, difficult-to-reach city, though it had long been a lively center of trade and learning.

Buffalo is a city in western New York at the northeastern end of Lake Erie, near the Canadian border. The Niagara River flows from Lake Erie toward Lake Ontario, and the Peace Bridge crosses it to connect Buffalo with Fort Erie, Ontario. Opened in 1927, the bridge was named to celebrate a century of peaceful relations between the United States and Canada. About 20 miles northwest of Buffalo, Niagara Falls is a group of powerful waterfalls on the same river. Buffalo grew as a center of shipping and industry because of its location on the Great Lakes and the Erie Canal. Today, it is also known for the Buffalo Bills football team, whose fans support them in the National Football League.

Stalagmites are mineral formations that grow upward from cave floors, often beneath places where water drips from the ceiling. As water moves through limestone, it dissolves some of the rock’s calcium carbonate. When the water reaches a cave and drips onto the floor, it can leave a tiny mineral deposit behind. Over many years, these deposits build up into a stalagmite. The mineral commonly deposited is calcite, a crystalline form of calcium carbonate. Stalagmites are different from stalactites, which hang down from cave ceilings. Both are found in caves, including those formed when water dissolves limestone in landscapes called karst. A simple way to remember the difference is that a stalagmite rises from the ground, while a stalactite clings to the ceiling.

Wales is a constituent country of the United Kingdom, lying west of England and bordered by the Irish Sea and the Bristol Channel. Its flag shows a red dragon, a symbol closely associated with Welsh history and identity. Welsh is an indigenous Celtic language and is still widely used, especially in parts of the north and west; public signs often appear in both Welsh and English. Wales’s capital and largest city is Cardiff, near the mouth of the River Taff on the Bristol Channel. Cardiff is home to the Senedd, where Wales’s elected parliament meets, and Principality Stadium, a major venue for rugby and other events. The traditional title Prince of Wales is usually given to the heir to the British throne; it is currently held by Prince William.

Staten Island is the southwesternmost of New York City’s five boroughs. It lies southwest of Brooklyn, separated from it by a tidal strait called the Narrows; the Arthur Kill separates Staten Island from New Jersey. Much of the borough has a suburban feel, with residential neighborhoods and parks. Visitors can see the Staten Island Zoo or ride the Staten Island Ferry, which connects the borough to Manhattan and offers views of New York Harbor. On Staten Island’s eastern edge, the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge crosses the Narrows to Brooklyn. This suspension bridge opened in 1964 and is named for Giovanni da Verrazzano, an Italian explorer who reached New York Harbor in 1524.

Elizabeth Tower is the 96-meter clock tower at the north end of the Palace of Westminster in London, where the Houses of Parliament meet. It has four illuminated clock faces, one on each side, so people can see the time from different directions. The tower was formerly known simply as the Clock Tower, but it was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 to honor Queen Elizabeth II. Inside hangs the 13.7-tonne Great Bell, which strikes the hour. Its familiar nickname is Big Ben, and its deep chimes are one of London’s best-known sounds. People often call the whole tower “Big Ben,” but the tower’s official name is Elizabeth Tower; Big Ben is the bell.

Lake Victoria is Africa’s largest lake by surface area. It lies in East Africa and is shared by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. Named after the British queen, the lake is traditionally regarded as a source of the White Nile, which flows north from the lake through Uganda. In the nineteenth century, explorers debated where the Nile began; John Hanning Speke argued that Lake Victoria was its source, and Henry Morton Stanley later supported his claim. The lake is also home to many cichlids, a diverse group of freshwater fish. In the 1950s, people introduced the large predatory Nile perch to support commercial fishing. As Nile perch spread, populations of many native cichlids fell sharply, and some species became extinct.

Genoa is a port city in Liguria, on Italy’s northwestern coast. During the Middle Ages, it was an independent maritime republic with a powerful fleet and trading network. Genoa competed with Venice for control of Mediterranean trade routes and ports. Genoese merchants and soldiers also had close ties to Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire. When the Ottoman Empire besieged Constantinople in 1453, Genoese troops helped defend it. Their commander, Giovanni Giustiniani, was wounded during the final assault, as Ottoman forces broke through the city’s defenses. Constantinople fell, bringing the Byzantine Empire to an end. The siege connects the histories of Genoa and Constantinople: one was an Italian seafaring republic, while the other was the Byzantine imperial capital its citizens helped defend.

Kuwait is a small Arab country on the northwestern shore of the Persian Gulf. Iraq borders it to the north and west, while Saudi Arabia borders it to the south. Kuwait has large oil reserves, which have played an important role in its economy and history. In August 1990, Iraq, then led by Saddam Hussein, invaded and occupied Kuwait. The invasion led to the First Gulf War, in which a coalition of countries, including the United States, fought to free Kuwait. The coalition used Saudi Arabia as a major base for its operations. Saudi Arabia is the largest country on the Arabian Peninsula and has coastlines on both the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.

Liverpool is a major city and port in northwest England, on the eastern bank of the River Mersey estuary. Across the tidal river lies the Wirral Peninsula. Ferries have long crossed the Mersey, and the river’s name appears in the Gerry and the Pacemakers song “Ferry Cross the Mersey.” Liverpool grew through maritime trade, and its historic waterfront includes the Royal Albert Dock, a former complex of docks and warehouses. The city is also famous as the birthplace of the Beatles and as the home of Liverpool Football Club, whose supporters sing “You’ll Never Walk Alone.” These landmarks, musicians and sporting traditions make Liverpool one of Britain’s best-known cities.

Montréal is the most populous city in Quebec, Canada. It occupies the Island of Montreal near the meeting of the Ottawa and St. Lawrence Rivers. The city hosted the 1976 Summer Olympics and, earlier, Expo 67, a world’s fair that left landmarks such as the Biosphere and the unusual Habitat 67 apartment building. Montréal takes its name from Mount Royal, a prominent hill near the city center. Today, the hill is the centerpiece of Mount Royal Park, where people can walk, cycle, and enjoy views of the city. A large cross near its summit is illuminated at night. Montréal is also known for McGill University and its Underground City, a network of passages that helps people move around during cold winters.

Bathymetry is the measurement and mapping of underwater depth in oceans, lakes, and other bodies of water. By measuring depths at many locations, scientists can create bathymetric maps showing the shape, or relief, of the seabed or lakebed, much as topographic maps show hills and valleys on land. An early method lowered a weighted line into the water, but modern surveys often use sonar. Sonar sends out sound pulses and detects their echoes after the sound bounces off the bottom. The time it takes for an echo to return helps determine the depth. Multibeam sonar sends out many pulses in different directions, allowing it to measure a broad swath of the seafloor at once. Bathymetric maps help with navigation and the study of underwater landscapes.

Nova Scotia is a Canadian province on the Atlantic coast. Its capital and largest city, Halifax, is home to Citadel Hill and the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic. Halifax was also the site of a devastating ship explosion in 1917. Along the coast, Peggy’s Cove is a seaside community known for its lighthouse. Nova Scotia includes Cape Breton Island, which is separated from the province’s mainland by the Strait of Canso and connected to it by the Canso Causeway. In the island’s north, the Cabot Trail passes through Cape Breton Highlands National Park. Nova Scotia was once part of the French colony of Acadia; the mainland area that is now New Brunswick was also part of that colony.

Tigray Region is a mountainous administrative division in Ethiopia’s northern highlands, along the border with Eritrea. Its administrative capital is Mekelle, a major city in northern Ethiopia. Many people in Tigray speak Tigrinya, and the region has a distinct local culture and history. Tigray was the main theater of a war that began in 2020 between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF. Federal forces took Mekelle in November 2020, though control of the city later changed again. The fighting caused widespread hunger and displacement, making it difficult for many residents to obtain food and other necessities. A ceasefire in 2022 was followed by renewed hostilities, and the African Union helped lead peace efforts.

The Trevi Fountain is a monumental Baroque fountain in Rome, the capital of Italy. Designed by Nicola Salvi and completed in 1762, it is built against the façade of a palace and combines dramatic sculptures with flowing water. Its central figure is Oceanus, an ancient Roman deity associated with the world’s waters. He stands above a shell-shaped chariot drawn by sea horses, beneath a large arch. Statues representing Abundance and Salubrity flank him. Visitors often toss a coin into the fountain’s pool because, according to a popular legend, doing so means they will return to Rome. The fountain also appears in the Italian film La Dolce Vita, helping make it one of the city’s best-known landmarks.

Big Ben is one of London’s most famous landmarks, but the name originally refers to the Great Bell inside a clock tower, not to the tower itself. The tower stands at the north end of the Palace of Westminster, home of the Houses of Parliament, and has four large clock faces that can be seen from different directions. Its official name is Elizabeth Tower, given in honour of Queen Elizabeth II; before that, it was known as the Clock Tower. The Great Bell rings to mark each hour, while smaller bells sound the quarter-hours. In everyday speech, people often call the whole tower “Big Ben.” So if a question asks for the landmark’s familiar name, answer Big Ben; if it asks for the tower’s official name, answer Elizabeth Tower.

The Standing Rock Sioux Reservation is the federally recognized homeland of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, spanning the border between North Dakota and South Dakota. Its tribal government is headquartered in Fort Yates, North Dakota. In 2016, the reservation became known worldwide because of protests against the Dakota Access Pipeline. Tribal members and other supporters worried that a pipeline crossing beneath the nearby Missouri River could threaten their water supply and harm culturally important sites. One major protest encampment was near Cannon Ball, North Dakota, where the Cannonball River flows into the Missouri River. The protests brought attention not only to the pipeline but also to tribal sovereignty—the right of Native American nations to govern their own lands and affairs—and the importance of protecting water.

America is the name of a vast landmass often described as two continents, North America and South America, connected by Central America. The name appeared on a world map published in 1507 by the German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller. He chose it to honor Amerigo Vespucci, a Florentine merchant and navigator whose accounts of voyages across the Atlantic helped Europeans understand that the lands they had encountered were not part of Asia. Waldseemüller first placed the name on what we now call South America, and it later came to be used more widely. Maps like his helped spread new geographic ideas, so the name became familiar. Remember the connection: Waldseemüller put America on the map, and America was named for Amerigo Vespucci.

Indian reservations are areas of land in the United States set aside for Native American tribes. They are governed by tribal governments, which have authority over many local matters, while the federal government also has responsibilities and authority. Reservations vary greatly in size and location. The Navajo Nation is the largest Indian reservation by land area, stretching across parts of Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah. Its capital is Window Rock, Arizona. Most of Arizona does not observe daylight saving time, but the Navajo Nation does, helping it keep the same time across its territory in all three states. Other reservations include Standing Rock, which spans parts of North and South Dakota and has been a focus of protests over oil pipelines.

The Humboldt Current is a cold ocean current that flows northward along the Pacific coast of South America, especially past Peru and Chile. It brings nutrient-rich water up from the depths, feeding plankton and supporting large populations of fish and other marine life. The current also cools the air above it. Along the coast of northern Chile, this can produce fog called camanchaca, which provides moisture for some plants despite the region’s extreme dryness. That region is the Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth. The Andes Mountains to its east help keep it dry by creating a rain shadow that blocks moisture from reaching the desert. Mining cities in the Atacama include Iquique and Antofagasta.

The Aegean Sea is an arm of the Mediterranean Sea between mainland Greece and western Turkey. It is dotted with islands, including the Cyclades, which contain Delos and Naxos, and the Sporades, northeast of the large Greek island of Euboea. The Cyclades were home to an ancient civilization known for marble figurines with folded arms. Another Aegean island, Thera, now commonly called Santorini, was reshaped by a huge volcanic eruption around 1600 BC. At the sea’s northeastern end, the narrow Dardanelles strait leads toward the Sea of Marmara. The Gallipoli Peninsula forms its western shore, while its eastern shore is part of northwestern Turkey. Together, these waterways provide a route between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.

Everglades National Park protects a vast subtropical wetland at the southern tip of Florida. Often called the “River of Grass,” the Everglades is a slow-moving flow of water, historically fed by Lake Okeechobee, that passes through wide sawgrass marshes toward the coast. The park also includes mangrove forests and coastal habitats that shelter manatees, birds, and many other animals. It is one of the rare places where American alligators and American crocodiles live in the same region. Along the park’s southern edge is Florida Bay, a large, shallow tropical lagoon dotted with mangrove islands. The bay lies between the Florida mainland and the Florida Keys, the chain of islands stretching southwest from near Miami.

Mount Mitchell is a mountain summit in western North Carolina. At 6,684 feet (2,037 meters), it is the highest point in the United States east of the Mississippi River. It lies in the Black Mountains, a rugged subrange of the southern Appalachian Mountains that contains several of the tallest peaks in the eastern United States. Mount Mitchell is protected within Mount Mitchell State Park, where visitors can reach an observation deck near the summit. Its high elevation brings cooler temperatures and different plants and animals than those found in the surrounding lowlands. The mountain is named for Elisha Mitchell, a scientist who measured its height in the 1800s. If asked for the name of the summit, answer Mount Mitchell; if asked for its subrange, answer the Black Mountains.

Paraguay is a landlocked country in South America, north of Argentina and bordered by Bolivia and Brazil. Its capital, Asunción, lies on the Paraguay River. Another major waterway, the Paraná River, forms part of Paraguay’s border with Brazil. The two countries share the Itaipu Dam, a huge hydroelectric project that crosses the Paraná and generates electricity for both nations. Western Paraguay includes part of the Gran Chaco, a vast region of plains and dry forests. Many Paraguayans speak Guaraní as well as Spanish, and the Guarani Aquifer beneath parts of South America takes its name from the Guaraní people. Paraguay and Bolivia are the only South American countries without a coastline.

The Arkansas River begins high in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains and flows east and southeast across the central United States. It passes through Kansas and Oklahoma, then crosses Arkansas before joining the Mississippi River near the former settlement of Napoleon, Arkansas. Because it flows into the Mississippi, the Arkansas is one of that river’s major tributaries. Along its route, it passes through Tulsa, Oklahoma, and the Arkansas cities of Fort Smith, Little Rock, and Pine Bluff. Tulsa is home to Oral Roberts University and the historic Greenwood District, a thriving Black business community once known as Black Wall Street. The river’s long course links mountain headwaters, Great Plains communities, and the Mississippi River drainage basin.

Amazonia is a vast region of northern South America centered on the Amazon River basin. It includes the world’s largest tropical rainforest as well as rivers, wetlands, and other surrounding landscapes. Although much of Amazonia lies in Brazil, it extends across several countries, including substantial parts of Peru and Colombia. Warm temperatures and heavy rainfall support its rich variety of plants and animals. The Amazon River flows east across the region to the Atlantic Ocean and carries more water by average discharge than any other river on Earth. Near the Brazilian city of Manaus, it meets the Rio Negro. The Rio Negro’s dark water and the Amazon’s lighter, sediment-rich water remain visibly separate for a stretch before mixing.

Oxford is a city in southern England where the River Cherwell meets the River Thames. It is home to the University of Oxford, one of the world’s oldest universities. For centuries, students and teachers lived alongside local townspeople, but the two groups did not always get along. In 1209, a violent “town-and-gown” dispute led some Oxford scholars to leave the city. Some settled in Cambridge, a city on the River Cam, where they helped establish the University of Cambridge. Oxford is also known for the Oxford Martyrs: Protestant bishops Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, who were executed there during the reign of the Catholic queen Mary I.

Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba. This port city lies on the island’s northern coast, beside the Straits of Florida, and has long been a center of Cuban government and trade. During the Cuban Revolution, opponents of President Fulgencio Batista tried to overthrow his government. On March 13, 1957, student members of the Revolutionary Directorate stormed Havana’s Presidential Palace in an unsuccessful attempt to kill Batista. The attack was separate from Fidel Castro’s 26th of July Movement, which eventually defeated Batista’s government. Today, the former Presidential Palace houses the Museum of the Revolution, where visitors can learn about this period of Cuban history.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo, often called the DRC, is a large French-speaking country in Central Africa. It covers much of the Congo River basin, the vast area drained by Africa’s second-longest river, and has a short coastline on the Atlantic Ocean. Its capital, Kinshasa, stands on the Congo River directly across from Brazzaville, the capital of the neighboring Republic of the Congo. Despite their similar names, these are two different countries. The DRC’s Kasai region is associated with an urban legend about a football match in 1998: according to the story, a single lightning flash killed all eleven players on one team. The story is a legend, not an established fact, but it is commonly linked to Kasai Province.

Thessaloniki is Greece’s second-largest city by population, after Athens, and an important port in the north of the country. It stands at the head, or northwestern end, of the Thermaic Gulf, an inlet that opens into the northern Aegean Sea. The Chalkidiki peninsula borders the gulf to the east. Thessaloniki is the largest city in the historic region of Macedonia and has long been a center of trade because its harbor connects inland routes with the sea. Founded in ancient times, the city later became an important part of the Byzantine and Ottoman empires. Today it is a busy center for business, education, and culture, as well as a gateway to northern Greece.

The Shenandoah River flows through Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley and into West Virginia. Formed by the meeting of its North and South forks, it runs roughly northeast alongside the Blue Ridge Mountains before joining the Potomac River near Harpers Ferry, West Virginia. The Shenandoah is the Potomac’s largest tributary: a tributary is a smaller river that flows into a larger one. The Potomac continues past Washington, D.C., and empties into the Chesapeake Bay; it is the largest river in the Chesapeake Bay watershed, the area of land that drains into the bay. The Shenandoah and the Blue Ridge Mountains are mentioned together in the second line of “Take Me Home, Country Roads,” a song closely associated with West Virginia.

The Mosquito Coast is a historic region along the Caribbean shores of present-day Honduras and Nicaragua. Its name is associated with the Miskito people, who have long lived in the area, rather than the mosquito insect. Britain developed strong trading and political ties with the Miskito and treated the coast as a protectorate until the 19th century. On the Nicaraguan part of the coast, the port of Bluefields became an important center of British trade. Bluefields is now the capital of Nicaragua’s South Caribbean Coast Autonomous Region. The city’s name is often linked to Abraham Blauvelt, a Dutch privateer active in the Caribbean. The region’s history reflects the influence of Indigenous communities and European powers on Central America’s Caribbean coast.

Micronesia is a region of many small islands in the western Pacific Ocean. Its name means “small islands,” and it is one of the Pacific’s three broad cultural and geographic regions, alongside Melanesia and Polynesia. Micronesia includes the Caroline, Gilbert, Mariana, and Marshall island groups. The region contains several countries and territories, so it is not the same thing as the Federated States of Micronesia, which is one country within it. That country includes islands in the Caroline group. Its national government is based in Palikir, the capital, on the island of Pohnpei. Remembering the difference between the region and the country helps: Micronesia names the wider island region, while Palikir is the capital of the Federated States of Micronesia.

Mobile is a port city in southwestern Alabama at the head of Mobile Bay. The bay is a broad estuary: it receives water from the Mobile and Tensaw rivers and opens southward into the Gulf of Mexico. This location has long made Mobile an important place for shipping and trade. Interstate 10 runs east–west through the city and meets Interstate 65 there, linking Mobile to other parts of Alabama and the Gulf Coast. Mobile is also known for its Mardi Gras celebrations, which began before the better-known celebrations in New Orleans and are among the oldest in the United States. If a question asks for the Alabama city where I-10 meets I-65 beside a namesake bay, the answer is Mobile; the bay is Mobile Bay.

Cornwall is a historic county at the southwestern tip of England, on the peninsula west of Devon. It is also considered a Celtic nation, with a distinct heritage and its own Celtic language, Cornish. The county is bordered by the sea on three sides, and its rugged coast includes Land’s End, a granite headland at the far western tip. Land’s End is commonly identified as the westernmost point of mainland England, though it is not the westernmost point of the entire United Kingdom. Cornwall also appears in Arthurian legend: Tristan, a knight whose story is linked to King Arthur’s world, is traditionally associated with the region. If a question describes England’s southwestern peninsula and mentions Tristan, the county is Cornwall; if it asks for the granite headland at its western tip, the answer is Land’s End.

The Australian Outback is the name commonly given to Australia’s vast, remote, sparsely populated interior. Much of it is dry, and settlements can be far apart. Large cattle stations became a defining feature of rural life there; jackaroos, young workers learning to manage livestock, were part of that station culture. The 1932 Emu War, when soldiers were sent to deal with emus damaging crops in Western Australia, is another episode associated with the Outback. At an Outback station, the poet Banjo Paterson wrote “Waltzing Matilda,” a song often called Australia’s unofficial anthem. It tells of a swagman, or travelling worker, camping beside a billabong, a waterhole. He carries a tucker bag for food and takes a jumbuck, or sheep.

Guyana is a country on the northern Atlantic coast of South America. Its capital, Georgetown, lies near the coast, while much of the interior is covered by rainforest. Guyana borders Venezuela to the west, Brazil to the south, and Suriname to the east. The Corentyne River forms much of its border with Suriname, which lies between Guyana and French Guiana. Guyana’s population reflects South Asian, African, Indigenous, and European influences, shaped in part by migration during the colonial era. Those influences also appear in its food: pepperpot is a traditional stew flavored with cassareep, while dal, a dish made from split pulses such as lentils, shows the influence of Indian cooking.

Aden is a major port city in southern Yemen, on a volcanic peninsula beside the Gulf of Aden. Its location made it an important stop for ships traveling between Europe and Asia. After Britain seized Aden in 1839, the city became a key coaling station where steamships could refuel on the route to India. To Aden’s west is the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. It separates Yemen, on the Arabian Peninsula, from Djibouti and Eritrea in Africa. Ships passing through the strait can continue across the Gulf of Aden toward the Indian Ocean, making the area important to world trade. Aden was also the site of the 2000 bombing of the USS Cole while the American warship was in port.

Guangzhou is a major port city on the Pearl River in southern China. Western traders historically called it Canton, a name still used in phrases such as the Canton System. Under the Qing dynasty, Guangzhou was the only Chinese port authorized for most maritime trade with Western merchants. This restrictive arrangement, known as the Canton System, required foreign traders to deal with licensed Chinese merchants called the Cohong, while a customs official called the Hoppo oversaw trade regulations. Western merchants bought Chinese goods such as tea, silk, and porcelain, at first paying largely in silver. Later, British traders sold opium illegally in China, contributing to the Opium Wars. China’s defeat in those wars ended the Canton System and forced it to open additional ports to foreign trade.

Honduras is a Central American country with a long coastline on the Caribbean Sea to the north and El Salvador along its southwestern border. It has the region’s largest Garifuna population, estimated at about 200,000. The Garifuna are a people of African and Indigenous Caribbean ancestry whose communities live along the coasts of several Central American countries. Honduras is also known for the brief 1969 conflict with El Salvador called the Soccer War, although tensions over land and migration were more important causes than soccer itself. Another Central American country with a substantial Garifuna community is Belize, where many Garifuna live in and around the coastal town of Dangriga. Belize lies east of Guatemala and has its own Caribbean coastline.

The Dominican Republic is a Spanish-speaking country in the Caribbean. It occupies the eastern, larger part of the island of Hispaniola, while Haiti occupies the western part. Knowing the difference between the country and the island is important: the Dominican Republic is one of two countries on Hispaniola, not another name for the whole island. Its capital, Santo Domingo, lies on the southern coast and is one of the oldest European-founded cities in the Americas. The country’s landscapes include Pico Duarte, the highest mountain in the Caribbean, and Lake Enriquillo, a large saltwater lake below sea level. Baseball is its most popular sport, and many Dominican players have become famous internationally. Dominica is a different Caribbean island country and should not be confused with the Dominican Republic.

Cairo is the capital and largest city of Egypt. It stands on the Nile River near the southern edge of the Nile Delta, where the river begins to spread into branches before reaching the Mediterranean Sea. The Nile flows north through Egypt and has long supplied water for farming, travel, and settlement in a country with large desert regions. Cairo is a major center of government, education, and culture in Egypt and the wider Arab world. Its streets, markets, museums, and historic buildings reflect many centuries of history. The city is also the setting of the Cairo Trilogy by Egyptian writer Naguib Mahfouz, whose novels portray family life during a period of political and social change.

The Sargasso Sea is a region of the North Atlantic Ocean with no land boundaries. Instead, currents of the North Atlantic subtropical gyre surround it. Its name comes from Sargassum, a floating brown seaweed that forms mats on the surface and shelters many marine animals. The sea is also the spawning area of the European eel, a long, snake-like fish. European eels spend much of their adult lives in freshwater rivers and coastal waters, then migrate thousands of kilometers to the Sargasso Sea to reproduce. Their transparent, leaf-shaped larvae drift across the Atlantic toward Europe and North Africa, eventually reaching rivers from Iceland and Norway south to North Africa. Because no one saw the eels breed, their reproductive cycle puzzled people for centuries.

Vatican City is an independent city-state entirely surrounded by Rome, Italy. Covering less than half a square kilometer, it is the world’s smallest country by area. It is the seat of the pope and the headquarters of the Catholic Church. Its principal church, St. Peter’s Basilica, is famous for its great Renaissance-era dome. In front of the basilica is St. Peter’s Square, a monumental plaza where large crowds gather for papal events. Sweeping rows of columns, called colonnades, frame the square; they were designed by the Italian artist and architect Gian Lorenzo Bernini. An ancient Egyptian obelisk stands at the center of the square. Although Vatican City lies within Rome, it governs itself as a sovereign state.

Tiananmen Square is a vast public plaza in central Beijing, directly south of the Forbidden City. Major state buildings stand around it, making it an important setting for national ceremonies and gatherings. At its center stands the Monument to the People’s Heroes, a granite obelisk completed in 1958. It bears an inscription by Mao Zedong and honors people who died in China’s revolutionary struggles. The square is also known worldwide for the 1989 protests, when students and others called for political reforms. After the government used force to end the protests, photographer Jeff Widener captured an image of a lone man facing a column of tanks near the square. The photograph made “Tank Man” an enduring symbol of the events.

The Volga River is Europe’s longest river, stretching about 3,500 kilometers across western Russia. It begins in the Valdai Hills, an upland region in Tver Oblast near the village of Volgoverkhovye. From there, it flows generally east and southeast through major cities including Nizhny Novgorod, Kazan, and Volgograd before emptying into the Caspian Sea. The Volga and its tributaries form a large drainage basin that supplies water and transportation routes to much of Russia. A canal links the Volga to the Don River, giving boats a route toward the Sea of Azov and, eventually, the ocean. Because it connects so many places, the Volga has long been important to Russian trade and culture.

Rhodes is a Greek island in the eastern Mediterranean, near the coast of southwestern Turkey. It is the largest island in the Dodecanese archipelago. In medieval times, the Knights Hospitaller governed Rhodes and built defenses there, but Ottoman forces under Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent captured it in 1522. Rhodes is also famous for the Colossus of Rhodes, an enormous bronze statue of the sun god Helios. Erected in the 3rd century BCE after the island resisted a siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes, the statue was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. An earthquake toppled it several decades later. Although the statue no longer stands, its name remains closely linked with the island.

Tunisia is a North African country on the Mediterranean Sea, bordered by Algeria to the west and Libya to the southeast. It includes the island of Djerba in the Gulf of Gabès. Near Tunisia’s capital, Tunis, lie the ruins of Carthage, an ancient city founded by Phoenician settlers. Carthage grew into a powerful trading center and became Rome’s chief rival in the Punic Wars. Rome eventually destroyed the city, then built a Roman city on the site. Its surviving archaeological remains include the Baths of Antoninus, one of the largest Roman bath complexes in Africa. Tunisia is also part of the Maghreb, a region of northwestern Africa that includes Algeria, Libya, and Morocco.

Johannesburg is the largest urban center in Gauteng province, South Africa, and one of the country’s main financial and commercial hubs. It grew rapidly after gold was discovered nearby in 1886, attracting people seeking work and opportunity. Its history also reflects deep racial inequality: under apartheid, South Africa’s system of legally enforced racial segregation, many Black residents were forced to live in separate townships. In Alan Paton’s novel Cry, the Beloved Country, Stephen Kumalo travels to Johannesburg to search for his son Absalom, and the city’s divisions shape the story. Southwest of central Johannesburg lies Soweto, a name formed from the initials of “South Western Townships.” In 1976, Soweto became the focal point of a student uprising against apartheid-era education policies.

The Gulf of Bothnia is the northern arm of the Baltic Sea, stretching between Sweden to the west and Finland to the east. It has two main subdivisions: the Bothnian Sea in the south and the Bothnian Bay in the north. Between them lies the Kvarken, a narrow stretch of water between the Swedish and Finnish coasts. The Bothnian Bay, north of the Kvarken, is bordered by northern Sweden and Finland. At its southern end, the Gulf of Bothnia connects to the rest of the Baltic Sea near the Åland Islands. Because the gulf reaches far north and its water is less salty than ocean water, parts of it freeze over in winter.

Cape Town is a major city on South Africa’s southwestern coast, where the Atlantic Ocean meets the Cape Peninsula. It is one of South Africa’s three capitals, each with a different government role: Pretoria is the administrative capital, Bloemfontein is the judicial capital, and Cape Town is the legislative capital. This means Cape Town is the seat of the Parliament of South Africa, the institution that makes national laws. Parliament has two chambers: the National Assembly, whose members are elected by voters, and the National Council of Provinces, which represents the country’s nine provinces. Cape Town is also known for Table Mountain, which rises above the city, and for its history as an important port on sea routes around southern Africa.

The Bonneville Salt Flats are a vast, remarkably level stretch of salt-covered ground in northwestern Utah. They formed from minerals and sediments left behind by Lake Bonneville, a huge prehistoric lake that covered much of present-day Utah during the Ice Age. As the climate changed and the lake receded, water evaporated and left a crust of salt across the lakebed. The flat, open surface makes the salt flats a famous place for drivers to attempt land-speed records, especially at the Bonneville Speedway. The two names are closely connected: Lake Bonneville was the ancient lake, while the Bonneville Salt Flats are part of the landscape it left behind.

Alabama is a state in the southeastern United States. It borders Tennessee to the north, while Florida and the Gulf of Mexico lie to its south. Its capital, Montgomery, was the site of a major turning point in the Civil Rights Movement: after Rosa Parks was arrested there in 1955 for refusing to give up her bus seat, Black residents organized the Montgomery bus boycott to challenge segregation. In 1965, voting-rights marchers traveled from Selma to Montgomery to demand equal access to the ballot. Birmingham was another important Civil Rights Movement site; in 1963, members of the Ku Klux Klan bombed a church there, killing four African American girls. These events make Alabama central to the history of the struggle for civil rights in the United States.

Kyoto is a historic city in central Japan that served as the imperial capital for more than a thousand years. Emperor Kanmu established it as the capital in 794, originally naming it Heian-kyō, meaning “Capital of Peace and Tranquility.” Its streets followed a grid plan inspired by Chang’an, a capital of ancient China. Although military rulers called shoguns held much of Japan’s political power for centuries, the emperor’s court remained in Kyoto. After imperial rule was restored in 1868, Emperor Meiji moved the court to Tokyo, ending Kyoto’s role as the capital. Today, Kyoto is known for its temples, shrines, and traditional neighborhoods. Landmarks include Kiyomizu-dera, a famous Buddhist temple, and Gion, a district associated with traditional arts.

The Appalachian Trail is a long-distance hiking route through the Appalachian Mountains of the eastern United States. It runs for more than 2,000 miles (about 3,500 kilometers) from Springer Mountain in Georgia, its southern terminus, to Mount Katahdin in Maine, its northern terminus. Mount Katahdin is also the highest peak in Maine. The trail passes through 14 states and crosses forests, valleys, and mountain ridges. Hikers can explore a short section in a day or spend several months attempting to walk the entire route, a journey known as a thru-hike. The Appalachians are a much larger mountain system that includes ranges such as the Blue Ridge Mountains. Although the trail is named for these mountains, it follows a particular marked route rather than covering the whole range.

Notre-Dame de Paris is a medieval Gothic Catholic cathedral in the heart of Paris, France. It stands on the Île de la Cité, an island in the River Seine that is also home to the Sainte-Chapelle and the Palais de Justice. Construction began in the 12th century, and the cathedral became famous for its large stained-glass rose windows and flying buttresses, exterior supports that helped builders create tall walls and spacious interiors. Victor Hugo’s novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, featuring the bell-ringer Quasimodo, helped inspire public interest in preserving the building. In 2019, a major fire destroyed much of its roof and spire, prompting a large restoration effort.

Kentucky is a state in the southeastern United States. Its capital is Frankfort, and it borders seven states: Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, West Virginia, Virginia, Tennessee, and Missouri. The Ohio River forms much of Kentucky’s northern boundary. Louisville, the state’s largest city, sits on that river across from southern Indiana. Each year, Louisville hosts the Kentucky Derby, a famous horse race held at Churchill Downs. Louisville was also the site of the 2020 police killing of Breonna Taylor, which drew national attention to questions about policing and racial justice. Kentucky’s two U.S. senators are Mitch McConnell, who served as Senate Majority Leader from 2015 to 2021, and Rand Paul.

The White House is the official residence and workplace of the president of the United States. It stands at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., and is known for its neoclassical design, inspired by ancient Greek and Roman architecture. John Adams became the first president to live there when he moved in during 1800. The building is part of a larger complex that includes the West Wing, which was created during a 1902 renovation under President Theodore Roosevelt. The West Wing contains the Oval Office, where the president works, and offices for senior staff. Because it is both a home and a center of government, the White House is also a setting for important meetings, speeches, and public events.

The Trans-Siberian Railway is a major east-west rail route linking Moscow, Russia’s capital, with the country’s Far East. Its main line crosses Siberia and northern Asia, carrying passenger and freight trains across thousands of kilometres. Built mainly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it helped connect distant parts of Russia and made it easier for people and goods to travel between European Russia and the Pacific coast. The main route’s eastern terminus is Vladivostok, a Russian port city on the Sea of Japan and an important gateway to the Pacific Ocean. Although many travellers think of the Trans-Siberian Railway as a single long train journey, it is a railway line used by different trains serving communities along the way.

The Anne Frank House is a museum at Prinsengracht 263 in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. During the German occupation in World War II, Jewish teenager Anne Frank hid in a concealed part of the building called the Secret Annex with her parents, her sister, and four other Jewish people. She wrote much of her famous diary there, describing daily life in hiding and her hopes for the future. Several trusted employees of Anne’s father, Otto Frank, helped prepare the hiding place and brought its occupants food and supplies. One of these helpers was Victor Kugler, whom Anne called “Mr. Kraler” in her diary. Today, visitors can see the historic building and learn about the people who hid there and those who helped them during the Holocaust.

Tel Aviv is a major Israeli city on the Mediterranean coast and the center of the country’s largest metropolitan area. It is also a leading center of Israel’s technology sector, with many startups and other businesses. The city’s full municipal name is Tel Aviv-Yafo. Yafo is the Hebrew name of Jaffa, an ancient port settlement beside Tel Aviv. Tel Aviv was founded in the early 1900s, while Yafo has a much longer history as a Mediterranean port. The two were joined into one municipality, which is why both names appear together. If a question asks for the modern coastal city known for technology, the answer is Tel Aviv; if it asks for the older port named in Tel Aviv-Yafo, the Hebrew name is Yafo.

Salem is a city in Essex County, Massachusetts, on the coast north of Boston. It was a major colonial seaport, and merchants who sailed to Asia brought back objects that helped form the collections of the East India Marine Society. Those collections became part of Salem’s Peabody Essex Museum, which displays art and objects from around the world. One of its most unusual exhibits is Yin Yu Tang, a Qing-era merchant’s house originally built in China’s Anhui Province. The house was dismantled, shipped to the United States, and reconstructed at the museum. Salem is also known for the 1692–1693 witch trials, when fear and false accusations led to the execution of twenty people.

Hampshire is a county on England’s southern coast. It contains the New Forest, an area of woodland and open heath where local people known as commoners have long held rights to graze ponies and other animals. Hampshire also gave its name to the U.S. state of New Hampshire, which lies east of Vermont and southwest of Maine. One of Hampshire’s major cities is Southampton, a busy port on the south coast. In April 1912, the Titanic departed from Southampton on its maiden voyage across the Atlantic. Many of its crew members lived in the city, so the ship’s sinking had a deep impact there. Today, Southampton’s SeaCity Museum tells the story of the city’s connection to the Titanic.

Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? is a 1962 American play by Edward Albee. It follows George and Martha, a married couple who invite a younger couple, Nick and Honey, to their home after a party. As the night goes on, drinking and seemingly playful party games turn into cruel arguments and psychological battles. Their tense exchanges reveal deep problems in George and Martha’s marriage and draw their guests into the conflict. The play explores how people use stories, illusions, and harsh truths to cope with disappointment. Its title echoes a children’s song, but the question becomes a serious one about facing reality. Albee also wrote Seascape, in which two humans, Nancy and Charlie, talk with two reptiles, Leslie and Sarah.

J. K. Rowling is a British novelist born in Yate, Gloucestershire. She is best known for the seven-book Harry Potter series, which follows an orphaned boy who learns that he is a wizard. Harry studies magic at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, makes close friends, and faces the dark wizard Voldemort. Beginning with Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone, the novels grew into a worldwide publishing phenomenon and inspired a popular film series. Rowling has also written detective novels featuring the private investigator Cormoran Strike under the pen name Robert Galbraith.

Antigone is a tragedy by the ancient Greek playwright Sophocles. Its title character is a princess of Thebes and the daughter of Oedipus. After her brother Polynices dies fighting against Thebes, King Creon forbids anyone to bury him. Antigone believes that honoring her brother with burial rites is a sacred duty, so she defies Creon’s order. Creon sentences her to death, setting off a conflict between the king’s law and what Antigone believes the gods require. The blind prophet Tiresias warns Creon that the gods reject his sacrifices while Polynices remains unburied and predicts disaster for his family. Tiresias also appears in Sophocles’ Oedipus Rex, where he tells Oedipus that he killed the former king, Laius. Creon changes his mind too late: Antigone kills herself, and further deaths follow.

The Oresteia is the only complete trilogy of ancient Greek tragedies to survive. Written by Aeschylus, it consists of Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers, and The Eumenides. The plays follow a cycle of violence in one family. First, Agamemnon returns from the Trojan War and is murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra. Their son Orestes then kills Clytemnestra to avenge his father, but he is pursued by the Furies, who punish family murder. In the final play, Orestes is tried in Athens before a court on the Areopagus established by the goddess Athena. When the jurors are evenly divided, Athena casts the deciding vote to acquit him. The trilogy moves from personal revenge toward judgment by a court.

The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian is a 2007 young-adult novel by Sherman Alexie, a Native American writer with Spokane and Coeur d’Alene heritage. It follows Arnold Spirit Jr., usually called Junior, a Spokane teenager who leaves his reservation school in Wellpinit to attend the mostly white Reardan High School. Junior loves drawing cartoons, which appear throughout the book and help show his humor, fears, and hopes. At Reardan, he finds new opportunities but also feels caught between his new classmates and his community at home. Through Junior’s experiences with friendship, basketball, family, and loss, the novel explores identity and belonging. Alexie also wrote the short-story collection The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven.

The Shahnameh, meaning “Book of Kings,” is the Persian national epic written by the poet Ferdowsi. Born in Tus, in the region of Khorasan, Ferdowsi spent decades composing the poem and completed it around 1010 CE. It tells the story of Iran through the reigns of legendary and historical rulers, mixing battles and adventures with questions about loyalty, family, and fate. One of its most famous episodes concerns the hero Rostam and the young warrior Sohrab. They fight without knowing that they are father and son, and Rostam kills Sohrab before discovering the truth. This tragedy is one reason the Shahnameh remains widely read and remembered.

“I, Too” is a poem by Langston Hughes, a leading writer of the Harlem Renaissance, a Black cultural movement of the early 20th century. Its speaker calls himself “the darker brother” and says he is sent to eat in the kitchen when company comes. Despite this exclusion, he imagines a future when he will sit at the table and others will recognize his beauty and feel ashamed of how they treated him. The poem’s title comes from its opening words, “I, too,” which introduce the speaker’s claim that he belongs to America. Hughes wrote the poem in response to “I Hear America Singing” by Walt Whitman, a 19th-century poet who also wrote Leaves of Grass. Where Whitman celebrates American voices, Hughes insists that Black Americans must be heard among them.

G. K. Chesterton (1874–1936) was an English writer and Catholic thinker whose work ranged from detective stories to novels and religious essays. He created Father Brown, a priest-detective who solves mysteries by understanding human nature and the motives behind crimes. Chesterton’s 1908 novel The Man Who Was Thursday follows the poet Gabriel Syme, who joins a secret police force and infiltrates an anarchist council. Its members use the days of the week as names, and Syme discovers that many of them are undercover police officers too. In The Everlasting Man, Chesterton explored human history and argued for the importance of Christianity. That book later helped move the writer C. S. Lewis toward Christian belief.

Carrie White is the main character of Carrie, a 1974 horror novel by American author Stephen King, who also wrote The Shining. Carrie is a bullied high-school student in the fictional Maine town of Chamberlain. She discovers that she has telekinesis, the ability to move objects with her mind. At the school prom, her classmates play a cruel prank: after she is crowned prom queen, they dump pig’s blood on her. Humiliated and overwhelmed, Carrie uses her powers to attack the people at the dance and unleash destruction across the town. Her story is a work of horror, but it also explores the effects of bullying, isolation, and cruelty.

Mario Vargas Llosa is a Peruvian novelist and essayist who won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Literature. His novels often explore power, politics, and the ways people respond to authority. In Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter, he draws on his early life to tell a story involving a young writer, his older relative by marriage, and a radio-script writer. His historical novel The Feast of the Goat is set around the final days of Rafael Trujillo’s dictatorship in the Dominican Republic. It follows an exiled woman returning to the country while also revisiting the events surrounding Trujillo’s assassination. Vargas Llosa was a prominent literary rival of Colombian novelist Gabriel García Márquez, although both became major figures in Latin American literature.

Charles Perrault was a French writer who, in the late seventeenth century, turned traditional folktales into written fairy tales. His collection The Tales of Mother Goose includes versions of Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, Puss in Boots, and Little Red Riding Hood. Mother Goose is the fictional storyteller associated with the collection, while Perrault was its real author. His Little Red Riding Hood follows a girl carrying food to her grandmother. On the way, she talks to a wolf, who reaches the grandmother’s house first and eats her. The wolf then eats the girl too. Unlike some later versions, Perrault’s story has no rescue; its warning is about the danger of trusting strangers.

George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, a British novelist who wrote during the Victorian era. She used a male name when publishing her fiction, at a time when women writers were often taken less seriously. Her novels are known for realistic characters, complicated relationships, and the pressures of family and society. In Middlemarch, one of her best-known books, she writes about the lives and ambitions of people including Dorothea Brooke. Another novel, The Mill on the Floss, follows Maggie Tulliver and her brother Tom as their family faces debt and other hardships near the River Floss. After years of conflict between them, a flood brings the siblings together again, and both drown in the river.

Flarf poetry is an experimental form that turns internet search results into poems. A poet might search for a phrase, collect surprising bits of text from the results, and rearrange them rather than write every line from scratch. The finished poem may keep awkward wording, mistakes, clichés, or strange changes in tone because those accidents can create humor or reveal unexpected connections. This use of found language has a precedent in Dadaism, an early 20th-century avant-garde movement that challenged traditional ideas of art. Dada artists used methods such as collage and the cut-up technique to make new works from existing material. Hugo Ball and Tristan Tzara were Dadaists, and the movement’s name is said to come from a French word for “hobbyhorse.”

Edgar Allan Poe’s Gothic short story The Fall of the House of Usher follows an unnamed narrator who visits his childhood friend Roderick Usher at the family’s decaying mansion. Roderick has written to him about a nervous illness, and when the narrator arrives, Roderick welcomes him inside. Roderick is deeply fearful and unusually sensitive to light and sound, yet he plays music as his condition worsens. His twin sister, Madeline, is also mysteriously ill and seems to die. Roderick and the narrator place her body in a vault beneath the house, but she was buried alive and eventually breaks free. She collapses onto Roderick, and both siblings die. As the narrator flees, the mansion splits apart and sinks, bringing the Usher family’s story to a terrifying end.

Mr. Bennet is the witty but often detached father of five daughters in Jane Austen’s novel Pride and Prejudice. He enjoys teasing his anxious wife, joking that her frequently mentioned nerves are his “old friends.” His favorite daughter, Elizabeth, refuses a marriage proposal from the pompous clergyman Mr. Collins. While Mrs. Bennet threatens to disown Elizabeth for refusing him, Mr. Bennet says he would disown her if she accepted. His humor shows his affection for Elizabeth, but he often withdraws from family problems instead of dealing with them. Elizabeth also rejects the first proposal of the wealthy Mr. Darcy, who speaks critically of her family. After she learns that Darcy helped her sister Lydia, Elizabeth comes to understand him better and accepts his second proposal.

The Merchant of Venice is a Shakespeare play that combines romance with a troubling courtroom drama. Antonio, a Venetian merchant, borrows money from the Jewish moneylender Shylock so his friend Bassanio can court Portia, a wealthy heiress. Portia’s suitors must choose correctly among three caskets to win her hand. When Antonio cannot repay the loan, Shylock demands the bond’s penalty: a pound of Antonio’s flesh. At the trial, Portia disguises herself as a young male legal scholar named Balthazar. Arguing before the Duke, she points out that the bond allows Shylock to take flesh but permits no blood to be shed. The play ends happily for Antonio and the lovers, yet its treatment of Shylock and the hostility between Christians and Jews remain subjects of debate.

“Disillusionment of Ten O’Clock” is a poem by American poet Wallace Stevens, who also wrote “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird.” It opens with houses “haunted by white night-gowns,” suggesting people dressed alike and ready for bed. Stevens contrasts their ordinary domestic lives with the colorful possibilities of imagination: the nightgowns are not decorated with the vivid patterns and colors he lists, and their wearers do not dream extraordinary dreams. At the end, however, “an old sailor, drunk and asleep in his boots” dreams that he “catches tigers in red weather.” The sailor’s strange, vivid dream makes him stand out from the quiet houses and shows how imagination can transform an ordinary night.

My Life as a Fake is a novel by Australian writer Peter Carey about a literary hoax that takes on a life of its own. Christopher Chubb invents a poet named Bob McCorkle and submits supposedly brilliant poems under his name, hoping to expose what he sees as the foolishness of the literary world. But McCorkle appears to become real, forcing Chubb to face the consequences of his deception. A literary editor, Sarah Wode-Douglass, later investigates the strange story. Carey drew inspiration from the real Ern Malley hoax: in the 1940s, two Australian poets invented Ern Malley, a fictional modernist writer, and sent his poems to the journal Angry Penguins, which published them. The novel asks whether art’s value changes when its creator is not who readers think.

L. Frank Baum was an American author born in 1856 in Chittenango, New York. He is best known for The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, a children’s fantasy published in 1900. In the novel, a cyclone carries Dorothy from her home in Kansas to the magical Land of Oz. Hoping to get home, she follows the yellow-brick road with three new friends: a Scarecrow, a Tin Woodman, and a Cowardly Lion. Each hopes the ruler known as the Wizard of Oz can help them. Baum went on to write thirteen sequels, turning Oz into a long-running fantasy series. He also wrote books under other names, including the pseudonym Edith Van Dyne.

Orlando: A Biography is a 1928 novel by British modernist writer Virginia Woolf. It tells the imaginary life of Orlando, an English noble who begins as a young man in the Elizabethan era, lives for centuries without growing old in the usual way, and becomes a woman. As Orlando moves through different periods of English history, Woolf explores how expectations about gender, love, writing, and social status change over time. The subtitle A Biography is playful: a biography normally tells the life story of a real person, but Orlando is fictional. Woolf drew inspiration for Orlando from her close friend and lover Vita Sackville-West, a poet and novelist whose family owned the country estate Knole.

All My Sons is a drama by American playwright Arthur Miller, set in Ohio after World War II. Its central character, factory owner Joe Keller, authorized the shipment of defective aircraft engine parts during the war, causing the deaths of 21 pilots. At first, Joe lets his business partner take the blame and tries to protect his family and his reputation. His son Chris, who survived the war, presses him to admit what he did and recognize the harm caused to the pilots’ families. Joe’s struggle shows how a decision made for personal gain can have devastating consequences for others. Overcome by guilt, he kills himself. The title reflects the idea that Joe owed a duty not only to his own sons but also to the young men who died.

“The Book of Sand” is a short story by the Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges, who also wrote “The Aleph” and “The Garden of Forking Paths.” In the story, a Bible seller brings the narrator a strange volume and trades it for a Wycliffe Bible. The seller calls it the Book of Sand because, like sand, it seems to have no beginning or end: however many pages the narrator turns, more appear. Even more unsettling, once he turns away from a page, he can never find that exact page again. The impossible book fascinates the narrator, but it also makes him anxious and obsessed. Through this mysterious object, Borges invites readers to imagine what it would mean to encounter something truly infinite.

Ozymandias is a sonnet by the English Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. In the poem, a traveler tells the speaker about the broken statue of a once-powerful ruler standing in a barren desert. Its face has a “sneer of cold command,” and an inscription on its pedestal boasts, “Look on my works, ye mighty, and despair!” Yet no great works can be seen: only “lone and level sands” stretch around the ruins. This contrast makes the ruler’s pride seem foolish and suggests that power and fame do not last forever. Shelley also wrote “Mont Blanc” and “Ode to the West Wind.” His wife, Mary Shelley, wrote Frankenstein.

Kate Chopin’s short story “The Storm” takes place in Louisiana during a sudden downpour. Calixta is sewing at home when her former lover Alcée arrives seeking shelter. Her husband, Bobinôt, and their young son, Bibi, are away at Friedheimer’s store, where they wait for the weather to pass; Bobinôt also buys shrimp for Calixta. Alone together, Calixta and Alcée rekindle their intimacy, even though both are married to other people. As the rain ends, Alcée leaves, and Calixta warmly welcomes Bobinôt and Bibi home. The story closes with the surprising observation that the storm passed and everyone was happy. Chopin uses the changing weather to reflect the characters’ passion and to explore desire, marriage, and the social expectations placed on women.

The Consolation of Philosophy is a sixth-century work by Boethius, a Roman statesman and philosopher. He wrote it while imprisoned after falling out of favor with the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. The book takes the form of a dialogue between Boethius, who is grieving over his sudden loss of power and freedom, and Lady Philosophy, a woman who personifies wisdom. Moving between poetry and reasoned argument, she challenges him to look beyond his misfortune. She explains that fortune is changeable, so lasting happiness cannot depend on wealth or status. Their conversation also explores divine providence—how God understands and orders events—and whether people can still make free choices. The work became an important text for medieval readers seeking comfort and guidance in difficult times.

Ovid, whose full name was Publius Ovidius Naso, was a Roman poet who wrote in Latin during the reign of Augustus. His Ars Amatoria, or The Art of Love, is a didactic poem: it presents advice about love in a playful, instructional style. Ovid is best known for Metamorphoses, a fifteen-book narrative poem that gathers myths about transformation.
