It begins with the creation of the world and moves through stories of gods and humans before ending with the deification of Julius Caesar, when Caesar is made divine. Later in his life, Augustus banished Ovid to Tomis, a town on the Black Sea. Ovid continued writing there, but Metamorphoses remains his most famous work.

In George Orwell’s Animal Farm, the pigs lead the animals’ rebellion against the human farmer, Mr. Jones. Old Major inspires the revolt with his vision of a farm run by animals, while Snowball and Napoleon help organize it. After the humans are driven out, the pigs take charge, claiming they need the farm’s milk and windfall apples because their work is especially important. Their growing privileges show how leaders who promise equality can become a ruling class. Napoleon eventually drives Snowball away and rules as a dictator. Another pig, Squealer, acts as Napoleon’s spokesman and chief propagandist. He uses persuasive speeches and selective claims to explain away changes to the farm’s commandments and convince the other animals that Napoleon’s decisions benefit them.

Songs of Innocence and of Experience is an illuminated poetry collection by the British Romantic poet William Blake, who combined his poems with illustrations he made himself. Its two sections present what Blake called “contrary states” of human life. Songs of Innocence often speaks through children and explores trust, joy, and faith, while Songs of Experience confronts fear, suffering, injustice, and corruption. In “The Lamb,” a gentle speaker asks a young animal who made it and connects its creator with a loving God. In “The Tyger,” Blake asks what “immortal hand or eye” could create the tiger’s “fearful symmetry.” By setting these poems beside each other, Blake invites readers to consider how innocence and experience offer different ways of seeing the same world.

John Gardner’s 1971 novel Grendel retells the Old English epic Beowulf from the viewpoint of the monster who terrorizes Heorot, the mead-hall of King Hrothgar. Instead of seeing Grendel only as an enemy for the hero to defeat, readers hear his thoughts as he watches the Danes, meets a dragon, and struggles to understand his place in the world. One figure who fascinates him is the Shaper, a blind poet at Hrothgar’s court. The Shaper turns the Danes’ often violent history into heroic songs, making their lives seem grand and meaningful. His music briefly draws Grendel toward the human community, even though Grendel knows the songs leave out darker truths. Through the monster’s perspective, Gardner explores how stories can shape what people believe about themselves.

Artemis Fowl II is the young Irish heir and supergenius at the center of Eoin Colfer’s Artemis Fowl fantasy series. Hoping to restore his family’s fortune, Artemis discovers a hidden fairy world whose inhabitants possess advanced technology. In the first novel, he uses his intelligence and careful planning to capture Holly Short, an elf police officer and captain in the Lower Elements Police Reconnaissance unit, known as LEPrecon. He holds her for a ransom of fairy gold, setting off a struggle between his household and the fairy authorities. Artemis is aided by Butler, his loyal bodyguard. Although he begins the series willing to exploit others to reach his goals, his encounters with Holly and the fairy world gradually challenge him to think about loyalty, friendship, and the consequences of his schemes.

Plato’s Symposium is a dialogue set at a banquet hosted by the poet Agathon in ancient Athens. Socrates and the other guests take turns giving speeches in praise of Eros, the Greek god of love, while exploring why people fall in love and what love can teach them. One speaker, the comic playwright Aristophanes, tells a myth in which humans were once double-bodied beings. Zeus split them apart, he says, leaving each person longing to find their missing half. Socrates later describes love as a desire for beauty and goodness. When Alcibiades arrives late, he breaks from the plan: instead of praising Eros, he gives a speech praising Socrates. Through these different voices, Plato invites readers to think about love as more than simple attraction.

Blanche DuBois is the tragic protagonist of Tennessee Williams’s play A Streetcar Named Desire. A former schoolteacher from Laurel, Mississippi, she arrives in New Orleans to stay with her younger sister, Stella Kowalski, and Stella’s husband, Stanley, in their cramped French Quarter apartment. Blanche tries to appear refined and youthful, hiding her age and avoiding bright light. She covers a bare light bulb with a paper lantern and insists, “I don’t want realism! I want magic!” Her illusions help her escape painful memories, including her young husband’s suicide, but they also bring her into conflict with the blunt, suspicious Stanley. As Stanley exposes her past and abuses her, Blanche loses her grip on reality. Her story explores the clash between comforting fantasy and harsh truth.

The Dunciad is a satirical mock-epic poem by the eighteenth-century English writer Alexander Pope. A mock-epic uses the grand style of ancient heroic poems to describe less noble events, making its targets look ridiculous. In The Dunciad, Pope imagines the goddess Dulness leading writers, critics, and other agents who spread stupidity, cultural decay, and bad taste across Britain. Rather than celebrating a brave hero, the poem gives a central role to a figure Pope considers an example of dullness. Lewis Theobald filled that role in an earlier version, but Pope replaced him with Colley Cibber in the 1742 version after Cibber insulted his writing. Through this exaggerated struggle between learning and Dulness, Pope criticizes what he sees as declining standards in literature and public life.

“Musée des Beaux Arts” is a poem by W. H. Auden about how people often continue their ordinary lives while someone else suffers. Its title refers to an art museum in Brussels, where Auden saw paintings by the Old Masters. The poem begins, “About suffering they were never wrong, / The Old Masters,” then turns to a landscape painting by the Flemish artist Pieter Bruegel the Elder. In Landscape with the Fall of Icarus, a boy from Greek myth falls from the sky into the sea, but a nearby ship sails calmly on. By describing this painting in words, Auden uses a technique called ekphrasis. The contrast between Icarus’s disaster and the ship’s indifference shows how easily suffering can go unnoticed.

George R. R. Martin is an American novelist best known for A Song of Ice and Fire, a fantasy series about rival families struggling for power in a world of political intrigue, dragons, and magic. The books inspired the television series Game of Thrones. Martin also helped create the mythology and ancient history of Elden Ring, a 2022 open-world role-playing game made by FromSoftware. In the game, players take the role of a Tarnished who travels through the Lands Between, fights powerful demigods, and seeks to restore the shattered Elden Ring, a source of power that shapes the world. Martin worked on the game’s background and setting, while FromSoftware developed the gameplay and the story players experience.

Elizabeth Bennet is the witty, independent-minded second daughter of Mr. Bennet, a gentleman with five daughters, in Jane Austen’s novel Pride and Prejudice. When wealthy bachelor Charles Bingley rents Netherfield, Elizabeth meets his friend Fitzwilliam Darcy. Darcy’s first impression of her is insulting, and Elizabeth comes to see him as proud and unpleasant. She rejects his first proposal of marriage, partly because she believes he has mistreated others. As the story continues, Elizabeth learns that some of her judgments were mistaken, while Darcy becomes less arrogant. Meanwhile, Bingley falls in love with Elizabeth’s sister Jane, and her younger sister Lydia elopes with George Wickham. By the end, Elizabeth and Darcy understand each other better and marry.

A Room of One’s Own is a 1929 extended essay by British writer Virginia Woolf, based on lectures she gave at women’s colleges in Cambridge. Its first-person speaker visits the fictional university of Oxbridge and the women’s college Fernham, noticing how unequal access to education and resources has limited women’s writing. Woolf argues that a woman needs money and a private room if she is to write fiction freely: without income, time, and space, talent may never have a chance to develop. The speaker says her own identity is unimportant and suggests several names readers may call her, beginning with Mary Beton. Through this invented voice, Woolf explores why so few women had been able to become celebrated writers.

The Brownings were Elizabeth Barrett Browning and Robert Browning, a married pair of Victorian English poets. Elizabeth is celebrated for her love poems, especially a sequence of sonnets that includes “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.” A sonnet is a fourteen-line poem. Robert became known for dramatic monologues, poems in which a character speaks and gradually reveals their thoughts and personality. In his poem “My Last Duchess,” a duke shows an emissary a portrait of his deceased wife. As he talks about her, his jealousy and possessiveness become clear, and he implies that he ordered her death. The poem lets readers judge the duke by what he says, even though he does not seem to recognize how cruel he sounds.

Holly Hills is a popular student in Jeff Kinney’s Diary of a Wimpy Kid series and Greg Heffley’s main love interest. Greg is the series’ protagonist, and his diary-style stories follow the awkward and often funny experiences of growing up. Holly is considered the most popular girl in her grade, which makes Greg especially eager to impress her. In one memorable exchange, Greg introduces himself, but Holly asks whether his name is “Fregley,” confusing him with another student. That mix-up captures the kind of embarrassing moment Greg frequently faces. Holly appears in the same series as books such as Dog Days and Cabin Fever. If you are asked to name Greg’s popular love interest, the answer is Holly Hills; if you are asked to name the series, it is Diary of a Wimpy Kid.

Mother Goose is a fictional storyteller associated with traditional nursery rhymes and fairy tales, not a single known author. Illustrations often show her as a kindly grandmother telling stories to children or as a wise, maternal goose. Her name became especially important in French literature in 1697, when the writer Charles Perrault published a collection called Histoires ou contes du temps passé, also known as Tales of Mother Goose. Perrault gathered and adapted older European folktales into literary stories, including “Sleeping Beauty,” “Puss in Boots,” and “Little Red Riding Hood.” The collection helped preserve and popularize these tales, while the name Mother Goose became a familiar symbol of storytelling for children.

The Time Machine is a Victorian science-fiction novel by the English author H. G. Wells, who also wrote The War of the Worlds, about invading Martians, and The Island of Doctor Moreau. Its unnamed protagonist, known as the Time Traveller, builds a machine that carries him to the year 802,701. There he meets the gentle, childlike Eloi and the Morlocks, who live underground and prey on them. He befriends an Eloi named Weena after saving her from drowning. While exploring the ruins of a museum he calls the Palace of Green Porcelain, he finds matches that help him survive. Through this imagined future, Wells explores how social divisions and human evolution might change life on Earth.

Marius Pontmercy is a young nobleman and student in Victor Hugo’s novel Les Misérables. Living in Paris, he becomes involved with the Friends of the ABC, a circle of republican students led by Enjolras. The group wants political change and builds a barricade during the June Rebellion of 1832. Marius joins them there and is badly wounded in the fighting. He also falls in love with Cosette, the adopted daughter of Jean Valjean. Although Valjean fears losing Cosette, he saves Marius from the barricade and carries him to safety. Marius recovers, and he and Cosette marry near the end of the novel. His story connects the novel’s political conflict with its themes of love, sacrifice, and family.

A simile is a figure of speech that compares two unlike things using words such as “like” or “as.” For example, “The warrior stood like a tree in a storm” compares a warrior’s strength to a tree’s without saying the warrior actually is a tree. A metaphor makes the comparison more directly, as in “The warrior was a tree in a storm.” In ancient epic poetry, poets often use a longer form called a Homeric simile, named for the poet associated with the Iliad and the Odyssey. A Homeric simile may pause the action for several lines to compare a heroic event with a familiar scene from nature or everyday life. The extended image helps readers picture the action and understand its force or emotion.

Akaky Akakievich Bashmachkin is the timid, impoverished copying clerk at the center of Nikolai Gogol’s Russian short story The Overcoat. He works in a government office in St. Petersburg, where other clerks mock him, but he takes quiet pleasure in transcribing documents. When the tailor Petrovich says his worn-out overcoat is beyond repair, Akaky saves carefully for a new one. His coworkers celebrate the purchase, but thieves steal the coat soon afterward. Desperate for help, Akaky approaches a high-ranking official known as the “Very Important Personage,” who scolds and humiliates him instead. Akaky falls ill and dies, and the story ends with reports of a ghost stealing overcoats. Through Akaky’s fate, Gogol criticizes cruelty and indifference toward people with little money or status. Gogol also wrote the novel Dead Souls.

The Hunger Games trilogy is Suzanne Collins’s three-book dystopian series about Panem, a country ruled by a powerful Capitol. Each year, the Capitol forces children from its districts to compete in the Hunger Games, a televised fight to the death. In the first book, Katniss Everdeen volunteers as a tribute from District 12 to save her younger sister, Prim, from being sent into the arena. Skilled with a bow, Katniss survives alongside fellow District 12 tribute Peeta Mellark. Her compassion for other tributes and her defiance of the Capitol make her a symbol of resistance known as the Mockingjay. Across The Hunger Games, Catching Fire, and Mockingjay, her story grows from a struggle to survive into a fight against the Capitol’s rule.

In Harper Lee’s novel To Kill a Mockingbird, the trial of Tom Robinson reveals how racial prejudice can shape a courtroom verdict. Mayella Ewell, a white woman, falsely accuses Tom, a Black farmhand, of raping her. Atticus Finch, the father of Scout and Jem, represents Tom and cross-examines Mayella about the injuries on the right side of her face. Tom’s left arm was badly injured in a cotton gin and is nearly unusable, making it unlikely that he struck her as described. Atticus presents this evidence to challenge her account, but the jury convicts Tom anyway. The trial is a central event in the novel, showing the gap between the evidence presented in court and the justice Tom receives.

Kate DiCamillo is an American author best known for children’s novels that mix adventure, humor, and difficult emotions such as loneliness. Her debut novel, Because of Winn-Dixie, follows Opal Buloni, a girl who moves to Naomi, Florida, to live with her preacher father. After finding a stray dog and naming him Winn-Dixie, Opal begins making friends in her new town. In DiCamillo’s 2003 fantasy novel The Tale of Despereaux, the hero is a large-eared mouse named Despereaux Tilling. Unlike other mice, he loves stories and music and becomes fascinated by a human princess, Princess Pea. When he speaks to her, the other mice punish him by sending him to the dungeon. Both books feature unusual friendships and characters who find courage in difficult circumstances.

Norton Juster was an American author best known for The Phantom Tollbooth, a children’s fantasy novel full of wordplay and jokes about language and learning. Its main character, Milo, is a bored boy who drives through a mysterious tollbooth and enters the Kingdom of Wisdom. There he meets Tock, a watchdog with a clock in his body, and discovers that the princesses Rhyme and Reason have been imprisoned in the Mountains of Ignorance. Milo sets out to rescue them, facing obstacles such as the Terrible Trivium, a demon who distracts people with pointless tasks. The novel turns ideas into characters and places: for example, a request for a “short sentence” is answered with the words “I am.” Milo’s adventure shows how curiosity can make the world more interesting.

Dubliners is a 1914 collection of short stories by Irish writer James Joyce. Set in early twentieth-century Dublin, it portrays ordinary people whose routines, fears, and social pressures often leave them feeling stuck, a condition Joyce called paralysis. The stories are arranged to move through four stages of life: childhood, adolescence, maturity, and public life. The collection ends with “The Dead,” which follows Gabriel Conroy at the Morkan sisters’ annual dance. When a guest sings “The Lass of Aughrim,” Gabriel’s wife, Gretta, remembers Michael Furey, a young man who loved her and died years before. Gabriel’s reflections lead to the story’s famous closing image of snow falling across Ireland. Joyce later wrote the novel Ulysses, which also explores life in Dublin.

A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning is a poem by John Donne, an English poet known for metaphysical poetry, which uses surprising comparisons to explore ideas such as love and faith. A “valediction” is a farewell, and the speaker asks his beloved not to mourn openly when they part: “let us melt, and make no noise.” He believes their love is more than physical closeness, so distance cannot break their bond. Donne compares the lovers to the two legs of a drawing compass. One leg stays fixed while the other travels, yet they remain joined; the fixed leg leans toward the moving one and helps bring it home. Donne also wrote “The Flea” and the Holy Sonnet “Death, be not proud.” He later became Dean of St Paul’s Cathedral in London.

Constantine Cavafy was a Greek poet who lived in Alexandria, Egypt, and wrote in modern Greek. His poems often draw on ancient history and mythology while exploring questions about hope, disappointment, and what gives life meaning. In “Ithaka,” inspired by Odysseus’s journey home in the ancient Greek epic The Odyssey, the speaker urges the traveler to “hope your road is a long one.” The poem suggests that the experiences gained along the way matter more than reaching the destination quickly. In “Waiting for the Barbarians,” a city expects outsiders to arrive, but when they do not, its people wonder what they will do without them: the barbarians had seemed “a kind of solution.” Cavafy’s language, Greek, also has an ancient form in which Sophocles wrote Oedipus Rex.

The Call of the Wild is a 1903 adventure novel by American author Jack London, who also wrote White Fang. Its main character, Buck, begins life as a comfortable household dog in California. After he is kidnapped and sold, he is taken north to work as a sled dog during the Klondike Gold Rush, when dogs hauled people and supplies through the cold. Buck passes through the hands of several owners and must learn to survive harsh weather, exhausting work, and fights with other dogs. As he becomes stronger and more independent, he feels an increasing pull toward life in the wild. London drew on his own experiences in the Klondike to portray the northern setting, including Alaska, where part of Buck’s journey takes place.

A Series of Unfortunate Events is a thirteen-novel children’s series by Lemony Snicket about Violet, Klaus, and Sunny Baudelaire. After a fire destroys their home and kills their parents, the three children become orphans and are sent to live with different guardians. Their chief enemy is Count Olaf, a theatrical villain who wants to steal their family fortune. Olaf repeatedly disguises himself to get close to the children; in The Reptile Room, he poses as an assistant named Stephano. The series begins with The Bad Beginning and follows the siblings as they use Violet’s inventing skills, Klaus’s love of reading, and Sunny’s sharp teeth and growing abilities to survive danger and uncover secrets connected to their parents and the mysterious organization V.F.D.

Alan Paton was a South African writer and opponent of apartheid, the system of racial segregation enforced in South Africa. His 1948 debut novel, Cry, the Beloved Country, became internationally known for showing how racial injustice and poverty affected families and communities. Its main character, Stephen Kumalo, is a Zulu Anglican pastor from the rural area near Ixopo. After receiving troubling news about his family, Kumalo travels to Johannesburg to search for his son Absalom and his sister Gertrude. He discovers that Absalom is accused of killing Arthur Jarvis, a white man who had worked for racial justice. Through Kumalo’s journey, Paton explores grief, forgiveness, and the divisions in South African society. Paton later helped found South Africa’s Liberal Party and continued to speak out against apartheid.

A bard is a poet and storyteller who performs inherited stories and helps preserve them for future generations. In oral traditions, bards passed on poems, genealogies (records of family ancestry), and historical tales by speaking or singing them, sometimes with musical accompaniment. They could use repeated phrases and familiar patterns to help remember long works. Bards are especially associated with Celtic traditions and are similar to the griots who have preserved and performed West African epics such as the Epic of Sundiata. Shakespeare’s nickname, the “Bard of Avon,” reflects his fame as a poet and playwright. The ancient Greek poet Homer is traditionally credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, but scholars debate whether those epics were created by one poet or developed through generations of oral storytelling.

In H.G. Wells’s science-fiction novel The Time Machine, the Time Traveller journeys to a distant future where humanity has split into two groups. The Morlocks are pale people who live underground beneath the ruins of London, tending machinery and coming to the surface at night. Aboveground live the Eloi, a gentle, childlike people who are physically weak and largely unaware of the danger below them. The Morlocks hunt the Eloi for food, reversing the Time Traveller’s first impression that the pleasant world aboveground is peaceful. One Eloi, Weena, becomes his companion after he rescues her from drowning. The contrast between the two groups helps Wells explore how divisions between rich and poor might shape humanity’s future.

“The Zahir” is a short story by the Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges, who also wrote “The Aleph” and “Funes the Memorious.” Set in Buenos Aires, it is told by a fictionalized version of Borges. After attending a funeral, the narrator receives a coin as change. At first, it seems ordinary, but he finds himself thinking about it more and more. He tries to get rid of the coin, yet its image remains in his mind and begins to crowd out his other thoughts. The story explores obsession: how can one small object come to dominate a person’s attention until the rest of the world seems to fade? Borges leaves readers wondering whether the coin has a mysterious power or whether the narrator’s own mind gives it that power.

Horace Smith’s “Ozymandias” was published in The Examiner in 1818 as part of a friendly poetry competition with Percy Bysshe Shelley, who wrote a more famous poem with the same title. Ozymandias is a Greek name for an ancient Egyptian ruler, and both poems explore how even great power can disappear with time. Smith describes the ruins of a vanished Egyptian civilization, then imagines a future hunter finding fragments where London once stood. The hunter might wonder what “powerful but unrecorded race” lived in that “annihilated place.” By linking ancient Egypt with a possible future London, Smith suggests that no civilization, however impressive it seems to its people, is guaranteed to be remembered forever.

A ghazal is a lyric poem made of couplets, or pairs of lines, that share a mood but can often stand on their own. It commonly explores longing for an unattainable beloved, though that beloved may also represent a spiritual connection. The form originated in Arabic poetry and became especially important in Persian and Urdu literature. Ghazals often use repeated words or phrases and a pattern of rhyme; in the final couplet, the poet may include a pen name. Rumi, a 13th-century Persian poet and mystic, wrote thousands of ghazals collected in his Divan-e Shams, named for Shams of Tabriz, who deeply influenced him. Ghazals are also performed in South Asian musical traditions.

Atticus Finch is a widowed lawyer in Harper Lee’s 1960 novel To Kill a Mockingbird. He lives in the fictional town of Maycomb, Alabama, and raises his two children, Jem and Scout. Scout narrates the story, which follows the family as Atticus defends Tom Robinson, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman from the Ewell family. Although many townspeople judge Tom unfairly because of his race, Atticus works to give him a fair defense. He also teaches Scout to consider other people’s points of view, telling her that she cannot truly understand someone until she imagines walking around in that person’s skin. Through Atticus and Tom’s trial, the novel explores prejudice, justice, and the courage to stand up for what is right.

Phoebe Caulfield is Holden Caulfield’s younger sister in J.D. Salinger’s novel The Catcher in the Rye. After Holden is expelled from his school, Pencey Prep, he wanders around New York City feeling lonely and frustrated. Phoebe is intelligent, perceptive, and affectionate, and she is one of the few people who understands him and listens to what he is going through. Holden buys her a “Little Shirley Beans” record, showing how much he cares about her, though the record breaks before he can give it to her. Near the end of the novel, Phoebe rides a carousel in Central Park while Holden watches. Central Park is the long, narrow green space that runs through the middle of Manhattan and includes the Central Park Zoo.

The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is a narrative poem by the British Romantic writer Samuel Taylor Coleridge. An old sailor stops a Wedding Guest and tells him about a disastrous voyage. When the ship is trapped among fog and ice, an albatross appears and seems to bring good luck. The mariner shoots the seabird with his crossbow, and his crew faces a supernatural curse. Their ship becomes becalmed, leaving them desperately thirsty despite being surrounded by seawater: “Water, water, everywhere, nor any drop to drink.” Death and Life-in-Death play dice for the sailors’ fates, and the mariner survives to suffer guilt and tell his story. The poem explores humanity’s relationship with nature, the consequences of a thoughtless act, and the possibility of spiritual change.

The Bluest Eye is the first novel by American writer Toni Morrison, published in 1970. It follows Pecola Breedlove, a Black girl growing up in Ohio who wishes for blue eyes because she has come to believe that blue eyes would make her beautiful and loved. Through Pecola’s experiences, Morrison shows how racism and narrow beauty standards can damage a person’s sense of self. The novel opens with words from a “Dick and Jane” reading book, presenting an idealized white family; increasingly fragmented versions of the passage also appear as chapter headings, contrasting that image with Pecola’s life. Morrison later won the Pulitzer Prize for her novel Beloved and the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Katherine Mansfield was a New Zealand modernist writer best known for her short stories. She was born in Wellington, New Zealand, in 1888 and often drew on memories of her childhood there. Rather than relying on dramatic plots, her stories explore characters’ feelings and the small moments that change how they see their lives. In “Bliss,” Bertha Young feels overwhelming happiness, which is associated with a flowering pear tree. Mansfield also wrote “Prelude,” about family life, and “How Pearl Button Was Kidnapped,” in which two Māori women take a young girl to see the sea. Māori are the Indigenous people of New Zealand, also called Aotearoa. Mansfield’s attention to shifting emotions and points of view helped make her an important figure in modernist literature.

Elizabeth Bishop was an American poet known for precise descriptions and poems about travel, memory, and loss. In “One Art,” a villanelle, the speaker repeats the claim that “the art of losing isn’t hard to master,” even as the losses she describes become increasingly painful. In “Crusoe in England,” Bishop uses a dramatic monologue: the poem is spoken by a character rather than by the poet herself. Its speaker is Robinson Crusoe, the castaway from Daniel Defoe’s novel. After spending twenty-eight years stranded on an island with his companion Friday, Crusoe has returned to England and looks back on his life there. By giving this familiar character a reflective voice, Bishop explores loneliness and the difficulty of leaving a place behind.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge was an English Romantic poet who explored imagination, nature, and the supernatural. In “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” a sailor stops a wedding guest to tell him how he shot an albatross and then suffered terrifying consequences. The poem includes the famous lines “Water, water, everywhere / Nor any drop to drink.” Coleridge also wrote the unfinished “Kubla Khan,” a dreamlike vision of a pleasure dome in Xanadu that he said came to him in a dream influenced by opium, a drug made from poppies. In 1798, he and fellow poet William Wordsworth published Lyrical Ballads, a landmark collection often linked to the beginning of British Romanticism. Wordsworth also wrote “Tintern Abbey” and “I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud.”

Inherit the Wind is a stage play by Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee that reimagines the 1925 Scopes trial, a court case about teaching evolution in Tennessee. In the play, schoolteacher Bertram Cates is prosecuted for teaching Darwin’s theory of evolution, and defense attorney Henry Drummond argues his case. Cates is a fictional counterpart of John T. Scopes, the real high-school science teacher charged in 1925. The courtroom conflict sets religious beliefs against scientific ideas and asks whether people should be free to think and question for themselves. The title echoes a passage from the Bible’s Book of Proverbs. Although the play draws on a real trial, its characters and dialogue are fictionalized rather than a historical record.

The Song of Roland is a medieval French epic poem about Roland, a knight in the army of Charlemagne, king of the Franks. On the army’s return from Spain, Roland commands the rearguard through the Roncevaux Pass. A Frankish baron named Ganelon betrays him by conspiring with the Saracen ruler Marsile to arrange an ambush. Roland fights bravely and sounds his ivory horn to summon Charlemagne, but he dies before help arrives. The poem turns a real defeat at Roncevaux, where Charlemagne’s rearguard was attacked by Basques, into a dramatic story of loyalty, courage, and treachery. After Ganelon’s betrayal is proved through a trial by combat, he is executed by being drawn and quartered.

“maggie and milly and molly and may” is a short poem by the American poet E. E. Cummings, who also wrote “anyone lived in a pretty how town.” It follows four girls on a trip to the beach, where each has a different encounter with the sea. Maggie finds a singing shell, Milly befriends a stranded starfish, Molly is chased by a bubble-blowing creature, and May brings home a smooth round stone. These discoveries suggest that people can experience the same place in very different ways. The poem ends by saying that “it’s always ourselves we find in the sea,” inviting readers to think about what each girl’s discovery reveals about her. Cummings’s use of lowercase letters, even for the girls’ names, is a distinctive feature of his writing.

In Emily Dickinson’s poem “Because I could not stop for Death—,” Death is personified as a courteous visitor who “kindly stopped” for the speaker when she could not pause for him. He takes her on a slow carriage ride past a school where children play, fields of grain, and the setting sun. These scenes suggest the passage through life and toward its end. The first stanza also names a third passenger: Immortality, the idea of living forever. Its presence hints that death may lead to an existence beyond earthly life. Rather than portraying Death as a frightening figure, Dickinson presents him as a calm companion, making the journey feel both polite and mysterious.

Tony Kushner is an American playwright known for plays that connect personal lives with major political and historical events. His two-part drama Angels in America is set during the AIDS epidemic in the 1980s. Prior Walter receives an AIDS diagnosis and has visions of an angel, while the powerful lawyer Roy Cohn faces his own illness. Through these characters, Kushner explores fear, identity, illness, and the ways people care for or abandon one another. Kushner also wrote A Bright Room Called Day, which follows Agnes Eggling, an actress in Berlin, as the Nazis rise to power in Germany. Later scenes feature contemporary Americans debating political responsibility. By moving between past and present, the play asks how people should respond when they see injustice growing around them.

“The Negro Speaks of Rivers” is a poem by Langston Hughes that connects African-American history and identity to rivers across the world. Its speaker says, “I’ve known rivers,” then remembers bathing in the Euphrates and hearing the Mississippi sing. The rivers are “ancient as the world,” suggesting a connection between the speaker, human history, and generations of people who came before him. Hughes links places in Africa and the Americas, giving the speaker a voice that reaches across time. Hughes was a major poet of the Harlem Renaissance, a 1920s flowering of African-American art and writing centered in New York City’s Harlem neighborhood. He also wrote “Harlem,” which asks what happens to a dream deferred, and published the poetry collection The Weary Blues.

Dr. Pangloss is a philosopher and tutor to the main character in Candide, a satirical work by the French Enlightenment writer Voltaire. Published with the subtitle “Optimism,” Candide follows a young man through wars, disasters, and other hardships. Pangloss repeatedly argues that they live in “the best of all possible worlds,” even after an earthquake and fire destroy Lisbon. His confidence seems increasingly absurd when compared with the suffering around him. Voltaire uses Pangloss to make fun of an overly simple kind of optimism: the belief that everything must happen for the best, no matter how terrible it appears. As Candide gains experience, he begins to question his tutor’s teachings. Remember that Pangloss is the philosopher, while Candide is both his student and the title of the work.

And the Band Played On is a 1987 nonfiction book by journalist Randy Shilts about the early years of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in the United States. Shilts describes how the disease spread, how scientists worked to understand it, and how fear and prejudice affected people with AIDS. The book also examines the actions of public health agencies, the media, and political leaders. It argues that delays and a lack of urgency made the crisis worse. Shilts is especially critical of the federal government’s slow response under President Ronald Reagan, a Republican who served two terms from 1981 to 1989. The book remains an important account of both the epidemic and the social and political decisions that shaped the response to it.

“The Ransom of Red Chief” is a comic short story by the American writer O. Henry, the pen name of William Sydney Porter. In the story, two men kidnap a boy from Summit, Alabama, hoping to collect a ransom from his father, Ebenezer Dorset. The boy calls himself “Red Chief” and turns the tables on his captors with nonstop games and rough make-believe. Exhausted by his behavior, the kidnappers end up offering Dorset money to take his son back. This reversal makes the attempted crime a joke at the kidnappers’ expense. O. Henry is also known for “The Cop and the Anthem,” about a homeless man named Soapy who tries to get arrested to escape the cold, and “The Gift of the Magi,” about a young married couple.

Tess of the d’Urbervilles is an 1891 novel by the English writer Thomas Hardy, who also wrote The Return of the Native and the poem “The Darkling Thrush.” Its main character, Tess Durbeyfield, comes from a poor family that believes it is descended from the aristocratic d’Urbervilles. Hoping to benefit from this connection, her family sends her to meet Alec d’Urberville, who sexually assaults her. Later, Tess works as a milkmaid at Talbothays Dairy and falls in love with Angel Clare. Their marriage is troubled when Angel learns about her past. After Tess kills Alec at the seaside resort of Sandbourne, she briefly reunites with Angel, but the authorities capture her at Stonehenge and she is executed. Hardy uses her story to question Victorian judgments about women, class, and morality.

Light in August is a 1932 novel by American writer William Faulkner. It takes place partly in Yoknapatawpha County, the fictional Mississippi setting Faulkner used in many of his books. The novel follows two contrasting journeys. Joe Christmas, an itinerant worker and bootlegger troubled by uncertainty about his ancestry, kills Joanna Burden, and her house is later burned. Meanwhile, Lena Grove travels through Mississippi while pregnant, hoping to find Lucas Burch, the father of her child. Their stories bring questions of identity, race, religion, and belonging into focus. Faulkner also wrote The Sound and the Fury and As I Lay Dying, both set in the American South.

Death, the end of life, is a major subject in poetry because it raises questions about memory, loss, and what may happen afterward. In Emily Dickinson’s “Because I could not stop for Death,” Death is personified as a courteous visitor who stops for the speaker and takes her on a carriage ride. They pass a school, fields, and the setting sun before reaching a grave, suggesting a journey through life toward its end. A. E. Housman’s “To an Athlete Dying Young” focuses on how a person is remembered after death. A champion runner is carried shoulder-high in his coffin, just as townspeople once carried him in celebration after he won their race. The repeated image makes the poem’s contrast between triumph and loss especially striking.

Gaius Valerius Catullus was a Roman lyric poet who wrote in Latin during the late Roman Republic. His poems often focus on love, friendship, jealousy, and sharp personal attacks. Many address a woman he calls Lesbia; poems 2 and 3 describe her pet sparrow and mourn its death. In another poem, Catullus attacks two critics named Aurelius and Furius. He also drew on earlier Greek poetry. His poem 51 reworks a poem by Sappho, a lyric poet from the island of Lesbos who was sometimes called the “tenth muse.” Both poems describe the speaker’s overwhelming physical reactions while watching a beloved person converse with someone else. Catullus’s full name was Gaius Valerius Catullus.

Faust is a legendary German scholar who longs for knowledge and power beyond what ordinary learning can provide. He becomes the subject of major dramas by the English playwright Christopher Marlowe and the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. In these works, Faust bargains with a demonic tempter named Mephistopheles, who offers him extraordinary experiences and magical power. The details of their pact differ between versions, but Faust’s desire for forbidden knowledge drives the story in each. His legend raises questions about ambition, temptation, and what a person might sacrifice to get what they want. If you see the name Doctor Faustus, it refers to the same legendary figure.

Holes is a 1998 novel by Louis Sachar about Stanley Yelnats, a boy sent to the desert juvenile detention camp called Camp Green Lake. Although the camp’s leaders claim that digging a hole every day builds character, Stanley discovers that they are really searching for buried treasure. The story moves between Stanley’s experiences, a supposed curse on his family, and the history of Green Lake. Years earlier, a schoolteacher named Katherine Barlow fell in love with Sam. After Sam was murdered, she became the outlaw known as Kissin’ Kate Barlow and buried her stolen fortune. A lipstick tube found in one of the holes provides a clue to it. Stanley eventually helps his friend Hector Zeroni, also called Zero, by carrying him up a mountain, an act that breaks the family curse.

Brobdingnag is the land of giants that Lemuel Gulliver visits in the second part of Jonathan Swift’s satirical novel Gulliver’s Travels. Unlike in Lilliput, where Gulliver towers over the inhabitants, in Brobdingnag he is tiny by comparison. A farmer finds him and exhibits him for money as a curiosity. The farmer’s young daughter, Glumdalclitch, looks after Gulliver and protects him; he calls her his “little nurse,” though she is enormous to him. When Gulliver is taken to the royal court, Glumdalclitch goes with him and continues to care for him. By reversing Gulliver’s size and status, Swift makes him vulnerable and invites readers to think about how people treat those who seem different or powerless.

The House of the Spirits is Isabel Allende’s debut novel. It follows several generations of the Trueba family through love, conflict, and political upheaval in an unnamed Latin American country. The story blends ordinary family life with supernatural events, a style often called magical realism. One of its central characters is Clara del Valle, who marries Esteban Trueba after remaining silent for nine years. Clara can foresee events and move objects with her mind, abilities known as clairvoyance and telekinesis. She also keeps notebooks recording her family’s experiences. Those notebooks help later generations piece together their history as the country changes around them. Through Clara and the Truebas, Allende connects private family memories with wider social and political events.

A Bend in the River is a 1979 novel by V. S. Naipaul. Its narrator and protagonist, Salim, is a merchant who leaves his coastal home to run a shop in an inland town beside a river in an unnamed, newly independent African country. He hopes the move will give him a fresh start, but the country is changing rapidly. Salim watches as the ruler known as the Big Man gains power and his authoritarian regime reshapes everyday life. Through Salim’s experiences as a trader and an outsider, the novel explores political upheaval, uncertainty after colonial rule, and the struggle to find a place in a changing society.

Literary realism is a movement and style that aims to show life as it is rather than as an idealized adventure. Realist writers focus on ordinary characters, recognizable social settings, and plausible events, using concrete details to explore how people behave and how society affects them. Instead of relying on perfect heroes or supernatural explanations, they make familiar experiences feel believable. Magical realism is a related mode that keeps this close attention to everyday life but includes fantastic or supernatural events as if they were ordinary. In stories by Gabriel García Márquez, for example, remarkable happenings appear alongside detailed descriptions of communities and daily routines. The key difference is that literary realism portrays a believable world without magic, while magical realism makes magic part of that world.

Wallace Stevens’s poem “The Snow Man” explores how we see the natural world and how our feelings can shape what we think is there. It opens, “One must have a mind of winter,” to regard the frost and the boughs of pine trees. That phrase describes the calm, detached attitude needed to look at a cold landscape without imagining that it shares human sadness. As the poem continues, a listener hears the wind among the bare trees without treating its sound as a voice of misery. At the end, the listener is “nothing himself” and perceives both “nothing that is not there” and “the nothing that is.” Stevens asks whether we can observe winter as it is, rather than filling its emptiness with our own emotions.

Amanda Gorman is an American poet and activist who became the first U.S. National Youth Poet Laureate in 2017. The title recognizes a young poet whose writing and public work help engage people across the country. Gorman often writes about identity, justice, and the possibility of change. At President Joe Biden’s inauguration in January 2021, she recited her original poem “The Hill We Climb.” Written at a time of deep political division, the poem acknowledges the country’s difficulties while urging Americans to work toward unity and a more hopeful future. Her performance brought poetry to a huge national audience and made her one of the best-known young poets in the United States.

The Goose Girl is a fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm in their Children’s and Household Tales. A princess travels to another kingdom to marry a prince, accompanied by her maid and her talking horse, Falada. Along the way, the maid forces the princess to exchange clothes and identities with her. At the palace, the maid pretends to be the bride, while the real princess is sent to herd geese with a boy named Conrad. The false bride has Falada killed, but his severed head is hung beneath a gateway and still speaks. Each day, as the princess passes, she says, “Falada, Falada, thou art dead,” and he answers her. Their strange exchange helps the king uncover the deception and restore the princess’s identity.

Jean de La Fontaine was a 17th-century French poet who published the first collection of his verse Fables in 1668. He adapted stories from Aesop and other earlier traditions, retelling them as poems with lively animal characters. A fable is a short story that teaches a lesson, or moral, about human behavior. In La Fontaine’s “The Crow and the Fox,” a crow sits in a tree holding a piece of food in its beak. A fox praises the crow’s appearance and asks to hear it sing. When the crow opens its beak, the food falls, and the fox takes it. The story warns readers not to be fooled by flattery.

Thomas Pynchon is an American novelist known for complex, playful stories and for keeping his life out of the public eye. His writing is often called postmodern because it mixes different styles, questions what is real, and follows characters searching for meaning in a confusing world. In his shorter novel The Crying of Lot 49, a woman investigates clues that may point to a secret postal network. His sprawling 1973 novel Gravity’s Rainbow is set largely in Europe near the end of World War II. One of its characters, former U.S. Army lieutenant Tyrone Slothrop, discovers that the places where he has had sexual encounters seem to match the locations of V-2 rocket impacts. That strange pattern helps drive the novel’s mysteries.

The Iceman Cometh is a drama by American playwright Eugene O’Neill, who also wrote Long Day’s Journey into Night and Mourning Becomes Electra. Set in Harry Hope’s Greenwich Village saloon, it follows a group of regulars who spend their days drinking and clinging to “pipe dreams”—comforting hopes that keep them from facing their unhappy lives. Their routine is disrupted when a traveling salesman named Hickey arrives and urges them to give up those dreams and confront reality. Hickey claims that doing so has brought him peace, but he eventually reveals that he murdered his wife, Evelyn, and asks to be sent to the electric chair. The play explores whether people can live without the hopes they use to comfort themselves.

The Awakening is an 1899 novel by Kate Chopin, a Louisiana-born writer who also wrote the short stories “The Story of an Hour” and “Désirée’s Baby.” Its main character, Edna Pontellier, is a married mother living in New Orleans. As she becomes more aware of her own desires and ambitions, Edna begins to question the expectation that she devote her life entirely to her husband and children. Her growing independence puts her at odds with the social rules of her time, especially those governing women’s behavior. Edna also develops feelings for Robert Lebrun, but their relationship cannot give her the freedom she seeks. The novel ends with Edna drowning in the Gulf of Mexico. Its title refers to her awakening to her own identity and wishes.

Elizabeth Barrett Browning was a major Victorian English poet whose writing explored love, social injustice, and women’s lives. She wrote the verse novel Aurora Leigh and the 44-poem love sequence Sonnets from the Portuguese, published in 1850. The sonnets grew out of poems she had privately given to fellow poet Robert Browning during their courtship. The couple married and settled in Italy. Despite its title, Sonnets from the Portuguese was written in English; “Portuguese” was a nickname Robert used for Elizabeth. Its best-known poem begins “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways,” then describes love in everyday life and in the speaker’s deepest feelings. The sequence remains one of the best-known expressions of love in Victorian poetry.

Octavio Paz was a Mexican poet and essayist who wrote in Spanish and explored questions of identity, history, and human experience. In his essay collection The Labyrinth of Solitude, he examined what it means to be Mexican, considering the country’s culture and past. His long poem Sunstone has 584 lines, a number linked to the cycle of Venus, and uses vivid images to explore love, time, and connection. Paz’s writing reached readers far beyond Mexico. In 1990, he became the first Mexican writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. The award honored his passionate writing, which the Nobel committee described as having “wide horizons” and “sensuous intelligence.”

Emily Brontë was a nineteenth-century English novelist and poet whose only novel, Wuthering Heights, was published in 1847 under the pseudonym Ellis Bell. She used a male pen name at a time when women writers often faced prejudice. The novel is set on the windswept Yorkshire moors and follows the intense, destructive bond between Catherine Earnshaw and Heathcliff. Heathcliff is a foundling brought to live with Catherine’s family at Wuthering Heights. The two grow deeply attached, but Catherine chooses to marry someone else. Heathcliff disappears for several years, then returns wealthy and determined to take revenge on those he believes wronged him. Brontë’s novel explores love, cruelty, class, and the lasting effects of revenge.

Katniss Everdeen is the protagonist of Suzanne Collins’s dystopian Hunger Games trilogy. A skilled archer from the impoverished District 12, she volunteers to take her younger sister Prim’s place in the Hunger Games, a televised contest in which teenagers are forced to fight to the death. Her fellow District 12 tribute is Peeta Mellark, a baker’s son who once secretly gave Katniss bread when her family was struggling. Peeta’s talent for camouflage later helps him hide from opponents in the arena. Katniss earns the nickname “the Girl on Fire” and becomes known as the Mockingjay, a symbol of rebellion against the Capitol. Her compassion also sets her apart: after Rue dies, Katniss sings to her and covers her body with flowers.

Margaret Mitchell was an American novelist born in Atlanta, Georgia, in 1900. Before becoming famous, she worked as a reporter for the Atlanta Journal. Her only published novel, Gone with the Wind, became a major bestseller and was adapted into a 1939 film. Set in Georgia during the Civil War and Reconstruction, the story follows Scarlett O’Hara as she struggles to survive and save her family’s plantation, Tara. Other important characters include Ashley Wilkes and Rhett Butler. The novel ends with Scarlett’s famous thought, “After all, tomorrow is another day.” Although it is a well-known work of historical fiction, its romanticized picture of the antebellum South and its portrayal of slavery and race have drawn criticism.

The Prelude is a long autobiographical poem by the English Romantic poet William Wordsworth. Subtitled “Growth of a Poet’s Mind,” it traces how his experiences, especially in nature, shaped his imagination and ideas from childhood into adulthood. Wordsworth intended it as an introduction to a larger philosophical poem called The Recluse, which explains the title The Prelude. He worked with Samuel Taylor Coleridge on the influential collection Lyrical Ballads, which includes Coleridge’s The Rime of the Ancient Mariner. Wordsworth also wrote “Tintern Abbey,” a poem reflecting on his return to the Wye Valley with his sister Dorothy. Like The Prelude, it explores how memories of nature can influence a person’s thoughts and feelings.

Wole Soyinka is a Nigerian playwright, novelist, and poet who became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986. His comedy The Lion and the Jewel is set in the village of Ilujinle, where Lakunle, a schoolteacher who favors Western ideas, and Baroka, a traditional village elder, both want to marry Sidi, the village beauty. Their rivalry explores the tension between modernity and local traditions. Soyinka’s tragedy Death and the King’s Horseman centers on Elesin Oba, who is expected to die by suicide after the king’s death as part of a ritual duty, but whose plans are disrupted by British colonial authorities. Through these plays, Soyinka examines how people respond to social expectations, cultural change, and colonial rule.

Ficciones is a 1944 collection of short stories by the Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges. It brings together two earlier groups of stories, El jardín de senderos que se bifurcan and Artificios, and uses puzzles, imaginary worlds, and philosophical questions to explore ideas about knowledge, time, and reality. In “The Library of Babel,” the universe is an apparently endless library of hexagonal chambers. Its books contain every possible combination of letters, so they include both meaningful texts and vast amounts of nonsense. Another story, “The Garden of Forking Paths,” connects a labyrinthine Chinese garden with the idea that time can branch into different possibilities. Borges’s unusual settings make abstract questions feel like mysteries that readers can explore.

Boule de Suif is a short story by French writer Guy de Maupassant set during the Franco-Prussian War. A mixed group of French passengers flees the occupied city of Rouen by coach. Among them is Élisabeth Rousset, a prostitute nicknamed Boule de Suif, or “Ball of Fat.” She generously shares her food with the others, but when a Prussian officer refuses to let the coach continue unless she sleeps with him, the supposedly respectable passengers pressure her to give in. After she does, they shun her, exposing their selfishness and hypocrisy. Another passenger, Cornudet, is a radical democrat who repeatedly whistles “La Marseillaise,” the French national anthem, while the group is delayed.

Troilus and Cressida is a play by William Shakespeare set during the Trojan War. It follows Troilus, a Trojan prince, as he falls in love with Cressida, the daughter of the priest Calchas. Cressida’s uncle, Pandarus, helps bring the two together: he arranges a secret meeting and urges Cressida toward Troilus when they meet. Their relationship does not last. After Cressida is sent to the Greek camp, Troilus sees her with another man and feels betrayed. The play is often called a “problem play” because it mixes romance, comedy, and tragedy without offering a simple moral or a happy ending. Shakespeare drew on earlier versions of the story, including Geoffrey Chaucer’s poem Troilus and Criseyde, which uses a different spelling of Cressida’s name.

“Tomorrow, at Dawn” is a lyric poem by the French writer Victor Hugo, also known for the novel Les Misérables. It is an elegy, a poem of mourning, written for his daughter Léopoldine Hugo. In 1843, Léopoldine and her husband, Charles Vacquerie, drowned near Villequier when their boat overturned. In the poem, the speaker vows to leave at first light and walk alone to her grave. Though he passes through a landscape at sunrise, he is so absorbed in grief that he will not look at the scenery or “the gold of evening.” The poem ends quietly: he reaches the grave and lays down a bouquet of green holly and flowering heather. That simple gesture makes his love and loss especially moving.

Anne Bradstreet was a 17th-century poet born in England who moved to the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Her collection The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America was published in 1650, making her one of the first poets in colonial America to have a book published. She wrote about family, faith, and the challenges of colonial life, as well as women’s ability to think and write. In one poem, she rebuked men who belittled women, noting that doing so during Queen Elizabeth I’s reign would have been considered treason. Bradstreet’s “To My Dear and Loving Husband” begins, “If ever two were one, then surely we.” In it, the speaker says she values her husband’s love more than riches.

Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird is a poem by the American modernist poet Wallace Stevens. It has thirteen brief, numbered sections, each presenting a different scene or way of seeing a blackbird. In one section, the bird “whirled in the autumn winds,” becoming “a small part of the pantomime.” The opening section notices a blackbird’s moving eye among twenty snowy mountains, while the final section places a blackbird in cedar limbs as snow falls. Rather than telling one continuous story, the poem moves between images and ideas. Its changing views suggest that what we notice, think, and feel can shape our understanding of the world.

The Gold-Bug is an 1843 mystery and adventure short story by American writer Edgar Allan Poe. Its central character, William Legrand, is an impoverished former Charleston resident who lives on Sullivan’s Island, South Carolina. After finding a strange gold-colored beetle, Legrand becomes involved in a search for treasure linked to the pirate Captain Kidd. A drawing of the beetle helps reveal a hidden message, and Legrand deciphers its cryptogram to work out where the treasure is buried. His friend, who narrates the story, and his servant Jupiter join him in the search. The story combines a treasure hunt with a puzzle: its mystery is solved through Legrand’s careful observation and code-breaking, rather than luck alone.

Life on the Mississippi is an 1883 memoir and travel narrative by American writer Mark Twain. It recounts his experiences learning to pilot a steamboat on the Mississippi River, the great North American river that flows past St. Louis and New Orleans. A pilot had to know the river’s changing channels, currents, and hazards well enough to guide a vessel safely. Twain combines memories of his training with observations of river travel and the communities along its banks. Steamboats transformed nineteenth-century river transportation because steam engines powered by heated water could move boats without relying on wind or human muscle. Their development drew on improvements to James Watt’s steam-engine designs, and Robert Fulton’s Clermont became an early commercially successful example.

Children’s literature is writing created mainly for children, from picture books for beginning readers to longer stories for older children and young teens. Picture books often use illustrations to help tell the story, while novels can explore more complex characters and ideas. Eric Carle’s The Very Hungry Caterpillar is a picture book about a small larva that eats its way through different foods over a week before becoming a butterfly. Holes in its pages show where the caterpillar has eaten. Neil Gaiman’s Coraline is a longer, darker story about a girl who discovers a sinister parallel version of her home. Although these books are very different, both are examples of children’s literature because they are written for younger audiences.

Nick Carraway is the first-person narrator of F. Scott Fitzgerald’s novel The Great Gatsby, set during the Jazz Age of the 1920s. Originally from the Midwest and educated at Yale, Nick moves east to work as a bond salesman. He rents a modest house in West Egg, Long Island, next to the mansion of Jay Gatsby, a self-made millionaire known for his extravagant parties. Nick is also the cousin of Daisy Buchanan, whom Gatsby hopes to win back. The green light across the bay on Daisy’s dock becomes a symbol of Gatsby’s longing for her. As Nick witnesses the wealthy characters’ dishonesty and carelessness, he grows disillusioned with life in the East. After Gatsby’s death, Nick returns to the Midwest.

In F. Scott Fitzgerald’s novel The Great Gatsby, a faded billboard shows the enormous eyes of Dr. T. J. Eckleburg, a fictional optometrist, or eye doctor. His name is printed on the advertisement, and the eyes stare out from behind huge spectacles. The billboard stands over the Valley of Ashes, a bleak, gray industrial area between West Egg and New York City. Nick Carraway passes through this region when he travels toward the city; George Wilson runs a garage there. Although the billboard was meant to advertise an eye doctor, its watchful eyes have become one of the novel’s most memorable images. They can suggest that someone is watching the characters even as people around them ignore the poverty and suffering in the valley.

The Bell Jar is a semi-autobiographical novel by American poet Sylvia Plath, who also wrote the poems “Daddy” and “Lady Lazarus.” Its narrator, Esther Greenwood, spends a summer interning at a women’s magazine in New York City. Although the opportunity looks exciting, Esther feels increasingly disconnected from the life others expect her to want. She imagines her possible futures as figs on a tree, unable to choose one without losing the others. As she struggles with her ambitions, relationships, and the restrictive expectations placed on women, her mental health worsens. The novel’s title describes how depression can make Esther feel trapped and cut off from the world around her. Through Esther’s experience, Plath explores identity, illness, and the pressure to follow a prescribed path.

Interpreter of Maladies is Jhumpa Lahiri’s debut short-story collection, published in 1999 and awarded the 2000 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. Its stories explore family, marriage, loss, and the experience of living between Indian and American cultures. In “A Temporary Matter,” a Bengali American couple share painful revelations during scheduled power outages. In the title story, Mr. Kapasi works as a driver and interpreter for a doctor while guiding an Indian American family around India. Lahiri was born in London to Bengali parents and grew up in Rhode Island, experiences that helped shape her interest in identity and belonging. She later wrote the novels The Namesake and The Lowland.

Man and Superman is a four-act play by the Irish playwright George Bernard Shaw. Its central character, John Tanner, is a revolutionary thinker who has written The Revolutionist’s Handbook to explain his political ideas. The play mixes comedy with debates about love, freedom, and how people should live. In a dream sequence called “Don Juan in Hell,” Tanner appears as Don Juan and takes part in a philosophical conversation rather than a conventional scene of punishment. Shaw also wrote Pygmalion, a play about Professor Henry Higgins and his bet with Colonel Pickering that he can teach Eliza Doolittle to speak and behave well enough to pass as a duchess. Both plays use lively dialogue to explore ideas about society and human behavior.

Ender Wiggin, whose full name is Andrew Wiggin, is the young protagonist of Orson Scott Card’s science-fiction novel Ender’s Game. Chosen for his unusual intelligence and skill at strategy, he trains at Battle School, where children practice commanding teams in a weightless battle room. Ender teaches his soldiers to think differently about direction, reminding them that “the enemy’s gate is down.” He is put in charge of Dragon Army, a newly formed unit with younger-than-usual members. With gifted soldiers such as Bean, Dragon Army remains undefeated under his command. After Battle School, Ender trains with Mazer Rackham and commands what he believes are simulated campaigns against the alien Formics. He later discovers that the battles were real and that his decisions defeated them.

Gypsy Ballads is a poetry collection published in 1928 by Federico García Lorca, a poet born in Granada, Spain. Lorca reworks the Spanish romance, a traditional ballad form that tells stories in verse, using the landscapes and folklore of Andalusia, the region where he grew up. The poems mix vivid images of the moon, horses, and the color green with myths and stories about the lives of Romani people. One of the best-known poems, “Romance Sonámbulo,” repeats the refrain “green, how I want you green.” Lorca also wrote the play Blood Wedding and the elegy “Lament for Ignacio Sánchez Mejías,” about a bullfighter’s death. Together, these works show his interest in powerful emotions, symbolism, and tragedy.

If Beale Street Could Talk is a 1974 novel by African American writer James Baldwin. It is narrated by Tish, a young woman living in Harlem who is pregnant with her fiancé’s child. Her fiancé, Alonzo Hunt, is a sculptor known by the nickname Fonny. After Victoria Rogers identifies Fonny as the man who raped her, he is imprisoned, although he is innocent. Tish and her family work to clear his name and bring him home before the baby is born. Through their struggle, Baldwin shows how racism and an unfair justice system can threaten a family’s future. The novel also focuses on the love and determination that help Tish and Fonny face their separation.

The Unbearable Lightness of Being is a philosophical novel by Milan Kundera, a Czech-born writer from Brno who moved to France in 1975 after the Soviet-led crackdown on reform in Czechoslovakia. Set around the 1968 Prague Spring and the invasion that followed, the story follows Tomas, a surgeon; his wife, Tereza; Sabina, an artist; and Franz, a professor. Their relationships unfold as political repression disrupts their work and private lives. Kundera explores whether life feels “light” when people are free from lasting commitments or “heavy” when love, responsibility, and history give their choices weight. Through the characters’ different views of freedom and loyalty, the novel asks how people can find meaning when they have only one life to live.

Winston Smith is the main character of George Orwell’s dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four. He lives in Airstrip One, a province of Oceania, where the Party watches citizens closely and demands loyalty to its leader, Big Brother. Winston is an Outer Party employee at the Ministry of Truth, where he changes old records to match whatever the Party currently claims is true. Privately, he doubts the Party and begins keeping a forbidden diary. Julia, a fellow Outer Party member who works in the Fiction Department, secretly passes Winston a note saying “I love you.” They begin an affair and meet in a room above Mr. Charrington’s shop. Their rebellion is discovered, and Winston is tortured in Room 101, where he betrays Julia.

Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is an anonymous Middle English Arthurian romance about courage, honesty, and the difficulty of living up to a knight’s ideals. At King Arthur’s court, a mysterious green visitor challenges anyone to strike him with an axe, on the condition that he may return the blow in a year. Sir Gawain beheads him, but the Green Knight picks up his head and reminds Gawain of their bargain. On his journey to the remote Green Chapel, Gawain spends Christmas at the castle of Sir Bertilak, also called Hautdesert. There, Gawain and his host agree to exchange whatever each wins during three days. At the chapel, Gawain discovers that Sir Bertilak is the Green Knight. The poem uses alliteration, repeating sounds at the beginnings of stressed words.

Mustapha Mond is the World Controller for Western Europe in Aldous Huxley’s 1932 dystopian novel Brave New World. The World State divides people into biologically engineered castes—Alphas, Betas, Gammas, Deltas, and Epsilons—and conditions them to consume goods, avoid strong emotions, and use the drug soma to escape discomfort. When Mond meets John the Savage, who grew up outside this society, he explains why the government censors challenging books and ideas: it believes that freedom, great art, and deep personal relationships could threaten stability. Mond understands what has been lost but argues that social order is worth the sacrifice. John disagrees, insisting on “the right to be unhappy” rather than accepting a life controlled by the State.

Murasaki is an important character in The Tale of Genji, an 11th-century Japanese novel set among the aristocrats of the Heian-period court. As a child, she is taken into the household of Hikaru Genji, the “Shining Prince,” who raises her. She is the niece of Lady Fujitsubo, a woman Genji loves, and her resemblance to Fujitsubo helps explain his interest in her. Murasaki later becomes Genji’s principal companion and one of the most important people in his life. When she dies, he is overwhelmed by grief. Remembering the connection between Murasaki and Genji helps identify her character; remembering that their story appears in The Tale of Genji helps identify the novel.

Sinbad the Sailor is a legendary Baghdad adventurer whose tales are commonly associated with One Thousand and One Nights, also known as The Arabian Nights. After seven extraordinary voyages filled with shipwrecks, strange islands, and dangerous encounters, Sinbad returns home and recounts his adventures to a poor porter who shares his name. In one famous episode, a giant bird called a roc carries him out of a valley filled with diamonds. One Thousand and One Nights is a framed collection: its central story follows Scheherazade, who tells a new tale each night to postpone her execution. She stops at a suspenseful moment so the ruler will let her live to continue the story. The collection is also associated with tales of Aladdin and Ali Baba.

Othello is a tragedy by William Shakespeare set mainly in Venice and Cyprus. Its title character is a Moorish general serving Venice who has married Desdemona. His ensign, Iago, secretly plots against him and suggests that Desdemona is having an affair with Cassio, one of Othello’s officers. Iago warns Othello that jealousy is a “green-eyed monster,” even as he deliberately feeds it. When Desdemona loses a handkerchief Othello gave her, Iago arranges for it to appear in Cassio’s possession, making it seem like proof of an affair. Othello believes the lie and kills Desdemona. Iago’s wife, Emilia, then reveals how the handkerchief was used in the plot. Realizing that Desdemona was innocent, Othello takes his own life.

Renascence is the breakthrough poem by American poet Edna St. Vincent Millay. It opens with the speaker looking out at “three long mountains and a wood,” but her view soon seems to expand until she can take in the whole world. Feeling the weight of its suffering overwhelms her, and she imagines sinking into a grave. While lying there, she hears rain, which begins to draw her back to life. A gust of wind brings the scent of an orchard, and she says, “I breathed my soul back into me.” By the end, the speaker celebrates the many forms of beauty around her. The poem’s title suggests a rebirth: through rain, nature, and beauty, she finds a new way to face the world.

Walden; or, Life in the Woods is an 1854 book by Henry David Thoreau about his experiment in living simply beside Walden Pond in Massachusetts. Thoreau built a small cabin on land owned by his friend and mentor Ralph Waldo Emerson, a Concord essayist whose book Nature helped shape American Transcendentalism. In Walden’s opening chapter, “Economy,” Thoreau describes the practical necessities of life as food, shelter, clothing, and fuel. He also questions why people work so hard to gain things they may not need, observing that many “lead lives of quiet desperation.” By writing about his daily routines and the natural world around him, Thoreau encourages readers to think carefully about what matters and to make room for a simpler, more deliberate life.

Elizabeth Lavenza is a character in Mary Shelley’s Gothic novel Frankenstein, also titled Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. Raised in the Frankenstein household, Elizabeth grows up as Victor Frankenstein’s beloved companion and later marries him. Victor is a scientist from Geneva who studies at the University of Ingolstadt, where he creates a living being and then abandons it. Angry at Victor for rejecting him, the creature seeks revenge by killing people Victor loves. On Victor and Elizabeth’s wedding night, the creature murders Elizabeth, bringing their hoped-for happiness to a tragic end. Victor later tells his story to Robert Walton, an Arctic explorer whose letters frame the novel. Elizabeth’s fate shows how Victor’s choices harm those closest to him.

The Lord of the Rings is an epic fantasy novel by British author J. R. R. Tolkien, set in the imagined world of Middle-earth. It follows Frodo Baggins, a hobbit who leaves his peaceful home in the Shire carrying the One Ring. The Ring gives great power to the Dark Lord Sauron, so Frodo must take it to Mount Doom in Mordor, the only place it can be destroyed. Early in the journey, Frodo reaches Rivendell, an Elven refuge ruled by Elrond. There, Elrond holds a council where representatives of Middle-earth’s peoples decide that the Ring must be destroyed and form the Fellowship to help Frodo. Tolkien also wrote The Hobbit, which takes place earlier in the same world.

Snow Country is a novel by Yasunari Kawabata, a Japanese writer who received the 1968 Nobel Prize in Literature. First published in installments, it follows Shimamura, a detached visitor from Tokyo who studies ballet but has never seen a performance. On repeated trips to a remote hot-spring town in Japan’s snowy mountains, he becomes involved with Komako, a geisha whose feelings for him are much deeper than his for her. The novel uses a spare modernist style: rather than explaining every emotion, Kawabata lets brief conversations, striking images, and the wintry landscape suggest what the characters feel. The snow and isolation make the beauty of their encounters seem fragile and fleeting. Kawabata also wrote the novels The Sound of the Mountain and Thousand Cranes.

Jordan Baker is a character in F. Scott Fitzgerald’s 1925 novel The Great Gatsby. A friend of Daisy Buchanan, she is a competitive golfer and a flapper, a young woman whose fashionable clothes and independent behavior reflect the changing social rules of the 1920s. Jordan often seems cool and socially detached, rarely showing strong emotion about the people around her. Nick Carraway, the novel’s narrator, recalls a report that she moved her ball during a golf tournament, suggesting that she may have cheated. This incident contributes to her reputation for dishonesty. Through Jordan, Fitzgerald shows some of the glamour and carelessness of the wealthy world around Jay Gatsby, a Long Island host known for his lavish parties and his pursuit of Daisy.

The Aeneid is a Latin epic poem by the Roman poet Virgil. It follows Aeneas, a Trojan survivor who escapes the fall of Troy and leads other refugees across the Mediterranean in search of a new home. In Carthage, Queen Dido welcomes them and falls in love with Aeneas. He later leaves her to fulfill his destiny in Italy, and she dies on a funeral pyre. During his journey, Aeneas also enters the underworld, where he meets his father, Anchises, who shows him a vision of Rome’s future. In Italy, Aeneas fights Turnus and marries Lavinia. His son Ascanius later founds Alba Longa, a city linked to the legendary founders of Rome. The poem connects Aeneas’s adventures to Rome’s origins.

King Arthur is a legendary British ruler whose stories became popular in medieval romances. His court is often set at Camelot, where his knights gather at the Round Table, a symbol of their fellowship. Arthur is also associated with the sword Excalibur and with Queen Guinevere. One of his knights, Gawain, is the hero of the Middle English poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, in which he accepts the Green Knight’s strange challenge to a beheading game. Another important figure in Arthurian legend is Merlin, a prophetic enchanter who advises Arthur. In many versions of the story, Merlin arranges for the infant Arthur, the hidden heir to the throne, to be raised in the household of Sir Ector.

The Odd Couple is a 1965 comedy play by American playwright Neil Simon, who also wrote Barefoot in the Park and Plaza Suite. After his marriage breaks down, the anxious, neat Felix Ungar moves into the apartment of his friend Oscar Madison, a sportswriter whose messy habits are almost the opposite of Felix’s. Oscar’s regular poker games bring their friends into the apartment, where Felix’s fussiness and Oscar’s disorder soon lead to arguments. Much of the humor comes from watching two people who care about each other struggle to share a home. The play opened on Broadway and became one of Simon’s best-known works.

Pip, whose full name is Philip Pirrip, is the orphaned narrator and main character of Charles Dickens’s novel Great Expectations. Raised in Kent by his older sister, Mrs. Joe, and her kind husband, Joe Gargery, Pip dreams of becoming a gentleman after visiting the wealthy but reclusive Miss Havisham at Satis House. There he meets Estella, whom he loves, although she often treats him coldly. When Pip receives money from a secret benefactor, he moves to London for a gentleman’s education. He assumes Miss Havisham is supporting him, but later learns that his benefactor is Abel Magwitch, an escaped convict he helped as a child. Pip’s changing fortunes and mistaken assumptions help him learn that loyalty and kindness matter more than wealth or social rank.

Ralph Ellison was an American novelist and essayist born in Oklahoma City in 1914. He studied music at Tuskegee Institute before moving to New York, where he became associated with the Harlem literary scene. His best-known novel, Invisible Man, won the 1953 National Book Award for Fiction. Its narrator is an unnamed Black man who tells his story from a hidden underground room in New York, where he secretly draws electricity from Monopolated Light & Power. He is “invisible” not because people cannot see his body, but because they refuse to recognize him as an individual. As he recounts his experiences at college and in New York, the novel explores racism, identity, and the struggle to be heard.
