W. H. Auden was an English-American poet born in York, England, in 1907 who later became a U.S. citizen. His poems often explore suffering, love, grief, and the way people respond to events around them. In “Musée des Beaux Arts,” he looks at paintings by the Old Masters and observes that they understood suffering: even when something terrible happens, ordinary life goes on nearby. “September 1, 1939” responds to the outbreak of World War II and includes the line “We must love one another or die.” In “Funeral Blues,” a speaker overwhelmed by a loved one’s death asks for clocks to be stopped and telephones cut off. The speaker calls the person who died “my North, my South, my East and West,” showing how central they were to his life.

In Margaret Atwood’s dystopian novel The Handmaid’s Tale, the Eyes are the secret police of Gilead, a theocratic state whose leaders claim religious authority over people’s lives. The Eyes spy on citizens, investigate suspected disobedience, and help enforce the regime’s rules. Because people cannot always tell who might be reporting to the Eyes, fear and suspicion become powerful ways to control them. This threat shapes the life of Offred, the novel’s narrator, who must be careful about what she says and whom she trusts. The name “Eyes” suggests that the government is always watching, even when its agents are not visible. Atwood, a Canadian author, also wrote The Testaments, a sequel that returns to the world of Gilead.

Profiles in Courage is a 1956 book published under the name of John F. Kennedy, then a U.S. senator from Massachusetts and later president of the United States. It tells the stories of senators who risked their careers or popularity to act on principle, exploring what political courage means when doing the right thing may cost someone votes or support. The book won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography. Kennedy’s longtime aide Ted Sorensen, a lawyer and speechwriter who later served as special counsel to the president, is often credited with substantial research and drafting for the book, although Kennedy was named as its author. Sorensen also helped write Kennedy’s speeches, including his 1961 inaugural address.

Haroun and the Sea of Stories is a 1990 children’s fantasy novel by British-Indian author Salman Rushdie. Its hero, Haroun, is the son of Rashid Khalifa, a storyteller who suddenly loses his gift for telling stories. Haroun travels to a magical world where stories flow through the Sea of Stories. There, he journeys to the dark land of Chup to stop the villain Khattam-Shud from poisoning the sea and silencing its stories. The adventure celebrates imagination and the freedom to speak and tell stories, while exploring the harm caused by censorship. Rushdie wrote the book after his earlier novel The Satanic Verses drew fierce controversy; in 1989, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa against him.

Edmund Pevensie is one of the four children who discover Narnia, a magical country reached through a wardrobe, in C.S. Lewis’s The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe. He is the younger brother of Peter and Susan and the older brother of Lucy. When Edmund first enters Narnia, the White Witch rules it and has kept it in a seemingly endless winter. She gives him enchanted Turkish delight and promises him more, tempting him to betray his siblings by revealing their plans. Edmund later realizes that the Witch has deceived him. Aslan, the great lion who returns to challenge her rule, forgives Edmund and saves him from the Witch’s claim over him. Edmund then joins his siblings in the battle that ends her reign.

Canto General is a fifteen-part poetry collection by the Chilean poet Pablo Neruda. Written in Spanish, it traces the history and landscapes of the Western Hemisphere from a Hispanic American perspective. Its opening section, “A Lamp on Earth,” describes the Americas before European conquest, while later poems explore their peoples, struggles, and natural world. The collection includes “The Heights of Macchu Picchu,” in which Neruda reflects on the ancient Inca city and the people whose labor built it. The speaker’s call, “Arise to birth with me, my brother,” invites those people to be remembered and to speak through his poetry. Neruda combines vivid descriptions of places with a concern for whose stories are told in history.

Captain Underpants is the unlikely superhero at the center of Dav Pilkey’s humorous children’s-book series. His ordinary identity is Mr. Krupp, the stern principal of Jerome Horwitz Elementary School. Two prank-loving students, George Beard and Harold Hutchins, use a 3-D Hypno Ring to make him believe he is the superhero they invented in their comic books. Dressed in a cape and underpants, he rushes into ridiculous adventures, often leaving George and Harold to help him out of trouble. After the hypnosis, snapping his fingers makes Mr. Krupp transform into Captain Underpants, while being splashed with water changes him back into the principal. The series mixes school life, comic-book action, and silly humor, especially the contrast between Mr. Krupp’s strict personality and his fearless superhero alter ego.

Edward Albee was an American playwright known for dramas that expose tension beneath ordinary conversations. His 1962 play Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? follows George and Martha as they host a younger couple, Nick and Honey, for an evening of drinking, cruel jokes, and confrontational party games. In Seascape, Albee takes a more unusual approach: the humans Nancy and Charlie talk with Leslie and Sarah, two lizard-like creatures. His one-act play The Zoo Story begins when Jerry approaches Peter, who is sitting on a bench in Central Park, Manhattan’s famous landscaped park. Their conversation grows increasingly disturbing and ends when Jerry impales himself on a knife Peter is holding. These plays show Albee’s interest in conflict, loneliness, and the difficulty of understanding other people.

In Charles Dickens’s novel Great Expectations, Miss Havisham is a wealthy woman who lives at Satis House. On the day she was to marry, she learned that her fiancé had abandoned her. The news arrived at twenty minutes to nine, so she stopped the clocks at that time and kept wearing her wedding dress, which gradually became tattered and yellowed. Her home, with its uneaten wedding feast, seems frozen on the day of her disappointment. Bitter about what happened, Miss Havisham raises a girl named Estella and teaches her to reject love and break men’s hearts. Estella later meets Pip, the novel’s young orphan narrator. Miss Havisham’s abandoned wedding helps explain both the strange state of Satis House and the way she treats Estella.

Christopher Paolini is an American author best known for the Inheritance Cycle, a four-volume young-adult fantasy series set in the fictional land of Alagaësia. The books are Eragon, Eldest, Brisingr, and Inheritance. In the first book, a farm boy named Eragon discovers a dragon egg. When the dragon Saphira hatches, their bond draws him into the ancient order of Dragon Riders, whose members are linked to dragons. Eragon and Saphira become involved in the struggle against Galbatorix, a tyrant king who has nearly destroyed the Riders. Paolini began writing Eragon as a teenager, and its success launched the series. If a question describes Alagaësia and these four books, the author is Christopher Paolini; if it asks for the series about Eragon and Saphira, the answer is the Inheritance Cycle.

Ishmael is the first-person narrator of Herman Melville’s novel Moby-Dick, which opens with the words “Call me Ishmael.” He signs on as a sailor aboard the whaling ship Pequod and becomes friends with Queequeg, a harpooneer he first meets at the Spouter-Inn. The ship’s captain, Ahab, is obsessed with hunting Moby Dick, a giant white whale. He nails a gold doubloon to the Pequod’s mast as a reward for whoever first spots the whale. During the final pursuit, the whale destroys the Pequod, killing everyone aboard except Ishmael. Queequeg’s coffin has been turned into a life buoy, and Ishmael survives by clinging to it until another ship, the Rachel, rescues him. Because he survives, Ishmael can tell the story of the voyage.

Thornton Wilder was an American playwright and novelist who wrote about everyday life, love, and death. His Pulitzer Prize-winning three-act play Our Town takes place in Grover’s Corners, a small New Hampshire town. A character called the Stage Manager speaks to the audience and guides them through the lives of the townspeople, especially Emily Webb and George Gibbs, from their youth to their marriage. The stage is mostly bare, and actors mime many objects rather than using real props. After Emily dies, she returns to revisit an ordinary day and realizes how easily people overlook the value of being alive. Wilder also wrote The Bridge of San Luis Rey, a novel in which a friar investigates the deaths of five people when a bridge collapses in Peru.

Anne of Green Gables is a Canadian novel by L. M. Montgomery about Anne Shirley, a red-haired orphan with a lively imagination. Anne is sent by mistake to live at Green Gables, a farmhouse on Prince Edward Island, with siblings Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert, who had expected to adopt a boy to help with farm work. Anne’s talkative nature and frequent mishaps surprise them, but she gradually wins their affection and finds a home. Matthew, the older sibling, becomes a devoted father figure to Anne. He notices how much she longs for a fashionable dress with puffed sleeves and gives her one. The novel follows Anne as she makes friends, faces challenges at school, and grows up in her new community.

Uncle Vanya is a Russian drama by Anton Chekhov about Ivan Voynitsky, known as Uncle Vanya, who manages a country estate with his niece, Sonia. Their routine is disrupted when Sonia’s father, Professor Serebryakov, returns with his much younger wife. Vanya grows bitter because he feels he has wasted years working to support the professor, and his resentment leads him to fire a gun at Serebryakov. He misses. Sonia, meanwhile, quietly loves Dr. Astrov, but he does not return her feelings. At the end of the play, Vanya and Sonia go back to managing the estate. Sonia comforts her uncle by saying that they will keep working through their troubles and, one day, finally rest.

Porphyria’s Lover is a Victorian dramatic monologue by Robert Browning, who also wrote My Last Duchess and Andrea del Sarto. In a dramatic monologue, one character speaks while readers work out what is happening and what the speaker may not understand about himself. The poem opens on a stormy night, with wind and rain outside a cottage. Porphyria enters, makes the fire, and sits close to the unnamed speaker, arranging her long hair around him. Believing he can preserve their moment of happiness forever, he strangles her with her own hair. He then sits beside her body through the night, calmly insisting that she felt no pain. His disturbing account makes readers question his claims and see the gap between his view of the murder and its horror.

In medias res is a Latin term meaning “in the middle of things.” It describes a story that opens after important events have already happened, rather than starting at the beginning of the timeline. The writer may reveal earlier events later through memories, dialogue, or flashbacks. This approach can create immediate interest because readers enter a conflict already in progress and gradually discover how it began. The Roman poet Horace discussed the technique in his Ars Poetica, and it is common in epic poetry. Homer’s Odyssey is a classic example: when the poem begins, Odysseus has already spent years trying to return home after the Trojan War. He is detained on the island of Calypso while the gods debate his return to Ithaca.

Dream of the Red Chamber is an 18th-century Chinese novel by Cao Xueqin and one of China’s Four Great Classical Novels. Set during the Qing dynasty, it follows Jia Baoyu, a young man born into the wealthy, aristocratic Jia family. His name includes the word for jade, a precious material valued in Chinese traditions for its beauty and associations with virtue and protection. Baoyu is born with a piece of jade in his mouth, and the novel connects him to a magical stone from a heavenly realm. Alongside Baoyu’s friendships and romances, the story explores family expectations, social class, and the lives of the women around him. As the Jia family’s fortunes decline, the novel shows how wealth and status can disappear.

Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s 1892 short story The Yellow Wallpaper follows an unnamed woman struggling with her mental health after childbirth. Her husband, John, is a physician who takes her to a rented house and confines her to an upstairs room. He forbids her from writing and insists on isolation and almost complete inactivity. This treatment is called the rest cure, a nineteenth-century regimen associated with physician Silas Weir Mitchell. With little to occupy her mind, the narrator studies the room’s yellow wallpaper and becomes convinced that a woman is trapped behind its pattern. Her obsession grows as her mental state worsens. The story uses this unsettling image to criticize a treatment that silenced women and dismissed their understanding of their own health.

A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court is a satirical novel by Mark Twain. Its main character, Hank Morgan, is a nineteenth-century superintendent at a Connecticut firearms factory. After he is knocked unconscious in a fight, he wakes up in the Britain of the legendary King Arthur. Hank tries to use his knowledge of modern technology and ideas to transform medieval society. For example, he gains influence at Arthur’s court by predicting an eclipse that others believe he has caused. Twain uses Hank’s adventures among kings and knights to make fun of chivalric romances, which often portray knights as noble heroes. The novel also asks whether inventions and claims of progress really make a society wiser or fairer.

In Search of Lost Time is a vast modernist novel by French writer Marcel Proust. It follows its narrator from childhood in Combray through his friendships, love affairs, and gradual discovery of his calling as a writer. Early in the novel, the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea unexpectedly brings back vivid memories of Combray, showing how an ordinary sensation can unlock the past. Another childhood scene features a magic lantern that projects the story of Golo and Geneviève de Brabant onto the narrator’s bedroom wall. Proust also fills the novel with conversations about literature and art. The narrator’s friend Bloch, for example, praises the line “The daughter of Minos and Pasiphaë” from Phèdre, a tragedy by the French playwright Jean Racine, joking that its merit is “meaning absolutely nothing.”

The Testaments is Margaret Atwood’s sequel to The Handmaid’s Tale, set years later in Gilead, a harsh society that controls women’s lives. The novel tells its story through three accounts: those of Aunt Lydia, Agnes, and Daisy. Agnes has grown up inside Gilead, while Daisy has grown up in Canada, so their experiences reveal different sides of the regime. Aunt Lydia is a powerful figure within Gilead’s leadership, but she secretly records its abuses and helps bring about its downfall. Her account is called the Ardua Hall Holograph, a hidden history named after the place where she works. Together, the three testimonies show how people living both inside and outside Gilead challenge its rule.

Paterson is a five-book modernist poem by the American poet William Carlos Williams, named for the city of Paterson, New Jersey. Rather than telling one continuous story, it brings together descriptions of streets and landscapes, pieces of local history, and different voices to explore how people experience a place and put that experience into words. Williams’s phrase “no ideas but in things” points to his belief that poetry can find meaning in concrete details, not just abstract thoughts. That approach also appears in his much shorter poems “The Red Wheelbarrow,” which begins “so much depends on,” and “This Is Just to Say,” in which the speaker apologizes for eating plums from an icebox. In Paterson, Williams uses similar attention to everyday life on the scale of an entire city.

The Bacchae is a tragedy by the ancient Greek playwright Euripides. Its title refers to the Bacchae, the ecstatic female worshippers of Dionysus, the god of wine and revelry, who are also called Maenads. When Dionysus arrives in Thebes, the young king Pentheus refuses to recognize him as a god and tries to stop his rites. Dionysus persuades Pentheus to disguise himself as a woman and spy on the worshippers gathered on Mount Cithaeron. The women, driven into a frenzy, mistake Pentheus for a wild animal and tear him apart. His mother, Agave, joins in the killing and carries his severed head back to the city before realizing what she has done. The play explores the danger of denying divine power and losing control of reason.

“Everybody’s Protest Novel” is an essay by James Baldwin about the limits of fiction written to promote social reform. Baldwin argues that even books opposing injustice can reduce complex people to symbols if they focus more on a message than on fully imagined human lives. He criticizes the “self-righteous, virtuous sentimentality” of Harriet Beecher Stowe’s antislavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin and the violence in Richard Wright’s Native Son. Baldwin calls Bigger Thomas, the protagonist of Native Son, a descendant of Stowe’s Uncle Tom. Although the two characters seem very different, Baldwin sees both as shaped by novels that define Black characters too narrowly through their responses to racism. His essay asks readers to look beyond a book’s good intentions and consider whether it portrays people in all their complexity.

The Book Thief is a World War II novel by Australian author Markus Zusak, who also wrote I Am the Messenger and Bridge of Clay. Its narrator is Death, who tells the story of Liesel Meminger, a girl living with foster parents in Nazi Germany. Liesel steals books and learns to love reading, even as the war brings danger and loss to her neighborhood. Her foster family hides a Jewish man, Max, in their basement, and Liesel shares stories with him. Her friend Rudy once covers himself in charcoal and runs a race to imitate the athlete Jesse Owens. After an Allied bombing destroys Liesel’s neighborhood, she is its sole survivor. Through her story, the novel explores the cruelty of war and the comfort and power of words.

“I’m Nobody! Who are you?” is a short, playful poem by Emily Dickinson, a 19th-century American poet from Amherst, Massachusetts, who lived a largely private life. Its speaker is delighted to meet someone else who is “Nobody” and proposes that they keep their shared identity secret. Being unknown feels like a kind of freedom: they can be themselves without performing for a crowd. By contrast, the speaker calls it dreary to be “Somebody,” comparing a publicly admired person to a frog that repeatedly announces its name to an admiring bog. The joke gently mocks fame and the desire for attention. Dickinson also explored more serious subjects, especially death, in poems such as “Because I could not stop for Death” and “I heard a Fly buzz—when I died.”

In Ernest Cline’s novel Ready Player One, people escape a troubled world by entering the OASIS, a vast virtual reality universe created by James Halliday. After Halliday dies, players begin searching the OASIS for an Easter Egg he hid there; whoever finds it will inherit his fortune and control of the OASIS. These dedicated “egg hunters” are informally called Gunters. The main character, Wade Watts, joins the hunt using the avatar name Parzival. Gunters compete not only with one another but also with the Sixers, a well-funded team recruited and equipped by the corporation IOI. Unlike the Gunters, IOI wants to take control of the OASIS for its own profit. Near the end of the novel, Gunters unite against IOI’s forces.

Poor Richard’s Almanack was an annual publication that Benjamin Franklin began publishing in 1732. Like other almanacs of the time, it offered useful information such as calendars and weather forecasts, but it also included practical advice about work, money, and everyday life. Franklin presented it as the work of Richard Saunders, a fictional almanac-maker and astrologer, rather than signing it with his own name. The invented character helped give the book a lively, humorous voice. Poor Richard’s Almanack became especially famous for its witty aphorisms: short, memorable sayings that express advice or observations about life. Many were repeated so often that they entered common use. The almanac’s mix of helpful information and humor made it one of Franklin’s best-known works.

Bertha Mason is a central figure in the Gothic mystery of Charlotte Brontë’s novel Jane Eyre. She is Edward Rochester’s first wife, but Jane does not know Bertha exists when Rochester asks to marry her. Rochester keeps Bertha confined in an upper room of his estate, Thornfield Hall, under the watch of Grace Poole. Strange events in the house, including unexplained noises and a fire, create a sense of danger before Jane learns the truth. Because Rochester is already married to Bertha, he cannot legally marry Jane, and Jane leaves Thornfield. Later, Bertha escapes confinement and sets fire to Thornfield Hall, destroying the estate. Her story exposes Rochester’s secret and changes the course of Jane and Rochester’s relationship.

Becky Thatcher is a character in The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, an 1876 novel by American author Mark Twain, who also wrote The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. The story takes place in the fictional town of St. Petersburg, Missouri. Becky is the daughter of a local judge and becomes Tom Sawyer’s love interest. Tom tries to propose to her with a brass knob from a fire grate, but Becky rejects him when she learns he had previously been engaged to another girl, Amy Lawrence. Later, Becky and Tom get lost together in McDougal’s Cave, where they struggle to find their way out. Their adventure is one of the novel’s most suspenseful episodes and helps show how the two characters grow closer.

In Margaret Atwood’s novel The Handmaid’s Tale, the Republic of Gilead assigns women called Aunts to train and control the Handmaids. Handmaids are fertile women forced to bear children for powerful households, and the Aunts teach them Gilead’s rules at a training facility known as the Red Center. Although “Aunt” sounds like a caring family title, these women indoctrinate, discipline, and supervise the Handmaids, helping the government enforce its strict limits on women’s freedom. The best-known is Aunt Lydia, a stern instructor who oversees the Red Center where Offred and other Handmaids are trained. Lydia also narrates part of Atwood’s sequel, The Testaments, which explores her background and role in Gilead.

A Wrinkle in Time is a 1962 science-fiction novel by Madeleine L’Engle. It follows Meg Murry, her younger brother Charles Wallace, and their friend Calvin O’Keefe as they travel across vast distances to rescue Meg’s missing father, a scientist. Three mysterious guides—Mrs. Whatsit, Mrs. Who, and Mrs. Which—help them cross space and time using a “tesseract,” a shortcut that brings faraway places close together. Their journey leads to Camazotz, a planet ruled by a tyrannical intelligence called IT. There, identical houses and children bouncing balls in perfect unison show how the rulers force everyone to conform. Charles Wallace falls under IT’s control, leaving Meg to confront its power. The story combines an interstellar adventure with questions about individuality, love, and the courage to resist control.

“Fog” is a short poem by the American poet Carl Sandburg. It begins, “The fog comes in on little cat feet,” comparing the quiet arrival of fog to a cat’s silent steps. The fog sits looking over the harbor and city, then moves on, much as a cat might pause to watch its surroundings before leaving. Sandburg uses just a few words to create a clear image rather than explaining what the fog means, a style associated with imagist poetry. The poem’s title names the atmospheric phenomenon it describes: fog. Sandburg also wrote “Chicago,” a poem that celebrates the energy of his home city and calls it “Hog Butcher for the World” and “City of the Big Shoulders.”

The Tin Drum is a 1959 novel by German writer Günter Grass. Its central character, Oskar Matzerath, receives a tin drum on his third birthday and decides to stop growing. He keeps drumming as he narrates his life, and his extraordinarily shrill screams can shatter glass. Oskar’s unusual abilities and his child-sized view of the world give the story a strange, sometimes darkly comic tone. Much of the novel takes place in and around Danzig, a city shaped by both German and Polish history, as Europe moves through the rise of Nazism, the Second World War, and its aftermath. Through Oskar’s story, Grass explores how people remember the past and respond to violence and guilt.

In Harper Lee’s To Kill a Mockingbird, the Finch family lives in the fictional town of Maycomb, Alabama. The family includes Atticus Finch, a lawyer, and his children, Jem and Scout. Scout narrates the novel as she and Jem learn about prejudice and fairness. Atticus defends Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman, even though many townspeople disapprove. He teaches his children that it is wrong to harm innocent people, comparing them to mockingbirds, which “do one thing except make music for us to enjoy.” Near the Finch home lives Boo Radley, a reclusive man the children are curious about. He quietly leaves them small gifts in a tree’s knothole and later carries them to safety after Bob Ewell attacks them.

Mourning Becomes Electra is a trilogy of plays by American playwright Eugene O’Neill. Set in New England just after the Civil War, it retells the Oresteia, an ancient Greek tragedy about a family torn apart by betrayal, murder, and revenge. O’Neill replaces the Greek House of Atreus with the Mannon family. Lavinia Mannon confronts her mother’s infidelity, and the family’s conflicts unfold across three plays. O’Neill also wrote The Iceman Cometh, which takes place in Harry Hope’s Greenwich Village saloon. In that play, a traveling salesman named Hickey challenges the regulars’ comforting dreams and confesses that he killed his wife, Evelyn. Remembering the Mannons helps identify Mourning Becomes Electra, while Hickey and Harry Hope’s saloon point to its author, Eugene O’Neill.

“The Veldt” is a science fiction short story by American writer Ray Bradbury, who also wrote the novel Fahrenheit 451. It follows George and Lydia Hadley, whose automated Happylife Home does nearly everything for their family. Its nursery can turn their children’s thoughts into convincing sights, sounds, and smells. Their children, Peter and Wendy, become obsessed with a scene of the African veldt, a grassy landscape where lions hunt. Troubled by the scene and by the children’s behavior, George and Lydia consult psychologist David McClean and decide to shut down the nursery. Peter and Wendy resist. They lure their parents inside, lock them in, and leave them to the lions. The story explores the dangers of relying on technology to replace care and attention within a family.

The Fudge series is a group of children’s novels by Judy Blume about the Hatcher family. Its main narrator is Peter Hatcher, an older brother who is often exasperated by the antics of his mischievous younger brother, Farley Drexel Hatcher, nicknamed “Fudge.” In Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing, Peter tries to deal with Fudge’s unpredictable behavior while also caring for his pet turtle, Dribble. Peter often feels that Fudge gets too much attention and that adults do not understand how frustrating life with a little brother can be. The books use humor and everyday family problems to show Peter and Fudge growing up. The series is named for Fudge, even though Peter tells much of the story.

The Sound and the Fury is a 1929 novel by American writer William Faulkner about the decline of the Compson family in Mississippi. It takes place in Faulkner’s fictional Yoknapatawpha County, the setting of many of his books. The novel is divided into four sections that show events from different perspectives rather than telling the story in a simple timeline. The first three sections follow the Compson brothers Benjy, Quentin, and Jason; the final section centers on Dilsey, a longtime Black servant in the Compson household. Faulkner’s shifting viewpoints and unusual treatment of time make the book an important work of modernist literature. He also wrote As I Lay Dying, in which the Bundren family travels to bury their mother, Addie.

Bret Harte was a 19th-century American writer known for regionalist stories set in California Gold Rush mining camps and frontier towns. Regionalist writers show what life is like in a particular place, often using local settings, customs, and characters. Two of Harte’s best-known stories are “The Outcasts of Poker Flat” and “The Luck of Roaring Camp.” In “The Luck of Roaring Camp,” a baby is born to Cherokee Sal in an isolated mining settlement. After his mother dies, the miners take responsibility for raising him and name him Thomas Luck. His arrival brings out a gentler side of the rough camp. Harte’s stories helped readers across the United States imagine the people and daily life of the American frontier.

The Golden Shovel is both a pool hall in Gwendolyn Brooks’s poem “We Real Cool” and the name of a poetic form inspired by that poem. Brooks introduces its speakers as “THE POOL PLAYERS. SEVEN AT THE GOLDEN SHOVEL.” Their short, defiant lines describe how they “lurk late” and “strike straight,” while hinting at the risks of their choices. American poet Terrance Hayes introduced the Golden Shovel form in his 2010 collection Lighthead. To write one, a poet takes words from an existing poem and places them, in their original order, at the ends of the lines of a new poem. Reading those end words downward reveals the borrowed text. Hayes used this structure to honor Brooks and respond creatively to her work.

In Alan Paton’s novel Cry, the Beloved Country, Absalom Kumalo is the son of Stephen Kumalo, a Zulu Anglican priest from the rural village of Ndotsheni. When Stephen learns that Absalom is missing, he travels to Johannesburg to search for him. There he discovers that Absalom has become involved in crime. During a burglary at the home of Arthur Jarvis, a white man, Absalom shoots and kills Jarvis; he is later sentenced to death. Stephen’s grief recalls the biblical King David mourning his son Absalom with the words “my son! my son!” Through the Kumalo family, Paton explores how poverty, migration to cities, and racial injustice strain families in South Africa just before apartheid became official policy.

On His Blindness is a sonnet by the English poet John Milton. It begins, “When I consider how my light is spent,” as the speaker reflects on losing his sight. He worries that blindness may prevent him from using his talents to serve God, but the poem suggests that patient faith can be a form of service too. The sonnet is also known by its opening line, since Milton did not give it the title On His Blindness. Milton later wrote Paradise Lost, an epic poem about Satan’s rebellion against God and the Fall of humanity through Adam and Eve. In that work, he aimed to “justify the ways of God to men.” Both poems explore questions about faith, duty, and how people respond to hardship.

Lennie Small is a powerful ranch laborer in John Steinbeck’s novella Of Mice and Men. He travels with his close companion, George Milton, a quick-witted ranch hand who protects him when his strength and difficulty understanding situations lead to trouble. The two men dream of owning a small farm, where Lennie hopes to tend rabbits and live “off the fatta’ the lan.” Lennie loves soft things, but he does not always realize how easily he can hurt them. After he accidentally kills a puppy, he panics while touching Curley’s wife’s hair and accidentally kills her too. He flees to a riverside clearing where George had told him to wait if he got into trouble. George finds Lennie before the other ranch hands arrive, talks to him about their farm, and then shoots him.

Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, published in 1962, warned that synthetic pesticides could harm living things far beyond the insects they were meant to kill. Carson focused especially on DDT, a chemical widely used after World War II to control pests. DDT could spread through the environment and build up in animals that ate contaminated prey. In birds, exposure caused eggshells to become abnormally thin and fragile, so eggs could break before the chicks inside hatched. The title Silent Spring imagines a spring without birdsong because bird populations have declined. Carson’s book made the ecological and wildlife dangers of pesticides widely known, helped inspire the modern environmental movement, and contributed to the United States’ 1972 ban on DDT.

Endgame is a bleak absurdist play by the Irish writer Samuel Beckett. Almost all the action takes place in a bare, sealed room, where Hamm sits blind and unable to walk in a wheelchair at its center. He gives orders to his servant Clov, who can move around but cannot sit down. Hamm’s parents, Nagg and Nell, live in ashbins and occasionally emerge to talk; they cannot even reach each other to kiss. Little happens in a conventional sense, but the characters’ repeated arguments, jokes, and routines reveal their dependence on one another. Through this strange situation, Beckett explores loneliness, the passage of time, and the difficulty of finding meaning when life seems to be nearing its end.

Clara Godfrey is a social studies teacher at Public School 38 in Lincoln Peirce’s comic series Big Nate. She is stern and expects students to follow the rules, which puts her at odds with the series’ class-clown protagonist, Nate Wright. Nate often goofs around with his friends Teddy and Francis, and his behavior earns him detentions from Mrs. Godfrey. He sees her as one of his greatest enemies and gives her dramatic nicknames, including “Godzilla” and “She Who Must Not Be Named.” Their clashes are a recurring source of humor in Big Nate: readers see both Nate’s dislike of being disciplined and Mrs. Godfrey’s frustration with his antics. If a question asks for Nate’s social studies teacher, the answer is Clara Godfrey; if it asks for the series, it is Big Nate.

In Emily Dickinson’s poetry, the Soul is an independent inner self that decides whom to welcome and whom to exclude. In “The Soul selects her own Society,” she chooses her companions and then “shuts the Door,” refusing even an important visitor. In another poem, Dickinson says the Soul “should always stand ajar,” suggesting that the inner self can also remain open to new experiences. Dickinson often explores such mysterious subjects through brief scenes and striking images. In “Because I could not stop for Death,” Death appears as a courteous driver who stops for the speaker and takes her on a carriage ride. They pass a school, fields, and the setting sun, images that suggest the stages of life and its ending.

Warriors is a children’s fantasy novel series written by several authors under the shared name Erin Hunter. It follows wild cats living in four rival groups: ThunderClan, RiverClan, WindClan, and ShadowClan. The cats have their own rules, leaders, and territories, and their stories involve friendships, battles, and difficult choices about loyalty. The first subseries, The Prophecies Begin, follows a young cat who joins ThunderClan and becomes known as Fireheart. He uncovers Tigerstar’s treachery and later faces a threat from BloodClan. The four Clans believe that their deceased ancestors live on in a spiritual group called StarClan. Medicine cats care for sick or injured cats, but they also seek guidance from StarClan, interpreting dreams and signs that may help their Clans make decisions.

The Iceberg Theory is a minimalist writing technique associated with American novelist Ernest Hemingway, who wrote The Old Man and the Sea and A Farewell to Arms. Hemingway compared a story to an iceberg: only a small part is visible above the water, while most lies hidden beneath it. In his prose, characters may speak plainly or describe events without directly explaining their deepest feelings. Readers use clues in the dialogue, actions, and setting to infer what remains unstated. This approach is also called the theory of omission because the writer deliberately leaves out details while still knowing what they mean. In A Farewell to Arms, for example, readers must often infer narrator Frederic Henry’s thoughts and emotions from what he says and does.

The Human Stain is a 2000 novel by American writer Philip Roth. It centers on Coleman Silk, a longtime classics professor and former dean at the fictional Athena College. When two students repeatedly miss class, Silk asks whether they are “spooks,” meaning ghosts because he has never seen them. The students are Black, however, and his remark is interpreted as a racial insult, leading to a scandal that ends his career. The narrator, Nathan Zuckerman, gradually uncovers a secret Silk has kept for decades: he was born into a Black family but has lived his adult life as a white man. Through Silk’s story, the novel explores racial identity, passing, public judgment, and the gap between what people believe about someone and the truth of that person’s life.

Casino Royale, published in 1953, is Ian Fleming’s first novel about James Bond, the British intelligence agent whose codename is 007. Bond works for MI6, Britain’s foreign intelligence service. In this story, his mission is unusual: instead of stealing secrets or chasing an enemy, he must defeat Le Chiffre at baccarat, a high-stakes card game, and bankrupt him. Le Chiffre is an agent of SMERSH, a Soviet counterintelligence organization, and has lost money he needs to repay. He hopes to recover it at the gaming table. Bond’s attempt to ruin Le Chiffre financially drives the novel’s suspense and introduces the resourceful spy who would become one of fiction’s most famous characters.

Italo Calvino was an Italian novelist and short-story writer who often mixed imaginative storytelling with unusual literary structures. In Cosmicomics, a recurring character named Qfwfq tells stories that turn scientific ideas, such as the origins of the universe, into playful fables. Calvino also experimented with how readers experience a book. His novel If on a Winter’s Night a Traveler opens by addressing “you,” the reader, as you sit down to read a book with that very title. This is called second-person narration. In his 1972 novel Invisible Cities, the explorer Marco Polo describes fantastical cities to the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan. Rather than following a straightforward plot, its short chapters return to recurring themes, inviting readers to think about memory, imagination, and the meaning of a city.

The Hunger Games is a dystopian novel by Suzanne Collins set in Panem, a future nation divided into twelve districts ruled by a wealthy Capitol. Each year, the Capitol forces every district to send two young “tributes” into an arena for a televised fight to the death. In the 74th Hunger Games, District 12’s tributes are Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark. Their mentor is Haymitch Abernathy, the only living victor from their district. Though he is cynical and drinks heavily, Haymitch gives them advice that could save their lives: when the Games begin, they should run away from the Cornucopia, where supplies are piled up, to avoid the deadly rush of tributes trying to seize them.

Edith Wharton was an American novelist who drew on her experience of upper-class New York society to write about its strict rules and the pressure to fit in. Her best-known works include The Age of Innocence and Ethan Frome, and she won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for The Age of Innocence. That novel follows Newland Archer, a young New York lawyer engaged to May Welland. After seeing May’s cousin, Ellen Olenska, at a performance of Faust, he becomes increasingly drawn to her. Newland’s feelings force him to choose between the life his family and society expect him to lead and the life he might want for himself. Wharton used stories like his to explore how social expectations can limit people’s freedom.

J. Alfred Prufrock is the fictional speaker of T. S. Eliot’s poem “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock,” a landmark work of early-20th-century modernist poetry. The poem is a dramatic monologue, so readers hear Prufrock’s thoughts as he imagines social encounters and struggles to say what he feels. Although the title calls it a love song, he is hesitant and self-conscious rather than confidently romantic. He notices women who “come and go, talking of Michelangelo,” worries about growing older, and asks, “Do I dare to eat a peach?” Near the end, he imagines mermaids singing to one another but doubts they will sing to him. Eliot, whose full name was Thomas Stearns Eliot, also wrote the modernist poem “The Waste Land.”

The Turn of the Screw is an 1898 Gothic novella by Henry James, an American-born writer known for exploring characters’ thoughts and fears. It first appeared in installments in Collier’s Weekly and was later published alongside James’s story “The Jolly Corner” in a volume called The Two Magics. The story follows an unnamed governess hired to care for two children, Miles and Flora, at an isolated English estate. She becomes convinced that the children are being visited by the ghosts of Peter Quint, a former valet, and Miss Jessel, a former governess. But because readers see events mainly through the governess’s account, they must decide whether the ghosts are real or whether her fears have shaped what she believes she sees.

D’Artagnan is the young Gascon hero of Alexandre Dumas’s 1844 adventure novel The Three Musketeers. He travels from southwestern France to Paris hoping to join the king’s musketeers, an elite group of soldiers. Soon after arriving, he angers three musketeers—Athos, Porthos, and Aramis—and each challenges him to a duel. Instead, they become close friends and join forces in adventures involving political intrigue, sword fights, and the schemes of Cardinal Richelieu’s agents. Although d’Artagnan is the main character, the novel’s title refers to his three companions, not to him. Dumas continued their story in two sequels, making d’Artagnan one of the best-known heroes of French adventure fiction.

The Harry Potter series is a set of seven fantasy novels by British author J. K. Rowling. The story follows Harry, a young wizard who learns that the dark wizard Lord Voldemort killed his parents. Harry attends Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, a boarding school where he studies magic and makes close friends, including Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger. When students arrive at Hogwarts, they are sorted into one of four houses: Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, or Slytherin. Across the series, Harry and his friends face mysteries and dangers as Voldemort tries to regain power. The books combine school life, friendship, and magical adventure with Harry’s struggle against the wizard responsible for his parents’ deaths.

Aeschylus was a fifth-century BCE Athenian playwright and one of ancient Greece’s most important writers of tragedy. His best-known surviving work is the Oresteia, a trilogy of plays about a family trapped in a cycle of revenge. In its first play, Agamemnon returns home from the Trojan War and is murdered by his wife, Clytemnestra. In the second, their son Orestes kills her to avenge his father. In the third, Orestes is judged by a court established in Athens, offering a way to settle violence through justice rather than further revenge. Aeschylus also appears as a character in The Frogs, a comedy by Aristophanes. There, he defeats the tragedian Euripides in a contest, and Dionysus chooses to bring Aeschylus back from the underworld.

Harold Pinter was a British playwright whose spare dialogue, charged pauses, and unsettling silences made ordinary conversations feel threatening. His plays often leave characters’ motives unclear, creating an atmosphere of menace and ambiguity. Pinter won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Literature and wrote The Birthday Party and The Homecoming. In his one-act play The Dumb Waiter, two hitmen, Ben and Gus, wait in a basement for instructions from their employer, Wilson. Instead, they receive increasingly strange food orders through a dumb waiter, a small lift used to carry food between floors. They also communicate through a speaking tube, which carries voices between rooms. The play’s absurd situation becomes more disturbing as the men wait, and it ends with a whistle from the tube.

Ars Poetica, Latin for “The Art of Poetry,” is a poem about how to write well by the ancient Roman poet Horace, who also wrote the Odes. Addressed to the Piso family, it advises poets to choose a suitable subject, keep their work consistent, and revise it carefully. Horace opens with a deliberately absurd image: a painter joins a horse’s neck to a human head, creating a figure whose parts do not belong together. He uses it to show why a poem should feel like a coherent whole rather than a jumble of mismatched ideas. Horace also discusses earlier poets such as Homer and the kinds of subjects they wrote about. One famous line from Horace’s Odes is “dulce et decorum est pro patria mori,” meaning that it is sweet and fitting to die for one’s country.

In “Caged Bird,” American poet and memoirist Maya Angelou contrasts two birds to explore freedom and oppression. The free bird flies through the sky and “dares to claim” it, while the caged bird cannot escape its bars. Although the caged bird is afraid and has little room to move, it sings of freedom. The birds are symbols: the free bird represents people who can live and act without unfair limits, and the caged bird represents people whose freedom is denied. By returning to the caged bird’s song, Angelou emphasizes both the pain of confinement and the determination to hope for something better. Angelou also wrote I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, an autobiography about her life through age seventeen, but “Caged Bird” is the title of the poem.

In Book 18 of Homer’s Iliad, Achilles needs new armor after his friend Patroclus dies wearing Achilles’ old armor, which the Trojans seize. Achilles’ mother, Thetis, asks Hephaestus, the Olympian god of fire and metalworking, to make replacement armor for him. Hephaestus creates an extraordinary shield as part of the set. Homer describes its surface in detail: it shows the sun, moon, and stars; two cities, one celebrating a wedding and one under siege; and scenes of farming, herding, and dancing. The pictures bring together peaceful work, celebration, conflict, and the wider cosmos. Although Achilles will carry the shield into battle, its images show much more than war: they portray the varied world he is fighting in.

Fantasy is a broad genre of imaginative literature in which magic, supernatural forces, invented worlds, or mythic heroes play important roles. Its stories may follow quests, battles, or ordinary people facing extraordinary events. In J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings, Frodo Baggins journeys to destroy the powerful One Ring, making the trilogy a famous example of fantasy. British author Terry Pratchett took a more humorous approach in his Discworld books. Discworld is a world carried by four elephants standing on the back of a giant turtle. Pratchett’s first Discworld novel, The Colour of Magic, introduces the inept wizard Rincewind, who becomes a guide to a tourist named Twoflower. Both Tolkien’s epic adventure and Pratchett’s comic stories show how varied fantasy can be.

The Cheshire Cat is a mysterious, grinning character in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, a fantasy novel first published in 1865 by the English author who used the pen name Lewis Carroll. Alice meets the Cat perched in a tree and asks which way she should go. Instead of giving a simple answer, it offers puzzling directions and talks with her about the strange logic of Wonderland. The Cat can appear and disappear gradually, sometimes leaving only its famous smile visible. That image—“a grin without a cat”—is one of the book’s most memorable moments. The Cheshire Cat’s playful, confusing conversation helps show how Wonderland challenges the ordinary rules Alice expects the world to follow.

“Hope is the thing with feathers” is a lyric poem by Emily Dickinson, a reclusive American poet from Amherst, Massachusetts. In the poem, Dickinson imagines hope as a small bird that perches in the soul and keeps singing, even during fierce storms. Its song represents the comfort and strength hope can give people in difficult times. The speaker says the bird has helped many people stay warm, yet it has never asked her for even a crumb in return. Dickinson often explored big ideas through vivid images. In another of her poems, “Because I could not stop for Death,” she imagines riding in a carriage with Death and Immortality.

Kate Chopin was an American realist writer who explored women’s lives, desires, and the limits placed on them by marriage and society. Her novel The Awakening is set in Louisiana and follows Edna Pontellier, a married woman who spends a summer on Grand Isle. As Edna discovers new interests and longs for independence, she feels increasingly trapped by the expectations that she should devote herself to her husband and children. The novel ends with Edna entering the Gulf of Mexico alone. Chopin also wrote “The Story of an Hour,” in which a woman briefly imagines a life of freedom after hearing that her husband has died. Through these characters, Chopin challenged conventional ideas about women’s roles in the late nineteenth century.

Scarlett O’Hara is the headstrong protagonist of Margaret Mitchell’s novel Gone with the Wind, set in Georgia during the Civil War and Reconstruction. The daughter of an Irish-born planter, Scarlett grows up at her family’s plantation, Tara. After the war devastates the South, she returns to Tara and vows to keep the estate from being lost, even if she must scheme or marry for money. Scarlett loves Ashley Wilkes, although he marries Melanie, and she later has a complicated relationship with Rhett Butler. Her determination helps her survive, but her choices often hurt other people. The novel ends with Scarlett putting off her troubles by saying, “After all, tomorrow is another day.” It also romanticizes the antebellum South, so readers should consider whose experiences that portrayal leaves out.

Shakuntala is a classical Sanskrit drama from India by the poet and playwright Kalidasa. Its heroine, Shakuntala, is raised in a forest hermitage and falls in love with King Dushyanta. When a visiting sage curses her, Dushyanta forgets her, and a lost ring becomes the key to restoring his memory. A fisherman later finds the ring, allowing the king to recognize Shakuntala again. The play’s story also appears in the Mahabharata, the Indian epic about the Pandavas and Kauravas. Shakuntala is one of three surviving dramas attributed to Kalidasa; the others are Malavikagnimitram and Vikramorvashiyam. He also wrote Meghaduta, a poem in which a cloud carries a message to a distant loved one.

Emma Bovary is the title character of Gustave Flaubert’s novel Madame Bovary. Married to Charles Bovary, a country doctor, she feels trapped by ordinary life and dreams of romance, luxury, and excitement. After the couple moves to the provincial town of Yonville, Emma has affairs with Rodolphe Boulanger and Léon Dupuis. She also spends lavishly and falls deeply into debt. Charles, meanwhile, tries to cure the ostler Hippolyte’s clubfoot after the pharmacist Homais encourages him to operate. The operation fails, and Hippolyte eventually needs an amputation. When Emma cannot repay the moneylender, she takes arsenic and dies. Through Emma’s hopes and disappointments, Flaubert explores the gap between romantic fantasies and everyday reality.

The Cherry Orchard is the final play by Russian writer Anton Chekhov. It follows Madame Ranevskaya and her debt-ridden aristocratic family as they return to their estate in Russia after years abroad. They love its beautiful cherry orchard but cannot afford to keep the property. Lopakhin, a wealthy merchant whose father had been a serf on the estate, suggests cutting down the trees and renting the land for summer cottages. The family does not act in time, and Lopakhin buys the estate at auction. As the family leaves, the sound of axes cutting down the orchard signals the end of their old way of life. The play mixes humor and sadness while showing how Russian society was changing.

Patrick White was an Australian novelist who won the 1973 Nobel Prize in Literature. His 1957 novel Voss tells the story of a dangerous expedition across Australia’s remote interior, often called the Outback. Its leader, Johann Ulrich Voss, is a German explorer determined to cross the continent, but the journey becomes a disaster. Alongside the expedition, the novel follows Laura Trevelyan, a young woman who remains in colonial society in Sydney. Although Voss and Laura are physically separated, their intense connection is central to the story. White uses their experiences to explore ambition, isolation, and the difficulty European settlers faced in understanding the Australian landscape. If a question mentions White, a German-led expedition, and Laura Trevelyan, the novel is Voss.

The Mousetrap is a stage mystery by British writer Agatha Christie. It opened in London’s West End in 1952 and became the world’s longest-running play, with more than 27,000 performances. The story takes place at Monkswell Manor, a country guesthouse run by a young couple. Heavy snow traps the guests inside, and news of a murder raises fears that the killer may be among them. Sergeant Trotter arrives to investigate and questions everyone at the house, uncovering secrets and suspicious connections between the visitors. Christie builds tension by making several characters seem capable of the crime, so the audience must weigh each clue carefully. The song “Three Blind Mice” is a recurring part of the mystery.

Superheroes Are Everywhere is a picture book by Kamala Harris that invites young readers to look beyond comic-book characters when they think about heroes. Harris shows how family members, friends, teachers, neighbors, and public figures can be superheroes through everyday acts of courage, kindness, and service. The book encourages children to notice the people who help others and to recognize that they, too, can make a difference. Harris served as a U.S. senator from California before becoming vice president of the United States in 2021. She was the first woman to hold that office. Knowing both the book’s title and its author connects its message about everyday heroes with Harris’s own career in public service.

Mr. Hyde is the violent, cruel alter ego of the respected Dr. Henry Jekyll in Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, a Gothic novella by the Scottish author Robert Louis Stevenson. The story follows London lawyer Gabriel Utterson as he tries to understand Jekyll’s troubling connection to Hyde. Utterson’s friend Richard Enfield recalls seeing Hyde trample a young girl; after a confrontation, Hyde pays her family a hundred pounds. Later, Hyde is suspected of murdering Sir Danvers Carew. Utterson notices that a note supposedly written by Hyde resembles Jekyll’s handwriting, deepening the mystery. Jekyll has used a potion to transform himself into Hyde, hoping to separate his darker impulses from his respectable public life. Stevenson also wrote the adventure novels Kidnapped and Treasure Island.

Like Water for Chocolate is a novel by Mexican author Laura Esquivel, set in Mexico during the Mexican Revolution. Its main character, Tita, loves Pedro, but her strict mother, Mamá Elena, forbids them to marry. Mamá Elena insists on a family tradition: the youngest daughter must remain unmarried and care for her mother until her mother dies. Pedro marries Tita’s sister so he can stay close to Tita, making family life even more painful. Each chapter begins with a recipe, and cooking becomes Tita’s way of expressing feelings she cannot speak aloud. In the novel’s magical events, her emotions pass into the food she prepares and affect the people who eat it. Through Tita’s story, Esquivel explores love, family duty, and the struggle for freedom.

In Madeleine L’Engle’s A Wrinkle in Time, Meg Murry, her brother Charles Wallace, and their friend Calvin travel through space and time with Mrs. Whatsit, Mrs. Who, and Mrs. Which. Their search for Meg’s missing father takes them to Camazotz, a planet ruled by IT. IT is a disembodied, tyrannical intelligence that controls people’s thoughts and actions. The children see its power in a neighborhood where residents bounce balls in eerie unison, as though no one is free to act differently. IT captures Charles Wallace and tries to bend Meg to its will as well. To rescue her brother, Meg must resist IT’s demand for obedience and sameness.

The Baby-Sitters Club is a long-running series of children’s novels created by Ann M. Martin. Set in fictional Stoneybrook, Connecticut, it follows adolescent friends whose babysitting jobs bring them together and lead to stories about friendship, family, and growing up. The club begins when Kristy Thomas realizes that neighborhood families need a reliable way to find babysitters and proposes organizing a service they can call. Kristy becomes the club’s president and is often shown wearing a baseball cap. The original core members are Kristy, her best friend Mary Anne Spier, artistic Claudia Kishi, and Stacey McGill. Together, they arrange babysitting jobs, solve problems that arise while caring for children, and learn how to work as a team.

The Prince is a Renaissance political treatise by Niccolò Machiavelli, a Florentine diplomat and political thinker who served the Republic of Florence before the Medici family returned to power. Written in 1513 and published in 1532, it examines how rulers gain power, keep control of their states, and respond to threats. Machiavelli argues that a ruler must understand both force and deception: like a lion, the ruler should be strong enough to frighten enemies, and like a fox, clever enough to recognize traps. He also suggests that, when a ruler cannot be both loved and feared, being feared is safer, though the ruler should avoid being hated. His examples include Cesare Borgia. Machiavelli later wrote the Discourses on Livy, another work about politics and government.

Antigone is the daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta in Greek myth and the central character of Sophocles’ tragedy Antigone. After her brothers, Eteocles and Polynices, kill each other while fighting over Thebes, their uncle Creon becomes king. Creon allows Eteocles to be buried but orders that Polynices’ body be left unburied as punishment for attacking the city. Antigone believes that honoring the dead is a sacred duty, so she defies Creon’s order and scatters earth over her brother’s body. Creon sentences his niece to be sealed alive in a cave. The blind prophet Tiresias later warns Creon that his decree offends the gods. Creon changes his mind, but he acts too late to save Antigone, making the play a tragedy about family loyalty, religious duty, and the limits of a ruler’s power.

Celeste Ng is a Chinese-American novelist whose books explore family secrets, identity, race, and the pressure to meet other people’s expectations. Her debut novel, Everything I Never Told You, is set in 1970s Ohio. It follows the Lee family after their middle daughter, Lydia, is found dead in a lake, revealing tensions that her parents and siblings had struggled to discuss. Ng’s next novel, Little Fires Everywhere, takes place in Shaker Heights, a planned suburb near Cleveland, Ohio. It follows the wealthy Richardson family and artist Mia Warren, whose arrival with her daughter disrupts their carefully ordered lives. The novel became a number-one New York Times bestseller and was adapted into a Hulu television series.

The Grinch is the Christmas-hating main character of Dr. Seuss’s 1957 book How the Grinch Stole Christmas! He lives alone in a cave on Mount Crumpit, above the cheerful town of Whoville. Hoping to stop the Whos from celebrating, he disguises himself as Santa Claus and sneaks into their homes on Christmas Eve to steal their presents, decorations, and food. He ties an antler onto his loyal dog, Max, so Max can pretend to be a reindeer pulling the sleigh. During the theft, the Grinch meets a little Who named Cindy-Lou Who. But when the Whos wake up, they sing together despite having lost their things. The Grinch realizes Christmas means more than gifts, and his heart grows “three sizes.”

“The Wife of Bath’s Tale” is a story in Geoffrey Chaucer’s medieval collection The Canterbury Tales. It begins when a knight assaults a maiden and is condemned to death at King Arthur’s court. Queen Guinevere intervenes: she will spare him if, within a year and a day, he can discover what women desire most. The knight travels widely and hears many different answers, but none seems certain. Near the end of his quest, an old woman promises to tell him the answer if he agrees to grant her a request. She teaches him that women most desire control over their own lives and choices. The tale uses the knight’s quest to explore power, marriage, and respect.

Eugene Ionesco was born in Romania and later became a French citizen. He wrote his plays in French and became a leading figure in the Theatre of the Absurd, a style that uses strange events and illogical dialogue to show how confusing or meaningless everyday life can seem. In his landmark one-act play The Bald Soprano, two English couples meet in a comfortable middle-class living room. Their ordinary conversation gradually falls apart into disconnected speech and escalating nonsense. The play’s title is first mentioned by a fireman who visits them. Ionesco also wrote Rhinoceros, in which townspeople turn into rhinoceroses while one man resists joining them. Through these unusual stories, Ionesco challenged audiences to think about communication, conformity, and what it means to remain an individual.

The Ant and the Grasshopper is a short animal fable traditionally attributed to Aesop, a storyteller said to have been enslaved in ancient Greece. During the warm summer months, the ant works hard to gather and store food, while the grasshopper spends its time singing. When winter arrives, the grasshopper has nothing to eat and asks the ant for help. In some versions, the ant refuses and tells the grasshopper that, since it sang all summer, it should dance through the winter. The story is often used to teach the value of preparing for the future, though readers may also question the ant’s lack of generosity. Like Aesop’s The Tortoise and the Hare, it uses animals to illustrate human choices and their consequences.

Lady Macbeth is a central character in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Macbeth. After reading a letter from her husband about the Weird Sisters’ prophecy that he will become king, she calls on spirits to strip away her compassion so she can help him seize the throne. When King Duncan visits their castle at Inverness, she challenges Macbeth’s courage and helps plan Duncan’s murder. She drugs Duncan’s attendants, and after Macbeth kills the king, the couple makes it look as though the attendants are guilty. At first Lady Macbeth seems more determined than her husband, but guilt gradually overwhelms her. She begins to sleepwalk and rub her hands as if trying to wash away blood that only she can see, crying, “Out, damned spot!”

In Margaret Atwood’s dystopian novel The Handmaid’s Tale, Handmaids are fertile women forced to bear children for powerful households in the Republic of Gilead. Because infertility is widespread, Gilead’s rulers treat them as essential while denying them freedom and control over their bodies. Handmaids wear red uniforms and are assigned names that show which Commander they serve: the story’s narrator is called Offred, meaning “of Fred.” Her experiences reveal how Gilead uses religion and strict rules to control women. Atwood, a Canadian author, later returned to Gilead in the novel The Testaments. She also wrote the science-fiction novel Oryx and Crake.

Hermione Granger is a Muggle-born witch in J. K. Rowling’s Harry Potter series. Although her parents are not magical, she becomes one of the most knowledgeable students at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, where she is sorted into Gryffindor. Hermione’s careful study, quick thinking, and courage help her close friends Harry Potter and Ron Weasley face many dangers. Ron is a red-haired wizard and the youngest son of Arthur and Molly Weasley, whose large family lives at a home called the Burrow. He becomes one of Harry’s closest friends, and his friendship with Hermione eventually grows into a romance. After the events of the main series, Hermione and Ron marry.

The Giving Tree is a 1964 picture book written and illustrated by Shel Silverstein, an American poet and cartoonist who also wrote the poetry collections Where the Sidewalk Ends and A Light in the Attic. It follows a boy and a tree that loves him as their relationship changes over his lifetime. As a child, he plays in its branches and eats its apples. When he grows older, the tree gives him its apples to sell, its branches to build a house, and its trunk to make a boat. Eventually, only a stump remains. The boy returns as an elderly man, and the stump offers him a place to sit and rest. The story invites readers to think about generosity, love, and what it means to give.

The Death of Ivan Ilyich is a novella by Russian author Leo Tolstoy about a successful judge forced to confront his own death. It opens with Ivan’s fellow judges discussing a newspaper notice of his death, then looks back over his life. Ivan has followed society’s rules, seeking a respectable career, a comfortable home, and the approval of others. While hanging curtains in his new house, he suffers what seems like a minor injury, but his health steadily worsens. As Ivan becomes frightened and isolated, his family avoids speaking honestly about his condition. Gerasim, a young household servant, offers him genuine compassion and eases his pain by supporting Ivan’s legs on his shoulders. Through Ivan’s suffering, Tolstoy asks what makes a life meaningful.

E. E. Cummings was an American modernist poet who experimented with how poems look and sound on the page. He often used lowercase letters where readers might expect capitals, including at the start of sentences and in names, and played with punctuation, word order, and spacing. In “maggie and milly and molly and may,” four girls visit the sea and find different things there; the poem suggests that what each person discovers reflects something about herself. Another poem, “anyone lived in a pretty how town,” follows a man called anyone and a woman called noone through courtship, marriage, aging, and death. As the town’s seasons return, their lives move forward while many neighbors barely notice them. Cummings’s unusual style helps readers pay attention to familiar experiences in new ways.

Death in Venice is a novella by the German writer Thomas Mann. Its main character, Gustav von Aschenbach, is an aging, disciplined author who travels to Venice, an Italian city built around canals. There he becomes captivated by Tadzio, a beautiful boy staying at the same hotel. Aschenbach watches him from a distance, and his fascination grows into an obsession. Meanwhile, a cholera outbreak spreads through the city. Although Aschenbach notices signs of danger, including the smell of disinfectant, he stays in Venice rather than leave Tadzio behind. First published in 1912, the novella explores the conflict between self-control and desire, as well as the attraction of beauty in the face of death. Mann also wrote the novel The Magic Mountain.

The Ramayana is an ancient Sanskrit Hindu epic traditionally attributed to the poet Valmiki. It tells the story of Prince Rama, whose exile from his kingdom leads him into the forest with his wife, Sita, and his brother Lakshmana. When the demon king Ravana abducts Sita and takes her to Lanka, Rama sets out to rescue her. One of Rama’s most devoted allies is Hanuman, a vanara, or monkey-like hero. Hanuman leaps across the ocean to Lanka to find Sita and later carries a mountain of medicinal herbs to save the wounded Lakshmana. Rama and his allies eventually wage war in Lanka and defeat Ravana. The epic is also valued for its exploration of loyalty, courage, and duty.

Jean Racine was a 17th-century French playwright and a leading figure in neoclassical drama, which valued carefully structured plots and powerful, controlled language. He is best known for tragedies in which characters struggle with passions they cannot easily control. His plays include Andromaque and Britannicus, and he was elected to the Académie française in 1673. His 1677 tragedy Phèdre draws on Greek mythology. Its central character is a queen of Athens who falls in love with her stepson, Hippolytus. When her husband, Theseus, is believed dead, she confesses this forbidden passion, setting off events that end in disaster. Racine’s portrayal of her guilt and desire helped make Phèdre one of the most celebrated plays in French classical drama.

Autobiography of Red is a 1998 novel-in-verse by Canadian writer Anne Carson. It retells an ancient Greek myth in which Herakles slays Geryon, a red monster, but turns Geryon into a modern adolescent with red wings. As Geryon grows up, he writes poetry, takes photographs, falls in love with Herakles, and travels with him. Carson’s version focuses less on a hero defeating a monster than on what life feels like from the so-called monster’s point of view. The title suggests that Geryon is telling the story of his own life, though the book mixes poetry, myth, and fiction rather than following the usual form of an autobiography.

The Secret Life of Walter Mitty is a comic short story by American humorist James Thurber, first published in The New Yorker in 1939. Walter Mitty is an ordinary husband running errands while his wife gets her hair done, but his imagination repeatedly turns everyday sights and sounds into dramatic adventures. In his daydreams, he pilots a Navy hydroplane through danger, becomes a brilliant surgeon performing a difficult operation, and plays other heroic roles. Meanwhile, he struggles with small real-life demands, such as remembering to buy overshoes. The contrast between Mitty’s spectacular fantasies and his frustratingly ordinary day creates much of the story’s humor. It also suggests why someone who feels overlooked or powerless might imagine being brave, skilled, and admired.

Andrew Clements was an American author whose novels often show how students’ ideas can change their schools. His books include No Talking, The Landry News, and Lunch Money, in which Greg Kenton and his childhood rival Maura Shaw make and sell comic books. Clements’s novel Frindle follows fifth-grader Nick Allen, who starts thinking about how words are created after a discussion in English class. Nick decides to call a pen a “frindle,” and his classmates begin using the new word too. What starts as a classroom idea spreads far beyond the school, gains national attention, and eventually reaches a dictionary. The story explores who gets to decide what words mean and how an ordinary idea can grow when people choose to use it.

E. B. White was an American author and essayist who contributed to The New Yorker for decades. He also helped revise The Elements of Style, a concise guide to English writing first written by his former Cornell professor, William Strunk Jr. White wrote the children’s books Stuart Little, about a mouse-like boy, and Charlotte’s Web, about a farm pig named Wilbur. In Charlotte’s Web, Wilbur faces slaughter until his friend Charlotte, a spider, weaves admiring words such as “SOME PIG!” and “TERRIFIC” into her web. The messages make people see Wilbur as special. Templeton, a rat, helps Charlotte find words for her plan, but only when he is offered food.

Peter Carey is an Australian novelist who has won the Booker Prize twice. His novel Oscar and Lucinda follows two unusual characters whose lives become linked by gambling. A wager to transport a glass church across the Australian landscape becomes a central part of their story. Carey’s other Booker Prize-winning novel, True History of the Kelly Gang, is a fictionalized account of Ned Kelly, a notorious nineteenth-century Australian bushranger, or outlaw who lived in the bush. Carey tells the story as if Kelly were writing letters for his daughter, giving readers an imagined version of the outlaw’s own voice. The book blends historical events with fiction rather than presenting itself as a straightforward biography.

The Souls of Black Folk is a 1903 collection of essays by W. E. B. Du Bois about African American life and the racism that shaped it after slavery. Its opening essay, “Of Our Spiritual Strivings,” introduces the image of a veil: a barrier that separates Black Americans from white society and affects how they are seen and understood. Du Bois also calls this division the “color line.” He describes double consciousness as a sense of “two-ness”: seeing yourself through your own eyes while also being aware of how a society that devalues Black people sees you. Throughout the book, Du Bois combines personal stories, history, and arguments for education and civil rights to show both the challenges Black Americans faced and the richness of their lives.

“Harlem,” a 1951 poem by Langston Hughes, asks, “What happens to a dream deferred?” A deferred dream is a hope or goal that someone has been forced to put off. Hughes explores the question through vivid images: the dream might dry up “like a raisin in the sun,” fester like a sore, or sag like a heavy load. The poem’s final question raises the possibility that it might explode. These images suggest the pain and pressure caused when hopes are repeatedly denied, especially for Black Americans facing racism. The raisin image inspired the title of Lorraine Hansberry’s 1959 play A Raisin in the Sun, which follows the Younger family as they pursue their dreams, including a move to a predominantly white neighborhood.

Robin Hood is a legendary English outlaw and folk hero whose stories began in medieval ballads and grew through centuries of retelling. He is famous for his skill with a bow and for leading a band of companions called the Merry Men, often portrayed as living in Sherwood Forest. In many versions of the legend, they rob the rich and give to the poor, making Robin a symbol of resistance to unfair authority. Robin Hood also appears in Sir Walter Scott’s historical novel Ivanhoe, published in 1819. There, he uses the name Locksley and helps the novel’s hero, Wilfred of Ivanhoe, a disinherited Saxon knight who has returned from the Crusades. Scott’s novel helped bring the Robin Hood legend to new readers.

In Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the play opens with Roman tribunes scolding citizens for celebrating Caesar’s triumph. As Caesar gains power, several Romans plot to kill him because they fear he will become a tyrant. He ignores warnings from a soothsayer to “beware the Ides of March,” from his wife Calpurnia, and from Artemidorus, who tries to give him a note naming conspirators. On the Ides of March, March 15, the conspirators stab Caesar, including Cassius and Caesar’s friend Brutus. After the murder, Brutus addresses the Roman crowd. He explains that he loved Caesar but loved Rome more, arguing that Caesar’s death protected the republic. Mark Antony then gives an opposing funeral speech that turns the crowd against the conspirators.

Pyramus and Thisbe is a tragic love story about two young people in Babylon whose families forbid them to meet. They secretly speak through a crack in the wall between their homes and arrange to meet outside the city. Thisbe arrives first but flees when she sees a lioness, leaving behind her veil. The lioness bloodies it, and Pyramus, finding the veil, mistakenly believes Thisbe has been killed. He takes his own life; when Thisbe returns and finds him, she does the same. The Roman poet Ovid retells their story in Book IV of the Metamorphoses, his Latin poem of interconnected myths and transformations. Centuries later, Shakespeare’s craftsmen perform a comic version of the tragedy as a play within A Midsummer Night’s Dream.

Mark Antony is a Roman statesman and a loyal ally of Julius Caesar in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar. After Brutus and Cassius lead a conspiracy to assassinate Caesar, Antony survives and asks to speak at Caesar’s funeral. Brutus gives him permission on the condition that he not openly condemn the conspirators. Antony begins, “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears,” then repeatedly calls the assassins “honourable men.” The phrase sounds respectful at first, but Antony’s praise becomes increasingly ironic as he describes Caesar’s wounds and reminds the crowd of Caesar’s generosity. His speech turns the citizens against the conspirators. The play follows the consequences of the murder and ends after Brutus and Cassius are defeated at the Battle of Philippi.

Sense and Sensibility is an 1811 novel by Jane Austen about two sisters, Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, and their contrasting experiences of love. After their father dies, the Dashwood women must leave their childhood home, Norland Park, and move to Barton Cottage, which they rent from Sir John Middleton. Elinor tends to be guided by “sense”: she is practical and careful about expressing her feelings. Marianne embodies “sensibility,” meaning she openly follows her emotions and romantic hopes. As the sisters face disappointment and make choices about their futures, the novel explores love, family, money, and expectations for women in their society. It was first published under the name “A Lady,” rather than Austen’s own name. Austen also wrote Pride and Prejudice, Mansfield Park, and Northanger Abbey.

The Bean Eaters is a 1960 poetry collection by Gwendolyn Brooks, a poet known for portraying African American life with close attention to ordinary people. In the collection’s title poem, an elderly couple eat beans in a rented back room. Their dinner is simple, but the beads, receipts, dolls, and cloth around them suggest a lifetime of memories and experiences. The collection also includes “We Real Cool,” a short poem about seven young pool players at the Golden Shovel who have left school. Brooks often used vivid details and distinctive rhythms to make readers think about people they might otherwise overlook. Her earlier book Annie Allen won the 1950 Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, making Brooks the first African American to receive that award.

Milo Minderbinder is a mess officer in Joseph Heller’s satirical World War II novel Catch-22.
