While his bomber squadron flies dangerous missions from the island of Pianosa, Milo sees chances to make money everywhere. He builds a trading syndicate called M&M Enterprises and claims its profits benefit everyone, even when his deals put fellow airmen at risk. In one absurd example, he buys eggs for seven cents each, sells them for five, and insists he still makes a profit. His schemes run alongside the story of bombardier John Yossarian, who desperately tries to escape combat missions. The novel’s title refers to a contradictory rule that traps airmen in military bureaucracy. Through Milo, Heller makes fun of greed and the idea that profit justifies any action.

Cats appear throughout the fiction of modern Japanese author Haruki Murakami, often as missing pets or mysterious presences. In his novel The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, the protagonist, Toru Okada, is asked to search for his household cat, which is named after his wife’s brother. What begins as an ordinary search becomes part of Okada’s increasingly strange life, in which familiar routines give way to unsettling events. The missing cat helps draw him into that mystery, showing how Murakami can use an everyday animal to connect ordinary life with the unknown. Remember the key pairing: the recurring animal is a cat, and the novel in which Toru Okada searches for one is The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle.

In George Orwell’s dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, Julia is a young woman living under the Party’s constant surveillance and the rule of Big Brother. She secretly defies the Party by beginning an affair with Winston Smith, a worker at the Ministry of Truth. Winston’s job is to rewrite historical records so they match whatever the Party currently claims, but in private he keeps a diary criticizing its control over people’s lives. Julia first approaches him by passing him a note that says “I love you.” Their relationship is dangerous because the Party forbids personal loyalties that might compete with loyalty to Big Brother. Through Julia and Winston, the novel shows how even love and private thoughts can become acts of rebellion in a society that tries to control everything.

In Nathaniel Hawthorne’s novel The Scarlet Letter, Hester Prynne lives in a Puritan community that punishes her for adultery. She is forced to wear an embroidered red A on her clothing, known as the scarlet letter A, so everyone can see what she has done. Hester’s daughter, Pearl Prynne, is the child of her relationship with the minister Arthur Dimmesdale. Pearl is lively and spirited, and she often accompanies Hester, including on visits to the forest. Her name is also the name of a precious gemstone. Although the letter begins as a mark of public shame, Hester’s care for Pearl and her work helping others show that she is more than the wrongdoing it represents.

Vardaman Bundren is the youngest child in William Faulkner’s novel As I Lay Dying. After his mother, Addie, dies, the Bundren family carries her coffin on a difficult journey to Jefferson, where she wanted to be buried with her family. Vardaman struggles to understand her death. Thinking Addie might need air, he drills holes in the lid of her coffin, but accidentally drills into her face. After seeing a dead fish he has been asked to clean, he says, “My mother is a fish,” a strange but memorable line that shows how he tries to make sense of losing her. The novel is set in Faulkner’s fictional Yoknapatawpha County and tells the story through the shifting thoughts and voices of different characters.

Gather Together in My Name is Maya Angelou’s second autobiographical memoir, published in 1974. It continues the life story she began in I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, the first book in her seven-volume autobiographical series. In this memoir, Angelou writes about her early adulthood as Rita, a young Black mother trying to support herself and her son in postwar California. She moves between jobs and faces poverty, racism, and difficult choices while searching for security and independence. For example, the army rejects Rita because it suspects her of being a communist. By describing both her mistakes and her determination to survive, Angelou gives readers a personal view of the challenges facing a young Black woman and mother in the United States after World War II.

Paul Revere’s Ride is an 1860 narrative poem by American poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, who also wrote The Song of Hiawatha and Evangeline. It tells the story of Boston silversmith Paul Revere’s warning ride on the night of April 18, 1775, before the Battles of Lexington and Concord. In the poem, Revere arranges for lanterns in the Old North Church tower to signal how British troops are leaving Boston: “one if by land, and two if by sea.” After seeing the signal, he rides through Middlesex County, warning towns such as Medford, Lexington, and Concord that the British are coming. Longfellow dramatized the ride to celebrate courage and the spread of an urgent warning, so the poem is not an exact historical account.

Macduff is the Thane of Fife in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Macbeth. After Macbeth murders King Duncan and seizes the Scottish throne, Macduff grows suspicious of him and flees to England to help Duncan’s son Malcolm challenge his rule. In revenge, Macbeth has Macduff’s wife and children killed. Macduff joins Malcolm and an English-backed army to reclaim Scotland, and he ultimately kills Macbeth in battle, avenging his family. The three witches had told Macbeth that no one “of woman born” could harm him, making him feel safe. But Macduff reveals that he was “untimely ripped” from his mother’s womb—born by caesarean section—so he does not fit the prophecy in the way Macbeth expected.

In George Orwell’s dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, the ruling Party develops Newspeak, an official language designed to limit what people can think and say. Party linguists repeatedly revise its dictionary, deleting words and narrowing meanings so that ideas such as political rebellion become harder to express. Syme, a philologist working on the Newspeak dictionary, enthusiastically tells the protagonist, Winston Smith, that a future edition will contain far fewer words. Syme understands that the Party wants to make rebellious thoughts nearly impossible by removing the language needed to describe them. Despite his loyalty to the Party, he later disappears and becomes an “unperson”: someone erased from official records as though he had never existed. Newspeak shows how controlling language can help a government control people.

Master Harold...and the Boys is a play by South African writer Athol Fugard, set in a Port Elizabeth tea room during apartheid, when South Africa enforced racial segregation. Hally, a white teenager, has grown up close to two Black employees, Sam and Willie, but his treatment of them becomes increasingly cruel. Sam remembers building a kite with Hally when he was younger, a memory that shows how much their friendship once meant to them. Sam is also an enthusiastic ballroom dancer. He imagines a world like a well-run dance competition, where people move gracefully without colliding, as a contrast to the harm caused by racism. The play’s turning point comes when Hally spits in Sam’s face and insists that Sam call him “Master Harold” instead of Hally.

Doubt: A Parable is a play by John Patrick Shanley set at a Catholic school in the Bronx, New York, in the 1960s. Sister Aloysius, the strict principal, becomes suspicious of Father Flynn’s relationship with a student and worries that he may have behaved inappropriately. A younger nun, Sister James, is caught between Sister Aloysius’s suspicions and Father Flynn’s explanations. The play never gives the audience a definite answer about what happened, so its title points to a central question: how should people act when they cannot be certain of the truth? Alongside this conflict, the characters plan a school pageant and debate whether it should include secular or religious songs for Christmas. The Christmas season is also the setting for the family gathering in James Joyce’s short story “The Dead.”

“A Sound of Thunder” is a science-fiction short story by American author Ray Bradbury. Eckels, a wealthy client, pays to join a commercial Time Safari that travels millions of years into the past to hunt a Tyrannosaurus rex. The guides warn him to stay on a raised path so he will not disturb anything that could change the future. When Eckels sees the dinosaur, he panics and steps off the path. After the group returns to the present, they notice that language has changed and that the presidential election has had a different outcome: Deutscher, a candidate described as a fascist, has defeated Keith. Eckels then discovers a crushed butterfly on his boot. The story shows how even a tiny change in the past can have enormous consequences.

Owl Creek Bridge is the fictional wooden railroad bridge in Alabama where Ambrose Bierce sets his short story “An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge.” During the American Civil War, Union soldiers prepare to hang Peyton Farquhar, an Alabama planter and Confederate sympathizer, from the bridge. As he waits, Farquhar’s senses seem unusually sharp: the ticking of his watch sounds to him like loud hammer blows. He then appears to escape into the creek below and make his way toward home. The story’s ending reveals that this escape happened only in his imagination in the moments before his death. Farquhar has been hanged and is swinging beneath the bridge’s timbers.

In Gabriel García Márquez’s short story A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings, a poor couple, Pelayo and his wife Elisenda, find a frail elderly man lying in their courtyard after a storm. His enormous feathered wings lead villagers to argue about whether he is an angel, though no one can explain who he is. As crowds gather to see him, Elisenda charges admission. The couple later uses the money to build a mansion, while the old man remains neglected in their yard. The story is an example of magical realism: it places something seemingly supernatural in an ordinary setting and shows people responding to it as part of everyday life. It also asks readers to consider how curiosity and greed can affect the way people treat someone vulnerable.

Father Mapple is a former whaleman who becomes a preacher in Herman Melville’s novel Moby-Dick. Before Ishmael and Queequeg sail with Captain Ahab, they hear him speak at the Whaleman’s Chapel in New Bedford. Mapple climbs a rope ladder to a pulpit shaped like a ship’s bow, making the chapel feel closely connected to life at sea. His sermon tells the biblical story of Jonah, a prophet who tries to escape by ship after God commands him to preach in the city of Nineveh. A storm strikes, Jonah is thrown overboard and swallowed by a great fish. After he is released, he carries out God’s command. Mapple uses Jonah’s story to urge his listeners to face their duties rather than run from them.

The Emperor’s New Clothes is a fairy tale by the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen, who also wrote The Snow Queen and The Little Mermaid. In the story, two swindlers promise an emperor a magnificent new outfit. They claim its fabric is invisible to anyone who is foolish or unfit for their job. Afraid of looking foolish, the emperor and his officials pretend they can see the clothes, even though the swindlers have made nothing. The emperor then parades through the city wearing no clothes, while the crowd praises his supposed outfit. Finally, a child says aloud that the emperor is naked. The tale shows how fear of embarrassment and pressure to agree with others can keep people from telling the truth.

Matilda is a children’s novel by Roald Dahl about Matilda Wormwood, a book-loving girl whose extraordinary intelligence goes unnoticed by her neglectful parents. At Crunchem Hall Primary School, she finds support from her kind teacher, Miss Honey, but must also face the terrifying headmistress, Miss Trunchbull. A former Olympic hammer thrower, Miss Trunchbull bullies pupils and treats Miss Honey cruelly. Matilda discovers that she can use telekinesis to move objects with her mind. She uses this power to make chalk write a message on the classroom board, convincing Miss Trunchbull that she is being haunted. Miss Trunchbull flees, and Miss Honey eventually adopts Matilda. The novel celebrates reading, kindness, and the courage to stand up to unfair adults.

Timaeus is a philosophical dialogue by the ancient Greek thinker Plato. It opens with Socrates recalling an earlier discussion of an ideal city. Timaeus, a Pythagorean philosopher from southern Italy, then explains how the cosmos was created and how it is structured. The dialogue also introduces a story that continues in Plato’s unfinished Critias: Egyptian priests told the Athenian lawgiver Solon about a war between ancient Athens and Atlantis, a powerful island civilization. They said Atlantis lay beyond the Pillars of Heracles, near the entrance to the Mediterranean Sea, and was larger than Libya and Asia put together. According to the story, earthquakes and floods destroyed the island. Atlantis is generally understood as part of Plato’s philosophical storytelling, not a confirmed historical place.

My Ántonia is a 1918 novel by American author Willa Cather, who also wrote O Pioneers! and The Song of the Lark. Its first-person narrator, Jim Burden, looks back on his childhood on the Nebraska prairie and his friendship with Ántonia Shimerda, a girl whose Czech family has immigrated to farm the land. Jim’s memories follow Ántonia through hard work, family struggles, and changes in her life, including a job as a housekeeper for the Harlings. She eventually marries Anton Cuzak and raises a large family. Through Jim’s account, Cather portrays immigrant homesteaders and explores how people build a sense of home in a new place.

Diedrich Knickerbocker is a fictional Dutch antiquarian created by American author Washington Irving. Irving presented him as the supposed author of A History of New York, a humorous account of the city’s Dutch past. Knickerbocker also appears as a source for stories in Irving’s collection The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., published in installments in 1819–20. That collection includes “Rip Van Winkle” and “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,” which are presented as tales drawn from Knickerbocker’s papers. In “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,” schoolteacher Ichabod Crane hears of the Headless Horseman, a ghost said to search for his missing head. By attributing stories to Knickerbocker, Irving gave them the feel of old local legends.

“God’s Grandeur” is a sonnet by Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Victorian poet and Jesuit priest who also wrote “The Windhover” and “Pied Beauty.” The poem says that God’s presence fills the world, sometimes flashing out like light and sometimes gathering slowly, like oil pressed from olives. Hopkins asks why people fail to recognize this power. Generations of work and industry have worn down the earth, leaving it marked by human footsteps, but they have not used up nature’s freshness. Each morning offers a new beginning because the Holy Spirit watches over the world, “broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings.” Hopkins’s distinctive sprung rhythm gives the sonnet an energetic, speech-like sound that matches its sense of wonder and hope.

“I heard a Fly buzz—when I died—” is a lyric poem by Emily Dickinson, a 19th-century American poet known for exploring death, hope, and the mysteries of the mind. The speaker describes a deathbed scene: mourners have gathered, and the room is so still that everyone seems to be waiting for the final moment. Instead of a grand or comforting vision, the speaker hears a fly buzzing. It crosses the speaker’s field of vision as the light fades and the speaker’s sight fails. This ordinary, distracting insect makes the moment of death feel strange and uncertain. Dickinson wrote other well-known poems, including “Because I could not stop for Death” and “Hope is the thing with feathers.”

Island of the Blue Dolphins is a 1960 historical novel for young readers by Scott O’Dell. It follows Karana, a Native American girl living on an island off the California coast. When her people leave for the mainland, Karana stays behind to look for her younger brother, Ramo. After a pack of wild dogs kills him, she must survive alone by finding food, building shelter, and making tools. Karana first sees the dogs as enemies, but she later captures their leader and gradually earns his trust. She names him Rontu, and he becomes her companion. The story explores Karana’s courage, loneliness, and changing relationship with the animals and landscape around her.

Wide Sargasso Sea is a 1966 novel by Jean Rhys that reimagines the life of a character from Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre. In Brontë’s novel, Mr. Rochester’s first wife, Bertha Mason, is confined in the attic of his English home. Rhys tells the story from the perspective of that woman before she becomes known as Bertha. Born Antoinette Cosway, she grows up in the Caribbean amid tensions shaped by slavery and colonialism. After marrying an Englishman, she faces his suspicion and rejection of her Caribbean identity. He begins calling her Bertha, a name she does not choose. By giving Antoinette a voice and a history, Wide Sargasso Sea asks readers to reconsider the woman whom Jane Eyre presents mainly through her husband’s account.

Breakfast of Champions is a satirical novel by American author Kurt Vonnegut. Its title borrows the slogan “Breakfast of Champions,” used to advertise Wheaties cereal. The story brings together Dwayne Hoover, a wealthy car dealer, and Kilgore Trout, a science-fiction writer whose work Dwayne takes dangerously literally. Through their encounter, Vonnegut uses dark humor, drawings, and interruptions to poke fun at advertising, consumer culture, and ideas about success in America. Vonnegut also wrote Slaughterhouse-Five, whose protagonist, Billy Pilgrim, becomes “unstuck in time” and experiences events out of order. Both novels show Vonnegut’s unusual style: he mixes serious concerns with absurd situations to make readers question the world around them.

An epithet is a descriptive word or phrase regularly attached to a person or thing. In ancient Greek epic poetry, Homer uses stock epithets such as “swift-footed Achilles” to emphasize a hero’s speed and “rosy-fingered Dawn” to describe the appearance of daybreak. Because these phrases recur, they help listeners recognize familiar figures and give the poem a rhythmic pattern. Epics also use another device called the Homeric simile: an extended comparison that may run for several lines. Like other similes, it uses “like” or “as,” but it develops the image in more detail, perhaps comparing a battle scene to a storm or an event from everyday life. An epithet supplies a recurring description; a Homeric simile builds a longer comparison.

Four Quartets is a sequence of four interrelated poems by T. S. Eliot, first published separately and later gathered into one work. Its opening poem, “Burnt Norton,” imagines a path into a garden the speaker never entered, using that unrealized possibility to explore memory and the relationship between past, present, and future. The second poem, “East Coker,” is named for a village in Somerset, England, connected to Eliot’s family history. Its refrain, “In my beginning is my end,” suggests that beginnings and endings are linked in the cycles of life. The other poems are “The Dry Salvages” and “Little Gidding.” Together, the four poems consider time, loss, faith, and the possibility of spiritual renewal.

A Handful of Dust is a 1934 novel by British writer Evelyn Waugh. It follows Tony Last, an English country gentleman whose comfortable life collapses when his marriage falls apart. After leaving England, Tony becomes stranded in the Brazilian jungle. Waugh uses Tony’s misfortunes to satirize the wealthy society around him, showing the cruelty and emptiness beneath its polite appearance. The novel’s title alludes to the line “I will show you fear in a handful of dust” from The Waste Land, a 1922 poem by T. S. Eliot. That poem includes sections called “The Burial of the Dead” and “A Game of Chess.” Knowing Tony’s story and the source of the title helps identify both Waugh’s novel and Eliot’s poem.

The Magic Mountain is a 1924 German-language novel by Thomas Mann. Its main character, Hans Castorp, is a young engineer who visits his cousin at the Berghof, a sanatorium in the Swiss Alps, intending to stay only a few weeks. After doctors find signs of illness, he remains there for seven years. Life at the sanatorium gives Hans time to think about sickness, death, love, and the world beyond the mountain. Among the people who influence him is Lodovico Settembrini, an Italian humanist who champions reason, progress, and democratic ideals. Settembrini frequently argues with Leo Naphta, a Jesuit-trained thinker whose views challenge his own. Through Hans’s long stay and these debates, Mann explores competing ideas in European society before the First World War.

Shakuntala is a heroine in the Mahabharata, an ancient Indian epic, and in a later Sanskrit play by the poet Kālidāsa. She is the daughter of the sage Vishvamitra and the celestial nymph Menaka, but she grows up in the forest hermitage of the sage Kanva. Shakuntala marries King Dushyanta, and their son Bharata becomes an important figure in Indian legend. In Kālidāsa’s play, often called The Recognition of Shakuntala, a curse causes Dushyanta to forget their marriage. He has given Shakuntala a signet ring, but she loses it in a river. A fish swallows the ring, and a fisherman later finds it inside the fish and brings it to court. Seeing the ring restores Dushyanta’s memory, allowing the couple to reunite.

Henry Fleming is the young Union private at the center of Stephen Crane’s 1895 Civil War novel The Red Badge of Courage. He enlists imagining that battle will prove his courage, but when fighting becomes terrifying, he runs from his first major engagement. Henry envies wounded soldiers because he thinks a wound would be a “red badge” proving bravery. He later receives a head wound from another soldier, not from enemy fire, and returns to his regiment. As the fighting continues, Henry helps lead an advance alongside his friend Wilson and carries the regiment’s flag. Even as he grows more confident, he remembers abandoning a tattered soldier and regrets the death of Jim Conklin. His experiences show that courage is more complicated than the heroic image he first imagined.

The Three Witches, also called the weird sisters, are supernatural figures in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Macbeth. They meet Macbeth, a Scottish thane, on a heath and predict that he will become king. Their prophecies help spark his ambition, but their later predictions are dangerously misleading. They tell Macbeth that no man “of woman born” can harm him, making him believe he cannot be killed. Macduff, the Thane of Fife, defeats and kills Macbeth because he was delivered by an early surgical birth: he was “from his mother’s womb untimely ripped.” The witches also predict that Banquo’s descendants will become kings. Their words shape the play’s events while raising a question: do the witches control the future, or do people bring it about through their choices?

Horace, whose full name was Quintus Horatius Flaccus, was a Roman poet of the Augustan era. His works include the Odes, Epodes, Satires, and Epistles. In the Odes, he wrote the Latin line “dulce et decorum est pro patria mori,” meaning “it is sweet and fitting to die for one’s country.” One of his verse epistles, addressed to the Piso family, is called Ars Poetica, or “The Art of Poetry.” It offers advice on poetic composition, including how writers can make their work coherent and effective. Horace opens it with a deliberately ridiculous image: a painter joining a horse’s neck to a human head. He uses this mismatched creature to show why the parts of a poem should fit together.

Piggy is an intelligent, asthmatic boy in William Golding’s 1954 novel Lord of the Flies. After a crash strands a group of British schoolboys on an uninhabited island, Piggy helps Ralph try to keep the group organized. He values rules, reason, and cooperation, while other boys become more interested in hunting and power. Piggy’s spectacles are especially important: the boys use their lenses to start a signal fire that might attract rescuers. When Jack’s tribe takes the glasses, they gain control over the group’s ability to make fire. Piggy continues to argue for order, but Roger, one of Jack’s followers, kills him by rolling a boulder onto him. His death marks how far the boys have moved from the rules they once tried to follow.

Eliza Doolittle is the young Cockney flower seller at the center of George Bernard Shaw’s play Pygmalion. Professor Henry Higgins, an expert in phonetics, notices her speech at Covent Garden, where she initially mistakes him for a policeman. Higgins and Colonel Pickering make a wager: Higgins will teach Eliza to speak and behave so convincingly like a wealthy lady that she can pass as a duchess. As Eliza learns, she also begins to question how Higgins treats her and what kind of life she wants for herself. Shaw uses her story to explore class, language, and the unfair judgments people make based on how someone speaks. The play’s title comes from a Greek myth about a sculptor who creates an ideal woman, but Eliza is a person with choices of her own.

In Harper Lee’s To Kill a Mockingbird, Calpurnia is the longtime cook in Atticus Finch’s household in Maycomb, Alabama. She helps raise his children, Scout and Jem, and is a trusted maternal figure to them. Calpurnia is also part of Maycomb’s Black community, giving the children a view of life beyond their own household. One Sunday, she takes Scout and Jem to worship with her at First Purchase African M.E. Church, where Reverend Sykes leads the service. The visit helps the children see Calpurnia as someone with a life and community of her own, while also showing them how racial divisions shape Maycomb.

August Strindberg was a Swedish playwright and novelist whose experiments with dramatic form helped shape modernist theater. His chamber play The Ghost Sonata creates a dreamlike, unsettling world in which the ghost of a milkmaid haunts Jacob Hummel, a vengeful man who uses a wheelchair. Strindberg also wrote Miss Julie, an 1888 naturalistic tragedy set during a Midsummer’s Eve celebration. It follows Julie, a count’s daughter, and Jean, her father’s valet, as their attraction develops into a destructive struggle shaped by class and power. In one shocking moment, Jean kills Julie’s pet canary. The two plays show different sides of Strindberg’s work: The Ghost Sonata is mysterious and symbolic, while Miss Julie focuses on human behavior and social pressures.

Rapunzel is a German fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm, Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, for their collection Children’s and Household Tales, first published in 1812. The story begins when a pregnant woman craves a leafy vegetable called rapunzel from an enchantress’s garden. After her husband takes some for her, the enchantress demands their child in return and names the girl Rapunzel. She later imprisons Rapunzel in a tower with no door or stairs. To enter, the enchantress calls for Rapunzel to let down her extraordinarily long hair, which a prince also uses to climb up to her. When the enchantress discovers their meetings, she cuts Rapunzel’s hair and sends her away. The prince falls from the tower into thorns and is blinded, but he eventually finds Rapunzel again.

Lyrical Ballads is a poetry collection first published in 1798 by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge. It helped launch English Romanticism, a movement that valued emotion, imagination, nature, and individual experience. The collection includes Coleridge’s mysterious “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” and Wordsworth’s “Tintern Abbey,” which reflects on memory, nature, and a visit with his sister. For the 1800 edition, Wordsworth wrote an influential preface arguing that poetry could focus on ordinary people and experiences and use language close to everyday speech. His ideas challenged the formal style many readers expected from poetry at the time. Wordsworth also wrote The Prelude, a long autobiographical poem about the growth of his mind as a poet.

David Copperfield is a Victorian novel by Charles Dickens, told in the first person by its title character as he looks back on his life. David’s childhood is shaped by a cruel stepfather, work in a factory, and a journey to live with his aunt, Betsey Trotwood. The story follows his education, friendships, love, and gradual moral growth, making it a bildungsroman, or coming-of-age novel. As an adult, David helps expose the dishonest Uriah Heep and eventually marries Agnes Wickfield. Dickens also created Ebenezer Scrooge in A Christmas Carol and Pip in Great Expectations, and wrote A Tale of Two Cities, a novel set during the French Revolution.

Il Canzoniere is a collection of lyric poems written in Italian by the fourteenth-century poet Petrarch, an important figure in early humanism. It includes sonnets, canzoni (songs), and other poems, many of them addressed to or inspired by a woman named Laura. Petrarch presents Laura as an idealized beloved: her presence brings him joy, while her absence causes longing and sorrow. His poems often explore conflicting feelings about love, as in the line “I burn and yet I freeze.” The collection opens by asking readers to listen to his “scattered rhymes.” Through its personal voice and careful treatment of emotion, Il Canzoniere became a major influence on later European love poetry.

“To His Coy Mistress” is a carpe diem poem by the English poet Andrew Marvell. Its speaker tells a woman that, if they had endless time, he could spend centuries admiring her: his “vegetable love” would grow slowly and become “vaster than empires.” But they do not have forever. He hears “Time’s winged chariot hurrying near” and argues that youth and life will end, so they should enjoy love and pleasure now. The poem moves from an imaginary world of unlimited time to the urgent reality of mortality. Marvell also wrote “The Garden” and the country-house poem “Upon Appleton House.” Beyond poetry, he served as a Member of Parliament and held a government post under Oliver Cromwell.

Daniel Keyes was an American writer who studied psychology at Brooklyn College and became best known for Flowers for Algernon. First published as a short story and later expanded into a novel, it follows Charlie Gordon, a bakery worker with an intellectual disability who undergoes an experimental operation intended to increase his intelligence. Charlie tells the story through “progress reports,” which show how his writing and understanding change as he becomes a genius. A laboratory mouse named Algernon has undergone the same experiment, and changes in Algernon’s abilities offer a warning about what may happen to Charlie. As Charlie’s intelligence declines, he asks that flowers be placed on Algernon’s grave. Keyes also wrote The Fifth Sally, a novel about a woman with multiple personalities.

Samuel Beckett was an Irish avant-garde playwright and novelist whose work often explores uncertainty, isolation, and the search for meaning. He is especially known for absurdist drama, in which characters repeat actions or conversations while little seems to change. In Waiting for Godot, Vladimir and Estragon spend their time beside a nearly bare tree, waiting for a mysterious person named Godot who never arrives. They encounter Pozzo and Lucky, but remain unsure what to do next. Another major Beckett play, Endgame, takes place in a sparse shelter. Hamm, who cannot walk, depends on his servant Clov, while Hamm’s parents, Nagg and Nell, live in ashbins and cannot even kiss. These unusual settings and relationships help Beckett show people trying to connect with one another in a confusing world.

Tarzan is a fictional hero created by American writer Edgar Rice Burroughs. Raised by apes in the African jungle, he first appeared in Burroughs’s 1912 novel Tarzan of the Apes. His adventures made him a famous character in books, films, and comics, and his habit of swinging through trees is one of his best-known traits. Tarzan is also mentioned in The House on Mango Street, a novel by Sandra Cisneros about Esperanza, a girl growing up in Chicago. Esperanza breaks her arm while trying to imitate Tarzan. Later, she gets a job working with film negatives at Peter Pan Photo Finishers. These details connect the two books: Tarzan is Burroughs’s jungle-raised hero, while The House on Mango Street is the novel about Esperanza.

The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky is a short story by American writer Stephen Crane. Jack Potter, the marshal of the Texas town of Yellow Sky, returns by train with the woman he has just married. He worries that he did not tell the townspeople about the wedding. Meanwhile, Scratchy Wilson, a local gunfighter, is looking for the kind of confrontation he and Potter have had before. When Scratchy meets Potter and sees his new wife, he learns that the marshal is unarmed and newly married. The expected showdown no longer makes sense, and Scratchy walks away. The story shows how marriage and ordinary life can change the old customs of a frontier town. Crane also wrote The Red Badge of Courage, about the young Union soldier Henry Fleming, and the shipwreck story The Open Boat.

The Lightning Thief is the first novel in Rick Riordan’s Percy Jackson & the Olympians series. It follows Percy Jackson, a twelve-year-old New York schoolboy who discovers that the gods of ancient Greece are real and that he is a son of Poseidon. After Zeus’s powerful master bolt goes missing, Percy is accused of stealing it. His friend Grover Underwood takes him to Camp Half-Blood, a refuge for children of Greek gods, where Percy begins to understand his identity. Percy then sets out across the United States with Grover and Annabeth Chase to find the bolt and prevent a conflict among the gods. Along the way, he faces mythological dangers and uses Anaklusmos, a sword that appears as a pen until he uncaps it.

Voltaire was the pen name of François-Marie Arouet, an eighteenth-century French writer and philosopher of the Enlightenment. He used sharp satire to question powerful institutions and defend freedom of religion. His best-known satirical novel, Candide, follows a young man who is expelled from Baron Thunder-ten-Tronckh’s castle and encounters war, cruelty, and other hardships as he travels. Among his companions are his tutor Pangloss and the servant Cacambo. Pangloss insists that everything happens for the best in “the best of all possible worlds,” an optimistic view that the novel repeatedly challenges. After searching for answers in many places, Candide ends by saying that “we must cultivate our garden.” This suggests that practical work and improving the world around us matter more than simply claiming that everything is already good.

David Levithan is an American author and editor known for young adult novels that put LGBTQ+ teenagers and their relationships at the center of the story. He worked as an editor at Scholastic, a publisher of children’s books. His 2003 debut novel, Boy Meets Boy, follows Paul, a gay teenager navigating first love at an unusually accepting high school where a student who plays quarterback is also elected homecoming queen. Levithan also wrote Two Boys Kissing, which explores the lives of several gay teens. With John Green, he cowrote Will Grayson, Will Grayson, a novel told by two teenage narrators—one straight and one gay—who share the same name. His books give young readers stories about love, identity, and finding a place to belong.

“The Interlopers” is a short story by the British writer Saki, the pen name of Hector Hugh Munro. It follows Ulrich von Gradwitz and Georg Znaeym, two landowners whose families have feuded for generations over a strip of forest. While hunting on the disputed land, they confront each other, but a falling tree pins them both to the ground. At first each hopes his own men will arrive first, but as they wait, they put aside their hatred and agree to become friends. When figures finally appear in the distance, Ulrich realizes they are wolves, not rescuers. The ending gives the story its dark twist: the men stop treating each other as enemies just as a greater danger arrives. Saki also wrote “The Open Window,” in which Framton Nuttel is told that three hunters died in a bog.

A Clockwork Orange is a 1962 dystopian novel by British writer Anthony Burgess. Its teenage narrator, Alex, leads a gang of “droogs,” or close friends, who gather at the Korova Milk Bar and commit acts of violence. After Alex is arrested, the authorities try to stop his violent behavior through an experimental treatment that makes him feel sick whenever he thinks about violence. The story asks whether someone can truly be good if they have no freedom to choose between right and wrong. Alex tells the story in Nadsat, a fictional youth argot that mixes English with words drawn mainly from Russian. For example, “droog” means friend, while “tolchock” refers to a blow or hit.

Long John Silver is a memorable pirate in Robert Louis Stevenson’s adventure novel Treasure Island. He serves as the cook aboard the Hispaniola, the ship that carries young Jim Hawkins and an expedition funded by Squire Trelawney to an island where pirate treasure is buried. Captain Smollett commands the ship, but Silver secretly organizes a mutiny among its crew. A former seaman with one leg, Silver is friendly and persuasive, and he initially wins Jim’s trust. Jim later discovers that the cook is plotting to seize the treasure for himself and the other pirates. Silver can be charming one moment and dangerous the next, making it hard to know what he will do. By the end of the story, he escapes with some of the treasure.

The Brontë sisters were three nineteenth-century English novelists: Anne, Charlotte, and Emily Brontë. They published under the pen names Acton, Currer, and Ellis Bell, partly because women writers faced prejudice at the time. Anne wrote Agnes Grey, while Emily wrote Wuthering Heights, a dark novel about Heathcliff and the Earnshaw and Linton families. Charlotte’s best-known novel is Jane Eyre. Its heroine is an orphan who becomes a governess at Thornfield Hall, the home of Edward Rochester. Jane and Rochester fall in love, but she discovers that his wife, Bertha Mason, is confined in the house. The sisters’ novels explore love, independence, family conflict, and the limits placed on women in their society.

The Comedy of Errors is a comedy by William Shakespeare built around two pairs of identical twins. After a shipwreck separates their family, one Antipholus grows up in Syracuse with his servant Dromio, while their twins, also named Antipholus and Dromio, live in Ephesus. Years later, Antipholus of Syracuse and his Dromio enter Ephesus without knowing their brothers are there. Because the twins look alike and share names, townspeople repeatedly mistake one brother for the other, leading to arguments, strange encounters, and comic confusion. At the start of the play, the Duke of Ephesus judges Egeon, the twins’ father, who has come searching for his lost family. The mix-ups eventually end when the family is reunited.

Khaled Hosseini is an Afghan-American novelist born in Kabul, Afghanistan. After his family settled in the United States, he trained as a physician in California before becoming a writer. His novels include A Thousand Splendid Suns and And the Mountains Echoed, but his best-known book is The Kite Runner, published in 2003. It follows Amir, who grows up in Afghanistan with his childhood friend Hassan. After Amir witnesses Hassan being attacked and fails to help him, guilt shapes much of his life. Years later, Amir returns from the United States to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan to rescue Sohrab, Hassan’s son. The novel’s title refers to the kite-flying tournaments of Amir’s childhood, when Hassan ran to retrieve fallen kites. Through Amir’s story, Hosseini explores friendship, betrayal, and the possibility of making amends.

In William Shakespeare’s play The Tempest, Caliban is an enslaved inhabitant of the island ruled by Prospero, the former Duke of Milan. Caliban is the son of the dead witch Sycorax and believes the island belongs to him. He resents Prospero’s control, including being taught Prospero’s language, which he says he can now use to curse. When the shipwrecked Trinculo first sees Caliban, he mistakes him for a fish. Caliban later drinks wine offered by another newcomer, Stephano, and pledges to be Stephano’s “true subject.” Prospero, meanwhile, uses magic and the help of the spirit Ariel to bring his brother Antonio’s ship to the island. Before leaving, Prospero gives up his magic and frees Ariel.

Hwæt is the Old English word that opens Beowulf, a medieval poem about the Spear-Danes and the hero’s battles with Grendel, Grendel’s mother, and a dragon. At the start of the poem, it calls for the audience’s attention, much like “Listen!” or “Lo!” Because it has no single perfect modern equivalent, translators choose different openings to set the tone. J.R.R. Tolkien used “Lo!”, while the Irish poet Seamus Heaney chose “So!” In her 2020 translation, American novelist Maria Dahvana Headley rendered Hwæt! as “Bro!” to capture a bold, conversational voice. She compared its force to a man in a bar pounding his glass and demanding another drink. These choices show how one word can shape a reader’s first impression of a story.

Gerard Manley Hopkins was a nineteenth-century English poet and Jesuit priest whose faith shaped much of his writing. He developed sprung rhythm, a style that counts stressed beats but allows the number of unstressed syllables to vary, giving his poems an energetic, speech-like sound. His verse also uses striking alliteration and vivid images. In “The Windhover,” he describes a falcon in flight as the “morning morning’s minion” and a “dapple-dawn-drawn Falcon.” Hopkins wrote his long poem “The Wreck of the Deutschland” in response to an 1875 shipwreck in which five Franciscan nuns traveling to America died. Dedicated to the nuns, the poem opens by addressing “God! giver of breath and bread” and explores suffering, faith, and divine power.

John Steinbeck’s 1952 novel East of Eden follows the intertwined Trask and Hamilton families across generations in California’s Salinas Valley. Much of the story centers on the Trask family, whose conflicts echo the biblical story of Cain and Abel: one brother feels rejected while another is favored. Steinbeck uses these family struggles to ask whether people are trapped by their past and their mistakes or can choose a different path. Lee, a member of the Trask household, studies a Hebrew passage about Cain with his Chinese relatives. They interpret the word “timshel” as “thou mayest.” For Lee, this means that a person is not required to give in to wrongdoing; each person has the possibility of choosing how to act.

Sherman Alexie is an American writer and filmmaker of Spokane and Coeur d’Alene heritage. His poetry and fiction often explore Native American life, including family, friendship, poverty, and the challenges of living between different communities. His story collection The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven became the basis for the film Smoke Signals, for which Alexie wrote the screenplay. His novel The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian follows Arnold Spirit Jr., usually called Junior, a Spokane teenager who leaves his reservation school to attend Reardan, a mostly white school. Junior draws cartoons to express his thoughts and joins Reardan’s basketball team. Through his experiences at school and at home, the novel explores identity, belonging, and the difficult choices involved in seeking new opportunities.

Lord Voldemort is the main villain of J. K. Rowling’s Harry Potter series and the leader of the Death Eaters, a group of dark witches and wizards. Born Tom Riddle, he attended Hogwarts, where he opened the Chamber of Secrets; years later, a memory of his younger self, preserved in a diary, helped open it again. Obsessed with escaping death, Voldemort committed murders to split his soul and hid its fragments in objects and a living creature. Each receptacle for a soul fragment is called a Horcrux, and it helps keep its creator tied to life. Voldemort gave Harry Potter his lightning-bolt scar when he tried to kill him as a baby. Harry eventually defeats him at the Battle of Hogwarts.

In Shakespeare’s tragedy Hamlet, Claudius becomes king of Denmark after secretly murdering his brother, King Hamlet, and marrying the dead king’s widow, Gertrude. At the royal castle of Elsinore, Claudius presents the marriage as a way to steady the kingdom, but he privately admits that guilt over his crime still troubles him. King Hamlet’s Ghost appears to his son, Prince Hamlet, on the battlements of Elsinore and reveals how he died: Claudius poured poison into his ear while he slept. The ghost urges the prince to avenge the murder. Claudius is therefore both Hamlet’s uncle and his chief enemy, even as he tries to appear to be a capable ruler.

Andrew Marvell was a 17th-century English metaphysical poet and political writer. He represented Kingston upon Hull in the House of Commons and served as Latin secretary to the poet John Milton. Marvell’s best-known poem, “To His Coy Mistress,” is a carpe diem poem, meaning it urges someone to seize the day. It opens, “Had we but world enough and time,” as the speaker imagines how slowly he could court his beloved if their lives were unlimited. The mood then changes: he hears “Time’s winged chariot” approaching and reminds her that life will end. Because they cannot stop time, he urges them to enjoy love in the present. The poem’s clever argument, vivid imagery, and contrasts between desire and death are characteristic of metaphysical poetry.

John the Savage is an outsider in Aldous Huxley’s novel Brave New World. His mother, Linda, was left behind during a visit to the Savage Reservation in New Mexico, and John grows up in its community of Malpais, beyond the World State’s control. Linda teaches him English and gives him a copy of Shakespeare’s works, which shapes how he thinks about love, suffering and freedom. When Bernard Marx and Lenina Crowne visit the reservation, they meet John and bring him to London. There, he is shocked by a society that produces people in hatcheries, encourages them to take the drug soma and controls much of their lives. Quoting Shakespeare, John challenges its values and struggles to find a place in either world.

Our Man in Havana is a comic espionage novel by British writer Graham Greene. Its main character, James Wormold, is a British vacuum-cleaner salesman living in Havana, Cuba, with his teenage daughter, Milly. When British intelligence recruits him as a spy, Wormold accepts the job partly because he needs more money to support her. Instead of gathering real secrets, he invents agents and sends fabricated reports to his employers, turning his ordinary sales work into a dangerous game of make-believe. The novel uses humor and suspense to show how easily intelligence officers can believe information they want to hear. Greene also wrote The Power and the Glory, about a fugitive whiskey priest in Mexico, and Brighton Rock, which centers on a young criminal named Pinkie Brown.

Dill Harris, whose full name is Charles Baker Harris, is an imaginative boy in Harper Lee’s novel To Kill a Mockingbird. He travels from Meridian, Mississippi, to Maycomb, Alabama, each summer and becomes close friends with Scout and Jem Finch. Together, the children invent games and grow curious about their mysterious neighbor, Boo Radley. Dill is also affected by the injustice he witnesses when Scout and Jem’s father, the lawyer Atticus Finch, defends Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of raping Mayella Ewell. Although Atticus shows that the accusation is false, Tom is convicted. Dill’s reactions help readers see how disturbing prejudice can be, especially through a child’s eyes. Lee drew partly on her childhood friendship with writer Truman Capote when creating Dill.

Umberto Eco was an Italian novelist and scholar of semiotics, the study of signs and how people create meaning. He became internationally famous for The Name of the Rose, a medieval murder mystery set in a monastery. In it, the Franciscan friar William of Baskerville and his novice investigate a series of deaths connected to a forbidden book. Eco also wrote Foucault’s Pendulum, in which three Milanese editors invent an elaborate secret history linking the Knights Templar to modern events. What begins as a private game becomes dangerous when others believe the conspiracy is real. Eco’s novels mix historical settings, puzzles, and ideas about interpretation, showing how a search for hidden meanings can lead people to mistake fiction for fact.

Stream of consciousness is a literary technique that presents a character’s private thoughts as they unfold, almost as if readers could listen to the character’s mind. Rather than explaining events in a neat order, the writing may move suddenly between present sensations, memories, feelings, and unexpected associations. It can resemble an interior monologue and may use sentence fragments, unusual punctuation, or few conventional grammatical breaks to suggest the continuous flow of thought. Writers use it to show how a character experiences the world from the inside. The Argentinian author Julio Cortázar uses stream of consciousness in much of his experimental novel Hopscotch. Its form is unusual too: readers can follow the chapters in printed order or use a “Table of Instructions” to jump between chapters, beginning with Chapter 73.

Dracula is an 1897 Gothic horror novel by Irish writer Bram Stoker, who spent nearly three decades as business manager of London’s Lyceum Theatre and worked closely with actor Henry Irving. The story begins when English solicitor Jonathan Harker visits Count Dracula, a Transylvanian nobleman, and discovers that his host is a vampire. Dracula then travels to England, where he threatens to spread vampirism. Among his victims are Lucy Westenra and Mina Harker, whose mysterious weakness leads Professor Abraham Van Helsing to recognize the danger and use garlic to help protect them. The novel is told through diaries, letters, newspaper reports, and other documents rather than by a single narrator. This form lets readers piece together the frightening events as the characters uncover Dracula’s plans.

Mowgli is a human boy raised by the Seeonee wolf pack in Rudyard Kipling’s jungle stories. Although he grows up among animals, he must learn how to survive in their world. Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther teach him the Law of the Jungle, while Shere Khan, a tiger who resents Mowgli’s presence, becomes his enemy. Mowgli uses fire to drive Shere Khan away and later defeats him by leading a stampede into a ravine. Mowgli’s adventures appear in The Jungle Book, Kipling’s 1894 collection of stories. The book also includes “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi,” about a brave mongoose, and “Toomai of the Elephants.” Kipling later wrote about Mowgli as an adult in “In the Rukh.”

Judy Blume is an American author known for writing children’s and young-adult novels about growing up, family, friendship, and difficult feelings. In Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret., Margaret Simon asks questions about religion and puberty as she waits for her first period. Blume’s Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing introduces Peter Hatcher, who is often exasperated by his mischievous younger brother, Fudge; Peter’s pet turtle, Dribble, also appears in the story. Another Blume novel, Blubber, follows fifth-grader Jill Brenner as she joins classmates in bullying Linda Fischer and later becomes a target of their cruelty herself. Blume’s books remain popular because they treat young people’s worries honestly and show how their choices can affect others.

“The Darkling Thrush” is a poem by Thomas Hardy, an English poet and novelist whose works include The Return of the Native and Tess of the d’Urbervilles. Set at the close of the nineteenth century, the poem follows a speaker looking across a frost-stricken countryside. Winter has made the landscape seem bleak and lifeless, reflecting the speaker’s gloomy thoughts about an era coming to an end. Then an old, frail thrush perched among tangled branches suddenly begins to sing, seeming to fling its soul into the growing darkness. Its joyful song surprises the speaker because he can see no reason for hope. He wonders whether the bird knows of some “blessed Hope” that he himself cannot recognize. The contrast between the desolate scene and the bird’s song makes hope the poem’s central question.

Cabbages and Kings is a collection of linked stories by the American writer O. Henry, the pen name of William Sydney Porter. Published in 1904, the stories take place in Anchuria, a fictional Central American republic. They follow politicians, businesspeople, and Americans living abroad as they become caught up in political maneuvering, commercial schemes, and everyday adventures. Characters and events recur across the stories, making the collection feel like a larger connected tale rather than a set of completely separate pieces. O. Henry is also known for “The Gift of the Magi,” in which Della sells her hair to buy Jim a Christmas present, and “The Cop and the Anthem,” in which a homeless man named Soapy tries to get arrested so he will have shelter for the winter.

The Lost World is a 1912 adventure novel by Arthur Conan Doyle, who also created Sherlock Holmes. It follows Edward “Ned” Malone, a reporter for the Daily Gazette, as he joins an expedition to a remote plateau in South America. The expedition is led by Professor Challenger, a brilliant but combative scientist who insists that prehistoric animals still live there. Malone, hunter Lord John Roxton, and the skeptical scientist Professor Summerlee travel with him to test his claim. On the isolated plateau, they encounter creatures thought to be extinct, including dinosaurs. The novel combines exploration, scientific debate, and danger as the group tries to survive and bring evidence of its discoveries back to the wider world.

Magnus Chase is the main character of Rick Riordan’s Magnus Chase and the Gods of Asgard series, which draws on Norse mythology. At the start of the story, Magnus is a homeless teenager living in Boston. He discovers that his father is Freyr, a Norse god, making Magnus a demigod. In a confrontation with the fire giant Surt, Magnus dies and is taken to Valhalla, the hall where warriors prepare for a future battle. These events happen in The Sword of Summer, the 2015 novel that introduces him and begins the series. Magnus is also the cousin of Annabeth Chase, a daughter of Athena from Riordan’s Percy Jackson books.

Karel Čapek was a Czech writer whose science fiction explored what can happen when people use new technologies without thinking about the consequences. His 1920 play R.U.R., short for Rossum’s Universal Robots, takes place around a factory that makes artificial workers. These workers eventually revolt against humanity. The play introduced the word “robot” to a wide audience; it comes from a Czech word connected with forced labor. Čapek also wrote the novel The War with the Newts, in which humans discover intelligent amphibians, exploit them as workers, and face disaster when the newts grow powerful and wage war. Both stories use imaginary beings to ask questions about labor, greed, and human responsibility.

Epistolary literature tells a story through written communications rather than a narrator describing events directly. These communications may be exchanged between characters or addressed to a particular recipient. Letters are common, but diaries, telegrams, emails, and other documents can also carry the plot. By reading what characters write, readers learn about events and see how different people understand them. Jane Austen’s Lady Susan is told through correspondence, while Bram Stoker’s Dracula combines letters, diary entries, and telegrams. In C. S. Lewis’s The Screwtape Letters, a senior demon named Screwtape sends advice to his nephew Wormwood, a junior tempter trying to influence a human. Anne Frank also addressed many entries in her diary to “Kitty,” giving them the form of letters.

Hiawatha is the central character of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s 1855 narrative poem The Song of Hiawatha. Longfellow portrays him as an Ojibwe warrior whose adventures include courting Minnehaha and encountering the mischievous Pau-Puk-Keewis. The poem draws on Indigenous stories and traditions, though Longfellow reshaped them into a fictional account rather than presenting an authentic traditional tale. Its strong, repeated rhythm comes from trochaic tetrameter, a pattern of four stressed-then-unstressed beats in each line. Hiawatha and Minnehaha also inspired sculptures by the nineteenth-century American artist Edmonia Lewis, whose family had African-American and Ojibwe roots. If asked for the warrior’s name, the answer is Hiawatha; if asked for the title of Longfellow’s poem, it is The Song of Hiawatha.

Sunstone is a major poem published in 1957 by Octavio Paz, a Mexican poet and diplomat. Its 584 lines echo a 584-day cycle associated with Venus in Aztec astronomy, linking the poem to the calendar and symbolism of Mexico’s Indigenous past. Rather than telling a straightforward story, Sunstone moves through images of love, memory, time, and human connection. Its flowing structure suggests that time can feel circular: experiences end, return, and begin again. Paz explored questions of Mexican identity in his prose book The Labyrinth of Solitude, and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1990. Remembering the poem’s unusual length and its Aztec connection can help you identify Sunstone, while Paz’s other book and Nobel Prize can help you identify its author.

A Shakespearean sonnet is a fourteen-line poem associated with William Shakespeare, the English poet and playwright who wrote Macbeth. It is usually arranged in three quatrains, or four-line sections, followed by a closing couplet of two lines. Its typical rhyme scheme is ABAB CDCD EFEF GG: the letters show which line endings rhyme. Shakespearean sonnets commonly use iambic pentameter, a rhythm with five pairs of syllables in each line, each pair moving from an unstressed syllable to a stressed one. The quatrains can develop an idea or argument, while the final couplet often offers a conclusion or surprise. In Sonnet 18, Shakespeare asks, “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?” and calls his subject “more lovely and more temperate.”

Alice Munro was a Canadian writer celebrated for short stories that explore everyday life, relationships, and the choices people make. Many of her stories are set in small-town Ontario, where she grew up. Her characters may seem ordinary, but Munro reveals how their memories and experiences shape who they become. In 2013, she won the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming one of the few writers best known for short stories to receive the award. Her 1971 book Lives of Girls and Women is a sequence of linked stories about Del Jordan as she grows up in the fictional Ontario town of Jubilee. By following Del through different stages of her coming of age, the book shows Munro’s skill at finding meaning in the details of daily life.

Jim Casy is a former preacher in John Steinbeck’s novel The Grapes of Wrath, which follows the Joad family as they leave drought-stricken Oklahoma for California in search of work. Casy travels with the family and becomes concerned about the unfair treatment of migrant workers. He turns to labor organizing, helping workers join together to demand better conditions. Casy is often described as a Christ figure because he puts others’ needs before his own and dies while standing up for them. Tom Joad, a recently paroled son of the Joad family, witnesses Casy being beaten to death while Casy is involved in a strike. In anger, Tom kills the attacker.

Faust, Part One is a dramatic tragedy by the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. Its central character, Faust, is a scholar who despairs because years of study have not given him the understanding or fulfillment he seeks. Mephistopheles, a demonic tempter who first appears to Faust as a black poodle, offers to serve him in a bargain for his soul. Faust then pursues a young woman named Gretchen, also called Margarete. Their relationship becomes tragic: Faust gives Gretchen a sleeping potion for her mother, but it causes her mother’s death. Gretchen later kills her infant and is imprisoned. When Faust and Mephistopheles come to free her, she refuses to escape with the tempter. Although she faces punishment, a voice from heaven declares that Gretchen is saved.

Chekhov’s gun is a storytelling principle named after Russian playwright Anton Chekhov. It says that if a story draws attention to an important object or detail, that detail should later matter to the plot rather than be included for no reason. Chekhov illustrated the idea with a gun displayed onstage: if the audience notices it, they will expect it to be fired later. The principle is about making conspicuous details meaningful, not about requiring every object in a story to have a dramatic payoff. Chekhov wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya, The Three Sisters, and The Seagull. In The Seagull, Konstantin Treplev shoots a seagull and gives the dead bird to Nina; later, he dies by suicide.

Tybalt is Juliet’s hot-tempered cousin and a member of the Capulet family in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Romeo and Juliet. He fiercely defends his family’s honor in its feud with the Montagues. After Romeo, a Montague, attends a Capulet masquerade ball, Tybalt challenges him to a duel. Romeo refuses to fight because he has secretly married Juliet and now considers Tybalt family. Romeo’s witty friend Mercutio steps in and fights Tybalt instead. Tybalt fatally wounds Mercutio, prompting an angry Romeo to kill Tybalt. As punishment, Romeo is banished from Verona, making it harder for him and Juliet to be together. Earlier in the play, Mercutio delivers the imaginative Queen Mab speech while teasing Romeo about his love for Rosaline.

Pedro Páramo is a 1955 novel by Mexican writer Juan Rulfo. It begins when Juan Preciado travels to Comala to find the father he has never known, Pedro Páramo. Juan makes the journey because he promised his dying mother, Dolores, that he would seek him out. At first, Comala seems like a town full of people who can tell Juan about his father, but its inhabitants gradually reveal themselves as voices of the dead. Their memories piece together the story of Pedro Páramo, a powerful man whose actions shaped the town. Rather than telling events in a simple order, the novel shifts among speakers and moments in time. Juan’s search provides its opening frame, while the voices of Comala bring its past to life.

The Call of Cthulhu is a horror short story by American writer H. P. Lovecraft. Rather than showing its monster right away, the story builds suspense by piecing together separate reports. A sculptor named Henry Wilcox makes a clay relief of a strange creature after a disturbing dream. Professor Angell investigates the relief and records similar dreams among artists and poets, along with evidence of a secretive cult that worships the creature. Later, Norwegian sailor Gustaf Johansen describes a monstrous city rising from the Pacific Ocean. Its name is R’lyeh, and its enormous buildings seem to defy ordinary rules of geometry. There, explorers open the tomb of Cthulhu, an ancient being known as a Great Old One. The story’s scattered clues make the discovery feel both mysterious and terrifying.

“The Garden Party” is a short story by Katherine Mansfield, who was born in Wellington, New Zealand, where Māori are Indigenous. It follows Laura Sheridan as her wealthy family prepares an outdoor party. During the preparations, Laura learns that Mr. Scott, a working-class neighbor, has died in an accident. She wonders whether it is right to celebrate so close to his grieving family, but her family decides to hold the party anyway. Afterward, Laura visits the Scotts’ home with leftover food and sees Mr. Scott’s body. The visit leaves her struggling to put into words what she feels about life and death. Through Laura’s experience, Mansfield explores the distance between rich and poor people, as well as the uneasy way joy and grief can exist side by side.

Tim O’Brien is an American author and Vietnam War veteran whose fiction explores combat, memory, guilt, and the ways people tell stories about difficult experiences. His novel Going After Cacciato follows a soldier who imagines that a deserter from his unit might walk all the way from Vietnam to Paris. O’Brien’s best-known book, The Things They Carried, is a collection of linked stories about American soldiers in the Vietnam War and the burdens they carry, both physical and emotional. In its title story, Lieutenant Jimmy Cross burns letters from Martha after fellow soldier Ted Lavender is killed. Another story in the collection, “Field Trip,” follows the narrator’s return to Vietnam years later with his daughter Kathleen. He takes her to the place where his friend Kiowa died.

Gone with the Wind is a 1936 novel by Margaret Mitchell about Scarlett O’Hara, a young woman from Georgia whose life is transformed by the American Civil War and the Reconstruction years that follow. Scarlett grows up at Tara, her family’s plantation. After Atlanta falls during the war, she returns to Tara, faces hunger and hardship, and vows that she will never go hungry again. Much of the story follows her efforts to keep the plantation and rebuild her life. Ashley Wilkes and Rhett Butler are important figures in her complicated relationships. The novel ends with Scarlett’s hopeful words, “After all, tomorrow is another day.” Although it is a famous work of historical fiction, its romantic picture of the prewar South overlooks the brutality of slavery.

Boo Radley, whose real name is Arthur Radley, is a mysterious neighbor in Harper Lee’s novel To Kill a Mockingbird. The story takes place in Maycomb, Alabama, where Scout Finch and her brother Jem grow up while their father, Atticus, defends Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of a crime. Because Boo rarely leaves his house, the children try to catch a glimpse of him and hear frightening rumors about him. Small gifts left in a tree’s knot-hole suggest that he has been watching them with kindness. After a Halloween pageant, Bob Ewell attacks Scout and Jem, and Boo saves them. Scout’s changing view of Boo shows why it is important to look beyond rumors and try to understand other people.

Gabriela Mistral was the pen name of Lucila Godoy Alcayaga, a Chilean poet and educator who wrote in Spanish. Her poems often explore love, grief, motherhood, and care for children, drawing on her experiences as a teacher. She first gained wide attention for “Los sonetos de la muerte” (“Sonnets of Death”), a sequence of poems mourning a lost lover. These sonnets appeared in her first major poetry collection, Desolación, published in New York in 1922. Mistral later worked to improve education and represented Chile abroad. In 1945, she became the first Latin American to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. Along with fellow Chilean poet Pablo Neruda, she is one of the best-known writers of Spanish-language poetry from Latin America.

The Stage Manager is the unnamed narrator and guide in Thornton Wilder’s play Our Town. Set in the fictional town of Grover’s Corners, New Hampshire, the play follows ordinary people through growing up, marriage, and death. The Stage Manager speaks directly to the audience, introduces the townspeople, and helps move the story between scenes. Our Town uses a nearly bare stage, with just a few pieces of furniture and ladders as props, so the audience must imagine much of the setting. The Stage Manager presides over the wedding of Emily Webb and George Gibbs. After Emily dies in childbirth, he reluctantly allows her to revisit her twelfth birthday. Her return helps reveal the play’s central idea: people often fail to appreciate everyday life while they are living it.

Wiglaf is a young Geatish warrior in Beowulf, an Old English epic poem. Near the end of the story, his king, Beowulf, goes to fight a dragon that threatens his people. Beowulf’s other companions flee, but Wiglaf returns to stand beside him. Together they kill the dragon, although Beowulf is fatally wounded. Wiglaf stays with Beowulf as he dies and later rebukes the warriors who abandoned their king. His courage and loyalty stand out against their fear. Earlier in the poem, Beowulf defeated the monster Grendel and Grendel’s mother; the final battle shows the aging hero facing one last enemy. After Beowulf’s death, his people mourn him, and Wiglaf is left to face an uncertain future with them.

Jurassic Park is a 1990 science-fiction thriller novel by Michael Crichton. InGen, a genetic engineering company, brings extinct dinosaurs back to life using DNA recovered from the blood of mosquitoes preserved in amber. It builds a theme park on Isla Nublar, a fictional island off the coast of Costa Rica, where visitors can see the animals. But the park’s safety systems fail, and the dinosaurs escape their enclosures, putting the visitors and staff in danger. The story combines adventure and suspense with questions about whether people can control the powerful technologies they create. Isla Nublar is the island of the original Jurassic Park; the larger island featured in the sequel is a different place.

Phileas Fogg is the wealthy London gentleman at the center of Around the World in Eighty Days, an adventure novel published in 1872 by the French author Jules Verne. At London’s Reform Club, Fogg wagers 20,000 pounds that he can travel around the globe and return within 80 days. He sets off with his French valet, Passepartout, who handles much of the practical work along the way. Their route takes them through places including India, Hong Kong, and the United States. In India, they rescue a woman named Aouda, who joins their journey. Fogg is famously calm and precise, even when unexpected delays threaten his schedule. The novel’s French title is Le Tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours, and its race against time makes Fogg’s journey a classic adventure story.

Rapunzel is the young woman at the center of a fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm. Before she is born, her mother longs for greens called rapunzel from an enchantress’s garden. Her father steals some, and the enchantress demands their child in exchange. Named after the plant, Rapunzel is taken and raised by the enchantress, Dame Gothel. When Rapunzel grows older, Gothel shuts her in a tall tower with no door or stairs. Gothel enters by calling for Rapunzel to let down her long hair, which she then climbs. A prince hears Rapunzel singing and later reaches her the same way. The tale draws on older European stories, including the Italian story of Petrosinella.

Isaac Asimov’s science fiction short story “The Last Question” begins with two technicians, Alexander Adell and Bertram Lupov, asking a planet-spanning computer called Multivac whether entropy can be reversed. Entropy is the tendency for usable energy to spread out, raising the troubling possibility that the universe will eventually run out of energy for stars and life. Across billions of years, later generations ask increasingly advanced descendants of Multivac the same question, but the computers cannot yet answer it. Eventually, the stars go dark and the universe reaches its end. The final computer, still working on the problem, discovers how to reverse entropy. With no humans left to hear its answer, it begins a new creation by declaring, “Let there be light!”

The Hunger Games is a 2008 dystopian novel by Suzanne Collins. It is set in Panem, a post-apocalyptic nation divided into districts and ruled by the wealthy Capitol. Each year, the Capitol forces children from the districts to compete in the Hunger Games, a televised fight to the death meant to remind the districts of its power. When Katniss Everdeen’s younger sister, Prim, is chosen, Katniss volunteers to take her place. She enters the arena alongside Peeta Mellark, another child from their district, and must survive dangerous challenges while knowing that viewers across Panem are watching. Katniss’s choices turn her into a symbol of defiance, and the novel explores survival, inequality, and the power of those who control what people see.

Othello is a tragedy by William Shakespeare about a respected military commander in the service of Venice, often called the “Moor of Venice.” He secretly marries Desdemona, but his ensign, Iago, resents him and plots to ruin their marriage. Iago gains Othello’s trust while planting the false idea that Desdemona has been unfaithful. He uses her lost handkerchief as supposed evidence and warns Othello about jealousy even as he encourages it. Iago also manipulates another man, Roderigo, repeatedly urging him to “put money in thy purse” to support his schemes. Overcome by suspicion, Othello kills Desdemona. When he learns that Iago deceived him and that she was innocent, he kills himself. The play explores how jealousy and misplaced trust can lead to tragedy.

Anthills of Savannah is a 1987 novel by Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe, who also wrote Things Fall Apart. It takes place in Kangan, a fictional West African country ruled by a military government. The story follows three people whose lives become entangled with its power struggles: Chris Oriko, a government commissioner; Ikem Osodi, a journalist who criticizes the regime; and Beatrice Okoh, a civil servant. Chris and Ikem were once friends with Sam, Kangan’s military Head of State, but his growing distrust of others puts them in danger. Through their experiences, Achebe explores political repression, the risks of speaking out, and the ways people respond to injustice. Beatrice’s role also brings questions about women’s voices and hopes for the country’s future into the story.

Eva Luna is a 1987 novel by the Chilean writer Isabel Allende. Its narrator, Eva, is an orphan with a talent for inventing stories. As she recounts her life, she describes the people she meets and the political upheaval and personal struggles that shape her world. Storytelling helps Eva make sense of these experiences and gives her a way to influence the lives of others. The novel takes its title from her name. Allende made her fiction debut with The House of the Spirits, a family saga about the Trueba family, and later wrote Daughter of Fortune. These books often bring personal lives into contact with larger historical events, but Eva Luna stands out for placing a storyteller’s voice at the center.

Daisy Buchanan is a central character in F. Scott Fitzgerald’s Jazz Age novel The Great Gatsby. She lives in wealthy East Egg with her husband, Tom Buchanan, a rich former Yale football player. Years earlier, Daisy and Jay Gatsby fell in love, and Gatsby still longs for her. From his home across the bay in West Egg, he looks toward the green light at the end of her dock. Gatsby connects Daisy with the upper-class life he hopes to enter; he even says her voice is “full of money.” Daisy’s cousin, Nick Carraway, narrates the novel. Nick works in the bond business and rents a modest West Egg house next door to Gatsby’s mansion. Through Nick’s account, Daisy’s charm and privilege become part of the novel’s examination of wealth and the American Dream.

Charlotte's Web is a children’s novel by E. B. White about friendship, kindness, and the cycle of life. When a newborn runt pig is in danger of being killed, a girl named Fern Arable insists that he be allowed to live. She raises him and names him Wilbur, but he is later moved to her uncle’s farm. There, Wilbur befriends Charlotte, a spider who tries to save him from being slaughtered by weaving praise such as “SOME PIG!” and “TERRIFIC” into her web. Templeton, a food-loving rat, helps find words for Charlotte, though he usually expects food in return. Fern continues to care about Wilbur and visits him at the county fair. After Charlotte dies, Wilbur protects her egg sac and later watches many of her spiderlings float away on silk threads.

Murasaki Shikibu was a writer at the Japanese imperial court during the Heian period, around the early 1000s. She served Empress Shōshi and kept a diary describing court life, including celebrations for the birth of the empress’s son. Murasaki is traditionally credited with writing The Tale of Genji, one of Japan’s most famous works of literature. Its main character, Genji, is a fictional imperial prince who is made a commoner. The story follows his romantic relationships, family ties, and political fortunes in the elegant but complicated world of the court. Genji’s death is marked by a blank chapter titled “Vanished into the Clouds.” The later Uji chapters shift attention to a younger generation, showing that the story continues beyond its original hero.

Piggy is a bespectacled, asthmatic schoolboy in William Golding’s novel Lord of the Flies. After a group of British boys are stranded on an uninhabited island, Piggy argues for reason, rules, and cooperation. He supports Ralph’s efforts to hold assemblies using a conch shell, which gives each speaker a turn. Piggy’s glasses are especially important because the boys use them to start fires, both for warmth and to make smoke that might signal a passing ship. As the boys’ fragile order breaks down, Jack’s group steals the glasses to control the fire. At Castle Rock, Roger sends a boulder crashing down on Piggy, killing him. Piggy’s death marks the collapse of the boys’ attempts to live by fair rules.

Honoré de Balzac was a nineteenth-century French novelist whose vast cycle of linked stories and novels, La Comédie humaine (The Human Comedy), portrays French society through characters who sometimes appear in more than one book. His detailed accounts of money, ambition, and social class helped establish literary realism. The cycle includes The Wild Ass’s Skin, about a magical object that grants wishes but shortens its owner’s life, and Eugénie Grandet, about a young woman whose wealthy, miserly father controls her life. Another novel, Père Goriot (Father Goriot), follows an aging former vermicelli maker living at the Maison Vauquer boarding house. There, law student Eugène de Rastignac witnesses Goriot’s devotion to his daughters, Anastasie and Delphine, who neglect him as his fortune dwindles.

The Tenant of Wildfell Hall is an 1848 novel by Anne Brontë, published under the pseudonym Acton Bell. The story is framed as Gilbert Markham’s account of his mysterious new neighbour, Helen Graham, who has moved into Wildfell Hall with her young son. Helen’s diary then reveals why she left her previous life: her husband, Arthur Huntingdon, was charming at first but became selfish, unfaithful and dependent on alcohol. Fearing his influence on their son, Helen fled their home and supported herself through painting.
