The novel’s realistic portrayal of addiction and an unhappy marriage challenged Victorian expectations that wives should endure their husbands’ behaviour. By telling Helen’s story through both Gilbert’s account and her own diary, Brontë shows how easily outsiders can misjudge her.

Oedipus at Colonus is a tragedy by the ancient Greek playwright Sophocles. It follows Oedipus, the former king of Thebes, years after he discovered that he had unknowingly killed his father and married his mother. Now blind, aged, and exiled, he arrives with his daughter Antigone at Colonus, a village near Athens. They enter a grove sacred to the Eumenides, also called the Furies, and are warned that the ground is holy. Creon, Oedipus’s brother-in-law, tries to force him back to Thebes, but Theseus, the king of Athens, grants Oedipus refuge and protection. Oedipus believes his final resting place will bring a blessing to Athens. The play ends with his mysterious death at Colonus.

Little Red Riding Hood is a traditional fairy tale about a girl carrying food through a forest to her grandmother. A wolf speaks to her, learns where she is going, and reaches the house first. It eats the grandmother, disguises itself in her clothes, and waits for the girl. In the version published by the French writer Charles Perrault in his 1697 collection Histoires ou contes du temps passé, also known as The Tales of Mother Goose, the wolf eats the girl too. No huntsman arrives to rescue either of them. Perrault’s ending warns readers about the danger of trusting strangers. Later versions often change the ending by having a huntsman save the girl and her grandmother.

Disgrace is a 1999 novel by J. M. Coetzee set in post-apartheid South Africa. Its central character, David Lurie, is a professor at a university in Cape Town. After he sexually assaults his student Melanie Isaacs, the university investigates him. David refuses to offer a sincere apology and resigns, then travels to his daughter Lucy’s farm in the Eastern Cape. There, a violent attack on Lucy and David forces them to confront questions about power, safety and how to live alongside others. The novel connects David’s personal disgrace with wider tensions in a country still dealing with the legacy of apartheid. Its title is Disgrace, and David Lurie is the professor whose actions begin the story.

Quasimodo is the central character of Victor Hugo’s French novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, also called Notre-Dame de Paris. He lives in Notre-Dame Cathedral, a Gothic landmark on the Île de la Cité in Paris whose construction began in 1163. Raised by Archdeacon Claude Frollo, Quasimodo becomes the cathedral’s bell-ringer; years of ringing its enormous bells have left him deaf. People often judge him harshly because of his unusual appearance, but Hugo shows his capacity for kindness and loyalty, especially in his efforts to protect Esmeralda, a Romani dancer. Frollo and Captain Phoebus are also drawn to Esmeralda, creating conflict in the story. Through Quasimodo, Hugo explores how a person’s character matters more than outward appearance.

Jean Valjean is the central character of Victor Hugo’s novel Les Misérables. He is sent to prison for stealing a loaf of bread to feed his sister’s children, and repeated escape attempts extend his sentence to nineteen years. After his release, he steals silverware from Bishop Myriel, the elderly bishop of Digne. When the police bring Valjean back, Myriel says the silver was a gift and gives him two candlesticks as well. This act of compassion inspires Valjean to change his life. Using the name Monsieur Madeleine, he becomes a successful factory owner and the mayor of a town. Although Inspector Javert pursues him because of his criminal past, Valjean tries to live generously and care for others.

The Joad family is at the center of John Steinbeck’s 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath. During the Dust Bowl and the Great Depression, the Joads lose their Oklahoma tenant farm and travel west along Route 66 to California, hoping to find work. Instead, they face poverty, hunger, and unfair treatment alongside other migrant laborers. Family members include Tom Joad, who is close to the former preacher Jim Casy, and Tom’s sister Rose of Sharon. In the novel’s final scene, Rose of Sharon nurses a starving man, an act of compassion despite her family’s hardship. Steinbeck was born in Salinas, California, also wrote Of Mice and Men and East of Eden, and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962.

Point Counter Point is a 1928 novel by British author Aldous Huxley. It follows a group of people in English society whose relationships overlap as they argue about love, politics, art, and the meaning of life. Rather than telling one straightforward story, Huxley moves between different characters and points of view, letting their ideas and experiences contrast with one another, much like voices in a piece of music. One important strand follows Walter Bidlake, a journalist who falls in love with Lucy Tantamount, a socially adventurous woman who does not share his feelings in the same way. Their difficult relationship is part of the novel’s wider picture of a society full of competing beliefs and desires. Huxley later wrote the dystopian novel Brave New World.

The Knight’s Tale is a story in Geoffrey Chaucer’s The Canterbury Tales, a collection told by pilgrims travelling to Canterbury. Written in Middle English, it is narrated by a knight and follows Palamon and Arcite, two cousins from Thebes. After a battle, Theseus, the duke of Athens, takes them prisoner. While imprisoned, both men see and fall in love with Emily, an Athenian woman, turning the cousins into rivals. Arcite is released, and Palamon later escapes. When Theseus discovers them fighting in the woods, he stops their duel and arranges a tournament to decide which man may marry Emily. The tale explores love, rivalry, honour, and the limits of human control over fate.

Marvin the Paranoid Android is a robot in Douglas Adams’s comic science-fiction series The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. Although he is extraordinarily intelligent, his personality circuits leave him constantly miserable, and he often complains that no one gives him work worthy of his abilities. Marvin travels with Arthur Dent, Ford Prefect, and their companions aboard the Heart of Gold. This starship has an experimental Infinite Improbability Drive, which allows it to travel by passing through every point in the universe at once. Marvin’s gloomy outlook contrasts with the ship’s cheerful computer, Eddie, and helps make him one of the series’ most memorable characters.

Neil Gaiman is a British writer known for fantasy novels, comics, and stories that bring myths into the modern world. In his novel American Gods, an ex-convict named Shadow Moon becomes the bodyguard of the mysterious Mr. Wednesday. As they travel across the United States, Shadow discovers that ancient gods are struggling against new figures representing parts of modern life, such as media and technology. Gaiman also created the comic series The Sandman, whose central character, Dream, is one of the Endless. After being captured, Dream must reclaim his realm and restore what he has lost. Gaiman co-wrote Good Omens with Terry Pratchett; it follows an angel and a demon trying to prevent the apocalypse. His other works include The Ocean at the End of the Lane.

Ozymandias is a sonnet by the English Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, who also wrote “Mont Blanc” and “To a Skylark.” Rather than seeing the statue himself, the poem’s speaker hears about it from “a traveller from an antique land.” The traveler describes a shattered statue of a ruler standing in the desert: its face still shows a “sneer of cold command,” but little else remains. An inscription names the ruler Ozymandias, calls him “King of Kings,” and commands others to “look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!” Around the ruins, however, there is only empty sand. The contrast between the king’s boast and his vanished empire suggests that even great power and monuments cannot last forever.

The War with the Newts is a 1936 satirical science-fiction novel by Czech writer Karel Čapek. It begins when Captain van Toch discovers intelligent newts and puts them to work collecting pearls. Humans soon exploit the amphibians on a much larger scale, using their labor while also giving them tools and weapons. As their numbers and power grow, the newts demand “lebensraum,” a German word meaning “living space,” and begin destroying land to create more coastal habitat. Their expansion threatens human civilization. Through this strange conflict, Čapek criticizes greed, colonial exploitation, and the aggressive politics of his time. He also wrote the play R.U.R., which introduced the word “robot.”

The Hunchback of Notre-Dame is an 1831 French Romantic novel by Victor Hugo, originally titled Notre-Dame de Paris. Set in medieval Paris, it centers on Quasimodo, the bell-ringer of Notre-Dame Cathedral, and Esmeralda, a young Romani dancer. Quasimodo cares deeply for Esmeralda, but she is drawn to the handsome Captain Phoebus. Claude Frollo, the cathedral’s archdeacon and Quasimodo’s guardian, also becomes obsessed with her. When Frollo finds Esmeralda with Phoebus, he stabs the captain and lets Esmeralda take the blame. The novel follows the tragic consequences of their tangled relationships while exploring prejudice, injustice, and the difference between outward appearance and inner character. Notre-Dame itself is so important to the story that Hugo named the novel after the cathedral in French.

In Haruki Murakami’s fiction, the ordinary task of finding lost cats can lead characters into strange, mysterious experiences. In The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle, Toru Okada’s wife, Kumiko, worries about their missing cat. Toru’s search brings him into contact with Malta Kano, a psychic who helps him explore connections between dreams and reality. In Kafka on the Shore, an elderly man named Satoru Nakata earns money by finding other people’s lost cats. After a mysterious incident during World War II, Nakata lost the ability to read and write, but he gained the unusual ability to speak with cats. These searches are more than simple errands: they show how Murakami uses everyday events to open the door to the supernatural.

The Kingdom of This World is a 1949 novel by Cuban writer Alejo Carpentier. It follows Ti Noël, an enslaved man, through the Haitian Revolution and its aftermath, when enslaved people fought French colonial rule. One figure Ti Noël encounters is Macandal, an escaped slave who plans to poison white settlers. Carpentier tells this history through marvelous realism, a style that presents extraordinary events and beliefs as part of everyday life rather than separating them from reality. The novel draws on the spiritual traditions and perspectives of Haiti’s people, showing how they understood the upheaval around them. To remember the key facts: The Kingdom of This World is the title, Alejo Carpentier is its author, and Ti Noël’s story is set amid the Haitian Revolution.

Ready Player One is a science-fiction novel by Ernest Cline set in 2045, when many people escape a troubled real world by spending time in a vast virtual-reality world called the OASIS. Its creator, James Halliday, has died and left a hidden Easter egg—a secret prize—for players to find. The story follows teenager Wade Watts, who uses the avatar name Parzival inside the OASIS. Wade and other egg hunters, known as gunters, solve puzzles inspired by Halliday’s favorite games and pop culture while competing against a powerful corporation called IOI. Wade’s adventures include winning a coin in a perfect game of Pac-Man that later gives him an extra life. The novel combines a virtual treasure hunt with a dystopian setting, meaning a society in serious decline.

An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge is a short story by American writer Ambrose Bierce, who served as a Union officer during the Civil War and later wrote the satirical work The Devil’s Dictionary. The story follows Peyton Farquhar, a Confederate civilian captured by Union soldiers after trying to sabotage a railroad bridge. As he is about to be hanged from Owl Creek Bridge, the rope seems to break, and he appears to escape into the river. He makes his way home, where he sees his wife waiting for him. But this escape never happens: it is an experience he imagines in the moments before his death. Bierce’s sudden ending makes readers reconsider what seemed real and shows how powerfully Farquhar longs to survive.

“Harlem” is a poem by Langston Hughes that opens with the question, “What happens to a dream deferred?” A deferred dream is a hope or goal that has been postponed or denied. Rather than giving one answer, Hughes offers a series of vivid possibilities: the dream might dry up like a raisin in the sun, fester like a sore, stink like rotten meat, become crusty like a syrupy sweet, or sag like a heavy load. The poem ends by asking whether it might explode. These images suggest that denied hopes can cause pain and frustration, especially when people face barriers to opportunity. Hughes was an African-American poet who also wrote “The Weary Blues” and “Theme for English B.”

The Phantom Tollbooth is a children’s fantasy novel by Norton Juster about Milo, a bored boy who drives his toy car through a mysterious tollbooth and enters the Lands Beyond. There, ordinary ideas become strange places and characters, and wordplay is part of nearly every adventure. In the Doldrums, Milo meets Tock, a “watchdog” with a clock built into his body, who joins him on his journey. Together, they set out to rescue the princesses Rhyme and Reason, who were banished to the Mountains of Ignorance by King Azaz and the Mathemagician after a disagreement. Along the way, Milo learns to think carefully, stay curious, and value knowledge instead of letting boredom or meaningless busywork control him.

Tom Buchanan is a wealthy former Yale football star in F. Scott Fitzgerald’s Jazz Age novel The Great Gatsby. He lives in East Egg with his wife, Daisy, but has an affair with Myrtle Wilson, whom he takes the narrator, Nick Carraway, to meet in the Valley of Ashes. Tom uses his wealth and social position to dominate others, and his racist arguments show his fear of social change. Across the bay, the mysterious Jay Gatsby throws lavish parties while hoping to reunite with Daisy; a green light on her dock symbolizes his longing. After Myrtle is killed by a car Daisy is driving, Tom tells Myrtle’s husband, George, that Gatsby owned the car. George then kills Gatsby. Disillusioned, Nick returns to the Midwest, ending the novel with an image of boats borne back into the past.

Published in 1901, Frank Norris’s naturalist novel The Octopus: A California Story follows wheat farmers in California’s San Joaquin Valley as they struggle against a powerful railroad. The fictional Pacific and Southwestern Railroad, led by its president Shelgrim, charges freight rates that make it hard for farmers to profit and uses its land policies to threaten their farms. The title compares the railroad’s far-reaching power to an octopus whose arms grip the region. Norris drew on real tensions between California farmers and railroad companies, including those behind the deadly Mussel Slough Tragedy. As a work of naturalism, the novel shows people trying to control their lives while facing larger economic forces. Norris intended it to be the first book in his unfinished Epic of the Wheat trilogy.

“To be, or not to be, that is the question” is the opening line of a famous soliloquy in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Hamlet. The speaker is Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, whose father has died and whose uncle Claudius has become king. Hamlet learns that Claudius murdered his father and struggles with whether and how to take revenge. In this speech, Hamlet asks whether it is better to keep living and endure life’s suffering or to die and escape it. Yet he worries about what might happen after death, making the choice harder. The line’s simple contrast between “to be” and “not to be” expresses his uncertainty about existence itself.

Gene Luen Yang is an American graphic novelist and comics writer whose stories often explore identity, family, and culture. His graphic novel American Born Chinese, a National Book Award finalist, weaves together stories about growing up Chinese American, while Boxers tells part of the story of the Boxer Rebellion in China. Yang also wrote comic-book sequels to the animated series Avatar: The Last Airbender, continuing the adventures of Aang and his friends after the show ended. For DC Comics, he wrote New Super-Man and co-created Kong Kenan, a teenager from Beijing chosen for a government program that gives him powers inspired by Superman. Kong Kenan is sometimes called the “Superman of China.” Yang’s work shows how comics can combine words and images to tell stories about both imagined heroes and real-world history.

Northanger Abbey is a novel by British author Jane Austen that gently makes fun of Gothic romances, stories filled with mysterious houses and frightening secrets. Its heroine, Catherine Morland, is a clergyman’s daughter who loves reading such novels but has little experience of the wider world. While visiting the fashionable city of Bath, she befriends Isabella Thorpe and meets Henry Tilney, to whom she becomes romantically attached. Catherine later visits Henry’s family at their country home, Northanger Abbey. Influenced by books such as The Mysteries of Udolpho, she imagines that ordinary objects and events point to a dark secret involving Henry’s father, General Tilney. Her mistakes are humorous, but they also show how stories can shape the way people interpret real life.

The Snow Queen is an 1844 fairy tale by the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen. It follows two children, Gerda and Kay, whose friendship is broken when shards of a magic mirror lodge in Kay’s eye and heart. The mirror makes good things seem ugly to him and leaves his heart cold. When the Snow Queen takes Kay to her icy palace, Gerda sets out to find him. She travels through strange lands and meets people and animals who help her along the way. Gerda’s love and determination finally free Kay from the mirror’s spell and bring him home. Andersen also wrote The Ugly Duckling, The Little Mermaid, and The Little Match Girl, making him one of the best-known authors of fairy tales.

The Rape of the Lock is a mock-epic poem by the eighteenth-century writer Alexander Pope. It tells how a suitor called the Baron secretly cuts a lock of hair from Belinda, a fashionable young woman, causing outrage among their social circle. A mock-epic treats a small or ordinary event as if it were a grand heroic adventure. Pope describes the stolen curl using the elevated language, battles, and supernatural interventions associated with epic poems about legendary heroes. For example, airy spirits watch over Belinda, while a goddess gathers her fears and tears. The contrast between the poem’s grand style and its relatively minor dispute makes the story funny. It also satirizes a society that places enormous importance on appearance and reputation.

Werther is the young protagonist of The Sorrows of Young Werther, an epistolary novel by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. An epistolary novel tells its story through letters, allowing readers to follow Werther’s thoughts and feelings closely. He falls in love with Charlotte, often called Lotte, but she is engaged to Albert and later marries him. Unable to accept that Charlotte cannot return his love in the way he hopes, Werther becomes increasingly distressed. Near the end of the novel, he asks Albert for two pistols and dies by suicide. Goethe wrote the novel in German, the language in which fellow writer Friedrich Schiller wrote the play William Tell and the poem “Ode to Joy.”

Imagism was an early twentieth-century poetry movement that grew from a London-based circle of writers. Imagist poets wanted to present a precise image of a thing or moment instead of explaining it in vague or flowery language. They favored direct expression, concise wording, and rhythms that followed natural speech rather than a fixed pattern. The American-born poet Ezra Pound helped launch the movement and set out its principles in his 1913 essay “A Few Don’ts by an Imagiste.” He later wrote the long poem The Cantos. William Carlos Williams was another poet associated with Imagism. His short poem “This Is Just to Say,” about plums eaten from an icebox, shows how an ordinary object and a few carefully chosen words can become poetry.

Enjambment happens when a thought or sentence runs past the end of a line of poetry and continues on the next line without a grammatical pause. The line break arrives before the phrase is complete, so readers move forward to find out how the words fit together. A poet might write “We walk beneath the” on one line and “trees” on the next: the word “the” leaves us waiting for the noun. Enjambment can quicken the pace, create suspense, or draw attention to a word at the start of the next line. Gwendolyn Brooks uses it memorably in “We Real Cool.” Its opposite is end-stopping, in which a line ends at a natural syntactic or rhetorical pause, often marked by punctuation, rather than running into the next line.

The Conference of the Birds is a Persian allegorical poem by the poet and Sufi mystic Farid ud-Din Attar. In the story, birds set out to find the Simurgh, a great bird they hope will be their ruler. Their difficult journey represents a spiritual search: each bird must overcome fears, desires, and doubts along the way. Only thirty birds reach the end, where they discover that the Simurgh they sought is a reflection of themselves together. This ending uses a Persian wordplay linking “Simurgh” with “thirty birds.” Rather than finding a separate ruler, the birds come to understand themselves through their shared journey. The poem uses this surprising discovery to explore Sufi ideas about self-knowledge and the search for a deeper truth.

Eoin Colfer is an Irish author best known for the Artemis Fowl series, which blends fantasy, science fiction, and crime stories. Its title character, Artemis Fowl II, is a teenage criminal mastermind who discovers that a technologically advanced fairy civilization exists underground. In the first novel, Artemis and his bodyguard, Butler, abduct Holly Short, an elf officer in the fairy police force known as LEPrecon, and demand a ransom in gold. As the series continues, Artemis’s relationship with the fairy world becomes more complicated. Colfer also wrote The Supernaturalist, about an orphan named Cosmo Hill, and And Another Thing..., a continuation of Douglas Adams’s The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy series.

Thus Spoke Zarathustra is a philosophical and literary work by the German thinker Friedrich Nietzsche, subtitled A Book for All and None. It follows Zarathustra, a prophet who leaves his mountain retreat to speak to humanity. Through his speeches and stories, Nietzsche explores the Übermensch, or “overhuman”: someone who creates values rather than simply accepting those handed down by society. Another central idea is eternal recurrence. It asks you to imagine living your life again and again, with every event happening in exactly the same order. Could you embrace life so fully that you would welcome that possibility? Nietzsche uses this question to challenge readers to think about how they live and what they value.

Newland Archer is the protagonist of Edith Wharton’s 1920 novel The Age of Innocence, set among the wealthy families of New York in the 1870s. A privileged young lawyer, Newland is engaged to May Welland, whose family expects him to follow society’s rules and marry her. But he becomes increasingly drawn to May’s cousin, Ellen Olenska, whose independence challenges those rules. Newland must decide whether to pursue a life with Ellen or protect his reputation and place in Manhattan society. The novel’s title points to a world that claims to value innocence while enforcing strict expectations about marriage and behavior. Drawing on Wharton’s knowledge of New York’s “old money” families, The Age of Innocence won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

Cormac McCarthy was an American novelist known for stark descriptions of violence, moral choices, and harsh landscapes. His 1985 novel Blood Meridian follows a Tennessee-born teenager known as “the kid” through the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. The kid joins the Glanton gang, a group of scalp hunters whose members include the disturbing and mysterious Judge Holden. McCarthy’s work often draws on the Western genre, but it questions the familiar idea of heroic frontier adventures. In The Road, a father and son travel toward the coast through a devastated landscape after an unexplained apocalypse, struggling to survive while trying to remain compassionate. Another novel, No Country for Old Men, begins with a drug deal gone wrong in West Texas and features the relentless killer Anton Chigurh, played by Javier Bardem in the film adaptation.

Alliteration is the repetition of the same initial sound in nearby words, especially words that receive strong stress in a line of poetry. It depends on sound rather than spelling: “knight” and “night,” for example, begin with the same sound. Alliteration helps give verse a memorable rhythm and can draw attention to important images or ideas. It is especially prominent in two anonymous Middle English poems, Pearl and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Pearl is a dream vision about a grieving father who falls asleep after searching a garden for his lost “precious pearl.” In his dream, he meets his young daughter in Heaven. Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is an Arthurian romance featuring a beheading challenge. Both poems use repeated initial sounds in stressed words as a key part of their verse.

Into Thin Air is Jon Krakauer’s nonfiction account of the deadly 1996 expedition to summit Mount Everest, the world’s tallest mountain. Krakauer, an American journalist and mountaineer, joined the climb while reporting for Outside magazine. A powerful storm and delays near the summit left climbers struggling to descend, and eight people died. Krakauer survived and later reconstructed what happened, including the decisions that may have contributed to the disaster. Because he tells the story as someone who was there, the book combines firsthand experience with reporting and reflection on the risks of high-altitude climbing. Krakauer also wrote Into the Wild and Under the Banner of Heaven.

Gregor the Overlander is a middle-grade fantasy novel by Suzanne Collins, who also wrote The Hunger Games. It follows Gregor, a boy from New York City, and his toddler sister, Boots. When they fall through a grate in their apartment building, they enter the Underland, a hidden civilization beneath the city. Pale humans live there alongside enormous creatures, including rats, bats, cockroaches, and spiders. Gregor wants to get himself and Boots safely home, but he becomes caught up in a prophecy involving the Underland’s rats and bats. As he explores this strange world, he must learn whom to trust and find the courage to face its dangers.

In William Golding’s postwar novel Lord of the Flies, a group of British schoolboys is stranded on an uninhabited island after a plane crash. As their attempts to govern themselves break down, Roger joins Jack Merridew’s tribe of hunters and becomes increasingly cruel. Early in the story, he throws stones near a younger boy but deliberately misses, still restrained by the rules he learned at home. Later, he tortures another boy, Wilfred, and helps Jack’s tribe terrorize Ralph and his friends. At Castle Rock, Roger deliberately dislodges a huge boulder that kills Piggy, Ralph’s bespectacled friend, who has asthma. Piggy’s glasses had been used to start signal fires, and Jack’s group steals them to control fire. Roger’s change shows how unchecked power and the loss of social rules can lead to violence.

Winesburg, Ohio is a 1919 short-story cycle by American writer Sherwood Anderson. Rather than following one continuous plot, its linked stories portray people living in the fictional Midwestern town of Winesburg, Ohio. Many of their experiences are connected through George Willard, a young newspaper reporter who listens to townspeople and hopes to become a writer. Anderson explores their loneliness, hidden desires, and difficulty communicating with others, themes associated with modernist literature. In the story “The Strength of God,” Reverend Curtis Hartman, a minister, watches Kate Swift through a window from his church’s bell tower. The experience unsettles him but also inspires him to work harder on his sermons. Together, the stories create a portrait of a small town and the complicated inner lives of its residents.

Kireji are “cutting words” used in traditional Japanese poetry, especially haiku. A kireji such as ya creates a pause or emphasizes a thought, often dividing the poem into two parts that the reader is invited to connect. In English translations, punctuation such as a dash or colon may stand in for the effect of a kireji. Haiku also traditionally contain a different kind of marker called a kigo, or seasonal word. A kigo points to a time of year through an image or event: “first snow,” for example, suggests winter. The two have different jobs: a kireji shapes how the poem’s ideas meet, while a kigo places its scene in a season. Matsuo Basho, an Edo-period master of haiku, used these conventions in poems about nature and everyday life.

Phillis Wheatley was born in West Africa and trafficked to Boston as an enslaved child. She learned to read and write and became an accomplished poet at a time when enslaved people were often denied an education. Her collection Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral appeared in 1773, making her one of the first African American authors to publish a book. She was emancipated after its publication. Wheatley wrote about religion, slavery, and events in colonial America; one of her poems is titled “On Being Brought from Africa to America.” In her 1775 poem “To His Excellency, General Washington,” she addresses George Washington, commander of the Continental Army. She urges him to “Proceed, great chief, with virtue on thy side” and connects his leadership with Columbia, a poetic name for America, and its cause of freedom.

Much Ado About Nothing is an Elizabethan comedy by William Shakespeare about love, gossip, and the harm caused by deception. Two of its central characters, Benedick and Beatrice, enjoy trading sharp jokes and claim they will never fall in love. Don Pedro and their friends arrange conversations for each of them to overhear, making each believe the other is secretly in love. A more cruel trick comes from Don John, who makes Claudio believe that his bride-to-be, Hero, has been unfaithful. Claudio publicly rejects her at their wedding, but the truth eventually comes out. The play mixes painful misunderstandings with humor and ends in reconciliation. In a 1993 film adaptation, Northern Irish actor Kenneth Branagh played Benedick and directed the film; he also directed film versions of Shakespeare’s Hamlet and Henry V.

E. M. Forster (Edward Morgan Forster) was a British novelist who explored relationships across differences of class, culture, and background. In Howards End, the lives of the Schlegel, Wilcox, and Bast families become entangled. One memorable incident begins when Helen Schlegel is absorbed in Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony at a concert and accidentally takes Leonard Bast’s umbrella. Forster also wrote A Room with a View and A Passage to India. Set during British rule in India, A Passage to India follows tensions between Indian and British characters. Dr. Aziz arranges an excursion for Adela Quested and Mrs. Moore to the Marabar Caves, a series of limestone hollows. The caves’ strange echo becomes central to a disputed accusation against Aziz.

Among School Children is a poem by the Irish poet William Butler Yeats. Its aging speaker visits a convent school, where the sight of young pupils makes him remember a woman he loved in his youth and consider how people change over time. He then thinks about education and the ideas of the ancient philosophers Plato, Aristotle, and Pythagoras, questioning whether their theories can fully explain living people. In the final stanza, Yeats describes a chestnut tree whose parts belong to one growing whole. He closes by asking, “How can we know the dancer from the dance?” The question suggests that a person and what they do, like a dancer and a dance, may be impossible to separate.

The Color Purple is an epistolary novel by Alice Walker, meaning its story is told through letters. It follows Celie, an African American woman living in the early-20th-century South, as she survives abuse and gradually finds friendship, independence, and a voice of her own. Celie first writes letters to God and later exchanges letters with her sister Nettie, from whom she has been separated. Much of Celie’s life unfolds in rural Georgia, the Deep South state where Margaret Mitchell’s Gone with the Wind is also set. Celie calls her husband “Mister,” though his real name is Albert, and her relationship with the singer Shug Avery helps her imagine a different future. Through Celie’s letters, Walker explores racism, sexism, family, and the power of love and self-expression.

The Wayward Bus is a 1947 novel by John Steinbeck, a California-born writer who later received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature. It follows a group of travelers on a bus route through California whose journey is interrupted when the bus becomes stranded. The passengers bring different personalities and problems with them, and their unexpected delay gives Steinbeck a chance to show how they behave around one another. One chapter shifts away from the travelers to the perspective of crooked car salesmen who peddle defective old vehicles called “jalopies.” Steinbeck also wrote Of Mice and Men and The Grapes of Wrath, a novel about the Joad family’s migration to California during the Great Depression.

Maya Angelou’s seven autobiographies tell the story of her life across different ages and places. The first volume, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, was published in 1969. It recounts her childhood as a Black girl in the segregated town of Stamps, Arkansas, and describes how she became largely silent for years after a traumatic experience. Through her memories, Angelou explores racism, family, identity, and the power of language to help her find her voice. The series continues into her adult life and ends with Mom & Me & Mom, published in 2013. That final book focuses on Angelou’s relationship with her mother, Vivian Baxter. Together, the seven books are known as Maya Angelou’s autobiographies.

Greek tragedy was a form of ancient Greek drama that presented serious stories about conflict, human error, and misfortune. Unlike comedy, it often showed a character making a fatal mistake or facing a sudden reversal of fortune. In Poetics, the philosopher Aristotle wrote that tragedy portrays a serious action and arouses pity and fear in the audience, leading to catharsis, or a release of those emotions. Tragedies were performed in ancient Athens, especially during the fifth century BCE, and playwrights included Aeschylus, Euripides, and Sophocles. Sophocles wrote Oedipus Rex and Antigone, two tragedies still widely read and performed today. Ancient tradition also credits him with introducing a third actor to the stage, allowing playwrights to create more complex interactions between characters.

The Republic is a philosophical dialogue by the ancient Greek thinker Plato. In it, Socrates and his companions ask what justice is, then imagine building a city from the ground up to see how a just society might work. Their discussion covers education, political rule, and the idea that the best rulers should be philosopher-kings: people trained to seek wisdom rather than power for its own sake. The dialogue also contains the Allegory of the Cave. Socrates describes prisoners who have been confined since childhood and see only shadows, which they mistake for reality. When one prisoner is freed and turns toward the light, he gradually discovers a wider world. His journey illustrates how learning can lead a person from ignorance toward knowledge.

Anne Frank was a German-Jewish teenager whose family fled to the Netherlands as the Nazis persecuted Jewish people. In 1942, they went into hiding in a concealed annex behind her father’s business in Amsterdam. During the two years they spent there, Anne wrote a diary about daily life in hiding, her fears, her hopes, and her thoughts about growing up. After the family was discovered in 1944, Anne was sent to Nazi concentration camps and died at Bergen-Belsen in 1945. Her father, Otto, survived and arranged for her diary to be published in Dutch in 1947 as Het Achterhuis. Known in English as The Diary of a Young Girl, it became one of the most widely read firsthand accounts of the Holocaust.

Uncle Tom is the enslaved Christian protagonist of Harriet Beecher Stowe’s 1852 anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin; or, Life Among the Lowly. Sold to the cruel plantation owner Simon Legree, Tom remains faithful to his beliefs despite brutal pressure to help Legree control other enslaved people. When Cassy and Emmeline escape, Tom refuses to reveal where they have gone, and Legree has him beaten to death. His story helped Stowe show readers the cruelty of slavery, but later writers questioned how she portrayed him. In his 1949 essay “Everybody’s Protest Novel,” James Baldwin criticizes the novel’s “self-righteous, virtuous sentimentality.” Baldwin also calls Bigger Thomas, the protagonist of Richard Wright’s Native Son, a descendant of Uncle Tom, linking two very different literary portrayals of Black characters confronting racism.

Kalidasa was an influential poet and playwright of ancient India who wrote in Sanskrit, a classical language also used to compose the Vedas, a collection of Hindu sacred texts. His drama The Recognition of Shakuntala tells the story of Shakuntala and King Dushyanta. After Shakuntala loses a signet ring in a river, a curse causes the king to forget her; the ring later helps him recognize her again. In Kalidasa’s lyric poem The Cloud Messenger, an exiled yaksha, or nature spirit, asks a passing cloud to carry a message to his wife in the Himalayas, the mountain range that includes Mount Everest. Kalidasa is celebrated for his imaginative storytelling and vivid descriptions of nature.

In William Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, Cassius is a Roman senator who fears that Caesar is becoming too powerful. He tries to persuade Brutus to join a plot to assassinate Caesar, arguing that Romans can choose their own future: “the fault… is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings.” Cassius also recalls rescuing Caesar from the Tiber River to suggest that Caesar is an ordinary man, not someone who deserves absolute power. After Cassius, Brutus, and the other conspirators kill Caesar, Caesar’s political ally Mark Antony speaks at his funeral. Antony begins, “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears,” then turns the crowd against the assassins.

Petrarch was a 14th-century Italian poet and early humanist, a thinker interested in classical learning and human experience. His best-known work, Il Canzoniere, is a collection of 366 lyric poems written in Italian rather than Latin. Most are sonnets about his love for Laura, and the collection is traditionally divided into poems written as if she were alive and poems reflecting on her after her death. Petrarch explores longing through striking contradictions, such as feeling both burning and freezing. He also wrote a letter describing his 1336 climb of Mont Ventoux. Its attention to the landscape and to his own thoughts has made the account a famous example of humanist curiosity and inward reflection.

“The Weary Blues” is a poem by Langston Hughes about a musician performing in Harlem beneath the pale light of an old gaslight. As the musician plays a droning, syncopated blues tune, the poem echoes the uneven rhythm of the music and conveys his weariness and sorrow. After the performance, he sleeps “like a rock or a man that’s dead.” Hughes was an important African American poet of the Harlem Renaissance, a period when Black writers and artists celebrated their culture and explored their experiences. He also wrote “Harlem,” which asks, “What happens to a dream deferred?” and “Theme for English B,” a poem about identity and learning across differences.

Watership Down is a 1972 adventure novel by British writer Richard Adams about rabbits searching for a safe home in the English countryside. The story begins when Fiver has a frightening vision that their warren will be destroyed. His brother Hazel trusts the warning and leads a small group away before the danger arrives. Their journey brings them into contact with other warrens, predators, and rabbits who threaten their freedom. Hazel becomes the group’s leader not because he is the strongest or oldest, but because he makes good decisions, listens to others, and helps the rabbits work together. They eventually establish a new warren at Watership Down, where Hazel serves as chief rabbit. When the powerful General Woundwort attacks, the rabbits help defend their home by unleashing a watchdog.

Ariel is a poetry collection by the American poet Sylvia Plath, published after her death in 1965. It includes “Lady Lazarus,” whose speaker says that “dying is an art,” and “Daddy,” whose speaker addresses a frightening father figure and describes a “man in black with a Meinkampf look.” Plath also wrote “The Colossus,” the title poem of her first poetry collection. Her work is often called Confessional poetry because it uses personal experiences and intense emotions as material, though the speakers in her poems are not necessarily Plath herself. In Ariel, vivid images and startling language explore subjects such as identity, suffering, death, and survival. Remember the link between the title and the poet: Ariel is the collection, and Sylvia Plath wrote it.

In Charles Dickens’s Victorian novel Oliver Twist, the Artful Dodger is the nickname of Jack Dawkins, a confident young pickpocket who brings Oliver into Fagin’s gang of thieves in London. “Artful” suggests how clever he is at stealing without being noticed. Oliver is an orphan who grows up in a workhouse, where poor children receive little food and harsh treatment. In one of the novel’s most famous scenes, he asks for another serving of gruel, saying, “Please, sir, I want some more.” After this, Oliver is sent to apprentice with an undertaker. His later encounter with the Dodger draws him into a dangerous world of crime, even though Oliver himself does not want to become a thief.

The Stone Raft is a novel by Portuguese writer José Saramago, who also wrote Blindness and The Gospel According to Jesus Christ. Its unusual premise is that the entire Iberian Peninsula, home to Portugal and Spain, breaks away from the rest of Europe and drifts into the Atlantic Ocean. As this impossible event unfolds, several travelers are drawn together by strange experiences. One woman scratches a line in the earth shortly before the land splits, while a man is followed by a flock of starlings. Their journey combines adventure with questions about identity and where people belong. The title compares the drifting peninsula to a huge stone raft, carrying its inhabitants toward an uncertain future.

Samuel Johnson was an eighteenth-century English writer, critic, and lexicographer, someone who studies and writes dictionaries. After years of work, he published A Dictionary of the English Language in 1755. It did more than define words: it used quotations from literature to show how they were used. Johnson later wrote Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets, a collection of biographies and criticism that discussed writers including John Milton, John Dryden, and Alexander Pope. His close companion James Boswell was a Scottish lawyer who traveled with Johnson through the Hebrides, a group of islands off Scotland’s west coast. Boswell later published The Life of Samuel Johnson, a celebrated biography that helped preserve Johnson’s conversations and reputation.

“She Walks in Beauty” is a lyric poem by the British poet Lord Byron. It opens, “She walks in beauty, like the night / Of cloudless climes and starry skies,” comparing a woman’s graceful appearance to a clear, star-filled night. Byron says that “all that’s best of dark and bright” meets in her face and eyes. Rather than treating darkness and light as opposites, he presents their balance as the source of her beauty. As the poem continues, her outward appearance suggests a peaceful mind and a kind heart. This focus on feeling, nature-inspired imagery, and idealized beauty makes the poem an example of Romanticism, a major nineteenth-century literary movement also associated with poets such as William Wordsworth and Percy Bysshe Shelley.

Cat’s Cradle is a satirical science fiction novel by Kurt Vonnegut. Its narrator, a writer named John, begins researching the people who helped create the atomic bomb, including the fictional scientist Felix Hoenikker. His search takes him to the island of San Lorenzo, where he encounters Bokononism, a made-up religion whose teachings help people cope with a harsh world. Hoenikker also invented ice-nine, a fictional form of ice that acts as a seed crystal: when it touches liquid water, the water freezes at room temperature. Because the process can spread from one body of water to another, ice-nine sets a global catastrophe in motion. Through this dangerous invention, Vonnegut uses dark humor to question scientific irresponsibility and humanity’s faith in technology.

Iambic pentameter is a rhythm often used in English poetry and drama. “Iambic” means that each metrical foot, or small unit of rhythm, typically moves from an unstressed syllable to a stressed syllable, like the word “today.” “Pentameter” means there are five feet in a line, usually making ten syllables in all. Poets may vary the pattern so their lines sound more natural or expressive. When lines of iambic pentameter do not rhyme, the form is called blank verse. Shakespeare used blank verse extensively for dialogue in his plays, and John Milton used it in his epic poem Paradise Lost. Listening for the five repeated beats can help you recognize the meter, while checking whether the lines rhyme can help you identify blank verse.

Flowers for Algernon is a science-fiction story by Daniel Keyes, first published as a short story and later expanded into a novel. Its narrator, Charlie Gordon, is an adult bakery worker with an intellectual disability who wants to learn. His teacher, Alice Kinnian, recommends him to researchers testing an experimental brain operation. The procedure has already increased the intelligence of a mouse named Algernon, and it soon makes Charlie a genius. Charlie records his experiences in “progress reports,” whose changing language shows how his thinking develops. But when Algernon begins to lose his new abilities, Charlie realizes the operation’s effects are temporary. His intelligence also declines, leaving him to face the loss of what he has gained. The novel explores how intelligence affects relationships and how people treat those who think differently.

Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard is a poem by the eighteenth-century English poet Thomas Gray, who also wrote “The Bard” and “Ode on a Distant Prospect of Eton College.” It opens, “The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,” as evening falls over a village burial ground. Gray imagines the lives of the ordinary people buried there and considers how death comes to everyone, regardless of wealth or fame. He suggests that some villagers may have had remarkable talents but never had the chance to develop them. Among them might have been “some mute inglorious Milton,” an unknown great poet, or “some Cromwell guiltless of his country’s blood.” The poem is an elegy, a work that reflects on death and loss.

The Romantic Movement, also called Romanticism, emerged in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Its writers and artists valued imagination, individual emotion, and the beauty and power of nature. They reacted against the Enlightenment’s emphasis on reason and against industrialization, which was changing landscapes and daily life. Rather than treating feelings as less important than logic, Romantic poets explored how personal experiences and encounters with nature could inspire wonder and insight. One leading figure was the English poet William Wordsworth, often called a Lake Poet because of his connection to England’s Lake District. He collaborated with his friend Samuel Taylor Coleridge on the poetry collection Lyrical Ballads and wrote Tintern Abbey. His poem I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud uses golden daffodils to capture a memorable experience in nature.

Nadine Gordimer was a South African novelist and short-story writer who explored how apartheid, the system of racial segregation enforced in South Africa, shaped people’s lives. Her fiction examined race, inequality, and political change, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991. In Burger’s Daughter, she writes about a young woman living with the legacy of her father’s anti-apartheid activism. Her 1981 novel July’s People imagines an uprising in Johannesburg that forces the white Smales family to flee their home. They take refuge in a rural village with the help of July, their Black servant. As the family adjusts to depending on him, the novel asks how their relationships might change if the political system that gave them power were overturned.

Edna St. Vincent Millay was an American poet and playwright who became known for vivid lyric poetry and an openly bisexual public identity. She won early acclaim for “Renascence,” which begins, “All I could see from where I stood / Was three long mountains and a wood.” The poem’s speaker starts with a limited view of the world, then has an overwhelming experience that leads her to feel buried in a grave. She remains there until she hears rain falling overhead. After the rainstorm, a breeze carries the scent of an orchard to her, and she says, “I breathed my soul back into me.” The poem moves from a sense of confinement toward a renewed appreciation of life and beauty.

Ford Madox Ford was an English novelist, editor, and critic who helped shape modernist literature, a movement that experimented with how stories could be told. His novel The Good Soldier explores the troubled marriage of Edward and Leonora Ashburnham through a narrator whose account reveals the truth gradually. Ford also wrote Parade’s End, a sequence of four novels following Christopher Tietjens through World War I and its aftermath. Beyond his own writing, Ford supported other writers as editor of The English Review. This influential literary magazine published early work by Ezra Pound and gave modernist writers a place to reach readers. Ford is remembered both for his inventive fiction and for helping new literary voices gain attention.

“The Lake Isle of Innisfree” is a lyric poem by the Irish poet W. B. Yeats. Its speaker longs to leave the noise of the city and live alone on a small island, where he imagines building a modest cabin of clay and wattles, planting nine rows of beans, and keeping a beehive. He expects to find peace there among the sounds and changing light of nature. Yeats drew on memories of Innisfree, a real island in Lough Gill near Sligo town in Ireland. Even while standing on a city road, the speaker can hear the lake’s water in his mind, showing how strongly he longs for the place.

Henry Miller was an American novelist who turned his own experiences into bold, semi-autobiographical fiction. His best-known novel, Tropic of Cancer, follows an American writer living among artists and other expatriates in Paris between the two world wars. It was first published in Paris in 1934, but its explicit language and sexual content kept it from being legally published in the United States until 1961. The American edition led to obscenity prosecutions and a major court ruling about freedom of expression. Miller also wrote The Rosy Crucifixion, a trilogy of autobiographical novels that faced censorship. His work challenged ideas about what subjects and language were acceptable in literature, making him an important figure in debates over literary freedom.

The Dumb Waiter is a one-act play by British playwright Harold Pinter. It follows two hired killers, Ben and Gus, who wait in a basement room for instructions from their unseen employer, Wilson. Their ordinary conversation, including an argument about whether to say “light the kettle,” is interrupted when a dumb waiter—a small service lift—begins delivering puzzling food orders. The men have little food to send back and do not know who is making the requests or why. Pinter’s clipped dialogue, awkward pauses, and unexplained events make the room feel increasingly threatening. As Ben and Gus try to follow orders without understanding them, the play raises questions about power, obedience, and the fear of what might happen next.

Alcman was an Archaic Greek lyric poet, probably active in the seventh century BCE. He is especially known for choral poetry: songs written to be sung and danced by a group rather than read silently. His best-known works are partheneia, or “maiden-songs,” performed by choruses of girls. These songs are closely associated with Sparta, a city-state in the Peloponnese. Although Sparta is often remembered for its military training, Alcman’s poetry shows that music, dance, and public performances were also part of its culture. Centuries after Alcman’s time, the Spartan king Leonidas led a famous defense against a Persian army at Thermopylae. Thus, the poet linked to girls’ choral maiden-songs is Alcman, and the city-state linked to those performances is Sparta.

Ta-Nehisi Coates is an American writer whose essays, memoirs, and fiction explore race and the history of slavery in the United States. His essay “The Case for Reparations” argues that the country should address the lasting harms of slavery and racist policies. His memoir Between the World and Me is written as a letter to his son about what it means to live in a Black body in America. Coates’s historical novel The Water Dancer follows Hiram Walker, an enslaved man with a mysterious ability called Conduction. In the novel, enslaved people are called “the Tasked,” while slave owners are called “the Quality.” Hiram encounters Harriet Tubman, a real-life leader who helped enslaved people escape. She tells him that “memory is the chariot,” and her role parallels Moses, the biblical leader who led the Israelites out of Egypt.

Ernest Hemingway’s 1926 modernist novel The Sun Also Rises follows Jake Barnes, an American veteran wounded in World War I, and his circle of expatriate friends living in Paris. Among them is Lady Brett Ashley, whom Jake loves, though his war injury makes a relationship between them difficult. The group travels from France to Pamplona, Spain, for the San Fermín fiesta, a festival known for bullfighting and the running of the bulls. There, rivalries and disappointments strain the friendships as the characters search for purpose and pleasure after the war. Hemingway’s spare writing style and focus on people unsettled by World War I make the novel a famous portrait of the “Lost Generation.”

Les Fleurs du mal is a landmark collection of poems by Charles Baudelaire, a French poet born in Paris in 1821. First published in 1857, its title means “The Flowers of Evil,” suggesting that poetry can find beauty even in troubling experiences. The collection opens with “To the Reader,” which condemns folly, sin, and ennui—a deep feeling of boredom and dissatisfaction—and challenges readers to recognize these faults in themselves. Other poems include “The Albatross,” in which a majestic bird becomes a symbol of a poet who feels out of place in ordinary life, and “Correspondences,” which explores connections between nature and the senses. Through images of beauty, decay, desire, and city life, Baudelaire helped shape modern poetry.

Schindler’s Ark is a historical novel by Thomas Keneally, an Australian author born in Sydney in 1935. It follows Oskar Schindler, a German industrialist who used his factories, money and connections to protect Jewish prisoners from Nazi persecution during the Holocaust. Keneally drew on real people and events, giving the book a nonfiction-like style. It won the Booker Prize and was originally published as Schindler’s Ark, though it appeared in the United States under the title Schindler’s List. Keneally also wrote The Chant of Jimmie Blacksmith, a novel about an Indigenous Australian bushranger. Knowing both the book’s original title and its author helps distinguish it from other accounts of Schindler’s actions.

Calypso is a character in Rick Riordan’s Percy Jackson universe and a daughter of the Titan Atlas. As punishment, she is confined to the remote island of Ogygia, where heroes sometimes arrive but cannot stay with her. She falls in love with some of them, including Odysseus, a hero from ancient Greek myth. When Percy Jackson reaches Ogygia, Calypso offers him a peaceful life there, but he chooses to leave and continue his quest. Percy later thinks of her as his “biggest what if,” wondering how his life might have changed if he had stayed. In The Heroes of Olympus series, Leo Valdez also arrives on Ogygia, and he and Calypso fall in love.

A House for Mr Biswas is a 1961 novel by V. S. Naipaul set in colonial Trinidad. It follows Mohun Biswas, a man who longs for a place of his own and a life he can shape for himself. After marrying Shama, he becomes entangled with her large, powerful Tulsi family. The newlyweds are drawn into Hanuman House, the family’s crowded residence in Arwacas, where Mrs. Tulsi presides over a busy household. Biswas repeatedly tries to live apart from his in-laws and build or buy a house, but money troubles and family demands frustrate him. His search for a home is also a search for independence and dignity. Through his struggles, the novel explores family, class, and life under colonial rule.

The War of the Worlds is an 1898 British science-fiction novel by H. G. Wells. Its unnamed narrator witnesses Martians arrive in cylinders that land in southern England. The invaders emerge and attack people with towering, three-legged fighting machines called tripods, using heat-rays to burn through human defenses. A fast-growing “red weed” from Mars also spreads across the landscape. Although people struggle to resist the invasion, human weapons cannot stop the Martians. Instead, the invaders die after exposure to Earth’s microorganisms: unlike humans, they have not developed resistance to these tiny living things. The novel imagines how frightening it would be for humanity to face a more powerful enemy, while showing that something as small as a microbe can change the outcome.

Richard Brinsley Sheridan was an Irish-born playwright and Whig politician who became one of the leading comic dramatists of the late 18th century. His best-known play, The School for Scandal, is a comedy of manners: it uses witty dialogue and tangled relationships to make fun of gossip, hypocrisy, and fashionable society. Sheridan was also connected to the literary world of Samuel Johnson, whose major reference work was titled A Dictionary of the English Language. Sheridan praised Johnson’s dictionary in a prologue to Richard Savage’s play The Tragedy of Sir Thomas Overbury. Johnson’s dictionary did more than define words; it included quotations from literature to show how words were used. For example, its entry for “oats” quotes the Irish writer Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver’s Travels.

Published in 1755, Samuel Johnson’s A Dictionary of the English Language was a landmark reference work that explained English words and illustrated their meanings with quotations from literature. Johnson had outlined his plans in 1747, when he proposed a dictionary that would help preserve what he saw as the purity of English. Although he worked with assistants, the project was closely associated with his own scholarship and judgment. Some definitions also reveal his wit. His entry for “oats” calls them “a grain which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people.” The entry includes a quotation from Jonathan Swift, the Anglo-Irish satirist who wrote Gulliver’s Travels and created its traveler, Lemuel Gulliver.

James and the Giant Peach is a children’s fantasy novel by Roald Dahl. Its hero, James Henry Trotter, is sent to live with his cruel aunts, Spiker and Sponge, after a rhinoceros kills his parents. His life changes when a peach in the garden grows to an enormous size. Inside it, James meets a group of talking insects, including Miss Spider and Old-Green-Grasshopper. The peach rolls away from the aunts’ house and eventually carries its passengers through the air across the Atlantic Ocean, from England to New York. Along the way, the travelers face dangers and learn to work together. Old-Green-Grasshopper, the elderly musician of the group, plays violin music during their airborne journey.

The picaresque is a form of episodic fiction that follows a poor, socially marginal rogue, often called a picaro, through a series of jobs, households, and encounters. Instead of winning through noble birth or heroic strength, the main character survives by using wit, trickery, and improvisation. These stories often use humor to expose hypocrisy and unfairness in society. A landmark Spanish example is Lazarillo de Tormes, published anonymously in 1554. Its narrator is a poor boy who serves several masters, including a blind man, a miserly cleric, and an impoverished squire. Each household brings new hardships and teaches him another way to get by. Miguel de Cervantes’s Don Quixote is not a typical picaresque, but its wandering adventures are closely allied to the form.

Aristophanes was a fifth-century BCE playwright from Athens whose surviving plays are among the best examples of Old Comedy, a style known for bold jokes and sharp satire of politics and public life. In Peace, a farmer named Trygaeus rides a giant dung beetle to heaven to rescue Peace. In The Wasps, a man named Philocleon is so obsessed with serving on juries that his family tries to stop him. Another comedy, The Frogs, follows the god Dionysus and his slave Xanthias on a journey to Hades, the Greek underworld. Dionysus hopes to bring a great tragic poet back to Athens, so he judges a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides. The play takes its title from a chorus of croaking frogs they encounter along the way.

Charlie Gordon is the narrator and main character of Daniel Keyes’s Flowers for Algernon, a science-fiction story first published as a short story and later expanded into a novel. Charlie works at a New York bakery and writes progress reports that let readers follow changes in his thoughts and writing. Doctors Strauss and Nemur give him an experimental operation intended to increase his intelligence. A white laboratory mouse named Algernon has already undergone the same operation, and Charlie races him through maze tests. Charlie’s intelligence rises dramatically, but Algernon begins to lose his new abilities and dies, warning Charlie that the treatment’s effects may not last. As Charlie’s own intelligence declines, his final report asks someone to put flowers on Algernon’s grave.

Count Paris is a nobleman of Verona in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Romeo and Juliet. Lord Capulet approves of Paris as a suitor for his daughter, Juliet, and later plans for them to marry. Juliet, however, has secretly married Romeo, a member of the rival Montague family. To avoid marrying Paris, she takes a potion that makes her appear dead. Paris visits the Capulet tomb to mourn her and encounters Romeo, who believes Juliet has truly died. Paris confronts him, and Romeo kills Paris in the fight that follows. Earlier in the play, Juliet’s cousin Tybalt kills Mercutio, a friend of Romeo and a relative of Paris. The play’s prologue calls Romeo and Juliet “star-cross’d lovers,” and their deaths finally bring the Montague–Capulet feud to an end.

Nate Wright is the mischievous sixth-grader at the center of Lincoln Peirce’s Big Nate newspaper comic strip and children’s book series. With his spiky black hair and yellow-and-blue shirt, Nate is usually easy to spot at Public School 38, where he jokes around with his best friends, Teddy and Francis, and often gets into trouble. He also sings in a garage band called Enslave the Mollusk. Nate’s confidence and dislike of rules frequently put him at odds with his teachers, especially Clara Godfrey, his social-studies teacher. She gives him so many detentions that Nate calls her “Godzilla” and “She Who Must Not Be Named.” Through Nate’s school days, friendships, and clashes with adults, the series turns everyday sixth-grade problems into comedy.

Second-person narration tells a story by addressing someone as “you.” That “you” may be the reader or a character within the story, making the addressee the focus of the action: “You open the door” instead of “She opens the door.” It is one of the three standard narrative persons, alongside first person (“I”) and third person (“he,” “she,” or “they”), and is the least common of the three. It can make readers feel as if they are taking part in events, though “you” does not always mean the real person holding the book. Italo Calvino uses second-person narration in his metafictional novel If on a Winter’s Night a Traveler, which begins by addressing a reader sitting down to read it. That reader then tries to finish a series of books whose beginnings keep being interrupted.

Long Day’s Journey into Night is an autobiographical drama by American playwright Eugene O’Neill. Set during a single day in 1912 at the Tyrone family’s summer home, it follows parents James and Mary and their sons, Jamie and Edmund, as illness and addiction bring painful memories and resentments into the open. Mary struggles with morphine dependence, while Edmund has tuberculosis. James, an actor, worries about money, and Jamie’s drinking adds to the family’s conflicts. They argue, blame one another, and try to explain their choices, but they also show moments of love. O’Neill drew on his own family history to create the Tyrones. Although the play was written earlier, it was first published and performed in 1956, after his death.

Oedipus Rex is a tragedy by the ancient Greek playwright Sophocles. It begins as a plague devastates Thebes, and its king, Oedipus, promises to find the cause of the city’s suffering. He sends his brother-in-law Creon to the Oracle of Delphi, which says the plague will end only when the murderer of the former king, Laius, is found and punished. Oedipus calls on Tiresias, a blind Theban prophet, for help. Tiresias at first refuses to name the killer, but when Oedipus presses him, he accuses Oedipus himself. As Oedipus investigates further, he discovers that Laius was his father and that he killed him without knowing it. He also learns that he has married his own mother, Jocasta.

My Last Duchess is a Victorian dramatic monologue by the British poet Robert Browning, who also wrote Porphyria’s Lover and The Bishop Orders His Tomb at Saint Praxed’s Church. In the poem, a duke shows a visiting envoy a portrait of his late wife while discussing plans for another marriage. As he talks, the duke complains that his former duchess smiled easily and treated other people’s kindness as warmly as she treated his attention. He wanted her admiration to be reserved for him. His chilling remark that he “gave commands” and then “all smiles stopped together” suggests that he ordered her death. Browning lets readers discover the duke’s jealousy and cruelty through the duke’s own words, even though the duke seems to think he is presenting himself well.

Saleem Sinai is the narrator and central character of Salman Rushdie’s novel Midnight’s Children. He is born in Bombay at the stroke of midnight on 15 August 1947, the moment India becomes independent from British rule. As Saleem tells his family’s story, his life becomes entwined with the political upheavals of India’s first decades as an independent nation. His unusually large, perpetually runny nose helps him discover telepathic powers, which let him communicate with other children born during the first hour of independence. Many of these “midnight’s children” have extraordinary abilities, giving the novel its title. Saleem’s story blends personal experience with national history, showing how the events of a country can shape one person’s life.

C. S. Lewis was an English writer and Christian apologist, someone who explained and defended Christian beliefs. He is best known for The Chronicles of Narnia, a series of fantasy books in which children enter a magical world. In The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, the lion Aslan sacrifices himself and returns to life, echoing the Christian story of Jesus. Lewis also wrote Surprised by Joy, a memoir about his early life and his journey from atheism toward Christianity. In it, he describes the influence of The Everlasting Man, a book by the English writer G. K. Chesterton. Chesterton also created Father Brown, a priest who solves mysteries.

“Crossing the Bar” is a four-stanza lyric by Alfred, Lord Tennyson, a Victorian British Poet Laureate who also wrote “Ulysses,” “In Memoriam A.H.H.,” and “The Lady of Shalott.” The poem begins with sunset and the evening star, images that suggest the end of a life. Its speaker imagines leaving shore, crossing a sandbar, and sailing into the “boundless deep.” The voyage is a metaphor for death: the sandbar marks the boundary between life and what lies beyond it. Rather than dwelling on grief, the speaker hopes there will be “no sadness of Farewell” when he embarks. He also hopes to meet his “Pilot” face to face, a figure commonly understood to represent God.

Albus Dumbledore is a powerful wizard and the headmaster of Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry for much of Harry Potter’s time there. Hogwarts students are sorted into four houses: Gryffindor, Hufflepuff, Ravenclaw, and Slytherin. Dumbledore guides Harry in his struggle against Lord Voldemort, but he also has a complicated past. As a young man, he formed a close relationship and alliance with Gellert Grindelwald, who later became a dangerous dark wizard. Dumbledore defeated Grindelwald in a famous duel in 1945, though their earlier connection remained a painful part of his history. In the sixth novel, Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, Severus Snape kills Dumbledore. Later books reveal more about Dumbledore’s past and the choices that shaped him.

“The Patient Griselda” is the final tale of Day Ten of Giovanni Boccaccio’s Decameron, a collection of stories told by young people sheltering from the Black Death in fourteenth-century Florence. Griselda is a poor young woman who marries Gualtieri, the Marquis of Saluzzo. To test her obedience, Gualtieri subjects her to years of cruel ordeals. He takes away their daughter and son and falsely tells Griselda that he has had the children killed. Later, he pretends to cast Griselda aside and marry someone else. Griselda remains patient throughout, and Gualtieri eventually reveals that their children are alive. The tale is remembered both for Griselda’s endurance and for the troubling cruelty of her husband’s tests.

The Faerie Queene is an unfinished epic poem by the English writer Edmund Spenser, first published in 1590. Spenser planned twelve books, each exploring a virtue through a knight’s adventures, but completed only six. The poem is an allegory: its characters and events represent ideas as well as telling a fantasy story. Its idealized fairy queen, Gloriana, celebrates Queen Elizabeth I. In Book One, the Redcrosse Knight represents holiness and sets out with Una, a virtuous princess who represents truth, to free her parents from a dragon. Their journey tests Redcrosse as he faces enemies such as the monster Error and the deceitful wizard Archimago. When Una and Redcrosse become separated, a lion comes to Una’s aid.

“Jabberwocky” is a nonsense poem by Lewis Carroll, the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson. It appeared in his 1871 book Through the Looking-Glass, the sequel to Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland. In the story, Alice enters a strange world on the other side of a mirror, where familiar things often seem reversed. The poem opens, “’Twas brillig, and the slithy toves,” introducing invented words whose sounds help readers imagine its eerie setting. Its story is easier to follow than its vocabulary: a father warns his son about the fearsome Jabberwock, and the son sets out with a sword to kill it. Carroll’s playful language makes the poem a famous example of literary nonsense, while its adventure gives readers a clear story to follow.

Knights-errant are wandering knights in medieval romances who leave their homes to seek quests and adventures. Guided by the code of chivalry, they are expected to show courage, defend vulnerable people, and win honor through their deeds. Later writers parodied these tales by showing what happens when someone takes their grand adventures too seriously. In Miguel de Cervantes’s Don Quixote, an aging Spanish hidalgo, or lesser nobleman, renames himself Don Quixote and sets out as a knight-errant with Sancho Panza as his companion. He mistakes an inn for a castle and windmills for giants, turning ordinary sights into imagined challenges. Mark Twain’s A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court also makes fun of romantic ideas about knights and their world.

Elie Wiesel was a Jewish writer born in Sighet, in what is now Romania. During the Holocaust, he was deported with his family to Nazi concentration camps and survived Auschwitz and Buchenwald. His best-known book, Night, is an autobiographical account of those experiences. Early in the memoir, Moishe the Beadle escapes a cattle train and returns to Sighet to warn its people about mass killings, but they do not believe him. Wiesel then describes being deported with his father to Auschwitz; his father later dies in Buchenwald. The book uses darkness as a recurring image to convey fear, suffering, and questions about faith. After the war, Wiesel became an internationally recognized witness to the Holocaust and won the 1986 Nobel Peace Prize for his work promoting human dignity and peace.

Go Tell It on the Mountain is a 1953 semi-autobiographical novel by African-American writer James Baldwin. It follows John Grimes, a fourteen-year-old boy growing up in Harlem, New York, as he struggles with his family, his faith, and his sense of who he is. John lives under the strict religious authority of his stepfather, Gabriel, whose expectations make their relationship difficult. On John’s fourteenth birthday, his brother Roy is stabbed, adding to the family’s troubles. Much of the novel centers on a church service where John experiences intense visions and a spiritual crisis. By exploring John’s thoughts alongside his family’s history, Baldwin shows how religion can offer hope while also becoming a source of fear and conflict.

Ali Baba is a poor woodcutter in the folktale Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves, often included in collections of One Thousand and One Nights, also called The Arabian Nights. While working in the forest, he hears a band of robbers say “Open Sesame!” to open the entrance to a cave where they hide their treasure. Ali Baba takes some of the riches, but his greedy brother tries to take more and is killed by the thieves. When the robbers come after Ali Baba, his quick-thinking servant Morgiana protects him. She discovers thieves hiding in large oil jars and pours boiling oil into the jars. Later, she recognizes their leader when he returns disguised as a merchant, preventing another attack.

Lokasenna is an Eddic poem from medieval Norse literature. Its title means “Loki’s Quarrel,” and it takes the form of a flyting: a contest of sharp insults and accusations. The gods have gathered for a feast in the hall of Aegir, a figure associated with the sea who brews ale for them. After a dispute, Loki enters and invokes the rules of hospitality to demand a place at the feast. He then quarrels with the assembled gods, accusing them of dishonesty and other wrongdoing. They answer with accusations of their own, including criticism of Loki’s practice of sorcery, which was sometimes considered unmanly in Norse culture. The poem uses this heated exchange to reveal tensions among the gods and show Loki as a disruptive trickster.

Vanity Fair is a dangerous marketplace in John Bunyan’s allegorical novel The Pilgrim’s Progress. The story follows a pilgrim named Christian as he travels from the City of Destruction toward the Celestial City, which represents heaven. On the way, Christian and his companion Faithful must pass through the fair, established by Beelzebub, Apollyon, and Legion to tempt travelers. Its merchants sell worldly goods and pleasures, including riches, entertainment, and power. Christian and Faithful refuse to buy anything because they value their spiritual journey more than the fair’s offerings. Their refusal angers the townspeople, who put them on trial. Faithful is executed, while Christian eventually continues his journey. The episode shows how difficult it can be to resist temptation and remain true to one’s beliefs.

“Bartleby, the Scrivener” is a short story by American author Herman Melville. Its narrator is a Wall Street lawyer who hires Bartleby to copy legal documents. At first, Bartleby works quietly, but he begins answering requests with “I would prefer not to.” He eventually refuses to work at all, leaving the lawyer unsure how to help him or make him leave. Bartleby’s passive resistance disrupts the office and raises questions about isolation, work, and responsibility for others. Near the end, the lawyer learns that Bartleby once worked in a dead-letter office, handling mail that could not be delivered. Melville also wrote Moby Dick, the novel narrated by Ishmael about Captain Ahab’s obsessive pursuit of a white whale aboard the Pequod.

An elegy is a poem that mourns a death or another profound loss. Rather than simply reporting what happened, it explores grief and often reflects on mortality, memory, and how a person’s life should be remembered. A famous example is Thomas Gray’s Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard. It opens with the line “the curfew tolls the knell of parting day” and imagines the lives of ordinary villagers buried in a rural churchyard. Gray considers the talents they may have had, even though they never became famous. Near the end, an epitaph describes “a youth to Fortune and Fame unknown.” The poem shows how an elegy can turn mourning into a thoughtful reflection on lives that might otherwise be forgotten.

The Picture of Dorian Gray is the only novel by Irish writer Oscar Wilde. First published in an 1890 issue of Lippincott’s Monthly Magazine, it tells the story of Dorian Gray, a handsome young aristocrat who wishes to stay young while his painted portrait grows old instead.
