The artist Basil Hallward paints the portrait and introduces Dorian to Lord Henry Wotton, whose ideas about pleasure strongly influence him. As Dorian makes cruel and selfish choices, his face remains youthful, but the portrait changes to show his aging and moral corruption. By hiding the painting, Dorian tries to conceal the consequences of his actions. The novel uses this supernatural idea to explore beauty, temptation, and the difference between outward appearance and a person’s character.

Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish writer known for stories of adventure, mystery, and the darker side of human nature. In his novella Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, a respectable doctor discovers a way to become Mr. Hyde, a secret persona who commits violent crimes. Stevenson’s novel Kidnapped follows David Balfour, a young man who is abducted and taken aboard a ship while trying to claim his inheritance. Another famous adventure novel, Treasure Island, begins when Jim Hawkins finds a map connected to the dead pirate Captain Flint’s buried riches. Jim joins a voyage to the island where the treasure is believed to be hidden. Among the people he meets is Long John Silver, a pirate whose parrot cries, “Pieces of Eight!”

Ian Fleming was a British writer who had worked as a journalist and a wartime intelligence officer before creating James Bond, the fictional MI6 agent known by the codename 007. Fleming introduced Bond in his first spy novel, Casino Royale, published in 1953. In that story, Bond travels to a French gaming resort to defeat Le Chiffre, a man linked to the Soviet organization SMERSH, at baccarat, a card game. He also meets Vesper Lynd, whose name inspires his famous “Vesper” martini. Fleming went on to write the original series of Bond novels, including Moonraker, in which Bond investigates Hugo Drax. Many of these books were written at Fleming’s Goldeneye estate in Jamaica. Other authors later continued the series, but Fleming was Bond’s creator.

The Houyhnhnms are a race of intelligent, rational horses in the final voyage of Jonathan Swift’s eighteenth-century satirical novel Gulliver’s Travels. The narrator, Lemuel Gulliver, reaches their land after earlier journeys to Lilliput, where he is a giant among tiny people; Brobdingnag, where he is tiny among giants; and Laputa, a flying island. The Houyhnhnms value reason and honesty so highly that they have no word for lying. They are repulsed by the Yahoos, brutish creatures that look like humans, and Gulliver is disturbed by how much he resembles them. Swift uses this contrast to make readers question whether people behave as wisely and morally as they believe they do.

Published in 1920, F. Scott Fitzgerald’s first novel, This Side of Paradise, follows Amory Blaine as he grows from a self-absorbed young man into someone questioning love, success, and his place in the world. Much of his intellectual and social development takes place at Princeton University, where he forms friendships and explores new ideas. After college, Amory falls deeply in love with the wealthy socialite Rosalind Connage, and they become engaged. Rosalind fears that Amory cannot provide the comfortable life she expects, so she ends their engagement and marries the richer Dawson Ryder instead. Amory’s painful loss is a turning point in the novel, which captures the ambitions and uncertainties of young Americans in the years around World War I.

Zorro is a masked swordsman and folk hero who fights injustice in Spanish colonial California. Johnston McCulley created him in the 1919 novel The Curse of Capistrano, set in southern California during the period of Spanish rule. Beneath the mask, Zorro is Don Diego de la Vega, a nobleman who keeps his heroic activities secret. By appearing to be an ordinary, unthreatening gentleman in daily life, Diego can protect his identity while challenging corrupt officials and defending people who are treated unfairly. Zorro’s skill with a sword and his daring escapes made him a popular adventure hero. His story has since been retold in books, films, and television shows, but the two key facts are his secret identity, Don Diego de la Vega, and the title of his first novel, The Curse of Capistrano.

Frindle is a children’s novel by American author Andrew Clements. Its main character, fifth grader Nick Allen, invents a new word for a pen: “frindle.” What starts as a playful classroom rebellion puts him at odds with his English teacher, Mrs. Granger, who insists that students use proper vocabulary. Nick’s classmates begin using his word, and it spreads beyond their school, attracts national attention, and eventually appears in a dictionary. The story explores how language can change when enough people choose to use a new word. Clements also wrote No Talking, about a fifth-grade boys-versus-girls silence challenge, as well as The Landry News and Lunch Money.

Walt Whitman wrote When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d after President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in April 1865. The poem is an elegy, a work that mourns someone who has died, but Whitman also expresses the grief of a nation recovering from the Civil War. Three images return throughout it: lilacs blooming in spring, a bright western star that has fallen, and a hermit thrush singing in a quiet place. The star represents Lincoln, while the lilacs and the thrush’s song help Whitman remember him and face his loss. Although the poem does not often name Lincoln directly, his death is at its center. Its images connect one man’s mourning with a country’s sorrow.

A fable is a short story that teaches a moral or practical lesson, often through animals that speak and behave like people. Many famous fables are credited to the ancient Greek storyteller Aesop, and they have been retold for centuries. In “The Tortoise and the Hare,” a fast, overconfident hare races a slow tortoise. The hare stops to rest, while the tortoise keeps going and wins, showing that steady effort can beat careless confidence. Other well-known examples include “The Ant and the Grasshopper” and “The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse.” Aesop’s fables are cataloged in the Perry Index, a list used to identify their different stories. The French writer Jean de La Fontaine also collected and retold fables.

Iago is the chief plotter in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Othello, which takes place partly in Venice and Cyprus. An ensign serving under the Venetian military commander Othello, Iago pretends to be loyal while secretly working to destroy him. His line “I am not what I am” reveals how different his outward appearance is from his true intentions. Iago exploits Othello’s fears about his wife, Desdemona, and encourages him to suspect that she is unfaithful with Cassio, another officer. He makes a handkerchief that Othello gave Desdemona seem like proof of an affair, although it proves nothing. Overcome by jealousy, Othello kills Desdemona and then himself after learning the truth. The play shows how Iago’s lies can turn trust into suspicion and cause tragedy.

Lenore is the deceased woman mourned by the speaker in “The Raven,” a narrative poem by American writer Edgar Allan Poe. Alone at midnight, the speaker tries to distract himself from his grief by reading, but a raven enters his room and perches on a bust of Pallas, a figure associated with wisdom. The bird repeatedly says “Nevermore,” and the speaker begins asking whether he will ever see Lenore again. He calls her a “rare and radiant maiden,” but readers learn about her only through his memories and longing. Her absence drives the poem’s sorrow and makes the raven’s repeated answer seem increasingly cruel. Some readers connect Lenore with Poe’s wife, Virginia, though the poem does not identify her as its model.

Dover Beach is a lyric poem by the Victorian writer Matthew Arnold. It opens with a peaceful view across the moonlit English Channel: the speaker can see the coast of France from the shore near Dover, known for its white cliffs. As he listens to waves dragging pebbles back and forth, their sound suggests an “eternal note of sadness.” Arnold says that the ancient Greek tragedian Sophocles heard the same sadness beside the Aegean Sea. The poem then imagines the “Sea of Faith” withdrawing from the world, expressing a sense that religious certainty is fading. Faced with a world that seems confusing and full of conflict, the speaker asks his beloved to be true to him. The poem ends with the unsettling image of “ignorant armies” clashing at night.

“Young Goodman Brown” is a short story by Nathaniel Hawthorne about a newly married Puritan who leaves his wife, Faith, at sunset and walks into a forest near Salem. There he meets a mysterious stranger carrying a staff that resembles a snake. Brown is shocked when Goody Cloyse, the elderly woman who taught him his catechism, recognizes him on the path and takes the stranger’s staff. Farther into the woods, Brown finds a pink ribbon like one Faith wears and witnesses a nighttime gathering that seems to include many people he had considered virtuous. Afterward, he returns to Salem unable to trust his neighbors or even his wife. Hawthorne leaves open whether the gathering really happened or was a dream, but Brown’s distrust lasts the rest of his life.

And Then There Were None is a mystery novel by British writer Agatha Christie. Ten people with seemingly unrelated pasts are invited by the mysterious U. N. Owen to an isolated island off the coast of Devon, England. Once they arrive, they learn that each has been accused of causing someone’s death. With no easy way to leave, the guests begin to die one by one. Their deaths follow the pattern of a nursery rhyme displayed in their rooms, while the number of small figurines on the dining room table decreases with each death. Christie builds suspense by making the survivors suspect one another. She also created the detectives Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple, and wrote other mysteries including The Murder of Roger Ackroyd and Death on the Nile.

In Markus Zusak’s World War II novel The Book Thief, the narrator is Death, imagined as a being who gathers the souls of people who die. Death tells the story of Liesel Meminger, a girl sent to live with her foster parents, Hans and Rosa Hubermann, in Nazi Germany. As Liesel steals books and learns to love words, Death describes both the kindness and the cruelty of the people around her. Her friend Rudy even covers himself in charcoal and runs a race to imitate the athlete Jesse Owens. Later, an Allied bombing destroys Liesel’s neighborhood, leaving her its sole survivor. Death sees many losses during the war, but is especially struck by human behavior, ending the novel with the words, “I am haunted by humans.”

The Hobbit is a 1937 fantasy novel by J. R. R. Tolkien. Its main character, Bilbo Baggins, is a comfort-loving hobbit from the Shire who would rather stay at home than seek adventure. Nevertheless, he joins a company of thirteen dwarves led by Thorin Oakenshield. They travel to the Lonely Mountain to reclaim the dwarves’ ancestral home and treasure from Smaug, the dragon guarding it. Along the way, Bilbo becomes separated from the group in tunnels beneath the Misty Mountains. There he finds a mysterious ring and meets Gollum, who challenges him to a contest of riddles. Bilbo escapes the underground passages and continues the journey, growing more resourceful and courageous as the story unfolds.

Number the Stars is a 1989 historical novel by Lois Lowry set in Nazi-occupied Denmark during World War II. It follows Danish schoolgirl Annemarie Johansen as she helps protect her Jewish friend Ellen Rosen from Nazi persecution. Ellen stays with Annemarie’s family, who pretend she is their daughter while helping her reach safety. Through Annemarie’s experience, the novel shows how ordinary people can act bravely even when they are afraid. Its title refers to a biblical image of God numbering the stars, a source of comfort and hope in a dangerous time. Lowry also wrote The Giver, the dystopian novel in which a boy named Jonas is chosen to become the Receiver of Memory.

The Baudelaire family is at the center of Lemony Snicket’s novel series A Series of Unfortunate Events. After a fire destroys their home and apparently kills their parents, Bertrand and Beatrice, the three Baudelaire children become orphans. Violet, the eldest, is a gifted inventor; Klaus, the middle child, loves books and research; and Sunny, the youngest, is known for her sharp teeth. In the first book, The Bad Beginning, the children are sent to live with Count Olaf, who wants to steal the fortune their parents left them. The siblings spend the series moving between guardians while Olaf repeatedly schemes to capture them. Their parents’ connection to a mysterious organization called the Volunteer Fire Department, or V.F.D., becomes part of the story’s larger mystery.

Smaug is an intelligent, fire-breathing dragon in J. R. R. Tolkien’s novel The Hobbit. Long before the story begins, he drives the Dwarves from their home beneath the Lonely Mountain and takes possession of their vast treasure. Thorin Oakenshield leads an expedition to reclaim the mountain, and Bilbo Baggins enters Smaug’s lair to investigate. Although Smaug’s body is protected by tough scales and gems stuck to his underside, Bilbo notices an unarmored patch on the dragon’s left breast. A thrush passes this information to Bard the Bowman when Smaug attacks nearby Lake-town. Bard uses his last arrow, the Black Arrow, to strike the exposed spot and kill the dragon. Smaug’s death allows Thorin’s company to reclaim the mountain, but it also leads to conflict over the treasure.

The Power and the Glory is a novel by British writer Graham Greene. Set in the Mexican state of Tabasco during a government campaign against the Catholic Church, it follows a fugitive priest who travels from place to place while trying to avoid capture. He is nicknamed the “whisky priest” because he drinks, despite his religious duties. He also struggles to find wine, which a priest needs to celebrate Mass. The priest is flawed and afraid, but he continues to serve people who need him. A mestizo guide suspects his identity and says he could test him by asking for confession. Through the priest’s journey, Greene explores faith, guilt, and moral courage—concerns that also appear in his other novels, including The End of the Affair and Brighton Rock.

The Sorrows of Young Werther is a 1774 German epistolary novel, meaning that much of its story is told through letters. Its sensitive young protagonist, Werther, writes to his friend Wilhelm about his feelings and experiences. He falls deeply in love with Charlotte, but she cannot return his love because she is committed to another man. As Werther struggles with his unreturned feelings, his emotions grow increasingly intense, and the novel ends with his suicide. The book made its author, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, widely famous and became an important work of German literature. Goethe later spent much of his career in Weimar and also wrote the play Faust, in which the title scholar makes a deal with Mephistopheles.

Okonkwo is the tragic protagonist of Things Fall Apart, a novel by Nigerian author Chinua Achebe. A celebrated wrestler and warrior, he works hard to earn respect in the Igbo community of Umuofia. Because he fears being seen as weak, however, he often acts harshly. He takes part in the killing of Ikemefuna, a boy who has lived with his family, and beats his wife Ojiugo during the Week of Peace. This sacred period before the planting season is meant to preserve harmony and help secure a good harvest; Ezeani, the priest of Ani, rebukes Okonkwo for breaking it. Later, an accidental killing sends Okonkwo into exile for seven years. When he returns, his resistance to colonial rule ends in his suicide.

Angels in America is Tony Kushner’s two-part drama, subtitled “A Gay Fantasia on National Themes.” Set during the AIDS crisis of the 1980s, it explores sexuality, religion, and politics in Ronald Reagan’s America. Prior Walter learns he has AIDS and experiences visions of an angel who announces that “The Great Work begins.” The angels want people to stop moving and changing, but Prior challenges their message; they grant him more life without curing him. Another central character is Joe Pitt, a closeted Mormon law clerk. Joe is married to Harper, who struggles with anxiety and loneliness, while the powerful lawyer Roy Cohn tries to draw Joe into a career in Washington. By mixing realistic relationships with supernatural events, the play asks how people can face illness and injustice while imagining a different future.

Ryu Murakami is a Japanese novelist and filmmaker known for dark stories about troubled young people and modern society. His novel Coin Locker Babies follows Hashi and Kiku, two boys abandoned as infants in separate coin lockers at a railway station. They survive and grow up together, but their experiences shape them in different ways. Their story leads them to Toxitown, a polluted, dangerous part of the city that reflects the novel’s harsh view of urban life. Hashi later becomes a rock star, while Kiku follows a different, more violent path. The book uses their unusual beginnings and the disturbing world around them to explore identity, abandonment, and anger. Ryu Murakami is not the same writer as Haruki Murakami, who wrote Norwegian Wood.

The lamppost is one of the first landmarks Lucy Pevensie sees when she enters the snowy land of Narnia through a wardrobe in C.S. Lewis’s The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe. It burns steadily in the middle of the wood, and Lucy meets the faun Mr. Tumnus nearby. Although it looks like an ordinary street lamp, its origin is magical. In The Magician’s Nephew, which tells how Narnia began, Queen Jadis, the former ruler of Charn, plants an iron bar in the ground of the newly created world. Because things grow in Narnia’s fresh soil, the bar grows into the lamppost. The lamp links the two stories and serves as a recognizable sign of the way into Narnia.

In the Harry Potter series, a Horcrux is an object that holds a fragment of a wizard’s soul. Creating one requires murder, which damages the soul and allows part of it to be hidden away. As long as a Horcrux survives, its creator cannot truly die, even if their body is destroyed. Lord Voldemort, also known as Tom Riddle, made multiple Horcruxes to protect himself from death. One was Tom Riddle’s diary, which preserved a memory of him as a teenager. Through the diary, that memory manipulated Ginny Weasley into reopening the Chamber of Secrets at Hogwarts. Harry discovered what the diary was and destroyed it with a basilisk fang, whose venom could damage a Horcrux beyond repair.

The odes by John Keats are a group of lyric poems in which the British Romantic poet explores beauty, imagination, joy, and the passing of time. They include “Ode to a Nightingale,” “Ode on a Grecian Urn,” and “Ode on Melancholy.” In “Ode on Melancholy,” Keats warns readers not to seek forgetfulness in Lethe, a river of oblivion in Greek mythology, and suggests that beauty and joy cannot last forever. “Ode to a Nightingale” addresses the bird as a “light-winged Dryad of the trees.” Its song leads the speaker to imagine Ruth standing “in tears amid the alien corn.” When the song fades, he wonders whether his experience was a vision or a waking dream.

An epistolary novel tells its story mainly through written documents, such as letters, diary entries, emails, or messages, rather than through a conventional narrator. These documents can make the story feel personal because readers learn what characters choose to reveal, hide, or misunderstand. An epistolary novel may contain exchanges between several people, but it can also take the form of one long letter. Ocean Vuong’s 2019 novel On Earth We’re Briefly Gorgeous is an example: its narrator, Little Dog, addresses an open letter to his mother, Rose, even though she cannot read it. Through that letter, he explores their family history, the effects of the Vietnam War, and his coming of age in Connecticut.

Robinson Crusoe is the narrator and main character of Daniel Defoe’s novel Robinson Crusoe, a landmark of British adventure fiction. After a shipwreck, the English sailor finds himself stranded on a remote island, where he spends twenty-eight years. He builds shelter, grows food, and learns to survive largely on his own. Later, he rescues a man from a group of cannibals and names him Friday after the day they meet. Friday becomes Crusoe’s close companion, and Crusoe recounts their life together on the island. The character has inspired later writers, including poet Elizabeth Bishop, whose poem “Crusoe in England” imagines him looking back on his island years after returning home.

Joseph Heller was an American novelist born in Coney Island, New York. During World War II, he served as a B-25 bombardier in the U.S. Army Air Forces and flew 60 missions over Italy. That experience helped inspire his first novel, Catch-22, a satire of war and military bureaucracy. Its main character, bombardier Yossarian, wants to survive, but his officers keep raising the number of missions he must fly. He hopes to be excused by claiming he is insane, yet the rule known as “Catch-22” says that wanting to avoid dangerous missions proves he is sane enough to fly them. The novel also features Milo Minderbinder, a mess officer who runs a sprawling business syndicate. Through absurd situations like these, Heller shows how confusing rules can trap people in a system.

Brandon Sanderson is an American fantasy novelist who created the Cosmere, a fictional universe shared by several of his book series. His Cosmere stories include Warbreaker and The Stormlight Archive, both known for detailed worlds and carefully developed systems of magic. In Warbreaker, magic called BioChromatic Breath can give life and awareness to objects. One such object is Nightblood, a sentient sword that speaks in a blunt, distinctive voice and urges its wielder to “destroy evil.” Nightblood also appears in The Stormlight Archive. Sanderson attracted attention in 2022 when he revealed that, during the COVID-19 pandemic, he had secretly written five additional novels alongside his publicly announced work.

Annabel Lee is a lyric poem by the 19th-century American writer Edgar Allan Poe, who also wrote The Raven and The Bells. Its speaker remembers loving Annabel Lee in a “kingdom by the sea.” He believes their love was so powerful that angels in heaven became jealous. After a chilling wind makes Annabel Lee ill and she dies, her family places her in a tomb beside the sea. The speaker insists that even death cannot separate their souls. Each night, he lies beside her tomb, mourning her but feeling that their bond endures. The poem’s repeated phrases and musical rhythm give it the sound of a song, while its seaside tomb and supernatural imagery create the eerie mood associated with Gothic literature.

The Song of the Lark is a novel by Willa Cather about Thea Kronborg, a girl growing up in the fictional town of Moonstone, Nebraska. People in town notice her remarkable singing voice, and she leaves home to study music and pursue a career as an opera singer. Dr. Howard Archie, a physician in Moonstone, recognizes her gift early and encourages her ambitions; he remains a supporter as her career develops. Thea’s journey also takes her to Arizona, where time spent among artists and in the desert helps shape her understanding of herself and her work. By following Thea from childhood to success on the opera stage, Cather explores the talent, determination, and sacrifices involved in becoming an artist.

The Theogony is an ancient Greek didactic poem attributed to Hesiod. Its title means “birth of the gods,” and it begins by invoking the Muses, divine figures associated with poetry and inspiration. The poem traces the origins and family lines of the gods, starting with early cosmic beings such as Chaos and Gaia (Earth). It then tells of later generations, including the Titans, and explains how Zeus rose to power. These stories helped ancient Greeks describe the order of the universe and the relationships among their gods. Zeus rules from Mount Olympus, the gods’ home in Greek mythology. To show how far Olympus stands above the earth, the Theogony says that an anvil dropped from there would take nine days to reach the ground.

Pinocchio is the wooden puppet at the center of an Italian children’s novel by Carlo Collodi. An elderly woodcarver named Geppetto makes him from a piece of wood and cares for him like a father. Pinocchio wants to become a real boy, but his curiosity and poor choices repeatedly get him into trouble. His nose famously grows when he lies, making it a memorable symbol of dishonesty. As he travels through a world of tempting promises and dangerous adventures, Pinocchio must learn to tell the truth, take responsibility for his actions, and care about others. His story has inspired many adaptations, but the central relationship remains the same: Pinocchio is the puppet, and Geppetto is the woodcarver who made him.

Charlie Bucket is the kind-hearted hero of Roald Dahl’s novel Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. He lives in poverty with his parents and four grandparents, and his family can rarely afford treats. Charlie treasures the chocolate bar he receives for his birthday, eating it slowly over several weeks. His luck changes when he finds one of five Golden Tickets that the reclusive candy maker Willy Wonka has hidden inside chocolate-bar wrappers. The tickets invite their finders to tour Wonka’s mysterious factory. During the visit, other children, including Veruca Salt and Violet Beauregarde, ignore warnings and get into trouble. Charlie remains honest and considerate, and Wonka eventually chooses him to inherit the factory.

Joan Didion was an American writer known for essays, novels, and memoirs that examine social change and the stories people tell about their lives. Her 1968 essay “Slouching Towards Bethlehem” reports on the hippie counterculture in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury district, showing its confusion and darker side rather than treating it as a carefree movement. The essay gives its name to one of her collections; another collection, The White Album, appeared in 1979 and explores California life and the upheavals of the 1960s. Didion borrowed the title “Slouching Towards Bethlehem” from “The Second Coming,” a poem by W. B. Yeats. That poem opens with an image of a falcon “turning and turning in the widening gyre,” suggesting a world slipping out of control.

The Lowell family was a prominent Boston family that produced several important American writers. Amy Lowell was an early-20th-century poet associated with Imagism, a movement that favored clear images and precise language. She helped promote the movement but disagreed with Ezra Pound about its direction; Pound mockingly called her version “Amygism.” A later member of the family, Robert Lowell, became a major poet known for writing about personal experience, family, and mental illness. His collection Life Studies includes “Skunk Hour,” a landmark of confessional poetry, which explores private struggles in a direct, revealing way. Remember the two names together: Amy Lowell is linked to Imagism, while Robert Lowell wrote “Skunk Hour.”

Tom Stoppard, born in Zlín in 1937 as Tomáš Straussler, is a Czech-born British playwright whose family fled Europe during World War II. His plays often combine wit, wordplay, and big questions about knowledge and chance. In Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead, he retells parts of Hamlet from the viewpoint of two minor courtiers, who at one point flip a coin that lands heads 92 times in a row. His play Arcadia moves between 1809 and the present at Sidley Park, an English country estate. There, the teenage mathematical prodigy Thomasina Coverly and her tutor, Septimus Hodge, explore ideas about heat, whether events are determined, and changes to the landscape. By showing people in different eras trying to understand the same place, Arcadia connects scientific discovery with human curiosity and loss.

The Wizard of Oz is the mysterious ruler of the Emerald City in L. Frank Baum’s Oz stories. Dorothy and her companions believe he can grant their wishes, but he is actually an ordinary man from Omaha, Nebraska, who once worked as a performer. He arrived in Oz by hot air balloon, and its people took him for a powerful wizard. To maintain that reputation, he uses stage tricks and elaborate effects to make himself seem magical when visitors come to see him. His story contrasts the appearance of power with real magic: despite his impressive title, he cannot perform the wonders people expect of him. His full name is Oscar Zoroaster Phadrig Isaac Norman Henkle Emmannuel Ambroise Diggs.

Sweeney Todd is a fictional barber on London’s Fleet Street who first appeared in The String of Pearls, a Victorian “penny dreadful” published in serial form in 1846–47. Penny dreadfuls were cheap, sensational stories that often featured crime and horror. In the tale, Todd murders customers in his barber shop, and their bodies are sent to Mrs. Lovett, who uses them as filling for her meat pies. This gruesome plot helped make Todd a lasting figure in British horror literature. Known as the “demon barber of Fleet Street,” he has appeared in many stage and screen adaptations, including a musical by Stephen Sondheim. The String of Pearls is the story that introduced him, even though later adaptations may tell his story differently.

A Brief History of Time: From the Big Bang to Black Holes is a popular-science book by British theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking. It introduces readers to questions about how the universe began, how it might end, and how space and time are connected. Chapters include “Space and Time” and “The Origin and Fate of the Universe.” Hawking wanted people without advanced training in physics to enjoy the book, so he included just one equation, believing that every additional equation would cut its readership in half. The book also explores black holes, regions whose gravity is so strong that light cannot escape past a boundary called the event horizon. Hawking predicted that black holes emit radiation, now called Hawking radiation, causing them to gradually lose mass.

Thomas Mann was a German-language novelist who won the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature. His first major novel, Buddenbrooks, follows the decline of a wealthy German family across several generations. In Death in Venice, a writer becomes obsessed with a beautiful young bather while a disease spreads through the city. Mann’s novel The Magic Mountain follows young Hans Castorp, who travels to a sanatorium in the Swiss mountains to visit his cousin. Although he expects a short stay, he remains there for seven years, encountering debates about politics, illness, life, and death. Mann also wrote The Confessions of Felix Krull, a playful novel about a charming impostor. His works often explore the tensions between art and ordinary life.

In Ambrose Bierce’s short story “An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge,” Peyton Farquhar stands on a bridge awaiting execution by hanging. As he listens, he hears a sharp, metallic sound like a blacksmith’s hammer striking an anvil. The sound is the ticking of his own watch, which seems unnaturally loud and slow because his senses are heightened in the moments before death. Farquhar then appears to escape when the rope breaks and he falls into the river. He swims away, travels through the countryside, and nearly reaches home. At the end, Bierce reveals that the escape happened only in Farquhar’s mind: he never got away and is hanging beneath Owl Creek Bridge. The watch’s ticking helps show how strangely Farquhar experiences time during his final moments.

Zadie Smith is a British novelist who grew up in northwest London. Her debut novel, White Teeth, follows Jamaican, Bangladeshi, and English families across generations in North London, exploring immigration, identity, friendship, and the ways families change over time. She later wrote NW, which also draws on life in northwest London. Another of her novels, On Beauty, follows two rival academic families in a fictional New England college town. It reworks Howards End, a novel by the earlier British writer E. M. Forster. Forster’s book is named for an English country house and examines differences in class and values through the Schlegel, Wilcox, and Bast families. Smith uses a similar family-centered story to explore race, beauty, and cultural conflict.

Because of Winn-Dixie is a children’s novel by American author Kate DiCamillo, who also wrote The Tale of Despereaux. Its main character, ten-year-old India Opal Buloni, has moved with her preacher father to the small town of Naomi, Florida. Feeling lonely, Opal finds a stray dog causing trouble in a grocery store called Winn-Dixie. She claims him as her own and names him after the store. Winn-Dixie’s friendly nature helps Opal meet people in her new town, including a librarian who tells her about Littmus Lozenges, candies said to taste both sweet and sad. As Opal builds friendships and learns about other people’s lives, she also begins to understand her own feelings about her absent mother.

Charles Bingley is a wealthy, good-natured young man in Jane Austen’s 1813 novel Pride and Prejudice. When he leases Netherfield Park, an estate near the Bennet family’s home at Longbourn, his arrival excites their neighbors, especially because he is unmarried. Bingley soon grows fond of Jane Bennet, the eldest Bennet daughter, but his friend Mr. Darcy and Bingley’s sisters persuade him to leave, believing Jane does not return his feelings. After he comes back, Bingley proposes to Jane, and they marry. Darcy, meanwhile, marries Jane’s younger sister Elizabeth, often called Lizzie. Bingley’s warmth and openness contrast with Darcy’s initially reserved manner. Jane Austen, who created both characters, also wrote Emma and Sense and Sensibility.

Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, historian, and political writer of the Italian Renaissance. After he was removed from public office, he wrote The Prince, a book about how rulers can gain and keep power. It argues that a ruler may need both the strength of a lion and the cunning of a fox, and that being feared can be safer than being loved. Machiavelli also wrote The Art of War and Discourses on Livy. In Discourses on Livy, he examines the history of ancient Rome to explore republican government, in which citizens have a role in public affairs. He discusses how conflict between Rome’s patricians, or wealthy elites, and plebeians, or ordinary citizens, helped shape its republic.

Percy Jackson & the Olympians is a young-adult fantasy series by Rick Riordan that brings ancient Greek mythology into the modern world. Its main character, Percy Jackson, discovers that he is a demigod: his mother is human, and his father is Poseidon, the Greek god of the sea. Percy trains at Camp Half-Blood, a refuge for demigods, and joins friends on dangerous quests involving monsters and the Greek gods. One of his closest friends is Annabeth Chase, a daughter of Athena, the goddess of wisdom. When Annabeth was seven, Thalia Grace and Luke Castellan found her and brought her to Camp Half-Blood. As a child, Annabeth was plagued by spiders in her room, but they hid whenever her stepmother came in.

Death of a Salesman, first staged on Broadway in 1949, is a tragedy by American playwright Arthur Miller. It follows Willy Loman, an aging traveling salesman who believes that being well liked will bring success. His confidence in charm and popularity hides a failing career and strained relationships with his wife, Linda, and their sons, Biff and Happy. Willy especially struggles to accept that Biff, once a promising high school football player, does not share his ambitions. After Willy loses his job, he sees no way to achieve the future he imagined for his family. He deliberately crashes his car, hoping that the life insurance money will help them. The play questions the idea that success and personal worth depend on wealth, popularity, or a prestigious career.

Blindness is a 1995 novel by Portuguese writer José Saramago, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1998. In the story, an unexplained epidemic makes people suddenly lose their sight. They experience a bright white emptiness, so the condition becomes known as the “white sickness.” As more people are affected, everyday services break down and society nears collapse. An ophthalmologist is among the first to go blind, but his wife remains able to see. She hides this fact so she can stay with him when the authorities isolate the infected. Through what she witnesses, including both cruelty and acts of kindness, the novel asks how people behave when familiar rules disappear and they must depend on one another to survive.

Ebenezer Scrooge is the central character of A Christmas Carol, a short novel by Charles Dickens set in Victorian London. At first, Scrooge cares more about money than people: he refuses his nephew’s Christmas invitation and treats his clerk, Bob Cratchit, harshly. On Christmas Eve, the ghost of his deceased former business partner, Jacob Marley, appears wearing chains made from ledgers and cashboxes. Marley warns Scrooge to change and tells him that three spirits will visit. The Ghosts of Christmas Past, Present, and Yet to Come show Scrooge memories, the hardships of others, and a possible future that includes his own lonely grave. Frightened and moved by what he sees, Scrooge becomes kinder and more generous, including toward Bob Cratchit and his son Tiny Tim.

As I Lay Dying is a 1930 modernist novel by William Faulkner, a Mississippi-born American writer who also wrote The Sound and the Fury and “A Rose for Emily.” Like many of his works, it is set in the fictional Yoknapatawpha County. After Addie Bundren dies, her husband and children carry her coffin through floods, fire, and other hardships to Jefferson, where she wanted to be buried with her family. Faulkner tells the story through the thoughts of different characters rather than through a single narrator, so readers see how each person understands the journey differently. Addie’s youngest child, Vardaman, struggles to understand her death and famously says, “My mother is a fish.” The unusual narration and attention to the characters’ inner lives make the novel an example of modernist literature.

Isaac Asimov’s Foundation series is a science-fiction cycle set in a distant future when a Galactic Empire rules much of humanity. Hari Seldon, a mathematician, predicts that the empire will collapse and that its fall could be followed by thousands of years of chaos. To shorten this dark age and preserve knowledge, he establishes the Foundation as part of a long-term plan. Seldon makes his forecasts using psychohistory, a fictional mathematical discipline that combines statistics, history, and the study of human behavior. Psychohistory can predict broad trends among enormous populations, but it cannot reliably predict what one individual will choose to do. The series explores how Seldon’s plan unfolds as later generations face political struggles, unexpected events, and changes across the galaxy.

Edwin Arlington Robinson was an American poet born in Head Tide, Maine, who won three Pulitzer Prizes for Poetry. He first gained attention for his sonnets, a poetic form traditionally made up of fourteen lines. He later became especially known for dramatic character poems that reveal a person’s inner struggles through a brief story. In “Miniver Cheevy,” he portrays a man who feels out of place in his own time. In “Richard Cory,” the townspeople admire a wealthy, courteous man and envy what seems to be his perfect life. The poem’s shocking final line reveals that Richard Cory dies by suicide, showing how little the townspeople understood about his unhappiness. Robinson’s poems often contrast public appearances with private feelings.

Lord Jim is a novel by Joseph Conrad, a Polish-born British writer who also wrote Heart of Darkness and Nostromo. Its main character, Jim, is a young seaman who dreams of being brave. When he believes the pilgrim ship Patna is about to sink, he abandons it with other crew members, leaving the passengers behind. The ship survives, but Jim’s decision fills him with shame and drives him to seek a chance to prove his courage. Much of his story is told by Charles Marlow, a recurring narrator in Conrad’s fiction. Jim eventually becomes a respected leader in Patusan, a remote region in Southeast Asia. There, his decision to trust the pirate Gentleman Brown leads to an attack in which Jim’s trusted companion Dain Waris is killed, bringing Jim’s struggle with guilt to a tragic end.

Ronald “Ron” Weasley is one of Harry Potter’s closest friends in J. K. Rowling’s Harry Potter novels. A red-haired member of a large wizarding family, Ron has five older brothers, including the twins Fred and George, who often tease him. He meets Harry on the Hogwarts Express, and both are sorted into Gryffindor house, where they become friends with Hermione Granger. In their first year, Ron’s skill at wizard chess helps the three friends cross a dangerous life-sized chessboard. Ron also brings his pet rat, Scabbers, to Hogwarts. For years, Ron believes Scabbers is an ordinary rat, but the animal is later revealed to be Peter Pettigrew, a wizard long thought dead. Ron and Hermione eventually marry.

Psychiatric hospitals provide residential treatment and support for people experiencing serious mental health difficulties. Older names include mental hospitals, asylums, and sanatoriums, though those terms can carry different historical meanings. Two Japanese novels use such settings. In Ryu Murakami’s Coin Locker Babies, Hashi’s story ends in a psychiatric hospital. In Haruki Murakami’s Norwegian Wood, Naoko stays at the Ami Hostel, a residential psychiatric facility, where she meets a music teacher named Reiko. Norwegian Wood follows Toru Watanabe as he remembers his university years, including the effect of his friend Kizuki’s suicide and his relationship with Naoko. Although the two authors share the surname Murakami, they are different writers.

Scheherazade is the storyteller at the center of the frame narrative of One Thousand and One Nights, also called The Arabian Nights. King Shahryar has been marrying a new bride each day and ordering her execution at dawn. Scheherazade chooses to marry him and begins telling him a tale at night, but stops at a suspenseful moment before morning. Eager to hear what happens next, Shahryar postpones her execution. She continues this pattern night after night, using her stories to keep herself alive and gradually change the king’s mind. The collection brings together many tales from Middle Eastern storytelling traditions. Its frame narrative explains why Scheherazade tells them and links the separate stories into a larger work.

“Sailing to Byzantium” is a poem by the Irish poet William Butler Yeats. Its aging speaker begins, “That is no country for old men,” rejecting a world absorbed in youth, desire, and the cycle of birth and death. He imagines traveling to Byzantium, an ancient city whose religious art represents something more lasting than the human body. There, he calls on holy sages to free his soul from its aging body. Rather than return to nature, he imagines becoming a golden bird perched on a bough, singing to an emperor and his court. The bird represents his hope that art can endure beyond a human lifetime. Yeats also wrote “Easter, 1916” and “The Second Coming,” and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923.

Foucault’s Pendulum is a 1988 novel by Umberto Eco, an Italian novelist and semiotician who studied how signs create meaning. Its story follows three publishing editors in Milan who encounter a manuscript from a supposed Knights Templar researcher named Ardenti. Amused by its claims, they use a computer and their knowledge of history to invent “the Plan,” an enormous conspiracy linking the Templars, occult groups, secret events and mysterious forces called telluric currents. What begins as a game turns dangerous when people who believe in conspiracies take the invented Plan seriously. The novel explores how easily people can find patterns in unrelated facts and mistake a compelling story for the truth. Eco also wrote The Name of the Rose, whose investigator is the Franciscan friar William of Baskerville.

12 Angry Men is a drama by American writer Reginald Rose. It was first written for live television and aired on CBS’s Studio One in 1954; Rose later adapted it for the stage. The story takes place during a jury’s deliberations after a murder trial. At first, eleven jurors vote guilty and only one votes not guilty. That juror does not claim to know the defendant is innocent, but argues that they should examine the evidence carefully before deciding. As the jurors discuss the case, they question witness testimony, consider how a switchblade was used, and confront their own assumptions and prejudices. Their votes gradually change, and all twelve ultimately agree on a not-guilty verdict. The drama shows why a jury must take reasonable doubt seriously.

Sonnet 43 is one of the best-known poems in Sonnets from the Portuguese, a sequence by the Victorian poet Elizabeth Barrett Browning, who was married to fellow poet Robert Browning. It opens with the question “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways,” then describes love through a series of comparisons. The speaker loves as deeply, broadly, and highly as her soul can reach, but also in everyday life, “to the level of every day’s / Most quiet need.” She loves freely, as people strive for what is right, and with the faith she had as a child. The collection’s first sonnet begins “I thought once how Theocritus had sung.” Together, these details identify both the numbered poem, Sonnet 43, and its author.

Gringotts Wizarding Bank is the main bank for witches and wizards in J. K. Rowling’s Harry Potter novels. Run by goblins, it manages the magical community’s gold and other valuables in heavily guarded underground vaults beneath Diagon Alley in London. Harry first visits Gringotts when he learns about the wizarding world, and the bank later becomes important in his search for Voldemort’s Horcruxes: objects containing fragments of Voldemort’s soul. Harry, Ron, and Hermione discover that a golden cup once owned by Helga Hufflepuff, one of Hogwarts’ four founders, is hidden in the Lestrange family vault. Known as the Cup of Hufflepuff, it is one of Voldemort’s Horcruxes, so they must retrieve and destroy it to help defeat him.

Richard III is a history play by William Shakespeare about a Yorkist duke who schemes his way onto the English throne. At the start, Richard tells the audience he is “determined to prove a villain,” and he manipulates and murders people who stand between him and the crown. After his brother King Edward IV dies, Richard takes custody of Edward’s two young sons, including the briefly crowned Edward V. The boys are kept in the Tower of London and disappear from public view in 1483. They are known together as the Princes in the Tower, and the play portrays Richard as responsible for their deaths. Shakespeare’s Richard is a memorable villain, but the play is a dramatized account of history rather than a reliable record of exactly what happened.

In the Middle English poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight, a mysterious green rider arrives on horseback at King Arthur’s court in Camelot during a New Year’s feast. Carrying a great axe, he proposes a “beheading game”: someone may strike him once, but must seek him out a year later to receive a return blow. Arthur’s nephew Sir Gawain accepts the challenge so the king does not have to. Gawain cuts off the rider’s head, but the Green Knight picks it up and rides away, reminding Gawain of their agreement. A year later, Gawain travels to the Green Chapel to keep his promise. The story tests his courage and honesty, and eventually reveals that the Green Knight is Bertilak de Hautdesert, a lord Gawain meets on his journey.

Palace Walk is a novel by the Egyptian writer Naguib Mahfouz and the first book in his Cairo Trilogy. It follows the al-Jawad family in Cairo during the years surrounding the 1919 Egyptian uprising against British rule. The family’s patriarch, Ahmad Abd al-Jawad, demands strict obedience at home, especially from his wife, Amina, and their children. When Amina visits the Al-Husayn Mosque without his permission, he punishes her. Meanwhile, their son Fahmy joins the nationalist movement and is killed by British soldiers during a demonstration. By showing both the family’s private struggles and the political upheaval outside their home, the novel explores authority and change in Egyptian society. Mahfouz also wrote Midaq Alley and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988.

Poetics is an ancient Greek treatise by the philosopher Aristotle that studies poetry and drama as forms of imitation: they represent human actions rather than simply report facts. Aristotle gives special attention to tragedy, a kind of play that portrays serious conflicts and suffering, such as those in Aeschylus’s Oresteia. He argues that a tragedy needs a well-constructed plot in which events connect through cause and effect. Important moments may include a reversal, when a character’s fortunes change, and recognition, when a character discovers a crucial truth. According to Aristotle, tragedy arouses pity for those who suffer and fear that similar misfortune could happen to us. He calls the resulting purging or clarification of these emotions catharsis. Poetics remains a foundational work of literary criticism.

Faust is the scholar at the center of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe’s two-part drama Faust. Although he has spent years studying, he feels that books cannot give him the understanding or fulfillment he wants. In despair, he considers drinking poison, but Easter bells and a chorus recalling his childhood turn him away from suicide. He then makes a wager with Mephistopheles, a supernatural tempter who offers to help him seek a moment of complete satisfaction. With Mephistopheles’s help, Faust seduces a young woman named Margarete, commonly called Gretchen. Their relationship ends tragically: after drowning her newborn child, Gretchen is imprisoned. Faust’s story explores the desire for knowledge and experience, the temptation to pursue them at any cost, and the harm that selfish choices can cause.

My Side of the Mountain is a novel by Jean Craighead George about Sam Gribley, a boy who leaves New York City to live on his own in the Catskill Mountains of New York State. Near the village of Delhi, Sam makes a home inside a hollow tree and learns to find food, build fires, and cope with changing seasons. He also raises and trains a peregrine falcon named Frightful, who helps him hunt. Although Sam wants to be self-sufficient, he forms friendships, including one with an English professor he calls Bando. The story combines an adventure in the wilderness with questions about independence, loneliness, and the skills people need to survive.

Janie Crawford is the protagonist of Zora Neale Hurston’s novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. After the death of her third husband, Tea Cake, Janie returns to Eatonville, Florida, where neighbors gossip about her. She chooses to tell her life story to her trusted friend Pheoby Watson, who listens without condemning her. Janie’s story follows her search for love, independence, and a voice of her own through three marriages. When she is young, watching a blossoming pear tree gives her an image of the loving, natural relationship she hopes to find. As Janie recounts the choices she made and the hardships she faced, readers see how she grows into someone able to speak for herself.

In Milan Kundera’s novel The Unbearable Lightness of Being, Tereza is married to Tomas, a surgeon whose relationships with other women leave her feeling insecure. Her recurring dreams, often nightmares, turn those fears into disturbing scenes. In one, cats scratch her; in another, she is forced to parade with other women around a swimming pool while being watched and humiliated. She also dreams of being buried in a hearse filled with dead women. Tereza wakes from these episodes shaken. The dreams are not ordinary events in the novel: they reveal how vulnerable she feels about her body, her dignity, and her place in Tomas’s life.

The Montague family is one of the two feuding households in William Shakespeare’s tragedy Romeo and Juliet, set in Verona, Italy. Their long-running conflict with the Capulet family causes fights in the streets and makes it dangerous for Romeo Montague and Juliet Capulet to fall in love. The play opens with a street fight between servants of the two families. Romeo’s cousin Benvolio, also a Montague, tries to stop the fighting and restore peace. Later, Benvolio urges Romeo to attend a feast hosted by the Capulets, where Romeo first sees Juliet. Although Romeo and Juliet hope their love might bring the families together, the feud contributes to the tragic deaths of both young lovers.

“The Cop and the Anthem” is a short story by O. Henry, the pen name of William Sydney Porter. As winter approaches in New York City, a homeless man named Soapy wants to be arrested so he can spend the cold months in jail on Blackwell’s Island. He tries several ways to attract a police officer’s attention, but each attempt fails. Then he hears an anthem, or hymn, coming from a church. Moved by the music, Soapy decides to change his life and find work. Ironically, a police officer arrests him for loitering just as he makes that decision. The story appears in O. Henry’s collection The Four Million, which also includes “The Gift of the Magi,” a story about a couple who each sacrifice a treasured possession to buy the other a Christmas gift.

The Haunting of Hill House is a 1959 Gothic horror novel by American writer Shirley Jackson. Dr. Montague invites several people to an isolated mansion with a reputation for supernatural activity: Eleanor Vance, Theodora, and Luke Sanderson. Eleanor joins the study after years of caring for her invalid mother and drives to Hill House in a car she has borrowed from her sister without permission. The novel opens by suggesting that no living organism can remain sane under “conditions of absolute reality,” setting an uneasy tone. Inside the house, strange sounds and messages frighten the visitors, while Eleanor becomes increasingly drawn to Hill House. Jackson leaves readers unsure whether the haunting is supernatural, shaped by Eleanor’s troubled mind, or both.

Pearl Prynne is the daughter of Hester Prynne and the minister Arthur Dimmesdale in Nathaniel Hawthorne’s 1850 novel The Scarlet Letter. Set in a strict Puritan community, the novel begins after Hester has been condemned to wear an embroidered scarlet A on her clothing as punishment for adultery. Hester refuses to name Pearl’s father, so Dimmesdale’s role remains a secret for much of the story. Pearl is lively, curious, and sometimes defiant; her behavior often draws attention to Hester’s letter and raises questions about her birth. Her name refers to a precious gemstone, suggesting how valuable she is to Hester despite the hardship surrounding her birth. Pearl is also a living reminder of the secret that shapes the novel.

The Road is a 2006 novel by American author Cormac McCarthy. After an unexplained catastrophe, an unnamed father and his young son travel across a burned, ash-covered United States, pushing their supplies in a shopping cart. They head toward the coast, hoping it may offer food, safety, or other survivors, but they face hunger, cold, and dangerous people along the way. The story focuses on their bond and the father’s effort to protect the boy and teach him to remain kind in a harsh world. The Road won the 2007 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. McCarthy also wrote Blood Meridian and No Country for Old Men; his fiction often portrays violence and survival, sometimes drawing on the traditions of the Western genre.

A graphic novel is a book-length story told through a sequence of illustrated panels, often with dialogue, captions, and other text. Unlike a prose novel, it uses the order and appearance of images as well as words to show events, emotions, and the passage of time. Graphic novels can tell fictional stories or explore real experiences. One important example is Art Spiegelman’s Maus: A Survivor’s Tale, in which Spiegelman’s father, Vladek, recounts his experiences during the Holocaust. The book portrays Jewish people as mice, Germans as cats, and Polish people as pigs. Other examples of graphic novels include Persepolis and the Amulet series.

Liesel Meminger is the central character of Markus Zusak’s novel The Book Thief, set in Nazi Germany during World War II. After her younger brother dies on the journey to foster care, Liesel is placed with Hans and Rosa Hubermann on Himmel Street. Hans helps her learn to read, and books become a source of comfort as she faces loss, war, and the dangers of life under Nazi rule. She steals books and shares stories with others, including Max, a Jewish man hidden by the Hubermanns. Her friend Rudy once covers himself in charcoal and pretends to be athlete Jesse Owens. Death narrates the novel and watches Liesel survive an Allied air raid that destroys her neighborhood. At the end, Death reflects, “I am haunted by humans.”

Lady Susan is an early novella by British author Jane Austen. It tells its story entirely through letters exchanged among Lady Susan Vernon, her relatives, and their acquaintances, rather than through a conventional third-person narrator. Fiction told through letters or similar documents is called epistolary fiction, and Lady Susan is an epistolary novel. The title character is a clever, manipulative widow who wants her reluctant daughter, Frederica, to marry the wealthy but foolish Sir James Martin. At the same time, Lady Susan attracts the attention of Reginald De Courcy, whose family distrusts her. Because readers see events through different people’s letters, they can compare what characters say about one another and notice how Lady Susan tries to influence them.

“The Gift Outright” is a poem by the American poet Robert Frost about how the American people came to identify with the land they lived on. It opens with the line “the land was ours before we were the land’s,” suggesting that possessing land and feeling a deep sense of belonging to it are not the same thing. Frost recited the poem at President John F. Kennedy’s inauguration in 1961, bringing it to a national audience. He also wrote “The Road Not Taken,” about a choice between two paths, and “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening,” in which a traveler pauses to watch snow fall before remembering the promises he must keep.

True Allegiance is a political-thriller novel published in 2016 by Ben Shapiro. It belongs to the broad category of mystery, crime, and adventure fiction, in which danger and political conflict help drive the story. Shapiro is also known as a conservative commentator. He became the youngest nationally syndicated columnist in the United States at age 17, meaning newspapers across the country published his writing while he was still a teenager. He later co-founded The Daily Wire, a conservative news and opinion website, and became widely associated with the phrase “facts don’t care about your feelings.” To keep the key facts straight, remember the connection in both directions: True Allegiance is the name of the 2016 novel, and Ben Shapiro is its author.

Journey to the Center of the Earth is an adventure novel by French author Jules Verne. Professor Otto Lidenbrock discovers a coded message left by the explorer Arne Saknussemm and realizes it must be read in a mirror. The message points to a route beneath the Icelandic volcano Snæfellsjökull. Eager to explore, Lidenbrock sets out with his nephew Axel and an Icelandic guide named Hans. As they descend, they encounter vast underground spaces and strange prehistoric life. Verne combines scientific ideas with an imaginary expedition to create a story about curiosity and the unknown. He also wrote Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, which features Captain Nemo and his submarine, the Nautilus.

Oliver Twist is a Victorian novel by the English writer Charles Dickens, first published in serial installments from 1837 to 1839. Its main character, Oliver, is an orphan raised in a parish workhouse, where poor children receive little food and harsh treatment. In a famous scene, he asks for more gruel by saying, “Please, sir, I want some more.” After being apprenticed to an undertaker, Oliver runs away to London. There, a boy called the Artful Dodger, whose real name is Jack Dawkins, introduces him to Fagin’s gang of young pickpockets. Oliver’s experiences show the dangers faced by poor children in Victorian England. Dickens also wrote other novels about life in that era, including David Copperfield, Bleak House, and Great Expectations.

Billy Pilgrim is the central character of Kurt Vonnegut’s novel Slaughterhouse-Five. An optometrist from Ilium, New York, and a World War II veteran, Billy is captured by German forces during the Battle of the Bulge. As a prisoner of war, he survives the Allied firebombing of Dresden by sheltering in the cellar of a slaughterhouse. The novel tells his story out of order because Billy has become “unstuck in time,” moving unpredictably among moments of his life. He also claims that aliens called Tralfamadorians abduct him and display him in a zoo. By mixing Billy’s wartime experiences with time travel and science fiction, Vonnegut explores the lasting effects of war. Accounts of death are repeatedly followed by the refrain “so it goes.”

The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle is a novel by Japanese author Haruki Murakami. Its main character, Toru Okada, begins by searching for his lost cat, but the mystery deepens when his wife, Kumiko, disappears. As Toru tries to find her, he meets unusual people and encounters strange events that blur the line between everyday life and dreams. The novel also draws on painful episodes from Japan’s past, connecting Toru’s personal search to larger questions about memory and violence. To keep the central details straight: The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle is the title of the novel, Toru Okada is the person searching, and Kumiko is the wife he hopes to find.

The Ugly Duckling is a fairy tale by the Danish author Hans Christian Andersen, who also wrote The Snow Queen and The Little Mermaid. The story follows a young bird who looks different from the ducklings around him. Other animals mock and reject him, so he leaves and spends a lonely, difficult winter trying to survive. When spring arrives, he sees his reflection and discovers that he has grown into a swan. He was never an ugly duck; he belonged to a different kind of bird. The tale is often read as a story about feeling like an outsider and finding a place where you belong. Its ending shows that the other animals’ cruel judgments did not define who he was.

On the Pulse of Morning is a poem by American writer Maya Angelou, who read it at President Bill Clinton’s 1993 inauguration. It opens with the words “A Rock, A River, A Tree,” giving these enduring parts of the natural world voices that speak to humanity. Through them, Angelou asks people to face the harm caused by history, including violence and oppression, rather than hide from it. The poem also offers hope: people from different backgrounds can choose to live together more justly and create a better future. Angelou was known for both her poetry and her writing about her own life. Her autobiographical book I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings is another of her best-known works.

“Rappaccini’s Daughter” is a Gothic short story by 19th-century American author Nathaniel Hawthorne, who also wrote The Scarlet Letter and The House of the Seven Gables. Set in Padua, Italy, it follows a student named Giovanni Guasconti, who rents a room overlooking a secluded garden. There, Dr. Rappaccini grows deadly plants and keeps his daughter Beatrice apart from other people. Giovanni becomes fascinated by Beatrice, but he discovers that her father’s experiments have made her poisonous, like the plants she tends. As Giovanni tries to understand and help her, the story raises questions about love, trust, and the danger of using science without considering its human cost.

When We Dead Awaken is the final play by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen. Its central character, Arnold Rubek, is a renowned sculptor who meets Irene, a woman who once modeled for his most famous work. Their reunion brings back painful memories: Rubek devoted himself to creating art, while Irene felt that the experience cost her a fuller life. As they talk, both wonder whether they have truly lived or have been emotionally “dead” for years. Rubek and Irene climb a mountain together, hoping for a new beginning, but an avalanche kills them both. The play’s title, When We Dead Awaken, points to their late realization of what they have lost.

“1914” is a sonnet by the English soldier-poet Wilfred Owen. Its title names the year World War I began. Rather than describing a single soldier’s death, the poem presents the outbreak of war as a turning point that threatens the great civilizations of Europe and the culture they created. That image also points toward the millions of people who would die in the conflict. Owen served in the war and became known for poetry that challenged idealized ideas about battle. His better-known poem “Dulce et Decorum Est” describes a gas attack and questions the claim that dying for one’s country is glorious. To remember the key facts, connect the year 1914 with the start of World War I and Wilfred Owen with the sonnet of that name.

The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy is a comic science-fiction novel by Douglas Adams that uses absurd adventures to poke fun at human assumptions about the universe. Arthur Dent, an ordinary Englishman, escapes just before Earth is demolished to make way for a hyperspatial express route. His companion, Ford Prefect, is an alien researcher updating an entry about Earth for an electronic travel guide. They eventually reach the Heart of Gold, a starship powered by the Improbability Drive, where they meet Marvin, a famously gloomy robot. The guide offers odd but useful advice, including the importance of carrying a towel. One of the novel’s best-known jokes concerns Deep Thought, a colossal computer that spends millions of years calculating the answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything. Its answer is simply 42.

Nadsat is the fictional youth slang spoken by Alex and his gang in Anthony Burgess’s dystopian novel A Clockwork Orange. It uses mostly English grammar but includes many words adapted from Russian, giving the characters a way of speaking that sets them apart from adults. The name Nadsat comes from a Russian suffix used in the words for the numbers 11 through 19, much like “teen” in English. One important Nadsat word is “droog,” meaning a close friend; it comes from the Russian word drug, which means “friend.” Alex calls the other members of his gang his droogs. Burgess uses this unfamiliar vocabulary to draw readers into Alex’s world while making them work out meanings from context.

Br’er Rabbit is a clever rabbit in African American folktales who survives by outsmarting stronger animals, including Br’er Fox and Br’er Wolf. His stories draw on African oral traditions of trickster characters, such as Anansi the spider. In one famous tale, Br’er Fox uses a figure covered in sticky tar to trap him. Br’er Rabbit begs not to be thrown into a briar patch, so his captors throw him there as a punishment. But he has tricked them: he knows how to move through the thorns and escapes. These tales reached a broad audience through the Uncle Remus stories, written and popularized by Joel Chandler Harris, a Georgia-born journalist and folklorist who drew on African American oral storytelling.

The Screwtape Letters is a 1942 novel by C. S. Lewis, an Oxford scholar and Christian writer who also wrote The Chronicles of Narnia and Mere Christianity. The novel takes the form of letters from Screwtape, an experienced demon, to his nephew Wormwood, a younger demon assigned to tempt a human man. Screwtape advises Wormwood on how to distract the man from his Christian faith and lead him toward selfishness, pride, and despair. Because readers see the story through a demon’s advice, Lewis explores moral choices and religious belief from an unusual, often humorous angle. A story told through letters is called an epistolary work; in this one, the letters reveal both the demons’ plans and the human struggles they hope to exploit.

Omar Khayyam was an 11th-century Persian scholar and poet who studied mathematics and astronomy as well as writing verse. English readers know him chiefly through the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, a collection of four-line poems called quatrains, especially in Edward FitzGerald’s translation. One famous passage imagines a book of verses, a jug of wine, a loaf of bread, and a companion beneath a tree branch, suggesting the pleasure of sharing a simple moment. Other quatrains ask larger questions about life and death. In one, a potter thumps clay; in another, clay shaped on a pottery wheel suggests human forms. These images invite readers to think about how people, like pottery, are formed from earth and eventually return to it.

Ben Jonson was an English playwright and poet of the late 1500s and early 1600s, when theatre was a popular form of entertainment. He is known for the comedies Every Man in His Humour and The Alchemist, which use wit and deception to make fun of human weaknesses. In another comedy, Bartholomew Fair, Jonson created Zeal-of-the-Land Busy, a character whose religious claims contrast with his behavior. The play takes its name from an annual fair held in London, England’s capital. London was also home to the Globe Theatre, where many people watched plays by Shakespeare and other dramatists. Audience members called groundlings paid less to stand in the open yard near the stage. Jonson’s plays offer a lively picture of the crowds, arguments, and ambitions of his time.

Willa Cather was an American novelist born in Virginia and raised in Red Cloud, Nebraska. Her experience of life on the Great Plains helped her write about pioneers, immigrants, and the challenges of building a home in a new place. In My Ántonia, she tells the story of Ántonia Shimerda, the daughter of Czech immigrants who settle in Nebraska. Another of Cather’s novels, The Song of the Lark, follows Thea Kronborg, a young woman from Moonstone, Colorado, who dreams of becoming an opera singer. Dr. Howard Archie supports Thea as she leaves home to pursue her talent. Through characters like Ántonia and Thea, Cather explored determination, ambition, and the ways a person’s home can shape their life.

“Quiet Night Thoughts” is a short poem by Li Bai, also known as Li Po, a celebrated poet of China’s Tang dynasty and a contemporary of Du Fu. In the poem, the speaker sees moonlight near the foot of his bed and, for a moment, thinks it is frost on the ground. He lifts his head to look at the moon, then lowers it as he thinks of his homeland. These simple movements turn a quiet scene into an expression of homesickness: the moon is beautiful, but it also reminds him of the place and people he misses. The poem is famous for expressing this feeling in just a few lines. Li Bai’s work later became known to English-language readers through translations by writers including Ezra Pound.

“The Fox and the Grapes” is a short fable attributed to Aesop, an ancient Greek storyteller traditionally described as enslaved. In the story, a hungry fox sees a bunch of ripe grapes hanging high on a vine. It leaps again and again to reach them, but every attempt fails. As the fox walks away, it claims that the grapes are probably sour and not worth eating. The fox has no reason to think this is true; saying it helps the fox feel better about failing. This reaction gives us the expression “sour grapes,” used when someone dismisses something they wanted but could not get. Like other fables associated with Aesop, including “The Tortoise and the Hare,” the story uses animals to show a recognizable human behavior.

The Cyropaedia is a prose work by Xenophon, an Athenian writer and soldier. Its title means “The Education of Cyrus,” and it follows Cyrus the Great from his childhood and training through his rise to power as founder of the Persian Achaemenid Empire. Rather than giving a strictly factual biography, Xenophon presents an idealized portrait of Cyrus as a wise, disciplined, and effective ruler. The work explores how education and character can help a leader win loyalty and govern an empire. Xenophon also wrote the Anabasis, which describes the retreat of Greek mercenaries after an expedition led by a different Persian prince, Cyrus the Younger.

Julio Cortázar was an Argentine writer celebrated for stories that blur the line between ordinary life and the strange. In “Axolotl,” a man repeatedly visits an aquarium to watch the axolotls, amphibians that fascinate him. One day, the story’s viewpoint shifts: he experiences life as an axolotl on the other side of the glass. Cortázar also wrote “Blow-Up” and the experimental novel Hopscotch. Its “Table of Instructions” offers a reading order that begins at Chapter 73 and then jumps between chapters, rather than proceeding from start to finish. Much of Hopscotch uses stream of consciousness to follow characters’ thoughts. Both “Axolotl” and part of Hopscotch are set in Paris, the capital of France, where Cortázar is buried in Montparnasse Cemetery.

A diary is a form of autobiographical nonfiction in which a person records their own experiences, thoughts, and observations close to when they happen. Diaries often consist of dated entries, allowing readers to follow events and see how the writer’s feelings change over time. They may begin as private writing but later become important literary or historical records. In Japan, Sei Shonagon’s Pillow Book describes life at the imperial court and includes lists of things she found annoying or beautiful; another court writer, Murasaki Shikibu, kept a diary about court life. A famous modern example is Anne Frank’s diary, written while she and her family hid from the Nazis in occupied Amsterdam during World War II. Anne addressed many entries to an imagined confidante named Kitty.

The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe is a 1950 fantasy novel by C. S. Lewis. Four siblings—Peter, Susan, Edmund, and Lucy Pevensie—enter the magical land of Narnia through a wardrobe. Lucy is the first to visit Narnia, where she meets Mr. Tumnus, a faun who lives near a lamppost. He invites her to tea, but admits that he has promised to turn any human he finds over to the White Witch. Instead, he lets Lucy go and later helps the children. The Witch has trapped Narnia in endless winter and tempts Edmund with Turkish Delight. The children join the lion Aslan in opposing her. After Aslan sacrifices himself at the Stone Table, a deeper magic brings him back to life; the Witch is defeated, and the Pevensies become kings and queens of Narnia.

The Master Builder is an 1892 drama by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, who also wrote A Doll’s House and Ghosts. Its central character, Halvard Solness, is a successful architect whose ambition is mixed with fear that younger builders will replace him. He is also troubled by the belief that he somehow willed his old house to burn down, an event that helped his career but devastated his family. Hilda Wangel encourages Solness to prove himself by climbing to the top of a newly built house, despite his fear of heights. He reaches the top but falls to his death. Ibsen’s plays often explore the pressures people face at home and in society. In A Doll’s House, the sound of a door slamming marks Nora’s departure from her husband, Torvald.

Welcome to the Monkey House is a 1968 collection of short stories by American author Kurt Vonnegut. His stories often use science fiction, satire, and dark humor to question rules that are supposed to improve society. In the title story, “Welcome to the Monkey House,” the government uses a program called “ethical birth control” to limit population growth. Billy the Poet rebels against it, though his actions also harm others. Another story in the collection, “Harrison Bergeron,” imagines a future in which the government forces people with unusual abilities to wear handicaps so that everyone will appear equal. For example, talented ballerinas must wear weights and masks. By taking these ideas to extremes, Vonnegut asks readers to think about freedom, equality, and the dangers of government control.

A Supermarket in California is a poem by Allen Ginsberg, a leading writer of the Beat Generation. Its speaker wanders through a brightly lit grocery store at night and imagines meeting Walt Whitman among the aisles. Whitman was a nineteenth-century American poet whose landmark collection is Leaves of Grass. Ginsberg addresses him as if they could walk and talk together, asking questions as Whitman pokes among the meats and looks at the shoppers. The imagined meeting connects two poets from different eras who wrote about American life and freedom. Yet the crowded store also leaves the speaker feeling lonely. By placing Whitman in an ordinary supermarket, Ginsberg contrasts the abundance of things to buy with a longing for human connection and a sense of direction.

Walter Mitty is the mild-mannered protagonist of “The Secret Life of Walter Mitty,” a short story by American writer and cartoonist James Thurber, first published in The New Yorker in 1939. As Mitty goes about ordinary errands with his wife, his imagination transforms him into a series of daring, capable heroes. While she gets her hair done and tells him to buy overshoes, he daydreams about piloting a Navy hydroplane and performing a difficult operation, even fixing a surgical device with a fountain pen. These fantasies contrast with his quiet, often bewildered behavior in everyday life. Thurber uses that contrast for humor while showing how daydreams can offer an escape from routine and make an ordinary person feel extraordinary.

Suzanne Collins is an American author known for two popular series for young readers: The Underland Chronicles and The Hunger Games trilogy. The Underland Chronicles begins with Gregor the Overlander, in which a boy named Gregor falls through an air duct in his New York City apartment building and discovers a hidden world beneath the city. There, humans live alongside giant creatures such as bats and rats, and Gregor becomes caught up in dangerous conflicts. Collins later created Katniss Everdeen, the main character of The Hunger Games, a dystopian science-fiction trilogy set in a future nation where children are forced to compete in a deadly televised contest. Across both series, Collins explores courage, loyalty, war, and the difficult choices young people face when others depend on them.
