In H. G. Wells’s science-fiction novel The Time Machine, the Time Traveller journeys far into the future and meets the Eloi, a frail, gentle group of humans who live on the Earth’s surface. Their lives seem carefree at first, but they are vulnerable to the Morlocks, another group of future humans who live underground and hunt the Eloi for food. One Eloi woman, Weena, becomes the Time Traveller’s companion after he rescues her from drowning. She later gives him two white flowers, which he brings back as evidence of his journey. The contrast between the Eloi and the Morlocks helps Wells explore how differences between social classes might shape humanity’s future.

Paddington Bear is a polite fictional bear created by British author Michael Bond. He first appeared in the 1958 children’s book A Bear Called Paddington. Paddington comes from “darkest Peru,” where he was cared for by his Aunt Lucy and Uncle Pastuzo. After traveling to London with a small suitcase, he is found alone at Paddington railway station by the Brown family, who take him home and give him his name. Paddington is known for his old hat, his good manners, and his love of marmalade sandwiches, which he often keeps handy for emergencies. Although he tries to be helpful, his curiosity can lead to comic mishaps. His stories show how a newcomer can become part of a family.

Haymitch Abernathy is a character in The Hunger Games series, set in the future country of Panem. He comes from District 12, a poor coal-mining region in Appalachia that is also home to Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark. Haymitch won the 50th Hunger Games, a special competition called a Quarter Quell, and by the time of the 74th Games he is the only living victor in District 12. As a former winner, he becomes Katniss and Peeta’s mentor when they are chosen to compete. Although he is known for heavy drinking and a sharp, cynical attitude, he understands how dangerous the Games are. He advises them to run away from the Cornucopia at the start, rather than risk being killed in the opening bloodbath.

Oral literature is made up of stories, poems, and other compositions passed between generations through speaking, singing, memorization, and performance rather than primarily through writing. Performers may use repeated phrases, familiar patterns, and rhythm to help them remember a work and share it with an audience. One example is the Epic of Sundiata, a story about the founder of the Mali Empire that has been performed by West African griots, who preserve and tell their communities’ histories. Scholars also study spoken transmission in religious texts. They point to repeated formulas in the Quran as evidence of its connection to recitation. Its recognized qira’at are distinct traditions for reciting the text. Oral literature can therefore include both long narrative epics and works preserved through religious recitation.

The Short Happy Life of Francis Macomber is a short story by American writer Ernest Hemingway, set during an African safari. Francis Macomber, an American tourist, panics and runs away during a lion hunt, leaving the experienced professional hunter Robert Wilson to shoot the wounded lion. Macomber’s wife, Margot, is ashamed of his fear and grows close to Wilson. Later, Wilson leads them on a buffalo hunt. When a wounded buffalo charges, Macomber stands his ground instead of fleeing, showing that he has begun to overcome his fear. Margot fires at the buffalo but hits Macomber in the back of the head, killing him. The story leaves open whether she meant to shoot him. Its title points to the brief period of courage and confidence Macomber finds just before his death.

First published in 1897, H. G. Wells’s science-fiction novel The Invisible Man follows Griffin, a scientist whose experiments with light make his body impossible to see. He arrives in the English village of Iping wrapped in bandages and rents a room at the Coach and Horses inn, where his strange behavior alarms the locals. Griffin’s invisibility lets him move unseen, but it also makes ordinary life difficult and leaves him increasingly desperate and violent. He later explains his optical experiments to Dr. Kemp and tries to recruit him for a “Reign of Terror.” Kemp refuses, recognizing the danger Griffin poses. The novel uses Griffin’s story to explore how scientific power can become destructive when it is used without concern for others.

Bridge to Terabithia is a 1977 novel by American author Katherine Paterson, who also won the Newbery Medal for Jacob Have I Loved. Its main character, Jess Aarons, is a fifth-grade boy who spends the summer training to become the fastest runner in his class. When a new girl, Leslie Burke, beats him in a race, the two become friends. They invent a secret kingdom called Terabithia in the woods and reach it by swinging on a rope over a creek. In their imaginary world, Jess and Leslie can be brave and powerful as they face the difficulties of school and family life. Their friendship is at the heart of a story about imagination, loss, and growing up.

Nikolai Gogol’s satirical short story The Overcoat follows Akaky Akakievich, a timid, poorly paid government copyist in St. Petersburg who spends his days recopying official documents. When his old coat wears out, he saves for months to buy a warm, tailor-made overcoat from a tailor named Petrovich. The new coat briefly earns Akaky attention and an invitation to an office party, but thieves steal it soon afterward. Akaky asks a senior official, known as the “Very Important Personage,” for help, only to be harshly dismissed. He falls ill and dies, then returns as a ghost who takes overcoats from passersby. Through Akaky’s small hopes and the cruel response to his loss, Gogol mocks a society that values rank more than kindness.

Eugene Onegin is a Russian novel in verse by Alexander Pushkin, a poet often regarded as a founder of modern Russian literature. Its main character, Eugene Onegin, is a detached young aristocrat who moves to the countryside. There he meets Tatyana Larina, who writes him a letter confessing her love, but he rejects her. Onegin later flirts with Tatyana’s younger sister, Olga, upsetting his friend Vladimir Lensky, who is engaged to her. Their quarrel leads to a duel in which Onegin kills Lensky. Years later, Onegin falls in love with Tatyana, but she has married someone else and refuses him despite still having feelings for him. Pushkin also wrote the poem The Bronze Horseman and the play Boris Godunov.

Rebecca is a Gothic novel by British author Daphne du Maurier, first published in 1938. Its young narrator, whose name is never revealed, marries the wealthy widower Maxim de Winter and moves to his imposing estate, Manderley, on the coast of Cornwall. There she finds that Maxim’s first wife, Rebecca, still seems to dominate the house, even though she is dead. The housekeeper, Mrs. Danvers, was devoted to Rebecca and makes the new Mrs. de Winter feel unwelcome. Manderley’s grand rooms and grounds hold reminders of Rebecca, creating the uneasy atmosphere typical of Gothic fiction. As the narrator tries to understand her husband and his past, secrets about Rebecca’s life and death come to light.

Ralph Waldo Emerson was a 19th-century American essayist and lecturer and a leading figure in Transcendentalism, a movement that valued nature, individual thought, and spiritual insight. In his essay Nature, Emerson imagined himself as a “transparent eye-ball” while contemplating the natural world: with his ordinary sense of self fading, he felt connected to something larger. His essay “Self-Reliance” urged readers to trust their own judgment rather than simply follow others. Emerson made a similar argument about American culture in an 1837 address to Harvard’s Phi Beta Kappa Society. Titled “The American Scholar,” the speech called on thinkers in the United States to develop their own intellectual voice instead of depending on European models.

Sisterhood is the relationship and sense of connection among sisters. In Anton Chekhov’s play Three Sisters, Olga, Masha, and Irina share a life in a provincial Russian town and repeatedly dream of returning to Moscow, where they spent their childhood. Their longing for the city brings them together even as each sister faces different disappointments. When a fire breaks out in the town, they help its victims, showing their concern for others. Shakespeare’s Macbeth offers a very different trio: the Weird Sisters, three witches who make prophecies and chant “Double, double, toil and trouble.” Comparing these groups shows how literature can portray sisterhood in different ways, from the everyday bonds of family to a mysterious supernatural alliance.

Moll Flanders is a 1722 novel by the English writer and pamphleteer Daniel Defoe. Presented as though it were the heroine’s true life story, it begins with Moll’s birth in London’s Newgate Prison. As she struggles to survive, she enters a succession of marriages and turns to theft, eventually being caught and sent to the American colonies. There she reunites with Jemmy, her “Lancashire husband,” before the story ends with her repentance. Moll’s adventures explore poverty, crime, and the limited choices available to women in eighteenth-century society. Defoe also wrote Robinson Crusoe, about a castaway who spends 28 years on an island, and A Journal of the Plague Year, a fictionalized account of London’s 1665 epidemic.

Oscar and Lucinda is a 1988 novel by Australian writer Peter Carey. Set in the nineteenth century, it follows Oscar Hopkins, an English clergyman, and Lucinda Leplastrier, an Australian heiress who owns a glass factory. Both are fascinated by gambling, and their friendship leads to an extraordinary wager: Oscar bets that he can transport a glass church to Bellingen, a town in New South Wales. The fragile church and the difficult journey make the bet a major test for both characters. Carey uses their story to explore faith, chance, love and life in colonial Australia. He later wrote another Booker Prize-winning novel, True History of the Kelly Gang, about the Australian outlaw Ned Kelly.

Kahlil Gibran was a Lebanese-American poet, writer, and artist best known for The Prophet, published in 1923. In this book, Almustafa prepares to leave the fictional island of Orphalese, and its people ask him to share his thoughts on subjects such as love, work, freedom, and death. His answers form a series of poetic teachings rather than a conventional story. Gibran also wrote The Earth Gods, a work that has been suggested to draw inspiration from The Four Zoas, an unfinished mythological poem by the English poet William Blake. Blake was a painter and printmaker as well as a poet, and he illustrated his own collection Songs of Innocence and of Experience. Both writers combined poetry with spiritual and philosophical ideas.

Stephen King is an American author best known for horror novels and short stories. His first published novel, Carrie, appeared in 1974, and his later works include The Shining, in which Jack Torrance descends into madness, as well as It and Cujo. King often connects his stories through recurring places, especially the fictional Maine town of Castle Rock. Not all of his writing focuses on supernatural horror: his novella The Body follows four boys in 1959 as they walk along railroad tracks in search of a missing boy’s body. Director Rob Reiner adapted The Body into the 1986 film Stand By Me, starring Wil Wheaton and River Phoenix. The film places the boys’ hometown in Castle Rock, Oregon.

Father Goriot is an 1835 novel by French writer Honoré de Balzac and part of his larger collection of connected stories, La Comédie humaine. Set mainly in a Paris boarding house run by Madame Vauquer, it follows Père Goriot, a former vermicelli-maker who has spent his fortune helping his two daughters. They neglect him as he grows poor and ill, revealing the selfishness beneath fashionable Parisian society. Another boarder, Eugène de Rastignac, is an ambitious law student from the provinces who hopes to rise in that society. Unlike Goriot’s daughters, Rastignac attends the old man’s funeral. After the burial, he looks out over Paris and defiantly challenges the city, marking his determination to succeed. Rastignac appears again in other works of La Comédie humaine.

Are You There God? It’s Me, Margaret. is a 1970 coming-of-age novel by American author Judy Blume. It follows Margaret Simon, a sixth-grader whose family moves from New York City to suburban New Jersey. Margaret becomes friends with Nancy, Janie, and Gretchen, and the girls form a club where they talk about growing up. As Margaret navigates friendship, puberty, and her first period, she also tries to decide what religion means to her. Her mother was raised Christian and her father Jewish, but Margaret has not been raised in either faith, so she speaks privately to God while exploring both traditions. Blume also wrote Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing, about Peter Hatcher and his frustrating younger brother, Fudge.

Poets are writers who use language, rhythm, and imagery to express ideas and feelings. In Thornton Wilder’s play Our Town, Emily Webb dies after giving birth and is allowed to revisit her twelfth birthday. Seeing an ordinary day again makes her wonder whether people truly appreciate life while they are living it. She asks the Stage Manager, the play’s narrator, if anyone ever realizes life in that way. He answers, “The saints and poets, maybe.” Robert Frost and Emily Dickinson are examples of poets. Dickinson was a 19th-century American writer from Amherst, Massachusetts. Her poems are known for unusual capitalization and punctuation, and many were published only after her death.

Uncle Remus is the fictional storyteller who frames Joel Chandler Harris’s collections of African American folktales. Harris, a Georgia-born journalist, introduced him in Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (1880). In the stories, Uncle Remus tells a young listener about animals such as Br’er Rabbit, a clever trickster who often outwits stronger opponents. Harris collected and adapted tales from Black oral traditions, many of which had been passed down during slavery. His books helped bring those stories to a wide audience, but they also raise questions about a white author’s use of Black storytellers’ work and his portrayal of Black speech and life in the South. Remember the distinction: Uncle Remus is the fictional narrator; Joel Chandler Harris is the author who created him.

Rick Riordan is an American author best known for Percy Jackson & the Olympians, a fantasy series that brings Greek mythology into the modern world. Its first book, The Lightning Thief, follows Percy Jackson, a boy who discovers that his father is Poseidon, the Greek god of the sea. Percy’s friend Grover Underwood brings him to Camp Half-Blood, a refuge where young demigods—children of gods and humans—learn about their powers. Percy carries a sword called Anaklusmos, also known as Riptide, which looks like a pen until he uncaps it. His mother’s habit of making blue-colored food is another memorable detail. Riordan has written other mythology-inspired series, including The Kane Chronicles, based on Egyptian mythology, and Magnus Chase and the Gods of Asgard, based on Norse mythology.

In Daniel Defoe’s adventure novel Robinson Crusoe, an English sailor survives a shipwreck and spends twenty-eight years on an island near the mouth of the Orinoco River. He builds a shelter and learns to find food and protect himself. Later, he rescues a man who is being pursued by cannibals. Crusoe names him Friday because he saves him on that day of the week. He teaches Friday English, and the two become companions, although Crusoe also treats Friday as his servant. Friday’s arrival changes Crusoe’s lonely life and gives him someone to work and speak with. The character is an important part of the novel’s story of survival, but their unequal relationship also reflects the colonial attitudes of Defoe’s time.

The Pillow Book is a work of Japanese literature written by Sei Shōnagon, a court lady who served Empress Teishi during the Heian period in the late tenth century. It is a diary-like collection rather than a continuous story: Shōnagon records observations of palace life, anecdotes about people at court, personal impressions, and lists of things she finds striking. Some lists have titles such as “Hateful Things” and “Things That Make One’s Heart Beat Faster,” giving readers a sense of her wit and attention to everyday details. Her accounts also reveal the customs and relationships of the imperial court, including a story about a palace cat and a dog. The Pillow Book remains valuable both as literature and as a glimpse into life at the Heian court.

Travel literature is nonfiction writing about journeys. Writers use their own experiences to describe places they visit, people they meet, and cultures they encounter. It can take the form of essays, memoirs, or travelogues, combining firsthand observation with storytelling and reflection. A travel writer might describe a landscape while also explaining how a journey changed their understanding of it. Mark Twain’s 1869 book The Innocents Abroad is a well-known example. It draws on his voyage aboard the Quaker City, a steamship tour that included Europe and the Holy Land. Twain turned the travelers’ sightseeing, observations, and comic reactions into a satirical account that makes fun of their expectations as well as what they saw.

Middle English was the form of English used in England from roughly the late eleventh to the late fifteenth century, after Old English, the language of the Anglo-Saxons, and before Early Modern English. It was not identical everywhere: writers used different regional forms. Famous Middle English works include Geoffrey Chaucer’s The Canterbury Tales and the anonymous poems Pearl and Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. In Pearl, a grieving father dreams of meeting his lost daughter in Heaven. Sir Gawain and the Green Knight is an Arthurian romance generally attributed to the same anonymous poet. Gawain accepts a beheading challenge at King Arthur’s court and is later tested at Sir Bertilak’s castle. The poem’s long stanzas use alliteration, repeating initial sounds in stressed words, and end with a short “bob” followed by a rhyming “wheel.”

“Chicago” is a free-verse poem by American poet Carl Sandburg. It speaks directly to the Midwestern city, calling it “Hog Butcher for the World” and “City of the Big Shoulders.” These nicknames reflect Chicago’s meatpacking industry and its image as a place of demanding physical work. Sandburg also describes the city as a “Tool maker, stacker of wheat, player with railroads,” showing its importance as an industrial and transportation center. The poem does not ignore Chicago’s poverty, crime, or harshness, but it celebrates the energy and confidence of the people who work there. By combining criticism with civic pride, Sandburg portrays Chicago as a rough yet powerful city. Sandburg also wrote the poems “Grass” and “Fog.”

Death and the King’s Horseman is a tragedy by Nigerian playwright Wole Soyinka, who became the first African to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986. Set in colonial Nigeria, the play draws on Yoruba beliefs about the duties of a king’s horseman. After the king dies, his horseman, Elesin Oba, is expected to die in a ritual act so he can accompany the king into the spirit world. British colonial officer Simon Pilkings intervenes and prevents the rite, with devastating consequences. The play explores the conflict between Yoruba traditions and colonial authority, but it also asks whether Elesin’s own choices contribute to the tragedy.

The Alchemist is a novel by Brazilian author Paulo Coelho about Santiago, a young shepherd living in Spain. After recurring dreams suggest that treasure awaits him near the Egyptian pyramids, he sets out to find it. Santiago’s journey becomes a search for his Personal Legend, the purpose he feels called to fulfill. Along the way, he learns about the Soul of the World, a force that connects all things, and about alchemy, the ancient pursuit of transformation. An alchemist teaches him that alchemy’s Master Work involves making the Elixir of Life and the philosopher’s stone, a substance said to turn lead into gold. Santiago’s adventures encourage him to trust his dreams and learn from the people and places he encounters.

V. S. Naipaul was a novelist and essayist born in Chaguanas, Trinidad, in 1932. He later moved to Britain, became a British citizen, and won the 2001 Nobel Prize in Literature. His writing often explores identity, family, and the effects of colonialism. One of his best-known novels is A House for Mr. Biswas, published in 1961. Its main character, Mohun Biswas, is an Indo-Trinidadian journalist who marries into the powerful Tulsi family. Living under his in-laws’ influence leaves him longing for independence. His struggle to own a house is about more than finding somewhere to live: it represents his wish to make a life that belongs to him.

Georg Cantor (1845–1918) was a German mathematician who founded modern set theory, the study of collections of objects called sets. He investigated cardinality, or the number of elements in a set, and showed that infinite sets can have different sizes. The counting numbers can be listed in order, but the real numbers, which include all decimal values, cannot. To prove this, Cantor imagined a complete list of real numbers and built a new number by changing the first decimal digit of the first number, the second digit of the second number, and so on. The new number differs from every listed number in at least one digit, so it cannot be on the supposedly complete list. This proof technique is called Cantor’s diagonal argument, and it shows that the real numbers are uncountable.

A function is a mathematical rule that assigns exactly one output to each allowed input. You can picture it as a machine: put in a value x, and the function produces a result written f(x), read as “f of x.” The set of all allowed inputs is called the domain. The outputs the function actually produces form its range, which may be smaller than its codomain, the set of possible outputs specified for the function. For example, if f(x) = x² and the domain is all real numbers, then f(3) = 9, and the range is all nonnegative real numbers. Functions can also be continuous, meaning their graphs have no breaks over an interval. The Intermediate Value Theorem applies when a function is continuous on a closed interval.

The Green–Tao theorem says that the prime numbers contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length. An arithmetic progression is a sequence in which the difference between consecutive terms stays the same, such as 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, where the common difference is 2. Primes may seem too scattered to form long, regular patterns, but the theorem guarantees that, for any length you choose, some progression of primes has that many terms. It does not say that a single progression goes on forever. Announced in 2004, the result was proved by Ben Green and Terence Tao, building on ideas connected to Szemerédi’s theorem about arithmetic patterns. Tao is an Australian-American number theorist who received the Fields Medal in 2006.

Gaussian curvature describes how a smooth surface bends near a particular point. To calculate it, multiply the surface’s two principal curvatures: its bending rates in the directions of greatest and least normal bending. A sphere has positive Gaussian curvature, a saddle-shaped surface has negative curvature, and a flat plane has zero. The key surprise is that Gaussian curvature is intrinsic: it can be determined from distances measured along the surface, without looking at how the surface sits in space. Bending a sheet of paper without stretching or tearing it therefore leaves its Gaussian curvature unchanged. This result is central to the Theorema Egregium, published in 1827 by the German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, for whom Gaussian curvature is named.

Cardinality is the number of elements in a set, often called its size and written with vertical bars: for example, if A = {2, 4, 6}, then |A| = 3. Two sets have the same cardinality if their elements can be paired one-to-one with none left over; such a pairing is called a bijection. Cardinality also applies to infinite sets. The natural numbers are countably infinite because they can be listed in order, but not every infinite set has the same size. Georg Cantor, the original formulator of set theory, used his diagonal argument to show that no list can contain every real number. Therefore, the real numbers are uncountable and have a larger cardinality than the natural numbers.

A fixed point of a function is an element that stays the same when the function is applied. If a function f maps a set into itself, x is a fixed point when f(x) = x. For example, if f(x) = x², then 1 is a fixed point because 1² = 1. A permutation rearranges the elements of a set, with each element sent to exactly one position and each position filled by exactly one element. In a permutation of the letters A, B, and C, an arrangement that leaves A in its original position has A as a fixed point. A permutation with no fixed points is called a derangement: every element moves to a different position.

A cylinder is a three-dimensional solid with two parallel, congruent circular bases joined by a curved surface. In a right circular cylinder, one base sits directly above the other, and the perpendicular distance between them is called the height. Since each circular base has area πr², where r is its radius, the cylinder’s volume is the base area multiplied by the height: V = πr²h. Archimedes studied a sphere inscribed in a cylinder, meaning the sphere fits inside and touches the cylinder’s top, bottom, and curved side. In this case, the cylinder’s height equals the sphere’s diameter, and the sphere’s volume is two-thirds of the cylinder’s volume.

A quadratic equation is a degree-two equation usually written as ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, and c are numbers and a cannot be zero. The x² term makes it quadratic. If you graph the related function y = ax² + bx + c, its shape is a parabola: it opens upward when a is positive and downward when a is negative. Solving the equation means finding its roots, the x-values where the parabola meets the x-axis. You can sometimes find them by factoring or completing the square, or you can use the quadratic formula, x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a). The expression b² − 4ac is called the discriminant. A positive discriminant gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated real root, and a negative discriminant gives two complex-conjugate roots.

The Division Algorithm is a theorem about dividing one integer by another. For any integer a and any nonzero integer b, there is exactly one pair of integers q and r such that a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < |b|. Here, a is the number being divided, b is the divisor, q is the quotient, and r is the remainder. The symbol |b| means the absolute value of b, so the remainder is always nonnegative and smaller than the size of the divisor, even if b is negative. For example, 17 = 5 × 3 + 2, so dividing 17 by 5 gives a quotient of 3 and a remainder of 2. The requirement on the remainder makes q and r unique. Division by zero is not allowed.

A hypersphere is the higher-dimensional analogue of a circle or an ordinary sphere. It consists of all points in Euclidean space that are a fixed distance, called the radius, from a center. In two-dimensional space, those points form a circle; in three-dimensional space, they form the familiar spherical surface. Mathematicians also study how to pack equal balls—the filled-in regions bounded by hyperspheres—as tightly as possible without overlap. This is called hypersphere packing, and the best arrangements can be difficult to find in higher dimensions. Ukrainian mathematician Maryna Viazovska proved that an arrangement based on the E8 lattice gives the densest packing in eight-dimensional space. Her breakthrough helped earn her a Fields Medal in 2022.

Euler’s identity is the equation e^(iπ) + 1 = 0. It brings together five important mathematical constants: 0 and 1, the imaginary unit i (whose square is −1), pi (π), and Euler’s number e. Pi is approximately 3.14 and is the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter; an angle of π radians is a half-turn, or 180 degrees. Euler’s number, approximately 2.71828, is the base of natural logarithms, so ln(e) = 1. In the identity, e is the base of the exponential term e^(iπ), not pi. Euler’s formula connects exponentials with angles and shows that e^(iπ) = −1. Adding 1 to both sides gives Euler’s identity, a compact link between algebra, geometry, and mathematical analysis.

Tetration is repeated exponentiation, much as multiplication is repeated addition and exponentiation is repeated multiplication. It is the operation after exponentiation in the hyperoperation sequence, so its name uses “tetra,” meaning four. In tetration, a base is stacked into a power tower, and the height tells you how many copies of the base appear. For example, “three to the height of two” is 3³, or 27, while three to the height of three is 3^(3³), or 3²⁷. Power towers are evaluated from the top down, so the order matters. One common way to write tetration is a↑↑b, where a is the base and b is the height. This is called Knuth up-arrow notation, after American computer scientist Donald Knuth.

A spherical triangle is a closed figure on the surface of a sphere whose three sides are arcs of great circles. A great circle is the largest circle that can be drawn on a sphere, like the equator on Earth. Unlike the straight sides of a flat triangle, these sides follow the sphere’s curved surface. Because of that curvature, a spherical triangle’s three interior angles add up to more than 180°. The amount above 180° is called its spherical excess. For example, if the angles total 200°, the spherical excess is 20°. To use spherical excess in the area formula, convert it to radians: the triangle’s area equals its spherical excess multiplied by the square of the sphere’s radius, R².

A reciprocal is the multiplicative inverse of a nonzero number: multiply the two together, and the result is 1. To find a reciprocal, divide 1 by the original number. For example, the reciprocal of 2 is 1/2, and the reciprocal of 1/2 is 2. Zero has no reciprocal because division by zero is undefined. Reciprocals also help describe the golden ratio, a positive number called phi that equals 1 plus its own reciprocal. Its value is approximately 1.618. The golden ratio appears when you divide consecutive Fibonacci numbers, a sequence in which each number is the sum of the two before it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and so on. As the sequence continues, those quotients approach phi.

Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that studies how the angles and side lengths of triangles are related. It is especially useful for finding an unknown side or angle in a right triangle, which has one 90-degree angle. Three important trigonometric functions are sine, cosine, and tangent. Each compares two side lengths relative to a chosen acute angle. The hypotenuse is the longest side and lies opposite the right angle; the adjacent side touches the chosen angle. Cosine is the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse. You can remember this using “CAH” in the mnemonic SOHCAHTOA: cosine equals adjacent divided by hypotenuse. For example, the cosine of zero degrees is one.

Degrees of freedom are the number of values that can vary independently in a statistical calculation after any constraints are taken into account. For example, if you have n observations and calculate each one’s deviation from the sample mean, the deviations must add to zero. Once n−1 deviations are known, the last is fixed, so there are n−1 degrees of freedom. This number helps determine the shape of distributions used for statistical tests. When a sample is used to estimate an unknown population variance, one-sample inference often uses Student’s t-distribution, a symmetric curve with heavier tails than the normal distribution. Its shape depends on the degrees of freedom, typically n−1: as that number grows, the curve gets closer to the normal distribution.

A rotation is a transformation that turns an object around a fixed point or axis without changing its shape or size. In a flat plane, rotations are commonly described as clockwise or counterclockwise. In three dimensions, an object can rotate around an axis, such as a spinning globe turning around the line through its poles. To describe three-dimensional rotations, mathematicians and computer graphics programmers often use quaternions. Invented by the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton, quaternions extend complex numbers from two dimensions to four. A quaternion has one real component and three components associated with the non-real units i, j, and k. These units are related to the three coordinate axes, making quaternions useful for representing rotations in space.

A system of linear equations is a collection of two or more first-degree equations involving the same unknowns. To solve the system, you must find values that make every equation true at once. For example, x + y = 5 and x − y = 1 have the unique solution x = 3, y = 2. Other systems have infinitely many solutions because their equations describe the same line, or no solution because the lines never meet; a contradiction such as 1 = 2 signals an inconsistent system. Systems can be solved by substitution or elimination. In Gaussian elimination, named for mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, the equations are written as an augmented matrix. Elementary row operations put it in row-echelon form, and back-substitution then finds the unknowns.

Seven is the largest single-digit prime number: it is greater than one and has no positive divisors except one and itself. A polygon with seven sides is called a heptagon, and each interior angle of a regular heptagon measures about 128.6 degrees. Seven is also the most likely sum when rolling two standard six-sided dice. It can be made in six ways, such as 1 + 6 or 2 + 5, giving it a probability of one-sixth. In mathematics, the cross product is commonly defined in three dimensions and can also be defined in seven dimensions. Seven appears in a famous puzzle about the seven bridges of Königsberg, a Prussian city. By studying whether someone could cross each bridge exactly once, Leonhard Euler helped establish graph theory.

The Law of Sines connects the sides and angles of any triangle. Label the sides a, b, and c, and their opposite angles A, B, and C. The law states that a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Here, sine is a trigonometric function: in a right triangle, it is the length of the side opposite an angle divided by the hypotenuse; on the unit circle, it gives the vertical coordinate. The common value of the three ratios is 2R, where R is the radius of the triangle’s circumcircle—the circle that passes through all three vertices. So that value is the circumcircle’s diameter. You can use the Law of Sines to find a missing side or angle when you know an opposite side-angle pair.

A graph is a collection of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines). A proper vertex coloring assigns a color to each vertex so that the two endpoints of every edge have different colors. Vertices that are not joined by an edge may share a color. The colors are simply labels: what matters is how many distinct labels are used, not their names. The smallest number of colors that can produce a proper vertex coloring of a graph G is its chromatic number, written χ(G). For example, a triangle needs three colors because every vertex is adjacent to both of the others. A square needs only two: you can alternate the colors as you move around its edges. Finding χ(G) means finding a valid coloring and checking that fewer colors cannot work.

A Möbius strip is made by giving one end of a paper strip a half-twist and joining the ends to form a loop. Unlike an ordinary paper loop, it has only one continuous side: if you draw a line along its surface without lifting your pen, you can reach every part of it and return to where you started. It is also non-orientable, meaning there is no consistent way to label one side “front” and the other “back” across the whole surface. Möbius strips are studied in topology, a branch of mathematics concerned with properties of shapes and spaces that remain unchanged when they are continuously stretched, bent, or twisted, without cutting or gluing.

A regular hexagon is a six-sided polygon with all sides equal and all interior angles equal. The sum of its interior angles is 720°, so each angle measures 120°. It has nine diagonals in total, three of which are the longest: they join pairs of opposite vertices and pass through the center. Drawing these three diagonals divides the hexagon into six equilateral triangles. Three regular hexagons fit around a point because their 120° angles add up to 360°. This lets copies be placed edge to edge across the Euclidean plane with no gaps or overlaps. A repeating arrangement of congruent polygons like this is called a tiling; for regular hexagons, it is a regular hexagonal tiling.

Dimension describes how many independent directions are needed to locate a point in a space. On a line, one number gives a position, so a line is one-dimensional. On a plane, two numbers are needed, so it is two-dimensional; ordinary space needs three. A refinement called Hausdorff dimension can also describe shapes that do not fit neatly into whole-number dimensions. It examines how many tiny sets are needed to cover a shape as the sets become arbitrarily small. Fractals, which often repeat similar patterns at smaller and smaller scales, can have non-integer Hausdorff dimensions. For example, the Koch snowflake’s boundary is more intricate than an ordinary line, even though it does not fill a plane.

The parallel postulate is Euclid’s fifth postulate, a basic assumption of ordinary plane geometry. Euclid stated it using a transversal, a line that crosses two other lines: if the interior angles on one side add up to less than two right angles (180 degrees), those two lines will meet on that side when extended. An equivalent way to express the postulate is that exactly one line through a point outside a given line is parallel to it, meaning the two lines never meet. Other kinds of geometry arise when this assumption is changed. In hyperbolic geometry, infinitely many distinct lines through a point outside a given line do not intersect it. The Poincaré disk is a model of hyperbolic geometry.

Twin primes are pairs of prime numbers that differ by exactly 2. A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 that is divisible only by 1 and itself, so both numbers in a twin-prime pair must meet that rule. For example, 3 and 5 are twin primes, as are 11 and 13. By contrast, 7 and 9 differ by 2 but are not twin primes because 9 is divisible by 3. The distance between two primes is called a prime gap; twin primes have a gap of 2. Mathematicians study these gaps to understand how primes are spread among whole numbers. The English number theorist James Maynard received a 2022 Fields Medal for work that included major contributions to prime gaps, building on Yitang Zhang’s research related to twin primes.

An even number is an integer that can be divided by 2 with no remainder, so it can be written as 2 times another integer. Examples include 0, 2, 8, and −6; numbers such as 3 and 7 are odd instead. Mathematicians describe an even number as having parity zero. Even numbers also appear in a famous unsolved problem called Goldbach’s conjecture. It says that every even number greater than 2 can be written as the sum of two prime numbers, such as 10 = 3 + 7 or 28 = 5 + 23. A prime number is a positive integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. The conjecture is named after Christian Goldbach, who proposed the idea in a letter to Leonhard Euler.

A directrix is a fixed line used with a fixed point called the focus to define a conic section. For any point on the curve, the ratio of its distance from the focus to its perpendicular distance from the directrix is constant; this ratio is called the eccentricity. A parabola has an eccentricity of one, so every point on it is equally far from the focus and the directrix. The parabola’s vertex lies halfway between them, and its axis of symmetry runs through the focus at a right angle to the directrix. A chord called the latus rectum passes through the focus, has both endpoints on the parabola, and is perpendicular to the axis of symmetry. Therefore, the latus rectum is parallel to the directrix.

Division finds how many times one number is contained in another. It is the inverse of multiplication: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 because 4 × 3 = 12. The answer is called the quotient. A rational number is any number that can be written as the quotient of two integers, such as 3/4 or −6/2, provided the denominator is not zero. When division does not give a whole-number answer, there may be a remainder: 14 divided by 3 gives a quotient of 4 and a remainder of 2, since 14 = 3 × 4 + 2. Division by zero is undefined. For a nonzero number such as 5, no quotient multiplied by zero can equal 5; 0 ÷ 0 is also undefined because it does not have one unique answer.

Newton’s method is an algorithm for finding an approximate root, or zero, of an equation f(x) = 0. Start with a guess x₀ and draw the tangent line to the graph of f at that point. Where the tangent line crosses the x-axis becomes the next guess. Repeat this process to get successively better estimates when the method works well. The slope of the tangent line is the derivative, written f′(x), so each step subtracts the function’s value divided by its derivative: new guess = current guess − f(current guess)/f′(current guess). For example, if the current guess is x, the correction is f(x)/f′(x). Newton’s method can converge quickly near a root, but it may fail if the derivative is zero or the starting guess is poorly chosen.

A group is a set of elements together with an operation for combining any two of them, such as addition. To be a group, it must satisfy four rules. Closure means combining two elements of the set always gives another element in the set. Associativity means that when combining three elements, changing the placement of parentheses does not change the result: (a ⋆ b) ⋆ c = a ⋆ (b ⋆ c). The group must also have an identity element, which leaves any element unchanged when combined with it, and every element must have an inverse that combines with it to give the identity. For example, the integers form a group under addition: zero is the identity, and the inverse of 5 is −5.

A Markov chain is a model for a sequence of events in which the next outcome depends on the current state, but not on how the process reached that state. For example, a simple weather model might use today’s weather to predict the chances of sun or rain tomorrow without considering earlier days. This is called the Markov property. The possible states can be drawn as vertices in a directed graph, with arrows labeled by the probabilities of moving between states. For a finite set of states, the same probabilities can be organized in a transition matrix: a square array whose entry in each row gives the chance of moving from that row’s current state to a particular next state. The probabilities in each row add up to 1.

One-half is the fraction 1/2: multiplying by it means taking half of a quantity. It appears in several area formulas. A parallelogram is a four-sided shape with two pairs of opposite sides that are parallel, meaning each pair would never meet even if the sides were extended. Its area is usually found by multiplying its base by its perpendicular height. If you know the lengths of its two diagonals instead, multiply those lengths by the sine of the angle between the diagonals, then multiply by one-half: area = 1/2 × diagonal 1 × diagonal 2 × sin(angle). The same coefficient appears in a triangle’s area formula when two side lengths and their included angle are known: area = 1/2 × side 1 × side 2 × sin(angle).

The number 3 is the smallest odd prime: a prime number has exactly two positive divisors, 1 and itself, and the only smaller prime is the even number 2. A useful divisibility rule says that a base-ten integer is divisible by 3 whenever its digits add up to a multiple of 3. For example, the digits of 39 add to 12, so 39 is divisible by 3. Any four-digit number made from two 7s and two 8s has a digit sum of 7 + 7 + 8 + 8 = 30. Because 30 is a multiple of 3, all six possible arrangements are divisible by 3. Two of them, 7887 and 8778, read the same forwards and backwards. A number with that property is called a palindrome.

The spherical coordinate system describes a point in three-dimensional space using a distance and two angles instead of x-, y-, and z-values. The radial distance tells how far the point is from the origin. The polar angle tells how far its direction tilts away from the positive z-axis, while the azimuthal angle tells how far it turns around that axis, measured in the xy-plane. Together, these three values locate the point. Letter conventions can differ: in a common physics convention, theta denotes the polar angle and phi denotes the azimuthal angle; mathematicians often use theta for the azimuthal angle instead. So when reading spherical coordinates, check which convention is being used.

A polygon is a closed, two-dimensional shape made from a finite number of straight line segments joined end to end. These segments are its sides, and the points where they meet are its vertices. The sides must form a complete boundary with no gaps, and curved edges do not count. Triangles, which have three sides, and quadrilaterals, which have four, are familiar polygons. A polygon lies in a flat plane, but related shapes called polytopes can exist in other dimensions. The simplest polygon is a triangle. The simplest three-dimensional polytope is a tetrahedron: a solid shaped like a triangular pyramid, with four triangular faces. Unlike a polygon, it occupies space rather than lying in a plane.

A saddle point is a stationary point that is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. For a differentiable function of two variables, it can occur where both first partial derivatives are zero, making the gradient zero, but nearby values rise in one direction and fall in another. Picture the middle of a horse’s saddle: it curves upward from front to back and downward from side to side. To investigate a critical point, mathematicians often use the Hessian matrix, a square array containing all the function’s second partial derivatives. These derivatives describe how the function curves in different directions. Identifying saddle points matters in optimization, where the goal is to find minima or maxima; for example, a machine-learning algorithm minimizing a loss function may encounter a point with zero gradient that is not a minimum.

Quaternions are a number system that extends complex numbers from two dimensions to four. A quaternion has the form a + bi + cj + dk, where a, b, c, and d are real numbers. The three distinct non-real basis elements, called the quaternion units, are i, j, and k. Each squares to −1, and their product in that order also equals −1: i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1. Order matters when multiplying them; for example, ij = k, but ji = −k. Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton devised quaternions and famously carved their defining relation into a bridge in Dublin in 1843. Quaternions are useful for describing rotations in three-dimensional space, such as the orientation of a spacecraft or a character in a video game.

The kissing number is the greatest number of identical, non-overlapping circles or spheres that can touch one identical circle or sphere. “Kissing” simply means touching at a point, without overlapping. In the plane, which is two-dimensional, the kissing number is six: six equal circles fit around a central equal circle, each touching it and its two neighbors. A seventh cannot fit without overlapping one of the others. One way to see why is to draw lines from the central circle’s center to the centers of the outer circles. Each pair of neighboring outer circles needs at least 60 degrees of space, and a full turn has 360 degrees, leaving room for at most six.

The square knot is a knot studied in topology, the branch of mathematics concerned with shapes and how they can be continuously deformed. In knot theory, a knot is a closed loop embedded in three-dimensional space. The square knot is made by taking the connected sum of two trefoil knots: one trefoil and its mirror image. To form a connected sum, imagine cutting a small section from each loop and joining the loose ends to make one loop. Because the two trefoils have opposite handedness, the resulting knot is equivalent to its own reflection: it can be smoothly moved and reshaped in three-dimensional space to match its mirror image without cutting the loop or letting it pass through itself. This mirror-related property is called amphichirality.

A kite is a quadrilateral with two pairs of congruent adjacent sides. “Congruent” means equal in length, and “adjacent” means the sides in each pair meet at a shared vertex. Draw a diagonal between those two meeting vertices: it crosses the kite’s other diagonal at a right angle and divides that diagonal into two equal segments. A line that does both is called a perpendicular bisector, so this diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other one. A kite does not need to have all four sides equal. If it does, it is also a rhombus; a square is an example of a rhombus that is also a kite.

Dirichlet’s theorem on arithmetic progressions, published in 1837, says that an arithmetic progression contains infinitely many primes if its positive starting number and positive common difference are coprime, meaning they share no divisor greater than 1. An arithmetic progression is a sequence formed by repeatedly adding the same number: for example, 5, 9, 13, 17, … has a common difference of 4. Since 5 and 4 are coprime, Dirichlet’s theorem guarantees infinitely many primes in that progression, even though many terms are composite. The theorem’s standard analytic proof uses Dirichlet characters. These are functions that repeat according to remainders modulo an integer and are completely multiplicative, meaning the value at a product equals the product of the values. They help distinguish residue classes and define Dirichlet L-functions.

A parallelogram is a quadrilateral, or four-sided plane shape, with two pairs of opposite sides that are parallel. Parallel sides stay the same distance apart and never meet, even if extended. In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal in length, opposite angles are equal, and the diagonals bisect each other: each diagonal cuts the other into two equal parts. Its area is usually found by multiplying a base by the perpendicular height. Another area formula uses the lengths of its two diagonals and the angle between them: area equals one-half times the first diagonal length times the second diagonal length times the sine of that angle. Rectangles, rhombuses, and squares are special kinds of parallelograms.

The denominator is the number or expression below the fraction bar. In a fraction such as 3/4, the denominator, 4, tells you that the whole is divided into four equal parts, while the numerator, 3, tells you how many parts are being counted. A denominator cannot be zero, because division by zero is undefined. To simplify a fraction, you can divide its numerator and denominator by the same nonzero factor. In more advanced math, a denominator may contain a complex number, which has a real part and an imaginary part involving i. The complex conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part: the conjugate of 5 + i is 5 − i. Multiplying both parts of a fraction by that conjugate can make its denominator real.

A bipartite graph is a graph whose vertices can be divided into two disjoint groups, or parts, so that every edge connects a vertex in one part to a vertex in the other. No two vertices in the same part are connected by an edge. This means the vertices can be colored with two colors, one for each part, without adjacent vertices sharing a color. A complete bipartite graph has every possible edge between its two parts. The graph called K₃,₃ has three vertices in each part, so it has nine edges connecting the parts. K₃,₃ is also important in the study of planar graphs: together with K₅, it appears in Kuratowski’s theorem, which characterizes graphs that cannot be drawn on a flat surface without edges crossing.

The Euler characteristic is a number that describes the structure of a shape or graph. To calculate it, count the vertices (corner points), edges (lines joining vertices), and faces (regions enclosed by edges), then use the formula vertices minus edges plus faces, or V − E + F. For example, a cube has 8 vertices, 12 edges, and 6 faces, so its Euler characteristic is 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. Every convex polyhedron has an Euler characteristic of 2. The same rule applies to a connected planar graph, which can be drawn on a flat surface without edges crossing. When counting its faces, include the unbounded region outside the graph. Its Euler characteristic is also always 2.

A parabola is a U-shaped curve that appears when a quadratic function such as y = x² is graphed. It is also a conic section with an eccentricity of exactly one. A parabola can be defined using a fixed point called the focus and a fixed line called the directrix: every point on the curve is the same distance from the focus as it is from the directrix. The vertex is the point where the parabola turns, and it lies halfway between the focus and the directrix. The directrix is on the opposite side of the vertex from the focus. A segment called the latus rectum passes through the focus, has endpoints on the parabola, and is parallel to the directrix.

Negative one, written -1, is the number one unit below zero on the number line. It is important in both complex numbers and quaternions. In the complex number system, the imaginary unit i is defined so that i squared equals -1; in other words, i is a square root of negative one. Quaternions extend complex numbers by adding two more units, j and k. A quaternion can be written as a combination of a real number and multiples of i, j, and k. These units follow special multiplication rules: i times j equals k, and k times k equals -1, so i times j times k equals -1. Unlike ordinary number multiplication, quaternion multiplication is noncommutative: changing the order can change the result.

A time integral adds up a quantity over an interval of time, rather than over a distance or position. You can think of it as combining many tiny contributions, each equal to the quantity’s value multiplied by a tiny amount of elapsed time. For example, power measures how quickly energy is transferred, so the time integral of power gives the total change in energy. In Lagrangian mechanics, developed by Joseph-Louis Lagrange, the Lagrangian is kinetic energy minus potential energy. Taking its time integral along a system’s history gives a scalar quantity called action. The principle of stationary action says that, for the path a system actually follows, small changes to the path do not change the action to first order. This principle leads to the system’s equations of motion.

The Power of a Point Theorem describes a relationship between a fixed point and a circle. Draw any line through the point that crosses the circle at two points. Multiply the directed distances from the fixed point to those intersections; the result is the same no matter which line you choose. This constant is called the point’s power. If the fixed point is outside the circle, both distances are positive: one reaches the nearer intersection and the other reaches the farther one. A line from the same point may instead touch the circle at exactly one point, T; this line is a tangent. If a secant from the point crosses the circle at A and B, then PT squared equals PA times PB. This special case is called the tangent-secant theorem.

Eight is the positive integer after seven and before nine. In chemistry, oxygen has atomic number eight, meaning each oxygen atom has eight protons. Eight also describes a full outer shell, or octet, of valence electrons in most noble-gas atoms; helium is an exception because its outer shell is full with two. The prefix “oct-” means eight, which helps explain the name octane, an alkane with eight carbon atoms. Octane gives its name to the octane rating, a measure of how well gasoline resists knocking, or igniting too early under compression in an engine. A higher octane rating means the fuel can withstand more compression before knocking. The number eight therefore connects a counting number to both atomic structure and an everyday measure of fuel performance.

The Law of Cosines extends the Pythagorean theorem to any triangle, including oblique triangles, which have no right angle. If two sides have lengths a and b, and the angle where they meet is C, then the opposite side has length c, where c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. Angle C is called the included angle because it lies between the two known sides, rather than opposite either one. When C is 90 degrees, cos C equals zero, so the equation becomes a² + b² = c². Cosine is a trigonometric function: in a right triangle, the cosine of an acute angle is the length of the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse.

Inverse proportionality is a relationship in which two quantities change in opposite directions while their product stays constant. It can be written as y = k/x, or xy = k, where k is a fixed number. If one quantity doubles, the other halves; if one triples, the other becomes one-third as large. For example, a light wave’s frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional when the speed of light is fixed. Another example is Wien’s displacement law, which describes radiation from a blackbody, an ideal object that absorbs all wavelengths of light. The law says that a blackbody’s absolute temperature, measured in kelvins, multiplied by the wavelength at which its emission is strongest remains constant. As the blackbody gets hotter, that peak wavelength gets shorter.

A diameter is a line segment that connects two points on a circle and passes through its center. It is a special kind of chord, which is any segment joining two points on a circle. The diameter is the longest chord because it stretches all the way across the circle through the center. A radius runs from the center to the circle, so a diameter is made of two radii and has twice the radius’s length. It is also related to Thales’ theorem, named for the ancient Greek mathematician Thales. The theorem says that if a triangle is inscribed in a circle and one of its sides is a diameter, then the angle at the opposite vertex is a right angle. The diameter is therefore the triangle’s hypotenuse.

A rhombus is a quadrilateral, or four-sided shape, with all four sides equal in length. It is sometimes called a diamond or lozenge, but rhombus is its standard geometric name. Its angles do not all have to be right angles: opposite angles are equal, while neighboring angles add up to 180 degrees. A square is a special rhombus in which all four angles are right angles. Like every parallelogram, a rhombus has two pairs of parallel opposite sides. It also has two diagonals, line segments that connect opposite corners. Each diagonal divides the angle at each of its endpoints into two equal angles, so each diagonal is an angle bisector of those corner angles.

Graham's number is an enormously large but finite integer that was used as an upper bound in a problem from Ramsey theory, the study of patterns that must appear when objects are arranged or colored. Imagine the vertices of a hypercube in a very high number of dimensions, with every pair of vertices joined by an edge. Color each edge either red or blue. The problem asks how many dimensions are enough to guarantee a square whose edges are all the same color. Graham's number provided an upper bound: at least by that enormous dimension, the desired pattern must occur. In 1977, mathematics writer and puzzle columnist Martin Gardner popularized Graham's number in a Scientific American column, describing it as the largest number then used in a serious mathematical proof.

Benoît Mandelbrot was a mathematician born in Warsaw who later worked in France and the United States. Using computers to explore shapes that ordinary geometry struggled to describe, he helped develop fractal geometry, the study of patterns that remain intricate at smaller and smaller scales. He coined the term fractal for such structures. The Cantor set is one example: start with a line segment, remove its middle third, and keep repeating that step on the pieces left behind. Many fractals show similar patterns when magnified. Mandelbrot argued that the rough outlines of coastlines, mountains, and clouds can be described more usefully with fractals than with smooth shapes such as circles or cubes. The famous Mandelbrot set is named after him.

An even function gives the same output for opposite inputs: f(−x) = f(x). For example, if f(3) = 9, then f(−3) must also equal 9. This makes its graph symmetric about the y-axis, the vertical line through the origin. If you folded the graph along that line, its left and right sides would match. The function f(x) = x² is even because squaring either 3 or −3 gives 9. Not every function is even: f(x) = x is not, because 3 and −3 have different outputs. To check whether a function is even, replace x with −x and see whether the result is unchanged. An even function must be defined at both x and −x for the inputs you are comparing.

Oddness has related meanings in arithmetic and in functions. An odd integer cannot be divided evenly by 2: if you pair up that many objects, one is left over. Examples include 3, 7, and −5. A function is odd when f(−x) = −f(x) for every x in its domain, so changing the sign of the input changes the sign of the output. For example, f(x) = x³ is odd because (−x)³ = −x³. On a graph, each point (x, y) is matched by a point (−x, −y). This relationship is called origin symmetry: rotating the graph halfway around the origin, (0, 0), leaves it looking unchanged. It differs from the symmetry of an even function, whose graph reflects across the y-axis.

Euclid’s theorem on the infinitude of primes says that there are infinitely many prime numbers. A prime is a whole number greater than one that can be evenly divided only by one and itself. In Book IX, Proposition 20 of the Elements, Euclid showed why no list of primes can be complete. Imagine listing every prime, multiplying them all together, and adding one to the product. Each prime on the list divides the product exactly, but leaves a remainder of one when you divide this new number by it. The new number does not have to be prime itself. However, every whole number greater than one has a prime factor, so this number must have a prime factor missing from the original list. That contradiction shows there is no largest prime.

Rational numbers are numbers that can be written as a quotient a/b, where a and b are integers and b is not zero. The operation that forms this quotient is division, the inverse of multiplication. For example, 3/4 is rational because it is 3 divided by 4, and the integer 5 is rational because it can be written as 5/1. Rational numbers also include negative fractions and decimals that terminate, such as 0.25, or repeat a pattern forever, such as 0.333…. Dividing by zero is undefined, so zero can be the numerator, as in 0/7, but it cannot be the denominator.

A hypercube, also called a tesseract, is the four-dimensional version of a square or cube. A square has four line segments as edges, while a cube has six square faces. A hypercube has eight cubes as its three-dimensional boundary pieces, called cells or facets. Although we cannot see all four dimensions at once, drawings can show a hypercube as one cube connected to another, much as a drawing of a cube can show one square connected to another. Geometers also study a shape’s dual, which swaps the roles of vertices and facets. The hypercube has 16 vertices and eight cubic facets. Its dual therefore has 16 tetrahedral facets and eight vertices. This regular four-dimensional polytope is commonly called the 16-cell.

A composite number is a positive integer greater than 1 that can be written as a product of smaller positive integers. For example, 12 is composite because 12 = 3 × 4; it can also be broken down into the prime factors 2 × 2 × 3. A prime number, such as 2 or 3, cannot be broken into smaller positive integer factors in this way. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic explains how these numbers fit together: every integer greater than 1 can be expressed as a product of primes, and that prime factorization is unique apart from the order of the factors. So 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 12 = 3 × 2 × 2 are the same prime factorization.

The Law of the Excluded Middle is a principle of classical logic stating that, for any proposition P, either P is true or its negation, “not P,” is true. It is written P ∨ ¬P, where ∨ means “or” and ¬ means “not.” For example, a whole number is either even or not even; there is no third possibility. Classical mathematicians can use this law in a proof by contradiction: they assume a claim is false, show that this leads to an impossibility, and conclude that the claim is true. Intuitionistic logic, a constructive approach to reasoning, does not accept the Law of the Excluded Middle for every proposition automatically. It requires a proof of P or a proof of ¬P before asserting that one of them holds.

A derivative tells how quickly a function is changing at a particular input. For example, if a function gives a car’s distance traveled over time, its derivative at one moment gives the car’s instantaneous speed. On a graph, the derivative is the slope of the tangent line: the straight line that passes through a point on the curve and matches the curve’s direction there. This differs from the slope between two points, which gives an average rate of change. Mathematicians find a derivative by considering the slopes between points that get closer and closer together. Differentiation is the process of finding derivatives; useful methods include the power rule for polynomials and the chain rule for functions built from other functions.

Coprimality is a relationship between two integers: they are coprime, or relatively prime, when their greatest common divisor (GCD) is 1. This means they share no prime factor, although either number can be composite. For example, 8 and 15 are coprime because 8 has only 2 as a prime factor, while 15 has 3 and 5. A fraction is in simplest terms when its numerator and denominator are coprime. You can test coprimality with the Euclidean algorithm: divide the larger number by the smaller, then replace the pair with the smaller number and the remainder. Repeat until the remainder is zero. The last nonzero remainder is the GCD; if it is 1, the original numbers are coprime.

Parallelism is the relationship between distinct lines in the same plane that never meet, no matter how far they extend. Such lines have the same direction and remain a constant distance apart. On a coordinate graph, the slope of a line measures its rate of rise over run: how much y changes compared with a change in x. In the equation y = mx + b, the coefficient m is the slope, while b tells where the line crosses the y-axis. Two distinct nonvertical lines are parallel when their m-values, or slopes, are equal. Vertical lines are parallel to one another too, even though their slopes are undefined. In three dimensions, lines that never meet are not necessarily parallel: they may instead be skew lines that lie in different planes.

An infinite set is a collection with no finite number of elements. The natural numbers, 1, 2, 3, and so on, form an infinite set because the list never ends. The number of elements in a set is called its cardinality, or size. Two sets have the same cardinality if their elements can be paired one-to-one, even if both sets are infinite. An infinite set is countable if its elements can be listed in a sequence that matches them with the natural numbers. The real numbers are uncountable: no such list can include them all. Georg Cantor, a German mathematician and founder of set theory, demonstrated this with his diagonal argument, showing that the real numbers have a greater cardinality than the natural numbers.

Probability is the branch of mathematics that measures how likely an event is to happen. A probability is a number from 0 to 1: 0 means the event is impossible, 1 means it is certain, and values in between describe different degrees of likelihood. For example, a fair coin has a probability of 1/2 of landing heads. Probability gives us a formal way to study random outcomes and uncertainty, and its results are used in statistics, science, and many other fields. French mathematician Hugo Duminil-Copin uses probability to investigate problems in mathematical physics, including phase transitions, when a material changes state, and critical phenomena near the point where such changes occur. He received the Fields Medal in 2022 for this work.

The harmonic mean is a type of average that is especially useful for rates, such as speed. To calculate it for n nonzero values, first find the reciprocal of each value: the reciprocal of x is 1 divided by x, and multiplying x by its reciprocal gives 1. Add these reciprocals, divide the sum by n, and then take the reciprocal of that result. Equivalently, the harmonic mean is n divided by the sum of the reciprocals. For example, if you travel one mile at 30 miles per hour and another mile at 60 miles per hour, your average speed is the harmonic mean of 30 and 60, or 40 miles per hour. This works because the two legs cover equal distances, while the slower leg takes more time.

Four is the natural number after three and before five. It is an even number, equal to two times two, and a square has four sides and four corners. In chemistry, four is the atomic number of beryllium, meaning that each beryllium atom has four protons in its nucleus. Physics also uses four in several ways: scientists recognize four fundamental interactions—gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong and weak nuclear forces—although the Standard Model describes only the last three. Time is often treated as a fourth dimension alongside the three dimensions of space. A Wheatstone bridge is a circuit with four resistors arranged in a diamond. A detector connected across one diagonal helps compare resistances and find an unknown resistance.

A latus rectum is a chord of a conic section that passes through a focus and is perpendicular to the conic’s main axis. A chord is a line segment whose endpoints lie on the curve. In an ellipse, the main axis is called the major axis; in a hyperbola, it is called the transverse axis. An ellipse has two foci and can have a latus rectum through each one. It is defined by a special distance rule: for every point on the ellipse, the sum of its distances to the two foci is constant. This rule distinguishes an ellipse from a hyperbola, for which the difference between those distances is constant. The eccentricity of an ellipse, a number describing its shape, is between zero and one.

Graph coloring is the assignment of colors or labels to parts of a graph while following rules about which parts may match. In vertex coloring, vertices joined by an edge must have different colors. In edge coloring, edges that meet at a vertex must have different colors. A map can also be treated as a graph: each region becomes a vertex, and two vertices are joined if their regions share a boundary. The four-color theorem says that every planar map can be colored with no more than four colors so that neighboring regions have different colors, no matter how many regions there are. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken first proved this theorem in 1976 using computer assistance. Graph coloring also appears in Ramsey theory, which studies patterns that must emerge when parts of a graph are colored.

A regular pentagon is a five-sided polygon with all sides equal and all interior angles equal. Each interior angle measures 108°. A diagonal connects two vertices that are not next to each other; a regular pentagon has five diagonals, all the same length and all longer than its sides. If you divide the length of a diagonal by the length of a side, the result is the golden ratio, commonly written as φ. Its exact value is (1 + √5) / 2, or approximately 1.618, and it is the positive solution to x² − x − 1 = 0. Regular pentagons cannot tile a flat plane without gaps or overlaps because 108° does not divide evenly into 360° around a point.

The greatest common divisor (GCD) of two or more integers is the largest positive integer that divides each one evenly. For example, the GCD of 18 and 24 is 6. Dividing a fraction’s numerator and denominator by their GCD reduces it to simplest form: 18/24 becomes 3/4. Bézout’s identity says the GCD can be written as an integer linear combination of the original numbers; for example, 6 = 24 − 18. A way to find the GCD is the Euclidean algorithm. Divide the larger number by the smaller, then replace the pair with the divisor and the remainder. Repeat until the remainder is zero; the last nonzero remainder is the GCD. For 24 and 18, the remainders are 6 and then 0, so their GCD is 6.

The Sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient method for finding prime numbers, named after Eratosthenes, a Greek mathematician from Cyrene who worked in Alexandria. A prime number is an integer greater than 1 that is evenly divisible only by 1 and itself, such as 7 or 11. To use the sieve, write down the integers from 2 up to a chosen limit. Start with 2, the smallest unmarked number: it is prime, so cross out its multiples, such as 4, 6, and 8. Then move to the next unmarked number, 3, and cross out its multiples. Continue in the same way with each newly identified prime. The crossed-out numbers are composite numbers: integers greater than 1 that have a divisor besides 1 and themselves. The numbers left unmarked are prime.

The chi-squared test checks whether observed counts in categories differ more than expected from counts predicted by a hypothesis. For example, if a die is fair, each of its six faces should appear about equally often. To calculate the test statistic, subtract the expected count from the observed count for each category, square the difference, divide by that category’s expected count, and add the results. A large total suggests the observations may not fit the hypothesis well. The total is compared with a chi-squared distribution, named for the Greek letter chi. This distribution depends on its degrees of freedom. In an ordinary goodness-of-fit test with no parameters estimated from the data, the degrees of freedom equal the number of categories minus one, because knowing all but one count fixes the last count when the total is fixed.

Quaternions are a four-dimensional number system that extends the complex numbers. A quaternion has the form a + bi + cj + dk, where a, b, c, and d are real numbers and i, j, and k are special units. Unlike ordinary numbers, quaternion multiplication is noncommutative: changing the order can change the result. Their defining rules include i² = j² = k² = ijk = −1, while ij = k but ji = −k. Quaternions are useful for describing rotations in three-dimensional space, such as those used in computer graphics and robotics. Their discovery is traditionally linked to the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton. In 1843, during a walk along Dublin’s Royal Canal, he reportedly realized the key rules and carved them into Brougham Bridge.

The error function, written erf(x), is a special function defined as (2/√π) times the integral of e^(−t²) from 0 to x. An integral measures the area under a curve, so the error function helps describe how much probability lies below a chosen value in a normal distribution. The normal distribution, also called the Gaussian distribution, is a continuous, symmetric distribution with a bell-shaped curve. Its cumulative distribution function—the probability of getting a value at or below x—can be written using erf. The central limit theorem explains why normal distributions appear so often: suitably standardized sums or averages of many independent observations tend toward a normal distribution. In a normal distribution, about 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of values lie within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean, respectively.

Geometry is the branch of mathematics that studies points, lines, shapes, distances, areas, and objects in two or three dimensions. It helps us understand figures such as circles and triangles, as well as three-dimensional objects like cubes and spheres. Around 300 BCE, Euclid organized much of geometry in his book Elements, using basic assumptions called postulates to prove other statements. His fifth postulate, commonly expressed as the parallel postulate, says that through a point outside a given line, exactly one line can be drawn that never intersects the original line. In Euclidean geometry, this helps establish that the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees, or two right angles. Other geometries use different rules about parallel lines; in hyperbolic geometry, for example, triangle angles add up to less than 180 degrees.

The Nine-Point Circle is a circle associated with every triangle. Its name comes from the nine special points it passes through: the midpoint of each of the three sides, the foot of each altitude (where a perpendicular from a vertex meets the opposite side or its extension), and the midpoint of each segment joining a vertex to the orthocenter. The orthocenter is where the triangle’s three altitudes meet. Another important point is the circumcenter, the center of the circle that passes through all three vertices. The center of the Nine-Point Circle lies halfway between the orthocenter and the circumcenter. When those two centers are distinct, the straight line through them is called the Euler line.

Euclid’s Elements is an ancient Greek mathematical treatise arranged in thirteen books. It begins with definitions, postulates, and common notions, then uses logical proofs to build a system of geometry. Its best-known geometric result appears in Book I, Proposition 47: the Pythagorean theorem. This states that, in a right triangle, the areas of the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the area of the square on the longest side, called the hypotenuse. In symbols, a² + b² = c². Elements also covers proportion and number theory. Books VII and IX contain ideas behind the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, which says that every integer greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes in only one way, apart from the order of the factors.
