Tiling the plane, also called tessellation, means covering an entire flat surface with shapes that fit together without gaps or overlaps. A floor covered with repeating tiles is a familiar example. At every point where corners meet, their angles must add up to 360 degrees. A regular pentagon has five equal sides and five equal angles, each measuring 108 degrees. Because 108 does not divide evenly into 360, regular pentagons alone cannot tile the plane. The length of a regular pentagon’s diagonal divided by its side length is the golden ratio, about 1.618. Regular octagons cannot tile the plane by themselves either, but they can do so when squares fill the spaces between them.

The Law of Large Numbers explains why averages become more reliable as data accumulates. A random variable is a quantity whose value depends on chance, such as the number shown on a rolled die. Its expected value is the average predicted by its probability distribution; for a fair six-sided die, it is 3.5. After several rolls, you can calculate the sample mean by adding the results and dividing by the number of rolls. This mean may be far from 3.5 at first, but as the number of independent rolls grows, it tends to get closer to 3.5. The Law of Large Numbers describes this approach toward the expected value. Its weak and strong forms differ in how they define convergence, but both concern the stabilization of sample averages.

A complex number has the form a + bi, where a and b are real numbers and i² = −1. Its complex conjugate keeps the real part, a, unchanged and reverses the sign of the imaginary part: the conjugate of a + bi is a − bi. Multiplying a complex number by its conjugate gives a real number because the terms containing i cancel: (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b². This is useful when simplifying a fraction with a complex number in the denominator. For example, if the denominator is 5 + i, multiply both the numerator and denominator by its conjugate, 5 − i. The denominator then becomes (5 + i)(5 − i) = 26, with no imaginary part.

A mathematical knot is a loop of string with its ends joined, placed in three-dimensional space. More precisely, it is a circle embedded in that space without crossing through itself. Knot theory, a part of topology, treats two knots as equivalent if one can be continuously reshaped into the other without cutting the loop or passing one strand through another. The unknot is a simple, untangled loop; the trefoil and figure-eight are examples of nontrivial knots. Mathematicians use invariants—properties that stay the same during these allowed deformations—to help tell knots apart. One important invariant is the Alexander polynomial, a Laurent polynomial derived from relations in the knot group. It does not change under ambient isotopy, the formal name for such reshaping, and it can distinguish a trefoil from the unknot.

A proof is a logical argument that uses accepted rules to establish a claim. In a proof by contradiction, also called an indirect proof, you temporarily assume that the claim is false. You then reason from that assumption until you reach an impossibility, such as concluding both that a statement is true and that it is not true. Since the assumption led to a contradiction, you reject it and conclude that the original claim is true. In classical logic, this method relies on the law of the excluded middle: for any proposition P, either P is true or its negation, “not P,” is true. This is why ruling out “not P” establishes P.

The orthocenter is the point where a triangle’s three altitudes meet. An altitude is a line drawn from a vertex (corner) perpendicular to the opposite side or to a line extending that side. “Perpendicular” means the lines meet at 90 degrees. Every triangle has three altitudes, one from each vertex, and all three pass through the orthocenter. In an acute triangle, whose angles are all less than 90 degrees, the orthocenter is inside the triangle. In an obtuse triangle, which has an angle greater than 90 degrees, it is outside. A right triangle has one 90-degree corner, called a right angle. Its two sides that form the right angle are also altitudes, so its orthocenter is exactly at the right-angle vertex.

The factorial of a positive integer n, written n!, is the product 1 × 2 × … × n; it counts the ways to arrange n distinct objects. The gamma function extends this idea to non-integer and complex inputs. Its definition is shifted by one: for every positive integer n, Γ(n) = (n−1)!, so Γ(n+1) = n!. Like factorials, it follows a step-by-step rule, Γ(z+1) = zΓ(z). The gamma function is meromorphic, meaning it is defined across the complex plane except at certain isolated points where it has poles. A related two-variable function is the beta function, written B(x,y). For positive x and y, it equals the integral from 0 to 1 of t^(x−1)(1−t)^(y−1), and it is connected to gamma by B(x,y) = Γ(x)Γ(y)/Γ(x+y).

Matrix multiplication combines two matrices, which are rectangular arrays of numbers, to make a new matrix. To multiply a left matrix by a right matrix, the number of columns in the left matrix must equal the number of rows in the right matrix. Each entry in the result comes from pairing one row of the left matrix with one column of the right matrix: multiply their corresponding numbers, then add those products. For example, if the left matrix has dimensions m × n and the right matrix has dimensions n × p, the result has dimensions m × p. The shared n tells you the multiplication is possible; the outside numbers give the result’s size. Transition matrices in Markov chains can be multiplied repeatedly to model changes over several steps.

Euler’s Prime-Generating Polynomial is the expression n² + n + 41, noticed by the 18th-century Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler. It produces a prime number for forty consecutive whole-number inputs, from n = 0 through n = 39. A prime is a whole number greater than 1 divisible only by 1 and itself. The pattern does not continue forever: at n = 40, the expression equals 1,681, or 41², which is not prime. Because the highest exponent of n is 2, this expression is a quadratic polynomial. Like other quadratic functions, its graph is a parabola. Quadratic equations can often be solved by completing the square or by using the quadratic formula, which includes the term √(b² − 4ac).

A logarithm tells you what exponent is needed to produce a number from a chosen base. For example, because 2 raised to the power 3 equals 8, the base-two logarithm of 8 is 3. In general, if b raised to the power x equals y, then the logarithm of y to base b equals x. Logarithms also describe how quickly some algorithms work. Binary search looks for a target in a sorted array by comparing it with the middle entry. If the target is smaller, it discards the upper half; if larger, it discards the lower half. Each comparison roughly halves the remaining entries, so searching an array of n entries takes a number of comparisons proportional to the logarithm of n.

Eratosthenes of Cyrene was an ancient Greek mathematician who made an early calculation of Earth’s circumference. On a midsummer day, he noted that the noon Sun was nearly overhead in Syene, Egypt, while it cast a shadow in Alexandria, where he served as chief librarian. He used the shadow to measure the Sun’s angle at Alexandria, then combined that angle with the distance between the two cities to estimate the distance around Earth. Eratosthenes also devised the sieve of Eratosthenes, a method for finding prime numbers. Starting with a list of whole numbers, the sieve repeatedly crosses out multiples of each prime, beginning with 2. The numbers left uncrossed are primes: numbers greater than 1 that have no divisors other than 1 and themselves.

A physical dimension describes the kind of measurement a quantity represents in terms of fundamental quantities such as length, time, and mass. For example, a distance has the dimension of length, an area has length squared because it is found by multiplying two lengths, and a volume has length cubed because it involves three lengths. Dimensional analysis is a way to check whether a proposed equation could be correct: the dimensions on both sides must agree, including the powers of the fundamental units. For instance, the area of a triangle is one-half its base times its altitude, so its dimension is length squared. Heron’s formula also gives an area: it takes the square root of four factors measured in lengths, turning length to the fourth power into length squared. Matching dimensions does not prove an equation is correct, but mismatched dimensions show it is wrong.

A Mersenne prime is a prime number of the form 2^p − 1, where p is also prime. For example, when p = 3, the result is 2^3 − 1 = 7, which is prime. The exponent must be prime: if it is composite, 2^p − 1 can be factored. But a prime exponent does not guarantee a Mersenne prime; 2^11 − 1 = 2047 is divisible by 23. Prime numbers have exactly two positive divisors, 1 and themselves, and they are the building blocks of all positive integers greater than 1. Mersenne primes are named after Marin Mersenne, a 17th-century French cleric, mathematician, and music theorist who studied these numbers and corresponded with many leading scholars.

Polynomial roots are values of a variable that make a polynomial equal to zero. A polynomial is an expression such as x² − 5x + 6, built from numbers and nonnegative integer powers of a variable. Setting this example equal to zero gives roots of 2 and 3, because substituting either value makes the expression zero. Roots are also called solutions or zeroes. Simple equations can often be solved by factoring, and there are general formulas for polynomials up to degree four. The Abel–Ruffini theorem says there is no universal formula using only arithmetic operations and radicals, such as square roots, that solves every general polynomial equation of degree five or higher. This does not mean those roots cannot be found: many specific equations can be solved exactly, and numerical methods can approximate others.

Algebra is a branch of mathematics that uses numbers, variables, and operations to describe patterns and solve equations. A variable, such as x, stands for an unknown value. In the equation 3x + 4 = 0, subtracting 4 from both sides and then dividing by 3 gives x = −4/3. Beyond these elementary problems, linear algebra studies vector spaces, while abstract algebra investigates structures defined by rules for operations. Polynomials are another important topic; the fundamental theorem of algebra says that every nonconstant polynomial has a complex root. The word “algebra” comes from the title of a ninth-century treatise by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi. Its title includes al-jabr wa’l-muqabala, meaning “completion and balancing.” The Latinized form of al-Khwarizmi’s name also gave English the word “algorithm.”

Johann Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet was a 19th-century German mathematician known for important work in number theory. He proved that an arithmetic progression—a sequence formed by repeatedly adding the same number—contains infinitely many prime numbers if its first term and common difference are coprime, meaning they share no factor greater than 1. For example, the progression 5, 11, 17, 23, and so on adds 6 each time; because 5 and 6 are coprime, Dirichlet’s theorem guarantees that primes keep appearing in it. Dirichlet is also credited with formulating the pigeonhole principle: if more objects are placed into containers than there are containers, at least one container must hold two or more objects.

The Empirical Rule is a shortcut for describing how values are spread in a normal distribution, a bell-shaped pattern centered on its mean. Standard deviation measures how far values typically are from that mean; it is the square root of the variance, which is the average of the squared differences from the mean. According to the rule, about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% lie within two, and about 99.7% lie within three. For example, if a normally distributed set of test scores has a mean of 80 and a standard deviation of 5, about 68% of scores would fall between 75 and 85. These percentages are estimates, not exact guarantees for every data set.

Fractal dimension measures how completely a fractal fills space as you look at it on smaller and smaller scales. Ordinary shapes have whole-number dimensions: a line has dimension 1, a plane has dimension 2, and a solid such as a cube has dimension 3. Fractals often repeat similar patterns at many scales and can have dimensions between those numbers. For example, the Cantor set is made by repeatedly removing the middle third of each remaining line segment; its fractal dimension is between 0 and 1. One precise measure of fractal dimension is Hausdorff dimension, named for the German mathematician Felix Hausdorff. It examines coverings of a shape made from increasingly small pieces and finds the critical exponent where a related measure changes from infinite to zero.

Irrational numbers are numbers that cannot be written as a ratio of two integers, such as a fraction with whole-number numerator and denominator. The square root of two is a familiar example: no fraction equals it exactly. Its decimal digits continue forever without settling into a repeating pattern. This differs from rational numbers, such as 3/4 or 2, which can be written as fractions. Stories about Pythagoras sometimes claim that he rejected irrational numbers, though these stories are not established history. Ancient Babylonian mathematicians used the sexagesimal, or base-sixty, system for arithmetic. A Babylonian clay tablet records fifteen Pythagorean triples—sets of whole numbers that can be the sides of a right triangle. The Babylonian use of base sixty is also often linked to the convention of dividing a circle into 360 degrees.

A hyperbola is a conic section made of two separate, curved branches. Its eccentricity, a number that describes a conic’s shape, is greater than 1; by comparison, a circle has eccentricity 0, an ellipse has eccentricity between 0 and 1, and a parabola has eccentricity 1. In a standard coordinate equation for a hyperbola, the squared x and y terms have opposite signs. For example, x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 describes a hyperbola centered at the origin whose branches open to the left and right along the x-axis. As the branches extend outward, they get closer and closer to two diagonal lines called asymptotes. For this equation, the asymptotes are y = (b/a)x and y = −(b/a)x.

The Koch snowflake is a fractal made by starting with an equilateral triangle. To create the next stage, divide each side into thirds and replace its middle third with two sides of a smaller, outward-pointing equilateral triangle. Repeat this process on every straight segment, again and again. The pattern is self-similar: smaller parts resemble the larger shape. At each stage, every boundary segment is replaced by four segments, each one-third as long, so the total boundary length is multiplied by 4/3. Repeating this indefinitely makes the boundary length grow without limit, even though the area enclosed by the snowflake stays finite. This surprising combination—a finite area surrounded by an infinitely long boundary—is one reason the Koch snowflake is a famous example of a fractal.

Optimization is the mathematical task of finding inputs that make a function as small or as large as possible. These values are called minima and maxima. In single-variable calculus, setting the derivative equal to zero helps locate critical points that might be minima or maxima. For a function with several inputs, the gradient—a collection of partial derivatives—plays a similar role: a zero gradient identifies a candidate, but does not prove it is an extreme value. The Hessian matrix describes how the function curves near that point. If it shows upward curvature in some directions and downward curvature in others, the point is a saddle point, not a local minimum or maximum. Optimization is also important in artificial intelligence, where algorithms such as gradient descent adjust a model to reduce its error, or loss.

A limit is the value a function approaches as its input gets close to a particular number, even if the function never reaches that value. Some limits involve a quotient whose numerator and denominator both approach zero, written as the 0/0 indeterminate form. Another indeterminate form occurs when both become unbounded, often written as infinity/infinity. In these cases, L'Hôpital's rule can sometimes help: differentiate the numerator and denominator separately, then find the limit of the quotient of those derivatives. The result equals the original limit when the rule’s conditions are met, including that the functions are differentiable nearby and the derivative of the denominator is not zero there. The forms 0/0 and infinity/infinity do not give answers by themselves; they signal that more work is needed.

The sexagesimal number system is a base-sixty system used by scribes in ancient Mesopotamia, including Babylonia. It is positional: a symbol’s value depends on where it appears, much as the digit 2 means different things in 2, 20, and 200. In a base-sixty system, each place is worth sixty times the place to its right. Sixty was useful because it can be divided evenly by many numbers, including 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. Babylonian mathematics helped shape conventions still used today. A full turn is divided into 360 degrees, so one complete revolution measures 360 degrees. We also see a legacy of counting by sixty when we divide an hour into 60 minutes and a minute into 60 seconds.

A random variable assigns a numerical value to each possible outcome of a chance process. For example, if you roll a six-sided die, a random variable X could be the number shown, so X can take the values 1 through 6. Each value has a probability: for a fair die, every face has probability 1/6. The expected value of a random variable is its probability-weighted average, found by multiplying each possible value by its probability and adding the results. For the fair die, this is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 3.5. You cannot roll a 3.5, but over many rolls, the average result tends to get closer to 3.5.

Statistical independence means that learning the outcome of one event does not change the probability of another. For example, if you roll a fair die twice, the first result does not affect the second. Events A and B are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B), where A ∩ B means that both events occur. For a collection of random variables, pairwise independence means every pair is independent. Mutual independence is stronger: the joint probabilities for every finite subcollection must equal the product of the corresponding individual probabilities. Mutual independence therefore guarantees pairwise independence, but pairwise independence does not always guarantee mutual independence. Independent variables have zero covariance when their covariance is defined, although zero covariance alone does not generally prove independence.

A vector is a mathematical quantity with both magnitude (size) and direction. You can picture a vector as an arrow: its length shows its magnitude, and the way it points shows its direction. Vectors can describe quantities such as displacement or velocity and can be written as lists of numbers called components. Two operations involving vectors are the dot product and the cross product. The dot product gives a number and can help find the angle between two vectors. The cross product of two vectors in three-dimensional space gives another vector perpendicular to both. A unit vector is a vector with a magnitude of exactly one. To make a unit vector pointing in the same direction as a nonzero vector, divide that vector by its magnitude.

The secant function is a trigonometric function written as sec(θ), where θ is an angle. It is defined as the reciprocal of cosine: sec(θ) = 1/cos(θ). This means secant is defined only where cosine is not zero, because division by zero is undefined. For example, cos(0°) = 1, so sec(0°) = 1. Cosine is one of the basic functions of trigonometry, the branch of mathematics that studies relationships between the angles and side lengths of triangles. In a right triangle, the “CAH” part of the mnemonic SOHCAHTOA tells you that cosine equals the length of the side adjacent to an angle divided by the hypotenuse. Secant reverses that ratio: hypotenuse divided by adjacent side.

The Cartesian coordinate system locates points on a flat plane using two number lines that meet at a right angle. The horizontal line is the x-axis, the vertical line is the y-axis, and their meeting point is the origin, written (0, 0). Each point has an ordered pair (x, y): the first number gives its horizontal position, and the second gives its vertical position. For example, (3, 2) is three units right and two units up from the origin. This system connects geometry with algebra, making it possible to describe shapes and lines with equations. It is named for René Descartes, a French philosopher and mathematician who helped develop analytic geometry. He wrote La Géométrie as an appendix to Discourse on the Method and is famous for saying, “I think, therefore I am.”

A full turn measures 360 degrees: a ray rotates all the way around a circle and points in its starting direction again. If perpendicular rays divide that turn into four equal parts, each part is a right angle measuring 90 degrees. Half a turn is a straight angle of 180 degrees, so two straight angles also make 360 degrees. The interior angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees, whether or not its sides and angles are equal. In another system for measuring angles, a full turn is 2π radians. The sine and cosine functions repeat their values every 360 degrees. On the complex plane, multiplying a number by i rotates it 90 degrees counterclockwise, so multiplying by i four times completes a full turn.

Differentiability means a function has a well-defined derivative at a point. The derivative gives the slope of the graph’s tangent line there and is found by taking the limit of a difference quotient: the change in output divided by a small change in input. For a function to be differentiable, this quotient must approach the same finite value from both sides of the point. The absolute value function, f(x) = |x|, is differentiable everywhere except at x = 0: its graph has a sharp corner there, with different slopes on either side. Differentiability implies continuity, meaning the function’s value at a point matches the limit of nearby values. The reverse is not always true: |x| is continuous at zero despite not being differentiable there.

Recursion is a way to define a mathematical object or solve a problem by referring to earlier or smaller versions of the same thing. A recursive rule for a sequence, for example, tells you how to find a term from terms that came before it. It also needs a starting value, called a base case, so you can calculate actual numbers rather than going backward forever. The Fibonacci sequence is a familiar example: it starts with 0 and 1, and each later term is the sum of the two immediately before it. Its first terms are 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, and 8. Recursion can also solve problems by repeatedly applying the same procedure to smaller cases until it reaches a base case.

The fundamental theorem of calculus connects differentiation and integration, showing that they can undo each other. A derivative measures how quickly a function changes at a point, such as the slope of its graph. An integral can measure the accumulated area under a graph. The first part of the theorem says that if you make a function by accumulating area under the graph of f from a fixed starting point to x, the derivative of that new function is f(x). The second part makes definite integrals easier to calculate: find an antiderivative F, a function whose derivative is the integrand f. Then the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) − F(a): the antiderivative’s value at the upper endpoint minus its value at the lower endpoint.

A palindromic number reads the same from left to right as it does from right to left. For example, reversing the digits of 7887 gives 7887 again, so it is a palindrome. The same is true of 8778: it begins and ends with 8, with two 7s in the middle. If you arrange exactly two 7s and two 8s into a four-digit number, there are six possible arrangements, but only 7887 and 8778 are palindromic. Each arrangement has the same digit sum, 7 + 7 + 8 + 8 = 30. Since 30 is divisible by 3, all six numbers are divisible by 3, whether or not they are palindromes.

The integers, written ℤ, are zero, the positive whole numbers (1, 2, 3, …), and their negatives (−1, −2, −3, …). They do not include fractions or decimals that are not whole numbers. In number theory, mathematicians often study remainders when integers are divided by other integers. For example, 17 has remainder 2 when divided by 5, so 17 is congruent to 2 modulo 5. The Chinese remainder theorem connects several such statements: if the divisors, called moduli, are pairwise coprime (no two share a factor greater than 1), then knowing a number’s remainder modulo each divisor determines exactly one remainder modulo their product. For instance, a number with remainder 2 modulo 3 and remainder 3 modulo 5 must have remainder 8 modulo 15.

Rolle’s theorem says that if a function is continuous on a closed interval [a, b], differentiable at every point inside it, and has equal values at the endpoints, f(a) = f(b), then there is at least one point c between a and b where f′(c) = 0. The derivative gives the slope of a tangent line, so the theorem guarantees a horizontal tangent somewhere in the interval. Imagine walking along a smooth path that starts and ends at the same height: at some point, the path must briefly be level. Rolle’s theorem is a special case of the Mean Value Theorem, which says that at some interior point the derivative equals the secant slope, (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). When the endpoint values are equal, that slope is zero.

Calculus is the branch of mathematics that studies change and accumulation. It uses limits to describe what happens as a quantity approaches a value, derivatives to measure an instantaneous rate of change, and integrals to find accumulated quantities, such as the area under a curve. For example, the derivative of a car’s position tells you its speed at a particular moment, while an integral can give the distance traveled from its changing speed. Isaac Newton and the German mathematician and philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed calculus independently in the seventeenth century. Leibniz, who also wrote Monadology, introduced notation still used today: dy/dx for a derivative and the elongated S symbol, ∫, for an integral.

A polynomial is an algebraic expression made of terms containing numbers, variables, and whole-number exponents, combined by addition or subtraction. A term might be a number such as 2 or a product such as 5x⁷. Polynomials can be named by how many terms they have after like terms are combined: 2x is a monomial because it has one term, 2x + 2 is a binomial because it has two, and x² + 3x + 1 is a trinomial because it has three. The degree of a polynomial is a different property: it is the greatest exponent on its variable among its terms. For example, 5x⁷ − 3x² is a binomial with degree 7.

A regular tetrahedron is a three-dimensional solid made of four identical equilateral triangles. It has four faces, six edges, and four vertices, or corners. Three faces meet at each vertex. The word “tetrahedron” means “four-faced solid,” and “regular” means its faces are congruent regular polygons, with the same arrangement at every vertex. It is the simplest of the five Platonic solids: convex solids whose faces are all identical regular polygons. You can also picture it as a triangular pyramid with an equilateral triangle for its base and three matching triangular sides. In tabletop role-playing games such as Dungeons and Dragons, a four-sided die often has this shape. It is called a d4: the “d” stands for die, and the 4 tells you how many faces it has.

A set is a collection of distinct elements, usually written inside curly braces, such as {2, 4, 6}. The empty set is the set with no elements at all. It is written as {} or with the special symbol ∅, which looks like a circle crossed by a diagonal stroke. It is also called the null set. There is only one empty set: if two sets have no elements, they contain exactly the same elements and are therefore equal. Be careful not to confuse the empty set, {}, with a set containing the empty set, {∅}; the latter has one element. If two sets have nothing in common, their intersection is the empty set. On a Venn diagram, those sets can be shown as non-overlapping circles.

A tangent line shows the direction a smooth curve is heading at a particular point. Its slope describes the curve’s instantaneous steepness there. On a straight line, slope is always the same and is calculated as rise over run: the change in vertical position divided by the change in horizontal position. On a curve, the slope can change from point to point, so calculus finds the tangent line’s slope by looking at the slopes of secant lines through two points as those points get closer together. “Tangent” also has a related use in trigonometry: the tangent of an angle is its sine divided by its cosine, provided the cosine is not zero. Thus, tangent can mean either a line associated with a curve or a trigonometric function.

Dot notation is a way to show how a quantity changes over time by placing dots above its symbol. One dot means the first derivative with respect to time: if x is an object’s position, ẋ represents its velocity, or how quickly its position is changing. Two dots mean the second derivative, so ẍ represents its acceleration, or how quickly its velocity is changing. This notation is especially common in physics and mechanics, where motion is often described as a function of time. It is associated with Isaac Newton, who developed a way of studying changing quantities called the method of fluxions. Another common way to write a time derivative is dx/dt, using notation associated with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.

Hilbert’s Grand Hotel is a thought experiment about infinity. Imagine a hotel with one room for every positive integer: rooms 1, 2, 3, and so on. Every room is occupied, yet a new guest can still check in. The manager moves the guest in room n to room n+1, sending the guest in room 1 to room 2, the guest in room 2 to room 3, and so forth. This frees room 1 without leaving any original guest without a room. The move creates a bijection, or one-to-one matching, between all the original rooms and the destination rooms numbered 2, 3, 4, and onward. It shows why an infinite set can match a smaller-looking part of itself, unlike a finite set.

An eigenvalue describes how a square matrix acts on a particular nonzero vector. Usually, multiplying a vector by a matrix changes both its length and direction. But for some vectors, the result stays on the same line: the matrix may stretch, shrink, reverse, or collapse the vector to zero. Such a vector is called an eigenvector, and the number describing the change is its eigenvalue. If the matrix is A, the eigenvector is v, and the eigenvalue is λ, their relationship is Av = λv. Eigenvalues can be found by solving det(A − λI) = 0, where I is the identity matrix. Each solution for λ is an eigenvalue, and a corresponding nonzero vector v is an eigenvector.

The mode is the value that appears most often in a data set. For example, in 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, the mode is 3 because it appears twice, while every other value appears once. Unlike the arithmetic mean, which is found by adding the values and dividing by how many there are, a mode must be one of the observed values. A data set can have more than one mode: if two values tie for the greatest number of appearances, both are modes. A frequency graph shows how often values occur, so a mode often appears as a peak. A distribution with two distinct peaks is called bimodal. If every value occurs equally often, the data set has no single mode.

Positivity means being strictly greater than zero. For example, 3 and 0.5 are positive, but zero is not. This distinction matters because “nonnegative” includes zero. In linear algebra, the inner product of any nonzero vector with itself must be positive, as must the norm, or length, of that vector. A real symmetric matrix is called positive definite when its quadratic form xᵀAx is greater than zero for every nonzero real vector x. Equivalently, all its eigenvalues are positive. Positivity also appears in calculus: when a function’s second derivative is positive, its slope is increasing and its graph bends upward, so the function is called concave-up.

Commutativity is the property of an operation that gives the same result when you swap the order of two inputs, called operands. For example, addition of real numbers is commutative because a + b = b + a; 3 + 5 and 5 + 3 both equal 8. Matrices are arrangements of numbers in rows and columns. Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative: multiplying matrix A by matrix B can give a different result from multiplying B by A. There is, however, a special square matrix called the identity matrix. It has 1s along its main diagonal and 0s everywhere else. Multiplying a compatible matrix by an identity matrix of the appropriate size, on either side, leaves that matrix unchanged. This is like multiplying an ordinary number by 1.

The Fibonacci sequence is a pattern of whole numbers that begins 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and continues by adding the two previous terms to get the next one. For example, 5 + 8 = 13. As the numbers grow, the ratio of each term to the one before it gets closer to about 1.618, a value called the golden ratio. The sequence is named after Fibonacci, also known as Leonardo of Pisa. In his 1202 treatise Liber Abaci, he described an idealized rabbit-breeding problem whose population counts follow this pattern. Liber Abaci also helped popularize Hindu-Arabic numerals, including the digits we use today, in Europe.

The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says that every integer greater than 1 can be written as a product of prime numbers in exactly one way, apart from the order of the factors. A prime number has exactly two positive divisors, 1 and itself. For example, 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5; rearranging those primes does not create a different factorization. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite: it is not a prime, and it cannot be expressed as a product of two or more primes. If 1 counted as prime, multiplying by extra 1s would also spoil the theorem’s uniqueness. An ancient proof of the theorem appears in Books VII and IX of Euclid’s Elements, a Greek mathematical work best known for its systematic treatment of geometry.

A square pyramid is a three-dimensional shape with a square base and four triangular side faces. Each triangle shares one edge with the base, and all four triangles meet at a single point called the apex. Because it has flat polygonal faces, it is a polyhedron. A square pyramid has five faces in total: one square and four triangles. The shape also appears in architecture. Architect I. M. Pei initially considered a square pyramid for the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library. He later used the form in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and Museum in Cleveland, Ohio, and designed the glass pyramid at the Louvre in Paris.

The geometric mean is a type of average used for positive numbers. To find it, multiply all the values together, then take the root that matches how many values there are. For two values, multiply them and take the square root; for three values, multiply them and take the cube root. For example, the geometric mean of 4 and 9 is the square root of 4 × 9, or 6. This differs from the arithmetic mean, which you find by adding the values and dividing by how many there are: for 4 and 9, that is 6.5. The geometric mean is useful when comparing growth rates or quantities that change by multiplication, such as repeated percentage increases.

Arithmetic is the branch of mathematics that studies basic operations on numbers, especially addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. With whole numbers, these operations let you combine quantities, find differences, make equal groups, and share amounts. Arithmetic provides calculation skills used throughout everyday life and forms a foundation for later subjects such as algebra. Mathematicians can also study arithmetic through a formal system of axioms, or starting rules. Peano arithmetic is one such system: it describes the natural numbers using a successor operation, which gives the next number, along with rules for addition and multiplication. Gödel’s incompleteness theorems show that a sufficiently expressive, consistent formal system of arithmetic cannot prove every true statement about the natural numbers.

A probability distribution describes how likely each possible value of a random variable is, accounting for all possible outcomes. For a discrete variable, such as the result of a coin toss, it assigns a probability to each value, and those probabilities add up to 1. The Bernoulli distribution models one trial with two possible values: 1 for success, with probability p, and 0 for failure, with probability 1−p. A binomial distribution builds on this idea by counting successes across a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials. Continuous variables, such as height, can take values within a range; their probabilities are described using a density curve. One common continuous model is the Gaussian, or normal, distribution, whose bell-shaped curve is centered on its mean.

The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says that every nonconstant polynomial in one variable with complex coefficients has at least one complex root. A root is a value that makes the polynomial equal zero. For example, x² + 1 has no real roots, but it has the complex roots i and −i, where i² = −1. Once one complex root is found, its linear factor can be removed; repeating this shows that a polynomial of degree n factors into n linear factors over the complex numbers, counting repeated roots. A field with the property that every nonconstant polynomial over it has a root—and therefore splits completely into linear factors—is called algebraically closed. Thus, the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra says that the field of complex numbers is algebraically closed.

Five is the integer between four and six, and in music it also names the fifth degree of a scale. To count scale degrees, start with the tonic, or home note, as one and count upward. In a major key, the fifth degree is called the dominant, and a dominant triad is built on that note. A pentatonic scale has five distinct notes: “penta” means five. A standard major scale has more notes. Its pattern of steps is whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Starting on the tonic and following that pattern takes you through seven distinct notes before the eighth note repeats the tonic at a higher pitch, called an octave.

A triangle is a polygon with three sides, and its interior angles add up to 180 degrees. Its area is half its base multiplied by its height. To find a triangle’s centroid, first locate the midpoint of each side. Then draw a segment from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. Each of these segments is called a median. Every triangle has three medians, and they all meet at one point: the centroid. The centroid is the triangle’s geometric center of gravity, meaning a triangular sheet of uniform material could balance at that point. It lies on each median and divides it in a 2:1 ratio: the distance from the vertex to the centroid is twice the distance from the centroid to the opposite side’s midpoint.

A Venn diagram uses closed curves, often circles, to show how sets relate to one another. A set is a collection of distinct elements, such as numbers, usually written inside braces. Each curve represents a set, and an element’s position shows which set or sets it belongs to. In a diagram of sets A and B, the overlapping region represents their intersection, written A ∩ B: the elements that belong to both sets. The regions inside just one circle contain elements belonging to only that set, while elements outside both circles belong to neither set. Everything inside either circle is the union of A and B. If the circles do not overlap, the sets have no elements in common, so their intersection is the empty set.

Variance measures how widely values in a data set or probability distribution are spread around the mean, or average. To calculate it, find each value’s difference from the mean, square those differences, and average the results. Squaring prevents positive and negative differences from canceling out and gives more weight to values far from the mean. In probability, variance is also called the second central moment. Because the differences are squared, variance is measured in squared units: if heights are measured in centimeters, their variance is in square centimeters. Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance. It describes spread in the original units, making it easier to interpret as a typical distance from the mean. A larger variance or standard deviation means the values are more spread out.

Gödel’s incompleteness theorems reveal limits of formal systems: collections of axioms and rules used to prove mathematical statements. The first theorem says that if such a system has a mechanical way to list its axioms, is consistent (does not prove contradictions), and can express enough arithmetic involving whole numbers, then some statements in its language can be neither proved nor disproved using its rules. Gödel showed this by constructing a statement that, in effect, says it cannot be proved within the system. The second theorem says that a sufficiently strong system cannot prove its own consistency, assuming it really is consistent. These ideas are often discussed alongside work by Alan Turing, a British mathematician and logician. In 1936, Turing introduced an idealized computing machine and showed that no algorithm can always determine whether a program will eventually stop.

A tetrahedron is a three-dimensional polyhedron with four triangular faces, six edges, and four vertices. It looks like a pyramid with a triangular base: any one of its faces can be chosen as the base, and the remaining vertex is its tip. Its faces do not have to be equilateral triangles; a tetrahedron with four equilateral faces is called a regular tetrahedron. In each triangular face, a median runs from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The three medians meet at that triangle’s centroid. Now join each vertex of the tetrahedron to the centroid of the opposite face. These four segments all meet at one point, called the tetrahedron centroid, which is the balance point of a uniform solid tetrahedron.

The reciprocal function is f(x) = 1/x: it takes a nonzero number and returns its multiplicative inverse. For example, f(4) = 1/4, while f(−2) = −1/2. Since division by zero is undefined, x cannot equal zero. Multiplying each input by its output gives 1, so the graph also has the equation xy = 1. It is a hyperbola with one branch in the first quadrant and another in the third. As x moves far from zero, the graph approaches the x-axis; as x approaches zero, it approaches the y-axis. These two coordinate axes are asymptotes, which the graph approaches but never touches. For positive numbers, adding their reciprocals gives the denominator in the formula for their harmonic mean. The reciprocal function is also the derivative of ln x for x > 0.

Symmetry means that an object or pattern looks unchanged after a transformation such as a rotation, reflection, or translation. A snowflake has rotational symmetry if a partial turn makes it look the same, while a human body has approximate bilateral symmetry because its left and right sides are roughly mirror images. Some symmetries occur in continuous families: a circle, for example, looks the same after a rotation through any angle. Mathematicians use structures called Lie groups to study these continuous symmetries. Functions can have symmetry too. An odd function satisfies f(-x) = -f(x), so its graph looks unchanged after a half-turn about the origin. The function f(x) = x³ is an example. This differs from symmetry across the y-axis, which an odd function generally does not have.

A Klein bottle is a closed surface with no edge and only one side. It is non-orientable: if you travel around it, your sense of which direction is “up” can reverse without crossing an edge. You can imagine making one by joining the ends of a cylinder after reversing one end. Unlike a Möbius strip, which also has one side but has an edge, a Klein bottle has no boundary. It is studied in topology, the branch of mathematics concerned with properties that survive stretching and bending. A Klein bottle cannot be embedded in ordinary three-dimensional space without passing through itself. Familiar models therefore show a self-intersection. Such a model is an immersion: each small patch remains a smooth, regular piece of surface, even though separate patches intersect.

The semiperimeter is half the perimeter of a polygon. For a triangle with side lengths a, b, and c, its perimeter is a + b + c, so its semiperimeter is s = (a + b + c)/2. This measurement is useful when you know a triangle’s three side lengths but do not know its height. Heron’s formula uses the semiperimeter to find the triangle’s area: area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)]. To use it, add the side lengths and divide by two to find s, then substitute s and the three side lengths into the formula. The result is an area, measured in square units, rather than a length.

Aleph numbers are cardinal numbers that describe the sizes of infinite sets. The first, aleph-zero, is the size of the natural numbers (0, 1, 2, 3, and so on). A set is countably infinite if its members can be matched one-to-one with the natural numbers; the integers and rational numbers are examples. Not every infinite set is countable, however. Cantor’s diagonal argument shows that the real numbers cannot be listed this way, so they form a larger infinity. The next size after aleph-zero is called aleph-one. The continuum hypothesis proposes that the real numbers have size aleph-one: there is no size of infinity strictly between that of the natural numbers and that of the real numbers.

The central limit theorem explains what happens when we repeatedly take large, independent samples from a population and calculate each sample’s mean. If the population has a finite variance, the distribution of those sample means becomes approximately bell-shaped as the sample size grows, even when the original population is not bell-shaped. To compare sample means, we can standardize them by subtracting the population mean and dividing by the standard deviation of the sample mean. The resulting values approach the standard normal distribution, a symmetric bell-shaped curve centered at 0 with variance 1. About 68% of the area under this curve lies between -1 and 1; about 95% lies within two standard deviations of 0, and about 99.7% lies within three.

Polar coordinates are a way to locate points on a plane using a distance and an angle instead of the usual x- and y-coordinates. The fixed starting point is called the origin, where the x- and y-axes meet at (0, 0). A point’s distance from the origin is called its radius and is usually written as r. Its angle, often written as θ, is measured from a reference direction, usually the positive x-axis. Together, the radius and angle tell you where the point is: for example, a radius of 5 and an angle of 90° place it 5 units directly above the origin. If the radius stays constant while the angle changes, the points trace a circle centered at the origin.

A tensor is a mathematical object that extends the ideas of scalars (single numbers), vectors (lists of numbers), and matrices (rectangular tables of numbers). Its components can be arranged in a multidimensional array, but the array alone does not define the tensor: when coordinates change, the components must change according to specific rules so that the underlying object stays the same. Mathematicians may name a tensor with one letter, while physicists often display its indices, such as Tᵢʲ. Indices identify components and can appear above or below the letter. In Einstein summation convention, an index repeated once above and once below in a term means to add the contributions for every allowed value of that index, without writing a summation symbol.

Eight is the natural number after seven and before nine. In geometry, it appears in several familiar shapes: an octagon has eight sides, so a standard stop sign, which is usually shaped like a regular octagon, has eight sides too. A cube has eight vertices, or corners, where its edges meet. Eight is also the number of faces on an octahedron, a three-dimensional solid with six vertices and twelve edges. A regular octahedron is one of the five Platonic solids, meaning all its faces are identical regular polygons arranged in the same way around each vertex. Its eight faces are equilateral triangles. The prefix “oct-” in octagon and octahedron is a useful clue that both shapes are connected to the number eight.

The area of a triangle measures the amount of flat space inside the triangle. You can find it by multiplying the length of a base by the corresponding altitude (the perpendicular height from that base to the opposite vertex) and dividing by two. The result is measured in square units, such as square centimetres. If you know the lengths of all three sides but not the altitude, you can use Heron’s formula instead. First, add the side lengths a, b, and c, then divide by two. This gives s, the semiperimeter, which is half the triangle’s perimeter. Heron’s formula says that the area is the square root of s times (s − a) times (s − b) times (s − c).

Perimeter is the total distance around a closed plane figure. For a polygon, find it by adding the lengths of all its sides. A rectangle has two sides of each length, so its perimeter is twice its length plus twice its width: P = 2l + 2w. In a regular polygon, all sides are equal, so you can multiply one side length by the number of sides. Its area can also be found by multiplying half its perimeter by its apothem, the perpendicular distance from the center to a side. The distance around a circle is called its circumference. Since a circle has no straight sides to add, calculate its circumference using C = 2πr, where r is the radius.

William Rowan Hamilton was an Irish mathematician who invented quaternions in 1843. Ordinary complex numbers have a real part and one imaginary part, often written using i. Hamilton extended this idea to a four-dimensional algebraic system: a quaternion has one real component and three imaginary components, conventionally written with i, j, and k. These units follow special multiplication rules, including ijk = −1, and the order in which they are multiplied matters. Quaternions are useful for describing rotations in three-dimensional space, such as the orientation of a spacecraft or a character in a video game. Hamilton’s name also appears in physics: the Hamiltonian is the operator that acts on the wavefunction in the Schrödinger equation and represents a system’s energy.

Parentheses are matched curved marks, ( and ), placed around part of an expression to show that it should be handled as a unit. They can override the usual order of operations, in which exponents come before multiplication and division, and multiplication and division come before addition and subtraction. For example, 3 + (4 − 5) means subtract 5 from 4 first, then add 3. Parentheses can also show how numbers are grouped even when the answer stays the same: (3 + 4) + 5 and 3 + (4 + 5) both equal 12. This is the associative property of addition. Multiplication is associative too, but subtraction is not: (10 − 4) − 2 and 10 − (4 − 2) give different answers.

The Chinese remainder theorem helps solve problems involving several remainders at once. Suppose an integer leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3, remainder 3 when divided by 5, and remainder 2 when divided by 7. Because 3, 5, and 7 are pairwise coprime—no two share a factor greater than 1—the theorem says these conditions determine one unique residue class modulo their product, 105. One solution is 23, and every other solution differs from 23 by a multiple of 105. More generally, any specified remainders for pairwise coprime moduli lead to exactly one residue class modulo the product. The classic problem with remainders 2, 3, and 2 is preserved in an ancient Chinese mathematical work called the Sunzi Suanjing.

Graph theory is the branch of mathematics that studies networks called graphs. A graph consists of vertices, which represent places or objects, and edges, which connect pairs of vertices. Graph theorists study questions such as whether a path exists between two vertices and whether a network is connected. One early landmark was Leonhard Euler’s 18th-century investigation of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg, a Prussian city now called Kaliningrad. The bridges crossed the Pregel River and connected its islands with the surrounding land. Euler asked whether someone could take a single walk that crossed each of the seven bridges exactly once. By treating land areas as vertices and bridges as edges, he showed that such a walk was impossible.

Eleven is the natural number after ten and before twelve. It is also the usual point target in squash, an indoor racket sport in which two players take turns hitting a small ball against a front wall. Players try to control the T-shaped area near the center of the court because it gives them a good position for reaching the next shot. In a standard rally-scoring squash game, either player can score a point on each rally, and the first player to reach eleven points wins if they lead by at least two. If the score reaches 10-all, play continues until one player gains a two-point lead, such as 12–10 or 13–11. Some versions of squash are played to fifteen points instead.

Surface area measures the total two-dimensional extent of a three-dimensional object’s exterior: how much material would be needed to cover its outside. It is measured in square units, such as square centimeters. Different solids have different surface-area formulas. For a sphere, the formula is 4πr², where r is the radius—the distance from the sphere’s center to any point on its surface. Because the radius is squared, doubling a sphere’s radius makes its surface area four times as large. Surface area also appears in physics. For a flat surface in a uniform magnetic field, magnetic flux depends on the surface’s area and its orientation relative to the field.

A right triangle is a three-sided figure with one 90-degree angle, called a right angle. The two sides that meet at that angle are the legs, and the side opposite it is the hypotenuse, which is always the longest side. The Pythagorean theorem describes how their lengths are related: if the legs have lengths a and b and the hypotenuse has length c, then a² + b² = c². In geometric terms, the areas of squares built on the two legs add up to the area of a square built on the hypotenuse. This theorem helps solve practical problems. For example, a ladder leaning against a wall forms a right triangle with the wall and ground; knowing the ladder’s length and its distance from the wall lets you calculate the height it reaches.

Countability describes whether the elements of a set can be listed in a sequence and matched one-to-one with the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on. An infinite set that can be matched this way is called countably infinite and has a size, or cardinality, called aleph-zero. The integers and rational numbers are countably infinite, even though a simple list of them might seem impossible at first. The real numbers, which include fractions and numbers such as π, are too numerous to list this way. Cantor’s diagonal argument proves this by assuming there is a complete list of real numbers written as decimal expansions. It then changes the nth digit of the nth number to make a new number that differs from every entry on the list.

Arctangent, written arctan(x) or tan⁻¹(x), is the inverse of tangent: it gives an angle whose tangent is x. Because tangent repeats every π radians, many angles can have the same tangent. The standard arctangent chooses just one, called the principal angle, in the open interval (−π/2, π/2), or between −90° and 90°. The endpoints are excluded because tangent is undefined there. Arctangent can take any real number as its input; for example, arctan(1) = π/4 because tan(π/4) = 1. It also appears in mechanics. The angle of repose is the steepest slope on which an object can remain at rest without sliding. If μs is the coefficient of static friction, that angle is arctan(μs).

Eccentricity is a dimensionless number, usually written as e, that describes the shape of a conic section. A circle has eccentricity 0. An ellipse has an eccentricity strictly between 0 and 1: values close to 0 describe nearly circular ellipses, while values close to 1 describe more stretched-out ones. An ellipse also has two focal points, and the sum of the distances from any point on the ellipse to those points is constant. A parabola has eccentricity exactly 1, placing it between ellipses and hyperbolas in this classification. A hyperbola has eccentricity greater than 1. Because eccentricity is a ratio rather than a measurement of length, enlarging or shrinking a conic section does not change its eccentricity.

Euler’s number, written e, is an irrational constant approximately equal to 2.71828. It is the base of the natural logarithm, written ln, and can be found by calculating (1 + 1/n)^n as n grows larger and larger: the values approach e. Euler’s number also appears in counting rearrangements. A permutation is a way to arrange distinct objects; for n objects, there are n! possible permutations. An object that stays in its original position is called a fixed point. A derangement is a permutation with no fixed points, so every object moves to a different position. As the number of objects increases, the fraction of all permutations that are derangements approaches 1/e, or about 0.368.

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. An identity matrix is a special square matrix, meaning it has the same number of rows and columns. It has 1s on its main diagonal, which runs from the top left to the bottom right, and 0s everywhere else. For example, the 2-by-2 identity matrix has 1s in its top-left and bottom-right positions. Multiplying a matrix by an identity matrix of the appropriate size leaves the original matrix unchanged, whether the identity matrix is on the left or the right. This makes it a multiplicative identity for matrices, just as the number 1 is the multiplicative identity for ordinary numbers: multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged.

The Intermediate Value Theorem describes what happens when a function changes continuously across an interval. A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input; the notation f(x) means the output of the function f for the input x. Imagine drawing the graph of a continuous function from x = a to x = b without lifting your pencil. If its output is 2 at one endpoint and 7 at the other, the graph must reach every value between 2 and 7 somewhere along the way. More precisely, if a function is continuous on the closed interval from a to b, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that it takes every real-number value between f(a) and f(b) at least once. Without continuity, the function could jump over a value.

Georg Friedrich Bernhard Riemann was a 19th-century German mathematician who made major contributions to geometry and complex analysis, the study of functions involving complex numbers. His ideas about curved spaces later became important to Einstein’s theory of gravity. In number theory, Riemann studied the zeta function, which has a deep connection to the distribution of prime numbers. A zero of this function is a value where its output equals zero. The Riemann Hypothesis predicts that every nontrivial zero has a real part of one-half. Because complex numbers can be plotted using their real and imaginary parts, the points with real part one-half form a vertical line, written Re(s) = 1/2. This is called the critical line.

A parallelepiped is a three-dimensional solid with six faces, each shaped like a parallelogram. A parallelogram is a four-sided shape with two pairs of opposite sides that stay parallel, even if the sides are extended. The opposite faces of a parallelepiped are also parallel and equal in size and shape. Cubes and rectangular prisms are special kinds of parallelepipeds: their faces are rectangles, and a cube’s faces are all squares. A body diagonal runs through the inside of the solid from one corner to the opposite corner. A parallelepiped has four body diagonals, and they all cross at the same midpoint. This point is called the center of symmetry because every point on the solid has a matching point equally far away on the opposite side of it.

Viète’s formulas connect the coefficients of a polynomial to its roots. For a monic polynomial, whose leading coefficient is 1, imagine writing it as a product of factors such as (x − r₁)(x − r₂)(x − r₃). Expanding these factors shows that the coefficient of x² is −(r₁ + r₂ + r₃), the coefficient of x is r₁r₂ + r₁r₃ + r₂r₃, and the constant term is −r₁r₂r₃. The sums of products made by choosing one root, two distinct roots, and so on are called elementary symmetric polynomials. Viète’s formulas say that these expressions equal the polynomial’s coefficients, with alternating signs. For a quadratic, they can help find roots without completing the square or using the quadratic formula.

Complex numbers extend the real number line by including an imaginary unit, i, defined by i² = −1. A complex number is written a + bi, where a and b are real numbers: a is the real part, and bi is the imaginary part. The set of complex numbers is denoted by a double-struck C, written ℂ. For example, 3 + 2i is complex, while an ordinary real number such as 3 can be written 3 + 0i. William Rowan Hamilton later extended this idea to create quaternions, which use three imaginary units, i, j, and k. Unlike ordinary number multiplication, quaternion multiplication is noncommutative: changing the order can change the result. Hamilton famously carved a defining multiplication relation for quaternions onto Broom Bridge in Dublin.

Seven is the integer after six and before eight. In Western music theory, a major scale contains seven distinct notes before the first note, called the tonic, repeats at the octave. For example, C major has C, D, E, F, G, A, and B, followed by a higher C. Its pattern of steps between notes is whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. The major scale’s seventh note is therefore the note just below the octave. A dominant seventh chord also gets its name from adding a seventh to a three-note chord, or triad, built on the fifth degree of a scale. This added note makes a four-note chord that sounds tense and often leads back to the tonic chord.

Least squares is a method for fitting a model, such as a straight line, to observed data. For each data point, the difference between its observed value and the value predicted by the model is called a residual. Least squares chooses the model parameters, such as a line’s slope and intercept, to make the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible. Squaring makes negative and positive differences both count and gives larger errors more weight. The method is widely used in regression, though an unusually extreme data point can strongly affect the result. Least squares also has a place in mathematical history: the French mathematician Adrien-Marie Legendre first published it in 1805 in a treatise called Nouvelles méthodes pour la détermination des orbites des comètes, about determining comet orbits.

The brachistochrone problem asks which curved path lets a frictionless bead, released from rest, travel between two fixed points in the shortest time under gravity. The fastest path is not a straight line: it is part of a cycloid, the curve traced by a point on the rim of a rolling wheel. A cycloid drops steeply at first, allowing the bead to gain speed quickly, then bends toward its destination. Johann Bernoulli posed the problem as a challenge in 1696, and his brother Jakob was among those who worked on it. The English physicist Isaac Newton also submitted a solution. Newton later formulated three laws of motion, including the third law: for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, or GRH, is an unsolved conjecture about where certain complex numbers called zeros occur. The original Riemann Hypothesis says that every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function lies on a vertical line in the complex plane where the real part is one-half. GRH extends this claim to a broader family called Dirichlet L-functions. These functions come from series whose coefficients are Dirichlet characters: arithmetic functions that repeat modulo an integer and are completely multiplicative, meaning the value at a product equals the product of the values. After the series are analytically continued, GRH predicts that all their nontrivial zeros also have real part one-half. If true, it would give mathematicians powerful tools for studying how prime numbers are distributed.

A triangle is a polygon with three sides. A median of a triangle is a line segment drawn from one vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. A midpoint divides a side into two equal lengths, so each median also divides the triangle into two smaller triangles of equal area. Every triangle has three medians, one from each vertex, and they all meet at a single point called the centroid. The centroid is the triangle’s center of gravity: if a flat triangular shape had an even thickness, it could balance at that point. Along each median, the centroid lies two-thirds of the way from the vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

Jeopardy! is an American television quiz show created by Merv Griffin. Contestants choose clues from a board of categories and dollar values, then try to respond before their opponents. Unlike in most quiz shows, each clue is presented as a statement of information, and contestants must phrase their responses as questions. For example, a clue saying “This planet is known as the Red Planet” calls for the response “What is Mars?” The syndicated version of Jeopardy! premiered in 1984 with Canadian-born Alex Trebek as host. He remained in that role until his death in 2020, becoming the show’s longest-serving and most recognizable host. Jeopardy! is also familiar enough to have inspired comedy sketches, including a Saturday Night Live parody of its celebrity edition.

The Catbus is a magical, cat-shaped vehicle in the 1988 animated film My Neighbor Totoro. It has twelve legs, glowing eyes that work like headlights, and a furry body with windows and seats inside. It races through the countryside, carrying passengers such as the sisters Satsuki and Mei, who discover forest spirits after moving to a rural home. Although it looks like a bus, the Catbus is a living creature and a major supporting character in their adventure. My Neighbor Totoro was written and directed by Japanese filmmaker Hayao Miyazaki, whose films often mix everyday childhood experiences with imaginative, magical beings.

Disco music is a dance-oriented genre that rose to prominence in the 1970s. Its steady beat and lively rhythms made it popular in nightclubs, where people danced beneath spinning mirrored disco balls. The film Saturday Night Fever helped make disco’s club culture and fashions, including flashy suits, widely recognizable. People danced to disco in groups or with partners, often performing the hustle. Some disco partner routines included dramatic dips, in which one dancer lowers the other toward the floor. These moves drew inspiration from the tango, a partner dance that developed in dance halls along the Río de la Plata in South America. Tango music is closely associated with the bandoneón, an instrument related to the accordion, and the composer Astor Piazzolla wrote music for it.

The Great British Bake Off, also known in the United States as The Great British Baking Show, is a British reality competition in which amateur bakers meet in a large tent, or marquee, each week. They make breads, pastries, cakes, and other desserts in three rounds. In the signature challenge, bakers use their own recipes to show what they do best. In the technical challenge, everyone makes the same item from a judge’s recipe, often with only sparse directions, so they must rely on their baking knowledge. The showstopper challenge asks them to create an elaborate centerpiece. Judges Paul Hollywood and Prue Leith assess the results, name a standout baker, and send one contestant home each week. The show is known for its friendly, relatively relaxed atmosphere.

“Running Up That Hill (A Deal with God)” is a 1985 single by British musician Kate Bush from her album Hounds of Love. Its pulsing synthesizers drive a song about wanting to make a deal to trade places with another person, hoping that experiencing each other’s lives would help them understand one another. The song found a new audience in 2022 when it appeared in the fourth season of the Netflix series Stranger Things. Set mainly in Hawkins, Indiana, the supernatural drama follows young friends facing dangers linked to a mysterious dimension called the Upside Down. In season four, Kate Bush’s song becomes a lifeline for Max Mayfield, helping her break free from the villain Vecna’s curse. Its appearance on the show sent the decades-old track back up the charts.

Björk is an Icelandic singer-songwriter known for combining pop with electronic, experimental, and other musical styles. She first gained international attention as a member of the alternative-rock band The Sugarcubes. Their 1988 album Life’s Too Good introduced many listeners outside Iceland to the group and included the songs “Birthday” and “Motorcrash.” After The Sugarcubes broke up in 1992, Björk built a solo career with adventurous records and striking music videos. She worked with director Michel Gondry on surreal videos for “Human Behaviour” and “Army of Me.” Her unusual vocals, bold visual style, and willingness to try new sounds have made her one of Iceland’s best-known musicians.

The Coen brothers, Joel and Ethan Coen, are American filmmakers known for directing films together. Their acclaimed movies include Fargo, the Western True Grit, and No Country for Old Men, which won the Academy Award for Best Picture. Their distinctive storytelling and use of dark humor have made them influential figures in modern American cinema. After years of working as a team, the brothers began pursuing separate projects. Joel Coen directed The Tragedy of Macbeth without Ethan. Based on William Shakespeare’s play Macbeth, the film stars Denzel Washington as Macbeth and Frances McDormand as Lady Macbeth. In the story, Macbeth murders King Duncan in a bid to take Scotland’s throne. Joel filmed his adaptation in black and white, giving it a stark look unlike most modern films.

Nope is a 2022 science-fiction horror film about siblings OJ and Emerald Haywood, who run their family’s horse ranch in Agua Dulce, California. After strange events disrupt the ranch, they discover a mysterious presence in the sky and try to capture evidence of it on camera. The film mixes suspense with questions about why people risk their safety to record something spectacular. It was written and directed by Jordan Peele, who also wrote and directed the horror films Get Out and Us. Before becoming a filmmaker, Peele was known for performing sketch comedy with Keegan-Michael Key. Daniel Kaluuya plays OJ; he also starred in Get Out.

Dragons are winged, fire-breathing creatures in George R. R. Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire and its television adaptation, Game of Thrones. Their power helped Aegon the Conqueror and his sisters unite much of Westeros under House Targaryen. After dragons disappeared for generations, the exiled Daenerys Targaryen, daughter of King Aerys II, received three seemingly petrified dragon eggs as a wedding gift from Illyrio Mopatis. She cared for the eggs and later placed them on her husband Khal Drogo’s funeral pyre. Three dragons hatched from the flames, bringing the creatures back into the world and earning Daenerys the title “Mother of Dragons.” Dragons remain closely linked to Targaryen power and identity; the Game of Thrones prequel is called House of the Dragon.

Stop-motion animation makes real objects appear to move by photographing them one frame at a time. Between photographs, animators shift a figure or part of a set slightly. When the frames play quickly in sequence, the small changes create the illusion of continuous movement. The figures may be made from clay, puppets, or other materials, and even a short scene can require hundreds of careful adjustments. One example is Isle of Dogs, Wes Anderson’s film about dogs exiled to a trash island. Another is the 1993 dark fantasy musical The Nightmare Before Christmas, directed by Henry Selick. It follows Jack Skellington, the skeletal ruler of Halloween Town, and features his ghost dog, Zero. Its songs include “This Is Halloween” and “What’s This?”

OVO Sound is a record label and entertainment company founded in Toronto by rapper Drake, producer and engineer Noah “40” Shebib, and executive Oliver El-Khatib. Its name comes from October’s Very Own, a phrase linked to Drake, whose birthday is in October. The company is strongly associated with an owl emblem that appears on its clothing and other merchandise. OVO Sound releases music by Drake and other artists while helping develop their careers. Shebib, often called “40,” has played a major role in shaping Drake’s atmospheric sound through his production and recording work. Drake is known for hits such as “One Dance” and “Hotline Bling,” but OVO Sound is the name of the company he co-founded, not his stage name.

Kirby’s Dream Land is a platform game released for the Nintendo Game Boy in 1992. It introduced Kirby, a round hero who later became famous for his pink color. In his first adventure, Kirby sets out to recover food stolen from Dream Land by its ruler, King Dedede. To reach Dedede, players guide Kirby through a series of stages filled with enemies such as Waddle Dees. Kirby can inhale enemies and puff himself up like a balloon to float over obstacles. He also battles Whispy Woods, an apple-dropping tree. At the end of the game, Kirby faces King Dedede, who wields a giant hammer and serves as the final boss.

Horror film is a genre designed to make audiences feel fear, dread, or unease. Its stories often involve disturbing events, dangerous people, or supernatural threats such as ghosts and monsters. Filmmakers may build tension with eerie settings, unsettling sounds, and jump scares—sudden moments meant to startle viewers. Horror often overlaps with suspense and thriller films, which also keep audiences anxious about what might happen next. One example is Get Out, directed by Jordan Peele. In the film, Chris visits his girlfriend’s family and is hypnotized into a dark mental void called the Sunken Place. He later discovers that the family plans to transplant the brains of older white people into the bodies of young Black people.

Master Wu is the wise teacher who trains the ninja heroes in LEGO Ninjago. Often seen carrying a staff and enjoying a cup of tea, he guides the team as they use Spinjitzu to face threats across their world. Wu is the younger brother of Lord Garmadon, whose shifting loyalties sometimes put the brothers on opposite sides. Both are sons of the First Spinjitzu Master, the ancient figure credited with creating Ninjago and devising Spinjitzu, a martial art whose fighters spin like tornadoes. This family connection links Wu not only to the ninja he teaches but also to the origins of the world and the skill they work to master.

Keanu Reeves is a Canadian actor who was born in Beirut, Lebanon, and raised in Toronto. He is best known for playing Neo in The Matrix films. Neo begins as a hacker who discovers that the world he knows is a computer-generated simulation. Reeves returned to the role in the 2021 science-fiction film The Matrix Resurrections, directed by Lana Wachowski. Carrie-Anne Moss also returned as Trinity, Neo’s close ally. Reeves stars in another major film series as John Wick, a retired assassin drawn back into violence while seeking revenge. He also appeared in the Bill and Ted comedy films, where his character’s frequent “Whoa” became a memorable part of his screen image.

A graphic novel tells a sustained story through a sequence of illustrated panels, usually combining pictures with dialogue, captions, or other text. Unlike a short comic strip, it develops its characters and plot over a book-length work. Readers follow both the words and the artwork: a character’s expression, a change in setting, or the arrangement of panels can reveal information that the text does not state directly. Graphic novels can tell many kinds of stories, including superhero adventures, memoirs, and historical fiction. A well-known example is Watchmen, written by Alan Moore and illustrated by Dave Gibbons. Its masked characters include Rorschach, Doctor Manhattan, and Silk Spectre. In the story, Adrian Veidt teleports a gigantic squid into New York City as part of an attempt to prevent nuclear war.

Jimmy Page is an English guitarist, songwriter, and producer best known for co-founding Led Zeppelin. Before becoming a rock star, he was an in-demand session musician in London, playing guitar on recordings for other artists. In 1966, he joined the Yardbirds, a British rock band. When the Yardbirds dissolved, Page formed Led Zeppelin with singer Robert Plant, bassist and keyboardist John Paul Jones, and drummer John Bonham. The band became one of the most influential rock groups of the 1970s. Its songs include “Immigrant Song,” with lyrics about the “land of the ice and snow,” and “Stairway to Heaven,” which opens with a lady buying a stairway. Page was known for experimenting with guitar sounds: during the recording of “Whole Lotta Love,” he played his guitar using a cello bow.

SpongeBob SquarePants is an animated comedy series about an optimistic, energetic sea sponge named SpongeBob. He lives in a pineapple under the sea in the town of Bikini Bottom and works as a fry cook at the Krusty Krab, where Squidward is his coworker. Although SpongeBob is excellent at making Krabby Patties, he struggles to learn how to drive a boat. His teacher, Mrs. Puff, is a pufferfish who runs the local boating school and gives him repeated driving lessons, but he keeps failing his tests. Other characters include SpongeBob’s friend Patrick and Plankton, who tries to steal the Krusty Krab’s secret recipe.
