Guild Navigators consume it to help them perceive safe paths through space, making interstellar travel possible. Because so many people depend on spice and Arrakis is its source, control of the planet is central to the struggle between powerful families in Dune.

La Dolce Vita is a 1960 Italian drama directed by Federico Fellini. It follows Marcello Rubini, a gossip journalist played by Marcello Mastroianni, as he moves through the wealthy and fashionable circles of Rome. Rather than telling one simple story, the film shows a series of Marcello’s encounters with celebrities, aristocrats, and other people seeking excitement or meaning in their lives. Its title means “the sweet life,” but the glamorous parties often leave Marcello feeling dissatisfied. Rome is an important part of the film: scenes take place along the fashionable Via Veneto and at the ancient Baths of Caracalla. Its most famous sequence, filmed at the Trevi Fountain, became one of cinema’s defining images. Mastroianni’s performance is among the best known from his long collaboration with Fellini.

Keegan-Michael Key is an American comedian and actor known for energetic characters and sharp impressions. He co-created and starred with Jordan Peele in Key & Peele, a Comedy Central sketch comedy series named after the pair. Before that, Key appeared on the sketch show MADtv, where he played Coach Hines, an intense, often angry gym teacher. One recurring Key & Peele sketch featured Key as Luther, the “anger translator” for President Barack Obama, played by Peele. Luther loudly expressed the frustration that the calm, careful president supposedly kept hidden. Obama was the 44th president of the United States. Another famous sketch featured Key as a substitute teacher who mispronounced students’ names, including Aaron, whom he called “A-A-ron.”

Apocalypse Now is a 1979 Vietnam War film directed by Francis Ford Coppola. It follows U.S. Army Captain Benjamin Willard as he travels upriver on a secret mission to find Colonel Walter Kurtz, a renegade officer living deep in the jungle. One of the film’s best-known scenes shows American helicopters attacking a village while “Ride of the Valkyries,” music by Richard Wagner, plays over loudspeakers. Coppola loosely based the film on Heart of Darkness, a novella by Joseph Conrad. In Conrad’s story, a seaman named Charles Marlow travels up the Congo River to meet another Kurtz, an ivory agent. By moving that journey to the Vietnam War, Apocalypse Now explores the violence and moral confusion of war.

Clone troopers were genetically engineered soldiers in Star Wars, created from the DNA of bounty hunter Jango Fett. They were raised in vast cloning facilities in Tipoca City on Kamino, a remote planet covered almost entirely by water. The troopers formed the Grand Army of the Galactic Republic and fought Separatist droid armies during the Clone Wars. Although they shared the same genetic template, individual troopers developed distinct personalities and skills. A group with unusual mutations became known as the Bad Batch, led by Hunter. The troopers also carried inhibitor chips that compelled them to obey Order 66 and turn against the Jedi they had served alongside.

Sonic the Hedgehog is Sega’s speedy blue video game hero, first introduced in 1991. In his original platform game, he runs through levels, collects golden rings, and battles the villain Dr. Robotnik, also known as Doctor Eggman. The game’s opening stage is Green Hill Zone, recognizable by its checkerboard cliffs, palm trees, loops, and waterfalls. Sonic often works with his friend Miles “Tails” Prower, a fox who can fly using his two tails. His adventures have expanded beyond the original games: in Sonic Colors, he joins an alien Wisp named Yacker to investigate Eggman’s amusement park, while the cartoon Sonic Boom features Sonic and his team on Seaside Island. Ben Schwartz voices Sonic in the live-action films, whose first installment was delayed so Sonic’s design could be changed after fans criticized it.

Old Town Road is a hit song by rapper Lil Nas X that blends trap music’s beats and rhythms with country imagery, including horses and cowboy life. It first spread widely through videos on TikTok, where people used it in a viral challenge. A remix featuring country singer Billy Ray Cyrus helped the song reach an even wider audience. Cyrus was already known for his earlier hit “Achy Breaky Heart.” The remix also drew attention to debates about whether Old Town Road belonged on country music charts, since it combined sounds from different genres. In 2019, the song spent a record-setting 19 weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100, making it one of the most successful examples of a song growing from internet popularity into a mainstream hit.

Ingmar Bergman was a Swedish filmmaker known for exploring questions about life, death, faith, and identity. In his 1957 film The Seventh Seal, a knight named Antonius Block returns to a land struck by the Black Plague and plays chess with Death to delay his own end while he searches for meaning. Bergman also directed Wild Strawberries, a film about an elderly professor reflecting on his life. His 1966 psychological drama Persona follows nurse Alma as she cares for actress Elisabet Vogler, who has suddenly stopped speaking. As the two women spend time together, the boundaries between their identities become increasingly blurred. These films helped make Bergman one of the most influential directors in film history.

The Phantom of the Opera is a masked, disfigured musical genius who secretly lives beneath a Paris opera house. In Gaston Leroux’s novel The Phantom of the Opera, he becomes obsessed with the young soprano Christine Daaé and tries to control her singing career, presenting himself as her mysterious “Angel of Music.” He is also called Erik. Andrew Lloyd Webber’s stage musical made the character especially famous, with songs in which Christine hears his voice and feels his presence in her mind. The story’s opera house is based on a real Paris landmark: the Palais Garnier, an ornate theater commissioned by Napoleon III and opened in 1875. Its grand spaces and hidden passages make a fitting setting for the Phantom’s story.

Team Rocket is a recurring criminal organization in the Pokémon games and anime. Its members steal Pokémon and use them to gain power and money. The group is led by Giovanni, a crime boss who is also the Viridian City Gym Leader in the original games. He specializes in Ground-type Pokémon, and after the player defeats him at his Gym, he announces that he is disbanding Team Rocket. In the anime, Team Rocket is best known through Jessie, James, and their talking Meowth. This bumbling trio often tries to capture Ash’s Pikachu, introduces itself with the line “Prepare for trouble, and make it double,” and usually ends up “blasting off again” when its plans fail.

In Among Us, venting means entering a floor vent and traveling through connected vents to reach another part of the map without walking through the corridors. Impostors use this ability to move quickly, escape after killing a crewmate, or approach someone unnoticed. Because ordinary crewmates cannot vent, seeing a player use one may make them seem suspicious. However, the Engineer is a crewmate role that can also vent, so venting alone does not always prove that a player is an impostor. This difference matters in Among Us, a social deduction game in which crewmates complete tasks and try to identify the impostors, while impostors try to eliminate crewmates and sabotage the map.

“Congratulations” is a song cut from the stage musical Hamilton. In it, Angelica Schuyler sharply criticizes Alexander Hamilton after he publishes the Reynolds Pamphlet, a public account of his affair with Maria Reynolds. Hamilton wrote the pamphlet to defend himself against accusations of financial wrongdoing, but it also exposed his infidelity to the public and deeply hurt his wife, Eliza, who is Angelica’s sister. Angelica calls his decision “a new kind of stupid” because, in her view, responding to the accusations in such detail made the scandal worse. The song’s title is sarcastic: Angelica is not praising Hamilton but condemning the damage he has done to his family.

A-Force is an all-female Marvel superhero team that debuted in a 2015 comic as an offshoot of the Avengers. Its members work together to protect people from powerful threats, bringing heroes with different abilities and backgrounds onto one team. One of its central members is She-Hulk, a green-skinned hero whose everyday identity is Jennifer Walters, a lawyer. Jennifer is also the cousin of Bruce Banner, the scientist who becomes the Hulk. Like her cousin, she can transform into a much stronger, green-skinned form, but her legal skills and judgment are important parts of her character too. Remembering the connection between the team and its central hero makes both names easier to identify: the team is A-Force, and Jennifer Walters is She-Hulk.

“I Know What You Did Last Summer” is a 2015 pop duet by Shawn Mendes and Camila Cabello, who was then a member of the girl group Fifth Harmony. Cabello was born in Cuba and later became a solo pop star. In the song, the two singers trade lines about a troubled relationship, returning to the repeated refrain “I know, I know, I know” and the line “can’t seem to hold you close.” Its title alludes to the 1997 teen slasher film I Know What You Did Last Summer, about friends haunted after covering up a fatal hit-and-run. Although it shares the film’s title, the song focuses on suspicion and heartbreak in a relationship rather than the movie’s plot.

Kenneth Branagh is a Northern Irish actor and director especially known for bringing William Shakespeare’s plays to the screen. In his 1993 film adaptation of the comedy Much Ado About Nothing, Branagh both directed the film and played Benedick, a witty bachelor who often trades sharp remarks with Beatrice. Their friends arrange staged conversations for each of them to overhear, making Benedick believe Beatrice loves him and Beatrice believe Benedick loves her. The trick helps them admit their real feelings for each other. Branagh also directed film versions of Shakespeare’s Henry V and Hamlet, two plays very different from the lighthearted Much Ado About Nothing. His work as both a performer and filmmaker has helped introduce Shakespeare’s characters and stories to modern movie audiences.

Happier Than Ever is Billie Eilish’s second studio album, released in 2021 after her debut, When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go? Eilish made it with her brother and longtime collaborator Finneas. The album includes “Your Power,” a song about someone misusing their influence, and “Therefore I Am.” Its title track begins as a quiet piano ballad before building into a loud, guitar-driven rock ending. “Therefore I Am” takes its name from part of the Latin philosophical statement “I think, therefore I am,” which is about the certainty of one’s own existence. In the song’s music video, Eilish wanders through an almost-empty shopping mall, taking food from its shops and eating fries.

Grey’s Anatomy is a long-running American medical drama created by television writer and producer Shonda Rhimes. It begins as surgical intern Meredith Grey starts work at Seattle Grace Hospital and discovers that Derek Shepherd, the man she met during a one-night stand, is an attending surgeon there. The series follows Meredith and her colleagues as they treat patients, train as surgeons, and navigate friendships and relationships. The hospital is later known as Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital. The show’s title refers both to Meredith’s surname and to Gray’s Anatomy, a famous medical textbook. Grey’s Anatomy also became the parent series of Station 19, a drama about Seattle firefighters. Rhimes later created Scandal and How to Get Away with Murder, and her production company is called Shondaland.

Twitter is a social media platform where people share short public posts, long known as “tweets,” and respond to news, celebrities, and one another. Its posts were historically limited to 280 characters, encouraging brief messages. Twitter was later rebranded as X, but many people still recognize its former name. The platform has also been part of debates about how social media companies handle misleading or harmful content. In May 2020, Twitter labeled some claims about mail-in voting made by U.S. President Donald Trump as disputed. Trump responded with an executive order aimed at changing the legal protections social media platforms receive under Section 230, a U.S. law that generally shields websites from liability for content posted by their users.

Waymond Wang is Evelyn Wang’s husband in the 2022 science-fiction comedy-drama Everything Everywhere All at Once. They run a family laundromat, but their marriage is strained, and Waymond is considering divorce. The film explores a multiverse: many different universes in which people’s lives can take different paths. A more assertive version of Waymond, called Alpha Waymond, reveals the multiverse to Evelyn and recruits her to fight a threat that reaches across realities. Despite his ordinary life and gentle manner, Waymond’s kindness becomes important to the story. He is played by Ke Huy Quan, who won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for the role. As a child actor, Quan played Short Round in Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Data in The Goonies.

No Time to Die is a James Bond action film starring Daniel Craig in his fifth and final appearance as the British secret agent 007. Bond has retired from active service and is living quietly in Jamaica, but an old friend from the CIA asks for his help rescuing a kidnapped scientist. The mission draws Bond into a dangerous plot involving a new villain and a powerful weapon. Although the film was originally planned for release in 2020, delays meant it reached cinemas in 2021. Its title song, also called “No Time to Die,” was co-written and performed by Billie Eilish, who became the youngest artist to write and record a Bond theme. Eilish is also known for the hits “bad guy” and “everything i wanted.”

Ludwig Anders Ahgren, usually known simply as Ludwig, is an American YouTuber and livestreamer who makes gaming videos, variety shows, and large online events. He drew widespread attention in 2021 with a 30-day Twitch “subathon,” a livestream that stayed on longer as viewers bought subscriptions. In 2022, he won Streamer of the Year at the Streamer Awards. Ludwig’s streams also helped bring more attention to GeoGuessr, a game in which players are dropped into a panoramic Street View scene and use clues such as road signs, landscapes, and buildings to guess their location on a map. Other creators, including Trevor Rainbolt, have helped popularize GeoGuessr by showing how much can be learned from a single street-level image.

Breaking Bad is an American television crime drama about Walter White, a high-school chemistry teacher who learns he has cancer. Hoping to provide money for his family, Walt begins making methamphetamine with Jesse Pinkman, a former student and small-time drug dealer whose early batches earned him the nickname “Cap’n Cook.” Walt uses his chemistry skills to produce a distinctive blue methamphetamine nicknamed “Blue Sky.” As their illegal business grows, Walt becomes known as “Heisenberg” and changes from an ordinary teacher into a powerful, dangerous figure in the drug world. The series follows the consequences of his choices for Jesse, Walt’s family, and the people caught up in their business.

“Boyfriend” is a synth-pop single released by Dove Cameron in February 2022. It became her breakout hit, introducing many listeners to a darker, synth-led sound than they might have expected from the actor and singer. In the song, the narrator flirts with someone who already has a boyfriend and argues that she could be a better romantic partner. The title comes from her offer to “be a better boyfriend than him.” Its playful, confident lyrics include the lines “I don’t need to tell you twice” and “all my clothes would fit.” Songwriter-producer Evan Blair co-wrote and produced “Boyfriend,” helping shape the moody electronic arrangement that contrasts with the song’s teasing tone.

“See You Again” is a pop song Miley Cyrus released in 2007 on her album Meet Miley Cyrus. In the lyrics, she describes feeling a deep connection when someone looks into her eyes and says she “can’t wait” to see that person again. Its energetic sound helped make it one of her early hits. A remix by Rock Mafia, a production team associated with Antonina Armato and Tim James, later brought the song to a new audience on TikTok. If you are trying to identify the song, the clues are Cyrus’s 2007 album, the lyrics about eye contact and a future reunion, and the Rock Mafia remix. Don’t confuse it with other songs called “See You Again,” including those by Carrie Underwood and Wiz Khalifa featuring Charlie Puth.

Alex Jones is an American media personality who founded Infowars in 1999. The outlet became the main platform for his broadcasts, which often promote conspiracy theories. After the 2012 shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Connecticut, where 20 children and six educators were killed, Jones falsely claimed that the attack was a hoax. Families of victims sued him for defamation, arguing that his claims harmed them and led to harassment. Courts found Jones liable, and juries ordered him to pay substantial damages. The case shows how false claims spread through popular media can have serious consequences for the people they target.

In Avatar: The Last Airbender, bending is the ability to control an element through movement and training. Most benders can control only one of four elements: water, earth, fire, or air. The Avatar is the exception: a reincarnating guardian who can master all four and has a duty to keep balance in the world. Aang is the Avatar during the main animated series, while Korra holds the title in a later series. Earlier Avatars include Wan, the first Avatar, and Kyoshi. The Avatar immediately before Aang was Roku, a Fire Nation Avatar. Roku grew up as a friend of Sozin, who became Fire Lord, but they later clashed over Sozin’s plans for conquest. Roku also traveled with a dragon named Fang.

Tatiana Maslany is a Canadian actress known for playing many genetically identical but very different women in the science-fiction drama Orphan Black. The story begins when Sarah Manning discovers that she is part of a cloning experiment. Maslany also plays clones such as Alison Hendrix, giving each character a distinct personality, voice, and way of moving. Her work on the series earned her an Emmy Award. She later starred in the Disney+ Marvel series She-Hulk: Attorney at Law as Jennifer Walters, a lawyer who can transform into the green-skinned superhero She-Hulk. These two roles show Maslany playing different versions of a person in very different kinds of television shows: a mystery-driven science-fiction drama and a superhero comedy.

American Psycho is a 2000 black-comedy psychological thriller directed by Mary Harron and adapted from Bret Easton Ellis’s novel. Christian Bale stars as Patrick Bateman, a wealthy Manhattan investment banker who appears polished and successful but hides a violent private life. The film uses dark humor and unsettling scenes to satirize wealth, status, and the pressure to maintain a perfect image. Harron had previously directed I Shot Andy Warhol, a film dramatizing the life of Valerie Solanas. To remember the film and its director, connect Bale’s character Patrick Bateman with the title American Psycho and Mary Harron with both American Psycho and I Shot Andy Warhol.

Parasite is a 2019 South Korean film directed by Bong Joon-ho, whose earlier films include Memories of Murder, The Host, and Snowpiercer. It follows the struggling Kim family as they find ways to work for the wealthy Park family without revealing that they are related. The son first becomes a tutor for the Parks’ daughter; through forged qualifications and carefully staged situations, his relatives then gain jobs as an art therapist, chauffeur, and housekeeper. What begins with clever schemes and dark comedy grows into a suspenseful story about inequality and the gulf between rich and poor. The contrast between the families’ homes, especially during a heavy rainstorm, makes that divide vivid. Parasite won several Academy Awards, including Best Director for Bong Joon-ho.

Sanditon is a British period-romance television series based on an unfinished novel by Jane Austen. Set in the Regency era, it follows Charlotte Heywood, a young woman from the village of Willingden. After Charlotte helps members of the Parker family following a carriage accident, they invite her to visit Sanditon, a seaside resort they hope to develop into a fashionable destination. There, Charlotte meets residents and visitors whose ambitions, friendships, and romances shape the town’s future. Her own relationships, including a dramatic romance with Sidney Parker, become central to the story. The series explores how a growing resort can bring together people from different backgrounds while giving Charlotte a chance to discover more about herself and the world beyond her village.

Schindler’s List is a 1993 historical drama directed by Steven Spielberg, who had earlier made Jaws and later directed Saving Private Ryan. The film tells the story of Oskar Schindler, a German industrialist who used his factory, money, and influence to protect Jewish workers from Nazi persecution during the Holocaust. Its title refers to a list of people selected to work in his factory, helping them avoid deportation to death camps. Spielberg filmed most of the story in black and white. One striking exception is a young girl in a red coat whom Schindler sees during the violent liquidation of the Kraków ghetto. Her appearance makes the suffering of individual victims stand out amid the vast scale of the tragedy.

Hecate was a goddess in Greek mythology associated with witchcraft, ghosts, crossroads, and the underworld. Some ancient Greeks considered her a Titaness, a member of the older generation of divine beings who came before the Olympian gods. Crossroads were important to her because they were seen as places of choice and mystery; people sometimes left offerings there for her. Hecate also appears in the story of Persephone, the daughter of the harvest goddess Demeter. After Hades abducted Persephone and took her to the underworld, Hecate helped Demeter search for her. When Persephone later became queen of the dead, Hecate accompanied her in the underworld and was described as her handmaiden or attendant.

Syrinx was an Arcadian nymph in Greek mythology who loved the wild places of the countryside. One day, Pan, the Greek god of shepherds and pastures, pursued her. Syrinx fled until she reached the river Ladon, where she could go no farther. To escape Pan, she was transformed into water reeds growing by the river. When Pan arrived, he heard the wind blowing through the reeds and making a beautiful sound. He gathered some of them and joined them together to make a set of reed pipes. This instrument became known as the panpipe, or syrinx, after the nymph. The story explains the mythical origin of Pan’s famous instrument and connects its music to the reeds into which Syrinx was transformed.

Eris was the Greek goddess of strife and discord. In one famous myth, she was not invited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, so she disrupted the celebration by throwing a golden apple marked “To the Fairest” among three goddesses: Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite. Each claimed the apple, and their quarrel was referred to Paris, a mortal prince of Troy. In the episode known as the Judgment of Paris, the goddesses offered him rewards for choosing them. Paris chose Aphrodite because she promised him Helen, a woman famed for her beauty. The dispute helped set in motion the events that led to the Trojan War. Eris’s apple is one of several golden apples in Greek mythology, but this one is especially associated with discord.

A psalm is a sacred poem or song used to express praise, prayer, sorrow, or trust in God. The Hebrew Bible contains a collection called the Book of Psalms. One of its best-known poems, Psalm 23, begins, “The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want,” comparing God’s care for people to a shepherd’s care for sheep. The word psalm also appears in the titles of later poems inspired by religious or moral themes. The American poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote “A Psalm of Life,” in which the speaker declares, “Life is real! Life is earnest! / And the grave is not its goal.” Longfellow also wrote “The Wreck of the Hesperus,” a poem about a ship caught in a storm.

Religious head coverings are hats or other garments worn on the head as part of worship or religious identity. In Tibetan Buddhism, “Red Hat” and “Yellow Hat” are labels associated with different traditions. The Yellow Hat tradition is the Gelug school, founded by the teacher Tsongkhapa in the 1400s. The lineage of the Dalai Lama, a leading figure in Tibetan Buddhism, belongs to this school. “Red Hat” can refer to several other Tibetan Buddhist traditions rather than one single school. In Islam, some Muslims wear a small, close-fitting skullcap called a taqiyah, including during prayer. These Buddhist hats and the Muslim taqiyah have different meanings and histories, but they are all examples of religious head coverings.

Soma is both a sacred drink in the ancient Vedic tradition and the name of the deity associated with it. Vedic priests prepared and offered Soma during rituals, and hymns in the Rigveda describe it as a source of divine strength and immortality for the gods. One god especially connected with Soma is Indra, a powerful, thunder-wielding deity who is repeatedly praised for drinking it before his great deeds. Indra uses his thunderbolt, called the vajra, to defeat the serpent Vritra, who had held back the waters. By slaying Vritra, Indra releases the waters. The name Soma also appears in Aldous Huxley’s novel Brave New World, where it is used for a fictional drug, but its much older religious meaning comes from the Vedas.

In Homer’s Odyssey, moly is a magical herb that protects Odysseus from the enchantress Circe. Odysseus reaches her island, Aeaea, while trying to return home to Ithaca after the Trojan War. Circe has turned some of his companions into pigs, and Odysseus sets out to rescue them. Before he enters her home, Hermes, the Olympian messenger god, meets him and gives him moly. Hermes also explains how to resist Circe’s magic. Protected by the herb, Odysseus drinks her potion without being transformed, surprising Circe and making it possible for him to secure his companions’ release. “Moly” is the Greek name used for the herb in the Odyssey.

In Roman legend, the twins Romulus and Remus were sons of Mars, the god of war, and Rhea Silvia. After they were abandoned near the Tiber River, a she-wolf found them and suckled them, keeping them alive until a shepherd took them in. The wolf became an important symbol of Rome’s beginnings. As adults, the brothers decided to establish a city, but they quarreled over its founding. Romulus survived the dispute and became Rome’s legendary founder and first king; the city was named after him. Wolves also appear in Greek mythology: Lycaon was transformed into a wolf after he tried to deceive Zeus. Although these are separate stories, the wolf is the animal that connects them.

The Malleus Maleficarum, or “Hammer of Witches,” is a Latin treatise written in the late 15th century by the German inquisitor Heinrich Kramer. It presents witchcraft as a form of Christian heresy and urges authorities to investigate and punish people accused of it, including by burning them at the stake. The book helped spread fears about witches and was used to justify persecution, especially of women. Kramer repeatedly cites Saint Thomas Aquinas, a 13th-century Dominican friar and Scholastic theologian. Aquinas wrote the Summa Theologica, a major work that brings together teachings and arguments about Catholic theology. Although Kramer drew on Aquinas’s authority, the Malleus Maleficarum was Kramer’s own work, written more than two centuries after Aquinas lived.

Pope Francis, born Jorge Mario Bergoglio, is the leader of the Roman Catholic Church who issued the 2015 encyclical Laudato si’, a letter calling for care of “our common home,” Earth. Its Italian title means “Praise be to you” and echoes the opening words of the Canticle of the Sun, a poem by Francis of Assisi, the saint whose name the pope chose. In Laudato si’, Pope Francis criticizes a “throwaway culture” that wastes resources and treats people as disposable. He argues that environmental damage, including pollution and climate change, is closely connected to poverty and social injustice. He returned to these concerns in Querida Amazonia, an exhortation published after a Church synod focused on the Amazon region and its people.

Jannah is the paradise promised to the righteous in Islamic teachings about the afterlife. Its name is often translated as “garden,” and descriptions of it include beautiful gardens, flowing rivers, peace, and the company of houris, beings often described as having large eyes. Jannah is contrasted with Jahannam, the place of punishment. Muslims believe that entry into Jannah depends on God’s mercy and judgment. In accounts of the Prophet Muhammad’s heavenly ascent, a lote tree called the Sidrat al-Muntaha stands at the furthest boundary of the heavens. It is described as marking the upper boundary of Jannah. These details help identify Jannah as the promised heavenly abode and the Sidrat al-Muntaha as the named tree associated with its boundary.

Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi, meaning “Grass-Cutting Sword,” is a legendary sword and one of Japan’s three Imperial Regalia, alongside a mirror and a jewel. In Japanese myth, the storm god Susanoo encounters Yamata no Orochi, a monstrous serpent with eight heads and eight tails. Susanoo gives the serpent sake, a Japanese alcoholic drink, and kills it after it becomes drunk. While cutting through the creature’s tails, he discovers the sword inside one of them. Susanoo later presents it to his sister Amaterasu, the sun goddess. The sword eventually becomes part of the regalia associated with Japan’s imperial family and its legendary descent from Amaterasu. Its name recalls a later story in which the sword is used to cut grass and escape a fire.

Gabriel, called Jibril in Arabic, is an archangel who serves as a messenger from God in Islamic belief. Muslims believe that he brought God’s revelations to the prophet Muhammad, beginning with a command to recite. These revelations were later collected in the Qur’an, Islam’s holy book. Muhammad first preached in Mecca, but he and his followers faced opposition there. In 622 CE, they migrated to Medina, an event called the Hijra. This migration marks the starting point of the Islamic calendar. Gabriel’s role in delivering the revelations connects him closely with Muhammad and with the origins of Islam.

Bhai Dooj is a Hindu festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters. It falls on the second lunar day of the bright fortnight after Diwali’s main celebration and traditionally marks the close of the Diwali festival period. Sisters often welcome their brothers by placing a ceremonial mark, called a tilak, on their foreheads, praying for their well-being, and sharing a meal with them. Brothers may give their sisters gifts in return. One traditional story explains the custom: Yama, the Hindu god of death, visited his sister Yamuna, who greeted him with a tilak and a meal. Bhai Dooj is a time for siblings to show affection and wish each other a long, happy life.

Atalanta was a swift runner and skilled huntress in Greek mythology. She joined the Calydonian Boar Hunt, organized after Artemis sent a fierce boar to punish a king who had failed to honor her. Atalanta was the only woman among the hunters and drew first blood by striking the boar with an arrow. After Meleager killed it, he awarded her its hide in recognition of her role. Atalanta later declared that she would marry only a man who could beat her in a footrace. Hippomenes asked Aphrodite for help, and the goddess gave him three golden apples. During the race, he tossed them onto the course one by one. Atalanta paused to pick them up, allowing Hippomenes to win and become her husband.

In Catholic teaching, an indulgence is a remission of the temporal punishment that remains after the guilt of a sin has been forgiven. It does not forgive the sin itself: forgiveness is associated with repentance and confession. Catholics may obtain indulgences through certain prayers or religious acts, but in the early 1500s, some preachers promoted them in connection with payments. This led many people to think they could buy relief from punishment for sin. The practice became a major issue in the Protestant Reformation. In 1517, Martin Luther, a German Augustinian friar, challenged the preaching and sale of indulgences in his Ninety-Five Theses, traditionally associated with Wittenberg’s Castle Church. His criticism helped spark a wider debate about Catholic teaching and authority.

The Church of England is the established Christian church in England and the mother church of Anglicanism, a worldwide family of churches that includes the Episcopal Church in the United States. It broke from the authority of the pope in Rome during Henry VIII’s reign, especially after the 1534 Act of Supremacy declared the king head of the English church. The Archbishop of Canterbury is its leading bishop. Under Henry’s son Edward VI, the church adopted the Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549 and largely compiled by Archbishop Thomas Cranmer. This book standardized worship in English, including prayers and services, and later shaped Anglican worship around the world. Its funeral service is the source of the familiar phrase “ashes to ashes, dust to dust.”

Solomon was an Israelite king who ruled from Jerusalem after his father, David, during the united monarchy, when Israel and Judah were one kingdom. According to the Hebrew Bible, God offered Solomon a gift, and Solomon asked for an understanding heart to govern his people rather than long life or riches. His wisdom is illustrated by his judgment in a dispute between two women who each claimed to be a baby’s mother. Solomon also built the First Temple in Jerusalem, using materials that included cedar supplied by Hiram of Tyre. His wealth and reputation drew the Queen of Sheba to Jerusalem. She arrived with spices, gold, and precious stones to test him with difficult questions; impressed by his answers and his prosperous court, she praised Israel’s God.

Quakers, also known as the Religious Society of Friends, are a Christian group that began in England in the 1600s. They emphasize the “inner light,” the belief that people can experience God’s guidance inwardly, and they teach that people can worship and communicate with God without a separate class of priests. Many Quakers also stress spiritual equality, peace, and freedom of conscience. Because Quakers faced religious persecution, the Quaker William Penn established Pennsylvania as a colony where they and others could practice their faith more freely. Philadelphia grew into Pennsylvania’s largest city, and Quakers later helped found colleges in the area, including Swarthmore College near Philadelphia.

Saraswati is the Hindu goddess of wisdom, learning, music, and the arts. Students, writers, and musicians may honor her when seeking knowledge or inspiration. In traditional accounts, she is the wife of Brahma, the god associated with creation. She is also one of the Tridevi, a group of three prominent Hindu goddesses that includes Lakshmi and Parvati. Saraswati is often shown dressed in white and holding a veena, a stringed instrument used in Indian classical music and commonly described as a type of lute. The veena represents her connection to music and artistic skill. Some images show her with four arms, holding objects that reflect different forms of knowledge and creativity.

The Crucifixion of Jesus is the execution described in the New Testament accounts of his Passion. Jesus was nailed to a cross at Golgotha, a place outside Jerusalem, with two other condemned men crucified beside him. Christians understand his death, followed by his resurrection, as central to their faith, and artists have depicted the scene for centuries. Marc Chagall painted versions called the White Crucifixion and Yellow Crucifixion, while Francis Bacon drew on its imagery in Three Studies for Figures at the Base of a Crucifixion. In 1954, the Surrealist Salvador Dalí painted Corpus Hypercubus, showing Christ against an unfolded net of a four-dimensional hypercube made of eight cubes. Dalí’s wife, Gala, appears below him.

Bellona was a Roman goddess of war and armed conflict, often shown carrying weapons and associated with the violence of battle. She was distinct from Mars, Rome’s best-known war god, though both were linked to warfare. Her temple stood near the Circus Flaminius, outside the pomerium, the sacred boundary of Rome. The statesman Appius Claudius Caecus vowed to build it during the Third Samnite War, and it was dedicated in 296 BCE. The temple’s location mattered because Roman leaders could meet there to discuss military affairs without crossing into the city’s sacred center. Bellona was also honored during the festival of Dies Sanguinis, or “Day of Blood.” Her ecstatic priests, called the Bellonarii, cut themselves and offered their blood to the goddess.

Runes are symbols used in the writing systems of early Germanic peoples, including the Norse. In Norse mythology, they also held mysterious power and could be used for divination, or seeking knowledge about the future. The god Odin wanted to understand their secrets. According to the story, he hung from Yggdrasil, the great world-tree that connects the different worlds, while pierced by his own spear. After this ordeal, he gained knowledge of the runes. This was one of several sacrifices Odin made in his search for wisdom: he also gave up an eye to drink from a well of wisdom guarded by Mimir. The key names to remember are runes for the symbols and Yggdrasil for the world-tree.

The Sanhedrin, also called the Great Sanhedrin, was the highest Jewish religious court and assembly in ancient Jerusalem. According to tradition, it had 71 members, including a presiding leader, and dealt with important questions of Jewish law and religious practice. It traditionally met in the Temple in Jerusalem. During the first century CE, that sanctuary was the Second Temple, built after the earlier Temple had been destroyed. The Temple was the center of Jewish worship and contained the Holy of Holies, a sacred inner chamber that only the High Priest could enter. Roman forces destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE. Remembering that the assembly was the Sanhedrin and that its Jerusalem meeting place was the Second Temple helps distinguish the court from the sanctuary itself.

Babe the Blue Ox is an enormous blue animal in American tall tales and the loyal companion of Paul Bunyan, a giant lumberjack. Tall tales use playful exaggeration to make their characters’ adventures seem larger than life. One story says Babe appeared during the Winter of the Blue Snow, when everything was so cold that the snow turned blue. Paul Bunyan’s own size is just as extraordinary: according to a tale, five giant storks were needed to deliver him to his parents. Stories also credit him with creating famous features of the landscape, including the Grand Canyon, which he supposedly carved by dragging his ax across the ground. Babe and Paul’s impossible size and feats make them memorable figures in American folklore.

In Roman legend, the twin brothers Romulus and Remus were the sons of Mars, the god of war, and Rhea Silvia, a Vestal Virgin. Rhea Silvia was the daughter of Numitor, the rightful king of Alba Longa. After Numitor’s brother Amulius seized the throne, he forced her to become a priestess to prevent her from having children who might challenge him. When the twins were born, Amulius ordered them abandoned on the Tiber River. A she-wolf found and suckled them, and they later grew up and overthrew Amulius. The brothers then disagreed about where to build a new city, near the Palatine or Aventine Hill. After a dispute involving bird omens, Remus jumped over a wall Romulus had built. Romulus killed Remus and founded Rome.

The Nation of Islam is an African American religious and political movement founded in Detroit in 1930 by Wallace Fard Muhammad. It grew under Elijah Muhammad, who led it from 1934 until his death in 1975. The movement taught Black pride, identity, and self-reliance, while promoting a distinct interpretation of Islam. One of its best-known members was Malcolm X, a powerful speaker whom Elijah Muhammad mentored. Malcolm X later broke with the organization and was assassinated in 1965 by men associated with it. Elijah Muhammad was also the father of Warith Deen Mohammed, who succeeded him as leader and guided many members toward mainstream Sunni Islam. The Nation of Islam remains an important part of the history of Black religious and political activism in the United States.

A parable is a short story that uses familiar people and situations to teach a moral or spiritual lesson. Rather than stating the lesson directly, it invites listeners to think about what the story means. Jesus often taught through parables in the Gospels. One well-known example is the Parable of the Prodigal Son: a younger son takes his share of his father’s property, wastes it in a distant land, and returns home hoping to be treated as a servant. Instead, his father welcomes him with a feast. The older brother objects because he has stayed and worked faithfully. The story encourages listeners to consider forgiveness, mercy, and how people respond when someone who has done wrong is welcomed back.

Jacob is a patriarch in the Book of Genesis and a grandson of Abraham. He married the sisters Leah and Rachel and fathered twelve sons whose names became associated with the Twelve Tribes of Israel. His sons included Joseph, whom his brothers sold into slavery in Egypt, and Benjamin, Rachel’s youngest son. Jacob’s story also explains why he is called Israel. At Penuel, he wrestled through the night with a mysterious figure and received the new name Israel, which the biblical account connects with his having striven with God and with people. Near the end of his life, Jacob gave blessings to his sons, including Benjamin. When a question mentions either Jacob’s twelve sons or his new name after the wrestling match, it is referring to this same patriarch.

Cinderella is a folk tale told in many versions across Europe. Its heroine is mistreated by her stepmother and stepsisters and made to work as a servant in her own home. Supernatural help lets her attend a royal celebration, where she meets a prince. She leaves behind a slipper, which the prince uses to find her, and they eventually marry. In a familiar version, a fairy godmother helps Cinderella get to the ball and gives her glass slippers. The German folklorists Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, known as the Brothers Grimm, included a version called Aschenputtel in their collection Children’s and Household Tales. In their telling, birds near a tree planted on the heroine’s mother’s grave help her instead of a fairy godmother.

Pelagianism is a Christian theological position associated with Pelagius, a teacher active in the early fifth century. It emphasizes human free will: people can choose to do good rather than evil. Pelagius rejected the view that Adam and Eve’s fall left everyone with original sin, an inherited condition that prevents them from making good moral choices without God’s help. This sparked a major debate about sin, freedom, and salvation. Augustine of Hippo, a North African bishop and theologian who wrote Confessions and The City of God, argued against Pelagianism. He taught that humans inherit sin from Adam and therefore need divine grace—God’s help—to overcome sin and be saved. The disagreement became one of the most important controversies in early Christian theology.

Purim is a Jewish festival celebrating the survival of the Jews of the Persian Empire after Haman, a powerful official, plotted to kill them. According to the Book of Esther, Queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai helped defeat his plan. The name Purim means “lots,” referring to the lots Haman cast to choose a date for his decree. Most Jewish communities observe Purim on the 14th of the Hebrew month of Adar. The Book of Esther, also called the Megillah, is read aloud, and listeners often use noisemakers called groggers when Haman’s name is mentioned. People also eat triangular pastries called hamantaschen. Jerusalem and other traditionally walled cities celebrate on the 15th of Adar, recalling an extra day of fighting in the Persian capital, Shushan. This later observance is called Shushan Purim.

In Islam, haram is an Arabic term meaning “forbidden.” It describes actions or things prohibited by Islamic religious law; eating pork and drinking alcohol are common examples. Its opposite is halal, meaning “permitted,” a word often used on food labels to show that food meets Islamic requirements. Muslims look to the Quran, Islam’s central scripture, when considering what is permitted or forbidden. They also draw on the teachings and example of the Prophet Muhammad. The Quran is organized into chapters called surahs and begins with a surah named Al-Fatiha. These sources guide Islamic jurisprudence, the study and interpretation of religious law, which addresses not only food and drink but many other aspects of conduct.

A leprechaun is a small fairy-like being from Irish folklore, usually portrayed as a bearded shoemaker who enjoys playing tricks. Traditional stories describe leprechauns as solitary and hard to catch. They are also associated with hidden wealth, especially pots of gold. In modern stories, a leprechaun’s treasure is often said to lie at the end of a rainbow, the colorful arc that appears in the sky when sunlight shines through raindrops. That makes the gold impossible to reach by simply following the rainbow: as you move, its apparent endpoint moves too. Although leprechauns are commonly shown wearing green today, older depictions often dressed them in red.

Yoga is a school of Hindu philosophy that seeks liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth through disciplined practice. It is traditionally associated with Samkhya, a school that distinguishes between consciousness and the material world. In these discussions, the Sanskrit word Atman names the individual self or soul. Yoga teaches that understanding the self and training the mind can help a person move toward liberation. Its practices include meditation, concentration, ethical conduct, and control of the senses. In the West, “yoga” is also the name for a system commonly associated with physical postures and breathing exercises, but the philosophical tradition is broader than exercise alone.

Luke the Evangelist was an early Christian associated with the apostle Paul. A letter attributed to Paul calls Luke “the beloved physician,” suggesting that he practiced medicine. Early Christian tradition credits Luke with writing two New Testament books addressed to Theophilus. The Gospel of Luke tells the story of Jesus’ life, teachings, death, and resurrection. Its sequel, Acts of the Apostles, is the fifth book of the New Testament and describes what Jesus’ followers did afterward. Acts follows the growth of the early Christian community from Jerusalem, including the selection of Matthias to replace Judas and the death of the first Christian martyr, Stephen. It also tells of Saul’s conversion and traces Paul’s missionary journeys until he reaches Rome.

Rocks and stones appear in Greek myths as dangerous obstacles, sacred markers, and punishments. The Planctae, or “Wandering Rocks,” were a deadly sea hazard. Another pair, the Symplegades, were clashing rocks that blocked the Argonauts’ route at the entrance to the Black Sea. The crew sent a dove through the gap to test whether their ship could pass. At Delphi, a stone called the Omphalos marked what the ancient Greeks considered the center of the world. In another myth, the Cyclops Polyphemus killed Acis, the lover of Galatea, with a rock. Sisyphus, who had tricked Thanatos and briefly stopped people from dying, was punished by having to roll a boulder uphill forever. Together, these stories show the many roles rocks played in Greek mythology.

In Greek mythology, the Hecatoncheires were three primordial giants born to Gaia, the earth, and Uranus, the sky. Their names were Cottus, Gyges, and Briareus. Each had fifty heads and one hundred hands, which is why they were also called the Hundred-Handed Ones. Uranus imprisoned them, but Zeus later freed them and gained powerful allies in his war against the Titans. The Hecatoncheires hurled huge rocks at the Titans, helping Zeus and the other Olympians win. After the victory, they guarded the defeated Titans in Tartarus, a deep part of the underworld. Homer gives one of the brothers another name: the gods called him Briareus, while mortals knew him as Aegaeon.

A cathedral is the main church of a Christian diocese, the area overseen by a bishop. It contains the bishop’s official seat, or “cathedra,” which gives the building its name. Cathedrals are often large and richly decorated, but their role as the bishop’s church—not their size or appearance—is what makes them cathedrals. Many have tall spires, stained-glass windows, and other striking architectural features. Mexico City’s Metropolitan Cathedral is one example. Another stands in Guadalajara, the capital of the Mexican state of Jalisco and Mexico’s second-most-populous city. Guadalajara’s central cathedral combines Gothic features, such as pointed forms and tall spires, with Baroque influences, which often include elaborate decoration.

The Wendigo is a dangerous supernatural being in the oral traditions of several Indigenous peoples of North America. It is associated with bitter winter, starvation, and an endless hunger for human flesh. Some accounts portray it as a giant with ice inside its body; others describe a spirit that drives people toward cannibalism or a person transformed into a Wendigo. No matter how much it eats, its appetite only grows. Wendigo stories vary between communities, so there is no single version of the creature. They are found among peoples including the Cree, Ojibwe, and Innu, whose ancestral languages belong to the Algonquian language family, spoken across parts of the Great Lakes region and northeastern North America.

Fáfnir is a dragon or serpent in Norse and Germanic legend whose story appears in the Völsunga saga. He is a son of Hreiðmarr and takes possession of a cursed treasure taken from the dwarf Andvari, including a ring. His greed transforms him into a dragon, and he guards the treasure. The hero Sigurd learns Fáfnir’s route to a stream where the dragon drinks, digs a trench beneath that path, and waits there to strike him from below. After killing Fáfnir, Sigurd roasts the dragon’s heart. When he tastes its blood, he gains the ability to understand birds. Fáfnir’s story links greed and cursed wealth with Sigurd’s rise as a legendary hero.

“Lamb of God” is a Christian title for Jesus that presents him as an innocent, blameless sacrifice for human sin. In ancient Jewish worship, lambs were among the animals offered as sacrifices, especially at Passover. Christians connect this imagery with Isaiah 53, which describes a suffering servant led to slaughter like a lamb, and with Jesus’ death on the cross. In the Gospel of John, John the Baptist sees Jesus and calls him “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” John the Baptist is also the figure who baptized Jesus in the Jordan River. The title expresses the Christian belief that Jesus willingly gave his life to bring forgiveness and reconciliation with God.

Halal is an Arabic term meaning “permissible” or “allowed” under Islamic law. It can describe actions and behavior, but it is especially common when discussing food Muslims may eat. For example, pork and alcohol are not halal; they are haram, meaning forbidden. Meat from permitted animals must also be prepared according to Islamic dietary rules to be considered halal. Another Islamic practice concerns preparation for prayer rather than food: Muslims ordinarily perform wudu, a ritual washing of specified parts of the body, including the hands, face, arms, and feet. When water is unavailable or cannot be used, a dry form of purification called tayammum may be performed using clean earth, such as dust or sand.

In Greek mythology, the eagle is a powerful bird closely associated with Zeus, king of the gods. After the Titan Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans, Zeus had him chained to a mountain in the Caucasus. An eagle came each day to eat Prometheus’s liver, which grew back overnight, making the punishment repeat. The eagle appears in another story about Ganymede, a beautiful Trojan youth. Zeus took the form of an eagle and carried Ganymede to Mount Olympus, home of the gods, where the youth became their cupbearer, serving them drinks. These two myths connect the eagle with Zeus’s power, but its role differs: it punishes Prometheus and carries Ganymede to Olympus.

Sawm is the Arabic name for Islamic fasting, one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Its obligatory observance takes place during Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar. From dawn until sunset each day, Muslims who are able to fast abstain from food and drink. They end each day’s fast after sunset with a meal called iftar and may eat again before dawn. Fasting is a way to practice self-discipline, strengthen devotion to God, and remember people who lack enough to eat. People who are ill, traveling, pregnant, or otherwise unable to fast may be excused under Islamic rules. Ramadan concludes with Eid al-Fitr, a festival marking the end of the month of fasting.

Stealing fire is a recurring mythological motif in which a trickster or culture hero takes fire from a god or another supernatural keeper and brings it to human beings. The gift changes human life: fire provides warmth and light, helps people cook food, and makes many crafts possible. Because the flame belongs to a powerful being, taking it often brings punishment. In Greek mythology, the Titan Prometheus defied Zeus by giving divine fire to humanity. Zeus had Prometheus bound to a mountain, where an eagle repeatedly ate his liver, which grew back each day. In some Native American stories, Coyote also steals fire and is punished when his tail turns white. These stories explore both the benefits of fire and the risks of challenging supernatural authority.

In ancient Egyptian belief, a person’s heart held a record of their thoughts and actions, so it was left in the body during mummification as evidence of how they had lived. After death, the jackal-headed god Anubis oversaw the weighing of the heart against the feather of Ma’at, who represented truth and justice. A heart that balanced with the feather showed that the person was worthy to enter the afterlife; a heart made too heavy by wrongdoing could be devoured by the creature Ammit. This judgment scene appears in the Book of the Dead, a collection of funerary texts that became widely used during the New Kingdom. It developed from older Egyptian traditions found in the Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts.

Prayer is a way of communicating with or worshiping God, either alone or with others. It can include spoken words, silent reflection, praise, or requests for help. In the Baháʼí Faith, believers choose from prescribed obligatory prayers and recite one each day; these are distinct from other prayers they may say whenever they wish. In Islam, the formal prayer called ṣalāh, or salat, is performed five times daily at prescribed times. Its beginning is traditionally announced by the muezzin’s call to prayer, known as the adhan. During ṣalāh, Muslims face Mecca and follow a sequence of recitations and movements. This structured worship differs from informal personal supplication, called duʿāʾ, which can be offered at other times.

Gilgamesh is the legendary king of Uruk and the hero of a Mesopotamian epic. At first, he is so powerful that the goddess Aruru creates a wild man, Enkidu, to challenge him. After wrestling, the two become close friends. Together they defeat Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest, and kill the Bull of Heaven, which a goddess sends against Uruk after Gilgamesh rejects her. The gods sentence Enkidu to die, and his death leaves Gilgamesh terrified of his own mortality. Seeking everlasting life, Gilgamesh travels across the Waters of Death to find Utnapishtim, a survivor of a great flood. Gilgamesh obtains a plant that can restore youth, but a serpent steals it. He returns to Uruk without the immortality he sought.

A magic ring is a recurring object in myths and stories that gives its wearer supernatural powers, such as protection, transformation, or invisibility. In some Arthurian legends, rings make the knights Perceval or Gareth invulnerable, meaning they cannot be harmed. A ring also appears in the Middle English poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight: while Gawain is staying at the Green Knight’s castle, the knight’s disguised wife offers him a ring, but he refuses it and later accepts a silk belt instead. One of the most famous magic rings is the One Ring in J. R. R. Tolkien’s stories. Sauron forged it in the fires of Orodruin, or Mount Doom, to control the other Rings of Power. Its inscription is written in Black Speech, and wearing it can make someone invisible.

Canonization is the Catholic Church’s formal declaration that a deceased person is a saint and may be honored by the Church. It normally follows beatification, an earlier step that permits more limited public veneration. The Church investigates the person’s life, and the process usually includes confirmation of miracles attributed to that person’s intercession, meaning prayers asking the person to appeal to God on someone’s behalf. One famous example is Stephen I, Hungary’s first king, who was canonized in 1083. At that time, Pope Gregory VII was the head of the Catholic Church. Gregory VII is also remembered for his conflict with Emperor Henry IV during the Investiture Controversy, a dispute over who had the authority to appoint church leaders.

The Pyramid Texts are a collection of ancient Egyptian funerary spells inscribed on the walls of royal pyramid burial chambers during the Old Kingdom. Their earliest known examples appear in the pyramid of King Unas at Saqqara. The spells were meant to help a deceased ruler reach the afterlife, overcome dangers, and gain a place among the gods. One famous composition within the Pyramid Texts is the Cannibal Hymn, also found in Unas’s pyramid. It describes the dead king consuming gods to take in their powers. This startling image is symbolic: it expresses the belief that the king could become powerful enough to live forever in the divine world.

Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God is a sermon preached by the minister Jonathan Edwards in 1741 at Enfield, Connecticut. It became one of the best-known sermons of the First Great Awakening, a period of intense Christian religious revival in colonial America. Edwards warned his listeners that sinners faced God’s judgment and could not save themselves through their own strength. In a striking image, he compared a sinner to a spider held by a thread over a fiery pit, showing how close that person was to Hell and how completely they depended on God’s mercy. The sermon urged listeners to recognize the danger of sin and turn to God. Its vivid language and urgent message helped make Edwards a leading voice of the revival.

Speaking in tongues, also called glossolalia, is a Christian practice in which a person speaks in words or sounds believed to be inspired by God. In the New Testament book of Acts, a sound like a mighty rushing wind accompanies the arrival of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost. Jesus’s followers then speak in languages that visitors from many regions recognize as their own. The apostle Paul later discusses speaking in tongues and interpreting them in his First Letter to the Corinthians. Some Christians understand tongues as human languages, while others describe them as spiritual speech. In Pentecostal Christianity, speaking in tongues is often seen as evidence that a believer has been baptized by the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is a member of the Trinity and is often pictured as a dove in Christian art.

Death is the end of a living being’s life, but people also explore it as a question about what, if anything, comes afterward. Religions and philosophies offer different views, including an afterlife, rebirth, or the belief that life simply ends. In The Prophet, Lebanese-American poet and painter Kahlil Gibran presents these questions through Almustafa’s farewell conversations with the people of the fictional island of Orphalese. Speaking about death, Almustafa compares fear of it to “the trembling of the shepherd when he stands before the king,” suggesting that fear can accompany an encounter with something profound. Near the book’s end, he calls departure “a moment of rest upon the wind” and says “another woman shall bear me,” expressing hope for renewal rather than treating death only as an ending.

Witchcraft is the supposed use of supernatural or magical powers, often by people called witches. Ideas about witchcraft vary across cultures: some traditions describe magic as helpful or protective, while others portray it as harmful or forbidden. Fear of harmful witchcraft has sometimes led to accusations and persecution. A famous example is the Salem witch trials in colonial Massachusetts in 1692. The panic began after Betty Parris and Abigail Williams reported strange afflictions that people blamed on witches. Tituba, an enslaved woman from the West Indies, was accused and then named Sarah Good and Sarah Osborne as witches. The accusations spread, and 19 people were executed after being convicted of witchcraft. Today, the trials are often studied as an example of how fear and unsupported accusations can have devastating consequences.

Pork is the meat of a pig. Jewish and Islamic dietary laws both prohibit eating it. In the Torah’s book of Leviticus, animals must have split hooves and chew their cud to be permitted as food. Pigs have split hooves but do not chew their cud, so pork is forbidden. The Hebrew name for the broader system of Jewish dietary laws is kashrut. Food that meets its rules, which also cover how some foods are prepared, is called kosher; food that does not is called treif. In Islam, permitted food is called halal, and pork is not halal. These rules help observant Jews and Muslims make choices about what they eat as part of their religious practice.

Shabbat candles are traditionally lit in Jewish homes shortly before sunset on Friday to welcome Shabbat, the weekly day of rest. They are often placed near the table for the evening meal, and their lighting is accompanied by a blessing. At that meal, a separate blessing called kiddush is recited over wine or grape juice. Shabbat continues through Saturday and ends after nightfall with a ceremony called Havdalah, which marks the transition back to the ordinary week. Havdalah uses wine or grape juice, fragrant spices, and a special candle with several wicks that make a braided flame. The flame is held up during the ceremony, and the candle is often extinguished in the wine afterward. Unlike the Friday candles, the Havdalah candle is lit at the end of Shabbat.

Horse sacrifice was a ritual in several ancient Indo-European traditions, often linked to warfare, royal power, and claims of sovereignty. In Rome, the Equus October involved sacrificing a horse from a victorious chariot team after a race held in honor of Mars, the god of war. In Vedic tradition, the Ashvamedha was a royal horse sacrifice. A consecrated stallion roamed for a year, protected by the ruler’s warriors; allowing it to pass through a territory signaled acceptance of the ruler’s authority, while stopping it could lead to battle. The horse was then brought back for a ceremony conducted by Brahmin priests. Scholars have suggested that such rites may share roots in older Proto-Indo-European practices, though the Roman and Vedic ceremonies were not identical.

The Prose Edda, also called the Younger Edda, is a medieval Icelandic work compiled by Snorri Sturluson. It preserves many Norse myths and helped later generations learn about the gods. One of its main sections, Gylfaginning, tells stories about the creation of the world and the death of Baldr, a beloved god. In its creation story, Odin, the chief of the Norse gods, and his brothers Vili and Vé kill the primordial giant Ymir. They then use parts of Ymir’s body to make the world, including the sky from his skull. Odin is also known for hanging himself from Yggdrasil, the world tree, to gain wisdom. The Prose Edda is different from the Poetic Edda, a separate collection of Norse poems.

Kitsune are fox spirits in Japanese folklore that can change shape, sometimes taking human form. They appear in stories as clever, mysterious beings that may help people or trick them. Some legends say a kitsune grows additional tails as it becomes older and wiser, with the most powerful having as many as nine. Kitsune are especially associated with Inari, a kami, or divine spirit, in Shinto, Japan’s native religion. Inari is linked with rice, agriculture, and prosperity, and foxes are often portrayed as Inari’s messengers rather than as Inari itself. Statues of foxes can be seen at shrines dedicated to Inari, including the major Fushimi Inari shrine complex in Kyoto.

Sokushinbutsu was a rare Japanese Buddhist ascetic practice in which monks tried to preserve their own bodies after death through years of extreme fasting and ritual austerities. Practitioners gradually reduced what they ate, sometimes living on nuts, roots, and bark, while continuing to meditate and perform religious rites. Near death, a monk might enter a small chamber to meditate; afterward, others would check whether the body had remained preserved. Not every attempt succeeded. Sokushinbutsu is often discussed alongside Shugendo, a Japanese mountain-ascetic tradition that blends Buddhist practices with other religious traditions. Its practitioners, called yamabushi, train in sacred mountains and perform demanding physical disciplines and esoteric Buddhist rites. Both traditions emphasize spiritual training through hardship, though not all yamabushi practiced sokushinbutsu.

Al-Baqarah, meaning “The Cow,” is the second and longest surah, or chapter, of the Quran. It covers many subjects, including faith, worship, moral guidance, and stories of earlier communities. One passage mentions Harut and Marut, two figures associated with a test involving magic; scholars have debated whether they should be understood as fallen angels. Al-Baqarah also contains verse 2:255, known in Arabic as Ayat al-Kursi, or the Throne Verse. This verse describes God’s complete knowledge and authority over the heavens and the earth. Many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi for protection and as a reminder of God’s power.

Jah is a name for God used in Rastafari, also called Rastafarianism. It comes from a shortened form of the Hebrew divine name represented by the tetragrammaton, the four Hebrew letters used to write God’s personal name in the ancient Israelite tradition. Rastafari is an Afrocentric Abrahamic religious movement that developed in Jamaica in the early 20th century. It draws on the Bible and emphasizes African identity and connections to Ethiopia. Many Rastafari followers regard Haile Selassie I, who became emperor of Ethiopia in 1930, as the second coming of Christ, though beliefs vary among followers. Rastafari has no single central authority and includes groups known as “mansions,” such as the Nyabinghi, Bobo Ashanti, and Twelve Tribes of Israel.

Cernunnos was a Celtic or Gallo-Roman deity associated with animals, the natural world, and fertility. He is usually shown with antlers, suggesting a close connection to wild creatures and the forests where they live. One of the few surviving ancient images of him appears on the Pillar of the Nautes, a Gallo-Roman monument commissioned by a guild of boatmen in ancient Paris during the reign of the Roman emperor Tiberius. The pillar’s carved blocks were discovered beneath Notre-Dame Cathedral in 1710. Because so little written evidence about Cernunnos survives, images like this are important clues to how people in Roman-era Gaul pictured and honored him.

Inti was the Inca god of the Sun, whose light and warmth helped crops grow. He was also important to Inca rule: emperors traced their ancestry to him, presenting their authority as divinely given. Inti’s principal sanctuary was Qorikancha in Cusco, the Inca capital. The temple complex’s Quechua name is commonly translated as “Golden Enclosure,” and its walls were once sheathed in gold, a metal associated with the Sun. After the Spanish conquest, the Church of Santo Domingo was built on Qorikancha’s foundations. Worship of Inti shows how the Incas connected the Sun’s importance in daily life with the power of their rulers.

Scylla is a sea monster in Greek mythology who appears in Book 12 of Homer’s Odyssey. She lurks beside a narrow sea passage traditionally identified with the Strait of Messina, between Italy and Sicily. Across the water is Charybdis, a dangerous whirlpool that can swallow an entire ship. Odysseus must steer between these two threats on his journey home from the Trojan War. Following advice from the sorceress Circe, he sails closer to Scylla rather than risk losing his whole ship to Charybdis. Scylla reaches down with her six heads and seizes six of his sailors, one for each head. Their story gives us the expression “between Scylla and Charybdis,” meaning a choice between two dangers.

The City of God is a major work by Augustine of Hippo, a North African bishop and influential Christian theologian. He began writing it after Rome was sacked in 410, when some people blamed Christianity for the empire’s troubles. Augustine argued that history involves two “cities”: the City of God, shaped by love of God, and the earthly city, shaped by selfish ambition and the desire for power. These are not simply two places on a map; they describe different ways people live and what they value. The work also explores government, justice, war, and humanity’s ultimate destiny. Augustine wrote another famous book, Confessions, in which he recalls stealing pears as a teenager and describes his conversion from Manichaeism to Christianity.

In Christian theology, Hell is the realm of punishment for the wicked after death, though Christians differ in how they understand its nature. It is also the setting of Inferno, the first part of Dante Alighieri’s 14th-century poem The Divine Comedy. Dante imagines Hell as nine descending circles, where sinners receive punishments suited to their misdeeds. In the second circle, for example, those punished for lust are tossed about by an endless storm. The pilgrim Dante travels through Hell with Virgil, an ancient Roman poet whose writing Dante admired. Virgil represents human reason and helps Dante understand what he sees, but he cannot accompany him into Paradise. Dante’s vivid nine-circle journey is a literary vision, not a description that all Christians accept as doctrine.

A shimenawa is a sacred rope used in Shinto, a Japanese religious tradition. Traditionally made from rice straw or hemp, it marks a place or object as sacred. You might see one wrapped around a tree or rock, or hung at a shrine. These ropes show that the marked place is connected with kami, beings often described as gods or spirits in Shinto. Kami may be associated with natural features as well as shrine spaces. Shimenawa can vary in size, and some are several feet thick. By marking a boundary, the rope reminds visitors to treat the place with respect.

The Book of Daniel is part of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. Its stories follow Daniel, a Jewish exile living in Babylon, who interprets dreams and remains faithful to God despite pressure from powerful rulers. One ruler, King Nebuchadnezzar II, dreams of a colossal statue with a golden head, a silver chest and arms, a bronze middle, iron legs, and feet made partly of iron and clay. Daniel explains that the golden head represents Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom and that the other parts represent kingdoms that will follow it. Later, Daniel sees a vision of four beasts rising from the sea, including one with a “little horn.” Readers have interpreted these mysterious images in different ways, but both visions concern the rise and fall of earthly powers.

Cassandra was a princess of Troy and the daughter of King Priam and Queen Hecuba. In Greek mythology, Apollo, the god of light and prophecy and twin brother of Artemis, gave her the power to see the future. When Cassandra rejected his romantic advances, Apollo cursed her so that no one would believe her predictions, even when they were true. She warned the Trojans that their city would be destroyed by the Greek army, but they ignored her. Her story is tragic because she could see disaster coming yet could not persuade anyone to stop it. Today, calling someone a “Cassandra” can mean that they give accurate warnings that others refuse to take seriously.

Coatlicue is an earth and mother goddess in Aztec mythology. Her name means “Snake Skirt,” referring to the serpents shown in many images of her. According to a famous myth, Coatlicue was sweeping a temple when a ball of feathers fell from the sky. She tucked it into her clothing and became miraculously pregnant with Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec war god. Her daughter Coyolxauhqui and her four hundred sons, collectively called the Centzon Huitznahua, were outraged by the pregnancy and attacked her. The Centzon Huitznahua are associated with the southern stars. Huitzilopochtli was born ready for battle and defeated his siblings, making the story an important part of Aztec beliefs about the gods and the heavens.

Leto was a Titaness in Greek mythology and the daughter of the Titans Coeus and Phoebe. She became the mother of Apollo and Artemis, the twin children of Zeus. Zeus’s wife, Hera, was angry about Leto’s pregnancy and pursued her, so many places were afraid to offer Leto shelter. The island of Delos finally gave her refuge, and there she gave birth to the twins. Delos later became an important religious sanctuary dedicated to Apollo. Leto also appears in the story of Niobe, a queen who mocked her for having only two children while Niobe had many. Apollo and Artemis defended their mother’s honor by killing Niobe’s children. These stories connect Leto to both the birth of two major Greek gods and the sacred island of Delos.

The First Vatican Council was a major meeting of Catholic bishops convened by Pope Pius IX. It opened in December 1869 at Saint Peter’s Basilica in Rome, near the Vatican, the center of the papacy. The bishops discussed the authority of the pope and how the Church should respond to changes in the modern world. In 1870, they adopted a dogmatic constitution called Pastor aeternus, Latin for “Eternal Shepherd.” It affirmed the pope’s primacy and defined papal infallibility: under specific conditions, when the pope makes a definitive ruling on faith or morals for the whole Church, his teaching is held to be free from error. The council’s proceedings were suspended later in 1870 when the Kingdom of Italy captured Rome.

The Tridevi is a grouping of three major Hindu goddesses: Saraswati, Lakshmi, and Parvati. Its name means “three goddesses,” and it is often described as the feminine counterpart to the Trimurti, the grouping of the male deities Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. Saraswati is associated with wisdom, learning, music, and the arts. Traditionally the consort of Brahma, she is often shown holding or playing a veena, a stringed instrument. Lakshmi, the consort of Vishnu, is associated with wealth, prosperity, and good fortune. Parvati, the consort of Shiva, is associated with love, strength, and motherhood. Together, the Tridevi show how Hindu traditions honor divine power in feminine forms.

Tezcatlipoca was one of the most powerful deities in Aztec religion. His name means “Smoking Mirror,” a reference to the dark, reflective obsidian mirrors used in divination. He was associated with night, fate, rulership, sorcery, and conflict. Aztec stories describe several successive ages, each ruled by a different sun. In some accounts, Tezcatlipoca and Quetzalcoatl clashed over who would serve as the sun, and their struggle helped bring one age to an end and another into being. Quetzalcoatl, whose name means “Feathered Serpent,” was also associated with wind. These stories were part of a wider Aztec understanding of a changing world in which gods played a direct role in the creation and destruction of each age.

Idolatry means worshiping an idol or treating something created as if it were God. Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions condemn it because worship should be directed to God alone. The First Commandment forbids having other gods, and in Islam, associating anything with God in worship is called shirk. A famous example appears in the book of Exodus: while Moses is on Mount Sinai receiving the tablets of the Law, Aaron makes a golden calf from the Israelites’ jewelry. The people worship the calf, and when Moses returns and sees them, he breaks the tablets in anger. Religious traditions have also debated whether using images in worship counts as idolatry; the key issue is whether the image itself is being treated as divine.

Māui’s fish hook is a magical object in stories about Māui, a clever hero found in many Polynesian traditions. It is often described as being made from a jawbone. In one story, Māui uses the hook to catch the sun and slow its journey across the sky. The sun had been moving so quickly that people had too little daylight to work, prepare food, and finish their daily tasks. By restraining it, Māui gives them longer days. In other traditions, he casts his hook into the ocean and hauls up land, helping explain how islands came to exist. Details differ among Polynesian communities, but the hook is a symbol of Māui’s strength and ingenuity.

Dionysus, the Greek god of wine, is often called “twice-born” because his origin story includes two births. His mother, Semele, was a mortal woman who became pregnant by Zeus, the ruler of Olympus. According to the myth, Semele died when Zeus appeared before her in his full divine glory, but their unborn child survived. Zeus rescued the fetus and sewed it into his own thigh, where Dionysus continued to grow until he was ready to be born. His emergence from Zeus’s thigh is known as Dionysus’s second birth. This unusual story emphasizes Dionysus’s connection to both a mortal mother and a divine father, while explaining the name “twice-born.”
