The Trimurti is a Hindu grouping of three major deities linked to the cycle of the universe: Brahma is associated with creation, Vishnu with preservation, and Shiva with destruction or transformation. These roles describe how the world comes into being, continues, and changes, although Hindu traditions do not all understand the three gods in exactly the same way. Vishnu, the preserver, is especially important to his devotees and is worshipped through avatars, or earthly incarnations, including Rama and Krishna. Shiva is particularly revered in Shaivism, a major tradition within Hinduism. He is also known as the father of Ganesha and Kartikeya and is often shown with a blue throat, which tradition says he gained after drinking a dangerous poison.

Jhator is a Tibetan Buddhist funerary practice in which a dead person’s body is taken to a designated outdoor site and offered to scavenger birds, traditionally vultures, rather than being buried or cremated. It is sometimes called a “sky burial,” although the body is not buried. Ritual attendants called rogyapa prepare the remains by cutting the body into pieces so the birds can consume it. They may also break up the bones and mix them with tsampa, a flour made from roasted barley, so that little remains. The practice reflects Buddhist teachings about impermanence: after death, the body is no longer needed, and giving it to other living beings can be understood as an act of generosity.

Kiddush is a Jewish blessing recited over a cup of wine or grape juice to mark the holiness of Shabbat and festivals. Shabbat begins at sunset on Friday and continues until nightfall on Saturday. At the Friday-night meal, a person usually says Kiddush before the family begins eating, thanking God for the gift of Shabbat and recalling the creation of the world and the departure from Egypt. During Kiddush, the braided bread called challah is traditionally kept covered. After the blessing over the wine or grape juice, the challah is uncovered and a blessing is said over it before the meal. Kiddush is different from Kaddish, another Jewish prayer with a similar-sounding name.

Cadmus was a Phoenician prince whose father, Agenor, sent him to search for his abducted sister Europa. Unable to find her, Cadmus consulted Apollo’s oracle at Delphi and was told to follow a cow and build a city where it lay down. The cow led him to Boeotia, where he founded Thebes and became its first king. Before establishing the city, Cadmus killed a dragon sacred to the god Ares. Athena then advised him to sow the dragon’s teeth in the ground. Armed warriors sprang up from the earth and fought one another; the survivors were called the Spartoi and became ancestors of Theban noble families. Cadmus later married Harmonia, and their children included Ino, who became a figure in other Greek myths.

Narcissus was a beautiful youth in Greek mythology, the son of the river god Cephissus. A seer predicted that he would live to old age only if he never came to know himself. In the Roman poet Ovid’s telling, Narcissus rejects those who love him, including the nymph Echo. One rejected admirer prays that Narcissus will suffer the pain of loving someone who cannot love him back. Nemesis, the goddess of retribution, answers the prayer. At a pool, Narcissus sees his reflection but does not at first realize it is his own image. He falls in love with it and cannot turn away. He eventually dies, and a narcissus flower grows where he had been.

Muslims are people who follow Islam, a religion centered on belief in one God and the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad. Islam has long been practiced in West Africa, and enslaved West Africans carried their faith to the Americas. In January 1835, enslaved and freed Africans, many of them Muslims, rose up in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, against slavery and the authorities who upheld it. This uprising is called the Malê Rebellion because “Malê” was a term used in Brazil for Muslims. Their history is also part of North American history: Estevanico, an explorer who traveled with Spanish expeditions, and Bilali Fula, an enslaved man in what is now the United States, are among the earliest documented Muslims in North America whose names are known.

Draupnir was a magical gold ring belonging to Odin, the one-eyed god of the Aesir and the father of Baldr. Like an ordinary ring, it was a round band, but it had an extraordinary power: every ninth night, eight new rings of the same size and weight came from it. The dwarven brothers Brokkr and Eitri forged Draupnir during a contest sparked by Loki’s wager with dwarf smiths. Their rivals, the Sons of Ivaldi, made other treasures, including Odin’s spear Gungnir, which never missed its target. Draupnir later appeared in the story of Baldr’s death, when Odin placed the ring on his son’s funeral pyre. Its ability to multiply made it a symbol of abundance as well as a remarkable example of dwarven craftsmanship.

Bastet was an ancient Egyptian goddess associated with cats, protection, fertility, and the home. She was often shown as a woman with the head of a domestic cat, an animal Egyptians valued partly because it caught mice that threatened stored grain. Her principal cult center was Bubastis, a city in the eastern Nile Delta that hosted a major annual festival in her honor. Worshippers brought offerings to Bastet and sometimes dedicated cat statues or mummified cats to her. She could be seen as a gentle guardian, especially in contrast to Sekhmet, a fierce goddess usually shown with a lioness’s head. In Greek, Bastet was sometimes called Ailuros, a name connected with cats.

Ishtar was a major goddess in ancient Mesopotamian religion, associated with love, fertility, and war. She was closely identified with Inanna, a goddess worshipped in Sumer. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Ishtar proposes to the hero Gilgamesh, but he rejects her and criticizes the way she has treated past lovers. Angered, she asks Anu, a sky god, to send the Bull of Heaven against Gilgamesh’s city of Uruk. The bull causes destruction, but Gilgamesh and his companion Enkidu fight and kill it. Their victory has a serious consequence: the gods decide that Enkidu must die. This story shows both Ishtar’s power and the danger of angering a deity in Mesopotamian mythology.

Pope Pius IX led the Catholic Church from 1846 until his death in 1878, one of the longest papal reigns in history. During this period, Italy was becoming a unified country. In 1870, the Kingdom of Italy annexed Rome, ending the pope’s rule over the Papal States. Pius IX also issued the Syllabus of Errors, a document condemning ideas he saw as threats to Catholic teaching and authority, including the separation of church and state. An earlier event in his reign caused lasting controversy: in 1858, papal authorities took six-year-old Edgardo Mortara from his Jewish family in Bologna after learning that a household servant had secretly baptized him as an infant. Pius IX supported keeping the boy in Catholic care despite his parents’ protests.

Aegeus was a mythological king of Athens and the father of the hero Theseus. Before Theseus was born, Aegeus left a sword and sandals beneath a great rock at Troezen. He told the boy’s mother, Aethra, daughter of King Pittheus, that their son should retrieve them when he was strong enough to move the rock. Aethra raised Theseus there, and he later traveled to Athens. When Theseus sailed to Crete to face the Minotaur, Aegeus arranged for him to use white sails on the journey home if he survived, rather than the black sails carried on the outward voyage. Theseus succeeded but forgot to change the sails. Seeing the returning ship’s black sails, Aegeus mistakenly believed his son was dead and leapt into the sea in grief.

The Stoning of the Devil is a ritual performed during Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca. Pilgrims travel to Mina, a place near Mecca, where they throw small stones or pebbles at three targets called the jamarat, traditionally described as pillars. The action recalls the story of Ibrahim (Abraham), who rejected Satan’s attempts to lead him away from obeying God. Each throw symbolizes a refusal to give in to temptation and a commitment to do what is right. The ritual takes place during the days of Eid al-Adha, an important festival connected with Ibrahim’s faith and obedience. Although it is called “stoning,” pilgrims are not throwing stones at a person: the jamarat are symbolic targets.

Mount Athos is a mountain and self-governing monastic community on a peninsula in northern Greece, overlooking the Aegean Sea. Its twenty monasteries make it an important center of Eastern Orthodox Christianity. Monks there have long practiced hesychasm, a tradition of quiet, focused prayer that seeks closeness to God. The oldest monastery on Mount Athos is Great Lavra Monastery, founded in 963 by Athanasius the Athonite at the peninsula’s southeastern end. Its founding helped establish Mount Athos as a major center of monastic life, where communities of monks devote their days to prayer, worship, and work.

In the Book of Revelation, the last book of the New Testament, a vision describes four horsemen who appear as the first four seals of a scroll are opened. They are commonly associated with conquest, war, famine, and death. The fourth rider comes on a pale horse, a color that suggests sickness or a corpse. Unlike the other riders, he is explicitly named: he is Death. Revelation also says that Hades follows him. Here, Hades personifies the realm of the dead, rather than being another horseman. In Greek mythology, Hades is also the name of the god who rules the underworld. Together, Death and Hades make the final horseman’s arrival an image of widespread mortality.

Bifröst is a fiery, rainbow-like bridge in Norse mythology that connects Asgard, the realm of the gods, with Midgard, the world of humans. It allows the gods to travel between the two realms. Heimdall, a god known for his extraordinary sight and hearing, guards the bridge and watches for threats. He also carries the Gjallarhorn, a horn he is said to sound at the beginning of Ragnarök, the great battle that brings destruction to the Norse gods and their world. According to prophecy, Bifröst will be destroyed during Ragnarök. Although it is often called a rainbow bridge, its fiery nature makes it more than an ordinary rainbow: it is a vital link between worlds and a passage that must be protected.

Aliyah is the Hebrew term for the immigration of Jews to the Land of Israel. It literally means “going up,” reflecting the religious and historical importance of the land in Jewish life. Jews have moved there for many reasons, including religious commitment, family ties, and the hope of safety from persecution. Pogroms, or violent attacks on Jewish communities, and other forms of antisemitism led some Jews, including many from the Soviet Union, to make aliyah. After Israel became a state in 1948, it passed the Law of Return in 1950. This law gives Jews the right to immigrate to Israel and helped make aliyah a central part of the country’s approach to Jewish immigration.

Miaphysitism is a Christian teaching about the nature of Jesus Christ, especially associated with the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, and Ethiopian Orthodox churches. It says that Christ’s divinity and humanity are united in one incarnate nature: Jesus is fully God and fully human, and his humanity is not swallowed up by his divinity. The study of questions about who Christ is is called Christology. In 451, bishops meeting at the Council of Chalcedon in Bithynia defined Christ as existing in two natures, divine and human. Oriental Orthodox churches do not accept that definition. The disagreement concerns how best to describe the relationship between Christ’s divinity and humanity, not whether both are real.

Candomblé is an Afro-Brazilian religion that developed when enslaved Africans brought their religious traditions to Brazil, where those traditions interacted with local beliefs and Catholicism. Its followers honor orishas, spiritual beings associated with forces of nature and aspects of human life. Many of the orishas honored in Candomblé come from the religious heritage of the Yoruba people, whose traditional homeland, Yorubaland, lies mainly in southwestern Nigeria and extends into neighboring Benin. Candomblé ceremonies take place in temples called terreiros. There, a religious community may gather to sing, drum, dance, make offerings, and seek a connection with the orishas. Although practices vary among communities, these shared ceremonies and the honoring of orishas are central to the religion.

Ash Wednesday is a Christian observance that begins Lent, a season of repentance and preparation for Easter, when Christians celebrate Jesus’ resurrection. During Ash Wednesday services, a minister may mark a cross of ashes on each worshiper’s forehead. The ashes symbolize human mortality, and the minister may say, “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return,” echoing the Book of Genesis. Lent lasts roughly 40 days, not counting Sundays, recalling the 40 days Jesus spent fasting and facing temptation in the wilderness. During Lent, some Christians fast, give up luxuries, pray more often, or help others as ways to reflect on their lives and faith.

The Book of Esther is a book of the Hebrew Bible set at the Persian royal court. It tells how Esther, a Jewish woman who becomes queen, helps save her people with the aid of her cousin Mordecai. The king’s powerful vizier, Haman, becomes furious when Mordecai refuses to bow to him. Haman then persuades the king to issue a decree allowing the destruction of Jews throughout the empire. Esther risks approaching the king to reveal her identity and expose Haman’s plot. The danger is reversed, and Haman is executed on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai. These events are celebrated at Purim, the “Festival of Lots,” when the Book of Esther is read aloud as the Megillah.

The First Council of Nicaea was a meeting of Christian bishops convened by Emperor Constantine in 325 CE at Nicaea, in the Roman province of Bithynia. It addressed a dispute sparked by Arius, who taught that the Son was created and was not eternal in the same way as God the Father. The bishops rejected this teaching and produced the first version of the Nicene Creed, a statement of Christian belief. The creed declared that the Son is “of one substance” with the Father, meaning that Christ shares the Father’s divine nature. The creed was later expanded and is still recited in many churches today. A later tradition says Saint Nicholas slapped Arius at the council, but historians are uncertain whether that happened.

The Opening of the Mouth was an ancient Egyptian funerary ritual performed after mummification on a mummy or a statue of the deceased. Egyptians believed that death left a person unable to use their senses or perform basic actions in the afterlife. During the ceremony, priests touched the figure’s mouth with ritual tools while reciting prayers, symbolically restoring the person’s ability to eat, drink, breathe, and speak. One distinctive tool was the peseshkef, a forked implement that was often made of flint in early examples. The ritual helped prepare the deceased to live in the afterlife, where they would need these abilities again.

Bird metamorphoses in Greek mythology are stories in which people are transformed into birds, often after violence or a challenge to the gods. In one tale, Tereus assaults his wife Procne’s sister, Philomela, and cuts out her tongue to keep her silent. Philomela weaves a message revealing what happened. In revenge, Procne kills her son Itys and serves his flesh to Tereus. The gods eventually transform Procne, Philomela, and Tereus into birds, though accounts differ about which bird each becomes. Another story concerns the Pierides, a group of sisters who challenge the Muses to a singing contest. After losing, the Pierides are turned into birds, often identified as magpies, as punishment for their musical arrogance.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is a restorationist Christian church founded by Joseph Smith in 1830. Its members believe that God restored the original Christian church through Smith, whose teachings include the Book of Mormon and the Doctrine and Covenants. After Smith was killed in 1844, several groups formed. Brigham Young became the leader of the largest group of his followers and led them west to the Salt Lake Valley, in what is now Utah. The church is headquartered in Salt Lake City and is often called the LDS Church; its members are also sometimes called Mormons. In the nineteenth century, the church faced criticism over practices including polygamy, which it later officially abandoned. In 1978, it ended a restriction that had prevented Black men from being ordained to its priesthood.

Fire appears in many myths as a force that can destroy, transform, and give life. In Greek mythology, the Titan Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans, allowing them to cook, keep warm, and develop crafts. Zeus punished him by chaining him to a rock, where an eagle devoured his liver each day; it grew back each night. Fire also appears in the Greek underworld, where the river Phlegethon was said to flow with flames. The phoenix, a mythical bird that burns and rises again from its ashes, symbolizes fire’s power of destruction and renewal. In Norse mythology, Muspellheim is a realm of fire whose giant Surtr plays a destructive role at Ragnarok.

The Seven Deadly Sins are a traditional Christian list of seven principal vices: lust, wrath, pride, greed, envy, gluttony, and sloth. They are called “deadly” because they can lead people toward other sins and away from a virtuous life. The familiar list developed over time rather than appearing as a single list in the Bible. An important early influence was Evagrius Ponticus, a fourth-century Christian monk who lived among monks in the Egyptian desert. He described eight destructive thoughts that could distract people from spiritual life. His list included vainglory, or an excessive desire for praise, and dejection, a form of discouragement. Evagrius’s ideas later influenced John Cassian and helped shape the Christian teaching that became known as the Seven Deadly Sins.

In Norse mythology, crying plays a part in two stories. After the beloved god Baldr dies, the ruler of the realm of the dead agrees to let him return if every living thing weeps for him. Almost everyone does, but Loki disguises himself as a giantess named Þökk and refuses to cry. Because one being has withheld her tears, Baldr cannot return from Hel. Crying is also linked to Freyja, a goddess associated with love and beauty. When her husband, Óðr, is away, she searches for him and weeps; her tears are said to become red gold. In one story, refusing to cry keeps a god among the dead, while in the other, a goddess’s tears become something precious.

Atlantis is a legendary island civilization described by the ancient Athenian philosopher Plato in his dialogues Timaeus and Critias. In the story, Egyptian priests tell the Athenian lawmaker Solon about an island beyond the Pillars of Hercules, the strait now called Gibraltar. Plato says Atlantis was “larger than Libya and Asia put together” and became a powerful kingdom that fought ancient Athens. Its people eventually grew arrogant and sought to conquer other lands, making the tale a warning about pride and the misuse of power. According to the account, great earthquakes and floods caused Atlantis to sink beneath the sea. Although people have searched for it, there is no reliable evidence that Atlantis existed as Plato described it.

Moksha is a spiritual goal in many Hindu traditions: liberation from samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. Actions create karma, which can keep a person bound to that cycle. Different Hindu traditions describe the path to moksha in different ways, including spiritual knowledge, devotion, and selfless action. In Sikh teachings, liberation from rebirth and the bonds of karma is commonly called mukti. Sikhs seek to overcome the Five Thieves—harmful tendencies such as anger, greed, and pride—by developing virtues and living in remembrance of God. Moksha and mukti are often compared with Buddhist nirvana because all involve freedom from rebirth, but Hindu, Sikh, and Buddhist traditions explain that freedom in different ways.

Helios was the Greek god and personification of the Sun. Each day, he was said to drive a shining chariot across the sky, bringing daylight to the world. He was traditionally named as the father of Phaethon, whose story is told in Ovid’s Metamorphoses. Wanting to prove that Helios was his father, Phaethon asked to drive the solar chariot for one day. Helios warned him that even the gods would struggle to control its powerful horses, but Phaethon insisted. Once in the sky, he lost control: the chariot veered too high and then too close to the earth, scorching it. To stop the destruction, Zeus struck Phaethon with a thunderbolt, killing him. The story shows why guiding the Sun was a task only Helios could safely perform.

The Five Suns is an Aztec creation account that describes history as a series of cosmic ages, each called a “sun.” According to the story, four earlier worlds were created and then destroyed by catastrophes, including floods and violent winds. The present world is the fifth Sun. Its Nahuatl name is Nahui Ollin, meaning “Four Movement,” after a day sign in the Aztec calendar. “Movement” also points to this age’s predicted end: earthquakes. The account presents the world as something that has changed dramatically before and could change again, rather than as a place that has always existed in its present form.

Water is important in several New Testament accounts of Jesus and the early Christian community. At a wedding feast in Cana, Jesus performed a miracle by turning water into wine. In another Gospel account, he walked on the water of the Sea of Galilee during a storm. Water also became central to baptism, a rite of initiation into the Christian community associated with repentance and a new life of faith. A person could be baptized by being immersed in water or by having water poured over them. John the Baptist baptized people as a sign of repentance, and the Gospels describe him baptizing Jesus in the Jordan River. These stories and practices give water a meaning beyond its everyday role as a substance essential to life.

A sermon is a spoken religious message, often delivered by a minister during Christian worship. It may explain a passage from the Bible, teach a belief, or ask listeners to think about their actions and their relationship with God. Sermons can also be delivered outside a church, especially by evangelists who hope to reach new audiences. During the First Great Awakening, a period of intense religious enthusiasm in colonial America, preachers such as George Whitefield and Jonathan Edwards gave sermons that urged people to examine their faith. In 1741, Edwards delivered a famous sermon called Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God. He pictured a sinner held above the fiery pit of Hell like a spider, using the image to warn listeners about divine judgment.

Cupid’s arrows are magical weapons carried by Cupid, the winged Roman god of desire and the counterpart of the Greek god Eros. He is often shown with a bow and a quiver of arrows, which he uses to change how people feel rather than to injure them. In particular, a gold-tipped arrow makes the person it strikes fall in love, sometimes suddenly and intensely. Other versions of the myth describe a lead-tipped arrow that makes someone reject love instead. These arrows help explain why attraction can seem unexpected or beyond a person’s control. Cupid also appears in the story of Psyche, a mortal who becomes his lover and is eventually made immortal. When a myth describes Cupid using a golden arrow to kindle an emotion, that emotion is love.

Frashokereti is the final renewal of the world in Zoroastrianism. It is sometimes compared with an apocalypse or the end times in other religions, but its main purpose is not simply to destroy the Earth: it is to free creation from evil and make it perfect and immortal. Zoroastrian accounts describe a future savior called the Saoshyant, who is associated with the resurrection of the dead and the world’s final purification. The dead return to life, evil is defeated, and the harm and suffering that have marked the world come to an end. Frashokereti therefore marks both the end of the present struggle between good and evil and the beginning of a renewed existence in which creation is restored.

A princess is the daughter of a king or queen and a familiar character in folktales. Stories often use princesses to explore questions of identity, kindness, and who is considered worthy of marriage. In Hans Christian Andersen’s tale The Princess and the Pea, a queen tests a visitor who claims to be a princess by hiding a pea beneath twenty mattresses and twenty featherbeds. The visitor feels it despite all the bedding, which the queen takes as proof that she is truly royal. In an Italian folktale, a cloven-footed youth earns the chance to marry a princess after treating a talking eel kindly. Though the plots differ, both stories feature a princess as a royal bride and use an unusual event to shape her future.

Sodom is a city in the Book of Genesis, the first book of the Bible. It is usually named alongside Gomorrah, another city destroyed by God with fire and sulfur, traditionally called “fire and brimstone.” Before the destruction, Abraham asks God to spare Sodom if ten righteous people can be found there, but the city is not spared. Abraham’s nephew Lot lives in Sodom and is warned to leave with his family. Lot escapes with his daughters, but his wife looks back toward the city despite a warning not to and becomes a pillar of salt. Later Jewish writings, including the Talmud, also describe the people of Sodom as cruel and inhospitable to strangers.

The Samaritans are a small ethnoreligious community that traces its ancestry to the ancient Israelites. Their religion is based on the Torah, but unlike Judaism, Samaritan tradition identifies Mount Gerizim, near the city of Nablus, rather than Jerusalem as the place God chose for worship. Samaritans have their own priesthood and still gather on Mount Gerizim to offer a Passover sacrifice each year. According to one Samaritan account of their history, their ancestors rejected Eli as high priest and followed Uzzi to Mount Gerizim. Samaritans also appear in the New Testament: in Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan, a Samaritan helps an injured traveller whom others have passed by.

Isra and Mi'raj is the Islamic account of the Night Journey and Ascension of the Prophet Muhammad. In the first part, called Isra, Muhammad travels by night from Mecca to Jerusalem on Buraq, a miraculous mount described in hadith as a white creature larger than a donkey but smaller than a mule. The journey ends at the sacred precinct in Jerusalem where the Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock stand today. In the second part, called Mi'raj, Muhammad ascends through the heavens, encounters earlier prophets, and comes into God’s presence. Islamic tradition connects this experience with the establishment of the five daily prayers. The account is an important expression of Jerusalem’s sacred place in Islam.

The Epistle to the Romans is a New Testament letter attributed to Paul the Apostle. He wrote it to Christians in Rome, a community he had not yet visited, to explain important ideas about faith and salvation. Paul argues that God makes people righteous, or puts them in a right relationship with him, through faith in Jesus Christ rather than through obeying religious law alone. He also explores how God’s grace relates to the law and discusses Israel’s place in God’s purposes. Romans later became especially important to Christian thinkers such as Martin Luther, who drew on it when teaching justification by faith. Although Paul is named as the letter’s author, someone else wrote down his words: near the end, in Romans 16:22, the scribe greets the readers and gives his name as Tertius.

Magical rings in Norse mythology can bring wealth, but they can also carry a curse. Andvari, a dwarf, owned a ring that Loki took while gathering gold to pay a ransom for accidentally killing Otr, who had taken the shape of an otter. The gods had to cover Otr’s pelt with gold, and Andvari’s ring was used to hide its final uncovered hair. Andvari cursed the treasure, which later came into the possession of Fafnir, a dragon who guarded it greedily. Another famous magical ring is Draupnir, which belongs to Odin. Every ninth night, eight new rings of equal weight appear from it. The dwarf smiths Brokkr and Eitri forged Draupnir as one of the gifts they made during a contest with Loki.

Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth, the fire at the center of a home where families gathered and cooked. She was also linked to the safety and stability of Rome itself. In her sanctuary in the Roman Forum, a sacred flame was kept burning as a symbol of the city’s well-being. The six priestesses who tended this fire were called the Vestal Virgins. Chosen as girls, they took a vow of chastity and traditionally served for thirty years. One Vestal Virgin in Roman legend was Rhea Silvia, the mother of Romulus and Remus. Vesta was the Roman equivalent of the Greek goddess Hestia, who was also associated with the hearth.

Lydia of Thyatira appears in the Book of Acts, the New Testament book about the early Christian church and the travels of the apostles. She was a seller of purple goods, which were valuable because purple dye was expensive. Although she came from Thyatira, Paul met her in Philippi, a city in Macedonia. There, Lydia listened as Paul spoke to a group gathered near a river. Acts says that she accepted his message, and she and her household were baptized. She then persuaded Paul and his companions to stay at her home, offering them a place to gather and rest. Later in Philippi, the city’s magistrates ordered Paul and Silas beaten and jailed. Lydia is remembered as an early Christian convert whose hospitality helped the missionaries.

A mythic hero is a central figure in a traditional story whose life or adventures follow patterns found in many cultures. In a comparative study, Lord Raglan described 22 incidents that often appear in heroic legends, such as an unusual birth, a struggle for power, and a remarkable death. Not every hero fits all 22 incidents. Joseph Campbell explored another pattern, the monomyth or Hero’s Journey, in his 1949 book The Hero with a Thousand Faces. Campbell organized the journey into departure, initiation, and return: a hero leaves the familiar world, faces trials and transformation, then comes back changed. Some stories include a descent into the underworld followed by a return. These patterns help scholars compare myths without claiming that every heroic tale is identical.

Guru Gobind Singh was the tenth and final human Guru, or spiritual teacher, of Sikhism. In 1699, at Anandpur Sahib, he initiated the Khalsa, a community of Sikhs committed to a shared religious discipline. Members of the Khalsa wear the Five Ks as visible signs of that commitment: kesh (uncut hair), kangha (a comb), kara (a steel bracelet), kachera (special shorts), and kirpan (a ceremonial sword). Guru Gobind Singh also decided that no human Guru would succeed him. Instead, he declared the Guru Granth Sahib, Sikhism’s sacred scripture, to be the community’s eternal Guru and spiritual authority. His leadership helped shape Sikh identity through both the founding of the Khalsa and the lasting importance he gave to the scripture.

Sati was a historical practice in some Hindu communities in which a widow died on her deceased husband’s funeral pyre, usually by being burned alive. It was never followed by all Hindus, and its prevalence varied across regions and periods. Some accounts described widows as choosing sati, but others faced strong social pressure or coercion, so it is important not to assume every death was voluntary. Hindu reformers challenged the practice, including Ram Mohan Roy, who argued against it in the early nineteenth century. In 1829, Lord William Bentinck, the British governor-general of India, issued a regulation prohibiting sati in the Bengal Presidency. The ban later extended to other areas under British rule. Today, sati is illegal in India.

Minos was a mythological king of Crete, an island in Greece. When Athens came under his power, he required it to send seven young men and seven young women as tribute to the Minotaur, a creature with a human body and a bull’s head. The Minotaur was born to Minos’s wife, Pasiphaë, and a bull. To keep the creature confined, Minos commissioned the ingenious craftsman Daedalus to build the Labyrinth, a winding maze at Knossos. The Athenian hero Theseus eventually entered the Labyrinth and killed the Minotaur. After Daedalus helped Theseus escape, Minos kept the craftsman and his son Icarus from leaving Crete. They fled by flying on wings Daedalus made from feathers and wax.

Scientology is a modern religion founded in the United States by L. Ron Hubbard in the 1950s. It teaches that people are immortal spiritual beings, called thetans, whose experiences can affect their present lives. Scientologists use a practice called auditing to address those experiences. One account in Scientology’s teachings describes an extraterrestrial ruler named Xenu, who brought billions of beings to Earth about 75 million years ago. According to the account, Xenu arranged their deaths by placing them near volcanoes and setting off hydrogen bombs. Knowing both the religion’s name, Scientology, and the ruler’s name, Xenu, helps distinguish this story from other religious or science-fiction accounts involving extraterrestrials.

Horses appear often in Norse mythology, but the most famous is Sleipnir, the eight-legged steed ridden by the god Odin. Sleipnir’s unusual birth began when a builder offered to construct a wall around Asgard, the home of the gods, with help from his powerful stallion, Svaðilfari. The gods had agreed to a deadline, and when the builder came close to finishing on time, they told the trickster god Loki to stop him. Loki transformed into a female horse, or mare, and lured Svaðilfari away from the work. The wall was not completed by the deadline, and Loki later gave birth to Sleipnir. In this story, a horse is both the animal Loki becomes and the form of Odin’s remarkable mount.

Roman Catholicism is a branch of Christianity centered on the Roman Catholic Church. It recognizes the pope, the bishop of Rome, as its supreme earthly pastor and teaches that bishops carry on the ministry of Jesus’s apostles. Catholics worship through prayer and the Mass, which includes the Eucharist, and recognize seven sacraments, including baptism and confession. An important event in Catholic history was the Council of Trent, a gathering of church leaders that met in several sessions from 1545 to 1563. It was part of the church’s response to the Protestant Reformation. The council clarified Catholic teachings on justification, or how people are made right with God, and on the sacraments. It also called for reforms in the education of clergy.

Guinevere is the legendary queen of Britain and the wife of King Arthur in Arthurian tradition. Arthur’s court is associated with Camelot, where his knights gather as the Knights of the Round Table. His story also features the wizard Merlin, who advises him, and the famous sword Excalibur. In many later versions of the legend, Guinevere falls in love with Sir Lancelot, one of Arthur’s most celebrated knights. Their relationship causes conflict because it breaks the trust between Guinevere, Arthur, and Lancelot and threatens the unity of Arthur’s court. Stories about Guinevere vary, but her role as Arthur’s queen and her connection to Lancelot make her an important figure in the legends of King Arthur.

Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp tells of a poor young man who gains a magical lamp containing a genie able to grant his wishes. After an encounter with a scheming magician, Aladdin uses the lamp to change his fortunes, but must also protect it from someone who wants its power. Although the tale is widely associated with the Middle Eastern collection known as The Thousand and One Nights, it entered the European version through Antoine Galland’s early-18th-century French edition, rather than appearing in the earliest known Arabic manuscripts of the collection. Galland recorded hearing the story in Paris in 1709 from Hanna Diyab, a Syrian storyteller from Aleppo. Today, many people know Aladdin through Disney’s animated film and its 2019 live-action remake, which feature a street urchin, a genie, and the song “A Whole New World.”

The Thunderbird is a powerful supernatural bird found in many Indigenous North American traditions, including those of peoples of the Pacific Northwest. In some stories, its enormous wings create thunder when they beat, while its eyes or movements bring lightning. Stories about the Thunderbird differ among communities, so it does not have one fixed appearance or meaning. The Thunderbird also appears in the traditions of the Haida, whose homeland includes Haida Gwaii, a large archipelago off the northern coast of British Columbia. Haida artists are known for carving cedar poles that display family crests and tell stories connected to their histories. Bird figures, including the Thunderbird, may appear on such poles. These traditions show how the Thunderbird can connect powerful events in the sky with stories and artwork passed down through generations.

In Irish folklore, a banshee is a female spirit whose mournful cry warns that someone in a particular family is about to die. Her name comes from an Irish phrase meaning “woman of the fairy mound,” reflecting her connection to the spirit world. Stories describe her crying, shrieking, or wailing near a family’s home, sometimes with red eyes from continual weeping. The banshee does not usually cause the death; her voice is an omen, or sign, that it is approaching. Her lament resembles keening, a traditional Irish practice in which mourners voice their grief through wailing and song at a death or funeral. Knowing the difference helps: the spirit is the banshee, while the mournful vocal lament is called keening.

Creation ex nihilo is the Jewish and Christian doctrine that God brought the universe into existence from nothing, without using any preexisting matter. The Latin phrase ex nihilo means “from nothing.” The doctrine is commonly associated with the opening of Genesis, the first book of the Hebrew Bible, which begins, “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” Genesis chapter 1 describes God creating by divine command over six days, including light, the sky, land, plants, animals, and human beings. God then rests on the seventh day. The passage does not use the phrase “from nothing,” but Jewish and Christian thinkers have interpreted it, along with other teachings, as support for the belief that everything ultimately depends on God for its existence.

The Four Cups are four ritual cups of wine, or grape juice, drunk during the Passover Seder, the meal that retells the Israelites’ escape from slavery in Egypt. They mark important stages of the Seder: the opening blessing, the end of the retelling, the blessing after the meal, and the conclusion. The cups are linked to four promises God makes to the Israelites in Exodus 6:6–7: “I will bring you out” from Egypt, “I will rescue you” from slavery, “I will redeem you,” and “I will take you” as my people. Drinking the Four Cups helps participants celebrate and remember these promises of freedom and a lasting relationship with God.

Polyphemus is a one-eyed giant called a Cyclops and a son of Poseidon, the Greek god of the sea. In Homer’s Odyssey, Polyphemus lives on an island with other Cyclopes and traps the Ithacan king Odysseus and his crew inside his cave. Odysseus tells him that his name is “Nobody,” then gives him wine. While Polyphemus sleeps, Odysseus and his men blind him by driving a sharpened stake into his single eye. When the injured Cyclops calls for help, he says that “Nobody” is hurting him, so the other Cyclopes do not come to his aid. Odysseus and his surviving men escape the cave by clinging to the undersides of Polyphemus’s sheep as they leave to graze.

In Roman legend, the twin brothers Romulus and Remus were abandoned as infants beside the Tiber River, which flows through modern-day Rome. A female wolf, known as the she-wolf of Rome, found the babies and nursed them until a shepherd took them in. As adults, the brothers disagreed about where to build a city. Romulus was eventually credited with founding Rome, which was named after him. The image of the she-wolf feeding the twins became an enduring symbol of the city and its legendary beginnings. The story was important to Romans because it connected their city’s founding to divine protection: their father was said to be Mars, the god of war, and the river god Tiberinus was said to have saved them.

A shofar is a wind instrument used in Jewish worship, traditionally made from a ram’s horn. Unlike a trumpet, it has no valves; the player makes sounds by blowing through its narrow end. The shofar is sounded on Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, where its piercing blasts call people to reflect on their actions, repent, and remember their shared traditions. It is also heard at the end of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, which comes ten days after Rosh Hashanah. On Yom Kippur, many Jews fast and pray as they seek forgiveness and consider how to live better. After nightfall, a final shofar blast marks the end of the holy day and its fast.

Mary Magdalene was a follower of Jesus in the New Testament. Her name likely links her to Magdala, a town near the Sea of Galilee. Luke says that Jesus had driven seven demons out of her, and the Gospels place her among the women who followed him and went to his tomb after his crucifixion. She is a key witness to the empty tomb and the news of Jesus’s resurrection. In the Gospel of John, Mary finds the tomb empty and later sees the risen Jesus but mistakes him for a gardener. She recognizes him when he speaks her name, and he sends her to tell his disciples what she has seen. Mary Magdalene is distinct from Mary, the mother of Jesus, and Mary of Bethany, Martha’s sister.

Jocasta was the queen of Thebes in Greek mythology and the wife of King Laius. A prophecy warned that their infant son would kill Laius and marry Jocasta, so the baby was left to die. He survived and was raised in Corinth, unaware of his birth parents. Years later, he killed Laius at a crossroads without knowing the man was his father. He then solved the riddle of the Sphinx, a creature with a lion’s body and a human head, and became king of Thebes. As the new king, Oedipus married Jocasta. Neither knew that she was his birth mother, so the prophecy came true despite their attempt to prevent it. Their story is central to plays by the ancient Greek writer Sophocles.

Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was a Christian bishop in Roman North Africa whose ideas strongly shaped Western Christianity. He wrote about grace, human freedom, and evil, arguing that evil is not a substance of its own but an absence of good. In his autobiographical Confessions, he described his spiritual struggles and conversion to Christianity, including a youthful theft of pears that taught him about the attraction of doing wrong. After Rome was sacked in 410, some people blamed Christianity for the empire’s troubles. Augustine responded in The City of God, a work of theological history that contrasts the “earthly city,” shaped by love of self, with the “heavenly city,” shaped by love of God.

The Book of the Dead is a collection of ancient Egyptian funerary spells and instructions meant to help a deceased person travel safely through the afterlife. It became especially prominent during the New Kingdom and later periods, building on older traditions such as the Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts. Families often had its spells copied onto papyrus and placed in a burial for the dead person to use. One famous scene describes the judgment of the deceased before Osiris’s tribunal. Anubis, a god often shown with a jackal’s head, oversees the weighing of the person’s heart against the feather of Ma’at, which represents truth and justice. Egyptians believed the heart reflected a person’s conduct in life, so its weight helped determine whether that person was worthy of entering the afterlife.

In Greek mythology, the underworld is the realm where the dead go, ruled by Hades and his wife, Persephone. It is sometimes called Hades, after its ruler. Myths describe several regions within it: the Fields of Asphodel, where many ordinary souls dwell; Elysium, a place for favored souls; and Tartarus, a vast abyss far below the world of the living. After Zeus and the Olympian gods defeated the Titans, the Titans were imprisoned in Tartarus. Souls entering the underworld had to pass rivers such as the Styx, while the three-headed dog Cerberus guarded its entrance. Persephone spent part of each year there because she had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld.

Troy was an ancient city in northwestern Anatolia, at the site called Hisarlik in modern Turkey. In Greek mythology, it was the setting of the Trojan War, fought after Paris took Helen to Troy. The story of the war begins with the Judgment of Paris at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis. Their son Achilles led the Myrmidons, a group of Greek warriors. In the Iliad, Achilles kills the Trojan prince Hector to avenge the death of his close companion Patroclus. Another story tells how the Greeks finally captured Troy by hiding soldiers inside a huge wooden horse that the Trojans brought into the city. The priest Laocoön warned against the horse, but sea serpents attacked him and his sons.

The Eye of Horus is an ancient Egyptian emblem showing a stylized eye with distinctive markings. People wore it as an amulet because they believed it offered protection, healing, and restoration. Horus was a falcon-headed god who struggled with his rival Set. In one version of the myth, Horus’s eye was injured during their conflict, then restored by Thoth, the ibis-headed god of wisdom and writing. This story made the eye a symbol of becoming whole again after harm. The emblem appeared on jewelry and other objects, where it could represent both Horus’s restored eye and the hope that its protective power would help the person who carried it.

Romulus is the legendary founder and first king of Rome. According to Roman myth, he and his twin brother Remus were the sons of Rhea Silvia and the god Mars. After the twins were abandoned near the Tiber River, a she-wolf suckled them, and a shepherd later raised them. As adults, the brothers decided to found a city but disagreed about its location and who should rule it. They sought an answer through augury, interpreting the flight of birds as a sign from the gods. Romulus won the contest, but the quarrel continued. In a common version of the story, Remus crossed or mocked the boundary wall Romulus had marked out, and Romulus killed him. Romulus then named the new city Rome and became its first king.

John the Baptist was a Jewish prophet who appears in the New Testament Gospels. He preached in the wilderness, urging people to repent, or turn away from wrongdoing, and prepared them for Jesus’s arrival. The Gospels describe him wearing clothing made of camel hair and eating locusts and wild honey. Luke identifies him as the son of Elizabeth. John is called “the Baptist” because he baptized people with water as a sign of repentance. He also baptized Jesus in the Jordan River, which flows south from the Sea of Galilee into the Dead Sea. After Jesus’s baptism, the Gospels describe a voice from heaven calling Jesus beloved and saying it is well pleased with him. Baptism remains an important Christian practice.

A Hanukkah menorah is a nine-branched candleholder used during the eight nights of Hanukkah. The holiday celebrates the Maccabees’ rededication of the Second Temple in Jerusalem and recalls the tradition that a small supply of oil kept its lamp burning for eight days. Eight places on the menorah hold the festival lights, one for each night. On the first night, one light is kindled; another is added each night until all eight are lit. The ninth light, called the shamash, is set apart from the others, often at a different height. Shamash means “helper”: it is lit first and used to kindle the festival lights each night. Lighting the menorah helps families remember the events and meaning of Hanukkah.

In the Warriors series, the wild cats of the Clans believe that many of their deceased ancestors live on as StarClan, a spiritual community that watches over the living. StarClan cats may send warnings, guidance, and prophecies through dreams and visions, especially to medicine cats, who care for their Clanmates and act as a link to the ancestral spirits. In the Clans’ original forest territories, medicine cats traveled to a cave to seek StarClan’s guidance. There, they touched their noses to the Moonstone, a pale quartz formation that shone in moonlight, before sleeping and receiving dreams. These visits helped medicine cats bring StarClan’s messages back to their Clans.

Bismillah is an Arabic invocation meaning “In the name of God.” Muslims commonly say it before reading the Qur’an, praying, eating, or beginning another good action to show that they are acting with awareness of God. It is also said when an animal is slaughtered for halal meat. The longer form, “Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim,” means “In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful” and appears at the start of nearly every chapter, or surah, of the Qur’an. Surah An-Naml, meaning “The Ants,” is notable because Bismillah appears both at its opening and in verse 30, where it begins a letter from the prophet Solomon to the Queen of Sheba.

Utnapishtim is a flood survivor in Mesopotamian mythology. In the Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, he tells Gilgamesh how the god Ea, also known as Enki, warned him that a great flood was coming. Utnapishtim built a large vessel and took his family and living creatures aboard so they could survive the deluge. After the waters receded, the gods granted him and his wife immortality. Gilgamesh, the king of Uruk, visits Utnapishtim while searching for a way to escape death. His search begins after his close companion Enkidu dies. Utnapishtim’s story helps Gilgamesh understand that immortality is an extraordinary gift, not something most humans can gain.

Yin and yang are a Chinese philosophical idea describing two complementary, interdependent forces found throughout nature. Yin is often associated with darkness, coolness, and rest, while yang is associated with light, warmth, and activity. They are not enemies or fixed categories: each can give way to the other, as night turns into day, and both are needed for balance. The familiar circular black-and-white symbol is called the taijitu. Its two curved halves show yin and yang in a changing relationship, while the dot of the opposite color in each half suggests that each contains a part of the other. Yin and yang are important in Daoism, a Chinese tradition concerned with living in harmony with the Dao, or “the way.”

In Greek mythology, a nymph is a feminine spirit connected with a part of the natural world, such as a spring, river, tree, forest, mountain, or sea. Nymphs often appear in stories as companions of gods and as guardians of the places where they live. Different kinds of nymphs are named for their surroundings: Naiads belong to freshwater places such as springs, streams, and rivers, while Dryads are associated with trees. Echo, whose voice was said to repeat the words of others, was also a nymph. Although artists often pictured nymphs as young women, they were supernatural beings rather than ordinary humans. Knowing that “nymph” is the general term and “Naiad” means a freshwater nymph helps distinguish them from spirits linked to trees or mountains.

Hippolyta was a queen of the Amazons, a group of warrior women in Greek mythology. She ruled at Themyscira and possessed a prized belt, sometimes called a girdle, that symbolized her authority. For his ninth labor, Heracles was ordered by King Eurystheus to obtain it. He traveled to Themyscira, the Amazon stronghold, to meet Hippolyta. Different versions of the story describe what happened next: in some, Hippolyta was willing to give him the belt, but a conflict broke out among the Amazons; in others, Heracles fought for it. In every version, the belt is the object Heracles seeks, Hippolyta is the Amazon queen who owns it, and Themyscira is the city where he goes to find her.

Crucifixion was an ancient method of execution in which a condemned person was fastened to a wooden cross with ropes or nails and left suspended until death. The Romans used it to punish people they considered criminals or rebels and to warn others against defying their authority. According to the New Testament, the Roman governor Pontius Pilate ordered the crucifixion of Jesus, an event central to Christianity. Crucifixion also appears in the history of Spartacus, a former gladiator who led a major slave revolt against the Roman Republic beginning in 73 BC. After the revolt was defeated, the Roman commander Crassus had thousands of captured rebels crucified along the Appian Way, the road leading from Capua to Rome.

The Monkey is the ninth sign in the Chinese zodiac’s repeating cycle of twelve animals, coming after the goat (also called the sheep) and before the rooster. The zodiac is used to name years in a traditional Chinese calendar, and each animal sign is also associated with yin or yang and one of the Five Phases: wood, fire, earth, metal, or water. The Monkey has a famous counterpart in Chinese literature: Sun Wukong, the Monkey King in the classic novel Journey to the West. Born from a stone, Sun Wukong is a clever trickster and skilled fighter who learns to change shape, rebels against Heaven, and carries a magical staff that can grow or shrink. His adventures make him one of Chinese mythology’s best-known figures.

In Greek mythology, dragon’s teeth are the teeth of a slain serpent that grow into armed warriors when sown in the ground. Jason encountered them during his quest for the Golden Fleece. In Colchis, King Aeëtes ordered him to plant dragon’s teeth as one of his tasks; the warriors that sprang up were a danger he had to overcome. A similar story concerns Cadmus, a Phoenician prince whose father, Agenor, sent him to search for his sister Europa. Near a spring in Boeotia, Cadmus killed a serpent sacred to Ares and sowed its teeth. The warriors who emerged fought one another, and the survivors helped Cadmus found the city of Thebes. These stories make dragon’s teeth a symbol of conflict that can arise from a single act.

Europa was a Phoenician princess in Greek mythology. Zeus took the form of a gentle white bull and approached her while she was gathering flowers. When she climbed onto his back, he carried her across the sea to Crete. There, Europa became the mother of several sons, including Minos, who later became king of Crete. Minos was the father of Ariadne and Phaedra, and his palace at Knossos became associated with the labyrinth that held the Minotaur. Europa’s brother Cadmus searched for her; in Greek tradition, he was also credited with bringing the alphabet to Greece. Europa’s name is associated with the name of the continent Europe.

The African Methodist Episcopal Church, often called the AME Church, is an independent Black Christian denomination rooted in Methodism, a movement associated with John and Charles Wesley. It was organized in the United States in 1816 after Black worshippers faced racial segregation at a Philadelphia church. Richard Allen helped establish the denomination and became its first bishop. The AME Church gave Black Christians a place to worship and lead their own congregations. Allen also supported Jarena Lee, a Philadelphia-born itinerant preacher who traveled to share her faith. In 1819, he gave her permission to preach, making her the first woman authorized to preach in the AME Church. Lee later wrote an autobiography describing her religious conversion and travels as an evangelist.

Medea is a princess of Colchis and a powerful sorceress in Greek mythology. When Jason, the Greek hero who led the Argonauts, sailed to Colchis in search of the Golden Fleece, Medea fell in love with him and used her magic to help him. She gave Jason the means to survive a challenge involving fire-breathing bulls and to defeat warriors that sprang from dragon’s teeth he had sown. Her help allowed him to obtain the fleece, and she left her homeland to become his wife. Their story did not have a happy ending: Jason later abandoned Medea to marry another woman, leading to a tragic conflict. Medea’s story is often told as one about love, betrayal, and the dangerous power of revenge.

Aztec human sacrifice was a religious practice in which priests offered people to the gods. The Aztecs believed such offerings helped sustain the gods and keep the world in balance. Many victims were captives taken in war, including conflicts called Flower Wars, which could provide prisoners for ceremonies. Some accounts describe priests using a blade to remove a victim’s heart. Major ceremonies took place in Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital built on an island in Lake Texcoco. According to tradition, the city was founded where an eagle landed on a cactus. The ruins of Tenochtitlan lie beneath present-day Mexico City. These details identify both the ritual practice, Aztec human sacrifice, and the city where many ceremonies took place.

Misogi is a Shinto rite of purification using water. Its best-known mythic example appears in the Kojiki, an early collection of Japanese myths. After escaping Yomi, the land of the dead, the creator deity Izanagi bathed in a river to cleanse himself of the impurity associated with death. During this purification, three important kami, or divine beings, were born from parts of his body: Amaterasu from his left eye, Tsukuyomi from his right eye, and Susanoo from his nose. Misogi shows how washing can prepare a person to approach the sacred. Before visiting a Shinto shrine’s main worship area, visitors commonly rinse their hands and mouth at a water basin in a related purification practice.

The perpetual virginity of Mary is the Christian teaching that Mary, the mother of Jesus, remained a virgin before, during, and after his birth. Christians believe she conceived Jesus through the Holy Spirit rather than through sexual intercourse; the word “perpetual” means that her virginity continued for the rest of her life. This teaching is especially important in Catholic and Orthodox Christianity. It is different from the Immaculate Conception, which concerns Mary’s freedom from original sin from the beginning of her own life. It is also different from the Assumption of Mary: in Catholic teaching, the Assumption means that, at the end of her earthly life, Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory.

Jinn are supernatural beings in Islamic tradition, mentioned in the Quran. They are created from smokeless fire, unlike humans, who are associated with clay, and angels, who are associated with light. Jinn are often described as having free will: like humans, they can make choices, follow a religion, and act in helpful or harmful ways. Islamic teachings therefore do not treat all jinn as evil. In folklore, some jinn have extraordinary powers, and stories sometimes show them being confined by magic in objects such as lamps or talismans. The word “genie” is often used for a jinn in popular stories, though those tales do not represent every Islamic belief about them. The key fact to remember is that jinn are beings made from smokeless fire.

The Fall of Troy is the legendary capture and destruction of Troy at the end of the Trojan War. Troy was ruled by King Priam, and the Greeks had struggled for years to take the city. They finally used a trick: Greek warriors hid inside a huge wooden horse that their army appeared to leave behind as an offering or victory trophy. The Trojans brought the Trojan Horse inside their walls, allowing the hidden warriors to emerge and help the Greeks sack the city. The prophet Cassandra warned of the danger, but a curse from Apollo meant no one believed her. Aeneas escaped with other survivors and later traveled to Italy, a journey told in Virgil’s Aeneid.

Tantalus was a king of Sipylus in Greek mythology and a son of Zeus and the nymph Plouto. Invited to dine with the gods, he committed a terrible crime: he killed his son Pelops and served him as food to test whether the gods would notice. They discovered what he had done and restored Pelops to life. Demeter had unknowingly eaten part of Pelops’s shoulder, so the missing piece was replaced with ivory. As punishment, Tantalus was sent to the underworld, where he stood in water beneath fruit-laden branches. Whenever he tried to drink, the water slipped away; whenever he reached for fruit, the branches moved out of reach. His endless hunger and thirst gave rise to the word “tantalize,” meaning to torment someone with something they cannot obtain.

Real Presence is the Christian belief that Christ is truly present in the consecrated bread and wine of the Eucharist, which become or contain his body and blood rather than serving only as symbols. The Eucharist recalls the Last Supper, when Jesus shared bread and wine with his apostles before his death. Catholic theology explains the Real Presence through transubstantiation: the substance, or underlying reality, of the bread and wine changes into Christ’s body and blood, while their outward appearances, such as taste and texture, remain the same. The Fourth Lateran Council affirmed this teaching in 1215. Orthodox Christians also affirm Christ’s real presence but generally do not define exactly how it occurs. Christian denominations differ on this question; some understand the bread and wine primarily as symbols.

Zamzam water comes from the Zamzam Well near the Kaaba in Mecca and is sacred to Muslims. In Islamic tradition, Hajar, the wife of Ibrahim, was left in the dry Meccan valley with their infant son, Isma’il. When their water ran out, she hurried between the hills of Safa and Marwa seven times, searching for help. Allah provided water for them when the angel Jibreel struck the ground, causing a spring to appear. Pilgrims remember Hajar’s search by traveling between Safa and Marwa during the hajj and umrah pilgrimages. Many also drink Zamzam water at the sanctuary and carry some home. The story connects the water with trust in Allah and care for those in need.

Filial piety is a central virtue in Confucian ethics. Known in Chinese as xiao, it means honoring, respecting, and caring for parents and elders. It includes listening to them, helping them as they age, and treating them with gratitude. These duties can continue after death through remembrance and rites for ancestors, the deceased family members from whom a person is descended. In some Chinese homes, an ancestor’s name is written on a tablet kept at a family shrine. During the Qingming festival, families may sweep ancestors’ graves and make offerings. Filial piety is also the subject of a short Confucian work called The Classic of Filial Piety, traditionally presented as a dialogue between Confucius and his disciple Zengzi.

Caves often serve as places of refuge in mythology, but what happens inside them can affect the wider world. In Japanese myth, the sun goddess Amaterasu hid in a cave called Ama-no-Iwato after her brother Susanoo offended her. With the sun goddess out of sight, the world fell into darkness. The other deities gathered outside the cave and devised a way to draw her out, restoring light. In Greek myth, a cave on Mount Ida sheltered the infant Zeus while Amalthea raised him, keeping him safe from his father, Cronus. Both stories feature caves as hiding places, though one cave conceals a goddess whose absence changes the world, while the other protects a child who will become a powerful god.

The Jade Emperor is the supreme celestial ruler in Chinese mythology. He presides over Heaven as the head of a vast hierarchy of divine officials, much like an emperor governing through ministers. Also called the Heavenly Emperor, he is honored in Daoist and Chinese popular religious traditions. Stories about him belong to the wider world of Chinese mythology, which also includes the Eight Immortals, the moon goddess Chang’e, and the archer Houyi, who shot down nine of ten suns. In many Chinese communities, the ninth day of the first lunar month is celebrated as the Jade Emperor’s Birthday. Worshippers may mark the occasion with temple ceremonies, prayers, and offerings to honor Heaven’s ruler and seek blessings for the year ahead.

Yu the Great is a legendary Chinese ruler remembered for bringing a devastating flood under control. According to tradition, his father, Gun, tried to stop the water by building barriers, but failed. Yu took a different approach: he organized people to dig channels and clear waterways so the floodwaters could flow away. Stories say he worked for years and even passed his own home without stopping because the task was so urgent. His success made him a model of determination and leadership. Yu is also traditionally regarded as the founder of the Xia Dynasty, often described as ancient China’s first hereditary royal house, in which rule passed from one family member to another. The details of his life are difficult to verify, but his story remains important in Chinese tradition.

The Pandavas are five brothers in the ancient Indian epic the Mahabharata: Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva. Yudhishthira, the eldest, leads them and is said to be the son of Yama, the god of death. All five brothers are married to Draupadi. Their rivals are their cousins, the Kauravas, who gain control of the kingdom after Yudhishthira loses a game of dice. As a result, the Pandavas are forced into exile. Their struggle with the Kauravas eventually leads to the Battle of Kurukshetra, a central event in the Mahabharata. The epic also contains the Bhagavad Gita, a conversation in which the god Krishna teaches Arjuna about duty before the battle.

The Ninety-Five Theses were a set of 95 propositions written in 1517 by Martin Luther, a German theologian, Augustinian friar, and teacher at the University of Wittenberg. Luther questioned the religious basis of indulgences, which were presented as reducing the punishment for sins, including time in purgatory. He especially objected to the way they were being sold to raise money for the Church and to claims that buying them could help people in purgatory. According to tradition, Luther posted the theses on the door of All Saints’ Church in Wittenberg, a place where notices could be displayed for public debate. His challenge to indulgences grew into a wider dispute about Church authority and helped launch the Protestant Reformation.

Kwanzaa is a weeklong celebration of African-American culture and shared African heritage, observed each year from December 26 through January 1. It was created in 1966 by Maulana Karenga, who wanted to give African Americans a way to honor their history, community, and values. Each day focuses on one of seven principles, such as unity, creativity, and faith. A central symbol is the kinara, a candleholder with seven spaces: one black candle in the center, with three red and three green candles on either side. The candles represent the seven principles and are lit during the celebration. Kwanzaa may also include music, storytelling, gifts, and a feast called Karamu. Although it begins the day after Christmas, Kwanzaa is a cultural holiday, and some families celebrate both.

Ammit was a fearsome being in ancient Egyptian beliefs about the afterlife. She was usually shown with a crocodile’s head, a lion’s forequarters, and a hippopotamus’s hindquarters. Egyptians believed that after death, a person’s heart was weighed against the feather of Ma’at, which represented truth and justice. The jackal-headed god Anubis, who guided the dead, oversaw the weighing. If the heart was heavier than the feather, it was judged unworthy, and Ammit, waiting beside the scales, devoured it. This meant the person could not enjoy the afterlife. Unlike organs placed in canopic jars, the heart was generally left in the mummy’s body because Egyptians believed it was needed for this judgment.

Athena was the Greek goddess of wisdom, crafts, and strategic warfare. According to myth, she sprang fully grown and armed from the head of her father, Zeus. She became the patron goddess of Athens after a contest with Poseidon to win the city’s favor: Athena offered its people an olive tree, a source of food, oil, and wood. Although Athena was skilled in many crafts, one musical invention did not please her. She fashioned the aulos, a double-reed woodwind instrument, but threw it away when she saw that blowing into it made her cheeks bulge. These stories show Athena’s connection to clever inventions as well as to the city that bears her name.

In Sikh teaching, the Five Thieves are five inner vices: lust, anger, greed, attachment, and ego. They are called “thieves” because they can draw a person away from living truthfully, serving others, and remembering God. Sikhs seek to recognize and overcome these tendencies through prayer, honest work, selfless service, and guidance from the Gurus, the spiritual teachers of Sikhism. Cultivating the Five Virtues—truth, compassion, contentment, humility, and love—helps counter the Thieves and supports spiritual growth. The goal of this growth is mukti, also called moksha: liberation from the cycle of rebirth and the effects of karma, and union with God.

Asha Vahista is one of the six Amesha Spentas, divine beings associated with Ahura Mazda in Zoroastrianism. The name means “Best Truth” or “Best Righteousness.” Asha Vahista represents asha: truth, right order, and the righteous way to live. This divine being is also closely linked to sacred fire, which symbolizes light, wisdom, and purity. In Zoroastrian fire temples, priests tend consecrated flames as a focus for prayer and worship; the fire itself is not considered a god. The highest grade of consecrated fire is called Atash Bahram, meaning “Fire of Victory.” It is established through elaborate purification and consecration rites and is carefully kept burning.

The Churning of the Ocean of Milk is a Hindu myth about the devas (gods) and asuras (powerful beings who often oppose them) working together to obtain amrita, the nectar of immortality. They placed Mount Mandara in the cosmic ocean and rotated it like a churning rod, using the serpent Vasuki as a rope to pull it back and forth. When the mountain began to sink, Vishnu took the form of Kurma, a giant tortoise, and supported it from below. The churning brought forth many things, including the deadly poison halahala. Shiva swallowed the poison to protect the world, and it turned his throat blue. At last, the churning produced the amrita that the devas and asuras had sought.

Adonis was an exceptionally handsome mortal in Greek mythology who was loved by Aphrodite, the goddess of love and beauty. He died after a wild boar wounded him during a hunt. In one account, Aphrodite mourned him, and anemone flowers sprang from his spilled blood. The name “anemone” comes from the Greek word for wind, so the flower is sometimes called a windflower; its genus belongs to the buttercup family. Like other Greek myths in which a death is linked to a flower, the story uses a change in nature to remember someone who was lost. To identify Adonis in a quiz, remember his connection to Aphrodite and the boar; to identify the flower, remember the anemone.

Coyote is a trickster figure in the stories of many Indigenous peoples of North America. Named for the wild canine, Coyote is often clever, mischievous, and able to change shape. Coyote’s actions may cause trouble, but the stories can also explain features of the world or teach lessons about behavior. Because these traditions belong to different peoples, Coyote’s character and adventures vary from one community to another. Another trickster is Iktomi, who appears in Lakota religious tales. Iktomi usually takes the form of a spider rather than a canine. A Lakota story connects Iktomi with the origin of hoops containing string webs, used as protective charms for children. Both figures are tricksters, but Coyote is named for an animal of the dog family, while Iktomi is associated with a spider.

Valhalla is Odin’s great hall in Asgard, the home of the gods in Norse mythology. Valkyries, female figures who choose warriors slain in battle, bring some of the dead there. These warriors are called the einherjar. In Valhalla, they feast and train for Ragnarök, the final battle in which gods and their enemies will fight. One story says the goat Heiðrún grazes on the tree Læraðr above the hall and produces enough mead, a drink made from honey, for the warriors to enjoy. Valhalla is therefore both a place where fallen warriors spend the afterlife and a gathering place for Odin’s fighters as they prepare for Ragnarök.

The Beatitudes are a series of short blessings taught by Jesus near the beginning of the Sermon on the Mount. They appear in the Gospel of Matthew, a New Testament account of Jesus’ life traditionally attributed to Matthew, one of the Twelve Apostles who had worked as a tax collector. Each Beatitude names a group of people and pairs them with a promise. The first says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Others say that the meek will inherit the earth and that the merciful will receive mercy. Together, the Beatitudes teach that qualities such as humility, compassion, and a desire for justice matter in God’s kingdom. Matthew is one of the four canonical Gospels, alongside Mark, Luke, and John.

The Trojan Horse was a huge wooden horse used by the Greeks to capture Troy after years of war. The Greeks pretended to sail away, leaving the horse outside the city as if it were a victory trophy. The Trojans brought it inside their walls, unaware that Greek soldiers were hiding within it. Cassandra, a Trojan princess and prophetess, warned her people not to trust the horse. She could foresee disaster, but a curse from the god Apollo meant that no one believed her predictions. That night, the hidden soldiers emerged and helped the Greek army enter the city, leading to the sack, or destruction, of Troy. The story of the horse appears in the Odyssey, an ancient Greek epic attributed to Homer.

In Greek mythology, Tartarus is a primordial abyss deep below Hades, the realm of the dead. In the Iliad, Zeus describes it as being as far beneath Hades as heaven is above the earth. Tartarus was not simply another name for the underworld: it was its deepest, darkest region and a place of imprisonment. After the Titanomachy, a war between the younger Olympian gods and the older generation of gods called the Titans, Zeus confined the defeated Titans there. They became Tartarus’s best-known prisoners. Greek myths also describe Tartarus as a dungeon for beings punished for exceptionally wicked deeds. When a question asks for the abyss beneath Hades, the answer is Tartarus; when it asks for the older gods imprisoned there, the answer is the Titans.

Eid is a name shared by two major Islamic holidays: Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. Eid al-Fitr, sometimes called the “Lesser Eid,” begins when Ramadan, the month of fasting, ends. Muslims celebrate with a special communal prayer, visits with family and friends, and festive meals. Before the prayer, they give a charitable contribution called zakat al-fitr so that people in need can share in the celebration. Eid al-Adha, sometimes called the “Greater Eid,” commemorates Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God. It is associated with the Hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. Although the two holidays have different meanings, both are important occasions for worship, generosity, and community.

L. Ron Hubbard was an American pulp-fiction author who became the founder of Scientology. In 1950, he published Dianetics: The Modern Science of Mental Health, introducing a self-help system called Dianetics. Hubbard taught that painful experiences could leave harmful mental impressions, which Dianetics aimed to address through a process called auditing. In this system, a person who has overcome those impressions is said to be “Clear.” Hubbard later established Scientology, a religious movement that developed from his ideas about the mind and human potential. Remember the distinction: L. Ron Hubbard is the founder, Dianetics is the system he introduced in his 1950 book, and Scientology is the religious movement he founded.

Laka is a Hawaiian deity traditionally regarded as the patron of hula, a ceremonial art that combines dance, meaningful gestures, and chant to tell stories and honor gods and ancestors. In the traditional style called hula kahiko, dancers perform to chanting and percussion rather than modern songs. Hula is therefore more than entertainment: it helps preserve Hawaiian history, beliefs, and language. Dancers may wear leis and other adornments, and plants associated with Laka have a special place in hula traditions. Hawaiian stories also connect hula with Hiʻiaka and her sister Pele, the volcano goddess. In the nineteenth century, Christian missionaries opposed hula, and it was suppressed for a time, but Hawaiians continued to practice and revive it. If asked for hula’s patron deity, the answer is Laka; if asked for the art associated with Laka, it is hula.

Hathor was an ancient Egyptian goddess associated with love, fertility, motherhood, music, and joy. Artists often showed her as a cow or as a woman wearing a solar disk between two cow horns, making her easy to recognize. She was also linked with dancing and celebration, and Egyptians asked for her protection during childbirth. In some traditions, Hathor was the wife of Horus, a falcon-associated god closely connected with Egyptian kingship. Horus was the son of Osiris, who became lord of the underworld after his brother Set killed him. To avenge his father, Horus fought and defeated his uncle Set. These stories place Hathor within a family of gods whose myths helped Egyptians explain both the afterlife and the power of their rulers.

The Anabaptists were a 16th-century Radical Reformation movement that rejected infant baptism. They believed baptism should take place only after a person was old enough to understand and consciously profess Christian faith, an idea often called believer’s baptism. Their beliefs challenged established churches and authorities, and some early Anabaptists were involved in the unrest surrounding the German Peasants’ War of 1525. Anabaptist communities later took different paths, but many emphasized peaceful living, mutual support, and separation from state-controlled churches.
