Menno Simons, a Dutch theologian from Friesland, had been a Catholic priest before leaving the priesthood in 1536. He became an influential organizer of peaceful Anabaptist congregations, and his writings helped shape the movement in the Low Countries. Mennonites are named after him; the Amish later developed from the Mennonite tradition.

Druids were religious authorities in ancient Celtic societies, especially in parts of Britain and Gaul. They are known mainly through accounts written by outsiders, including Roman authors, so some details of their beliefs and rituals remain uncertain. Julius Caesar described druids as overseeing religious ceremonies, while Pliny the Elder associated them with ritually gathering mistletoe from oak trees. Modern groups inspired by druids have held ceremonies at Stonehenge, a prehistoric stone circle on Salisbury Plain in southern England. Stonehenge was built in stages beginning more than 4,000 years ago, long before the period when Roman writers described Celtic druids. Although the monument may have had religious or timekeeping purposes, archaeologists have not established that ancient druids built it or used it for rituals.

John Henry Newman (1801–1890) was an English theologian and priest who became a leading figure in the Oxford Movement. This movement urged the Church of England, or Anglican Church, to recover older traditions and emphasize its historical links to early Christianity. While still an Anglican, Newman argued that the church’s Thirty-nine Articles could be understood in a way compatible with Catholic beliefs. His study eventually led him to enter the Catholic Church in 1845. Pope Leo XIII made him a cardinal in 1879. Newman also wrote Apologia Pro Vita Sua, a spiritual autobiography published in 1864. He wrote it to explain and defend his religious journey after the writer Charles Kingsley accused him of being untruthful.

Baron Samedi is a prominent loa, or spirit, in Haitian Vodou. He is associated with death, cemeteries, and the realm of the dead, and is often pictured wearing a black tailcoat, a top hat, and dark glasses while holding a cigar. Haitian Vodou has a supreme god called Bondye, but people commonly approach Bondye through loa. Another widely invoked loa is Papa Legba, who is linked to crossroads and opens the way for communication with other spirits. He is commonly depicted carrying a cane. These details help distinguish Baron Samedi, the death spirit, from Papa Legba, the intermediary at the crossroads. Haitian Vodou is a religion with African and Catholic influences, not a practice centered on sticking pins into dolls.

The Jersey Devil is a legendary creature said to roam the Pine Barrens, a vast, sparsely settled region of southern New Jersey. Descriptions vary, but it is often pictured with a horse-like head, batlike wings, and cloven hooves. One well-known story says it began as the thirteenth child of a woman called Mother Leeds and transformed into a frightening creature soon after birth. The Pine Barrens provide an eerie setting for such tales: their sandy soil supports pine and scrub-oak woodlands, while cedar swamps add to the sense of a remote wilderness. For centuries, reported sightings and strange sounds have kept the legend alive. The Jersey Devil is a figure of folklore, not an animal known to science.

Hell is a general name for a realm associated with the dead, punishment, or suffering after death. Its meaning varies across religions and mythologies: some traditions describe it as a place where people are punished for wrongdoing, while others have an underworld where the dead go regardless of how they lived. In Greek mythology, the underworld is ruled by Hades, a son of Cronus and Rhea, brother of Zeus and Poseidon, and husband of Persephone. The Greek underworld is not exactly the same as every religious idea of hell, but the two are often compared. The word “hell” can also be used figuratively for a place of terrible suffering, as in the name “Ashoka’s Hell” for a torture chamber associated with the Mauryan emperor Ashoka before his conversion to Buddhism.

Ancient Egyptian mythology was the religious tradition of ancient Egypt, with stories about gods, the natural world, death, and the afterlife. Egyptians believed that preserving a body through mummification helped prepare a person for life after death. They pictured the dead facing judgment: a person’s heart was weighed against the feather of Ma’at, which represented truth and justice. Anubis, often shown with a jackal’s head, guided and protected the dead. Osiris ruled the underworld and was commonly shown with green skin, a color linked to new life. According to myth, his brother Seth murdered him, but his wife Isis restored him. Osiris therefore became a symbol of resurrection and hope for life after death. Egyptian gods were also often pictured holding an ankh, a symbol of life.

Noah’s Ark is the large vessel Noah builds at God’s command in the Book of Genesis. God warns Noah that a great flood will cover the earth, so Noah brings his family and representatives of the animals aboard to keep them safe. Rain falls for forty days and forty nights, and the ark floats while the floodwaters cover the land. When the waters finally recede, the ark comes to rest in the mountains of Ararat. Noah, his family, and the animals then leave the vessel. God makes a promise never again to destroy all life with a flood and names the rainbow in the clouds as the visible sign of that promise.

Jansenism was a 17th-century Catholic theological movement named after Cornelius Jansen, a Dutch-born bishop and theologian. Drawing on the teachings of Saint Augustine, Jansen argued that human beings are deeply affected by original sin, the sinful condition inherited from Adam and Eve. Jansenists therefore stressed the limits of human freedom: people cannot overcome sin or choose what is good without God’s grace. They also emphasized predestination, the idea that God knows or determines who will be saved. Jansen’s major work, Augustinus, was published after his death and sparked a major dispute within the Catholic Church. Church authorities condemned propositions about grace and free will attributed to the book, while Jansen’s supporters argued that those propositions did not accurately represent his teaching.

Confessions is a spiritual autobiography written in Latin by Augustine of Hippo, a North African bishop and major Christian theologian of the late fourth and early fifth centuries. Addressing God directly, Augustine looks back on his life to explore why people do wrong and how faith changed him. He recalls stealing pears with friends as a teenager, even though he did not want the fruit, because the thrill lay in breaking the rules. He also describes his earlier involvement with Manichaeism, a religion he eventually rejected. While struggling to convert to Christianity in Milan, Augustine heard a child’s voice say “take and read.” He opened a book of the Bible, read a passage, and decided to embrace the Christian faith.

The Council of Chalcedon was a meeting of Christian bishops held in 451 in Chalcedon, a city across the Bosporus from Constantinople. It addressed a central question of Christology: how Jesus Christ could be both God and human. The council taught that Christ is one person with two distinct natures, one divine and one human. Its doctrinal statement, commonly called the Definition of Chalcedon, says that these natures exist without confusion or separation: neither is blended into the other, but Christ is not divided into two people. This teaching became standard in many Christian churches. Oriental Orthodox churches rejected the council’s formula and follow a different understanding of how Christ’s divinity and humanity are united.

Christian missionaries are people who travel to share Christianity, teach its beliefs, and establish churches and Christian communities. In Chinua Achebe’s Nigerian novel Things Fall Apart, missionaries arrive in the Igbo village of Umuofia during British colonial rule. The villagers give them land in the Evil Forest, expecting that living there will bring them harm, but the missionaries survive and gain followers. Their presence challenges local religious beliefs and unsettles the community’s social order. Two missionaries in the novel are the more understanding Mr. Brown and the hostile Mr. Smith; another speaks through an interpreter who mistakenly says “my buttocks” when he means “myself.” After the protagonist, Okonkwo, hangs himself, a British District Commissioner considers reducing his story to a brief passage in a book about the “pacification” of “primitive tribes.”

Mithras was the central deity of a Roman mystery cult that flourished across the Roman Empire. Its members met in small, often underground temples and advanced through seven grades of initiation. Mithras was commonly shown being born from a rock while carrying a dagger and a torch. The cult’s best-known image shows him killing a bull. This scene is called the tauroctony, a term derived from Greek words connected with bull-killing. It appeared in Mithraic temples and was central to the cult’s religious imagery, though historians do not know exactly what it meant to worshippers. Roman Mithras was related in name and some traditions to Mithra, a deity in ancient Iranian religion, but the Roman cult developed its own distinctive practices.

The Feather of Ma’at was an ostrich feather used in ancient Egyptian beliefs about judgment after death. It represented Ma’at, the goddess and principle of truth, justice, and order. Egyptians believed that, in the Hall of Two Truths, a dead person’s heart was placed on one side of a scale and the Feather of Ma’at on the other. Anubis, the jackal-headed god associated with mummification and the dead, performed the weighing. The heart was thought to reveal how a person had lived: a heart balanced with the feather showed that the person was worthy of continuing into the afterlife. A heart weighed down by wrongdoing failed the test and could be devoured by the creature Ammit.

Houyi is a legendary archer in Chinese mythology. In one famous story, ten suns appeared in the sky at once, making the earth unbearably hot and threatening all living things. Houyi used his bow to shoot down nine of them, leaving one sun to provide light and warmth. Another story links Houyi to Chang’e, his wife. When Houyi obtained an elixir of immortality, Chang’e drank it and ascended to the moon, where she became known as a moon goddess. Versions of the story differ about why she drank the elixir: some say she was protecting it from a thief, while others tell the event differently. Together, the stories of Houyi and Chang’e are among the best-known legends of China.

Shia Islam is the second-largest branch of Islam, after Sunni Islam. It began with a disagreement over who should lead the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad died in 632. Shia Muslims believe that Ali, Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law, was his rightful successor and that leadership should continue through Ali’s descendants. These leaders are called imams; in Shia belief, they have a special role in guiding the community. Twelver Shia Muslims recognize twelve imams and believe the twelfth entered occultation, meaning he is hidden from the world. They expect him to return near the end of time as the Mahdi, a restorer who will establish justice. Shia communities include the Alawites of Syria. In the 19th century, a Sudanese leader who claimed to be the Mahdi led a revolt against Egyptian rule.

Shabbat is the Jewish weekly day of rest and religious observance. It begins at sunset on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday, marking the seventh day of the week. Shabbat recalls the biblical account of God resting after creation and gives families and communities time for prayer, meals, and rest. Observant Jews refrain from certain kinds of work during this time. A Friday-night Shabbat meal often begins with Kiddush, a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to sanctify the day. The challah, a braided bread traditionally served at the meal, is covered while Kiddush is said. Some families also eat cholent, a slow-cooked stew prepared before Shabbat so it can be served without cooking during the day of rest.

Around 1000 CE, Iceland faced a dispute between followers of the traditional Norse gods and supporters of Christianity. Rather than let the disagreement divide the island, the Althing, Iceland’s national assembly, asked its law speaker, Thorgeir Thorkelsson, to decide which religion the law would recognize. According to tradition, Thorgeir spent time thinking beneath a cloak before declaring that Iceland would adopt Christianity. This religious transformation is called the Christianization of Iceland. The ruling helped preserve a shared legal system, although some older pagan practices were initially allowed in private. Later accounts say Thorgeir cast idols of the Norse gods into a waterfall called Goðafoss, or “waterfall of the gods,” to mark the change.

Black cat superstitions are beliefs that black cats can be signs, or omens, of bad luck. In some European folklore, especially stories about witches, a black cat was imagined as a familiar: a supernatural animal companion that helped a witch perform magic. Gothic literature uses similar images to create an eerie mood or hint that something frightening may happen. These stories reflect people’s fears and traditions, not facts about cats; a black cat is an ordinary animal, and seeing one does not cause misfortune. Beliefs also vary by place: in some traditions, black cats are considered lucky instead. The color black often signals danger in gothic stories, but its meaning depends on the story or culture.

Antyesti is the Hindu funeral rite performed after a person dies. Its name means “last sacrifice,” and it is traditionally the final samskara, or life-cycle ceremony. In a traditional Antyesti, the deceased person’s body is placed on a funeral pyre, a structure made of stacked wood, and cremated. Family members may take part in prayers and other rites to honor the deceased and help mark the person’s passage from this life. Practices vary among Hindu communities, and some people are buried rather than cremated. Antyesti is an example of a funeral: a set of ceremonies held after someone’s death. Other religions have their own funeral customs, but Antyesti is the name of this Hindu last rite, and the wooden structure used for cremation is called a funeral pyre.

Religious syncretism is the blending of beliefs, rituals, or symbols from different religions into a shared tradition. It often develops when communities with different faiths come into contact and find ways to practice inherited traditions alongside newer ones. One example is Santería, an Afro-Cuban religion that combines Yoruba-derived traditions honoring spiritual beings called orishas with Catholic practices and saints. Another possible example is devotion to Our Lady of Guadalupe, a form of the Virgin Mary said to have appeared to Juan Diego in Mexico in 1531. Some scholars see this devotion as blending Catholic and Indigenous Mexican religious traditions. Syncretism does not mean that all the original religions become identical; it describes how particular ideas and practices can come together in a new religious tradition.

Sacramental wine is wine made from grapes and used alongside bread in the Eucharist, also called Holy Communion or, in Catholic worship, the Mass. Christians use these elements to remember Jesus’s Last Supper, when he shared bread and wine with his disciples. Different Christian traditions understand the wine in different ways: some see it as a symbol of Christ’s blood, while Catholics believe it becomes his blood during the Mass. Sacramental wine also matters in Graham Greene’s novel The Power and the Glory. Set in the Mexican state of Tabasco during a revolutionary government’s persecution of the Church, it follows a fugitive priest nicknamed the “whisky priest” who struggles to obtain wine so he can continue celebrating Mass.

George Whitefield was an English Anglican minister who became one of the most famous preachers of the eighteenth century. Rather than staying in one church, he traveled widely as an itinerant evangelist, preaching to huge outdoor audiences in Britain and the North American colonies. His energetic sermons urged people to seek a personal religious conversion, helping make the colonial revival part of a wider transatlantic movement. That wave of evangelical revivals, especially strong in the 1730s and 1740s, is called the First Great Awakening. Another leading preacher was Jonathan Edwards, whose sermon “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” used vivid warnings about divine judgment. Supporters of the revival were sometimes called “New Lights,” while critics objected to its emotional style.

In Haitian Vodou, Bondye is the supreme creator and source of all life. The name comes from the French phrase bon Dieu, meaning “good God.” Bondye is generally understood to be distant from everyday human affairs, so practitioners usually seek help and guidance through spirits called lwa. The lwa are not the supreme god; they are spirits that people may approach in ceremonies for matters such as health, family, and protection. Vodou priests, called houngans, and priestesses, called mambos, lead rituals that honor the lwa and help people communicate with them. This distinction is important: Bondye is the supreme deity, while the lwa are the spirits with whom practitioners interact more directly.

The Church of Scientology is a religious organization founded by L. Ron Hubbard. It grew from Dianetics, a system Hubbard introduced in a 1950 book. Dianetics teaches that a “reactive mind” holds painful experiences that can affect a person’s thoughts and behavior. In a process called auditing, a person answers questions about their experiences with the aim of reducing that influence. Scientology describes someone who has reached an important stage in this process as “clear.” Hubbard later developed further spiritual teachings about thetans, which Scientologists understand as immortal spiritual beings. The church has attracted well-known members, including actors John Travolta and Tom Cruise, and has also faced controversy over its practices. If asked for the organization’s name, the answer is the Church of Scientology; Hubbard’s earlier system is called Dianetics.

Zarathustra was an ancient Iranian religious teacher traditionally regarded as the founder and prophet of Zoroastrianism. His teachings center on Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity associated with wisdom and goodness. Zarathustra is also known as Zoroaster, the Greek form of his name. The Gathas, a group of hymns traditionally attributed to him, are the oldest and most revered part of the Avesta, Zoroastrianism’s sacred collection. The Avesta also preserves liturgical prayers and instructions for religious rituals. Together, these writings are an important source for understanding Zoroastrian beliefs and practices. If asked to name the teacher associated with the Gathas, the answer is Zarathustra; if asked to name the collection that contains them, the answer is the Avesta.

Uranus, also called Ouranos, was the primordial Greek personification of the sky. He was the consort of Gaia, the Earth, and together they had many children, including the Titans. Uranus feared some of their other children and kept them imprisoned, angering Gaia. She persuaded their Titan son Kronos to attack his father, and Kronos overthrew Uranus, beginning a new generation of divine rulers. Among the children of Gaia and Uranus were three giants called the Hekatonkheires, or Hundred-Handed Ones. Each had a hundred hands and fifty heads. Their names were Cottus, Gyges, and Briareus. Much later, they helped Zeus and the other Olympians defeat the Titans.

Demons are supernatural beings that many religious traditions associate with evil, temptation, or punishment. Some traditions hold that a demon can possess a person, and an exorcism is a ritual intended to drive it out. Ideas about demons vary across religions and historical periods. In some medieval Christian interpretations, Leviathan was considered a demon charged with punishing envious sinners. Leviathan is also a fearsome sea creature in the Book of Job, where its extraordinary power helps emphasize how much greater God’s power is. The Book of Job describes another mighty creature, Behemoth, alongside Leviathan. Some readers have suggested that Leviathan resembles a crocodile, while others understand it as a mythical monster.

Niobe was a queen of Thebes in Greek mythology who had seven sons and seven daughters. She proudly compared her fourteen children with the two children of the goddess Leto and mocked Leto for having so few. But Leto’s children were the divine twins Artemis and Apollo, born on the island of Delos. To avenge their mother, Apollo killed Niobe’s sons and Artemis killed her daughters. Overcome with grief, Niobe wept until she was turned to stone. Her story warns against hubris, or excessive pride: Niobe’s boast insulted a goddess, and she lost the family she had been so proud of.

The High Holy Days are a ten-day period of Jewish observance that begins with Rosh Hashanah and ends with Yom Kippur. Also called the Days of Awe, this is a time for reflecting on the past year, making amends, and seeking forgiveness. Rosh Hashanah begins on the first day of Tishrei, a month in the Jewish calendar, and marks the Jewish New Year. It is traditionally celebrated with the sounding of the shofar, a horn that calls people to reflection. Yom Kippur falls on the tenth day of Tishrei. Known as the Day of Atonement, it is a solemn day of fasting and prayer. In Jewish tradition, a person’s fate for the new year is sealed on Yom Kippur.

Shechita is the Jewish method of ritual slaughter used to prepare permitted animals for kosher meat. It is performed by a trained practitioner called a shochet, who checks an exceptionally sharp knife for imperfections and makes a swift, uninterrupted cut at the animal’s neck. A shochet performs the slaughter; a person who supervises whether food follows kosher rules is called a mashgiach. Shechita is one part of kashrut, the system of Jewish dietary laws. “Kosher” means “fit” or suitable under those laws. For example, permitted land mammals must have cloven hooves and chew their cud. Pigs have cloven hooves but do not chew their cud, so pork is not kosher. Kosher rules also prohibit mixing meat and dairy in a meal.

Robin Hood is a legendary English outlaw and folk hero whose adventures appear in ballads, stories, and later books and films. He leads a band of companions called the Merry Men, who hide in Sherwood Forest, a historic woodland in Nottinghamshire, England. In many tales, Robin is a skilled archer who resists corrupt officials, especially the Sheriff of Nottingham, and helps ordinary people. The familiar idea that he steals from the rich to give to the poor became an important part of his legend. Robin Hood’s stories have changed over centuries, so they are best understood as folklore rather than a reliable account of one historical person. His forest refuge, loyal companions, and defiance of unjust authority have made him an enduring hero.

A Shabbos goy is a non-Jew who helps Jewish people with certain tasks on Shabbat, the weekly day of rest that runs from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Traditional Jewish law forbids Jews from doing particular kinds of work, called melakhot, during this time. In some communities, a Shabbos goy was hired to tend a fire or do another needed task that Jewish residents could not do themselves. Historically, some impoverished women who served in this role were paid with a piece of challah, the braided bread traditionally eaten at Shabbat meals. The term combines Shabbos, a Yiddish word for Shabbat, with goy, a word for a non-Jew. Jewish rules about requesting such help have limits, so the practice was not simply a way around every Shabbat restriction.

The Exodus is the biblical account of the Israelites’ escape from slavery in Egypt, led by the prophet Moses. After Moses confronted Pharaoh and demanded their freedom, God sent a series of plagues upon Egypt. Before the final plague killed Egypt’s firstborn, Israelite families marked their doorposts with the blood of a sacrificial lamb so their homes would be passed over, an event remembered at Passover. Pharaoh then allowed the Israelites to leave, but his army pursued them. God parted the sea so the Israelites could cross, and the waters closed over the pursuing forces. During their journey, Moses went up Mount Sinai to receive God’s commandments. The Israelites later wandered in the wilderness for forty years before reaching the land promised to their ancestors.

In the Gospel of Luke, Jesus tells the Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus. The rich man wears purple and fine linen and feasts every day, while Lazarus, a beggar covered in sores, lies at his gate hoping for scraps. After they die, angels carry Lazarus to Abraham’s bosom, a traditional phrase for a place of comfort beside the patriarch Abraham. The rich man, meanwhile, is in torment. He asks Abraham to send Lazarus with a drop of water to cool his tongue, but a great chasm separates them and cannot be crossed. The story contrasts the two men’s lives and afterlives, warning listeners to pay attention to people in need. This beggar Lazarus is not the Lazarus of Bethany whom Jesus raises from the dead in the Gospel of John.

In Hinduism, death is usually understood as a transition rather than the end of the soul’s existence. Many Hindus believe the soul is reborn after death, with its future shaped by karma, or the consequences of a person’s actions. In Hindu mythology, Kali is a goddess associated with death, destruction, and powerful change. Yama is the god of death who judges the departed and rules Naraka, a realm often compared to Hell. Yama also appears in the Mahabharata as the divine father of Yudhishthira, the eldest of the five Pandava brothers. These stories connect ideas about death and the afterlife with characters from one of Hinduism’s great epics.

Our Lady of Guadalupe is a title for the Virgin Mary, the mother of Jesus, associated with a reported appearance on Tepeyac Hill in present-day Mexico City in 1531. According to Catholic tradition, Mary appeared to Juan Diego, an Indigenous convert, and asked him to have a church built there. When the bishop sought a sign, Juan Diego gathered roses and carried them in his tilma, or cloak. As he presented the roses to the bishop, an image of Mary was said to appear on the cloth. The image is now displayed at the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, one of the world’s major Catholic pilgrimage destinations. Her feast day is December 12, when many pilgrims visit the basilica.

Zoroastrian weddings are marriage ceremonies in communities that follow Zoroastrianism, an ancient Persian religion whose supreme being is Ahura Mazda. The bride and groom make a commitment to one another, and a priest blesses their bond. The ceremony also includes symbolic actions that express hopes for a happy life together. In some Zoroastrian communities, especially among Parsis in India, the partners sprinkle rice on each other. The rice represents good luck and their new union as a married couple. Customs can vary between families and communities, but the priest’s blessing and the exchange of rice are two features associated with these weddings.

Hanukkah candles are ritual lights lit during Hanukkah, an eight-night Jewish festival. They are placed in a special holder called a hanukkiah, often also called a menorah. On the first night, one candle is lit; another is added each evening until eight candles are lit on the final night. The candles for the festival nights are placed from right to left, but lit from left to right, so the newest candle is lit first. An additional light, called the shamash, is used to light the others. It is usually set apart, often higher or lower than the eight main candles. The lights recall a tradition that, when the Temple in Jerusalem was rededicated, a small supply of oil lasted for eight nights.

A frog is a tailless amphibian that lives in or near water. Frogs also appear in stories from different cultures. In a well-known version of the Brothers Grimm fairy tale “The Frog Prince,” a prince is changed into a frog and returns to human form after a princess kisses him. In ancient Egyptian mythology, Kek, a personification of primordial darkness, could be shown with a frog’s head. Another Egyptian deity, the goddess Heket, also had a frog’s head and was associated with birth and fertility. Heket was linked to the Nile River, whose yearly floods helped crops grow. One Egyptian story says the Nile’s waters came from the tears of Isis as she mourned the death of Osiris.

The Haggadah is the Jewish text that guides the Passover Seder, a ritual meal at which families retell the Israelites’ Exodus from slavery in Egypt. It sets out the order of the ceremony and includes readings, questions, songs, and instructions for symbolic foods and other rituals. Passover is also a time when observant Jews avoid leavened bread, recalling the Israelites’ hurried departure from Egypt. One part of the Seder recounts the ten plagues that, according to the biblical story, struck Egypt before the Israelites were freed. As each plague is named, participants traditionally remove a drop of wine from their cups. The number ten is also associated with the Ten Commandments given to Moses at Mount Sinai.

Nemesis was the Greek goddess who personified divine retribution: the punishment that comes to people who overstep proper bounds, especially through arrogance or undeserved good fortune. She was not simply a goddess of anger; she represented the idea that actions have consequences and that excessive pride should be brought back into balance. An important sanctuary dedicated to her stood at Rhamnous in Attica, so she was also called Rhamnousia. Another name used for Nemesis was Adrasteia, meaning “the inescapable.” In one tradition, Adrasteia was also the name of a nurse who cared for the infant Zeus. To protect him from his father Cronus, the Curetes clashed their weapons together, making enough noise to drown out the baby’s cries.

The Arba'een Pilgrimage is an annual Shia Muslim observance centered on Karbala, a city in present-day Iraq. It takes place forty days after Ashura, the day that marks the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn was a grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and an important figure in Shia Islam. Millions of pilgrims travel to Karbala for Arba'een, and many make part of the journey on foot. They visit Husayn’s shrine to remember his death and reflect on the values of courage and standing against injustice that his story represents. Arba'een is one of the world’s largest regular religious gatherings.

The Temple in Jerusalem was the central sanctuary of ancient Jewish worship. It stood on a hilltop sacred precinct in Jerusalem, the ancient capital of Judah. According to biblical tradition, King Solomon built the First Temple. After that Temple was destroyed, a Second Temple was built on the site; Roman forces destroyed it in 70 CE. The Temple contained the Holy of Holies, its most sacred inner chamber, which only the High Priest could enter, and only on the Day of Atonement. The Great Sanhedrin was a 71-member Jewish council regarded as the highest court in ancient Jewish tradition. It is described as meeting in the Temple and appointing the High Priest.

The laying on of hands is a Christian practice in which one or more people place their hands on someone while praying. It can express a blessing, a prayer for healing, or the granting of a role in the church. In Acts 8, Peter and John visit newly baptized believers in Samaria, pray for them, and lay their hands on them; the believers then receive the Holy Spirit. The gesture is also used in ordination, when a person is appointed to serve as a minister or bishop. In Catholic teaching, the laying on of hands at a bishop’s ordination expresses apostolic succession: the belief that bishops’ authority has been passed down through an unbroken chain from Jesus’s apostles. The church of Rome claims special standing because of its association with the apostle Peter.

A monastery is a religious community where monks live together, follow a shared rule of life, and gather regularly for prayer and worship. In medieval Christian Europe, monks also worked, studied, and sometimes copied manuscripts by hand, helping to preserve religious texts and other learning. One influential guide to monastic life was the Rule of Benedict, written by Benedict of Nursia in the sixth century. Benedict founded a monastery at Monte Cassino in Italy, which became the mother house of the Benedictine order and a model for many later monasteries. During World War II, Allied bombing heavily damaged Monte Cassino in 1944, as armies fought in the Italian campaign. The monastery was later rebuilt.

In Greek mythology, the Calydonian Boar was a monstrous wild pig that terrorized Calydon, a kingdom in Aetolia. Its king, Oeneus, had offered sacrifices to the gods after a successful harvest but neglected Artemis, the goddess of the hunt and wilderness. Angered by the omission, Artemis sent the boar to ravage the land, destroying crops and threatening its people. Oeneus’s son Meleager gathered a group of heroes to hunt it, including Atalanta, a skilled huntress. Atalanta was the first to wound the boar, and Meleager dealt the killing blow. The hunt became a famous Greek myth not only because of the dangerous beast, but also because arguments over who deserved its hide led to further tragedy.

In Greek religion and mythology, the Anemoi were gods who personified the winds from the four main directions. They were said to be children of Eos, goddess of the dawn, and Astraeus, a god associated with the stars. Each wind had its own character and effect on the weather. Boreas, the north wind, brought cold winter air and was often shown as a winged, bearded god. In one myth, he abducted Oreithyia, an Athenian princess. Zephyrus, the west wind, was linked with gentler breezes and spring. Notus, the south wind, could bring storms and rain, while Eurus, the east wind, was often associated with unsettled weather. These figures helped the ancient Greeks explain the changing winds they experienced.

In Chinese traditions, ancestors are deceased family members who remain important to the living. Families may place tablets bearing their names in household shrines and offer food, incense, or other gifts as signs of remembrance and respect. Honoring ancestors is connected to filial piety, the duty to care for and respect one’s parents and older relatives. A major spring observance is the Qingming Festival, also called Tomb-Sweeping Day. It falls about 15 days after the spring equinox, usually in early April. During Qingming, relatives visit and clean family graves, make offerings, and may burn paper money as a symbolic gift for the dead. These practices help families remember earlier generations and maintain a sense of connection with them.

The Black Stone is a revered stone set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba, the sacred building at the center of Islam’s most important mosque in Mecca. During the Hajj pilgrimage, and also during the smaller pilgrimage called Umrah, Muslims perform tawaf: they walk around the Kaaba seven times, with each circuit beginning and ending at the corner marked by the Black Stone. Pilgrims traditionally try to touch or kiss the stone as they pass it, a practice called istilam. When crowds make that impossible, they may gesture toward it instead. The Black Stone helps mark where each circuit starts and finishes; Muslims do not worship the stone itself.

Circe is an enchantress in Greek mythology who lives on the island of Aeaea. In Homer’s Odyssey, the Greek hero Odysseus lands there with his crew while trying to return to his home in Ithaca after the Trojan War. Circe uses magic to turn some of his companions into pigs. The god Hermes gives Odysseus a protective herb called moly, which helps him resist her spell. Odysseus persuades Circe to restore his men to human form, but he and his crew remain on Aeaea for about a year before continuing their journey. Circe later helps Odysseus by advising him about dangers he will face on the way home.

Ayatollah is an honorific for an especially learned, high-ranking cleric in Twelver Shia Islam, the largest branch of Shia Islam. The word means “sign of God” in Arabic. Ayatollahs study Islamic teachings and law for many years, and some are recognized as authorities whose interpretations of religious law guide other Muslims. One of the best-known ayatollahs was Ruhollah Khomeini. After years in exile, including time in France, he returned to Iran during the 1979 Iranian Revolution. That revolution overthrew Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, Iran’s monarch, and established the Islamic Republic. Khomeini became its first Supreme Leader, giving him enormous political as well as religious influence. His prominence made the title Ayatollah familiar to many people outside the Shia Muslim world.

A human corpse is the body of a person who has died. Religions have different ways of caring for corpses, often to honor the dead and follow beliefs about purity or the afterlife. In the Tibetan sky-burial rite called jhator, specialists known as rogyapa prepare a corpse for vultures; afterward, they may grind the bones and mix them with tsampa, a barley flour. Zoroastrians have traditionally placed corpses on circular structures called dakhmas, commonly known in English as Towers of Silence. There, scavenging birds consume the remains, keeping the dead from contact with earth and fire, which Zoroastrians consider sacred. Other religious funerals may involve burying or cremating a corpse instead.

The Synod of Whitby was a church council held in 664 at a Northumbrian monastery led by Abbess Hilda. Christians in the kingdom followed different customs: some used practices associated with the monastery on Iona, while others followed those of the Roman Church. Their most important disagreement was how to calculate the date of Easter, Christianity’s celebration of Jesus’s resurrection. At the council, Colman argued for the Ionan tradition, while Wilfrid argued for the Roman method. After hearing both sides, Northumbrian King Oswiu chose the Roman customs, including the Roman calculation of Easter. The decision helped bring the Northumbrian church into closer agreement with churches elsewhere in western Europe. The historian Bede later described the debate in his history of the English church.

Puruṣārtha is a Hindu framework describing four proper aims of human life. Dharma means living according to moral duty and doing what is right. Artha is the pursuit of material well-being, including the resources needed to support yourself and others. Kāma refers to desire, pleasure, and enjoyment, including love and the arts. Mokṣa is spiritual liberation: freedom from the cycle of death and rebirth, called samsara. The four aims show that Hindu thought recognizes both everyday needs and a deeper spiritual goal. A person may pursue prosperity and enjoyment while also respecting dharma, with mokṣa understood as the aim that goes beyond ordinary worldly life.

Laozi was an ancient Chinese sage traditionally regarded as a founder of Taoism, or Daoism. Later stories portray him as a contemporary of Confucius, though historians are uncertain whether he was a single historical person. Laozi is credited with writing the Tao Te Ching, also called the Daodejing, a classic arranged in 81 short chapters. Its title is commonly translated as “The Book of the Way and Its Virtue.” The text explores the Dao, or “the Way,” and how people can live in harmony with it. One teaching associated with Laozi is wu wei, meaning non-forcing action: instead of trying to control everything, a person acts in a way that fits the natural course of events. The Tao Te Ching also values compassion, simplicity, and humility.

Qingming Festival, also called Tomb-Sweeping Day, is observed in China in early April, about 15 days after the spring equinox. Families visit the graves of their ancestors—deceased relatives—to sweep and tidy them, pay their respects, and leave offerings such as food. They may also burn joss paper, an imitation currency sometimes called “ghost money,” as a symbolic gift for relatives in the afterlife. Some families eat green dumplings made with mugwort, a spring herb. These customs reflect the importance of remembering ancestors and showing filial piety, or respect and care for one’s family, including those who have died. Qingming is both a time of remembrance and a way for families to maintain a connection with earlier generations.

Christology is the branch of Christian theology that studies who Jesus Christ is, especially how he can be both fully divine and fully human. To explain this, theologians distinguish between a “person,” or who someone is, and a “nature,” or what someone is. At the Council of Chalcedon in 451, church leaders affirmed that Jesus is one person with two natures, divine and human, united “without confusion” or “division.” This became the standard teaching of many major churches, but Oriental Orthodox churches reject the council’s definition and describe their position as miaphysite. Christology is closely connected to Christian teachings about the Trinity, which describe the relationship between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret religious initiation rites held in ancient Greece at Eleusis, near Athens. They centered on Demeter, the goddess of grain and agriculture, and her daughter Persephone. According to the myth, Hades abducted Persephone and took her to the underworld. As Demeter searched for her, she grieved so deeply that crops stopped growing. Persephone’s return brought renewed growth, although she had to spend part of each year in the underworld. The rites honored the bond between mother and daughter and connected their story to the cycle of life, death, and renewal. Initiates were promised hope for a better fate after death, but they were required to keep the ceremonies secret, so many details remain unknown.

Narasimha is an avatar, or earthly form, of Vishnu, the Hindu god associated with preserving the universe. He appears with a human body and a lion’s head to protect Prahlada, a young prince who remains devoted to Vishnu. Prahlada’s father, the demon king Hiranyakasipu, tries to destroy him because he refuses to abandon his faith. The king believes he cannot be killed by a human or an animal, indoors or outdoors, or during the day or night. Narasimha defeats him at twilight on a threshold, a place that is neither fully inside nor outside. As a being who is part human and part lion, Narasimha also escapes the king’s protection against either kind of attacker. The story shows Vishnu protecting a faithful devotee.

The Argo was the ship that carried the Greek hero Jason and his crew on their voyage to Colchis, where they sought the Golden Fleece. The crew were called the Argonauts, meaning sailors of the Argo. One of their most dangerous obstacles was the Symplegades, a pair of rocks that slammed together and could crush a passing ship. The Argonauts sent a dove ahead to test the timing of the rocks. After it flew through, they rowed hard and passed through safely. In the myth, Hera, the wife of Zeus, helped Jason on his quest because he had once helped her. When Jason reached Colchis, he faced further challenges before he could claim the fleece, including sowing a dragon’s teeth in the ground.

Kosher is the Hebrew word for food that is permitted under Jewish dietary law, known as kashrut. Food that is not permitted is often called treif; kosher is roughly comparable to halal, the term for what is permitted under Islamic rules. Jewish dietary laws specify which animals may be eaten and how food must be prepared. For example, pigs are not kosher, so observant Jews do not eat pork. Most insects are also forbidden, but certain locusts are a traditional exception. Locusts appear in the Bible as the eighth plague sent against Egypt in the book of Exodus. The New Testament also describes John the Baptist eating locusts while living in the wilderness.

The Assumption of Mary is the Catholic teaching that Mary, the mother of Jesus, was taken body and soul into heavenly glory at the end of her earthly life. Catholic doctrine does not say whether she died before this happened. The Assumption is different from the Immaculate Conception, which teaches that Mary herself was conceived without original sin, and from the belief that she conceived Jesus through the Holy Spirit while remaining a virgin. Catholics also distinguish Mary’s Assumption from Jesus’s Ascension: Jesus ascended to heaven by his own power, while Mary was taken there by God. In 1950, Pope Pius XII formally defined the Assumption as Catholic dogma in an apostolic constitution titled Munificentissimus Deus, Latin opening words meaning “Most Bountiful God.”

Religious fasting means giving up food, and sometimes drink or other activities, for a time as an act of worship. In Islam, fasting is called sawm. During Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, Muslims remember the first revelation of the Quran to Muhammad and spend time in prayer and reflection. Muslims who are healthy enough fast each day from dawn until sunset. They eat a meal called suhur before dawn and break the fast after sunset with a meal called iftar, often beginning with dates. Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. Christians also practice fasting, especially during Lent, a season of preparation for Easter. Some Eastern Orthodox Christians observe a partial fast during Lent by avoiding animal products.

Hou Yi is a legendary archer in Chinese mythology. In one famous story, ten suns appeared in the sky at the same time, bringing terrible heat that scorched the land and threatened the people. To save the world, Hou Yi used his bow to shoot down nine of the suns, leaving just one to provide light and warmth. Some versions of the myth say the ten suns were the children of the goddess Xihe and took turns crossing the sky before they appeared together. The story explains why only one sun is visible today and presents Hou Yi as a hero who restored balance when the world was in danger.

Níðhöggr is a serpent-like dragon in Norse mythology. It lives beneath Yggdrasil, the immense ash tree at the center of the Norse cosmos, and gnaws at one of its roots. Yggdrasil’s roots reach into multiple realms, linking different parts of the mythological world. A squirrel named Ratatoskr runs along the tree’s trunk, carrying messages between Níðhöggr below and an eagle perched high above. Níðhöggr is also associated with Náströnd, a place where it chews on the corpses of the dead. In the poem Völuspá, it is pictured emerging from below with corpses in its wings. These images make Níðhöggr a memorable creature: a dragon beneath the world-tree that attacks its roots and feeds on the dead.

The Argonauts were a band of Greek heroes led by Jason on a voyage to find the Golden Fleece. Their destination was Colchis, a kingdom on the eastern shore of the Black Sea, where the fleece was guarded by a dragon. The heroes traveled aboard the Argo, a ship built by Argus with the help of the goddess Athena. According to myth, its prow contained a beam of oak from Dodona that could speak and offer prophecies. The Argonauts’ adventures include dangerous encounters at sea, while Jason’s success in Colchis depended on help from Medea. The poet Apollonius of Rhodes told their story in an epic called the Argonautica, named for the heroes who sailed on the Argo.

Ablution is the ritual washing of all or part of the body with water to express purification or prepare for worship. The practice appears in many religions, though its meaning and steps vary. In Islam, the ablution often performed before salah, or prayer, is called wudu: it includes washing the face and arms, wiping the head, and washing the feet in a prescribed order. Jewish worshippers may wash their hands in a rite called netilat yadayim, sometimes using a cup. Christians use water in baptism as a sign of spiritual cleansing and entry into the faith. Hindus may bathe in the Ganges River as a sacred act, while Zen Buddhists may use a stone basin called a tsukubai to wash before entering a sacred space.

In Christian moral teaching, lust is a capital vice: sexual desire that becomes excessive or disordered, especially when it leads someone to treat another person as an object rather than with care and respect. The idea does not mean that all attraction is sinful; it concerns desire that overwhelms judgment or conflicts with moral commitments. Dante Alighieri gives lust a vivid place in the Inferno, the first part of his 14th-century poem the Divine Comedy. Guided by the ancient Roman poet Virgil, Dante travels through Hell and sees souls punished for different sins. In the second circle, people condemned for lust are swept endlessly through a violent storm. Among them are Paolo and Francesca, whose forbidden love led to an affair and their deaths.

Sukkot is a Jewish harvest festival that begins on the 15th of Tishrei, five days after Yom Kippur. It celebrates the harvest and recalls the Israelites’ years of wandering in the wilderness after leaving Egypt. A central custom is building a sukkah, a temporary outdoor booth that reminds people of the shelters used during those wanderings. Families eat meals in the sukkah, and some also sleep there. Its roof is made from plant material, with gaps through which the sky can be seen. Another custom is to hold and shake the “four species,” which include a lulav, or palm branch, and an etrog, a citron. Sukkot lasts seven days; in many communities, the following day, Shemini Atzeret, is counted with it as an eighth day.

Cults are religious or ideological groups often described as having a powerful leader, beliefs outside the mainstream, and strong demands for members’ loyalty. The word can be controversial because people sometimes use it to dismiss unfamiliar religions, so it is more useful to look at a group’s specific beliefs and practices. Two groups often discussed in connection with events of the 1990s are the Branch Davidians and Heaven’s Gate. The Branch Davidians lived at the Mount Carmel Center near Waco, Texas. In 1993, federal agents besieged the site after an attempted raid, and the standoff ended in a deadly fire. Heaven’s Gate taught that its members could reach a higher existence connected to a spacecraft; in 1997, 39 members died in a mass suicide.

The Sermon on the Mount is a collection of teachings attributed to Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew, chapters 5–7. A sermon is a religious speech, often given to teach people how to live, and Matthew describes Jesus teaching a crowd from a mountainside. The sermon opens with the Beatitudes, a series of blessings that begins “Blessed are the poor in spirit” and includes “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.” Jesus then teaches about subjects such as anger, forgiveness, giving to the needy (almsgiving), and prayer. The sermon also contains the Lord’s Prayer, which begins “Our Father in heaven.” Together, these teachings emphasize humility, mercy, sincere worship, and care for others.

A wizard is a figure in stories and folklore who uses supernatural powers, often gained through learning, spells, or secret knowledge. Wizards can be helpful guides or dangerous deceivers. In legends of King Arthur, Merlin is a powerful wizard who advises and aids Arthur; he is also connected with the earlier king Vortigern. A very different wizard appears in Edmund Spenser’s epic poem The Faerie Queene. Archimago is an evil trickster who uses magic to mislead the Redcrosse Knight. He sends Redcrosse a false dream that makes him doubt the chastity and faithfulness of Una, his companion. This deception helps separate them. Merlin and Archimago show why “wizard” describes a type of magical character, not someone who is necessarily good or evil.

Spiders appear in myths around the world, often as creators, storytellers, or skilled weavers. In Navajo tradition, two spider deities debated what to call their invention, while the Hopi tell of Grandmother Spider, who helped create humanity. The web connects these sacred beings with ideas of making and shaping the world. In West African stories, the spider Anansi bought the world’s stories from the sky god Nyame and became a famous trickster and storyteller. Greek mythology tells a different spider story: Arachne, a mortal weaver from Lydia, challenged the goddess Athena to a tapestry contest. Arachne’s tapestry showed the gods’ misdeeds; after Athena destroyed it, Arachne was transformed into a spider. These stories show why spiders are associated with weaving across many cultures.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church is a Protestant Christian denomination that grew out of the Millerite movement in the 1840s. Millerites expected the return, or “advent,” of Jesus Christ; Adventists continue to emphasize his future return. “Seventh-day” refers to Saturday, the seventh day of the week, which members observe as the Sabbath rather than the Sunday worship day more common among Christians. This practice connects to the biblical account of God resting on the seventh day of creation. One of the church’s most influential pioneers was Ellen G. White, a 19th-century American author who reported religious visions and wrote books including Steps to Christ and The Great Controversy. Today, the church has members around the world, and its world headquarters are in Silver Spring, Maryland.

Brynhild is a legendary Valkyrie in the Volsunga Saga, a story from Norse mythology. Valkyries are female figures who choose warriors killed in battle and guide them to Valhalla, the hall of the slain. Brynhild meets Sigurd, a hero famous for slaying a dragon, and teaches him how to use magical runes. Their story becomes tragic when Sigurd is drawn into a tangled conflict over love and marriage. After Sigurd is killed, Brynhild dies and is placed with him on his funeral pyre, where their bodies are burned together. Remembering their connection makes both names easier to recall: Brynhild is the Valkyrie who teaches the runes, and Sigurd is the dragon-slaying hero who learns them.

Cupid is the Roman god of love and desire, corresponding to Eros in Greek mythology. Artists often show him as a winged boy carrying a bow and arrows; his gold-tipped arrows can make people fall in love. In a famous story, Cupid falls in love with Psyche, a mortal woman, but asks her not to look at him. When she breaks that promise, hot oil from her lamp burns him, and they are separated. Psyche faces difficult trials before they are reunited. Cupid then asks Jupiter, the chief Roman god, to make her immortal so they can remain together. Jupiter grants the request, and Psyche receives ambrosia, the divine food associated with immortality. Ambrosia is distinct from nectar, the drink of the gods.

Wudu is a ritual washing that Muslims perform before prayer to prepare themselves in a state of ritual purity. It is a form of ablution, or cleansing, that normally uses water to wash specified body parts, including the face, arms, and feet, and to wipe the head. Muslims also perform wudu before some other acts of worship. Wudu is about spiritual readiness as well as physical cleanliness, but it does not mean that washing alone removes every sin. If water is unavailable or using it would be harmful, a Muslim may perform tayammum instead. Tayammum is a dry purification rite that uses clean earth, such as dust, in place of water. Both practices allow a person to prepare for prayer according to Islamic rules of purification.

Bodhidharma was a semi-legendary Buddhist monk whom Chinese Chan tradition credits with bringing its lineage from India to China. Chan emphasizes meditation and became known as Zen in Japan. Many stories about Bodhidharma were written long after he lived, so historians cannot confirm every detail. One famous legend says he spent nine years meditating while facing a wall. He is also traditionally associated with the Shaolin Temple, which later became famous for its martial arts. In a later Chan account, a student named Huike stood in the snow outside Bodhidharma’s cave, hoping to be accepted as his disciple. Huike then cut off his own arm to show his determination. According to Chan tradition, Bodhidharma accepted him, and Huike became the Second Patriarch of Chan in China.

The Chimera was a monster in Greek mythology with a lion’s head and body, a goat’s head rising from its back, and a serpent for a tail. It was said to breathe fire and to be a child of Typhon and Echidna, the parents of several other famous monsters. The Chimera terrorized the kingdom of Lycia, so King Iobates sent the hero Bellerophon to kill it. With the help of the goddess Athena, Bellerophon gained the winged horse Pegasus. Riding Pegasus let him attack the Chimera from above while staying out of reach of its claws and fire. Bellerophon’s victory made him a celebrated hero, but the creature remains memorable because it combines parts of three very different animals.

Yomi is the underworld in Japanese mythology, a realm of the dead described in the Kojiki. The creator goddess Izanami goes there after dying while giving birth to Kagutsuchi, the fire deity. Her husband, the creator god Izanagi, journeys to Yomi hoping to bring her back to the land of the living. Izanami tells him that she has eaten the food of Yomi and cannot simply leave. Izanagi is warned not to look at her, but he does and sees that her body has decayed. Frightened, he flees as she pursues him, then seals Yomi’s entrance with a massive boulder. Their separation marks a boundary between the living and the dead. Izanami vows to kill a thousand people each day, and Izanagi replies that he will bring fifteen hundred into the world.

Hayagriva is a manifestation, or avatar, of the Hindu god Vishnu, usually shown with a human body and a horse’s head. He is revered as a divine source of knowledge and wisdom. In Hindu tradition, Hayagriva is closely connected with preserving and passing on the Vedas, the foundational sacred scriptures of Hinduism. The Vedas are traditionally grouped into four collections: the Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda, and Atharvaveda. They contain hymns, chants, and formulas used in religious rituals. Stories about Hayagriva often describe him protecting or recovering this sacred knowledge, showing why learning and the scriptures are central to his identity.

Polygamy is a marriage system in which a person has more than one spouse at the same time. In the early Latter Day Saint movement, it was often called plural marriage and usually meant one man having multiple wives. Joseph Smith, the movement’s founder, taught that the practice was permitted by God, but it became highly controversial and contributed to tensions surrounding his death in 1844. Some Latter-day Saints continued to practice plural marriage after following Brigham Young west to Utah. In 1890, Wilford Woodruff, then president of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, issued a declaration known as the Manifesto. It led the mainline church to stop authorizing new plural marriages, although ending the practice entirely took more time.

Ancient Egyptian mummification was a funerary process that preserved a body for the afterlife. Egyptians believed a person’s spirit needed a recognizable body to return to, so embalmers worked to prevent decay. They removed many internal organs, which could be stored in canopic jars, then covered the body with natron, a naturally occurring salt mixture that drew out moisture. After the body had dried, embalmers wrapped it in layers of linen bandages. The finished mummy was placed in a coffin or tomb, often with objects and prayers intended to help the dead person in the afterlife. Animals, including cats, were sometimes mummified too.

In Greek mythology, the Judges of the Underworld assessed souls after death and decided where they would go. Their best-known members were Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus, all sons of Zeus. Souls judged worthy of a blessed afterlife could enter the Elysian Fields, while ordinary souls might go to the Asphodel Fields. Minos had also been a king of Crete during his life. After his son Androgeus died in Athens, Minos demanded tribute from the Athenians: young people sent to Crete to face the Minotaur, a creature kept in a labyrinth. This story connects Minos’s life as a ruler with his later role as a judge of the dead.

Brahmins are the priestly varna, or social class, in the traditional Hindu varna system. They are associated with studying and teaching sacred texts, preserving religious knowledge, and performing rituals. In the traditional ranking of the four varnas, Brahmins stand above the Kshatriyas, the warrior and ruler class. In ancient Vedic religion, Brahmin priests officiated at the Ashvamedha, a royal horse sacrifice. For this ritual, a consecrated stallion was allowed to roam for a year before the sacrifice was completed. The rite was intended to demonstrate a king’s power and authority. Brahmins’ role in ceremonies such as the Ashvamedha reflects the importance traditionally placed on their ritual knowledge.

In Norse mythology, Odin, the chief god, was determined to gain wisdom even at great personal cost. Beneath the roots of Yggdrasil, the world-tree, lay Mímir’s Well, a spring whose water granted knowledge to those who drank it. Mímir guarded the well and demanded a price before allowing Odin a drink. Odin surrendered one of his eyes, leaving it in the well in exchange for the wisdom-granting water. This episode is known as Odin’s Eye Sacrifice. It shows that Odin’s knowledge did not come easily: he was willing to lose part of himself to understand more about the world. His search for wisdom continued in other stories, including one in which he hung from Yggdrasil to discover the runes, symbols used for writing and divination.

Death is often personified, or shown as a humanlike figure, to make the idea of mortality easier to imagine. In the medieval Danse macabre, or “dance of death,” Death leads people of every social rank into a final dance, showing that no one can escape dying. This image inspired the ending of The Seventh Seal, a 1957 Swedish film directed by Ingmar Bergman. Set during the Black Plague, the film follows the knight Antonius Block, played by Max von Sydow, as he returns from the Crusades and searches for meaning. Block plays chess with Death in an attempt to prolong his life. The film closes with a famous silhouetted procession that recalls the medieval dance and its message that death comes for everyone.

Xenu is a figure in an advanced teaching of Scientology, a religion founded by L. Ron Hubbard. According to this account, about 75 million years ago Xenu ruled a Galactic Confederacy and transported billions of people to Earth. There, they were killed with hydrogen bombs. Scientology teaches that the effects of these events still affect people today. The Xenu story is not part of the introductory teachings that newcomers study; it appears in a confidential advanced level called Operating Thetan III, usually shortened to OT III and sometimes nicknamed the “Wall of Fire.” These claims are part of Scientology’s religious account, not established historical or scientific facts.

Chinese mythology is the body of traditional stories from China about how the world began, how nature works, and the deeds of gods and heroes. In one creation story, the giant Pangu emerges from a cosmic egg and separates the sky from the earth. The goddess Nüwa repairs the damaged sky, using the legs of a giant turtle to support it. Another story tells how the archer Hou Yi saves the world by shooting down nine of ten suns. He receives an elixir of immortality, but his wife, Chang’e, drinks it and becomes associated with the Moon. Her story is recalled during the Mid-Autumn Festival, when people traditionally eat mooncakes. Chinese mythology also includes the race that determines the order of the twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac.

Cthulhu is a fictional monster created by horror writer H. P. Lovecraft. It is one of the Great Old Ones, immensely ancient beings in the connected stories often called the Cthulhu Mythos. Cthulhu is commonly pictured as a gigantic creature with a tentacled head and enormous wings. According to Lovecraft’s story “The Call of Cthulhu,” it lies dormant in R’lyeh, a sunken city beneath the Pacific Ocean. When the city briefly rises above the water, Cthulhu can awaken. Lovecraft’s stories often suggest that humans know very little about the universe and that discovering beings like Cthulhu can be terrifying. Although it has become a familiar figure in books, games, and films, Cthulhu and R’lyeh are inventions of fiction, not creatures or places from an ancient religion.

The Mandaeans are an ethnoreligious community, meaning they share both a religious tradition and a cultural identity. Their religion, Mandaeism, is a Gnostic tradition that emphasizes spiritual knowledge and the contrast between a world of light and a world of darkness. Mandaeans revere John the Baptist as their final prophet, but their beliefs and practices are distinct from Christianity. For centuries, many Mandaeans lived in what is now Iraq, especially near rivers. Flowing water remains central to their religious life: an important ritual called masbuta involves full immersion in a river or other flowing water. Unlike a baptism performed only once, masbuta can be repeated throughout a person’s life for spiritual purification. Thus, Mandaeans are the community, while Mandaeism is the religion they practice.

Frigg is a goddess in Norse mythology and the wife of Odin, ruler of the Aesir gods. She is associated with marriage, family life, prophecy, and clairvoyance—the ability to know things beyond ordinary sight. Frigg is also the mother of Baldr, a god whose death plays an important part in Norse myths. Some traditions describe her using a mystical spinning wheel to create clouds. Her husband Odin is associated with wisdom, war, poetry, and magic. His search for knowledge leads him to give up one eye for a drink from Mimir’s well and to hang from the world tree, Yggdrasil, to learn the secrets of the runes. Frigg should not be confused with Freyja, another Norse goddess who owns a falcon-feather cloak.

The Tribe of Judah was one of the twelve tribes of Israel, traditionally descended from Judah, a son of Jacob. It became especially important because it was the tribe of David, a shepherd who became king. David captured Jerusalem and made it his capital, and biblical tradition says that God promised his royal dynasty an enduring throne. David’s son Solomon inherited the kingship and built the First Temple in Jerusalem. After the kingdom split, Judah was the leading tribe of the southern Kingdom of Judah. In the New Testament’s Book of Revelation, Jesus is called the “Lion of the tribe of Judah,” an image of strength and messianic victory that connects him with David’s royal line.

Heimdallr is an Aesir god in Norse mythology who guards Bifrost, the rainbow bridge linking Midgard, the world of humans, with Asgard, the stronghold of the gods. He watches for threats approaching Asgard and is known for his extraordinarily keen sight and hearing: stories say he can see for great distances and hear even the faintest sounds. His watchful role becomes especially important at Ragnarök, the great conflict that brings an end to the old order of the gods. Heimdallr keeps a horn called Gjallarhorn, whose blast will be heard throughout the worlds when Ragnarök begins. Together, his sharp senses and his horn make him the gods’ lookout and the one who sounds the warning when danger arrives.

Delphi was an ancient Greek sanctuary and settlement in Phocis, on the slopes of Mount Parnassus. People traveled there to seek guidance from the Pythia, a priestess who delivered prophecies at the oracle of Apollo. Pilgrims could wash in the nearby Castalian Spring before entering the sanctuary and making offerings. According to myth, Apollo claimed Delphi by slaying a serpent called the Python, from which the Pythia took her name. Apollo was also the twin brother of Artemis and the god of music and archery. Another sacred object at Delphi was the omphalos, a stone said to mark the center of the world: Zeus had released two eagles from opposite ends of the earth, and they met there.

Jason is a hero of Greek mythology who led the Argonauts aboard the ship Argo on a quest for the Golden Fleece. King Pelias sent him to retrieve it from Colchis, where King Aeëtes guarded it and set Jason dangerous challenges. Aeëtes’ daughter Medea, who knew magic, helped Jason yoke fire-breathing bulls, sow dragon’s teeth that grew into armed warriors, and overcome the dragon guarding the fleece. Medea then left Colchis with Jason. On the voyage, the musician Orpheus played his lyre to protect the crew from the Sirens’ song. Jason and Medea’s story later turned tragic: after Jason abandoned her despite his promise to remain faithful, some versions of the myth say he died when the rotting Argo fell on him.

Saint Nicholas of Myra was a fourth-century Christian bishop in Lycia, a region in what is now Turkey. Later stories celebrated him for helping people in need, especially by giving gifts secretly to the poor. These traditions helped make him the historical inspiration for Santa Claus, the figure who brings children gifts at Christmas. Nicholas is also linked to a story about the First Council of Nicaea, an assembly of bishops held in 325 CE to debate Christian beliefs, including the nature of Christ. According to a later legend, Nicholas became so angry with Arius during the debate that he struck him. Historians do not know whether this incident happened, but the legend remains part of Nicholas’s story.

The Mahdi, meaning “the rightly guided one,” is an expected leader in Islamic beliefs about the end times. Many Muslims believe he will appear before the final judgment to fight injustice and restore justice, although traditions differ about who he is and what he will do. In Twelver Shia Islam, the Mahdi is identified with the twelfth imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, who is believed to be hidden and will return. Sunni traditions also describe a future Mahdi, but generally do not identify him as this hidden imam. Throughout history, some people have claimed the title. In 1881, the Sudanese religious leader Muhammad Ahmad proclaimed himself the Mahdi. He led a revolt against Egyptian rule in Sudan, and his followers captured the city of Khartoum in 1885.

Golden apples appear in several Norse and Greek myths. In Norse mythology, the goddess Iðunn keeps apples that preserve the gods’ youth; without them, the gods begin to grow old. In Greek mythology, golden apples grow in the Garden of the Hesperides at the edge of the world, where a dragon named Ladon guards them. A different golden apple, marked “To the Fairest,” was thrown by Eris, the goddess of discord, and led to a contest among three goddesses. Golden apples also feature in the story of Atalanta, a swift huntress who agreed to marry only someone who could beat her in a footrace. Her challenger, Melanion, dropped three golden apples given to him by Aphrodite. Atalanta stopped to pick them up, allowing him to win.

The Book of Jonah is a short book of the Hebrew Bible about a prophet whom God commands to warn Nineveh, a great Assyrian city, that it faces destruction. Jonah tries to escape this mission by sailing toward Tarshish, but a storm strikes the ship. After the sailors throw him overboard, a great fish swallows him and later releases him onto dry land. Jonah then goes to Nineveh and delivers the warning. Its people, including their king, fast and turn from their evil ways, so God spares the city. Jonah is upset by this mercy, and the book ends by challenging him to care about the people of Nineveh. The entire Book of Jonah is read during Yom Kippur, Judaism’s Day of Atonement.

The Styx is a river of the Greek underworld that marks a boundary the dead must cross on their way to the realm of Hades. It was sacred to the gods: after the war against the Titans, Zeus declared that an oath sworn on the Styx could not be broken without severe punishment. In a later story about the hero Achilles, his mother Thetis, a sea nymph called a Nereid, dipped him into the Styx as an infant to make him invulnerable. She held him by one heel, so that spot did not touch the water and remained vulnerable. This story is the source of the expression “Achilles’ heel,” meaning a weakness that can bring down someone otherwise strong.

Tiresias is a blind prophet from Thebes who appears in several Greek myths and tragedies. In Sophocles’ Oedipus Rex, King Oedipus investigates a plague afflicting Thebes and searches for the murderer of the former king, Laius. Tiresias initially refuses to reveal what he knows, but eventually tells Oedipus that he himself killed Laius. Oedipus angrily accuses the prophet of plotting against him. As the truth emerges, Oedipus learns that Laius was his father and that Jocasta, whom he married, is his mother. Jocasta dies, and Oedipus blinds himself. Tiresias also appears in Sophocles’ Antigone, where he warns the ruler Creon that refusing to bury Polynices has offended the gods. In both plays, Tiresias sees truths that powerful rulers resist hearing.

Iðunn is a goddess in Norse mythology who keeps the apples that preserve the gods’ youth. When the giant Þjazi, a jötunn, captures Loki, he forces Loki to lure Iðunn outside Asgard. Þjazi then carries her and her apples away to his home, Þrymheimr. Without Iðunn’s apples, the gods begin to grow old, so they demand that Loki bring her back. Loki rescues Iðunn, but Þjazi pursues them and is killed by the gods. Þjazi’s daughter, Skaði, later comes to Asgard to demand compensation for her father’s death. Iðunn’s story shows why the apples matter: even the Norse gods depend on them to remain young.

The sacred lotus is an aquatic flowering plant whose roots grow in muddy water while its blossoms rise above the surface. In Buddhism, this makes it a symbol of purity and awakening: a person can live in a troubled world yet develop wisdom and compassion. Buddhist art often shows Buddhas seated on lotus flowers to represent their enlightenment. The lotus also appears in Buddhist names and teachings. The Lotus Sutra is an important text that teaches that everyone has the potential to become a Buddha. In China, a Buddhist religious organization called the White Lotus Society took its name from the flower. It was associated with the 14th-century Red Turban Rebellion.

In Zoroastrian belief, the Chinvat Bridge is the crossing that every soul reaches after death. It is a place of judgment: a person’s good and bad thoughts, words, and actions determine what happens as the soul tries to cross. For a righteous person, the bridge is broad and safe, leading toward a joyful afterlife. For a wicked person, it becomes narrow and dangerous, and the soul falls toward a place of suffering. Mithra, a Zoroastrian deity associated with truth and keeping promises, is linked with guarding the bridge and taking part in judgment. The bridge therefore represents an important Zoroastrian idea: how people live has consequences beyond death.

Protestantism is a broad Christian movement that began during the 16th-century Reformation. Protestants challenged the authority of the pope and taught that the Bible, rather than the pope, was the highest authority in matters of faith. The movement developed into several branches, including Calvinism. In France, Protestants who followed Calvinist teachings were known as Huguenots. They sought the right to practice their religion in a mostly Catholic country, and conflict between Catholics and Huguenots led to the French Wars of Religion, which lasted from 1562 to 1598. Henry of Navarre was a Huguenot leader during these wars. He later became King Henry IV of France and converted to Catholicism to secure his rule.

Martin Luther was a German Augustinian friar and theologian whose ideas helped launch the Protestant Reformation, a movement that changed Christianity in Europe. In 1517, he wrote a set of propositions called the Ninety-Five Theses to invite debate about indulgences. Church officials offered indulgences as a way to reduce punishment for sin, but Luther objected to how they were being sold. He especially challenged claims associated with the preacher Johann Tetzel that payments could shorten a person’s time in purgatory. Money from indulgence sales also helped fund the rebuilding of St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome. According to tradition, Luther posted the Ninety-Five Theses on the door of All Saints’ Church in Wittenberg, Germany. Their rapid spread brought his criticism to a wide audience.

Lot is a figure in the Book of Genesis, the first book of the Hebrew Bible. He is Abraham’s nephew and lives in Sodom, a city whose inhabitants are described as wicked and inhospitable. When visitors come to Sodom, Lot welcomes them into his home. God decides to destroy Sodom and the nearby city of Gomorrah, but Lot is warned and led away with his wife and daughters before the destruction. They are told to flee without looking back. Lot’s wife does look back at Sodom and becomes a pillar of salt, one of the story’s best-known details. Remembering that Lot is Abraham’s nephew and that the city he escapes is Sodom helps distinguish the man from the place.

A torii is a traditional Japanese gate that marks the entrance to a sacred place, especially a Shinto shrine. Its familiar shape has two upright pillars supporting one or more horizontal beams. Passing through a torii symbolizes leaving the everyday world and entering sacred grounds. Torii are often painted red or orange, though they can also be made of unpainted wood or stone. The religion associated with torii is Shinto, the indigenous religion of Japan. Shinto practices center on respect for kami, spiritual beings or powers associated with nature, places, and ancestors. One of Shinto’s most important sites is Ise Grand Shrine, which is dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu.

Bread is a staple food usually made by baking dough from flour and water. It also has an important place in the Gospels and Christian worship. In one miracle known as the feeding of the four thousand, Jesus feeds a large crowd with just seven loaves of bread and a few fish, with food left over afterward. Bread is also central to the Eucharist, or Communion. At the Last Supper, the final meal Jesus shared with his disciples before his arrest, he gave them bread and wine and told them to continue the practice in remembrance of him. In the Eucharist, bread is identified with Christ’s body, though Christian traditions differ in how they explain what happens to it.
