A troll is a supernatural, humanlike creature from Scandinavian folklore, especially the stories of Norway, Sweden, and Denmark. Trolls are often linked to mountains, caves, and wild places. Their appearance varies from tale to tale: some are huge and frightening, while others are smaller, and some are described as having tails. In certain stories, a troll caught in sunlight turns to stone. Trolls also appear in Henrik Ibsen’s Norwegian play Peer Gynt, in which the hero encounters a troll king. The Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg wrote music to accompany the play and later arranged some of it into orchestral suites. His pieces include “Morning Mood” and “In the Hall of the Mountain King,” whose music grows faster and louder as Peer is chased.

In Buddhism, nirvana is liberation from suffering and from the cycle of death and rebirth. Its name is commonly explained as meaning “blowing out,” like extinguishing a flame. What is extinguished is not a person, but the craving, hatred, and ignorance that keep suffering going. Buddhists seek nirvana by following the Buddha’s teachings, including the Noble Eightfold Path. An ancient Greek skeptic, Pyrrho of Elis, is sometimes discussed alongside this Buddhist idea. Pyrrho traveled to India with Alexander the Great’s expedition and later taught Timon of Phlius. His ideal of ataraxia, or freedom from mental disturbance, has been compared with nirvana. The two ideas come from different traditions, however, and scholars cannot be certain that Pyrrho learned his ideal from Buddhist ascetics.

Brigham Young was an early leader of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, often called the LDS or Mormon Church. After the church’s founder, Joseph Smith, was killed in 1844, Young led many members west to escape conflict and find a place to settle. In 1847, he chose the Salt Lake Valley as the site of their main settlement, which became Salt Lake City. Young became the church’s second president and directed the growth of its communities across the American West. In 1850, Congress established Utah Territory, a U.S. jurisdiction that was much larger than today’s state of Utah and included much of the Great Basin. Young served as its first governor while continuing to lead the church.

Apostolic succession is the Christian belief that bishops receive their spiritual and church authority through a continuous line of bishops reaching back to Jesus Christ’s apostles, his first followers. This line of succession supports the legitimacy of the episcopate, or the office of bishop. In the Catholic Church, a new bishop is ordained when other bishops pray over him and lay their hands on his head. This laying on of hands is a visible sign of passing on the authority entrusted to the apostles. Catholics also connect apostolic succession to the authority of the pope: they regard Saint Peter as the first pope and believe that the bishops of Rome succeed him. Other churches with bishops, including Eastern Orthodox churches, also teach apostolic succession.

In Greek mythology, the Sphinx was a dangerous creature with a lion’s body and a human head. It stopped travelers near the city of Thebes and challenged them to answer a riddle, killing those who failed. Its most famous question asked what walks on four legs in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening. Oedipus answered “a human”: people crawl as babies, walk on two legs as adults, and may use a cane in old age. His correct answer ended the Sphinx’s threat, and he became king of Thebes. Oedipus was the son of Laius and Jocasta, though he did not know who his parents were when he arrived at Thebes. Sophocles later told his tragic story in plays.

Sharia is the body of Islamic religious law and ethical guidance that helps Muslims decide how to worship and conduct everyday life. It draws on the Quran and the Sunnah, the teachings and example of the Prophet Muhammad. Sharia addresses matters such as prayer, fasting, family life, business dealings, and food. Islamic teachings classify some actions and foods as haram, meaning forbidden, while halal means permitted. For example, food described as halal is allowed for Muslims to eat; pork is haram. Sharia is not a single rulebook applied in exactly the same way everywhere. Muslim scholars interpret its sources, and practices and legal systems can differ among communities and countries.

The Wesley family played a central role in the rise of Methodism, a Christian movement that emphasized personal faith, regular prayer, and helping others. Susanna Wesley, the daughter of minister Samuel Annesley, raised her children in a home where religious study was important. Two of her sons, John and Charles Wesley, helped establish the Methodist movement in 18th-century England. John became known for his preaching and for organizing Methodist groups, while Charles spread their beliefs through hymns. Charles was a prolific writer who composed thousands of hymns, including “And Can It Be” and “O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing.” Their work helped Methodism grow beyond England and influenced many later Christian churches.

In ancient Egyptian religion, the Eye of Ra was the personified power of Ra, the sun god. It could take the form of a goddess who protected him and punished his enemies. One such goddess was Sekhmet, often shown with the head of a lioness. In one myth, Ra sent her to punish humanity after people conspired against him. Her attack became so fierce that she had to be stopped: beer was colored red to look like blood, and she drank it until she could no longer continue her rampage. The Eye of Ra belongs to a wider Egyptian tradition of divine eyes, but it is distinct from the Eye of Horus, also called the wedjat, which the god Thoth restored in another myth.

Atheism is a position about belief in gods: an atheist may explicitly hold that no gods exist or may simply not believe in gods because they find the evidence unconvincing. It differs from agnosticism, which focuses on whether the existence of gods can be known. Atheism does not, by itself, tell someone how to live or what gives life meaning. Those questions are central to existentialism, a philosophical movement associated with Albert Camus and Jean-Paul Sartre. Sartre described existentialism as “a humanism,” emphasizing human freedom and responsibility. Camus explored how people might live in a seemingly meaningless universe in his essay The Myth of Sisyphus. Both Camus and Sartre were atheists, unlike the Christian existentialist Søren Kierkegaard.

Mulan, also called Hua Mulan, is a heroine of Chinese folklore. Her story is told in an anonymous poem commonly known in English as The Ballad of Mulan. When a military draft orders someone from her family to serve, Mulan fears that her aging father cannot survive the fighting. She disguises herself as a man and joins the army in his place, serving for years without her fellow soldiers discovering her identity. After the war, she declines the official honors offered for her service and asks instead to return home. Only when she puts on her usual clothes do her comrades realize she is a woman. The tale celebrates her courage and devotion to her family and has been retold in books, films, and other works.

Iftar is the evening meal with which Muslims break their daily fast during Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. During Ramadan, Muslims who are able to fast abstain from food and drink from dawn until sunset as part of a practice called sawm. They eat a meal called suhur before dawn, then wait until sunset to eat again. Iftar traditionally begins with dates, often followed by water, before a larger meal. Eating dates to break the fast is a practice associated with the Prophet Muhammad. Iftar may be shared with family, friends, or a wider community, and it is often a time for prayer and gratitude. Ramadan ends with the celebration of Eid al-Fitr.

Jonathan Edwards was an 18th-century New England Congregationalist minister and theologian who helped lead the First Great Awakening, a wave of religious revival in the American colonies. While serving a church in Northampton, Massachusetts, he wrote about the many people there who had experienced religious conversion. Edwards urged listeners to recognize their need for God’s mercy and change their lives. His most famous sermon, Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, was delivered in Enfield, Connecticut, in 1741. It warned of divine judgment through vivid images, including a bow aimed at sinners and a spider held over a fire. Near the end of his life, Edwards became president of the College of New Jersey, now Princeton University.

In Celtic traditions and other folklore, witches are people believed to practice magic, sometimes to heal or protect others and sometimes to cause harm. Stories about witches vary widely, but fear of harmful witchcraft led to accusations against real people in medieval and early modern Europe. Many of those accused were women, and suspicion could grow from local disputes or someone’s misfortune rather than evidence of magic. In the late 15th century, the German writer Heinrich Kramer produced a Latin treatise called Malleus Maleficarum, usually translated as “The Hammer of Witches.” It portrayed witchcraft as a serious religious threat and argued for harsh punishment. The book helped spread ideas used to justify witch trials, though beliefs about witches and responses to accusations differed across places and periods.

The Guru Granth Sahib is the central scripture of Sikhism, a religion founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab region of South Asia. It contains hymns by Sikh Gurus and devotional poets from other religious traditions, bringing together teachings about devotion to one God, equality, and honest living. The fifth Sikh Guru, Guru Arjan, oversaw its original compilation, known as the Adi Granth, in 1604 and had it installed at the Harmandir Sahib, also called the Golden Temple, in Amritsar. Later, the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, declared the scripture the final Guru. Sikhs therefore honor the Guru Granth Sahib not simply as a holy book, but as their eternal, living spiritual guide.

The Book of Proverbs is a book of wisdom in the Hebrew Bible traditionally attributed to King Solomon. Its opening verses say that its teachings offer wisdom and instruction, helping readers understand good judgment and live rightly. A central lesson is that “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge.” Here, fear means deep reverence and respect for God, not simply being frightened. Proverbs often contrasts wise choices, such as honesty, self-control, and kindness, with foolish choices that harm people. In chapter 8, Wisdom is personified as a woman who calls out to the inexperienced and urges them to learn. She says the Lord possessed her at the beginning of creation and describes being present before the earth’s foundations were laid.

Mythological twins are a recurring motif in stories from many cultures: two closely linked siblings, often heroes or divine figures, face dangers and accomplish great deeds together. A famous example is Hunahpu and Xbalanque, the Hero Twins of the K’iche’ Maya. Their story appears in the Popol Vuh, a sacred narrative that preserves Maya myths and traditions. In it, the twins descend to Xibalba, the Maya underworld, where they face dangerous trials, play a ball game, and outwit its powerful lords. Their adventures show how twin characters can work together to overcome forces that seem stronger than they are. If asked to name the motif, the answer is mythological twins; if asked which narrative tells their story, it is the Popol Vuh.

The Rabbit is the fourth animal in the Chinese zodiac’s repeating cycle of twelve signs. It comes after the Tiger and before the Dragon. Chinese tradition connects zodiac signs with years in a calendar based on the moon, and each sign also has associations with yin or yang and one of the Five Phases: wood, fire, earth, metal, or water. The Rabbit is linked to a famous moon legend. In this story, an immortal woman named Chang’e lives on the moon with the Jade Rabbit. The rabbit is often shown using a mortar and pestle to pound herbs, sometimes to make an elixir of immortality. So if you see clues about the fourth zodiac animal or a jade animal working beside Chang’e on the moon, the answer is Rabbit.

Buddhist monks are ordained religious practitioners who devote their lives to studying and practicing the Buddha’s teachings. Traditionally, they give up many ordinary possessions, wear robes, and live together in a monastic community called the sangha. Monks seek liberation from suffering, often described as attaining nirvana, through meditation, ethical conduct, and wisdom. Their daily lives are guided by the Vinaya, a collection of disciplinary rules covering matters such as behavior, possessions, and life in the community. The Vinaya is one of the three main divisions of the Buddhist canon, a collection of sacred texts. Monastic traditions vary across Buddhist cultures: for example, Shaolin monks in China are associated with martial arts. The sangha is also counted as one of Buddhism’s Three Jewels, alongside the Buddha and his teachings.

The Michigan Dogman is a creature from Michigan folklore, often described as a large, dog-like being that walks on two legs and resembles a werewolf. Stories say its howl sounds like a human scream. It is a cryptid: an animal whose existence some people claim but science has not confirmed. The Dogman is a local legend rather than a creature known to exist, and descriptions of it vary from one story to another. The legend gained wider attention in 1987 when Steve Cook, a Michigan radio personality, wrote and recorded a song called “The Legend” for Traverse City radio station WTCM-FM. The song helped turn stories of the Dogman into a well-known part of Michigan folklore.

Tithonus was a Trojan prince whom Eos, the Greek goddess of the dawn, fell in love with and carried away. Wanting them to stay together forever, Eos asked Zeus, king of the gods, to make Tithonus immortal. But she forgot to ask for eternal youth. Tithonus could never die, yet he continued to grow older, becoming frail and withered while Eos remained young. In some versions of the myth, he eventually became a cicada, an insect known for its persistent song. His story shows why immortality and eternal youth are not the same thing: living forever might seem like a gift, but for Tithonus it became a burden.

Baldr is a beloved god of the Aesir, the son of Odin and Frigg. Famous for his beauty and goodness, he was thought to be safe from harm after Frigg persuaded nearly everything in the world to swear not to hurt him. But she had overlooked a young mistletoe plant. Loki, a shape-shifting trickster god, discovered this weakness and made a weapon from mistletoe. While the gods amused themselves by throwing harmless objects at Baldr, Loki guided Baldr’s blind brother Höðr to throw the mistletoe at him. It struck and killed Baldr, though Höðr did not know it could cause harm. Baldr’s death was a terrible loss to the gods and became one of the events leading toward Ragnarök, the destruction and renewal of the world.

A unicorn is a mythical creature usually pictured as a horse with one long horn rising from its forehead. In European legends, unicorns symbolize purity and are often linked with magic and healing. Medieval people believed the horn could cure illness and protect against poison; the traditional name for a unicorn’s horn is an alicorn. Objects sold as alicorns were sometimes actually narwhal tusks, which may help explain why narwhals are called “unicorns of the sea.” Although unicorns belong to legend rather than the natural world, they remain popular in stories and art. The unicorn is also the national animal of Scotland.

Maenads were female followers of Dionysus, the ancient Greek god of wine, celebration, and transformation. Their name is linked to a state of frenzy, and Greek stories describe them dancing, singing, and leaving ordinary social rules behind during his worship. They were also called Bacchae or Bacchantes, after Bacchus, another name for Dionysus. Some accounts describe their rituals as reaching a violent climax in two distinct acts: sparagmos, the tearing apart of a living victim, and omophagia, the eating of its flesh raw. These accounts appear especially in myth and drama, so they should not be taken as proof that every group of Dionysus’s worshippers performed such acts. In myth, Maenads embody both the joy and the frightening loss of control associated with Dionysus.

Garuda is a powerful eagle-like figure in Hindu mythology, often shown with a human body and the wings, beak, and claws of a bird. He is the king of birds and the son of Vinata. Garuda serves as the mount, or vehicle, of Vishnu, carrying the god through the sky. His sworn enemies are the nāgas, serpent beings sometimes depicted as snakes or as beings with both human and snake features. One important nāga is Shesha, the serpent king on whom Vishnu is often shown resting. This creates two memorable images of Vishnu: riding through the sky on Garuda and reclining on Shesha. Garuda’s brother Aruna is the charioteer of Surya, the sun god.

Penelope is the queen of Ithaca and the wife of the Greek hero Odysseus in Homer’s Odyssey. While Odysseus spends ten years fighting in the Trojan War and another ten years trying to return home, many suitors crowd his palace, hoping to marry Penelope and become king. Unsure whether Odysseus is alive, she finds a clever way to delay choosing a new husband. She says she must first finish weaving a funeral cloth for Laertes, Odysseus’s elderly father. Each day she works on the textile, but each night she secretly unravels what she has woven, so it never gets finished. Her plan holds off the suitors for years, though it eventually comes to light. Penelope is remembered for her loyalty, patience, and resourcefulness.

Juno was the Roman queen of the gods and the wife of Jupiter. Romans honored her alongside Jupiter and Minerva as part of the Capitoline Triad, a group of three major gods worshipped at a temple on Rome’s Capitoline Hill. She was also associated with marriage and the protection of women. In Virgil’s epic poem the Aeneid, Juno’s anger at the Trojans drives the opening conflict. She opposes Aeneas as he leads Trojan survivors toward the land where their descendants will eventually found Rome. In Book 1, Juno approaches Aeolus, the ruler of the winds, and persuades him to unleash a storm against Aeneas’s fleet. She promises Aeolus the nymph Deiopea in return, but Aeneas and his companions survive the storm.

Horses appear in many Greek myths, sometimes with extraordinary powers or unusual forms. Achilles’ chariot was pulled by Balius and Xanthus, two immortal horses; Xanthus could even speak. In one of his labors, Heracles captured the Mares of Diomedes, horses that had been trained to eat human flesh. Another famous horse was Pegasus, who had wings and could fly. The hero Bellerophon rode Pegasus when he fought the Chimera and later tried to reach Mount Olympus. Not every mythological horse lived on land: the hippocampus was a sea creature with the front half of a horse and the tail of a fish. Hippocampi are often pictured pulling the sea god Poseidon’s chariot. Together, these creatures are examples of mythological horses.

The Three Jewels, also called the Triple Gem or Three Refuges, are the three foundational supports in which Buddhists take refuge: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Taking refuge means looking to them for guidance on the path toward awakening. The Buddha is the awakened teacher; Siddhartha Gautama is the historical Buddha whose teachings began Buddhism. The Dharma is his teaching, including ideas and practices that help people understand suffering and work toward freedom from it. The Sangha is the Buddhist community that preserves and practices those teachings. Traditionally, it centers on ordained monks and nuns, though the word can also include a wider community of practitioners. Together, the Three Jewels provide a teacher, a path, and a community of support.

The Eucharist is a Christian act of worship that recalls the Last Supper, when Jesus shared bread and wine with his disciples before his death. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning “thanksgiving,” and it is also called Holy Communion or the Lord’s Supper. During the service, Christians eat bread and drink wine, or sometimes grape juice, in remembrance of Jesus. Different churches explain the meaning of the bread and wine in different ways. In Catholic teaching, the doctrine of transubstantiation says that they become Christ’s body and blood in substance, even though they still look, taste, and feel like bread and wine. Lutherans teach sacramental union, which says that Christ’s body and blood are truly present with the bread and wine.

Wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting grapes or grape juice. It has an important place in both Jewish and Christian rituals. In Jewish practice, a blessing called Kiddush is commonly recited over a cup of wine at the Friday-evening meal to sanctify Shabbat; Kiddush is also said on festivals. During the Passover Seder, participants traditionally drink four cups of wine at different points in the meal. Wine also appears in Jewish teachings about the Nazirite vow, which requires a person taking the vow to avoid wine and other grape products. In many Christian communities, wine is used alongside bread in the Eucharist, a ritual remembering Jesus’s Last Supper. These uses give wine religious meaning beyond its role as an everyday drink.

Momotaro, whose name means “Peach Boy,” is a hero of Japanese folklore. In a familiar version of the story, an elderly woman finds a giant peach floating down a river and brings it home to her husband. When they open it, they discover a baby boy inside and raise him as their son. As Momotaro grows up, he sets out to confront the oni, or ogres, who live on an island called Onigashima, meaning “Ogre Island.” Along the way, he shares food with a dog, a monkey, and a pheasant. They become his companions and help him defeat the ogres. The tale is often told as a story about courage, teamwork, and the strength of friendship.

A fairy is a supernatural being from European folklore, often linked to magic and an otherworldly realm. Fairy stories vary widely: some fairies help humans, while others play tricks or cause trouble. In modern stories they may be pictured as tiny creatures with wings, but older traditions describe them in many different ways. Tinker Bell, from J. M. Barrie’s Peter Pan, is a famous fairy. Fairies also appear in William Shakespeare’s play A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Oberon and Titania are their king and queen, and Oberon’s mischievous jester, Puck, creates confusion among the human characters. One of Puck’s tricks is to transform the head of a man named Nick Bottom into that of a donkey.

Puja is a devotional worship ritual practiced in several Indian religions. It may take place at home or in a temple and often includes prayers, offerings of flowers, food, or light, and other acts of respect. In Jainism, bhava puja refers to inward worship focused on a person’s thoughts and intentions, while dravya puja uses physical offerings and ceremonial actions. Puja is also part of important festivals. During Diwali, a South Asian festival often called the festival of lights, many Hindus perform Lakshmi puja to honor the goddess of prosperity, commonly on the festival’s third day. Jains also observe Diwali, but they connect it with the nirvana, or spiritual liberation, of Mahavira, a major teacher of Jainism.

Peleus was a mortal king, and Thetis was a sea goddess. Their wedding became an important event in Greek mythology because Eris, the goddess of discord, brought a golden apple meant for “the fairest.” Three goddesses claimed it, and the Trojan prince Paris was asked to choose between them. His choice in the Judgment of Paris helped set in motion the Trojan War. Peleus and Thetis’s son was Achilles, the leader of the Myrmidons and the foremost Greek warrior in that war. In the Iliad, Achilles withdraws from battle after a dispute with the Greek commander Agamemnon. When the Trojan warrior Hector kills Achilles’s close friend Patroclus, Achilles returns to the fighting and kills Hector in revenge.

Zoroastrian sky burial is a traditional funeral practice in Zoroastrianism, a religion that began in ancient Persia. Zoroastrians have regarded earth, fire, and water as sacred, so burying or cremating a body could be seen as contaminating those elements. Instead, the body is taken to a Tower of Silence, a circular, open-air stone enclosure raised above the surrounding ground. There it is exposed to scavenger birds, which consume the flesh. Afterward, the remaining bones are collected. This practice gives the dead a place of rest while keeping the body separate from the sacred elements. Although customs vary today, the rite is known as Zoroastrian sky burial, and the structure used for it is called a Tower of Silence.

Hyacinthus was a beautiful young man in Greek mythology who was loved by Apollo, the god of music and light. According to one version of the story, Zephyrus, the personification of the west wind, also loved Hyacinthus and grew jealous of Apollo’s affection for him. While Apollo and Hyacinthus were throwing a discus together, Zephyrus blew it off course so that it struck Hyacinthus and killed him. Apollo was overcome with grief. He caused a flower to grow from Hyacinthus’s blood, giving the youth’s name to the hyacinth. The myth links a tragic death with the appearance of a new flower, a common way Greek stories explained features of the natural world.

In Norse mythology, Midgard is the world where humans live. Its name is often translated as “Middle Earth” because it is imagined as a central realm among the nine worlds. These worlds are linked by Yggdrasil, a great ash tree known as the World Tree. Midgard is separate from Asgard, the home of gods such as Odin and Thor, but the two realms are connected by Bifrost. Bifrost is a bridge described as looking like a rainbow, and it provides a passage between the human world and the gods’ world. So if a question asks for the human realm, the answer is Midgard; if it asks for the rainbow bridge connecting Midgard to Asgard, the answer is Bifrost.

In Greek mythology, Echo was a nymph known for her skill at conversation. While Zeus pursued affairs with other women, Echo kept his wife, Hera, distracted by talking to her at length. When Hera discovered the trick, she cursed Echo so that she could no longer speak her own thoughts and could only repeat the last words spoken by someone else. Echo later fell in love with Narcissus, a beautiful young man, but he rejected her. Grieving, she faded away until only her repeating voice remained, explaining the echoes people hear. Narcissus then became transfixed by his own reflection in a pool. His name gives us the word “narcissistic,” used to describe someone who is excessively self-admiring.

Indra is a major deity in Vedic and Hindu mythology and the king of the Devas, a group of divine beings. He is associated with storms, rain and warfare, and his weapon is the Vajra, a powerful thunderbolt. In traditional images and stories, Indra rides Airavata, a white elephant. One of his best-known myths describes how he defeats Vritra, a serpent-like being that holds back the waters, allowing the waters to flow again. Indra is praised more often than any other deity in the Rigveda, an ancient Sanskrit collection of hymns used in Vedic religious tradition. The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas, sacred texts that are important to Hinduism.

A kachina doll is a carved figure that represents a katsina spirit in Hopi religious and ceremonial traditions. Katsinas are spiritual beings associated with aspects of the natural world and community life, and they appear in ceremonies through masked dancers. Hopi artists traditionally carve the dolls from cottonwood, a tree whose wood is light and relatively easy to shape. The figures may be painted and decorated to show the features of particular katsinas. They are often given to children to help them learn to recognize these beings and understand their place in Hopi teachings. Although they are called “dolls” in English, kachina dolls are teaching objects connected to living cultural traditions, not simply toys.

The Jewish Messiah, or mashiach, is a future leader and redeemer awaited in traditional Jewish belief. The word “messiah” means “anointed one,” recalling the anointing of ancient kings. Traditional accounts say the Messiah will gather Jews from the diaspora back to Israel, restore Jewish national life, rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, and reestablish the Sanhedrin, a council that served as a high court. Across history, figures including Simon bar Kokhba and Sabbatai Zevi have been claimed to be the Messiah, but neither is accepted as having fulfilled these hopes. Belief in the Messiah’s coming is the twelfth of the Thirteen Principles of Faith formulated by the medieval Jewish philosopher and legal scholar Maimonides. The traditional hymn “Ani Ma’amin” draws on this principle.

A funeral is a ceremony or set of customs held after someone dies. It gives family and friends a way to mourn, honor the person’s life, and care for or dispose of their remains. Funeral practices vary across religions and cultures. In Hinduism, the funeral rite called Antyesti means “last sacrifice” and is considered the final samskara, or rite of passage. It commonly involves cremation. At Jewish funerals, close mourners may perform keriah by tearing a garment as a sign of grief. A Catholic funeral may include a Requiem Mass, with prayers for the deceased. Islamic funerals include burial rather than cremation. Although these traditions differ, each uses ritual to help people respond to death and remember the person who has died.

The Lady of the Lake is a mysterious enchantress in the legends of King Arthur, the ruler of Camelot and leader of the Knights of the Round Table. In some versions of the story, Arthur’s first sword, drawn from a stone, breaks during a fight. The Lady of the Lake then gives him a new magical sword called Excalibur, which rises from the water. Although different stories give her different names, including Nimue, she is closely linked to the lake and to Arthur’s fate. After Arthur is mortally wounded in his final battle, Excalibur is thrown back into the water, where the Lady receives it. She also helps carry Arthur to Avalon, a mysterious island associated with healing.

Kriah is a Jewish mourning practice in which a person tears or cuts a garment after the death of a close relative. The tear makes grief visible and expresses the pain of the loss. It is commonly performed before the funeral or burial, often with the guidance of a rabbi or funeral attendant. Close relatives who may observe kriah include a parent, child, sibling, or spouse of the person who died. After burial, mourners traditionally begin shiva, a seven-day period of mourning. During shiva, they commonly stay at home, pause many ordinary activities, and receive visitors who come to comfort them. Kriah and shiva are different practices: kriah is the act of tearing clothing, while shiva is the mourning period that follows burial.

Calaveras are skull and skeleton figures that appear throughout Mexican Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead, art. The Spanish word calaveras means “skulls,” but it can also refer to the playful skeleton characters seen in satirical prints and painted decorations, as well as to decorated sugar skulls given as offerings. These images are not simply meant to be frightening: they can humorously remind people that death is part of life while honoring those who have died. Mexican printmaker José Guadalupe Posada created the etching La Calavera Garbancera, showing a skeleton dressed in an elegant hat. The figure later became known as La Catrina and grew into one of the best-known calaveras images. Artist Diego Rivera included her in his mural Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in Alameda Park.

In Greek mythology, Leda was a queen of Sparta whose story is closely tied to Zeus. According to a famous account, Zeus approached her in the form of a swan, and she later laid eggs from which some of her children hatched. Myths differ about exactly which children were Zeus’s and which were fathered by Leda’s husband, King Tyndareus, but Leda is commonly named as the mother of Helen of Troy, Clytemnestra, and the twin brothers Castor and Pollux. Helen’s departure for Troy helped spark the Trojan War. Clytemnestra married Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, who led the Greek forces in that war. After Agamemnon returned home, Clytemnestra killed him, making her a central figure in later Greek tragic stories.

The Holy Spirit, also called the Holy Ghost, is the third person of the Christian Trinity, alongside God the Father and God the Son, Jesus Christ. Christians associate the Holy Spirit with God’s presence, guidance, and gifts to believers; a dove often symbolizes it. In the New Testament book of Acts, Jesus’ disciples are gathered in Jerusalem when the Holy Spirit comes upon them with a sound like a mighty rushing wind. They begin speaking in languages they had not learned, and visitors from many regions hear the message in their own languages. This event is commemorated by Pentecost, a Christian feast celebrated fifty days after Easter. Some Christians, especially Pentecostals, also associate speaking in tongues with the Holy Spirit’s power.

Aztec mythology is the collection of sacred stories told by the Aztec, or Mexica, people of central Mexico. Its Five Suns creation story describes a series of worlds, each ruled by a different sun, that were destroyed and replaced. In one version, the gods sacrifice themselves to set the sun of the fifth age in motion. Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent, travels to Mictlan, the underworld, to retrieve bones from earlier generations of humans. He mixes the bones with his blood to create humanity again. Quetzalcoatl often clashes with Tezcatlipoca over the succession of the Suns. Tezcatlipoca’s name means “Smoking Mirror,” a reference to obsidian mirrors. He is also associated with night and jaguars.

Nimrod is a ruler named in the Hebrew Bible’s Book of Genesis. In the Table of Nations, he is identified as a son of Cush and described as a “mighty hunter before the Lord.” Genesis says his kingdom began with Babel, Erech, and Akkad in the land of Shinar. The biblical text does not describe Nimrod meeting Abraham, but later Jewish and Islamic interpretive traditions portray him as a king who opposes the patriarch Abraham, called Ibrahim in Arabic. In those traditions, Nimrod orders Abraham cast into a fire because Abraham rejects idol worship; Abraham is miraculously saved. The Quran also tells how Abraham considers the stars, moon, and sun, recognizes that each disappears, and turns instead to worship the Creator.

Dogs appear in several Greek myths as loyal companions and extraordinary creatures. In Homer’s Odyssey, Odysseus returns to his home on Ithaca after many years away. His old dog Argos recognizes him despite his disguise, then dies soon afterward. Another mythical dog, Laelaps, is fated to catch anything she chases. This creates a puzzle when she pursues the Teumessian Fox, which is fated never to be caught: neither creature’s fate can come true without contradicting the other’s. In one version of the story, Zeus ends the impossible chase by turning both animals to stone, then placing them in the sky as constellations. Laelaps becomes Canis Major, and the fox becomes Canis Minor.

In Homer’s Odyssey, Calypso is a nymph who keeps the Greek hero Odysseus on her remote island, Ogygia, for seven years. Odysseus has been trying to return to his home in Ithaca after the Trojan War, but Calypso wants him to stay with her and even offers him immortality. He longs instead to see his wife, Penelope, and their family again. The goddess Athena appeals to Zeus on his behalf, and Zeus sends the messenger god Hermes to Ogygia with an order that Calypso must let Odysseus go. She helps him build a raft so he can continue his journey. Calypso is traditionally described in some accounts as a daughter of the sun god Helios, though other accounts name the Titan Atlas as her father.

Mary of Bethany is a follower of Jesus in the New Testament and the sister of Martha and Lazarus. In Luke’s Gospel, Jesus visits the sisters’ home. Martha is busy serving and complains that Mary has left her to do the work alone, while Mary sits at Jesus’s feet and listens to him. Jesus praises Mary for choosing to learn from him. In John’s Gospel, the family lives in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem. When their brother Lazarus becomes ill and dies, Jesus comes to Bethany. Lazarus has been in his tomb for four days when Jesus calls him out, bringing him back to life. Mary of Bethany is not the same person as Mary, Jesus’s mother, or Mary Magdalene, another follower of Jesus.

In Judaism, God is the one creator of the universe and the deity worshipped by the Jewish people. The Hebrew Bible describes God making a covenant, or sacred agreement, with Abraham and his descendants. Later, God speaks to Moses from a burning bush and gives a name often translated as “I am who I am.” The Hebrew Bible also represents God’s name with four consonants, transliterated as YHWH. This four-letter form is called the Tetragrammaton, a term meaning “four letters.” Because Jewish tradition treats the name as especially holy, readers generally do not pronounce it as written. When reading scripture aloud, they commonly say Adonai, meaning “Lord,” instead; Hashem, meaning “the Name,” is another respectful way to refer to God.

The Bhagavad Gita, meaning “Song of the Lord,” is a Sanskrit work within the Hindu epic Mahabharata. It takes the form of a conversation just before the Kurukshetra War. Arjuna, a warrior fighting for the Pandavas, is distressed at the thought of battling his relatives and teachers. His charioteer, Krishna, is also a divine figure, and he counsels Arjuna about dharma, or duty: Arjuna must decide how to act rightly even when the choice is painful. Krishna explains paths toward spiritual understanding, including knowledge, devotion to God, and disciplined action without attachment to its rewards. He also teaches that the self is more than the physical body. The dialogue has become one of Hinduism’s most influential texts because it connects spiritual ideas to difficult choices in everyday life.

In the Book of Exodus, God sends the Ten Plagues upon Egypt after Pharaoh refuses Moses and Aaron’s demand to free the enslaved Israelites. The disasters begin when the Nile turns to blood. They continue with frogs, gnats or lice, flies, disease among livestock, boils, hail, locusts, and darkness. During the ninth plague, darkness covers Egypt for three days, leaving Egyptians unable to see one another, while the Israelites have light in their homes. The final plague is the death of Egypt’s firstborn. Afterward, Pharaoh allows the Israelites to leave. Jews remember their departure from Egypt during Passover, a holiday whose Seder meal includes recounting the ten plagues.

Exorcism is a ritual or action intended to drive demons or evil spirits out of a person or place. In Christian tradition, Jesus performs exorcisms in the Gospels, where they show his authority over evil spirits. In one account, Jesus meets a man believed to be possessed and asks the spirit its name. The answer is “Legion,” with the explanation, “for we are many”: the name refers to the many spirits that have entered the man. Jesus then expels them, freeing the man from their control. Different Christian traditions have their own prayers and practices for exorcism, but the central idea is the same: expelling what is believed to be an evil spiritual presence.

Falun Gong is a modern spiritual movement introduced publicly in China in 1992 by the teacher Li Hongzhi. Also called Falun Dafa, it combines meditation and five slow exercises with teachings about living according to truthfulness, compassion, and forbearance. Its name refers to the “Dharma wheel,” or falun, a spiritual concept central to its beliefs. Li later wrote Zhuan Falun, one of the movement’s central texts, which explains its practices and moral teachings. Falun Gong grew rapidly in China during the 1990s, but the Chinese government banned it in 1999 and began persecuting its practitioners. Today, people practice Falun Gong in many countries. It is a distinct modern movement, not the same religion as Daoism, although both originated in China.

Names of God are words or titles that religious communities use to identify or describe a deity. They can express beliefs about the deity’s nature, such as wisdom, power, or holiness. In Zoroastrianism, an ancient Persian religion whose sacred texts are collected in the Avesta, the supreme being is Ahura Mazda, a name often translated as “Wise Lord.” A Zoroastrian tradition lists 101 names of God that praise divine qualities. In the Hebrew Bible, the distinctive four-consonant name of God is written YHWH and is called the tetragrammaton, meaning “four letters.” It is sometimes rendered as Yahweh or Jehovah, though many Jewish readers say “Adonai” (“Lord”) instead out of reverence. These traditions show how a divine name can both identify God and convey respect.

Valkyries are supernatural women in Norse mythology who choose warriors slain in battle. Their name is commonly translated as “choosers of the slain.” They escort some of the fallen warriors to Valhalla, the great hall of the god Odin. There, the warriors feast and prepare to fight at Ragnarök, the final battle in Norse myth. Valkyries are often pictured as armed riders or shieldmaidens, and some stories say they serve mead to the warriors in Valhalla. A famous valkyrie named Brynhild appears in stories about the hero Sigurd. Valkyries are also sometimes linked with the goddess Freyja, who receives some of the battle dead.

A mantra is a sacred syllable, word, or phrase repeated aloud, chanted, or recited silently during religious practice. Mantras are used in Buddhism and other traditions to focus the mind, support meditation, and express devotion. In Tibetan Buddhism, one of the best-known mantras is the six-syllable phrase “om mani padme hum.” It is especially associated with Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. A bodhisattva is someone who seeks enlightenment while helping other beings. By repeating this mantra, practitioners may focus on compassion for themselves and others. Not every mantra has the same purpose or meaning, but repetition is a common feature of the practice.

Daphne was a nymph in Greek mythology who wanted to remain free from romantic relationships. After Eros, also called Cupid, struck Apollo with an arrow that made him fall in love with her, Apollo pursued Daphne, but she did not return his feelings. As he was about to catch her, Daphne prayed to her father, the river god Peneus, for help. Peneus answered by transforming her into a laurel tree. Apollo, the god of light and music, could not turn her back, so he made the laurel sacred to him. This story explains why Apollo is often shown wearing a wreath of laurel leaves. Daphne’s transformation saved her from Apollo’s pursuit, though it also meant she could no longer live as a nymph.

Benjamin was the youngest son of Jacob and Rachel in the Hebrew Bible. His older brother Joseph was sold into slavery in Egypt by their other brothers, but Benjamin did not take part. Jacob, who was also called Israel, gave blessings to his sons before he died. In his blessing, he compared Benjamin to a “ravenous wolf” that devours prey in the morning and divides the spoil in the evening. Benjamin became the ancestor of the Tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve Tribes of Israel named for Jacob’s sons. Many generations later, a man from this tribe named Saul, the son of Kish, was chosen by the prophet Samuel to become Israel’s first king.

The ason is a hand-held ritual rattle used in Haitian Vodou, a religion that developed in Haiti from West and Central African traditions alongside elements of Catholicism. It is often covered or wound with colorful beads and makes a distinctive sound when shaken. High-ranking Vodou priests, called houngans, and priestesses, called mambos, use the ason during ceremonies to help call and engage with spirits known as lwa. In Vodou, the lwa serve as intermediaries between people and the supreme god, Bondye. The ason is more than a musical instrument: it is a sign of a priest’s religious authority and an important part of ceremonial practice. Haitian Vodou should not be confused with fictional portrayals of “voodoo” centered on dolls and curses.

In Islam, angels are unseen beings created from light who carry out God’s commands. Belief in angels is commonly listed as the second of the six articles of faith, alongside beliefs such as God’s oneness and the prophets. One of the best-known angels is Jibril, or Gabriel, who conveyed the Quran to the prophet Muhammad. Two figures named Harut and Marut are mentioned in Al-Baqarah, the Quran’s second and longest surah, whose name is often translated as “The Cow.” Al-Baqarah also contains the Throne Verse, a passage about God’s power and knowledge. Scholars have debated the nature of Harut and Marut, but their mention in this chapter is a useful way to remember where they appear.

Janus was the Roman god of doors, gates, beginnings, and transitions. He was usually shown with two faces looking in opposite directions, a fitting image for a god connected with moving from one place or state to another. Romans invoked him at the start of important activities, and the month of January takes its name from him. Janus was also linked to the change between war and peace. Near the Roman Forum stood a sanctuary called the Temple of Janus, whose doors were traditionally kept open while Rome was at war and closed when the state was at peace. This custom made the temple’s doors a visible symbol of the transition between those two conditions.

Medb, also spelled Maeve, is a warrior queen of Connacht in the Ulster Cycle, a group of stories from Irish mythology. In the Táin, or Cattle Raid of Cooley, she compares her wealth with that of her husband and co-ruler, Ailill mac Máta. Ailill owns the valuable White-Horned Bull, and Medb wants a bull of equal worth. She therefore leads an army into Ulster to seize the Brown Bull of Cooley. The young Ulster warrior Cu Chulainn holds off her forces by fighting their champions one at a time. Medb is not simply a background character: her determination to match Ailill’s wealth drives the raid and makes her one of the best-known figures in Irish legend.

Heaven’s Gate was a UFO-oriented religious movement founded in the United States by Marshall Applewhite and Bonnie Nettles. Among their followers, Applewhite was known as Do and Nettles as Ti. The group taught that humans could leave their earthly lives behind and reach a higher level of existence connected with extraterrestrial beings. In 1997, a bright comet called Hale-Bopp appeared in the night sky. Heaven’s Gate members believed a spacecraft was traveling behind it and that dying would allow them to join it. That March, 39 members, including Applewhite, died by suicide at a residence in California. Their deaths made Heaven’s Gate one of the best-known examples of a modern religious movement shaped by beliefs about UFOs.

A mosque is a Muslim house of worship where people gather for prayer, especially the communal Friday prayer. Worshippers pray facing the qibla, the direction of Mecca, and a niche called a mihrab in the prayer hall marks that direction. Mosques may also have a minaret, a tower traditionally used for the call to prayer, though their designs vary widely. In the Ottoman Empire, rulers and wealthy patrons commissioned mosques, including one built in Istanbul for Nurbanu Sultan by the architect Mimar Sinan. The Ottomans also converted some existing churches into mosques. A famous example is the Hagia Sophia, a former Byzantine cathedral in Constantinople. After the Ottomans captured the city in 1453, they converted the Hagia Sophia into a mosque; its enormous central dome remains a defining feature.

Salat is the formal ritual prayer that is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. Muslims perform it at five appointed times each day, using set recitations and bodily postures such as standing, bowing, and prostrating. This makes Salat different from spontaneous personal supplication, which can be offered at any time. Before praying, worshippers prepare through ritual washing and face toward the Kaaba in Mecca. A muezzin announces the time for a scheduled prayer by reciting the adhan, the Islamic call to prayer. The adhan is distinct from the iqama, a shorter announcement made immediately before a congregational prayer begins. Salat may be performed alone or with others, often in a mosque.

Confucianism is a Chinese ethical, philosophical, and religious tradition associated with Confucius, an ancient teacher who taught that people could build a harmonious society by acting with kindness, respect, and a sense of responsibility. It emphasizes learning and the cultivation of virtue, as well as filial piety—respect and care for parents and elders—and ritual propriety, or behaving appropriately in relationships and ceremonies. Confucius’s sayings and conversations with his disciples were collected in the Analects, a foundational text of Confucianism. Its ideas have influenced Chinese family life, education, and government for centuries, and have also reached other traditions. For example, Sun Myung Moon, founder of the Unification Church, reportedly drew on Confucian ideas after reading the Analects as a child.

The Ark of the Covenant was a sacred chest that accompanied the Israelites during their journey through the wilderness. According to the Hebrew Bible, it held the stone tablets bearing the Ten Commandments and served as a sign of God’s presence among the people. In the book of Exodus, Moses received the first tablets from God but shattered them when he found the Israelites worshipping a golden calf. God then gave Moses a replacement set, which was kept in the Ark. The Ten Commandments are laws about how people should relate to God and one another. They include a ban on making and worshipping idols, sometimes called “graven images,” and a commandment against murder, traditionally worded “thou shalt not kill.”

The bunyip is a legendary creature in some Aboriginal Australian traditions, said to live in billabongs, swamps, and other waterways. A billabong is a pool or stretch of water left behind when a river changes course. Stories often portray the bunyip as dangerous to people who come too close, and descriptions of its appearance vary: it may have features resembling a bird, frog, or crocodile. The Rainbow Serpent is a different being in many Aboriginal Australian traditions. In Dreamtime stories, this ancestral serpent is associated with rainfall and is said to have shaped rivers and waterholes as it moved across the land. Aboriginal peoples have diverse traditions, so stories and details about both beings differ between communities.

Mount Olympus is the home of the Olympian gods in Greek mythology, with Zeus as their king. The Greeks also knew Mount Olympus as a real mountain, but in myth it was a divine dwelling high above the human world. Hesiod’s Theogony describes its height by saying that a bronze anvil would take nine days to fall from Olympus to Earth. In one story, the hero Bellerophon tries to reach it on the winged horse Pegasus, but Zeus sends a gadfly to startle Pegasus, and Bellerophon falls. Zeus became king of the gods after overthrowing his father, Cronus, and his signature weapon was the thunderbolt. Other gods associated with Olympus include Ares and Aphrodite, while Hebe and Ganymede serve the gods as cupbearers.

Krishna is a major Hindu deity traditionally regarded as an avatar, or earthly form, of Vishnu. He plays a central role in the Bhagavad Gita, a famous section of the ancient Indian epic the Mahabharata. The epic tells of a conflict between two branches of a family, the Pandavas and the Kauravas. Just before battle at Kurukshetra, Arjuna, the third Pandava prince and a skilled archer, sees that he must fight his relatives and hesitates. Krishna, serving as Arjuna’s charioteer, becomes his spiritual teacher. He explains ideas about duty, action, and devotion, encouraging Arjuna to do what he believes is right. Krishna also reveals his divine form to Arjuna, showing that he is far more than an ordinary charioteer.

The Torah is the foundational Jewish scripture and consists of five books: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. These are also called the Five Books of Moses and correspond to the first five books of the Christian Old Testament. The books tell of the creation of the world, the beginnings of the people of Israel, their escape from slavery in Egypt, and the laws and teachings they are to follow. In synagogue services, a portion of the Torah is read each week from a handwritten scroll. Trained scribes called soferim copy these scrolls, which are kept in a special cabinet called an ark. To follow the words without touching the parchment, the reader uses a pointer called a yad, often shaped like a small hand.

In many Hindu traditions, cows are regarded as sacred because they provide milk and have long symbolized nourishment, generosity, and nonviolence. This reverence is often described by the familiar term “sacred cow.” It does not mean that every Hindu worships cows, but many consider cattle worthy of protection, and cow slaughter is taboo or legally restricted in numerous parts of India. Cattle also appear in stories and images of Hindu gods. Shiva, for example, is often shown with Nandi, a white bull who serves as his mount and devoted companion. Recognizing Nandi helps connect the broader sacred cow tradition with a specific figure in Hindu mythology: the revered animal associated with Shiva is a bull, and his name is Nandi.

The Last Supper was the final meal Jesus shared with his twelve apostles before his arrest and crucifixion. In the Synoptic Gospels—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—Jesus breaks bread and shares wine with them, telling them to remember him. Christians commemorate this meal in the Eucharist, also called Communion or the Lord’s Supper. Christian traditions differ in how they understand the bread and wine: some teach that Christ is truly present in them, while others see them mainly as symbols. The Last Supper is also the subject of a famous mural painted in the 1490s by the Renaissance artist Leonardo da Vinci. Created for the dining hall, or refectory, of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, it shows the apostles reacting to Jesus’s words and is known for its perspective and deteriorating paint.

The Zamzam Well is a sacred source of water in Mecca, near the Kaaba. According to Islamic tradition, Hajar was in the barren valley with her infant son, Isma'il, when she desperately searched for water. She went back and forth between the hills of Safa and Marwah until water appeared at the place now known as the Zamzam Well. Muslim pilgrims remember her determination by performing sa'i, a rite in which they travel seven times between Safa and Marwah. Sa'i is part of the Hajj pilgrimage and can also be performed during Umrah, a shorter pilgrimage. Pilgrims may drink Zamzam water or take some home. The well reminds Muslims of Hajar’s trust in God and of God’s care for her and Isma'il.

The Yoruba are a major ethnic group concentrated in southwestern Nigeria and neighboring parts of West Africa, especially Benin and Togo. They have a rich history of kingdoms, art, language, and religious traditions. In traditional Yoruba religion, divine beings called orishas are honored through rituals, prayers, music, and offerings. Different orishas are associated with aspects of nature and human life, such as rivers, thunder, wisdom, and healing. During the transatlantic slave trade, Yoruba people and their descendants carried these beliefs to the Americas. Their traditions helped shape African diasporic religions, including Candomblé in Brazil, where orishas remain central figures. Yoruba religious practices also influenced Haitian Vodou. Today, Yoruba people follow a range of religions, including Christianity, Islam, and traditional Yoruba religion.

In Jain cosmology, time has no beginning or end. It moves through an eternal cycle with two halves: utsarpini, an ascending phase in which conditions gradually improve, and avasarpini, a descending phase in which they gradually worsen. Each half contains six periods. Jains believe we now live in the sixth period of avasarpini, which traditionally began three years after the death of Mahavira. Mahavira was the twenty-fourth tirthankara, a revered spiritual teacher who taught a path to liberation and helped shape the Jain tradition as it is known today. This vast cycle is part of a worldview in which living beings undergo repeated death and rebirth, called samsara, until they achieve liberation.

A koan is a brief question, statement, or exchange used in Zen Buddhist training to challenge ordinary reasoning. A famous example asks, “What is the sound of one hand clapping?” Rather than looking for a clever logical answer, a student reflects on the koan during meditation to develop insight into the nature of the mind and reality. Zen, called Chan in China, places strong emphasis on meditation and is traditionally associated with Bodhidharma. It belongs to Mahayana Buddhism, a broad branch whose name means “Great Vehicle.” Mahayana is often contrasted with Theravada, another major branch of Buddhism. So, the puzzling prompt is called a koan, and the wider Buddhist branch to which Zen belongs is Mahayana.

Judas Iscariot was one of Jesus’s twelve apostles, the close followers who traveled with him during his ministry. At the Last Supper, Jesus told the disciples that one of them would betray him. According to the Gospel of Matthew, Judas agreed to hand Jesus over to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. He later led an arresting party to Jesus and identified him with a kiss, a greeting that became a symbol of betrayal. Judas’s actions helped lead to Jesus’s arrest and crucifixion. The New Testament gives differing accounts of Judas’s death, but both Matthew and Acts connect it with a place called the Field of Blood, also known as the Potter’s Field.

Holi is a Hindu spring festival that celebrates the arrival of spring, joyful community gatherings, and the triumph of good over evil. On the evening before the main celebration, people light bonfires in a ritual called Holika Dahan. The ritual recalls the story of Prahlada, a young devotee of the god Vishnu. His aunt Holika tried to kill him by sitting with him in a fire, but she perished while Prahlada emerged unharmed. The next day, people celebrate by playfully throwing brightly colored powder and spraying water on one another. Families and friends also gather to share food and greetings. Some adults may drink bhang, a cannabis-based beverage, during Holi, though it is not central to the festival.

The Aboriginal peoples of Australia are the many distinct Indigenous communities of mainland Australia and Tasmania, whose cultures, languages, and histories stretch back thousands of years before European colonization. Their traditions vary from community to community, but some describe songlines: routes across the land connected to ancestral journeys, stories, and songs. Stories of the Rainbow Serpent, a powerful ancestral being, are also found in several traditions. In 1770, British naval captain James Cook sailed along and charted Australia’s east coast aboard the Endeavour and claimed it for Britain. His voyage preceded British settlement and major disruptions to Aboriginal peoples’ lands and lives. Despite colonization, Aboriginal communities continue to maintain and renew their cultures today.

The Dome of the Rock is a major Islamic shrine on Jerusalem’s Temple Mount. Built in the late seventh century under the Umayyad dynasty, it is known for its octagonal shape, richly decorated exterior, and golden dome. At its center lies a sacred rock commonly called the Foundation Stone. In Islamic tradition, the rock is associated with the Prophet Muhammad’s Night Journey, during which he traveled to Jerusalem and ascended to heaven. The site is also important in Jewish tradition, which links the stone to the ancient Temple and the creation of the world. The Dome of the Rock is a shrine built around this sacred place, not a mosque used mainly for congregational prayer.

In the Kojiki, an early collection of Japanese myths, Izanami is a primordial Shinto goddess who helps create the islands of Japan with her brother and husband, Izanagi. They circle a pillar in opposite directions as part of their marriage ceremony, then bring forth islands and many kami, or divine spirits. Izanami dies after giving birth to Kagutsuchi, the fire deity, and enters Yomi, the shadowy land of the dead. Izanagi travels there hoping to bring her home, but she has eaten food cooked in Yomi and cannot return to the living world. When Izanagi flees, Izanami vows to kill a thousand people each day; he replies that he will cause fifteen hundred people to be born each day. Their story connects creation with death and the continuing renewal of life.

Ambrosia is the food of the gods in Greek mythology and was also known in Roman tradition. It is associated with immortality: when a mortal receives ambrosia, it can help them become divine. Ambrosia is usually distinguished from nectar, the drink of the gods, though ancient stories do not always describe them in exactly the same way. In the Roman story of Cupid and Psyche, Jupiter grants Psyche immortality and gives her ambrosia after Cupid pleads for her. The gods are also said to have ichor flowing through their veins instead of ordinary human blood. These ideas mark the difference between mortals and immortals: humans need everyday food and have blood, while the gods consume ambrosia and have ichor.

The Hail Mary is a traditional Catholic prayer addressed to Mary, the mother of Jesus. It is also called Ave Maria, from its opening words in Latin. The prayer begins with a greeting drawn from the Gospel of Luke’s account of the Annunciation. In that story, the archangel Gabriel tells Mary that she will conceive Jesus. The prayer goes on to call Mary the “Mother of God” and asks her to pray for sinners “now and at the hour of our death.” Catholics call this request for Mary’s prayers intercession. The Hail Mary has also inspired music, including settings of Ave Maria; Franz Schubert’s “Ellen’s Third Song” is a famous example associated with the prayer.

Fionn mac Cumhaill is a legendary Irish warrior and the leader of the Fianna, a band of warriors whose adventures are told in the Fenian Cycle. He gained supernatural wisdom through the Salmon of Knowledge: while cooking the fish for his teacher, he burned his thumb and put it in his mouth, accidentally receiving the wisdom meant for whoever ate the salmon. Fionn’s son Oisín is both a warrior of the Fianna and a poet who tells some of their stories. He narrates the tale of Diarmuid and Gráinne, in which Gráinne runs away with Diarmuid despite being promised to Fionn. In another famous story, Oisín travels with Niamh to Tír na nÓg, a magical land of youth.

Hadith are reports that preserve the Prophet Muhammad’s sayings, actions, and approvals, including things he allowed others to do without objecting. Muslims study them alongside the Quran to understand how to put Islamic teachings into practice, such as how to pray and behave toward others. The Quran is believed to be revelation from God, while hadith record reports about Muhammad’s example; the two are not the same kind of text. Scholars collected and examined hadith to judge how reliably each report had been passed down. One especially important Sunni collection is Sahih al-Bukhari, compiled in the ninth century by Muhammad ibn Ismail al-Bukhari. Many Sunni Muslims regard it as the most authoritative collection of hadith.

A pi bond is a covalent bond formed when two parallel p orbitals overlap side by side. In an alkene, the two carbon atoms of a C=C double bond share two bonds: a sigma bond and a pi bond. The sigma bond forms by head-on overlap along the line joining the carbon nuclei, while the pi bond has electron density above and below that line. Each carbon in the double bond is sp2 hybridized, leaving an unhybridized p orbital to form the pi bond. Because rotating one carbon relative to the other would disrupt the overlap of these p orbitals, a carbon–carbon double bond restricts rotation. The name “pi” uses the same Greek letter as the mathematical constant approximately equal to 3.14.

Aircraft are vehicles designed to travel through Earth’s atmosphere. Many use engines or propellers for propulsion and wings or other aerodynamic surfaces to produce lift, the upward force that keeps them flying. Fixed-wing aircraft, such as airplanes, have wings that stay in place, while rotary-wing aircraft, such as helicopters, use spinning blades to generate lift. Jet airliners often cruise near the lower stratosphere, above much of the turbulent weather in the troposphere; their engines provide thrust, and their wings provide lift. An important early aircraft was the Wright Flyer, a powered biplane built by Orville and Wilbur Wright. In 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, it made the first successful sustained, controlled flight by a powered, heavier-than-air machine.

An internal combustion engine is a heat machine that burns fuel inside its working chambers. Burning a fuel-air mixture creates hot, expanding gases that produce mechanical work, making internal combustion engines the broad category that powers most gasoline and diesel cars. In a common piston engine, the gases push pistons back and forth, and a crankshaft converts that motion into rotation to turn the wheels. A four-stroke piston engine repeatedly takes in air and fuel, compresses them, uses combustion to deliver power, and expels exhaust. A Wankel engine performs these stages differently: instead of pistons moving back and forth, it uses a roughly triangular rotor spinning inside a curved housing. The rotor’s tips form moving chambers for intake, compression, power, and exhaust. Mazda used Wankel engines in its RX-7 and RX-8 cars.

Chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, are a family of compounds containing carbon, chlorine, and fluorine. They were once widely used as refrigerants in cooling systems, propellants in aerosol cans, and solvents for cleaning. CFCs are stable near Earth’s surface, but when they reach the stratosphere, ultraviolet sunlight can break them apart and release chlorine radicals. These radicals repeatedly destroy ozone, a gas made of three oxygen atoms (O3). The stratospheric ozone layer absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation, so its depletion increases the amount that reaches Earth’s surface. Ozone loss is especially severe over Antarctica each spring, creating what is commonly called the ozone hole. The 1987 Montreal Protocol led countries to phase out CFCs to protect the ozone layer.

The citric acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle, is a series of enzyme-catalyzed reactions in the matrix of mitochondria, the organelles where cells produce much of their energy. It begins when the enzyme citrate synthase joins the two-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to four-carbon oxaloacetate. This forms six-carbon citrate and releases coenzyme A. As citrate moves through the cycle, its carbon atoms are released as carbon dioxide, and energy from its chemical bonds is captured in NADH and FADH₂. These molecules carry electrons to the electron transport chain in the mitochondrion’s inner membrane, helping the cell make ATP. The cycle also regenerates oxaloacetate, allowing another acetyl group to enter.

Anthony Fauci is an American physician and immunologist, a scientist who studies how the immune system fights disease. He directed the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) from 1984 to 2022. In that role, he helped guide research on infectious diseases such as HIV/AIDS and advised every U.S. president from Ronald Reagan onward on public health. Fauci became especially well known during the COVID-19 pandemic, when he explained the science behind measures to limit the virus’s spread and the development of vaccines. His long career in public health earned him the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2008. President George W. Bush presented him with the award, recognizing his work to advance research and treatment for HIV/AIDS.

The plant cuticle is a thin, waxy layer covering the outside of the epidermal cells on many leaves. It is hydrophobic, meaning it repels water, so it slows evaporation from the leaf’s surface and helps prevent the plant from drying out. The cuticle also provides some protection from damage and disease. Leaves still need to exchange gases with the air for photosynthesis: they take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. This exchange happens mainly through microscopic pores in the epidermis called stomata. Each stoma is controlled by a pair of guard cells that can open or close the pore. When stomata are open, water vapor can escape, so closing them helps the plant conserve water.

Jonas Salk was an American medical researcher at the University of Pittsburgh who developed the first successful vaccine against polio, or poliomyelitis. Polio is a viral disease that mainly affects children and can cause paralysis; some patients once needed an iron lung to help them breathe. With support from the March of Dimes, Salk created an injectable inactivated polio vaccine. Its virus particles were treated with formalin so they could not replicate, but they could still teach the immune system to recognize the virus. This differed from later oral polio vaccines, which used weakened live virus. A field trial involving nearly two million children tested Salk’s vaccine, and in 1955 it was declared safe and effective.

Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats, meaning their carbon chains contain more than one carbon–carbon double bond. Their defining feature is that the first double bond is at the third carbon when counted from the terminal methyl end of the chain. This is different from saturated fats, which have no carbon–carbon double bonds. Two omega-3 fatty acids are EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) and DHA (docosahexaenoic acid). DHA has 22 carbon atoms and six double bonds. It is an important part of cell membranes in the brain and retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Omega-3s occur in foods such as fatty fish, and DHA may also be added to fortified foods.

Positive electric charge is one of two types of electric charge; the other is negative charge. Opposite charges attract, so a positively charged object attracts a negatively charged one, while two positive charges repel. Protons carry positive charge, and an object can become positively charged when it loses electrons. Electric field lines show the direction a small positive test charge would be pushed: they point outward from positive charges and toward negative charges. In the 18th century, American experimenter Benjamin Franklin proposed a “one-fluid” theory of electricity and helped establish the terms positive and negative. Although his explanation of electricity has been replaced by modern physics, the names remain in use today. In electrostatics, the electric field inside a conductor is zero.

The plant cell wall is a rigid layer outside the plasma membrane of cells in trees, grasses, and flowering herbs. It supports the cell, helps give the plant its shape, and resists turgor pressure—the outward push created when water fills the cell. The wall is made mainly of cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. Cellulose is a polysaccharide built from long chains of glucose; its chains form strong fibers that reinforce the wall. Hemicellulose helps connect those fibers, while pectin helps bind wall materials together and is also used to make jams and jellies set. Animal cells do not have cell walls, and fungal cell walls contain chitin rather than cellulose. Some plant walls, especially in wood, also gain strength from lignin.

Focal length describes how strongly a lens bends light. For a converging lens, it is the distance from the lens’s principal plane to the focal point, where incoming rays parallel to the optical axis meet. For a diverging lens, those rays spread out after passing through it; the focal point is where they appear to have come from. Focal length helps determine where a lens forms an image: the thin lens equation says that the reciprocal of the object distance plus the reciprocal of the image distance equals the reciprocal of the focal length. A lens’s optical power is also the reciprocal of its focal length when that length is measured in meters. Optical power is measured in diopters, with one diopter equal to one inverse meter. Eyeglass prescriptions commonly use diopters to state lens strength.

Atomic radius is a measure of an atom’s size, commonly defined as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded or adjacent atoms. Atoms have no sharp outer edge, so chemists use different definitions for different situations. For example, the van der Waals radius is half the closest distance between two atoms that are not bonded. Atomic radius generally increases down a group because atoms gain electron shells, and decreases from left to right across a period because the growing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer. A notable example is the lanthanide contraction: as protons are added while 4f orbitals fill, the 4f electrons shield the outer electrons poorly, so atomic sizes progressively shrink. Atoms also often become smaller when they lose electrons to form positive ions called cations.

COVID-19 vaccines help protect people from serious illness caused by SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. They train the immune system to recognize the virus so it can respond more quickly if a person is exposed. Companies such as BioNTech helped develop these vaccines, which have been offered at clinics and pharmacies. In the United States, CDC recommendations have included vaccination for people as young as six months. New York nurse Sandra Lindsay became the first American to receive a COVID-19 vaccine outside a clinical trial, an event later recognized with the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Vaccines remain important as the virus changes. Omicron, a variant first detected in Botswana in 2021, spread more easily than the earlier Delta variant; its BA.5 sublineage later became dominant in the United States.

Stokes’ law describes the drag force a fluid exerts on a small sphere moving slowly through it. The force equals six pi times the fluid’s viscosity, the sphere’s radius, and its speed relative to the fluid. Viscosity measures how strongly a fluid resists flowing; the law works when the motion is gentle enough that the Reynolds number is small. Robert Millikan and Harvey Fletcher used Stokes’ law to analyze tiny oil droplets in the 1909 Millikan oil-drop experiment. By observing droplets falling through air, they could account for air resistance and determine their weight. They then adjusted an electric field between two plates to balance a charged droplet’s weight. From that balance, they determined the electron’s electric charge, about negative 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs.

Scientists investigate the natural world by asking questions, making careful observations, testing ideas through experiments, and analyzing evidence. They work in many fields, including physics, chemistry, and biology. Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist whose research on radioactivity helped scientists understand how some atoms release energy. She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics and won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Rosalind Franklin was another scientist; her X-ray diffraction studies produced important evidence about the structure of DNA. Scientists also appear in fiction: Meg and Charles Wallace Murry’s parents in Madeleine L’Engle’s novel A Wrinkle in Time are scientists. Whether studying radioactive materials, examining DNA, or appearing in a story, scientists are defined by their work investigating the world using evidence.

Elon Musk is a technology entrepreneur born in Pretoria, South Africa. He founded SpaceX, a private company that develops rockets and spacecraft, and leads Tesla, a major maker of electric cars. In 2022, he completed a $44 billion purchase of Twitter, which was later renamed X. One of SpaceX’s rockets, Falcon Heavy, has three booster cores that work together to lift heavy payloads. On its first flight in February 2018, Falcon Heavy carried a Tesla Roadster sports car into space with a mannequin nicknamed Starman in the driver’s seat. Musk has also pursued other projects, including the Boring Company, which aims to build transportation tunnels. His work links engineering, space exploration, and electric vehicles.

Deafness is a substantial loss or complete absence of hearing. It can affect how a person communicates and gains access to spoken language, though deaf people use a range of methods, including sign languages, writing, and spoken language. Hearing loss can be present at birth or develop later because of illness, injury, aging, or exposure to loud sounds. In Washington, D.C., Gallaudet University was founded in 1864 as the first college for deaf students. Its programs and services are designed to be accessible to deaf and hard-of-hearing people. On its grounds stands a memorial statue by Daniel Chester French showing Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet seated and teaching Alice Cogswell, a deaf student whose education helped inspire early schools for deaf children in the United States.

Hydrothermal vents are openings in the seafloor that release hot, mineral-rich water. They often form near divergent plate boundaries, where tectonic plates move apart and volcanic activity heats seawater that has seeped into cracks in the ocean floor. When the heated water rises, its dissolved minerals can build chimney-like structures called “black smokers” or “white smokers.” Although sunlight does not reach these deep-sea habitats, life thrives around the vents. Bacteria use chemicals in the vent water to produce food through chemosynthesis, forming the base of the ecosystem. Giant tube worms are among the best-known vent animals. They live in long, pale casings and have bright red plumes. As adults, they lack a functional digestive tract and depend on chemosynthetic bacteria living inside their bodies for food.

Obsidian is a naturally occurring volcanic glass formed when lava, or molten rock at Earth’s surface, cools so quickly that crystals have little or no time to grow. It is often dark and shiny, though its color can vary. Unlike rocks made of interlocking mineral crystals, obsidian is glassy and brittle.
