When it breaks, it can leave curved, shell-like surfaces and exceptionally sharp edges. This breakage pattern is called conchoidal fracture, and it also occurs in flint and other glassy materials. It differs from mineral cleavage, in which a crystal splits along flat planes determined by its internal structure. People have used obsidian’s sharp edges to make tools, including blades and arrowheads.

Data types are categories that tell a program what kind of value a variable can hold and what operations make sense for that value. An integer stores a whole number, so it can be used in arithmetic; a string stores a sequence of characters, such as a name; and a Boolean represents a logical condition with one of two values, true or false. For example, a program might store a person’s age as an integer and whether they are old enough to vote as a Boolean. Compilers and programs running your code can use data types to catch mistakes, such as trying to add a number to a name. Some languages also let programmers convert values between types, a process that may be called casting or coercion.

Bioluminescence is light made by living organisms through chemical reactions, rather than light reflected from an outside source such as the Sun. It occurs in many ocean animals, especially in the deep sea, where sunlight does not reach. Some animals use this glow to communicate, hide from predators, or attract prey. The anglerfish is a deep-sea predator with a modified dorsal-fin ray that extends in front of its mouth like a fishing rod. At its tip is a lure that, in some anglerfish, glows with the help of symbiotic bacteria. Smaller fish may swim toward the light, allowing the anglerfish to catch them. Other organisms, including some jellyfish and plankton, can produce their own light without bacterial help.

A cryptographic hash function takes data of any length, such as a word, file, or password, and turns it into a fixed-size output called a digest or hash. It is designed to be one-way: knowing the digest should not let someone recover the original input. It should also be difficult to find two different inputs that produce the same digest, an event called a collision. Hashes can help check whether a file has changed and support other security tools, but a hash is not encryption because it is not meant to be reversed with a key. MD5, designed by Ron Rivest in 1992, produces a 128-bit digest. It was once widely used for checksums and password storage, but practical collision attacks have made it unsuitable for security-sensitive use.

A meniscus is the curved surface at the top of a liquid in a container. Its shape depends on adhesion, the attraction between the liquid and the container, and cohesion, the attraction among the liquid’s own molecules. In a narrow glass tube, water clings to the walls and rises there, making a dip in the center called a concave meniscus. Mercury’s cohesion is stronger than its adhesion to glass, so it bulges upward in the center, forming a convex meniscus. To measure a liquid in a graduated cylinder accurately, place your eye level with the meniscus and, for liquids like water, read the scale at the bottom of the curve. Viewing it from above or below can make the level seem to shift, causing parallax error.

Nitric acid is a strong, corrosive acid with the chemical formula HNO3. It contains nitrogen and is widely used in industry, especially to make fertilizers and explosives. Most nitric acid is produced by the Ostwald process, which begins by reacting ammonia with oxygen. A platinum-rhodium catalyst helps this reaction take place; later steps produce nitric acid. Nitric acid is also known for its role in aqua regia, a highly corrosive mixture made by combining it with hydrochloric acid. Gold resists attack by either acid on its own, but aqua regia can dissolve it because the two acids work together. Because nitric acid and aqua regia can cause serious burns, they must be handled with great care.

The Lebanon cedar, or Cedrus libani, is an evergreen conifer native to the mountains of the eastern Mediterranean. Young trees often have a cone-shaped outline, but as they mature, their branches spread into a broad, tiered crown. Their needle-like leaves remain green throughout the year, and their seeds develop in upright cones. The tree is a national emblem of Lebanon and appears at the center of its flag; Lebanon’s capital is Beirut. Cedar forests in the region were important in ancient cultures, and Mesopotamian mythology described a forest of cedars in what is now Lebanon as a home of the gods. The Lebanon cedar belongs to the genus Cedrus, which also includes the deodar cedar and the Atlas cedar.

Mach number describes how fast an object moves compared with the local speed of sound. To calculate it, divide the object’s speed by the speed of sound in the surrounding fluid, such as air. Because both speeds use the same units, the result is a dimensionless ratio. A Mach number below 1 means the object is traveling slower than sound, Mach 1 means it is traveling at the speed of sound, and above Mach 1 means it is traveling faster than sound, or supersonically. The speed of sound varies with conditions such as temperature, so the local value matters; in air at 20 degrees Celsius, it is about 343 meters per second. A supersonic aircraft creates shock waves that can reach an observer as a sudden, sharp sound called a sonic boom.

Mineral hardness is a mineral’s resistance to being scratched. The Mohs scale ranks hardness from 1 to 10 by comparing which minerals can scratch others: a harder mineral scratches a softer one. Talc, a hydrated magnesium silicate, is the softest mineral on the scale, with a value of 1. Its soft, white form can be ground into talcum powder, traditionally used in baby powder. Diamond is at the opposite end, with a value of 10, and can scratch every other mineral on the scale. Apatite, a group of calcium phosphate minerals, has a hardness of 5; hydroxyapatite is a major component of human bones. The numbers show an order of hardness, not equal steps in how hard the minerals are.

Wood is a natural structural material found mainly in the stems and branches of trees and other woody plants. Trees build wood from cells whose walls contain cellulose and lignin. Cellulose forms strong fibers, while lignin is a complex polymer that binds those fibers together and helps make wood rigid. This combination lets a tree support its branches and grow tall. It also makes wood useful to people: after a tree is cut and processed, its wood can become lumber for buildings, furniture, and other products. In the United States, many houses use “stick” framing, in which pieces of lumber such as two-by-fours form the structure of walls and floors. Wood is widely used in construction because it is strong, relatively inexpensive, and easy to shape.

A space telescope is an observatory placed above Earth’s atmosphere to study objects such as stars and galaxies. From the ground, moving air can blur images, and the atmosphere absorbs some kinds of light before they reach a telescope. Space telescopes avoid these problems, helping astronomers collect clearer images and observe light that is difficult to detect from Earth. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, is one example. Another is the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in December 2021. Webb observes primarily in infrared light, which has wavelengths longer than visible light. Its first science images, released in July 2022, included a deep-field view of the galaxy cluster SMACS 0723, revealing many distant galaxies.

An F-center is a point defect in an ionic crystal: a missing negatively charged ion, or anion, leaves a vacancy that traps an electron. For example, in an alkali-halide crystal such as sodium chloride, a missing chloride ion can leave a site where an electron becomes trapped. The trapped electron can absorb some colors of visible light, causing an otherwise clear or white crystal to appear colored. If a second electron occupies the same anion vacancy, the defect is called an F′ center (“F-prime center”). These defects interrupt the regular arrangement of ions in a crystal lattice, but they do not destroy the crystal’s overall ordered structure. Studying them helps scientists understand how tiny changes in a material’s structure can affect its appearance and other properties.

HTTP, short for Hypertext Transfer Protocol, is an application-layer standard that defines how web clients and servers communicate. When you open a website, your browser sends an HTTP request to a server, and the server sends back a response, such as a web page, image, or error message. These resources are identified by URLs; you may see “http://” at the start of one. A common HTTP request method is GET, which asks the server to return a representation of a resource, such as an HTML page. GET is considered safe because it is meant only to retrieve information, not change it. It is also idempotent: making the same GET request repeatedly should have the same intended effect as making it once.

Camels are large, hoofed mammals that people have domesticated to carry riders and goods across dry regions. Their broad, padded feet help them walk on sand, and their bodies can cope with long periods when water is scarce. The two best-known domesticated species are the one-humped dromedary camel, common in North Africa and the Middle East, and the two-humped Bactrian camel of Central Asia. Bactrian camels have thick coats that help them withstand the region’s frigid winters as well as its hot summers. Camels’ humps store fat, not water, giving them a source of energy when food is limited. Because they could transport supplies over long desert routes, camels were important to trade caravans on the Silk Road and across the Sahara, earning the nickname “ships of the desert.”

An axon is a long, usually single extension of a neuron, or nerve cell. It carries electrical impulses away from the cell body, also called the soma, toward other neurons, muscles, or glands. Dendrites are different: a neuron usually has many of them, and they mainly receive incoming signals. Some axons are wrapped in a myelin sheath, an insulating layer that helps impulses travel faster. The sheath has regularly spaced gaps called nodes of Ranvier. At these gaps, clusters of ion channels renew the electrical signal, so it appears to jump from node to node. This process is called saltatory conduction. Axons are part of the nervous system, which includes the brain, spinal cord, and nerves throughout the body.

Glenn T. Seaborg was an American chemist who helped discover ten transuranium elements, elements with atomic numbers greater than uranium’s 92. He shared the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Edwin McMillan for their work on these elements. One of them, the synthetic element seaborgium, has atomic number 106 and was named in Seaborg’s honor while he was still alive. In 1949, Seaborg and his colleagues discovered another synthetic element, atomic number 97, at the University of California, Berkeley. They named it berkelium after the university. Berkelium sits just after curium on the periodic table; curium was named for Marie Curie and her husband, Pierre. Seaborg later served as chancellor of UC Berkeley and worked on science education and nuclear policy.

Carl Linnaeus was a Swedish naturalist born in 1707 who helped create the system scientists use to classify and name living things. In his influential book Systema Naturae, first published in 1735, he organized nature into a hierarchy of groups. One broad rank is kingdom, which comes below domain and above phylum; familiar kingdoms include plants and animals. Linnaeus also made binomial nomenclature central to scientific naming. Under this system, each species has a two-part Latinized name: the first part is its genus, and the second is its specific epithet. For example, humans are Homo sapiens. Giving species consistent names helps scientists around the world communicate clearly, even when they use different everyday names for the same organism.

The de Broglie wavelength is the wavelength associated with a moving particle. French physicist Louis de Broglie proposed that particles such as electrons can behave like waves, just as light can behave as both a wave and particles called photons. A particle’s de Broglie wavelength is found using the equation λ = h/p, where λ is wavelength, h is Planck’s constant, and p is the particle’s momentum. Momentum measures a particle’s motion and depends on its mass and velocity. Because momentum is in the denominator, a particle with greater momentum has a shorter wavelength. This wave behavior is easier to observe for tiny particles than for everyday objects, whose de Broglie wavelengths are far too short to notice.

Agriculture, or farming, is the practice and industry of growing crops and raising livestock for food and other products. Farmers prepare soil, plant seeds, care for crops and animals, and harvest produce. Agriculture has supported civilizations by providing a steadier food supply, and technologies such as tractors, synthetic fertilizers, and high-yield crop varieties have greatly increased productivity. Governments also influence farming through policies. In Europe, the Common Agricultural Policy, or CAP, was established in 1962 to coordinate support for farmers and markets for farm produce among member states. Disagreement over how to finance the CAP helped lead French president Charles de Gaulle to withdraw France from European Community meetings during the 1965–66 Empty Chair Crisis.

A hot-air balloon is an aircraft that rises because the air inside its large fabric envelope is heated. Warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it lifts the balloon and the basket carrying people or cargo. Unlike a powered aircraft, a balloon generally travels with the wind. During the Prussian Siege of Paris in 1870–71, enemy forces surrounded the city and blocked ordinary routes out. Balloons became a way to carry mail and passengers beyond the blockade, although pilots could not precisely control where they would land. The French politician Léon Gambetta left Paris in a balloon named Armand-Barbès and traveled to Tours, where he helped organize resistance to the Prussians.

Surface tension is a property that makes the surface of a liquid behave somewhat like a stretched elastic film. It arises because molecules attract one another: water molecules at the surface are pulled toward the water beneath and beside them. This cohesion helps round droplets and lets small insects such as water striders stand on a pond without sinking. Soaps and detergents contain surfactants, substances that reduce surface tension by gathering at the boundary between water and air or between water and oil. A surfactant molecule has a water-attracting part and an oil-attracting part. By helping water spread and oily grime mix with it, surfactants make cleaning easier.

The Titius–Bode law is a historical numerical rule that estimates planets’ distances from the Sun using a pattern based largely on doubling numbers. It placed a possible orbit about 2.8 astronomical units from the Sun, in the apparent gap between Mars and Jupiter. An astronomical unit is roughly the distance from Earth to the Sun. The prediction encouraged astronomers to search that region for a “missing” planet. In 1801, they discovered Ceres there. Rather than being a major planet, Ceres is now classified as a dwarf planet and is the largest object in the asteroid belt, a region containing many rocky asteroids between Mars and Jupiter. The Titius–Bode law is not a reliable law of nature: although some predicted distances were close, it does not accurately describe all planetary orbits.

The Crab Nebula is a cloud of glowing gas and dust in the constellation Taurus. It is a supernova remnant: the expanding debris left behind when a star exploded in a powerful event called a supernova. Chinese astronomers recorded the explosion in 1054 CE, when the star became bright enough to be seen in the daytime. At the center of the nebula is a pulsar, a rapidly rotating neutron star formed from the collapsed core of the original star. As it spins, the pulsar sends energy into the surrounding debris, helping the cloud glow. The Crab Nebula lets astronomers study what happens after a supernova, as material thrown out by the explosion continues to spread through space.

The Arrhenius equation describes how a chemical reaction’s rate constant changes with temperature. It is written as k = A × e^(−Ea/RT), where k is the rate constant, A is the pre-exponential factor, R is the gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature in kelvins. Ea is the activation energy, measured in joules per mole: it represents the minimum energy reacting particles need for a reaction to occur. In the equation, activation energy appears in the exponent as −Ea divided by RT. At a higher temperature, more particles have enough energy to react, so the rate constant usually increases. The equation is named after the Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius.

Édouard Roche was a 19th-century French astronomer who studied how gravity shapes planets, moons, and rings. He is best known for the Roche limit, a critical distance from a planet. If a moon held together mainly by its own gravity orbits closer than this limit, the planet’s unequal gravitational pull on its near and far sides—called tidal force—can tear it apart. The resulting debris may spread into a planetary ring, although a strong, solid object can sometimes survive closer in. Roche’s name also appears in Saturn’s ring system: the Roche Division separates the A ring from the more distant F ring. This is different from the Cassini Division, which separates Saturn’s A and B rings. Saturn, the sixth planet from the Sun, has the Solar System’s most visible rings.

A decomposer is an organism that gets nutrients by breaking down dead organic matter, such as fallen leaves, dead trees, and animal remains. Fungi and bacteria release substances that digest this material and then absorb the nutrients. Detritivores, such as earthworms, eat bits of dead matter and help break them into smaller pieces. Together, these organisms return nutrients to soil and water, where plants and other living things can use them again. Wood, the structural material in tree trunks and branches, is also broken down by decomposers. It contains cellulose and lignin, tough substances that help support trees. Some fungi can digest lignin, while fungi and termites can break down parts of wood to obtain food.

The Kinetic Theory of Gases explains large-scale properties of a gas, such as pressure and temperature, through the motion of its tiny particles. In a simple version of the model, particles are treated as hard spheres that move freely between brief interactions called collisions. When a particle collides with a container wall, it transfers momentum to the wall; many such collisions produce the gas’s pressure. Temperature is related to the particles’ average kinetic energy, so hotter gases have faster-moving particles on average. Gas particles can also collide with one another and exchange momentum. In an elastic collision, total kinetic energy as well as total momentum is conserved. In an inelastic collision, momentum is still conserved, but some kinetic energy changes into other forms, such as heat or sound.

A fault is a break or zone of breaks in Earth’s crust where rock on either side has moved, leaving the layers displaced. Faults are classified by the direction of that movement. In a normal fault, one block drops relative to the other; in a reverse fault, one block rises; and in a strike-slip fault, the blocks slide sideways past each other. Faults often occur where tectonic plates meet. Some offset segments of mid-ocean ridges, underwater mountain chains where magma rises and cools to form new oceanic crust. As more crust forms, older crust gradually moves away from the ridge. This process is called seafloor spreading. The Vine–Matthews–Morley hypothesis used patterns in the magnetic record of ocean-floor rocks as evidence for seafloor spreading.

Hominin fossils are preserved remains of humans and our extinct close relatives. Researchers study their bones and teeth to learn how different species lived and how human traits evolved over millions of years. Many important hominin fossils have been found at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, where Mary and Louis Leakey worked. These finds include remains assigned to Homo habilis, Homo erectus, and Paranthropus boisei. In 1959, Mary Leakey discovered a Paranthropus boisei skull with unusually large molars and powerful jaws, which led to its nickname, “Nutcracker Man.” The skull’s catalog designation is OH 5: “OH” stands for Olduvai Hominid, and “5” identifies it as the fifth hominin find cataloged from the gorge.

Valentina Tereshkova was a Soviet cosmonaut who became the first woman to travel in space. She launched alone aboard the spacecraft Vostok 6 on June 16, 1963, and orbited Earth 48 times before landing nearly three days later. A cosmonaut is the Soviet or Russian term for a person trained to travel in space; Yuri Gagarin had become the first human in space two years earlier aboard Vostok 1. Tereshkova’s flight was a milestone because no woman had gone into space before her. It also showed that a woman could complete a demanding orbital mission. If asked to name the first woman in space, the answer is Valentina Tereshkova; if asked which spacecraft carried her, the answer is Vostok 6.

Lindlar’s catalyst is a substance used in organic chemistry to turn an alkyne, which has a carbon–carbon triple bond, into a cis-alkene, which has a double bond with key groups on the same side. It is made from palladium supported on calcium carbonate and is used with hydrogen gas. The palladium is partially “poisoned,” or made less active, commonly with quinoline and lead acetate. Lead acetate is a salt of lead, a heavy metal once widely used in plumbing, and acetate comes from ethanoic acid. This reduced activity helps stop the reaction at the alkene instead of continuing to an alkane. Like other catalysts, Lindlar’s catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering its activation energy without being consumed.

Galileo Galilei was an Italian astronomer and physicist whose telescope observations changed how people understood the solar system. In 1610, he reported that Jupiter has four moons orbiting it: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. He also described mountains and craters on the Moon in his Latin book Sidereus Nuncius, published that year. Its title means “Starry Messenger.” Galileo later observed that Venus goes through phases, much like the Moon. These phases challenged the traditional Earth-centered model and supported the idea that planets orbit the Sun, as Copernicus had proposed. Galileo improved the telescope for astronomical use, but he did not invent it. His support for heliocentrism brought him into conflict with the Catholic Church, which placed him under house arrest.

Cassini–Huygens was a joint mission by NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA), and the Italian Space Agency (ASI) to explore Saturn and its moons. In 2004, Cassini became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, giving scientists years of close-up observations of the planet, its rings, and its moons. It carried the Huygens lander, which descended through the thick, nitrogen-rich atmosphere of Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, and sent back data from the surface in 2005. Titan is the second-largest moon in the solar system and has lakes and seas of liquid hydrocarbons, mainly methane and ethane, near its poles. Cassini–Huygens helped scientists understand this unusual world and why its chemistry might offer clues about conditions before life began on Earth.

Mud is a mixture of water, soil, and fine sediment that often forms after heavy rain. When mud flows downhill, it can become a mudslide and bury roads, buildings, and farmland. Volcanic eruptions can also trigger fast-moving flows called lahars, in which mud, water, and volcanic debris rush down a volcano’s slopes. Mud volcanoes are different from ordinary volcanoes: they release mud and gases rather than molten rock. Azerbaijan’s Gobustan State Reserve has many mud volcanoes near the shore of the Caspian Sea. Although it is called a sea, the Caspian is an inland body of water and technically the world’s largest lake. The Volga River flows into it.

A gluon is a massless, spin-1 particle that carries the strong force, one of the fundamental forces of nature. Gluons bind quarks together inside hadrons, such as protons and neutrons. They are called gauge bosons, like photons, which carry the electromagnetic force. Unlike photons, however, gluons carry the kind of charge involved in their own force, called color charge. This means gluons can interact with one another as well as with quarks. The Standard Model theory that describes these interactions is quantum chromodynamics, or QCD. Its rules are based on a mathematical symmetry called SU(3), associated with three types of color charge. In the extremely hot early universe, quarks and gluons existed in a state called quark-gluon plasma.

Spiral galaxies are vast systems of stars, gas, and dust shaped like flattened disks. They have a central bulge surrounded by winding spiral arms, where many young stars form. Because the inner parts of a galaxy orbit faster than the outer parts, astronomers once wondered why the arms do not wind up and disappear. Density wave theory explains that the arms are long-lasting regions of increased density: stars and gas move into and out of them as they orbit, rather than remaining in the same arm forever. Our own galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral galaxy. In some spiral galaxies, an elongated structure of stars and gas called a bar crosses the central bulge, with arms extending from its ends. These barred spiral galaxies are labeled “SB” in Hubble’s tuning-fork classification.

An artificial neural network (ANN) is a computational model that learns patterns from data. It is loosely inspired by the way neurons connect in the human brain, though its artificial “neurons” are much simpler. These processing units are arranged in layers: an input layer receives data, hidden layers process it, and an output layer produces a prediction. Connections between units have adjustable values called weights, which determine how strongly signals affect later units. During training, the network compares its prediction with the correct answer to measure an error. An algorithm called backpropagation sends information about that error backward through the layers. Using a mathematical rule called the chain rule, it calculates how each weight contributed to the error, allowing the network to update its weights and improve its predictions.

Le Chatelier’s principle predicts how a system at chemical equilibrium responds when its conditions change: it shifts in a direction that tends to oppose a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature. At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the concentrations remain constant. The equilibrium constant, K, describes the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, with each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. The reaction quotient, Q, is calculated in the same way but uses the mixture’s current concentrations, which may not be at equilibrium. Comparing Q with K shows which way the reaction will shift: if Q is less than K, it shifts toward products; if Q is greater than K, it shifts toward reactants.

Lactic acid is a three-carbon organic acid produced when cells or certain bacteria break down sugars without enough oxygen. Bacteria such as Lactobacillus ferment sugars in milk, giving yogurt and other cultured dairy products their tangy taste. During intense exercise, muscle cells produce lactate, a form of lactic acid, through anaerobic glycolysis. Lactate travels in the blood to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose; the glucose can then return to muscles for energy. This liver-muscle pathway is called the Cori cycle. Lactic acid buildup is associated with the burning feeling during strenuous exercise, but it does not cause soreness that appears a day or two later. Lactic acid units can also be linked to make polylactic acid, a biodegradable plastic used in 3-D printing.

Hemoglobin is an iron-containing protein in red blood cells that gives them their oxygen-carrying capacity. It is a tetramer made of four subunits, each with a heme group: an iron atom held in a ring called a porphyrin. In the lungs, hemoglobin binds oxygen and carries it to tissues that need it. Active tissues produce carbon dioxide, which helps lower blood pH. This reduces hemoglobin’s attraction to oxygen, encouraging it to release oxygen where it is needed. This relationship is called the Bohr effect. In the lungs, carbon dioxide is expelled and pH rises, favoring oxygen loading. Hemoglobin also helps transport some carbon dioxide and regulate blood acidity. Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds to hemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does.

Electrodialysis is a method of desalination, which means removing dissolved salts from water to make it more suitable for drinking or other uses. It works by applying a direct-current electric field to salty water. The field pulls positively charged ions, called cations, in one direction and negatively charged ions, called anions, in the other. The water passes between alternating ion-exchange membranes: cation-exchange membranes let cations through, while anion-exchange membranes let anions through. Because each membrane blocks the opposite type of ion, the ions collect in some compartments and leave others. This produces neighboring salt-enriched streams, called concentrate, and salt-depleted streams, called dilute water. Unlike a solar still or reverse osmosis, electrodialysis separates salt mainly by moving its dissolved ions with electricity.

Black is an achromatic appearance, meaning it has no hue. We perceive it when little or no visible light reaches our eyes from a surface. A black surface absorbs most of the visible light that falls on it and reflects very little, while a completely dark space has no visible light to reflect. Black also gave an early name to the Golgi stain, or Golgi reaction, a technique developed by Italian scientist Camillo Golgi to study neurons. This silver-chromate method impregnates only a small subset of the nerve cells in a tissue sample. Those cells appear dark against a pale background, making their cell bodies, branching dendrites, and long axons easier to see and trace.

Phase space is an abstract way to represent every possible instantaneous state of a moving system. For a particle traveling in one dimension, each point in phase space has two coordinates: its position and its linear momentum. As the particle moves, its state changes and the point traces a path through phase space. Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, so it describes both how much motion an object has and its direction. A force acting over time produces an impulse, which equals the change in momentum. Momentum is conserved when a system has translational symmetry, meaning the laws governing it do not change from one location to another. In a collision with no external force, total momentum is conserved even if the collision is inelastic.

An inelastic collision is an impact in which the objects’ total linear momentum is conserved, but their total kinetic energy decreases. In an isolated system, no outside force changes the total momentum during the collision. The “lost” kinetic energy is not destroyed; it is transformed into other forms, such as heat, sound, or energy used to bend or dent the objects. A way to describe how much the objects rebound is the coefficient of restitution. This dimensionless number compares their relative speed as they move apart after impact with their relative speed as they move toward each other before impact. If the objects stick together and move as one, their relative speed afterward is zero, so the coefficient of restitution is zero.

Regeneration is the biological process of replacing lost or damaged tissues, organs, or body parts. Many animals can repair wounds, but some can rebuild complex structures: lizards grow replacement tails, starfish regrow arms, and salamanders can replace amputated limbs. African spiny mice are unusually good at regenerating damaged skin for mammals, healing with much less scarring than most other mammals. In a salamander, cells gather at the site of a lost limb and form a mass called a blastema. The blastema’s cells multiply and develop into the tissues needed for the replacement limb, including bone, muscle, and skin. Scientists study these animals to understand why some species can regenerate body parts while humans usually heal major injuries with scars instead.

Parthenogenesis is a form of asexual reproduction in which an embryo develops from an unfertilized egg, without sperm fertilizing it. Because no mating is needed, an animal can produce offspring on its own. One example is the marbled crayfish, a freshwater crustacean whose name refers to the marbled pattern on its shell. Marbled crayfish reproduce through parthenogenesis: females lay eggs that develop into new crayfish without fertilization. They are also triploid, meaning their cells have three sets of chromosomes rather than the two sets typical of diploid animals. Chromosomes carry genetic information, and having three sets is a separate trait from reproducing by parthenogenesis. The key distinction is that parthenogenesis names the reproductive process, while marbled crayfish names an animal that uses it.

Sirius A is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. Located in the constellation Canis Major, it is often called the Dog Star and forms the Winter Triangle with Betelgeuse and Procyon. Sirius A is a main-sequence star, meaning it produces energy by fusing hydrogen in its core. It is also part of a binary system: two stars orbiting each other. In the 1800s, Friedrich Bessel noticed small irregularities in Sirius A’s motion and inferred that an unseen companion was pulling on it. That companion, Sirius B, was later observed. Although Sirius B has roughly the Sun’s mass, it is only about the size of Earth and much fainter than Sirius A. It is a white dwarf, the dense remnant left after a star has used up its nuclear fuel.

Honey bees are social insects in the genus Apis that live in colonies centered around a queen. Most members of a colony are female workers, which gather nectar and pollen from flowers. As they move between blossoms, they transfer pollen and help plants reproduce. Workers turn nectar into honey, a food the colony stores in wax comb inside its hive. A worker that finds a good food source can tell other bees where to go by performing a waggle dance. It moves in a repeating figure-eight pattern; the angle of its central run indicates the food’s direction relative to the sun, and the run’s duration indicates roughly how far away it is. Honey bees can be threatened by disease and parasites, including Varroa mites.

The Burmese python is one of the world’s largest snakes. Native to South and Southeast Asia, it is a constrictor: it coils around prey and squeezes until the animal can no longer breathe. Burmese pythons have established an invasive population in the Everglades, a vast subtropical wetland in southern Florida known for its sawgrass marshes and mangrove habitats. Some were released or escaped from captivity, and the warm climate allowed them to survive and reproduce. They prey on native mammals and birds, threatening wildlife and disrupting the wetland’s food web. Unlike venomous snakes such as cobras, Burmese pythons rely on their strength to capture prey. Efforts to control their population are difficult because the snakes are well camouflaged and can spread across large, hard-to-reach areas.

Rod cells are photoreceptors in the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that sends visual information to the brain through the optic nerve. Rods are especially sensitive to faint light, making them important for night vision. They also contribute strongly to peripheral vision, helping you notice something off to the side. Unlike cone cells, which work best in brighter light and help you see colors and fine detail, rods favor light sensitivity over color discrimination. Each rod contains a light-sensitive protein called rhodopsin, also known as “visual purple.” Rhodopsin is a G-protein-coupled receptor: when it absorbs a photon, its retinal chromophore changes shape. This starts phototransduction, the process that turns light into an electrical signal the nervous system can use.

Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth’s rigid outer shell, called the lithosphere, is divided into large plates that move slowly over the layer beneath. Where plates pull apart, new ocean floor can form; where they collide or slide past each other, they can reshape continents, build mountains, and cause earthquakes and volcanoes. Plate movement also explains why continents that are far apart today were once joined. Alfred Wegener proposed that they had formed a prehistoric supercontinent called Pangaea, a name from Greek roots meaning “all” and “Earth.” He pointed to coastlines that seemed to fit together like puzzle pieces and to Glossopteris fern fossils found on widely separated continents. Over millions of years, Pangaea broke apart, eventually producing today’s continents and ocean basins.

A helicopter is an aircraft that uses a powered rotor with spinning blades to generate lift. Unlike a fixed-wing airplane, it can take off and land vertically, hover nearly motionless over one place, and maneuver without a runway. These abilities make helicopters useful for rescues, transporting people, and reaching places where airplanes cannot land. Helicopters also have a way to descend if the engine fails. In an emergency procedure called autorotation, the pilot adjusts the rotor blades so that air flowing upward through them as the helicopter descends keeps the rotor spinning. Although the engine is no longer driving the rotor, autorotation helps the pilot maintain control and make a landing.

Isotopes are forms of the same chemical element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. The number of protons determines the element, while the total number of protons and neutrons is its mass number. Changing the number of neutrons therefore changes an atom’s mass number without changing its element. Hydrogen provides a clear example: its most common isotope has one proton and no neutrons, while deuterium has one proton and one neutron in its nucleus. A neutral deuterium atom also has one electron, balancing the positive charge of its proton. Both of these hydrogen isotopes are stable. Isotopes can behave differently in reactions; the kinetic isotope effect describes a change in reaction rate when one isotope is substituted for another.

ITER is an international experimental fusion project being built at Saint-Paul-lès-Durance in France by the European Union, China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia, and the United States. Its tokamak uses powerful magnets to confine extremely hot plasma, allowing researchers to study nuclear fusion, the process in which light atomic nuclei join together. ITER’s planned high-performance experiments will use deuterium–tritium fusion: deuterium and tritium, two isotopes of hydrogen, combine to produce a helium-4 nucleus and a 14.1-MeV neutron. A lithium-bearing blanket is intended to help breed tritium for the fuel cycle. ITER is designed to produce 500 megawatts of fusion power from 50 megawatts of heating input. Its goal is to demonstrate high-performance plasma operation, not to generate commercial electricity.

Pathfinding is the computational task of finding a route between two locations, often the shortest or least-cost route. A map can be represented as a graph: locations are points called vertices, and connections between them are edges. In a weighted graph, each edge has a numerical cost, such as distance, travel time, or the energy needed to cross it. The best path may therefore have the lowest total cost rather than the fewest edges. Dijkstra’s algorithm searches for lowest-cost paths using the known edge costs, while A* also uses an estimate of the remaining cost to guide its search toward a destination. Pathfinding is used in video games to move characters around obstacles and in mapping software to plan routes.

Monkeys are a diverse group of primates that are not apes. They include New World monkeys, such as capuchins, howlers, and spider monkeys, which live in Central and South America, and Old World monkeys, such as macaques, which live in Africa and Asia. Most monkeys have tails, unlike apes, but not all monkey tails can grip. Many New World species, including spider monkeys, have a prehensile tail: they can wrap its tip around branches and use it like a fifth limb while climbing. Monkeys also appear in stories. Sun Wukong, the supernatural Monkey King, is a character in Journey to the West, a Chinese novel about a journey to India to collect Buddhist texts.

Corals are marine animals in the cnidarian group, related to jellyfish and sea anemones. Many live in colonies of tiny individuals called polyps, which secrete hard calcium-carbonate skeletons. Over time, these skeletons build coral reefs that provide food and shelter for a huge variety of ocean life. Many reef-building corals also contain photosynthetic dinoflagellates called zooxanthellae in their tissues. The algae use sunlight to make food and pass much of that energy to the coral; in return, the coral provides a protected place to live. When seawater becomes too warm, this partnership can break down, and corals may lose their zooxanthellae. The exposed white skeleton shows through their tissues, making the corals look pale—a process called coral bleaching.

A peptic ulcer is an open sore in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine. This lining is normally protected from strong digestive acid by a layer of mucus. One cause of peptic ulcers is frequent or excessive use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs, a class of pain relievers that includes aspirin, ibuprofen, and naproxen. NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation by blocking enzymes called cyclooxygenases. However, they can also reduce the production of protective mucus, leaving the digestive lining more vulnerable to acid damage. Another common cause of peptic ulcers is infection with the bacterium Helicobacter pylori. Symptoms may include burning pain in the upper abdomen, though some people have few symptoms.

The Magdeburg hemispheres were two copper half-spheres used by Otto von Guericke in a famous 1654 demonstration in Regensburg. When joined, they formed a hollow sphere. Guericke pumped most of the air out, leaving a near-vacuum inside. The air outside still pressed on the hemispheres, but there was very little gas inside to push back. This difference in pressure held the halves together so tightly that teams of horses could not pull them apart. The inward force came from atmospheric pressure—the pressure exerted by the air surrounding Earth—not from the vacuum pulling the shells together. When air was allowed back inside, the pressure on both sides became nearly equal, and the hemispheres could be separated easily.

Human hair consists of thin filaments that grow from follicles, small structures embedded in the skin. Hair is found across much of the body, but it is especially abundant on the scalp. Each hair has a root within its follicle and a visible shaft extending above the skin. The shaft is made mostly of keratin, a tough structural protein that is also a major component of fingernails and the outer layer of skin. Keratin gives hair strength and helps it withstand everyday activities such as washing and combing. Although the visible shaft is made of dead, keratin-filled cells, living cells in the follicle produce new hair as it grows. Hair can help protect the scalp from sunlight, and people also style it to express personal or cultural identity.

Olfaction is the sense of smell. When you breathe in, airborne chemicals called odorants enter the nose and bind to receptors on sensory neurons in the olfactory epithelium. These neurons send signals along their axons to the olfactory bulbs, a pair of structures at the front of the brain. In each bulb, axons from neurons that detect the same kind of odorant meet in small groups called glomeruli. The bulbs then send processed signals to brain regions including the piriform cortex, which helps identify odors. Most senses pass through the thalamus before reaching the cerebral cortex, but smell is unusual: its early pathway reaches the olfactory bulb and then the piriform cortex without an initial stop in the thalamus.

A space station is an artificial facility that orbits Earth and allows astronauts to live and work in space for extended periods. Unlike a spacecraft built mainly for a short journey, it has space for daily activities as well as scientific research. Astronauts aboard space stations can study how living things and materials behave in the weak gravity experienced in orbit and can observe Earth and space. Skylab, launched in 1973, was the first U.S. space station. Three crews lived and worked aboard it before it reentered Earth’s atmosphere in 1979. Later space stations included Russia’s Mir, which was assembled from modules, and the International Space Station, where crews from different countries have worked together.

Cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR, is an emergency procedure used when someone is in cardiac arrest and their heart is no longer pumping blood effectively. Chest compressions push blood toward the brain and other vital organs; rescue breaths, when given, help supply oxygen. An adult’s chest should be compressed at least 2 inches deep at a steady rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Call emergency services and begin CPR promptly. A portable device called an automated external defibrillator, or AED, can help too. It analyzes the person’s heart rhythm and gives voice instructions to the rescuer. If it detects a rhythm that can be treated with a shock, it delivers an electrical shock that may help the heart return to an effective rhythm.

Strip mining is a way to extract coal and other minerals that lie close to Earth’s surface. Instead of digging deep tunnels, miners remove long strips of soil and rock above a deposit, then take out the exposed material. This can greatly change the shape of the land, destroy habitats, and leave loose soil vulnerable to erosion, especially if the site is not restored afterward. Coal, a carbon-rich sedimentary rock used as a fossil fuel, can also be mined underground or in open pits. After mining, coal may be ground up and mixed with water to make a pumpable solid-liquid mixture called slurry, which can travel through pipelines. A flood of coal slurry at Buffalo Creek, West Virginia, killed more than 100 people in 1972.

Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive disorder in which brain cells become damaged and die over time. It is the most common cause of dementia in older adults, often beginning with memory problems and later affecting language, reasoning, and everyday activities. Two characteristic changes in the brain are beta-amyloid plaques, which build up between nerve cells, and neurofibrillary tangles made of tau protein, which form inside them. Researchers can study brain activity and, with specialized tracers, detect these protein deposits in living patients using positron emission tomography, or PET. In a PET scan, a radioactive tracer releases positrons as it decays. When a positron meets an electron, they produce two photons that the scanner detects to create an image.

Oscillation is repeated motion back and forth around an equilibrium position, where an object would rest if it were not disturbed. A swinging pendulum is one example: it moves to one side, passes through its equilibrium position, moves to the other side, and swings back. If this motion repeats in regular cycles, it is periodic. The time needed to complete one full cycle and return to the same point in the motion, moving in the same direction, is called the period, usually written T. Frequency tells us how many cycles occur each second, so frequency is one divided by the period. In a real pendulum, friction and air resistance gradually reduce the size of the swings, an effect called damping.

The mesosphere is the layer of Earth’s atmosphere above the stratosphere and below the thermosphere. It begins at the stratopause, about 50 kilometers above the ground, and extends to roughly 85 kilometers. Temperatures generally fall with height, making its upper region the coldest part of the atmosphere. Many meteors heat up and ablate, or break apart and vaporize, as they pass through the mesosphere. Near its upper edge, delicate blue-white clouds made of ice crystals can still catch sunlight after sunset, when the sky below is dark. These are called noctilucent clouds. The mesosphere is difficult to study because it is too high for ordinary weather balloons and too low for most satellites to orbit.

Hendrik Lorentz was a Dutch theoretical physicist whose work helped prepare the way for Einstein’s theory of special relativity. The Lorentz factor, written with the Greek letter gamma, describes how measurements of time and length change when an object moves close to the speed of light. It is used to calculate time dilation, in which a moving clock appears to run more slowly, and length contraction, in which a moving object appears shorter in its direction of travel. Lorentz also explained why a magnetic field can split a single spectral line—the light emitted or absorbed at a particular wavelength—into several lines. Another Dutch physicist, Pieter Zeeman, had observed this effect experimentally. Lorentz and Zeeman shared the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work on magnetism and radiation.

Strontium is a chemical element with the symbol Sr and atomic number 38, meaning each atom has 38 protons. It belongs to the alkaline-earth metals, a group that also includes calcium. Strontium compounds produce a vivid red color when heated, so they are used in fireworks and burn red in a flame test. While ordinary strontium has some practical uses, its radioactive isotope strontium-90 is dangerous. Strontium-90 can be released in nuclear fallout and spread through the environment. Because strontium is chemically similar to calcium, the body may absorb it and deposit it in bones, where calcium is normally stored. Radiation from strontium-90 can then damage nearby cells and increase the risk of cancer.

A solenoid is a long, helix-shaped coil of wire. When electric current flows through it, each turn produces a magnetic field, and the fields from successive turns reinforce one another. This creates a strong field along the coil’s axis, especially inside the coil. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field, and switching off the current removes the field produced by the current. A solenoid can therefore act as an electromagnet; placing an iron core inside it makes the magnetic effect stronger. Solenoids are used in devices such as electric door locks and valves. The French physicist André-Marie Ampère gave the solenoid its name. His work helped establish the relationship between electric currents and magnetism, and the ampere, the SI unit of electric current, is named in his honor.

The whale shark is the world’s largest living fish. Despite its name, it is a shark, not a whale: it breathes through gills and has a skeleton made mainly of cartilage rather than bone. Whale sharks live in tropical and warm-temperate oceans, often swimming near the surface where food is plentiful. They eat tiny organisms such as plankton, along with small fish. To feed, a whale shark takes in seawater through its wide mouth, traps food particles as the water passes through its filtering structures, and expels the water through its gills. This way of obtaining food is called filter feeding. Although whale sharks can grow to enormous sizes, they do not hunt large prey like some other sharks.

Hardness is a material’s resistance to being scratched, indented, or permanently deformed. Scientists measure it in different ways depending on what they want to compare. In a Vickers test, a diamond-shaped tip is pressed into a material, and the size of the indentation is used to calculate a hardness value. A scratch test instead checks whether one material can scratch another; an instrument called a sclerometer can be used for this. The Mohs scale is a scratch-hardness scale for minerals. It ranks talc at 1 and diamond at 10, with each higher-ranked mineral able to scratch lower-ranked ones. Mohs ranks show the order of scratch resistance, not equal-sized steps in hardness.

A precipitation reaction happens when ions dissolved in water combine to form an insoluble solid called a precipitate. Because the solid does not stay dissolved, it separates from the surrounding liquid and may sink to the bottom of a test tube. Scientists use these reactions in qualitative analysis to identify ions in an unknown solution: they add a substance containing a known ion and watch for a solid to form. For example, table salt dissolves into sodium ions and chloride ions. Chloride is the negatively charged ion, written Cl−, and it forms insoluble compounds with lead, silver, and mercury ions. A precipitate after chloride is added can therefore help scientists narrow down which ions are present. Chloride ion is not the same thing as elemental chlorine.

The speed of sound is the rate at which a sound wave travels through a medium such as air, water, or a solid. In dry air at 20°C, it is commonly rounded to 343 meters per second. Its value changes with conditions and with the medium’s properties: for example, sound generally travels faster in warmer air. In the ocean, changes in temperature and pressure create a depth region called the SOFAR channel, where the speed of sound reaches a minimum. To compare an object’s speed with the speed of sound around it, divide the object’s speed by the local speed of sound. The result is a dimensionless number called the Mach number. A jet traveling at twice the local speed of sound is moving at Mach 2.

Ctenophora is a phylum of marine invertebrates commonly called comb jellies. They usually have transparent, jelly-like bodies and swim using eight longitudinal rows of comb plates. Each comb plate is made of many cilia, tiny hair-like structures, joined together. As the cilia beat in coordinated waves, they push water backward and propel the animal forward. Light reflecting and scattering from the moving comb plates can make the rows look like shimmering, rainbow-colored bands. Despite their name and appearance, comb jellies are not true jellyfish, which belong to a different phylum. Ctenophores often catch small animals with sticky cells on their tentacles or body surfaces. If a question asks for the phylum of animals with eight rows of beating “combs,” the answer is Ctenophora; the specialized rows are called comb plates.

The JAK-STAT signaling pathway lets a cell respond quickly to signals from outside, especially cytokines, which are proteins that help coordinate immune responses. When a cytokine binds to its receptor on the cell surface, receptor-associated enzymes called Janus kinases (JAKs) add phosphate groups to proteins called STATs. The activated STAT proteins pair up and move into the nucleus, where they bind DNA and regulate transcription: the process of making an RNA copy of a gene. This changes which proteins the cell produces. Different cytokines can activate different STATs. For example, interleukin-6 activates STAT3, which promotes transcription of acute-phase response genes involved in the body’s early response to infection or injury.

The pituitary gland is a small endocrine organ at the base of the brain. Endocrine organs release hormones, chemical signals that travel through the blood and affect other parts of the body. The pituitary has two main parts. Its anterior lobe produces hormones such as human growth hormone (HGH), which supports growth, and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which helps regulate reproduction. Its posterior lobe releases hormones made in the hypothalamus, a nearby part of the brain. One of these is oxytocin, a peptide hormone involved in childbirth, milk release during breastfeeding, and social bonding between parents and newborns. This distinction matters: the posterior pituitary releases oxytocin, but the hypothalamus makes it.

The sperm whale is the largest living toothed cetacean, a group of aquatic mammals that includes whales, dolphins, and porpoises. It can dive more than a kilometer deep to hunt prey such as squid, using echolocation to navigate and find food in the darkness. Its enormous, block-shaped head contains a waxy substance called spermaceti. Whalers once extracted spermaceti to make candles and ointments. Early observers mistook it for a reproductive fluid, which led to the name “sperm whale,” though it is not sperm. The species is also traditionally identified as the massive white whale pursued by Captain Ahab and the crew of the Pequod in Herman Melville’s novel Moby-Dick.

Peptidoglycan, also called murein, is the tough, mesh-like polymer that gives most bacterial cell walls their shape and rigidity. It surrounds the cell membrane and helps keep a bacterium from bursting as water enters the cell. The mesh consists of long strands of alternating sugar units connected by short peptide chains; links between neighboring strands make it strong. Peptidoglycan makes up much of the dry weight of the thick cell walls of Gram-positive bacteria. Cell walls are not unique to bacteria, but their materials differ: plant cell walls are mainly cellulose, fungal cell walls contain chitin, and animal cells have no cell wall. Penicillins, a family of antibiotics first discovered by Alexander Fleming, stop bacteria from building strong walls by blocking the enzymes that cross-link peptidoglycan.

Pineapple is a tropical plant in the bromeliad family, whose other members include many plants grown for their colorful leaves and flowers. A pineapple fruit is not formed from just one flower: it is a compound fruit made when the fruits of many small flowers fuse together. Native to South America, pineapples were later grown in many warm regions. In Hawaiʻi, James Dole helped develop large-scale pineapple cultivation, making the crop an important plantation industry alongside sugar. Plantation businesses had major influence over the islands’ economy and politics; a group of powerful companies known as the “Big Five” was especially prominent. Hawaiʻi, now a U.S. state in the Pacific Ocean, became closely associated with pineapple production, even though pineapples did not originate there.

Carl Friedrich Gauss was a German mathematician, physicist, and astronomer whose discoveries shaped several branches of science. He made major contributions to number theory and geometry, and Gaussian elimination, named after him, is a method for solving systems of linear equations. His name also appears in Gauss’s law for magnetism, one of Maxwell’s equations. Magnetic flux measures how much magnetic field passes through a surface; for a closed surface, such as an imaginary sphere, it is found by adding up the field passing through every small part of the boundary. Gauss’s law says the total magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. Magnetic field lines have no beginnings or endings, so every line that enters a closed surface must also leave it.

Vitamin E is a group of fat-soluble compounds that act as antioxidants, helping protect cells from damage caused by unstable molecules called free radicals. Alpha-tocopherol is one of its main forms in the human body. Foods that provide vitamin E include plant oils, nuts, and seeds. Because it dissolves in fat, vitamin E can be stored in the body. Vitamin E acetate is a related ester form that was found in many THC-containing vaping products during investigations of EVALI, which stands for e-cigarette or vaping use-associated lung injury. Inhaling vitamin E acetate is different from eating foods that contain vitamin E: when inhaled, it can harm the lungs.

A power outage, also called a blackout, is a temporary loss of electrical service. It happens when electricity stops reaching a home or other building, whether because of a problem with the power system or a planned interruption for maintenance. In Jhumpa Lahiri’s short story “A Temporary Matter,” the utility company schedules one-hour power outages beginning at 8 p.m. each evening. Shukumar and his wife, Shoba, spend these hours without electric lights and begin sharing secrets with each other. Their conversations reveal the grief and distance between them after their baby was stillborn. During the couple’s final evening without electricity, Shukumar tells Shoba that their baby was a boy. The scheduled outages are temporary, but they create moments in which the couple confronts painful truths.

Thomas Young was an English physician and polymath who made important contributions to both optics and the study of materials. In his double-slit experiment, light passed through two narrow openings and produced alternating bright and dark bands. This interference pattern showed that light behaves like a wave: waves from the two slits can reinforce or cancel each other. Young’s name is also attached to Young’s modulus, a measure of a material’s stiffness. When a material is stretched or compressed within its elastic range, it can return to its original shape after the force is removed. Young’s modulus equals normal stress divided by longitudinal strain. Stress is force per unit area, while strain describes the relative change in length. A larger Young’s modulus means a stiffer material.

Adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, is a nucleotide that acts as an energy currency for cells. It stores usable chemical energy in bonds between its three phosphate groups. When a cell removes one phosphate group, ATP becomes ADP and releases energy that can power cellular reactions. During photosynthesis, the light-dependent reactions occur on the membranes of disk-shaped thylakoids inside chloroplasts and produce ATP. The ATP is then used in the chloroplast stroma, the fluid surrounding the thylakoids, by the Calvin cycle. Named for American chemist Melvin Calvin, this pathway fixes carbon dioxide and uses energy from ATP to help make carbohydrate precursors. The Calvin cycle also uses NADPH, another product of the light-dependent reactions.

Fluid velocity describes how fast a fluid, such as water or air, moves and in what direction. It is a vector: at each point in the fluid, it has both a speed and a direction. For a tiny parcel of fluid, velocity is the rate at which its position changes with time, usually measured in meters per second. Fluid motion is also affected by viscosity, a fluid’s internal resistance to flow. Dynamic viscosity is measured in pascal-seconds; a more viscous fluid resists motion more strongly. For a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid, Stokes’ law relates the drag force opposing its motion to the sphere’s radius, the dynamic viscosity, and the sphere’s velocity relative to the fluid.

A software bug is an error or flaw in a program that makes it behave in an unintended way. A bug might cause an app to crash, display the wrong answer, or fail only under certain conditions. Programmers look for bugs by testing their code and then fix them through a process called debugging. One famous story involves an actual moth found in a switch of the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947. The moth was taped into the computer’s logbook, and U.S. Navy computer scientist Grace Hopper later recounted the episode. Hopper, who became a rear admiral, also helped develop the work that led to COBOL, a programming language. People sometimes credit her with inventing the term “bug,” but it had been used to describe technical problems before the moth was found.

Cascading Style Sheets, or CSS, is a language for controlling how a webpage looks while HTML provides its content and structure. A web author can use CSS to set colors, fonts, spacing, and layouts without changing the meaning or order of the HTML content. CSS works through rules: a selector identifies the elements to style, and declarations specify properties and values, such as a text color or margin size. If multiple rules apply to the same element, the “cascade” determines which one wins, using factors such as selector specificity and the order of the rules. CSS also includes media queries, which apply styles only when conditions are met. For example, a media query can change a layout for a narrow phone screen, a different screen orientation, or a printed page.

Radio waves are electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than microwaves, at the long-wavelength end of the electromagnetic spectrum. Like microwaves and infrared light, they are non-ionizing: their photons do not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms. Radio waves can travel through space and carry information, making them useful for broadcasting and other wireless communications. In AM (amplitude modulation) broadcasting, the strength of a radio wave changes to encode sound; in FM (frequency modulation), its frequency changes instead. The Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell predicted that electromagnetic waves could travel through space. In the late 1880s, German physicist Heinrich Hertz produced and detected radio waves experimentally, confirming Maxwell’s prediction. The unit of frequency, the hertz, is named after him.

A meteorite is a piece of space rock or metal that survives its journey through Earth’s atmosphere and lands on the ground. Before it enters the atmosphere, the object is called a meteoroid; the bright streak seen as it speeds through the air is a meteor. Many meteoroids burn up completely, but any material that reaches the surface is a meteorite. Meteorites can come from asteroids, which are small rocky bodies, or from comets. One famous example is the Hoba meteorite, a massive iron meteorite discovered near Grootfontein, Namibia, in 1920. It remains where it was found and is considered the largest known intact meteorite.

The Y chromosome is one of the two human sex chromosomes and is usually passed from father to son. Unlike mitochondrial DNA, which can help trace a person’s maternal line, DNA on the Y chromosome can help trace a direct paternal line through many generations. Most people with a Y chromosome also have an X chromosome. An important DNA sequence on the Y chromosome is the SRY gene. It produces a transcription factor, a protein that helps control the activity of other genes. During embryonic development, SRY normally helps direct the developing gonads to become testes, beginning a typical male sex-determination pathway. If SRY does not work, a person with a Y chromosome may develop gonads differently.

Magnetism is a physical phenomenon in which magnetic fields exert forces on certain materials and on magnetic dipoles, such as compass needles. Earth’s magnetic field makes a compass needle align roughly north–south. Magnets have north and south poles: opposite poles attract, while like poles repel. At the atomic level, many particles act like tiny magnets. In ferromagnetic materials such as iron, neighboring atomic magnetic moments can align spontaneously in groups called domains. When many domains point the same way, the material produces a strong magnetic field and may remain magnetized after an external field is removed. This ability to “remember” a field is called hysteresis. Refrigerator magnets can be made from materials such as alnico or neodymium alloys. Above a ferromagnet’s Curie temperature, heat disrupts its ordered alignment, and it loses its ferromagnetism.

An inferior conjunction occurs when an inner planet, Mercury or Venus, passes between Earth and the Sun. From Earth, the planet’s sunlit side then faces mostly away from us, so it appears in a new phase. Venus also looks relatively large at this time because it is closer to Earth than when it appears full on the far side of the Sun. Inferior conjunction does not usually mean the three bodies line up perfectly in our sky: the planet generally passes above or below the Sun’s disk. If Venus crosses directly in front of the Sun, it appears as a small dark dot. This rare event is called a transit of Venus. One occurred in 2012, and the next is expected in 2117.

Pressure is the force pushing on each unit of area, so the same force creates more pressure when it acts on a smaller area. Its SI unit is the pascal, equal to one newton per square meter; other units include torr and pounds per square inch (psi). Air has weight, so it exerts atmospheric pressure, which can be measured with a barometer. Gases also exert pressure as their moving particles collide with the walls of a container. For a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, Boyle’s law says pressure and volume vary inversely: squeezing the gas into a smaller volume increases its pressure. Their product stays constant, written as P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, where the subscripts identify two different states of the gas.

Acid–base titration is a laboratory method for finding the concentration of an acid or base by reacting it with a solution of known concentration. A measured amount of the unknown solution is placed in a flask, and the known solution is added slowly from a burette. As they react, the acid and base neutralize each other. The equivalence point is the theoretical stage when they have reacted in exactly the proportions required by the chemical equation. For a monoprotic acid reacting with a base that supplies one hydroxide ion per molecule, this means equal numbers of moles. An indicator’s color change or an instrument reading marks the observed endpoint, which may be slightly before or after the equivalence point. The volume added is then used to calculate the unknown concentration.

Xylitol is a naturally occurring sugar alcohol used to sweeten foods without ordinary sugar. Despite its name, it is not the kind of alcohol found in drinks: it is a five-carbon compound with the chemical formula C₅H₁₂O₅. Xylitol tastes sweet but provides fewer calories than sugar, so it appears in many sugar-free products. It is especially common in chewing gum, including products sold by brands such as Orbit and Extra; some types of gum are made for blowing bubbles. Xylitol can also support dental health because bacteria in the mouth do not readily ferment it to produce the acids that contribute to tooth decay. Chewing gum itself is meant to be chewed rather than swallowed.

A decision tree is a supervised machine-learning model that predicts an outcome by following a series of branching choices. It starts at a root node; each internal node tests a feature, such as whether a temperature is above a certain value. The result determines which branch an example follows, until it reaches a terminal node, or leaf, that gives a prediction. In a classifier, the prediction is a category, and a good split separates examples of different categories into groups that are more uniform. One way to measure how mixed a group is uses its class probabilities: take each probability, multiply it by its logarithm, add the results, and change the sign. This measure is called entropy. A random forest combines predictions from many decision trees.

Messenger RNA, or mRNA, is a single-stranded molecule that carries instructions for making a protein. A cell produces it by copying the information in a gene’s DNA sequence through a process called transcription. In eukaryotic cells, the mRNA then leaves the nucleus and reaches the cytoplasm, where it associates with a ribosome. A ribosome is a molecular machine made of a small and a large subunit; ribosomes can float freely in the cytoplasm or attach to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. During translation, the ribosome reads the mRNA in three-base groups called codons. Each codon helps specify which amino acid comes next, allowing the ribosome to link amino acids into a growing polypeptide that can become a protein.

The common ion effect occurs when adding a soluble compound reduces the solubility of another ionic compound because both supply the same ion. In a saturated solution, an ionic solid is in equilibrium with its dissolved ions: some solid dissolves while some ions rejoin the solid. For lead(II) chloride, PbCl₂, this balance involves lead ions and chloride ions. Adding ordinary table salt, sodium chloride (NaCl), supplies more chloride ions, which are negatively charged. Because chloride is the ion shared by NaCl and PbCl₂, the balance shifts toward forming solid PbCl₂. Its solubility decreases, and some lead(II) chloride may precipitate, meaning it comes out of the solution as a solid. This change is called the common ion effect.

A calorie is a unit of energy used to describe heat. One small calorie is approximately 4.18 joules and is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one gram of water by one degree Celsius. This relationship reflects water’s specific heat capacity: about one calorie per gram per degree Celsius. Specific heat capacity tells you how much energy is needed to change the temperature of a given mass of a substance. Food labels usually use a larger unit, the Calorie with a capital C, which equals 1,000 small calories and is also called a kilocalorie. Scientists can measure heat changes during chemical reactions with a calorimeter, a device that tracks how much heat is released or absorbed.

The controlled use of fire was one of early humanity’s most important technologies. Rather than relying only on wildfires, early humans learned to keep fires burning and use them for cooking food, warming shelters, and lighting the darkness, which let them stay active after sunset. Heat could also harden wooden hunting tools, including spears. Cooking made some foods easier to chew and digest, and it may have contributed to the gradual shrinking of molar teeth in human ancestors such as Homo erectus. Evidence of ancient fire use has been found at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa’s Northern Cape, where researchers identified microscopic ash in cave sediments. Fire helped early humans survive cold conditions and develop new ways of living and making tools.

Mucus is a thick, slippery secretion that lines much of the respiratory tract, including the nose and trachea. It helps keep inhaled air moist and traps dust, bacteria, and other particles before they can reach the lungs. Mucus is released by goblet cells, specialized cells in the lining of the airways. Each goblet cell has a widened, cup-shaped upper end, which gives it its name. Tiny hairlike structures called cilia beat in coordinated waves to move the mucus and the particles trapped in it toward the throat, where they can be swallowed or coughed out. This process is called mucociliary clearance. In cystic fibrosis, a disorder involving the CFTR protein, mucus becomes unusually thick and difficult to clear.

A parallel circuit has two or more branches, with each branch connected between the same two nodes, or connection points. Because every branch starts and ends at the same points, the voltage, also called potential difference, is identical across every branch. The current can differ between branches: a branch with less resistance generally carries more current. Resistors, which limit current and are often shown as zigzag lines in circuit diagrams, can be connected this way. To find their equivalent resistance, add the reciprocals of the branch resistances: 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + and so on. Adding another parallel branch gives current an additional path, so the equivalent resistance decreases. The total current supplied by the source is the sum of the currents in the branches.

A stack is a data structure that follows the last-in, first-out rule: the most recently added item is the first one removed, like the top plate in a pile. Adding an item is called pushing it onto the stack, and removing the top item is called popping it off. Computers also use a call stack to keep track of active function calls and their local variables. This is especially important in recursion, a programming technique in which a function calls itself to solve smaller versions of a problem. Each call adds a new record to the stack, and that record is removed when the call finishes. If too many calls build up before returning, the stack can run out of space, causing a stack overflow error.

A shield volcano is a broad volcano with gently sloping sides, shaped like a wide shield resting on the ground. It forms through repeated eruptions of basaltic lava, which is relatively fluid and can travel far before cooling and hardening. As successive flows spread outward and pile up, they build a wide landform rather than a steep cone. Lava is molten rock that has reached Earth’s surface; while it is still underground, it is called magma. Shield volcanoes differ from steeper cinder cone volcanoes and stratovolcanoes because their lava flows so easily. Hawaiʻi has several shield volcanoes, including Mauna Loa, which forms much of the Big Island and is recognized as the world’s largest active volcano by volume.

Reginald Punnett was a British geneticist at the University of Cambridge who worked with William Bateson to study Mendelian heredity: how traits pass from parents to offspring. He is best known for the Punnett square, a grid that shows the possible combinations of gene versions, or alleles, an offspring could inherit from its parents. The grid helps predict the probability of particular traits, although real inheritance can be more complicated when genes are linked. Punnett also studied poultry genetics to improve agricultural breeding. One goal was to develop autosexing chickens: breeds whose newly hatched males and females have visibly different plumage, such as different feather colors or patterns. This lets breeders identify a chick’s sex soon after it hatches without waiting for it to grow.

An electronic filter is a circuit network that changes a signal according to its frequency. It lets some frequencies pass through while attenuating, or weakening, others. A cutoff frequency marks the boundary where the filter’s behavior begins to change. A low-pass filter passes frequencies below the cutoff and weakens higher ones; a high-pass filter does the opposite. One simple way to build an electronic filter is with an RC network, made of a resistor and a capacitor. The resistor limits current flow, while the capacitor stores energy in an electric field. On a circuit diagram, a capacitor is often shown as two parallel plates. By arranging the resistor and capacitor in different ways, an RC network can act as either a low-pass or a high-pass filter.

A character is one unit of text in a computer program, such as a letter, digit, punctuation mark, or special symbol.
