Some characters, such as a newline, control how text is displayed rather than appearing as a visible mark. Computers use encodings such as ASCII and Unicode to assign numeric values to characters. In Python, the ord function returns the Unicode number for a character. An ordered sequence of characters is called a string: for example, "cat" is a string of three characters, while "" is an empty string with none. Strings are used to store text, and in Python they are immutable, meaning an existing string cannot be changed in place.

Chromium is a hard, shiny transition metal with the chemical symbol Cr and atomic number 24. It is often added to steel to help it resist corrosion; stainless steel contains chromium, which forms a thin protective layer on its surface. Chromium also helps give some gemstones their colors. Ruby is mostly the mineral corundum, but small amounts of chromium in it produce its characteristic red color. Chromium forms many compounds, including chromium trioxide, whose formula is CrO₃: each unit contains one chromium atom and three oxygen atoms. Chromium trioxide is typically purple but turns orange when wet. Its name comes from “tri-,” meaning three, and “oxide,” indicating oxygen combined with another element.

Textual data is information made of written words and other characters, such as sentences, messages, or web pages. Computers commonly store it as strings of characters rather than as audio waveforms or measurements. Before a language-processing system can analyze text, it often performs tokenization: splitting a character sequence into smaller units called tokens, which may be words, parts of words, or punctuation marks. Another step, stemming, reduces related word forms to a common root; for example, “running” might become “run.” Embeddings turn tokens into numerical representations that help a model recognize similarities in meaning. These techniques help systems search documents, classify messages, and generate text.

Lunar maria are the broad, dark plains visible on the Moon, especially on the side facing Earth. Early astronomers thought these smooth-looking areas might be bodies of water, so they called them maria, the Latin word for “seas.” In fact, they are dry, rocky surfaces. Long ago, large asteroids struck the Moon and left deep impact basins. Later, molten rock rose from inside the Moon and spread across many of those basins. When the lava cooled, it formed basalt, a dark volcanic rock also common in Earth’s oceanic crust. This basalt makes the maria look darker than the Moon’s older, more heavily cratered highlands. A single one of these plains is called a mare; together, they are lunar maria.

A lymph node is a small, bean-shaped organ in the lymphatic system. Lymph nodes lie along one-way vessels that collect excess fluid from body tissues and eventually return it to the bloodstream. Once this clear fluid enters the vessels, it is called lymph. As lymph passes through a node, the node traps debris and germs. It also brings immune cells, including white blood cells, together so they can recognize and respond to threats. Lymph nodes are found throughout the body, with groups in the neck, armpits, and groin. They may become enlarged or tender during an infection because immune cells are becoming active inside them. Doctors also check lymph nodes when assessing whether a cancer has spread.

An antibody, also called an immunoglobulin, is a Y-shaped protein made by B cells to help the immune system recognize threats. It consists of two heavy protein chains and two light protein chains. At the tips of the Y, variable regions from a heavy chain and a light chain form an antigen-binding site called a paratope. Each paratope recognizes a particular small part of an antigen, called an epitope, much like a key fitting a lock. The antibody’s constant regions do not form this specific binding site; instead, they help determine how the immune system responds after binding. Antibodies can mark microbes for destruction or help block them from entering cells. B cells can also change their antibody genes, sometimes improving how tightly the antibodies bind their targets.

Sand is a loose, grainy material made mostly of tiny pieces of minerals and rock. It forms when larger rocks are broken down over time by wind, water, and changes in temperature. Wind can carry sand and pile it into dunes, like those found in parts of the Sahara Desert. The Sahara stretches across northern Africa from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea and is the world’s largest hot desert, although much of it is rocky rather than sandy. Sand also has a political role in Western Sahara, a disputed territory on the desert’s western edge. There, a long berm made partly of sand separates the area controlled by Morocco from an area controlled by the Sahrawi people.

Chaos is behavior in a deterministic dynamical system that follows fixed rules but is extremely sensitive to its initial conditions. If two trajectories start almost identically, tiny differences between them can grow rapidly, making long-term predictions difficult. This sensitivity is often called the butterfly effect: a small change now can lead to a very different outcome later. Chaos does not mean that the system is random; its evolution is still governed by rules. Scientists measure how quickly nearby trajectories separate using Lyapunov exponents. The largest Lyapunov exponent gives the average growth rate of separation along the most unstable direction. When it is positive, nearby trajectories tend to move apart, a key sign of chaos. Examples include some weather models, the logistic map, and electronic circuits.

Subduction happens at a convergent boundary, where two tectonic plates move toward each other and one descends beneath the other. Usually, a denser oceanic plate sinks below another plate, creating a deep ocean trench where the plates meet. As the sinking plate moves deeper, it releases water into the hot rock above it, helping some of that rock melt into magma. The magma can rise through the overriding plate and form volcanoes. A chain of these volcanoes is called a volcanic arc. Volcanic arcs often lie inland and run roughly parallel to the trench; the Cascade Range in western North America is an example. Subduction zones can also produce powerful earthquakes as the plates push against each other and sometimes suddenly slip.

The cosmological constant is a term in Einstein’s field equations of general relativity, often written with the Greek letter lambda (Λ). It can be understood as a uniform energy density of empty space that affects how the universe expands. In 1917, physicist Albert Einstein added it to his equations because he believed the universe was static, or unchanging in size. He hoped its effect would balance gravity, which would otherwise pull matter together. Astronomers later found that the universe is expanding, so Einstein’s original reason for adding the term no longer applied. Today, a cosmological constant is one possible explanation for why that expansion is speeding up. Einstein also developed special relativity and the famous equation E = mc².

A McLeod gauge is a precision laboratory instrument used to measure very low gas pressures, such as those in equipment kept under a vacuum. It traps a known volume of the remaining gas and uses rising mercury to compress that gas into a much smaller space. By comparing the heights of mercury columns, a scientist can calculate the gas’s original pressure. A vacuum is a space with little or no matter; even a strong laboratory vacuum may contain a few gas particles, which is why its pressure can be measured. Sound cannot travel through a complete vacuum because it needs matter to carry vibrations. The space above the mercury in a Torricelli barometer is also a vacuum.

Leukemia is a group of cancers that affect blood-forming tissues, usually the bone marrow, where blood cells are made. It causes abnormal blood cells, often white blood cells, to multiply and crowd out healthy cells. This can disrupt the production of red blood cells, platelets, and working white blood cells, leading to tiredness, easy bruising, and infections. Leukemias are classified as acute or chronic, depending on how quickly they develop, and as lymphoid or myeloid, depending on the type of blood-forming cell affected. In chronic myeloid leukemia, pieces of chromosomes 9 and 22 exchange places. The altered chromosome 22 is called the Philadelphia chromosome, named after the U.S. city where it was first identified. This exchange creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene, which helps drive uncontrolled cell growth.

The tongue is a muscular organ in the mouth that helps you taste food, form words, move food while chewing, and swallow. Small bumps called papillae cover much of its surface; many papillae contain taste buds. Muscles within the tongue change its shape, while other muscles attached to nearby structures, including the hyoid bone, move it around. A fold of tissue called the frenulum anchors the underside of the tongue to the floor of the mouth. If it is unusually short or restrictive, it can cause ankyloglossia, often called tongue-tie. Saliva, a fluid produced by glands including the parotid and submandibular glands, keeps the tongue and mouth moist. It dissolves food chemicals so they can reach taste receptors and contains amylase, an enzyme that begins breaking down starch.

Coronaviruses are a family of RNA viruses that can infect humans and other animals. Each virus has a fatty outer envelope with spike proteins that give it a crownlike appearance; “corona” means crown. Different coronaviruses cause different illnesses, ranging from some common colds to serious respiratory diseases. Members of this family caused the SARS and MERS outbreaks. The coronavirus identified in 2019 that causes COVID-19 is called SARS-CoV-2. It was the seventh known coronavirus to infect humans and the third to cause a major disease outbreak in humans, after the viruses responsible for SARS and MERS. SARS-CoV-2 spreads mainly through the air when infected people breathe, speak, cough, or sneeze. Vaccines, including the mRNA vaccines made by Pfizer and Moderna, help protect against severe COVID-19.

Adaptive radiation is the rapid diversification of one ancestral lineage into several species, each adapted to a different ecological niche, or way of life. It often happens when a group reaches a place with many unoccupied niches and encounters little competition. Over generations, different populations may evolve traits that help them use different food sources or habitats. If they become unable to interbreed, they have formed separate species through a process called speciation. A classic example is the finches Charles Darwin observed on the Galápagos Islands, a Pacific archipelago. These birds evolved different beak shapes suited to different foods, such as seeds or insects. Their diversity shows how one ancestral group can branch into multiple species as its descendants adapt to different opportunities in their environment.

A liquid is a state of matter with a definite volume but no fixed shape: it flows and takes the shape of its container. A gas can become a liquid when it cools and condenses. Liquid molecules stay close together but can move past one another; their attraction to each other is called cohesion. Cohesion helps hold water droplets together and contributes to surface tension at a liquid’s surface. Liquids also show capillary action, which can draw fluid upward through a narrow tube even against gravity. This happens when adhesion, the attraction between the liquid and the tube walls, works together with cohesion within the liquid. Capillary action helps water rise through the narrow tubes called xylem in plants.

Post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD, is a mental health condition that can develop after someone experiences or witnesses a traumatic event, such as abuse, assault, a serious accident, or war. Its symptoms last beyond the immediate danger and may include unwanted, intrusive memories or nightmares, avoiding reminders of the event, and feeling constantly on guard or easily startled. Not everyone who experiences trauma develops PTSD, and effective treatments are available. One psychotherapy is eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, or EMDR. During EMDR, a therapist guides a person to recall traumatic memories while following side-to-side eye movements or using other forms of alternating, or bilateral, stimulation. The goal is to reduce the distress linked to those memories. Researchers are also studying whether psychedelic drugs could help treat PTSD.

Sagittarius A* is the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, the galaxy that contains our Solar System. Astronomers first identified it as a compact source of radio waves. By tracking stars that orbit close to it, they found that about four million times the Sun’s mass is concentrated in a tiny region, providing strong evidence that it is a black hole. A black hole’s gravity is so strong that light cannot escape from inside its event horizon. In 2022, the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration released the first image of Sagittarius A*. This planet-scale network of millimeter and submillimeter radio observatories did not photograph the black hole directly. Instead, it captured bright emission from hot gas around a dark central region called its shadow.

El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, a recurring pattern involving both the tropical Pacific Ocean and the atmosphere above it. During El Niño, a broad band of surface water across the central and eastern tropical Pacific becomes unusually warm. This change affects winds and rainfall, shifting weather patterns far beyond the Pacific. For example, El Niño can bring wetter conditions to the southern United States while contributing to drier, warmer weather in parts of Southeast Asia. ENSO also has a cool phase called La Niña, when those Pacific waters are unusually cool. El Niño and La Niña do not produce exactly the same weather every time, but they help explain why rainfall and temperatures can vary from year to year.

S waves, also called secondary or shear waves, are seismic waves that travel through Earth after an earthquake. They are transverse waves: as an S wave moves forward, it shakes rock perpendicular to its direction of travel. This differs from a P wave, which compresses and stretches material along its direction of travel. S waves can move through solid rock but cannot pass through liquids, because liquids do not resist the shearing motion these waves require. Beneath Earth’s mantle lies the liquid outer core, so S waves cannot cross it to reach a broad region on the far side of the planet. This region is called the S-wave shadow zone, and it helped scientists establish that the outer core is liquid. Movement of liquid metal in the outer core also helps generate Earth’s magnetic field.

Fingerprints are patterns made by the friction ridges on the skin of your fingers. Their loops, whorls, and arches form arrangements that can be used to identify a person. Edward Henry developed a system for classifying fingerprints by recording these patterns on each digit. Today, biometric sensors, such as those used to unlock phones, compare ridge patterns to verify someone’s identity. Fingers can also leave behind invisible, or latent, prints when they touch an object. In forensic investigations, powders can make some prints visible, while the chemical reagent ninhydrin is useful on porous surfaces such as paper. Ninhydrin reacts with amino acids in residue left by the skin and produces a purple compound called Ruhemann’s purple, revealing the fingerprint.

Speech is the ability to turn intended words into meaningful spoken sounds. To speak, the brain coordinates breathing with movements of the vocal folds, tongue, and lips. Language-related regions help make this possible. Broca’s area, in the dominant frontal lobe, is especially important for producing speech, while Wernicke’s area helps people understand language. Damage to these regions can cause aphasia, a language disorder that makes speaking, understanding, or both difficult. A person with damage to Broca’s area may know what they want to say but speak slowly and with great effort, producing short phrases; their understanding is often better preserved than their ability to speak. Broca’s area is named after Pierre Paul Broca, a French physician who studied patients with this pattern.

Nickel is a metallic chemical element with the symbol Ni and atomic number 28, meaning each nickel atom has 28 protons. It is used in stainless steel, coins, and rechargeable batteries. In qualitative analysis, chemists identify ions in a solution by observing how they react with added chemicals. Some reactions produce a precipitate, an insoluble solid that separates from the liquid. Nickel can be difficult to identify this way because it behaves much like iron in several tests. A more specific test involves adding the organic reagent dimethylglyoxime to an ammoniacal solution containing nickel ions. Dimethylglyoxime reacts with the nickel ions to form a distinctive rose-red precipitate. That visible result helps chemists confirm that nickel is present.

Brownian motion is the continual, irregular movement of tiny particles suspended in a fluid, such as pollen grains in water. The particles appear to jiggle and change direction unpredictably because fast-moving molecules of the surrounding liquid or gas collide with them from all sides. These collisions do not balance perfectly at every instant, so the particles wander. In 1905, physicist Albert Einstein developed a mathematical explanation of Brownian motion using diffusion, the spreading of particles over time. He showed that a suspended particle’s mean-square displacement, a measure of how far it moves from its starting point, increases with elapsed time. Measurements that matched his theory provided strong evidence that matter is made of molecules, even though individual molecules were too small to observe directly at the time.

Charles’s Law describes how a fixed amount of gas behaves when its pressure stays constant: its volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature. If the temperature doubles in kelvins, the gas’s volume doubles; if the temperature falls, the volume shrinks. Temperature reflects the average kinetic energy, or motion, of particles, so heating a gas makes its particles move faster and spread out when they can. The law is named for Jacques Charles, a French physicist and ballooning pioneer who studied hydrogen-filled balloons. To use Charles’s Law, temperature must be measured on the Kelvin scale, not in degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit. Kelvin is an absolute scale: 0 kelvin is absolute zero, equal to −273.15°C, and a change of one kelvin is the same size as a change of one degree Celsius.

A eutectic system is a mixture of two substances with a special composition that melts at a lower temperature than either pure substance. At this composition, called the eutectic composition, the mixture changes between solid and liquid at one specific temperature rather than melting over a range of temperatures. A useful example is tin and lead, a dense metal with atomic number 82 and the symbol Pb. Their eutectic mixture contains 61.9% tin and 38.1% lead by mass and melts at about 183 °C. Tin–lead alloys have been used as solder: the alloy melts and flows into a joint to connect metal parts without melting the parts themselves. Because lead is toxic, many products now use lead-free solders.

The decibel (dB) is a logarithmic unit used to compare levels or ratios. In acoustics, it describes sound levels; in electronics, it can describe signal gain or attenuation. An increase of 10 dB means a tenfold increase in power, not an increase of ten fixed units of power. One common acoustic measurement is sound pressure level, or SPL. It compares the root-mean-square (RMS) pressure of a sound wave with a standard reference pressure of 20 micropascals in air, roughly the threshold of human hearing. Because pressure and power are related differently, a 20 dB rise in sound pressure level corresponds to ten times the RMS pressure. Decibels make it easier to describe the enormous range between very quiet sounds and noises such as a jet engine.

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the Moon’s gravity pulling on Earth’s oceans. The Sun’s gravity also contributes, though the Moon has the stronger effect because it is much closer to Earth. As Earth rotates, most coastal places experience two high tides and two low tides each day, but local patterns vary. The difference in height between high and low tide is called the tidal range. Near a new or full moon, the Sun, Earth, and Moon lie roughly along one line. This alignment is called syzygy, and their combined gravitational effects produce spring tides, which have the greatest tidal ranges. When the Sun and Moon pull from roughly right angles, neap tides occur, with smaller ranges.

Supersymmetry, often shortened to SUSY, is a proposed extension of particle physics in which every elementary particle has a superpartner. Each boson, a particle with whole-number spin, is paired with a fermion, which has half-number spin, and each fermion is paired with a boson. The partners’ spins differ by one-half unit. Physicists study supersymmetry partly because it could help explain why the Higgs boson’s mass is relatively small. In quantum calculations, contributions from bosons and fermions can cancel, preventing the Higgs mass from being driven toward a much larger scale. This could address the hierarchy problem: the puzzle of why the electroweak scale is so much smaller than the Planck scale. Supersymmetry also appears in some versions of string theory, but no superpartner has yet been observed.

Kepler’s Laws of Planetary Motion are three principles that describe how planets orbit the Sun. The first law says that each planet follows an ellipse, a slightly stretched circle, with the Sun at one focus rather than at the center. The second law says that an imaginary line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal amounts of time. This means a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun and slower when it is farther away. The equal-area rule follows from the conservation of angular momentum, an orbital quantity commonly symbolized by L. The third law connects a planet’s orbital period, the time it takes to complete one orbit, to its orbit’s size: the period squared is proportional to the cube of the ellipse’s semimajor axis.

Coal slurry is a mixture of finely ground coal particles and water. The water keeps the particles suspended, making the mixture fluid enough to pump through dedicated pipelines over long distances. This offers a way to move coal, a fossil fuel used in power stations, without carrying every load by train or truck. Slurry can also be produced as waste when coal is mined or processed. That waste is sometimes stored behind dams in impoundments, where a failure can release a dangerous flood of water, mud, and coal particles. In February 1972, a coal-waste impoundment failed in Logan County, West Virginia. The resulting surge killed 125 people in a disaster known as the Buffalo Creek flood.

The Carnot cycle is an ideal, reversible process that shows the greatest possible efficiency of a heat engine operating between a hot reservoir and a cold reservoir. It is named after the French engineer and physicist Sadi Carnot, whose 1824 treatise Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire helped establish the study of heat engines. The cycle has four steps: two isothermal steps, during which temperature stays constant as heat enters or leaves the engine, and two adiabatic steps, during which no heat enters or leaves. As heat flows from the hotter reservoir toward the colder one, some of its energy is converted into useful work. Real engines cannot achieve the Carnot cycle’s maximum efficiency because their processes are not perfectly reversible.

The circadian rhythm is the body’s internal timing system, running on a cycle of approximately 24 hours. It helps regulate when you feel sleepy or alert, as well as other daily changes in the body. Its “master clock” is the suprachiasmatic nucleus, a small group of nerve cells in the hypothalamus just above the optic chiasm, where the optic nerves cross. It receives light-related signals from the retina in your eyes, allowing daylight to keep the internal clock synchronized with the outside world. As darkness falls, the clock helps signal the pineal gland to release melatonin, a hormone that encourages sleepiness. Changes in light exposure, such as staying up late with bright screens or traveling across time zones, can disrupt this rhythm and make sleep harder.

Scattering is the deflection of particles or electromagnetic radiation, such as light, from their original paths when they interact with matter. Different interactions produce different kinds of scattering. In Compton scattering, a photon collides with a charged particle, usually an electron, and changes direction while transferring some energy to it. Rayleigh scattering occurs when light interacts with particles much smaller than its wavelength, such as molecules in Earth’s atmosphere. These molecules scatter shorter visible wavelengths, especially blue light, more strongly than longer wavelengths such as red light. Sunlight arrives from many directions after passing through the atmosphere, so scattered blue light reaches our eyes from across the sky. That is why a clear daytime sky appears blue.

Species richness is the number of distinct species in a particular area or ecosystem. If a pond contains five species of fish, its fish species richness is five, regardless of how many individuals belong to each species. Richness is one part of biodiversity, but it does not show whether species are equally common. That balance is called species evenness: a pond with similar numbers of each fish species has higher evenness than one dominated by a single species. Ecologists use both richness and evenness to describe a community’s diversity. The Shannon diversity index combines them by accounting for each species’ proportional abundance; its formula is −Σpᵢ ln pᵢ, where pᵢ is the proportion of individuals belonging to species i.

Telomeres are protective caps made of repeated DNA sequences and associated proteins at the ends of chromosomes. They help keep chromosome ends from being damaged or joining to other chromosomes. Each time many cells copy their DNA before dividing, the copying process cannot fully reproduce the very ends, so their telomeres gradually shorten. When telomeres become too short, the cell may stop dividing, which helps prevent damaged cells from multiplying. An enzyme called telomerase can rebuild telomeres by adding repeated DNA sequences to chromosome ends. It uses its own RNA as a template for the new DNA. Telomerase is active in many germ cells, which give rise to eggs or sperm, and in many cancer cells, where it can help cells keep dividing.

String theory is a proposed framework in physics in which the basic ingredients of nature are tiny, one-dimensional strings rather than dimensionless points. Different ways these strings vibrate would appear to us as different elementary particles, with properties such as mass and charge. Physicists study string theory partly because it may help connect quantum physics, which describes very small things, with gravity. One theoretical achievement is that it can account for some features of black hole thermodynamics, including how black holes can have entropy. A black hole is an extremely compact object whose gravity creates a boundary called an event horizon: once something crosses it, not even light can escape. Despite its mathematical promise, string theory has not yet been confirmed by experiments.

Ada Lovelace was a British mathematician and an early pioneer of computing. Born Augusta Ada Byron, she became known as Ada Lovelace after inheriting the title Countess of Lovelace through marriage. In the 1840s, she wrote extensive notes about Charles Babbage’s proposed Analytical Engine, a mechanical machine designed to carry out calculations using instructions. Although the engine was never completed, Lovelace recognized that it might do more than ordinary arithmetic if information could be represented as symbols. In one section of her notes, called Note G, she described a sequence of operations for the engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers. These rational numbers appear in formulas for finding sums of powers, such as the sum of the squares of consecutive integers. Her instructions are often regarded as the first computer program.

Filtration separates suspended solid particles from a fluid by passing the mixture through a porous material. The material lets the liquid or gas through but traps particles too large to pass through its pores. In a laboratory, filter paper is commonly used to separate an insoluble solid from a liquid. The liquid that passes through is called the filtrate, while the solid left on the paper is the residue. Gravity can pull the liquid through the filter, but a vacuum speeds up the process by drawing it through. For vacuum filtration, a Büchner funnel fits onto a side-arm flask connected to a vacuum source. The funnel has a broad, straight-sided cylindrical cup with a perforated plate that supports the filter paper.

Methane is a naturally occurring gas with the molecular formula CH₄: each molecule has one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms. It is the simplest hydrocarbon, meaning it contains only carbon and hydrogen, and the simplest alkane, a type of hydrocarbon with single bonds between atoms. Methane is released when organic matter breaks down in oxygen-poor places such as wetlands, and it is also produced during livestock digestion. It is the main component of natural gas, which people burn for heating and electricity. In the atmosphere, methane is a greenhouse gas: it absorbs heat that would otherwise escape into space. Over a 100-year period, it traps substantially more heat per unit of gas than carbon dioxide, so methane emissions contribute to climate change.

Primates are a mammalian order that includes lemurs, tarsiers, bush babies, monkeys, apes, and humans. Many primates have grasping hands or feet, which help them hold branches or handle food, and forward-facing eyes, which help them judge distances. Primates live in many habitats and include several distinct groups. Lemurs, including ring-tailed lemurs and sifakas, are especially diverse on the island of Madagascar. New World monkeys are primates native to Central and South America. Unlike monkeys from Africa and Asia, they have widely spaced nostrils that face outward. This group includes capuchins and spider monkeys; some New World monkeys have prehensile tails that can grip branches, almost like an extra hand.

The polio vaccine protects people from poliomyelitis, or polio, a viral disease that can damage the nervous system and sometimes cause permanent paralysis. American physician Jonas Salk developed an inactivated polio vaccine, made with poliovirus that had been killed so it could not cause polio but could still teach the immune system to recognize the virus. Salk led the large field trial that tested the vaccine, and it was announced as effective in 1955. The vaccine was an important public health breakthrough because widespread vaccination greatly reduced polio cases. The March of Dimes, founded by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, helped fund polio research, including Salk’s work.

A fly is an insect in the order Diptera, a name meaning “two wings.” Unlike many other flying insects, adult flies have just one functional pair of wings. Their hindwings are reduced to small balancing organs called halteres, which help them stay stable and steer in flight. The word “fly” also appears in a famous poem by Emily Dickinson, a reclusive 19th-century American poet whose poems often have no formal titles and are identified by their opening lines. In “I heard a Fly buzz - when I died -,” the speaker notices the fly’s “Blue—uncertain—stumbling Buzz” interrupting the “Stillness in the Room” at the moment of death. The ordinary insect creates a striking contrast with the seriousness of the scene.

Aphids are small, soft-bodied insects that use needlelike mouthparts to pierce plants and drink their sap. They often gather on stems and the undersides of leaves, where large numbers can weaken plants. Plant sap contains more sugar than aphids need, so they excrete the excess as a sweet, sugar-rich liquid called honeydew. Many ants feed on this honeydew and protect the aphids from predators in return. Ants may even move aphids to fresh plants, making the relationship seem a little like dairy farming. Aphids are also sometimes called greenflies or blackflies, though they can be other colors. If a question asks for the sap-sucking insects tended by ants, the answer is aphids; if it asks for the sweet liquid ants collect, the answer is honeydew.

A piston is a close-fitting part that slides back and forth inside an engine cylinder. In a combustion engine, burning fuel produces hot, expanding gases that push the piston along the cylinder’s bore. Piston rings help seal the small gap around it so pressure does not easily escape. A connecting rod links the piston to an offset point, called a crankpin, on the crankshaft. As the piston repeats its straight-line strokes, it pushes and pulls the rod, turning the crankshaft and producing rotary motion that can drive a vehicle or machine. A V-8 engine has eight cylinders, each with its own piston. Steam engines also use pistons: instead of burning fuel inside the cylinder, they use steam pressure to move them.

Planck’s constant, written h, is a universal number that connects energy with wave behavior in quantum physics. For a photon, a particle of light, its energy is E = hν, where ν is the light’s frequency. This means higher-frequency light has more energetic photons. Max Planck introduced the idea that energy is exchanged in discrete amounts, or quanta, to explain the radiation emitted by hot objects, known as blackbody radiation. Planck’s constant also helps describe matter waves. Louis de Broglie proposed that particles such as electrons can behave like waves as well as particles. Their de Broglie wavelength is found by dividing Planck’s constant by the particle’s momentum: λ = h/p. A particle with greater momentum therefore has a shorter wavelength.

Centrifugation is a laboratory technique that spins samples at high speed to separate or study their components. As the sample spins, particles move through the liquid at different rates, so scientists can observe their sedimentation behavior. How quickly a particle sediments depends on factors including its mass, shape, and density, not just its physical dimensions. Scientists describe this behavior with a sedimentation coefficient measured in Svedberg units, abbreviated S. For example, the two subunits of a eukaryotic ribosome are called 60S and 40S because they sediment at different rates during centrifugation; those numbers are not measurements of their size. Ribosomes make proteins, and this technique helps scientists study their parts as well as many other structures in cells.

A crocodile is a large, semiaquatic reptile found in warm regions, often near rivers, lakes, and wetlands. It is a powerful predator with armored skin and jaws lined with sharp teeth. Compared with an alligator, a crocodile generally has a narrower, more V-shaped snout, and some of its lower teeth remain visible when its mouth is closed. Crocodiles also appear in ancient Egyptian mythology. Ammit, a creature that devoured unworthy souls, had the head of a crocodile, the forequarters of a lion, and the hindquarters of a hippopotamus. During the weighing of the heart, a dead person’s heart was compared with the feather of Maat, representing truth and justice. If the heart failed the test, Ammit devoured it.

The paranasal sinuses are four pairs of air-filled spaces in the skull, located in the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones. Each sinus connects to the nasal cavity and is lined with a mucous membrane that makes mucus. Normally, mucus drains into the nose, helping keep these spaces clear. If the lining becomes swollen, often because of an infection or allergies, mucus may not drain easily. Inflammation of the paranasal sinuses is called sinusitis. It can cause a blocked or runny nose, facial pressure, and a headache, especially around the forehead or cheeks. Sinus headaches are different from migraines, which often involve sensitivity to light and sound and may begin with a warning sensation called an aura.

John von Neumann was a Hungarian-born mathematician who emigrated to the United States and made important contributions to game theory and computing. In 1945, his First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC described a stored-program design: a computer could keep instructions in memory alongside data, rather than requiring people to rewire it for each new task. The report helped shape EDVAC, an early electronic computer developed at the University of Pennsylvania as a successor to ENIAC. EDVAC used binary arithmetic and stored-program control. Von Neumann’s ideas also influenced how modern computers work: a central processing unit, or CPU, repeatedly fetches instructions from memory, decodes them, and executes them. Today’s CPUs, including Apple’s M2 and Intel’s i9, are much more advanced, but they still carry out programs using this basic process.

Caffeine is a naturally occurring stimulant found in coffee beans, tea leaves, and some other plants. Chemically, it belongs to a group of organic compounds called methylxanthines. Caffeine helps people feel more alert partly by blocking receptors for adenosine, a neuromodulator that builds up while you are awake and helps make you feel sleepy. Its effects can include improved concentration and a faster heartbeat, though too much may cause jitters or interfere with sleep. In 1819, the German chemist Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge isolated caffeine from coffee beans after the writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe encouraged him to investigate them. Today, caffeine is also found in products such as energy drinks, soft drinks, and some medicines.

Steam is water in its gaseous form, produced when liquid water is heated. In a steam engine or power plant, steam acts as a working fluid: it carries energy from a boiler and uses that energy to create motion. Early steam engines used its pressure to move pistons back and forth, powering pumps that removed water from mines. Thomas Newcomen built a practical pumping engine, but it used a great deal of fuel. In the 1700s, Scottish engineer James Watt added a separate condenser, which cooled the used steam without repeatedly cooling the main cylinder. This greatly reduced fuel consumption and helped make steam power useful across industry. In a modern Rankine-cycle power plant, steam expands through turbine blades, spinning a generator to produce electricity.

Reaction rate describes how quickly a chemical reaction proceeds. It is measured by how much a reactant’s concentration decreases, or a product’s concentration increases, per unit time. A rate law relates the reaction rate to reactant concentrations, and the sum of the exponents on those concentrations gives the reaction’s overall order. In a first-order reaction, the rate is proportional to the concentration of one reactant: as that concentration falls, the reaction slows. A plot of the natural logarithm of that reactant’s concentration against time is a straight line with a negative slope. First-order reactions also have a constant half-life, meaning it takes the same amount of time for half the remaining reactant to be used up, regardless of its starting concentration.

Molarity measures how concentrated a solution is by dividing the moles of dissolved substance, called the solute, by the total volume of the solution in liters. Its unit is moles per liter, often written as M. For example, a solution containing 2 moles of salt in 1 liter of solution has a molarity of 2 M. Chemists commonly use molarity when working with the law of mass action, which relates reaction behavior to concentrations. Molality is a different scale: it divides moles of solute by kilograms of solvent, the substance doing the dissolving. Because mass stays the same when temperature changes but volume can expand or shrink, molality is especially useful for temperature-related calculations such as boiling-point elevation.

Vesicles are small, membrane-bound sacs that move or store substances inside cells. They bud from one membrane, carry cargo such as proteins, and can fuse with another membrane to deliver it. Some vesicles have coats made of clathrin, a protein shaped like a three-legged triskelion; the coat helps the vesicle form. Proteins called SNAREs on vesicle surfaces help them recognize and fuse with the correct target membrane. For example, vesicles carry newly made proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus. There, the proteins are modified, sorted, and packaged into new vesicles for delivery elsewhere. The Golgi apparatus is named after Camillo Golgi, the Italian biologist who first described it. In neurons, secretion vesicles also release chemical signals at synapses.

Sandstone is a clastic sedimentary rock made mainly of sand-sized grains, about 0.0625 to 2 millimeters across. The grains may be fragments of older rocks or minerals such as quartz. Sand can collect in deserts, rivers, or beaches, then become buried beneath more sediment. The weight of the overlying layers presses the grains closer together, a step called compaction. Minerals carried by water can fill the spaces between grains and bind them together, a step called cementation. Together, these changes turn loose sediment into solid rock through a process called lithification. Sandstone is common in desert landscapes, where its layers can form prominent cliffs and flat-topped mesas.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition, meaning it affects how the brain develops and processes information. Autistic people may communicate and interact socially in different ways, and they may have repetitive behaviors, strong preferences for routines, or focused interests in particular topics. Traits and support needs vary widely from person to person, which is why autism is described as a spectrum. Some autistic people also experience sensory differences, such as being especially sensitive to sounds or lights. Autism is not caused by bad parenting. Bruno Bettelheim, an Austrian-born psychoanalyst, promoted the now-discredited claim that emotionally cold parents—especially mothers he called “refrigerator mothers”—caused autism. Research has rejected that idea. Asperger’s syndrome was once used as a separate diagnosis but is now generally included under ASD.

Gold mining is the work of extracting gold from rock ore or from placer deposits, where loose gold particles have collected in river gravel and sediment. Miners can crush and process ore, but placer miners often use water to separate dense gold from lighter material. A hand-held pan lets a miner swirl small amounts of gravel in water so the gold settles to the bottom. A sluice box is a water-fed trough that handles a steady flow of gravel; ridges called riffles catch dense gold particles while lighter sediment washes away. Rockers are another tool for washing placer deposits. In 1848, James Marshall discovered gold at Sutter’s Mill near California’s American River, setting off the Gold Rush and attracting hundreds of thousands of “forty-niners.” Some miners used mercury to collect gold, leaving lasting contamination.

Bubonic plague is a serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Its most recognizable symptom is painful swelling of the lymph nodes, producing lumps called buboes, often in the groin, armpit, or neck. The disease commonly reaches people through the bites of infected fleas, especially fleas that have fed on rodents such as rats. When an infected flea bites, it can pass the bacteria into a person’s body. Other symptoms may include fever, chills, and weakness. Alexandre Yersin first isolated the bacterium in Hong Kong in 1894, and it was later named Yersinia pestis in his honor. Bubonic plague caused devastating outbreaks in history, but today it can usually be treated with antibiotics if diagnosed promptly.

Recessive alleles are versions of genes whose effects are usually hidden when a dominant allele is present. In diploid organisms, an individual normally has two copies of each gene, one inherited from each parent. If both copies are recessive, the recessive trait can appear in the phenotype, or observable characteristics; if one copy is dominant, the individual may carry the recessive allele without showing its trait. Gregor Mendel discovered this pattern through experiments with pea plants, and Punnett squares can help predict how alleles pass to offspring. Later, American geneticist Thomas Hunt Morgan studied fruit flies and found that a gene for white eyes was linked to the X chromosome. His work helped establish that genes are carried on chromosomes.

Tianwen-1 was China’s first independently conducted mission to Mars. Launched in 2020 by the China National Space Administration, it carried an orbiter, a lander, and a rover together on one spacecraft. Tianwen-1 entered orbit around Mars in February 2021. The orbiter studied the planet from above and helped relay communications, while the lander descended to the surface. In May 2021, the lander touched down in the southern part of Utopia Planitia, a vast plain on Mars, and delivered a solar-powered rover named Zhurong. The rover explored the ground, taking images and studying Martian soil and rocks. Tianwen-1 was an important step in China’s planetary exploration because it combined orbiting, landing, and roving in a single mission.

Human breast milk is a nutrient-rich fluid made by the mammary glands during lactation. It gives newborns water, fats, carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, and minerals needed for growth. It also helps protect infants while their own immune systems are developing. One important protective antibody in breast milk is secretory immunoglobulin A, or IgA. It coats moist surfaces such as those in a baby’s digestive tract, helping block germs and providing passive immunity—protection received from the mother rather than made by the baby. Two hormones have different roles in breastfeeding: prolactin supports milk production, while oxytocin triggers the “let-down reflex,” which moves milk out of the breast so the baby can drink it. When breast milk is unavailable, infant formula may be used as a substitute.

Kinetic friction is the contact force that acts when two surfaces slide past each other. It points opposite their relative sliding motion, so a block sliding down a ramp experiences kinetic friction up the ramp. In the usual model, its magnitude is Fₖ = μₖN, where N is the normal force—the push from the surface perpendicular to it—and μₖ is the coefficient of kinetic friction. This coefficient is a dimensionless number that depends on the materials and condition of the surfaces. On a flat surface, the normal force often equals an object’s weight, mg, but on an inclined plane it is smaller. Kinetic friction differs from static friction, which acts when surfaces are not sliding and can provide traction for running shoes.

A bomb calorimeter measures the heat released when a substance burns or undergoes another reaction. The sample is placed in a sealed, rigid vessel, called the bomb, which is immersed in a water bath. Because the vessel cannot expand, the reaction takes place at constant volume. As the reaction releases energy, the surrounding water warms. Scientists use the water’s temperature increase, its mass, and its specific heat capacity to calculate how much energy it absorbed. Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius; for water, it is about 4.18 joules per gram per degree Celsius, or 1 calorie per gram per degree Celsius. The calorimeter itself also absorbs some heat, so its heat capacity must be included in accurate calculations.

Colligative properties are properties of a solution that depend on how many dissolved particles it contains, rather than on what those particles are made of. Examples include freezing-point depression, osmotic pressure, and boiling-point elevation. Boiling-point elevation occurs when a nonvolatile solute, such as salt, is dissolved in a solvent: the solution must reach a higher temperature than the pure solvent before it boils. For dilute solutions, the increase in boiling point depends on molality, which measures moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, and on the number of particles the solute forms when it dissolves. For example, dissolved salt separates into ions, so it can produce a larger effect than the same number of moles of a substance that stays as whole molecules.

The kilogram, written kg, is the SI base unit of mass. It is about the mass of one liter of water, although water’s exact mass varies slightly with temperature. In chemistry, the kilogram is used to describe molality: the number of moles of dissolved substance, or solute, divided by the mass of the solvent in kilograms. This differs from molarity, which divides moles of solute by the volume of the entire solution in liters. Molality is especially useful when temperature changes because mass stays the same while volume can expand or shrink. For many years, the kilogram was defined using a metal prototype. Since 2019, it has instead been defined by fixing the numerical value of the Planck constant, a fundamental constant measured in joule-seconds.

A hard disk drive (HDD), often called a hard drive, stores files and programs even when a computer is turned off. It records data magnetically on one or more rigid circular disks called platters. The platters spin around a central spindle while a read/write head moves across their surfaces to find or record information. In the traditional computer memory hierarchy, an HDD sits below main memory (RAM): it can hold much more data for long-term storage, but retrieving that data is slower. Unlike RAM, an HDD does not lose its contents when power is removed. Hard disk drives have become less common in some computers because solid-state drives (SSDs) access data faster and have no moving parts, but HDDs are still used when large storage capacity is needed.

A buffer solution is a mixture that resists large changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. It usually contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, the substance formed when that acid loses a hydrogen ion. If extra acid is added, the conjugate base reacts with much of it; if extra base is added, the weak acid reacts with much of that instead. This helps keep the pH relatively steady. In blood, carbonic acid and bicarbonate form an important buffer system. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation calculates a buffer’s pH: pH = pKa + log([conjugate base]/[weak acid]). Here, pKa describes the weak acid’s tendency to release hydrogen ions, and the bracketed terms are the concentrations of the two buffer components.

Yttrium is a silvery metal with the chemical symbol Y and atomic number 39. It is often grouped with the rare-earth elements and is used in advanced materials, including ceramics. One important example is yttrium barium copper oxide, commonly called YBCO. This ceramic contains yttrium, barium, copper, and oxygen. It became famous because it can act as a superconductor above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, about −196°C. A superconductor carries electric current with zero electrical resistance, so it does not lose energy as heat in the usual way. YBCO still needs to be extremely cold, but liquid nitrogen can cool it more easily and cheaply than the colder liquids required for many earlier superconductors.

Attraction is an interaction that pulls two objects toward each other. In electromagnetism, a positive electric charge and a negative electric charge attract, as do the north and south poles of two magnets. Two charges with the same sign, or two like magnetic poles, repel instead: they push apart. Coulomb’s law describes the force between two point charges, which are charges treated as if they are concentrated at single points. It says the force’s magnitude is proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Bigger charges exert a stronger force, while increasing the distance makes it weaker. For example, doubling the distance reduces the force to one-quarter of its original strength.

Slit pupils are elongated openings in the center of the eye, found in some vertebrates, including cats and foxes. A pupil lets light enter the eye, while the iris, the colored ring around it, changes the pupil’s size. In bright light, a slit pupil can narrow to a very thin opening, limiting the amount of light that reaches the retina and helping protect the animal’s vision. It can also improve image sharpness by reducing chromatic aberration. This optical flaw occurs because different wavelengths, or colors, of light bend by slightly different amounts and do not focus at exactly the same point. In dim light, the pupil widens to admit more light, helping the animal see when illumination is low.

Positron emission tomography, or PET, is a medical imaging technique that shows how tissues are functioning, rather than just what they look like. A patient receives a small amount of a radioactive tracer that collects in particular tissues. Its radioactive atoms emit positrons, which are positively charged particles. When a positron meets an ordinary electron, they annihilate and produce two gamma rays traveling in opposite directions. A PET scanner detects these rays and reconstructs a three-dimensional map of tracer uptake. One common tracer, 18F-FDG, combines fluorine-18 with a glucose-like molecule to map glucose metabolism. Many tumors use glucose rapidly, so they may show increased PET signal. Other tracers can help researchers study processes in the brain, including changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease.

Gregor Mendel was an Austrian monk and scientist who studied how traits pass from parents to offspring. At St. Thomas’s Abbey in Brno, he made controlled crosses between pea plants with different traits, such as purple or white flowers. In an 1866 paper on plant hybrids, he described patterns that became the foundations of genetics. His law of segregation says that an offspring receives one version of a gene, called an allele, from each parent. His law of independent assortment says that alleles for different traits can be inherited independently. Mendel also observed that a dominant allele can hide the effect of another allele. The hidden version is called a recessive allele; its trait generally appears only when an organism inherits two recessive copies.

The female sex is defined in reproductive biology by the production of ova, or egg cells, rather than sperm. In mammals, females commonly make a greater investment in each offspring: pregnancy requires time and energy, the placenta allows nutrients and oxygen to pass to a developing embryo, and lactation provides milk after birth. These costs can affect how animals compete for mates and care for young, although reproductive roles vary among species and individuals. In a 1972 paper on sexual selection, evolutionary biologist Robert Trivers introduced the concept of parental investment: the time, energy, and other resources a parent puts into an offspring that improve its chances of survival, often at the expense of the parent’s ability to produce or support other offspring.

Molecular mass describes how heavy a single molecule is. You can find it by adding the atomic masses of all the atoms in the molecule. For example, a water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so its molecular mass is about 18 daltons. The dalton, abbreviated Da, is a unit used for masses at the scale of atoms and molecules. Chemists also often give the mass of one mole of a substance in grams per mole; this is called its molar mass and has the same numerical value as its molecular mass in daltons. Molecular mass can help chemists identify substances and choose ways to separate mixtures. In size-exclusion chromatography, for instance, molecules can be separated according to their size, which is often related to molecular mass.

Dyes are substances that give color to materials such as fabrics, paper, food, and hair. Many dyes dissolve in a liquid, making them useful in inks and other coloring products. An ink that looks like one color may actually contain a mixture of dyes. Paper chromatography can separate that mixture: a small spot of ink is placed near the bottom of a sheet of cellulose paper, and the paper’s edge is dipped in a solvent. As the solvent climbs the paper, it carries the dyes upward. Different dyes travel different distances because they dissolve in the solvent and stick to the paper to different degrees. They form separate colored bands, revealing some of the components in the original ink.

A dwarf star is a term used for several kinds of relatively small stellar objects. Many ordinary stars, including red and orange dwarfs, are main-sequence stars that produce energy by fusing hydrogen. A white dwarf is different: it is the small, dense remnant left after a star like the Sun runs out of fuel and sheds its outer layers. Brown dwarfs are too small to sustain ordinary hydrogen fusion, while black dwarfs are hypothetical white dwarfs that have cooled so much they no longer shine visibly. Sirius A is the brightest star in the night sky, but it has a much fainter companion, Sirius B. Friedrich Bessel inferred the companion from its gravitational effect on Sirius A’s motion. Sirius B is a white dwarf.

Crystal Field Theory explains how ligands, the ions or molecules surrounding a metal ion, affect its d orbitals. It is especially useful for understanding complexes of transition metals, the elements found mainly in groups 3–12 of the periodic table. Before ligands approach, a metal ion’s five d orbitals have the same energy. The ligands’ electric fields interact with those orbitals differently, splitting them into groups with different energies. In an octahedral complex, six ligands sit along three perpendicular axes around the metal ion. Three d orbitals form a lower-energy group called t₂g, while two form a higher-energy group called eᵍ. The energy gap between them is the octahedral crystal-field splitting energy, written Δₒ. This gap helps explain why many transition-metal complexes have particular colors and magnetic properties.

A centrifuge is a laboratory device that spins sample tubes rapidly in a rotor. In a clinical lab, spinning a tube of blood causes its components to separate by density: the denser blood cells move toward the outside of the rotor and collect at the bottom of the tube when it stops, while the less dense liquid remains above them. If the blood has been treated with an anticoagulant to prevent clotting, that pale-yellow liquid is called plasma. Plasma still contains clotting proteins, including fibrinogen. This makes it different from serum, the liquid left after blood has clotted, which lacks most of those clotting proteins. Centrifuges help laboratory workers isolate blood components for testing and other uses.

The coelacanth is a rare lobe-finned fish with fleshy, limb-like fins. Scientists knew the lineage from fossils and believed it had vanished about 60 million years ago. That changed in 1938, when a fishing trawler caught an unusual fish off South Africa and brought it to the town of East London. Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, the curator of the local museum, recognized that it was unusual, preserved it, and alerted ichthyologist J.L.B. Smith, who identified it as a coelacanth. This discovery brought the supposedly extinct lineage to scientific attention and earned the coelacanth the nickname “living fossil.” The name does not mean the fish has remained unchanged for millions of years; it means its lineage survived long after scientists thought it had disappeared.

Bent molecular geometry describes a molecule in which two atoms are bonded to a central atom, with the bonds forming an angle rather than a straight line. Water is a familiar example: its oxygen atom is bonded to two hydrogen atoms and also has two lone pairs of electrons that are not used in bonds. VSEPR theory, short for valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, predicts molecular shapes by treating regions of electrons around a central atom as repelling one another. In water, the two bonding pairs and two lone pairs spread out, but the lone pairs push strongly on the bonding pairs. This gives water its bent shape and an angle of about 104.5° between its two oxygen–hydrogen bonds.

First ionization energy is the minimum energy needed to remove the least tightly bound electron from a neutral atom in the gas phase, leaving a singly charged positive ion. It measures how strongly an atom holds its outermost electron. Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period because the growing nuclear charge attracts electrons more strongly, though electron arrangements create exceptions. For example, nitrogen has a half-filled 2p subshell, with one electron in each of its three 2p orbitals. Oxygen has one pair of electrons sharing a 2p orbital; their repulsion makes an electron easier to remove. As a result, nitrogen’s first ionization energy is higher than oxygen’s. In the Bohr model, the ionization energy of a hydrogen-like atom scales with the square of its nuclear charge.

Endosymbiotic theory explains how some parts of complex cells may have evolved from bacteria that once lived independently. According to the theory, an ancestral cell took in certain bacteria but did not digest them. Instead, the bacteria and their host formed a lasting partnership. Over many generations, the bacteria became organelles: mitochondria, which help cells release usable energy from food, and chloroplasts, where plants carry out photosynthesis. In chloroplasts, light and dark reactions help convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose; the pigment chlorophyll gives leaves their green color. Mitochondria and chloroplasts support the theory because they have bacterial-like features, including their own DNA. American evolutionary biologist Lynn Margulis made a landmark case for endosymbiotic theory in her 1967 paper “On the Origin of Mitosing Cells” and became one of its best-known advocates.

Wolff’s law describes how bones adapt to the mechanical stresses placed on them. When a bone is loaded repeatedly, as during walking or exercise, it can become denser and stronger along the lines that bear the most force. When loading is reduced, such as during prolonged bed rest, bone can lose mass. This happens through bone remodeling, an ongoing process in which osteoblasts build new bone and osteoclasts break down, or resorb, existing bone. Repeated loading can shift this balance toward formation where extra strength is needed, while reduced loading can favor resorption. The process helps the skeleton support the body efficiently, but it also means that regular weight-bearing activity is important for maintaining bone strength.

Xenon is a heavy, colorless noble gas with atomic number 54. It belongs to Group 18, on the far right of the periodic table. Noble gases were once called “inert” because their outer electron shells are full, making them unlikely to react with other elements. Xenon was isolated by Sir William Ramsay and was long thought unable to form stable compounds. In 1962, chemist Neil Bartlett challenged that belief by reacting xenon with platinum hexafluoride, a substance that readily accepts electrons. The reaction produced an ionic compound known as xenon hexafluoroplatinate. This was the first synthesized noble gas compound and showed that even elements considered nearly unreactive can form chemical bonds under the right conditions.

The Mercury Program, also called Project Mercury, was the United States’ first effort to send people into space. NASA selected seven military test pilots, known as the Mercury Seven, to become its astronauts. On May 5, 1961, one of them, Alan Shepard, became the first American to travel to space aboard a Mercury spacecraft named Freedom 7. His flight was suborbital: he reached space but did not circle Earth before returning. Later Mercury missions did orbit Earth, helping NASA learn how to launch astronauts, keep them safe in space, and bring them home. The program laid important groundwork for the Gemini and Apollo programs, which eventually led to astronauts walking on the Moon.

A screw is a simple machine made from an inclined plane wrapped in a spiral, or helix, around a cylinder. Its raised spiral ridge is called a thread. When you turn a screw, the thread helps convert rotation into straight-line motion: a fastener moves into wood, for example, or a load rises along a threaded shaft. This lets a screw move or hold heavy objects with less effort, though it must turn through a greater distance. Screws can also lift liquids. Archimedes’ screw, named for the ancient Greek inventor, is a water-lifting device with a rotating helix inside a trough or tube. As it turns, water is trapped between the turns of the helix and carried upward, making it useful for irrigation and drainage.

Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, or EPR, is a technique for studying substances with unpaired electrons. An electron acts like a tiny magnet because of a property called spin. In EPR, a sample is placed in a magnetic field that is gradually changed while microwaves shine on it. At a particular field strength, the energy difference between the electron’s spin states matches the microwave energy, so the sample absorbs the microwaves. This signal helps scientists identify and study the unpaired electrons and their surroundings. EPR is especially useful for detecting free radicals: atoms or molecules with unpaired electrons that are often highly reactive. TEMPO and Fremy’s salt are unusually stable examples. In chemical reactions, the movement of a single electron, such as when a bond splits to form radicals, is shown with a fishhook arrow.

The urban heat island effect is the pattern in which a city is warmer than nearby rural areas. Roads, roofs, and buildings absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly, sometimes keeping cities especially warm at night. A surface’s albedo is the fraction of incoming sunlight it reflects. Dark asphalt has a low albedo, so it reflects little sunlight and absorbs more energy; a pale roof has a higher albedo and reflects more. Cities can also have fewer trees than rural areas, reducing the shade and cooling provided by plants. Planting trees and using lighter-colored roofs and pavements can help reduce urban heat.

Blood pressure is the force of circulating blood pushing against the walls of blood vessels. It is usually recorded as two numbers in millimeters of mercury, such as 120/80. The first number, systolic pressure, measures pressure when the heart’s ventricles contract and pump blood. The second, diastolic pressure, measures pressure when the ventricles relax between beats. A prolonged rise in blood pressure is called hypertension. The body adjusts blood pressure through several mechanisms. Stretch-sensitive nerve cells called baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect changes in pressure and send signals to the brainstem, which helps control heart rate and blood-vessel width. The brainstem consists of the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata. Hormones in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system also help regulate blood pressure.

The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event was a mass extinction about 66 million years ago, at the boundary between the Cretaceous, the final period of the Mesozoic Era, and the Paleogene, the first period of the Cenozoic Era. It wiped out many species worldwide, including all non-avian dinosaurs, although birds survived. The event is strongly linked to an asteroid impact that formed the Chicxulub crater, a roughly 180-kilometer-wide structure buried beneath Mexico’s northern Yucatán Peninsula. A ring of cenotes, or water-filled sinkholes, traces part of the crater’s rim. Dust and gases thrown into the atmosphere by the impact likely blocked sunlight, disrupted food chains, and caused rapid climate change. This was one of several mass extinctions in Earth’s history, but it is especially famous for ending the age of non-avian dinosaurs.

Biological staining is a laboratory practice that uses dyes or other reagents to make cells, tissue sections, and microorganisms easier to see under a microscope. Many structures are nearly transparent, so staining adds contrast and helps scientists tell them apart. Different stains highlight different features. The Golgi stain, developed by Italian biologist Camillo Golgi, is a silver-based method for studying nerve cells, or neurons. It uses potassium dichromate and silver nitrate to darken only a small subset of neurons. Because most nearby cells remain unstained, scientists can see each darkened neuron’s complete outline and branching processes even in crowded nervous tissue. Another example is Gram staining, which helps classify bacteria according to differences in their cell walls.

The top quark is one of six flavors of quark, a family of fundamental particles first proposed by Murray Gell-Mann. Quarks usually bind together to form larger particles called hadrons: for example, a proton contains two up quarks and one down quark. The top quark, symbolized t, is a third-generation quark and is by far the heaviest of the six flavors. It is also extremely short-lived. Before it has time to bind with other quarks, it decays into other particles. The process in which quarks bind to form hadrons is called hadronization. Because the top quark decays before hadronization can occur, it does not become part of a hadron, which makes it unusual among quarks.

Nuclear pasta is a predicted form of ultra-dense matter inside neutron stars, the compact remains of massive stars. It is thought to occur in the inner crust, a transitional layer beneath the star’s outer crust of nuclei and electrons and above its core of more uniform matter. In this region, protons and neutrons are squeezed so closely together that the strong nuclear force pulls them into clusters, while electrostatic repulsion between protons pushes them apart. Instead of forming only ordinary, roughly spherical nuclei, the matter may arrange itself into rods, slabs, tubes, and bubbles. Scientists call these shapes nuclear pasta because some resemble foods such as spaghetti or lasagna. These structures are predicted to be extremely strong, but their exact properties are still being studied.

Project Pigeon was a World War II research effort to see whether trained pigeons could guide missiles toward targets. Psychologist B. F. Skinner devised and led the project, applying operant conditioning: he rewarded pigeons for pecking at images of targets so they would learn to repeat the behavior. The plan was to place the birds in a missile’s nose cone, where a projected image would show what lay ahead. As a pigeon pecked at the target’s position on the image, a mechanism would use those pecks to adjust the missile’s course. Skinner is also known for studying learning and behavior with an operant-conditioning chamber, often called a Skinner box. Project Pigeon was an unusual attempt to use animal behavior in military technology, but its guidance system was never used in combat.

A honey bee drone is a male honey bee in a colony of Apis mellifera. It develops from an unfertilized egg, unlike female workers and queens, which develop from fertilized eggs. Because the drone receives only one set of chromosomes, its chromosome condition is called haploidy; an organism with this condition is described as haploid. Workers and queens have two sets of chromosomes. Drones do not gather nectar, build the hive, or defend it, and they have no stinger. Their main role is to mate with a queen from another colony, helping pass on their genes. A drone that mates dies soon afterward. Although the word “drone” can also mean an unmanned aircraft, in a honey bee colony it refers specifically to the male bee.

Sedimentary rock forms when particles of minerals, pieces of older rocks, or organic material accumulate and are compacted or cemented together over time. Water, wind, and ice can carry these particles, called sediment, to places where they settle in layers known as strata. Fossils may be preserved in the strata, giving scientists clues about past life and environments. Weathering breaks rock into smaller particles that can contribute to soil formation. Soil also contains organic matter, and its texture depends on the proportions of sand, silt, and clay. The fertile soil layer called topsoil, or the A horizon, lies near the surface and usually contains abundant humus, which is decomposed organic matter. Topsoil is important because it supports much of the plant growth on land.

Wasps are insects in the order Hymenoptera, which also includes bees and ants. Many wasps hunt other insects, helping keep prey populations in check. Some social wasps make papery nests by chewing wood fibers, mixing them with saliva, and shaping the pulp into chambers that harden as they dry. Caterpillars are the leaf-eating larvae of butterflies and moths, and some wasps prey on them or lay eggs in them. In a reported food-web disruption on Borneo, use of the pesticide DDT reduced wasps that preyed on caterpillars. With fewer wasps to limit their numbers, caterpillar populations rose and damaged plants. This illustrates how a chemical meant to kill pests can also harm helpful predators and have unexpected effects throughout an ecosystem.

Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. CFTR makes a protein that acts as a chloride channel in the cells lining the airways and other organs, helping control the movement of salt and water. A common mutation, called delta F508, deletes the amino acid phenylalanine at position 508 of the protein. When CFTR does not work properly, mucus becomes unusually thick and sticky. Normally, mucus traps dust and bacteria, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it out of the airways. In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus is difficult to clear, so it can block airways and increase the risk of lung infections. It can also obstruct ducts in the pancreas, interfering with digestion.

Abiogenesis is the scientific idea that life first emerged from nonliving matter through natural chemical processes. One proposed setting is Earth’s early oceans, sometimes called a “primordial soup,” where simple chemicals may have combined to form more complex molecules. A famous study related to this idea is the Miller-Urey experiment, conducted in 1953 by Stanley Miller and Harold Urey. They exposed a mixture of gases thought to resemble Earth’s early atmosphere to electrical sparks that simulated lightning. The experiment produced amino acids, molecules that can join through peptide bonds to form proteins. It did not create life or prove exactly how life began, but it showed that some of life’s building blocks could form from simpler, nonliving substances under certain conditions.

Newton’s rings are concentric bright and dark circles seen when a curved lens rests on a flat glass plate and light shines on them. The lens touches the plate at the center, but farther out, the thin air gap between them becomes gradually thicker. Some light reflects from the bottom of the lens, while some reflects from the top of the glass plate. These reflected waves overlap, producing an interference pattern: where they reinforce each other, a bright ring appears; where they cancel, a dark ring appears. In reflected light, the center is dark even though the air film there has zero thickness. That is because one reflected wave undergoes a half-cycle phase reversal, causing destructive interference. The pattern is named after Isaac Newton, although Robert Hooke observed it earlier.

Git is a distributed version control system that helps programmers track changes to a project over time. Each developer can keep a full copy of the project and its history on their own computer. Developers save snapshots of their work as commits, then push commits to a shared repository or pull changes made by others. Git also supports branches, which let people work on new features separately, and merging, which combines their changes. GitHub is a web platform for hosting Git repositories and collaborating on them. On GitHub, developers can propose changes through pull requests so others can review them before merging. GitHub launched in 2008 and became a major home for software projects; Microsoft acquired it in 2018.

A genome is the complete set of genetic information in an organism or cell. In humans, it is stored in DNA and includes genes, which provide instructions for making proteins, as well as noncoding DNA. Genome size does not necessarily reflect how complex an organism is: some simpler organisms have more DNA than humans. This surprising pattern is called the C-value paradox. Scientists can determine the order of DNA’s building blocks through sequencing, then piece overlapping sections together to assemble a genome. The Human Genome Project was an international research initiative launched in 1990 to map and sequence the human genome. It was declared complete in 2003, after 13 years of work, and gave researchers a reference for studying human biology and disease.

Mammatus clouds are recognized by rounded, pouch-like bulges hanging from the underside of a cloud. They often appear beneath the anvil cloud of a powerful thunderstorm. The anvil is the broad, flattened top that forms when rising air reaches a stable layer of the atmosphere and spreads outward. Strong convection—the movement of warm air upward and cooler air downward—helps create the turbulent conditions associated with mammatus. The pouches themselves can form as air and cloud particles sink and mix with drier air below. Mammatus may look dramatic, but they do not always mean severe weather is happening directly overhead. Like other clouds, they contain tiny water droplets or ice crystals, which form when moist air cools enough for water vapor to condense or freeze.

The Human Genome Project was an international research effort that began in 1990 and was declared complete in 2003. Scientists worked to map and sequence the human genome: the full set of genetic information carried in our DNA. The project produced a reference sequence of roughly three billion DNA bases, organized into 23 chromosome pairs. This reference gave researchers a shared starting point for studying genes, inherited traits, and disease, although any one person’s DNA may differ from it. The project also changed how scientists shared their work.
