In 1996, participating sequencing centers adopted the Bermuda Principles, an agreement to release newly determined DNA sequences to public databases promptly, generally within 24 hours, so researchers around the world could use the data.

Stardust was a NASA mission launched in 1999 to bring samples from a comet back to Earth. Its main target was Comet Wild 2, a short-period comet discovered in 1978 and catalogued as 81P. In 2004, the spacecraft flew through the comet’s coma, the cloud of gas and dust surrounding its nucleus. It caught tiny particles in aerogel, a very light material that slowed the fast-moving grains without destroying them. Stardust also collected particles of interstellar dust during its journey. Its return capsule landed in Utah in 2006, giving scientists samples they could study in laboratories. Because comets contain ice mixed with dust, these grains offered clues about the materials present when the solar system formed.

Cnidaria is a phylum of mostly marine invertebrates that includes jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydras. Cnidarians have radial symmetry, meaning their body parts are arranged around a central axis. Many have two body forms: a polyp, which is usually attached to a surface with its mouth facing upward, and a medusa, which swims with its mouth facing downward. Some species change from a polyp to a medusa during their life cycle, while others have only one form. Their defining feature is the cnidocyte, a specialized stinging cell used to capture prey or deter predators. Each cnidocyte contains a stinging organelle called a nematocyst, which can rapidly fire a thread. The cell is the cnidocyte; the organelle inside it is the nematocyst.

Static friction is the contact force that prevents two touching surfaces from starting to slide past each other. It acts opposite the direction in which they would slip: on a block resting on a slope, for example, it can act up the slope to resist the block’s tendency to slide down. Static friction also provides the grip that lets running shoes push backward on the ground so a runner can move forward. Its strength is not always the same; it increases as needed to prevent slipping, but only up to a maximum. That maximum equals the normal force, which presses the surfaces together, multiplied by the coefficient of static friction, often written μₛ. This coefficient is a dimensionless property of the pair of surfaces, not a force.

The Schwarzschild radius is the distance from the center of an idealized, nonrotating black hole to its event horizon. The event horizon is the boundary beyond which light cannot escape to the outside universe. For a black hole of mass M, the radius is 2GM/c², where G is the gravitational constant and c is the speed of light. This means a more massive black hole has a larger event horizon. The radius is named after German physicist Karl Schwarzschild, who found an exact, spherically symmetric solution to Albert Einstein’s equations of general relativity while serving on the Eastern Front during World War I. His solution showed how spacetime behaves around a spherical mass and provided the basis for calculating this radius.

Food poisoning is an illness caused by eating food contaminated with disease-causing organisms, such as bacteria, or with toxins they produce. Sometimes the organisms grow in the body after the meal; in other cases, toxins already present in the food cause the illness. Symptoms vary but may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and stomach cramps. One especially dangerous form of food poisoning is botulism, which can occur when food is improperly canned. In oxygen-free conditions inside a sealed container, certain bacteria can produce botulinum toxin. This toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine, a chemical that carries signals from nerves to muscles. Botulism may begin with blurred vision and difficulty swallowing, then cause muscle paralysis and, without urgent treatment, respiratory failure.

Regression analysis is a statistical method for estimating how one variable changes in relation to one or more others. For example, it can help predict a student’s test score from the number of hours they studied. In linear regression, the estimated relationship is shown as a straight line fitted through observed data points. The difference between an observed value and the value predicted by the line is called a residual. One common way to choose the line’s coefficients, such as its slope and starting value, is ordinary least squares. This method gives every observation equal weight and chooses coefficients that make the sum of the squared residuals as small as possible. Squaring keeps positive and negative errors from canceling out and makes larger errors count more.

In saturated carbon compounds, carbon often forms four single covalent bonds. To do this, one s orbital and three p orbitals combine to make four equivalent, directional orbitals, a bonding scheme called sp³ hybridization. These orbitals point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, spreading the bonds as far apart as possible. In methane (CH₄), each orbital forms a bond with a hydrogen atom, so the four C–H bonds are equivalent. The hydrogen atoms form a tetrahedral arrangement around the central carbon, and each H–C–H bond angle is about 109.5°. A carbon with sp³ hybridization can also bond to four different groups; such a carbon may be a chiral center, meaning its molecule and mirror image cannot be placed on top of each other exactly.

A globular cluster is a densely packed, roughly spherical collection of stars held together by gravity. It can contain hundreds of thousands of stars, most of which are very old. Globular clusters are often found around galaxies, including the Milky Way. Their stars are commonly classified as Population II stars: stars that formed early in a galaxy’s history and generally contain relatively small amounts of elements heavier than helium. Astronomers call those heavier elements “metals,” so Population II stars are described as metal-poor. Globular clusters help scientists study the early history of galaxies because many of their stars formed billions of years ago. If a question describes a dense, round group of old stars, it is likely asking for a globular cluster; if it asks for the type of old, metal-poor stars found there, the answer is Population II.

The baiji was a pale, long-beaked freshwater dolphin found only in China’s Yangtze River, the country’s longest river. It was the sole living member of the family Lipotidae. As shipping, fishing, pollution, and dam construction changed the river, the baiji’s population declined sharply. In 2006, an international team spent six weeks searching the Yangtze’s main channel from two vessels. This search, called the Yangtze Freshwater Dolphin Expedition, found no confirmed baiji. Although an occasional reported sighting makes it difficult to prove that every individual is gone, the species is widely regarded as functionally extinct: too few, if any, remain to sustain a breeding population. The baiji is often described as the first cetacean species driven to extinction by human activity.

Saturated fats are dietary fats whose fatty-acid chains have only carbon–carbon single bonds. Each carbon holds as many hydrogen atoms as its bonds allow, so the chains are “saturated” with hydrogen and contain no carbon–carbon double bonds. They are listed separately from monounsaturated fats, which have one double bond, and polyunsaturated fats, which have more than one. Saturated fats occur in foods such as whole milk, butter, meat, and some plant oils. One common saturated fatty acid is palmitic acid, which is especially abundant in palm oil. Its name comes from the palm, and its shorthand designation, C16:0, means it has 16 carbon atoms and zero double bonds. Although saturated fats are part of many diets, nutrition guidance generally recommends limiting them rather than eating them in excess.

A partial charge is a small, non-integer electric charge that develops when atoms in a covalent bond share electrons unequally. The atom that attracts the shared electrons more strongly becomes slightly negative, written δ−, while the other becomes slightly positive, written δ+. These atoms are not full ions because the electrons have not been completely transferred. In water, oxygen attracts electrons more strongly than hydrogen, so oxygen has a partial negative charge and each hydrogen has a partial positive charge. Water is bent, with a bond angle of about 104.5 degrees, so its bond polarities do not cancel. The resulting separation of positive and negative charge is measured by the electric dipole moment, a vector quantity commonly expressed in debyes. Water’s partial charges also help its molecules form hydrogen bonds.

Esters are a family of organic compounds often recognized by their fruity or fragrant smells. They can form when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, releasing water in a reaction called esterification. The acid and alcohol determine which ester is produced: salicylic acid reacts with methanol, the simplest alcohol, to form methyl salicylate. Methyl salicylate has the characteristic scent of wintergreen, while other esters contribute to the aromas of many fruits. Alcohols contain an –OH group, and a carboxylic acid has a –COOH group. During esterification, parts of these groups combine to make water, and the remaining parts join to form the ester. Salicylic acid can also be used to make aspirin, but aspirin and methyl salicylate are different compounds.

Rigel is a bright blue supergiant star in Orion, the constellation that represents a hunter in Greek mythology. It marks one of the hunter’s feet and is commonly described as the brightest star in Orion, although the red supergiant Betelgeuse can sometimes rival it in brightness. To find Orion, look for its distinctive belt: three stars in a nearly straight line named Alnitak, Alnilam, and Mintaka. Rigel lies below the belt, on the opposite side from Betelgeuse, which marks one of the hunter’s shoulders. Orion also contains the star Bellatrix and the Trapezium Cluster, a group of young stars. In stories and star maps, the hunter is often shown facing Taurus the Bull, with the constellations Canis Major and Canis Minor representing his dogs.

Coherence is the property of waves whose phase relationship stays stable over time. A wave’s phase describes where it is in its cycle, such as at a peak or a trough. Coherent light has a well-defined frequency, and its waves maintain a predictable phase relationship. Lasers are a common source of highly coherent light. When two light waves overlap, their peaks and troughs combine in a process called interference. Where the waves reinforce each other, they produce bright regions; where they cancel each other, they produce dark regions. If the light is coherent, these bright and dark regions form a persistent interference pattern. If the phase relationship keeps changing, the pattern shifts and may become too blurred to see.

An ideal gas is a simplified model of a gas whose particles take up negligible space and exert no forces on one another except during collisions. Its pressure (P), volume (V), amount in moles (n), and temperature (T) are related by the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, where R is a constant and temperature is measured in kelvins. Real gases behave most like ideal gases at high temperatures and low pressures, when their particles are far apart and intermolecular forces matter less. If the amount of gas and its temperature stay fixed, the ideal gas law shows that pressure and volume change in opposite directions. This relationship is called Boyle’s law: halving the volume doubles the pressure.

Cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, is a clear liquid that circulates through spaces inside the brain called ventricles and around the brain and spinal cord. It cushions these delicate parts of the central nervous system, helps carry away waste, and provides a stable environment for nerve cells. Around the spinal cord, CSF flows through a space between protective membranes called the subarachnoid space. Near the lower back, the spinal cord tapers to an end called the conus medullaris, but a bundle of nerve roots called the cauda equina continues below it. The enlarged CSF-filled subarachnoid space in this region is the lumbar cistern. Doctors commonly collect CSF from the lumbar cistern during a spinal tap because it lies below the end of the spinal cord.

A white dwarf is the small, extremely dense core left behind when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel and expels its outer layers. Although it may be about the size of Earth, it contains a large amount of mass. With no ordinary fusion to support it, gravity pulls inward, while electron degeneracy pressure—a resistance created when electrons are packed tightly together—keeps it from collapsing. This balance works only below an upper mass of about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass, called the Chandrasekhar limit after astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. If a white dwarf gains too much mass from a companion star and approaches this limit, it can become unstable and explode as a Type Ia supernova.

The Right-Hand Rule uses your right hand to work out directions in electromagnetism. In 1820, Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted noticed that an electric current in a nearby wire deflected a compass needle, showing that current produces a magnetic field. For a straight wire, point your right thumb in the direction of conventional current (the direction positive charge would flow). Your curled fingers show the direction of the circular magnetic field around the wire. A related version helps find the magnetic force on a moving positive charge: point your index finger along the charge’s velocity and your middle finger along the magnetic field, B. Your thumb then points in the direction of the magnetic force. For a negative charge, the force points the opposite way.

Face masks are protective coverings worn over the mouth and nose to help reduce the spread of respiratory infections such as COVID-19. They work by blocking some of the tiny droplets and particles people release when they breathe, speak, cough, or sneeze. A surgical mask is generally loose-fitting and helps contain droplets, but it does not seal closely around the face. An N95 respirator is a U.S.-certified type of mask designed to fit snugly and filter at least 95% of airborne particles when worn correctly. A good fit matters because air can flow through gaps instead of passing through the mask’s filtering material. Wearing a mask in crowded indoor places, especially when infection risk is high, can be one part of protecting yourself and others, alongside measures such as vaccination.

Length contraction is the shortening of an object’s measured length along its direction of motion when it moves very fast relative to an observer. For example, a stationary observer would measure a rapidly moving rod as shorter than someone traveling with the rod would measure it. The rod does not become shorter in its own rest frame; the two observers measure its length from different frames of reference. This effect becomes noticeable only at speeds close to the speed of light. Length contraction is predicted by Albert Einstein’s theory of special relativity, which is based in part on the idea that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers—observers moving at constant velocity. Einstein later developed general relativity, which also accounts for gravity.

Tidal locking occurs when gravity gradually makes an orbiting body rotate once on its axis for each orbit around its parent body. As a result, the same side continually faces the parent. Earth’s Moon is tidally locked to Earth, which is why we usually see the same lunar hemisphere, although sunlight still reaches different parts of the Moon as it orbits. Tidal locking can also be mutual: Pluto and its large moon Charon each keep the same hemisphere facing the other. Pluto, once classified as the ninth planet, was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. Some planets orbiting other stars may be tidally locked too, leaving one side facing the star and the other facing away.

Cats are mammals in the felid family, a group that includes domestic cats and wild species such as ocelots and servals. Like other felids, they have sharp claws and teeth suited to hunting. Cats are also central to the Warriors novels, written by several authors under the shared name Erin Hunter. The stories follow four Clans of wild cats, who call cats kept by humans “kittypets.” In the books, the Clans believe that their deceased ancestors live on in a spiritual group called StarClan. Medicine cats care for their Clan members and can receive guidance from StarClan. So “cats” names the animals that make up the Clans, while “StarClan” names the ancestral Clan they look to for guidance.

An android is an artificial being designed to look and often behave like a human. In science fiction, androids may speak, make decisions and interact with people so naturally that their true nature is not immediately obvious. Ash, a crew member aboard the spaceship Nostromo in Ridley Scott’s 1979 film Alien, is an android. In the film, an alien creature first attaches itself to another crew member, Kane, by latching onto his face. Androids also appear in stories connected to Blade Runner: its humanlike replicants are based on characters in Philip K. Dick’s novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? Although stories often use the terms “robot” and “android” loosely, “android” specifically emphasizes a humanlike appearance.

Stuxnet was a sophisticated computer worm discovered in 2010. A worm is a type of malware that can spread between computers, but Stuxnet was unusual because it targeted industrial control systems rather than ordinary desktop files. Its best-known target was the underground uranium-enrichment facility at Natanz, Iran. There, software made by Siemens helped control centrifuges, machines that spin rapidly to enrich uranium. Stuxnet secretly changed how those centrifuges operated, potentially damaging them, while feeding operators misleading information that made the equipment appear to be working normally. The attack showed that malicious software could affect physical machinery, not just steal data or disrupt computer files. It also raised concerns about the use of cyberattacks to sabotage important infrastructure.

The hippocampus is a small, curved structure deep inside each of the brain’s medial temporal lobes. Its name comes from the Greek word for “seahorse,” which it resembles in shape. Humans have two hippocampi, one on each side of the brain. They help consolidate new experiences and facts: after you learn something, the hippocampus helps turn it into a memory that can last beyond the short time you are actively thinking about it. This more durable store is called long-term memory. For example, remembering a phone number just long enough to dial it uses short-term memory, while remembering what you learned in class last week involves long-term memory. Damage to the hippocampus can make it difficult to form new long-term memories.

A lobotomy was a brain operation once used to treat severe mental illness. It involved cutting connections in the frontal lobes, areas involved in planning, emotions, and behavior. Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz developed an early form called prefrontal leucotomy in the 1930s and received the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work. In the United States, Walter Freeman and James Watts adapted the procedure, which was performed in mental asylums and psychiatric hospitals. Lobotomies sometimes made patients seem calmer, but they could also cause serious, permanent changes in personality, thinking, and independence. The procedure fell out of use as its harms became clearer and other treatments, including psychiatric medications, became available.

Paul Dirac was an English theoretical physicist who combined quantum mechanics with Einstein’s special relativity to describe particles moving at very high speeds. His Dirac equation describes spin-one-half particles, including electrons, and led him to predict a counterpart to the electron with the same mass but opposite electric charge. An electron has a negative charge; its positively charged antimatter counterpart is called a positron. Dirac tried to explain positrons as “holes” left in a sea of filled electron states, an idea known as the Dirac sea. In 1932, Carl Anderson detected positrons in cosmic rays, providing evidence for Dirac’s prediction. Positrons can also be emitted during beta-plus radioactive decay.

Raman spectroscopy is a way to study materials by shining a laser on a sample and examining the light that scatters back. Most scattered photons keep their original energy, but a small number exchange energy with the sample’s molecules. This is called inelastic scattering. The resulting shifts in the light’s frequency reveal molecular vibrational modes and create a spectrum that can help identify the material. The technique is named for Indian physicist C. V. Raman, who discovered this effect in 1928. When a molecule gains vibrational energy, the outgoing photon has less energy, a lower frequency, and a longer wavelength than the incoming photon. This particular change is called Stokes scattering. Raman spectroscopy can also help determine the diameter of a carbon nanotube.

A cathode is the electrode where reduction occurs: ions or other particles gain electrons there. In a galvanic cell, such as a battery producing electricity from a chemical reaction, the cathode is the positive electrode and the anode is the negative electrode, where oxidation releases electrons. A wire connects the electrodes so electrons can travel from the anode to the cathode. In a zinc-copper galvanic cell, the copper electrode is the cathode. The two parts of the cell, called half-cells, also need a path for ions to move so charge does not build up and stop the reaction. This path is often a salt bridge: a U-shaped glass tube filled with an electrolyte solution that allows ions to migrate between the half-cells.

The nose is the facial organ that lets you breathe and smell. As air passes through it, the nasal passages warm and humidify the air before it reaches the lungs. Goblet cells in the lining produce mucus, which traps dust, bacteria, and other particles. Tiny hairlike cilia move this mucus toward the throat, where it can be swallowed or expelled; this process is called mucociliary clearance. High in the nasal cavity, sensory neurons detect airborne chemicals that we experience as odors. Their nerve fibers pass through small openings in the cribriform plate, a bone between the nose and brain, to reach the paired olfactory bulbs at the front of the brain. There, signals are organized in clusters called glomeruli before being relayed to other brain areas.

A computer keyboard is an input device that lets you enter text and commands by pressing physical keys or touching keys on a screen. Its keys include letters, numbers, punctuation, and controls such as Enter, Shift, and Backspace. The most common English-language layout is called QWERTY, named for the first six letters in the top row of alphabetic keys: Q, W, E, R, T, and Y. Keyboards send your keystrokes to a computer, which interprets them as characters or actions. On a full-size keyboard, a separate block of keys usually sits to the right of the main typing area. This numeric keypad is arranged much like a calculator and makes it convenient to enter numbers and arithmetic operators such as +, −, ×, and ÷.

Chien-Shiung Wu was a Chinese-American experimental physicist who helped reveal a surprising property of the weak force, one of the four fundamental forces of nature. In 1956, she and her collaborators cooled cobalt-60 atoms and aligned their nuclei so their spins pointed in the same direction. They then observed the beta particles, or electrons, released as the nuclei underwent radioactive decay. The electrons were emitted more often opposite to the direction of the nuclei’s spin. If the weak interaction obeyed parity conservation, this pattern would have looked the same in a mirror; instead, the mirror image would reverse it. Wu’s experiment showed that the weak interaction violates parity conservation, confirming a prediction by physicists Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang.

Bilirubin is a yellow-orange pigment made when the body breaks down heme, a part of the hemoglobin in old red blood cells. At first, bilirubin is unconjugated, meaning the liver has not yet processed it. Because this form dissolves poorly in water, it travels through the bloodstream attached to albumin, a major plasma protein that also helps keep fluid inside blood vessels by maintaining oncotic pressure. The liver changes bilirubin into a more water-soluble form and releases it into bile, the fluid that helps digest fats. Bile is stored in the gallbladder before entering the small intestine. In the gut, products formed from bilirubin help give stool its brown color. If too much bilirubin builds up in the body, it can cause jaundice, which makes the skin and whites of the eyes look yellow.

An OR gate is a basic building block of digital circuits. It takes two or more inputs, each represented as 0 (false or low) or 1 (true or high), and produces 1 if at least one input is 1. For a two-input OR gate, the pairs 01, 10, and 11 all give an output of 1; only 00 gives 0. This differs from an AND gate, which produces 1 only when both inputs are 1, so 11 is its only true two-input case. You can model these gates in Minecraft using redstone: two input wires of redstone dust feeding one output act like an OR gate, while a circuit made with three redstone torches linked by dust can act like an AND gate.

The Boeing B-29 Superfortress was an American heavy bomber built for long-range missions during World War II. It had four Wright R-3350 engines, a pressurized crew compartment that helped crews fly at high altitude, and remotely operated defensive gun turrets. Introduced into combat in the Pacific in 1944, B-29s carried out bombing raids against Japan. On August 6, 1945, pilot Paul Tibbets flew a B-29 named Enola Gay, after his mother, to drop the atomic bomb Little Boy on Hiroshima. Three days later, another B-29, Bockscar, dropped an atomic bomb on Nagasaki. The aircraft also has a connection to Lake Mead in Nevada: a B-29 crashed into the lake during a flight in 1948 and remains submerged there.

Boolean logic uses two truth values: true means a statement or condition holds, while false means it does not. For example, the comparison 1 == 2 evaluates to false because 1 and 2 are not equal. Programs use these values to decide what to do next. A conventional while loop repeats a block of code as long as its condition is true; when the condition becomes false, the loop stops. An if statement makes a different kind of decision: it chooses a path without repeating code. In Java, if the condition in an if statement is false, the program skips the if block and may run an optional else block instead.

A nurse is a healthcare professional trained to care for patients, give treatments, and work with doctors and other medical staff. Nurses may check a patient’s condition, administer medicines, explain care instructions, and offer emotional support. Fictional nurses can show different sides of the profession. In Tony Kushner’s two-part play Angels in America, Belize is a nurse and drag performer who cares for Prior Walter during the AIDS epidemic. Kushner also wrote the play A Bright Room Called Day. By contrast, Mildred Ratched is an authoritarian nurse in Ken Kesey’s novel One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. Both characters are nurses, even though they treat the people in their care very differently.

A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, blocking some or all of the Sun from view. This alignment of three objects is called a syzygy. In a partial solar eclipse, the Moon covers only part of the Sun. In a total solar eclipse, it completely covers the Sun’s bright visible surface, called the photosphere. For a short time, observers in the path of totality can then see the corona, the Sun’s outer atmosphere, as a faint, pearly halo around the Moon’s dark silhouette. The corona is usually hidden by the photosphere’s brightness. A solar eclipse can occur only at a new moon, but not every new moon produces one because the Moon’s orbit is tilted relative to Earth’s orbit around the Sun.

The trachea, also called the windpipe, is the airway that carries air from the larynx in the throat toward the lungs. At its lower end, it divides into two main bronchi, one leading to each lung. Its walls are supported by incomplete C-shaped rings made of hyaline cartilage, a firm but flexible tissue. These rings help keep the airway open so air can pass through, even as the neck moves. The open part of each ring faces backward, toward the esophagus, which lies behind the trachea. This arrangement lets the esophagus expand when food is swallowed. In an emergency, medical professionals may insert a breathing tube into the trachea to help a person breathe.

Microscopy is the practice of using instruments to examine cells and other structures too small to see clearly with the unaided eye. Light, or optical, microscopes use lenses to magnify specimens; early users such as Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek helped reveal a previously unseen world of cells and microorganisms. Electron microscopes instead use beams of electrons to show much finer details. They include transmission microscopes, which image electrons passing through thin samples, and scanning microscopes, which reveal surface features. A specialized optical technique called confocal microscopy uses a focused laser to scan a fluorescent specimen. A pinhole blocks much of the light from outside the focal plane, producing a sharp image of one thin layer. Combining images from different depths can create a three-dimensional view of a thick sample.

A magnetic monopole is a hypothetical particle with a single magnetic pole: either north or south. Ordinary magnets always have both poles, and cutting one in half makes two smaller magnets, each with a north and south pole. No magnetic monopole has been confirmed, but its discovery would make Maxwell’s equations, which describe electricity and magnetism, more symmetric. In 1931, physicist Paul Dirac showed that if even one magnetic monopole exists, electric charge must occur in fixed units rather than take any value. The rule behind this result is called the Dirac quantization condition. In Gaussian units, it says that the product of an electric charge and a magnetic charge must equal an integer multiple of ℏc/2, where ℏ and c are physical constants.

Karl Fischer titration is a laboratory method for measuring how much water is in a sample, even when the amount is very small. It is named after the chemist Karl Fischer. In the test, water takes part in a chemical reaction involving iodine and sulfur dioxide. The amount of iodine used tells scientists how much water the sample contained, making the method useful for checking moisture in medicines, foods, and chemicals. There are two main ways to supply the iodine. In volumetric Karl Fischer titration, a measured volume of reagent is added, often from a burette. In coulometric titration, iodine is generated electrochemically inside the test cell. The instrument calculates the water content from the electrical charge passed during that process.

Marine snow is a steady shower of tiny particles that sink from the ocean’s sunlit surface toward the deep sea. It includes dead organisms, waste, and bits of organic material that may stick together as they fall. Some of this material comes from phytoplankton: microscopic organisms that drift in the water and use sunlight to photosynthesize. Phytoplankton form the base of many marine food webs, but sunlight does not reach the deepest parts of the ocean. As marine snow sinks, it carries nutrients and food from the surface to animals living far below, including bottom-feeders on the seafloor. Much of it is eaten or broken down on the way, but the particles that reach the deep ocean help support life there.

Edwin Hubble was an American astronomer whose work changed how scientists understand galaxies and the universe. In the 1920s, he used the Mount Wilson Observatory to study Cepheid variable stars in Andromeda. Because these stars reveal their distances through the pattern of their changing brightness, Hubble showed that Andromeda lies far beyond the Milky Way and is a separate galaxy. He later found that more distant galaxies generally move away from us faster, providing important evidence that the universe is expanding. Hubble also classified galaxies by shape in a chart known as the tuning-fork diagram. Elliptical galaxies form one sequence, while the two branches show spiral galaxies with and without central bars.

Robert Hooke was an English natural philosopher who became the Royal Society’s Curator of Experiments in 1662. He studied small objects with a microscope, an instrument that magnifies things too tiny to see clearly with the unaided eye. In 1665, Hooke published Micrographia, an illustrated book of his observations that helped make microscopy widely known. Its detailed images included a flea and a thin slice of cork. Looking at the cork, Hooke saw many tiny, boxlike compartments and called them “cells” because they reminded him of small rooms. He was seeing the walls of dead plant cells, not living cells themselves. Hooke’s work helped people recognize that microscopes could reveal an unseen world and laid important groundwork for the later study of cells.

Ganymede is Jupiter’s largest moon and the largest natural satellite in the Solar System. It is bigger than the planet Mercury, though much less massive. Beneath Ganymede’s icy surface, scientists think a salty ocean lies sandwiched between layers of ice. Ganymede also has its own intrinsic magnetic field, meaning it generates a magnetic field inside itself—a rare feature for a moon. During its mission in the 1990s, NASA’s Galileo spacecraft made several close flybys of Ganymede. Its magnetic measurements provided evidence for the hidden ocean because salty water conducts electricity and can produce a detectable magnetic response. The spacecraft was named after Galileo Galilei, who made the first telescopic observations of Jupiter’s four large moons, including Ganymede.

The solar corona is the Sun’s outermost atmosphere. It stretches millions of kilometers into space but is usually hidden by the bright solar disk. During a total solar eclipse, when the Moon blocks that disk, the corona appears as a pearly halo around the Sun. Although it is much less dense than the Sun’s visible surface, the corona is extremely hot and contains plasma, a gas of electrically charged particles. The Sun’s magnetic fields can suddenly release huge amounts of energy in the corona, launching a vast bubble of magnetized plasma into interplanetary space. This event is called a coronal mass ejection. If one travels toward Earth, it can disturb Earth’s magnetic field, causing a geomagnetic storm and sometimes producing bright auroras.

A phospholipid is a type of lipid that forms the main structure of cell membranes. It has a phosphate-containing head that is hydrophilic, meaning it attracts water, and fatty-acid tails that are hydrophobic, meaning they avoid water. A molecule with both water-attracting and water-repelling regions is called amphipathic. In the watery environment inside and outside a cell, phospholipids arrange themselves in two layers: their heads face the water on either side, while their tails point inward toward one another. This phospholipid bilayer helps separate the cell’s interior from its surroundings. The membrane is flexible rather than rigid; in animal cells, cholesterol helps regulate its fluidity.

The Mössbauer effect occurs when an atomic nucleus in a solid emits or absorbs a gamma ray without losing energy to recoil. The whole solid takes up the recoil instead, so the gamma ray’s energy remains extremely precise. This produces an exceptionally narrow resonance: absorption happens only when the gamma ray has almost exactly the right energy. Scientists can therefore use the effect to detect tiny shifts in energy caused by motion or gravity. In the Pound–Rebka experiment, conducted at Harvard in 1959–1960, researchers compared gamma rays traveling between the top and bottom of a 22.5-meter tower. They used the Mössbauer effect to measure gravitational redshift, the small change in a gamma ray’s frequency caused by moving through Earth’s gravitational field.

The spleen is an organ in the upper-left abdomen, next to the stomach. It resembles a large lymph node, but instead of filtering lymph fluid, it filters blood. The spleen removes old or damaged red blood cells and helps the immune system detect and fight infections. About 10 percent of people also have a much smaller, extra spleen called an accessory spleen. Some illnesses, including mononucleosis and Hodgkin’s disease, can cause the spleen to become enlarged, a condition called splenomegaly. The stomach, which lies beside the spleen, is a hollow digestive organ. It mixes food with gastric acid to help break it down, then passes the resulting contents into the small intestine.

Norman Borlaug was an American agronomist, a scientist who studies crops and farming. While working in Mexico, he bred semi-dwarf wheat that produced high yields and resisted rust, a disease that can destroy wheat crops. Because the plants had shorter, stronger stems, they were less likely to fall over when they produced heavy heads of grain. Borlaug’s wheat varieties spread to other countries and became a hallmark of the Green Revolution, a mid-20th-century transformation that sharply increased crop production through improved seeds and farming methods, including wider use of fertilizers and pesticides. These advances helped reduce the risk of famine, earning Borlaug the nickname “father of the Green Revolution.” He received the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts to address world hunger.

Trinitrotoluene, usually called TNT, is an aromatic compound best known as an explosive. It is made from toluene, a chemical also called methylbenzene because it has a CH3 group attached to a benzene ring. Adding three nitro groups, each written as NO2, produces trinitrotoluene, with the formula C7H5N3O6. The nitro groups give TNT its explosive properties. Scientists often compare the energy released by other explosions with the energy released by TNT, so “TNT equivalent” is a common way to describe explosive power. The German chemist Julius Wilbrand first prepared trinitrotoluene in 1863, but it was not widely used as a military explosive until decades later.

Global Mean Surface Temperature is the average temperature at Earth’s surface. Scientists estimate it by combining air-temperature readings taken near the ground over land with temperatures measured in the ocean’s uppermost waters, then averaging them across the planet. Unlike a local weather reading, it describes a global pattern. Its long-term rise is a key measure of warming caused by greenhouse gases. Scientists often report that change as a temperature anomaly: the signed difference between a measured temperature and the average for a chosen baseline period. A positive anomaly means warmer than the baseline; a negative one means cooler. To study times before thermometers, scientists use clues in ice and sediment cores, including the ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16.

Venus is the second planet from the Sun and completes one orbit in about 225 Earth days. Like Earth’s Moon, it appears to change shape as we see different amounts of its sunlit half. In 1610, Galileo observed Venus showing phases from crescent to gibbous. These phases provided strong evidence that Venus orbits the Sun, supporting the heliocentric model of the solar system. When Venus lies between Earth and the Sun, the alignment is called inferior conjunction. Venus is then relatively close to Earth, so it can appear larger through a telescope, although little of its sunlit side faces us. The opposite alignment, with the Sun between Earth and Venus, is called superior conjunction.

Ice is the solid phase of water. At ordinary atmospheric pressure, liquid water freezes into ice at about 0°C (32°F). Glaciers are huge masses made mostly of ice, formed when layers of snow build up, are compressed, and gradually turn into dense ice. Found in polar regions and high mountains, glaciers move slowly under their own weight. As they advance, the moving ice can pick up rocks and boulders and carry them far from the bedrock where they began. When a glacier shrinks or retreats, often because its ice melts into water, it leaves some of those rocks behind. Large boulders deposited this way are called glacial erratics; they can weigh hundreds of tons and may look very different from the rocks around them.

Random-access memory, or RAM, is the computer’s temporary working area for programs and data that the processor is currently using. “Random access” means the computer can retrieve data directly from any memory location without reading through earlier locations first; it does not mean the data is chosen randomly. RAM is much faster than a hard drive or solid-state drive, but it is volatile: its contents disappear when electrical power is removed. A widely used type of RAM called dynamic random-access memory, or DRAM, serves as the main memory in many computers. In DRAM, each bit is stored as an electrical charge in a tiny capacitor paired with a transistor. Because that charge gradually leaks away, the computer must refresh DRAM regularly to preserve its data while the power is on.

Age-related macular degeneration, or AMD, is an eye disease that damages the macula, the central part of the retina. The retina is a layer at the back of the eye that detects light, and the macula provides the sharp central vision needed for reading and recognizing faces. AMD has two forms. In dry AMD, deposits called drusen build up beneath the retina, and vision often worsens gradually. In wet AMD, fragile abnormal blood vessels grow beneath the retina and can leak fluid or blood, causing faster damage to central vision. A growth signal called VEGF encourages these vessels to form. Medicines called VEGF inhibitors block that signal and can slow vision loss from wet AMD.

A collision is an interaction in which two objects exert forces on each other for a short time, often changing their speeds or directions. If the objects form an isolated system, their total momentum is conserved: momentum gained by one is balanced by momentum lost by the other. Collisions are classified by what happens to kinetic energy, the energy of motion. In an elastic collision, total kinetic energy is conserved, and the objects bounce apart. In an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy is converted into other forms, such as heat, sound, or deformation. The coefficient of restitution describes how strongly objects rebound. In a one-dimensional collision, it is the relative speed at which they separate divided by the relative speed at which they approach. It is 1 for an ideal elastic collision and 0 when the objects stick together.

Herbivory is the feeding interaction in which animals eat plant tissues, in contrast to carnivory, which involves eating other animals. Herbivores that graze eat grasses and other low-growing plants, while browsers feed on leaves and shoots higher above the ground, often from shrubs or trees. Plants resist being eaten with physical defenses such as thorns and cactus spines and chemical defenses such as tannins and alkaloids. Herbivores have ways to cope: some can break down plant toxins, and many rely on microbes to digest cellulose, a tough material in plant cell walls. Ruminants such as cattle have a four-part stomach. Its largest chamber, the rumen, contains microbes that ferment plant material; cattle also regurgitate food and rechew it as cud.

Trigonal bipyramidal molecular geometry describes a molecule with five atoms bonded to a central atom and no lone pairs on that atom. Three bonds point toward the corners of a triangle in one plane, 120° apart; these are the equatorial positions. The other two bonds point above and below the plane and are called axial positions. Each axial bond makes a 90° angle with the equatorial bonds. Phosphorus pentachloride, PCl5, is an example: its phosphorus atom forms five bonds to chlorine atoms, giving it ten electrons around it rather than the eight predicted by the octet rule. In some trigonal bipyramidal molecules, the atoms attached to the center can move together so that axial and equatorial positions exchange. This rearrangement is called Berry pseudorotation.

An adiabatic process is a change in a system, such as a gas, in which no heat is exchanged with its surroundings. The gas can still change temperature: when it is compressed, work done on it can raise its temperature, while expansion can lower it. For a reversible adiabatic process involving an ideal gas, pressure P and volume V obey the relation PV^γ = constant. Volume is the space the gas occupies, measured in units such as liters or cubic meters. The exponent γ is called the adiabatic index. It has no units because it is a ratio: the gas’s heat capacity at constant pressure divided by its heat capacity at constant volume. Heat capacity describes how much energy is needed to raise a system’s temperature by one degree.

pKa measures an acid’s strength and is defined as the negative base-ten logarithm of its acid dissociation constant, Ka: pKa = −log10(Ka). A lower pKa means a stronger acid because more of its molecules release hydrogen ions in water. In a titration, a measured amount of base is added to an acid, and the changing pH can be plotted against the volume of base added. For a weak acid titrated with a strong base, half-equivalence is the point where half the acid has been converted into its conjugate base; there, pH equals pKa. This also follows from the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log10([conjugate base]/[acid]). The equation helps estimate the pH of a buffer, a solution that resists changes in pH.

The dodo was a large, flightless bird found only on Mauritius, an island nation in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar. A species found naturally in just one place is called endemic, so the dodo was endemic to Mauritius. It evolved from flying pigeon ancestors, but on an island with few land predators, flight became less important. After people settled Mauritius, they hunted dodos and changed their habitat. They also brought animals such as rats, pigs and monkeys, which likely ate dodo eggs and competed for food. These combined pressures drove the dodo to extinction by the late 1600s. Its story shows how vulnerable island species can be when humans and unfamiliar animals arrive.

Sea urchins are rounded marine animals related to sea stars and sand dollars. They belong to a group called echinoderms, meaning “spiny-skinned” animals, and live on the seafloor in oceans around the world. Their bodies have a hard shell covered with dense, movable spines that help protect them from predators and can also help them move. The name “urchin” comes from an old word for “hedgehog,” another animal known for its spines. On the underside of a sea urchin is a hard mouth apparatus with five teeth, traditionally called Aristotle’s lantern. The teeth scrape algae from rocks and other surfaces, though some sea urchins eat other small organisms too. Sea urchins are important members of marine ecosystems because their grazing can affect how much algae grows.

The Great Red Spot is a huge, long-lived storm in the atmosphere of Jupiter, the largest planet in the Solar System. It has been observed for centuries and appears as a reddish oval among Jupiter’s bands of clouds. The storm is an anticyclone, meaning its winds rotate around an area of high atmospheric pressure. Although it has been shrinking, it is still larger than Earth. Jupiter is a rapidly rotating gas giant with no solid surface like Earth’s, so the Great Red Spot is a feature of its atmosphere rather than a mark on the ground. Scientists are still studying its reddish color; one possible explanation involves chemicals such as ammonium hydrosulfide reacting with ultraviolet light from the Sun.

A locust is a type of grasshopper that can change its behavior when many locusts crowd together. In its solitary phase, it lives much like an ordinary grasshopper. Crowding can trigger a gregarious phase in which locusts gather, move together, and form enormous migratory swarms. These swarms eat large amounts of vegetation and have repeatedly devastated crops, making locusts serious agricultural pests. Locusts also appear in religious texts: in the Book of Exodus, they are the eighth plague sent against Egypt. In the Gospels, John the Baptist, a wilderness preacher who later baptized Jesus in the Jordan River, is described as eating locusts and wild honey. Some Jewish traditions also permit certain locusts as kosher food, although most invertebrates are not kosher.

The capture-recapture method, also called mark-recapture, helps ecologists estimate the size of an animal population without counting every individual. Researchers capture and harmlessly mark a first group, then release them. After the animals have had time to mix with the rest of the population, researchers capture a second group and count how many carry marks. If many are marked, the population is probably relatively small; if few are marked, it is probably larger. The Lincoln–Petersen estimator gives a numerical estimate: multiply the number marked in the first sample by the total number caught in the second sample, then divide by the number of marked animals caught again. The estimate works best when marks remain visible, marked and unmarked animals are equally likely to be caught, and the population changes little between samples.

Wave velocity is the speed at which a wave disturbance travels through space or a material. For a periodic wave, it equals wavelength multiplied by frequency: wavelength is the distance between repeating points, such as crests, and frequency is the number of cycles per second. In a dispersive medium, different frequencies can travel at different speeds, so two kinds of wave velocity matter. Phase velocity describes how fast a particular point in a wave’s repeating pattern, such as a crest, moves. Group velocity describes how fast the overall envelope of a wave packet moves; mathematically, it is the derivative of angular frequency with respect to wavenumber. Light travels at about 3 × 10⁸ metres per second in a vacuum, but its velocity changes in materials such as glass.

The Curie family made major discoveries about radioactivity, the energy and particles released by unstable atoms. Inspired by Henri Becquerel’s finding that uranium gave off radiation, Marie Curie and her husband Pierre studied pitchblende, a uranium-rich mineral. They found that it contained substances more radioactive than uranium and, in 1898, identified two new elements: radium and polonium. Marie, who was born in Poland and later worked in France, named polonium after her homeland. Polonium’s atomic number is 84, meaning each of its atoms has 84 protons. Marie also coined the term “radioactivity.” Pierre and Marie shared a Nobel Prize in Physics, and Marie later won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry, becoming the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

A telescope is an optical instrument that gathers and focuses light from distant objects, making them easier to see. Some telescopes use lenses to bend light, a process called refraction, while others use mirrors to reflect it. Astronomers use telescopes to study planets, stars, and other objects in space. In 1610, the Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei reported seeing four moons orbiting Jupiter through his telescope in a work called Sidereus Nuncius. These moons are now known as the Galilean moons. His observation showed that not everything in space orbits Earth. Another astronomer, Simon Marius, discovered the moons independently, while Johannes Kepler later improved the design of refracting telescopes.

Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that send beams of electromagnetic radiation into space. As a pulsar spins, its beams sweep past Earth like the light from a lighthouse, producing flashes at remarkably regular intervals. A neutron star is the compact remnant left behind when some massive stars explode. It packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere only about the size of a city, making it far denser than a white dwarf. Neutron stars are made mostly of neutrons, and pressure associated with these particles helps keep them from collapsing further into black holes. Their solid outer crust can sometimes crack and shift in events called starquakes. Thus, a pulsar is a type of neutron star, but not every neutron star is observed as a pulsar.

CRISPR-Cas9 is a gene-editing technique adapted from a defense system that bacteria use against viruses. Researchers design a guide RNA to match a chosen DNA sequence. The guide directs Cas9, a DNA-cutting protein, to that location, where Cas9 makes a cut. As the cell repairs the cut, researchers can disrupt a gene or make a planned change to its DNA. A widely used Cas9 protein comes from the bacterium Streptococcus pyogenes. French microbiologist Emmanuelle Charpentier studied bacterial immunity and an RNA molecule called tracrRNA, which helps Cas9 work. She collaborated with Jennifer Doudna to develop CRISPR-Cas9 into a programmable gene-editing tool. Charpentier and Doudna shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this work.

When the body breaks down proteins, it also breaks down their building blocks, amino acids, producing nitrogen-containing waste. This process can release ammonia, which is toxic if it builds up. In mammals, the liver converts ammonia into a safer compound called urea through a series of chemical reactions known as the urea cycle. Urea has the molecular formula CH4N2O and is also called carbamide. It travels in the blood from the liver to the kidneys, which filter it out and remove it from the body in urine. Urea is the waste compound, while urine is the liquid that carries it away. The liver also performs other important jobs, including detoxifying alcohol and making many proteins found in blood plasma.

Endosymbiosis is an evolutionary process in which one cell takes up another but, instead of digesting it, keeps it as an internal partner. Over many generations, the two cells become closely dependent on each other. Scientists think this process helped produce eukaryotic cells, the complex cells found in animals, plants, and fungi. According to this explanation, an ancient cell took in an oxygen-using bacterium that became the mitochondrion, an organelle that releases energy from food and produces most of a cell’s ATP. Mitochondria have their own DNA and a double membrane, which are clues to their bacterial origin. Their DNA is usually inherited from the mother. A similar endosymbiotic event is thought to have produced chloroplasts, the organelles that carry out photosynthesis in plants and algae.

The Andromeda Galaxy is an enormous spiral galaxy about 2.5 million light-years from Earth. It is the nearest major galaxy to our own, the Milky Way, which contains the Solar System. Also called Messier 31 or M31, Andromeda is visible as a faint, fuzzy patch in the night sky under dark conditions, although most of its stars are too far away to see individually. Gravity is drawing Andromeda and the Milky Way toward each other, and astronomers predict they will collide and eventually merge, beginning in roughly 4.5 billion years. Andromeda has several smaller satellite galaxies. One of them, Messier 32 or M32, is a compact elliptical galaxy near Andromeda’s central region. Its stars are crowded closely together, giving its center an unusually high surface brightness.

Tyrannosaurus rex was a large meat-eating dinosaur that lived in what is now North America during the Late Cretaceous, about 68 to 66 million years ago. Its scientific name means “tyrant lizard king,” and it belonged to a group of dinosaurs called tyrannosaurids. T. rex had powerful jaws, large teeth, strong hind legs, and unusually short arms. One of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found is nicknamed Sue, after fossil hunter Sue Hendrickson, who discovered it in South Dakota in 1990. Sue is exhibited at the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago, on the lakefront near the Shedd Aquarium and Adler Planetarium. Fossils like Sue help scientists study how this enormous predator lived.

The 1964 Alaska earthquake struck south-central Alaska on Good Friday, March 27, 1964. Also called the Great Alaska earthquake, it measured magnitude 9.2, making it the strongest earthquake recorded in North America. It was a megathrust earthquake: one tectonic plate suddenly slipped beneath another along a fault under the seafloor. The main rupture occurred offshore in Prince William Sound, a large coastal inlet east of Anchorage. Violent shaking caused landslides and ground collapse, while sudden movement of the seafloor and underwater landslides generated destructive tsunamis. Coastal communities including Valdez and Chenega suffered severe damage, and tsunami waves reached other parts of the Pacific. The disaster shows how a major offshore earthquake can threaten people both through shaking and through waves that arrive afterward.

An electric field describes the electric force that a charged object would experience at each point in space. It is a vector, meaning it has both a size and a direction. To define it, imagine placing a tiny positive test charge at a point: the electric field is the force on that charge divided by its charge, and it points in the direction the charge would be pushed. Field lines therefore point away from positive charges and toward negative charges. In electrostatics, the field is also the negative spatial gradient of electric potential: it points toward lower potential. Electric fields can also be produced by changing magnetic fields, as described by Faraday’s law. Inside a conductor at electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field is zero.

Pregnancy is the period when an embryo or fetus develops in a person’s uterus, usually beginning after implantation and ending with childbirth. Home pregnancy tests detect hCG, a hormone that rises early in pregnancy, while an obstetric ultrasound can show whether an embryo or fetus is developing in the uterus. Pregnant people are advised to take folic acid because it lowers the risk of neural-tube defects, including spina bifida and anencephaly. Some experience Braxton Hicks contractions: episodes of uterine tightening that remain irregular, do not steadily grow stronger, and do not open the cervix as labor contractions do. An ectopic pregnancy occurs when implantation happens outside the uterus, often in a fallopian tube, and requires prompt medical care because it can be life-threatening.

The Kodiak bear is a very large subspecies of brown bear native to the Kodiak Archipelago, a group of islands in the Gulf of Alaska off the state’s southern coast. The largest island in the group is Kodiak Island. Kodiak bears have been isolated from mainland brown bears for thousands of years, helping them become a distinct subspecies. They are closely related to grizzly bears but are generally larger, making them among the largest bears in the world. Their size is supported by abundant food, especially salmon, which they catch in the islands’ rivers. Like other brown bears, Kodiak bears are omnivores: they also eat plants, berries, and other animals.

Yuri Gagarin was a Soviet pilot and cosmonaut who became the first human to travel into space. On April 12, 1961, he launched aboard Vostok 1, a single-seat Soviet spacecraft with a spherical module designed to return through Earth’s atmosphere. The flight lasted about 108 minutes and carried Gagarin once around Earth before the spacecraft came down near Engels, in the Soviet Union. During the final descent, Gagarin ejected from the capsule and landed separately by parachute. His flight showed that a person could survive launch, orbit, and the return to Earth, making it a major milestone in space exploration. Gagarin’s achievement also drew worldwide attention to the Soviet space program during the space race.

A lysosome is a membrane-bound organelle that acts as a cell’s recycling center. It contains digestive enzymes that break down large molecules, such as proteins and fats, as well as worn-out cellular components. The Golgi apparatus sorts many of these enzymes by adding a sugar-phosphate tag called mannose-6-phosphate. Sorting receptors recognize this tag and help direct the enzymes to lysosomes, where they can carry out intracellular digestion. If a lysosomal enzyme is missing or defective, substances it normally breaks down can build up inside cells. For example, in Gaucher’s disease, a defective enzyme prevents cells from properly breaking down the fatty substance glucocerebroside. Lysosomes therefore help cells both remove waste and reuse useful materials.

Polylactic acid, or PLA, is a biodegradable thermoplastic polyester made from lactic acid. Its long chains contain ester bonds linking units derived from lactic acid, and its raw materials can come from renewable sources such as corn starch or sugarcane. One common way to make PLA starts by joining two lactic acid molecules into a small ring-shaped compound called lactide. In ring-opening polymerization, lactide rings open and link together to form long PLA chains. PLA is widely used as filament in fused-deposition 3-D printing because it is relatively easy to print and tends to warp less than many other plastics. Lactic acid is also produced by bacteria during fermentation, which is why it is associated with sour dairy foods such as yogurt.

Plants, or Plantae, are a kingdom of organisms that includes trees, grasses, mosses, and the small flowering plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Most plants make their own food through photosynthesis, using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to produce sugars. Arabidopsis is a model organism: scientists study it because it grows quickly and helps them understand processes shared by many plants. One such process is RNA interference, which helps cells control which genes are active. In this process, small RNA molecules guide a group of proteins called the RNA-induced silencing complex, or RISC, to matching messenger RNA. Proteins in the Argonaute family, first discovered in Arabidopsis, can then cleave that messenger RNA, preventing it from being used to make a protein.

The angle of incidence describes the direction from which a light ray reaches a surface. It is measured between the incoming ray and an imaginary line called the normal, which is perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray arrives. It is not measured from the surface itself. Like other angles, it can be expressed in degrees or radians. When light passes between materials such as air and water, it may change direction, a process called refraction. Each material has a refractive index related to how fast light travels through it. Snell’s law uses these indices and the angles on either side of the boundary to predict the bending: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where θ₁ is the angle of incidence and θ₂ is the angle of refraction.

A force is a push or pull that can change an object’s motion. Force is a vector, which means it has both a size and a direction. On a free-body diagram, arrows show the forces acting on an object. In Newtonian mechanics, Newton’s second law says that the net force—the combined effect of all those forces—equals the object’s mass multiplied by its acceleration. A spring provides a useful example: when an ideal spring is stretched or compressed, it exerts a restoring force that points back toward its equilibrium position. The farther the spring is displaced, the greater this force becomes. Hooke’s law describes this relationship: the spring force equals minus the spring constant times the displacement, where the minus sign shows that the force points opposite to the displacement.

Yeasts are single-celled fungi that feed on sugars. When they ferment sugar, they produce carbon dioxide gas and alcohol. The gas forms bubbles that make bread dough rise, while the alcohol produced during fermentation is important in brewing beer and making wine. The species most widely used in baking and brewing is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, also called baker’s yeast. In 1996, it became the first eukaryote—an organism whose cells have a nucleus—to have its entire genome sequenced. Scientists study yeast because it is easy to grow and shares many basic cell processes with other eukaryotes. Yeasts are also used to make biofuels, and genetically engineered strains can produce medicines such as insulin and components of hepatitis B vaccines.

The greenhouse effect is the warming of Earth’s surface and lower atmosphere when gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapor, and methane absorb infrared radiation emitted by the warm surface and re-emit some of it toward Earth. This natural process keeps the planet warm enough for life, but increasing greenhouse gas concentrations strengthens it and raises global temperatures. Warming can also trigger positive feedback loops: for example, warmer air can hold more water vapor, which is itself a greenhouse gas and can cause further warming. Ozone, a molecule made of three oxygen atoms, is another greenhouse gas. Most atmospheric ozone is found in a layer in the stratosphere, where it absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation. That protective role is different from the greenhouse effect, which involves infrared radiation.

The troposphere is the lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere, beginning at the surface and extending roughly 8 to 15 kilometers upward, depending on location. It contains most of the atmosphere’s water vapor, so clouds, rain, storms, and nearly all other weather occur there. Air in the troposphere normally gets cooler as altitude increases, allowing warmer air near the ground to rise and mix with the air above. Sometimes, however, a layer of warmer air sits over cooler air at the surface. This temperature inversion prevents much of that vertical mixing. In cities, an inversion can trap pollutants near the ground, including smog, a visible and harmful form of air pollution.

An AND gate is a basic building block of digital circuits. It takes two or more inputs, each represented as 1 (true) or 0 (false), and produces a 1 only when every input is 1. For a two-input AND gate, the output is 1 for the pair 1,1 and 0 for 0,0, 0,1, or 1,0. This makes it useful when two conditions must both be met, such as a machine running only if its power is on and its safety switch is closed. A NAND gate is an AND gate followed by a NOT operation, which inverts the output. A two-input NAND gate therefore produces 0 only for 1,1. NAND is called a universal gate because other logic gates and entire circuits can be built using NAND gates alone.

Fructose is a monosaccharide, or simple sugar, found naturally in many fruits and in honey. It tastes sweeter than glucose, another simple sugar. When fructose and glucose bond together, they form sucrose, the sugar commonly used at the table. Fructose is also found alongside glucose in high-fructose corn syrup, a sweetener used in many foods and drinks. To make it, producers first break down starch from corn, also called maize or Zea mays, into a glucose-rich syrup. Enzymes then convert some of that glucose into fructose. Common versions of high-fructose corn syrup contain about 42% or 55% fructose; most of the remaining sugar is glucose. Its name describes its fructose content compared with ordinary corn syrup, not a syrup made entirely of fructose.

Omicron is a variant of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. It was identified in southern Africa in late 2021, with early cases detected in Botswana and South Africa, and was quickly designated a variant of concern because it spread rapidly. Omicron has many mutations in its spike protein, the part of the virus that helps it enter human cells. These changes helped it spread more easily than earlier variants, including Delta. As Omicron continued to evolve, it produced related subvariants. After BA.2 and BA.4 circulated, the Omicron subvariant BA.5 became the dominant SARS-CoV-2 strain in the United States during the summer of 2022. Vaccination and well-fitting masks can help reduce the risk of severe illness and transmission.

The Reynolds number is a dimensionless quantity that helps engineers predict how a fluid, such as water or air, will move. Named after British physicist Osborne Reynolds, it combines the fluid’s speed and density with a characteristic length, such as a pipe’s diameter, and its viscosity, or resistance to flowing. At low Reynolds numbers, flow tends to be laminar: the fluid moves smoothly in orderly layers. At higher numbers, it can become turbulent, with swirling motion and unpredictable changes in velocity and pressure. In a circular pipe, a Reynolds number above about 4,000 generally indicates turbulent flow. Engineers use this distinction when designing pipes, aircraft, and other systems where fluid movement matters.

Active galactic nuclei, or AGNs, are exceptionally bright, energetic regions at the centers of some galaxies. They are powered by supermassive black holes surrounded by accretion disks of gas and other matter. As matter spirals inward, it heats up and releases enormous amounts of energy before crossing the black hole’s boundary. AGNs can outshine the rest of their galaxies and send energy into surrounding gas, sometimes heating it enough to slow the formation of new stars. Quasars and blazars are types of AGN. Some AGNs also launch narrow jets of particles moving at nearly the speed of light. A blazar is an AGN whose jet points almost directly toward Earth, making its emission appear especially strong and rapidly variable.

The Navier–Stokes equations describe how fluids such as water and air move. They relate a fluid’s velocity and pressure to the forces acting on it, including friction within the fluid, called viscosity, while expressing conservation of momentum. Scientists and engineers use these equations to study fluid flow, but their solutions can be difficult to calculate when the flow is turbulent. Turbulence is chaotic flow with irregular swirling motions called eddies, which occur at many sizes. At the smallest sizes, known as Kolmogorov microscales, the swirling energy is dissipated by viscosity. Turbulent flow is common at high Reynolds numbers and contrasts with laminar flow, in which fluid moves in smooth layers. Averaging the Navier–Stokes equations over time helps computers model turbulence, such as the air movements that cause bumpy airplane rides.

A prism is a transparent object with angled faces, often shaped like a triangle, that bends light as it enters and leaves. This bending is called refraction. When white light passes through a glass prism, it spreads into a spectrum of colors because different wavelengths bend by different amounts. Wavelength is the distance between successive peaks of a light wave; red light has a longer wavelength than blue light. How strongly light bends also depends on the material’s index of refraction, a number that compares the speed of light in a vacuum with its speed in that material. A vacuum has an index of refraction of exactly 1, air’s is almost 1, and water’s is about 1.33.

The Three-Body Problem is the challenge of predicting how three objects, such as stars or planets, move when each pulls on the others through gravity. Newton’s law says that gravitational attraction grows with the objects’ masses and weakens with the square of the distance between them. With two bodies, their orbits can be described by a general formula, but adding a third makes their motions interdependent, so there is generally no closed-form solution for arbitrary starting positions and speeds. Mathematicians have found special cases, however. Joseph-Louis Lagrange described a solution in which the three bodies remain at the corners of an equilateral triangle as they orbit their common center of mass. His name is also attached to five equilibrium points in the restricted three-body problem, where a much smaller third body moves under the influence of two larger ones.

Corundum is a crystalline mineral made mainly of aluminum oxide. It is best known for its colorful gem varieties: red corundum is ruby, while corundum of other gem colors is called sapphire. Corundum has a hardness of 9 on the Mohs scale, a ranking of minerals by their ability to scratch one another. On this scale, a harder mineral can scratch a softer one. Talc is the softest reference mineral, at 1, and diamond is the hardest, at 10. Because the numbers are ranks rather than equal steps in hardness, the difference between 9 and 10 is not necessarily the same as the difference between 1 and 2. Corundum’s high hardness makes it useful not only as a gemstone but also as an abrasive for grinding and polishing.

The kinetic isotope effect is a change in a chemical reaction’s rate when an atom in a reacting molecule is replaced by a different isotope of the same element. Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different masses. In hydrogen-transfer reactions, researchers often replace ordinary hydrogen, called protium, with deuterium. Deuterium is a stable hydrogen isotope whose nucleus has one proton and one neutron, making it roughly twice as massive as protium. The heavier atom changes how bonds vibrate and can make it less likely that a hydrogen atom will pass through an energy barrier by quantum tunneling. By comparing reaction rates with different isotopes, scientists can learn how a reaction works, including whether tunneling occurs in an enzyme.

Electricity is a form of energy carried by moving electric charges. In the heart, electrical signals spread through specialized cells, including Purkinje cells, to coordinate each heartbeat. During cardiac arrest, the heart may stop pumping blood effectively, sometimes because its electrical activity has become chaotic. An automated external defibrillator (AED) uses pads placed on the chest to check the heart’s rhythm. If a shock is needed, the AED delivers a brief, controlled burst of electricity that can interrupt the chaotic rhythm and give the heart a chance to resume coordinated contractions. While an AED is being prepared, responders should begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). CPR uses repeated chest compressions, at least 2 inches deep for an adult, to help keep blood circulating.

Molecular hydrogen is the gaseous form of hydrogen, the element with atomic number 1. Its formula is H₂ because each molecule contains two hydrogen atoms bonded together. This colorless, odorless gas is an important fuel and industrial raw material. In a fuel cell, hydrogen reacts with oxygen to produce electricity, with water as the main product. Industry also uses molecular hydrogen to make ammonia, which is needed for many fertilizers. In the Haber–Bosch process, hydrogen reacts with nitrogen over an iron-based catalyst at high temperature and pressure to produce ammonia on a large scale. Hydrogen can also be added to other substances in reactions called hydrogenation; for example, it can react with an alkyne using Lindlar’s catalyst.

Ayurveda is a traditional system of healing that developed in South Asia. Its Sanskrit name is commonly translated as “knowledge of life.” Ayurvedic practitioners use dietary guidance, herbal remedies, massage, and other practices to support health. A central idea is that the body has three functional principles, collectively called the doshas: vata is associated with movement, pitta with transformation and digestion, and kapha with structure and stability. Traditionally, health is understood as a balance among these doshas, though they are not the same as structures or processes identified by modern medical science. Some Ayurvedic practices may help people feel better, but many treatments have not been shown to work in rigorous studies, and some herbal products can be unsafe or interact with medicines.

Bitcoin is a digital currency that lets people send money directly to one another over the internet without relying on a central bank. It was described in a 2008 white paper under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto and launched in 2009. The real identity of its creator, who stopped communicating publicly around 2011, remains unknown. Bitcoin transactions are recorded on a public blockchain: a shared ledger that many computers can check. To add new groups of transactions, miners compete to solve computational puzzles in a process called proof-of-work. This helps secure the network but uses substantial electricity. In 2021, El Salvador became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender, meaning it could officially be used to pay debts.

Blue light is the short-wavelength part of visible light, near the violet end of the spectrum. Sunlight contains many colors, but as it travels through Earth’s atmosphere, air molecules redirect some of it in different directions. This redirection is called scattering. When the molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of the light, the process is called Rayleigh scattering. It affects shorter wavelengths much more strongly than longer ones, so blue light is scattered far more than red light. The scattered blue light reaches your eyes from across the sky, giving a clear daytime sky its familiar color. Violet light is scattered even more strongly, but the Sun produces less of it, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet, so the sky looks blue rather than violet.

Vitamin B12, also called cobalamin, is an essential vitamin with a cobalt atom at its center. It is found naturally mainly in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs, and milk, though some foods are fortified with it. The body needs B12 to make DNA, form normal red blood cells, and keep nerves healthy. Absorbing it takes several steps: in the stomach, B12 eventually binds to intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein made by cells called parietal cells. This partnership lets B12 be absorbed in the terminal ileum, the last part of the small intestine. If the immune system destroys the parietal cells, too little intrinsic factor is produced, so B12 cannot be absorbed properly. The resulting deficiency can cause pernicious anemia and may also damage nerves.

Environmental protection means caring for the natural world and reducing the harm people cause to it. It includes conserving ecosystems, protecting wildlife and habitats, reducing pollution, and using resources in ways that can continue into the future. Cutting carbon emissions is an important part of this effort because gases released by burning fossil fuels contribute to climate change, which can damage ecosystems. Environmental protection is also a central goal of green politics, a political approach that puts ecological concerns, such as conservation and climate action, alongside social priorities.
