For example, Australia’s “teal” independent politicians have been associated with green politics and liberal social positions. Whether people act through government policy, businesses, or everyday choices, the broad goal is to protect the environment for current and future generations.

The El Niño–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO, is a recurring climate pattern in which ocean temperatures and atmospheric conditions change together across the tropical Pacific. Shifts in sea-surface temperature affect air pressure and wind circulation, which can alter rainfall and storms far beyond the Pacific. ENSO’s warm phase is called El Niño: surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific become warmer than usual, often weakening the trade winds and changing weather patterns worldwide. Its cool phase is called La Niña, when those waters become cooler than usual. ENSO’s effects vary from year to year. In 2010, an El Niño-related drought in Venezuela was linked to a temporary disappearance of the frequent lightning over Lake Maracaibo.

DNA replication is the process by which a cell copies its DNA before division. It occurs during S phase of the cell cycle and begins at specific locations called origins of replication. As the DNA double helix unwinds, it forms fork-shaped junctions called replication forks. Topoisomerases relieve the twisting strain caused by this unwinding. Each original strand serves as a template for a new strand, so each finished DNA molecule contains one old strand and one new strand; this is why replication is called semiconservative. DNA polymerases build the new strands, but they work differently at the two sides of a fork. The leading strand is made continuously, while the lagging strand is made in short segments called Okazaki fragments. Each fragment starts with an RNA primer, and DNA ligase joins the fragments together.

Parrots are birds in the order Psittaciformes, a group that includes macaws, cockatoos, and parakeets. Many have bright feathers, and their strong, hooked bills help them crack seeds and nuts and climb among branches. Parrots are also known for their intelligence and, in some species, their ability to imitate sounds, including human speech. A famous fictional example appears in Robert Louis Stevenson’s Treasure Island: the pirate Long John Silver keeps a talkative parrot named Captain Flint. The bird is named after the deceased pirate whose buried treasure drives the story. Another parrot appears in Julian Barnes’s novel Flaubert’s Parrot, in which a doctor searches for a stuffed parrot connected to the French writer Gustave Flaubert.

A software project often depends on knowledge held by its contributors: how the code works, why certain decisions were made, and how to fix problems. The bus factor is the smallest number of contributors whose sudden unavailability would seriously stall development or stop the project. Its name comes from the imagined example of team members being hit by a bus, but any reason for leaving or becoming unavailable counts. A low bus factor means greater risk: if only one or two people understand crucial parts of a project, losing them could cause major delays. Teams can reduce this risk by documenting their work, sharing responsibilities, and helping more contributors learn the code. A 2016 study of 133 popular projects hosted on GitHub estimated that 65 percent had a bus factor below three.

James Watt was a Scottish engineer and instrument maker who made steam engines much more efficient during the Industrial Revolution. Earlier engines, including Thomas Newcomen’s practical design, used steam to move a piston inside a cylinder, often to pump water out of mines. Watt noticed that these engines wasted fuel because the cylinder had to be heated by incoming steam and then cooled each time the steam condensed. His solution was the separate condenser, a chamber where steam could cool and turn back into water while the working cylinder stayed hot. Watt patented this improved design in 1769. It reduced heat loss and fuel consumption, helping steam power become useful for more kinds of machinery. Although Watt is sometimes called the inventor of the steam engine, he improved an existing invention.

Psychiatric hospitals provide inpatient housing and treatment for people with mental illness. Unlike outpatient clinics, where patients visit for appointments and then go home, psychiatric hospitals can provide care around the clock. They have also been called mental hospitals or asylums, especially in the past. During the 1800s, reformers pushed for better treatment of patients, but conditions varied widely. In 1887, journalist Nellie Bly pretended to have a mental illness so she could enter a psychiatric hospital on Blackwell’s Island in New York City, now called Roosevelt Island. After leaving, she described the harsh conditions she had witnessed in Ten Days in a Mad-House. Her investigation helped draw public attention to how patients were treated.

Mitosis is the process in which a cell divides its nucleus so that two daughter cells receive genetically similar sets of chromosomes. Before mitosis begins, the cell copies its DNA, creating duplicated chromosomes made of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. During metaphase, these chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell, and spindle fibers attach to them. The next stage, anaphase, begins when the sister chromatids separate and the spindle fibers pull them toward opposite poles. The nuclei then reform, and the cell usually divides into two. Checkpoints help ensure that DNA has been copied correctly before division continues. Mitosis supports growth and repair and differs from meiosis, which produces sex cells with half the usual number of chromosomes.

Mustard gas is a chemical warfare agent used in World War I. Its molecules contain a sulfur atom attached to two 2-chloroethyl groups, so it contains both sulfur and chlorine. It is a blister agent: exposure can cause severe burns and blisters on the skin and damage the eyes and lungs. Despite its name, mustard gas is usually a liquid at room temperature; its common name comes from an odor sometimes compared to mustard. Its wartime history is linked to chemist Fritz Haber, who helped develop the use of chlorine as a weapon. Haber also helped create the Haber–Bosch process, which combines nitrogen from the air with hydrogen under high pressure to make ammonia. That ammonia made large-scale fertilizer production possible.

Nucleotides are the small molecules that join together to form DNA and RNA. Each nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and one or more phosphate groups. The sugar is deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA. Neighboring nucleotides connect through phosphodiester bonds, forming a long sugar-phosphate backbone. Their bases include adenine and guanine, which are purines, and cytosine and thymine, which are pyrimidines; RNA uses uracil instead of thymine. Bases on opposite DNA strands pair through hydrogen bonds, helping the molecule store and copy genetic information. Nucleotides also have other jobs in cells. Adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, is a nucleotide made of adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups. It is widely known as the cell’s primary energy currency because cells use it to power many activities.

Saliva is a watery fluid made mainly by salivary glands around the mouth, including the parotid and submandibular glands. It keeps the tongue and mouth moist, lubricates food so it is easier to chew and swallow, and dissolves chemicals in food so they can reach taste receptors. Saliva also begins digestion before food reaches the stomach. An enzyme called salivary amylase starts breaking down starch, a carbohydrate, into smaller sugars. Once swallowed food reaches the stomach, acidic conditions greatly reduce this enzyme’s activity. Saliva contains antimicrobial substances that help control microbes in the mouth. It also carries minerals such as calcium, phosphate, and fluoride that help repair tooth enamel, the hard outer covering of teeth.

An algorithm is a finite, precisely specified sequence of instructions for solving a problem or producing an output. Each step must be clear enough to follow without guessing, and the process must eventually stop. Long division is an everyday example: it gives a set of steps for calculating an answer. In computer science, algorithms tell computers how to process information, but an algorithm does not have to be written as a computer program. British mathematician Alan Turing introduced an abstract model of computation called the Turing machine. It has an unbounded tape divided into spaces, a head that reads and writes symbols on the tape, and a finite set of rules that determine what it does next. This model helps scientists study what algorithms can compute.

Rubber is an elastomer, a polymer that can stretch and return to its original shape. Natural rubber is harvested as a milky liquid called latex from rubber trees, while synthetic rubbers are made from chemicals; neoprene is one example. Rubber’s flexibility makes it useful for tires, hoses, and elastic bands, but untreated rubber can become sticky in heat or brittle in cold. The American inventor Charles Goodyear discovered that heating rubber with sulfur makes it stronger and more durable. This process, called vulcanization, creates links between the polymer chains so they hold together better while still allowing the rubber to stretch. Too many sulfur links can produce a hard material called ebonite. Ozone in the air can also damage some rubbers, causing cracks over time.

Sediment is loose material, such as sand, silt, pebbles, and mud, that forms when rocks are broken down by weathering. Weathering breaks rock apart or changes it, while erosion moves the resulting particles from one place to another by water, wind, or ice. When sediment is deposited and builds up in layers, pressure may compact it, and minerals may cement the particles together to form sedimentary rock. Glaciers also pick up and carry sediment and larger pieces of rock. This mixed, unsorted material is called till. As a glacier melts or retreats, it can leave till in long ridges along its sides or near the farthest point it reached. These glacial deposits are called moraines.

Sterilization is a medical procedure intended to provide permanent contraception, meaning it prevents pregnancy without requiring a method to be used each time someone has sex. In male sterilization, called a vasectomy, a surgeon cuts or seals the vas deferens, the tubes that carry sperm from the testes. Sperm can then no longer enter the semen. Female sterilization, often called tubal ligation or tubectomy, blocks or cuts the fallopian tubes so sperm and an egg cannot meet. These procedures are intended to be permanent and do not protect against sexually transmitted infections. Sterilization should be a voluntary, informed choice. During India’s Emergency in the 1970s, however, the government’s population-control campaign forced many people, especially poor men and women, to undergo sterilization.

In a reversible reaction, equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. The equilibrium constant, K, describes that mixture at a specified temperature. For a balanced reaction, chemists calculate K by multiplying the product concentrations, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, and dividing by the similarly calculated reactant terms. The reaction quotient, Q, uses the same calculation but applies to a mixture at any moment, even before equilibrium. Comparing Q with K predicts the direction of net change: if Q is less than K, the reaction tends to produce more products; if Q is greater than K, it tends to produce more reactants. At equilibrium, Q equals K.

Insulin is a peptide hormone made by beta cells in the pancreas that helps keep blood glucose, or blood sugar, at a healthy level. When insulin binds to its receptor on a cell, the receptor’s tyrosine kinase activity starts signals that help cells take up glucose from the bloodstream. Insulin also encourages the liver and muscles to store glucose as glycogen, lowering blood glucose. It works alongside glucagon, a hormone that raises blood glucose when it is too low. Beta cells first make insulin as a larger molecule called proinsulin. They then cut out a connecting segment called C-peptide, releasing it alongside mature insulin. Measuring C-peptide helps doctors assess how much insulin a person’s own pancreas makes. In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys beta cells, causing an insulin deficiency.

Dark energy is the name for a poorly understood component of the universe that appears to make its expansion speed up. Scientists estimate that it accounts for about 68 percent of the universe’s total energy content, compared with about 27 percent for dark matter. Key evidence came in the late 1990s from observations of distant Type Ia supernovae, a class of stellar explosions whose brightness can be used to estimate distance. Astronomers compared how bright these supernovae appeared with predictions for a universe whose expansion was slowing down. The explosions appeared dimmer, and therefore farther away, than expected. This showed that the universe’s expansion was accelerating instead. Scientists call the cause dark energy, but they do not yet know exactly what it is.

Rabies is a viral disease that affects the nervous system of mammals, including humans and dogs. It usually spreads when saliva from an infected animal enters a bite wound. The virus travels along nerves toward the brain, where it can cause agitation, confusion, difficulty swallowing, and hydrophobia—a fear of water caused by painful swallowing spasms. Dogs with rabies may become unusually aggressive and bite, spreading the virus to others. Once symptoms appear, rabies is nearly always fatal, so someone bitten by a possibly rabid animal needs urgent medical care. In 1885, the French chemist and microbiologist Louis Pasteur gave a pioneering post-exposure rabies vaccine to Joseph Meister, a boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog.

Tapeworms are long, ribbon-shaped parasitic flatworms that mature in the intestines of vertebrates, including humans and pigs. Their bodies consist of many segments, but unlike most animals, they have no digestive tract. Instead, they absorb nutrients from food already digested by their host through their outer covering. At the front of a tapeworm is an anchoring organ called the scolex, which attaches to the intestinal wall using suckers and, in some species, hooks. A person can acquire certain tapeworms by eating undercooked infected meat, including pork, so cooking meat thoroughly helps prevent infection. Although tapeworms may grow to remarkable lengths, most of that length consists of repeated body segments rather than a complex system of organs.

Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is a peptide messenger released by four small parathyroid glands on the back of the thyroid gland when blood calcium levels fall. Calcium is needed for muscle movement, nerve signaling, and other body functions, so PTH helps bring its level back up. In bones such as the femur and tibia, PTH signals bone-forming cells called osteoblasts, which in turn increase the activity of osteoclasts. Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells that break down mineralized bone in a process called bone resorption, releasing calcium into the blood. PTH also acts on the kidneys to reduce calcium loss in urine and stimulate production of active vitamin D, which helps the intestines absorb calcium from food. If PTH remains too high for too long, bone density and strength can decrease.

Hormones are chemical messengers that help coordinate activities throughout the body. Glands in the endocrine system release them into the bloodstream, which carries them to cells with matching receptors. Different hormones regulate growth, metabolism, reproduction, and other processes. They include protein or peptide hormones, such as insulin, and lipid-based hormones, such as testosterone. The pituitary gland sits at the base of the brain and releases many hormones, including human growth hormone (HGH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). One peptide hormone, oxytocin, is made in a nearby brain region called the hypothalamus but is stored and released by the posterior pituitary. Oxytocin helps trigger uterine contractions during childbirth and milk ejection during breastfeeding. It is also associated with social bonding, including bonds between parents and newborns.

A bacteriophage, or phage, is a virus that infects bacteria. Many phages attach to a bacterial cell and inject their genetic material, using the cell’s machinery to make more viruses. The T2 bacteriophage infects E. coli and played a key role in the 1952 Hershey–Chase experiment, which helped scientists identify DNA as genetic material. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase labeled the phage’s DNA with radioactive phosphorus and its protein coat with radioactive sulfur. After the phages infected bacteria, the researchers found that the DNA had entered the cells while most of the protein coats remained outside. This showed that DNA, rather than protein, carries the instructions a phage passes on when it reproduces.

Silver is a precious metal with atomic number 47 and the chemical symbol Ag. It has the highest electrical conductivity of any metal, making it useful in electronic contacts and circuits. Silver is also used in jewelry, coins, and medals, including many second-place awards. Unlike iron, it does not rust, but it can tarnish: sulfur-containing compounds in the air react with its surface to form a dark layer of silver sulfide. Silver iodide, a crystalline compound made from silver and iodine, has a different use. Its crystals can help ice form, so they are dispersed into clouds in a process called cloud seeding. Silver iodide was also used in photographic materials because it reacts to light.

A fluid is a substance that flows and continuously changes shape when a shear force pushes one part of it sideways relative to another. Liquids and gases are both fluids: a liquid keeps nearly the same volume but takes the shape of its container, while a gas can expand to fill the container. Fluid motion can be described by the Navier–Stokes equations, which account for forces such as pressure and internal friction. That internal resistance to flow is called viscosity. Honey, for example, has a higher viscosity than water and flows more slowly under similar conditions. The Reynolds number compares inertial effects with the effects of viscosity. If viscosity is set to zero in the Navier–Stokes equations, they become the idealized Euler equations.

The Iron Hand of Götz von Berlichingen was an early prosthetic hand made for a German knight after he lost his right hand to a cannonball during the 1504 siege of Landshut, a city in Bavaria. Built in the early sixteenth century, the metal device had articulated fingers that could be moved into position, allowing Götz to grip objects rather than simply cover his injury. Its mechanical design made it a remarkable example of replacement technology for its time. Götz became known as “Götz of the Iron Hand” and later took part in the German Peasants’ War. The hand shows how craftspeople used engineering to help someone adapt to a serious injury centuries before modern prosthetics existed.

Neanderthals were an extinct group of close human relatives who lived across Europe and Asia, a region called Eurasia, until roughly 40,000 years ago. They made tools, adapted to cold environments, and sometimes had children with the ancestors of modern humans. Because of this interbreeding, many people living today carry small fragments of Neanderthal DNA. Researchers can identify those fragments by comparing DNA sequences from living people with DNA recovered from Neanderthal fossils. Before sequencing a particular stretch of DNA, scientists may make many copies of it using polymerase chain reaction, or PCR. PCR repeatedly heats and cools a sample in a machine called a thermal cycler. A heat-stable enzyme, often Taq polymerase, builds new DNA strands during each cycle.

A galactic bar is an elongated concentration of stars stretching across the center of some spiral galaxies. Spiral arms often begin near the ends of the bar, giving these galaxies their distinctive shape. In the Hubble tuning fork, a system for classifying galaxies by appearance, barred spiral galaxies lie on the lower branch and have the two-letter designation SB. The Milky Way is an example of a barred spiral galaxy. Although the bar looks like a solid structure, it is made of stars that orbit the galactic center. Patterns in the movement of stars and gas help the bar persist over long periods, despite the fact that different parts of the galaxy rotate at different speeds.

Acceleration due to gravity describes how quickly an object’s velocity changes when it falls freely under Earth’s gravitational pull. Near Earth’s surface, it is usually written as g and approximated as 9.8 meters per second squared. That means a falling object’s downward velocity increases by about 9.8 meters per second each second, if air resistance is ignored. The actual value varies slightly from place to place because of factors such as latitude and elevation. To provide a consistent reference for calculations, scientists also use standard gravity, defined as exactly 9.80665 meters per second squared. Standard gravity is a fixed, agreed-upon value, not a measurement that must match the gravitational acceleration at every location.

The Grashof number is a dimensionless quantity engineers use to describe natural convection: fluid motion caused by heating rather than by a pump or fan. When a fluid warms, it usually expands and becomes less dense. Gravity then causes the warmer fluid to rise relative to cooler, denser fluid. This upward effect is called buoyancy, and viscous forces resist the motion. The Grashof number compares buoyancy-driven forces with that viscous resistance. A larger value means buoyancy has a stronger influence on the flow. Its value depends on gravity, how much the fluid expands with temperature, the temperature difference, a characteristic length such as the height of a heated surface, and the fluid’s kinematic viscosity. Engineers use it to predict how heat moves through fluids.

The bonobo is an endangered great ape that lives in forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River. It is one of two living species in the genus Pan; the other is the common chimpanzee. Bonobos are generally smaller and more slender than common chimpanzees, but the two are close relatives. The Congo River is a major Central African river that flows westward into the Atlantic Ocean. It separates the bonobo’s range from areas where common chimpanzees live. Because these apes do not swim well, scientists think the river may have helped separate their ancestors, allowing the two species to evolve independently. Bonobos are threatened by habitat loss and hunting.

Physicians are medical professionals who diagnose illnesses, recommend treatments, and care for patients. Some physicians specialize in surgery, treating injuries or disease through operations. In the nineteenth century, surgeons often taught in operating theaters, where students watched procedures from rows of seats. American artist Thomas Eakins painted two famous scenes of physicians at work: The Gross Clinic and The Agnew Clinic. In The Gross Clinic, painted in 1875, surgeon Samuel Gross leads an operation on a patient’s thigh before an audience at Jefferson Medical College. Eakins later painted surgeon Hayes Agnew demonstrating an operation. These paintings show how physicians combined patient care with teaching future doctors.

A binary star system consists of two stars held together by gravity. Rather than one star simply circling the other, both orbit a shared center of mass, although the more massive star usually moves less. The stars may look close together in the sky, but a true binary is physically bound, unlike a chance alignment of distant stars. Astronomers often call the brighter or more massive member the primary and label it “A”; its companion is labeled “B.” A well-known example is the Sirius system. Sirius A is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky, while its much fainter companion, Sirius B, is a white dwarf nicknamed the Pup. Studying binary stars helps astronomers measure stellar masses by observing how the stars move around each other.

The Richter magnitude scale is a way to describe the size, or magnitude, of an earthquake using seismic waves recorded by instruments called seismographs. It was introduced in 1935 by American seismologist Charles F. Richter, who developed it with Beno Gutenberg at Caltech to study earthquakes in Southern California. The scale is logarithmic: an increase of one whole number means the recorded wave amplitude is ten times greater. An earthquake above magnitude 7.0 is generally considered major. Scientists now usually use the moment magnitude scale instead, especially for large earthquakes, because it estimates magnitude from seismic moment, which reflects the area of a fault that slipped, how far it moved, and the strength of the rock.

Unix is a family of operating systems that began as a Bell Labs project in the late 1960s. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie were key developers, and Ritchie also helped create the C programming language. Unix was later rewritten largely in C, making it easier to move to different kinds of computers and helping it spread beyond Bell Labs. Its design favors small, understandable programs that each do one job well. Users can connect these programs with “pipes,” which send the output of one program into another to handle more complex tasks. Dennis Ritchie later coauthored The C Programming Language with Brian Kernighan. Unix influenced many later operating systems, including Linux, but Linux is not Unix itself.

Fossil fuels are energy sources formed from the remains of prehistoric plants and other organisms that were buried and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years. The three main fossil fuels are coal, petroleum (crude oil), and natural gas. People burn them to generate electricity, power vehicles, and heat buildings. Natural gas is composed mainly of methane and, in its pure form, is colorless and odorless. It is commonly piped to homes for cooking and heating; suppliers add a strong-smelling substance so leaks are easier to detect. Fossil fuels are nonrenewable because they form far more slowly than we use them. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, which contributes to climate change, so efforts to reduce their use include switching to cleaner energy sources.

An Archimedean screw is a machine that raises water from a lower level to a higher one. It has a central shaft with a spiral, blade-like surface wrapped around it, often inside an inclined pipe or trough. As the screw rotates, water becomes trapped in pockets between the spiral’s turns and is carried upward until it flows out at the top. The spiral surface is called the helical flight: “helical” means spiral-shaped, and each turn of the flight helps hold and move the water. A screw is a simple machine formed by wrapping an inclined plane around a cylinder. Named after the ancient Greek scientist Archimedes, this design has long been used for irrigation and drainage, and it can also move materials such as grain.

Thunder is the sound made when lightning rapidly heats the air around it. The air expands so suddenly that it creates a sharp pressure disturbance called a shock wave. As this wave travels outward and weakens, it becomes an ordinary sound wave that reaches your ears as thunder. Nearby thunder may sound like a loud crack, while thunder from farther away often sounds like a long rumble. The rumbling happens partly because sound from different sections of a lightning bolt travels different distances to reach you. You see lightning before you hear thunder because light travels much faster than sound. Although thunder can be startling, the lightning that produces it is the main danger during a storm.

A positron is the antimatter counterpart of an electron. It has the same mass as an electron but the opposite electric charge: positive instead of negative. Its charge is plus one in units of the elementary charge. Positrons can be produced in beta-plus decay, a type of radioactive decay that occurs in some unstable atomic nuclei. In this process, a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron, and the nucleus emits a positron and an electron neutrino. The number of protons therefore decreases by one, changing the atom into a different element. If an emitted positron later meets an electron, the two can annihilate, converting their mass into energy, usually in the form of gamma rays.

The stomach is a muscular digestive organ between the esophagus and the small intestine. After you swallow, food travels down the esophagus into the stomach, where it is stored temporarily and mixed by the stomach’s muscular walls. Glands in its lining release gastric acid and digestive enzymes that help break food down before it moves into the small intestine. One of these enzymes is pepsin, which digests proteins. Cells called chief cells release it in an inactive form, pepsinogen; gastric acid then activates it, allowing it to work in the stomach. A protective mucus layer helps shield the stomach lining from the acid. The spleen, an organ that filters blood, lies next to the stomach.

A chariot was a light, horse-drawn vehicle with two spoked wheels, usually carrying a driver and sometimes a warrior. Spoked wheels were lighter than solid wheels, helping horses pull chariots quickly across suitable ground. Ancient peoples used chariots in warfare, transport, ceremonies, and racing. One of the most famous chariot battles was the Battle of Kadesh, fought near the Orontes River around 1274 BCE between the forces of Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Muwatalli II. It is often cited as the largest clash of chariots in history. Egypt and the Hittites later made one of the earliest surviving peace treaties. Chariot racing remained popular for centuries, including in the Byzantine Empire, where rival fans helped spark the Nika riots.

The Einstein–Smoluchowski relation connects two ways a tiny particle moves through a fluid at thermal equilibrium. Random collisions with surrounding molecules make the particle wander, a motion called Brownian motion. Its diffusion coefficient measures how quickly this wandering spreads it out. If an external force is applied, the particle also drifts in the force’s direction. Mobility is the particle’s drift velocity per unit applied force, so it measures how readily the particle responds. The relation states that the diffusion coefficient equals mobility multiplied by Boltzmann’s constant and the absolute temperature: D = μkBT. In other words, faster random spreading is linked to greater mobility or higher thermal energy. The relation is named after Albert Einstein and Marian Smoluchowski, who studied Brownian motion.

The Einstein tensor is a way to describe how spacetime curves in Albert Einstein’s theory of general relativity. It is built from the Ricci tensor, which measures aspects of curvature: subtract one-half of the Ricci scalar (a single-number measure of curvature) multiplied by the metric, which describes distances in spacetime. Mathematically, Gμν = Rμν − ½Rgμν. The Einstein tensor has zero covariant divergence, a property that fits with the conservation of energy and momentum. It appears on the geometric side of the Einstein field equations, opposite the stress-energy tensor, which describes matter and energy. In their simplest form, the equations say Gμν = (8πG/c⁴)Tμν; they can also include a cosmological-constant term.

The Three Gorges Dam is a huge hydroelectric dam built across the Yangtze River near Sandouping in China’s Hubei province. Water held behind the dam forms a reservoir that stretches far upstream. As water passes through turbines, it generates electricity; the dam also helps control floods and makes shipping easier. Building it flooded many towns and farmland, requiring more than a million people to relocate. The river it spans, the Yangtze, is China’s longest river. It begins on the Tibetan Plateau, flows eastward across the country, and empties into the East China Sea near Shanghai. The dam shows how a major engineering project can provide power while also changing landscapes, ecosystems, and people’s lives.

Optics is the branch of physics that studies light and how it behaves when it meets different materials. It includes reflection, when light bounces off a surface, and refraction, when light changes direction as it passes from one material to another. Lenses use refraction to focus light, while prisms can bend light and separate white light into colors. Isaac Newton investigated these effects in experiments with prisms. He described them in his 1704 book Opticks, whose title uses an older, Latinized spelling rather than the modern name of the field, optics. Newton also argued that light was made of tiny particles called corpuscles. Today, scientists describe light as having both wave-like and particle-like properties.

New World monkeys are primates native mainly to the forests of Central and South America. They include capuchins, howler monkeys, and spider monkeys, whose long arms help them swing through branches. Many spend much of their lives in trees, eating foods such as fruit, leaves, and insects. Some New World monkeys have prehensile tails that can curl around branches and help them climb. The family Atelidae includes spider monkeys, howler monkeys, woolly monkeys, and muriquis. Atelids have fully prehensile tails strong enough to help support their weight as they move through the treetops. Not every New World monkey has such a tail: capuchins, for example, belong to a different family.

Google Maps is a web-based mapping service made by Google. It lets users explore interactive maps, search for places, and get directions for driving, walking, cycling, or public transit. Users can switch from a standard road map to satellite imagery to see an area from above. For a view from the ground, Google Maps offers Street View, which shows panoramic images captured along streets and at other locations. The small yellow figure called Pegman helps users find these views: dragging Pegman onto a map highlights places where Street View imagery is available, and dropping him on one opens the panorama. Street View images are also used in GeoGuessr, a game in which players study their surroundings and try to guess where in the world they are.

Poliomyelitis, usually called polio, is an infectious disease caused by the poliovirus. It mainly affects children and spreads through contact with infected feces, often in contaminated food or water. Many infections cause few or no symptoms, but the virus can sometimes attack motor neurons, the nerve cells that control muscles. This can cause sudden, limp weakness known as acute flaccid paralysis. If the breathing muscles become paralyzed, a person may need mechanical ventilation; before modern ventilators, an iron lung could help them breathe. Franklin D. Roosevelt was famously associated with polio, and his efforts helped inspire the March of Dimes to fight the disease. With support from that organization, American researcher Jonas Salk developed an inactivated-virus polio vaccine. Large field trials of his vaccine were declared successful in 1955.

An unidentified flying object, or UFO, is something seen in the sky that observers cannot immediately identify. The name does not mean it is an alien spacecraft: a sighting might later turn out to be a balloon, aircraft, natural event, or another ordinary object. Still, UFOs are often linked to extraterrestrials in popular culture, especially through stories about “flying saucers,” the 1947 Roswell incident, and Area 51. The U.S. Air Force investigated UFO reports in three major studies: Project Sign, Project Grudge, and then Project Blue Book. Project Blue Book ran from 1952 to 1969 and was headquartered at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio. Its investigators collected and evaluated reports to see whether sightings could be explained and whether they posed a threat to national security.

A binary adder is a combinational digital circuit that adds bits, the 0s and 1s used by computers. Its outputs depend only on its current inputs. A half adder adds two input bits and produces two outputs: a sum bit and a carry-out bit. For example, 1 + 1 equals 10 in binary, so the sum bit is 0 and the carry-out is 1. A full adder accepts two input bits plus a carry-in from the previous bit position, and it also produces a sum bit and a carry-out. The carry-out can feed into the next position, allowing several full adders to work together to add larger binary numbers. Adders can be built from logic gates such as XOR, AND, and OR.

Hysteresis means that a system’s present state depends on what happened to it earlier, not just on the conditions acting on it now. In a ferromagnet, such as iron, groups of electron spins tend to align, creating magnetic regions called domains. As an applied magnetic field increases, more domains align with it and the material becomes magnetized. When the field is reduced, the domains do not simply retrace the same changes, so magnetizing and demagnetizing follow different paths on a hysteresis curve. Some magnetization remains even after the applied field reaches zero; this is called residual magnetization or remanence. To reduce it to zero, a magnetic field must be applied in the opposite direction. The magnitude of that reverse field is the material’s coercivity.

Calorimetry is a family of techniques that measures heat exchanged during a physical or chemical process. A calorimeter limits heat loss to the surroundings, allowing a measured temperature change to be used to calculate heat; in a simple setup, heat is related to mass, specific heat capacity, and temperature change. These measurements can reveal reaction enthalpy, a substance’s heat capacity, or properties of a phase change. Different instruments suit different questions: an insulated “coffee-cup” calorimeter can study reactions at constant pressure, while a sealed bomb calorimeter measures heat released when a fuel burns in oxygen. Differential scanning calorimetry tracks changes as temperature is varied. Isothermal titration calorimetry instead keeps a sample cell at constant temperature and measures heat signals from successive small injections of a ligand into a solution containing a macromolecule. Those signals can reveal how strongly they bind and other thermodynamic properties.

A lahar is a fast-moving mixture of water, volcanic ash, rock, and other debris that rushes down a volcano’s slopes and through nearby valleys. It is a type of landslide, or downslope movement of material. Lahars can begin during an eruption, when hot volcanic material melts snow or ice, but heavy rain can also loosen volcanic deposits and trigger one without a new eruption. As a lahar flows downhill, it may pick up more debris and become powerful enough to bury roads, buildings, and entire communities. In 1985, an eruption of Nevado del Ruiz in Colombia triggered a lahar that swept down the Lagunillas River valley. It buried the town of Armero and killed more than 20,000 people.

The moose is the largest living member of the deer family. It lives in boreal and mixed forests across northern Eurasia and North America, including areas near the U.S.–Canada border. Adult males, called bulls, grow broad, palm-shaped antlers that they shed and regrow each year. Moose often feed on leaves, twigs, and aquatic plants, and their long legs help them move through deep snow and wetlands. In Maine, visitors are more likely to spot moose in the inland Katahdin Woods and Waters area than in coastal Acadia National Park. Acadia is on Mount Desert Island and is known for Cadillac Mountain and the Beehive Loop, a hiking route with metal rungs.

A refrigerant is the working fluid that carries heat through a refrigerator, heat pump, or air conditioner. In a vapor-compression cooling system, the refrigerant absorbs heat from the space being cooled as it evaporates from a liquid into a gas. A compressor then helps move it through the system. When the refrigerant condenses back into a liquid, it releases that heat elsewhere, such as outdoors. An air conditioner uses this cycle to carry heat out of a room or vehicle cabin, making the inside cooler. It is often described as a heat pump operating in reverse: instead of moving heat into a space to warm it, it moves heat out to cool it.

In sp² hybridization, one s orbital and two p orbitals on an atom mix to form three equivalent hybrid orbitals. These orbitals point in three directions in the same plane, ideally about 120° apart, giving the atom trigonal planar geometry. One p orbital remains unhybridized and points above and below that plane. In ethene, each carbon uses its three sp² orbitals to form sigma bonds: two to hydrogen atoms and one to the other carbon. The remaining p orbitals on the two carbons overlap sideways to form a pi bond. Together, the sigma bond and pi bond make the carbon–carbon double bond. Carbon atoms in benzene are also sp² hybridized, with each carbon’s unhybridized p orbital contributing to the ring’s shared pi electrons.

Sheep are domesticated ruminants, meaning they have specialized stomachs that help them digest grass and other plants. Farmers usually keep them in flocks and raise them for their fleece, which is made into wool, as well as for meat and sometimes milk. Sheep farming has supported major wool industries in Australia and New Zealand. Different breeds can look quite different. The Racka is a Hungarian sheep breed famous for its long, corkscrew-shaped horns, which can grow on both males and females. Racka sheep are traditionally associated with the Hortobágy region of the Great Hungarian Plain, where herders have cared for livestock for centuries.

Lightning is a sudden electrical discharge in the atmosphere. It can occur between clouds or between a cloud and the ground when a buildup of electrical charge becomes strong enough to overcome the air’s resistance. A lightning bolt rapidly heats the surrounding air, causing it to expand and produce the sound we hear as thunder. Scientists have also studied whether lightning could have helped form the chemicals needed for life on early Earth. In the 1953 Miller-Urey experiment, researchers circulated water vapor, methane, ammonia, and hydrogen through a laboratory apparatus and exposed the mixture to electrical sparks that simulated lightning. The experiment produced amino acids, molecules that can join together to form proteins, and showed that some building blocks of life could form from simpler substances.

A crucible is a small, heat-resistant laboratory container used to heat substances to very high temperatures. It is often made of porcelain and can hold a sample, such as a metal, while the sample is strongly heated. For example, in a common chemistry experiment, a magnesium ribbon is burned in a crucible, and the crucible is weighed before and after heating to help measure the change in mass. A crucible can be heated over a Bunsen burner, an adjustable laboratory device that produces an open flame. The burner is named after German chemist Robert Bunsen and is commonly fueled by natural gas, which consists mainly of methane. Because crucibles remain hot after the flame is turned off, they should be handled with suitable tongs.

Opticks is a book about light published in 1704 by the English scientist Isaac Newton. It describes experiments with prisms, mirrors, and lenses to investigate color, reflection, refraction, diffraction, and spectra. Newton showed that when white sunlight passes through a prism, it separates into a band of colors called a spectrum. He argued that sunlight already contains rays of different colors, rather than the prism creating those colors. The rays also have different refrangibility, meaning they bend by different amounts as they pass through the prism. Newton further showed that a second prism could recombine the separated colors into white light. These experiments helped explain how prisms produce rainbow-like displays and made Opticks an important work in the study of light.

Pea plants are a garden crop that helped scientists discover how traits pass from parents to offspring. In the 19th century, Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar working in a monastery garden, studied different varieties of pea plants. He chose them because they grow easily, can self-pollinate, and have visible traits such as round or wrinkled seeds, flower color, and pod shape. Mendel also cross-pollinated plants himself, then counted which traits appeared in their offspring over several generations. He found that traits followed predictable patterns: some could seem to disappear in one generation and reappear in the next. His findings, published in 1866, became a foundation of genetics and helped explain dominant and recessive traits.

White-nose syndrome is a disease that affects bats hibernating in caves and other cold, sheltered places. It is caused by the cold-tolerant fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans, which grows on bats’ skin, especially around their noses, ears, and wings. Hibernating bats normally conserve energy by remaining inactive for long periods, relying on stored body fat until insects return in warmer weather. Infection can make them wake up repeatedly, using up those energy reserves too quickly. Some bats may even leave their caves during winter, when little food is available. As a result, white-nose syndrome can kill large numbers of bats. Its name comes from the pale fungal growth sometimes visible around an infected bat’s nose.

Osteoblasts are cells that build bone. They secrete osteoid, a soft, collagen-rich organic matrix that forms the framework of new bone. Mineral salts, especially calcium and phosphate, are then deposited in the osteoid, making the bone hard and strong. Osteoblasts are important as bones grow and when they repair damage such as fractures. They work alongside osteoclasts, cells that break down old bone, so the skeleton can continually renew itself and help regulate calcium levels. Bones such as the femur and tibia support the body and protect organs; their strength depends in part on this ongoing balance between bone formation and breakdown.

Earth’s crust is the planet’s outermost solid layer. It lies above the mantle and forms part of the lithosphere, a rigid shell that also includes the uppermost portion of the mantle. The crust is thinner beneath oceans and thicker beneath continents. It is broken into sections that move along with the uppermost mantle as tectonic plates. One process that helps drive this movement is mantle convection. Deep in the mantle, heat causes warmer material to rise, while cooler material sinks. Although mantle rock is solid, it can flow very slowly over long periods. This circulating movement transfers heat and helps move the plates, changing Earth’s surface over millions of years.

A neutron star is the compact remnant left when the core of a massive star collapses during a supernova. Although it is only about the size of a city, it can contain more mass than the Sun, making it far denser than a white dwarf. It consists mostly of neutrons, which are particles with no electric charge. Neutron degeneracy pressure helps prevent it from collapsing further into a black hole. Some neutron stars spin rapidly and send beams of radiation into space; when a beam sweeps past Earth, we detect regular pulses and call the object a pulsar. The Crab Pulsar, at the center of the Crab Nebula in Taurus (catalogued as M1), formed in the supernova observed in 1054 and spins about 30 times per second.

Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was a French naturalist who proposed an early explanation for evolution, the change in organisms over generations. In his 1809 book Philosophie zoologique, he argued that using an organ frequently could strengthen or enlarge it, while not using it could cause it to weaken or shrink. He also believed that organisms could pass such changes, acquired during their lifetimes, to their offspring. This theory is called Lamarckism, or the inheritance of acquired characteristics. For example, Lamarck suggested that giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves and passed longer necks to their young. His proposed mechanism is not the accepted explanation for most evolutionary change: Darwin later argued that natural selection acts on inherited variation already present in a population.

Dust storms occur when strong winds lift fine, dry particles from the ground and carry them through the air. They are common in dry regions on Earth, including the Bodélé Depression in the Sahara, and they also occur on Mars. Because Mars has a thin atmosphere and a dusty surface, its storms can spread across much of the planet, hiding surface features from view. In November 1971, the spacecraft Mariner 9 arrived at Mars during a planet-wide dust storm and initially saw little of the surface. As the dust cleared, it photographed features including Olympus Mons, the Solar System’s largest volcano. Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, and its observations revealed how dramatically dust storms can change the view of Mars.

The War of the Currents was a late-nineteenth-century rivalry over how to supply electricity to homes and businesses. Thomas Edison promoted direct current (DC), which flows in one direction. George Westinghouse backed alternating current (AC), which repeatedly reverses direction, and secured rights to use Nikola Tesla’s AC patents. AC could be transformed to higher voltages for efficient transmission over long distances, then lowered for use in buildings, giving it an important advantage. Edison argued that AC was dangerous and used public demonstrations involving the electrocution of animals to make his case. Westinghouse, an American industrialist who had earlier developed the railway air brake, helped build AC power systems. AC eventually became the main system used for electric power distribution, although DC remains useful in batteries and electronic devices.

Introduced in 1908 by Henry Ford’s automobile company, the Ford Model T was a rugged, affordable car nicknamed “Tin Lizzie.” Earlier cars were often expensive and built in small numbers, but the Model T was produced on a huge scale, making car ownership possible for many ordinary Americans. A major change happened at Ford’s Highland Park Plant, a factory that opened in 1910 in a suburb just north of Detroit. In 1913, Ford introduced a moving assembly-line system there: instead of workers building one car in a single place, the car moved past workers who each performed a specific task. This made production faster and helped lower the Model T’s price. The car became a symbol of how mass production could change everyday life.

The Indian peafowl is a large pheasant species native to South Asia. Males, called peacocks, have a bright blue-green neck and a long courtship train covered in eye-shaped spots. During courtship, a male spreads and displays this train to attract females, called peahens. The train is costly to grow and maintain, and it can make escaping predators harder. These costs help explain why it may be an honest signal of the male’s condition: a healthy male can better afford such an elaborate display than one in poor condition. This idea is called the handicap principle. It shows how a trait that seems disadvantageous for survival can still evolve if it helps its owner attract mates and reproduce.

An inclined plane is a sloping surface, such as a ramp, that helps raise or lower a load. Instead of lifting an object straight up, you move it along the slope. Because the path along the ramp is longer than the vertical height gained, less force is needed, though that force acts over a greater distance. In an ideal situation with no friction, the total work done—force multiplied by distance—is the same as for lifting the object vertically. The ideal mechanical advantage of an inclined plane measures how much it multiplies the input force. It is the distance traveled along the ramp divided by the vertical height gained, so it has no units. Real ramps have friction, which means they require more work than the ideal calculation predicts.

Sneezing is a reflex that forcefully pushes air out through the nose and mouth. It often begins when dust, pollen, or another irritant stimulates the lining of the nasal passages. Nerves send a signal to the brain, which coordinates a quick breath and contractions of the chest and throat muscles to expel the air. The familiar “achoo” imitates the sound of a sneeze, and people often respond by saying “Bless you.” Sneezing is usually protective because it helps clear irritants from the nose. For some people, though, a sudden change from dim light to bright light, such as stepping into sunshine, can also trigger sneezing. This light-triggered tendency is called the photic sneeze reflex.

Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev was a 19th-century Russian chemist who published an early periodic table of the elements in 1869. He arranged the known elements mainly by atomic weight and placed elements with similar chemical properties together. He noticed that these properties repeated in a pattern, a principle called the periodic law. Rather than force every known element into a space, Mendeleev left gaps where he believed undiscovered elements belonged. He predicted their properties and called three of them eka-aluminium, eka-boron, and eka-silicon. Scientists later discovered these elements and named them gallium, scandium, and germanium, respectively. Their properties closely matched his predictions, providing strong evidence that his table captured a real pattern in nature. Modern periodic tables arrange elements by atomic number instead of atomic weight.

Antoine Lavoisier was a French chemist whose careful measurements helped transform the study of chemical reactions. In the 1700s, many scientists thought burning released a substance called phlogiston. Lavoisier instead used quantitative experiments, including weighing substances before and after reactions, to show that combustion involves a component of air: oxygen. Oxygen makes up about 21% of Earth’s atmosphere and combines with hydrogen to form water. Lavoisier’s measurements also helped establish the law of conservation of mass, which says that matter is not created or destroyed in an ordinary chemical reaction: the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. He also helped develop modern chemical nomenclature, a systematic way of naming substances so scientists could describe them more clearly.

Bone density, also called bone mineral density, measures how much mineral matter is packed into bones. Minerals such as calcium help make bones strong, so this measurement helps doctors estimate a person’s risk of fractures. A dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scan, usually called a DEXA scan, measures bone density using low-dose X-rays. Bones are constantly being broken down and rebuilt, but if bone is lost faster than it is replaced, density falls. A substantial loss of bone density can lead to osteoporosis, a disease in which bones become weak and brittle and may fracture easily. Osteoporosis is especially common in older adults and in women after menopause. Exercise, enough calcium and vitamin D, and medical care when needed can help protect bone health.

Amedeo Avogadro was an early-19th-century Italian scientist who helped chemists understand gases. He proposed that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, no matter which gases they are. This idea, called Avogadro’s law, helped scientists distinguish molecules, which can contain more than one atom, from individual atoms. The particle-count constant named in his honor is Avogadro’s constant. It connects the tiny scale of atoms and molecules to amounts chemists can measure: one mole, the SI base unit for amount of substance, contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities, such as atoms, molecules, or ions. Historically, this quantity was linked to the number of atoms in 12 grams of carbon-12.

A carbon–carbon double bond joins two carbon atoms, which have atomic number 6. It is found in alkenes and consists of two different covalent bonds: a sigma bond formed by head-on orbital overlap and a pi bond formed by sideways overlap. Each carbon in a typical carbon–carbon double bond is sp² hybridized. This means it uses three hybrid orbitals to form bonds arranged in a flat, trigonal-planar shape, with about 120 degrees between them. One unhybridized p orbital remains on each carbon, pointing perpendicular to that plane; their sideways overlap creates the pi bond. Because rotating the carbons around their shared axis would disrupt this overlap, a carbon–carbon double bond restricts rotation.

Hans Christian Ørsted was a Danish physicist who made an important discovery in 1820. While demonstrating electricity, he noticed that a compass needle turned away from north when electric current flowed through a nearby wire. When the current stopped, the needle returned to its usual position. This showed that a current produces a magnetic field, an invisible influence that can push or pull on magnetic objects such as a compass needle. Ørsted’s observation helped scientists understand that electricity and magnetism are connected, paving the way for the study of electromagnetism. Magnetic fields are measured in teslas; Earth’s magnetic field is much weaker than one tesla, averaging about 50 microteslas. The magnetic field around a straight wire circles the wire, and its direction can be found using the right-hand rule.

A separatory funnel is a laboratory vessel used to separate liquids that do not mix, such as water and oil. It has a broad upper opening closed by a stopper and a narrow outlet at the bottom fitted with a manually operated tap called a stopcock. When the liquids are placed in the funnel and left to settle, they form layers according to their densities: the denser liquid is usually on the bottom. A scientist removes the stopper, opens the stopcock to drain the lower layer into a container, and closes it before the upper layer flows out. Separatory funnels are often used in liquid-liquid extraction, which moves a substance from one liquid into another. Water forms the aqueous layer; if the liquids have been shaken, they may need time to settle fully before draining.

A stoma is a microscopic opening in the epidermis, or outer layer, of a plant leaf. Stomata allow carbon dioxide to enter the leaf for photosynthesis, while oxygen produced during photosynthesis and water vapor leave through them. The loss of water vapor is called transpiration. Each stoma is bordered by a pair of specialized epidermal cells called guard cells. As the amount of water in these cells changes, they change shape and open or close the pore. This helps the plant take in the carbon dioxide it needs while limiting water loss, especially in dry conditions. Many stomata are found on the undersides of leaves, where they are less exposed to direct sunlight.

Apple silicon is the name for Apple’s family of custom-designed processors used in its computers and other devices. These chips use an ARM-based architecture and are systems on a chip, meaning they combine parts such as the central processor, graphics processor, and memory controllers in one package. In 2020, Apple began replacing Intel processors in many Mac computers with Apple silicon. The first chip in this Mac transition was the M1, which debuted in November 2020. It first appeared in the MacBook Air, the 13-inch MacBook Pro, and the Mac mini. Designing its own chips gives Apple more control over how its hardware and software work together, helping its computers balance performance and energy efficiency.

The HMS Beagle voyage was a British naval surveying expedition from 1831 to 1836. Commanded by Captain Robert FitzRoy, the ship charted coastlines, especially around South America, and visited the Galápagos Islands. Charles Darwin joined as the voyage’s naturalist, collecting specimens and recording observations of plants, animals, and fossils. On the Galápagos Islands, he noticed that related species differed from island to island; differences among finches’ beaks later became a well-known example of adaptation to different foods. After the voyage, Darwin developed his theory of evolution by natural selection, explaining how traits that help organisms survive and reproduce can become more common over generations. He published the theory in On the Origin of Species in 1859, while FitzRoy also published accounts of the expedition.

A pulley is a simple machine made of a grooved wheel mounted on an axle, with a taut rope or cable running over the wheel. Pulling one end of the rope can lift a load on the other end. A fixed pulley changes the direction of the force, so you can pull downward to lift something upward, but it does not reduce the force needed in an ideal system. A movable pulley rises with the load and can reduce the effort needed, though you must pull more rope. A block and tackle combines pulleys fixed to a support with pulleys that move with the load. Its mechanical advantage depends on how many rope segments support the moving load: more supporting segments mean less pulling force is needed, ignoring friction.

An instinct is an inborn pattern of behavior that an animal can perform without being taught. Instincts often help members of a species survive or care for their young. For example, hand-reared birds may become restless when it is time to migrate, even if they have never made the journey before. A greylag goose instinctively tries to roll an egg that has slipped out of its nest back inside. This egg-rolling behavior is a fixed action pattern: a predictable sequence of movements triggered by a particular stimulus, such as seeing the misplaced egg. Once the sequence begins, the goose may continue the rolling motion even if the egg is removed. Human babies’ palmar grasp reflex, in which they grip a finger placed in their palm, is another example of unlearned behavior.

Argon is a colorless, odorless gas with atomic number 18. It belongs to the noble gases, the group of elements with full outer electron shells that makes them unusually unreactive. Argon makes up just under 1% of Earth’s atmosphere, yet it is the third most abundant gas there, after nitrogen and oxygen. Its low reactivity makes it useful when a gas must not easily take part in chemical reactions. For example, argon can fill a Geiger–Müller tube, the gas-filled detector inside some Geiger counters. When radiation causes an ionizing event in the tube, it starts an electrical discharge that spreads through the gas. The tube produces a detectable pulse that is largely independent of how much energy the original event carried.

Technology is the practical use of knowledge to solve problems and meet human needs. It includes tools, equipment, machines, and designed systems, from early stone tools to computers, power grids, and other complex infrastructure. Technology is not just a collection of objects, however. In his essay The Question Concerning Technology, the philosopher Martin Heidegger argued that modern technology also shapes how people see the world. He called this way of seeing “enframing”: it reveals things mainly as resources to be measured, organized, and kept ready for use. For example, a river may be viewed primarily as a source of electricity rather than as a natural place. Heidegger warned that this outlook can also lead people to treat other people as resources.

Acetic acid is a weak carboxylic acid with the formula CH₃COOH. It is the main acid in vinegar, giving vinegar its sour taste. “Weak” means that only some of its molecules release hydrogen ions when dissolved in water. Acetic acid also forms when the body processes ethanol, the alcohol produced by yeast during fermentation. In the liver, an enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase first converts ethanol into acetaldehyde, a two-carbon compound known as an aldehyde. A second enzyme then oxidizes acetaldehyde into acetic acid, which can also be called acetate in the body. This sequence—ethanol to acetaldehyde to acetic acid—shows why acetaldehyde is the intermediate, while acetic acid is the weak acid formed in the next step.

David Albert Huffman was an American electrical engineer best known for creating Huffman coding, a method of lossless data compression. Compression makes information take up less storage space, and “lossless” means the original data can be recovered exactly. Huffman coding assigns short sequences of bits to symbols that appear often and longer sequences to less common symbols. These sequences are prefix codes: no complete code is the beginning of another, so a computer can tell where one symbol ends and the next begins. This produces a minimum-redundancy code for the symbol frequencies being used. Huffman also studied the mathematics of origami. His work explored the geometry of crease patterns and the conditions that allow a sheet of paper to fold flat.

Bumblebees are stout, often densely hairy bees in the genus Bombus. As they forage for nectar and pollen, they carry pollen between flowers, making them important pollinators. Many species live in annual colonies: a queen starts a nest in spring, workers help raise young through the summer, and new queens survive to start colonies the following year. One European species, Bombus terrestris, is raised commercially to pollinate greenhouse crops such as tomatoes. It is sometimes called the buff-tailed bumblebee because its queens have buff-colored tail tips, unlike the queens of a similar white-tailed species. Bumblebees are also known for their buzzing flight, which inspired Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov’s fast orchestral piece Flight of the Bumblebee.

Metalloids are chemical elements whose properties fall between those of metals and nonmetals. They are often found along the zigzag boundary that separates metals from nonmetals on the periodic table. Commonly listed metalloids include boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, and tellurium. Unlike good electrical conductors such as copper, many metalloids conduct electricity only under certain conditions, making them useful as semiconductors. Silicon, whose chemical symbol is Si and whose atomic number is 14, is especially important: its ability to control the flow of electricity makes it a key material in transistors and microchips. Germanium is another metalloid used in electronics. The name “metalloid” reflects this mixture of metal-like and nonmetal-like behavior.

Juno is a NASA spacecraft launched in 2011 that arrived at Jupiter in 2016. It follows a highly elliptical polar orbit, sweeping close to the planet and then moving far away. During these passes, Juno studies Jupiter’s atmosphere, interior, gravity, and magnetic field, which is the strongest of any planet in our solar system. One of its targets is the Great Red Spot, an enormous storm in Jupiter’s southern hemisphere that astronomers have observed for centuries. The storm is anticyclonic, meaning it rotates around a region of high pressure. Juno used an instrument called a microwave radiometer to look below the visible clouds and measure how far the Great Red Spot extends down into Jupiter’s atmosphere.

Aquaporins are proteins that form selective channels for water in cell membranes. Water can cross a membrane on its own, but aquaporins let it move much more quickly while largely excluding substances such as salts. They are especially important in the kidneys, the bean-shaped organs that filter blood and produce urine. Each kidney contains many nephrons, its functional filtering units. As fluid passes through a nephron and into a collecting duct, the body can reclaim water instead of losing it in urine. When the body needs to conserve water, the hormone vasopressin signals collecting-duct cells to insert Aquaporin-2 channels into the membrane facing the duct. This lets more water leave the fluid and return to the blood, producing more concentrated urine.

Enceladus is a small, icy moon of Saturn with an exceptionally bright surface that reflects more sunlight than any other known body in the Solar System. Its fresh ice is continually renewed by jets that spray water vapor and ice particles from long fractures near its south pole, nicknamed “tiger stripes.” Scientists think the jets draw material from a liquid-water ocean beneath the moon’s icy crust. That possibility makes Enceladus important in the search for places beyond Earth that might support life, although no life has been found there. The Cassini spacecraft made repeated close flybys of Enceladus and flew through its plumes to sample their material. After studying Saturn and its moons for years, Cassini ended its mission in 2017 by plunging into Saturn’s atmosphere.

Topsoil is the fertile upper layer of soil, usually called the A horizon. It lies above the subsoil and is where many plant roots grow. Like other soil, it contains particles of weathered rock, including sand, silt, and clay, but it is especially rich in nutrients and organic matter. Leaves, roots, and other remains of living things break down over time to form humus, a dark material that helps the soil hold moisture and supplies nutrients for plants. In places with a layer of fallen leaves or growing grass, that organic layer may sit above the topsoil. Healthy topsoil supports crops and natural vegetation, but it can be washed or blown away if the ground is left bare.

Chlorophyll is the green pigment that helps plants capture light energy for photosynthesis, the process of making sugars from carbon dioxide and water. It gives most leaves their familiar green color because it absorbs mainly red and blue light while reflecting green light. Chlorophyll molecules are found in chloroplasts, structures inside plant cells where photosynthesis takes place. At the center of each chlorophyll molecule is a magnesium ion, so plants need enough magnesium to make this pigment. If a plant lacks magnesium, its older leaves may turn yellow as their chlorophyll breaks down and the plant moves magnesium to newer growth. This yellowing is called chlorosis. Healthy soil or suitable fertilizer can help provide the nutrients plants need to keep making chlorophyll.

Blood type, or blood group, describes markers called antigens on the surface of red blood cells. The ABO system depends on whether those cells have A antigens, B antigens, both, or neither. A separate marker called the Rh factor determines whether a blood type is positive or negative. O-negative red blood cells have neither A nor B antigens and lack the Rh antigen. Because they lack these major markers, O-negative red cells are commonly called the universal red-cell donor type: in an emergency, they can often be transfused before a patient’s blood group is known. This designation refers specifically to red-cell transfusions, not to every blood component. Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the body and help transport carbon dioxide back to the lungs to be exhaled.

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was an Indian-American astrophysicist who studied how stars change over time. He calculated that a white dwarf, the dense remnant left by a star like the Sun, can remain stable only if its mass is below about 1.4 times the Sun’s mass. This maximum is called the Chandrasekhar limit. Gravity pulls a white dwarf’s matter inward, but electron degeneracy pressure pushes back. This quantum-mechanical resistance to compression arises from the Pauli exclusion principle, which prevents electrons from all occupying the same state. Above the limit, that pressure cannot support the white dwarf against gravity, and it may explode as a Type Ia supernova. Chandrasekhar received the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics for his theoretical work on the structure and evolution of stars.

Catalytic converters are devices fitted to automobile exhaust systems to make engine emissions less harmful before they leave the tailpipe. Inside, a thin coating called a washcoat spreads catalysts, often platinum-group metals, over a large surface area. These catalysts speed up chemical reactions without being used up. For example, they help oxidize poisonous carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide and, in modern three-way converters, help turn nitrogen oxides into nitrogen. A catalyst can stop working if other substances coat its surface, a problem called catalyst poisoning. Tetraethyl lead, an organometallic compound once added to gasoline to prevent engine knocking, leaves lead residues that poison catalytic converters. This was one reason leaded gasoline was phased out in favor of unleaded fuel.

A calendar is a system that organizes days into longer periods, such as weeks, months, and years. It lets people record dates, plan events, and track the seasons. Calendars are often based on repeating patterns in nature, especially the Sun’s yearly cycle and the Moon’s phases. Julius Caesar introduced the Julian calendar in 45 BCE as a reform of the Roman calendar. It used a 365-day year and added an extra day every fourth year, called a leap year, to help keep calendar dates aligned with the seasons. Scholars have also debated whether Stonehenge, a prehistoric stone circle in Britain, was used for a calendar or other kind of timekeeping, although its exact purpose remains uncertain.

The Minnesota Starvation Experiment was a World War II-era study led by American physiologist Ancel Keys at the University of Minnesota, a public university in Minneapolis. It examined what happens to the body and mind when people do not get enough food, and how they recover when they begin eating more. Thirty-six conscientious objectors volunteered for the study. After an initial period of normal eating, they underwent 24 weeks of severe calorie restriction, followed by controlled refeeding. The men lost weight and experienced effects such as fatigue, difficulty concentrating, and intense thoughts about food. Researchers hoped the findings would help relief workers care for people suffering from famine after the war. Keys later led the Seven Countries Study, which investigated links between diet and cardiovascular disease.

The Beaufort scale describes wind strength using numbered levels based on what the wind does, rather than on a direct instrument reading. It starts at 0 for calm conditions, when smoke rises almost straight up and the sea looks smooth. As the numbers increase, wind begins to move leaves and branches, raise waves, and eventually damage trees and buildings. The standard scale ends at 12, meaning hurricane-force winds that begin at about 73 miles per hour. Some regions prone to typhoons extend the scale to 17 to describe even stronger winds. A typhoon is a powerful tropical storm in the western Pacific; a similar storm in the Atlantic is called a hurricane. To measure wind speed directly, scientists use an anemometer, often fitted with rotating cups or a small propeller.

Bone tissue is the hard, mineralized connective tissue that forms most of the skeleton in humans and other vertebrates. It supports the body, protects organs, helps muscles produce movement, and stores minerals such as calcium. Although bones seem unchanging, they are continually remodeled: cells called osteoclasts break down old bone, while osteoblasts build new bone. Hormones, including parathyroid hormone and calcitonin, help regulate this process and the amount of calcium in the blood. Mechanical forces matter too. Wolff’s law, named for the 19th-century German surgeon Julius Wolff, states that bone structure and density adapt over time to the stresses placed on them. Regular weight-bearing activity can strengthen bones, while too little stress can weaken them. Vitamin D helps the body absorb the calcium needed to build strong bone.

Molecular vibrations are the motions of atoms within a molecule as they move around their equilibrium positions, the locations where the atoms are most stable. Atoms can stretch bonds or bend relative to one another, and these motions occur in distinct patterns called vibrational modes. The motions are quantized, meaning a molecule can have only certain vibrational energies rather than any value. Scientists can study them using spectroscopy. One technique, Raman spectroscopy, shines light on a sample and measures small changes in the frequency of the scattered light. Those shifts reveal information about vibrational modes. Nanotechnologist Millie Dresselhaus used Raman spectroscopy to study forms of carbon, called allotropes, including graphite and nanotubes.

Logistic growth is a model of how population size—the number of organisms in an area—changes when resources are limited. When a population is small, it may grow quickly because food, space, and other resources are plentiful. As more individuals compete for those resources, growth slows. On a graph, this pattern forms an S-shaped curve that levels off near the carrying capacity, often written as K. Carrying capacity is the maximum population an environment can sustain over time. Unlike exponential growth, which assumes a population keeps increasing rapidly, logistic growth accounts for environmental limits. The model does not mean population size always stays exactly at K; it may rise or fall as conditions change.

Superacids are acid systems stronger than pure, 100-percent sulfuric acid. Scientists often compare their strength using the Hammett acidity function, which is useful for extremely acidic solutions where the familiar pH scale is less helpful. A value below about −12 indicates superacidic conditions; the more negative the value, the greater the acidity. One famous example is magic acid, made by combining fluorosulfuric acid with antimony pentafluoride. This mixture can stabilize carbocations, which are positively charged carbon-containing ions that would usually react quickly. Magic acid has helped chemists study how these short-lived ions behave. Like other strong acids, superacids must be handled with great care because they can react dangerously with many materials.

Geysers are hot springs that periodically shoot jets of hot water and steam into the air. They form where groundwater seeps underground and is heated by hot rock, often near volcanoes. In some geysers, narrow passages trap the water as it heats, allowing pressure to build until the water erupts at the surface. After an eruption, more groundwater fills the passages and the cycle begins again. Yellowstone National Park in the United States has many geysers, including Old Faithful, which is known for its frequent eruptions. The word “geyser” comes from Geysir, the name of a hot spring in Iceland, a North Atlantic island nation. Iceland also has active volcanoes; an eruption there in 2010 sent ash into the air and disrupted flights across Europe.

X-chromosome inactivation is a process in most female mammals that switches off one of the two X chromosomes in each cell.
