Because males usually have only one X chromosome, this helps balance the activity of X-linked genes between females and males. The chromosome is silenced through epigenetic changes, which affect whether genes are used without changing their DNA sequence. Early in development, each cell generally makes a random choice about which X chromosome to silence, and its descendant cells keep that choice. This creates a mosaic of cell groups that use different X-linked genes. In female cats with one allele for black fur and another for orange fur on their X chromosomes, different skin-cell groups produce patches of each color. This coloration is called a tortoiseshell coat pattern.

Emerald is the green gemstone variety of the mineral beryl and the traditional birthstone for May. Beryl can form in several colors, and different gem varieties have different names: blue to blue-green beryl is called aquamarine, while pink beryl is called morganite. Emerald’s rich green color usually comes from small amounts of chromium or vanadium within the mineral. Like other minerals, beryl has an orderly crystal structure, and emerald crystals often grow as six-sided prisms. Many emeralds contain tiny cracks or inclusions, which are materials trapped inside the crystal as it forms. These features can help distinguish a natural emerald from a flawless-looking imitation. Remember that emerald, aquamarine, and morganite are all varieties of the same mineral species: beryl.

Charcoal is a black, porous, carbon-rich material made by heating wood with very little oxygen. Because the wood cannot burn completely, much of its carbon remains as charcoal. It is different from coal, which forms naturally underground over millions of years. Charcoal was the fuel in traditional gunpowder, an invention from China. The other two ingredients were potassium nitrate, which supplies oxygen to help the mixture burn rapidly, and sulfur, a yellow, brittle nonmetal that helps it ignite. When sulfur burns in air, it produces sulfur dioxide, a pungent gas that can contribute to acid rain. Charcoal also has uses outside gunpowder, including as a fuel for cooking and, when specially processed, in filters that trap impurities.

Cis–trans isomerism is a type of geometric isomerism, in which molecules have the same atoms joined in the same order but differ in how those atoms are arranged in space. It can occur around a carbon–carbon double bond or in a ring because these structures restrict rotation. If the groups being compared are on the same side, the isomer is called cis; if they are on opposite sides, it is called trans. For example, two groups attached to a double bond may point toward the same side in one molecule and toward opposite sides in another. Each carbon in the double bond must have two different groups attached for cis–trans isomers to be possible. These different arrangements can give the isomers different physical properties, even though their atoms are connected in the same way.

Rhodopsin, also called “visual purple,” is a light-sensitive pigment in the outer segments of rod cells in the retina. Rods help you see in dim light and contribute to peripheral vision. Rhodopsin is made of a protein called opsin attached to a light-absorbing molecule called retinal. Before light strikes it, retinal is in a bent configuration called 11-cis-retinal. When it absorbs a photon, it changes shape to all-trans-retinal. This change activates rhodopsin, a G-protein-coupled receptor, and begins a chain of signals inside the rod cell. The retina then sends information toward the brain through the optic nerve, allowing you to detect light even when conditions are too dark for cones to work well.

The Ideal Gas Law describes how the pressure, volume, amount, and temperature of an ideal gas are related: PV = nRT. Here, P is pressure, V is volume, n is the amount of gas in moles, T is absolute temperature measured in kelvins, and R is the universal gas constant. For example, if a gas is heated while its volume stays fixed, its pressure rises. The law assumes that gas particles have negligible size and do not attract one another, so it works best when those effects are small. Real gases can behave differently, especially at high pressures or low temperatures. The Van der Waals equation extends the Ideal Gas Law by using a constant called a to account for attractions between particles and a constant called b to account for their finite size.

Sagittarius is a constellation in the southern sky traditionally pictured as an archer; its name comes from the Latin word for “archer.” It lies in the direction of the Galactic Center, the center of our Milky Way galaxy. That does not mean the center is close to Earth: it is about 26,000 light-years away, and clouds of dust hide much of it from visible-light telescopes. Astronomers can study the region using radio waves and other forms of light that pass through the dust. Near the Galactic Center, they have detected a compact radio source called Sagittarius A*, which is associated with the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole. Sagittarius also contains the Sagittarius Star Cloud, listed as M24 in Charles Messier’s catalog.

E. O. Wilson was an American biologist born in Alabama who spent decades studying ants at Harvard University. His research showed how ant colonies cooperate: workers gather food, defend the nest, and care for young, often guided by chemical signals. Ants are eusocial insects, meaning they live in organized colonies whose members have different roles. Wilson used insights from ants and other animals to help establish sociobiology, a field that uses evolutionary biology to explain social behavior across species. It asks how behaviors such as cooperation, competition, and caring for relatives can develop through natural selection. Wilson’s work helped scientists connect the everyday activities of animal groups with the evolutionary forces that shaped them.

Cassini was a spacecraft built through a collaboration among NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA), and the Italian Space Agency (ASI). It began orbiting Saturn in 2004 and spent 13 years studying the planet, its rings, and its moons. Cassini also carried the separate Huygens probe, which descended through the atmosphere of Saturn’s moon Titan. Another important target was Enceladus, an icy moon that Cassini repeatedly observed ejecting plumes from its south polar region. The spacecraft detected silica grains in the plumes, suggesting that hot water from Enceladus’s subsurface ocean interacts with a rocky seafloor, possibly near hydrothermal vents. This made Enceladus a key place to investigate conditions that might support life. Cassini’s mission ended in 2017 when it entered Saturn’s atmosphere.

Hawking radiation is a predicted thermal glow produced by quantum effects near a black hole’s event horizon, the boundary beyond which light cannot escape. Physicist Stephen Hawking showed that, when quantum physics is taken into account, black holes should have a temperature and emit particles. That energy must come from the black hole, so it gradually loses mass and could eventually evaporate. The effect is expected to be extremely faint for large black holes and has not yet been directly observed. Hawking was a British physicist who later wrote the popular science book A Brief History of Time. After developing motor neurone disease, also known as ALS, he used a speech synthesizer to communicate.

Smog is a visible, often harmful haze made of air pollutants. It commonly forms over cities, where traffic and industry release nitrogen oxides, sulfur oxides, and other pollutants. Sunlight can also drive chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, a major part of some kinds of smog. These pollutants can irritate the eyes and lungs and make breathing harder. Smog may linger when the air cannot mix and carry pollution away. Normally, air temperature decreases with height through the troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere, where weather occurs. In a temperature inversion, however, a layer of warm air sits above cooler air near the surface. This warm layer acts like a lid, limiting vertical mixing and trapping smog close to the ground.

A simple harmonic oscillator is an idealized system that moves back and forth around an equilibrium position, where it would rest if undisturbed. Its restoring force always points toward equilibrium and is proportional to how far the object has moved from that position. A mass attached to a spring is a standard example: stretching or compressing the spring creates a force that pulls or pushes the mass back. This relationship is called Hooke’s law. As the mass passes through equilibrium, its momentum carries it onward, so the motion repeats. A pendulum—a weight suspended from a pivot—also behaves approximately like a simple harmonic oscillator when it swings through small angles. For larger swings, that approximation becomes less accurate.

Platinum is a dense, silvery-white transition metal with atomic number 78. Its chemical symbol on the periodic table is Pt: a capital P followed by a lowercase t. Platinum is rare, valuable, and resistant to corrosion, which helps make it useful for long-lasting jewelry. It is also used in automobile catalytic converters, where it acts as a catalyst to help change harmful exhaust gases into less harmful substances. Platinum sits near the bottom of the metal activity series, meaning it is much less likely to react with other substances than highly reactive metals such as lithium and potassium. Its low reactivity helps it remain stable while it performs these jobs.

A predator is an organism that hunts, kills, and eats another organism, called its prey. In a food chain, predators usually occupy a higher trophic level than the animals they eat: for example, a wolf can prey on a moose. Apex predators are at the top of a food chain and have few or no natural predators themselves. Not every animal that eats meat is acting as a predator, though. A scavenger feeds on the carcasses of animals that died naturally or were left behind after another animal’s kill, rather than hunting and killing that food itself. Vultures and flesh flies are examples of scavengers. Some animals can act as both predators and scavengers, depending on how they find their food.

A positive feedback loop is a self-reinforcing process: an initial change causes effects that make that change even stronger. In the climate system, greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide trap some of Earth’s outgoing heat. Warming can then trigger changes that increase warming further. One example is ice-albedo feedback. Albedo means how much sunlight a surface reflects. Bright sea ice has a high albedo, so it reflects much of the Sun’s energy. When rising temperatures melt sea ice, they expose darker ocean water, which absorbs more solar energy. The ocean warms, contributing to further ice melt and continuing the loop. “Positive” does not mean beneficial here; it means that the effects reinforce the original change rather than counteract it.

An observatory is a facility where astronomers systematically observe and measure objects in the sky, such as stars, planets, and the Moon. Observatories use instruments to track where these objects appear and how they move, helping astronomers make accurate records and predictions. In the medieval Islamic world, the caliph al-Ma’mun established an early observatory in Baghdad, a major center of learning. Centuries later, in the 15th century, the Timurid ruler Ulugh Beg founded a large observatory in Samarkand, in present-day Uzbekistan. He supported astronomers who measured the positions of stars and compiled the influential Zij-i Sultani star catalog. These observatories show how careful, repeated observations helped people improve their understanding of the night sky.

Coevolution happens when two interacting species each exert selective pressure on the other, leading to reciprocal evolutionary changes over many generations. For example, flowering plants may evolve shapes that suit particular pollinators, while those pollinators evolve body parts that help them reach the flowers’ nectar. Charles Darwin predicted that Madagascar’s long-spurred star orchid, whose nectar lies deep inside its flower, must have a pollinator with an exceptionally long feeding tube. A hawk moth called Xanthopan praedicta was later identified as that pollinator. Coevolution can also occur in mutualisms, where both species benefit, such as relationships between plants and fungi, and in antagonistic relationships, such as those between hosts and parasites. In each case, changes in one species can affect which traits help the other survive and reproduce.

Childbirth is the process of delivering a baby. It usually begins with labor, when coordinated contractions of the uterus gradually thin and open the cervix, the lower part of the uterus. The cervix dilates to about 10 centimeters, creating a passage for the baby to move through the birth canal. After the baby is born, contractions continue during the third stage of labor to push out the placenta. The placenta is a temporary organ that develops during pregnancy and connects to the fetus through the umbilical cord. It transfers oxygen and nutrients from the pregnant parent to the fetus and carries away some of the fetus’s waste products. Delivery of the placenta completes the main stages of childbirth.

An electronic display, also called a screen, is the hardware component that turns electrical signals into visible images. Displays let you read text, watch videos, and view pictures on phones, televisions, and computers. Older, bulky televisions and computer monitors often used cathode-ray tubes, or CRTs. Inside a CRT, an electron beam travels through a vacuum and is steered onto a phosphor-coated surface, which glows where the beam hits to form an image. Flat-panel displays replaced most CRTs because they take up less space. These include liquid-crystal displays (LCDs), plasma displays, and newer organic light-emitting diode (OLED) displays. Although these technologies produce images in different ways, they all serve the same basic purpose: presenting visual information to the viewer.

Polytetrafluoroethylene, usually shortened to PTFE and widely known by the brand name Teflon, is a thermoplastic fluoropolymer. Like all polymers, it consists of many repeating units joined into long chains. PTFE is made by chain-growth polymerization of tetrafluoroethylene, a two-carbon fluorinated alkene with the formula C₂F₄. During this process, the monomers link together to form the polymer. PTFE has exceptionally low friction, so other materials slide across it easily, and it resists reactions with a wide range of chemicals. These properties make it useful as a nonstick coating on cookware and in parts such as seals and bearings. As a thermoplastic, it can be shaped using heat, although processing it requires very high temperatures.

A stroke is a medical emergency that happens when part of the brain stops getting enough blood or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain cells need a constant supply of oxygen from blood, so they can begin to die within minutes if that supply is interrupted. In an ischemic stroke, a clot blocks an artery supplying the brain, preventing oxygen from reaching brain tissue. In a hemorrhagic stroke, a blood vessel ruptures and bleeds into or around the brain. Warning signs can include sudden weakness on one side of the body, trouble speaking, and a severe headache. If someone may be having a stroke, call emergency services immediately: fast treatment can limit brain damage.

The center of mass is the average position of an object’s mass, with heavier parts contributing more to its location than lighter parts. For a collection of particles, you find it by multiplying each particle’s position by its mass, adding those results, and dividing by the total mass. An extended object’s straight-line motion can be analyzed as though all its mass were concentrated at this point. It can also be a useful balance point: a flat object may balance on your finger if you support it directly beneath its center of mass. The center of gravity is a related but distinct point where the object’s total weight can be treated as acting. When the gravitational field is uniform, as it approximately is for everyday objects near Earth’s surface, the center of gravity and center of mass coincide.

A codon is a group of three nucleotide bases in messenger RNA (mRNA) that a ribosome reads while building a protein. DNA contains the instructions for a protein, but the ribosome uses an mRNA copy of those instructions during translation. Each codon usually specifies one amino acid, and the ribosome joins amino acids together in the order given by the codons. For example, the mRNA codon AUG specifies the amino acid methionine and commonly signals where translation begins. Not every codon specifies an amino acid, though. A stop codon tells the ribosome to end translation and release the completed protein. The three standard stop codons in mRNA are UAA, UAG, and UGA. Because codons are read three bases at a time, their order is essential to making the right protein.

The gray wolf is a widespread wild member of the dog family and the main large predator on Isle Royale, an island national park in Michigan. Wolves there hunt chiefly moose, large browsing animals in the deer family that feed on leaves, twigs, and other vegetation. In a food chain, a predator hunts and eats another animal, so wolves occupy a level above the moose they prey on. Scientists have studied Isle Royale’s wolves and moose for decades because the island offers a rare chance to observe how predator and prey populations affect each other. Changes in moose numbers can influence how much food is available to wolves, while wolf hunting can affect the moose population.

Domestication is the process by which a species changes over many generations as it lives alongside humans. People may encourage traits such as friendliness or usefulness by breeding animals that have them, while the animals also adapt to human environments. This differs from taming: a wild animal can become comfortable with people during its lifetime, but taming does not by itself change a species over generations. Dogs are generally considered the first domesticated animals; their ancestors formed a lasting relationship with humans thousands of years ago. Domestic cats later became valuable around early settlements because they hunted mice and other rodents attracted to stored food. Today, cats are familiar companions known for purring and meowing.

Cotton plants are cultivated members of the genus Gossypium, grown mainly for the soft fibers that surround their seeds. When the seed pods, called bolls, ripen and open, the fibers can be separated from the seeds and spun into yarn for clothing and other textiles. The most widely grown species is Gossypium hirsutum, commonly called upland cotton. It was domesticated in what is now Mexico and supplies most of the cotton fiber produced worldwide. Cotton is an important agricultural crop in countries including Uzbekistan. It also has a painful history: before the American Civil War, enslaved people were forced to grow and harvest cotton on large plantations in the southern United States.

Half-life is the time it takes for half of a sample to decay or be removed. After one half-life, 50 percent remains; after two, 25 percent remains. For a substance that undergoes first-order decay, its half-life equals the natural logarithm of 2 divided by its rate constant. Scientists use half-lives to describe radioactive materials, how long drugs remain in the body, and how slowly some pollutants are eliminated. Carbon dating uses the radioactive isotope carbon-14, which is continually produced when cosmic rays interact with Earth’s atmosphere. Living organisms take in carbon-14, but stop exchanging carbon with their surroundings after death. Because carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, measuring how much remains helps estimate when once-living material died.

Aqua regia is a highly corrosive mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid, usually combined in a ratio of three parts hydrochloric acid to one part nitric acid. Its name means “royal water” because it can dissolve noble metals such as gold and platinum, which resist many other acids. Gold is a lustrous yellow metal with the chemical symbol Au and atomic number 79. It was also central to Ernest Rutherford’s famous experiment: his team fired alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold. Most particles passed through, but a few bounced back or changed direction sharply. This showed that atoms contain a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. Aqua regia must be handled with great care because it is corrosive and gives off dangerous fumes.

Cypresses are evergreen coniferous trees that keep their foliage year-round and produce cones rather than flowers. Many grow in a tall, narrow shape, which makes them easy to recognize in landscapes. The Dutch artist Vincent van Gogh often painted cypresses, including ones standing near wheat fields. In his 1889 painting The Starry Night, a dark cypress rises in the foreground beneath a swirling blue night sky filled with bright stars. A golden crescent moon appears in the upper right. Van Gogh painted the scene while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, drawing inspiration from the view there. The cypress’s strong vertical shape contrasts with the sky’s sweeping curves, making the tree one of the painting’s most striking features.

The peroxide ion is a polyatomic anion with the formula O₂²⁻: it contains two oxygen atoms and has an overall charge of −2. The oxygen atoms are directly connected by an O–O single covalent bond, meaning they share one pair of electrons. Because the two oxygens are equivalent, each has an oxidation state of −1, rather than the −2 typical of oxygen in many other compounds. Salts containing this ion are called peroxides; sodium peroxide, for example, can form when sodium burns in excess oxygen. Adding two hydrogen ions to the peroxide ion produces hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, which the enzyme catalase breaks down into water and oxygen. The O–O bond and the −1 oxidation state help distinguish peroxide from other oxygen ions, such as oxide and superoxide.

In physics, work is the energy transferred when a force causes an object to move. To calculate it, multiply the component of the force in the direction of motion by the distance moved. Work is measured in joules, and one joule equals one newton of force acting over one meter. For example, lifting a box requires work because you apply an upward force while the box moves upward. You could also push the box up a ramp, which is a simple machine called an inclined plane. The ramp lets you use less force than lifting the box straight up, but the box must travel a greater distance. Ignoring friction, the total work needed to raise it to the same height does not decrease.

Perseverance is a NASA rover that landed in Mars’s Jezero Crater on February 18, 2021. Like other Mars rovers, it explores the planet’s surface with cameras and scientific instruments. Jezero is especially interesting because it once held a lake and a river delta, places where signs of ancient life might have been preserved. Perseverance searches rocks and soil for evidence of ancient microbial life and collects samples that could eventually be brought to Earth for closer study. The rover also carried Ingenuity, a small, solar-powered rotorcraft. Ingenuity was a technology demonstration, not a science rover: its purpose was to test whether powered flight was possible in Mars’s thin atmosphere. In April 2021, it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.

Click chemistry is a branch of chemistry that uses simple, reliable reactions to join molecules, as if they “click” into place. Scientists can use it to attach a reporter molecule, such as a fluorescent tag, to a biomolecule so they can locate or study it. One important target is proteins: polymers made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Proteins carry out many jobs in cells and can interact with small molecules, including drugs, so marking them helps researchers investigate those interactions. Some click reactions use copper, which can be toxic to living cells. Copper-free versions allow researchers to label molecules inside cells without disrupting normal cell chemistry; these are called bioorthogonal reactions.

Limb loss is the absence of part or all of an arm or leg. A person may be born without a limb, lose one in an accident, or have one surgically removed because of an injury or disease such as bone cancer. Someone who has lost a limb is also called an amputee. Limb loss can change how a person walks, handles objects, or takes part in activities, but rehabilitation can help them develop new skills. This may include exercises, mobility training, and learning to use a prosthesis, an artificial replacement for a missing body part. A limb prosthesis may have a socket that fits over the remaining limb, a supporting structure, and a specialized hand or foot. Prostheses can restore some functions, though they do not work exactly like natural limbs.

Ductility is a material’s ability to stretch when pulled and be drawn into a thin wire without breaking. A ductile solid can change shape under tension, the pulling force that tries to lengthen it. Ductility is different from malleability: a malleable material can be hammered or rolled into thin sheets. Aluminum is a lightweight metal with both properties, and its ductility helps make it useful for electrical conductors such as wires. Aluminum comes from the ore bauxite. In the Bayer process, bauxite is refined to obtain alumina, or aluminum oxide. To produce aluminum metal, the Hall-Héroult process dissolves alumina in molten cryolite and uses electrolysis—an electric current that drives a chemical reaction—to separate the aluminum from the oxygen.

The actinides are a series of 15 radioactive chemical elements, from actinium (atomic number 89) to lawrencium (atomic number 103). On most periodic tables, they appear in a separate row beneath the lanthanides, although they belong to period 7. Some actinides, such as uranium, occur naturally and are used as fuel in nuclear reactors; others have been made in laboratories. One synthetic actinide is mendelevium, element 101, first produced at Berkeley in 1955. It was named in honor of Dmitri Mendeleev, the Russian chemist who formulated the periodic law and developed an early periodic table. By recognizing patterns among elements, Mendeleev was able to predict the properties of elements that had not yet been discovered.

The Descent of Man is an 1871 book by the English naturalist Charles Darwin. In it, Darwin applied his theory of evolution to humans, arguing that humans and other animals share ancestors. He also examined sexual selection: how traits can spread because they help an animal attract a mate or compete for one. Darwin used this idea to discuss differences between the sexes. His thinking about evolution had developed during and after his voyage aboard HMS Beagle, when he observed plants and animals in South America and the Galápagos Islands. The different beak shapes of Galápagos finches helped him understand how species can adapt to different environments. Darwin is especially known for explaining natural selection, the process by which helpful inherited traits become more common over generations.

Anaphase is the stage of mitosis that begins just after metaphase, when duplicated chromosomes have lined up at the cell’s equator. Each duplicated chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at a region called the centromere. A protein complex called the kinetochore forms at each centromere and provides an attachment site for spindle microtubules, also called spindle fibers. Once the cell is ready to proceed, the sister chromatids separate. Spindle fibers shorten and pull the chromatids by their kinetochores toward opposite poles of the cell. This movement gives each end of the cell a matching set of chromosomes. The cell can then complete mitosis and divide into two daughter cells with the same genetic information.

Io is the innermost of Jupiter’s four large Galilean moons and the most volcanically active world in the solar system. Although Io is about the size of Earth’s Moon, it has hundreds of active volcanoes. Jupiter’s gravity stretches and squeezes Io as it orbits, while gravitational interactions with the moons Europa and Ganymede help keep its orbit slightly oval. This repeated flexing generates heat inside Io, melting rock that erupts as lava. Sulfur and other volcanic materials give its surface striking yellow, orange, red, and white colors. Io’s largest named volcanic depression is Loki Patera, a broad basin containing a lava lake. The lake periodically brightens during episodes of intense activity as hot material becomes exposed at its surface.

Irrigation is the controlled delivery of water to farmland to supplement rainfall. It helps crops grow when rain is scarce or arrives at the wrong time. Farmers can move water through canals, pipes, or channels and apply it to fields as needed. Around Angkor, engineers of the Khmer Empire built large reservoirs called baray to collect and store water for irrigation. These reservoirs were part of a wider water-management system that helped support farming in the region. Sri Lankan kingdoms also developed irrigation works, including underground canals that carried water to agricultural land. In both places, managing water allowed people to grow crops more reliably instead of depending entirely on rain.

The Kutta–Joukowski theorem explains how a wing or other airfoil generates lift as fluid flows around it. For idealized two-dimensional flow, it states that lift per unit span—the lift on each unit of wing length—equals the fluid’s density multiplied by the free-stream speed and the circulation around the airfoil. Free-stream speed is the speed of the fluid far from the wing. Circulation measures the overall tendency of the flow to move around the airfoil; mathematically, it is found by integrating the fluid’s velocity along a closed curve enclosing it. Although the word may suggest a whirlpool, circulation does not mean that air must travel in closed loops. A wing’s shape and angle to the airflow help establish circulation, producing a pressure difference and deflecting air downward.

Manatees, sometimes called sea cows, are large aquatic mammals that eat plants such as seagrass. They live in warm coastal waters and rivers, including those in Florida. Although they spend their lives in water, they breathe air and must regularly surface. Manatees often move slowly and feed in shallow areas where people also use boats. This puts them at risk of being struck by boats or injured by propellers; some surviving manatees have visible propeller scars. Boat collisions are a major human-caused cause of manatee deaths, so speed-restricted “no-wake” zones help protect them by requiring boats to travel slowly. Manatees also face threats from habitat loss and pollution, which can damage the waters and plants they depend on.

Sally Ride was an American physicist and NASA astronaut who became the first American woman in space in 1983. She flew aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger on that historic mission and returned to space on Challenger in 1984. In 1986, Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew members, including teacher Christa McAuliffe. Ride was appointed to the presidential panel that investigated the disaster and recommended safety reforms. This panel is commonly called the Rogers Commission, after its chair, William P. Rogers. The investigation found that an O-ring seal in one of the shuttle’s solid rocket boosters failed in the unusually cold conditions at launch. Another commission member, physicist Richard Feynman, demonstrated how cold could affect the rubber seal using ice water.

A diopter is a unit of optical power used to describe how strongly a lens bends light. One diopter equals one reciprocal meter. The lens property behind this measurement is focal length: the distance from a lens to the point where parallel rays of light come together, or appear to spread from. A lens’s optical power in diopters is the reciprocal of its focal length in meters. For example, a lens with a focal length of 0.5 meter has a power of 2 diopters. Focal length also appears in the thin-lens equation: the reciprocal of the object distance plus the reciprocal of the image distance equals the reciprocal of the focal length. Eyeglass prescriptions use diopters to specify the power of corrective lenses.

Transcription is the step of gene expression in which an RNA polymerase reads one strand of DNA as a template and builds a complementary RNA molecule. It produces RNA, not a new DNA molecule, and takes place before translation, when ribosomes use messenger RNA (mRNA) to make a protein. Transcription begins when RNA polymerase binds near a gene at a promoter. Proteins called transcription factors help control whether this happens; activators can bind enhancer sequences to increase a gene’s transcription. In eukaryotic cells, transcription occurs in the nucleus. RNA polymerase II makes the RNA precursors of most protein-coding mRNAs and is strongly inhibited by the mushroom toxin α-amanitin. Before these precursors become mature mRNA, they are processed, including the addition of a 5-prime cap and a poly-A tail.

A Western blot is a laboratory technique used to find a particular protein in a mixture. First, gel electrophoresis separates the proteins, usually by size. The proteins are then transferred from the gel onto a membrane, where they can be tested with antibodies. An antibody is a Y-shaped protein that recognizes a specific part of another molecule, called an epitope. In a Western blot, the primary antibody binds directly to an epitope on the target protein. A separately labeled secondary antibody then binds to the primary antibody. The label produces a detectable signal, showing whether the target protein is present and where it appears on the membrane. Scientists use Western blots to study proteins in cells and tissues.

Alveoli are microscopic air sacs at the ends of the smallest airways in the lungs. Each alveolus is surrounded by capillaries, or tiny blood vessels, and has a very thin wall. This allows oxygen from inhaled air to pass into the blood while carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the air to be exhaled. Keeping these sacs open is essential for breathing. Special cells in their walls, called type II pneumocytes, secrete pulmonary surfactant. This substance reduces surface tension—the force that would otherwise make the moist inner surfaces stick together—and helps prevent the alveoli from collapsing during exhalation. Smoking and vaping can damage lung tissue, including the alveoli, making it harder for the lungs to exchange gases effectively.

The gut microbiome is the community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, that live throughout the gastrointestinal tract, especially in the intestines. Members include species such as Escherichia coli (E. coli) and Bacteroides fragilis. As they help break down food, these microbes produce substances called metabolites. Some metabolites may affect the brain through the gut–brain axis, the two-way communication between the digestive system and the brain. Researchers are studying whether changes in the gut microbiome influence Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia in older adults. Alzheimer’s is a neurodegenerative disease, meaning brain cells gradually become damaged and die. It is characterized by beta-amyloid plaques, which build up between brain cells, and tangles of a protein called tau inside them. Scientists are investigating whether diet-related changes to gut microbes could help, but this remains experimental.

A tree is a data structure that organizes information in a hierarchy. It consists of nodes connected by edges, with one designated starting node called the root. A node can have children below it, and a node with no children is called a leaf. Unlike a family tree, each node in a data-structure tree has only one parent, except for the root, which has none. One example is the Document Object Model (DOM), which represents a web page as a tree of elements that can contain other elements. A binary tree is a particular kind of tree in which each node has at most two children, conventionally called the left child and the right child.

Zoom is a videoconferencing platform that lets people meet online using live video and audio. It can also be used for text chat and screen sharing, making it useful for remote classes, work meetings, and events such as online quizbowl matches. Zoom became especially popular during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many people could not meet in person. That rapid growth brought attention to problems with its digital security and privacy. In 2020, Zoom announced a 90-day pause on developing non-security features so it could focus on addressing those concerns. The company was founded in 2011 by Eric Yuan, a Chinese-American engineer who had previously been a vice president at Cisco. Yuan later led Zoom as its CEO.

An air conditioner cools an enclosed space, such as a room or a vehicle, by moving heat from inside to outside rather than creating cold. Most use a vapor-compression cycle, in which a working fluid called a refrigerant circulates through coils. In the indoor coil, the refrigerant evaporates from a liquid into a gas and absorbs heat from the surrounding air. A compressor then raises the gas’s pressure and temperature so it can release that heat outdoors. In the outdoor coil, the refrigerant condenses back into a liquid, giving off heat to the outside air. It then passes through a valve that lowers its pressure, ready to repeat the cycle. Fans move air across the coils to help transfer heat.

An echo is a sound heard again after its sound waves bounce off a surface and return to the listener. If you shout in a cave or canyon, the sound may reflect from a distant wall and come back after a noticeable delay. Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air, so the reflecting surface must be far enough away for the returning sound to be heard separately from the original. Many closely spaced reflections blend together instead, creating reverberation. Computers can simulate how sounds reflect in a space using ray tracing: they follow possible paths of sound and calculate when reflected sound would arrive. Ray tracing is also used to generate images by following paths of light rays and their reflections, though it is generally slower than scan-line rendering techniques.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the field of computing that develops methods to analyze, represent, and generate human language. It helps computers work with text for tasks such as searching documents, translating between languages, and generating responses. Before a system can analyze a sentence, it often performs tokenization: dividing the text into smaller units called tokens, which may be words, parts of words, or punctuation marks. Other methods include tagging words by their roles, such as noun or verb, and stemming, which reduces related words toward a common root. Statistical models and language models learn patterns from large amounts of text to predict or produce sequences of words. Modern systems such as GPT use transformer models to generate text that can sound remarkably human.

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid, meaning humans must get it from food because our bodies cannot make it. It is also called aromatic because part of its chemical structure contains a ring of atoms. When cells build proteins, the standard genetic code uses the RNA codon UGG to specify tryptophan; no other codon specifies it. Some bacteria can make their own tryptophan, and the genes involved are controlled by the trp operon, a repressible system that switches off when enough tryptophan is available. Tryptophan is also a starting material for serotonin and melatonin. Melatonin is a hormone secreted mainly by the pineal gland that helps regulate circadian rhythms, including the daily sleep–wake cycle.

Gauss’s law connects electric charge to the electric field it produces. Imagine a closed surface, such as an imaginary sphere, surrounding some charges. Electric flux measures how much of the electric field passes through the surface: to calculate it, you add up the field’s component perpendicular to each tiny part of the surface. Gauss’s law says that the net electric flux through the closed surface equals the total charge enclosed divided by the permittivity, a property of the surrounding material. Charges outside the surface can affect the field at points on it, but they do not change its net flux. In its differential form, Gauss’s law says that the divergence of the electric field at a point equals the charge density there divided by the permittivity.

A moraine is a ridge or pile of rock debris left behind by a glacier. As a glacier moves, it erodes the land, picking up and carrying material ranging from fine clay and sand to gravel and large stones. This material is called sediment while it is being transported. When the ice melts, it deposits some of the debris directly onto the ground. The unsorted mixture deposited this way is called till, and a buildup of till forms a moraine. Moraines can mark where the edge of a glacier once stood, helping scientists trace how glaciers moved and changed over time. Weathering is different from erosion: weathering breaks rock down, while erosion moves the broken material from one place to another.

Soldering joins metal pieces by heating a filler alloy, called solder, until it melts and flows into the joint. The pieces being joined, known as the base metals, stay solid because the solder melts at a lower temperature. This differs from welding, which melts the base metals, and from brazing, which uses a filler metal that melts at a higher temperature than solder. Soldering is widely used to attach electronic components to printed circuit boards; in large-scale production, boards may pass over a wave of molten solder. Traditional solder often contains tin and lead, a dense metal with the chemical symbol Pb. Because lead is toxic, lead-free solder alloys are now widely used. Some tin-lead mixtures have a lower melting point than either metal alone; these are called eutectic mixtures.

Kirchhoff’s Current Law describes what happens to electric current at a junction, or node, where circuit wires meet. Electric current is the rate at which electric charge passes a point. It is represented by the symbol I and measured in amperes, or amps. Because charge cannot disappear or pile up at an ordinary junction, the total current flowing into it must equal the total current flowing out. For example, if 5 amps enter a junction and one outgoing wire carries 2 amps, the other outgoing wires must carry a total of 3 amps. This rule follows from conservation of charge. It can also be written as an algebraic sum of zero when currents entering and leaving are given opposite signs.

Sociobiology is the interdisciplinary study of how evolution shapes social behavior in animals. It combines evolutionary biology with the study of animal behavior to ask why behaviors such as cooperation and altruism develop and persist. One important example is eusociality, in which animals live in organized colonies, care for young together, and divide tasks such as finding food and defending the nest. Ants are eusocial insects: worker ants cooperate to support their colonies, and some species farm fungi for food or protect acacia trees in exchange for shelter. The Harvard biologist E. O. Wilson studied ants extensively and helped establish sociobiology as a field. His influential 1975 book, Sociobiology: The New Synthesis, brought together research on the evolutionary roots of social behavior.

Pectin is a group of plant polysaccharides found in primary cell walls, especially in fruits such as apples and citrus fruits. Its main building blocks are related to galactose, a type of sugar. Pectin helps plant tissues hold together because it is an important part of the middle lamella, the thin layer between neighboring cells’ primary walls that acts like a cement. Primary walls also contain cellulose, which provides strength while allowing growing cells some flexibility. In cooking, pectin’s ability to form a gel makes it useful for setting jams and jellies. When fruit is cooked with the right amounts of sugar and acid, pectin molecules join into a network that traps water, turning a runny mixture into a spreadable preserve.

Snow is frozen precipitation that forms when water vapor in cold clouds becomes ice crystals. As the crystals grow and join together, they fall to the ground as snowflakes or clusters of flakes. Snow can cover the landscape, soften sounds, and create a quiet winter scene. That kind of scene appears in “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening,” a poem by the American poet Robert Frost. Its unnamed speaker pauses beside snow-filled woods but then remembers his responsibilities, saying, “I have promises to keep / and miles to go before I sleep.” Frost also wrote “The Road Not Taken,” a poem about choosing between two paths. Remember that snow is the weather phenomenon in the woods poem, while Robert Frost is the poet who wrote it.

Alkenes are hydrocarbons made of carbon and hydrogen that contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond. They are called unsaturated because the double bond can react to add other atoms, unlike the single bonds in alkanes. Ethene is a simple example of an alkene. One way to test for alkenes is to add an orange-brown solution of bromine, a halogen with the chemical symbol Br that is liquid at room temperature. If an alkene is present, bromine reacts with the carbon–carbon double bond and the solution loses its color. This color change is a qualitative test: it helps show that a reactive double bond is present, but it does not measure how much alkene is in the sample.

The Permian–Triassic Extinction Event, also called the Great Dying, occurred about 252 million years ago and was the largest known mass extinction in Earth’s history. A mass extinction happens when many species disappear across the world in a relatively short span of geologic time. During this event, most marine species and many organisms on land died out. It coincided with enormous eruptions in northern Siberia that formed a flood-basalt volcanic province called the Siberian Traps. These eruptions released large amounts of greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide, which warmed the planet and disrupted oceans and ecosystems. Scientists study the event to understand how rapid environmental changes can threaten life on a global scale.

The circumstellar habitable zone, also called the Goldilocks zone, is the range of orbital distances around a star where a planet could maintain liquid water on its surface if it has a suitable atmosphere. Closer to the star, water may evaporate; farther away, it may freeze. The zone’s inner and outer boundaries depend partly on the star’s luminosity, or brightness, and on how the planet’s climate and atmosphere trap heat. Being in this zone does not guarantee life or even liquid water. Some planets there may be tidally locked: their rotation and orbit are synchronized, so the same hemisphere always faces the star, leaving permanent day and night sides. Pluto and its moon Charon are also tidally locked. On such a planet, the strip between the hot and cold sides might offer more moderate conditions.

Camillo Golgi was an Italian physician and histologist who worked at the University of Pavia. He discovered the Golgi apparatus, a cell organelle that modifies and packages proteins into small sacs called vesicles for transport. He also developed a silver-based staining method, known as the Golgi stain or “black reaction,” that makes a small number of cells in nervous tissue appear dark. This allowed scientists to see individual neurons and their branching shapes more clearly. A neuron, or nerve cell, is an excitable cell with a cell body, branching dendrites that receive signals, and an axon that carries signals to other cells. Neurons communicate at junctions called synapses. Golgi shared the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Santiago Ramón y Cajal for their work on the nervous system.

Zebras are African equids, relatives of horses and donkeys, best known for their distinctive black-and-white stripes. Each zebra has a unique stripe pattern. As grazing animals, zebras eat grasses and move to find fresh food and water. Many plains zebras join wildebeest herds during the great migration across the Serengeti, a vast grassland ecosystem in Tanzania. The animals follow seasonal rains that bring new grass, and their route extends north into Kenya’s Maasai Mara. Traveling in large groups can help zebras spot predators such as lions, although river crossings and long journeys remain dangerous. When a question describes striped African equids migrating with wildebeest, the animals are zebras; when it asks for the Tanzanian grassland on their route toward the Maasai Mara, the answer is the Serengeti.

The Indian cobra is a venomous snake native to South Asia. Its scientific name is Naja naja, and it is known for the broad hood it displays when threatened. The cobra makes this hood by spreading the ribs in its neck, making itself look larger. Indian cobras appear in Rudyard Kipling’s story “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi” as Nag and his mate, Nagaina. Their opponent is Rikki-Tikki-Tavi, a mongoose that protects a family from the snakes. The story was published in Kipling’s 1894 collection The Jungle Book, which also includes stories about Mowgli and Baloo. Thus, Nag and Nagaina are Indian cobras, and the collection containing their story is The Jungle Book.

During Mars’s 1877 opposition, when the planet was especially well placed for observation from Earth, Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli studied its surface from Milan’s Brera Observatory. He drew detailed maps showing a network of narrow, straight-looking lines and called them canali, an Italian word meaning “channels.” In English-language accounts, canali was often translated as “canals,” suggesting waterways built by intelligent beings. The supposed features became known as the Martian canals, and some people imagined that Martians had constructed them to carry water for irrigation. Later, clearer observations and spacecraft images found no such network. The lines were an optical illusion caused by the difficulty of seeing fine details through telescopes, not evidence of Martian engineering.

Stem cells are unspecialized cells that can self-renew, making more stem cells, and differentiate, developing into specialized cells with particular jobs, such as blood or muscle cells. Different stem cells have different developmental potential: totipotent stem cells have the broadest potential and can produce all the cells needed to form an entire organism. Stem cells can be collected from the placenta, a temporary organ that develops during pregnancy. The placenta exchanges oxygen, nutrients, and waste between the mother and fetus, and the umbilical cord connects it to the fetus. After the baby is born, the placenta is expelled during the third stage of labor. Scientists study stem cells to understand development and explore ways to repair damaged tissues.

Weight is the gravitational force acting on an object. Near Earth’s surface, it points toward Earth’s center and has a magnitude equal to the object’s mass multiplied by the local acceleration due to gravity, often written as W = mg. Mass measures how much matter an object contains and stays the same wherever the object goes, but weight can change because gravity varies from place to place. For example, an object weighs less on the Moon than on Earth. When a book rests motionless on a level table, its weight pulls downward while the table pushes upward with an equal force. That upward support is called the normal force; “normal” means it acts perpendicular to the tabletop.

Müllerian mimicry occurs when two or more species that are genuinely toxic, venomous, unpalatable, or otherwise defended evolve similar, conspicuous warning signals. Bright colors or bold patterns can warn predators that an animal is unpleasant or dangerous to eat. If a predator learns to avoid one defended species, it may also avoid other species with the same pattern, benefiting them all. This is an example of honest signaling because each species really does have a defense; it is not a harmless animal pretending to be dangerous. One example is the neotropical red postman butterfly, Heliconius erato. It is itself unpalatable and shares striking red, yellow, and black warning patterns with another defended butterfly.

Terminal velocity is the constant speed an object reaches when the forces driving its motion are balanced by forces opposing it. A skydiver first accelerates because gravity pulls downward more strongly than air resistance pushes upward. As the skydiver speeds up, air resistance increases until it equals the skydiver’s weight. The net force and acceleration are then zero, but the skydiver keeps descending at terminal velocity. A tiny sphere settling slowly through a viscous fluid can reach terminal velocity too. In that case, its downward weight is balanced by an upward buoyant force and fluid drag. For a small sphere moving slowly under suitable conditions, Stokes’ law gives the drag force as 6π η r v, where η is the fluid’s viscosity, r is the sphere’s radius, and v is its speed.

Biological altruism is behavior that increases another organism’s fitness—its chances of surviving and reproducing—while reducing the fitness of the individual performing it. For example, an animal may give an alarm call that warns others of a predator but makes itself more noticeable. Biologists classify the behavior by these effects on fitness, not by whether the animal seems caring or intends to help. A costly act can still spread through a population if it helps relatives who share some of the actor’s genes. Hamilton’s rule predicts when this can happen: rb > c, where r is the genetic relatedness between actor and recipient, b is the fitness benefit to the recipient, and c is the fitness cost to the actor. The greater the relatedness or benefit, the more likely altruism is to be favored by natural selection.

A scavenger is an organism that feeds on dead animals rather than hunting and killing its own prey. Scavengers may eat animals that died naturally or the remains of prey left behind by predators. Vultures and flesh flies are examples. By consuming carcasses, scavengers help recycle nutrients through an ecosystem. One unusual scavenger is the bearded vulture, an Old World bird that feeds largely on bones. It carries bones into the air and drops them onto rocks to break them into pieces it can swallow. Its feathers are naturally pale, but they often look rusty orange because the bird bathes in iron-rich soil. Scavengers differ from predators, which hunt live prey, and from decomposers such as fungi and bacteria, which break down dead material.

The grizzly bear is a North American form of the brown bear. Its most recognizable feature is a prominent hump between its shoulders. This hump is made of muscle, not fat, and helps power the bear’s strong forelimbs as it digs for roots, plant bulbs, and other food. Grizzlies are omnivores, eating plants, insects, fish, and other animals. A closely related brown-bear population, the Kodiak brown bears, lives on the Kodiak Archipelago in Alaska. Kodiak bears are generally larger than grizzlies and are among the largest bears in the world. Both are brown bears, but their names help distinguish the grizzlies of mainland North America from the bears native to the Kodiak islands.

Pierre Curie was a French physicist whose work helped scientists understand both electricity and radioactivity. With his brother Jacques, he discovered piezoelectricity: the ability of some crystals, including Rochelle salt, to produce an electric charge when squeezed. Pierre later studied radioactive materials with his wife, Marie Curie, a Polish-born physicist and chemist. While investigating pitchblende, a uranium-rich ore, Marie and Pierre identified two new elements: polonium, named after Marie’s home country of Poland, and radium. In 1903, Pierre and Marie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Henri Becquerel for their research on radiation. Marie went on to win a second Nobel Prize, becoming the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

Tools are objects used to manipulate the environment or carry out tasks, such as hammers for striking and axes for cutting. Stone tools were important in early human evolution because they helped our ancestors process food and other materials. Humans are not the only tool users: some other primates use objects to solve problems. At Gombe Stream National Park, on the eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika in Tanzania, Jane Goodall observed chimpanzees using grass stems to “fish” termites from their nests. Her research helped show that tool use was not unique to humans. Gombe was also the site of a four-year conflict between the Kasakela and Kahama chimpanzee communities.

A volcanic hotspot is a relatively long-lasting area where hot material rises from deep within Earth’s mantle, producing magma that can feed volcanoes. Unlike many volcanoes, which form near the edges of tectonic plates, hotspot volcanoes can form far from plate boundaries. The hotspot stays roughly in place while a plate slowly moves over it. Magma breaks through the plate to build a volcano; as the plate carries that volcano away, a new one may form above the hotspot. This process creates a chain of volcanoes that become older farther from the active hotspot. The Hawaiian Islands formed this way as the Pacific Plate moved northwest. Hawaiʻi, the youngest major island, is volcanically active, while the islands farther northwest are progressively older.

Endorphins are short chains of amino acids, called peptides, that the body makes naturally. They act as opioids by binding to opioid receptors in the brain and nervous system, helping to reduce pain signaling. Endorphins can also contribute to feelings of pleasure or euphoria. Their release is associated with activities such as exercise and laughter, which may help explain why these activities can make people feel better. One specific endorphin, beta-endorphin, is a chain of 31 amino acids. The body produces it by cutting a larger protein called proopiomelanocortin into smaller pieces, a process known as cleavage. Beta-endorphin is associated with pain relief.

The Pleiades is a nearby open star cluster in the constellation Taurus. An open cluster is a group of stars that formed from the same cloud of gas and dust and remain loosely held together by gravity. The Pleiades is bright enough to see without a telescope, although most people can pick out only a few of its stars. It is traditionally called the Seven Sisters, a name drawn from Greek mythology. French astronomer Charles Messier included the cluster in his catalog of objects that might be mistaken for comets. It is the catalog’s 45th entry, so astronomers also call it Messier 45, or M45. If you see a small, sparkling group of stars in Taurus, you may be looking at the Pleiades.

Humphry Davy was an English chemist at the Royal Institution who pioneered the use of electrolysis to isolate elements. In electrolysis, an electric current supplies the energy needed to drive a chemical reaction that would not happen on its own. Davy used a voltaic pile, an early battery, to pass electricity through molten compounds and separate metals from them. In 1807, he electrolyzed molten potash and isolated potassium, a soft, highly reactive alkali metal with atomic number 19. Potassium is found in many mineral salts. Davy also isolated sodium that year and later helped isolate calcium, magnesium, and barium. His experiments showed that electricity could break compounds apart and reveal elements that had not previously been obtained in their pure forms.

Turtles are reptiles in the order Testudines, known for the hard shells that protect their bodies. The group includes species that live mostly in water and terrestrial tortoises, which spend most of their lives on land. Turtles appear in stories from many cultures. In some myths, a turtle carries the world on its back; in others, its shell supports the sky. They also feature in Aesop’s fable The Tortoise and the Hare. In that story, a hare is so confident it will win a race that it stops along the way. The tortoise keeps moving slowly and steadily, passes the hare, and wins. The tale is often used to show that persistence can matter more than speed.

A non-fungible token, or NFT, is a unique digital token recorded on a blockchain, a shared record maintained by a network of computers. “Non-fungible” means it is not interchangeable with another token in the way that one unit of a cryptocurrency can be exchanged for another. An NFT can be linked to a digital artwork or a physical object to help show ownership or authenticity. The token is distinct, but a digital file it represents, such as an image, can still be copied and shared; owning the NFT does not necessarily give someone copyright over the artwork. Ethereum is a blockchain network widely used for NFTs. It introduced the ERC-721 standard, which allows tokens to be individually identifiable, and its native cryptocurrency is called ether.

The Stern–Gerlach experiment, performed in 1922, showed that angular momentum in atoms can take only certain allowed values rather than any value. Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach sent a narrow beam of neutral silver atoms through a nonuniform magnetic field, whose strength varied across the beam. If the atoms’ magnetic orientations could vary freely, they would have formed a continuous spread on the detector. Instead, the beam split into two distinct paths. Each silver atom has a single outer, or valence, electron in a 5s orbital. The two paths correspond to the two possible orientations of that electron’s spin, a form of intrinsic angular momentum, relative to the field. The result provided striking evidence of quantization in the atomic world.

A spectral line is a narrow, distinct feature in a spectrum, the spread of light into its different wavelengths. Atoms and ions produce spectral lines when their electrons move between energy levels: they emit light at a particular wavelength when an electron drops to a lower level, or absorb it when an electron moves to a higher one. Because each element has its own set of possible energy changes, its pattern of spectral lines acts like a fingerprint. Astronomers use these lines to identify elements in distant stars and clouds of gas. One important example is the H-alpha line of hydrogen, at about 656.3 nanometers in the red part of the spectrum. It comes from an electron moving from the third energy level to the second and helps astronomers map glowing emission nebulae.

The photosphere is the Sun’s visible surface: the layer that forms the bright disk we see in ordinary visible-light images. The Sun is made of hot gas rather than solid material, so the photosphere is not a hard surface. Instead, it is the layer from which most sunlight escapes into space. Sunspots are patches on the photosphere that look dark against their brighter surroundings. They still give off plenty of light, but they are cooler than nearby areas. Strong magnetic fields in a sunspot interfere with convection, the movement of hot gas that normally carries energy toward the surface. With less heat reaching it, the spot emits less light than the surrounding photosphere and appears dark by comparison.

Ammonites were an extinct group of marine mollusks related to modern squid, octopuses, and nautiluses. As cephalopods, they had tentacles and lived in the sea, but unlike squid and octopuses, they had hard external shells. These shells were usually coiled into a distinctive spiral, and their fossils are common in rocks from the Mesozoic Era. Ammonites were affected by a major climate change during the Late Triassic Period called the Carnian Pluvial Event, or CPE. For several million years, the climate became warmer and wetter, with unusually heavy rainfall. This episode disrupted marine ecosystems and devastated many ammonite groups, although ammonites survived and later became abundant again.

Cluster headache is a neurological disorder that causes repeated attacks of extremely severe pain, usually around or behind one eye. Attacks often come in groups, or “clusters,” over weeks or months, with pain-free periods between them. During an attack, the eye on the painful side may water or turn red, and the nostril on that side may become blocked or runny. Unlike a migraine, a cluster headache often makes a person feel restless rather than wanting to lie still. One common treatment for an attack is high-flow oxygen: the person breathes nearly 100 percent oxygen through a non-rebreather mask, which can relieve the pain within minutes. Researchers are also studying whether psychedelic drugs could help prevent cluster headaches, but this remains experimental.

The cerebrum, the largest part of the brain, is divided into major regions called cerebral lobes. Each lobe has important jobs, although they work together. The frontal lobe helps with planning, decision-making, and voluntary movement. The temporal lobe helps process sound and supports memory, while the occipital lobe is mainly involved in vision. The parietal lobe lies behind the frontal lobe and above the temporal lobe. It processes information from the body, including touch, temperature, and the position of body parts. Its sensory association areas help you make sense of what you feel. For example, they help you recognize a letter or number traced on your skin without looking, an ability called graphesthesia.

An impact basin is an enormous, usually circular depression formed when a large asteroid or comet strikes the surface of a planet or moon. The collision releases tremendous energy, excavating rock and often leaving a raised rim and surrounding debris. Impact basins are generally much larger than ordinary impact craters, although the terms are sometimes used interchangeably. Mercury’s Caloris Basin is about 1,550 kilometers across and is the planet’s largest well-preserved impact structure. Its name comes from a Latin word meaning “heat.” Another example is the Herschel impact feature on Saturn’s moon Mimas. Herschel is so large compared with the moon that it gives Mimas an appearance resembling the Death Star from Star Wars. Studying these features helps scientists understand the collisions that shaped the Solar System.

Comets are small Solar System bodies made mainly of ice, dust, and rock. Their solid central part is called the nucleus. When a comet travels closer to the Sun, sunlight warms its surface, causing some ice to change directly into gas, a process called sublimation. The escaping gas carries dust with it and forms a large, fuzzy cloud around the nucleus called the coma. Sunlight and particles streaming from the Sun can then push material away from the coma, producing one or more tails that extend away from the Sun. Comets often become easier to see during this active stage. They can also leave trails of debris along their paths; when Earth passes through one, the debris burns up in our atmosphere and creates a meteor shower.

Basalt is a dark, fine-grained volcanic rock that forms when lava with a low proportion of silica cools and solidifies. Lava is molten rock on Earth’s surface; while it remains underground, it is called magma. Basaltic lava flows relatively easily, so repeated eruptions can build broad, gently sloping shield volcanoes, such as those in Hawaii. Basalt also forms at mid-ocean ridges, where tectonic plates spread apart and lava erupts onto the seafloor. There, seawater rapidly chills the outside of a lava flow while molten rock inside continues to push outward. This process creates a series of rounded lobes called pillow lava. Whether it forms underwater or on land, the rapidly cooled rock often has crystals too small to see without a microscope.

Cosmic expansion is the ongoing increase in distances between galaxies on the largest scales. As space expands, light traveling through it is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths, a change called redshift. More distant galaxies generally show greater redshifts, revealing that the universe is expanding. Expansion began in the early universe after the Big Bang and continues today; it does not mean that galaxies, stars, or planets themselves are growing. Observations of distant Type Ia supernovae helped show that cosmic expansion has been speeding up in the universe’s later history. Scientists commonly attribute this acceleration to dark energy, a nearly uniform component of the universe with negative pressure. What dark energy is remains one of cosmology’s major unanswered questions.

Greenhouse gases are gases in Earth’s atmosphere that absorb infrared radiation released by the warmed surface and re-radiate some of that energy, slowing the loss of heat to space. This natural greenhouse effect helps keep Earth warm enough for life, but increasing greenhouse gas concentrations contribute to global warming. Examples include water vapor, carbon dioxide and methane. Carbon dioxide is released by activities such as burning fossil fuels, while methane comes from sources including wetlands, livestock and leaks from natural gas systems. Methane has the chemical formula CH4: one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms. It is the simplest hydrocarbon, a compound made only of carbon and hydrogen, and the simplest alkane. Over a 100-year period, methane is estimated to trap about 25 times as much heat as an equal mass of carbon dioxide.

Oxytocin is a hormone made of nine amino acids, so it is called a peptide hormone. Neurons in the hypothalamus, a region of the brain, make oxytocin and carry it to the posterior pituitary, the back lobe of a small gland at the base of the brain. There, oxytocin is stored in nerve endings until it is released into the bloodstream. The posterior pituitary also releases another hormone called vasopressin. During labor, oxytocin strengthens contractions of the uterus, helping to deliver the baby. During breastfeeding, it causes milk to be pushed from the breast toward the nipple; this is called milk ejection. Oxytocin also helps support social bonding, including the bond between parents and newborns, which is why it is sometimes called the “love hormone.”

On the Origin of Species is an 1859 book by the British naturalist Charles Darwin that explained how populations change over generations through natural selection. Individuals vary, and those with traits that help them survive and reproduce tend to pass those traits to their offspring. Darwin opened the book by discussing variation among domesticated plants and animals, showing how breeders select desirable traits. Its first edition was published by John Murray and bore a subtitle ending “the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life”; here, “races” referred broadly to varieties of living things, not modern human racial categories. Before writing the book, Darwin spent years studying and classifying barnacles. On an earlier voyage aboard the British survey ship HMS Beagle, he visited the Galápagos Islands and collected finch specimens.

Aragonite is a mineral made of calcium carbonate, with the chemical formula CaCO3. It is a polymorph of calcite: the two minerals have the same chemical formula but different crystal structures. Aragonite is less stable than calcite under most conditions near Earth’s surface, and many reef-building corals use it to build their skeletons. Calcite has a trigonal crystal structure and is a major component of limestone and chalk. Scientists monitor aragonite’s saturation state in seawater to understand ocean acidification. This measurement indicates how readily aragonite can form or remain intact in the water. When carbon dioxide from the atmosphere dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid and changes the balance of dissolved carbonate compounds. As aragonite saturation falls, corals may have more difficulty building and maintaining their skeletons.

Kaposi sarcoma is a cancer that develops from cells lining blood and lymph vessels in connective tissue. It often appears as reddish-purple or brown patches or raised lesions on the skin, but it can also affect the mouth and internal organs. The disease is linked to human herpesvirus 8, commonly abbreviated HHV-8. Most people infected with HHV-8 do not develop Kaposi sarcoma, but the risk is higher when the immune system is weakened, especially in people with HIV/AIDS. HHV-8 is also associated with two other conditions: primary effusion lymphoma and multicentric Castleman disease. Although Kaposi sarcoma belongs to a group of cancers called sarcomas, which arise from connective tissues, its link to blood-vessel cells helps explain the color of its visible lesions.

A p orbital is a region around an atom’s nucleus described by a one-electron wavefunction, which tells us where an electron is likely to be found. It has angular momentum quantum number ℓ = 1 and is often drawn as two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, separated by a nodal plane where the probability of finding the electron is zero. Each shell with p orbitals has three orientations, which together form a p subshell. Each orbital can hold two electrons, so the subshell can hold six. Most noble gases have a filled p subshell in their outer shell; helium is the exception. Noble gases were once thought to be completely inert, but Neil Bartlett showed that xenon, the noble gas with atomic number 54, could react with platinum hexafluoride to form a compound.

Robert Ballard is an American oceanographer and marine archaeologist who explores the deep sea and studies historic shipwrecks. He led the 1985 expedition that located the Titanic, which had sunk in the North Atlantic in 1912. He also found the wreck of the German battleship Bismarck and helped locate the remains of PT-109, a patrol boat commanded by future U.S. president John F. Kennedy during World War II. Ballard used deep-sea technology, including remotely operated cameras, to search areas too deep for divers. His team also discovered the wrecks of the USS Yorktown and USS Hammann. Both American ships were sunk during the Battle of Midway, a major 1942 naval battle in the Pacific that helped shift the course of World War II.

A binary tree is a data structure that organizes information in a hierarchy of nodes. Each node can have no more than two children, called the left child and the right child; it may also have just one child or none. In a binary search tree, values are arranged so that smaller values lie to the left of a node and larger values lie to the right. To find a value, binary search compares the target with the current node, then follows only the left or right branch as appropriate. Binary search can also work on a sorted array by repeatedly halving the range that might contain the target. When a search tree is balanced, searching takes about logarithmic time, written O(log n), but a badly lopsided tree can be slower.

A quasar is an extremely bright, compact-looking center of a distant galaxy. It can outshine all the stars in its host galaxy, making quasars some of the most luminous objects in the universe. At a quasar’s center is a supermassive black hole, an object whose gravity is so strong that light cannot escape from inside its event horizon. The quasar’s light comes mainly from hot gas as it spirals toward the black hole, not from inside the black hole itself. In 1963, astronomer Maarten Schmidt studied the quasar 3C 273 and recognized familiar hydrogen lines in its spectrum shifted toward longer wavelengths. This shift is called redshift, and its large size showed that 3C 273 was extremely far from Earth.

Breccia is a sedimentary rock made of broken pieces of older rocks that have been cemented together. These pieces, called clasts, are angular, with sharp edges and corners. The shape of the clasts is the key difference between breccia and conglomerate, another coarse-grained sedimentary rock: conglomerate contains rounded clasts. Rock fragments usually become rounded as they are carried and rubbed against one another by water or other forces, so the angular pieces in breccia often indicate that they did not travel far before being buried and cemented. Breccia can form where rocks break apart, such as near faults or at the base of steep slopes. On geologic maps, its angular fragments may be shown by a pattern of jagged polygons.

Dogecoin is a cryptocurrency, a form of digital money that uses a shared record called a blockchain to track transactions. It was launched in 2013 by Billy Markus and Jackson Palmer as a playful, satirical alternative to Bitcoin. Its name comes from “Doge,” an intentionally misspelled word used in an internet meme featuring a dog. The dog in that meme, and on Dogecoin’s emblem, is a Shiba Inu. This breed of small hunting dog was developed on Honshu, Japan’s main island. Although Dogecoin began as a joke, people can use it to send and receive payments online. Its history shows how an internet meme can inspire a technology that people use in the real world.

Time dilation is an effect predicted by Albert Einstein’s special theory of relativity: an observer measures a clock moving relative to them as ticking more slowly than a clock at rest beside them. The effect becomes noticeable at speeds close to the speed of light. Observers following different paths through spacetime can therefore measure different elapsed times, even though each sees their own clock ticking normally. Special relativity also predicts length contraction, in which a fast-moving object is measured to be shorter along its direction of motion. Scientists tested time dilation in the 1971 Hafele–Keating experiment by carrying atomic clocks on eastbound and westbound commercial flights and comparing them with reference clocks at the U.S. Naval Observatory. The clocks showed differences consistent with relativity’s predictions.

Valence electrons are the negatively charged particles in an atom’s outermost occupied electron shell. They largely determine how the atom bonds with other atoms and how it reacts chemically. Atoms often become more stable when their outer shell is full, so they may gain, lose, or share valence electrons during a chemical reaction. Elements in the same column of the periodic table usually have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical behavior. Fluorine, chlorine, and bromine belong to a family called the halogens. Halogens typically have seven valence electrons, so they tend to gain one electron to fill their outer shell. Bromine is also one of only two elements that are liquid at standard temperature and pressure; the other is mercury.

Eggshell thinning is a reduction in the thickness and strength of bird eggshells.
