It is especially linked to DDT, a synthetic insecticide developed by Paul Hermann Müller and widely used in agriculture after World War II. DDT can persist in the environment and build up in food chains, so birds may be exposed when they eat contaminated prey. In their bodies, a breakdown product of DDT interferes with the formation of strong eggshells. Thin shells can crack when parent birds sit on their eggs, before the embryos have developed enough to hatch. This contributed to declines in some bird populations. Rachel Carson drew public attention to DDT’s environmental harms in her 1962 book Silent Spring, and most agricultural uses of DDT were banned in the United States in 1972.

A Transformer is a neural-network architecture introduced in the 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need.” It is especially useful for processing sequences of tokens, such as the words or parts of words in written text. Earlier approaches often used recurrent layers to handle a sequence one step at a time. Transformers instead use attention to relate different positions, allowing many tokens to be processed in parallel. Their central mechanism is self-attention: each token is represented by query, key, and value vectors. By comparing a token’s query with other tokens’ keys, the model assigns weights to their values and combines information from across the sequence. This helps a Transformer understand context—for example, which earlier word a pronoun refers to—and generate text, as GPT models do.

Light scattering happens when light encounters particles or irregularities in a material and is redirected in different directions. Rayleigh scattering is a type caused by particles much smaller than the wavelength of light. In Earth’s atmosphere, molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of visible light, such as blue, more strongly than longer wavelengths, making the daytime sky look blue. Scattering also occurs in colloids, mixtures in which tiny particles remain dispersed throughout another substance. Milk, for example, contains fat droplets dispersed in water. If a narrow beam of light passes through a colloid, its particles scatter some light toward an observer standing to the side, making the beam’s path visible. This visible-beam phenomenon is called the Tyndall effect.

Staphylococcus is a genus of round, Gram-positive bacteria, called cocci, that often grow in clusters resembling bunches of grapes. They are also catalase-positive, meaning they produce an enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide. Some species normally live on human skin, but others can cause infections. Clinical laboratories often distinguish species by testing for coagulase, an enzyme associated with blood clotting: Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-positive, while many other species are coagulase-negative. S. aureus can also produce clumping factor, a surface protein detected in some coagulase tests. Another molecule on the cell surface of S. aureus is Protein A. It binds the Fc region of immunoglobulin G (IgG), a type of antibody, and scientists use this binding ability to capture and purify antibodies in the laboratory.

Glutathione is a small molecule found in most cells and is one of their major antioxidants, helping protect them from damage caused by reactive oxygen compounds. It is a tripeptide made from three amino acids: glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. Glutamate and cysteine are joined by an unusual gamma linkage rather than the linkage found in most peptides. In its reduced form, glutathione is called GSH. When two GSH molecules are oxidized, the sulfur atoms in their cysteine residues join to form a disulfide bond, producing glutathione disulfide, or GSSG. Cells recycle GSSG back into two GSH molecules using the enzyme glutathione reductase. This enzyme is a flavoprotein that uses NADPH to provide the electrons needed for the reaction, helping maintain the cell’s supply of reduced glutathione.

The Chicxulub crater is a roughly 180-kilometer-wide impact structure buried beneath the northern Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico and extending offshore under the Gulf of Mexico. It formed about 66 million years ago when a large asteroid struck Earth. The impact blasted rock into the atmosphere and triggered fires, tsunamis, and major changes to the climate. Dust and other debris blocked sunlight, disrupting food chains worldwide. This event is closely linked to the extinction of the non-avian dinosaurs, along with many other species. The abrupt extinction horizon is called the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary: it marks the end of the Cretaceous Period and the Mesozoic Era, and the beginning of the Paleogene Period and the Cenozoic Era.

Eyjafjallajökull is a volcano partly covered by an ice cap on the south coast of Iceland, a North Atlantic island country. In 2010, it erupted beneath the ice, and the heat melted ice that mixed with rising magma. This helped break the magma into tiny fragments of rock and glass called volcanic ash. Winds carried the ash high into the atmosphere and across busy European flight routes. Unlike the soft ash left by a fire, volcanic ash is gritty and can damage aircraft. Its particles can melt inside hot jet engines, then stick to engine parts and interfere with their operation. Because flying through the ash could be dangerous, authorities cancelled thousands of flights across Europe.

A transition state is a fleeting, high-energy arrangement of atoms that forms as reactants change into products. It is also called an activated complex. In a transition state, some bonds may be partly broken while new bonds are partly formed. On a reaction-coordinate diagram, it sits at the top of an energy peak between the reactants and products. The energy difference between the reactants and that peak is called the activation energy: the barrier the reaction must overcome. A higher activation energy generally makes a reaction slower because fewer particles have enough energy to get over the barrier. Catalysts speed reactions up by providing a pathway with a lower activation energy. Enzymes are biological catalysts, usually made of proteins.

Position tells where an object is relative to a chosen reference frame, such as a classroom, a map, or a set of coordinate axes. In classical mechanics, a particle’s position is often written as x, while its momentum describes its motion. Laplace’s hypothetical demon was imagined to know every particle’s position and momentum exactly; under classical laws, it could then calculate their past and future. Quantum mechanics places a limit on that idea. Position and momentum are conjugate observables, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle says they cannot both be known with unlimited precision at the same time. Their uncertainties obey ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2, where Δx is uncertainty in position, Δp is uncertainty in momentum, and ℏ is a fundamental constant.

Erosion is the natural process that moves rock, soil, and other material from one place to another, where it may be deposited. It differs from weathering: weathering breaks down or changes rock where it sits, while erosion carries the loosened material away. That material is called sediment and can include pebbles, sand, and dust. Moving water, wind, and glaciers can all cause erosion. A glacier is a large mass of ice that moves slowly across the land, picking up rock fragments and soil as it goes. This debris is called till. When the glacier melts or retreats, it can leave till in piles or ridges called moraines. Over long periods, deposited sediment can also be compacted and cemented together to form sedimentary rock.

Cosmonauts are space travelers, especially those trained for Soviet or Russian missions. The word means much the same as “astronaut,” but it is traditionally used for people in those space programs and for some international crew members who flew with them. Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space when he orbited Earth aboard Vostok 1 in 1961. Two years later, Soviet pilot Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, launching aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963 and spending nearly three days in orbit. Soviet missions also carried travelers from other countries. In 1980, Cuban cosmonaut Arnaldo Tamayo Méndez flew aboard Soyuz 38, becoming the first Latin American to travel to space.

A wavefunction is a mathematical description of a quantum system and the possible results of measuring it. Before measurement, the system can be in a superposition, meaning its wavefunction includes several possible outcomes. In the Copenhagen interpretation, associated with Niels Bohr, measurement produces one definite result: the wavefunction is said to undergo wavefunction collapse, an irreversible reduction to the eigenstate corresponding to the observed value. The outcome cannot generally be predicted with certainty, although the wavefunction gives probabilities for different results. Bohr also emphasized complementarity: experiments can reveal different aspects of a quantum system, such as wave-like or particle-like behavior, depending on how they are set up. Hugh Everett’s many-worlds interpretation avoids collapse, instead proposing that different outcomes occur in branching worlds.

An IP address, short for Internet Protocol address, is a numerical label assigned to a device or network interface. It helps identify the device and route data to it across a network. When you enter a website name, the Domain Name System (DNS) finds the IP address associated with that name so your device can connect to the right destination. Some IP addresses are dynamic: a service called DHCP can automatically assign an address when a device joins a network. IPv4, the older widely used version, has 32-bit addresses often written as four numbers separated by dots, such as 127.0.0.1, which refers back to the device itself. Because the supply of IPv4 addresses is limited, IPv6 was developed with a much larger 128-bit address space. IPv6 addresses are commonly written as colon-separated groups of hexadecimal digits.

Clay is a naturally occurring, fine-grained material made largely of hydrous aluminum silicate minerals—minerals containing aluminum, silicon, oxygen, and water or hydroxyl groups. Its tiny particles hold water, so wet clay can be molded by hand or shaped on a potter’s wheel. As it dries, it becomes firmer; firing it in a hot kiln makes it hard and durable, as in pottery and ceramics. One common clay mineral is kaolinite, a soft, usually white aluminosilicate with the chemical formula Al₂Si₂O₅(OH)₄. Kaolinite is an important ingredient in porcelain, a type of ceramic, and is also used to coat paper, giving it a smoother surface. Clay can contain other minerals too, so its color and properties vary from place to place.

JPEG is a widely used format for storing photographs on digital cameras and websites. It uses lossy compression, which makes files smaller by discarding some image information that is less noticeable to the eye. In the common baseline JPEG process, the image is divided into 8×8 blocks of pixels. A mathematical operation called the discrete cosine transform, or DCT, converts each block’s pixel values into frequency coefficients. These coefficients describe patterns ranging from gradual changes in brightness to fine details. JPEG then quantizes the coefficients, rounding their values so that some detail can be stored less precisely or removed. This reduces the amount of data needed, but repeated saving or heavy compression can produce visible blockiness or blur. JPEG is especially useful for photographs, though it is less suitable for sharp text or simple graphics.

Yellow fever is a viral disease spread to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes, especially in parts of Africa and South America. It is caused by the yellow fever virus, an RNA virus in the flavivirus family. Many infected people have fever, headache, and muscle pain; severe cases can damage the liver and cause jaundice, a yellowing of the skin and eyes that gives the disease its name. There is no specific cure, so preventing mosquito bites and vaccination are important. Some countries require travelers to show proof of yellow fever vaccination before entering. Virologist Max Theiler developed the 17D strain used in the yellow fever vaccine. His discoveries about the disease and its treatment earned him the 1951 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Fire is a rapid combustion reaction that releases energy as heat and light and produces hot gases. It begins when a fuel, such as wood or a candle’s wax, gets hot enough to react with an oxidizer, usually oxygen in the air. The visible flames are glowing gases and tiny particles heated by the reaction. Fire is the phenomenon traditionally shown as a dragon’s breath in stories, though real fire depends on chemistry, not magic. The three basic requirements for a fire are called the fire triangle: fuel, heat, and an oxidizer. Remove any one of them and the fire goes out. Water can cool a fire by removing heat, while a fire blanket can block oxygen from reaching the fuel.

The van ’t Hoff factor describes how many dissolved particles a solute produces in a solution. It is conventionally written as the lowercase letter i, which also represents the square root of −1 in mathematics. When table salt dissolves, it separates into sodium ions and chloride ions, so its ideal van ’t Hoff factor is 2. Sugar molecules stay intact when they dissolve, giving sugar a factor of about 1. The factor matters because colligative properties depend on the number of dissolved particles, not just the amount of solute added. Scientists use i in equations to calculate effects such as boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, and osmotic pressure. In real solutions, particles can interact, so the measured factor may differ from its ideal value.

AND is a Boolean operation that checks whether two conditions are both true at the same time. It is written as p ∧ q, where p and q are statements that can each be true or false. The result is true only when p is true and q is true; if either one is false, the result is false. For example, “I have a ticket AND the concert has started” is true only if both parts are true. In digital hardware, an AND gate applies this rule to two input signals. A NAND gate combines “NOT” with “AND,” so it reverses the AND gate’s output: NAND is false when both inputs are true and true for the other three possible input combinations.

Light is electromagnetic radiation: energy that travels as linked electric and magnetic fields. The light humans can see is only a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Other wavelengths include infrared, ultraviolet, radio waves, and X-rays. Unlike sound, light does not need air or another material to travel; it can move through the vacuum of space. Light also has a quantum description: its energy comes in discrete packets rather than being carried as a perfectly continuous stream. One packet is called a photon. Different photons can have different energies, depending on the light’s wavelength. Stars and galaxies emit light, and astronomers study the photons that reach Earth to learn about these distant objects.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs, are medicines that relieve pain, reduce fever, and calm inflammation without being steroids. They work by blocking enzymes called cyclooxygenases, which the body uses to make prostaglandins. Prostaglandins help produce pain, fever, and swelling after an injury or during illness. Common NSAIDs include ibuprofen and aspirin. Aspirin, also called acetylsalicylic acid, was developed at Bayer in 1897. Besides treating pain and fever, low-dose aspirin can help prevent heart attacks in some people by making blood platelets less likely to clump together. However, NSAIDs can irritate the stomach and reduce its protective mucus. Taking too much or using them for a long time can increase the risk of a peptic ulcer, a break in the stomach or upper intestine’s lining.

Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), commonly called lye, is a strong base used to make soap. Industrially, it is produced alongside chlorine and hydrogen when salty water, or brine, is electrolyzed in the chlor-alkali process. Lye was traditionally associated with alkali obtained by leaching wood ash with water, although wood-ash lye often contains potassium hydroxide instead. In soapmaking, sodium hydroxide reacts with triglycerides, the main molecules in fats and oils. It breaks their ester bonds, producing glycerol (also called glycerin) and sodium salts of fatty acids, which are soap. This reaction is called saponification. Sodium hydroxide generally produces firmer soap bars than potassium hydroxide, which is often used for softer or liquid soaps. Soap helps water clean by reducing surface tension and lifting oily dirt.

Speciation is the evolutionary process in which populations descended from one ancestral species become distinct species. As they accumulate genetic and other differences, they may eventually become reproductively isolated, meaning they can no longer successfully interbreed to produce fertile offspring. In allopatric speciation, a physical barrier such as a mountain or stretch of water separates populations, allowing them to evolve independently. In sympatric speciation, barriers to interbreeding arise within the same geographic area, sometimes because groups use different resources or prefer different mates. Speciation can happen especially rapidly when many ecological opportunities become available. This pattern is called adaptive radiation: one ancestral lineage gives rise to many species, each adapted to a different ecological niche, such as different food sources or habitats on an island.

Vertebrata is a subphylum of chordates that includes fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Vertebrates are characterized by a vertebral column, or backbone, which helps support the body and protect the spinal cord. Most vertebrates also have jaws, though jawless fish such as lampreys and hagfish do not. Vertebrates breathe in different ways. Most fish use gills to take oxygen from water and lack lungs, but some fish do have lungs. Amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals use lungs to breathe air. Inside mammalian lungs are tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen passes into the blood. Pneumonia can affect the alveoli, making it harder to breathe.

Quantum tunneling is a quantum-physics effect in which a particle has a chance of passing through a potential-energy barrier even when it does not have enough energy to cross it according to classical mechanics. Particles such as electrons are described by wave-like probabilities, and their probability of being found can extend through a thin barrier to the other side. Tunneling does not mean the particle gains the energy needed to climb over the barrier. This effect makes the scanning tunneling microscope possible. Its atomically sharp conducting tip is held extremely close to a conducting surface, leaving a tiny gap. Electrons tunnel across the gap and produce an electric current. As the tip moves over the surface, changes in that current help reveal atomic-scale details. Such microscopes have also been used in experiments with molecular “nanocars.”

Hippocrates was an ancient Greek physician born on the island of Kos around the fifth century BCE. He is traditionally called the Father of Medicine because he helped establish the idea that illnesses have natural causes that doctors can observe and treat, rather than being punishments from the gods. A collection of ancient medical writings, known as the Hippocratic Corpus, is associated with him, although he probably did not write all of it. The Hippocratic Oath, named in his honor, sets out ethical duties for doctors. Hippocrates is also associated with humoral theory, an outdated medical framework that said health depended on balancing four bodily fluids, or “humors”: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Modern medicine no longer accepts this theory, but Hippocrates remains important in medical history.

Herpesviruses are a family of DNA viruses that can remain in the body after an initial infection and sometimes become active again later. One member, Epstein–Barr virus, can cause infectious mononucleosis, often called mono. Another, varicella-zoster virus, causes chickenpox, a childhood illness with an itchy, widespread rash of small, fluid-filled blisters. After the chickenpox rash clears, the virus can stay inactive in nerve cells for years. If it reactivates, it causes shingles, a painful rash that is more common in adults. Other members of the family include herpes simplex viruses, which can cause cold sores or genital herpes, and human herpesvirus 8, which is linked to a cancer called Kaposi’s sarcoma.

Seafloor spreading is the process that creates new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges, where tectonic plates pull apart and molten rock rises from below. As the rock cools, it becomes part of the seafloor and gradually moves outward on both sides of the ridge. This movement helps explain plate motion and continental drift. Cooling rocks also record the direction of Earth’s magnetic field. Because the field has reversed many times, oceanic rocks preserve alternating bands of magnetic direction that match on opposite sides of a ridge. In the early 1960s, three geophysicists independently proposed that these matching magnetic bands resulted from field reversals as new crust spread outward. Their explanation is called the Vine–Matthews–Morley hypothesis and provided strong evidence for seafloor spreading.

Mysorean rockets were military weapons developed in the Kingdom of Mysore in southern India under the rulers Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan during the 18th century. Each rocket used gunpowder packed inside an iron casing, with a long bamboo stick to help guide its flight. The strong iron casing allowed the rockets to build up pressure and travel farther than many earlier rockets, though they were not always accurate. Mysore’s forces launched them at British troops during the Anglo-Mysore Wars, sometimes firing many at once to disrupt enemy formations. British forces took examples of the rockets home, where artillery officer William Congreve studied their design. He developed the Congreve rocket system, which Britain used during the Napoleonic Wars.

Constellations are named areas of the night sky containing recognizable patterns of stars. People have long imagined these patterns as animals, people, or objects and used them to tell stories and find their way. The stars in a constellation may look close together from Earth, but they can be very far apart in space. Two constellations named for dogs are Canis Major, the “greater dog,” and Canis Minor, the “lesser dog.” Canis Major contains Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. In one Greek myth, Laelaps was a dog that always caught its prey, while the Teumessian Fox could never be caught. To end their impossible chase, Zeus turned them to stone and placed them in the sky: Laelaps became associated with Canis Major.

Influenza, commonly called the flu, is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses. It spreads mainly through droplets released when infected people cough, sneeze, or talk, and can cause fever, cough, sore throat, and body aches. Seasonal flu circulates each year, while avian flu mainly infects birds and swine flu mainly infects pigs; some strains can spread to humans and cause pandemics. Influenza viruses include types A and B. Strains of influenza A are named for two proteins on their surface: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). For example, H1N1 has hemagglutinin type 1 and neuraminidase type 1. An H1N1 strain caused the devastating 1918 flu pandemic, and another caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic.

The planetary twilight zone is the transition region between the permanently sunlit and permanently dark sides of a planet. This arrangement can occur because of tidal locking: the planet rotates once on its axis in the time it takes to orbit its star, so the same hemisphere always faces the star. Pluto and Charon are tidally locked with respect to each other. On a locked planet, the day side may be very hot while the night side is very cold. The twilight zone, also called the terminator zone, could have more moderate temperatures and might allow liquid water, a key ingredient for life. Being in a star’s Goldilocks zone helps a planet receive a suitable amount of energy, but scientists must also consider its atmosphere and other conditions when judging whether it could support life.

Male pregnancy is a form of reproduction in which a male carries developing young. It is unusual among vertebrates but occurs in seahorses and their pipefish relatives. In seahorses, the female transfers her eggs into a specialized chamber on the male’s underside called a brood pouch. The eggs are fertilized there, and the male protects and incubates the developing embryos until they hatch and are released as young seahorses. Some related pipefish carry eggs on their bodies rather than in a fully enclosed pouch. Because the male carries the embryos, he makes a substantial investment in the survival of the young. This differs from the pattern in most vertebrates, where females carry developing offspring or lay eggs that develop outside the body.

In a crystalline solid, electrons can occupy certain ranges of energy called bands. The lower, usually filled range is the valence band, and the higher range that can accept electrons is the conduction band. Between them is the energy band gap: a range of energies that electrons cannot have in that solid. Semiconductors have smaller band gaps than insulators, so electrons can more readily gain enough energy to reach the conduction band and carry current. In a light-emitting diode (LED), an electron falling from a higher-energy state into a lower-energy state can release a photon of light. The band gap helps determine that photon’s energy and therefore its color. Photon energy is inversely related to wavelength: red light has a longer wavelength and lower-energy photons than blue light.

The Zeeman effect occurs when an external magnetic field causes an atom’s or molecule’s spectral line to split into two or more lines. Spectral lines are specific colors of light emitted or absorbed when electrons move between energy levels. A magnetic field, represented by the vector B and measured in teslas, changes those energy levels slightly, so the transitions produce light at several nearby wavelengths instead of just one. The number and spacing of the lines can help scientists determine the strength of the magnetic field around the atom or molecule. Magnetic fields can be produced by electric currents, such as a current flowing through a coil of wire.

The California condor is a critically endangered New World vulture and the largest land bird in North America, with a wingspan approaching three meters. Like other vultures, it scavenges on carrion, or dead animals, and its mostly bare head helps it stay clean while feeding. By the 1980s, habitat loss, hunting, and lead poisoning had reduced the wild population to just 22 birds. Conservationists brought the remaining birds into captivity to breed them, then reintroduced their offspring into the wild, helping the population recover. In 2021, genetic tests revealed that two chicks hatched in captivity had no genetic father, although their mothers had access to fertile males. The chicks had developed from unfertilized eggs through a rare reproductive process called parthenogenesis.

Atomic emission spectroscopy is a technique for identifying elements by studying the light their atoms give off. A sample is energized, often by heating it, which raises electrons in its atoms to higher energy levels. As the electrons return to lower levels, they release light at specific wavelengths. An instrument separates that light into a pattern of bright emission lines. Because each element has its own characteristic pattern, scientists can compare the lines with known patterns to identify the elements in a sample. Sodium, an alkali metal with atomic number 11, is recognized by two closely spaced yellow lines called the D-lines. These lines are also seen when scientists analyze light from the Sun.

An egg is a reproductive structure that contains a developing embryo and a supply of nutrients to support its growth. In birds such as chickens, the embryo develops outside the parent’s body, so a shell helps protect it. People also use the word “egg” in other contexts: an “Easter egg” is a hidden surprise in a website, game, or film. Eggs play a satirical role in Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels. In the fictional country of Lilliput, the ruler orders people to crack their eggs at the small, pointed end. Those who reject the rule and insist on cracking the large end are called Big-Endians. Their dispute turns an everyday choice into a political and religious conflict.

Specific heat capacity describes how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of a unit mass of a substance by one degree Celsius. It is an intensive property, meaning it does not depend on how much of the substance you have. Its SI unit is joules per kilogram per kelvin; a rise of one kelvin is the same size as a rise of one degree Celsius. In calorimetry, water is a useful reference because its specific heat capacity is about 1 calorie per gram per degree Celsius, or 4.18 joules per gram per degree Celsius. This means one calorie of heat raises the temperature of one gram of water by about one degree Celsius. Calorimeters often contain water so that scientists can use its temperature change to calculate heat gained or lost.

Feldspar is a group of rock-forming aluminosilicate minerals that makes up more than half of Earth’s crust. It is a major component of familiar rocks such as granite, while anorthosite is made almost entirely of feldspar. Feldspar’s crystal framework contains silicon, aluminum, and oxygen, along with elements such as potassium, sodium, or calcium. This gives rise to potassium-rich feldspars and sodium-calcium feldspars called plagioclase. In a common feldspar formula, the framework contains eight oxygen atoms. Oxygen is also part of silica, the compound of silicon and oxygen that is a major constituent of sand. Aluminum, another key element in feldspar, is the most abundant metal in Earth’s crust.

Cosmic rays are extremely energetic particles that reach us from beyond the Solar System. Despite their name, they are mostly protons and heavier atomic nuclei, not rays of light. Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield us from many of them, but spacecraft are more exposed. When a cosmic ray strikes a satellite, it can deposit electrical charge in its circuits. If it passes through semiconductor memory, that charge may briefly change a stored 0 to a 1, or a 1 to a 0, without permanently damaging the chip. This radiation-induced bit flip is called a single-event upset. Cosmic rays are different from the solar wind, which consists of charged particles emitted by the Sun, but both can pose challenges for spacecraft electronics.

Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish physical chemist who made important contributions to both chemistry and climate science. The Arrhenius equation describes how a chemical reaction’s rate changes with temperature. It includes activation energy, the minimum energy needed for a reaction to proceed, and a pre-exponential factor related to how often molecules can react. Arrhenius also studied Earth’s climate. In 1896, he calculated how changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide could affect the planet’s temperature. Carbon dioxide helps trap heat in the atmosphere, a process called the greenhouse effect. His calculations were an early quantitative estimate of this effect, long before modern climate models existed. Arrhenius’s work connected mathematical ideas with questions about chemical reactions and the environment.

The spleen is an organ in the upper-left abdomen, next to the stomach. It filters blood, removes old red blood cells, and helps the immune system fight infections. Splenomegaly is the medical term for an abnormally enlarged spleen. It can occur when the spleen responds to an infection or is affected by a blood cancer, including Hodgkin lymphoma. One infection that can cause splenomegaly is infectious mononucleosis, often called “mono.” It is most often caused by the Epstein–Barr virus and is especially common in adolescents and young adults. Typical symptoms include fever, a sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, and tiredness. An enlarged spleen may be more easily injured, so someone with mono may be advised to avoid contact sports until a healthcare professional says it is safe.

NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test, or DART, was a planetary-defense mission launched in 2021 to test whether a spacecraft could change an asteroid’s motion by crashing into it. DART targeted the near-Earth asteroid system Didymos, which consists of a larger asteroid and a smaller moonlet called Dimorphos. In September 2022, the spacecraft deliberately struck Dimorphos. This “kinetic impactor” approach uses the force of a collision to alter an object’s path, rather than using explosives. Measurements showed that the impact shortened Dimorphos’s orbital period around Didymos by about 32 minutes. DART demonstrated a possible way to deflect an asteroid if one were ever found on a collision course with Earth.

Granite is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock that forms when felsic magma cools slowly beneath Earth’s surface. Because the magma cools underground over a long time, its minerals have time to grow into crystals large enough to see. Granite is made mainly of quartz and potassium feldspar, though it often contains smaller amounts of other minerals, such as mica. Quartz consists of silicon dioxide and commonly appears in granite as glassy, gray or translucent grains. It has a hardness of 7 on the Mohs scale, so it can scratch glass. Potassium feldspar may give granite a pink or cream color. Granite’s visible, interlocking crystals help distinguish it from rocks that form when lava cools quickly at the surface.

Mantle convection is the slow circulation of rock in Earth’s mantle that transfers heat from the planet’s interior. Although mantle rock is mostly solid, it can flow very slowly over millions of years. Hotter rock rises, while cooler rock sinks, creating a cycle beneath the lithosphere. The lithosphere is Earth’s rigid outer shell, made of the crust and the uppermost mantle, and it is broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. Mantle convection helps drive the movement of these plates, along with forces called ridge push and slab pull. Plates move apart at mid-ocean ridges, where new seafloor forms, and come together at subduction zones, where one plate sinks beneath another. These movements can cause earthquakes and volcanoes.

The European rabbit is a burrowing mammal native to the Iberian Peninsula in southwestern Europe. In 1859, Thomas Austin, an English-born pastoralist, released 24 European rabbits at his Barwon Park estate in Victoria, Australia, so he would have animals to hunt. He assumed the small group would do little harm, but rabbits breed quickly, and few effective predators kept their numbers in check. They spread across Australia, eating vegetation and damaging farmland and habitats used by native animals. Within about 50 years, Western Australia began building a long rabbit-proof fence to try to stop their spread. The European rabbit became a famous example of an invasive species: an animal introduced outside its native range that causes harm in its new environment.

Fleas are small, wingless insects that live on the outside of mammals and birds and feed on their blood, making them ectoparasites. Their powerful hind legs act like springs, letting them jump many times their body length to reach new hosts. Flea bites can cause itching and skin inflammation; in dogs, an allergic reaction to flea saliva is a common cause of dermatitis. Some fleas also spread diseases, including murine typhus and bubonic plague. The oriental rat flea, Xenopsylla cheopis, is a major plague vector associated with rats. When it feeds on an infected animal, the plague bacterium can multiply and block part of the flea’s digestive tract. During a later bite, the flea may regurgitate bacteria into a new host, spreading the infection.

Big O notation describes an upper bound on how an algorithm’s resource use grows as the input gets larger. It is often used to describe worst-case running time, but it can also describe memory use. For example, checking a list one item at a time may take O(n) steps for a list of n items, while binary search can find an item in a sorted list in O(log n) steps by repeatedly halving the part it searches. Big O focuses on the overall growth pattern, so it leaves out constant factors and smaller terms: O(2n + 3) is written as O(n). When Big O describes the extra memory an algorithm needs rather than its computational steps, it reports auxiliary space complexity.

Muscle tissue is made of cells specialized to contract, or shorten, to produce force. Its contractions rely on two proteins: thin actin filaments and thick myosin filaments, which slide past one another. There are three main types. Skeletal muscle attaches to bones and moves the body, as when you bend your arm using your biceps. Cardiac muscle makes the heart beat and pump blood, while smooth muscle moves materials through internal organs such as the intestines. Skeletal and cardiac muscle are striated, meaning they have a striped appearance caused by the orderly arrangement of their filaments. In striated muscle, the repeating contractile unit is called a sarcomere. Each sarcomere extends from one Z disc to the next and shortens as its actin and myosin filaments slide past one another.

The motherboard is the main printed circuit board in a computer. It holds the socket for the CPU (processor) and slots for memory, while connecting them to storage interfaces, expansion slots, and rear input/output (I/O) ports for devices such as a keyboard or monitor. Its chipset and other circuitry help the computer’s parts communicate, making the motherboard the system’s central connection platform. Motherboards come in different sizes and layouts, called form factors. A common desktop form factor is ATX, short for Advanced Technology Extended. Introduced by Intel in 1995 to replace the older AT layout, a full-size ATX motherboard measures 305 by 244 millimeters and has a defined area for rear I/O connectors.

Pyroclastic material is rock, glass, and other debris blasted from a volcano during an explosive eruption, rather than released as a flowing stream of lava. It can include tiny particles as well as larger pieces called clasts. The smallest common category is volcanic ash: fragments less than 2 millimeters across. Despite its name, volcanic ash is not the soft residue left by a fire; it consists of sharp particles of volcanic rock and glass. Powerful eruptions can carry ash high into the atmosphere, where winds transport it far downwind before it settles as a deposit. Larger pyroclastic fragments include lapilli and volcanic bombs or blocks. Studying the size and distribution of these deposits helps scientists understand how a volcano erupted.

Orville and Wilbur Wright were brothers and bicycle mechanics from Dayton, Ohio, who helped invent the airplane. They tested gliders and built a homemade wind tunnel to study how wings produce lift. Their key achievement was three-axis control, which let a pilot steer, climb or descend, and keep the aircraft balanced. On December 17, 1903, their powered aircraft, the Wright Flyer, made the first successful controlled, sustained airplane flights near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. It used a forward-mounted elevator, part of a layout called a canard design, and flew four times that day before wind damage ended its use. The flights took place at Kill Devil Hills, the neighboring coastal community where the Wright Brothers National Memorial now stands.

Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane, which lets water pass but blocks some dissolved substances, or solutes. Water moves net from the side with a lower solute concentration to the side with a higher solute concentration. This helps cells control how much water they contain. When the solutions on both sides are isotonic, water still moves in both directions, but there is no net movement. A solution’s tendency to draw water across the membrane is measured by its osmotic pressure, represented by the Greek letter π. For dilute solutions, the van ’t Hoff equation is π = iMRT, where i accounts for the number of dissolved particles, M is molar concentration, R is a constant, and T is temperature. Reverse osmosis uses applied pressure to purify salt water.

Barbed wire is steel fencing with sharp points, or barbs, spaced along it. In 1874, Joseph Glidden, a farmer from DeKalb, Illinois, patented a practical design that twisted two strands of wire together to hold the barbs in place. On the 19th-century American frontier, ranchers used it to keep cattle and other livestock from wandering or pushing through fences. It was much cheaper to build long stretches of barbed-wire fence than wooden fence, especially on the Great Plains, where trees were scarce. As barbed wire spread, ranchers and farmers could fence large areas and mark property boundaries more easily. This changed how land was used, but fences also restricted movement across lands that had previously been open, including lands used by Native Americans.

Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen. Like ordinary hydrogen, called protium, it has one proton, but tritium also has two neutrons. Its symbol is T. When a tritium atom replaces one ordinary hydrogen atom in a water molecule, the molecule contains one protium atom (H), one tritium atom (T), and one oxygen atom (O). Its conventional isotopic formula is HTO, and it is called tritiated water. Because HTO moves with other water molecules, scientists can measure its radioactivity to trace where water travels. Tritium gradually decays over time, with a half-life of about 12 years, so measuring how much remains can also help scientists estimate the age of relatively recent groundwater.

Magic acid is a superacid made by mixing fluorosulfuric acid, whose formula is HSO₃F, with antimony pentafluoride, SbF₅. It earned its unusual name because it can react with substances that ordinary acids cannot. Acids can donate protons, and this mixture is an exceptionally strong proton donor. Antimony pentafluoride helps make the mixture much more acidic than fluorosulfuric acid alone. Chemists use magic acid to create and stabilize carbocations, which are positively charged carbon-containing ions that might otherwise react too quickly to study. Superacids are stronger than ordinary strong acids, such as sulfuric acid. Although acids in water generally have a pH below seven, chemists use a different measure, called the Hammett acidity function, to describe the extreme acidity of mixtures like magic acid.

The diaphragm is a dome-shaped skeletal muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen and is the main muscle used for breathing. When it contracts, it flattens and moves downward, increasing the space in the chest, called the thoracic cavity. This helps draw air into the lungs. When it relaxes, it rises again, helping push air out. The diaphragm also contracts during laughter, which is why laughing can make your abdomen move. Its movement is controlled mainly by the paired phrenic nerves, one on each side. These nerves carry motor commands from the spinal cord at levels C3–C5 to the diaphragm. Damage to a phrenic nerve can weaken the diaphragm and make breathing more difficult.

Cryptocurrency is digital money that people can send and receive electronically. It uses cryptography, a way of protecting information with mathematical techniques, to help secure transactions. Many cryptocurrencies record transactions on a blockchain, a shared digital ledger that groups records into blocks. Bitcoin and Ethereum are prominent examples of cryptocurrency. Ethereum’s blockchain can also support other digital items, including NFTs, or non-fungible tokens, which represent unique items rather than interchangeable units of money. Dogecoin is another cryptocurrency. Billy Markus and Jackson Palmer created it as a humorous alternative to Bitcoin, and its logo features the Shiba Inu dog from the “Doge” internet meme. Despite its playful origins, Dogecoin can be transferred electronically like other cryptocurrencies.

Fritz Zwicky was a Swiss astronomer who worked at the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech. In the 1930s, he studied the Coma Cluster, a large group of galaxies, and measured how fast its galaxies moved. They were moving so quickly that the gravity of the stars and gas visible through telescopes did not seem strong enough to hold the cluster together. Zwicky concluded that the cluster must contain much more mass than astronomers could see. The invisible material invoked to explain this extra gravity is called dark matter. It does not give off or reflect light, but its gravitational effects can be measured. Zwicky also helped establish the term “supernova” for a powerful stellar explosion.

An orbit is the curved path an object follows around another body because of gravity. Earth orbits the Sun, and the Moon orbits Earth. An orbiting object is continually pulled toward the body it circles, but its forward motion keeps it from falling straight into it. Spacecraft can change their orbits by firing engines to change their velocity, or speed and direction. Because fuel is limited, a spacecraft may instead use a gravity assist, also called a gravitational slingshot. In this maneuver, it flies close to a moving planet or other massive body. The body’s gravity bends the spacecraft’s path, and its motion can change the spacecraft’s speed relative to the Sun. This helps the spacecraft reach a new destination while using less fuel.

Cloud seeding is a weather-modification technique that tries to increase rain or snow from existing clouds. Some clouds contain supercooled water droplets: liquid water that remains unfrozen even below 0°C. Meteorologists can release tiny ice-nucleating particles into suitable clouds using flares on aircraft or ground-based generators. A commonly used substance is silver iodide, a crystalline compound whose structure helps ice crystals begin to form. As the crystals grow, they may become heavy enough to fall as snow or melt into rain on the way down. Cloud seeding cannot create clouds from clear skies, and it does not guarantee precipitation; its success depends on the cloud’s temperature, moisture, and other conditions.

Synapses are specialized junctions where a neuron sends a signal to another neuron or to a target cell, such as a muscle cell. At a chemical synapse, the sending, or presynaptic, neuron stores neurotransmitters in small membrane-bound carriers called synaptic vesicles. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of the neuron, some vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their neurotransmitters into the narrow synaptic cleft. The chemicals cross the cleft and bind to receptors on the receiving cell, passing on the signal. Proteins called SNAREs help vesicles fuse with the membrane. After release, the neuron can retrieve and recycle vesicle membrane through a process called clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Some synapses transmit signals electrically instead of using neurotransmitters.

Deep-field images are made by pointing a telescope at a tiny patch of sky for a very long exposure. The telescope gathers more light over time, revealing faint, distant galaxies that shorter exposures might miss. A famous early example is the Hubble Deep Field. The Hubble Space Telescope, an orbiting observatory launched aboard the space shuttle Discovery in 1990, observed a seemingly empty region in the constellation Ursa Major for roughly ten days. When the image was released in 1995, it showed thousands of galaxies in that small area. More recently, the James Webb Space Telescope produced Webb’s First Deep Field, showing that this technique continues to help astronomers study the distant universe.

An artery is a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Each heartbeat pushes blood into the arteries at high pressure, so their thick, elastic walls stretch and spring back to help withstand that pressure. Veins, in contrast, carry blood toward the heart and generally have lower pressure. Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood to the body’s tissues, but the pulmonary arteries are an exception: they carry oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs. The body’s largest artery is the aorta. It begins at the heart’s left ventricle and delivers oxygen-rich blood into systemic circulation, the network that supplies the body. If a clot blocks an artery leading to the brain, the loss of oxygen can cause an ischemic stroke.

John James Audubon was a French-American naturalist, ornithologist, and artist who studied North American birds in the wild. In the 19th century, he combined field observations with dramatic, lifelike paintings that showed birds in natural poses and settings. His best-known work, Birds of America, was a four-volume collection published in London in parts from 1827 to 1838. It contained 435 hand-colored plates, many showing birds at life size. Audubon painted species that have since become extinct, including the passenger pigeon and Carolina parakeet; his collection also includes the great auk. His work remains an important record of North American birdlife, and the modern bird conservation organization called the Audubon Society is named after him.

Vultures are a group of roughly 23 species of birds of prey that feed mainly on carrion, the bodies of dead animals. They help ecosystems by removing carcasses. Vultures are called polyphyletic because Old World vultures and New World vultures belong to different families rather than forming one close evolutionary group. Both lineages independently evolved mostly bare heads, which can help keep feathers clean while feeding inside carcasses; this is an example of convergent evolution. One New World species, the turkey vulture, has an unusually well-developed sense of smell. Its large olfactory lobe helps it detect chemicals released as animals decay, including ethyl mercaptan, so it can find food even when a carcass is hidden from view.

SpaceX, short for Space Exploration Technologies Corp., is an American aerospace company founded by Elon Musk in 2002. It develops rockets and spacecraft, including the Falcon rockets and the Dragon capsule. SpaceX once proposed an uncrewed Mars mission called Red Dragon. The plan was to adapt its Dragon spacecraft, designed to carry people, so the capsule could land on Mars using rocket engines to slow its descent—a method called a propulsive landing. Red Dragon remained a concept and never flew. SpaceX later set it aside and shifted its Mars plans toward Starship, a much larger spacecraft being developed for missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. If asked to name the company, the answer is SpaceX; if asked to name the proposed capsule-based Mars mission, the answer is Red Dragon.

The RC time constant describes how quickly a circuit containing a resistor and capacitor charges or discharges. It equals resistance multiplied by capacitance (τ = RC), measured in seconds. After one time constant, a charging capacitor’s voltage has completed about 63% of its total change; a discharging capacitor retains about 37% of its initial voltage. This idea also helps explain how neurons carry signals. A neuron’s membrane separates electric charges and acts like a capacitor, while resistance limits the flow of current. Myelination adds an insulating sheath around an axon. Oligodendrocytes make this sheath in the central nervous system, and Schwann cells make it in the peripheral nervous system. Myelination can increase the distance an electrical signal travels along an axon, called the length constant, without changing the membrane’s RC time constant.

A microscope is an instrument that makes objects too small to see with the unaided eye appear larger and more detailed. An optical microscope uses visible light focused through lenses; a specimen may be placed on a transparent glass slide so light can pass through it. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light. Because electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light, these microscopes can resolve much finer details. In the 17th century, the Dutch naturalist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who lived in Delft, built powerful single-lens microscopes. He used them to observe tiny living organisms in water and reported his findings to the Royal Society, helping reveal a world of microscopic life.

The Wright Flyer was the airplane built by Wilbur and Orville Wright, two brothers from Dayton, Ohio, who ran a bicycle shop. On December 17, 1903, they flew it near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, making the first controlled, sustained flights in a powered aircraft. Its canard layout placed the elevator, a movable surface used to control pitch, ahead of the main wings rather than behind them. The brothers completed four flights that day. The longest lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet. Strong winds damaged the Flyer after the fourth flight, so it never flew again. The flights took place near the town of Kill Devil Hills, which now commemorates their achievement.

Coal mining is the industry of extracting coal, a combustible sedimentary rock, from underground seams or surface deposits. Coal has been used as fuel for heating and electricity generation and as a feedstock in industries such as steelmaking. Historically, coal mining has been concentrated in places including northern England, Wales, and the Appalachian region of the United States, especially West Virginia. Mines may remove coal from the surface or use tunnels to reach deeper seams. One underground method is longwall mining: a cutting machine moves along a long face of coal, shearing it from the seam. Hydraulic supports hold up the roof near the working face and advance as mining moves forward. This lets workers extract a large section of the seam in a systematic way.

Deciduous plants shed their leaves on a recurring seasonal schedule, unlike evergreens, which keep their foliage throughout the year. Many deciduous trees, such as maples and oaks, lose their leaves in autumn as temperatures fall; in other climates, plants may drop them when a dry season begins. Leaves help plants make food from sunlight and exchange gases with the air, but maintaining them through cold or drought can cost more water and energy than the plant can spare. Before a leaf falls, the plant forms a separation layer at the base of its stalk. This controlled process, called abscission, allows the leaf to detach while protecting the plant where it was attached. The plant then grows new leaves when conditions improve.

An anion is an atom or group of atoms with a net negative charge. It has more electrons than protons, often because it has gained one or more electrons. Anions are the opposite of positively charged ions, called cations. The attraction between anions and cations holds ionic compounds together. For example, when hydrogen combines with an electropositive metal such as sodium, the metal can lose an electron and hydrogen can gain it. The hydrogen atom then becomes H⁻, a monatomic anion called the hydride ion. Its negative charge balances the metal’s positive charge, helping form an ionic compound. Not all compounds containing hydrogen have hydride ions, but in ionic metal hydrides, hydrogen acts as an anion.

The Perseids are an annual meteor shower that occurs when Earth crosses a trail of debris left by Comet Swift–Tuttle. This icy comet takes about 133 years to orbit the Sun. It last passed closest to the Sun, a point called perihelion, in 1992 and is expected to return in 2126. As a comet approaches the Sun, some of its ice turns to gas and releases dust, leaving particles along its path. When Earth passes through that trail, the particles enter our atmosphere and burn up, making bright streaks often called “shooting stars.” The Perseids are usually most active in August. Their streaks appear to spread outward from a point in the constellation Perseus, which is why the shower is called the Perseids.

The seafloor is the bottom surface of the ocean, beneath the water column. It includes rocky areas, soft sediment, and deep-sea habitats such as hydrothermal vents. The organisms living on or within the seafloor are collectively called benthos. They include sponges attached to rocks, clams on or in the sediment, sea stars moving across the bottom, and worms burrowing beneath it. Some benthos feed on marine snow—tiny bits of dead organisms and waste that sink from above—or on the remains of large animals such as whales. Near hydrothermal vents, microbes use chemicals from the Earth instead of sunlight to make food, supporting animals such as tube worms. Burrowing worms also stir the sediment, helping oxygen reach organisms living below the surface.

A tumor is an abnormal mass of tissue that forms through neoplasia, when cells grow and divide in an uncontrolled way. Tumors can be benign, meaning they do not invade nearby tissues, or malignant, meaning they can invade and spread; malignant tumors are cancerous. Doctors may use the TNM system to describe how far a cancer has progressed. T describes the size and extent of the main tumor, N describes whether cancer has reached nearby lymph nodes, and M describes whether it has spread to distant parts of the body. Lymph nodes are small structures that filter lymph, a clear fluid from body tissues, and contain many immune cells. They occur in clusters, including in the armpits and along the head and neck.

Sodium bicarbonate, also called baking soda, is a mildly alkaline compound with the chemical formula NaHCO₃. Because it is a base, it can react with acids such as vinegar, lemon juice, or buttermilk. This reaction produces carbon dioxide gas, which forms bubbles. In baking, those bubbles expand in the batter or dough and help cakes, muffins, and other baked goods rise, so baking soda is called a leavener. Baking soda also has household uses: it can help remove odors from laundry and clean stains, such as coffee marks on cups. It is much weaker than the strong bases found in some oven and drain cleaners.

A pig is a domesticated mammal in the family Suidae. It is an even-toed ungulate, meaning it has hooves that bear weight mainly on two toes. Pigs are raised worldwide, especially for their meat, which is called pork. Their short, often curly tails also appear in stories: Wilbur, the main animal character in Charlotte’s Web, is a pig. In Gabriel García Márquez’s novel One Hundred Years of Solitude, the Buendía family fears that a child born to closely related parents might have a pig’s tail. In the family’s seventh and final generation, a baby boy is born with that unusual feature. His given name is Aureliano.

Simple harmonic motion is a repeating back-and-forth movement around an equilibrium position. In an ideal mass-spring system, pulling the mass away from equilibrium makes the spring exert a restoring force toward it. Hooke’s law describes this force as F = −kx, where x is displacement and k measures the spring’s stiffness; the minus sign shows that the force points opposite to the displacement. Because the force grows in direct proportion to displacement, the mass’s position varies sinusoidally over time, tracing the shape of a sine or cosine wave. The greatest distance the mass reaches from equilibrium is its amplitude. As long as the spring stays in its linear range, changing the amplitude does not change the period, or time needed for one complete oscillation.

Chemical weapons are armaments that use toxic substances to injure or kill, rather than relying mainly on the blast or impact of a conventional weapon. The substances may be dispersed as gases, vapors, or aerosols, allowing people to breathe them in or come into contact with them. Examples include nerve agents, which disrupt the nervous system, and mustard gas, which can cause severe burns and damage to the lungs. During Italy’s 1935–36 invasion of Ethiopia, Italian forces used chemical weapons against Ethiopians. Ethiopia’s emperor, Haile Selassie, appealed to the League of Nations and condemned their use. The League was an international organization founded after World War I to promote collective security. It was headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland, and dissolved in 1946.

The Permian Period lasted from about 299 to 252 million years ago and was the final period of the Paleozoic Era. During this time, most of Earth’s land was joined in the supercontinent Pangaea, which reached its greatest extent. The Permian ended with the Permian–Triassic mass extinction, the largest known extinction in Earth’s history. It wiped out an estimated 95 percent of species and sharply reduced the diversity of marine animals such as crinoids. Near the end of the period, immense volcanic eruptions in what is now Siberia formed a large igneous province called the Siberian Traps. The eruptions released vast amounts of gases that are thought to have contributed to global warming and disrupted ocean conditions, helping drive the extinction.

A single-displacement reaction, also called a single-replacement reaction, occurs when a free element takes the place of another element in a compound. Its general pattern is A + BC → B + AC: element A replaces element B in compound BC, leaving B on its own and forming the new compound AC. Whether this happens depends on the elements’ reactivity. For metals, the activity series ranks them from most reactive near the top to least reactive near the bottom. A metal can usually replace another metal below it in the series, but not one above it. Potassium and lithium are near the top of the series and belong to the alkali metals, the highly reactive elements in Group 1 of the periodic table.

The spring constant describes how stiff a spring is, or how strongly it resists being stretched or compressed. It is usually written as k and measured in newtons per meter (N/m). A larger k means more force is needed to change the spring’s length by a given amount. For an ideal spring, the relationship between force and displacement is Hooke’s law, written F = −kx. Here, x is the distance from the spring’s equilibrium position, where it is neither stretched nor compressed. The minus sign shows that the spring’s restoring force points opposite to the displacement: a stretched spring pulls back, while a compressed spring pushes outward. A mass attached to a spring can therefore move back and forth in a pattern called simple harmonic motion.

Chalk is a soft, porous type of limestone made mainly of calcite, a mineral form of calcium carbonate. It often forms from the remains of tiny sea organisms that built up on an ancient seabed. In parts of England, thick layers of white chalk lie beneath grassy hillsides. People have used this bright rock to make geoglyphs: huge figures that can be seen across the landscape. To create some hill figures, they dug trenches through the grass and soil to expose the chalk below or filled the trenches with chalk. Two examples are the Uffington White Horse and the Cerne Abbas Giant, a massive human figure cut into a hillside in Dorset. Although the Giant was once thought to be ancient, soil dating reported in 2021 suggested it was made in the Middle Ages.

The Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant was a generating station near Pripyat in northern Ukraine that used RBMK nuclear reactors to produce electricity. In April 1986, reactor number four was destroyed during a failed safety test, releasing large amounts of radioactive material. The disaster forced the evacuation of Pripyat and led to the creation of an exclusion zone around the plant. Workers first covered the damaged reactor with a concrete and steel shelter, often called a sarcophagus, to limit the spread of radiation. In 2016, an enormous arch-shaped structure called the New Safe Confinement was moved into place over that shelter. It was designed to contain radioactive material more effectively and provide space and equipment for the eventual dismantling of the damaged reactor.

The Boeing 737 MAX is a family of narrow-body passenger jets made by Boeing. It is a newer, re-engined generation of the long-running 737 line. In October 2018, Lion Air Flight 610 crashed, followed by Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in March 2019. Investigators linked both crashes to a flight-control feature called the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, or MCAS. MCAS used data from an angle-of-attack sensor, which measures how steeply a plane’s nose is pointed relative to the air flowing past it. Faulty sensor readings could cause MCAS to repeatedly command nose-down stabilizer trim, making the aircraft difficult for pilots to control. After the second crash, aviation authorities grounded 737 MAX airplanes worldwide in March 2019 while the system and pilot training were reviewed.

A sound wave is a mechanical disturbance that travels through a material medium, such as air, water, or a solid. It carries energy as alternating regions of higher and lower pressure, while the particles of the medium vibrate around their usual positions. Humans typically hear sound waves with frequencies from about 20 to 20,000 hertz, though this range varies with age and hearing ability. In air, sound is a longitudinal wave: air particles move back and forth parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. This differs from a transverse wave, whose particles move perpendicular to the wave’s direction. Sound travels through room-temperature air at roughly 343 meters per second, and sound levels are commonly expressed in decibels.

Electron affinity is the energy change when an isolated, neutral atom in the gas phase gains an electron, a negatively charged particle, to form a negative ion. For many atoms, this process releases energy and is called exothermic. Electron affinity is different from ionization energy, which concerns the energy needed to remove an electron. Halogens generally have favorable electron affinities because gaining one electron helps fill their outer shell. Chlorine has a more exothermic first electron-addition process than fluorine, even though fluorine is above it in the periodic table. Fluorine’s outer 2p subshell is small and crowded, so an incoming electron experiences strong repulsion from electrons already there. Chlorine’s larger 3p subshell gives the added electron more room and less repulsion.

The chambered nautilus is a cephalopod mollusk found in the Indo-Pacific Ocean. Unlike its relatives the octopus and squid, it has an external shell. The shell forms a tight coil shaped roughly like a logarithmic spiral and is divided by curved walls into chambers. The nautilus lives in the large, outermost chamber; the older chambers behind it help control buoyancy. A narrow tube called the siphuncle passes through the walls between chambers. By moving fluid out of these chambers and allowing gas to occupy the space, it helps the nautilus rise or sink. The animal also moves by jet propulsion, drawing water into its body and forcefully expelling it.

Goldfish are freshwater fish kept as pets in aquariums and garden ponds. They were domesticated from the Prussian carp, a fish native to Eurasia, and people have selectively bred them for centuries. Selective breeding means choosing fish with desired traits to produce offspring, which has led to goldfish varieties with different colors, body shapes, fins, and tails. Some populations of their Prussian carp ancestor can reproduce through an unusual process called gynogenesis. In this process, sperm from another fish triggers an egg to develop but does not contribute DNA to the offspring. Goldfish may look very different from their wild ancestors, but both belong to the carp family and live in freshwater.

Prophase is an early stage of mitosis, the process that divides one cell into two genetically identical cells. During prophase, long, loose strands of DNA called chromatin coil tightly and become visible as chromosomes. Each chromosome has already been copied, so it consists of two identical sister chromatids joined together. At the same time, structures called centrosomes move toward opposite sides of the cell, and microtubules begin organizing between them into a bipolar apparatus called the mitotic spindle. The spindle later attaches to chromosomes and helps pull sister chromatids apart. These changes prepare the cell to distribute a complete set of chromosomes to each new cell. Prophase also occurs in meiosis, the type of cell division that produces egg and sperm cells, although meiosis has some additional events.

Wildfires are uncontrolled fires that spread through vegetation such as forests, grasslands, and shrubs. They can start naturally, for example from lightning, or through human activity, and may spread quickly when conditions are hot, dry, and windy. Besides burning plants and threatening homes and wildlife, wildfires produce intense heat and smoke that can affect air quality far from the flames. Sometimes their heat drives rising air so powerfully that it forms a towering thundercloud called a pyrocumulonimbus cloud. These clouds can produce dangerous weather, including lightning and, rarely, tornadoes. In August 2020, the National Weather Service issued its first warning for a tornado produced by a pyrocumulonimbus cloud during wildfires in Lassen County, California. California’s capital is Sacramento.

Ions are atoms or molecules with an electric charge. An atom or molecule that loses electrons becomes a positively charged ion, or cation; one that gains electrons becomes a negatively charged ion, or anion. When dissolved in water, ions can carry electric current, which is why solutions containing them are called electrolytes. Scientists also use ions to identify substances in mass spectrometry, a technique that separates particles by their mass-to-charge ratio. One way to produce ions for this technique is MALDI, short for matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization. In MALDI, the sample is mixed with an energy-absorbing matrix. A laser pulse strikes the matrix, releasing and ionizing sample molecules while causing relatively little fragmentation, so large molecules can often be studied intact.

Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers that neurons use to communicate with other neurons, muscles, and glands. When an electrical signal reaches the end of a neuron, it can cause neurotransmitters to be released into the tiny gap called a synapse. The chemicals cross the gap and bind to receptors on the receiving cell, passing the signal along. Acetylcholine is one example of a neurotransmitter. Motor neurons release it at neuromuscular junctions, the places where nerves meet muscles, and it helps trigger muscle contraction. Botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine, so the muscle does not receive the usual signal to contract. This explains why botulism can cause muscle weakness, including drooping eyelids.

Rats are medium-sized rodents that are larger than mice. The Norway rat is one of the species most often used in laboratories because rats can learn tasks and adapt to different environments. Researchers have studied how rats find their way through mazes, respond to rewards or frightening experiences, and use drugs. In a well-known experiment by psychologist Bruce Alexander, some rats lived alone in small cages, while others lived together in a spacious setting with room to play and interact. The shared, enriched environment was called Rat Park. When offered morphine-laced water, the rats in Rat Park drank less of it than the rats housed alone. The experiment helped researchers explore how an animal’s surroundings and social opportunities can affect its behavior.

Jaws are paired skeletal structures that attach to the skull and let an animal seize, bite, and process food. They may support teeth or other surfaces that help break food into smaller pieces. Vertebrates are animals with backbones, and most living vertebrates have jaws. This includes sharks, bony fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Together, jawed vertebrates form the group called Gnathostomata; an individual member is called a gnathostome. Jaws help these animals eat a wide range of foods, from plants to prey. Not every vertebrate has them, though. Lampreys and hagfish are living jawless vertebrates, and many extinct fish also lacked jaws. The presence or absence of jaws is therefore an important way to distinguish major groups of vertebrates.

Monsanto was an American agricultural and chemical company founded in St. Louis in 1901. It first manufactured saccharin, an artificial sweetener, but later became known for herbicides and genetically engineered seeds. In 1974, Monsanto introduced Roundup, a broad-spectrum weed killer whose active ingredient is glyphosate. The company also developed crops designed to tolerate Roundup, including genetically modified soybeans, so farmers could spray weeds without killing the crop. Other Monsanto products included potato plants engineered to produce Bt, a substance that protects them from certain insects. These technologies made Monsanto influential in farming and sparked debate about their environmental and economic effects. German company Bayer completed its acquisition of Monsanto in 2018.

Published in 1687, Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, often called the Principia, is a landmark book by the English mathematician and scientist Isaac Newton. Its Latin title means “Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy,” a term then used for the study of nature. In the book, Newton set out his three laws of motion, which describe how objects move and how forces change their motion. He also presented a mathematical account of universal gravitation: the same force that makes an object fall toward Earth helps keep the Moon and planets in their orbits. By applying these ideas to objects on Earth and to planets, moons, and other celestial bodies, Newton laid the foundations of classical mechanics.

A tetrahedral arrangement forms when a central atom has four bonds that point toward the corners of a regular tetrahedron, a shape like a pyramid with a triangular base. According to VSEPR theory, the bonds spread out in three dimensions to keep their electron pairs as far apart as possible. The angle between any two bonds is called a bond angle; in an ideal tetrahedral arrangement, it is approximately 109.5 degrees, so it is known as the tetrahedral bond angle. Methane is a common example. It is the simplest hydrocarbon, with one carbon atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms. Its four equivalent carbon–hydrogen bonds form a tetrahedral shape, and every hydrogen–carbon–hydrogen bond angle is about 109.5 degrees.

Limestone is a sedimentary rock that forms when calcium-carbonate-rich material accumulates and hardens, often in oceans and lakes. It commonly contains the mineral calcite and may include the shells and skeletons of ancient sea creatures. If limestone is exposed to enough heat and pressure, it can change into the metamorphic rock marble. Limestone also dissolves slowly in slightly acidic groundwater. Over time, water moving through cracks can widen them into caves or caverns, and a cave roof may collapse to form a sinkhole. Dripping mineral-rich water inside caves can build stalactites and stalagmites. A limestone-rich landscape shaped by this dissolving process, with features such as caves, sinkholes, and underground streams, is called karst.

The Quantum Hall Effect occurs when electrons are confined to a nearly two-dimensional layer, cooled to a low temperature, and exposed to a strong magnetic field perpendicular to the layer. As current flows, the magnetic field pushes electrons sideways, creating a voltage across the layer. The resistance measured across the current’s direction, called Hall resistance, does not change smoothly as the magnetic field changes. Instead, it stays on remarkably precise, flat steps called plateaus. Their values are set by a universal resistance scale, h/e², where h is Planck’s constant and e is the elementary charge. This scale is called the von Klitzing constant. The plateaus occur at simple fractions of this constant, making the Quantum Hall Effect useful for precise electrical measurements.

The Kerr effect is an electro-optic phenomenon: applying an electric field to certain materials changes how light travels through them. The optical property that changes is the refractive index, also called the index of refraction. It describes how much light slows down in a material compared with its speed in a vacuum. To calculate it, divide the speed of light in a vacuum by its speed in the material, so it has no units. In the Kerr effect, the change in refractive index is typically proportional to the square of the electric field strength. For example, doubling the field strength would make the change about four times as large. By controlling the electric field, scientists and engineers can therefore control how light behaves in a material.

An aerodynamic stall occurs when an aircraft wing is tilted too steeply into the oncoming airflow. The angle between the wing and that airflow is called the angle of attack. As this angle increases, the wing initially produces more lift, but beyond a threshold, air can no longer flow smoothly along its upper surface. The airflow separates, and the wing loses substantial lift. The greatest angle of attack at which the airflow can remain attached is called the critical angle of attack. A stall is therefore caused by exceeding this angle, not simply by flying below a particular speed. Low speed can make a stall more likely because a pilot may need to raise the wing’s angle of attack to keep the aircraft aloft.

A dam is an engineered barrier built across a river or other watercourse to hold back and control water. The water stored behind it forms a reservoir, which can supply farms with water for irrigation and help manage the river’s flow. Some dams also generate hydroelectric power: water released through the dam spins turbines connected to generators, producing electricity. The Aswan High Dam is an example on the Nile River near Aswan, in Egypt, north of Sudan. It created the large artificial reservoir Lake Nasser, named after Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser, who ordered the dam’s construction. Rising water from the reservoir would have flooded the ancient Abu Simbel temples, so the temples were moved to higher ground.

The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin vaccine, usually called BCG, is used primarily to protect against tuberculosis, especially severe forms of the disease in children. It is a live attenuated vaccine, meaning it contains living bacteria that have been weakened so they can train the immune system without usually causing disease in healthy people. BCG is made from a weakened strain of Mycobacterium bovis, the species of bacterium that causes tuberculosis in cattle. Although Mycobacterium bovis is related to the bacterium responsible for most human tuberculosis, it is a different species.
