Like other vaccines, BCG helps the immune system recognize a threat and respond more effectively if exposed later. Its protection against tuberculosis varies, so its use differs between countries.

The Second Law of Thermodynamics says that the total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease over time: it may increase or, in an ideal case, stay the same. Entropy is often described as a measure of how spread out energy is. This law explains why heat flows spontaneously from a hotter object to a colder one, rather than the reverse. A famous challenge to the law is Maxwell’s demon, a hypothetical intelligent being that opens and closes a tiny door between two containers of gas. By letting fast molecules pass one way and slow molecules the other, the demon seems able to separate hot and cold gas and lower entropy without using energy. The puzzle is resolved by accounting for the physical costs of the demon’s work, including handling information.

The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialized form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum found in muscle cells. It is a membrane network that stores calcium ions, which muscle fibers need to contract. Pumps called SERCA move calcium from the cell fluid into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, keeping a supply ready for use. In skeletal muscle, enlarged storage regions called terminal cisternae lie next to transverse tubules, which carry electrical signals deep into the fiber. When a signal arrives, calcium flows out through channels called ryanodine receptors, helping start contraction. These channels are named for ryanodine, a plant alkaloid that affects them. Mutations in a ryanodine receptor can cause malignant hyperthermia, a dangerous reaction to certain anesthetic drugs.

A kingdom is a broad rank in biological taxonomy, the system scientists use to classify living things. It sits below domain and above phylum: a domain can contain several kingdoms, and a kingdom can contain several phyla. Familiar kingdoms include animals, plants, fungi, and protists. Classification systems have changed as scientists have learned more about organisms and their evolutionary relationships. For example, organisms once grouped together in a kingdom called Monera may instead be separated into Archaea and Bacteria. In the 1700s, Swedish taxonomist Carl Linnaeus used the Latin word regnum, meaning “kingdom,” for three major groups: animals, plants, and minerals. His mineral kingdom, Regnum Lapideum, included rocks, although rocks are not living things and are not classified in a biological kingdom today.

A laboratory funnel has a wide opening that narrows into a stem, making it easier to pour a liquid into a container with a small opening without spilling. In a simple funnel, filter paper can hold back solid particles while the liquid passes through. Funnels also come in specialized forms. A separatory funnel has a stopcock, or valve, near its outlet. It is used to separate immiscible liquids, such as oil and water, which form distinct layers after settling; the lower layer can be drained out first. A Büchner funnel has a flat, perforated surface that holds filter paper and is often connected to a vacuum pump to pull liquid through more quickly. A dropping funnel releases liquid gradually into a reaction, and some have a tube that equalizes pressure.

The Fermi paradox asks why we have found no convincing evidence of extraterrestrial civilizations, even though the universe is vast and ancient and many stars have planets where life might develop. It is often summed up as “Where is everybody?” The puzzle does not prove that aliens do not exist; they might be rare, too far away, or difficult for us to detect. One way scientists think about the question is the Drake equation, proposed in 1961. It estimates how many detectable civilizations might exist in the Milky Way by combining factors such as the rate at which stars form, the fraction with planets, the chances of life and intelligence developing, the development of detectable technology, and how long civilizations remain detectable. SETI projects search for possible signals from such civilizations.

Piezoelectricity is the ability of certain materials to produce an electric charge when they are squeezed, bent, or otherwise put under mechanical stress. The effect also works in reverse: applying an electric field can make a piezoelectric material change shape slightly. This happens because stress or an electric field shifts the positions of charged particles within the material. In the 1880s, the brothers Pierre and Jacques Curie investigated this effect in crystals, including Rochelle salt, whose chemical name is potassium sodium tartrate tetrahydrate. Piezoelectric materials are useful in devices that turn movement into electrical signals, such as some microphones and pressure sensors, and in devices that use electrical signals to create tiny movements, such as ultrasound equipment.

Eels are elongated, snake-like fish with flexible bodies that help them move through water and into narrow hiding places. True eels belong to the order Anguilliformes and include conger eels, moray eels, and European eels. The deep-sea gulper eel is another eel-like fish, known for its huge, pelican-like mouth and glowing tail. European eels spend much of their lives in European rivers and coastal waters, but they cross the Atlantic Ocean to reproduce in the Sargasso Sea. Their larvae then drift back toward Europe on ocean currents. Because no one had observed where they bred, the ancient Greek thinker Aristotle mistakenly believed eels arose spontaneously. Electric eels are also long and eel-shaped, but despite their name, they are not true eels.

In optics, the normal is an imaginary line drawn perpendicular to a surface at the point where a light ray strikes it. It provides a reference for describing the ray’s direction, even when the surface is tilted or curved. The angle between the incoming ray and the normal is called the angle of incidence. When light reflects from a plane mirror, the outgoing ray makes an angle with the normal called the angle of reflection. The law of reflection states that these two angles are equal. Both angles are measured from the normal, not from the mirror’s surface. For example, if an incoming ray makes a 30-degree angle with the normal, the reflected ray makes a 30-degree angle with it on the other side.

Opioids are a class of drugs that relieve pain by acting on receptors in the brain and body. They include prescription medicines such as oxycodone, as well as heroin and fentanyl. Opioids can be helpful when used under medical supervision, but they can also cause dependence, meaning a person may find it difficult to stop using them. Taking too much can slow or stop breathing, causing a life-threatening overdose. Widespread misuse and overprescription have contributed to the opioid epidemic in the United States. An overdose can often be reversed with naloxone, an opioid antagonist that blocks opioids’ effects. Naloxone is also sold under the brand name Narcan and can be given as a nasal spray. In 2022, Illinois eliminated co-pays for this medication to make it easier to access.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory is a U.S. Department of Energy research facility in Tennessee that grew out of the Manhattan Project, the World War II effort to develop the first nuclear bombs. The federal government acquired land at Oak Ridge for several secret wartime facilities. One of them, the X-10 Graphite Reactor, began operating in November 1943. It was a pilot-scale reactor: scientists used it to demonstrate how to produce plutonium and to gain experience before larger production facilities at Hanford, Washington, came online. The reactor also supplied material for research, while other Oak Ridge facilities worked on enriching uranium. Today, Oak Ridge National Laboratory continues to study nuclear science along with fields such as materials, energy, and computing.

Viscosity measures how strongly a fluid resists flowing or changing shape because of friction between its moving layers. Honey has a higher viscosity than water, so it pours more slowly. Liquids and gases are both fluids, and their motion can be described by the Navier–Stokes equations. If viscosity is treated as zero, these equations simplify to the Euler equations. Viscosity also helps determine the pattern of a fluid’s motion. The Reynolds number is a dimensionless ratio that compares inertial effects, which tend to keep a fluid moving, with viscous effects, which resist differences in motion. A low Reynolds number generally indicates smooth, orderly flow called laminar flow; a high Reynolds number makes chaotic, swirling flow called turbulent flow more likely.

Metals are a broad class of elements that occupy much of the left and center of the periodic table. They generally conduct heat and electricity well and have a shiny surface called metallic luster. Many metals can be shaped without breaking and combined with other elements to form alloys, which may be stronger or more resistant to corrosion than the original metal. Titanium and cobalt are examples of metals. Cobalt is a silvery-blue transition metal with atomic number 27, meaning each cobalt atom has 27 protons. It is used in some rechargeable battery cathodes, the parts of batteries involved in storing and releasing electrical energy, and in high-strength alloys. Not every metal looks the same or has exactly the same properties, but these shared traits help distinguish metals from other elements.

An evaporite is a chemical sedimentary deposit formed when water in a saline lake or shallow sea evaporates, leaving dissolved substances behind. This often happens in hot, dry basins where water flows in but little flows out. As the water level falls, the dissolved substances become more concentrated and eventually crystallize, or precipitate, into minerals. Evaporite deposits can contain gypsum, borax, and halite. Halite is sodium chloride (NaCl), the same substance as table salt. It commonly forms cubic crystals, and large deposits of it are mined as rock salt. Evaporation, the process that creates evaporites, is also part of the water cycle: liquid water becomes water vapor and enters the atmosphere.

A mirror is a smooth surface that reflects light to form an image. Flat mirrors, like those found in homes, let you see your appearance. Curved mirrors can make images look larger or smaller, and reflecting telescopes use them to collect light from distant objects. The process that makes mirrors work is reflection: when light reaches a surface, it changes direction and travels back into the medium it came from. On a smooth mirror, this is called specular reflection, which produces a clear image. The incoming light ray and the reflected ray make equal angles with an imaginary line called the normal, which is perpendicular to the mirror’s surface. Rough surfaces scatter reflected light in many directions, so they do not form clear images.

Beryllium is a lightweight metal with the chemical symbol Be and atomic number 4. Atomic number tells you how many protons are in an atom’s nucleus, so every beryllium atom has four protons. Beryllium is the first element in group 2 of the periodic table, a group called the alkaline-earth metals. It is strong for its low weight and is used in some aerospace equipment, but beryllium dust is dangerous to breathe. The number four also appears in two familiar molecules. Methane has the formula CH4, meaning each molecule contains one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. A molecule of white phosphorus has the formula P4, so it contains four phosphorus atoms. Thus, beryllium’s atomic number matches both counts.

Astronomical parallax is the apparent shift in a nearby star’s position when it is viewed from different places. To measure it, astronomers observe the star from opposite sides of Earth’s orbit around the Sun, about six months apart, and compare its position with much more distant background stars. The star has not actually moved back and forth; the shift is caused by the change in Earth’s viewpoint. Astronomers use half of the total observed shift as the star’s annual parallax angle. A larger angle means the star is closer, while a smaller angle means it is farther away. A parsec is the distance at which a star’s annual parallax is exactly one arcsecond, a tiny unit of angle. Distance in parsecs equals one divided by the parallax angle in arcseconds.

The Cori cycle is a metabolic process that links working muscles and the liver. During strenuous activity, muscles may need energy faster than oxygen can be supplied. They break down glucose through glycolysis, producing a three-carbon substance called pyruvate, which is then converted to lactate. Lactate is the ionized form of lactic acid and is the form commonly found in the body. It travels through the blood to the liver, where it is used to make glucose. That glucose can return through the blood to the muscles and be used for energy again. This recycling helps muscles keep working when oxygen is limited, although making glucose in the liver requires energy. Lactate can build up during intense exercise, but it is not the cause of delayed-onset muscle soreness.

Botulism is a serious illness caused by botulinum toxin, a protein made by certain Clostridium bacteria, especially Clostridium botulinum. It can develop after someone eats improperly preserved food containing the toxin or when bacteria contaminate a wound. The toxin acts at peripheral nerve endings, where nerves normally release acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter that signals muscles to contract. By cutting proteins called SNARE proteins, botulinum toxin prevents acetylcholine from being released. Without that signal, muscles become weak and limp. Symptoms can include drooping eyelids and paralysis that spreads downward from the face and neck to other parts of the body. If breathing muscles are affected, botulism can be life-threatening and requires urgent medical care. In carefully controlled doses, the same toxin is used in Botox treatments to reduce wrinkles.

Abortion is the deliberate ending of a pregnancy. It can involve medication or a medical procedure, and is different from birth control, which aims to prevent pregnancy. People may seek an abortion for many reasons, including health concerns or personal circumstances. Access to abortion is debated because people hold different views about pregnancy, bodily autonomy, and the role of government in medical decisions. In the United States, the 1973 Supreme Court decision Roe v. Wade recognized a constitutional right to abortion. In 2022, the Supreme Court overturned that decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, leaving states with greater power to regulate or ban abortion. Restrictions can also have public-health and social effects: when Romania banned abortion under Nicolae Ceaușescu, many children were abandoned.

Hydraulic fracturing, often called fracking, is a method of extracting oil and natural gas trapped in shale and other rock that does not let fluids flow through it easily. A well is drilled into the rock, and fluid is pumped down the well at high pressure. The pressure creates small cracks, or fissures, that give the trapped oil and gas a path toward the well. The injected fluid contains grains of sand or engineered ceramic called proppant. These grains lodge in the cracks and hold them open after pumping stops, so oil and gas can continue to flow. Fracking can make previously hard-to-reach reserves accessible, but it is controversial because of concerns about water use, pollution, and earthquakes linked especially to wastewater disposal.

The Casparian strip is a waterproof band of suberin in the walls of endodermal cells near the center of a plant root. The endodermis lies between the outer cortex and the vascular cylinder, or stele, which contains tissues that carry water and nutrients through the plant. Water and dissolved minerals can initially travel through spaces and cell walls without entering cells; this is the apoplastic pathway. The Casparian strip blocks that route, forcing the substances to cross an endodermal cell membrane before entering the stele. This helps the root regulate which minerals move inward. Once inside a cell, water and minerals can travel through the connected cytoplasm of neighboring cells via tiny channels called plasmodesmata. This cell-to-cell route is the symplastic pathway.

Theia is the name given to a hypothetical protoplanet that may have struck the early Earth more than four billion years ago. A protoplanet is a large, developing body that can grow into a planet. In the leading explanation for how Earth’s Moon formed, Theia’s impact blasted material from the young Earth and the colliding body into space. Some of that debris remained in orbit and gradually came together, or coalesced, to form the Moon, Earth’s natural satellite. Scientists call this the giant-impact hypothesis. Theia has not been directly observed; its existence is inferred from evidence about the Earth–Moon system. The key connection is that Theia was the proposed impactor, while the Moon was the satellite formed from the collision’s debris.

The Drake Equation is a way to estimate how many technological civilizations in the Milky Way might be detectable from Earth. It multiplies the galaxy’s rate of star formation by factors estimating how many stars have planets, how many planets could support life, how often life and intelligence develop, and how often intelligent societies produce technology that sends detectable signals. Most of these factors are uncertain probabilities, so the equation does not give a reliable single answer. Its final factor, called civilization lifetime and written L, is different: it is the average length of time a technological society emits signals detectable across interstellar distances. If societies stop transmitting quickly, fewer would be detectable at any given time, even if life is common.

Migraine is a neurological disorder that causes repeated attacks of head pain, often severe enough to disrupt daily activities. During an attack, a person may feel nauseated or become unusually sensitive to light and sound, so a bright room or ordinary noises can feel uncomfortable. Some people experience an aura before the headache begins. An aura is a temporary visual or sensory disturbance, such as flashing lights, blind spots, zigzag patterns, or tingling in part of the body. Not everyone with migraine has an aura, and some auras occur without a headache afterward. Migraine is different from a sinus headache, which can be caused by inflammation of the air-filled sinus cavities in the skull.

Hygroscopicity is a material’s ability to attract and hold water vapor from the surrounding air. A dry, hygroscopic salt can absorb moisture when exposed to humid air, causing it to clump or become wet. Some salts are so strongly hygroscopic that they dissolve in the water they take up; this behavior is called deliquescence. Hygroscopicity matters when storing chemicals and when considering particles people might breathe in. For example, sparkler smoke can contain potassium chloride, a salt that can take up moisture and pose an inhalation hazard. Potassium is an alkali metal with 19 protons in each atom, and its chemical symbol is K, so potassium chloride has the formula KCl. The name for the moisture-attracting property is hygroscopicity.

A quantum computer processes information using quantum bits, or qubits. Unlike a classical bit, which is either 0 or 1, a qubit can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 until it is measured. By controlling qubits and their interactions, a quantum computer can tackle some problems differently from an ordinary computer. One approach uses photons, the particles of light, instead of electrons in optical circuits. Photons belong to a larger group of particles called bosons. Bosons obey Bose-Einstein statistics and, unlike electrons, can share the same quantum state. In a technique called boson sampling, an optical network sends many indistinguishable photons through different paths, and researchers measure how often each possible output occurs. Controlling errors in such circuits remains a major challenge.

Nicolaus Copernicus was a Renaissance astronomer born in Toruń, then part of Royal Prussia, in 1473. At a time when many scholars believed Earth stood still at the center of the universe, he argued that Earth rotates once each day and travels around the Sun each year. This Sun-centered, or heliocentric, model also placed the other known planets in orbit around the Sun. Copernicus explained his ideas in De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, a Latin title meaning “On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres.” The book was printed in Nuremberg in 1543, the year he died. His model challenged the long-accepted Earth-centered view and helped transform astronomy. Later scientists, including Galileo Galilei, gathered evidence that supported the idea that Earth is a moving planet.

Energy is the capacity to cause change or do work. In mechanics, kinetic energy is the energy of motion, while potential energy is stored because of an object’s position or arrangement, such as a raised ball or a stretched spring. Energy can move between objects and change forms, but it cannot be created or destroyed. This conservation principle is the First Law of Thermodynamics. Energy is often discussed alongside entropy, a different quantity usually symbolized by S. Entropy is related to how many microscopic arrangements are possible in a system and is sometimes described as a measure of disorder. The Second Law of Thermodynamics says that the total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease, even though its energy remains conserved.

A weighted graph is a network of vertices, or points, connected by edges, or links. Each edge has a numerical weight that can represent a distance, travel time, cost, or another quantity. For example, in a map of roads, intersections could be vertices and roads could be edges weighted by driving time. Pathfinding algorithms use these weights to compare routes and find one with the smallest total weight, rather than simply the fewest edges. One shortest-path method is Dijkstra’s algorithm, named after Dutch computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra. Starting at a chosen vertex, it repeatedly selects the unsettled vertex with the lowest known distance and uses its edges to update the known distances to neighboring vertices. This method works when edge weights are nonnegative.

An egg cell, or ovum, is the large female gamete that can join with a sperm cell during fertilization. Egg cells develop from immature cells in the ovaries. During each menstrual cycle, one usually matures inside an ovarian follicle. A surge in luteinizing hormone (LH) triggers the follicle to release it in an event called ovulation, which occurs before the luteal phase. The egg cell then enters a fallopian tube, where fertilization may take place. After releasing the egg, the follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which produces hormones that help prepare the uterus for pregnancy. An unfertilized egg cell does not implant in the uterine lining; if fertilization occurs, the developing embryo may later implant there.

Chromatography separates the substances in a mixture by letting a liquid, called the mobile phase, move across a stationary phase such as paper or a thin coating on a plate. As the liquid moves, different substances travel different distances and form separate spots. In paper and thin-layer chromatography, the retention factor, abbreviated Rf, describes how far a spot moves compared with the liquid. To calculate it, measure from the starting line, or origin, to the center of the spot, then divide by the distance from the origin to the leading edge of the liquid. That leading edge is called the solvent front. Because both measurements use the same units, Rf has no units. It helps compare substances tested under the same conditions.

The rhesus macaque, also called the rhesus monkey, is an adaptable Old World monkey native to parts of Asia. Its range stretches from Afghanistan across northern India and into China. Rhesus macaques live in social groups and have been widely used in biomedical and behavioral research. In the 1950s, American psychologist Harry Harlow studied maternal attachment using infant rhesus macaques. He gave them two artificial “mothers”: one made of wire that could provide milk and another covered in soft cloth. The infants spent much more time clinging to the cloth mother, showing that comfort and physical contact are important to attachment, not just food. Harlow’s experiments, including later studies of social isolation, are now considered highly controversial because they caused serious distress to the animals.

The philosopher’s stone is a legendary substance sought by alchemists, people who studied how materials could be transformed. They believed the stone could transmute base metals such as lead into gold and help produce the Elixir of Life, a potion said to prolong life. No philosopher’s stone has ever been shown to exist, but the idea has remained popular in stories. In Paulo Coelho’s novel The Alchemist, the stone and the Elixir of Life are described as the goals of alchemy’s “Master Work.” In the first Harry Potter novel, the alchemist Nicolas Flamel is said to have made the Philosopher’s Stone. He and his wife, Perenelle, use its life-extending power to live for centuries. The book was published in the United States as Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone.

Tim Berners-Lee is a British computer scientist who invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN, a European physics research center. In 1989, he proposed a hypertext system to help researchers share and connect information. He then built the first web browser and web server. The World Wide Web lets people follow links between documents identified by web addresses, or URLs. Browsers use HTTP, a set of rules for requesting and receiving those documents from servers. Berners-Lee also developed HTML, the markup language that structures webpages using tags. The web is not the same as the internet: the internet is the underlying global network that carries data, while the World Wide Web is a system of linked pages and other resources that uses that network.

Punctuated equilibrium is a theory of evolution developed by paleontologists Stephen Jay Gould and Niles Eldredge to explain patterns in the fossil record. Many species appear to remain relatively unchanged for long stretches of geologic time, a pattern called stasis. These intervals are “punctuated” by geologically brief periods of rapid evolutionary change, often associated with speciation, when new species form. This differs from the idea that species always change slowly and continuously. “Rapid” is relative to geologic time: it can still mean thousands of years or more, not a sudden change in one organism. Punctuated equilibrium does not reject natural selection, the process by which inherited traits that improve survival and reproduction become more common. Instead, it describes when evolutionary change may be most noticeable in the history of a species.

Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble nutrient found in citrus fruits such as oranges and lemons, as well as in foods such as potatoes. The body needs it to make collagen, a protein that helps keep skin, gums, blood vessels, and other tissues strong. Because the body does not store much vitamin C, people need a regular supply from food. A severe lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, a disease that can lead to bleeding gums, weakness, and poor wound healing. Scurvy was once a major danger for sailors on long voyages because fresh foods were scarce. Carrying citrus fruits or other vitamin C-rich foods helped prevent it.

A collision is a brief interaction in which two or more objects strike one another and exert forces that change their motion. Billiard balls collide when they hit, and in the kinetic theory of gases, molecules repeatedly collide with one another and with the walls of their container. In an isolated collision, total momentum is conserved: the objects can exchange momentum, but their combined momentum stays the same. Kinetic energy is also conserved in an elastic collision, but some of it becomes heat, sound, or deformation in an inelastic collision. For a head-on collision, the coefficient of restitution compares the relative speed at which objects separate after impact with the relative speed at which they approached before impact. It is 1 for an ideal elastic collision and 0 for a perfectly inelastic one.

Orangutans are great apes with long arms and shaggy reddish hair. They live in the rainforests of two major Southeast Asian islands, Borneo and Sumatra, and spend much of their time in trees, a lifestyle called arboreal. Their long arms and grasping hands and feet help them climb through the forest canopy, where they find foods such as fruit, leaves, and insects. Unlike many other great apes, orangutans are usually solitary. Borneo, one of their island homes, is divided among Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brunei; the Indonesian part is called Kalimantan. Orangutans are threatened by habitat loss as rainforests are cleared, making protection of their forest homes important for their survival.

Parasitism is an ecological relationship in which one organism, called a parasite, benefits by living in or on another organism, called the host. The parasite takes resources such as nutrients or shelter, while the host is harmed. For example, some nematodes, or roundworms, live inside animals and feed at their hosts’ expense. Other parasites live on a host’s surface, as ticks do when they feed on blood. Unlike a predator, which usually kills and eats its prey, a parasite often depends on its host remaining alive for some time. The harm to a host can range from mild irritation to serious illness. When identifying this relationship, remember the roles: the parasite benefits, and the host provides the habitat or resources and is harmed.

Phenolphthalein is a synthetic pH indicator used in acid–base titrations. It is colorless in acidic solutions and turns pink or fuchsia in basic solutions, so it can show when the pH has changed. In a titration, a measured solution called the titrant is gradually added to another solution, the analyte, to help determine the analyte’s concentration. If phenolphthalein is the indicator, the first pale-pink color that remains after mixing signals that reagent addition should stop. This observed color change is the titration endpoint. It approximates the equivalence point, where the acid and base have reacted in the required proportions, though the two points are not always exactly the same.

Solubility describes how much of a substance can dissolve in a solvent, such as water, to form a solution. If a dissolved compound exceeds its solubility limit, some of it may separate from the solution as a solid called a precipitate. Many ionic compounds, or salts, dissolve because water can separate their positive and negative ions, though some salts are much less soluble than others. For example, nitrates and most alkali-metal compounds are soluble, while lead(II) chloride has limited solubility. When lead(II) chloride dissolves, it releases lead ions and chloride ions. Adding sodium chloride supplies extra chloride ions. Because chloride is an ion the two salts have in common, this shifts the balance toward solid lead(II) chloride, causing more to precipitate. This decrease in solubility is called the common ion effect.

Cyanobacteria are bacteria that use sunlight to make food through photosynthesis, releasing oxygen in the process. Although they are sometimes called “blue-green algae,” they are bacteria, not true algae. They live in freshwater, oceans, and on land, and some grow as chains of cells called filaments. A filament may contain specialized cells called heterocysts, which fix nitrogen: they convert nitrogen gas from the air into forms that living things can use. Heterocysts provide a low-oxygen environment for this process, since oxygen interferes with nitrogen fixation. Photosynthesis takes place on internal membranes called thylakoids. Researchers have reported that cyanobacterial membranes can contain pentadecane, a straight-chain hydrocarbon with 15 carbon atoms, which may help stabilize the thylakoids.

Worms are elongated, soft-bodied invertebrates, but the name describes a body shape rather than one closely related group of animals. Earthworms live in soil and help break down dead material, making them useful in composting. Other worms include flatworms and roundworms; some, such as pinworms, are parasites that live in animals or humans. Tapeworms are parasitic flatworms that can live in the gut, while roundworms belong to the phylum Nematoda. One tiny roundworm, Caenorhabditis elegans, is widely used by scientists to study how embryos develop. Its simple body and short life cycle make it easier to observe changes as it grows. So, although these animals are all commonly called worms, they belong to several different branches of the animal kingdom.

The International Space Station, or ISS, is a laboratory and living space that orbits Earth. Built through cooperation among several countries, it was assembled in low Earth orbit beginning in 1998 and has been continuously inhabited since 2000. Astronauts from different nations live and work there for months at a time, studying how microgravity affects people, plants, and other materials. Earlier space stations included Mir and Skylab. Visiting spacecraft, including Dragon, deliver supplies to the ISS. One part of the station is the Cupola, an observation module attached to the Tranquility module. Its seven windows give astronauts panoramic views of Earth and help them see what they are doing when operating the station’s robotic arm.

Chemical activity is a measure of a substance’s effective concentration: it describes how the substance behaves in reactions rather than simply how much of it is present. In an ideal solution, activity closely matches concentration. In a real solution, particles interact, so an activity coefficient adjusts the concentration to account for those interactions. Using activity in equilibrium expressions helps predict how nonideal solutions behave. For dilute electrolyte solutions, which contain charged particles called ions, the Debye–Hückel limiting law relates an ion’s activity coefficient to its charge and the solution’s ionic strength. Ionic strength measures the overall effect of dissolved ions. It is calculated as one-half the sum, over all ion types, of each ion’s concentration multiplied by the square of its charge. Thus, ions with larger charges contribute especially strongly.

Transposable elements, also called transposons or “jumping genes,” are DNA sequences that can move to new positions within a genome instead of staying at one fixed site. Some move directly as DNA, while others are copied into RNA before a new DNA copy is inserted elsewhere. LINEs and SINEs are examples, and transposable elements and their remnants make up about half of the human genome. Moving or copying a sequence can disrupt a gene or change how it works. Barbara McClintock discovered transposable elements while studying how kernel color is inherited in maize, or corn. Her work showed that genes could be affected by nearby mobile DNA, a surprising idea at the time. She later received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this discovery.

A Mars rover is a robotic vehicle that travels across the surface of Mars to investigate the planet. Unlike a stationary lander, it can drive to different sites; unlike an orbiting probe, it studies rocks, soil, and local conditions up close. Rovers carry cameras and scientific instruments that help researchers examine Martian geology and look for signs of past environments that might have supported life. NASA’s Perseverance rover landed in Jezero crater in February 2021. Scientists chose the site because it contains an ancient river delta, where water may once have deposited sediments that preserve clues about Mars’s past. Perseverance carries Mastcam-Z, a camera system that takes detailed images of the landscape and helps scientists choose places to explore.

A tulip is a flowering plant in the genus Tulipa. It grows from a bulb, an underground structure that stores food and helps the plant sprout again. Tulips are known for their brightly colored, cup-shaped flowers and are still widely cultivated in the Netherlands. During the Dutch Golden Age in the 1630s, some rare tulip bulbs became objects of intense speculation: people bought and sold them hoping their prices would keep rising. When prices fell sharply, the episode became known as “tulip mania.” Amsterdam had an active market in this trade. It was also an important trading port and housed the principal chamber of the Dutch East India Company, which shipped spices from Asia. Amsterdam later became the capital of the Netherlands.

Magnetohydrodynamics is the study of how electrically conducting fluids move and interact with magnetic fields. It combines fluid dynamics, which describes how liquids and gases flow, with electromagnetism, which describes electric currents and magnetic forces. A key example is plasma, often called the fourth state of matter. Plasma is a gas containing charged particles because some of its atoms have lost electrons. It makes up the Sun and appears in phenomena such as auroras and lightning. Because plasma conducts electricity, its motion can affect magnetic fields, while magnetic fields can guide or constrain its motion. Scientists use magnetohydrodynamics to understand these interactions in space and to design fusion devices called tokamaks, which use magnetic fields to confine hot plasma in a doughnut-shaped region.

Shoemaker–Levy 9 was a comet discovered in 1993 in images taken at Palomar Observatory. By then, Jupiter’s powerful gravity had pulled the comet apart into a chain of fragments. In July 1994, those pieces plunged one after another into Jupiter, creating enormous explosions and temporary dark marks in its cloud tops that astronomers could see from Earth. The impacts gave scientists a rare chance to study what happens when objects collide with a planet. Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the solar system’s first gas giant, a huge planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium. It is also known for the Great Red Spot, a long-lasting storm.

Luteinizing hormone, or LH, is a reproductive hormone released by the anterior pituitary gland in the brain. Around the middle of the menstrual cycle, LH levels rise sharply in what is called the LH surge. This surge triggers ovulation: an ovarian follicle releases a mature oocyte, or egg cell, which enters the fallopian tube and may be fertilized by sperm. The emptied follicle then develops into the corpus luteum, a temporary structure that secretes hormones, especially progesterone. Progesterone helps prepare the lining of the uterus for a possible pregnancy. Ovulation marks the transition toward the luteal phase, when the corpus luteum is active.

Robert Fulton was an American engineer and inventor who helped make steamboats a practical way to carry passengers and goods. A steamboat uses an engine powered by steam, or water vapor, to turn a paddle wheel and move through the water. In 1807, Fulton began a commercially successful service on the Hudson River between New York City and Albany. Its vessel was later popularly known as the Clermont, after the Hudson Valley estate of Fulton’s financial backer, Robert Livingston. Fulton did not invent the steam engine or the steamboat, but he showed that steam-powered river travel could work as a business. Steamboats went on to transform transportation on American rivers in the 19th century.

Ziegler–Natta catalysts are a family of substances used to make polymers, large molecules built from repeating units called monomers. They are especially important for turning olefins, such as propylene, into plastics through coordination polymerization. In this process, monomers attach to a metal center and join a growing chain. Early catalyst systems combined a transition-metal halide, such as titanium tetrachloride, with an organoaluminum compound. By controlling how each propylene unit joins the chain, these catalysts made it possible to produce highly stereoregular polypropylene, whose repeating units have an orderly arrangement. The catalysts are named after Karl Ziegler and the Italian chemist Giulio Natta. Natta developed stereospecific polymerization of propylene, and the two scientists shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

An amoeba is a single-celled protist often found in pond water. Unlike organisms with a fixed body shape, it constantly changes shape as it moves. It does this by pushing out temporary extensions of its cytoplasm called pseudopods, or “false feet,” then flowing into them. An amoeba also uses pseudopods to surround food particles or smaller organisms and draw them into the cell. This way of engulfing food is called phagocytosis. Amoebas move slowly, so they may take careful observation to spot on a slide under a light microscope. Their changing shape and use of pseudopods for both movement and feeding help distinguish them from pond organisms such as Paramecium, which swims using tiny hair-like structures called cilia.

Google Chrome is a web browser developed and distributed by Google, the company that also maintains the Android operating system. People use Chrome to visit websites, search the web, and run web apps. Like other browsers, it displays pages built with HTML and CSS and runs JavaScript to make them interactive. If Chrome cannot connect to the Internet, its error page may show a pixelated dinosaur; pressing the space bar starts a simple running game. Chrome shares much of its source code with Chromium, an open-source browser project. Developers can use Chromium’s code to build browsers, and Chromium is also the name of a browser build without Google’s proprietary branding and some of Chrome’s Google-specific features.

An array is a data structure that stores an ordered collection of elements, such as numbers or words. Each element has a position called an index, so a program can retrieve or change a particular element without searching through the whole collection. In Java, arrays use square brackets to access elements: scores[0] refers to the first element of an array named scores. This may seem surprising because people often count from 1, but Java arrays use zero-based indexing. The first element has index 0, the second has index 1, and each later index increases by one. For example, an array with five elements has indexes 0 through 4. A for loop is often used to visit each element in order.

Ray tracing is a computer-graphics technique for creating images by modeling how light travels through a virtual scene. A computer traces imaginary rays, often backward from a camera, to find where they hit objects and how the light reflects, bends through transparent materials (refraction), or casts shadows. These calculations can make images look realistic, but ray tracing is often slower and more computationally expensive than scan-line methods, which draw visible surfaces more directly. If too few rays are used, the image may show random speckles called noise; tracing more rays can reduce it. The same general idea can model sound waves traveling through a space. When sound reflects off a surface and reaches a listener noticeably after the original sound, the distinct repetition is called an echo.

Blood type describes the markers, called antigens, on a person’s red blood cells. The letters A, B, AB, or O describe one set of antigens, while the plus or minus sign describes the Rh factor. The Rh factor includes several red-cell antigens, but the D antigen is the most important for routine blood typing: if your red blood cells have D, you are Rh-positive; if they lack D, you are Rh-negative. Rh is short for rhesus, the monkey species associated with its discovery. Knowing both ABO and Rh type matters when giving a blood transfusion, in which donated blood enters a patient’s bloodstream. If the blood is incompatible, the patient’s immune system may attack the donated cells, causing a dangerous reaction.

The Keeling Curve is a graph of the amount of carbon dioxide, or CO2, in Earth’s atmosphere over time. It is named for American geochemist Charles David Keeling, who began a long-running measurement program at the Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii in 1958. The graph has a sawtooth pattern: carbon dioxide levels rise and fall slightly each year as plants absorb CO2 during growing seasons and release less of it during other seasons. Beneath these seasonal changes, the overall trend is a steady increase, mainly because burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide to the air. CO2 is a greenhouse gas that traps heat, so the Keeling Curve provides important evidence for studying human-caused climate change.

Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. The damage can cause gradual, irreversible vision loss, making glaucoma a leading cause of blindness. It is often linked to increased pressure inside the eye, although it can also occur when that pressure is normal. The eye produces a clear fluid called aqueous humor, which normally drains through a porous tissue called the trabecular meshwork near the junction of the cornea and iris. In open-angle glaucoma, the drainage angle remains open, but fluid does not flow out efficiently through this tissue. As fluid builds up, pressure may rise and harm the optic nerve. Because early vision loss may go unnoticed, regular eye exams are important.

Saturn, the sixth planet from the Sun, is famous for its wide, bright rings. Saturn looks pale yellow partly because of ammonia crystals in its clouds, but its rings are separate from the planet’s atmosphere. They are made mostly of countless pieces of ice, along with some rocky dust, all orbiting Saturn. The rings are not solid sheets: their particles range from tiny grains to large chunks. Astronomers divide the system into several main rings, including the bright A and B rings. The broad, darker gap between those two is called the Cassini Division. It is not completely empty, but it has far fewer particles than the neighboring rings. Gravitational interactions with Saturn’s moon Mimas, called orbital resonances, help keep parts of this division relatively clear.

An electrode is a conductive component that connects an external electrical circuit to an ionic solution, allowing charge to pass across the boundary between them. In a pH meter, electrodes help measure how acidic or basic a solution is more precisely than color-changing indicators such as litmus paper. The glass electrode is the sensing electrode: its thin glass membrane responds to hydrogen ions in the solution, changing its electrical potential. A second electrode, called the reference electrode, provides a stable potential for comparison. It contains an electrolyte of known composition, helping the meter measure the voltage difference between the two electrodes. The meter uses that difference to calculate the solution’s pH.

Electrolysis uses an external power supply to drive a chemical reaction that would not happen spontaneously. It takes place in a liquid or molten substance containing charged particles called ions. Positive ions move toward the negative electrode, called the cathode, where they gain electrons; negative ions move toward the positive electrode, called the anode, where they lose electrons. For example, when molten table salt (sodium chloride) undergoes electrolysis, sodium ions gain electrons at the cathode and form sodium metal. Electrolysis is also used in the Hall-Héroult process to produce aluminum. In that process, aluminum oxide, obtained from bauxite, is dissolved in molten cryolite, and an electric current helps convert aluminum ions into aluminum metal.

Joseph John Thomson was a British physicist whose experiments changed how scientists understood atoms. In the late 1890s, he studied cathode rays, beams produced inside glass tubes from which most of the air had been removed. By showing that the beams were deflected by electric and magnetic fields, he found that they consisted of tiny negatively charged particles. These particles, later called electrons, were much smaller than atoms, proving that atoms contain smaller parts. Thomson then proposed the “plum pudding model”: negatively charged electrons were embedded in a spread-out region of positive charge, rather like pieces of fruit in a pudding. His model was later disproved by Ernest Rutherford’s gold foil experiment, which showed that an atom’s positive charge is concentrated in a small nucleus.

A magnetic compass is a navigational instrument with a magnetized needle that can pivot freely. The needle lines up with Earth’s magnetic field, so its north-seeking end settles toward magnetic north and helps travelers find directions even when they cannot see landmarks. Magnetic north is not the same as true geographic north, the direction of the North Pole on a map. The angle between these two directions at a particular location is called magnetic declination. Declination varies from place to place, so someone using a compass with a map may need to adjust for it. A compass reading can also be disturbed by nearby magnets, iron objects, or electrical equipment, which can pull the needle away from the direction it would normally point.

Tetrahedral molecular geometry describes a molecule whose central atom is bonded to four atoms arranged toward the corners of a tetrahedron, a three-dimensional shape with four triangular faces. According to VSEPR theory, bonding pairs of electrons repel one another, so four bonding pairs around a central atom with no lone pairs spread out as far as possible. Methane, CH4, is a common example: its carbon atom forms four equivalent bonds to hydrogen atoms in a tetrahedral arrangement. The angle between any two C–H bonds is approximately 109.5 degrees, rounded to one decimal place. This angle is larger than a right angle because the bonds spread out in three dimensions rather than lying flat on a page.

Cross-coupling reactions are a family of organic reactions that join two molecular fragments, often forming a new carbon–carbon bond. They usually rely on a transition-metal catalyst, commonly palladium. In a typical catalytic cycle, the metal first undergoes oxidative addition, attaching to one starting material. During transmetalation, a group from the other starting material transfers to the metal. Reductive elimination then joins the two groups and releases the product, allowing the catalyst to be used again. One important example is Suzuki–Miyaura coupling, which uses a palladium catalyst and a base to join an organoboron reagent, such as a boronic acid, with an organic halide or pseudohalide. The organoboron partner distinguishes it from related couplings that use organotin, organozinc, or organomagnesium reagents.

A blackbody is an ideal object that absorbs all incoming light and emits radiation according to its temperature. Classical physics predicted that as the wavelength of this radiation became shorter, the emitted energy would grow without limit. That would mean an impossible amount of energy at ultraviolet wavelengths and beyond. This failure became known as the Ultraviolet Catastrophe. Real hot objects behave differently: their emission reaches a peak and then falls at shorter wavelengths. In 1900, the German physicist Max Planck explained the observed pattern by proposing that energy is emitted or absorbed only in discrete packets, later called quanta. The energy of each packet is proportional to its frequency, expressed as E = hf. Planck’s idea helped launch quantum theory.

A virus is a tiny infectious agent that cannot reproduce on its own. It must enter a living host cell and use that cell’s machinery to make copies of itself. The first virus discovered, tobacco mosaic virus, causes a mosaic-like pattern of discoloration on tobacco leaves. Viruses also infect animals and people; examples include HIV and coronaviruses. Some viruses that infect bacteria, called bacteriophages, can follow two different routes. In the lytic cycle, they quickly make new phages and cause the host cell to burst. In the lysogenic cycle, viral genetic material is inserted into the bacterium’s chromosome and copied as the bacterium divides, without immediately bursting the cell.

A frog is an amphibian belonging to the order Anura, whose name means “without a tail.” Adult frogs lack tails and usually have strong hind legs for jumping. Most begin life as eggs laid in water, hatch into aquatic tadpoles that breathe with gills, and change through metamorphosis into adults that breathe mainly with lungs and through their moist skin. Frogs also appear in literature. In Mark Twain’s comic story “The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County,” set around a California mining camp, Simon Wheeler tells of a gambler who trains a frog named Dan’l Webster to jump. The gambler loses a forty-dollar bet after his opponent secretly fills the frog’s mouth with lead shot, making it too heavy to jump. Mark Twain also wrote The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.

An emulsion is a mixture in which tiny droplets of one liquid are dispersed throughout another liquid that does not normally mix with it. In liquid-liquid extraction, chemists use two immiscible liquids, often water and an organic solvent, to separate substances according to which liquid they dissolve in better. Water forms the aqueous phase. After the liquids are shaken and left to settle, they usually form two distinct layers. Sometimes the shaking creates an emulsion that appears as a cloudy third layer between them, making separation harder. Chemists carry out this process in a separatory funnel, a pear-shaped glass container with a narrow bottom and a stopcock. Once the layers have separated, they can open the stopcock to drain the lower layer selectively.

Pangaea was a prehistoric supercontinent in which most of Earth’s land was joined as one immense landmass. Its name comes from Greek words meaning “all Earth.” In 1912, the German meteorologist and geophysicist Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift: the idea that continents move over time. He noticed that coastlines on opposite sides of the Atlantic seemed to fit together like puzzle pieces. Fossils of the same plants, including Glossopteris ferns, were also found on continents now separated by oceans. Wegener developed this evidence in his book The Origin of Continents and Oceans. Plate tectonics later explained how continents move. As Pangaea broke apart about 200 million years ago, it separated into two major landmasses: Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south.

Bicarbonate, also called hydrogen carbonate, is a negatively charged ion with the formula HCO₃⁻. It is part of seawater’s carbonic-acid buffering system, which helps resist sudden changes in acidity. When excess carbon dioxide from the atmosphere dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid. Bicarbonate can help neutralize added acid by taking up hydrogen ions, although increasing carbon dioxide can still make the ocean more acidic. Bicarbonate also has a familiar use in the kitchen: paired with sodium, it forms sodium bicarbonate, commonly called baking soda. This fine white powder is a leavening agent. When it reacts with an acid in batter or dough, it releases carbon dioxide gas, creating bubbles that help baked goods rise.

Yellow is a color in the visible spectrum that appears in several useful chemistry clues. When heated, an element can give off light at specific wavelengths, forming a pattern of bright lines called an emission spectrum. Sodium, an alkali metal, produces two closely spaced yellow lines near 589 nanometers. Known as the sodium D lines, they can also be identified as dark lines when sunlight is separated into a spectrum, because sodium in the Sun’s atmosphere absorbs light at those wavelengths. Potassium chromate solution is yellow, and solid lead iodide is yellow too. Their appearance provides two more clues to the same color, while the pair of D lines identifies the element sodium.

Dimorphos is a small asteroid moon that orbits Didymos, a larger near-Earth asteroid. In September 2022, NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft into Dimorphos to test whether a collision could change an asteroid’s motion. The spacecraft was sent by the DART mission, short for Double Asteroid Redirection Test. DART was the first full-scale test of a “kinetic impact,” which means using a spacecraft’s collision rather than an explosion to push an asteroid. After the impact, Dimorphos took about 32 minutes less to complete each orbit around Didymos. Scientists measured that change to learn whether this method might someday help deflect an asteroid that threatened Earth. Dimorphos itself was not a threat to our planet.

A liquid’s boiling point is the temperature at which its vapor pressure equals the pressure around it. At that temperature, bubbles of vapor can form throughout the liquid, rather than molecules escaping only from its surface. The boiling point depends on the surrounding pressure: water boils at 100 degrees Celsius under standard atmospheric pressure, but at a lower temperature where air pressure is lower. Water’s boiling point is unusually high for such a small molecule because its molecules attract one another through hydrogen bonding. A water molecule is bent, and its oxygen end has a partial negative charge while its hydrogen ends have partial positive charges. A partially positive hydrogen on one molecule is attracted to a lone pair of electrons on the oxygen of a neighboring molecule. These attractions require extra energy to overcome when water boils.

The Chernobyl disaster was a major nuclear accident on April 26, 1986, at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Soviet Ukraine. During a safety test, reactor four exploded and caught fire, releasing radioactive material into the air and surrounding environment. The accident forced many people to leave their homes, including residents of the nearby city of Pripyat, and led to the creation of a roughly 30-kilometer Exclusion Zone around the plant. Radioactive contamination spread beyond the immediate area, making Chernobyl one of the most serious nuclear disasters in history. At the time, Ukraine was a republic within the Soviet Union. It became independent in 1991, and its capital is Kyiv. Therefore, the plant was located in what is now Ukraine.

A hydrogenosome is an organelle found in certain eukaryotes that live where little or no oxygen is available, such as the single-celled organism Trichomonas. It is a modified descendant of a mitochondrion, the organelle that produces much of a cell’s ATP under oxygen-rich conditions. Hydrogenosomes also make ATP, but they do so through anaerobic metabolism and release molecular hydrogen gas (H2). The pathway begins with pyruvate, the three-carbon end product of glycolysis, which is the process that breaks down glucose. Inside the hydrogenosome, pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA. This reaction supplies electrons that are ultimately used to form hydrogen gas. Remembering that glycolysis produces pyruvate helps identify the molecule that enters this pathway.

Electrons occupy regions around an atom called orbitals, which describe where an electron is likely to be found. Atomic orbitals include s and p types, which have different shapes. When an atom forms bonds, its orbitals can mix to create new orbitals aimed toward other atoms; this process is called orbital hybridization. In sp² hybridization, one s orbital and two p orbitals combine to make three equivalent hybrid orbitals. These point in three directions within a single plane, 120 degrees apart, producing a trigonal planar geometry. One p orbital remains unhybridized. In ethene, each carbon uses its three sp² orbitals to form sigma bonds, while its remaining p orbital overlaps sideways with the other carbon’s p orbital to form a pi bond. Together, the sigma and pi bonds make a carbon–carbon double bond.

Radioactive decay happens when an unstable atomic nucleus spontaneously changes into a more stable one, releasing particles or electromagnetic radiation. Different kinds of decay release different things: alpha decay emits a cluster of two protons and two neutrons, while gamma decay releases high-energy electromagnetic radiation. In beta-minus decay, a neutron inside the nucleus turns into a proton and emits an electron and an antineutrino. Cobalt-60 undergoes this kind of decay. Radioactive decay is random for any single nucleus, but large groups of nuclei decay at a predictable rate. The half-life is the time it takes for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. For example, carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years.

The nightshade family, also called Solanaceae, is a group of flowering plants that includes familiar crops such as tomatoes, potatoes, peppers, and eggplants, as well as poisonous plants such as henbane and belladonna. Being in the same family means these plants share features inherited from common ancestors, but it does not mean every part of every plant is safe to eat. The potato is a nightshade crop originally cultivated in the Andes of South America. People grow it chiefly for its starchy underground tubers, which store energy for the plant and provide food for humans. After the Spanish introduced potatoes to Europe, they became a major staple crop there.

Oral administration means taking a medicine by mouth, usually by swallowing a pill, capsule, or liquid. After it is swallowed, the medicine travels through the gastrointestinal tract, where it is absorbed and can enter the bloodstream. This route does not require a needle and is often convenient for patients. Not every drug can be given this way: some must enter the bloodstream by another route, such as an intravenous (IV) injection. Lufotrelvir, a Pfizer antiviral candidate for treating COVID-19, was described as requiring IV delivery rather than oral administration. It was designed to inhibit viral proteases, enzymes that break proteins apart by cutting the bonds between their building blocks.

Heliocentrism is the astronomical model in which the Sun is at or near the center of the solar system and Earth and the other planets orbit it. This differs from the older geocentric model, which placed Earth at the center. In 1543, the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus advanced heliocentrism in his book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, presenting a Sun-centered arrangement of the planets. Later observations and scientific work helped strengthen the model, though it faced opposition. In the 1600s, Galileo Galilei was forced by the Catholic Church to recant his support for the idea that Earth moves around the Sun. Today, heliocentrism is a basic part of our understanding of the solar system, although the Sun is not the center of the universe.

Buckminsterfullerene is a molecule made of 60 carbon atoms, so its chemical formula is C₆₀. The atoms form a hollow, ball-shaped cage with 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, like the pattern on a soccer ball. Nicknamed the “buckyball,” it belongs to a family of carbon molecules called fullerenes. In 1985, British chemist Harry Kroto worked with Robert Curl, Richard Smalley, and colleagues on experiments involving carbon clusters. They identified C₆₀ in material produced by vaporizing graphite, a form of carbon. Kroto, Curl, and Smalley later shared the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of fullerenes. Buckminsterfullerene’s shape also made it useful in molecular engineering: James Tour used C₆₀ molecules as the wheels of an early nanocar, a tiny vehicle built from molecules.

General Relativity is Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity. It explains gravity not simply as a pull between objects, but as a result of mass and energy curving spacetime, the combined framework of space and time. Objects and light follow paths through this curved spacetime. For example, Earth’s mass curves spacetime around it, helping explain why the Moon orbits Earth and why objects fall toward the ground. The Sun’s gravity can also bend the path of light passing nearby. When a massive object, such as a galaxy, bends light from a more distant source, the effect is called gravitational lensing. It can make the distant source appear as a distorted arc or as multiple images. General Relativity also predicts gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime that detectors such as LIGO can measure.

Jaundice is a condition in which the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow because too much bilirubin builds up in the blood. Bilirubin is a yellow-orange pigment produced when old red blood cells break down. Normally, the liver processes bilirubin and releases it into bile, a fluid that helps with digestion. If the liver is damaged or the ducts that carry bile are blocked, bilirubin may not be removed properly. Jaundice can therefore be a sign of liver or biliary disease, including hepatitis, which is inflammation of the liver. The yellow colour is a symptom rather than a disease on its own, so doctors look for its underlying cause.

A loop is a programming construct that repeats a block of code according to a condition or an iteration rule. Common types include for, while, and do-while loops. A for loop is often useful when you know how many times to repeat an action, such as visiting each item in an array. A while loop checks its condition before each repetition and continues only while that condition is true. When the condition becomes false, the loop stops; for example, 1 == 2 evaluates to false because 1 and 2 are not equal. A do-while loop is similar, but it checks the condition after running the block, so the code runs at least once. Loops save programmers from writing the same instructions over and over.

Cholecystokinin, often shortened to CCK, is a peptide hormone that helps the body digest food. When fats and amino acids from a meal enter the duodenum and jejunum, the first two parts of the small intestine, specialized enteroendocrine cells called I cells release CCK into the bloodstream. CCK signals the gallbladder to contract, sending stored bile into the small intestine. Bile is a yellowish-green liquid made by the liver that helps break fats into tiny droplets so they are easier to digest. CCK also prompts the pancreas to release digestive enzymes that help break down fats, proteins, and carbohydrates. Together, these actions help the small intestine process food and absorb nutrients.

The polar bear is a large, white-coated bear that lives in and around the Arctic Circle. Its scientific name is Ursus maritimus: Ursus is Latin for “bear,” and maritimus means “of the sea.” Polar bears are classified as marine mammals because they depend on the ocean for food and spend much of their lives on sea ice. Their broad paws help them walk across ice and swim, while their thick fur and layer of fat protect them from the cold. They mainly hunt seals, often waiting near holes where seals surface to breathe. Climate change is melting Arctic sea ice, reducing the habitat polar bears need to travel and hunt.

A nuclear explosion occurs when an enormous amount of energy is released in a fraction of a second from changes in atomic nuclei. This can happen through fission, which splits heavy atoms, fusion, which combines light atoms, or both. The sudden release produces extreme heat and light, a destructive blast wave, and intense radiation. Radioactive material may also fall back to Earth as fallout, especially if the explosion draws soil and debris into the air. Nuclear explosions can be caused by nuclear weapons, rather than ordinary chemical bombs. The first full-scale nuclear explosion was the Trinity test, conducted by the Manhattan Project at a remote site in New Mexico on July 16, 1945. It tested a plutonium fission bomb before nuclear weapons were used in World War II.

Triglycerides are a type of fat, or lipid, made when one glycerol molecule bonds to three fatty acids in a process called esterification. They make up most of the fat in food and are the body’s main way of storing excess energy. After a meal, the body can use some triglycerides for energy and store the rest in fat cells. Clusters of these cells form adipose tissue, found mainly beneath the skin and around internal organs. Adipose tissue provides an energy reserve, cushions organs, and helps insulate the body to keep it warm. Triglycerides are different from cholesterol, another lipid that helps build cell membranes. High levels of triglycerides in the blood can be a sign of increased risk for heart disease.

Computer memory is the collection of hardware resources that holds the data and instructions a computer uses. It is organized as a hierarchy: smaller, faster levels sit closer to the CPU, while larger, slower levels hold more information. RAM, or random-access memory, provides working space for programs that are running, but its contents are usually lost when the computer is turned off. A cache is a smaller, faster area of memory that keeps data the CPU is likely to need soon, so the CPU does not have to retrieve it from RAM as often. Web browsers use a similar idea when they cache previously visited pages. At a slower, larger level, solid-state drives store files using flash memory and retain them when power is off.

A tachyon is a hypothetical particle that, if it existed freely, would always travel faster than light in a vacuum. In relativity, the speed of light in a vacuum, called c, is about 300,000 kilometers per second and is the speed limit for ordinary particles. Tachyons are associated with negative mass-squared in some physics equations, but none have been observed. This idea is different from what happens in a transparent material such as water: light travels more slowly there than it does in a vacuum, so an ordinary charged particle can move faster than light moves through that material without breaking relativity’s speed limit. When it does, it can produce a blue glow called Cherenkov radiation, often seen in nuclear reactors.

The eutectic point is the particular composition and temperature at which a mixture has its lowest melting or freezing point. On a binary phase diagram, which shows how two substances behave at different compositions and temperatures, a liquid at the eutectic point cools and solidifies into two different solid phases at the same time. It melts at a lower temperature than either pure component, making the composition useful when a low-melting alloy is needed. For example, the lead–tin system has a eutectic composition of about 61.9% tin by mass and 38.1% lead. This alloy melts or freezes at 183 °C, its minimum melting temperature. Changing the proportion of tin or lead raises the temperature at which the alloy becomes completely liquid.

Data compression is the process of encoding information so it takes up less storage space or is quicker to send. Lossless compression preserves every bit of the original data, so the file can be restored exactly. Lossy compression makes files smaller by discarding some information, which cannot be fully recovered. JPEG, also written JPG, is a widely used lossy format for photographs from digital cameras and images on websites. It reduces file size by removing some visual detail, but stronger compression can make an image look blurry or blocky. Another compression method, Huffman coding, assigns shorter codes to common pieces of data and longer codes to less common ones. Which method is best depends on whether an exact copy matters more than saving space.

A leaf vein is a bundle of transport tissues running through a leaf’s flattened blade. The largest vein often forms a central midrib, with smaller veins branching outward to reach the rest of the leaf. Together, these veins form a network that moves materials and helps support the blade. Each vein contains two main transport tissues: xylem and phloem. Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots into the leaf. The leaf uses that water during photosynthesis, when chlorophyll captures light energy to help make sugars. Phloem carries those sugars away from the leaf to other parts of the plant, where they can be used or stored.

A protein’s primary structure is the exact order of amino acids in its polypeptide chain. Scientists write this sequence from the amino terminus, or N-terminus, to the carboxyl terminus, or C-terminus. Adjacent amino acids are joined along the chain’s backbone by peptide bonds. Each peptide bond is a covalent amide linkage formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. Primary structure describes the sequence, not features such as helices or the protein’s overall three-dimensional shape. It is the foundation for higher levels of structure: as the chain folds, it can form secondary structures and then a more complex tertiary structure. The order of amino acids helps determine how the protein folds and functions.

A conservation law says that the total amount of a measurable quantity stays the same over time in a closed system, where it cannot enter or leave. The quantity may move between objects or change form, but its total remains constant. For example, energy can change from motion into heat, and electric charge can move through a circuit without being created or destroyed. In a collision, the total linear momentum of the objects is conserved if no external force acts on the system. An inelastic collision is one in which some kinetic energy—the energy of motion—changes into heat, sound, or deformation. The objects may bounce apart or stick together, but their total kinetic energy does not stay the same, even though their total linear momentum does.

The lens is a transparent, flexible structure just behind the iris and pupil. Light entering the eye passes through the lens, which helps focus it onto the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. To keep objects at different distances clear, the lens changes shape in a process called accommodation. When you look at something nearby, the ciliary muscle contracts, reducing tension in the suspensory fibers that hold the lens. The lens becomes rounder, increasing its optical power so it can focus the nearby object sharply on the retina. For distant objects, the lens becomes flatter. A cataract occurs when the lens becomes cloudy, scattering or blocking light and causing blurry vision.

pH is a logarithmic measure of how acidic or basic an aqueous solution is. It is defined as the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity, often approximated using hydrogen-ion concentration. A lower pH means greater acidity; at 25°C, a pH of 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is basic. Because the scale is logarithmic, a change of one pH unit corresponds to a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion activity. Buffers are solutions that resist changes in pH and commonly contain a weak acid and its conjugate base. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation estimates a buffer’s pH: pH equals the acid’s pKa plus the base-10 logarithm of the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid.

Psychedelic drugs are psychoactive substances that can change how a person perceives the world, thinks, and feels. They include psilocybin, found in certain mushrooms, and LSD. Their effects may include altered senses, a changed sense of time, and powerful emotions. Researchers are studying whether psychedelics, given in carefully controlled settings alongside psychological support, could help people with depression. They are also being investigated as possible treatments for post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD. PTSD can develop after a shocking or harmful event, such as combat, assault, or abuse. Someone with PTSD may have intrusive memories, avoid reminders of the event, or remain unusually alert long afterward. Psychedelics are also being studied for cluster headaches, but their possible medical uses do not mean they are safe to take without medical supervision.

Curiosity is a NASA rover that landed on Mars, the fourth planet from the Sun, in August 2012. It used a sky-crane system, which lowered the rover to the surface on cables during the final stage of landing. Since then, Curiosity has explored Gale Crater, a roughly 96-mile-wide impact basin, traveling toward Mount Sharp, the layered mountain rising from its floor. Its cameras and scientific instruments study Martian rocks, soil, geology, and climate for clues about the planet’s past. They also look for evidence that ancient environments had water and other conditions that could have supported tiny living things called microbes. Curiosity is investigating whether Mars was once habitable, not whether Martians built the canals that some people mistakenly imagined long ago.

Potassium is a soft, highly reactive alkali metal with atomic number 19 and the chemical symbol K. Because it reacts readily with water and air, it is usually found in compounds rather than as a pure metal in nature. Potassium compounds are essential nutrients for plants and are commonly added to fertilizers alongside nitrogen and phosphorus. Potassium also helps geologists determine the age of rocks. A small fraction of natural potassium is the radioactive isotope potassium-40, which slowly decays in minerals to form argon-40, an isotope of the noble gas argon. By measuring how much potassium-40 remains compared with the argon-40 produced, geologists can estimate how long ago a rock formed. This method is called potassium-argon radiometric dating.

K-selection is a reproductive strategy favored when a population lives near the carrying capacity of its environment: the largest population that available resources can support. In these relatively stable but crowded conditions, competition for food, space, and other resources is strong. Rather than producing many offspring, K-selected organisms tend to produce fewer and invest more time and energy in each one, increasing the offspring’s chances of survival. Parental care is one form of this investment. Competition also helps explain Georgy Gause’s competitive exclusion principle: two species competing for the same limiting resource cannot occupy exactly the same niche indefinitely. Over time, one may outcompete the other unless they adapt to use different resources or occupy different niches.

Archimedes’ principle states that an object wholly or partly immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. A fluid can be a liquid or a gas. Buoyant force arises because fluid pressure increases with depth, so the pressure pushing up on an object’s lower surface is greater than the pressure pushing down on its upper surface. If the buoyant force balances the object’s weight, the object can float; if its weight is greater, it sinks. The same object may float in one liquid but sink in another because denser liquids provide more buoyant force for the same displaced volume. Submarines adjust their buoyancy by taking water into ballast tanks to increase their weight or pumping it out to become lighter.
