A router connects different computer networks and forwards data packets between them. A home router, for example, links devices on a local network to the Internet, often through a modem. It may have Ethernet ports for wired connections and antennas that provide Wi-Fi on bands such as 2.4 or 5 gigahertz. Unlike a device that merely repeats signals within one network, a router reads each packet’s destination IP address and checks a routing table to decide where to send it next. Sometimes more than one table entry matches an address. A /16 route covers a broad range of addresses, while a /24 route covers a smaller, more specific range. The router chooses the most specific matching entry—the /24 in this case—using a rule called longest-prefix match.

Mangroves are salt-tolerant trees and shrubs that grow along warm coastlines, where seawater mixes with fresh water to make brackish water. Their tangled roots help hold muddy soil in place, reduce erosion, and provide shelter for fish, crabs, and birds. One of the world’s largest mangrove forests is the Sundarbans, in the Ganges Delta of South Asia. Mangroves also grow along the coast of Florida, a southeastern U.S. state whose island chain, the Florida Keys, includes Key West and Key Largo. Miami and Orlando are two of Florida’s major cities. In southern Florida, mangroves are also found in the Everglades, a vast wetland fed by water flowing from Lake Okeechobee.

Ticks are small arachnids related to spiders and mites. Adult ticks have four pairs of legs, and they feed by attaching to vertebrate animals, such as mammals, birds, or reptiles, and taking a blood meal. People may encounter ticks while hiking through grass or wooded areas, including along the Appalachian Trail. Some ticks carry pathogens that can infect the animals or people they bite. In North America, deer ticks can spread the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, the primary cause of Lyme disease. The illness is named after Lyme, Connecticut, where a cluster of cases was investigated in the 1970s. Wearing long clothing, using insect repellent, and checking for ticks after outdoor activities can reduce the risk of a bite.

A gear is a rotating machine part with teeth that mesh with the teeth of another gear. As one gear turns, it pushes the other, transferring motion and torque, or turning force, between shafts. Gears can change the speed, direction, or force of rotation. The gear ratio describes this change: it is a number found by comparing the gears’ tooth counts. For example, if a gear with 10 teeth drives one with 20 teeth, the driven gear turns once for every two turns of the first gear. It rotates more slowly but provides more torque. This is why selecting a low gear can make pedaling a bicycle uphill easier. Gears are also used in clocks, vehicle transmissions, and many other machines.

Earth’s magnetic field is an invisible region of magnetic influence surrounding our planet. It is generated mainly by a dynamo process in the liquid outer core, where moving, electrically conducting molten iron creates electric currents. The field guides compass needles toward magnetic north, which is not in the same place as the geographic North Pole. It also deflects many charged particles from the solar wind and traps some energetic particles in two broad, doughnut-shaped regions called the Van Allen radiation belts. Measurements from the Explorer 1 satellite helped scientists identify these belts in 1958. Over Earth’s history, the field has sometimes reversed direction, swapping its magnetic north and south poles. Alternating bands of magnetized rock on the ocean floor preserve a record of these ancient reversals.

Eagles are large birds of prey known for their sharp eyesight, hooked bills, and powerful talons. They use their talons to catch animals and their bills to tear food. Many species are called eagles, including the golden eagle and the bald eagle. Despite its name, the adult bald eagle is not bald: it has a white-feathered head and tail that contrast with its dark brown body. This North American species is the national bird of the United States and appears on the Great Seal of the United States. Eagles also appear as symbols in other countries; for example, a golden eagle on Egypt’s flag represents Saladin, a medieval ruler.

The Messier catalog is a list of 110 bright astronomical objects begun in the eighteenth century by French astronomer Charles Messier. While searching for comets, Messier recorded fixed objects that looked fuzzy through his telescope so he would not mistake them for comets again. Each entry has an “M” number: M31 is the Andromeda Galaxy, and M45 is the Pleiades star cluster. Messier commonly called many of these fuzzy objects nebulae, a broad term astronomers used at the time. Modern telescopes show that the catalog contains several kinds of objects, including galaxies and star clusters, and that only a minority are truly nebulae, or clouds of gas and dust in space. Examples include M1, the Crab Nebula, and M16, the Eagle Nebula.

Adrenaline, also called epinephrine, is a hormone and neurotransmitter that helps the body respond quickly to sudden danger or intense emotion. During acute stress, the inner part of the adrenal glands, called the adrenal medulla, releases adrenaline into the bloodstream. It is a catecholamine, a type of chemical messenger. Adrenaline increases heart rate and breathing, directs more blood toward the muscles, and helps release stored energy so the body can act quickly. These changes are part of the fight-or-flight response, the sympathetic nervous system’s pattern of raising alertness and preparing the body to confront a threat or escape it. Once the danger passes, adrenaline levels fall and the body gradually returns to its usual state.

Uranium is a radioactive chemical element with the symbol U and atomic number 92. It belongs to the actinide series of the periodic table and is found in minerals that can be processed into a concentrated material called yellowcake. Natural uranium is mostly uranium-238, an isotope that does not readily split when struck by slow-moving neutrons. Only about 0.7% is uranium-235, but this rarer isotope can undergo fission with slow-moving, or thermal, neutrons. When a uranium-235 nucleus splits, it releases energy and more neutrons, which can split other nuclei in a chain reaction. Many nuclear reactors use uranium fuel enriched to contain more uranium-235 than occurs naturally. The energy released by this controlled reaction is used to generate electricity.

Ionic compounds, also called salts, consist of positively charged ions and negatively charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction. In solid sodium chloride, for example, sodium and chloride ions form a repeating crystal structure. Many ionic compounds dissolve in water: their ions separate and spread through the liquid. A compound’s ability to dissolve is called solubility. If a solution contains more dissolved ions than it can hold under certain conditions, some may form a solid called a precipitate. Adding an ion already present in a dissolved salt can lower that salt’s solubility. For example, adding sodium chloride to a solution of lead(II) chloride supplies extra chloride ions, causing some lead(II) chloride to precipitate. This is called the common ion effect.

The Tasmanian devil is a carnivorous marsupial native only to Tasmania, an island south of mainland Australia separated from it by the Bass Strait. Although it is about the size of a small dog, it has powerful jaws and can make loud, harsh calls. Like other marsupials, females carry their young in a pouch. Tasmanian devils eat small animals and scavenge carcasses, helping to clean up their environment. Their populations have fallen severely because of devil facial tumor disease, commonly abbreviated DFTD. This unusual contagious cancer spreads mainly when devils bite one another, often while fighting over food or mates. It causes tumors around the face and mouth that can make eating difficult. Conservation efforts aim to protect the species from the disease.

Metastasis is the spread of cancer cells from a primary tumor, where the cancer first developed, to another part of the body. Some cancer cells break away from the original tumor and travel through the bloodstream or the lymphatic system. The lymphatic system is a network of vessels that collects excess fluid from body tissues, carries it through lymph nodes, and eventually returns it to the bloodstream. If traveling cancer cells settle in a new location and begin to grow, they form a secondary tumor. This tumor is still made of cells from the original cancer: for example, breast cancer that spreads to the lungs is called metastatic breast cancer, not lung cancer. Metastasis can make cancer harder to treat because tumors may develop in several parts of the body.

The Sputnik program was a series of Soviet spacecraft launched during the early years of space exploration. In October 1957, Sputnik 1 became the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth. Its launch amazed the world and helped start the Space Race between the Soviet Union and the United States. Sputnik 2 followed in November 1957, carrying Laika, a stray dog from Moscow who became the first living creature to orbit Earth. The spacecraft was not designed to bring her home, and she died during the mission. Sputnik 3 carried scientific instruments and was intended to study Earth’s radiation environment, including the Van Allen radiation belts, but faulty components prevented it from mapping those belts as planned. Together, these missions showed that spacecraft could reach orbit and gather information about space.

Jane Goodall is an English primatologist who began studying wild chimpanzees in 1960 at Gombe Stream, on the eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika in what is now Tanzania. The protected area, first established as a game reserve in 1943, is officially called Gombe Stream National Park. By patiently observing individual chimpanzees over many years, Goodall discovered that they make and use tools, such as twigs for catching termites. She also documented their family bonds, cooperation, and aggression, challenging the belief that complex social behavior was uniquely human. Her observations included violent conflict between chimpanzee groups, known as the Gombe Chimpanzee War, after which the Kahama community was destroyed. Goodall’s work transformed how scientists study and understand animal behavior.

A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom rather than being shared with another atom in a covalent bond. In a Lewis structure, it is usually shown as two dots beside the atom. Although lone pairs do not form bonds, they take up space and repel nearby bonding regions. According to VSEPR theory, these repulsions help determine a molecule’s shape. In water, the central oxygen has two O–H bonding regions and two lone pairs. The four regions have a tetrahedral electron-domain arrangement, but only the atoms determine the molecule’s visible shape. The lone pairs push the O–H bonds closer together, giving water a bent molecular geometry with an H–O–H bond angle of about 104.5°.

Sonar, short for sound navigation and ranging, uses sound waves to detect objects underwater. In active sonar, a ship or submarine sends out a short acoustic pulse and listens for the echo reflected by an object, such as another vessel or the seafloor. The interval between sending the pulse and receiving its echo is called the time of flight. Because sound travels through water at a known approximate speed, the system can use that interval to calculate the object’s range, or distance: it divides the total distance traveled by two because the pulse travels to the object and back. Ships also use sonar devices called echosounders to measure water depth. Multibeam echosounders take measurements across a wide area, helping scientists create detailed maps of the seafloor in a field called bathymetry.

Graphite is a soft allotrope of carbon, meaning it is a form of the element carbon with a particular atomic structure. Its atoms form flat sheets of hexagons. Strong bonds hold the carbon atoms together within each sheet, but much weaker forces hold the sheets together. Because the layers slide over one another and rub off easily, graphite leaves marks on paper when used in a pencil. A single sheet from graphite is called graphene: it is just one carbon atom thick and conducts electricity extremely well. Researchers Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov famously used ordinary adhesive tape to peel layers from graphite, eventually isolating graphene. Diamond is another carbon allotrope, but its atoms have a different arrangement, giving it very different properties.

Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which patterns of eating become persistently disrupted and harm a person’s physical health, emotions, or social life. They are not simply choices about food: thoughts about weight and body image can play a powerful role. Anorexia nervosa often involves severe restriction of food and an intense fear of gaining weight. Bulimia nervosa involves repeated binge episodes, in which a person eats an unusually large amount of food and feels unable to stop, followed by behaviors intended to compensate, such as self-induced vomiting, fasting, or misusing laxatives. Unlike anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa does not require a markedly low body weight. Eating disorders can affect people of many body sizes, and treatment may include medical care, nutrition support, and therapy.

The photoelectric effect occurs when light striking a material, often a metal, causes it to emit electrons. Albert Einstein explained it in a 1905 paper by proposing that light transfers energy in discrete packets called photons. Each photon has an energy determined by its frequency: higher-frequency light has more energetic photons. An electron can escape only if it absorbs enough energy from one photon, so the light must exceed a minimum frequency called the threshold frequency. Below that threshold, making the light brighter will not release electrons. Above it, greater intensity can produce more emitted electrons, but it does not increase their maximum kinetic energy; increasing the frequency does that. Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.

Qualitative analysis is the branch of analytical chemistry that finds out which substances are present in a sample, rather than how much of each substance there is. Chemists identify substances by observing characteristic reactions. For example, some metal ions produce distinctive colors in a flame test. Another method is to add a reagent, a chemical used to test the sample, to a solution. If dissolved ions combine to form an insoluble solid, the solid separates from the liquid and may settle at the bottom of the test tube. This process is called a precipitation reaction, and the solid is called a precipitate. Different ions form precipitates with different reagents, so the result can provide a clue to their identities. For instance, chloride ions can form precipitates with lead, silver, or mercury ions.

ILOVEYOU was a computer worm that spread rapidly by email in 2000. It arrived with the subject line “ILOVEYOU” and an attachment that appeared to be a love letter. Its filename used a misleading double extension, “.txt.vbs”: “.txt” made it look like a harmless text file, but “.vbs” meant it contained VBScript, a scripting language that Windows Script Host could run. When someone opened the attachment, the worm could overwrite certain files and email copies of itself to addresses in the person’s contacts. Those messages appeared to come from someone the recipients knew, making them more likely to open the attachment too. Unlike a computer virus, which typically attaches itself to another file, a worm can spread by copying itself.

Nonpolarity means a molecule has no overall separation of positive and negative charge, or net dipole. Its bonds may be nonpolar, or it may contain polar bonds whose dipoles cancel because of the molecule’s shape. Nonpolar molecules cannot attract one another through permanent dipole–dipole interactions, so dispersion forces are often their strongest intermolecular attraction. They tend to dissolve poorly in polar water but more readily in nonpolar liquids, following the rule “like dissolves like.” In a mixture of water and an organic solvent, nonpolar substances therefore tend to enter the organic layer. Surfactants show a related pattern: in water, their water-attracting heads face outward while their nonpolar hydrocarbon tails point inward. The water-excluding interior of the resulting spherical structure is called the micelle core.

Earth’s outer core is a thick layer of liquid metal beneath the mantle and around the solid inner core. It is made mainly of molten iron and nickel. Scientists know the outer core is liquid partly because seismic S waves, which are produced by earthquakes, cannot travel through liquids. As a result, there are regions on the far side of Earth where these waves are not detected, called S-wave shadow zones. The outer core also helps create Earth’s magnetic field. Heat drives the electrically conductive liquid metal to move, and Earth’s rotation helps organize that motion. This process, called the geodynamo, generates electric currents that sustain the magnetic field around our planet.

Max Planck was a German theoretical physicist born in Kiel in 1858. He studied blackbody radiation, the electromagnetic radiation emitted by an ideal object that absorbs all light falling on it. When such an object is in thermal equilibrium, the pattern of radiation it emits depends on its temperature. Planck found a mathematical formula for this pattern, now called Planck’s law. To make the formula work, he proposed that energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets, or quanta, rather than in any arbitrary amount. The energy of one quantum equals its frequency multiplied by h. This value, called Planck’s constant, is approximately 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds. Planck’s discovery helped launch quantum theory, which explains how matter and energy behave at very small scales.

SARS-CoV-2 is the enveloped coronavirus that causes COVID-19. It is closely related to, but not a direct descendant of, the coronavirus that caused the SARS outbreak beginning in southern China in 2002. The virus spreads mainly through respiratory particles and can infect cells in the lungs, where oxygen passes into the blood. To enter a cell, SARS-CoV-2 uses a prominent surface protein called the spike glycoprotein to attach to a receptor called ACE2. Changes in the spike protein have helped produce variants such as Delta and Omicron, which can spread differently or partly evade existing immunity. Many COVID-19 mRNA vaccines give the body instructions for making a harmless version of the spike protein, helping the immune system recognize the virus.

Varroa destructor is a tiny parasitic mite that poses a serious threat to honey bees. Female mites enter brood cells before worker bees cap them with wax, then reproduce inside while feeding on the developing bees. The mites also feed on adult bees, weakening them and spreading pathogens between bees and colonies. One especially important pathogen is deformed wing virus. Bees infected during development may emerge with shortened abdomens and malformed wings that cannot support flight. Because healthy workers are needed to gather food and care for young, heavy mite infestations and the viruses they spread can contribute to major colony losses. This matters beyond the hive: honey bees pollinate many flowering plants and crops, so protecting colonies helps support ecosystems and food production.

Wetlands are ecosystems where the soil stays saturated with water or is flooded for part of the year. They include marshes, bogs, fens, and swamps, with different plants and water conditions in each. Florida’s Everglades and Georgia’s Okefenokee Swamp are well-known wetlands. Wetland plants can trap pollutants such as iron and copper, while the habitat supports animals including muskrats, capybaras, and wading birds such as blue herons. Wetlands also help filter water and provide places for wildlife to feed and breed. Because these ecosystems are valuable and vulnerable, countries work together to protect them. The Ramsar Convention, adopted in 1971 and named for a city in Iran, is an international agreement to conserve wetlands and promote their “wise use.”

Earth’s core is the innermost major layer of the planet, lying beneath the rocky mantle. It is made mainly of iron and nickel and has two parts: a solid inner core at the center and a liquid outer core surrounding it. Scientists learn about these layers by studying seismic waves from earthquakes. P-waves can travel through both solids and liquids, but S-waves cannot travel through liquids. The fact that S-waves do not pass through the outer core is key evidence that it is liquid. As hot, electrically conducting metal moves through the outer core, it helps generate and sustain Earth’s magnetic field. So the entire metallic region is called the core, while its liquid shell is specifically called the outer core.

Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a single-celled fungus commonly called baker’s yeast or budding yeast. In bread dough, it ferments sugars and releases carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise. Fermentation by this species is also used to make beer and wine. Scientists study it because its cells are easy to grow and, like human cells, are eukaryotic: they have a nucleus. In 1996, S. cerevisiae became the first eukaryote to have its complete genome sequenced. Its cells can also contain a naturally occurring, circular piece of DNA outside their chromosomes called the 2-micron plasmid. This plasmid maintains many copies of itself in a cell partly through recombination at FRT sites, carried out by an enzyme called Flp recombinase.

Litmus paper is a simple way to test whether a solution is acidic or basic. It is made by treating narrow strips of paper with litmus dyes derived from lichens. These dyes change color depending on pH: litmus is red or pink in an acidic solution and blue in a basic solution. A neutral solution usually leaves the paper close to its original color. Because it reveals whether pH is below or above neutral through a visible color change, litmus paper is an acid-base indicator, also called a pH indicator. Red cabbage juice contains another indicator pigment, anthocyanin, while phenolphthalein is an indicator often used in titrations. Litmus paper gives a quick general result, but a pH meter is better when an exact pH measurement is needed.

Nitrogen fixation is the process of converting nitrogen gas (N₂) from the atmosphere into a form living things can use. Plants need nitrogen to make amino acids, proteins, and other important molecules, but they cannot use atmospheric N₂ directly. Certain soil bacteria use an enzyme called nitrogenase to turn N₂ into ammonia, which can then be incorporated into biological molecules. Some of these bacteria live in a partnership with legumes, such as peas and beans. They are housed in rounded swellings called root nodules, which form on the plant’s underground roots. The roots absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant in the soil. In this partnership, the bacteria supply usable nitrogen to the plant, while the plant provides sugars made through photosynthesis.

Carbon tetravalence is the usual ability of carbon, the element with atomic number 6, to form four covalent bonds. Carbon shares electrons with other atoms to make these bonds, allowing it to build chains, rings, and many other molecular frameworks. In a saturated carbon atom, such as one joined to four other atoms by single bonds, its orbitals mix through sp³ hybridization. This produces four equivalent bonding directions arranged in a tetrahedral shape, with bonds pointing toward the corners of a three-dimensional pyramid-like structure. If the carbon is bonded to four different groups, it can be a chiral center: its mirror image cannot be placed exactly on top of it. A carbon in a double bond does not have this tetrahedral arrangement, though some double bonds allow cis and trans isomers.

The Ives–Stilwell experiment was a 1938 spectroscopy test of Einstein’s special theory of relativity. Herbert Ives and G. R. Stilwell studied light emitted by rapidly moving hydrogen canal rays, which are streams of charged atoms or ions. Motion changes the observed frequency of light through the Doppler effect: light from a source moving toward an observer shifts one way, while light from a source moving away shifts the other. By comparing spectral shifts in both directions, the experimenters tested the extra change predicted by relativistic time dilation, in which a moving clock runs slower as seen by an observer. This correction is called the transverse Doppler effect because it also predicts a frequency shift when light is observed at right angles to the emitter’s motion.

The pistil is the female reproductive structure of a flower. It typically has three parts: the stigma, the style, and the ovary. The stigma sits at the tip of the style and receives pollen grains, often catching them on its sticky surface. The style is a stalk that connects the stigma to the ovary, which contains ovules. Pollinators such as bees and birds can carry pollen from a flower’s male structure, the stamen, to the stigma. Once a pollen grain lands there, it can grow a tube down through the style toward an ovule in the ovary, allowing fertilization to occur. Fertilized ovules can develop into seeds, while the ovary may develop into a fruit.

A stack overflow is a runtime error that happens when a program runs out of space in its call stack, the area of memory used to keep track of active function calls. Each time a function is called, the program adds information about that call to the stack. When the function finishes, that information is removed. A recursive function calls itself and normally stops when it reaches a base case, a condition that ends the repetition. If it never reaches a base case and keeps calling itself, this is called infinite recursion. The growing chain of calls can exhaust the stack and cause the program to crash. Stack Overflow is also the name of a website where programmers ask and answer questions.

Programming languages are formal systems people use to write instructions that computers can follow. Each language has rules for expressing commands, much as spoken languages have rules for forming sentences. Python, Java, C++, and Ada are all programming languages; Ada was named after Ada Lovelace, an early pioneer of computing. Another pioneer was Grace Hopper, a U.S. Navy rear admiral who helped develop COBOL, a language widely used for business data processing. Hopper is also associated with an incident in which a real moth was found in a computer relay, causing a malfunction. Programmers use the word “bug” for an error in software and “debugging” for the work of finding and fixing one.

Candida albicans is a species of yeast, a single-celled fungus that commonly lives on human mucosal surfaces, including the mouth and vagina. It usually causes no harm, but it can grow too much when the normal balance of microbes changes or the immune system is weakened. This can lead to oral thrush, which causes white patches in the mouth, or vulvovaginitis, often called a vaginal yeast infection. In people with seriously weakened defenses, Candida can also enter the bloodstream and cause dangerous invasive disease. Infections caused by Candida albicans or related Candida species are called candidiasis. In the laboratory, Candida albicans can be identified by a germ tube test: when incubated in serum at body temperature, its cells form short tube-like outgrowths.

Malware, short for “malicious software,” is deliberately created to harm computers or networks, steal information, disrupt operations, or gain access without permission. Unlike an ordinary software bug, malware is designed to cause problems. Common types include viruses, which attach to other files; worms, which can spread between computers on their own; trojans, which disguise themselves as harmless programs; and ransomware, which encrypts files and demands payment to unlock them. Malware can also target physical equipment controlled by computers. Stuxnet, a worm discovered in 2010, targeted Siemens Step7 software used to control industrial machinery. It manipulated the speeds of nuclear centrifuges at Iran’s Natanz facility, showing that malware can have consequences beyond a computer screen.

Saturn’s moons are natural satellites that orbit the ringed planet, and they vary greatly in size and appearance. Some interact with Saturn’s rings: the small moon Pan acts as a “shepherd,” helping maintain the Encke Gap in the A ring. Mimas has a huge impact crater called Herschel, which makes it look a little like the Death Star. Bright, icy Enceladus releases water-vapor plumes from fractures near its south pole known as “tiger stripes.” Titan is Saturn’s largest moon. It has a dense, nitrogen-rich atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane, substances that are gases under most conditions on Earth. The Huygens probe descended through Titan’s atmosphere and landed on its surface, while the Cassini spacecraft studied Saturn, its rings, and its moons.

Alfred Wegener was a German meteorologist and geophysicist who proposed the idea of continental drift: continents move slowly over Earth’s surface. He noticed that coastlines on opposite sides of the Atlantic Ocean seemed to fit together like puzzle pieces. He also found that matching fossils, including those of the Glossopteris fern, occurred on continents now separated by oceans. Wegener argued that these lands had once been joined in a supercontinent he called Pangaea, a name from Greek roots meaning “all” and “Earth.” Although he could not fully explain what moved the continents, later discoveries about plate tectonics supported the central idea behind his theory. Wegener died during a scientific expedition in Greenland.

Mount Etna is an active stratovolcano on the eastern coast of Sicily, a large Mediterranean island belonging to Italy. It is among Europe’s highest and most frequently erupting volcanoes. A stratovolcano is built from layers of lava and other volcanic material produced by repeated eruptions. Etna’s lava flows have sometimes threatened nearby towns, including Catania; one historic eruption sent lava into Catania’s harbor. Sicily lies just off the toe of mainland Italy’s “boot,” and the narrow Strait of Messina separates its northeastern tip from the mainland. Earthquakes and volcanoes are common in this region because moving tectonic plates interact beneath the Mediterranean. So, if asked to name the volcano, the answer is Mount Etna; if asked to name its island, the answer is Sicily.

A mid-ocean ridge is a vast underwater mountain system formed where two tectonic plates move apart at a divergent boundary. As the plates separate, molten rock rises from Earth’s interior, cools, and becomes new oceanic crust. This process, called seafloor spreading, gradually widens the ocean floor. Mid-ocean ridges extend through ocean basins and are associated with volcanic activity and shallow earthquakes. One major example is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which runs down the center of the Atlantic Ocean. In the northern Atlantic, it separates the North American and Eurasian plates; farther south, it separates the South American and African plates.

Convection is the transfer of heat by the bulk motion of a fluid, such as a liquid or gas. Unlike conduction, which transfers heat through matter without moving it as a whole, or radiation, which can transfer heat through empty space, convection carries thermal energy as the fluid flows. In natural convection, heating makes part of a fluid expand and become less dense, so it rises while cooler, denser fluid sinks. A fan or pump can also drive the flow, producing forced convection. Scientists use the Nusselt number to compare heat transfer across a fluid layer with what conduction alone would provide. A Nusselt number of 1 means conduction alone; a larger value means fluid motion has increased the heat transfer.

Drosophila melanogaster, commonly called the fruit fly or vinegar fly, is a small insect often found around fermenting fruit. Scientists use it to study genetics because it reproduces quickly and its traits and mutations are easy to observe. In its salivary glands, many copies of each chromosome remain joined together, forming unusually large polytene chromosomes that are useful for studying genes. At Columbia University, geneticist Thomas Hunt Morgan studied a white-eyed mutant of Drosophila melanogaster. His experiments showed that the gene affecting eye color was carried on the X chromosome, providing important evidence for sex-linked inheritance. Researchers have also used this species to investigate how genes control body development and circadian rhythms, the roughly 24-hour cycles that help regulate activity and sleep.

Vantablack is an extremely black coating that absorbs nearly all the visible light that strikes it. Its name comes from VANTA, short for “vertically aligned nanotube arrays”: a dense forest of tiny carbon tubes that traps incoming light instead of reflecting it back to your eyes. With so little light reflected, a coated object can appear unusually flat, making its curves and details hard to see. Vantablack also sparked controversy in the art world when British-Indian sculptor Anish Kapoor secured exclusive rights to use it for artistic purposes. Other artists objected to one person having special access to such a striking material. Kapoor also created Cloud Gate, the mirrorlike stainless-steel sculpture in Chicago’s Millennium Park that visitors call “the Bean.”

The Hubble Sequence is a system for classifying galaxies by their visible shapes, or morphology. It is often drawn as a tuning-fork diagram: elliptical galaxies form the handle, or central stem, while spiral galaxies appear on two branches. One branch contains ordinary spirals, and the other contains barred spirals, which have a straight bar of stars across their centers. Lenticular galaxies sit where the handle meets the branches. They have a disk like spiral galaxies but little or no visible spiral structure. The diagram helps astronomers compare galaxy shapes, but it does not mean that galaxies must change from one type into another in the order shown.

The Adler Planetarium is a center for learning about space and astronomy on Chicago’s Museum Campus, near the Field Museum and Shedd Aquarium. It opened in 1930 with support from businessman Max Adler and was the first planetarium in the Western Hemisphere. A planetarium helps visitors explore the sky through shows and exhibits, while Adler’s astronomy museum displays objects and ideas connected to the study of space. Adler also includes the Doane Observatory, a public observing facility with a 20-inch reflecting telescope. Unlike a planetarium show, which presents a simulated view of the sky, the observatory lets visitors look at real objects in the night sky when conditions allow.

The Ostwald process is an industrial method for making nitric acid from ammonia. It is named after the German chemist Wilhelm Ostwald. First, ammonia (NH3) is mixed with air and passed at high temperature over platinum-rhodium gauze, a thin, open mesh of noble metals that acts as a catalyst. This reaction produces nitric oxide (NO) and water. The nitric oxide then reacts with more oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide (NO2). Finally, the nitrogen dioxide is absorbed in water, producing nitric acid (HNO3). This process is important because nitric acid is used to make fertilizers and other chemicals. The ammonia that starts the process is often made by the Haber-Bosch process, which combines nitrogen and hydrogen under high pressure using an iron catalyst.

Orbital eccentricity is a number that describes how much an object’s orbit around a central body differs from a perfect circle. It has no units: an eccentricity of zero means the orbit is circular, while a larger value means it is more stretched out. For an elliptical orbit, eccentricity can be calculated by comparing the object’s closest and farthest distances from the central body. Among the eight major planets, Mercury has the greatest orbital eccentricity, so its distance from the Sun changes more over an orbit than any other planet’s. Mercury is also the smallest planet and the one closest to the Sun. Its rotation has a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance: Mercury turns three times on its axis for every two trips it makes around the Sun.

An acid-base indicator is a substance that changes color over a particular pH range, giving a quick way to tell whether a solution is acidic or basic. The pH scale describes how acidic or basic a solution is: values below 7 are acidic, 7 is neutral, and values above 7 are basic. Indicators can also help during a titration, in which one solution is gradually added to another. A visible color change signals that the reaction has reached its endpoint. Phenolphthalein is a common indicator used in titrations, and pigments called anthocyanins make red cabbage juice act as one too. Another familiar indicator is litmus paper, made with dyes from lichens. Its narrow strips turn red in acidic solutions and blue in basic solutions.

Intermolecular forces are attractions between separate molecules, unlike covalent or ionic bonds, which hold atoms together within a substance. These forces depend on how electrons are distributed: an uneven distribution gives a molecule partially positive and partially negative regions that can attract those of its neighbors. Even molecules without permanent positive or negative regions experience induced-dipole attractions when electrons briefly shift position. A particularly strong intermolecular force is hydrogen bonding. It occurs when a hydrogen atom bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine is attracted to a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine in a neighboring molecule. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another, so it takes more energy to separate them. This helps explain why water has an unusually high boiling point.

Paper is a thin, fibrous sheet made by breaking down plant materials into pulp, spreading the fibers in a layer, and drying them. It is used for writing, printing, crafts, and packaging. Invented in China, paper is counted among China’s Four Great Inventions. Papermaking later spread westward; according to a traditional account, Chinese prisoners shared the techniques that led to paper mills in Baghdad. Baghdad is the modern-day capital of Iraq and was once a major center of Islamic learning. It was home to the House of Wisdom, a place associated with scholarship and the translation of books. When Baghdad was sacked in 1258, a probably legendary story claimed that ink from destroyed books turned the Tigris River black.

Tusklessness is an inherited trait in which an elephant grows no tusks, the long ivory-bearing teeth that normally extend from its mouth. During Mozambique’s civil war, poachers killed many elephants for their ivory. Elephants without tusks were less likely to be killed, so they had more chances to survive and pass the trait to their offspring. This is an example of natural selection: a heritable trait becomes more common because it helps individuals survive in a particular environment. In Gorongosa National Park, tusklessness became unusually common, especially among female elephants, after the intense poaching. Poaching did not cause individual elephants to lose their tusks; instead, it changed which elephants were most likely to survive and reproduce.

Taq DNA polymerase is an enzyme originally isolated from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium that lives in hot environments. It is widely used in polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, a method for making many copies of a chosen DNA sequence. Each PCR cycle has three main steps: heating separates the two DNA strands (denaturation), cooling lets short DNA primers attach to the target sequence (annealing), and Taq extends those primers by adding DNA building blocks (extension). Ordinary DNA polymerases would lose their shape and stop working during the repeated high-temperature steps, but Taq is heat-stable and remains active. Repeating the cycle produces enough copies of the target DNA for scientists to study, often using techniques such as gel electrophoresis.

The asteroid belt is a broad region between the orbits of Mars, the fourth planet from the Sun, and Jupiter, the fifth. It contains many small rocky bodies, including asteroids, as well as Ceres, a dwarf planet, and Vesta, a large protoplanet. The belt lies near the divide between the inner terrestrial planets and the outer giant planets, but its asteroids are spread far apart rather than packed together. Jupiter, the gas giant at the belt’s outer edge, is the largest planet in the Solar System. It also has the largest known population of Trojan asteroids: objects that share Jupiter’s orbit around the Sun and cluster near stable locations called Lagrange points.

Wavelength is the distance between matching points on successive waves, such as one crest and the next or one trough and the next. It is usually measured in metres or smaller units, such as nanometres for visible light. Red light has a longer wavelength than blue light. A related property is frequency: the number of complete wave cycles that pass a point each second, measured in hertz. Wave speed equals wavelength multiplied by frequency. In a vacuum, all light travels at the same speed, so longer-wavelength red light has a lower frequency than shorter-wavelength blue light. When light enters a new medium, such as water or glass, its speed and wavelength change, while its frequency stays the same.

Blood clotting, also called coagulation, is the process that stops excessive bleeding after a blood vessel is injured. Platelets circulating in the blood stick to the damaged site and to one another, forming an initial plug. At the same time, a chain of reactions activates proteins called clotting factors. This cascade produces fibrin, a protein that forms a mesh to strengthen the plug and seal the injury. One important clotting protein is factor IX, also known as the Christmas factor. It is a vitamin K–dependent enzyme activated in the intrinsic pathway; it helps activate factor X, which begins the common pathway of coagulation. An inherited deficiency of factor IX causes hemophilia B, a disorder in which blood does not clot properly.

Kinases are enzymes that transfer phosphate groups, often from ATP, to other molecules such as proteins. Adding a phosphate group can change a molecule’s shape or activity, making kinases important switches for many cell processes. Cyclin-dependent kinases help control the cell cycle, guiding a cell through growth and division. Most human body cells divide by mitosis, which produces two cells with the same number of chromosomes as the original cell. Egg and sperm cells, called gametes, are produced instead by meiosis. Meiosis involves two successive divisions and reduces the chromosome number by half, so an egg and sperm can combine to give an offspring the usual number of chromosomes. During prophase I of meiosis, paired chromosomes can exchange pieces in a process called crossing over.

The peregrine falcon is a bird of prey found on every continent except Antarctica. It hunts other birds in flight, often climbing high above them before plunging downward in a steep hunting dive called a stoop. Peregrines can reach speeds of more than 200 miles per hour during a stoop, making them famous as one of the fastest animals on Earth. Their speed and hunting ability have also made them valuable in falconry, the practice of training birds of prey to hunt. In Jean Craighead George’s novel My Side of the Mountain, Sam Gribley leaves New York City to live in the Catskill Mountains. There he trains a peregrine falcon to help him hunt and names her Frightful.

Comments are notes programmers write in source code to explain what the code does, why a decision was made, or how to use a class or method. They are meant for people reading the code; the compiler or interpreter generally ignores them when running the program. In Python, a single-line comment begins with #, while in Java, it begins with //. Useful comments clarify things that may not be obvious from the code itself, helping programmers maintain it or work together. Java also supports specially formatted documentation comments, often placed before classes and methods. These can contain tags such as @param to describe an input parameter and @return to describe a method’s result. The standard tool called Javadoc reads these comments and generates API documentation.

Fish are aquatic vertebrates that typically breathe by passing water over gills, which absorb dissolved oxygen. They include bony fish, traditionally grouped as Osteichthyes, and cartilaginous fish, or Chondrichthyes, whose skeletons are made mainly of cartilage rather than bone. Sharks and rays are cartilaginous fish, while most living fish species are ray-finned bony fish. Another bony-fish lineage, the lobe-finned fish, has fins supported by fleshy, bone-filled structures. One member of this lineage is the coelacanth. Scientists knew coelacanths from fossils and believed they had been extinct for more than 60 million years. Then, in 1938, a living specimen was found off South Africa. This surprising discovery is why the coelacanth is often called a “living fossil.”

A circuit node is a point where two or more electrical components, such as resistors or batteries, connect through wires. In a circuit diagram, all points joined by ideal wires without a component between them are treated as the same node because they have the same electric potential. When several paths meet at a node, it may also be called a junction. Electric current is the rate at which charge flows, and charge cannot simply disappear or build up at a node in a steady circuit. Therefore, the total current flowing into a node equals the total current flowing out. This rule is Kirchhoff’s current law. It helps solve circuits with branching paths and is different from Kirchhoff’s loop rule, which concerns changes in electric potential around a closed path.

The Aswan High Dam is a massive barrier across the Nile River in southern Egypt, near the city of Aswan. Completed in 1970, it holds back the river to regulate flooding and provide a more reliable supply of water for farming. Water flowing through the dam also turns turbines to generate hydroelectric power. Behind it, the Nile formed Lake Nasser, a vast reservoir that extends south into Sudan, where its continuation is called Lake Nubia. Creating the reservoir flooded a large area and forced many people to move. It also threatened ancient monuments, including the temples at Abu Simbel. To save them from being submerged, workers cut the temples into sections and rebuilt them on higher ground.

Momentum describes how much motion an object has and how difficult it is to change that motion. Linear momentum equals mass times velocity, so a heavier or faster-moving object has more of it. Rotating objects have angular momentum, which equals moment of inertia times angular velocity. Moment of inertia depends on how an object’s mass is distributed around its axis, while angular velocity describes how quickly it spins. In an isolated system, where no external force or twisting effect acts, total momentum is conserved. Torque is different from momentum: it measures how strongly an applied force tends to change an object’s rotational motion. For a force applied perpendicular to a lever arm, torque equals the force multiplied by its distance from the axis of rotation.

Neurons are nerve cells that carry signals through the nervous system. Many neurons have a long extension called an axon, which sends electrical impulses toward other cells. Around many axons is a fatty insulating layer called the myelin sheath. Like insulation around a wire, myelin helps prevent signals from leaking away. The sheath has small, regularly spaced gaps called nodes of Ranvier. An impulse can jump from one node to the next, allowing it to travel much faster than it would along an uninsulated axon. In multiple sclerosis, or MS, the immune system damages myelin in the brain and spinal cord. This damage can leave scar-like patches, called plaques, in the nervous system’s white matter and disrupt signaling. MS often follows a relapsing-remitting pattern, with symptoms worsening and then improving.

Francis Crick was a British molecular biologist who, with James Watson, helped establish that DNA has a double-helical structure. He also proposed the Central Dogma, which describes how genetic information is used: information in DNA is copied into RNA, and RNA guides the production of proteins. During protein synthesis, transfer RNA (tRNA) carries amino acids to a ribosome. Each tRNA has an anticodon that pairs with a three-base codon on messenger RNA, helping the ribosome add the correct amino acid to a growing protein. Crick predicted that pairing at one position between a codon and anticodon is less strict than ordinary complementary base matching. This flexibility, called wobble pairing, allows a single tRNA to recognize more than one codon.

A louse is a small, wingless parasitic insect that lives on a human or other animal and feeds on its blood. The plural is lice. Lice can spread through close contact and often cause itching. A louse is also the subject of “To a Louse,” a poem by Robert Burns inspired by seeing one crawling on a woman’s bonnet at church. The speaker imagines how surprised she would be to know it was there and wishes for the gift “to see ourselves as others see us.” Burns calls the insect a “crowlan ferlie,” using Scots, a language closely related to English. Burns was born in Alloway, Scotland, the nation that joined England in 1707 to form Great Britain.

The Trinity Test was the first detonation of a nuclear weapon. It took place on July 16, 1945, at the Alamogordo Bombing and Gunnery Range in New Mexico. The test was the culmination of the Manhattan Project, the U.S. effort during World War II to develop an atomic bomb, directed by scientist J. Robert Oppenheimer. For the test, the Los Alamos team built a plutonium implosion device: conventional explosives squeezed its plutonium core until a nuclear chain reaction began. The scientists codenamed this device “the Gadget.” Its successful explosion showed that the implosion design worked; the same basic design was later used in the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki, Japan.

DNA has the shape of a double helix: two long strands that wind around each other like a twisted ladder. The sides of the ladder are made of sugar and phosphate molecules, while the rungs are pairs of nucleotide bases. These bases pair in a specific way: adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine. James Watson and Francis Crick proposed this model of DNA in 1953. An important piece of evidence was Photo 51, an image produced by chemist Rosalind Franklin using X-ray diffraction. By studying how X-rays scattered as they passed through DNA fibers, Franklin obtained a pattern that revealed DNA’s helical shape. The double-helix structure helps explain how DNA stores genetic information and how each strand can serve as a guide for making a new one.

In 1909, Robert Millikan and Harvey Fletcher carried out the oil-drop experiment to measure the elementary electric charge. An atomizer sprayed tiny oil droplets into a chamber, where some gained electrons from air ionized by X-rays. The researchers watched individual droplets fall through the air and then adjusted an electric field to balance the electric force against their weight. To work out each droplet’s mass from how it moved, they had to account for air resistance, or viscous drag. For a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid, Stokes’ law gives that drag force as six pi times the fluid’s viscosity, the sphere’s radius, and its speed. Comparing the droplets’ forces showed that their charges came in multiples of a smallest value: about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, negative for an electron.

An organic light-emitting diode, or OLED, is a technology used in screens that display images on phones, televisions, and computers. It contains thin films of carbon-based compounds that emit light when an electric current passes through them. Each OLED pixel produces its own visible light, so the screen can turn individual pixels off to show deep blacks and make bright areas stand out. This differs from a liquid crystal display, or LCD: its liquid crystals control how much light passes through them, but they do not produce that light themselves. An LCD therefore needs a separate light source behind the image-forming layer, called a backlight. Because OLED screens do not need a backlight, they can be made especially thin and flexible.

The rubber industry is the global network of businesses that produce natural and synthetic rubber and turn it into products such as tires, hoses, and seals. Natural rubber begins as latex, a milky liquid tapped from Hevea rubber trees grown on plantations. Factories process the latex into usable rubber, while chemical plants make synthetic elastomers—stretchy materials with rubber-like properties—from chemicals derived mainly from petroleum. One important step in making rubber useful is vulcanization. In this process, rubber is heated with sulfur, which links its long molecular chains together. Vulcanized rubber is more durable and elastic and better able to withstand heat and wear. The development of vulcanization is commonly credited to the American inventor Charles Goodyear in the 19th century.

Toluene is an aromatic hydrocarbon made of a benzene ring with one methyl group (CH3) attached. That is why it is also called methylbenzene. Its molecular formula is C7H8: the ring contributes six carbon atoms, and the methyl group adds a seventh. Toluene is a liquid that dissolves many other substances, so it is used as a solvent in products such as permanent markers and paint thinners. It is also a starting material for making other chemicals. For example, nitration can add three nitro groups (NO2) to toluene at the 2, 4, and 6 positions on the ring. The resulting compound, 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene, is a high explosive commonly known by the abbreviation TNT.

A glacial erratic is a boulder that a glacier picks up, carries, and leaves behind when the ice melts or retreats. Glaciers are huge, slowly moving masses of ice that form in cold regions and high mountains. As they move, they can break rocks from the ground and transport them far from where they formed. An erratic may therefore be a different rock type from the surrounding landscape, giving scientists a clue about the glacier’s path. Some erratics weigh hundreds of tons. Big Rock near Okotoks, Alberta, is a famous example: it is made of quartzite, a hard metamorphic rock that stands out on the nearby plains.

An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth, and Moon line up so that one body blocks sunlight and casts a shadow on another. In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, casting a shadow on Earth. In a lunar eclipse, Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, casting a shadow on the Moon. An observer in the darkest part of a solar eclipse’s shadow can see the Sun completely covered, while someone in the lighter outer shadow sees a partial eclipse. Just before or after a total solar eclipse, sunlight can shine through valleys along the Moon’s uneven edge, appearing as brief bright points called Baily’s beads. These can form part of the “diamond ring” effect seen near totality.

Echinoderms are a phylum of marine invertebrates that includes starfish, sea cucumbers, brittle stars, sea urchins, and crinoids. Their name means “rough-skinned,” referring to the spines or bumpy surfaces found on many species. Adult echinoderms commonly have five-part radial symmetry, meaning their body parts are arranged around a central point, although sea cucumbers may not look five-part at first glance. A feature of the group is the water vascular system, a network of fluid-filled canals connected to small tube feet. By changing fluid pressure, an echinoderm can extend and retract these feet to move, grip surfaces, or handle food. Echinoderms live only in the ocean, from shallow coastal waters to the deep sea.

Apatite is a group of calcium-phosphate minerals found in rocks and living things. Its best-known members include hydroxyapatite, which makes up most of the inorganic mineral material in human bones and teeth. Apatite has a standard hardness of 5 on the Mohs scale, a scale that ranks minerals from 1 to 10 by whether they can scratch one another. A harder mineral can scratch a softer one, so apatite can scratch minerals ranked below 5 but is scratched by those ranked above it. Talc, a very soft mineral used in powder, is ranked 1, while diamond is ranked 10. The scale measures resistance to scratching, not how easily a mineral breaks.

A convergent boundary, also called a destructive boundary, is a place where two tectonic plates move toward each other. Tectonic plates are large slabs of Earth’s outer rocky layer, the lithosphere, that move slowly over time. When the plates meet, their edges are compressed. If one plate contains denser oceanic lithosphere, it may bend and sink beneath the other plate into the mantle. This process is called subduction. Subduction zones can produce powerful earthquakes and volcanoes as the descending plate moves deeper into Earth. When two continents collide, neither plate sinks easily, so the crust can crumple and rise into mountain ranges. This mountain-building process is called orogeny. Thus, convergent boundaries can form mountains, volcanoes, and earthquakes, depending on the plates involved.

Disruptive selection is a type of natural selection that favors individuals at both extremes of a trait while individuals with intermediate traits leave fewer offspring. Natural selection occurs when inherited traits help organisms survive and reproduce in their environment, allowing those traits to become more common over generations. Unlike directional selection, which shifts a population toward one extreme, disruptive selection can maintain two contrasting forms. For example, finches on Santa Cruz Island in the Galápagos have either small or large beaks, while relatively few have medium-sized beaks. If small and large beaks are better suited to available foods than medium-sized beaks, birds with those extreme traits are more likely to survive and pass them on.

Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom’s nucleus. Protons are positively charged particles found alongside neutrons, which have no electric charge. Scientists use the letter Z to represent atomic number, and every element has its own value: hydrogen has one proton, so its atomic number is 1, while carbon has six protons, so its atomic number is 6. Changing the number of protons changes the element itself. In contrast, atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these forms are called isotopes, but they all have the same atomic number. On the periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. This makes atomic number a reliable way to identify an element, regardless of how many neutrons its atoms contain.

Vacuum permittivity, also called the permittivity of free space, is a physical constant written ε₀. It describes how electric fields behave in empty space. In SI units, electric displacement D equals ε₀ times the electric field E in a vacuum. Its value is about 8.85 × 10⁻¹² farads per meter. Vacuum permittivity also helps determine the force between two electric charges. In Coulomb’s law, that force depends on the product of the charges and decreases with the square of the distance between them. The proportionality factor is called the Coulomb constant, k, and in SI units it equals 1/(4π ε₀). Thus ε₀ is vacuum permittivity, while the constant formed from it, 1/(4π ε₀), is the Coulomb constant.

Bromine is a chemical element with the symbol Br. It belongs to the halogens and is unusual because it is a reddish-brown liquid at room temperature. In the laboratory, bromine dissolved in water or another solvent can be used to test for carbon–carbon unsaturation: bonds between carbon atoms that can react with bromine. When a sample contains a carbon–carbon double bond, bromine reacts with it and the solution’s reddish-brown color fades. Hydrocarbons with a carbon–carbon double bond are called alkenes, so a fading color can indicate that alkenes are present. Alkynes, which have carbon–carbon triple bonds, can also react with bromine; the test alone does not always distinguish them from alkenes.

Alfred Nobel was a Swedish chemist, engineer, and inventor born in Stockholm in 1833. He worked with nitroglycerin, a powerful but dangerously unstable explosive. By absorbing it into a material called diatomaceous earth, Nobel made it safer to handle and more practical to use. He patented the resulting explosive, dynamite, in 1867. Dynamite became important in mining, construction, and other work that required blasting, although explosives could also be used in war. Nobel earned a large fortune from his inventions and businesses. In his will, he directed that much of his money be used to fund annual prizes honoring achievements in fields including physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, and peace. These awards are known as the Nobel Prizes.

Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, the body’s largest internal organ. The liver produces bile to help digest fats, processes nutrients from food, and filters harmful substances from the blood. Hepatitis can have several causes, including viruses, heavy alcohol use, and certain medicines. The main viral forms are called hepatitis A, B, and C. Hepatitis A usually spreads through contaminated food or water, while hepatitis B and C can spread through infected blood; hepatitis B can also spread through other bodily fluids. Before blood donations were routinely screened, transfusions were an important way hepatitis C spread. Liver inflammation may cause tiredness, nausea, or jaundice—a yellowing of the skin and eyes. Long-lasting hepatitis can scar the liver, a condition called cirrhosis.

A chemical synapse is a junction where one neuron passes a signal to another using chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, rather than a direct electrical connection. When a nerve signal reaches the end of the sending, or presynaptic, neuron, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters. These molecules diffuse across a narrow space called the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the receiving, or postsynaptic, neuron. This can help start a new signal in the receiving cell. The neurotransmitters are then cleared from the cleft, sometimes by being taken back into the presynaptic neuron in a process called reuptake. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as Prozac and Celexa, slow the reuptake of serotonin, leaving more of it available in the synapse.

CERN is an international particle-physics research organization headquartered near Geneva, on the border between Switzerland and France. Its name comes from an earlier French title, but today it is known in English as the European Organization for Nuclear Research. CERN operates the Large Hadron Collider, a huge underground machine that accelerates particles to nearly the speed of light and collides them so scientists can study the fundamental building blocks of matter. In 2012, experiments at the collider announced the discovery of the Higgs boson. This particle is associated with the Higgs field, which helps explain how some fundamental particles, including the W and Z bosons, acquire mass. The discovery was an important confirmation of the Standard Model, scientists’ leading theory of fundamental particles and their interactions.

White phosphorus is a highly reactive form, or allotrope, of phosphorus, the element with atomic number 15. It is made of separate molecules, each containing four phosphorus atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron, so its molecular formula is P₄. This differs from more stable forms of phosphorus that have extended, polymeric structures rather than discrete molecules. The bonds in the small P₄ tetrahedron are strained, which helps explain why white phosphorus reacts so readily. When exposed to air, it can glow faintly as it reacts with oxygen and may even ignite spontaneously. For this reason, it must be handled carefully and is commonly stored under water to keep it away from air.

Island biogeography is the study of how island conditions shape the number and kinds of species that live there and how those species evolve. An island’s size matters because larger islands usually offer more habitats and resources, while its distance from other land affects how easily new species can arrive. Isolation can also allow a species that reaches an island to diversify into several species adapted to different ways of life, a process called adaptive radiation. Island animals sometimes undergo striking changes in body size. Foster’s rule, also called the island rule, describes a tendency for large-bodied mammals to evolve smaller forms and small-bodied mammals to evolve larger forms. These patterns help scientists understand how geography, available resources, predators, and competition influence evolution.

Hooke’s law describes how an ideal spring responds when it is stretched or compressed. Within its elastic limit, the farther the spring is displaced from its equilibrium position, the stronger the restoring force pulling or pushing it back. This relationship is written F = −kx, where x is the displacement and k is the spring constant, a measure of stiffness. The minus sign shows that the force acts opposite to the displacement. If a mass is attached to the spring and released, this force makes it move back and forth around equilibrium. Because the mass’s acceleration is proportional to its displacement and directed toward equilibrium, its oscillation is called simple harmonic motion. The amplitude is the greatest distance the mass reaches from equilibrium.

A calorimeter is a laboratory instrument that measures heat transferred during a physical change or chemical reaction. Different designs suit different experiments. A differential scanning calorimeter, or DSC, heats or cools a sample and a reference according to a programmed temperature schedule, then measures the difference in heat flow between them. Scientists use it to study polymers, the large molecules that make up many plastics, and to identify changes such as the glass transition, when a polymer softens as it warms. A bomb calorimeter measures the heat released when a substance burns inside a strong, sealed vessel called a bomb. Because the vessel has a fixed volume, this is a constant-volume method, not a constant-pressure one.

André-Marie Ampère was a French physicist and mathematician who helped establish electrodynamics, the study of how electricity and magnetism interact. In the early 1800s, he investigated the magnetic effects of electric currents. He showed that two wires carrying current can attract or repel each other, depending on the directions of the currents, and formulated a law describing the force between them. Ampère also introduced the name solenoid for a long, helical coil of wire. When electric current flows through its turns, each loop contributes to a magnetic field, making the coil act like a magnet; when the current stops, that field disappears. In recognition of his work, the ampere, or amp, is the SI unit of electric current.

The Saffir–Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale ranks hurricanes in five categories according to their maximum sustained wind speed, giving an idea of the damage their winds could cause. Category 1 is the lowest hurricane rating, while Category 5 is the highest. A storm reaches Category 5 when its sustained winds are at least 157 miles per hour (252 kilometers per hour); winds this powerful can cause catastrophic damage to buildings and trees. Hurricanes are tropical cyclones that form over warm ocean water, including in the Atlantic Ocean. They have a calm center called the eye, surrounded by an eyewall where some of the strongest winds occur. Although hurricanes can also produce dangerous storm surge and flooding, the Saffir–Simpson scale assigns their categories based on wind speed, not water levels.

Chickenpox is a contagious disease caused by varicella-zoster virus, a member of the herpesvirus family. It is most common in children and usually begins with fever, tiredness, and a rash. The rash becomes very itchy and develops into small, fluid-filled blisters that can spread across the body. Chickenpox spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, or through contact with blister fluid. After a person recovers, varicella-zoster virus can remain dormant in sensory nerve cells. Years later, it may reactivate and cause shingles, a painful rash. Vaccination helps prevent chickenpox and reduces the risk of serious illness.

The Daniell cell is a nineteenth-century galvanic cell, a device that turns chemical energy into electrical energy. It has two half-cells: a zinc electrode in zinc sulfate solution and a copper electrode in copper sulfate solution. At the zinc electrode, zinc atoms release electrons; those electrons travel through an external wire to the copper electrode, producing a steady electric current. Meanwhile, copper ions in the copper sulfate solution gain electrons and form copper metal. The solutions must not mix freely, but ions still need to move between them to prevent a buildup of charge. A salt bridge connects the solutions and lets ions pass, maintaining electrical neutrality. This arrangement helped make batteries a more reliable source of electricity.

The pancreas is an organ in the abdomen, located behind the stomach. It has two important jobs. Most of its tissue produces digestive enzymes, which travel through ducts to the small intestine and help break down food. The main pancreatic duct, also called the duct of Wirsung, joins the common bile duct before they empty into the small intestine. Scattered among the enzyme-producing tissue are small clusters of endocrine cells called the islets of Langerhans. These cells release hormones into the bloodstream rather than through ducts. Alpha cells in the islets release glucagon, which raises blood sugar, while beta cells release insulin, which helps lower it. When the body cannot produce enough insulin or use it effectively, blood sugar can become too high, as it does in diabetes.

A subsurface ocean is a body of liquid water hidden beneath the icy crust of a moon or another celestial body. Unlike Earth’s oceans, it cannot be seen from the surface. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, and Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, are well-known examples. Enceladus releases plumes of water vapor and ice into space, providing clues about the ocean below. Scientists study these oceans as possible habitats for life because liquid water is one of the key ingredients life needs. Ganymede, another moon of Jupiter, is also thought to have a subsurface ocean, possibly between layers of ice. Ganymede is the largest natural satellite in the Solar System and has its own intrinsic magnetic field, a rare feature among moons.

Superconductors are materials that can carry electrical current with zero resistance when cooled below a characteristic critical temperature. Unlike ordinary wires, they do not lose electrical energy as heat while current flows. They also expel magnetic fields, an effect that can make a magnet float above a superconductor. These properties could improve power transmission, electronics, and medical imaging, but most superconductors need very low temperatures. A material that worked at room temperature under practical conditions would be especially useful. In 2020, researchers reported possible room-temperature superconductivity in a compound made from carbon, sulfur, and hydrogen, but only under enormous pressure. They squeezed the sample between two diamond crystals in a device called a diamond anvil cell. The reported result was later disputed.

A red giant is a star in a late stage of its life. After it uses up the hydrogen fuel in its core, the core contracts while hydrogen continues to fuse in a shell around it. The star’s outer layers expand enormously and cool, making the star look reddish despite its great brightness. Our Sun is expected to become a red giant billions of years from now. In a low-mass red giant, the contracting core eventually becomes hot enough for helium fusion to begin. But electron-degeneracy pressure holds the core at nearly the same size as it heats, so the rising temperature makes fusion speed up rapidly. This sudden burst of helium fusion is called a helium flash.

Neon is a colorless, odorless element with the symbol Ne and atomic number 10. It belongs to the noble gases, a group whose atoms have full outer electron shells and rarely react with other elements. Neon occurs only in trace amounts in Earth’s atmosphere. In 1898, the Scottish chemist William Ramsay and his colleague Morris Travers isolated neon from liquefied air. They identified it as a new element by examining its distinctive spectral lines: specific colors of light emitted when its atoms gain energy. When an electric current passes through neon in a discharge tube, it produces a vivid red-orange glow. That glow made neon famous for its use in illuminated signs.

The Fluid Mosaic Model describes the cell membrane as a flexible, constantly changing boundary rather than a rigid structure. In a 1972 Science paper, S. Jonathan Singer and Garth L. Nicolson proposed that the membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it. Each phospholipid has a water-attracting polar head and water-repelling nonpolar tails. The heads face the watery surroundings inside and outside the cell, while the tails point toward each other. The membrane is “fluid” because many lipids and proteins can move sideways within the bilayer, and “mosaic” because its different components form a varied pattern. Cholesterol helps regulate membrane fluidity in animal cells. This structure allows the cell membrane to enclose the cell and control what enters and leaves it.

Lysergic acid diethylamide, commonly called LSD, is a powerful psychedelic drug that can alter a person’s perceptions, thoughts, and sense of time. Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann first synthesized it in 1938 while researching ergot alkaloids, chemicals found in a fungus that grows on grains, at the pharmaceutical company Sandoz. Its psychoactive effects were discovered in 1943, when Hofmann accidentally absorbed a small amount. He later deliberately took a dose and recorded his experiences during a bicycle ride home, an event often called “Bicycle Day.” In the 1950s and 1960s, the CIA studied LSD under Project MKULTRA and administered it to some people without their consent. Those experiments are now recognized as serious violations of medical ethics.

The cubic crystal system describes crystals whose repeating building block, called a unit cell, is shaped like a cube: its three axes are equal in length and meet at right angles. Crystals have orderly, repeating arrangements of atoms or ions, unlike amorphous materials such as glass. The cubic system has three Bravais lattices, distinguished by where lattice points occur. A primitive cubic lattice has points only at the eight corners. A body-centered cubic lattice also has a point at the cube’s center. A face-centered cubic lattice, often shortened to FCC, has points at the corners and at the centers of all six square faces. In an FCC lattice, each point has 12 nearest neighbors. These arrangements help scientists describe the structures and properties of crystalline materials.

Mollusca is a phylum of soft-bodied invertebrates that includes clams, scallops, snails, squids, and octopuses. Mollusks commonly have a mantle, which may produce a shell; a visceral mass containing internal organs; and a muscular foot used for movement or other tasks. Their bodies vary widely: bivalves such as clams and scallops have two hinged shells, gastropods such as snails usually move on a broad foot, and cephalopods such as octopuses and nautiluses have arms and can use jet propulsion. Some mollusks have reduced shells or no external shell at all. Many gastropods feed with a radula, a flexible, ribbon-like organ covered in rows of tiny teeth that scrape food from surfaces. Bivalves generally lack a radula and often feed by filtering particles from water.

A dipole is a separation of positive and negative charge. In a molecule, it forms when the centers of positive and negative charge do not line up, producing a dipole moment. Some molecules have permanent dipoles because their electrons are shared unevenly and their shape prevents the bond dipoles from canceling out; these are called polar molecules. Dipoles can also be temporary. Electrons are always moving, so an electron cloud may briefly become uneven, making one side of a particle slightly negative and the other slightly positive. This temporary dipole can shift the electrons in a nearby particle, inducing another dipole. The attraction between these temporary and induced dipoles is called a London dispersion force. These forces occur between all particles and are especially important in nonpolar substances, which lack permanent dipoles.

Superconductivity is a state that some materials enter when cooled below a critical temperature. In this state, their electrical resistance drops to zero, so an electric current can flow without losing energy as heat. Resistance is the opposition to the flow of current and is measured in ohms. A superconductor also pushes magnetic flux out of its interior as it enters the superconducting state. This magnetic response is called the Meissner effect. It distinguishes a superconductor from an ideal conductor that merely has zero resistance: an ideal conductor would not necessarily expel a magnetic field already inside it. In many superconductors, electrons form linked pairs called Cooper pairs, which help explain how current can flow without resistance.

The multiverse is the hypothetical idea that reality may contain many universes rather than just the one we observe. These universes might have different histories, physical laws, or conditions, although scientists have not confirmed that other universes exist. The idea is also popular in fiction, where characters can travel between alternate realities and meet different versions of themselves. In the 2022 film Everything Everywhere All at Once, Michelle Yeoh plays Evelyn, who moves between universes and discovers other versions of her life. The villain, Jobu Tupaki, uses a black bagel as a recurring symbol. The film uses the multiverse to explore how a person’s life might change if they had made different choices.

Hess’s Law says that the overall enthalpy change of a chemical reaction depends only on its starting reactants and final products, not on the steps taken between them.
