Enthalpy, represented by H, is a thermodynamic state function; its change, written ΔH, describes the heat absorbed or released by a reaction at constant pressure. To find ΔH for a target reaction, you can add the ΔH values of other reactions whose equations combine to produce it. If you reverse a reaction equation, you reverse the sign of its ΔH. If you multiply all the coefficients in an equation by a number, you multiply its ΔH by the same number. Any substances that appear on both sides of the combined equations cancel out.

The inverse-square law describes how a force weakens as the distance between two point sources increases: the force is proportional to 1 divided by the distance squared. If the separation doubles, the force becomes one quarter as strong; if it triples, the force becomes one ninth as strong. Newton’s law of universal gravitation follows this pattern for masses, and Coulomb’s law follows it for stationary electric charges. Coulomb’s law says that the magnitude of the electrostatic force is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. In a vacuum, its proportionality constant is 1/(4πε₀), where ε₀ is the permittivity of free space. Unlike gravity, electric forces can attract or repel, depending on the signs of the charges.

The steady-state approximation helps chemists work out rate laws for reactions that happen in several steps. These reactions may briefly produce an intermediate: a substance formed in one step and used up in another. After a short initial period called the transient, the intermediate may be produced and consumed at nearly equal rates. Chemists can then treat its concentration—the amount of it in a given volume, often expressed in molarity—as nearly constant, even though molecules of the intermediate are continually being made and removed. In mathematical terms, its rate of formation minus its rate of consumption is approximately zero. This assumption simplifies the equations for a multistep reaction and helps chemists predict how quickly the overall reaction proceeds.

Hydrogen sulfide is a colorless, toxic gas made of one sulfur atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, giving it the formula H2S. Hydrogen is the lightest element, and sulfur is the element with atomic number 16. Hydrogen sulfide is well known for its rotten-egg smell, although a strong exposure can make a person unable to detect the odor, so it should never be used as a safety warning. The bonds and lone pairs around sulfur help explain the molecule’s shape. Sulfur has two bonding pairs, one for each hydrogen, and two lone pairs that are not part of bonds. These four pairs of electrons repel one another, so the three atoms do not form a straight line. Instead, hydrogen sulfide has a bent molecular geometry, with an H–S–H angle of about 92°.

Visible light is the part of the electromagnetic spectrum that human eyes can detect. It includes the colors from violet to red and is emitted by sources such as the Sun, LEDs, and fluorescent lamps. When visible light enters the eye, it reaches the retina, a layer of light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. The retina contains two main kinds of photoreceptor cells: rods and cones. Rods are especially useful in dim light but do not provide detailed color vision. Cones work best under brighter conditions and allow us to distinguish colors. This is why colors can be hard to identify in a dark room, even when you can still make out shapes. Some people with migraines are unusually sensitive to light, which can make bright sources uncomfortable during a headache.

A blood transfusion is a medical procedure in which donated blood, or a blood component such as red blood cells, plasma, or platelets, is delivered into a patient’s vein. It may be needed after severe blood loss or when a person lacks enough healthy blood cells. Before a transfusion, clinicians check the donor’s and recipient’s blood types because incompatible blood can trigger a dangerous immune reaction. Blood types include an ABO group—A, B, AB, or O—and a positive or negative designation. The plus or minus sign refers to the Rh factor, an inherited antigen on red blood cells that was named for rhesus macaques, in which it was first studied. Careful matching of ABO and Rh types helps make transfusions safer.

Penicillins are a class of beta-lactam antibiotics used to treat infections caused by susceptible bacteria. Bacteria need a sturdy cell wall made of peptidoglycan, a polymer that makes up much of the dry weight of Gram-positive bacterial walls. Penicillins block enzymes that link peptidoglycan strands together, weakening the wall so the bacteria can die, especially as they grow and divide. Early penicillins came from substances produced by Penicillium molds. In 1928, Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold contaminating a laboratory plate had stopped nearby staphylococcal bacteria from growing. This observation led to the discovery of penicillin. Human cells lack cell walls, which helps explain why penicillins can target bacteria without attacking the same structure in our cells.

A windmill is a machine that captures the wind’s energy with large sails or blades. As the wind turns them, they rotate a shaft connected to a mechanism that can grind grain into flour or pump water. Some modern wind-powered machines use a generator to produce electricity; these are usually called wind turbines. Windmills also appear in literature, especially in Miguel de Cervantes’s Spanish novel Don Quixote. Its main character is an aging man so absorbed in tales of knights and heroic quests that he believes he is a knight himself. In a famous scene, he mistakes windmills for giants and attacks one. He undertakes his quests in the name of Dulcinea del Toboso, whom he imagines as his beloved lady.

The woodchuck, also called the groundhog, is a marmot native to eastern North America. Its scientific name is Marmota monax: Marmota is its genus, and monax identifies the species. Woodchucks are rodents related to squirrels, and they live in burrows they dig in the ground. They are often found in fields, meadows, and along woodland edges, where they eat grasses, leaves, and other plants. During winter, they hibernate in their burrows, slowing their body functions to conserve energy. The name “woodchuck” is familiar from the tongue twister “How much wood would a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood?” Despite the rhyme, woodchucks do not throw wood; “chuck” in the tongue twister is a playful word for tossing it.

A Bose-Einstein condensate, or BEC, is a state of matter that forms when a dilute gas of bosons is cooled extremely close to absolute zero. Bosons are particles with integer spin. At such low temperatures, many of them occupy the same lowest-energy quantum state, so they behave collectively rather than like separate atoms. This makes quantum effects, which are usually noticeable only at tiny scales, easier to study. The first dilute-gas BEC was created in 1995 at JILA by Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman. They used atoms of rubidium-87, a bosonic isotope of rubidium with a mass number of 87, and cooled the gas using techniques that included lasers.

Auxins are plant hormones that help control how plants grow and respond to their surroundings. The main naturally occurring auxin in most plants is indole-3-acetic acid, or IAA, which plants make from the amino acid tryptophan. Auxins promote stem elongation and help regulate root growth. They also play a role in phototropism: when light comes from one side, auxin builds up on the shaded side of a shoot, causing those cells to elongate more so the shoot bends toward the light. Proteins called PIN proteins move auxins directionally through plant tissues, a process known as polar auxin transport. Auxin produced near the tip of the main shoot also helps suppress the growth of lateral buds, an effect called apical dominance.

Published in 1632, Galileo Galilei’s Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems presents four days of discussion about two competing views of the cosmos. The Ptolemaic model places Earth at the center, while the Copernican model places the Sun at the center of the solar system, with Earth moving around it. Galileo wrote the work as a conversation among three characters rather than a straightforward textbook. Salviati, a learned defender of the Copernican model, argues for heliocentrism in debates with Simplicio, who favors traditional Aristotelian and geocentric ideas. A third speaker, Sagredo, listens and asks questions. Galileo’s telescopic observations, including the phases of Venus and moons orbiting Jupiter, had provided evidence that challenged the older Earth-centered view. The book brought Galileo into conflict with the Catholic Church.

The Triassic Period was the first period of the Mesozoic Era, lasting from about 252 to 201 million years ago. It began after the end-Permian mass extinction, the largest known extinction in Earth’s history, and came immediately before the Jurassic Period. During much of the Triassic, Earth’s landmasses were joined in the supercontinent Pangaea, and many regions were hot and dry. Later in the period, a several-million-year interval called the Carnian Pluvial Event brought unusually wet conditions to parts of Pangaea. Researchers have linked this climate change to intense volcanic eruptions in the Wrangellia terrane. The wetter climate reshaped ecosystems on land and may have helped dinosaurs become more widespread and dominant.

A covalent bond forms when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons, often helping each atom fill its outer electron shell. Covalent bonds commonly form between nonmetals. In a Lewis structure, a shared pair can be shown as two dots or a line between atoms. A single bond shares one pair of electrons, a double bond shares two pairs, and a triple bond shares three pairs. This sharing differs from ionic bonding, in which an electron is transferred from one atom to another. Covalent bonds are also important in living things. When two cysteine residues in a protein are oxidized, their sulfur atoms can form a covalent cross-link called a disulfide bond, which can help hold the protein’s shape.

Dynamite is a high explosive developed in the 19th century by Swedish inventor and industrialist Alfred Nobel, who patented it in 1867. Its main explosive ingredient is nitroglycerin, a powerful liquid that is dangerous to handle on its own because it can detonate unexpectedly. Nobel made it safer and more practical by absorbing the nitroglycerin into a porous material, allowing it to be shaped into sticks for transport and use. Dynamite became a powerful alternative to gunpowder and was widely used to blast rock for mining, tunnels, roads, and railways. Unlike gunpowder, which burns rapidly, dynamite detonates, producing a much faster and stronger shock wave. Nobel later established the Nobel Prizes, which bear his name.

A computer monitor is a visual output device that shows the text, images, and video generated by a computer. Unlike a printer, which puts output on paper, a monitor displays it on a screen so you can view it and interact with programs as they run. A laptop usually has a screen attached to the rest of the computer, while a desktop computer often uses a separate monitor. Many flat-panel monitors use LCD technology, short for liquid crystal display. In an LCD, a backlight shines through a layer of liquid crystals. The crystals control how much light passes through each pixel, and the pixels work together to form the picture you see.

A reactant is a starting substance in a chemical reaction. Reactants are written before the arrow in a chemical equation, while the substances formed, called products, appear after it. As the reaction proceeds, reactants are consumed or transformed into products. A balanced equation shows the mole ratio in which reactants combine. If the amounts available do not match that ratio, one reactant may be used up before the others. This is the limiting reactant: it determines the maximum amount of product that can form, even if some of the other reactants remain. In reactions that reach equilibrium, reactants and products are both present because the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.

The Golgi apparatus, or Golgi body, is an organelle in eukaryotic cells made of stacks of flattened membrane sacs. It acts like a processing and shipping center: it receives many newly made proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), modifies them, then sorts and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles for delivery elsewhere in the cell or release outside it. Vesicles are small, membrane-bound containers that carry cargo between cell compartments. Vesicles traveling from the ER to the Golgi form with a coat complex called COPII, which helps shape the vesicle and select its cargo. COPI is a different coat complex that commonly helps move cargo in the reverse direction, from the Golgi back toward the ER.

Landslides are movements of rock, soil, or debris downhill under the force of gravity. They include sudden rockfalls, slower-moving slopes, and fast debris flows. A slope may fail when heavy rain or melting snow soaks the ground and increases the pressure of water in the spaces between soil grains, making the material less stable. Earthquakes can also shake slopes and sometimes cause waterlogged ground to lose strength. Volcanic eruptions can trigger a special kind of fast-moving landslide called a lahar: a mixture of water, volcanic ash, and rock fragments that rushes down valleys. Lahars can form during an eruption or later, when rain washes loose volcanic deposits downhill. Because landslides can move quickly and travel far, they can threaten people, roads, and buildings.

The thalamus is a pair of structures deep in the brain that acts as a major relay station. It receives information from nearly all the senses and helps direct it to the cerebral cortex, the outer part of the brain where much of that information is processed. For example, signals about touch, vision, and hearing pass through the thalamus on their way to areas of the cortex. The thalamus also helps coordinate movement and supports functions such as attention and thinking. Smell is the important exception to its usual sensory relay role: odor signals first travel to the olfactory bulb and then reach areas including the piriform cortex without first passing through the thalamus. The hypothalamus, which lies below the thalamus, is a different structure that helps regulate body functions and controls the pituitary gland.

Noether’s theorem connects symmetries with conservation laws. A symmetry means that a system’s action, a quantity describing its motion, stays unchanged under a smooth, continuous transformation. The theorem says that each such symmetry has a corresponding conserved quantity—something that remains constant as the system evolves. If the laws governing a system do not change over time, energy is conserved. If they do not change when the system is shifted through space, linear momentum, the product of mass and velocity, is conserved. If they do not change when the system is rotated, angular momentum is conserved. German mathematician Emmy Noether established this result in her 1918 paper Invariante Variationsprobleme. She is also known for major contributions to abstract algebra.

Animal models in research are studies that use nonhuman animals, such as rats and monkeys, to investigate biology, behavior, and processes that may also occur in humans. Researchers can observe how animals learn, respond to stress, or react to treatments, then use the results to form and test ideas about human health and behavior. However, findings from animals do not always apply directly to people. Abraham Maslow, a humanistic psychologist, argued that behaviorist studies of animals could not fully explain human motivation. In his paper “A Theory of Human Motivation,” he proposed a theory later widely known as the hierarchy of needs. It describes needs ranging from basic physiological requirements, such as food, to self-actualization: the desire to fulfill one’s potential.

Project Orion was a late-1950s study at General Atomics of a spacecraft powered by nuclear explosions. Instead of burning fuel continuously like a conventional rocket, the craft would eject small nuclear bombs behind a broad, strong pusher plate. Each bomb would explode at a safe distance, and the blast would push the plate—and the spacecraft—forward. Shock absorbers between the plate and the rest of the vehicle would smooth out the repeated jolts. Engineers hoped this “nuclear pulse” approach could provide enough thrust for ambitious journeys through the solar system. It was never built, partly because of concerns about radioactive fallout and international restrictions on nuclear explosions. The key idea is that Project Orion proposed using repeated nuclear bomb blasts to propel a spacecraft.

Desalination is the process of removing dissolved salts from seawater or brackish water to make freshwater suitable for drinking, farming, or other uses. One common method is reverse osmosis: pumps apply pressure to salty water, pushing it against a semipermeable membrane. Water passes through the membrane, while most dissolved salts stay behind. A reverse-osmosis desalination plant helps supply Key West with freshwater. Other methods include electrodialysis, which uses electricity and specialized membranes to separate salt ions from water, and solar stills, which use sunlight to evaporate water and then collect it as freshwater when it condenses. Desalination is especially useful where freshwater is scarce, but it requires energy and leaves behind concentrated salty waste called brine.

Hadrons are composite subatomic particles built from quarks, rather than single elementary particles. The two main classes are baryons and mesons. Baryons have three valence quarks—the quarks that determine the particle’s basic identity. Protons and neutrons are familiar baryons; together, they make up the nuclei of ordinary atoms. Mesons instead have a valence quark and a valence antiquark. An antiquark is the antimatter counterpart of a quark. Quarks inside hadrons are held together by the strong force, one of the fundamental forces of nature. Physicist Richard Feynman proposed a “parton” model to help describe what happens inside hadrons during high-energy collisions. The key distinction is that protons and neutrons are three-quark baryons, while mesons have a quark–antiquark pair.

The competitive exclusion principle states that two species cannot coexist indefinitely if they occupy the same ecological niche and depend on the same limited resources under identical conditions. When food, space, or another resource is scarce, one species may use it more effectively and eventually displace the other. Coexistence is possible if the species differentiate their niches, such as by eating different foods or living in different parts of a habitat. The principle is associated with ecologist Georgy Gause, who tested it using Paramecium, a group of single-celled organisms. In his experiments, two competing Paramecium species grown together under the same conditions could not both persist. His results showed how competition can shape which species survive in an environment.

Radar, short for “radio detection and ranging,” detects objects by sending out radio waves or microwaves and listening for echoes that bounce back. Because these waves travel at a known speed, the time an echo takes to return tells a radar system how far away an object is. The direction of the returning signal helps locate it. Radar can track aircraft, locate storms and measure vehicle speeds, making it useful for aviation, weather forecasting and enforcing speed limits. It can also detect motion through the Doppler effect: when a target moves relative to the radar, the returning wave has a different observed frequency from the transmitted wave. Comparing those frequencies helps the system determine whether the target is moving toward or away from it and how fast it is moving.

Klinefelter syndrome is a chromosomal condition in which a person who is typically male has an extra X chromosome. Most males have 46 chromosomes, including one X and one Y sex chromosome, written as 46,XY. The most common chromosome pattern in Klinefelter syndrome has 47 chromosomes: two X chromosomes and one Y. Its standard shorthand is 47,XXY. The extra X chromosome usually arises by chance when reproductive cells form; it is not caused by anything a parent did. Effects vary, but they can include small testes, lower testosterone levels, reduced fertility, and differences in growth or learning. Some people have few noticeable symptoms. Knowing that Klinefelter syndrome is associated with an extra X chromosome and the 47,XXY pattern distinguishes it from other chromosomal conditions.

Kary Banks Mullis was an American biochemist who conceived the polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, while working at Cetus Corporation. The technique makes millions of copies of a selected DNA sequence from a small starting sample, making it a cornerstone of molecular biology. In each cycle, heat separates the two strands of DNA. As the sample cools, short pieces of DNA called primers bind to the target sequence; this step is called annealing. A DNA polymerase enzyme then extends the primers to build new strands. Repeating these steps rapidly increases the amount of target DNA. PCR commonly uses a heat-stable polymerase from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus, which survives the repeated heating. Mullis received the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing PCR.

The Chua circuit is an electronic oscillator that can produce chaos: complex, seemingly unpredictable behavior from a system that follows definite rules. Its behavior is highly sensitive to initial conditions, so a tiny difference in starting voltage can lead to a very different path over time. The circuit typically contains capacitors, an inductor, a resistor, and a special nonlinear element called the Chua diode. Despite its name, the Chua diode is not necessarily an ordinary one-way diode like an LED. It is a nonlinear resistor whose current-voltage relationship has straight-line sections, including a negative-resistance region. That region helps the circuit undergo period doubling, in which an oscillation’s pattern repeats only after twice as long. The circuit can also produce a distinctive chaotic pattern called a double-scroll attractor.

Angiosperms are flowering plants, a major group that includes orchids, daisies, grasses, and many trees. Unlike gymnosperms, which produce exposed seeds often found in cones, angiosperms enclose their seeds inside ovaries that develop into fruits. Flowers help them reproduce: pollen from a flower’s stamen can be carried by wind or by animals such as bees and birds to the stigma of a pistil, the female reproductive structure. The pistil also contains a style and an ovary. After pollen reaches the ovary, it delivers two sperm cells. One fertilizes an egg to form an embryo; the other joins with a central cell to form endosperm, tissue that nourishes the developing seed. This two-part process is called double fertilization.

Planetary rings are broad, flattened disks of ice, dust, and rocky fragments that orbit some planets. They are not solid sheets: each ring contains countless separate particles, from tiny grains to much larger chunks, moving around the planet. All four giant planets in our Solar System have rings, but Saturn’s are by far the brightest and easiest to see. Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, and its ring system stretches across a huge area despite being remarkably thin. Astronomers divide it into several main rings; a prominent gap called the Cassini Division separates the bright A and B rings. That gap is maintained partly by the gravitational pull of Mimas, one of Saturn’s moons.

Spectroscopy is the study of how matter interacts with electromagnetic radiation, such as visible or infrared light. Atoms and molecules can absorb, emit, or scatter radiation at particular energies, producing a spectrum that helps scientists identify a substance and learn about its structure. Infrared spectroscopy detects the absorption of infrared light by vibrating bonds in molecules; its spectra include regions useful for identifying chemical groups and a distinctive “fingerprint” region. Raman spectroscopy also reveals molecular vibrations, but it measures small energy shifts in laser light that scatters inelastically from a sample. Raman measurements can even help determine the diameter of a carbon nanotube. Another related analytical technique, mass spectrometry, identifies ions by their mass-to-charge ratios rather than by measuring light.

In the Rutherford Scattering Experiment, researchers fired alpha particles at an extremely thin sheet of gold foil. Alpha particles are helium-4 nuclei: each contains two protons and two neutrons and has a charge of +2. The experiment tested the plum-pudding model, which pictured an atom’s positive charge spread throughout it. Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil, showing that atoms are mostly empty space. A few bounced back or changed direction sharply. Ernest Rutherford interpreted these surprising deflections as evidence that nearly all an atom’s mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny, dense center called the nucleus. The experiment transformed scientists’ understanding of atomic structure.

Urine is a liquid waste product made by the kidneys as they filter the blood. It contains water and dissolved wastes, including urea, which forms when the body breaks down proteins. Inside each kidney, tiny filtering units called nephrons remove wastes and help control how much water and salt the body keeps. The resulting urine travels from the kidneys through two tubes called ureters to the urinary bladder. This hollow, muscular organ in the pelvis stores urine until it is time to eliminate it. When you urinate, the bladder wall contracts and pushes urine out of the body through another tube, the urethra. This process removes wastes while helping the body maintain a healthy balance of fluids.

Sleep is a recurring natural state in which consciousness and responsiveness to the surroundings decrease. It is essential for physical restoration, memory processing, and overall health. Sleep moves through stages of non-REM (NREM) sleep, including deep sleep, and REM sleep, when vivid dreaming is common. The timing of sleep is guided by a circadian rhythm, an internal cycle of about 24 hours that helps determine when you feel alert or drowsy. A brain region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus helps keep this rhythm aligned with the day–night cycle. In response to darkness, the pineal gland releases melatonin, a hormone that signals that it is time to sleep. Some people take melatonin supplements to help them fall asleep, although it does not replace healthy sleep habits.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, are medications commonly prescribed for depression and anxiety. Nerve cells communicate by releasing chemical messengers into the spaces between them. One messenger, serotonin, helps regulate mood, sleep, and other functions. After serotonin sends a signal, a nerve cell normally takes it back up, a process called reuptake. SSRIs block that reuptake, allowing serotonin to remain available longer. Examples include citalopram, sold as Celexa, and fluoxetine, sold as Prozac. Fluoxetine was the first SSRI approved in the United States, in 1987. It stands out because the body eliminates it slowly: it has a long elimination half-life, and an active substance formed as the body processes it can remain in the body for weeks.

Maxwell’s equations are four equations that describe how electric and magnetic fields behave and interact. Gauss’s law for electricity says that electric charge is a source of electric fields: the electric field’s divergence is related to charge density. Gauss’s law for magnetism says that magnetic-field divergence is zero, meaning there are no isolated magnetic poles. Faraday’s law describes electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. Ampère’s law, as corrected by Maxwell, says that electric currents and changing electric fields produce magnetic fields. Maxwell called the changing-electric-field contribution the displacement current. It allows a magnetic field to exist even where no charged particles flow, such as in the gap between the plates of a charging capacitor. Together, the four equations also explain how electromagnetic waves, including light, travel.

Microsoft Windows is a family of graphical operating systems developed by Microsoft and widely used on personal computers. An operating system manages a computer’s hardware and software, while a graphical interface lets people use windows, icons, menus, and a pointer to open programs and work with files. Windows XP and Windows Vista are two releases in this family. To store files, an operating system uses a file system, which organizes data on a drive and keeps track of where files are located. Windows NT 3.1 introduced a file system called NTFS, short for New Technology File System. NTFS uses a Master File Table, or MFT, to record information about files and directories, including their names and where their data is stored.

Bile is a yellowish-green digestive fluid made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder. When food containing fat enters the small intestine, the gallbladder releases bile to help with digestion. Bile salts break large fat droplets into smaller ones, making it easier for digestive enzymes to act on them. Bile also carries waste products from the liver, including bilirubin. Bilirubin is a yellow pigment formed when the body breaks down heme, a component of hemoglobin in aging red blood cells. It normally leaves the body through the intestines and helps give stool its brown color. If too much bilirubin builds up in the blood, it can cause jaundice, which makes the skin and whites of the eyes look yellow.

A first-order reaction is a chemical reaction whose rate is directly proportional to the concentration of one reactant. If the reactant’s concentration doubles, the reaction rate doubles; as the reactant is used up, the rate slows. The rate law is rate = k[A], where [A] is the reactant concentration and k is the rate constant. Because the rate depends on how much reactant remains, its concentration decreases exponentially over time rather than by the same amount each minute. The half-life is the time it takes for the concentration to fall to half its current value. In a first-order reaction, each halving takes the same amount of time, regardless of the starting concentration. This constant half-life equals ln 2 divided by k, or about 0.693/k.

A salt bridge connects the two half-cells of a galvanic cell, such as a zinc-copper battery. It is often a U-shaped glass tube filled with an electrolyte solution, sometimes held in place by a gel. As electrons travel from the anode to the cathode through an external wire, ions move through the salt bridge. This ion movement prevents charge from building up in either half-cell, maintains electrical neutrality, and allows the cell to keep producing current. The salt bridge does not carry the electrons between the electrodes; it provides a path for ions. A porous cup can serve a similar purpose. One common gel-forming substance in salt bridges is agar, a polysaccharide derived from red algae that forms a stable gel in water and helps keep the electrolyte in place.

The Document Object Model, or DOM, is a browser programming interface that represents a web page as a hierarchy of objects called nodes. These nodes can correspond to HTML elements such as headings, paragraphs, and buttons. The DOM is organized as a tree: it has one top-most node called the root, and nodes below it can have parent-child relationships. A node may have several children, creating branches, while a node with no children is called a leaf. JavaScript can use the DOM to inspect a page and change its content or appearance without loading a new page. For example, a script attached to a button can respond to a click by changing the text of a paragraph.

The turkey vulture is a New World bird that feeds mainly on carrion, the bodies of dead animals. Unlike many birds, it has an exceptionally strong sense of smell, helped by an unusually large olfactory lobe, the part of the brain that processes odors. This lets a turkey vulture find food even when it is hidden from view, such as beneath leaves or in a forest. One scent it can follow is ethyl mercaptan, a sulfur-containing compound released during decomposition. Turkey vultures often soar above the ground while searching for these odors. Their ability to detect carrion helps them find meals and plays a useful role in ecosystems by removing dead animals.

An improvised firearm is a gun assembled from nonstandard or readily available materials instead of being produced through conventional industrial manufacturing. It may also be described as homemade, makeshift, or DIY. Improvised does not mean harmless: such weapons can be deadly and may be especially unpredictable because they lack the testing and quality controls of factory-made firearms. A well-known example was used in Japan on July 8, 2022, when Tetsuya Yamagami shot former prime minister Shinzo Abe at a campaign event in Nara. The weapon was visibly homemade, with two pipes strapped together using electrical tape. Japan has strict gun control laws, and the attack drew attention both to the unusual weapon and to the death of a prominent political leader.

Marble is a crystalline carbonate rock that usually forms when limestone or dolostone is changed by heat and pressure. During this process, the original mineral crystals recrystallize into interlocking grains. These grains give marble its distinctive appearance and allow it to take a high polish, making it prized for sculpture, buildings, and monuments. White marble was used in the Taj Mahal, and marble is also found in the Lincoln Memorial statue and the US Supreme Court Building. One especially famous source is Carrara, Italy, whose marble has been used by sculptors for centuries. Between 1501 and 1504, Michelangelo carved his sculpture David from a single block of Carrara marble. The original David is displayed at the Galleria dell’Accademia in Florence.

Mechanical equilibrium occurs when all the forces acting on an object cancel, so the net force is zero and the object has no acceleration. It may remain at rest or continue moving at a constant velocity. Equilibrium can be stable or unstable. In stable equilibrium, a small displacement produces forces that tend to return the object to its original position. A ball at the bottom of a bowl is an example: if nudged up the side, gravity pulls it back down, and its potential energy is lowest at the bottom. In unstable equilibrium, a small displacement causes the object to move farther away, like a ball balanced on top of a hill. Both types can arise in systems where gravity acts between multiple bodies.

Orogeny is the geological process that builds mountain ranges when forces inside Earth push and reshape its crust. Earth’s outer shell is divided into huge moving slabs called tectonic plates. Where plates move toward each other at a convergent boundary, their edges can be compressed, folded, broken along faults, and lifted upward. In some collisions, one plate slides beneath another in a process called subduction; in others, two continents collide and their crust crumples and thickens. Orogeny usually takes millions of years, and the resulting mountains can continue to rise while the plates keep moving. The Himalayas are an example: the Indian Plate is still pushing into the Eurasian Plate, raising a range that includes Mount Everest and stretches across areas including Nepal, Bhutan, India, and China.

Hückel’s rule helps chemists predict whether a ring-shaped molecule is aromatic, meaning it has extra stability because its π electrons are spread around the ring. The rule applies when the molecule is cyclic (forms a closed ring), planar (its ring atoms lie roughly in one plane), and conjugated (each ring atom can take part in a continuous network of overlapping orbitals). Such a ring is aromatic if it has 4n + 2 π electrons, where n is a whole number starting at zero. This gives possible counts of 2, 6, 10, and so on. Benzene, a six-carbon hydrocarbon with the formula C₆H₆, is a familiar example: its conjugated ring has six π electrons. Since six equals 4(1) + 2, Hückel’s rule predicts that benzene is aromatic.

The Eddington experiment was a landmark 1919 test of Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity, which predicts that the Sun’s gravity bends light from distant stars. During the total solar eclipse on 29 May 1919, the Moon blocked the Sun’s bright disk, making stars near it visible. Astronomers photographed those stars and compared their apparent positions with photographs taken when the Sun was elsewhere in the sky. Arthur Eddington and Edwin Cottingham observed from the island of Príncipe in the Gulf of Guinea, while a separate British team worked in Brazil. The stars appeared slightly displaced, providing early experimental support for Einstein’s prediction.

Unit testing is a way to check small parts of a program, such as one function, method, or class, before they are combined into a larger application. A unit test gives a component a specific input and checks whether its output or behavior matches what the programmer expects. Testing components on their own helps programmers find bugs early and identify which part of the code needs fixing. It differs from integration testing, which checks whether multiple parts work together correctly. Programmers often run unit tests again after changing code to make sure earlier behavior still works. In Java, a popular unit-testing framework is JUnit. Its Jupiter API lets programmers mark test methods with @Test and use assertions such as assertEquals to compare an actual result with an expected one.

Global warming is the long-term rise in Earth’s average temperature. It has accelerated since the Industrial Revolution as people have burned large amounts of coal, oil, and natural gas for energy. Burning these fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, a gas that strengthens the greenhouse effect. In this natural process, gases in the atmosphere absorb infrared radiation given off by Earth’s surface and re-emit it, keeping some heat from escaping into space. The greenhouse effect makes Earth warm enough for life, but adding more heat-trapping gases causes extra warming. As temperatures rise, glaciers and ice sheets melt, contributing to sea-level rise. Warmer ocean water also expands, raising sea levels further. Global warming is one major part of climate change, which includes shifts in rainfall and more frequent or intense heat waves.

An aircraft carrier is a warship that acts as a floating airbase. Its long flight deck lets military aircraft take off and land at sea, while its crew stores, fuels, repairs, and arms the planes. Carriers allow a navy to launch air attacks and defend ships far from land-based airfields. Their importance became clear at the Battle of the Coral Sea in May 1942, near Papua New Guinea. In this battle, American and Australian forces opposed a Japanese advance toward Port Moresby. It was the first naval battle in which opposing aircraft carriers fought through planes launched from their decks without the surface fleets ever sighting one another. The battle halted Japan’s advance toward Port Moresby. The USS Abraham Lincoln is a modern Nimitz-class aircraft carrier.

Physical dimensions describe what kind of quantity a measurement represents, independently of the units used to measure it. Common fundamental dimensions are mass (M), length (L), and time (T). For example, speed has the dimension length divided by time, written L/T, whether it is measured in meters per second or miles per hour. In dimensional analysis, scientists combine dimensions like algebraic factors to check equations and understand how quantities relate. Sometimes every fundamental dimension cancels: distance divided by distance, for instance, has no remaining power of length. A value with zero net power of every fundamental dimension is called a dimensionless quantity. The Reynolds number, which helps describe fluid flow, and the coefficient of friction are examples.

The nervous system is the body’s communication network. It includes the brain and spinal cord, which process information, and nerves that extend throughout the body. Nerve cells called neurons carry electrical signals that let you sense your surroundings, move your muscles, and regulate functions such as breathing. A neuron usually has many branching dendrites that receive signals and one long projection called an axon that carries electrical impulses away from the cell body. Many axons are wrapped in a fatty insulating layer called the myelin sheath, which helps signals travel quickly and efficiently. In multiple sclerosis, damage to myelin disrupts these signals and can interfere with movement, sensation, and other functions.

Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who changed how scientists understand atoms and quantum physics. In 1913, he proposed an atomic model in which electrons occupy specific, or discrete, energy levels around a small, dense nucleus. Electrons can move between these levels by absorbing or releasing energy, which helped explain the distinct lines in hydrogen’s light spectrum. Bohr received the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on atomic structure. Later, he and Werner Heisenberg helped develop the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics. This account emphasizes that the way an experiment is arranged affects what can be measured and that quantum theory predicts probabilities for results rather than always giving a single certain outcome.

The water-gas shift reaction is an industrial process in which carbon monoxide reacts with water vapor, or steam, to produce carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas: CO + H2O ⇌ CO2 + H2. The double arrow shows that this is an equilibrium reaction, meaning it can run in both directions. Industry uses it to make more hydrogen from gas mixtures that contain carbon monoxide. Hydrogen gas is diatomic: each molecule contains two hydrogen atoms, so its formula is H2. It is useful as a fuel and as a raw material for other chemicals. For example, hydrogen combines with nitrogen in the Haber process to make ammonia, which is widely used to produce fertilizers.

Leafcutter ants are social insects native to the Americas, often called the New World. They live in large colonies with a queen and workers that perform different jobs. Some workers cut pieces from fresh leaves and other vegetation, while others carry the fragments back to an underground nest. Despite their name, leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves directly. Instead, they use the plant pieces as a growing material for a cultivated fungus. Workers care for this fungal crop by adding fresh fragments and keeping the garden clean. The colony eats the fungus, which provides its food. This partnership makes leafcutter ants a striking example of agriculture in the animal world: they gather raw materials, tend a crop, and depend on the harvest.

Transfer RNA, or tRNA, is an adaptor molecule that helps cells build proteins. Each tRNA carries a particular amino acid and has an anticodon, a three-base sequence that pairs with a matching codon on messenger RNA (mRNA). At a ribosome, the cell’s protein-building structure, tRNA delivers its amino acid so it can be joined to the growing protein chain. The incoming tRNA first binds at the ribosome’s A site. Some tRNAs can recognize more than one codon because pairing at one position is flexible. Molecular biologist Francis Crick proposed this “wobble pairing.” Crick also formulated the Central Dogma of molecular biology, which describes how genetic information is used to make proteins: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.

Gunpowder is a combustible mixture traditionally made from charcoal, sulfur, and potassium nitrate, also called saltpeter. When ignited, it burns rapidly and produces expanding gases that can propel a projectile or cause an explosion. Historically, makers dampened the mixture, pressed it into a paste, and broke it into grains in a process called corning. Gunpowder was used in weapons and became central to the Gunpowder Plot of 1605. Plotters, including Guy Fawkes, stored 36 barrels of gunpowder beneath England’s Parliament, intending to blow it up and kill King James I. Their plan was discovered before the explosion could happen. James I was the first Stuart king of England and commissioned the English Bible translation known as the King James Bible.

Scurvy is a disease caused by a severe lack of vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid. The body needs vitamin C to make collagen, a protein that helps hold tissues together and supports healthy gums, blood vessels, and skin. Without enough of it, people may develop bleeding gums, loose teeth, bruising, and wounds that heal slowly. Scurvy was once common among crews on long-distance sea voyages because fresh fruits and vegetables were hard to keep aboard ships. Eating foods that contain vitamin C, such as citrus fruits, prevents the disease. On land, scurvy became much less common in Europe after potatoes, a tuber brought from South America, became a widely eaten food. Potatoes provide vitamin C, especially when they are fresh and not overcooked.

A thylakoid is a flattened, disk-shaped compartment inside a chloroplast, the part of a plant cell that carries out photosynthesis. Thylakoids are surrounded by a membrane and are often arranged in stacks called grana. The light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis occur in the thylakoid membrane, where groups of proteins and pigments called photosystems capture light energy. Their main green pigment is chlorophyll, which absorbs mostly blue-violet and red light but reflects much of the green light we see in leaves. The captured energy helps make ATP, a molecule that supplies energy for the next stage of photosynthesis. That stage, the Calvin cycle, takes place in the fluid outside the thylakoids, called the stroma, where carbon dioxide is used to build sugars.

Naloxone is a medication that can rapidly reverse an opioid overdose. Opioids include prescription painkillers such as OxyContin, as well as heroin and fentanyl. During an overdose, opioids can slow or stop a person’s breathing. Naloxone is an opioid antagonist: it pushes opioids off receptors in the body, allowing breathing to return. It is often given as a nasal spray, commonly sold under the brand name Narcan. Its effects can wear off before the opioids do, so someone who receives naloxone still needs emergency medical care and may need another dose. In May 2022, Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker signed a law eliminating co-pays for a nasal-spray version of naloxone, making it easier for people to obtain this potentially lifesaving treatment.

A particle accelerator uses electric fields to speed up charged particles, such as ions or electrons, while magnetic fields can steer or confine their paths. Some accelerators send particles into a target; others make beams collide. Scientists study the results to learn about atomic nuclei and the smaller particles that make up matter. Accelerators can also help create synthetic elements—elements not normally found in nature—by forcing atomic nuclei together at high speeds. At Dubna, researchers used a particle accelerator to bombard americium-243 with calcium-48 ions. Some of the nuclei fused, producing atoms of moscovium, the synthetic element with atomic number 115. Moscovium is the heaviest element in group 15 of the periodic table, the group that also includes nitrogen.

Voyager 2 is a NASA spacecraft launched in 1977 to explore the outer solar system. It was the second of two Voyager probes to leave Earth, though it launched before Voyager 1. Voyager 2 flew past Jupiter and Saturn, then continued to Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989. It remains the only spacecraft to have visited both Uranus and Neptune, which are known as ice giants. During its Neptune flyby, Voyager 2 observed exceptionally fast winds and a large storm system called the Great Dark Spot. Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun, and its largest moon is Triton. After completing its planetary flybys, Voyager 2 continued outward, sending back information about the distant reaches of our solar system.

The period of a repeating motion is the time it takes to complete one full cycle. For a pendulum, a cycle means swinging from a starting position to the other side and back to the starting position, moving in the same direction as before. Period is usually measured in seconds and is often written as T. Frequency measures how many complete cycles happen each second; its unit is the hertz (Hz), meaning one cycle per second. Period and frequency are reciprocals: frequency equals 1 divided by period, and period equals 1 divided by frequency. For example, if a pendulum completes one cycle every 2 seconds, its period is 2 seconds and its frequency is 0.5 Hz.

Birch trees are deciduous trees in the genus Betula, meaning they shed their leaves each year. Many have pale trunks with bark that peels in thin layers, and they produce hanging clusters of flowers called catkins. One North American species, the paper birch, has especially bright white bark that curls away in thin sheets. Its scientific name is Betula papyrifera; “papyrifera” refers to its papery bark. Indigenous peoples traditionally used this light, flexible, water-resistant bark to make canoes. Birch trees also appear in literature: Robert Frost’s poem “Birches” imagines a boy swinging on their branches and describes a snow-white trunk. These features make birches recognizable in both forests and poetry.

A desert is a biome defined by very low precipitation, not necessarily by heat. Hot deserts include the Sahara, while Antarctica is a cold polar desert and the largest desert on Earth. With little available water, deserts usually have sparse vegetation and relatively low biodiversity, but plants and animals have adaptations that help them survive. Wind can shape sand into dunes or vast sand seas called ergs. In some places, groundwater from an underground layer called an aquifer reaches the surface, creating an oasis where plants and animals can find water. One Sahara animal is the fennec fox, a small canid whose oversized ears help release body heat and detect prey. Fur on its feet protects it from hot sand.

The placenta is a temporary organ that develops during pregnancy and forms an interface between the mother and the developing fetus. It attaches to the wall of the uterus and exchanges oxygen, nutrients, and waste products with the mother’s blood. The fetus is connected to the placenta by the umbilical cord, which carries oxygen and nutrients to the fetus and carries wastes away. The mother’s and fetus’s blood usually do not mix directly; substances pass across the placenta between them. After the baby is born, the umbilical cord is clamped and cut. The placenta is then expelled from the mother’s body during the third stage of labor. It is sometimes called the afterbirth.

Poinsot construction is a geometric way to picture how a rigid object, such as a spinning top, rotates when no outside torque acts on it. Without torque, its rotational kinetic energy and angular momentum stay constant. Angular momentum, symbolized L, is the rotational counterpart of ordinary momentum; torque is the rate at which it changes. In the construction, an imaginary shape called the inertia ellipsoid rolls without slipping on a fixed plane perpendicular to the conserved angular momentum. The point where the ellipsoid touches the plane traces two curves, depending on the viewpoint. On the ellipsoid, the curve is called the polhode and moves with the body. On the fixed plane, the curve is called the herpolhode.

Heat is energy transferred from one system or place to another because of a temperature difference. It normally flows from hotter regions to cooler ones. Unlike internal energy, which is energy stored within a system, heat describes energy in transit. Heat can travel by conduction, convection, or radiation. Conduction transfers energy through microscopic interactions between neighboring particles, without the material moving as a whole. For example, heat moves from the hot end of a metal spoon toward its cooler handle by conduction. Convection carries heat through the movement of a liquid or gas, while radiation transfers energy as electromagnetic waves and does not require matter. An adiabatic process allows no heat to enter or leave a system. Exothermic reactions release energy to their surroundings, often as heat.

Bay laurel is an evergreen tree native to the Mediterranean region. Its glossy, aromatic leaves are used in cooking as bay leaves, often to flavor soups and stews. In ancient Greece and Rome, laurel branches were woven into wreaths to crown winners, making the tree a symbol of victory and honor. Bay laurel was also sacred to Apollo, the Greek god associated with prophecy, music, and healing. According to a Greek myth, the nymph Daphne was transformed into a laurel tree while fleeing Apollo’s pursuit. Laurel was connected to Apollo’s oracle at Delphi, where a priestess called the Pythia delivered prophecies. Thus, the same tree links an everyday kitchen ingredient with ancient stories and ceremonies.

A chemical bond is an attractive interaction that holds atoms together to form substances. The three major types are ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds. An ionic bond commonly forms when a metal transfers one or more electrons to a nonmetal. The metal becomes a positively charged ion, and the nonmetal becomes a negatively charged ion; electrostatic attraction between these opposite charges holds them together. In a covalent bond, atoms share electrons rather than transfer them. If the atoms attract the shared electrons with different strengths, the bond can be polar, as in water. In a metallic bond, metal atoms are held together by attraction to a cloud of freely moving, delocalized electrons. Bonds join atoms, while weaker intermolecular forces act between molecules.

White blood cells are immune-system cells that circulate in the blood and help protect the body from infection. Unlike red blood cells, which carry oxygen, white blood cells recognize and respond to germs and other threats. They include several kinds of cells, such as neutrophils, basophils, and lymphocytes. One type of lymphocyte is the T cell, named for the thymus, the organ where it matures. Helper T cells coordinate immune responses by signaling to other immune cells, while cytotoxic, or “killer,” T cells destroy cells that have been infected. Different kinds of white blood cells work together, so the body can detect threats and fight them in more than one way.

Einsteinium is a synthetic, radioactive chemical element with the symbol Es and atomic number 99, meaning each atom has 99 protons. It belongs to the actinides, a group of heavy elements near the bottom of the periodic table. Einsteinium is named after physicist Albert Einstein, who developed the theory of special relativity and helped show how the motion of tiny particles in a liquid, called Brownian motion, provides evidence that atoms exist. Scientists first identified einsteinium in radioactive debris from Ivy Mike, a 1952 U.S. thermonuclear test at Enewetak Atoll. Ivy Mike was the first successful full-scale test of a hydrogen bomb. Only tiny amounts of einsteinium can be made, so it is used mainly in scientific research rather than everyday products.

Cygnus X-1 is a famous X-ray binary system in the constellation Cygnus. It consists of a massive, hot blue O-type supergiant star, cataloged as HDE 226868, and a compact object that is one of the strongest known stellar-mass black-hole candidates. The two objects orbit each other about once every 5.6 days. Gas from the supergiant’s powerful stellar wind is drawn toward the compact object, where it heats up as it flows inward and produces intense X-rays. Those X-rays, together with measurements of the orbit and the compact object’s mass, have made Cygnus X-1 a landmark in the study of black holes. Physicist Stephen Hawking famously lost a bet with Kip Thorne over whether the system contained a black hole.

Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state in a reversible reaction: reactants continue forming products, and products continue forming reactants, but the two processes occur at equal rates. As a result, their concentrations stay constant, although they are not necessarily equal. At a fixed temperature, the equilibrium constant, K, describes the ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium. If conditions change, the system may shift to counteract the change, as described by Le Châtelier’s principle. In electrochemistry, the Nernst equation relates an electrode’s potential to the activities or concentrations of the reacting species. It helps predict how the potential changes as a redox reaction proceeds. At equilibrium, it can also be used to relate the reaction’s standard electrode potential to its equilibrium constant, K.

A heterozygous genotype means an individual has two different versions, or alleles, of a gene at one location in their DNA. It is often written as Aa, with a capital and a lowercase letter. In the Hardy–Weinberg model, if the frequencies of two alleles are p and q, the expected frequency of heterozygous individuals is 2pq. Heterozygotes can sometimes have an evolutionary benefit over people with two identical alleles; this is called heterozygote advantage. For example, a person with one usual beta-globin allele and one sickle-cell allele has some protection against severe malaria. A person with two sickle-cell alleles, however, can develop sickle-cell disease. In regions where malaria is common, the benefit to heterozygotes helps keep the sickle-cell allele in the population.

RNA polymerase is the enzyme that carries out transcription, the process of making an RNA copy of a gene. It binds near the start of a gene at a DNA sequence called a promoter, reads one DNA strand as a template, and joins ribonucleotides together to build a growing RNA strand. The resulting messenger RNA, or mRNA, can carry instructions for making a protein. In bacteria, RNA polymerase relies on a detachable subunit called the sigma factor to find and recognize promoters. Sigma factor helps the enzyme identify characteristic promoter regions known as the −10 and −35 regions, named for their positions before the start of transcription. Once RNA polymerase begins making RNA, the sigma factor commonly detaches, while the enzyme continues along the gene.

A gravity-assist maneuver, also called a gravitational slingshot, lets a spacecraft change its speed and direction by flying close to a moving planet. The planet’s gravity bends the spacecraft’s path, while its motion around the Sun allows the spacecraft to exchange a tiny amount of momentum with it. Depending on the approach, the spacecraft can gain or lose speed relative to the Sun. The planet’s change in motion is too small to notice, but the spacecraft can save a great deal of fuel. This matters because spacecraft have limited propellant for changing their velocity, or “delta-v.” NASA’s Voyager 2 used a chain of gravity assists on its Grand Tour: it visited Jupiter and Saturn, then became the only spacecraft to fly past Uranus and Neptune.

The tesla (T) is the SI derived unit of magnetic flux density, which describes the strength and direction of a magnetic field. It is named after Nikola Tesla, a pioneer in electrical engineering and electromagnetism. Magnetic flux measures the total magnetic field passing through a surface, and its SI unit is the weber (Wb). Flux density describes how much magnetic flux passes through each unit of area, so one tesla equals one weber per square meter (1 T = 1 Wb/m²). For example, when electric current flows through a solenoid—a coil of wire—it creates a magnetic field. Each loop contributes to that field, whose flux density can be measured in teslas.

Photosystem II is the first major protein complex in the linear electron-transfer pathway of oxygenic photosynthesis. Embedded in the thylakoid membrane of plants, algae, and cyanobacteria, it absorbs light and uses that energy to extract electrons from water. Its reaction center, called P680, passes the energized electrons into an electron transport chain, helping the cell make energy-rich molecules for building sugars. On the side of Photosystem II facing the thylakoid lumen is the oxygen-evolving complex, a catalytic assembly containing a manganese-calcium cluster. This complex cycles through five stages, known as S-states, as it removes electrons from water. Splitting water replaces the electrons lost by P680 and releases molecular oxygen as a byproduct. It also releases protons into the lumen, helping drive ATP production.

Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and solidifies. Molten rock beneath Earth’s surface is called magma; when it erupts onto the surface, it is called lava. Magma that cools slowly underground forms intrusive igneous rocks, whose crystals have time to grow large. Granite is a coarse-grained intrusive rock that is usually felsic, meaning it is rich in silica, and it makes up large portions of the continents. Lava cools more quickly at the surface, forming extrusive igneous rocks such as basalt and rhyolite. Some extrusive rocks, including pumice and scoria, are full of holes left by trapped gas bubbles. Igneous rocks can also be classified by composition: basalt and scoria are generally mafic, or lower in silica, while granite and rhyolite are felsic.

Right ascension is a coordinate astronomers use to describe where an object appears on the celestial sphere, an imaginary sphere surrounding Earth. It plays the role that longitude plays on Earth, while declination plays the role of latitude. Right ascension starts at the vernal equinox, the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator moving north in March, and increases eastward around the sky. Instead of degrees, it is usually written in hours, minutes, and seconds: a full circle is 24 hours, so one hour of right ascension equals 15 degrees. Declination measures an object’s angular distance north or south of the celestial equator. It is expressed in degrees from −90° to +90°. Together, right ascension and declination let astronomers specify the position of a star or planet.

Thermohaline circulation is the planet-spanning movement of deep ocean water driven by differences in seawater density. “Thermo” refers to temperature, and “haline” refers to salinity, or the amount of dissolved salt. Cold water is generally denser than warm water, while saltier water is denser than fresher water. In some regions, cold, salty surface water sinks and then flows through the deep ocean, helping connect ocean basins. This differs from surface currents, which are driven mainly by wind. As ocean water moves, Earth’s rotation also affects its path. This apparent deflection is called the Coriolis effect: moving water bends to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

Nuclear fission occurs when a heavy atomic nucleus, such as uranium-235, absorbs a neutron and splits into smaller nuclei. The split releases energy and usually more neutrons, which can strike other nuclei and cause a chain reaction. If enough fissile material is assembled, the reaction can sustain itself; the minimum amount needed under particular conditions is called the critical mass. In a nuclear reactor, control rods containing materials such as boron-10 absorb neutrons to regulate the reaction rate. In December 1942, scientists built a graphite-and-uranium lattice called Chicago Pile-1 beneath Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. It produced the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. Fission differs from fusion, which releases energy by joining light nuclei rather than splitting a heavy one.

A comet is a small body made of ice, dust, and rock that travels around the Sun. Its solid center is called the nucleus. As the comet approaches the Sun, sunlight warms its frozen material. Some ice changes directly from a solid into a gas without becoming liquid first; this phase change is called sublimation. The escaping gas carries dust away from the nucleus, forming a diffuse, fuzzy cloud around it called the coma. A coma can grow much larger than the nucleus, even though its gas and dust are spread thinly through space. Sunlight and the stream of charged particles from the Sun push material away from the coma, helping form the comet’s tails.

Stainless steel is an iron-based alloy, meaning it is a mixture of iron and other elements. Like ordinary steel, it usually contains carbon, but it also contains a substantial amount of chromium. When chromium at the surface reacts with oxygen, it forms a thin protective oxide layer that helps prevent the iron underneath from rusting. If the surface is scratched, this layer can form again, helping stainless steel resist corrosion over time. Stainless steel can also be polished to a bright, mirror-like finish. Sculptor Anish Kapoor used it for the reflective exterior of Cloud Gate, the sculpture nicknamed “the Bean” in Chicago’s Millennium Park. Its curved surface reflects the city and the people standing around it, making it a popular place for photos.

Cumulonimbus clouds are towering storm clouds that can extend through much of the troposphere, the lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere. They form when warm, moist air rises, cools, and condenses into cloud droplets. Powerful upward currents can build these clouds high enough to produce thunderstorms, lightning, heavy rain, hail, and sometimes tornadoes. Strong winds near the cloud tops may spread them sideways into a broad, flattened cap called an anvil. A pyrocumulonimbus cloud forms when intense heat from a wildfire drives air upward, creating a thundercloud above the fire. In August 2020, a pyrocumulonimbus spawned a tornado in Lassen County, California, prompting the National Weather Service’s first warning for a tornado produced by this type of cloud.

Xylem is the vascular tissue that carries water and dissolved mineral ions from a plant’s roots toward its stems and leaves. Roots absorb water from the soil, and xylem moves it through long conducting cells called tracheids and vessel elements. In woody plants, the vascular cambium produces new xylem toward the inside of the stem; much of this xylem becomes wood. Xylem differs from phloem, which transports sugars made by photosynthesis. Water does not need an active pump in the stem to rise through xylem. As water evaporates from leaf surfaces during transpiration, it creates tension that pulls a continuous column of water upward. This mechanism is called transpiration pull.

The alkali metals are the highly reactive elements in Group 1 of the periodic table, including lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, cesium, and francium. Each has one electron in its outermost shell, which it can lose easily when forming compounds. Their reactivity generally increases down the group, so they are stored carefully, often under oil, to keep them from reacting with air or water. Alkali metals are also near the top of the metal activity series, meaning they can readily replace less reactive metals in some compounds. Cesium, the Group 1 element with atomic number 55, has a pale-gold appearance. A particular transition in cesium-133 atoms is used to define the second in atomic timekeeping.

Gymnosperms are seed-producing plants whose name means “naked seeds.” Their ovules and seeds are not enclosed inside an ovary; instead, the seeds often develop on the scales of cones. Gymnosperms include conifers, such as pines and firs, as well as cycads, ginkgo, and gnetophytes. Many conifers are evergreen, meaning they keep their leaves throughout the year, but being evergreen is not what defines a gymnosperm. The key difference is how the seeds are held. Angiosperms, the other major group of seed-producing plants, are flowering plants. Their ovules are enclosed within an ovary, which usually develops into a fruit containing the seeds. A pine cone and an apple show this contrast: the pine’s seeds are exposed on cone scales, while the apple’s seeds are enclosed in fruit.

The Curie point, also called the Curie temperature, is the temperature at which a ferromagnetic material loses its spontaneous magnetization and becomes paramagnetic. Below this point, interactions between atomic magnetic moments help keep many of them aligned, allowing materials such as iron to act as magnets. As the material heats up, thermal motion disrupts that alignment. Above the Curie point, the material can still respond to an external magnetic field, but it no longer stays magnetized on its own. The point is named for Pierre Curie, who studied how temperature affects magnetism. Another French physicist, Pierre Weiss, developed a molecular-field explanation of ferromagnetism and proposed that magnets contain domains: small regions in which magnetic moments point in the same direction.

A light microscope uses visible light and glass lenses to make small specimens appear larger. A typical compound light microscope has a stage that holds a slide, an objective lens near the specimen, and an eyepiece you look through; together, the lenses can magnify an image up to about 1,000 times. A drop of pond water on a slide may contain microorganisms such as Euglena, Paramecium, and amoebas. An amoeba is a single-celled organism with no fixed shape. It moves slowly by extending parts of its cell called pseudopodia, or “false feet,” and it can surround and engulf food by a process called phagocytosis. In contrast, a Paramecium moves quickly using many tiny, hair-like structures called cilia.

A fire is rapid combustion: fuel reacts with an oxidizer, usually oxygen in the air, releasing heat and often light and smoke. When a fire grows out of control, it can destroy buildings, industrial facilities, and forests, as well as threaten lives. Ordinary combustion needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and enough heat to start and sustain the reaction. These requirements form the fire triangle. Removing any one of them can suppress a fire: water can cool burning material, a fire blanket can block oxygen, and clearing dry vegetation can remove fuel. Fires have caused major disasters, including the 1871 Great Chicago Fire, the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire, and a 1969 fire on Ohio’s heavily polluted Cuyahoga River.

A series connection places electrical components one after another along a single path, with no branches between them. Because there is only one route for electric charge to travel, the same current passes through every component. Resistors oppose the flow of current, and in a series connection their resistances add directly: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3, and so on. This total is called the equivalent resistance because one resistor with that value would have the same overall effect on the circuit as the group of resistors. For example, a 2-ohm resistor and a 3-ohm resistor in series have an equivalent resistance of 5 ohms. This differs from a parallel connection, where components provide separate paths for current.

Penguins are flightless aquatic birds native to the Southern Hemisphere. Their wings have evolved into flippers that help them swim through the water, where they hunt fish, squid, and krill. Several species live in or around Antarctica, including Adélie penguins and emperor penguins, while the Galápagos penguin lives near the equator and is the northernmost penguin species. The emperor penguin is the largest living penguin. It breeds on Antarctic ice during the polar winter, when conditions are extremely cold and dark. After the female lays a single egg, the male balances it on his feet beneath a warm fold of skin called a brood pouch. He keeps the egg off the ice and incubates it while the female travels to sea to feed.

Dolphins are aquatic mammals in the cetacean group, which also includes whales and porpoises. Their streamlined bodies and powerful tails help them swim efficiently, while their intelligence and social behavior allow many species to live and hunt in groups called pods. Like other mammals, dolphins breathe air through lungs and must surface regularly. They can also find their way and locate prey when underwater visibility is poor by using echolocation. A dolphin produces a train of high-frequency clicks, then interprets the echoes that bounce back from fish, obstacles, or the seafloor. The time it takes for an echo to return helps the dolphin judge an object’s distance, while other features of the echo reveal its position and shape.

Mark Zuckerberg is an American technology entrepreneur best known for co-founding Facebook and serving as its chief executive. While studying at Harvard University, he created Facemash, a website that let students compare photos of their classmates. In 2004, he and fellow students launched Facebook as a social-networking service for college students. It later grew into a platform used around the world to share posts, photos, and messages. Facebook’s engineers developed Hack, a programming language based on PHP, to help build its services. The company has also faced criticism over how it handles personal information. In the Cambridge Analytica scandal, data from millions of Facebook users was obtained and used for political profiling, raising concerns about privacy and the responsibilities of social media companies.

Shedd Aquarium is a public aquarium on Chicago’s Museum Campus, beside Lake Michigan. It opened in 1930 after a major gift from Chicago businessman and philanthropist John G. Shedd, for whom it is named. Visitors can observe aquatic animals and learn about their habitats in exhibits such as Caribbean Reef and Waters of the World. The aquarium also supports research and conservation efforts that help scientists understand and protect aquatic life. Next door is the Field Museum of Natural History, whose collections include Sue, a famous and remarkably well-preserved Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton. Knowing these neighboring landmarks helps distinguish the aquarium, which focuses on life in water, from the Field Museum, which explores natural history more broadly.

Linear molecular geometry describes a molecule in which two atoms are bonded to a central atom and lie on opposite sides of it, forming a straight line with a bond angle of 180 degrees. VSEPR theory explains this shape: regions of electrons around a central atom repel one another and arrange themselves as far apart as possible. In gaseous beryllium fluoride, BeF₂, the central beryllium atom (atomic number 4) is bonded to two fluorine atoms. Its two bonding regions point in opposite directions, so the gas has linear molecular geometry. Beryllium fluoride can have a different arrangement in its liquid form, where beryllium has a tetrahedral arrangement with four surrounding fluorine atoms. By comparison, methane is tetrahedral and has bond angles of about 109.5 degrees.

Guano is the accumulated droppings of seabirds or bats. It is especially rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, nutrients that help plants grow, so farmers have long valued it as a powerful fertilizer. In the 19th century, huge seabird colonies left deep guano deposits on islands off the coast of Peru. Peru became the center of a major international trade, exporting the material to countries seeking to improve farmland. Guano was also valuable because its nitrogen compounds could be used to make saltpeter, an ingredient in gunpowder. Although even pigeon droppings were collected for this purpose, the word “guano” is most closely associated with large seabird and bat deposits.

Turbidity is a measure of how cloudy a liquid is, or how much its clarity is reduced by suspended particles. In water, tiny bits of sediment, algae, or other material can scatter light, making the water look cloudy. Turbidity is important in water-quality monitoring because high turbidity can signal pollution or make it harder for light to reach aquatic plants. A nephelometer measures turbidity by shining light into a water sample and detecting the light scattered at roughly a right angle to the beam. Cloudy mixtures called colloids also scatter light; this visible scattering is known as the Tyndall effect. Unlike a clear solution, in which a solute is dissolved in a solvent, a colloid contains particles dispersed throughout another substance.

Caenorhabditis elegans, often shortened to C. elegans, is a transparent soil-dwelling nematode, or roundworm, about one millimeter long. Scientists use it as a model organism because it is easy to raise in a laboratory, develops quickly, and lets researchers watch its cells as it grows. It has helped them study how genes control development, and in 1998 it became the first multicellular organism to have its complete genome sequenced. Working with C. elegans, Andrew Fire and Craig Mello found that introducing double-stranded RNA could silence a gene with a matching sequence. This process is called RNA interference, or RNAi: the RNA helps cells identify and break down matching messenger RNA before it can be used to make a protein. Fire and Mello shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discovery.

Vostok 1 was the Soviet spacecraft that carried Yuri Gagarin on the first human journey into space. On 12 April 1961, Gagarin, a Soviet Air Force pilot and cosmonaut, became the first person to orbit Earth. He completed one orbit in a flight lasting about 108 minutes before returning safely. Vostok 1 was a major achievement in the Space Race between the Soviet Union and the United States. It followed two earlier Soviet milestones: Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth, launched in 1957, and Sputnik 2, which carried the dog Laika, the first creature to orbit Earth. Gagarin’s flight showed that a human could travel into space and survive the journey home.

An aircraft wing extends outward from an airplane’s fuselage and generates the lift that helps keep it in the air. As the wing moves forward, its airfoil shape and angle to the airflow affect the pressure around it and deflect air downward, producing an upward force. A curved shape called camber can help a wing generate lift even at zero angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air. Wings often carry flaps, which change lift for takeoff and landing, and ailerons, which help the airplane roll or turn. In an idealized airflow, the Kutta–Joukowski theorem relates lift per unit span to air density, freestream speed, and circulation around the wing: L′ = ρVΓ.

Voltammetry is a family of electroanalytical techniques used to study how substances gain or lose electrons. An instrument varies the electrical potential, or voltage, applied to a sample and records the resulting current.
