Changes in current can reveal when an analyte, the substance being studied, undergoes reduction (gains electrons) or oxidation (loses electrons). A typical voltammetry cell has three electrodes. The working electrode is where the analyte is oxidized or reduced, and its potential is varied relative to the reference electrode, which provides a stable comparison. A third, counter electrode completes the electrical circuit. In cyclic voltammetry, the potential is swept in one direction and then reversed, helping scientists investigate redox behavior and estimate reduction potentials.

Chitin is a tough structural polysaccharide, or long chain of linked sugar molecules. It helps form the cell walls of many fungi and the protective outer skeletons, called exoskeletons, of arthropods such as insects, crabs, and spiders. Chitin is built from repeating units of N-acetylglucosamine, an amino sugar derived from glucose. “N-acetyl” refers to a small chemical group attached to its nitrogen-containing amino group. Many chitin chains can pack together to provide strength and support. Chitin has a role similar to cellulose, which strengthens plant cell walls, but the two polymers have different building blocks. Remember the distinction: chitin is the whole structural polymer, while N-acetylglucosamine is the repeating sugar unit that makes it up.

A wave function is a mathematical description of the quantum state of a particle, such as an electron. It is commonly symbolized by the Greek letter psi (ψ). Unlike a map showing exactly where a particle is, a wave function helps predict where it might be found: its squared magnitude gives the probability density, or how likely the particle is to be found near a particular location. The wave function can change over time according to the Schrödinger equation, named after Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger. He also imagined a cat sealed in a box with poison to explore a puzzling question in quantum mechanics: how can a system have several possible outcomes before it is observed, yet produce just one result when measured?

Steve Jobs was an American technology entrepreneur who co-founded Apple with Steve Wozniak in 1976. Wozniak designed the early Apple I and Apple II computers, while Jobs helped turn their work into a business. After a dispute with Apple executive John Sculley, Jobs left the company in 1985 and founded NeXT, which made computers and software. He also invested in the animation company that grew out of Lucasfilm’s computer division: Pixar Animation Studios. Pixar became famous for computer-animated films and for its logo, in which a hopping desk lamp squashes the letter I. Disney acquired Pixar in 2006. Apple later bought NeXT, bringing Jobs back; he became Apple’s CEO and helped lead the development of products such as the iMac and iPhone. He died in 2011.

Opportunity was a NASA rover that explored the surface of Mars. It landed in January 2004 at Meridiani Planum, inside a small impact crater called Eagle crater. There, it studied exposed bedrock and tiny iron-rich spheres nicknamed “blueberries,” which helped scientists investigate evidence that water had once been present. Opportunity was designed to work for just 90 sols, or Martian days, but it kept exploring for nearly 15 years and traveled much farther than expected. A planet-wide dust storm in 2018 blocked the sunlight its solar panels needed, and NASA lost contact with the rover. Its long mission gave scientists a much richer picture of Mars’s geology and past environment than they had originally planned.

Pewter is an alloy, meaning a material made by combining two or more elements. Its main ingredient is tin. In a traditional formulation, tin is blended with antimony, a metalloid whose chemical symbol is Sb. Metalloids have properties between those of metals and nonmetals; adding antimony makes pewter harder and more durable than pure tin. For centuries, people used pewter to make household vessels such as dishes, pitchers, and drinking tankards because it was easy to shape and had a silvery appearance. Some older pewter also contained lead, which is toxic, so it is not considered safe for food or drink. The key distinction is that pewter is the name of the finished tin-based alloy, while antimony is one of the elements mixed into it.

An organic compound is a carbon-containing chemical, usually built around bonds between carbon atoms and other elements such as hydrogen and oxygen. Organic compounds are often associated with living things and biological processes, but they can also be manufactured in factories. Sugars, benzene, and formaldehyde are all organic compounds, even though their structures and uses differ greatly. Formaldehyde is used mainly to make resins for products such as particle board and laminate flooring. Industry produces it by oxidizing methanol, the simplest alcohol. Methanol has just one carbon atom and the formula CH₃OH; it is also called methyl alcohol. Oxidation changes methanol into formaldehyde, showing how one organic compound can be converted into another.

Homolytic cleavage, also called homolytic fission, happens when a covalent bond breaks and the two atoms split its shared pair of electrons evenly: each atom keeps one electron. This produces fragments called free radicals, which have at least one unpaired electron and are often highly reactive. It does not produce the oppositely charged ions formed when both bonding electrons go to one atom. Chemists use single-headed “fishhook” arrows to show how individual electrons move during homolytic cleavage. Breaking a bond this way requires energy; the amount needed to separate one mole of bonded atoms into radical fragments is called the bond-dissociation energy, usually measured in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol). Light can supply the energy to split bonds in halogen molecules, producing radicals that react with alkanes.

A Bayer designation names a star using a Greek letter followed by the name of its constellation. Traditionally, the brightest star in a constellation is given the letter Alpha, the second-brightest Beta, and so on. For example, Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is Alpha Canis Majoris because it belongs to the constellation Canis Major. The lettering does not always match a star’s current brightness ranking. In Orion, Betelgeuse is called Alpha Orionis, but Rigel, called Beta Orionis, often appears brighter. Betelgeuse also varies in brightness over time. Orion is easy to recognize because three bright stars in a row form an asterism known as Orion’s Belt.

Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter, a chemical messenger that carries signals between cells. When you decide to move, motor neurons release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, the small gap between a nerve ending and a skeletal-muscle fiber. It binds to receptors on the muscle fiber, starting electrical changes that trigger contraction. Acetylcholine also sends signals in the nervous system, where one class of its receptors is called nicotinic receptors. These receptors are ligand-gated ion channels: when acetylcholine binds, they open and let charged particles flow through, helping pass on a signal. Nicotine can activate the same receptors in the brain, which contributes to its addictive effects. Thus, the messenger that triggers skeletal-muscle contraction is acetylcholine, and the receptor class activated by both acetylcholine and nicotine is nicotinic receptors.

Genetic linkage is the tendency of genes that lie close together on the same chromosome to be inherited together. Chromosomes carry genes, and during meiosis, the cell division that produces sperm or eggs, matching chromosomes can exchange sections in a process called crossing over. Crossing over may separate linked genes, but it is less likely to occur between genes that are very close together than between genes farther apart. By studying how often traits were inherited together in fruit flies, American geneticist Thomas Hunt Morgan helped show that genes are arranged on chromosomes. This work provided classic evidence for genetic linkage and helped scientists map the positions of genes. Morgan received the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his discoveries about the role of chromosomes in heredity.

Joseph Priestley was an English chemist and theologian who isolated oxygen in 1774. He focused sunlight through a lens to heat mercuric oxide, a compound of mercury and oxygen, and collected the gas it released. Priestley called it “dephlogisticated air” because he interpreted his results using phlogiston theory, an older explanation of burning. Antoine Lavoisier later showed that combustion requires this gas, helping replace phlogiston theory with a new understanding of chemical reactions. Today the gas is called oxygen. Its chemical symbol is O, it makes up about 21% of Earth’s atmosphere, and it combines with hydrogen to form water.

Molting is the process in which an animal sheds and replaces its outer covering. Snakes molt by loosening and shedding their old skin, often in one piece. Insects, spiders, and crustaceans are arthropods, animals with a hard outer covering called an exoskeleton. Because that covering cannot grow along with them, they periodically shed its outer layer, or cuticle, so a larger one can take its place. Molting is also called ecdysis. The cast-off covering is called exuviae; for example, the empty shell left clinging to a tree after a cicada emerges is its exuviae. A newly molted arthropod’s replacement covering is soft at first and then hardens, giving the animal room to grow until its next molt.

Alfred Russel Wallace was a British naturalist who studied how plants and animals vary across different places. While exploring the Malay Archipelago in Southeast Asia, he independently developed the idea of evolution by natural selection: individuals with traits that help them survive and reproduce are more likely to pass those traits to their offspring. In 1858, Wallace sent Charles Darwin an essay explaining this idea, prompting the two scientists to present their findings jointly. Wallace also noticed a striking difference in animal life between the nearby islands of Bali and Lombok. Animals west of this divide were mainly Asian, while those to the east were more closely related to Australasian species. The boundary became known as the Wallace Line, an important example of how geography shapes where species live.

Colony collapse disorder occurs when most adult worker bees suddenly disappear from a managed honey-bee colony, leaving the queen, developing young, and food stores behind. Worker bees are the caste that gathers nectar and pollen, cares for young bees, and performs much of the hive’s daily work. Without enough workers, a colony may be unable to survive, even if it still has food. Scientists have not identified one single cause of colony collapse disorder. Possible contributing factors include disease-causing pathogens spread by Varroa mites, poor nutrition, pesticide exposure, and other stresses. Honey bees, which belong to the genus Apis, pollinate many flowering plants and communicate the location of food through a waggle dance.

Reptiles are vertebrates, meaning they have backbones, and most are ectothermic: they rely largely on their surroundings to regulate body temperature. They usually have dry, scaly skin that helps reduce water loss. Reptiles include turtles, lizards, crocodilians, and snakes. Their young develop inside an amnion, a protective membrane; many reptiles lay shelled eggs on land, while some give birth to live young. Snakes are limbless reptiles that include the king cobra and Burmese python. They flick their forked tongues to collect chemical cues from the air and ground, helping them find prey. Many snakes swallow prey whole. Some, such as cobras, use venom to subdue prey, while others, such as pythons, use constriction. As snakes grow, they periodically shed their outer skin in a process called molting or ecdysis.

Krubera Cave is a deep natural cave in the Arabika Massif of Abkhazia, a territory in the Caucasus near the Black Sea whose principal city is Sukhumi. Long recognized as the world’s deepest known cave, Krubera extends more than two kilometers below its entrance. It formed in a karst landscape, where groundwater slowly dissolves limestone and other soluble rock, creating underground passages and shafts. Water can also deposit minerals inside caves, forming stalactites that hang from ceilings and stalagmites that grow upward from floors. Exploring Krubera’s steep passages requires specialized equipment and skill; people who explore caves are called spelunkers or cavers. Its great depth makes Krubera an important site for studying how water shapes the ground beneath Earth’s surface.

Grace Brewster Murray Hopper was an American computer scientist and U.S. Navy rear admiral who helped make computers easier to program. At a time when programmers often had to write instructions in forms close to machine code, she championed languages that used English-like words. Her work on FLOW-MATIC helped shape COBOL, a programming language designed for business data processing that became widely used in commercial applications. Hopper also helped popularize the terms “bug” and “debugging” for computer problems and the work of fixing them. In a famous incident, her team found an actual moth trapped in a computer relay and recorded it in a logbook. Hopper’s ideas influenced how people write programs and use computers today.

Steve Wozniak is an American computer engineer who co-founded Apple Computer with Steve Jobs and Ronald Wayne in 1976. Nicknamed “Woz,” he designed the Apple I, an early personal computer sold as an assembled circuit board. He then designed the Apple II, introduced in 1977. Unlike the Apple I, the Apple II came in a plastic case with a built-in keyboard and could display color graphics. Owners could also expand it by adding hardware for new functions. These features helped make the Apple II a successful home computer and established Apple’s reputation in personal computing. Jobs focused on selling and promoting the computers, while Wozniak’s engineering made the early machines possible.

The second, written with the symbol s, is the SI base unit of time. It measures duration: how long something lasts or how much time passes between two events. For example, a short race might take 12 seconds, and 60 seconds make one minute. Scientists define the second using cesium-133, a particular isotope of cesium. When a cesium-133 atom changes between two closely spaced energy states in its ground state, it is associated with microwave radiation of a very precise frequency. Exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles of that radiation occur in one second. This definition lets atomic clocks measure time consistently and with extraordinary precision. Time also appears in calculations such as speed, which equals distance divided by time.

Feathers are lightweight structures made chiefly of keratin, the protein also found in hair and nails. They cover modern birds, helping keep them warm, protect their skin, and create the aerodynamic surfaces needed for flight. Fossils show that some non-avian dinosaurs had feathers too, although scientists do not know whether Tyrannosaurus rex was fully feathered. A feather has a central shaft with branching parts that can form a broad, flexible surface. The flight feathers attached to a bird’s wings are collectively called remiges. These include the primaries, attached to the hand and especially important for forward thrust, and the secondaries, attached along the forearm and important for lift. Tail feathers have a different name, rectrices, and are not remiges.

Ciliophora is a phylum of mostly single-celled protists called ciliates. They have many tiny hairlike structures called cilia, which beat in coordinated waves to help them move through water or sweep food toward their mouths. Unlike most cells, ciliates typically have two kinds of nucleus: a large macronucleus that controls everyday activities and a smaller micronucleus involved in reproduction. Two ciliate genera are Vorticella and Stentor. Stentor includes large freshwater ciliates known as trumpet animalcules because their bodies often spread out like trumpets. They can attach to surfaces using a holdfast and rapidly contract into a compact shape when disturbed. Some Stentor species are a striking blue-green color.

The black mamba is a large, fast-moving venomous snake native to sub-Saharan Africa. Its scientific name is Dendroaspis polylepis. Despite its name, its scales are usually olive, gray, or brown; “black” refers to the dark lining inside its mouth, which it may display when threatened. Like other snakes, it is a legless reptile that moves by slithering and swallows prey whole. Its venom attacks the nervous system and can be deadly without prompt medical treatment. The black mamba belongs to Elapidae, a family of front-fanged venomous snakes that also includes cobras and kraits. These snakes use fixed fangs near the front of their mouths to inject venom into prey or in self-defense.

A chemical element is a pure substance whose atoms all have the same number of protons in their nuclei. That number is the element’s atomic number: every hydrogen atom has one proton, while every bismuth atom has 83. Elements appear on the periodic table, and modern chemistry recognizes 118 of them. Long before scientists understood atoms, the ancient Greek thinker Empedocles proposed that everything was made from four “roots”: air, water, earth, and fire. He believed that two forces, Love and Strife, governed how these roots came together or separated. His four roots were an early attempt to explain what matter is made of, but they are not chemical elements in the modern sense.

Self-driving cars, also called driverless cars, use sensors, cameras, maps, and computer systems to navigate roads and make driving decisions with limited or no human control. Their systems must detect other vehicles, pedestrians, and obstacles, then choose actions such as braking or steering. This raises difficult ethical questions when a crash appears unavoidable: what should the car do if one action might save its passengers but put pedestrians at greater risk? The Moral Machine project studies these dilemmas by asking people online to choose between outcomes in imagined crash scenarios, such as saving one group of road users rather than another. Researchers use the responses to explore people’s moral judgments, though deciding how a real car should act also involves safety rules, laws, and engineering.

An up quark is the lightest of the six quark flavors. Quarks are tiny particles that combine to form hadrons, including protons and neutrons. A proton has three valence quarks: two up quarks and one down quark. Each up quark has an electric charge of +2/3 of the elementary charge, written +2/3e, while a down quark has a charge of −1/3e. Adding the charges in a proton gives +2/3e + 2/3e − 1/3e = +1e. That is why a proton has one positive elementary charge. The up quark’s name describes its flavor, or type; it does not mean the particle points upward.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, are a large group of thousands of human-made chemicals whose strong carbon–fluorine bonds make many of them slow to break down. They have been used in nonstick coatings, water- and stain-resistant products, and some firefighting foams. Because some PFAS can remain in the environment for years, they are often called “forever chemicals.” Their persistence, along with concerns about possible health effects, has led to efforts to limit their use. One well-known PFAS is perfluorooctanesulfonic acid, abbreviated PFOS. It is an eight-carbon perfluoroalkane sulfonate that was a key ingredient in older Scotchgard formulations designed to repel water and stains. The manufacturer 3M began phasing out PFOS production in 2000.

Arsenic is a chemical element with the symbol As and atomic number 33. It is a metalloid, meaning it has some properties of both metals and nonmetals, and it belongs to group 15 of the periodic table. Nitrogen is also in group 15, two rows above arsenic. Arsenic and many of its compounds are poisonous to humans, but people did not always understand the danger. In the 19th century, arsenic compounds were used in cosmetics and colorful products. One example was Emerald Green, a vivid pigment made with arsenic and copper compounds. It appeared in wallpapers and was sometimes used in cosmetics. As its toxic effects became better known, these uses were abandoned.

Ecological succession is the gradual change in the species and structure of an ecosystem over time. In primary succession, life begins to establish itself on a surface with little or no soil, such as bare rock exposed when glaciers retreat. Glaciers are immense, slow-moving bodies of ice that can carve valleys and lose mass through melting or calving, when chunks of ice break off. Pioneer species, such as lichens and mosses, help break down rock and build soil, making the area suitable for other plants and animals. Secondary succession happens after a disturbance, such as a wildfire, in a place where soil remains. As species arrive, grow, and interact, the ecosystem changes and may eventually become relatively stable.

Soil liquefaction happens when loose, water-saturated sediment temporarily loses its strength and stiffness and behaves more like a fluid. The spaces between soil grains contain water; during strong earthquake shaking, pressure in that water can rise, reducing the contact between grains that normally helps the ground support weight. As a result, buildings may tilt or sink, and the ground may spread or crack. Liquefaction can also destabilize a slope, allowing soil and rock to move downhill. This downslope movement belongs to a broad hazard category called landslides, which also includes rockfalls and debris flows. Not every landslide involves liquefaction: heavy rain, erosion, volcanic activity, or earthquakes can trigger landslides in other ways.

Jade is a gemstone name used chiefly for two different materials: nephrite and jadeite. Both are tough enough to be shaped into detailed carvings, and their colors range from pale white to deep green. In Chinese history, jade was especially valued for ritual objects, burial goods, and ornaments, and it became a symbol of virtue, status, and spiritual power. Its cultural importance is reflected in the name of the Jade Emperor, a heavenly ruler in Chinese mythology. Jadeite is a sodium-aluminum mineral in the pyroxene group. Its vivid green varieties, colored by chromium, are prized as “imperial jade,” and major jadeite deposits are found in Myanmar. Although nephrite and jadeite are different materials, either may be sold or described as jade.

Benjamin Spock was an American pediatrician whose 1946 parenting manual, Baby and Child Care, became a trusted guide for families raising children after World War II, including many Baby Boomers. Instead of telling parents to follow strict rules, Spock encouraged them to trust their own judgment and respond warmly to their children’s needs. His reassuring advice helped shift parenting away from a more authoritarian approach. Spock was also interested in how children develop: he helped found the Arsenal center for child psychology in Pittsburgh with Erik Erikson and Margaret McFarland. Later in life, he became a prominent opponent of the Vietnam War and was the People’s Party’s presidential nominee in 1972.

Oysters are marine bivalve mollusks, relatives of clams and mussels. Their two-part shells protect their soft bodies, and many oysters attach to rocks or other hard surfaces as they grow. People cultivate oysters for food, while some varieties are raised for pearls, which form when the animal coats an irritant inside its shell. Oyster farmers sometimes produce triploid oysters. Triploidy means having three sets of chromosomes instead of the usual two sets, a condition called diploidy. Chromosomes carry genetic information, and their number affects how an animal develops and reproduces. Triploid oysters generally cannot reproduce normally, so they do not have the usual spawning period. This can help keep their meat suitable for eating throughout the year.

A solid-state drive, or SSD, is a computer storage device that keeps files, programs, and the operating system even when the power is off. It is called secondary storage because it holds data for the long term, unlike RAM, which temporarily holds data while a computer is running. SSDs commonly use NAND flash memory, a type of nonvolatile semiconductor memory. “NAND” is also the name of a logic gate that outputs false only when both inputs are true. Unlike a hard disk drive, an SSD has no spinning platters or moving read/write head, so it can usually access data faster. SSDs may connect to a computer through SATA or through PCIe using the NVMe protocol.

Dopamine is a chemical messenger, or neurotransmitter, that helps brain cells communicate. It is a catecholamine made in several brain regions and plays roles in controlling movement, motivation, and reward-related signaling. Dopamine is often linked with pleasure, but it is especially important in anticipating rewards and learning which actions may lead to them. In Parkinson’s disease, dopamine-producing neurons gradually degenerate in a midbrain region called the substantia nigra. This darkly pigmented nucleus gets its Latin name, meaning “black substance,” from its appearance, which is partly due to a pigment called neuromelanin. The loss of these neurons reduces dopamine signaling in circuits that control movement, contributing to symptoms such as tremor, stiffness, and slowed movement.

Cosmic dust is made of tiny solid grains found throughout space, including between stars, around planets, and in comets. Some grains form when material from stellar winds or supernovas cools and condenses. Dust between stars absorbs and scatters more blue light than red light, making distant stars appear redder; this effect is called interstellar reddening. Within our Solar System, cosmic dust is concentrated near the plane of the planets’ orbits, called the ecliptic. When these grains scatter sunlight, they produce zodiacal light, a faint, roughly triangular glow visible along the ecliptic after twilight or before dawn. Comets contain ice mixed with dust, and NASA’s Stardust mission returned dust samples from comet Wild 2 in 2006.

Heat capacity measures how much heat energy must be added to an object to raise its temperature by one degree Celsius or one kelvin. A larger heat capacity means the object needs more energy for the same temperature rise. Heat capacity depends on both the material and how much of it there is; specific heat capacity is measured per unit mass, while molar heat capacity is measured per mole. For many solid elements at sufficiently high temperatures, the molar heat capacity is approximately 3R, where R is the gas constant. This classical result is called the Dulong–Petit law, named after two French physicists. It is an approximation, not a rule that works equally well for every solid at every temperature, especially at low temperatures.

Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis that causes sudden attacks of intense joint pain, redness, warmth, and swelling. It often first affects the joint at the base of the big toe, although other joints can be affected. Gout happens when urate crystals build up in a joint and trigger inflammation. These crystals form from uric acid, a waste product the body makes when it breaks down purines, substances found naturally in our cells and in some foods. Normally, the kidneys filter uric acid from the blood so it can leave the body in urine. If too much uric acid builds up, crystals may form in joints and cause gout; uric acid crystals can also contribute to kidney stones.

Bill Gates is an American programmer and entrepreneur who left Harvard before completing his degree to start Microsoft with his former schoolmate Paul Allen. Microsoft became one of the world’s most influential software companies, developing the MS-DOS operating system and later Windows, which helped make personal computers widely used. Gates served as Microsoft’s CEO and became one of the world’s wealthiest people. He later focused much of his work on philanthropy through a foundation established with his then-wife Melinda, supporting projects such as public health and education. Bill and Melinda Gates also joined Warren Buffett, the Berkshire Hathaway chairman nicknamed the “Oracle of Omaha,” to launch the Giving Pledge. This campaign encourages the world’s wealthiest people to promise to give most of their fortunes to charitable causes.

An oxidation state, also called an oxidation number, is a formal value chemists assign to an atom to keep track of electrons in a compound or reaction. It represents the charge the atom would have if bonding electrons were assigned according to a set of rules. Changes in oxidation state help show whether an atom has been oxidized or reduced. In a neutral compound, the oxidation states of all its atoms add up to zero. For example, potassium permanganate has the formula KMnO₄. Potassium has an oxidation state of +1, and each of its four oxygen atoms has an oxidation state of −2, giving the oxygens a total of −8. For the sum to be zero, manganese must have an oxidation state of +7.

A transistor is a small semiconductor device that controls the flow of electric current in a circuit. It can act as an electronic switch, turning current on or off, or as an amplifier, making a weak signal stronger. Because transistors are solid-state devices with no moving parts, they replaced many bulky vacuum tubes and helped make radios, computers, and other electronics smaller and more reliable. The transistor radio was an early, well-known example. The first point-contact transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in 1947 by John Bardeen and Walter Brattain. Their colleague, physicist William Shockley, later developed a different type called the junction transistor. Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for their work on semiconductors and transistors.

Ocean acidification is the decrease in ocean pH that happens mainly when seawater absorbs carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas released in large amounts by burning fossil fuels. Its atmospheric concentration has been measured at the Mauna Loa Observatory and plotted over time on the Keeling Curve. When dissolved CO2 reacts with seawater, it forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions and lowers the water’s pH. These reactions also reduce the carbonate ions that many marine organisms need to build shells and skeletons. As a result, ocean acidification can make it harder for animals such as oysters and corals to grow and survive. The ocean is not necessarily becoming acidic; “acidification” means its pH is falling.

The parallel-axis theorem lets you find a rigid body’s moment of inertia about one axis when you know it about a parallel axis through the body’s center of mass. Moment of inertia, also called rotational inertia, measures how strongly an object resists changes in its rotation. It depends not just on the object’s mass but on how far that mass is from the axis: for a point mass, it equals the mass times the square of that distance. The theorem states that I = Icm + Md², where Icm is the moment of inertia about the center-of-mass axis, M is the body’s total mass, and d is the distance between the two parallel axes. Because Md² is never negative, shifting the axis away from the center of mass increases the moment of inertia.

Proteases are enzymes that break down proteins by cutting the peptide bonds that link amino acids together. They do this through hydrolysis, a chemical reaction that uses water to split a bond. Proteases have many jobs, including helping the body digest food. One digestive protease is trypsin, a member of the serine protease group. The pancreas produces trypsin as an inactive precursor called trypsinogen, which is released into the small intestine and activated there. This helps prevent it from damaging the pancreas. Trypsin preferentially cuts peptide bonds just after the amino acids lysine and arginine, breaking large proteins into smaller pieces that can be digested further.

A cryptographic key is a piece of data supplied to an algorithm to control how it encrypts, decrypts, signs, or authenticates information. You can think of it as a setting that changes the algorithm’s result: without the right key, encrypted data should be difficult to read. In a simple XOR cipher, for example, a key is combined with a message represented in binary, the 0s and 1s used by computers. Some systems use a pair of related keys with different access roles. The public key can be shared openly so others can encrypt messages for its owner or verify the owner’s digital signatures. The matching private key is kept secret; its owner uses it to decrypt those messages or create signatures.

A spider web is a structure made of silk by a spider, an eight-legged arachnid. Many spiders use webs to intercept insects and other prey, though webs can also provide shelter or protect eggs. Webs come in several shapes, including round orb webs, flat sheets, funnels, and irregular tangles. In many orb webs, strong supporting threads hold the structure together while a sticky spiral crosses them and traps prey that touches it. The silk comes from glands in the spider’s abdomen. As the spider builds, silk passes through small, movable organs on the underside of its abdomen called spinnerets. A spider can produce different kinds of silk for different jobs, such as strong draglines for support and sticky strands for catching prey.

The melting point is the temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid at a specified pressure. For a pure substance at the same pressure, its melting point and freezing point are the same temperature: pure water melts or freezes at 0°C under ordinary atmospheric pressure. Mixing substances can change this temperature. A eutectic mixture melts at a lower temperature than either of its pure components, while dissolved salt lowers water’s freezing point, helping reduce ice on winter roads. Melting point also helps determine which materials can withstand extreme heat. Tungsten, the element with chemical symbol W (from its alternate name, wolfram), has an exceptionally high melting point. That is why it was used for filaments in incandescent light bulbs, where the filament must become very hot without melting.

A wave packet is a group of waves that travel together, forming an overall shape called an envelope. The speed at which this envelope moves is the group velocity. It is found from how angular frequency changes with wavenumber, written as dω/dk. Individual crests, or points of constant phase, can move at a different speed called the phase velocity. For a monochromatic wave, which has just one frequency, phase velocity is angular frequency divided by wavenumber, or ω/k; it also equals wavelength times frequency. In a nondispersive medium, waves of different frequencies travel at the same speed, so group velocity and phase velocity match. In a dispersive medium, their speeds can differ, causing a wave packet to spread out as it travels.

The Hershey–Chase experiment, carried out in 1952, helped show that DNA is the hereditary material. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase studied bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. A phage has DNA inside a protein coat, so they used radioactive labels to track the two parts separately: phosphorus labeled the DNA, while sulfur labeled the protein. After the phages infected bacteria, the researchers used a blender to shake off the outer coats and a centrifuge to separate the bacterial cells from that material. Most of the radioactive phosphorus was found inside the cells, while most of the sulfur remained outside. The infected bacteria then produced new phages. These results showed that DNA, rather than the protein coat, entered the cells and supplied the instructions for making new viruses.

Kenneth Waltz was an American political scientist whose 1979 book Theory of International Politics helped establish neorealism, also called structural realism, in the study of international relations. Waltz argued that countries’ actions cannot be explained only by their leaders’ choices or goals. They are also shaped by the international system: it is “anarchic” because no world government has authority over all states. To protect themselves, states pay attention to the distribution of capabilities, such as military and economic strength, among countries. If one state becomes much stronger than others, rival states may build up their own strength or form alliances to balance its power. Waltz’s approach helps explain why countries may behave similarly under similar pressures, even when their governments have different beliefs.

Bertrand Russell was a British philosopher and logician who helped shape modern philosophy. With Alfred North Whitehead, he coauthored Principia Mathematica, a major work on the logical foundations of mathematics. Russell is also known for his theory of descriptions, which explains how phrases such as “the present king of France” work. Although the phrase sounds like a name, Russell argued that it makes two claims: a present king of France exists, and there is exactly one. The sentence “The present king of France is bald” adds a third claim: that this person is bald. Since France has no present king, the sentence can still be understood even though its description does not refer to a real person.

The demographic transition model explains how a population—the number of people living in an area—typically changes as a society develops. At first, birth rates and death rates are both high, so the population grows slowly. Improvements in food, sanitation, and health care then reduce deaths while births remain high, causing rapid growth. Later, people tend to have fewer children, so birth rates fall and growth slows. In some societies, births and deaths eventually become similarly low, or deaths may outnumber births. The rate of natural increase measures the difference between births and deaths, usually expressed as a percentage of the population. It does not include people moving into or out of an area; migration must be considered separately to calculate total population change.

Competition is the rivalry among firms or sellers for customers. It can limit market power because customers may switch to another seller if one firm charges too much. In perfect competition, an idealized market with many sellers offering similar products, no individual firm can set the market price. That lack of pricing power also means a firm cannot practice price discrimination, or charge different customers different prices for equivalent products. At the opposite extreme is a monopoly, a market supplied by just one firm. A monopolist has substantial power over price and could theoretically use first-degree price discrimination, charging each customer the most they are willing to pay. This would let the firm capture all consumer surplus, the benefit customers otherwise get when they pay less than they were willing to pay.

In Marxist theory, the proletariat is the class of people who own little or no productive property, such as factories or machinery, and must sell their ability to work for wages. Its members are called proletarians. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels contrasted them with the bourgeoisie, the class that owns and controls the means of production—the resources and equipment used to make goods. Marx argued that because the bourgeoisie controls these resources, it can profit from workers’ labor while paying them less than the value they create. He saw this conflict between wage workers and owners of capital as central to capitalism. In The Communist Manifesto, Marx and Engels argued that proletarians could unite to overthrow the existing class system, saying they had “nothing to lose but their chains.”

The Sicilian Mafia is an organized-crime network that emerged on the Italian island of Sicily. Also known as Cosa Nostra, or “our thing,” it has traditionally operated through local clan-like groups called cosche. These groups have used threats and violence to gain power and make money through activities such as extortion, while sometimes presenting themselves as a source of protection. An important part of the Mafia’s influence is omertà, a code of silence that pressures members, victims, and witnesses not to tell police about crimes or help investigators. Fear of retaliation has often made people reluctant to speak, making investigations and prosecutions more difficult. The Sicilian Mafia has also appeared in popular culture, including the film The Godfather, but fictional portrayals should not be confused with its real-world effects.

Dutch is a West Germanic language spoken mainly in the Netherlands and in northern Belgium, where it is also called Flemish. It is related to English and German. In the 1600s, Dutch settlers brought their language to the Cape of Good Hope in southern Africa. Over time, their Dutch developed into Afrikaans, influenced by other languages spoken in the region. Afrikaans is now one of South Africa’s official languages and is also spoken in Namibia. Language can be closely tied to power: during apartheid, South Africa’s government required many Black schools to teach in Afrikaans. Students protested this policy in the 1976 Soweto uprising. So, if a question asks for the European source language of Afrikaans, the answer is Dutch; if it asks for the language that grew from Dutch in southern Africa, the answer is Afrikaans.

Forced sterilization is a medical procedure that permanently prevents a person from having biological children without their freely given, informed consent. Governments have used it against people they considered undesirable, often targeting poor people, disabled people, and minority groups. During India’s 1975–77 Emergency, when Prime Minister Indira Gandhi ruled by decree, her son Sanjay Gandhi was associated with a mass sterilization campaign. Many people were pressured or forced into the procedures as part of a population-control effort. In the United States, sterilization laws were linked to eugenics, the discredited belief that society could be improved by stopping certain people from reproducing. In Buck v. Bell (1927), the Supreme Court upheld a Virginia law as applied to Carrie Buck. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote the majority opinion, including the notorious line, “Three generations of imbeciles are enough.”

Plato’s Phaedo tells the story of Socrates’ final day in an Athenian prison, before he is executed by drinking hemlock. The dialogue is framed as Phaedo’s report of those events to Echecrates. Rather than focusing only on his approaching death, Socrates discusses whether the soul survives after the body dies. Two of his main debate partners are Simmias and Cebes, who challenge his arguments for the soul’s immortality. Simmias, a Theban, compares the soul to the harmony produced by a lyre: if the instrument is destroyed, its harmony disappears too. By this analogy, he suggests that the soul might perish when the body dies. Socrates answers this objection as part of the dialogue’s wider search for what the soul is and whether it can survive death.

Indo-European is a large language family that includes Sanskrit, Persian, Greek, Russian, English, and the Romance languages, such as Spanish and French. These languages developed from a common ancestor called Proto-Indo-European, which scholars have reconstructed by comparing words and sounds across its branches. One way to group the branches is the centum–satem distinction, based on how an ancient consonant changed in words related to “hundred.” The Germanic branch, which includes English, also underwent a set of sound changes called Grimm’s law. It changed many inherited voiceless stops into fricatives: for example, the /p/ at the start of Latin pater corresponds to the /f/ at the start of English father. Such patterns help linguists trace how related languages changed over time.

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, or SEC, is a federal agency created in 1934 after the 1929 stock-market crash. It oversees U.S. securities markets, where investments such as stocks and bonds are bought and sold. The SEC requires companies to give investors accurate information and enforces laws against financial wrongdoing, including investment fraud, insider trading, and market manipulation. One company it investigated was Theranos, a health technology startup founded by Elizabeth Holmes. Theranos claimed its technology could perform many medical tests using just a few drops of blood, but those claims were misleading. The SEC accused Theranos and Holmes of deceiving investors, showing how the agency can act when companies make false claims to raise money.

Economic growth is a sustained increase in an economy’s real output of goods and services over time. “Real” means that output is adjusted for inflation, so higher prices alone do not count as growth. Economists study growth to understand why living standards rise and why some nations become wealthier than others. The Solow–Swan model explains growth using capital accumulation, labor, and technological progress. It assumes diminishing returns to capital: adding more machines helps, but each additional machine contributes less than the previous one. In this model, technological progress comes from outside the model and drives long-run growth in output per person. By contrast, endogenous growth theories explain technological advances through choices made within the economy, such as investment in education, research, and innovation.

The San peoples are a broad group of Indigenous peoples of southern Africa, not a single community with one language or way of life. They include hunter-gatherer communities such as the !Kung and Ju/'hoansi, whose cultures and languages differ from one another. Many San communities have longstanding ties to the Kalahari Desert, an arid region that covers much of Botswana and extends into neighboring countries. Anthropologists have studied San life there to learn about hunting, food sharing, and social relationships. For example, Richard B. Lee conducted fieldwork among !Kung communities in the Kalahari. Although “Bushmen” appears in older writing, “San peoples” is a common collective term today. Remember the connection: San names the peoples, while Kalahari names the desert region associated with many of their communities.

Auguste Comte was a 19th-century French philosopher who founded positivism, the view that reliable knowledge should be based on observation and scientific methods rather than speculation alone. His “law of three stages” described how human explanations develop: in the theological stage, people explain events through gods or spirits; in the metaphysical stage, they appeal to abstract forces or ideas; and in the positive stage, they use evidence to discover patterns and laws. Comte also coined the terms “sociology,” for the study of society, and “altruism,” for concern for others. Although he wanted to use science to improve society, John Stuart Mill worried that Comte’s proposed moral authority would restrict individual freedom. In his 1859 essay On Liberty, Mill warned against a “despotism of society over the individual.”

On Liberty is a short work of political philosophy by John Stuart Mill, first published in 1859. It defends individual freedom from both government repression and the “tyranny of the majority,” in which social pressure forces people to follow popular opinions or customs. Its central idea is the harm principle: society may use coercive power against a competent adult only to prevent harm to others, not merely because that adult’s choices seem unwise or harmful to themselves. Mill therefore supports freedom of thought, speech, and personal conduct, even when others strongly disapprove. He also recognizes a limit to voluntary choice: a person cannot sell themselves into slavery, because doing so would permanently give up the freedom that On Liberty seeks to protect.

A dictator is a ruler who concentrates political power in one person and suppresses meaningful opposition, often through censorship, intimidation, or violence. Some dictators gain power through elections or coups but then weaken the institutions that could limit their rule. Rafael Trujillo, who ruled the Dominican Republic, was a historical dictator. Latin American writers have explored such rulers in “dictator novels,” including Miguel Ángel Asturias’s El Señor Presidente, set in Guatemala. The novel was also an early example of magical realism, a literary mode that places fantastical or seemingly impossible events within an otherwise naturalistic setting. Writers such as Juan Rulfo and Isabel Allende are also associated with magical realism.

Émile, or On Education is a 1762 book by the French philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau. It follows the imagined upbringing of a boy named Émile from infancy toward adulthood and argues that education should fit each stage of a child’s growth. Rousseau believed children learn best by exploring the world and experiencing the results of their actions, rather than by memorizing lessons too early. He called his approach “negative education”: the tutor delays formal book learning and moral instruction while protecting the child from harmful social influences. This does not mean leaving Émile alone; the tutor carefully shapes his surroundings so he can learn through experience. In the final book, Rousseau considers Émile’s marriage and preparation for civic life.

The LGBTQ+ community includes people with diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, including lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer people. The “+” recognizes other identities, such as intersex and asexual. Many members and advocacy groups use the rainbow pride flag to express pride, solidarity, and a shared commitment to equal rights. LGBTQ+ people have faced discrimination in areas such as marriage, military service, and public life, and they have organized to challenge it. An important turning point came in June 1969, when police raided the Stonewall Inn, a bar in New York City’s Greenwich Village. People at the bar and in the surrounding neighborhood resisted, leading to several days of protests known as the Stonewall uprising. The event helped inspire modern LGBTQ+ rights activism.

Xi Jinping Thought is the political doctrine associated with Xi Jinping, China’s president and leader of the Chinese Communist Party. Its full official name is “Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.” It presents the party’s goals for governing China, including strengthening party leadership, pursuing economic development, and increasing China’s role in world affairs. In October 2017, the 19th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party, a major party meeting in Beijing, formally added the doctrine to the party’s constitution. Since then, it has been promoted through government policy and education; textbooks teaching Xi Jinping Thought were introduced in Chinese schools in 2021. Knowing both the doctrine’s name and the 2017 meeting where it was adopted helps explain its place in Chinese politics.

Realpolitik is an approach to politics and diplomacy that focuses on practical power and achievable results rather than strict loyalty to ideals or ideology. It asks leaders to consider what is possible in the circumstances and to choose actions that advance their goals. The approach is famously associated with Otto von Bismarck, a 19th-century Prussian statesman who said that “politics is the art of the possible.” Bismarck used diplomacy and limited wars to bring many German states together under Prussian leadership. After the German Empire was formed in 1871, he became its first chancellor. His statecraft illustrates Realpolitik because he adapted his methods to changing situations instead of following one fixed principle, while pursuing the practical goal of German unification.

Mixed-use zoning is a land-use approach that allows homes, shops, offices, and other activities to share a building or neighborhood. A common example is apartments above street-level stores, so residents can live close to places they visit regularly. This differs from single-use zoning, which separates areas by purpose, such as housing in one zone and businesses in another. City governments use zoning laws to decide which uses are allowed in different places. Planners often support mixed-use zoning because nearby shops and services can make it easier to walk instead of drive. The quality that describes how easily pedestrians can reach everyday destinations is called walkability. Mixed-use neighborhoods can also support public transit and reduce some car trips, though their success depends on features such as safe sidewalks and crossings.

Government spending is the money a government uses to provide goods and services, such as schools, roads, and public safety. It is one part of gross domestic product, or GDP, which measures the market value of final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a given period. In the expenditure approach, economists calculate GDP by adding consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports (exports minus imports). Government spending is also a tool of fiscal policy: changing it can affect economic activity. If a government spends more than it collects in tax revenue, it may run a budget deficit and borrow money, adding to the national debt. GDP is often used to judge an economy’s performance, while GDP divided by population gives GDP per capita.

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola was a 15th-century Italian humanist who believed ideas from different philosophical and religious traditions could be brought together. He wrote 900 theses, or statements for debate, drawing on sources such as ancient Greek philosophy, Christianity, and Jewish Kabbalah. In some of them, he tried to reconcile Kabbalistic teachings with Christian beliefs. Pico planned a public debate about the theses and prepared an introductory address that became known as the Oration on the Dignity of Man. In it, he argued that human beings have an unusual freedom to shape who they become through their choices and learning. Although the planned debate did not take place, the oration became a famous expression of the Renaissance interest in human potential.

Drug cartels are criminal organizations that coordinate the production, transport, and sale of illegal drugs such as heroin and cocaine. They often operate across national borders, using networks of growers, manufacturers, smugglers, and sellers to make money. Their activities can fuel violence and corruption as rival groups compete for control and try to evade law enforcement. One well-known example was the Medellín Cartel in Colombia, led by Pablo Escobar. In the 1990s, the vigilante group Los Pepes and a Colombian police unit called the Search Bloc pursued Escobar. Another example is Mexico’s Sinaloa Cartel, once led by Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán. Agencies such as the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration, or DEA, investigate and combat drug trafficking by these organizations.

The Little Albert experiment was a controversial psychology study conducted at Johns Hopkins by John B. Watson and his research assistant Rosalie Rayner. They described it in their 1920 report “Conditioned Emotional Reactions.” At first, an infant known as Little Albert showed no fear of a white rat. Watson and Rayner then repeatedly presented the rat while making a sudden, loud noise that frightened him. After these pairings, Albert became afraid of the rat even when there was no noise. His fear also generalized to some other furry objects. The study was meant to show that a fear response could be learned through classical conditioning, in which something previously harmless becomes linked to a frightening experience. Today, the experiment is considered unethical because it deliberately caused distress in an infant.

Barbara Ehrenreich was an American author and political activist who had previously worked as a biology researcher. To investigate whether people could meet their basic needs on low wages, she took jobs as a waitress, hotel housekeeper, and retail clerk. She described these experiences in her 2001 book Nickel and Dimed. Ehrenreich found that even full-time workers could struggle to afford rent, food, and other necessities, especially when wages were low and housing was expensive. Her account drew attention to the physical demands of service work and the difficulties workers face when they have little money or job security. Rather than treating poverty as a matter of individual effort alone, the book asks readers to consider how wages and living costs shape people’s lives.

bell hooks was the pen name of Gloria Jean Watkins, an American writer, feminist theorist, and cultural critic. She wrote her name in lowercase to honor her maternal great-grandmother and to keep attention on her ideas rather than herself. Her work explored how racism, sexism, and class inequality can combine, especially in the lives of Black women. In Ain’t I a Woman: Black Women and Feminism, whose title recalls a speech by Sojourner Truth, she examined the neglect of Black women within both feminism and movements for racial justice. In Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center, she argued that feminism should include people pushed to society’s margins. Her 2000 book All About Love describes love as an action, not just a feeling, built through care, commitment, knowledge, responsibility, respect, and trust.

Political order is the durable arrangement of authority, laws, and institutions through which a society makes and enforces public decisions. It includes rules for choosing leaders, government bodies such as legislatures and courts, and ways of resolving disputes. Political order is not the same as a particular leader or policy: leaders and policies may change while the basic framework of government remains in place. A stable political order helps people know who has authority and how decisions will be made. Political scientist Francis Fukuyama studied how such arrangements develop in his book The Origins of Political Order: From Prehuman Times to the French Revolution. He also wrote The End of History and the Last Man, which argues that liberal democracy could be the final form of political government.

History is the study of the human past. Historians investigate what happened, why it happened, and how people experienced it, using evidence such as written records, objects, buildings, and other artifacts. They compare sources and interpret them because accounts of the past can be incomplete or reflect a particular point of view. Studying history therefore means more than memorizing names and dates: it also involves understanding the lives of people who really lived and the societies they shaped. Herodotus, a Greek author of the fifth century BCE, is traditionally called the “Father of History.” In his work the Histories, he recounted the Greco-Persian Wars and described the customs of various peoples.

Hannah Arendt was a German-born Jewish political thinker who fled Nazi Germany in 1933 and later became a U.S. citizen. She studied totalitarianism, a form of rule in which a government seeks sweeping control over people’s lives, in her book The Origins of Totalitarianism. Arendt also asked how ordinary people could take part in terrible crimes such as the Holocaust. In 1961, she covered the trial in Israel of Adolf Eichmann, a former Nazi official who had organized the deportation of Jews. Her reports for The New Yorker became the book Eichmann in Jerusalem, subtitled A Report on the Banality of Evil. By this phrase, Arendt suggested that grave wrongdoing can be carried out by people who follow orders and fail to think critically about their actions.

Russian is an East Slavic language spoken primarily in Russia. It uses the Cyrillic alphabet and is closely related to Ukrainian and Belarusian. Many famous novels and plays were originally written in Russian, so translators help readers of other languages enjoy them. Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky are a married team known for translating Russian literature into English. Their translations include Crime and Punishment by Fyodor Dostoevsky. Their first major translation was another Dostoevsky novel, The Brothers Karamazov. It follows the troubled Karamazov family, including three brothers named Alyosha, Dmitri, and Ivan. The translators have also worked on writings by Anton Chekhov, a Russian author known for his short stories and plays.

Traffic congestion happens when more vehicles try to use a road than it can handle, causing drivers to slow down or wait in queues. It is especially common during commuting hours and can make trips longer, increase air pollution, and affect local businesses. Governments may respond by expanding roads, improving public transportation, or making walking and cycling easier. They can also change intersections so vehicles spend less time stopped. In Virginia, state delegate Danica Roem made congestion on Route 28, a busy road in Prince William County, a major issue in her 2017 campaign. Representing the 13th House District, she defeated longtime incumbent Bob Marshall and proposed fewer traffic lights and more overpasses to help traffic move more smoothly.

Killing means causing another person’s death. In ethics, people ask whether killing is ever justified and whether a person’s intentions or the consequences of an action matter most. The trolley problem explores this by asking whether it is right to divert a runaway trolley so that it kills one person instead of several. Killing also appears in a famous challenge to the ideas of Immanuel Kant, an Enlightenment philosopher who wrote the Critique of Pure Reason and the Critique of Practical Reason. Kant’s categorical imperative says that a moral rule should be one everyone could follow. Critics ask whether someone should tell the truth to a would-be murderer who asks where hidden children are, even though lying might save their lives.

Neoplatonism was a philosophical tradition that emerged in the third century CE and reinterpreted the ideas of Plato, the Greek philosopher who wrote the Timaeus. Its best-known thinker was Plotinus, who came from Lycopolis in Egypt. He studied in Alexandria under Ammonius Saccas before moving to Rome to teach. Plotinus described reality as flowing from the One, the ultimate source of everything. From the One comes Intellect, the realm of perfect ideas, and from Intellect comes Soul, which connects that higher reality to the changing world we experience. Neoplatonists believed people could turn their minds toward the One through thought and contemplation. After Plotinus’s death, his student Porphyry arranged his writings into six groups of nine, called the Enneads.

Race is a social construct: a way societies group people, often by visible traits such as skin color, and give those groups meaning. Although physical traits can be inherited, racial categories are not fixed biological divisions or a ranking of human worth. The boundaries and meanings of race have changed across places and times. False claims that some races are biologically superior have been used to justify discrimination and unequal treatment. Anthropology, the study of humans and their cultures, helps explain how these ideas develop and affect people’s lives. American anthropologist Ruth Benedict, who wrote The Chrysanthemum and the Sword after researching Japanese society during World War II, argued that anthropology’s purpose was “to make the world safe for human differences.”

New Urbanism is a movement in town planning that aims to make communities easier to live in without relying on a car for every trip. Instead of spreading homes, shops, schools, and public spaces far apart, it places them close together in compact neighborhoods. Sidewalks, connected streets, and shared spaces make walking and cycling more practical, while a mix of housing and businesses helps people meet everyday needs nearby. These ideas are meant to counter car-dependent suburban sprawl and support environmental sustainability by reducing long drives and making efficient use of land. An early example is Seaside, a planned community on Florida’s Gulf Coast designed by Andrés Duany and Elizabeth Plater-Zyberk. Miami is also in Florida.

Fear is an emotion that arises when you perceive danger or a threat. It can make your heart pound, your palms sweat, and your body feel alert and ready to respond. Horror films often provoke fear even though viewers know they are safe. Sometimes people notice these physical reactions but mistake what caused them. In a famous suspension-bridge study, participants who crossed a high, shaky bridge were more likely to report attraction to an interviewer than participants who crossed a low, sturdy bridge. One explanation is that they interpreted their racing hearts and other signs of fear as romantic interest. Assigning bodily arousal to the wrong source is called misattribution of arousal. The study shows how the situation around us can affect how we understand our emotions.

Sign languages are complete languages that convey meaning visually rather than through audible speech. Signers combine handshapes and movements with facial expressions and body position to express ideas, ask questions, and show grammatical information. Deaf communities around the world use different sign languages, each with its own vocabulary and grammar; there is no single universal sign language. American Sign Language, or ASL, is widely used in the United States and parts of Canada. Although people in the United States and Britain both commonly speak English, ASL is distinct from British Sign Language and has historical ties to French Sign Language. Some signs can also be understood by touch: Anne Sullivan taught Helen Keller, who was deaf and blind, by spelling words into her hand.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition involving differences in social communication and interaction, along with restricted or repetitive behaviors, routines, or interests. It is called a spectrum because autistic people differ in their strengths, experiences, and support needs. One way researchers have studied how children understand other people’s beliefs is the Sally-Anne test. In the story, Sally puts a marble in a basket and leaves. Anne moves it to a different place while Sally is away. The child is asked where Sally will look when she returns. The answer is the basket: Sally does not know the marble was moved. This is called a false-belief task because it tests whether someone can recognize that another person may believe something that is no longer true.

Vietnamese Americans are a U.S. community whose families came from Vietnam as immigrants or refugees. Many arrived after the fall of Saigon in 1975, which marked the end of the Vietnam War, and built new lives in the United States while maintaining connections to Vietnamese language and culture. Vietnamese American writers have explored experiences of war, migration, identity, and belonging. Ocean Vuong, a poet and novelist, wrote “Aubade with Burning City,” a poem set during the fall of Saigon. Viet Thanh Nguyen won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for his novel The Sympathizer. Its narrator is a communist double agent who leaves Vietnam for the United States after the fall of Saigon and struggles with divided loyalties.

Decision-making is the process of selecting one option from several alternatives, such as deciding what to buy or how to spend your time. Traditional economics often describes a “rational actor” who compares options and chooses the one that best meets their goals. Behavioral economics combines economics with psychology to study how people actually make decisions. Researchers such as Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that mental shortcuts, called heuristics, can influence choices. For example, anchoring occurs when the first price you see shapes your judgment of later prices. In his book The Paradox of Choice, Barry Schwartz argues that having more options is not always better: too many choices can make deciding harder and leave people less satisfied with what they select.

Simone de Beauvoir was a French existentialist philosopher and feminist whose work explored freedom, responsibility, and women’s place in society. In her 1949 book The Second Sex, she argued that women are often treated as the “Other”: men are seen as the standard, while women are defined in relation to them. She also examined how expectations about femininity are shaped by society, rather than determined entirely by biology. Her famous idea that “one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman” captures this point. In another book, The Ethics of Ambiguity, de Beauvoir considered what it means to be free and how people should act responsibly when their choices affect others. Both works ask how people can live freely in a world shaped by social pressures.

Rat Park was a research project led by Canadian psychologist Bruce Alexander in the 1970s. Earlier drug experiments often kept rats alone in small cages, where they could choose between plain water and water containing morphine. Alexander and his colleagues compared these isolated rats with rats living together in a spacious, stimulating colony called Rat Park, which offered room to explore, play, and socialize. The socially housed rats generally consumed less morphine than the isolated rats. These findings challenged the idea that a drug’s chemical properties alone explain addiction: an animal’s surroundings and social connections may also affect its drug use. Rat Park did not prove that environment is the only cause of addiction, but it helped researchers ask how isolation and enrichment influence behavior.

Hotelling’s Lemma connects a firm’s maximum profit to its supply and input choices. Profit is revenue minus total cost, and a firm chooses how much to produce and which inputs, such as labor and materials, to use to make profit as large as possible. Its optimized profit function records that maximum profit at different output and input prices. Holding input prices fixed, the derivative of this function with respect to the output price gives the firm’s output supplied, also called its firm supply. Differentiating with respect to an input price instead gives the negative of the firm’s demand for that input. The lemma is useful because economists can recover these choices from the optimized profit function without solving the firm’s profit-maximization problem again.

International relations is the study of how sovereign states and other actors interact across borders. It examines diplomacy, war, trade, alliances, and global institutions such as the United Nations. Scholars use different theories to explain these interactions: Realism emphasizes competition for security and power, Liberalism highlights cooperation and international institutions, and Constructivism explores how shared ideas and norms shape behavior. One influential American theorist, Kenneth Waltz, helped establish neorealism with his book Theory of International Politics. Waltz argued that the international system is anarchic, meaning no world government has authority over all states. Because states must look after their own security, the structure of that system strongly influences their choices, including whether they build military strength or form alliances.

Adam Smith was a Scottish Enlightenment philosopher and economist born in Kirkcaldy. In his 1776 book The Wealth of Nations, he explored how people produce and exchange goods. His example of a pin factory shows the division of labor: instead of each worker making an entire pin, workers specialize in separate steps. This can greatly increase output because they become skilled at their tasks and save time switching between them. Smith also described how people pursuing their own interests through market exchange can sometimes benefit society, an idea often called the invisible hand. In international trade, he discussed absolute advantage, which means one country can produce a good using fewer labor hours than another. Together, these ideas helped shape modern economics.

Wages are payments workers receive for their labor, such as hourly pay or a set amount for each item they produce, called piece-rate pay. They are labor income, unlike the profit earned by a business owner or the rent received by a property owner. Nominal wages are measured in current money, while real wages are adjusted for inflation to show what workers can actually buy. Governments may set a minimum wage, a legal floor on pay. Employers may also offer efficiency wages—pay above the usual level—to encourage effort and reduce turnover. In George Akerlof and Janet Yellen’s gift-exchange game, a worker responds to an employer’s generous wage offer by working harder, even though no enforceable contract requires that extra effort.

Mutual assured destruction, often shortened to MAD, was a Cold War doctrine of nuclear deterrence. It held that if two rival countries both had nuclear weapons and each could respond to an attack, neither would gain by striking first: the other could retaliate, causing catastrophic damage to both. The ability to survive an enemy’s initial nuclear attack and still launch a devastating response is called second-strike capability. To maintain it, a country might spread its nuclear forces among missile silos, submarines, and aircraft, making them harder to destroy all at once. MAD did not mean nuclear war was impossible; accidents, mistakes, or misjudgments could still cause one. Its central idea was that the threat of retaliation would discourage either side from starting a nuclear war.

Risk is the possibility of an unwanted outcome, considered alongside how large the loss could be. In investing, for example, a stock might offer a high expected reward but also carry a chance of losing money. Investors weigh that risk against the potential reward when deciding where to put their money. Risk matters outside finance, too. A software project can be at risk if only a few people know how to maintain it. Its bus factor is the minimum number of contributors whose sudden departure would stall the project; the name imagines them being hit by a bus. A low bus factor means the project depends heavily on a small group. A 2016 study found a bus factor below three for 65 percent of 133 popular GitHub projects.

A mirror is a smooth, reflective surface that forms an image by bouncing light back toward your eyes. People use mirrors for everyday tasks such as checking their appearance, but scientists also use them to study animal cognition. In a mirror mark test, researchers put a visible mark on an animal’s body where it cannot easily see the mark directly. They then watch what the animal does in front of a mirror. If it uses the reflection to investigate the mark on its own body, rather than reacting as though the reflection is another animal, researchers take this as evidence of self-recognition: the ability to identify the image as itself. Psychologist B. F. Skinner trained pigeons to perform a version of this task.

Impeachment is the process the U.S. Constitution provides for Congress to address serious misconduct by federal officials, including presidents. The House of Representatives decides whether to bring formal charges, called articles of impeachment. If it does, the Senate holds a trial and may vote to remove the official from office. Being impeached means being charged, not automatically removed. In 1868, the House impeached President Andrew Johnson after he dismissed Secretary of War Edwin Stanton. It alleged that the dismissal violated the Tenure of Office Act, a federal law that restricted the president’s ability to remove certain officials whose appointments had been confirmed by the Senate. The Senate tried Johnson but fell one vote short of removing him.

Jerome H. Powell is the chair of the Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States. A former investment banker, he served as undersecretary of the Treasury for domestic finance during President George H. W. Bush’s administration. Powell joined the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors in 2012 and became chair in 2018, succeeding Janet Yellen. The Federal Reserve guides monetary policy to pursue maximum employment and stable prices. Its monetary-policy committee adjusts a benchmark overnight lending rate, which influences borrowing costs throughout the economy. When inflation rose sharply in 2022, Powell supported raising interest rates to help slow price increases. The Federal Reserve can also use tools such as quantitative easing, which involves buying financial assets to put more money into the financial system.

In economics, labor is the human effort used to make goods or provide services. It includes physical work, such as building a house, and mental work, such as designing it. Economists study labor alongside other factors of production, including land, which provides natural resources, and capital, such as tools and machinery. Labor can become more productive when workers specialize in different tasks. In The Wealth of Nations, economist Adam Smith illustrated this idea with a workshop that made pins, small metal fasteners. Rather than having each person make an entire pin, workers divided the process into separate steps. By practicing one task and passing the work along, they could produce many more pins together.

A monopsony is a market with one buyer and many sellers. In a labor market, it can occur when many workers seek jobs but only one employer hires in their area or occupation. That employer has bargaining power: workers have few alternatives, so it may be able to pay lower wages or hire fewer people than it would in a more competitive market. This helps explain why a minimum wage does not always reduce employment. If an employer was already paying unusually low wages, a moderate wage increase might attract more workers without causing layoffs. Economists David Card and Alan Krueger studied this question by comparing fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which raised its minimum wage in 1992, with restaurants in neighboring Pennsylvania, which did not raise it at that time.

Irish is a Celtic language traditionally spoken in Ireland. Its name in Irish is Gaeilge, and Ireland’s constitution designates it the country’s national and first official language. Irish belongs to the Goidelic branch of the Celtic language family, so it is closely related to Scottish Gaelic and Manx, the traditional language of the Isle of Man. Welsh and Breton are also Celtic languages, but they belong to a different branch. Breton is spoken in Brittany, a region of France. Although most people in Ireland use English in daily life, Irish is still spoken in some communities, taught in schools, and used in public life. It is part of Ireland’s cultural heritage, connecting people with its history, stories, music, and place names.

Language acquisition is the process by which children learn to understand and use language.
