It begins early in life as babies listen to people around them, recognize sounds and patterns, and gradually learn words and grammar. Conversation and other everyday experiences help children develop these skills, alongside their growing ability to think and communicate. Researchers study how the timing of those experiences affects learning. The critical period hypothesis proposes that early childhood is a particularly favorable window for acquiring a language, especially for reaching native-like mastery. Learning a language after that window is still possible, but reaching the same level may be more difficult. This idea helps explain why early opportunities to hear and use language matter so much.

The Mundell–Tobin effect describes how expected inflation may affect interest rates. Inflation is the rate at which the overall prices of goods and services rise. A benchmark called the Fisher effect predicts that, if the real interest rate stays fixed, a one-percentage-point rise in expected inflation will raise the nominal interest rate—the rate quoted by a bank—by one percentage point. The Mundell–Tobin effect suggests the increase can be smaller. When people expect money to lose value faster, they may hold less cash and put more resources into investments such as equipment or buildings. This greater investment can lower the real interest rate, partly offsetting inflation’s upward pressure on the nominal rate. Thus, nominal interest rates may rise by less than one-for-one with expected inflation.

Substantive due process is a constitutional-law doctrine that allows courts to protect certain fundamental rights through the Due Process Clauses of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, even when those rights are not explicitly listed in the Constitution. Unlike procedural due process, which concerns whether the government follows fair steps before taking action, substantive due process asks whether some government actions violate basic freedoms regardless of the steps used. The doctrine has been important in cases about privacy and personal autonomy. In Griswold v. Connecticut (1965), the Supreme Court struck down a state ban on contraceptive use by married couples; the case is often discussed in connection with substantive due process. The doctrine remains contested, partly because judges disagree about which unlisted rights the Constitution protects.

Monadology is a short philosophical work written in 1714 by the German polymath Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Organized into numbered sections, it describes reality as made up of monads: simple, nonmaterial substances that cannot be divided into smaller parts. Each monad has its own perceptions and activity, so the world is more than a collection of physical objects moving like a machine. Leibniz argued that even if you could walk inside a thinking machine and inspect all its parts, you would not find a physical mechanism that explains conscious experience. He also independently developed calculus, alongside Isaac Newton. In his work on theodicy, which examines how evil can exist if God is good, Leibniz argued that ours is the “best of all possible worlds.”

Democritus was an ancient Greek philosopher from Abdera who studied under Leucippus. He is best known for atomism, the idea that everything is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms moving through empty space. He thought the different arrangements and movements of atoms could explain changes in the world without relying on the actions of gods. His account was deterministic: atomic motion followed causes rather than happening by chance, so events were the results of earlier events. Centuries later, the Roman thinker Lucretius proposed that atoms sometimes make a tiny, unpredictable change in direction. He called this deviation the clinamen, or atomic swerve. The swerve challenged strict determinism by making room for events that could not be completely predicted from earlier atomic motion.

Moral intuitions are judgments about right and wrong that seem to arise immediately, without extended step-by-step reasoning. For example, someone might feel at once that breaking a promise is wrong, then try to explain why. Philosophers debate whether these intuitions are reliable guides to morality. Ethical intuitionists, including G. E. Moore, give them an important role in thinking about moral truths. Experimental philosophers study how people report their intuitions when faced with ethical thought experiments, including whether small changes to a scenario affect their answers. Moral psychology investigates the mental processes behind these judgments, such as the influence of emotions, learning, and social experience. Jean Piaget’s studies of how children develop ideas about rules and fairness helped establish moral psychology as an area of research.

Capital: A Critique of Political Economy is Karl Marx’s multivolume study of how capitalism works. Its first volume appeared in 1867, and Friedrich Engels edited and published the later volumes after Marx’s death. Marx examines wage labor, commodity production, and capital: assets such as money and machinery used to produce more goods or wealth. He argues that workers create value through their labor but receive wages worth less than the value they produce; the difference is called surplus value. Marx also studies the commodity form, or how goods made for exchange acquire value in a market. He calls one effect commodity fetishism: the social relationships among the people who make and exchange goods appear instead to be relationships among the goods themselves, as if commodities possessed value and power on their own.

The Book of Five Rings is a seventeenth-century Japanese treatise on swordsmanship and strategy written by Miyamoto Musashi, a swordsman famed for his duels. Musashi founded Niten Ichi-ryū, a fighting style that uses two swords, and explained how careful training and good judgment could help a warrior respond to different situations. The treatise has five parts, named Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Void. Although it focuses on combat, Musashi also encourages students of swordsmanship to study arts such as calligraphy and to apply martial discipline beyond fighting. His teachings reflect the world of the samurai, the warrior class that served Japanese lords called daimyo and followed a moral code known as bushido.

Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals is a 1785 work by Immanuel Kant, a German Enlightenment philosopher who also wrote Critique of Pure Reason. In the Groundwork, Kant tries to identify principles of right conduct based on reason rather than on personal desires or the results of an action. His central idea is the categorical imperative: a moral rule that applies to everyone, regardless of what they want. One way to test an action is to ask whether you could will its maxim, or guiding rule, to become a universal law followed by everyone. If you could not consistently want everyone to act that way, Kant argues, you should not do it. His strict view of honesty later prompted debate about whether lying could be justified to protect someone from a murderer.

Banks are financial institutions that accept deposits, such as money in checking or savings accounts. They also make loans to households and businesses and process payments, including transfers and card transactions. Commercial banking mainly involves deposits and lending, while investment banking includes activities such as helping companies issue stocks and bonds, known as securities underwriting. In the United States, the Glass-Steagall Act historically kept many commercial-banking and investment-banking activities separate. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 repealed key parts of Glass-Steagall, allowing banks to affiliate with securities firms and insurers and loosening those restrictions. Because problems at very large banks can affect the wider economy, institutions considered globally systemically important face extra oversight under international standards developed by the Basel Committee.

De is a Chinese philosophical concept often translated as “virtue,” but its meaning changes with the tradition using it. In Confucian thought, de refers to moral character: the qualities that help a person act well and influence others through a good example. Mohist writers also used it in discussions of morality. In Daoist thought, de can mean the inner power or effectiveness that comes from living in harmony with the Dao, or “Way.” The term is the second element in the title Dao De Jing, commonly translated as “Classic of the Way and Virtue.” That text is traditionally attributed to Laozi, a sage linked to the ancient state of Chu. According to tradition, his surname was Li, and “Laozi” is an honorific meaning “Old Master.”

Law is the system of rules and institutions that defines rights and duties, resolves disputes, and guides the conduct of people and organizations. In the United States, students preparing to become lawyers often earn a J.D. degree. They study appellate court opinions in casebooks, with professors using Socratic questioning to test how they reason about decisions. One approach to studying law, formalism, treats legal decisions as the logical application of established rules and principles. Legal realism, an early 20th-century American movement associated with Karl Llewellyn and Jerome Frank, challenged that view. Legal realists examined how judges actually decide cases and argued that social conditions, personal judgments, and practical consequences can influence outcomes. This contrast helps explain why studying law involves more than memorizing rules.

Grimm’s law describes a regular pattern of consonant changes that occurred as Proto-Germanic developed from Proto-Indo-European, the ancestor of a language family that includes English, Latin, Greek, Sanskrit, and Russian. One part of the pattern changed the Proto-Indo-European voiceless stops p, t, and k into the Proto-Germanic voiceless fricatives f, th, and h. A stop briefly blocks airflow, while a fricative produces sound as air passes through a narrow opening. For example, Latin pater and Greek patēr begin with p, preserving the older sound in the word for “father.” English father begins with f because the ancestral p changed to f in the Germanic branch. These consistent correspondences help linguists trace relationships among languages.

Mandarin Chinese is a major Chinese language variety historically centered in northern China. Standard Mandarin is based largely on Beijing pronunciation and is the official spoken standard in mainland China, where it is called Putonghua. Mandarin uses tones, so a syllable’s pitch pattern can change its meaning. In some Beijing pronunciations, speakers add an “r” sound or rhotic coloring to the end of a syllable, usually without making a separate syllable. This process is called erhua. Mandarin also uses measure words when counting many nouns: for example, ge is a common measure word, while zhi is used with certain animals and objects. Mandarin is written with Chinese characters; simplified characters are used in mainland China, while traditional forms remain common in Taiwan.

Synonymy is the relationship between words or expressions that have the same or nearly the same meaning. For example, “begin” and “start” are often synonyms, though they may not fit equally well in every sentence. Synonymy matters in philosophy of language because it can help explain analytic truths: statements that seem true because of what their words mean, such as “All bachelors are unmarried.” In his essay “Two Dogmas of Empiricism,” the American philosopher W. V. O. Quine challenged the distinction between analytic truths and synthetic truths, which depend on facts about the world. He argued that defining analyticity by saying synonymous words can replace one another, while defining synonymy by appealing to analyticity, is circular: neither concept has been explained independently.

In Abraham Maslow’s theory of motivation, growth needs are motives that push people to develop their abilities, find meaning, and become more fully themselves. They differ from deficiency needs, which arise when something important is missing, such as food, safety, or connection with others. Satisfying a deficiency need reduces discomfort, but a growth need can continue to matter even when basic needs are met: learning a skill, creating something, or pursuing a meaningful goal may make someone want to keep growing. Maslow called the highest-level process self-actualization. It means realizing your potential and becoming what you are capable of becoming. His hierarchy of needs is often drawn as a pyramid, with basic physiological needs near the bottom and self-actualization at the top.

Death is the end of biological life, when a living body permanently stops functioning. Because everyone eventually dies, people have long asked what death means, how to face it, and whether anything follows it. Religions offer different beliefs about an afterlife, while philosophers consider questions about identity, meaning, and mortality. Poets often use images and stories to explore these ideas. In “Crossing the Bar,” the British poet Alfred, Lord Tennyson compares dying to a final sea voyage and hopes to meet his “Pilot,” often understood as God, after crossing. Tennyson also wrote “The Charge of the Light Brigade,” about a cavalry attack at the Battle of Balaclava during the Crimean War, in which soldiers ride into the “valley of Death.”

Lying means deliberately communicating something you believe is false in order to mislead someone. It differs from an honest mistake: a person who gives incorrect information while believing it is true is not lying. The Enlightenment philosopher Immanuel Kant argued that lying is morally wrong under his categorical imperative, a principle for testing the rule, or maxim, behind an action. One formulation asks whether you could consistently will everyone to follow that rule as a universal law. If everyone lied whenever it suited them, people would stop trusting what others said, undermining communication itself. Another formulation of the categorical imperative emphasizes treating people with respect rather than merely using them for your own purposes. Critics ask whether Kant’s strict view would still require telling the truth to someone intending to harm another person.

Meditations is a collection of twelve books of personal reflections by Marcus Aurelius, a Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher. He wrote them for himself, often while on military campaigns, rather than as a polished work for publication. In these notes, Aurelius practices self-discipline by reminding himself that hardship and death are natural parts of life. He urges himself to respond calmly to events he cannot control and to focus instead on his own judgments and actions. He also stresses the duty to act fairly and serve the human community. Aurelius ruled alongside Lucius Verus and later fought peoples along the Danube. His reflections show how he tried to apply Stoic ideas while facing the responsibilities of an emperor.

Anselm of Canterbury was an eleventh-century Benedictine monk, theologian, and philosopher. Born in Aosta, he became abbot of the monastery at Bec and later Archbishop of Canterbury, England’s highest church office. In his book Proslogion, Anselm offered a famous proof for God’s existence called the ontological argument. He described God as a being “than which nothing greater can be conceived.” Anselm reasoned that a being that exists in reality is greater than one that exists only as an idea in the mind. Therefore, he argued, the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality as well as in our understanding. His argument has been debated for centuries: the monk Gaunilo challenged it by asking whether similar reasoning could prove the existence of a perfect island.

The Oedipus complex is a concept in classical psychoanalytic theory, developed by the Austrian neurologist Sigmund Freud. Freud proposed that, during early childhood, a child may feel an unconscious attachment to the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the same-sex parent. He used the name Oedipus, a figure from Greek mythology, to describe this pattern, particularly in boys. Freud saw it as part of psychosexual development: his theory that early experiences and feelings help shape personality. He also founded psychoanalysis and proposed that personality involves the id, ego, and superego. The Oedipus complex is historically important because it influenced later discussions of childhood and family relationships, but it is not considered a well-supported explanation of how most children develop.

Zoning laws are local rules that divide a municipality’s land into districts and set limits on what can be built in each one. They may specify whether land can be used for homes, shops, or factories, as well as building height, size, and other development details. In the 1926 case Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of this kind of regulation. Traditional “Euclidean” zoning often separates uses into single-purpose districts, such as areas reserved for single-family homes. Mixed-use zoning takes a different approach: it allows different activities in the same building or development, such as street-level shops with apartments on the floors above. Supporters argue that placing homes near shops and services makes neighborhoods easier to walk around and can reduce the need to drive.

The Vice President of the United States holds the country’s second-highest executive office. Created by the Constitution, the vice president presides over the Senate but normally votes only to break a tie. The vice president is also first in line to become president if the president dies, resigns, or is removed from office. John Adams was the first vice president, serving under George Washington from 1789 to 1797, before becoming the nation’s second president. During Franklin D. Roosevelt’s presidency, his vice presidents included John Nance Garner, Henry A. Wallace, and Harry S. Truman. Truman became president when Roosevelt died in 1945, showing why the office’s place in the line of succession matters.

A paradox is a statement, argument, or situation that appears to lead to a contradiction or a conclusion that defeats itself. The ancient Greek thinker Zeno of Elea created famous paradoxes about motion. In one, an arrow in flight seems to be stationary at every single instant, raising the puzzling question of how it can move at all. In another, Achilles seems unable to catch a tortoise with a head start because he must first reach each place where the tortoise was, while the tortoise keeps moving ahead. A paradox does not necessarily prove that ordinary experience is wrong; it may reveal a hidden problem in how an argument is framed. When several explanations seem possible, Occam’s razor, associated with the 14th-century Franciscan William of Ockham, advises choosing the simplest adequate explanation without unnecessary assumptions.

Monads are the basic substances in the philosophy of Gottfried Wilhelm von Leibniz, a German philosopher and polymath. In his Monadology, Leibniz described them as simple and indivisible: they have no physical parts, occupy no space, and cannot be broken apart. He called them “windowless” because nothing enters or leaves them, yet each monad represents the whole universe from its own perspective. If monads cannot directly affect one another, how do events seem to fit together? Leibniz answered with “pre-established harmony”: God arranged their changes in advance so that they correspond, like clocks keeping the same time. This also explained for Leibniz why mind and body appear to interact. In his Theodicy, he argued that God created the best of all possible worlds.

The Enlightenment was a European intellectual movement of the 17th and 18th centuries that encouraged people to use reason and empirical inquiry—learning from observation and evidence—to understand the world. Its thinkers questioned inherited ideas and argued that knowledge could help improve society and government. The Scottish Enlightenment was an important branch of the movement, with figures including David Hume and Adam Smith. Smith was a moral philosopher and political economist who studied both how people treat one another and how economies work. In The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), he explored sympathy and moral judgment. In The Wealth of Nations (1776), he examined trade, labor, and the sources of national prosperity. His work shows how Enlightenment thinkers applied careful reasoning to human behavior and social reform.

Canadian Medicare is the commonly used name for Canada’s publicly funded health-care system. It provides universal coverage for medically necessary hospital and physician services, so patients generally do not pay for those services when they receive them. The provinces and territories run their own health plans, with support from the federal government. Medicare’s development began before it became a national system. In Saskatchewan, the provincial government led by Premier Tommy Douglas introduced a pioneering public hospital-insurance plan in 1947. Douglas belonged to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, a party that supported expanding public services. Saskatchewan later introduced public insurance for doctors’ services as well. These provincial programs helped inspire the federal government under Prime Minister Lester Pearson to establish Medicare across Canada in the 1960s.

The International Phonetic Alphabet, or IPA, is a standardized system for writing the sounds of spoken language. Unlike ordinary spelling, which can represent the same sound in different ways, IPA symbols let people record pronunciation consistently across languages. It uses letters and small marks called diacritics, which add detail about how a sound is made. A broad transcription shows the main sounds of a word, while a detailed transcription can show finer differences in pronunciation. Vowels are speech sounds made with an open vocal tract, unlike consonants, which involve some constriction or closure. A diphthong is one vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable, like the vowel in “boy.” In IPA, a diphthong is usually written with two vowel symbols.

Bookkeeping is the systematic recording and tracking of financial transactions, such as payments received, purchases made, and money owed. It helps individuals and organizations understand where their money comes from, where it goes, and what they own or owe. In double-entry bookkeeping, each transaction is recorded in two related accounts, helping bookkeepers check that their records balance. This method became closely associated with Renaissance commerce, when merchants needed reliable ways to manage trade. One early account of double-entry bookkeeping appears in Della mercatura e del mercante perfetto, a fifteenth-century treatise on merchants and trade by Benedetto Cotrugli. Cotrugli was a merchant and diplomat from the Republic of Ragusa, a maritime republic on the Dalmatian coast of what is now Croatia.

Warren Buffett is an American investor and business leader born in Omaha, Nebraska. Nicknamed the “Oracle of Omaha,” he is known for value investing: buying shares in businesses he believes are worth more than their current price and holding them for the long term. He has led Berkshire Hathaway for decades as its chairman and CEO, helping turn it into a company that owns many businesses and investments. Buffett is also known for philanthropy, or giving money to help others. With Bill and Melinda Gates, he co-founded the Giving Pledge, an initiative that encourages billionaires and other very wealthy people to commit to donating most of their fortunes to charitable causes. His career connects finance with questions about wealth and how it can benefit society.

Occam’s razor is a principle for choosing between explanations: do not add more assumptions or kinds of things than you need. When two explanations account for the same evidence equally well, prefer the simpler one. “Simpler” does not mean easiest to understand or always correct; an explanation must still fit the facts. The principle is named for William of Ockham, a 14th-century English Franciscan friar and philosopher born in the village of Ockham in Surrey. He was a major nominalist, meaning he questioned whether general categories, such as “redness,” exist as separate things beyond the individual objects we describe. Occam’s razor is useful in science and philosophy because it helps people avoid unnecessary claims while remaining open to new evidence.

Atheism is a form of nonbelief in gods. It can mean explicitly denying that any gods exist or holding that belief in gods is unwarranted. Philosophers distinguish this question from other beliefs about the soul, an afterlife, or sacred texts: someone’s view on one does not automatically determine their view on the others. In classical Indian philosophy, the Charvaka school is known for its materialist outlook. Charvaka thinkers rejected the authority of the Vedas, treated direct perception as the most reliable source of knowledge, and denied an afterlife. Charvaka is therefore often discussed alongside atheism. However, the Sanskrit term nastika, applied to schools that rejected Vedic authority, should not simply be translated as “atheist”: rejecting a scripture and rejecting gods are different positions.

Stranger anxiety is the wariness or fear an infant may show around people they do not know. It often appears as babies become better at recognizing familiar caregivers and noticing when someone is unfamiliar or unpredictable. A baby might cling to a parent, cry, or turn away when a stranger approaches. This is a common part of development, though its timing and intensity vary from child to child. Psychologist Jean Piaget associated stranger anxiety with the sensorimotor stage, the first of his four stages of cognitive development. This stage lasts from birth to roughly age two. During it, infants learn about the world through their senses and actions, and they gradually develop object permanence: the understanding that something still exists even when they cannot see it.

Greek is a language with a written history stretching back more than 3,000 years. Ancient and modern Greek are different stages of the same language, though their vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation have changed over time. The Alexandrian poet Constantine Cavafy wrote in modern Greek; his poems include “Ithaka” and “Waiting for the Barbarians.” Sophocles, who wrote the tragedy Oedipus Rex in the fifth century BCE, used ancient Greek. His plays are particularly associated with Attic Greek, a classical dialect named for Attica, the region centered on Athens. Knowing this distinction helps identify Greek as the language shared by Cavafy and Sophocles, and Attic Greek as the dialect linked to classical Athenian tragedy.

Art theft is the unlawful taking of artworks, such as paintings, sculptures, or drawings, from museums, galleries, or private collections. A thief may steal one famous work or remove several pieces from an institution. One of the best-known cases involved the Mona Lisa. In 1911, Vincenzo Peruggia, a former worker at the Louvre in Paris, took the painting from the museum. He kept it hidden for more than two years before approaching an art dealer in Florence, Italy, and was arrested. Other famous artworks have also been stolen: multiple versions of Edvard Munch’s painting The Scream have been victims of theft. Such crimes can deprive the public of access to art and make it difficult to protect, trace, and return valuable cultural objects.

Justice is the idea that people should be treated fairly, have their rights respected, and receive what they are owed. It matters in law, where a blindfolded woman holding scales symbolizes impartial judgment: decisions should be based on evidence rather than a person’s wealth or status. Justice also raises questions about how a society should distribute resources and opportunities. In A Theory of Justice, philosopher John Rawls argued that fair rules are ones people would choose if they did not know what position they would hold in society. Libertarian philosopher Robert Nozick challenged theories that aim to preserve a particular pattern of distribution. In Anarchy, State, and Utopia, he used the example of basketball star Wilt Chamberlain: if many people freely pay to watch Chamberlain play, he may become much wealthier than others without anyone being treated unjustly.

Liberty means freedom from arbitrary restraint: the ability to make choices and live your life without someone else controlling you without good reason. The English philosopher John Locke argued that people have natural rights, including life, liberty, health, and property. In his Two Treatises of Government, he explained that people form governments to protect these rights. If a government fails to do so or abuses its power, the people may resist it. Locke’s ideas influenced Thomas Jefferson, who named “life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness” as rights in the Declaration of Independence. In both Locke’s and Jefferson’s writing, liberty is a right that government should respect and protect, not a gift it can take away whenever it chooses.

In U.S. law, obscenity is a category of sexually explicit expression that can be excluded from the First Amendment’s protection of free speech. Not all pornography or sexual content is legally obscene; material that does not meet the legal definition is generally protected. In Roth v. United States, the Supreme Court linked obscenity to material that appeals to a “prurient interest,” meaning an unhealthy or excessive interest in sex. The current standard comes from Miller v. California. Under its three-part test, material must appeal to prurient interest by community standards, depict sexual conduct in a clearly offensive way as defined by law, and lack serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. All three conditions must be met before material can be classified as obscene under this test.

Profit is the money a firm has left after subtracting costs from the revenue it earns by selling goods or services. There are two important ways to measure it. Accounting profit subtracts explicit expenses that appear in financial records, such as wages, rent, and materials. Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, especially the opportunity cost of using resources in this business instead of their best alternative use. For example, an owner who works without a salary gives up the income they could have earned at another job. In a perfectly competitive market, high economic profits attract new firms, while losses cause firms to leave. Over time, this entry and exit tends to drive economic profit to zero, even though firms may still earn positive accounting profit.

Emotions are feelings such as fear, joy, and anger. They involve both changes in the body and how we understand what is happening around us. For example, a racing heart might feel like fear during a horror movie but excitement before a performance. Stanley Schachter and Jerome Singer’s two-factor theory of emotion says that people experience physiological arousal and then interpret it using cues from the situation. In a classic experiment, participants received an injection that caused arousal. What they were told about its effects, along with the behavior of another person in the room, influenced the emotions they reported. This helps explain why people can misidentify their feelings when situational cues are misleading. Alexithymia is difficulty recognizing and describing emotions.

Child soldiers are people under 18 who are recruited or used by armed forces or armed groups. They may fight, but they may also serve as scouts, messengers, or porters, so the term covers more than children carrying weapons. Recruiting and using children in war puts them at grave risk and can disrupt their education and development. One historical example comes from the War of the Triple Alliance, also called the Paraguayan War. In this conflict, fought in the 1860s and early 1870s, Paraguay battled a coalition of Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay. After heavy losses depleted Paraguay’s fighting-age population, its leader, Francisco Solano López, sent young people into combat. The example shows how pressure on an army can lead to the use of children in war.

Gender discrimination is unfair treatment of someone because of their gender or sex. It can include paying a woman less than a man for comparable work, denying someone a promotion, or offering fewer job opportunities. Lilly Ledbetter, a former Goodyear employee, sued after learning that she had been paid less than male coworkers. In 2007, the Supreme Court ruled against her because she had filed her claim too long after the original pay decisions. This deadline is called a statute of limitations. Congress responded with the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009, signed by President Barack Obama. The law allows each paycheck affected by discriminatory pay to start a new period for filing a claim, making it easier for workers to challenge ongoing pay discrimination.

A statute of limitations is a law that sets a deadline for bringing a legal claim. The time allowed depends on the type of claim, and a court may reject a case filed after the deadline even if the person’s complaint is valid. Lilly Ledbetter’s case shows why the starting point matters. She sued Goodyear over gender discrimination in her pay, but in 2007 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that she had filed too late. Ledbetter argued that each discriminatory paycheck should start a new 180-day period for filing a claim. The Court rejected that argument, but Congress later changed the rule for pay-discrimination claims through the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009. President Barack Obama signed the act into law.

Jean-Paul Sartre was a French philosopher, novelist, and playwright who became a leading figure in existentialism. In his book Being and Nothingness, he argued that “existence precedes essence”: people are not born with a fixed purpose or identity but shape who they are through their choices. Sartre believed this freedom brings responsibility, and he called it “bad faith” when people pretend they have no choice. His play No Exit places three characters together in a room where they cannot escape one another’s judgments. Its famous line, “Hell is other people,” reflects their struggle with how others see them. In 1964, Sartre was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, but he refused it because he believed a writer should not be turned into an institution.

The Sally–Anne test is a classic psychology task that explores whether children understand that someone else can believe something that is not true. Two dolls, Sally and Anne, represent the characters. Sally puts a marble in a basket and leaves the room. While she is away, Anne moves the marble to a box. The child is then asked where Sally will look for the marble when she returns. A child who understands Sally’s false belief will answer “the basket,” because Sally did not see Anne move it. Answering “the box” may mean the child is relying on what they know is true rather than considering Sally’s perspective. This ability to think about another person’s beliefs is part of what psychologists call theory of mind.

Virtue ethics is an approach to moral philosophy that asks what kind of person we should become, not just which rules we should follow or which action produces the best outcome. It focuses on developing good character traits, called virtues, such as courage, justice, kindness, and generosity. A virtue ethicist might ask, “What would a fair and compassionate person do?” The ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle explored this approach in Nicomachean Ethics. He described eudaimonia—the highest human good—as a flourishing life achieved through the practice of virtue. Interest in virtue ethics grew again in modern philosophy after G.E.M. Anscombe’s 1958 essay “Modern Moral Philosophy.” This approach contrasts with deontology, which emphasizes duties and rules, and consequentialism, which judges actions mainly by their results.

Lesbianism is a sexual orientation and identity involving women who experience romantic or sexual attraction to other women. A woman with this orientation may call herself a lesbian, although people choose the words that best describe their own experiences. The term comes from Lesbos, an island in the Aegean Sea where the ancient Greek poet Sappho lived. Sappho wrote poems expressing affection and desire for women, so her name also gave rise to the word “sapphic,” another term associated with love between women. Today, lesbian identities are part of discussions about relationships, culture, and equality. The “L” in LGBT stands for lesbian; the other letters refer to other sexual orientations and gender identities.

No-fault divorce allows a married couple to legally end their marriage without either spouse proving that the other committed adultery, cruelty, or another kind of wrongdoing. Instead, a court may accept a reason such as “irreconcilable differences,” meaning the spouses cannot resolve problems in their relationship. This changed earlier rules that often required one spouse to accuse the other of misconduct before a divorce could be granted. California’s 1969 Family Law Act helped establish no-fault divorce in the United States. It was signed by California’s governor, Ronald Reagan, who later became president. Reagan had himself been divorced before taking office, making him the first U.S. president to have been divorced.

David Ricardo was an English political economist whose 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation examined how income is divided among landowners, workers, and business owners through rent, wages, and profits. He is especially known for explaining comparative advantage, a principle of international trade. A country has an absolute advantage when it can produce a good using fewer resources, such as fewer labor hours, than another country. Comparative advantage asks a different question: what does each country give up to make one good instead of another? Even if one country can make every good more efficiently, both countries can benefit by specializing in goods they produce at the lowest relative cost and then trading. This idea helps explain why trade can benefit countries with different levels of productivity.

Subjective idealism is the view that sensible objects, such as trees and tables, depend on minds that perceive them rather than existing as mind-independent material things. Its best-known defender was George Berkeley, an Irish philosopher and Anglican bishop. In A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, he argued that “to be is to be perceived”: what we know of an object comes through experiences such as seeing and touching it. Berkeley also defended his ideas in Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous. But does a tree stop existing when nobody is nearby? Berkeley said no. He believed God perceives everything all the time, so objects continue to exist even when no human observes them. This account of reality is also called Berkeley’s immaterialism.

Francis Fukuyama is an American political scientist best known for The End of History and the Last Man. The book grew out of a 1989 essay in The National Interest and was published in 1992. Fukuyama argued that, after the Cold War, liberal democracy might be the endpoint of humanity’s ideological evolution—not that wars, disagreements, or other events would stop happening. He has also written two books about political order: how societies develop stable institutions that allow governments to function. These works trace the rise of capable states, the rule of law, and accountable government, while examining how institutions can weaken over time. Fukuyama was once associated with neoconservatism, a political movement known partly for supporting a forceful foreign policy, but he later distanced himself from it.

Yin and yang are paired ideas in classical Chinese philosophy that describe how apparent opposites depend on and complement each other. Yin is traditionally associated with darkness, coolness, stillness, and qualities described as feminine; yang is associated with light, warmth, activity, and qualities described as masculine. Neither is simply good or bad, and each can give way to the other, as night turns into day. Their changing balance helps explain patterns in the natural world and is important in practices such as feng shui, which aims to create harmony between people and their surroundings. The familiar circular symbol of yin and yang is called the taijitu. Its interlocking black and white, comma-shaped halves each contain a dot of the opposite color, showing that each force contains an aspect of the other.

The Bradley effect is a proposed problem in election polls: some people may tell pollsters they support a Black candidate because that answer seems socially acceptable, even though they intend to vote for a white opponent. If this happens, polls can make the Black candidate’s support look stronger than it really is. The effect is named after Tom Bradley, the mayor of Los Angeles, who ran for governor of California in 1982. Pre-election polls showed Bradley ahead, but he lost to Republican George Deukmejian, who was then California’s attorney general. Researchers debate how much voters’ unwillingness to reveal their preferences explains that result; polling errors can have several causes. The Bradley effect is therefore a hypothesis, not a rule that applies to every election.

Supply is the relationship between a good’s price and the quantity producers are willing and able to offer for sale. The law of supply says that, all else being equal (ceteris paribus), producers generally offer more when the price rises and less when it falls. A higher price can make producing and selling the good more profitable, encouraging businesses to increase output. Economists show this relationship with a supply curve, which usually slopes upward as price and quantity increase together. Supply works alongside demand, the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy, to help determine market prices. If demand rises while supply stays the same, prices often rise; if supply rises while demand stays the same, prices often fall.

The Medellín Cartel was a Colombian drug-trafficking organization based in the city of Medellín and led by Pablo Escobar. During the 1980s and early 1990s, it became one of the world’s most powerful criminal networks by producing and distributing cocaine, especially to the United States. Drug cartels are groups that organize the illegal trade of drugs; Escobar’s cartel also used bribery and violence to protect its business and influence officials. Colombian authorities pursued Escobar for years. An elite Colombian National Police task force called the Search Bloc tracked him to Medellín, where he was killed in December 1993. The cartel’s history shows how illegal drug profits can fuel violence and corruption, affecting communities and government institutions.

Heraclitus was an ancient Greek philosopher from Ephesus who lived before Socrates. He taught that the world is always changing, using fire as an image of a cosmos in continual transformation. His famous claim that no one can step into the same river twice illustrates this idea: the river’s water keeps flowing, so it is never exactly the same river from one moment to the next. Yet Heraclitus did not think change was random. He called the common rational principle that orders the changing cosmos the Logos, a Greek word often translated as “reason” or “account.” He believed this principle was shared by all, although most people failed to understand it.

Learned helplessness occurs when someone repeatedly experiences unpleasant events they cannot control and comes to believe that trying to change the situation is pointless. This belief can reduce their efforts to escape or solve a problem later, even when they have a real chance to succeed. In classic experiments, dogs that had experienced inescapable electric shocks often did not try to avoid later shocks, although escape was possible. American psychologist Martin Seligman co-developed this research. The idea can also help explain why a person facing repeated setbacks might stop trying, but it does not mean they are unable to learn or change. Seligman later became a leading advocate of positive psychology, which studies strengths and well-being, and served as president of the American Psychological Association.

Robert Nozick was an American philosopher who taught at Harvard. In his 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia, which won a National Book Award, he defended libertarianism and a minimal state limited mainly to protecting people from force, theft, and fraud. He argued that a more extensive state would violate individual rights. Nozick’s account of distributive justice is called entitlement theory. It asks how people came to own what they have: Was it acquired justly, transferred voluntarily, or corrected through rectification of a past injustice? If so, Nozick argued, the resulting distribution can be just even if it is unequal. His Wilt Chamberlain thought experiment illustrates how people’s voluntary choices can disrupt a planned pattern of wealth, challenging theories that judge fairness by the final pattern alone.

Abenomics was an economic program launched by Japanese prime minister Shinzō Abe after he returned to office in 2012. Japan had experienced years of slow growth and deflation, meaning that prices were falling or barely rising. Abe described his plan as three “arrows” meant to work together. The first, monetary easing, involved Japan’s central bank expanding the money supply by buying large amounts of financial assets and aiming for 2 percent inflation. The second, fiscal stimulus, used government spending to boost demand and create jobs. The third, structural reform, aimed to change rules and practices that limited long-term growth. Together, the arrows were intended to encourage spending, investment, and a stronger economy.

Moral psychology is the interdisciplinary study of how people decide what is right or wrong and how those decisions affect their behavior. It combines psychology’s study of emotions, reasoning, learning, development, and social interaction with philosophical questions about ethics. For example, researchers may ask whether people rely more on careful thought or immediate moral intuitions when judging an action. They also study how moral understanding changes as children grow and how other people influence our choices. One example is Moral Machine, a crowdsourced online study developed by researchers at MIT’s Media Lab. It presents unavoidable crash scenarios involving self-driving cars and asks people whose lives the cars should prioritize. The responses reveal public preferences, though they do not necessarily settle what an automated car ought to do.

Bankruptcy is a legal process for people or organizations that cannot repay their debts. Under court supervision, it provides an orderly way to address creditors’ claims rather than leaving each creditor to seek payment separately. In the United States, different chapters of bankruptcy law offer different approaches. Chapter 7 generally involves liquidation: selling assets and using the proceeds to pay creditors according to legal rules. Chapter 11 focuses on reorganization. It is commonly used by businesses that want to keep operating while they propose a plan to restructure their debts and repay creditors over time. Creditors can review and respond to the proposed terms, and the court oversees the process. Filing for bankruptcy does not automatically erase every debt or excuse someone from legal responsibilities.

The Secretary-General of the United Nations is the UN’s chief administrative officer under its founding charter and one of its leading diplomatic representatives. The Secretary-General manages the organization’s work and helps countries address conflicts through negotiation. One former holder of the position, Ghanaian diplomat Kofi Annan, served from 1997 to 2006. He gave his name to the Annan Plan, a 2004 proposal to reunify Cyprus, an island divided between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities; the plan was not adopted. Another former Secretary-General, Sweden’s Dag Hammarskjöld, worked to resolve international crises and died in a plane crash in 1961. The position’s title is Secretary-General of the United Nations, while Kofi Annan is the person associated with the Cyprus reunification plan.

The Giving Pledge is a campaign launched in 2010 by Bill and Melinda Gates and investor Warren Buffett. It invites billionaires and other extremely wealthy people to publicly promise to give more than half their wealth to philanthropic causes, either during their lives or after their deaths. Philanthropy means using money and other resources to help others, such as by supporting health care, education, or efforts to reduce poverty. The pledge is a public commitment, not a law, and its signers choose which causes to support. Buffett, a co-founder of the campaign, is the longtime chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and is nicknamed the “Oracle of Omaha” for his investing success. The campaign highlights how private wealth can be used to address social needs.

The College Board is an American educational organization best known for administering the SAT, a test used in college admissions, and for developing Advanced Placement (AP) courses and exams. AP courses let high school students study subjects at a college level and may help them earn college credit. In February 2023, the College Board announced that AP African American Studies would join its course offerings. Discussion of the course also drew attention to the 1619 Project, a journalism initiative created by Nikole Hannah-Jones. The project asks readers to examine U.S. history through the lasting effects of slavery. Its name refers to 1619, the year enslaved Africans first arrived in the English colony of Virginia. The 1619 Project and the College Board’s AP course are separate initiatives.

Counterfeiting is the crime of making fake money or altering real currency so it looks genuine and can be used as if it were real. For example, someone might print imitation banknotes or change a bill’s appearance to make it seem more valuable. Counterfeiting can undermine trust in money: if people cannot tell whether a bill is real, buying and selling become more difficult. In 1865, when counterfeit notes were a serious problem in the United States, the federal government created the United States Secret Service within the Treasury Department to investigate and combat the crime. The agency later gained a different, better-known responsibility. After President William McKinley was assassinated in 1901, Congress tasked the Secret Service with protecting the president.

A vowel is a speech sound made with a relatively open vocal tract, unlike a consonant, which involves narrowing or closing part of the tract. A diphthong is a vowel sound that glides from one vowel quality to another within a single syllable. For example, the “oy” in “toy” begins with one vowel quality and moves toward another, but we hear the glide as one syllable. Linguists can write this change using two symbols from the International Phonetic Alphabet, or IPA. The IPA is a standardized notation system for representing speech sounds across languages; its chart includes symbols for vowels and consonants, as well as diacritics that show additional details of pronunciation.

A witness is a person who gives testimony in a legal proceeding. An eyewitness describes something they personally saw or heard, while an expert witness uses specialized knowledge, such as medical or scientific training, to help the court understand evidence. Before an expert testifies, a court may question them about their qualifications and decide whether they may offer an expert opinion. This questioning can be called voir dire, a French-derived term often translated as “to speak the truth.” Voir dire is also used during jury selection, when lawyers and the judge question prospective jurors to find out whether they can be fair and impartial. Although witnesses and jurors have different roles, questioning them beforehand helps the court decide who is qualified to take part in a trial.

The Interpretation of Dreams is a book by Sigmund Freud, a Viennese neurologist who founded psychoanalysis, a way of studying how unconscious thoughts and feelings may shape behavior. Published in late 1899 with a title page dated 1900, the book argues that dreams recalled after sleep can express unconscious wishes, often in disguised form. Freud examined his own dreams to explain his ideas, including a dream about a patient known as Irma. He suggested that the events remembered from a dream can differ from the hidden thoughts behind them, so interpreting a dream means looking for those underlying meanings. Freud later proposed the id, ego, and superego as parts of the mind. His dream theories were influential, although many of their claims remain debated.

Pierre Teilhard de Chardin was a French Jesuit priest, paleontologist, and philosopher who belonged to the Roman Catholic Church. His study of fossils shaped his interest in evolution, but he believed evolution involved more than changes in living bodies. In his book The Phenomenon of Man, he argued that life develops toward greater complexity and that consciousness grows alongside it. He imagined humans becoming increasingly connected through shared thought and cooperation, eventually reaching a final state of spiritual unity. Teilhard called this destination the Omega Point, using “omega,” the last letter of the Greek alphabet, to suggest an ultimate endpoint. His ideas brought together science and religious belief, though his vision of evolution was a philosophical and theological interpretation rather than an established scientific prediction.

Mencius was a Confucian philosopher who lived during China’s Warring States period, centuries after Confucius. Traditionally honored as the “second sage,” he is known through a collection of conversations and teachings called the Mencius. He argued that human nature is fundamentally good, but that people must nurture their moral abilities, much as a gardener tends young plants. Mencius called the first stirrings of virtue the “four sprouts.” Compassion can grow into benevolence, or care for others; shame at wrongdoing into righteousness; deference, or respectful consideration, into propriety; and a sense of right and wrong into wisdom. For Mencius, these impulses exist naturally in everyone, but whether they flourish depends on how people learn and act.

Beauty is an aesthetic quality that can make a person, artwork, place, or idea seem pleasing or worthy of admiration. Philosophers who study aesthetics ask why we find things beautiful and whether beauty lies in the object itself or in the person experiencing it. The English Romantic poet John Keats explored beauty in several odes. At the end of “Ode on a Grecian Urn,” a poem about an ancient Greek vessel, he famously links beauty with truth. In “Ode to Melancholy,” he writes that melancholy “dwells with Beauty—Beauty that must die.” This suggests that beautiful things do not last forever and that awareness of their passing can bring sadness alongside pleasure.

Maria Montessori was an Italian physician and educator who became one of Italy’s earliest women to earn a medical degree, despite facing opposition to studying medicine. In 1907, she opened the Casa dei Bambini, or “Children’s House,” in Rome. Her work there led to the Montessori method, a child-centered approach that gives children opportunities to choose activities, use hands-on materials, and learn through discovery while teachers guide and observe them. Montessori believed that young children are naturally eager to learn and can develop independence when their environment supports exploration. She called their remarkable ability to take in language, culture, and other knowledge from everyday experience the “absorbent mind.” She considered this capacity especially important during the first six years of life, when children learn rapidly from the world around them.

Sociology is the systematic study of society: how people interact, form groups, build institutions, and behave collectively. Sociologists use evidence, such as surveys, interviews, and statistics, alongside theories to understand how families, schools, governments, and inequalities shape people’s lives. Sociology overlaps with anthropology, the study of humans and their cultures, but often focuses on social relationships and structures within societies. A founding figure, the French scholar Émile Durkheim, argued that “social facts,” such as shared rules and customs, should be studied as real forces that influence individuals. In his study of suicide, he compared rates among religious groups, including Protestants and Catholics. He argued that differences in social integration—how strongly people are connected to a community—helped explain differences in those rates.

Property means something a person owns or controls, such as land, a home, or personal belongings. It was an important idea for Enlightenment thinkers who asked what rights people have and how societies should be organized. John Locke treated property as a natural right, alongside life and liberty, that governments should protect. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, a Genevan philosopher, examined a different side of the issue. In Discourse on the Origin and Basis of Inequality, he argued that the establishment of private property helped create social inequality: once people claimed land and resources as their own, some gained wealth and power while others did not. Rousseau also wrote The Social Contract, which opens with the line “Man is born free, yet everywhere is in chains,” and Emile, a work about education.

A school is an institution where pupils and teachers come together for planned learning. Students often study subjects such as reading, mathematics, and science in classrooms, while also developing skills through discussion, practice, and activities with others. Schools can take many forms, from large public buildings to small schools based in homes. In Louisa May Alcott’s Little Women, Jo March is one of four sisters in the March family, alongside Meg, Beth, and Amy. In the sequel Little Men, Jo and Professor Bhaer establish a school for boys in the home Jo inherited from her aunt. That school is called Plumfield. The novel follows the lives and education of its pupils, showing that a school can be both a place for academic lessons and a community where children grow.

Saving is the part of income that households do not spend on goods and services now. Instead, they set it aside in bank deposits or other financial assets for future purchases or investment. Saving postpones current consumption and can help fund new capital, such as machines and buildings used in production. Economists study how saving affects an economy’s growth. In the Solow-Swan growth model, the share of income saved is generally treated as fixed. The Ramsey growth model instead examines how households choose between consuming now and saving for the future. First formulated by Frank Ramsey in a 1928 paper on the mathematical theory of thrift, it helps explain how choices about saving can shape capital accumulation over time.

The Slutsky equation explains why the quantity people buy changes when a price changes. It separates the overall change into a substitution effect and an income effect. The substitution effect occurs because a good becomes cheaper or more expensive relative to other goods, encouraging buyers to switch between them. The income effect occurs because the price change alters what buyers can afford with the same money. The equation relates the price derivatives, or rates of change, of two kinds of demand. Marshallian demand shows choices at given prices and income, so it is called uncompensated demand. Hicksian demand holds the buyer’s utility, or level of satisfaction, fixed while prices change. It finds the least expensive way to reach that utility level, making it compensated demand and allowing economists to isolate the substitution effect.

George Berkeley was an Irish early modern philosopher who argued that physical objects do not exist independently of minds. His view, called immaterialism or subjective idealism, is often summed up as “to be is to be perceived.” For example, you know a tree through experiences such as seeing its shape and feeling its bark, rather than through a material object existing apart from all perception. But what happens when no person is looking at the tree? Berkeley argued that it continues to exist because God perceives everything. He defended these ideas in A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge and in Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous, a work published in 1713 that presents the debate as conversations between two characters.

Personality is the characteristic pattern of how a person behaves, thinks, and responds emotionally. Psychologists study it in several ways. The Big Five model describes personality using five broad traits, often remembered by the acronym OCEAN: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism. Other approaches group people into types. The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, or MBTI, is a four-letter assessment that sorts people into 16 profiles, such as ESFP and INTJ. It uses four pairs of preferences, including introversion versus extraversion, and draws partly on Carl Jung’s ideas about psychological types. Unlike the Big Five, which measures traits along a range, the MBTI places people into categories. These frameworks offer different ways to describe personality, though no short test can capture everything about a person.

Inductive reasoning, or induction, uses particular observations to form a general rule or predict what will happen in cases not yet observed. If the sun has risen every morning you remember, you may expect it to rise tomorrow. Unlike deduction, which can guarantee a conclusion when its premises are true and its logic is valid, induction makes a conclusion likely but not certain. The philosopher David Hume highlighted the problem of induction: what justifies assuming that patterns observed in the past will continue in the future? Saying that induction has worked before does not solve the problem, because that argument itself uses induction. The sun’s past behavior therefore gives us a strong practical reason to expect another sunrise, but it does not logically prove one must occur.

The Sentinelese are an Indigenous people who live on North Sentinel Island, part of India’s Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal. They are also called the North Sentinel Islanders. They obtain food by hunting, fishing, and gathering, including collecting mud crabs. The Sentinelese have largely avoided contact with outsiders and have resisted attempts to visit their island. Indian law restricts access to protect them from intrusion and from diseases to which they may have little immunity. In 2018, an American missionary named John Allen Chau made an unauthorized landing on North Sentinel Island, hoping to contact the people who lived there. He was killed during that attempt. Their continued isolation makes it important to respect their choice to remain apart from outside society.

Being and Nothingness is a 1943 philosophical treatise by Jean-Paul Sartre, a leading French existentialist. Sartre argues that people are conscious of themselves and their surroundings and must make choices about how to live. This freedom can feel unsettling because we are responsible for our actions rather than simply following a fixed role. He calls it “bad faith” when people deceive themselves to avoid that responsibility. For example, he describes a waiter who acts as though being a waiter completely defines who he is, leaving no room for other possibilities. Sartre also wrote the novel Nausea and declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature. His work asks readers to consider how honestly they face their freedom.

American Sign Language, or ASL, is a natural visual language used mainly by Deaf communities in the United States and English-speaking parts of Canada. Instead of relying on spoken sounds, it uses handshapes, movements, facial expressions, and body position to communicate. ASL has its own grammar and is not simply English translated into signs. It developed in the 1800s through contact among signers at a school for Deaf students founded by Thomas Gallaudet. French Sign Language traditions and regional signing practices, including those used on Martha’s Vineyard, helped shape it. Like spoken languages, ASL allows for playful challenges similar to tongue twisters. Signing sequences such as “good blood, bad blood” can be difficult because they require quick, precise changes in handshape and movement. These signing tongue twisters are nicknamed finger fumblers.

The Second Treatise of Government is a late-17th-century work by the English philosopher John Locke. Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property. Governments are created to protect those rights, and their authority is legitimate only when the people consent to be governed. If rulers violate people’s rights or become tyrannical, the people may resist them and establish a new government. These ideas later influenced democratic movements, including the American Revolution. Locke also wrote An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, a work about how people gain knowledge. There, he challenged the idea that humans are born with certain ideas already in their minds.

The United Nations Security Council is the UN body with primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. Established by the UN Charter in 1945, it can respond to threats by calling for ceasefires, imposing sanctions, or authorizing peacekeeping missions. The council has 15 members: five permanent members—China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States—and ten others elected for two-year terms. Each permanent member has veto power, meaning it can block a substantive draft resolution even if most other members support it. The council’s presidency rotates among its members each month; holding the presidency does not give a country an extra vote or remove any other permanent member’s veto power.

Alexander Wendt is an American political scientist associated with constructivism, an approach to international relations that emphasizes how shared ideas shape the way countries behave. In his landmark 1992 article, “Anarchy Is What States Make of It,” Wendt argued that anarchy—the absence of a world government—does not automatically make states enemies. Instead, states give anarchy its meaning through their interactions: they may come to see one another as rivals, threats, or partners. He developed this argument in his 1999 book Social Theory of International Politics. There, Wendt explained that states’ identities and interests are not determined solely by material factors such as military power or resources. They are also shaped by shared understandings, expectations, and past relationships.

The social contract is the idea that a government’s authority comes from an agreement among the people it governs. People accept limits on some of their freedoms and agree to follow common rules in return for protection of their rights, public security, and a more orderly society. The English philosopher Thomas Hobbes argued that without a common authority, people would live in a “war of all against all,” with life “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.” He believed people could escape this dangerous condition by authorizing a sovereign, or ruler, to keep the peace. Other thinkers developed different versions of the social contract: John Locke emphasized the protection of natural rights, including life, liberty, and property, while Jean-Jacques Rousseau explored how political authority could reflect the will of the people.

Leviathan is a political-philosophical treatise published in 1651 by the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes, who was born in 1588 and spent time in exile in France around the English Civil Wars. Hobbes argued that without a common power to enforce rules, people would live in a dangerous “state of nature,” marked by insecurity and a “war of all against all.” To escape this condition, people make a social contract: they authorize a sovereign ruler to govern and keep the peace. Hobbes believed that this sovereign needed strong, even absolute, authority to prevent society from falling back into conflict. The book’s famous frontispiece shows a crowned giant holding a sword and staff, with a body made up of many smaller people. Its title comes from a biblical sea monster.

Manufacturing Consent: The Political Economy of the Mass Media is a 1988 book by Noam Chomsky and Edward S. Herman about how powerful institutions shape the news people see. The authors propose the propaganda model, a framework for explaining why news organizations may repeatedly favor certain viewpoints without journalists consciously coordinating or being ordered to lie. They describe five institutional “filters” that influence which stories are selected and how they are presented: media ownership, dependence on advertising revenue, reliance on powerful sources for information, “flak” or organized criticism that pressures outlets, and a dominant ideology that defines perceived threats. Together, these pressures can make some ideas seem natural or trustworthy while pushing others to the margins. The book asks readers to examine the economic and political structures behind news coverage, not just the intentions of individual reporters.

Proto-Indo-European is the reconstructed common ancestor of the Indo-European language family, which includes English, Greek, Latin, Sanskrit, Persian, and Russian. No written record of Proto-Indo-European survives, so linguists infer its sounds and grammar by comparing systematic similarities among its descendant languages. For example, related words may show regular sound correspondences, while shared grammatical forms can point to features inherited from an older language. Scholars have also used reconstructed vocabulary to explore what its speakers may have known, including livestock and wheeled vehicles. In 1868, the German linguist August Schleicher wrote a short fable in his reconstruction of Proto-Indo-European to demonstrate how it might have sounded. The fable is commonly called “The Sheep and the Horses.”

Water privatization is the process of transferring ownership or management of water services from a government to a private company. These services can include treating and distributing drinking water through pipes and collecting and treating wastewater. Supporters argue that private companies may bring investment and improve services, while critics worry that higher prices could make water harder for people to afford and that companies may not serve everyone fairly. Governments can set rules to protect access and regulate prices, but how well those rules work is often debated. A well-known example occurred in Cochabamba, Bolivia, where a concession involving the municipal water utility SEMAPA sparked major protests and riots in 1999–2000. The conflict made Cochabamba a landmark case in debates about who should control essential water services.

A monarchy is a system of government in which one person, usually a king or queen, serves as head of state. The position is often inherited through a royal family. In a constitutional monarchy, a constitution and laws limit the monarch’s powers, and elected officials usually make most political decisions. In an absolute monarchy, the ruler has much greater authority over government. Monarchs have claimed different reasons for their right to rule. Under the divine right of kings, a sovereign’s authority comes directly from God, rather than from the people or a legislature. This idea was used to defend royal power in Europe. A different tradition in China, the Mandate of Heaven, held that a ruler could lose the right to govern by ruling badly.

Human migration is the movement of people from one region or country to another, either temporarily or permanently. A common way to explain migration is the push-pull factors framework. Push factors are hardships that encourage people to leave their place of origin, such as unemployment, conflict, or limited opportunities. Pull factors are features that attract people to a destination, such as available jobs, safety, or better education. For example, someone might leave an area with few jobs and move to a city where employers are hiring. Migration can change the size and makeup of populations in both places. It can also affect labor supply: the area people leave may have fewer workers, while the destination may gain workers with a range of skills.

A jury trial is a court proceeding in which a group of citizens called jurors listens to evidence and decides disputed facts. The judge oversees the trial, rules on questions of law, and makes sure proper procedures are followed. After hearing the case, jurors discuss the evidence and reach a verdict, such as guilty or not guilty in a criminal case. Reginald Rose’s drama 12 Angry Men takes place almost entirely in a jury room during these discussions. At first, nearly all the jurors vote to convict, but one holdout urges them to examine the evidence more carefully. As they reconsider eyewitness testimony, a knife, and the prosecution’s timeline, the jurors come to doubt the defendant’s guilt and ultimately vote to acquit him.

The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, or MBTI, is a personality questionnaire that describes how people prefer to focus their attention, take in information, make decisions, and approach daily life. It was developed by American writer Isabel Briggs Myers and her mother, Katharine Cook Briggs, building on psychologist Carl Jung’s theory of psychological types. The questionnaire uses four pairs of preferences: introversion (I) or extraversion (E), sensing (S) or intuition (N), thinking (T) or feeling (F), and judging (J) or perceiving (P). Choosing one letter from each pair produces one of 16 four-letter types, such as INTJ or ESFP. These types can be useful for discussing preferences, but they should not be treated as fixed limits on what a person can do.

Gresham’s Law is a principle about what happens when two forms of money must be accepted at the same legally fixed value, even though one is worth more as a material or could be exchanged for more elsewhere. People tend to spend the less valuable money and save, melt down, or export the more valuable money. As a result, the less valuable form dominates everyday circulation. This is often summarized as “bad money drives out good,” but it depends on the two forms being treated as equal in payment; it does not mean people always prefer worse money. The law is named for Thomas Gresham, a 16th-century English merchant and royal financier. He served Elizabeth I as an agent in Antwerp and helped establish London’s Royal Exchange, which opened in 1571.

Esperanto is a planned language created by L. L. Zamenhof to help people from different countries communicate without having to learn many foreign languages. It is a constructed language, or conlang, but unlike languages invented for fictional worlds, it was designed for real-world use. Its grammar is deliberately regular: nouns typically end in -o, adjectives in -a, adverbs in -e, and verbs in their basic form in -i. Esperanto has just one definite article, la, meaning “the.” Its name means “one who hopes.” Zamenhof also left out grammatical gender, the system in some languages that classifies nouns as masculine, feminine, or neuter. Removing that requirement helps make Esperanto easier to learn.

War is organized armed conflict between states, political communities, or other organized groups. It can involve armies fighting over territory, political power, security, or resources, and it can cause great harm to civilians as well as soldiers. Scholars of international relations study why wars begin, how they are fought, and how they can be prevented or ended. For centuries, thinkers have also written about military strategy. The ancient Chinese strategist Sun Tzu is traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise that emphasizes deception and argues that subduing an opponent without battle is better than fighting. Much later, the Italian thinker Niccolò Machiavelli wrote a treatise called The Art of War. These works show that studying war involves decisions and strategy, not just battles.

Factors of production are the basic resources businesses use to make goods and provide services. In the traditional framework, they are land, labor, and capital. Land means natural resources, such as farmland, water, and minerals. Labor is the human effort, skills, and time people contribute to production. Capital means produced assets that help make other goods or services, including tools, machinery, and buildings. For example, a bakery uses land and natural resources to obtain ingredients, workers’ labor to prepare bread, and capital such as ovens and a bakery building. Economists also study how the supply and use of these inputs affect economic growth. Adding more workers or machines can raise production, while new technology can help the same resources produce more.

Aircraft hijacking is the unlawful seizure or control of an airplane, usually by people who threaten its crew or passengers. Hijackers may try to redirect the flight, take hostages, demand money, or pressure a government to meet political demands. Because aircraft often cross national borders, hijacking is a serious crime under both domestic and international law. A well-known case occurred in 1976, when members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and allied militants hijacked Air France Flight 139 and diverted it to Entebbe Airport in Uganda. Uganda’s dictator, Idi Amin, supported the hijackers. Israeli and Jewish passengers were among those held hostage. Israeli commandos later carried out the Entebbe Raid, a military operation that rescued many of the remaining hostages.

Click consonants are speech sounds made by sealing off a small pocket of air in the mouth with the tongue, then releasing one part of the seal to produce a sharp, suction-like sound. Unlike most consonants, they do not need air pushed out from the lungs. Linguists may write different clicks with symbols that look like a pipe, a bullseye, or an exclamation point. Clicks are especially characteristic of languages in southern Africa, including Xhosa and Zulu. These two closely related Bantu languages each use three types of clicks, made with the tongue in different positions. Zulu is the most common first language in South Africa. So, if a question asks for the sounds themselves, the answer is click consonants; if it asks for that widely spoken Bantu language, the answer is Zulu.
