This term describes harmful norms and behaviors, not masculinity or men as a whole. Researchers have linked pressure to follow such norms with a greater risk of depression and substance abuse in some men. They also discuss normative male alexithymia, a pattern in which social expectations may make it harder for some men to identify and describe their feelings. These are possible influences, not traits shared by all men.

Gross domestic product, or GDP, is the total market value of final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a given period, usually a quarter or a year. Economists use it as a broad measure of economic activity: when GDP rises, the economy is generally producing more. One way to calculate GDP is to add household consumption, business investment, government spending, and net exports, which are exports minus imports. To compare countries of different sizes, economists often calculate GDP per capita by dividing a country’s GDP by its population size, or number of people. This gives an average amount of economic output per person and can help compare standards of living, though it does not show how income is shared among citizens.

Middle English is the form of English used in England from roughly the late eleventh century to the late fifteenth century, between Old English and Early Modern English. It changed as English speakers came into closer contact with Norman French after the Norman Conquest, adding many French words to the language. Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in Middle English; its stories are told by pilgrims traveling to Canterbury. Other Middle English works include Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Pearl. Pearl is a poem in alliterative verse, which repeats sounds at the beginnings of nearby words. It takes the form of a father’s dream after the loss of a young girl. He sees her across a jeweled stream, where she explains Christian ideas about grace and salvation. Pearl survives in the same manuscript as Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.

An adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM, is a home loan whose interest rate can change over time. Unlike a fixed-rate mortgage, which keeps the same interest rate for the full term, an ARM often starts with a lower introductory rate. After that period ends, the rate may rise or fall under the loan’s terms, changing the borrower’s monthly payment. A sharp increase can make the loan difficult to afford, as happened to some borrowers during the 2008 financial crisis. The home is collateral: property pledged to secure the loan. If the borrower fails to make payments, the lender may have the right to seize it. The original amount borrowed is called the principal; interest is the extra cost of borrowing that money.

The World Bank Group is an international organization that supports economic development, especially in lower-income countries. It brings together five affiliated institutions: the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), International Development Association (IDA), International Finance Corporation (IFC), Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), and International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID). Together, they provide loans, grants, investment support, and policy advice for projects such as schools, roads, and water systems. Established in 1960, the IDA focuses on the world’s poorest countries. It offers grants and concessional credits—loans with favorable terms, often including low interest rates and long repayment periods. The World Bank Group has also faced criticism when its lending and policy recommendations, including support for privatizing public services, have been seen as unfair or harmful to local communities.

Fascism is an authoritarian, ultranationalist political ideology that puts the nation and a powerful leader above individual rights and democratic debate. It arose in Italy after World War I under Benito Mussolini. His movement used armed supporters called the Blackshirts to intimidate opponents and help it gain power. A turning point came in October 1922, when Fascist supporters converged on Italy’s capital in an event called the March on Rome. Their action created a political crisis, but it was not a straightforward military conquest of the city. King Victor Emmanuel III declined to authorize emergency rule and instead appointed Mussolini prime minister. Mussolini then used his position to dismantle democratic institutions and establish a dictatorship. Fascism also attracted supporters outside politics, including the American poet Ezra Pound, who praised Mussolini.

Nelson Goodman was an American philosopher who explored how we use past observations to predict the future, a process called induction. In his book Fact, Fiction, and Forecast, he presented the “new riddle of induction.” Imagine that every emerald examined so far has been green. We might predict that the next emerald will also be green. But Goodman invented the predicate “grue”: an object is grue if it is examined before a specified future time and is green, or examined afterward and is blue. Every emerald examined so far is therefore both green and grue, yet those descriptions lead to different predictions about emeralds examined later. Goodman paired grue with a contrasting predicate, “bleen,” to ask why some descriptions seem better suited to reliable predictions than others.

An oligarchy is a system of government in which power is held by a small, select group rather than shared broadly among the population. The word comes from Greek and means “rule of the few.” Members of the ruling group might gain influence through wealth, family connections, military power, or control of important institutions. Oligarchy contrasts with democracy, in which citizens have a role in making political decisions. Ancient Athens is famous for its democracy, although participation was limited and women, enslaved people, and foreigners were excluded. Athens did not remain democratic at all times: during the Peloponnesian War, an oligarchic group seized power in 411 BCE. This short-lived regime, known as the Four Hundred, briefly replaced the city’s democratic government.

The Second Sex is a landmark 1949 study by the French philosopher and novelist Simone de Beauvoir. Drawing on existentialism, a philosophy concerned with human freedom and the choices people make, de Beauvoir examines how society shapes women’s lives and opportunities. Her famous statement, “One is not born, but rather becomes a woman,” means that ideas about femininity are learned and enforced through upbringing, education, customs, and expectations, rather than simply fixed at birth. She argues that women have often been treated as the “Other”: defined in relation to men instead of recognized as full individuals. Originally written in French, The Second Sex helped inspire later feminist thought by asking how social structures limit women’s freedom and how those limits might be challenged.

Deadweight loss is the reduction in total economic welfare that occurs when some trades that would benefit both buyers and sellers do not happen. Economists measure it by comparing actual output with the socially optimal output: the quantity at which marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost. Up to that point, the benefit of each additional unit is greater than its cost, so producing it increases total surplus. A tax can raise the price buyers pay and lower the amount sellers receive, preventing some of these trades. A monopoly can restrict output to keep its price high. In a standard supply-and-demand diagram, the resulting deadweight loss appears as a triangle of lost surplus between the demand and supply curves, over the range of units that were not produced.

John Maynard Keynes was a British economist whose ideas changed how governments respond to recessions. In his 1936 book The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, he challenged the belief that markets would always return to full employment on their own. During the Great Depression, Keynes argued, too little spending could leave businesses with unsold goods, causing them to cut production and jobs. He called total planned spending on final goods and services at a given overall price level aggregate demand. It includes spending by households, businesses, and governments, as well as spending by foreign buyers on a country’s goods and services. Keynes believed that when private spending fell, government spending could help make up the shortfall, supporting output and employment.

Existence means being real rather than merely imagined or possible. In ontology, the branch of philosophy that studies what there is, philosophers distinguish what a thing is from whether it exists at all. A fictional dragon, for example, has describable features but does not exist in the world. Questions about existence are especially important in debates about God. In his medieval work Proslogion, the Benedictine monk Anselm of Canterbury offered an ontological argument: he described God as the greatest being we can conceive and argued that such a being cannot exist only in the mind, because existing in reality would be greater. Critics have challenged this reasoning, but it remains a famous attempt to argue for God’s existence from an idea of God.

The Sámi are an Indigenous people whose traditional homeland, Sápmi, stretches across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Russia’s Kola Peninsula. They speak several Sámi languages, which belong to the Finno-Ugric branch of the Uralic language family. Sámi communities have diverse traditions and livelihoods, including reindeer herding, fishing, and handicrafts, though many Sámi today live in towns and cities. Traditional clothing can include the brightly colored Four Winds hat. The older term “Lapps” is often considered offensive, so “Sámi” is preferred; “Lapland” remains a geographic name used for parts of the region, especially in Finland. Remember the distinction: Sámi names the people, while Sápmi names their homeland.

Published in 1966, Michel Foucault’s The Order of Things explores how ideas about knowledge change over time. Foucault argues that people in a given era share underlying ways of organizing what they know, even when they do not notice those assumptions. By tracing shifts from the Renaissance to the modern age, he examines the conditions that made the “human sciences,” such as the study of society and human behavior, possible. In the book’s preface, Foucault discusses Las Meninas, a painting by Diego Velázquez set in a Spanish court. It shows the young Infanta Margarita with her attendants, as well as a dwarf and a dog. Velázquez also paints himself at an easel. Foucault uses the scene to raise questions about who is looking, who is being represented, and how we understand what we see.

A taboo is an act, object, word, or practice that a society strongly forbids, often because people consider it sacred, dangerous, or polluting. The word comes from a Polynesian term meaning “forbidden.” Taboos vary across cultures: they can include prohibitions on cannibalism, restrictions involving sacred people, or rules against speaking or writing certain names. In ancient China, for example, people avoided writing the names of ancestors, respected figures, or the emperor. Taboos can help define a community’s values and boundaries, though the reasons for them differ. In his 1913 book Totem and Taboo, Sigmund Freud, a Viennese neurologist and founder of psychoanalysis, discussed totemism and rules against incest in Indigenous Australian societies.

Interest rates are the percentages charged on borrowed money, usually stated as an annual percentage of the principal, or original amount borrowed. They determine how much extra a borrower pays a lender. For example, a higher interest rate makes a loan more expensive, while a lower rate makes borrowing cheaper. In the United States, the Federal Reserve, or Fed, uses monetary policy to influence interest rates and the wider economy. During a downturn, when overall spending, or aggregate demand, is weak, the Fed may use expansionary monetary policy to encourage spending. It can buy bonds or lower a key borrowing rate, helping push interest rates down. Cheaper loans can encourage households to buy goods and businesses to invest, increasing aggregate demand.

Francis Bacon was an English philosopher, statesman, and Lord Chancellor who argued that knowledge should grow through careful observation and induction: using evidence from particular cases to reach broader conclusions. In The Advancement of Learning, he explored how different branches of knowledge could be organized, an idea that later influenced ways of classifying books. In Novum Organum, he set out an approach to investigating nature that helped shape the modern scientific method. Bacon also warned that reasoning can be distorted by four recurring kinds of error, which he called the Idols of the Mind. These include biases shared by all humans, biases formed by personal experience, confusion caused by language, and assumptions inherited from established philosophical systems. Recognizing these obstacles, he believed, helps people investigate the world more clearly.

The Critique of Pure Reason is a major work by the German Enlightenment philosopher Immanuel Kant. First published in 1781 and substantially revised in 1787, it asks what humans can know and whether metaphysics can provide reliable knowledge. Kant explores how synthetic a priori knowledge is possible: knowledge that adds something new but does not depend on particular experiences. He argues that the mind does not simply receive information from the world. Instead, it organizes experience through space and time, which he calls forms of intuition, and through basic concepts called categories. As a result, we know objects as they appear to us, not things in themselves as they might exist independently of our minds. This distinction sets limits on what human reason can claim to know.

Intelligence is the broad ability to learn, reason, solve problems, understand new ideas, and adapt to unfamiliar situations. Researchers often study it using standardized tests, such as the Stanford–Binet test, which was developed to assess children’s thinking abilities. A score from such a test is called an intelligence quotient, or IQ; on many IQ tests, the average score is set at 100. The score is a measurement, while intelligence is the underlying capacity the test aims to assess. Researchers have also observed the Flynn effect: in many countries, average scores on standardized cognitive tests rose across successive generations, especially during the twentieth century. This does not necessarily mean that each generation was born more intelligent; changes in education, health, and daily life may have helped people perform better on the tests.

Philosophical optimism is the early modern idea that the actual world is the best of all possible worlds. The philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz argued that a wise and good God would choose the best possible creation, even if people cannot understand why it contains suffering and other apparent evils. The French Enlightenment writer Voltaire mocked this doctrine in his satirical novel Candide. Dr. Pangloss, the title character’s teacher, repeatedly insists that “all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds,” even when terrible events happen around him. By making Pangloss defend this claim in the face of disaster, Voltaire challenges the idea that every misfortune must somehow contribute to an ultimately perfect plan.

Human infants are babies in the earliest stage of life, when their senses and relationships with caregivers are developing rapidly. Psychologists study infants to learn how they perceive the world and form attachments. In Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk’s visual cliff experiment, infants encountered a glass-covered platform whose patterned surface appeared to drop away on one side. Their behavior helped researchers investigate depth perception. Mary Ainsworth studied attachment using a procedure called the Strange Situation. In this structured observation, an infant spends time in a room with a caregiver, who briefly leaves and returns, while an unfamiliar adult also enters and leaves. Researchers watch how the infant responds, especially during separation and reunion, to understand the infant’s attachment to the caregiver.

Jury unanimity is the rule in many criminal trials that every juror must agree on the same verdict, such as guilty or not guilty. After hearing the evidence, jurors deliberate together, discussing the case and trying to reach a decision. If the trial requires unanimity, a majority vote is not enough: even one juror who disagrees prevents a verdict. A jury that remains unable to agree after deliberating is called a hung jury. The judge may then end the trial without a verdict, an outcome known as a mistrial. In some cases, prosecutors can choose to try the case again with a new jury. Unanimity rules vary by place and type of case, but where they apply, they require agreement from the entire deliberating jury.

Quantitative easing, or QE, is a policy central banks use to support an economy when short-term interest rates are already near zero and cannot easily be cut further. The central bank buys large amounts of government bonds and sometimes other financial assets, adding money and liquid assets to the financial system. These purchases can lower longer-term borrowing costs, making it easier for households and businesses to borrow and spend. Japan’s central bank, the Bank of Japan, launched a QE program in March 2001 to fight deflation, a sustained fall in prices. Instead of targeting the overnight call rate, a short-term interest rate, its initial program targeted the current-account balances that financial institutions held at the central bank. The U.S. Federal Reserve later used QE during the Great Recession.

Atomism is the ancient philosophical theory that everything is made of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms moving through empty space, or a void. Instead of treating matter as continuous and endlessly divisible, atomists argued that objects differ because their atoms have different shapes, arrangements, and positions. In ancient Greece, the theory is especially associated with Leucippus and his follower Democritus, a philosopher from Abdera and one of atomism’s major proponents. Democritus was nicknamed the “laughing philosopher” for his cheerful outlook. Ancient writers contrasted him with Heraclitus, the “weeping philosopher,” who emphasized that the world is constantly changing. Ancient atomism was a philosophical explanation of reality, not the same as the modern scientific theory of atoms, which describes particles that have smaller components.

The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision is an international forum where central banks and national banking regulators work together to make banks safer. It was created in 1974 after the Herstatt crisis showed that the failure of a bank operating across borders could expose gaps in financial oversight. Its secretariat is hosted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in Basel, Switzerland. The committee develops shared standards, including rules about capital adequacy: how much money banks must keep available to absorb losses. Some banks are designated global systemically important banks, or G-SIBs, because their failure could threaten the international financial system. Under the committee’s framework, these banks must hold an additional buffer of high-quality capital called Common Equity Tier 1. This extra requirement is the G-SIB surcharge, and its size depends on the bank’s systemic-importance category.

Tourism is the economic sector built around people traveling to places outside their usual surroundings for leisure, culture, or other purposes. Visitors spend money on lodging, food, guided excursions, and transport while exploring landmarks, cultural heritage sites, and natural attractions. That spending can provide jobs and bring foreign currency into a country, but an economy that depends heavily on tourism can suffer when travel suddenly declines. Sri Lanka, an island nation off the southern tip of India, experienced this problem during the COVID-19 pandemic, when international travel fell sharply. Its government, led by Gotabaya Rajapaksa, cited the loss of tourism revenue as one cause of a severe economic crisis. In 2022, protests over economic mismanagement culminated in demonstrators occupying the president’s and prime minister’s residences in Colombo, Sri Lanka’s largest city.

George Armitage Miller was an American psychologist and a pioneer of cognitive science, the study of how people think, learn, and remember. He is best known for the idea that short-term memory can keep about seven units of information readily accessible at once, give or take two. Short-term memory is the temporary store you use when holding a phone number in mind long enough to dial it or remembering a brief set of instructions. Miller also showed that these units can be “chunks”: meaningful groups rather than single letters or numbers. For example, familiar initials may be easier to remember as one group than as separate letters. The “seven plus or minus two” estimate is a classic rule of thumb, not a fixed limit for every person or task.

The Milgram obedience experiment was a landmark study of how people respond to orders from an authority figure. Beginning in 1961 at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut, psychologist Stanley Milgram recruited volunteers for what they were told was a study of learning and memory. Each volunteer acted as a “teacher” and was instructed to give a “learner” an increasingly strong electric shock after each mistake on a word-memory task. The shocks were not real, but the teachers believed they were, and many continued when the experimenter urged them to do so, despite the learner’s protests. Milgram wanted to understand how ordinary people might obey harmful orders, a question shaped by the Holocaust, in which Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered six million Jews.

The Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race is an annual endurance event in Alaska in which mushers guide teams of sled dogs across roughly 1,000 miles of wilderness. The race usually begins in early March near Anchorage and follows a historic trail through forests, mountains, frozen rivers, and remote communities. Mushers must care for their dogs throughout the journey, stopping at checkpoints for rest and veterinary checks while coping with snow, ice, wind, and extreme cold. The route can vary from year to year, but it traditionally finishes beneath a burled-wood arch in Nome, a coastal town on the Seward Peninsula beside the Bering Sea. The race celebrates the skills and traditions of sled-dog travel, which was once an important way to carry people and supplies across Alaska.

Pau Gasol is a Spanish basketball player known for his skill as a power forward and center. Selected third overall in the 2001 NBA draft, he began his career with the Memphis Grizzlies and won the NBA Rookie of the Year award. In 2008, Memphis traded Pau to the Los Angeles Lakers, where he teamed with star guard Kobe Bryant. Together, they helped the Lakers win consecutive NBA championships in 2009 and 2010. The trade also involved Pau’s younger brother, Marc Gasol: Memphis acquired the rights to Marc, a center who became a key player for the Grizzlies. Marc was named an NBA All-Star three times and won the league’s Defensive Player of the Year award in 2013.

Nyjah Huston is an American professional skateboarder known for his success in street competitions. In street skateboarding, athletes perform tricks on obstacles modeled after features of a city, such as handrails, stairs, and ledges. Skateboarding also has park events, which use a course with ramps and curved surfaces. Huston has won ten X Games Street gold medals, a record for that event. He was favored to win men’s street when skateboarding made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo 2020 Games, which were held in 2021. Instead, he finished seventh after failing to land four tricks in a row. Japan’s Yuto Horigome won the men’s street gold medal at those Games.

The International Federation of Bodybuilding and Fitness (IFBB) is an organization that oversees amateur bodybuilding and fitness competitions around the world. It was founded in Montreal, Canada, in 1946 by brothers Joe and Ben Weider. Joe Weider was a Canadian bodybuilding promoter who also launched the Mr. Olympia contest in 1965; Arnold Schwarzenegger later won that title seven times. In bodybuilding, competitors train to develop their muscles and then display their physiques through poses onstage. Judges assess qualities such as muscular development, balance, and presentation, rather than how much weight a competitor can lift. Competitors often apply tanning products and oil to make their muscles more visible under stage lights. The sport includes divisions such as Classic Physique and Men’s Physique.

The FIFA World Cup is the premier international tournament in men’s association football, also called soccer. National teams compete for the title, with the tournament usually held every four years in a different host country or countries. The 2002 World Cup was jointly hosted by South Korea and Japan, the first time it was held in Asia. Brazil won that tournament, with forward Ronaldinho among its stars. In the quarterfinal against England, he scored a memorable long-range free kick that went past goalkeeper David Seaman. Ronaldinho later played for FC Barcelona and won the 2005 Ballon d’Or, an award for outstanding individual performance. In the 2018 World Cup final, France defeated Croatia at Luzhniki Stadium in Moscow, Russia.

LeBron James is an American basketball player born in Ohio who was selected first overall by the Cleveland Cavaliers in the 2003 NBA draft. A versatile forward known for his scoring, passing, and leadership, he has won four NBA Most Valuable Player awards. After starting his career in Cleveland, he joined the Miami Heat and won his first two NBA championships there. He returned to the Cavaliers and helped bring Cleveland a championship in 2016, then moved to the Los Angeles Lakers in 2018. James also has a connection to soccer: in 2011, he acquired a minority stake in Liverpool Football Club. The Premier League team plays at Anfield in Merseyside, England, and its supporters are famous for singing “You’ll Never Walk Alone.”

Rugby union is a team sport played with an oval ball by 15 players on each side. Players move the ball upfield by carrying or kicking it, but they cannot pass it forward by hand. A team scores a try, worth five points, when a player grounds the ball in the opposition’s in-goal area. After a try, the team can attempt a conversion kick for two extra points; teams can also score with penalty kicks and drop goals. Rugby union is different from rugby sevens, a faster version with seven players per side that is played at the Olympics. Rugby union is Samoa’s national sport, and Samoa regularly ranks among the world’s top teams. New Zealand’s national team, the All Blacks, is also famous for its success in the sport.

Ronaldinho is a retired Brazilian soccer player famous for his creative passing, skillful dribbling, and playful style. He helped Brazil win the 2002 FIFA World Cup, held in South Korea and Japan. After playing for Paris Saint-Germain in France, he joined the Catalan club FC Barcelona in 2003. His performances there earned him the 2005 Ballon d’Or, an award given to the world’s best player. He also helped Barcelona win the 2005–06 UEFA Champions League, Europe’s leading club competition. Ronaldinho moved to Italy’s AC Milan in 2008. So, if a question mentions a Brazilian playmaker who won the 2005 Ballon d’Or and the 2002 World Cup, the player is Ronaldinho; the club where he won the Ballon d’Or was FC Barcelona.

Fielding Yost was a football coach who took charge of the University of Michigan’s team in 1901. His first Michigan squad went undefeated with an 11–0 record and outscored its opponents 550–0. Yost’s teams scored so quickly and often that they became known for their “Point-a-Minute” style of play. On January 1, 1902, he led Michigan to a 49–0 victory over Stanford in the first Rose Bowl. Michigan is in Ann Arbor, and its teams are called the Wolverines. They wear maize and blue and play home football games at Michigan Stadium, nicknamed “The Big House.” Yost’s success helped establish Michigan as one of college football’s leading programs.

Magnus Carlsen is a Norwegian chess grandmaster who became world champion in 2013 by defeating Viswanathan Anand. A grandmaster is a chess player awarded the game’s highest official title by FIDE, the International Chess Federation. Carlsen is known for finding strong moves in many kinds of positions and for his remarkable consistency against the world’s best players. He also holds the highest recorded FIDE rating in classical chess, reaching 2882. A rating is a number that estimates a player’s strength based on tournament results. Classical chess uses longer time controls than rapid or blitz chess, giving players more time to think through each move. Although Carlsen is a former world champion, his record classical rating remains a major achievement.

Fernando Alonso Díaz is a Spanish racing driver who won the Formula One World Drivers’ Championship in 2005 and 2006. He drove for Renault in both title-winning seasons, and his 2005 victory ended Michael Schumacher’s run of five consecutive championships. Alonso later raced for Ferrari from 2010 through 2014, competing for more titles with the Italian team known for its prancing-horse logo. He has also competed outside Formula One, including three attempts to enter the Indianapolis 500; he did not qualify for the 2019 race. His career has spanned several teams and types of racing, but his two consecutive championships with Renault remain among his best-known achievements.

The Michigan Wolverines are the varsity athletic teams of the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. Their football team competes in the Big Ten Conference and has a famous, longstanding rivalry with Ohio State. In 1902, coach Fielding Yost led Michigan to a 49–0 victory over Stanford in the first Rose Bowl game. The program has also produced well-known players such as Charles Woodson and Tom Brady. Michigan plays its home football games at Michigan Stadium, which opened in 1927. Because it holds more than 100,000 spectators, the stadium is often called “The Big House.” When a question asks for the nickname of the university’s teams, the answer is Michigan Wolverines; when it asks for the official name of their home venue, the answer is Michigan Stadium.

Super Bowl LI was the NFL championship game played in Houston, Texas, on February 5, 2017. The New England Patriots faced the Atlanta Falcons, who built a 28–3 lead during the third quarter. Led by quarterback Tom Brady, the Patriots scored 25 unanswered points to tie the game at 28–28. It became the first Super Bowl ever decided in overtime. New England won the coin toss, drove down the field, and scored a touchdown to win 34–28, completing the largest comeback in Super Bowl history. Brady threw for 466 yards and was named the game’s Most Valuable Player (MVP). The letters “LI” are Roman numerals for 51, so Super Bowl LI is also known as Super Bowl 51.

A stolen base is recorded when a baseball or softball runner advances to the next base without help from a hit, walk, or fielding error. Runners often try to steal while a pitch is being delivered, hoping to reach the next “bag” before the catcher’s throw. If the defense tags the runner out, it is called caught stealing instead. Speed and good timing make stealing bases easier, but runners must also judge when the pitcher is about to throw. Rickey Henderson, an Oakland Athletics outfielder and Hall of Famer, holds Major League Baseball’s career record with 1,406 stolen bases. He also set the single-season record by stealing 130 bases in 1982. In 2022, Julio Rodríguez became the first MLB rookie to hit 25 home runs and steal 25 bases.

Speedcubing is the competitive practice of solving Rubik’s Cubes and other twisty puzzles as quickly as possible. Competitors take part in events for different puzzles, including the 3×3×3 cube and the Pyraminx, as well as challenges such as one-handed solving, blindfolded solving, and finding a solution in the fewest moves. Solvers often start with a layer-by-layer approach, then learn faster methods such as CFOP, developed by Jessica Fridrich. They describe turns using letters for the cube’s faces: F for front, B for back, U for up, D for down, L for left, and R for right. The World Cube Association publishes competition regulations and recognizes official competitions, whose results contribute to international rankings and records.

Martial arts are systems of combat, self-defense, and physical training practiced around the world. They teach skills such as striking, blocking, movement, and control, while often building fitness, focus, and discipline. Karate developed in Okinawa, taekwondo in Korea, and kung fu is a broad term for Chinese martial arts. One Chinese martial art, Wing Chun, is known for protecting and controlling the centerline—an imaginary line down the front of the body—and for rapid sequences of straight punches called chain punches. The Wing Chun teacher Ip Man taught Bruce Lee, who later developed his own approach to fighting and became famous for the advice “Be water, my friend.” Although martial arts differ in their techniques and traditions, karate, taekwondo, kung fu, and Wing Chun all belong to this broad category.

The Houston Rockets are an NBA basketball team based in Houston, Texas. Led by Nigerian-born center Hakeem Olajuwon, they won their first two NBA championships in consecutive seasons, 1994 and 1995. Olajuwon was named NBA Finals Most Valuable Player both years. In 1994, the Rockets defeated the New York Knicks in a seven-game Finals series. Their comeback from a 2–0 deficit against the Phoenix Suns during those playoffs helped Houston earn the nickname “Clutch City.” In 1995, Houston again beat the Suns on its way to the Finals, where it defeated the top-seeded Orlando Magic. Years later, star guard James Harden won the league’s MVP award while playing for the Rockets. In 2021, Houston traded Harden to the Brooklyn Nets.

Leicester City F.C. is a professional soccer club from Leicester, England, nicknamed the Foxes. Before the 2015–16 season, bookmakers gave the club 5,000-to-1 odds of winning the Premier League, England’s highest division. Against those expectations, Leicester won its first top-flight title that season under manager Claudio Ranieri, with important contributions from players including striker Jamie Vardy and goalkeeper Kasper Schmeichel. The victory is remembered as one of soccer’s greatest upsets because clubs with much larger budgets were expected to finish ahead of Leicester. The team plays at King Power Stadium, which it moved into in 2002 after leaving its former ground, Filbert Street. The stadium’s current name comes from King Power, the retail brand associated with the club’s Thai ownership.

Tony Hawk is an American professional skateboarder nicknamed the “Birdman.” He became famous for vert skateboarding, in which riders perform aerial tricks above the curved walls of a large ramp. At the 1999 X Games, Hawk landed the first documented 900: a jump with two and a half complete spins before landing. His competition performances and the Tony Hawk video-game franchise helped introduce skateboarding to millions of people. Skateboarding also includes street events, where riders use obstacles such as stairs and handrails, and park events, which use a course of ramps and curves. The sport made its Olympic debut at the 2020 Summer Olympics, held in 2021, where Japan’s Yuto Horigome won the men’s street gold medal.

The San Diego Padres are a Major League Baseball team based in San Diego, California. They joined the National League as an expansion team in 1969 and now compete in its West division. Their home ballpark is Petco Park, which opened in 2004. The team’s name, “Padres,” is Spanish for “fathers” and refers to the Spanish missionaries who helped establish San Diego. Players associated with the Padres include Manny Machado, Yu Darvish, and Juan Soto, who arrived in a 2022 trade from the Washington Nationals. One of the most celebrated Padres is Hall of Fame outfielder Tony Gwynn. He spent all 20 seasons of his major-league career with San Diego, won eight National League batting titles, and wore No. 19, which the club later retired.

Kobe Bryant was an American basketball guard who spent all 20 of his NBA seasons with the Los Angeles Lakers. Known for his scoring and competitive drive, he helped the Lakers win five NBA championships. In 2006, he scored 81 points against the Toronto Raptors, the second-highest total in a single NBA game, and he scored 60 points in his final game in 2016. Early in his career, Bryant won the NBA slam dunk contest; he later adopted the nickname “Black Mamba.” Bryant won his last two championships, in 2009 and 2010, alongside Pau Gasol, a Spanish power forward whom the Lakers acquired from the Memphis Grizzlies in 2008. That trade also included the rights to Pau’s younger brother, Marc Gasol. Bryant died in a helicopter crash in 2020.

Giannis Antetokounmpo is a Greek-Nigerian basketball forward known for his speed, strength, and ability to score near the basket. Born in Athens, Greece, to Nigerian parents, he was selected 15th overall in the 2013 NBA draft and has played for the Milwaukee Bucks, a team from Wisconsin, since his NBA debut that year. Nicknamed the “Greek Freak,” Antetokounmpo helped lead the Bucks to the 2021 NBA championship. Milwaukee defeated the Phoenix Suns in six Finals games, winning its first title since 1971, when Kareem Abdul-Jabbar led the team. Antetokounmpo scored 50 points in the title-clinching Game 6 and was named the 2021 NBA Finals Most Valuable Player, or MVP.

Gary Gygax was a game designer from Wisconsin who helped create the modern tabletop role-playing game. He first developed Chainmail, a set of rules for fantasy battles with miniature figures. Gygax then worked with Dave Arneson to create Dungeons & Dragons, or D&D, which was published in 1974 by TSR. The original game came in three booklets: Men & Magic, Monsters & Treasure, and The Underworld & Wilderness Adventures. Gygax’s young daughter reportedly helped choose the name Dungeons & Dragons. In the game, players imagine characters such as fighters and rogues, describe what they do, and roll dice to find out what happens. Its twenty-sided die became especially important in later editions, including the third edition published by Wizards of the Coast.

Blackjack is a casino card game in which each player competes against the dealer, not the other players. The goal is to finish with a hand worth more than the dealer’s without going over 21, which is called a bust. Number cards are worth their printed values, while jacks, queens, and kings are worth 10. An ace can count as either 1 or 11. A hand with an ace counted as 11 without exceeding 21 is called a soft hand; if another card would cause a bust, the ace can instead count as 1. The strongest opening hand is an ace and a ten-valued card, which total 21 and are called a blackjack.

The Black Sox Scandal was a major crisis in American baseball after the 1919 World Series. Eight players on the Chicago White Sox were accused of working with gamblers to deliberately lose the championship to the Cincinnati Reds. The accusations shocked fans because they raised doubts about whether the games they watched were fair. One of the accused players was star outfielder “Shoeless” Joe Jackson. The players were acquitted in a criminal trial, but baseball still imposed its own punishment. In the scandal’s aftermath, federal judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis became baseball’s first commissioner and banned all eight accused players for life. The scandal remains a famous example of how gambling can threaten trust in sports.

The Edmonton Oilers are a National Hockey League (NHL) team based in Edmonton, the capital of Alberta, Canada. They have won five Stanley Cups, the NHL’s championship trophy, including four in the 1980s when Wayne Gretzky played for them. The Oilers were also part of a memorable moment in a 2007 game against the Dallas Stars. Dallas forward Patrik Štefan had a chance to score into an empty net, which had no goaltender guarding it, but he missed. Edmonton took the puck the other way and tied the game moments later. The play is often remembered as a reminder that even a seemingly easy empty-net goal is not guaranteed.

The Olympic Games are an international festival where athletes compete in many sports. They trace their roots to contests held at Olympia in ancient Greece, traditionally every four years. Ancient athletes competed without clothing, and the festival was an important part of Greek religious and cultural life. After the ancient Games ended, centuries passed before a French educator and historian, Pierre de Coubertin, campaigned to bring them back. He helped establish the International Olympic Committee in 1894, and the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in 1896. Today, the Games bring together competitors from around the world and remain the centerpiece of the modern Olympic movement.

Colombia’s men’s national football team represents the country in international soccer and is widely nicknamed “Los Cafeteros,” a reference to Colombia’s coffee-growing tradition. At the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, Colombia reached the round of 16, where it beat Uruguay 2–0. Midfielder James Rodríguez scored both goals. His first became one of the tournament’s most celebrated moments: after controlling the ball on his chest outside the penalty area, he struck a powerful left-footed volley that hit the underside of the crossbar and went into the goal. He scored again in the second half to secure Colombia’s victory. Rodríguez went on to win the Golden Boot as the tournament’s top scorer, with six goals.

An American football stadium is a large venue built around a rectangular field called a gridiron. The field has end zones at both ends and goalposts for kicks. Stadiums may be open-air or enclosed, and they provide seating so thousands of fans can watch games. One example is the Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana. It opened in 1975 and is the home field of the New Orleans Saints, a professional football team. Because the Superdome is a large enclosed building, it has also been used for purposes beyond sports. During Hurricane Katrina in 2005, it served as a public shelter for people seeking safety from the storm.

Baseball stadiums are large venues where teams play baseball and fans watch from seats around the field. The field has four bases arranged in a diamond, with dugouts for the teams and seating beyond the outfield. Stadiums can have distinctive features: Fenway Park in Boston, for example, has a towering left-field wall nicknamed the Green Monster. In 1992, Oriole Park at Camden Yards opened as the home of the Baltimore Orioles, an American League team. Located near Baltimore’s Inner Harbor in Maryland, it combined modern facilities with the look and feel of older baseball parks. Its design helped inspire a movement toward “retro-style” stadiums, which use features such as brickwork and views of the surrounding city to connect the ballpark to its setting.

The Seattle Mariners are a Major League Baseball team based in Seattle, the largest city in Washington state. They compete in the American League West and played their first home game at the Kingdome in April 1977. One of their best-known recent players is outfielder Julio Rodríguez. In 2022, his rookie season, Rodríguez became the first MLB rookie to hit at least 25 home runs and steal at least 25 bases in one season. A stolen base occurs when a runner advances to the next base while the pitcher is delivering the ball, without the help of a hit. Rodríguez also competed in the 2022 Home Run Derby, finishing second to Juan Soto.

The 2020 Summer Olympics were an international sports competition hosted by Tokyo, Japan. Although the Games are normally held every four years, the COVID-19 pandemic forced organizers to postpone this edition by one year. It took place in 2021 but kept the official name “2020 Summer Olympics.” The pandemic also raised concerns about the safety of bringing athletes and visitors together. Summer heat created another challenge: to protect competitors, organizers moved the marathon and racewalking events from Tokyo to Sapporo, a city on Japan’s northern island of Hokkaido where conditions were expected to be cooler. Sapporo had previously hosted the 1972 Winter Olympics. Despite the delays and changes, athletes from around the world competed in Tokyo and other venues across Japan.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are a Major League Baseball team that began in Brooklyn, New York, before moving west in 1958. While playing for the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1947, Jackie Robinson broke Major League Baseball’s color barrier, becoming its first Black player in the modern era. The team had won seven World Series championships by 2020. When the Dodgers first arrived in Los Angeles, they played home games at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum. In 1962, they moved to Dodger Stadium in the Elysian Park area of the city. Dodger Stadium remains their home ballpark and is the oldest Major League Baseball stadium west of the Mississippi River.

Klay Thompson is an American basketball guard known for his accurate three-point shooting and quick scoring. He spent 13 seasons with the Golden State Warriors, helping them win four NBA championships, before joining the Dallas Mavericks in 2024. With fellow Warriors guard Stephen Curry, he formed the “Splash Brothers,” a nickname inspired by the sound of their shots dropping through the net. Thompson can score at an extraordinary pace: in 2016, he scored 60 points in just 29 minutes against the Indiana Pacers. In 2018, he made 14 three-pointers against the Chicago Bulls, setting an NBA single-game record. Curry, Thompson’s Splash Brothers partner, became the first player to win the NBA Most Valuable Player award by a unanimous vote in 2016.

Zugzwang is a chess term from German for a position in which having to move is a disadvantage. Chess players cannot pass their turn, so a player in zugzwang must choose a legal move even though every choice makes their position worse. For example, moving a king might allow an opponent’s king to advance and capture an important pawn. Zugzwang can happen at any point in a game, but it is most common in the endgame, when few pieces remain and a player may have very few safe moves. Recognizing zugzwang helps players plan ahead: sometimes the goal is not to attack immediately, but to arrange the position so that the opponent is the one forced to move.

Association football, commonly called soccer in the United States and football in many other countries, is played by two teams of 11 players. Each team tries to put the ball into the opponent’s rectangular goal while defending its own. Players usually move the ball by kicking or heading it; most cannot deliberately use their hands or arms, though goalkeepers may handle the ball within their own penalty area. A standard match has two 45-minute halves, with extra time added for stoppages. The sport has inspired television shows as well as real-life rivalries. In the Apple TV+ comedy-drama Ted Lasso, Jason Sudeikis plays an upbeat American football coach hired to manage the fictional English soccer club AFC Richmond, even though he knows little about association football.

Rugby is a family of team sports played with an oval ball. Players advance the ball by running with it or kicking it, and they score by carrying it across the opposing team’s goal line or kicking it through the goalposts. The main forms include rugby union, rugby league, and rugby sevens. Sevens has seven players per side and shorter matches, making it a fast-paced version of the game. At the 2016 Rio Olympics, Fiji defeated Great Britain in the men’s rugby sevens final. That victory gave the Pacific island nation its first Olympic medal—and it was a gold. Another well-known rugby team is New Zealand’s All Blacks, who perform a haka, a traditional Māori dance, before matches.

Usain Bolt is a Jamaican sprinter famous for his speed in the 100-meter and 200-meter races. At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, he won gold in both events and set a 100-meter world record of 9.69 seconds. He lowered that record to 9.58 seconds at the 2009 World Championships, a mark that still stands, and went on to win eight Olympic gold medals. Bolt also holds the men’s 200-meter world record. He represented Jamaica, a Caribbean nation with a strong sprinting tradition. Other Jamaican stars include Yohan Blake, who won silver in both the 100 and 200 meters at the 2012 London Olympics, and Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, a three-time Olympic champion in the women’s 100 meters.

Russell Wilson is an American football quarterback who was selected by the Seattle Seahawks in the third round of the 2012 NFL Draft. He became Seattle’s starting quarterback and led the team to two Super Bowls. In Super Bowl XLVIII (48), played at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, Wilson and the Seahawks faced the Denver Broncos. The game began badly for Denver when a snap sailed over quarterback Peyton Manning’s head, giving Seattle a safety. The Seahawks went on to win 43–8, earning the franchise’s first Super Bowl championship. Wilson later left Seattle to play for the Broncos, joining the team in a 2022 trade.

Novak Djokovic is a Serbian tennis player who has won multiple Grand Slam singles titles and held the world No. 1 ranking for a record number of weeks. Tennis has four major tournaments, also called Grand Slams: the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and U.S. Open. Winning all four in the same January-to-December year is called a calendar-year Grand Slam. In 2021, Djokovic won the first three majors, leaving him one victory away from that rare achievement. He reached the U.S. Open final but lost to Daniil Medvedev, so he did not complete the sweep. Rod Laver, in 1969, was the last man to win a calendar-year Grand Slam in singles.

Eliud Kipchoge is a Kenyan distance runner and Olympic marathon champion. A marathon is a 26.2-mile (42.2-kilometer) race named after the ancient Greek Battle of Marathon. In 2019, Kipchoge became the first person to cover the marathon distance in under two hours, finishing in 1 hour, 59 minutes, and 40 seconds in Vienna, Austria. The event was called the INEOS 1:59 Challenge, after its sponsor. It was specially organized to help him reach the two-hour goal: pacemakers took turns running with him, and the course was designed for speed. Because those conditions did not meet the rules for an official race record, his time was a historic achievement but not an official marathon world record.

The European Super League was a proposed breakaway soccer competition announced in April 2021 by twelve major European clubs, including Liverpool, Manchester United, Real Madrid, and Juventus. Unlike most European competitions, in which teams must earn a place through their results, the Super League would have guaranteed its founding clubs permanent places. Its organizers argued that regular matches between famous clubs would attract more viewers and money. Many fans, players, and soccer authorities objected, saying the plan would reward wealthy clubs regardless of how they performed and weaken existing leagues. Several clubs withdrew within days, causing the project to collapse in its announced form. Florentino Pérez, the president of Real Madrid, was named the Super League’s inaugural chairman and remained one of its most prominent public defenders.

Playing cards is a pastime in which people use a deck of cards to play games with different rules and goals. A standard poker deck has 52 cards, not counting two optional jokers. Card games can be played casually or for money in casinos. The pastime appears in art, too: C. M. Coolidge’s famous paintings show dogs gathered around tables playing cards, sometimes while smoking cigars, and Paul Cézanne painted people doing the same in The Card Players. One popular casino card game is blackjack. In blackjack, each player competes against the dealer and tries to make a hand worth as close to 21 as possible without going over, or “busting.” Keeping track of which cards have been dealt, called card-counting, can help reduce the casino’s advantage.

The 2022 Winter Olympics were held in Beijing, China, in February 2022. The Winter Games are an international sporting event held every four years, with athletes competing in sports such as figure skating, snowboarding, and freestyle skiing. Beijing became the first city to host both the Summer and Winter Olympics, having previously staged the Summer Games in 2008. One of the best-known athletes at the 2022 Games was freestyle skier Eileen Gu. She was born in San Francisco but competed for China, her mother’s birth country. Gu won gold medals in women’s big air and halfpipe and a silver medal in slopestyle, giving her three medals in three different freestyle skiing events.

Reggie Miller was a shooting guard who spent all 18 of his NBA seasons with the Indiana Pacers, from 1987 to 2005. One of basketball’s best three-point shooters, he was especially dangerous late in close games. His clutch shots against the New York Knicks earned him the nickname “Knick Killer” and made him a central figure in the teams’ playoff rivalry. In Game 1 of the 1995 Eastern Conference semifinals, Miller scored an astonishing eight points in the final 8.9 seconds to help the Pacers beat the Knicks. He also famously traded taunts with Spike Lee, a film director and devoted Knicks fan who often sat courtside wearing Knicks gear. Miller was later inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame.

The Summer Olympic Games are the warm-weather edition of the modern Olympics, an international competition held every four years. Athletes representing countries around the world compete in many sports, including athletics (track and field), swimming, and gymnastics. A different host city organizes each Games, and the event brings together national delegations, spectators, and visitors. Atlanta, Georgia, hosted the 1996 Summer Olympic Games. During a concert at Centennial Olympic Park, a downtown gathering place for Olympic visitors, an explosive device detonated. The attack, commonly called the Centennial Olympic Park bombing, killed one person and injured more than 100 others. It was later linked to Eric Rudolph. The bombing is a tragic event associated with the 1996 Games, though it was not part of the sporting competition.

Sumo is a traditional Japanese form of wrestling in which two competitors face off on a raised clay ring called a dohyō. A wrestler wins by forcing their opponent out of the ring or making any part of the opponent’s body other than the soles of their feet touch the ground. Although a bout may last only seconds, wrestlers train for years to develop strength, balance, and technique. Sumo also has ties to Shinto, a Japanese religious tradition. Before bouts, wrestlers may throw salt into the ring as a purification ritual. The highest rank in sumo is yokozuna. Yokozuna wear a thick braided sacred rope, called a tsuna, during formal ring-entry ceremonies, when they perform symbolic stomps meant to drive away evil spirits.

The 2008 Summer Olympics were held in Beijing, the capital of China, marking the first time China hosted the Summer Games. This international multi-sport event, held every four years, opened on August 8, 2008, with a ceremony at Beijing National Stadium, nicknamed the Bird’s Nest because of its woven-looking structure. Athletes from around the world competed in sports such as swimming, gymnastics, and track and field. One of the Games’ biggest stars was American swimmer Michael Phelps, who won eight gold medals. He broke fellow American Mark Spitz’s record of seven gold medals at a single Olympics. Phelps’s victories included the 100-meter butterfly, which he won by just one hundredth of a second.

Table tennis, also called ping-pong, is a fast racket sport played by two people in singles or four people in doubles. Players use small paddles to hit a lightweight ball back and forth over a low net on a raised rectangular table. They try to make shots that their opponents cannot return legally. Two common ways to hold the paddle are the penhold grip, used by many East Asian players, and the shakehand grip, common among Western players. One of the sport’s most successful athletes is China’s Ma Long, nicknamed “the Dictator” for his commanding play. He has captained China’s national team since 2014 and became the first man to win a Double Grand Slam: two titles each in the Olympics, World Championships, and World Cup.

In 1901, American schoolteacher Annie Edson Taylor became the first person to survive a trip over Niagara Falls inside a barrel. She hoped the dangerous stunt would bring her fame and money. Niagara Falls is a waterfall system on the border between New York State in the United States and Ontario in Canada. It includes three waterfalls: the American Falls, Bridal Veil Falls, and Horseshoe Falls. Taylor’s descent helped make Niagara Falls famous for daredevil stunts, though going over the falls in a barrel is extremely dangerous and is now illegal. Other people have attempted risky feats there; in 2012, Nik Wallenda crossed the falls on a tightrope. Visitors can see the waterfalls from a safer perspective on Maid of the Mist boat tours.

Magic: The Gathering is a fantasy collectible card game in which players build decks of spells and creatures and compete to reduce an opponent’s life total to zero. Playing many cards requires mana, a resource associated with five colors: white, blue, black, red, and green. The game also includes card types such as artifacts, which represent magical objects, and planeswalkers, powerful characters who can help a player. Different deck strategies emphasize different cards; for example, a red “Burn” deck uses spells such as Lightning Bolt to deal damage quickly. Magic: The Gathering was first published by Wizards of the Coast, a game company founded in 1990 that also publishes Dungeons & Dragons. Wizards of the Coast later became a subsidiary of Hasbro.

A goaltender, often called a goalie, is the ice hockey player whose main job is to stop the opposing team’s shots from entering the goal. Goaltenders wear heavy protective equipment and use a stick, glove, and large leg pads to block or catch the puck. In the butterfly style, a goalie drops to both knees and spreads the pads across the lower part of the net. A hybrid style combines that move with other ways of making saves. Late in a game, a team that needs a goal may pull its goaltender for an extra skater, leaving an “empty net.” One of the most successful NHL goaltenders was Martin Brodeur. He spent most of his career with the New Jersey Devils, won three Stanley Cups with them, and holds the NHL regular-season career records for wins and shutouts.

The Chicago White Sox are a Major League Baseball team in the American League. They play on Chicago’s South Side and have a longtime crosstown rivalry with the Chicago Cubs. The team is closely linked to the “Black Sox” scandal: eight White Sox players, including “Shoeless” Joe Jackson, were accused of intentionally losing the 1919 World Series and were later banned from baseball for life. Another unusual moment in team history happened at Comiskey Park in July 1979. During a promotion called Disco Demolition Night, radio personality Steve Dahl invited fans to bring disco records to be destroyed between games of a doubleheader. After the records were blown up, fans rushed onto the field and caused enough damage that the White Sox had to forfeit the second game.

Cryptic crosswords are a type of crossword especially popular in Britain. Like standard crosswords, they have Across and Down clues that lead to words entered in a grid, but their clues work in two ways: each usually contains a straightforward definition and a separate piece of wordplay leading to the same answer. The wordplay might rearrange letters in an anagram, hide an answer inside other words, or join smaller words together in a “charade.” Cryptic grids also often have more black squares than standard crossword grids. The people who create crosswords are called setters or cruciverbalists. One influential British setter, Derrick Somerset Macnutt, used the pen name Ximenes for his long-running puzzle in The Observer. He also used that name on his 1966 handbook, On the Art of the Crossword.

A marathon is a long-distance road race covering 42.195 kilometers, or about 26.2 miles. Its name comes from the Battle of Marathon, where Athenians defeated a Persian army in 490 BCE, and from a legend about a messenger who ran to announce the victory. The marathon has been part of the modern Olympic Games since the first Games in Athens in 1896, although its distance was standardized later. Famous races include the Boston Marathon. In 2019, Kenyan runner Eliud Kipchoge completed the marathon distance in 1 hour, 59 minutes, and 40.2 seconds at the INEOS 1:59 Challenge in Vienna. He was the first person to run that distance in under two hours, but the specially arranged pacers and conditions meant his time did not count as an official world record.

A tier list ranks characters, items, or competitors by their relative strength or value. Instead of giving each one a separate numbered place, it groups them into tiers, often labeled S, A, B, and so on, with S above A. Players use tier lists to compare their options in competitive games, but the rankings can change as they discover new strategies or the game is updated. Fighting games are especially known for tier lists because a character’s abilities and matchups against other characters can affect tournament results. One often-discussed example is Super Smash Bros. Melee, a platform fighting game released for the GameCube in 2001. Its competitive tier lists commonly place Fox and Marth among the strongest characters.

Highland games are traditional gatherings in Scotland that combine athletic contests with celebrations of Scottish culture. Competitors test their strength in events such as the stone put, in which they throw a heavy stone, and the hammer throw. One of the best-known events is the caber toss. A caber is a long, tapered wooden pole that a competitor lifts upright, runs with, and throws so it flips end over end. Unlike many throwing events, the goal is not to send the caber as far as possible. Judges look at whether it turns over and how straight it lands. Highland games often feature bagpipe music, dancing, and kilts, making them both sporting competitions and community festivals.

Disco Demolition Night was a baseball promotion held on July 12, 1979, at Comiskey Park, home of the Chicago White Sox. Chicago radio personality and rock DJ Steve Dahl urged listeners to bring disco records to the ballpark, where the records would be blown up between games of a doubleheader against the Detroit Tigers. The stunt drew a much larger crowd than expected. After the explosion, thousands of fans rushed onto the field, damaging the playing surface and making it unsafe to continue. The White Sox had to forfeit the second game. The event became famous not only as a baseball promotion that went badly wrong, but also as an example of the strong backlash against disco music in the late 1970s.

Curling is a Winter Olympic team sport that originated in Scotland. Players take turns sliding heavy, polished granite stones down a sheet of ice toward a target of concentric circles called the house. Teammates sweep the ice in front of a moving stone to help control how far it travels and how much it curves. A round of play is called an end. After all the stones in an end have been thrown, the team with a stone closest to the center of the house scores points. The team that does not score generally throws the final stone of the next end. This last-stone advantage is called the hammer, and it gives that team a chance to respond to its opponent’s shots.

Juventus Football Club is a soccer team founded in Turin, Italy, in 1897. Often called “Juve” or “La Vecchia Signora” (“the Old Lady”), it competes in Serie A, Italy’s top division, and plays its home matches at Allianz Stadium. Juventus has featured stars from around the world, including Portuguese forward Cristiano Ronaldo, who joined from Real Madrid in 2018, Argentine attacker Paulo Dybala, and Italian goalkeeper Gianluigi Buffon. Another club legend is Italian forward Alessandro Del Piero. He scored 290 goals for Juventus, making him the club’s all-time leading scorer, and captained the team for many years. When Juventus was relegated to Serie B, Italy’s second division, in 2006, Del Piero stayed with the club and helped it return to Serie A.

The Texas Tech Red Raiders are the athletic teams of Texas Tech University, a public university in Lubbock, Texas. Their school colors are scarlet and black, and their football team competes in the Big 12 Conference. One of the program’s best-known former players is quarterback Patrick Mahomes. In a 2016 college game against Oklahoma, Mahomes completed 52 of 88 passes for 734 yards, but Texas Tech still lost 66–59. Mahomes later became the quarterback of the Kansas City Chiefs. He led the Chiefs to a win over the San Francisco 49ers in Super Bowl LIV and was named the game’s Most Valuable Player.

In Magic: The Gathering, players use mana to cast spells, and red mana is one of the game’s five types of mana. Its symbol is a fireball, reflecting red’s connection to fire, emotional impulse, and the freedom to act without restraint. Red cards often reward fast, aggressive play: creatures attack early, while spells deal damage directly to opponents or their creatures. A deck built around dealing damage quickly with instant and sorcery spells is called a burn deck. One of red’s best-known burn spells is Lightning Bolt. This instant costs one red mana and deals 3 damage to any target, making it a clear example of how red mana can turn a small resource investment into an immediate attack.

Grandmaster is the highest standard title a chess player can earn, apart from the separate distinction of world champion. It is awarded by the international chess federation, commonly called FIDE, using the initials of its French name, Fédération Internationale des Échecs. FIDE was founded in Paris in 1924. To become a grandmaster, a player typically must reach a required chess rating and achieve strong results in several qualifying tournaments, known as grandmaster norms. Unlike the world champion title, which belongs to the winner of the world championship, the grandmaster title can be held by many players at once and is generally held for life. Judit Polgár, a Hungarian chess prodigy, is one famous grandmaster.

A calendar-year Grand Slam is one of tennis’s rarest achievements: winning all four major singles tournaments in the same calendar year, from January through December. The four are the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and U.S. Open. Winning three majors is remarkable, but it does not count as a calendar-year Grand Slam; the player must win all four before the next January begins. In men’s singles, Rod Laver last accomplished the feat in 1969. Serbian player Novak Djokovic came close in 2021. He won the Australian Open, French Open, and Wimbledon, leaving only the U.S. Open. But he lost that tournament’s final to Daniil Medvedev, so he did not complete the calendar-year Grand Slam.

Shohei Ohtani is a Japanese-born Major League Baseball star known for succeeding at two jobs that most players do separately: starting pitcher and power hitter. As a pitcher, he tries to stop the other team from scoring; as a designated hitter, he bats without playing a fielding position. With the Los Angeles Angels in 2021, Ohtani hit 46 home runs while also pitching, earning the American League Most Valuable Player (MVP) award. His rare two-way success made him one of baseball’s most talked-about players. During Ohtani’s 2022 season, another major home run milestone came from St. Louis Cardinals slugger Albert Pujols. In his final MLB season, Pujols hit his 703rd career home run, passing Alex Rodriguez for fourth place on the all-time list.

A racket is a piece of sports equipment used to hit a ball or shuttlecock in games such as tennis, squash, and badminton. It has a handle for the player to grip and a frame that holds a tightly stretched web of strings, called the string bed. When the ball or shuttlecock meets the strings, the racket helps direct it across a net or, in squash, against a wall. On a tennis racket, a centered hit in a particular area of the string bed usually feels cleaner and transfers energy more efficiently than a hit near the frame. This area is called the sweet spot. Players try to make contact there for greater control and a more effective shot.

Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. in Louisville, Kentucky. A gifted boxer, he won a light heavyweight gold medal at the 1960 Olympics and defeated Sonny Liston in 1964 to become world heavyweight champion. After that victory, he changed his name to Muhammad Ali. Famous for his quick movements and confident words as well as his skill in the ring, Ali became an influential civil rights figure. He also opposed the Vietnam War and refused to serve in the military, a decision that cost him his boxing title for a time. His hometown honors his life and achievements at the Muhammad Ali Center. Louisville sits on the Ohio River, is Kentucky’s most populous city and the seat of Jefferson County, and is also home to Churchill Downs, where the Kentucky Derby is held.

A bull is a mature male bovine, or male member of the cattle family. Bulls are important in livestock farming, but they also appear in rodeo sports. In professional bull riding, competitors try to stay on a bucking bull for eight seconds while holding on with one hand. The Professional Bull Riders organization, often called the PBR, holds competitions featuring these powerful animals. One famous bull was Bodacious, who became notorious for throwing riders and causing serious injuries. He is often described as one of the most dangerous bulls in the sport’s history. The word “bull” can also appear outside rodeos: a “bull market” is a period when stock prices are rising, and the Charging Bull sculpture near Wall Street symbolizes financial strength.

Kevin Durant is an American basketball star known for his scoring and long-range shooting. He began his NBA career with the Seattle SuperSonics, who became the Oklahoma City Thunder in 2008. While playing for Oklahoma City, Durant won the 2014 NBA Most Valuable Player award. In his emotional acceptance speech, he thanked his mother for supporting him and told her, “You the real MVP.” In 2016, Durant left the Thunder to join the Golden State Warriors, who had just set an NBA record by winning 73 regular-season games. He helped Golden State win championships in 2017 and 2018 and was named NBA Finals MVP in both seasons. Durant later played for the Brooklyn Nets and Phoenix Suns.

Golf is a sport in which players try to complete each hole of a course in as few strokes as possible. They start from a teeing area and use clubs to hit a ball toward a green, where they putt it into a cup. Each hole has a par: the number of strokes an experienced player is expected to need. Taking three strokes on a par-four hole is one stroke under par, called a birdie. Because lower scores are better, players add up their strokes across all the holes to find their total score. In a related sport called disc golf, players throw flying discs rather than hit balls with clubs, aiming for targets in as few throws as possible.

The discus is a heavy, circular object thrown for distance. It was one of the five events in the ancient Greek pentathlon and remains an event in modern track and field. A thrower spins inside a marked circle to build momentum, then releases the discus toward a landing area. The event also inspired a famous ancient Greek sculpture by Myron called the Discobolus, meaning “discus thrower.” It shows an athlete twisting his body at the moment before he throws, capturing the movement and effort of the sport. Myron’s original bronze statue has been lost, but Roman marble copies preserve its appearance.

The Philadelphia Phillies are a Major League Baseball team founded in 1883. They compete in the National League East and play their home games at Citizens Bank Park in South Philadelphia. The ballpark opened in 2004, replacing the Phillies’ former home, Veterans Stadium. In 2022, the Phillies defeated the San Diego Padres to win the National League championship and advance to the World Series, baseball’s best-of-seven championship series. They played their home games at Citizens Bank Park during that run but lost the World Series to the Houston Astros. Phillies outfielder Nick Castellanos is known for hitting home runs at unexpectedly awkward moments during broadcasts.

The Connecticut Sun are a professional basketball team in the Women’s National Basketball Association, or WNBA. The franchise began as the Orlando Miracle and moved from Florida to Connecticut in 2003. The Sun play their home games at Mohegan Sun Arena in Uncasville, and Connecticut does not have an NBA team. One of the Sun’s standout players was Bahamian forward Jonquel Jones. In 2021, she led the WNBA in rebounding and was named the league’s Most Valuable Player. The Sun reached the WNBA Finals in 2022, but lost the championship series to the Las Vegas Aces. Jones later joined the New York Liberty in a 2023 trade. Although the Sun had an excellent 2021 season, they did not win that year’s WNBA championship.

O. J. Simpson was an American football running back known for his speed and powerful rushing. After starring at the University of Southern California (USC), he was selected first overall in the 1969 NFL draft by the Buffalo Bills. He played for Buffalo from 1969 to 1977, and in 1973 he rushed for 2,003 yards, becoming the first NFL player to gain more than 2,000 rushing yards in a single season and setting a Bills team record. He later played for the San Francisco 49ers and worked as an actor and television personality. Decades after his football success, Simpson became the focus of a highly publicized murder trial involving his former wife, Nicole Brown Simpson. He was found not guilty in the criminal trial.

The Kentucky Derby is an annual Thoroughbred horse race held each spring at Churchill Downs in Louisville, Kentucky. First run in 1875, it is the opening race of the American Triple Crown, a series of three major races for three-year-old Thoroughbreds. The Preakness Stakes and Belmont Stakes follow it; a horse must win all three to earn the Triple Crown. Churchill Downs has hosted the Derby since its beginning, and its grandstand is famous for its twin spires. The race is often called “the most exciting two minutes in sports” because the horses cover its 1¼-mile distance so quickly. Spectators also associate the event with colorful hats, mint juleps, and a garland of roses presented to the winning horse.

Lacrosse is a team sport played by Indigenous peoples of North America long before European contact. Players use sticks with small netted heads to catch, carry, pass, and shoot a ball into a goal. Modern lacrosse usually uses a hard rubber ball, but the sport grew from older Indigenous games with deep cultural meaning. Among the Haudenosaunee, lacrosse is known as the Creator’s Game and remains connected to community, tradition, and spirituality. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is an alliance of six Indigenous nations whose traditional homelands include parts of present-day New York and Ontario. Today, people play several forms of lacrosse, with rules and equipment that vary, but the stick, ball, goals, and teamwork remain central to the game.

A bicycle is a two-wheeled vehicle powered by a rider turning pedals. The pedals drive a chain connected to the rear wheel, making the bicycle move forward. Bicycles come in different designs: road bikes are built for speed on paved surfaces, mountain bikes are made for rough trails, and compact BMX bikes are used for racing and tricks. Many bicycles have gears that help riders pedal comfortably at different speeds or on hills. When a rider shifts gears, the chain moves between different-sized sprockets, or toothed wheels. On a multi-gear bicycle, the spring-loaded mechanism beside the back wheel that guides the chain across the rear cluster of sprockets is called the rear derailleur.

Chess pieces are the movable units used to play chess on an 8-by-8 board. Each player starts with 16 pieces: one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns. The pieces move in different ways, and players use them to attack and defend; a game often ends when a king is checkmated. The knight is the only type of piece that can jump over other pieces. It moves in an L shape: two squares in one direction and then one square perpendicular to it. In algebraic notation, which records chess moves, the knight is represented by N. Chess pieces can also be works of art: the medieval Lewis chessmen were carved from materials including walrus ivory and whale teeth.

The Ohio State University is a public research university in Columbus, Ohio. Its sports teams are called the Buckeyes, after the buckeye tree, a symbol of the state. Ohio State’s football program is one of the most successful in college football and has sent many players to the NFL, including Nick and Joey Bosa and Ezekiel Elliott. The Buckeyes have a long-running rivalry with the University of Michigan. Two other former Ohio State players, Malcolm Jenkins and Michael Thomas, both played for the New Orleans Saints, an NFL team based in Louisiana. Led by quarterback Drew Brees, the Saints won their first Super Bowl championship in Super Bowl XLIV, played in 2010 after the 2009 season.

The New Orleans Saints are an NFL team based in New Orleans, Louisiana’s largest city. Founded as an expansion team in 1967, the Saints use a fleur-de-lis, a stylized lily long associated with New Orleans, as their emblem. After decades without a championship, they won their first Super Bowl following the 2009 season. Led by quarterback Drew Brees, they defeated the Indianapolis Colts in Super Bowl XLIV. The Saints play their home games in a domed stadium in downtown New Orleans that opened in 1975. It has had several names over the years and is currently called the Caesars Superdome. The stadium has also hosted major events beyond Saints games, including Super Bowl XLVII.

Patrick Ewing was a dominant center who starred in college for the Georgetown Hoyas in Washington, D.C. Under coach John Thompson, the Hoyas reached the NCAA men’s championship game in 1982 and 1985 and won the national title in 1984. Ewing was selected first overall in the 1985 NBA draft by the New York Knicks.
