He spent 15 seasons with the Knicks, becoming one of the team’s best-known players and leading them to the NBA Finals in 1994. A center plays close to the basket, where Ewing’s size helped him score, rebound, and block shots. He later entered the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame.

Squash is a fast-paced racket sport played by two people on an enclosed court. Players take turns striking a small rubber ball against the front wall, and during a rally the ball can also rebound off the side and back walls. A player must return the ball before it bounces twice on the floor. Because shots can travel to different parts of the court, players try to move back toward the center after each hit. This central position is called the T, named for the shape made by court lines on the floor. Controlling the T helps a player reach shots on either side and can force an opponent to do more running. Squash games are commonly played to 11 points.

The first baseman is the baseball or softball player who defends first base, the bag at the right corner of the infield. In scorekeeping, the position is assigned number three. First basemen often catch throws from other infielders to record force outs: if a runner must advance to first base, the fielder can get the runner out by touching the bag with the ball before the runner arrives. They also field balls hit near first base and may catch throws from pitchers attempting to pick off runners. Two well-known first basemen are Freddie Freeman and Lou Gehrig. Gehrig played for the New York Yankees, earned the nickname “The Iron Horse,” and played 2,130 consecutive games, a record Cal Ripken Jr. broke in 1995.

Boxing is a combat sport in which two opponents use their fists to land punches while following rules about legal strikes, rounds, and safety. Boxers wear padded gloves and are matched by weight class so that opponents are closer in size. They can win by scoring more points than their opponent or by a knockout, when an opponent cannot continue. Boxing appears in films such as Rocky and Raging Bull, but it is also an Olympic sport. One of its most famous champions was American heavyweight Muhammad Ali. Competing under his birth name, Cassius Clay, he won the light-heavyweight gold medal at the 1960 Rome Olympics. As a professional, Ali later defeated George Foreman in the 1974 fight known as the “Rumble in the Jungle.”

Disc golf is a sport in which players throw flying discs along a course, trying to complete each marked hole in as few throws as possible. A hole begins at a tee area and ends at a target, usually a metal basket with hanging chains that help catch the disc. Players count every throw, and courses often have nine or eighteen holes. Like traditional golf, disc golf uses par as a guide to how many throws a hole should take. Players choose different discs for different shots: drivers are designed for long throws, while putters have blunt, rounded rims that help with short, accurate approaches and final throws into the basket. The player with the lowest total number of throws wins.

Rubik’s Cube solving is the practice of turning a three-by-three puzzle until each of its six faces shows just one color. Solvers do not usually turn pieces at random; they follow steps and use short, learned sequences of moves called algorithms. A popular speedsolving method is CFOP, which Jessica Fridrich helped popularize. Its name gives the order of its four stages: Cross, First Two Layers, Orientation of the Last Layer, and Permutation of the Last Layer. Solvers often start with a white cross, then pair corner and edge pieces to complete the first two layers. Finally, they turn the last-layer pieces so the top face has one color and move those pieces into their correct positions. With practice, speedsolvers can complete the puzzle in just seconds.

Whitewater rafting is a recreational sport in which a group travels down a river in an inflatable raft, using paddles to steer through fast-moving, turbulent water called rapids. Rafters work as a team and often follow a guide’s instructions to avoid rocks and other hazards. Rapids are commonly rated using the International Scale of River Difficulty, which has six grades, from Class I to Class VI. Class I means easy water with few obstacles, while higher classes involve stronger currents, larger waves, and more hazards. Class VI indicates extreme difficulty and may be too dangerous to attempt. In the United States, the New River near West Virginia’s New River Gorge Bridge is a popular place for whitewater rafting.

Skateboarding is a sport in which athletes ride a board with four wheels, using their balance and momentum to perform tricks. Skateboarders might jump and flip their boards, grind along handrails, or launch into the air from ramps. At the Summer Olympics, they compete in two disciplines: park, which uses a course with ramps and bowl-shaped sections, and street, which has obstacles inspired by city spaces, such as stairs and handrails. Judges score the difficulty and execution of their tricks. One of the sport’s best-known athletes is American skateboarder Tony Hawk, nicknamed the “Birdman.” In 1999, he became the first person to land a 900, an aerial trick involving two and a half full rotations on a ramp. A popular skateboarding video game series also bears his name.

Alex Ovechkin is a Russian ice hockey left winger born in Moscow. The Washington Capitals selected him first overall in the 2004 NHL Draft, and he has been their captain since 2010. One of the NHL’s most prolific goal scorers, Ovechkin is especially famous for his powerful one-timer: he shoots the puck immediately after receiving a pass, often from his familiar spot near the left faceoff circle. He helped the Capitals win their first Stanley Cup in 2018, when they defeated the Vegas Golden Knights in the Final. Ovechkin has also scored many empty-net goals, which happen when the opposing team takes its goaltender off the ice to add another attacking player.

Bill Russell was an American basketball center known for his defense, rebounding, and leadership. At the University of San Francisco, he captained his team to consecutive NCAA championships in 1955 and 1956. He then played his entire 13-season NBA career with the Boston Celtics, helping turn them into a basketball dynasty. Russell won five NBA Most Valuable Player awards and led the Celtics to 11 NBA championships. Eight of those titles came in a row, from 1959 through 1966, under coach Red Auerbach. Rather than relying mainly on scoring, Russell changed games by blocking shots, grabbing rebounds, and helping his teammates. His success made him one of the most important players in basketball history.

Secretariat was a chestnut American Thoroughbred racehorse famous for winning the 1973 Triple Crown. To earn that title, a horse must win three major races in the same year: the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness Stakes, and the Belmont Stakes. Secretariat was the first horse in 25 years to do it, and he set records in all three races. His most astonishing performance came in the Belmont Stakes, traditionally the final and longest race of the series. He finished 31 lengths ahead of the next horse, covering 1½ miles in 2 minutes 24 seconds. That time remains the American record for the distance on a dirt track. His speed and enormous winning margin made him one of the most celebrated horses in racing history.

Bill Belichick is an American football coach best known for leading the New England Patriots through a dominant period in the NFL. Before becoming the Patriots’ head coach in 2000, he coordinated the defense for the New York Giants teams that won Super Bowls XXI and XXV. With New England, Belichick won six Super Bowl titles, all with quarterback Tom Brady, whose nickname is “TB12.” Brady earned four Super Bowl MVP awards during those championship runs. The two were also linked to the Deflategate controversy, an investigation into whether Patriots footballs had been deliberately underinflated. Brady was suspended for the first four games of the 2016 season following the investigation.

The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal involved the team’s use of technology to learn what pitches opponents were about to throw during the 2017 season and postseason. Catchers give pitchers hand signals, or signs, to choose a pitch. Astros personnel used footage from a center-field camera and replay-room video to decode those signs. In some games, they relayed the information to batters by banging on a garbage can; different sounds could tell a batter which pitch to expect. Major League Baseball investigated the scheme after it became public in 2019 and identified Astros bench coach Alex Cora as a central figure in the sign-decoding system. Cora later managed the Boston Red Sox to a World Series title. The scandal raised questions about cheating and the fair use of video in baseball.

Mercedes-Benz is a German automaker with a long history in motor racing. Its factory Formula One team became especially successful during the hybrid era, which began in 2014, and often fought the Italian team Ferrari for championships. British driver Lewis Hamilton won six of his drivers’ world championships in Mercedes cars between 2014 and 2020. Mercedes racing cars and teams are nicknamed the Silver Arrows because of their metallic silver appearance. According to a famous story from the 1934 Eifelrennen race, the team removed paint from its cars to meet a weight limit, revealing the shiny aluminum bodywork beneath. Whether every detail of that story is accurate is debated, but the Silver Arrows nickname remains closely associated with Mercedes-Benz racing.

The CFOP Method is a popular way to solve a 3×3 Rubik’s Cube quickly. It is often associated with speedcuber Jessica Fridrich, so it is sometimes called the Fridrich method. Its name comes from the initials of its four stages: Cross, First Two Layers, Orientation of the Last Layer, and Permutation of the Last Layer. First, the solver makes a cross, often on the white face, while matching its edge pieces to the side centers. Next comes First Two Layers, or F2L: the solver pairs each unsolved corner with its matching edge and inserts them together into their shared slot. Finally, the solver turns the last-layer pieces so their top colors face upward, then moves those pieces into their correct positions to complete the cube.

Wizards of the Coast is a game publisher best known for creating Magic: The Gathering and publishing Dungeons & Dragons. It was founded in 1990 by entrepreneur Peter Adkison, who served as its CEO before Hasbro acquired the company in 1999. Magic: The Gathering is a fantasy trading card game in which players build decks and use five colors of mana to play spells and other cards. One common strategy, called Burn, uses red cards such as Lightning Bolt to deal damage quickly. Dungeons & Dragons is a tabletop role-playing game in which players create characters and tell an adventure together, guided by a Dungeon Master. These two games helped make Wizards of the Coast a major name in tabletop gaming.

ROC was the three-letter team label used by athletes from Russia at the 2020 Summer Olympics in Tokyo. Although the Games kept “2020” in their official name, they took place in 2021 after a one-year delay caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Russia could not compete under its national name or flag because of sanctions linked to a widespread, state-sponsored doping scandal. Athletes who were allowed to participate therefore competed under ROC, short for Russian Olympic Committee, and used a modified flag instead of Russia’s national flag. The label identified their team without presenting it as the official Russian national team. If a question asks for their three-letter designation, the answer is ROC; if it asks which postponed Tokyo Games they attended, the answer is the 2020 Summer Olympics.

A professional basketball player earns a living playing basketball, often in a league such as the National Basketball Association (NBA). Players have different roles on the court: a center is usually tall and plays near the basket, rebounding, defending shots, and scoring close to the hoop. Music sometimes refers to these athletes. Rapper Sheck Wes named his hit song “Mo Bamba” after Mohamed “Mo” Bamba, an NBA center drafted sixth overall in 2018. Shaquille O’Neal and Allen Iverson are also famous professional basketball players who released rap music. Gunna’s song “Yao Ming” refers to another player: Yao Ming, a 7-foot-6 center from China who played for the Houston Rockets after being selected first overall in the 2002 NBA draft.

A golf ball is the small, hard ball struck with clubs in the sport of golf. Unlike a smooth sphere, it has hundreds of shallow dimples that help it travel farther. As the ball flies, air moves around it. In laminar flow, the air moves in smooth, orderly layers; in turbulent flow, it mixes irregularly, with changing speeds and pressures. The dimples encourage turbulent flow in a thin layer of air next to the ball. This helps the moving air stay attached to the ball’s surface longer instead of separating early and leaving a large wake behind it. A smaller wake means less drag, or air resistance, so a dimpled golf ball can travel farther than a smooth one struck in the same way.

The Tuck Rule Game was a January 2002 AFC divisional playoff between the New England Patriots and Oakland Raiders, played in a snowstorm at New England’s home stadium. Late in the game, Raiders defender Charles Woodson hit Patriots quarterback Tom Brady, knocking the ball loose. Oakland recovered what appeared to be a fumble, but after a replay review, referee Walt Coleman announced that the play was an incomplete pass. Under the NFL’s tuck rule at the time, a quarterback’s forward passing motion still counted as a pass attempt even if he was bringing the ball back toward his body. New England kept possession, and Adam Vinatieri kicked a field goal to tie the game. His field goal in overtime gave the Patriots a 16–13 win.

Manchester United F.C. is a football club from northern England that plays in the Premier League, England’s top division. The club has played its home matches at Old Trafford since 1910. Nicknamed the “Theatre of Dreams,” the stadium also hosted matches during the 1966 FIFA World Cup. Manchester United is famous for its long period of success under manager Sir Alex Ferguson. During his 26 years in charge, Ferguson led the team to 13 Premier League titles. One of the club’s notable goalkeepers was Danish international Peter Schmeichel, whose son Kasper later helped Leicester City win the Premier League in 2015–16. Manchester United is sometimes called Man United or the Red Devils; it is a different club from Manchester City.

Albert Pujols is a Dominican-American baseball player known for his powerful hitting. He spent most of his Major League Baseball career with the St. Louis Cardinals and also played for the Los Angeles Angels and Dodgers. With the Cardinals, he won three National League Most Valuable Player (MVP) Awards and helped the team win the World Series in 2006 and 2011. A home run is a hit that lets the batter circle all the bases and score, usually by sending the ball over the outfield fence. In 2022, his final season, Pujols finished with 703 career home runs. That total put him fourth on MLB’s all-time list, ahead of Alex Rodriguez, another Dominican-born slugger, who finished his career with 696.

Michigan Stadium is the home field of the University of Michigan Wolverines football team in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Opened in 1927, it is nicknamed “The Big House” because it holds more than 100,000 spectators, making it one of the largest stadiums in the United States. The Wolverines play in the Big Ten Conference and have a fierce rivalry with Ohio State. Their football history began long before the stadium opened: coach Fielding Yost led Michigan’s famous 1901–05 “Point-a-Minute” teams, known for scoring at an extraordinary pace. In the first Rose Bowl, played in 1902, Yost coached Michigan to a 49–0 victory over Stanford. Michigan alumni who later became football stars include Charles Woodson and Tom Brady.

The Oakland Athletics, often called the Oakland A’s, are a Major League Baseball team in the American League West. They won three straight World Series championships from 1972 through 1974 while playing home games at Oakland’s Coliseum, a concrete stadium built for multiple sports. One of their biggest stars was slugging outfielder Reggie Jackson, whose powerful hitting helped drive those championship runs. Jackson later played for the New York Yankees and became known as “Mr. October” for his outstanding performances in postseason games. Decades later, the A’s drew attention for using statistics called sabermetrics to find undervalued players. That approach was the subject of Michael Lewis’s book Moneyball and a movie starring Brad Pitt.

The Mercedes-AMG Petronas Formula One Team is the works racing team of German carmaker Mercedes-Benz. Based in Brackley, England, it dominated Formula One after the sport introduced hybrid engines in 2014. Mercedes won the Constructors’ Championship, awarded to the team whose drivers score the most points together, every year from 2014 through 2021—eight titles in a row. British driver Lewis Hamilton joined Mercedes from McLaren in 2013 and won six Drivers’ Championships with the team between 2014 and 2020. His seventh career title in 2020 tied Michael Schumacher’s all-time record. In 2021, Red Bull driver Max Verstappen beat Hamilton to the Drivers’ Championship, but Mercedes still won the Constructors’ Championship.

Red Auerbach was a coach and executive who helped turn the Boston Celtics into one of basketball’s most successful teams. As head coach, he led the Celtics to nine NBA championships from 1957 through 1966, including eight titles in a row. His teams featured stars such as Bill Russell and John Havlicek. Auerbach became famous for lighting a cigar near the end of games when he was sure the Celtics would win. He also helped break a barrier in professional basketball: in the 1950 NBA draft, he selected Chuck Cooper, a center-forward from Duquesne University, with the 13th overall pick. Cooper became the first Black player drafted by an NBA team.

The University of Louisville is a public research university in Louisville, Kentucky’s largest city. It began in 1798 as Jefferson Seminary and grew into a university with varsity sports teams known as the Cardinals. Since 2014, those teams have competed in the Atlantic Coast Conference, or ACC, a major college sports league founded by seven schools in 1953. The conference’s name refers to the Atlantic Ocean, and many of its member schools are in states near the Atlantic coast. Louisville, however, is in north-central Kentucky, far inland. That makes its ACC membership an example of how a sports conference’s name does not always describe where all its member schools are located.

In chess, each player starts with eight pawns lined up in front of their other pieces on the 8-by-8 board. A pawn normally moves one square forward and cannot move through or onto another piece. On its first move, it may move two squares forward if both squares are clear. Unlike most chess pieces, a pawn captures on a different square from the one it moves toward: it takes an enemy piece one square diagonally forward. A special capture called en passant, French for “in passing,” is possible when an enemy pawn moves two squares from its starting square and lands beside your pawn. Your pawn may then capture it as if it had moved only one square, but only on your very next move.

Cricket is a bat-and-ball sport played by two teams on a large field. One team bats to score runs while the other bowls and fields. A bowler delivers the ball toward a batter, who tries to hit it while protecting a wicket made of three upright stumps topped by two small bails. Batters can score runs by running between wickets or hitting the ball to the field’s boundary. Cricket is especially popular in England, Australia, and other Commonwealth countries. The Ashes, a series of Test matches between England and Australia, is one of its best-known contests. Bowlers can make the ball spin: a right-arm leg-break turns from leg toward off for a right-handed batter, while a disguised delivery that turns the opposite way, from off toward leg, is called a googly.

The Lewis chessmen are a famous collection of medieval chess pieces discovered in 1831 near Uig, on the western shore of the Isle of Lewis in Scotland’s Outer Hebrides. Most date from the twelfth century and were carved from walrus ivory, while some were made from whale teeth. The pieces include kings, queens, bishops, knights, and pawns, along with figures called warders that served as rooks. Many have expressive faces and detailed clothing, offering clues about the art and culture of the time. The collection is named the Lewis chessmen after the island where it was found. Like the pieces in a modern chess set, these figures were used to play a game in which a player tries to checkmate the opponent’s king.

Dice are small objects rolled to produce random or nearly random results in board games, gambling, and tabletop role-playing games. The most familiar die is a cube with six faces, each marked with one to six dots called pips. “Die” means one object, while “dice” is the usual plural. Some games use dice with different numbers of sides: a “d20,” for example, is a twenty-sided die. Dungeons & Dragons, a fantasy tabletop role-playing game, uses dice with four, six, eight, ten, twelve, and twenty sides to help determine what happens during play. In its fifth edition, a character’s combat initiative, which helps determine when they act, is calculated by adding their Dexterity modifier to the result of a d20 roll.

Wilt Chamberlain was a 7-foot-1 center and one of the most dominant players in NBA history. On March 2, 1962, while playing for the Philadelphia Warriors, he scored 100 points against the New York Knicks in a single game. No other NBA player has matched that record. The Knicks are a New York City franchise whose home arena is Madison Square Garden. Years after Chamberlain’s record-setting game, the Knicks selected center Patrick Ewing with the first pick in the 1985 NBA draft. Chamberlain’s 100-point performance is still one of basketball’s most famous achievements, while the Knicks remain a well-known NBA team with a long history.

The Milwaukee Bucks are an NBA basketball team based in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. They won their first league championship in 1971, led by star center Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. Fifty years later, the Bucks claimed their second title in the 2021 NBA Finals by defeating the Phoenix Suns in six games. In the championship-clinching Game 6, Greek forward Giannis Antetokounmpo scored 50 points and was named Finals Most Valuable Player, or Finals MVP, for his outstanding performance throughout the series. His teammates Khris Middleton and Brook Lopez also helped Milwaukee win the title. The Bucks’ two championships, in 1971 and 2021, are key moments in the team’s history.

Mr. Olympia is a prestigious professional bodybuilding contest founded by Joe Weider. It was first held in 1965 at the Brooklyn Academy of Music in New York City. The first champion was American bodybuilder Larry Scott, who won again in 1966 before retiring from competitive bodybuilding. The contest has grown to include divisions such as Men’s Open, Classic Physique, and Men’s Physique, each with different standards for the competitors’ appearance. Bodybuilding is about displaying muscle size, shape, and definition rather than lifting the heaviest weight. At a show, competitors pose onstage, often wearing tanning products and oil to make their muscles easier to see. Arnold Schwarzenegger later became one of Mr. Olympia’s best-known champions, winning the title seven times.

Patrick Mahomes is an American football quarterback for the Kansas City Chiefs, an NFL team based in Missouri. Known for powerful throws and creative plays, he was named the NFL’s Most Valuable Player for the 2018 season. He later led the Chiefs to a victory over the San Francisco 49ers in Super Bowl LIV and earned that game’s MVP award. Before joining the NFL, Mahomes played college football at Texas Tech University, a Big 12 school whose teams are called the Red Raiders. In a remarkable 2016 game against Oklahoma, he threw for 734 yards, although Texas Tech lost 66–59. His ability to produce huge numbers even in a loss was also on display with the Chiefs in a 54–51 defeat against the Los Angeles Rams in 2018.

The Kansas City Chiefs are a professional American football team in the National Football League (NFL). Although their name includes “Kansas City,” they are based in Kansas City, Missouri, not the neighboring state of Kansas. They compete in the AFC West division and play their home games at Arrowhead Stadium, a venue known for its loud crowds. Their star quarterback, Patrick Mahomes, won the NFL’s Most Valuable Player award for the 2018 season. A quarterback directs the offense and often throws passes to move the ball downfield. Mahomes later led the Chiefs to a victory over the San Francisco 49ers in Super Bowl LIV, played after the 2019 season, and was named the game’s Most Valuable Player.

Max Verstappen is a Dutch Formula One driver who became the first person from the Netherlands to win the World Drivers’ Championship. Racing for Red Bull Racing, he claimed his first title in 2021 after a season-long battle with Lewis Hamilton, a driver for Mercedes. The championship came down to the final race, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, held at Yas Marina Circuit in the United Arab Emirates. Verstappen and Hamilton entered the race level on points. Near the end, a safety-car period brought the cars together, and Verstappen passed Hamilton on the final lap after racing restarted. The dramatic finish secured Verstappen’s title, although Mercedes won that season’s Constructors’ Championship, the award for the team whose two drivers score the most points combined.

Threefold repetition is a chess rule that lets a player claim a draw when the same position occurs for a third time. The positions do not have to occur on consecutive moves. They count as the same only if the same player is to move, the pieces occupy the same squares, and the same moves are legally available, including any rights to castle or capture en passant. A player can claim the draw when the position has appeared for the third time or when their next move will produce it, as long as they follow the proper claim procedure. The rule can be useful in an endgame when neither side can make progress. It appears in the Laws of Chess published by FIDE, the worldwide chess federation founded in Paris in 1924 and now based in Lausanne.

Gambling means risking money or something else valuable on an uncertain outcome in the hope of winning more. It includes betting on sports, playing casino games, and wagering on card games. In some games, skill affects the result, but there is still a risk of losing what you bet. Three-card monte is a street card hustle that may look like a simple gambling game. A dealer places three cards face down—usually one queen and two other cards—then moves them quickly. The bettor pays to guess where the queen has ended up. Although it seems possible to win by watching closely, the dealer often uses sleight of hand and may work with accomplices, making three-card monte a common scam.

The Rubik’s Cube is a handheld, three-dimensional puzzle invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik. A standard cube has six square faces, each divided into a 3-by-3 grid of colored squares. Twisting a layer moves pieces between faces, and the usual goal is to arrange them so that every face shows just one color. Many beginners learn to solve it layer by layer, while speedcubers practice methods designed to reduce the number of moves and the time needed. One popular speed-solving system is the CFOP method, developed by Jessica Fridrich. Its four stages are Cross, First Two Layers, Orientation of the Last Layer, and Permutation of the Last Layer. Other twisty puzzles, such as the Pyraminx, offer different shapes and challenges.

The rook is a chess piece that moves any number of unoccupied squares along a rank (row) or file (column), but never diagonally. Each player starts with two rooks, one in each corner of their back rank. A rook captures an opposing piece by moving onto its square, but it cannot jump over other pieces. Rooks also take part in castling, a special move involving the king. To castle, neither the king nor the chosen rook may have moved earlier, and the squares between them must be empty. The king moves two squares toward the rook, which then moves to the square immediately on the king’s other side. Castling is not allowed if the king is in check or would move through or into check.

The Old Firm rivalry is the long-running association-football contest between Celtic and Rangers, two clubs based in Glasgow, Scotland’s largest city. Their matches are among the country’s most prominent club fixtures, drawing intense support and attention far beyond Glasgow. The rivalry has roots in the clubs’ different histories and communities: Celtic has traditionally been associated with Irish Catholic immigrants, while Rangers has traditionally been associated with the Protestant community. These connections have sometimes contributed to sectarian hostility, though supporters have many different backgrounds today. Rangers play their home matches at Ibrox Stadium in southwest Glasgow, near the River Clyde. A memorial at the stadium remembers the 66 people who died in the 1971 Ibrox disaster, when a crowd crush occurred after an Old Firm match.

Von Miller is an American football linebacker best known for his time with the Denver Broncos. In Super Bowl 50, he helped Denver defeat the Carolina Panthers 24–10 and was named the game’s Most Valuable Player. Miller recorded 2.5 sacks, meaning he tackled the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage, and forced two fumbles, knocking the ball loose from a player’s hands. His pressure disrupted Carolina quarterback Cam Newton, who had led the Panthers to a 15–1 record during the regular season. Miller later joined the Los Angeles Rams and won another Super Bowl with them. His Super Bowl 50 performance is a major reason he is remembered as one of the NFL’s standout defensive players.

Ski jumping is a Winter Olympic sport in which athletes ski down a steep approach called an inrun, take off from a ramp, and fly toward a landing hill. Their scores combine how far they jump with judges’ ratings of their technique, including their position in the air and the quality of their landing. Distance is measured against a reference mark on the hill called the K-point. Olympic competitions include normal-hill and large-hill events, which use hills of different sizes. One famous ski jumper was British athlete Michael Edwards, nicknamed “Eddie the Eagle.” At the 1988 Calgary Winter Olympics, he finished last in both the normal-hill and large-hill events, but became well known for his determination to compete.

FC Barcelona is a football club based in Barcelona, the capital of Catalonia, a region of Spain. Its senior men’s team is famous for its blue-and-garnet colors, and its matches against Real Madrid, known as El Clásico, are among football’s best-known rivalries. The club’s Catalan slogan, “Més que un club,” means “More than a club” and reflects its importance to many people as a symbol of Catalan identity as well as a sports team. FC Barcelona is also known for developing young players through its academy, La Masia. The academy takes its name from the old farmhouse that originally housed its young players. Its graduates include Xavi and Andrés Iniesta, who went on to become stars for both Barcelona and Spain.

Super Bowl XLVIII was the NFL championship game played on February 2, 2014, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The Seattle Seahawks defeated the Denver Broncos 43–8 to win their first Super Bowl title. Denver, led by quarterback Peyton Manning, had a disastrous start: on its first play, the center snapped the ball over Manning’s head, giving Seattle a safety and a 2–0 lead. Seattle’s defense continued to dominate, forcing turnovers and keeping Denver from scoring until late in the game. Seahawks linebacker Malcolm Smith was named the game’s Most Valuable Player (MVP). He returned a Manning interception 69 yards for a touchdown and also recovered a fumble. The Roman numerals XLVIII mean 48, so the game’s formal name is Super Bowl XLVIII.

Cristiano Ronaldo is a Portuguese soccer forward known for his goal-scoring and long career at top clubs. He was born in Funchal on Madeira, an island that belongs to Portugal, and developed as a young player at Sporting CP. He then moved to Manchester United before joining Real Madrid, where he spent nine seasons and became one of the club’s greatest scorers. In 2018, Ronaldo left Real Madrid to join Juventus, a club based in Turin that plays in Italy’s Serie A. He later returned to Manchester United and now plays for Al-Nassr in Saudi Arabia. Ronaldo has also captained Portugal’s national team. Outside soccer, he has opened fashion boutiques and helped design clothing lines.

The National Collegiate Athletic Association, or NCAA, sets rules for college sports in the United States and oversees championship competitions in three divisions. One of its best-known events is the Division I men’s basketball tournament, popularly called March Madness. The NCAA has also faced disputes over how college athletes can be compensated. Former UCLA basketball player Ed O’Bannon became the lead plaintiff in a lawsuit after his likeness was used in a college basketball video game without his permission. A major federal antitrust ruling in 2014 found that NCAA restrictions on certain benefits for athletes broke competition law. Later legal challenges led the NCAA to allow athletes to earn money from endorsements using their names, images, and likenesses.

Ma Long is a Chinese table tennis star known for his powerful, precise play and his long period at the top of the sport. Table tennis is played by two or four people who use small rackets to hit a lightweight ball back and forth across a table. Ma Long was appointed captain of China’s national team in 2014 and became the first man to complete two singles Grand Slams, meaning he won the sport’s three major singles titles—the Olympics, World Championships, and World Cup—twice each. He is sometimes nicknamed “the Dictator” because of his dominance in matches. At the 2012 World Cup, he won gold by defeating Timo Boll, a player who represents Germany internationally and has played for the German club Borussia Düsseldorf.

The Boston Celtics are a professional basketball team from Boston, Massachusetts, that plays in the NBA. They became one of the league’s greatest dynasties during the 1950s and 1960s. From 1957 to 1966, coach Red Auerbach led the Celtics to nine NBA championships in ten seasons. Their success was built around center Bill Russell, whose defense and rebounding helped the team dominate, along with talented teammates such as John Havlicek. Auerbach was famous for lighting a victory cigar when he felt a game was already won. In later decades, the Celtics featured stars including Larry Bird, who won the NBA’s first three three-point contests, as well as Paul Pierce, Kevin Garnett, and Jayson Tatum.

The Women’s National Basketball Association, usually called the WNBA, is the premier professional women’s basketball league in the United States. Founded in 1996, it gives many of the world’s best players a place to compete at the highest level. Its teams include the Las Vegas Aces and the Connecticut Sun, which met in the 2022 WNBA Finals. The Aces won that championship with stars including A’ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum. Their coach was Becky Hammon, who had previously worked as an assistant coach under Gregg Popovich with the San Antonio Spurs in the men’s National Basketball Association (NBA). The Aces had played in San Antonio before moving to Las Vegas in 2017.

Argentina’s men’s national football team is known as La Albiceleste, meaning “the White and Sky Blue,” after the colors of its striped shirts. It has won the FIFA World Cup three times: in 1978, 1986, and 2022. Two of its most famous players are Diego Maradona, who led the team to the 1986 title, and Lionel Messi, who captained it to victory in 2022. Argentina is also remembered for a remarkable team goal at the 2006 World Cup. In a group match against Serbia and Montenegro, its players exchanged 25 consecutive passes before midfielder Esteban Cambiasso finished the move by scoring. The goal is celebrated because it showed how coordinated passing and teamwork can create a scoring chance.

The 2012 Summer Olympics were an international multi-sport competition held in London, England. London had previously hosted the Summer Games in 1908 and 1948, so 2012 made it the first city to host them three times. Athletes from around the world competed in events ranging from track and field to cycling and water sports. Swimming, diving, and synchronized swimming took place at the London Aquatics Centre in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. The centre was designed by British-Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid, who gave it a sweeping, wave-like roof inspired by the movement of water. After the Games, the venue continued to serve as a place for swimming competitions and public use.

Aaron Rodgers is an American football quarterback best known for his years with the Green Bay Packers. Green Bay drafted him 24th overall in 2005, and he spent three seasons as Brett Favre’s backup before becoming the team’s starter. Rodgers led the Packers to victory in Super Bowl XLV and won four NFL Most Valuable Player awards. He also became familiar to people who did not watch football through State Farm insurance commercials, including ads with the character Jake from State Farm. In a State Farm Super Bowl commercial featuring Rodgers and fellow quarterback Patrick Mahomes, the rapper Drake played Jake’s stand-in. Drake is a chart-topping musician who released the surprise album Honestly, Nevermind in 2022.

The New York Knicks are a professional basketball team founded in 1946. They play in the NBA and have played most of their home games at Madison Square Garden in New York City. The Knicks are the older of the city’s two current NBA teams and have a rivalry with the Brooklyn Nets. One of the most important players in Knicks history is Patrick Ewing, a center from Georgetown University. The Knicks selected him with the first overall pick in the 1985 NBA draft. Ewing spent 15 seasons with the team, led it to the NBA Finals in 1994 and 1999, and became its all-time leader in points and rebounds. Although the Knicks did not win either of those Finals, Ewing remains closely associated with the franchise.

Peyton Manning was a Hall of Fame NFL quarterback known for reading defenses and directing his team’s offense. The Indianapolis Colts selected him first overall in the 1998 draft, and he spent 14 seasons with them before joining the Denver Broncos in 2012. Denver released its previous quarterback, Tim Tebow, after signing Manning. With the Broncos, Manning reached two Super Bowls and ended his career with a championship. His final NFL game was Super Bowl 50, played on February 7, 2016, at Levi’s Stadium in Santa Clara, California. Denver defeated the Carolina Panthers 24–10. Although Manning was the quarterback, Broncos linebacker Von Miller was named the game’s Most Valuable Player after helping Denver’s defense dominate.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar is a Hall of Fame basketball center known for his nearly unstoppable skyhook shot. Before joining the NBA, he won three NCAA championships at UCLA under coach John Wooden. He entered the league with the Milwaukee Bucks, a team based in Wisconsin, and helped lead them to their first NBA championship in 1971 alongside star guard Oscar Robertson. Abdul-Jabbar later played for the Los Angeles Lakers and became the NBA’s all-time leading scorer, a record he held until LeBron James passed him in 2023. The Bucks did not win another championship until 2021, when Giannis Antetokounmpo led them to their second title. Abdul-Jabbar’s skill and long career made him one of basketball’s most celebrated players.

Reggie Jackson was a powerful American baseball outfielder known for hitting home runs in important games. He starred for the Oakland Athletics, also called the Oakland A’s, when the American League club won three straight World Series championships from 1972 through 1974. Jackson later played for the New York Yankees, where he earned the nickname “Mr. October” for his outstanding performances in the playoffs. In the deciding game of the 1977 World Series, he hit three home runs, helping the Yankees defeat the Los Angeles Dodgers. He was named the Most Valuable Player of that World Series. Jackson’s career is especially remembered for his role in Oakland’s championship run and his remarkable three-home-run game with New York.

Figure skating is a judged Winter Olympic sport in which athletes perform choreographed programs on an ice rink. Skaters combine movements set to music with technical elements such as jumps, spins, and step sequences. In the short program, they must include specific elements, which can include a double or triple jump and a double Axel. One well-known jump is the Axel, named after Norwegian skater Axel Paulsen, who introduced it in the late 19th century. Unlike most figure-skating jumps, an Axel takes off from a forward outside edge. A single Axel completes one and a half rotations before the skater lands backward. Judges consider both how well skaters perform the technical elements and the quality of their overall performance.

The Golden State Warriors are an NBA team based in the San Francisco Bay Area. The franchise began in Philadelphia in 1946, moved to the Bay Area in 1962, and adopted the name Golden State Warriors in 1971. Led by star guard Stephen Curry, the team won four championships from 2015 through 2022, becoming famous for its fast-paced play and three-point shooting. Another key player was Kevin Durant, a former NBA Most Valuable Player who left the Oklahoma City Thunder to join the Warriors in 2016. Durant helped the team win championships in 2017 and 2018 and was named Finals MVP both years. These victories were part of one of the most successful eras in Warriors history.

Grover Cleveland was a Democratic president who served as both the 22nd and 24th president of the United States. He is the only U.S. president to have served two nonconsecutive terms: he first held office from 1885 to 1889, Benjamin Harrison served next, and Cleveland returned from 1893 to 1897. His second term took place during a severe economic downturn that began with the Panic of 1893. In 1894, workers at the Pullman railroad-car company near Chicago, Illinois, protested wage cuts, and their dispute grew into a major railroad confrontation called the Pullman Strike. Eugene Debs and the American Railway Union led a boycott of trains carrying Pullman cars. Cleveland’s administration sent federal troops to break the strike, arguing that disrupted rail service was interfering with the delivery of U.S. mail.

Mexican Americans are people in the United States with roots in Mexico. Their history includes farm labor, discrimination, and campaigns for equal rights. During a World War II farm labor shortage, the 1942 Bracero Program brought Mexican workers to the United States on temporary contracts. In the 1960s, the Chicano movement pressed for better treatment in workplaces, schools, and communities; labor leaders César Chávez and Dolores Huerta helped organize farmworkers. Mexican American students also challenged unequal education. In 1968, students at Garfield, Lincoln, Roosevelt, Wilson, and Belmont high schools left class to protest overcrowding, poor facilities, and unfair treatment. These coordinated demonstrations are commonly called the East Los Angeles walkouts, or “blowouts.”

Virginia is a U.S. state with a central place in early English colonial history. In 1607, English settlers founded Jamestown there, the first permanent English settlement in North America. Its early years were difficult: many colonists died during the “Starving Time,” and settlers came into conflict with the Powhatan peoples. In 1619, Virginia’s House of Burgesses first met, becoming the first representative legislature in English America. Decades later, tensions over frontier defense, relations with Native peoples, and colonial leadership helped spark Bacon’s Rebellion. Led by Nathaniel Bacon in 1676, the uprising challenged Governor William Berkeley and culminated in the burning of Jamestown before royal forces restored order. These events connect Virginia to both the beginnings of English settlement and struggles over who held power in the colonies.

Roanoke Colony was an early English settlement founded in 1587 on Roanoke Island, in present-day North Carolina, as part of Sir Walter Raleigh’s efforts to establish a colony in North America. Its governor, John White, returned to England for supplies, but war with Spain delayed his trip back. When he reached Roanoke in 1590, the settlers had vanished. He found “CROATOAN” carved on a post and “CRO” on a tree, clues that may have pointed to the nearby Croatoan people and their island, but the colonists’ fate remains uncertain. The settlement became known as the Lost Colony. White’s granddaughter Virginia Dare was born there during the 1587 expedition and is traditionally regarded as the first English child born in the Americas.

George H. W. Bush became the 41st U.S. president in January 1989 and served one term, ending in 1993. His presidency came at a turning point in world history: the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, Germany reunified in 1990, and the Cold War ended as the Soviet Union collapsed. Bush worked with other countries to manage these changes. His secretary of state, James Baker, had previously been President Ronald Reagan’s chief of staff and was a key U.S. negotiator during German reunification. Baker also helped build international support during the 1991 Gulf War, when a U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait. Although Bush had promised “no new taxes,” he later agreed to a tax increase and lost his 1992 re-election bid to Bill Clinton.

James Monroe was the fifth president of the United States, serving from 1817 to 1825. His presidency is often called the Era of Good Feelings because the Federalist Party had faded and national politics briefly seemed less divided. But serious disagreements remained, especially over slavery. Monroe signed the Missouri Compromise in 1820, which admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state while setting a boundary for slavery in much of the Louisiana Purchase territory. In an 1823 message to Congress, Monroe announced the foreign-policy principle later called the Monroe Doctrine: the Americas were no longer open to European colonization, and attempts by European powers to extend their political control in the Western Hemisphere would be viewed as hostile to the United States.

After losing the election of 1800 to Thomas Jefferson, President John Adams tried to fill newly created judicial posts with members of his Federalist Party before leaving office. These last-minute appointees became known as the “midnight judges.” Adams signed their commissions, the documents confirming their appointments, but some were not delivered before Jefferson took office. One appointee, William Marbury, had been named a justice of the peace in the District of Columbia. When Jefferson’s administration refused to deliver his commission, Marbury asked the Supreme Court to order its delivery. In the 1803 case Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Court could not issue that order under an unconstitutional provision of the Judiciary Act of 1789. The decision established judicial review: the Supreme Court’s power to declare federal laws unconstitutional.

Ironclad warships were steam-powered naval vessels protected by thick iron or steel armor. During the American Civil War, both the Union and the Confederacy used them because their armor could resist many cannon shots that would badly damage wooden ships. Two famous examples were the Union’s USS Monitor, designed by Swedish inventor John Ericsson with a rotating gun turret, and the Confederacy’s CSS Virginia, built from the hull of a captured Union ship and fitted with an iron ram. In March 1862, these ships fought near Norfolk, Virginia, in the Battle of Hampton Roads. Their duel was the first famous clash between ironclads. Although neither ship won a decisive victory, the battle showed that armored, steam-powered vessels could change naval warfare.

Hawaiian annexation was the incorporation of the Hawaiian Islands into the United States in 1898. Hawaii had been an independent Pacific kingdom, united under King Kamehameha I, before American business interests gained growing influence there. In 1887, Lorrin Thurston helped force a new constitution on the Hawaiian king; it became known as the Bayonet Constitution because it was imposed under threat of force. In 1893, a group backed by U.S. interests overthrew Hawaii’s final monarch, Queen Liliʻuokalani, and Sanford Dole led the new government. Five years later, Congress passed the Newlands Resolution, a joint measure named for its Nevada sponsor, in July 1898. It authorized Hawaii’s annexation rather than restoring the monarchy. Hawaii later became a U.S. territory and, in 1959, the 50th state.

Lewis Cass was a nineteenth-century American politician who served in several major roles before the Civil War. He governed Michigan Territory, served as secretary of war under President Andrew Jackson, and became the Democratic Party’s presidential nominee in 1848, though he lost the election. Cass later served as secretary of state under President James Buchanan, a Democrat who won the 1856 election and served immediately before Abraham Lincoln. After Lincoln’s election in 1860, Southern states began to secede from the United States. Cass believed Buchanan’s administration was not responding firmly enough to the crisis, so he resigned as secretary of state in December 1860. His resignation reflected the deep disagreements in Washington as the country moved toward civil war.

Kent State University is a public university in northeastern Ohio remembered for a deadly confrontation during protests against the Vietnam War. In May 1970, students protested President Richard Nixon’s decision to expand the war into Cambodia. After several days of unrest, Ohio National Guardsmen were sent to campus, and officials declared martial law. On May 4, Guardsmen fired into a crowd, killing four students and wounding nine. One of the dead was Jeffrey Miller. Kent State student photojournalist John Filo captured a photograph of 14-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio kneeling and crying beside Miller’s body. The image won a Pulitzer Prize and became a powerful symbol of the war’s divisions at home. The shootings sparked student protests and campus closures across the United States.

The Mississauga Ojibwe are an Anishinaabe Indigenous people whose homelands lie around the Great Lakes, especially in what is now southern Ontario. They are part of the wider Ojibwe community and have their own histories, traditions, and communities today. American sculptor Edmonia Lewis claimed that one-quarter of her heritage was Mississauga Ojibwe. She drew on Indigenous themes in some of her art, including Old Arrow Maker. That sculpture shows an older man teaching a young child to make an arrow, a traditional hunting implement fashioned from materials such as wood and feathers. The scene emphasizes knowledge being passed from one generation to the next. Lewis’s work also explored other subjects, but Old Arrow Maker is the sculpture to remember when connecting her claimed Mississauga Ojibwe heritage with Indigenous themes.

The Mueller Report is the common name for a Justice Department document released publicly in April 2019. It presented the findings of an investigation led by Robert Mueller, a former FBI director, into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and possible coordination between Russia and Donald Trump’s campaign. Mueller also examined whether Trump had obstructed the investigation. The inquiry began after the election, amid concerns about Russian hacking and efforts to influence voters. In May 2017, Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein appointed Mueller as special counsel to lead it. Rosenstein signed the appointment order because Attorney General Jeff Sessions had recused himself from the Russia investigation, meaning he stepped aside from overseeing it. The report’s release sparked debate about its findings and how they were presented to the public.

The Kansas–Nebraska Act was an 1854 law that created the territories of Kansas and Nebraska west of the Missouri River. It was introduced in the U.S. Senate by Stephen A. Douglas, an Illinois Democrat who chaired the Committee on Territories. Douglas supported popular sovereignty, the idea that settlers in each territory should vote on whether to allow slavery. This overturned the Missouri Compromise of 1820, which had banned slavery in much of the land north of a set boundary. The possibility that Kansas could become a slave state brought pro-slavery and anti-slavery settlers into conflict. Their elections and violent clashes gave the territory the nickname “Bleeding Kansas.” The act deepened the national disagreement over slavery in the years before the Civil War.

Publius was the shared pen name used by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay when they wrote the Federalist Papers. Published in 1787 and 1788, these essays urged Americans to ratify the proposed U.S. Constitution. The name Publius referred to an ancient Roman figure associated with government by the people, giving the essays a sense of public-minded purpose. Although the three authors signed their essays with the same name, they wrote different numbers of them. Hamilton wrote the most, Madison wrote many important essays, and Jay contributed five. Jay later became the first Chief Justice of the United States, leading the Supreme Court in its early years. Remembering both the shared signature, Publius, and Jay’s five essays helps distinguish the pen name from the people who used it.

Sherman’s March to the Sea was a Union military campaign during the American Civil War. In November 1864, General William Tecumseh Sherman led his army from the captured city of Atlanta across Georgia toward the Atlantic coast. His troops destroyed railroads, supplies, and other resources that could help the Confederate army, while also taking food from the countryside. This strategy aimed to weaken the Confederacy’s ability and willingness to keep fighting. In December, Union forces occupied Savannah, a major Georgia port city. Sherman famously offered Savannah to President Abraham Lincoln as a “Christmas gift.” Supporters of the later Lost Cause interpretation of the war portrayed the march as an example of Northern aggression, but its main military purpose was to damage Confederate resources and hasten the war’s end.

The Missouri Compromise was a congressional agreement reached in 1820 to ease conflict between states that allowed slavery and states that did not. Missouri wanted to enter the Union as a slave state, which would have upset the balance between slave and free states in the Senate. Congress agreed to admit Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, preserving that balance. The agreement also drew a boundary across the Louisiana Purchase at the 36°30′ parallel of latitude. Slavery would be prohibited in the remaining territory north of that line, with an exception for Missouri, even though it lay north of the boundary. The compromise temporarily reduced tensions, but it did not resolve the growing national dispute over slavery or its expansion westward.

Mark Kelly is a former NASA astronaut who became a Democratic U.S. senator from Arizona. He flew on four Space Shuttle missions and commanded the final flight of the orbiter Endeavour in May 2011. That mission delivered the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, an instrument used to study particles in space, to the International Space Station. Kelly is married to Gabby Giffords, a former Arizona congresswoman who survived a shooting in Tucson in 2011. In 2020, he won a special Senate election against Republican Martha McSally, who had been appointed to fill the seat once held by longtime senator John McCain. Kelly’s career connects space exploration with Arizona politics.

The Freedom Riders were interracial groups of civil rights activists who traveled together on buses through the segregated South in 1961. They deliberately used seats and facilities that local customs tried to reserve for only white or Black people. Their rides tested whether federal rulings against segregation in interstate travel would actually be enforced. In the 1960 Supreme Court decision Boynton v. Virginia, the Court ruled that racial segregation in facilities serving interstate bus passengers, such as bus-terminal restaurants, violated federal law. Despite that ruling, segregation continued in many Southern terminals. Freedom Riders challenged it by entering waiting rooms and other facilities together. They faced arrests and violent attacks, but their actions drew national attention and helped push federal authorities to enforce desegregation in interstate bus travel.

The Navy SEALs are the U.S. Navy’s primary special operations force. Their name stands for Sea, Air, and Land, the environments in which they are trained to operate. SEALs carry out demanding missions such as reconnaissance, rescue, and raids, often in small teams and under dangerous conditions. To qualify, candidates must complete Basic Underwater Demolition/SEAL training, known as BUD/S, at a Navy base in Coronado, California. One of the SEALs’ best-known missions was Operation Neptune Spear in 2011. During that raid in Abbottabad, Pakistan, SEAL Team Six killed Osama bin Laden, the al-Qaeda leader responsible for orchestrating the September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States.

The Little Rock Nine were nine Black teenagers who enrolled at Little Rock Central High School, a formerly all-white public school in Arkansas, in 1957. Their enrollment tested the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling, which declared racial segregation in public schools unconstitutional. Arkansas governor Orval Faubus used the state’s National Guard to block the students from entering the school, while hostile crowds gathered outside. After the students were turned away, President Dwight D. Eisenhower sent federal troops from the 101st Airborne Division to protect them and enforce desegregation. The students attended classes despite harassment and threats. Their courage made the Little Rock school crisis a major event in the civil rights movement and showed the federal government’s role in upholding students’ right to equal education.

The McCloskey gun incident took place in June 2020 in St. Louis, Missouri, during protests against racial injustice following the killing of George Floyd. Mark and Patricia McCloskey, a husband-and-wife team of lawyers, stood outside their home holding firearms as Black Lives Matter demonstrators passed through their neighborhood. Images and video of the couple spread widely, making the incident a national controversy. Supporters said the McCloskeys were defending their property, while critics said their actions threatened protesters. The couple later spoke at the 2020 Republican National Convention. That convention faced a separate controversy when it used “Hallelujah” without permission from the estate of Leonard Cohen, the Canadian singer-songwriter who wrote the song.

Bacon’s Rebellion was a 1676 uprising in the Virginia Colony led by Nathaniel Bacon against the government of royal governor William Berkeley. Many colonists on the frontier believed Berkeley was not doing enough to protect them from attacks, and they opposed his policies toward Native peoples. Bacon gathered armed supporters, who fought Native communities and then turned against Berkeley’s administration. The rebellion reached Jamestown, Virginia’s colonial capital, which the rebels burned. Bacon died later that year, and the uprising collapsed, but Berkeley was recalled to England afterward. The revolt exposed deep tensions in colonial Virginia over frontier security, political power, and relations with Native peoples.

The January 6 Committee, formally the United States House Select Committee on the January 6 Attack, was formed by the House of Representatives in 2021. Chaired by Mississippi Democrat Bennie Thompson, the bipartisan panel investigated the January 6, 2021 storming of the U.S. Capitol and efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election. Its televised public hearings in 2022 examined what happened before and during the attack, when Congress was meeting to certify Joe Biden’s victory. Two Republicans served on the committee: Adam Kinzinger of Illinois and Liz Cheney of Wyoming. Cheney had supported Donald Trump’s impeachment after the attack, and House Republicans removed her as chair of the House Republican Conference.

Operation Eagle Claw was a secret U.S. military mission authorized by President Jimmy Carter in April 1980 to rescue Americans held hostage at the U.S. embassy in Tehran, Iran. The plan called for a rescue force to fly into Iran, refuel, and transfer personnel at a remote desert staging site codenamed Desert One before continuing toward Tehran. Eight RH-53D helicopters were assigned to the mission, but mechanical problems and a dust storm left too few helicopters able to continue. As the force prepared to leave Desert One, an RH-53D helicopter collided with an EC-130 transport aircraft, killing eight U.S. service members. Commanders abandoned the rescue attempt. The failure was a major setback for the United States during the hostage crisis.

The University of California, Berkeley, often called UC Berkeley or Cal, is a public research university in the San Francisco Bay Area and is regarded as the flagship campus of the University of California system. In 1969, after student strikes calling for courses that reflected the histories and experiences of underrepresented communities, Berkeley became the first U.S. university to establish an ethnic studies program. LaNada War Jack, the university’s first Native American student, was part of this era of activism. Later in 1969, she joined Indians of All Tribes in occupying Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay. The occupation lasted 19 months. The group invoked the Treaty of Fort Laramie to claim the island and proposed building a center there for the study of Native American history and culture.

The Palmer Raids were a series of U.S. government sweeps in late 1919 and early 1920, after World War I. Many Americans feared that revolution and political violence might spread to the United States, especially after the communist revolution in Russia and several bomb attacks at home. Under Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, federal agents arrested thousands of people suspected of being anarchists, communists, or other political radicals. Some were held without proper legal protections, and some immigrants were deported. The raids became a major example of the first Red Scare, a period when fear of communism led to harsh treatment of people with radical views. Palmer later sought the Democratic presidential nomination in 1920, but did not win it.

Angel Island Immigration Station was a federal immigration and detention facility on an island in California’s San Francisco Bay. Open from 1910 to 1940, it processed many people arriving from Asia, especially China and Japan, and became known as the “Ellis Island of the West.” Unlike many immigrants at Ellis Island on the East Coast, arrivals at Angel Island could be held for weeks or months while officials questioned them and checked their documents. Chinese immigrants faced especially strict scrutiny because of the Chinese Exclusion Act, a federal law first passed in 1882 that barred most laborers from China, then ruled by the Qing dynasty, from entering the United States. The station closed after a fire in 1940. Today, Angel Island helps tell the history of immigration and discrimination in the United States.

Massive Resistance was a coordinated campaign by white Southern politicians and institutions to block school desegregation after the Supreme Court’s 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education. The Court ruled that racially separated public schools were unconstitutional, rejecting the idea that “separate but equal” schools were acceptable. A later ruling directed schools to desegregate “with all deliberate speed,” but many officials used laws, court challenges, and other tactics to delay integration. In Virginia, Senator Harry F. Byrd Sr. led a powerful political organization that promoted Massive Resistance. Its leaders supported closing public schools rather than allowing Black and white students to attend them together. These efforts disrupted students’ education but did not overturn the Court’s ruling.

Thomas Paine was an English-born political writer who moved to the American colonies and became a powerful voice for independence during the American Revolution. In 1776, he published Common Sense, a pamphlet that urged the colonies to separate from Britain. Paine wrote in clear, direct language so ordinary readers could understand his argument. He argued that it was absurd for a vast continent to be ruled by a distant island, and he challenged the idea that kings had a right to govern. Later, as Americans fought the Revolutionary War, Paine wrote a series of pamphlets called The American Crisis to encourage them to keep going. Its first installment began with the famous words, “These are the times that try men’s souls.”

Italian Americans are people in the United States with roots in Italy. Their communities grew as many Italians immigrated in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Two Italian American anarchists, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were convicted of murders committed during a 1920 robbery in Braintree, Massachusetts, and executed in 1927. Their case sparked protests over whether prejudice against immigrants and their political beliefs had affected the trial. Another event linked to the era’s political violence was the 1920 Wall Street bombing: on September 16, a horse-drawn wagon exploded outside J.P. Morgan & Co. in Manhattan, killing 38 people. Investigators suspected members of Italian immigrant Luigi Galleani’s anarchist circle, but never conclusively identified the bombers. The bombing happened years before Sacco and Vanzetti’s execution.

The Watergate break-in was a 1972 burglary at the Democratic National Committee (DNC) headquarters in the Watergate office complex in Washington, D.C. The burglars were tied to President Richard Nixon’s reelection campaign and entered the offices to install surveillance equipment and gather information about political opponents. On June 17, security guard Frank Wills noticed tape placed over door latches so the doors would not lock. He removed it, but when he found that the tape had been replaced, he alerted police. Officers searched the building and caught the burglars inside the DNC offices. Investigations into the break-in uncovered a wider effort to hide the crime and misuse political power. The resulting Watergate scandal damaged Nixon’s presidency and led to his resignation in 1974.

The Thompson submachine gun was developed in the United States around World War I. Nicknamed the “Tommy gun,” this .45-caliber automatic firearm could fire rapidly and use a distinctive round drum magazine. It became a symbol of Prohibition, when the sale of alcohol was banned in the United States. Bootleggers, who illegally sold alcohol, and law enforcement officers both used Thompson guns; gangsters were sometimes said to carry them in violin cases. The weapon is especially associated with the 1929 St. Valentine’s Day Massacre in Chicago. Seven members of George “Bugs” Moran’s gang were shot in a garage by attackers, some disguised as police officers. The killings became one of the most notorious examples of Prohibition-era gang violence.

Samuel Alito is a conservative Associate Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court. President George W. Bush nominated him to replace Justice Sandra Day O’Connor, and he joined the Court in 2006. Alito wrote the majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, a 2022 case about a Mississippi abortion law. The ruling overturned two earlier Supreme Court decisions, Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey. Alito’s opinion held that the U.S. Constitution does not confer a right to abortion, so states could set their own abortion laws, including bans. A draft of the Dobbs opinion was leaked before the Court officially announced its decision.

The 1968 Democratic National Convention was held in Chicago that August as the party chose its presidential nominee during the Vietnam War. President Lyndon B. Johnson had decided not to run again, and many antiwar activists supported Senator Eugene McCarthy. Thousands of protesters gathered outside the convention, where clashes with police were broadcast on television. During one confrontation, known as the “Battle of Michigan Avenue,” demonstrators chanted, “The whole world is watching.” Inside the convention, Connecticut senator Abraham Ribicoff seconded McCarthy’s nomination and condemned the police response as “Gestapo tactics.” His remarks drew a furious reaction from Chicago mayor Richard J. Daley. The convention became a symbol of the deep divisions over the war and of the conflict between protesters and authorities.

The Oregon Trail was a historic overland route that carried thousands of European-American emigrants from the Missouri River region toward Oregon Country during nineteenth-century U.S. westward expansion. Many travelers began in Independence, Missouri, a river town east of Kansas City where they could buy supplies and prepare their wagons; later, more wagon traffic departed from St. Joseph, Missouri. The journey took months and led across the Great Plains and Rocky Mountains toward the fertile Willamette Valley in present-day Oregon. Travel increased sharply during the “Great Migration” of 1843, when a large group of families headed west together. Emigrants hoped to find farmland and new opportunities, but the trip brought serious dangers, including disease, difficult river crossings, and harsh weather.

Matthew Calbraith Perry was a career U.S. naval officer born in Newport, Rhode Island. Under President Millard Fillmore, he led a squadron of steam-powered warships to Edo Bay in 1853. The Japanese called them “black ships.” At the time, Japan’s Tokugawa shogunate had followed a policy of relative isolation for about two centuries, sharply limiting contact with other countries. Perry’s arrival put pressure on the Tokugawa government to negotiate, and he returned with a larger squadron in 1854. The resulting Treaty of Kanagawa opened the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships for supplies and included provisions to help shipwrecked American sailors. Perry’s expedition helped begin a wider opening of Japan to foreign trade and diplomacy in the years before the Meiji Restoration.

The Navajo Code Talkers were Navajo-speaking U.S. Marines who sent secure battlefield messages during World War II. Navajo is an Athabaskan language native to the American Southwest. The Marines developed a code based on it, using Navajo words for military terms and an alphabet system for other words. They sent messages by radio and telephone during battles in the Pacific, where quick communication could save lives. Enemy forces might intercept a message, but the code made it extremely difficult for them to understand it. Navajo Code Talkers served in several campaigns, including the 1945 Battle of Iwo Jima, fought for a volcanic island south of Japan. That battle is also remembered for the raising of an American flag on Mount Suribachi.

Blackbeard was a feared pirate who sailed in the Caribbean and along the eastern coast of North America in the early 1700s. Often called Edward Teach or Edward Thatch, he was best known by a nickname inspired by his thick, dark beard. In 1717, he captured a French slave ship and refitted it as his flagship, the Queen Anne’s Revenge. The next year, he blockaded Charles Town, South Carolina, seizing ships and prisoners until he received medical supplies in exchange for their release. After the Queen Anne’s Revenge ran aground near Beaufort Inlet in 1718, Blackbeard parted ways with fellow pirate Stede Bonnet and continued sailing aboard the Adventure. His blockade and his powerful flagship helped make him one of history’s most notorious pirates.

The Ancestral Puebloans were Indigenous peoples of the American Southwest whose descendants include modern Pueblo peoples, such as the Hopi and Zuni. Over many centuries, they developed farming communities and built settlements using stone and adobe. At Mesa Verde in present-day Colorado, they constructed villages in sheltered cliff alcoves. Another major center was Chaco Canyon in northwestern New Mexico. Chaco Canyon is known for monumental buildings called great houses, including Pueblo Bonito, and for a network of ancient roads linking it to other places. These sites show how Ancestral Puebloan communities organized large building projects and maintained connections across the region. Their history did not end when people left these settlements: Pueblo peoples continue to live in the Southwest today.

Frances Perkins became the first woman to serve in the U.S. Cabinet when President Franklin D. Roosevelt appointed her Secretary of Labor in 1933. During the Great Depression, millions of Americans were out of work, and Perkins helped shape the New Deal’s response to poverty and joblessness. She supported stronger labor protections and chaired Roosevelt’s 1934 Committee on Economic Security, which developed a plan for a national safety net. That plan helped produce the Social Security Act of 1935, a landmark law that established old-age benefits and unemployment insurance. Perkins’s work helped change the federal government’s role in supporting workers and families, while her appointment broke a barrier for women in national government.

The Sherman Antitrust Act is a federal law passed by Congress in 1890 to protect competition in interstate commerce. It outlaws contracts and combinations that unreasonably restrain trade and makes monopolization a federal offense. The law became a foundation for efforts to break up powerful business trusts, and courts still apply it to organizations that limit competition. In NCAA v. Alston, decided unanimously by the Supreme Court in 2021, former West Virginia University running back Shawne Alston and other student-athletes challenged NCAA limits on benefits tied to education. The Court upheld an injunction that prevented the NCAA from restricting certain education-related benefits, such as graduate-school scholarships and academic awards. The decision did not require colleges to pay athletes salaries or decide every question about athlete compensation.

The 1619 Project is a New York Times Magazine initiative first published in 2019, 400 years after the first enslaved Africans arrived in English Virginia in 1619. Developed by journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones, it asks readers to consider how slavery and its aftermath have shaped the United States, including its laws, economy, culture, and ideas about freedom and equality. Hannah-Jones wrote the project’s lead essay and received the 2020 Pulitzer Prize for Commentary for her work on it. The project includes essays and other materials, and an educational curriculum was created to help students study its themes. Its interpretation of American history has also sparked debate among historians, educators, and politicians, especially about how slavery and racism should be taught in schools.

William Penn was an English Quaker who founded the colony of Pennsylvania as a “holy experiment” in religious toleration. In 1681, King Charles II gave Penn a royal charter for land west of the Delaware River, partly to repay a debt owed to Penn’s late father, a prominent naval officer. As the colony’s proprietor, Penn promoted Quaker ideals, including freedom of worship and peaceful relations among people of different faiths. He also planned Philadelphia, Pennsylvania’s capital, with a grid of straight streets near the meeting of the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers. The colony attracted settlers from several religious backgrounds. Although Penn hoped to deal fairly with Native Americans, later colonial leaders took their land through actions such as the Walking Purchase of 1737.

The Zimmermann Telegram was a secret German diplomatic message sent to Mexico in 1917, during World War I. Germany proposed that Mexico join it in a war against the United States if the United States entered the conflict. In return, Germany promised to support Mexico in recovering territory it had lost to the United States, including Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. Much of that land had changed hands after the Mexican-American War through the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Germany hoped a war with Mexico would keep American forces occupied at home. British intelligence intercepted the telegram and shared it with the United States. When its contents became public, they increased American anger toward Germany. Along with Germany’s unrestricted submarine warfare, the telegram helped lead President Woodrow Wilson to ask Congress to declare war.

The My Lai massacre was a Vietnam War atrocity on March 16, 1968, when U.S. Army soldiers from Charlie Company killed hundreds of unarmed civilians in the South Vietnamese village of My Lai. The victims included women, children, and older people. Lieutenant William Calley led one of the units involved and was later convicted for his role. The killings were initially concealed, but journalist Seymour Hersh helped bring them to public attention, increasing opposition to the war. During the investigation, Major Colin Powell was assigned to review allegations of abuses described in a letter from U.S. soldier Tom Glen. Powell did not believe the letter showed widespread mistreatment of civilians. He later became chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and U.S. secretary of state.

The Bracero Program was an agreement between the United States and Mexico that brought Mexican workers to the United States on temporary contracts from 1942 to 1964. It began during World War II, when many U.S. workers had joined the military or taken factory jobs, leaving farms short of labor. Mexican braceros crossed north to plant and harvest crops, helping U.S. agriculture meet wartime and postwar demand. The program promised workers wages and basic protections, but many faced poor housing, low pay, and unfair treatment.
