Braceros were temporary workers, not permanent immigrants, though the program shaped Mexican migration and Mexican-American communities for years afterward. If asked to name the wartime guest-worker arrangement, the answer is the Bracero Program; its partner country was Mexico.

United States v. Wilson was an 1833 Supreme Court case about whether a person must accept a presidential pardon. George Wilson had been convicted of robbing the U.S. mail and endangering the life of the mail carrier. President Andrew Jackson issued him a pardon, but Wilson refused to accept it. Chief Justice John Marshall reasoned that a pardon is like a deed: delivering it is not enough to make it effective unless the recipient accepts it. The Court therefore held that a person may refuse a pardon. A presidential pardon is an act of clemency that can relieve someone of the legal consequences of a federal crime. The case is remembered for establishing that this form of clemency cannot be forced on its recipient.

Super PACs are political committees that can raise unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, and unions to support or oppose candidates in U.S. elections. They can pay for advertisements and other political messages, but their spending must be independent: they cannot coordinate it with candidates’ campaigns or political party committees. Super PACs became prominent after the 2010 Supreme Court decision Citizens United v. FEC. That case began with a dispute over whether a conservative group could distribute Hillary: The Movie, a film about Hillary Clinton, near the 2008 presidential primaries. The Court ruled that restrictions on independent political spending by corporations violated the First Amendment’s protection of free speech. The ruling helped set the stage for Super PACs, which can spend unlimited amounts independently but cannot give unlimited funds directly to candidates.

John Roberts is a lawyer who became the 17th Chief Justice of the United States in 2005 after President George W. Bush nominated him. He led the Supreme Court during its 2022 decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, a case involving a Mississippi law that banned most abortions after 15 weeks of pregnancy. A draft of the decision was leaked about a month before the Court released its ruling. In the final decision, the Court overturned Roe v. Wade, ending the federal constitutional protection for abortion that Roe had established and allowing states to set their own abortion laws. Justice Samuel Alito, another Bush appointee, wrote the majority opinion. Roberts supported upholding Mississippi’s law but did not agree that the Court needed to overturn Roe entirely.

Edgar Daniel Nixon, often called E. D. Nixon, was an Alabama labor organizer and civil rights leader. He worked for decades as a Pullman porter, serving passengers on railroad sleeping cars, and helped organize workers through the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. As a leader of the local NAACP, he also fought racial segregation in Montgomery, Alabama. After Rosa Parks was arrested in December 1955 for refusing to give up her seat on a segregated bus, Nixon helped organize a citywide bus boycott. He and other activists formed the Montgomery Improvement Association to coordinate the protest and helped bring the young minister Martin Luther King Jr. into its leadership. King became the association’s first president, while Nixon’s organizing experience helped sustain the boycott.

J. Edgar Hoover led the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the U.S. government’s main domestic investigative agency, from 1924 until his death in 1972. During the Cold War and the civil rights movement, he oversaw COINTELPRO, short for Counter Intelligence Program. This secret FBI initiative ran from 1956 to 1971 and used surveillance, infiltration, and other disruptive tactics against groups the bureau considered “subversive,” including civil rights and antiwar activists. At the same time, the FBI largely neglected white supremacist violence in the 1950s and 1960s. When Martin Luther King Jr. criticized the bureau for failing to confront that violence, Hoover publicly called him the “most notorious liar” in America. Hoover’s record remains controversial because the FBI used its power to target people exercising their rights.

Cahokia was a major center of Mississippian culture near present-day St. Louis, along the Mississippi River. At its height, around 1100 CE, it was the largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico. Its residents farmed crops such as corn, beans, and squash, built neighborhoods and plazas, and raised enormous earthen mounds for important buildings and ceremonies. The most imposing was Monks Mound, a four-terraced platform mound that dominates Cahokia’s central precinct. It is the largest prehistoric earthen structure north of Mexico and was later named for monks who lived nearby. Cahokia also had circles of tall wooden posts, often called Woodhenge, that may have helped people mark the changing seasons. Together, these features show the scale and organization of this Indigenous city.

The Great White Fleet was a group of sixteen U.S. Navy battleships that sailed around the world from 1907 to 1909. The ships left Hampton Roads, Virginia, and visited ports across the globe. Their white-painted hulls and buff-colored funnels gave the fleet its name. President Theodore Roosevelt ordered the voyage to show that the United States had a powerful navy capable of operating far from home. It was part of his approach to foreign policy, often summed up as “speak softly and carry a big stick”: negotiate peacefully, but be ready to use military strength. Roosevelt, the 26th U.S. president and a former governor of New York, believed a strong navy would help the nation protect its interests and earn respect abroad.

In the 1876 United States presidential election, Democrat Samuel J. Tilden won the popular vote over Republican Rutherford B. Hayes, but disputed returns in several states left the Electoral College result uncertain. Congress created an electoral commission to review the contested votes. The commission awarded them to Hayes, giving him a narrow victory and the presidency. Democrats accepted the result under an informal agreement known as the Compromise of 1877. In return, Hayes’s administration withdrew the remaining federal troops from the South. Their departure effectively ended Reconstruction, the period after the Civil War when the federal government had worked to rebuild the South and protect the rights of formerly enslaved people. The election showed how a dispute over votes could have major consequences beyond deciding who became president.

The 2020 Democratic National Convention was a four-day gathering in August 2020 at which the Democratic Party formally nominated Joe Biden for president and Kamala Harris for vice president. It had been planned for Milwaukee, Wisconsin, but the COVID-19 pandemic forced organizers to hold a mostly virtual program, with speeches and appearances broadcast from around the country. Harris was then a U.S. senator from California; before joining the Senate, she had served as California’s attorney general and San Francisco’s district attorney. The convention also featured Americans speaking about their experiences, including teenager Brayden Harrington, who discussed overcoming his stutter. In a lighter moment during the state-by-state nomination roll call, a Rhode Island restaurant owner held up fried squid and praised a “Calamari Comeback.”

Lee Harvey Oswald was a former U.S. Marine who had once defected to the Soviet Union before returning to the United States. On November 22, 1963, President John F. Kennedy was shot while riding in a motorcade in Dallas, Texas. Oswald was arrested that day, and investigators accused him of firing the shots from the Texas School Book Depository, where he worked. He was also accused of killing a Dallas police officer, J. D. Tippit, shortly after the assassination. Oswald denied killing Kennedy and never stood trial. Two days later, on November 24, Dallas nightclub owner Jack Ruby shot Oswald in the basement of Dallas police headquarters as officers were transferring him to another jail. The shooting was shown on live television.

The Kingdom of Hawaii was an independent monarchy in the Pacific Ocean, established when Kamehameha I united the Hawaiian Islands. Its final ruler, Queen Liliʻuokalani, succeeded her brother, King Kalākaua, in 1891. She was also a composer associated with the song “Aloha ʻOe.” In 1893, a group of businessmen and politicians called the Committee of Safety, supported by U.S. troops, deposed her and ended the monarchy. Sanford Dole later led the new government. The United States annexed Hawaii in 1898 through the Newlands Resolution, but it did not immediately become a state. After decades as a U.S. territory, Hawaii entered the Union in 1959 as the 50th state.

Nancy Pelosi is a Democratic politician who represented the San Francisco area of California in the U.S. House of Representatives. After Democrats won control of the House in the 2006 midterm elections, House members elected her Speaker of the House in 2007. She succeeded Dennis Hastert and became the first woman to hold this powerful post, saying she had broken the “marble ceiling.” The Speaker is chosen by members of the House, the lower chamber of Congress, at the start of each Congress. The office ranks second in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president. Pelosi later led House Democrats during the passage of the Affordable Care Act. She also drew attention when she tore up her copy of President Donald Trump’s 2020 State of the Union speech.

Richard Henry Lee was a Virginia delegate who played a key role in the American Revolution. On June 7, 1776, he presented a motion to the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia declaring that the colonies “are, and of right ought to be, free and independent States.” John Adams seconded the motion. Known as the Lee Resolution, it led Congress to vote for independence on July 2. The Second Continental Congress also appointed the committee that drafted the Declaration of Independence, which explained the decision to break from Britain and was adopted on July 4. During the Revolutionary War, this same assembly acted as the colonies’ national government, directing the war effort and handling relations with other countries.

Tituba was an enslaved woman from Barbados who lived in Salem, Massachusetts, when a witchcraft panic began there in 1692. She was among the first people accused of witchcraft. Under pressure, she confessed and named others, and her testimony helped fuel the Salem witch trials. Arthur Miller made Tituba a character in his play The Crucible, which dramatizes the trials. In the play, Abigail Williams and other girls are discovered dancing in the forest; Abigail then makes accusations that help spread the panic. Miller wrote The Crucible as an allegory for the McCarthy era, when Americans were accused of being communists, often with little evidence. Tituba’s story shows how fear and pressure could turn an accusation into a wider crisis.

Manzanar War Relocation Center was a World War II incarceration camp in California’s Owens Valley, near the town of Independence. It began receiving Japanese Americans in March 1942, after the U.S. government ordered people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast to leave their homes. Manzanar was one of ten federal camps where they were forcibly confined, even though many were U.S. citizens. Families lived in crowded barracks and tried to build daily routines despite losing their freedom. In 1943, photographer Ansel Adams visited Manzanar and made portraits of incarcerated people and photographs of camp life. He published many of these images in his 1944 book Born Free and Equal. Photographer Dorothea Lange also documented the wartime removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans.

Casey Jones was an Illinois Central Railroad engineer who became an American folk hero after a train wreck in 1900. He was driving a southbound passenger train nicknamed the Cannonball when it approached Vaughan, Mississippi, a community near Canton. A freight train had not fully cleared the main track, and Jones’s train collided with it. Accounts say he stayed at the controls, sounded the whistle, and applied the brakes instead of jumping to safety. Jones was killed, but his actions are credited with helping spare his passengers. The wreck inspired a famous American ballad, “The Ballad of Casey Jones,” which helped turn the railroad engineer into a lasting symbol of courage during the age of steam trains.

Minnesota is a state in the Upper Midwest known for its many lakes and for the Mississippi River, which begins at Lake Itasca. Its largest city, Minneapolis, became the focus of worldwide attention in May 2020 when George Floyd, a Black man, died during an arrest. Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin pinned Floyd to the pavement with his knee while Floyd repeatedly said, “I can’t breathe.” Chauvin was later convicted of murder. Video of Floyd’s death led to protests across the United States and around the world against police violence and racial injustice. Minnesota governor Tim Walz called for a period of silence to honor Floyd. These events made Minneapolis and Minnesota central to a major moment in the history of American civil rights.

Liz Cheney is a Republican politician who represented Wyoming’s at-large congressional district in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2017 to 2023. In 2019, fellow Republicans elected her to succeed Cathy McMorris Rodgers as chair of the House Republican Conference, making her the party’s third-ranking leader in the House. Cheney became a prominent critic of President Donald Trump after the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. She supported Trump’s second impeachment, arguing that he bore responsibility for the attack. House Republicans removed her as conference chair in May 2021 because of her continued criticism of Trump. Cheney later served alongside Adam Kinzinger as one of only two Republicans on the House committee investigating the January 6 attack.

James G. Blaine was a leading Republican politician from Maine during the late 1800s. He served in the U.S. House of Representatives, became Speaker of the House, and later served as secretary of state. In 1884, Republicans chose Blaine as their presidential nominee. His opponent was Grover Cleveland, a Democrat who had served as governor of New York. Both campaigns faced controversy: Blaine was criticized over allegations of political corruption, while Cleveland faced questions about his personal life. Cleveland narrowly won the election. After losing to Benjamin Harrison in 1888, Cleveland won the presidency again in 1892, making him the only U.S. president to serve two nonconsecutive terms. Blaine’s 1884 defeat is a key link between these two major political figures of the Gilded Age.

John White was an English artist and colonial governor who led a group of settlers to Roanoke Island, in present-day North Carolina, in 1587. The colony was part of an English effort sponsored by Sir Walter Raleigh, and it received help from Manteo, a local Indigenous leader. White’s granddaughter Virginia Dare was born there and is often described as the first English child born in the New World. White sailed back to England for supplies, but war delayed his return until 1590. When he reached Roanoke, the settlers had vanished. He found “CROATOAN” carved nearby, possibly pointing to an island associated with the Croatoan people. No one knows for certain what happened to the settlers, so Roanoke became known as the “Lost Colony.”

The Kitchen Debate was a televised Cold War exchange in Moscow in 1959 between U.S. vice president Richard Nixon and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev. It took place at an American exhibition inside a furnished model home, where the two men stood near a modern kitchen. Nixon pointed to American household goods as examples of what capitalism could provide for ordinary people. Khrushchev defended communism and argued that the Soviet Union could match or surpass the United States. Their lively discussion showed how the two countries competed not only through military power but also by claiming their way of life was better. Khrushchev was first secretary of the Soviet Communist Party and later led the USSR during the Cuban Missile Crisis. Nixon later became U.S. president.

Browder v. Gayle was the federal court case that ended legally enforced segregation on Montgomery, Alabama’s city buses. In 1955, Rosa Parks’s arrest for refusing to give up her seat helped spark the Montgomery bus boycott. Black residents walked or organized carpools while demanding bus desegregation. Instead of relying only on the boycott, five African American women challenged the bus rules in court. One plaintiff was Claudette Colvin, a 15-year-old student who had been arrested in March 1955 after refusing to give up her bus seat, months before Parks’s arrest. In 1956, a three-judge federal panel ruled that Alabama and Montgomery laws requiring separate seating for Black and white passengers violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of equal protection. The U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the ruling, bringing legal segregation on Montgomery’s buses to an end.

James Madison was a Virginia delegate to the Constitutional Convention in 1787 and a principal author of the Virginia Plan, which proposed a stronger national government. His ideas helped shape the Constitution of the United States, the charter whose seven articles set up the federal government, including its legislative, executive, and judicial branches. This work earned him the nickname “Father of the Constitution.” To persuade states to ratify it, Madison joined Alexander Hamilton and John Jay in writing The Federalist Papers under the shared pen name Publius. Madison later served as secretary of state under President Thomas Jefferson. In 1809, he became the fourth president of the United States.

The Homestead Strike was a major labor conflict in July 1892 at Carnegie Steel’s Homestead Works near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Workers were resisting wage cuts and a lockout ordered by company executive Henry Clay Frick. When armed Pinkerton agents arrived by river to take control of the plant, they clashed violently with striking steelworkers and local residents. Several people died, and the Pennsylvania state militia was later sent in to secure the works. During the dispute, anarchist Alexander Berkman shot and stabbed Frick in his Pittsburgh office. Frick survived, and Berkman’s attack was not organized by the workers’ union. The strike ended in defeat for the workers, weakening the union at Homestead and showing how fiercely companies and workers fought over wages and workplace power during the Gilded Age.

Gibbons v. Ogden was an 1824 Supreme Court case about competing steamboat services between New York and New Jersey. New York had granted an exclusive right to operate steamboats in its waters. Aaron Ogden, a former New Jersey governor, operated under that privilege and sued to stop Thomas Gibbons, whose boats ran under a federal coasting license. The dispute asked whether a state monopoly could block a vessel licensed by the federal government to travel between states. Chief Justice John Marshall’s Court ruled for Gibbons, holding that navigation was part of interstate commerce, which Congress had the power to regulate under the Constitution’s Commerce Clause. The decision struck down the New York monopoly where it conflicted with federal law and strengthened the federal government’s authority over trade between states.

Crispus Attucks was a dockworker of African and Native American descent who became the first person killed in the Boston Massacre. On March 5, 1770, tensions between colonists and British troops erupted on King Street in Boston, the capital of colonial Massachusetts. British soldiers fired into a crowd, killing Attucks and four other people. The shooting became known as the Boston Massacre, although it was also called the Incident on King Street. It intensified colonial anger toward British rule in the years before the American Revolution. Paul Revere made an engraving of the event that helped spread news of it, though his image was not a fully accurate account. Attucks is remembered as an early symbol of resistance to British authority.

At noon on September 16, 1920, a horse-drawn wagon packed with explosives blew up outside J.P. Morgan & Co.’s headquarters in Manhattan’s financial district. The attack, known as the Wall Street bombing of 1920, killed 38 people, injured hundreds, and spread fear during a period of intense concern about political violence. Investigators suspected followers of Luigi Galleani, an Italian-born anarchist who had urged revolution and promoted violence through his newspaper, Cronaca Sovversiva. U.S. authorities had deported Galleani in 1919, but his supporters remained active. No one was convicted of the bombing, so responsibility has never been proved. The attack occurred amid the same tensions that surrounded the arrests of Italian-American anarchists Sacco and Vanzetti earlier in 1920.

The Cuban Missile Crisis was a 13-day Cold War standoff in October 1962 that brought the United States and the Soviet Union dangerously close to nuclear war. U.S. surveillance photographs revealed that the Soviet Union was building nuclear missile sites in Cuba, just 90 miles from Florida. President John F. Kennedy announced a naval “quarantine” of Cuba in a televised address on October 22 to prevent more Soviet weapons from arriving. Kennedy and Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev then worked toward a settlement, while Kennedy’s younger brother Robert, the U.S. attorney general, served as a key adviser. The crisis ended when the Soviet Union agreed to remove its missiles from Cuba and the United States pledged not to invade the island.

James Bowie was a Kentucky-born American frontiersman who later joined the Texas Revolution against Mexico. He became nationally famous after surviving the Sandbar Fight, a bloody 1827 clash near Natchez, Mississippi. What began as a duel between two other men turned into a larger fight involving gunfire and knife attacks. Stories about Bowie’s skill with a large, fixed-blade knife helped build his frontier reputation, and that type of weapon became known as the Bowie knife. In 1836, Bowie helped defend the Alamo Mission in San Antonio while Mexican forces under General Santa Anna besieged it. Bowie died when the Alamo fell, along with fellow defenders William Travis and Davy Crockett.

Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University to found Theranos, a Silicon Valley health technology company, in 2003. As its chief executive and public face, she promised that the company’s Edison device could run many medical tests using only a few drops of blood from a finger prick. That claim attracted investors and helped Theranos pursue a major partnership with the pharmacy chain Walgreens, which planned to offer its testing services in stores. Investigations later showed that Theranos’s technology could not reliably do what Holmes claimed; the company often relied on conventional testing equipment instead. Theranos shut down in 2018, and Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors in 2022. Her story shows why medical claims need careful testing and why investors and patients need accurate information.

Elizabeth Peratrovich was a Tlingit civil rights activist who challenged discrimination against Alaska Native people. She and her husband, Roy, were leaders in the Alaska Native Sisterhood and Brotherhood. At the time, Alaska was a U.S. territory, and Native people could be turned away from restaurants, theaters, and other businesses open to the public. In 1945, Peratrovich spoke before Alaska’s territorial legislature in support of a bill to ban this kind of racial discrimination. Her testimony challenged lawmakers to recognize that Native Alaskans deserved the same treatment as other citizens, and it is widely credited with helping the bill pass. The resulting Alaska Anti-Discrimination Act prohibited race-based exclusion from public businesses, making it a landmark civil rights law years before Alaska became a state.

Osama bin Laden was a Saudi-born militant who founded al-Qaeda, a terrorist organization, and led it for many years. Al-Qaeda carried out the September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States, killing nearly 3,000 people. Bin Laden became one of the world’s most wanted fugitives, and the U.S. searched for him for nearly a decade. By 2011, he was living in a compound in Abbottabad, a city in Pakistan. In May of that year, U.S. Navy SEALs raided the compound and killed him. President Barack Obama, the 44th president of the United States, ordered the operation. Bin Laden’s death was a major moment in the U.S. campaign against al-Qaeda, though the organization continued to exist.

After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941, fear and prejudice led the U.S. government to forcibly remove more than 100,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast. Most were U.S. citizens, and they were confined in camps such as Manzanar and Tule Lake. This wartime policy is called Japanese American internment. In 1944, the Supreme Court decided Korematsu v. United States, upholding the conviction of Fred Korematsu, a California-born U.S. citizen who had refused to obey a military order excluding Japanese Americans from his area. Unlike earlier wartime cases that considered curfews, Korematsu directly reviewed an exclusion order. The ruling is now widely condemned as a violation of civil liberties driven by racial discrimination rather than evidence of individual wrongdoing.

Zachary Taylor was a career Army officer who became the 12th president of the United States. He served in the Second Seminole War, a conflict in Florida between U.S. forces and the Seminole people, a Native American group that had split from the Creek. Taylor commanded U.S. troops at the Battle of Lake Okeechobee in 1837. After the war, the United States forced many Seminoles to move, while some remained in the Everglades. Taylor later led American troops in the Mexican-American War, winning battles at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma in 1846. His reputation as a tough, practical commander helped earn him the nickname “Old Rough and Ready.” His military fame helped him win the presidential election of 1848.

Stuart v. Laird was an 1803 Supreme Court case decided shortly after Marbury v. Madison. Both cases grew out of disputes over changes to the federal courts during the early republic. The Judiciary Act of 1801 had created new judgeships and reduced the need for Supreme Court justices to sit on lower courts. Congress repealed much of that law in 1802, and a party in Stuart v. Laird challenged the restored requirement that justices travel to assigned regions to hear cases in federal circuit courts. This practice was called circuit riding. The Supreme Court upheld it, finding that Congress could organize the lower federal courts this way. While Marbury v. Madison is famous for establishing judicial review, Stuart v. Laird confirmed the constitutionality of circuit riding.

Tammany Hall began as a social club in New York City but became a powerful organization within the Democratic Party. One of its early leaders, Aaron Burr, helped turn it into a political machine: a group that organized voters and used its influence to win elections and gain government jobs. Burr later served as vice president under Thomas Jefferson and fatally shot Alexander Hamilton in a duel. During the 1800s, Tammany Hall became a major force in New York City and state politics. Its leaders held the title “Grand Sachem.” The organization helped candidates win office, including the New York City mayoralty, partly by providing assistance to immigrants and other voters. It also became notorious for corruption, especially under its most infamous leader, William “Boss” Tweed.

A Yankee is traditionally a person from New England and, more broadly, someone from the northern United States, especially when contrasted with a Southerner. The term became particularly useful for describing regional differences during and after the Civil War. In his essay “The Sahara of the Bozart,” H. L. Mencken criticized the South’s cultural achievements after its defeat and repeatedly contrasted Southerners with Yankees. The word also appears in the title of Mark Twain’s novel A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court. Its main character, Hank Morgan, is a Yankee who is transported back in time to King Arthur’s Britain. He uses his knowledge of modern technology to gain influence there and has a daughter named Hello Central.

Richard J. Daley was the Democratic mayor of Chicago from 1955 until his death in 1976. He led a powerful political organization that helped elect Democrats in Chicago and gave him influence in national politics. In the 1960 United States presidential election, Democrat John F. Kennedy narrowly defeated Republican Richard Nixon. Illinois was an important state in that close contest, and Nixon supporters accused Daley’s organization of manipulating Chicago votes to help Kennedy win it. The accusations became a lasting part of the story of the election, though they did not establish that Daley changed the national result. Nixon declined to challenge the election outcome. Daley remained a major figure in the Democratic Party for years afterward.

William Bradford was a leader of the Pilgrims, a group of English Separatists who sought freedom to practice their religion. After living in Leiden in the Netherlands, they crossed the Atlantic on the Mayflower in 1620. The ship was meant to reach Virginia but landed farther north, where its passengers founded Plymouth Colony. Bradford helped lead the new settlement and, after the death of its first governor, John Carver, became Plymouth’s longtime governor. Beginning in 1630, Bradford wrote Of Plymouth Plantation, a history of the Separatists’ departure from Leiden, their voyage, and the colony’s difficult early years. His account is one of the most important firsthand sources for understanding the Pilgrims and Plymouth Colony.

The Pentagon Papers were a classified U.S. Department of Defense study commissioned by Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara. They traced American involvement in Vietnam from 1945 to 1967 and showed that government officials had misled the public about the Vietnam War. Daniel Ellsberg, who had worked on the study, leaked it to newspapers, and The New York Times began publishing excerpts in 1971. President Richard Nixon’s administration tried to stop publication, arguing that releasing the documents would threaten national security. This was an attempt at prior restraint, meaning the government wanted to block information before it appeared in print. In New York Times Co. v. United States, the Supreme Court rejected the government’s attempt to block publication, making the case an important example of press freedom.

The Centennial Olympic Park bombing occurred during the 1996 Summer Olympics in Atlanta, Georgia. Centennial Olympic Park was a downtown gathering place where spectators watched events and celebrated. Late on July 27, a bomb planted there exploded, killing spectator Alice Hawthorne and injuring more than 100 people. Investigators later identified Eric Rudolph as the bomber. He also carried out other bombings in the southeastern United States and then hid in the Appalachian wilderness for more than five years. A police officer arrested him in Murphy, North Carolina, in 2003. The attack is commonly called the Centennial Olympic Park bombing because it took place in the park during the Olympic Games.

Common Sense was a widely read pamphlet published in January 1776 by Thomas Paine, an English-born political writer living in the American colonies. Paine urged the colonies to separate from Britain rather than seek a compromise with the king. He argued that it made no sense for a large continent to be ruled by a small island and that hereditary monarchy was irrational: a ruler should not gain power simply by being born into a royal family. Written in direct, accessible language, Common Sense helped persuade many colonists to support independence. Later that year, the United States declared independence. Paine also wrote the pamphlet series The American Crisis to encourage Americans during the Revolution. Its famous opening line is “These are the times that try men’s souls.”

James K. Polk, a Tennessee Democrat, was the 11th president of the United States, serving from 1845 to 1849. Known as the first “dark horse” president because he was an unexpected presidential nominee, he pursued an expansionist agenda. His campaign was associated with the slogan “Fifty-Four Forty or Fight,” referring to a proposed northern boundary for U.S. territory in Oregon. Rather than fight Britain over Oregon, Polk’s administration settled the boundary dispute through negotiation. The United States also fought the Mexican-American War during his presidency, from 1846 to 1848. Although President Polk recalled diplomat Nicholas Trist, Trist continued negotiating the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. That agreement formally ended the war and transferred California and much of the present-day Southwest from Mexico to the United States.

Tecumseh was a Shawnee leader who worked to unite Native nations in the Old Northwest, a region around the Great Lakes, to resist U.S. expansion into their lands. He believed that Native peoples could better defend their territory by acting together rather than making separate agreements with the United States. During the War of 1812, Tecumseh’s confederacy allied with Britain against U.S. forces. In 1813, an American naval victory at the Battle of Lake Erie, led by Oliver Hazard Perry, allowed U.S. forces to recapture Detroit and pursue the British and their Indigenous allies into present-day Ontario. Tecumseh was killed near Moraviantown at the Battle of the Thames, where the Americans won. His death weakened and effectively ended the confederacy he had built.

The XYZ Affair was a diplomatic crisis between the United States and France in 1797–1798. President John Adams sent Charles Cotesworth Pinckney, John Marshall, and Elbridge Gerry to France to resolve disputes over French attacks on American ships. Instead of meeting directly with France’s foreign minister, Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand, the envoys encountered intermediaries who said they must first arrange a loan to France and make a private payment. Talleyrand was a former bishop and a prominent diplomat under France’s Directory government. When the envoys’ reports became public, the intermediaries were identified only as X, Y, and Z, giving the affair its name. Many Americans were outraged by the demands, and tensions escalated into the Quasi-War, an undeclared naval conflict between the two countries.

Reconstruction was the period after the U.S. Civil War, generally dated from 1865 to 1877, when the federal government worked to rebuild the South and define the rights of formerly enslaved people. Federal troops remained in the South while Southern states formed new governments, and constitutional amendments ended slavery, established citizenship and equal protection under the law, and protected Black men’s voting rights. Congress also created the Freedmen’s Bureau, a federal agency that provided relief to formerly enslaved people and other refugees. It helped people obtain food and medical care, supported schools, offered legal assistance, and helped with labor contracts. Reconstruction brought important changes, but many white Southerners resisted Black equality, and its end in 1877 left many of those rights vulnerable.

Blackwater was an American private military company founded in 1997 by Erik Prince, a former U.S. Navy SEAL and the brother of former education secretary Betsy DeVos. It operated a major training facility in North Carolina and provided security services to the U.S. government, including during the Iraq War. Private military companies employ civilians to carry out work connected to military operations, raising questions about oversight and accountability. Blackwater drew international scrutiny in 2007 when its personnel fired on people at Baghdad’s Nisour Square, killing 17 Iraqi civilians. The incident became a prominent example in debates about the use of private contractors in war. Blackwater later operated under other names, including Xe Services and Academi.

The American Civil Liberties Union, or ACLU, is a U.S. nonprofit organization founded in 1920. It grew out of the Civil Liberties Bureau, a World War I-era group that defended conscientious objectors—people who refused military service because of their beliefs. The ACLU uses lawsuits and public advocacy to protect constitutional rights and civil liberties, including free speech and due process, the right to fair legal procedures. One of its founding members was Helen Keller, an Alabama-born writer and activist. Keller lost both her sight and hearing after an illness when she was very young. With the help of her teacher Anne Sullivan, she learned ways to communicate and later described her education in her autobiography, The Story of My Life.

The Big Dig was a major transportation project in Boston, the capital of Massachusetts. Its main goal was to move the elevated Central Artery, a busy section of Interstate 93, into tunnels beneath the city. The project also built roads and bridges to improve travel through downtown Boston. One important addition was a new crossing under Boston Harbor between South Boston and Logan International Airport. That crossing is the Ted Williams Tunnel, named for the celebrated Boston Red Sox hitter who wore number 9. Construction lasted for many years and cost far more than originally planned, making the Big Dig one of the largest and most debated highway projects in U.S. history. It also allowed the old elevated highway to be replaced with parks and open space.

Henry Ward Beecher was a famous 19th-century American Congregationalist minister and a leading opponent of slavery. As pastor of Plymouth Church in Brooklyn, New York, he used his widely heard sermons to argue that slavery was morally wrong. During the violent struggle over whether Kansas would enter the United States as a free or slave state, Beecher and his supporters helped provide weapons to anti-slavery fighters, including John Brown. The weapons were Sharps rifles, breech-loading firearms that could be reloaded more quickly than many older guns. They became known as “Beecher’s Bibles,” a nickname linking the preacher’s religious work to his support for armed resistance to slavery. Brown later became famous for his 1859 raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry.

Lynching is an extrajudicial killing: a person is killed without a trial or lawful sentence, often by a mob. In the United States, lynchings were used especially to terrorize African Americans and enforce racial inequality. Many victims were hanged, sometimes before crowds, and perpetrators were often not punished. Writers and artists drew attention to this violence. Jamaican-born poet Claude McKay wrote “The Lynching,” describing “little lads” who “danced round the dreadful thing in fiendish glee.” He also wrote “If We Must Die,” which begins, “If we must die, let it not be like hogs.” McKay became prominent during the Harlem Renaissance, a 1920s flowering of African American art and literature named for a New York City neighborhood.

Charles Curtis was a Kansas politician of Kaw, Osage, Potawatomi, and French-American ancestry. He served in both houses of Congress, became Senate majority leader, and then served as vice president under President Herbert Hoover from 1929 to 1933. He was the first U.S. vice president with Native American ancestry. Curtis’s career also shows the complexities of federal policy toward Indigenous peoples: an act bearing his name helped break up tribal landholdings, although he objected to the bill’s final version. While serving in Congress, Curtis introduced the first version of the Equal Rights Amendment, or ERA, a proposed change to the Constitution intended to guarantee equal legal rights regardless of sex. Congress approved the ERA in the 1970s, but it did not gain the required ratification by the states.

The Goliad Massacre was the execution of several hundred Texian prisoners by Mexican soldiers during the Texas Revolution. In March 1836, Colonel James Fannin’s troops were defeated at the Battle of Coleto Creek and surrendered near Goliad, Texas. The prisoners were held at Presidio La Bahía, a former Spanish fort. On March 27, acting on orders from Mexican general and president Antonio López de Santa Anna, soldiers marched many of the captives away and shot them. Fannin was also executed. The massacre happened about three weeks after Santa Anna’s forces defeated Texian defenders at the Alamo in San Antonio. Both events became powerful symbols for the Texians, who rallied with the cries “Remember the Alamo!” and “Remember Goliad!”

Peggy Eaton, born Margaret O’Neill, became the center of a political and social controversy during Andrew Jackson’s presidency. She first married Navy purser John B. Timberlake. After his death, she married John Henry Eaton, a U.S. senator whom Jackson appointed Secretary of War. Rumors about Peggy’s earlier relationship with Eaton led many wives of Jackson’s officials to refuse to socialize with her. Floride Calhoun, the wife of Vice President John C. Calhoun, was among those who ostracized her. Jackson defended Peggy, and the dispute, called the Petticoat Affair, deepened divisions within his administration. As relations with some official advisers worsened, Jackson increasingly turned to a separate, informal circle that included Francis Preston Blair and Martin Van Buren. This group became known as the Kitchen Cabinet.

The Communist Party USA was founded in 1919 after a split from the Socialist Party of America. It promoted Marxist-Leninist ideas, including a society in which workers would control the economy. During the Cold War, fear of Soviet influence fueled a Red Scare in the United States, and party members faced federal investigations and prosecutions. Prosecutors used the Smith Act, a 1940 law that banned advocating the violent overthrow of the U.S. government, to charge party leaders with conspiring to promote such an overthrow. The Supreme Court upheld their convictions in Dennis v. United States. The era’s suspicion also shaped literature: in Philip Roth’s novel I Married a Communist, actor Ira Ringold belongs to the Communist Party, and his marriage to Eve Frame becomes part of a story about political accusation and betrayal.

Illinois is a Midwestern state whose largest city, Chicago, was the setting for major events in U.S. history. In 1871, the Great Chicago Fire destroyed much of the city; a popular but unproven story blamed Mrs. O’Leary’s cow. Jane Addams later founded Hull House there to help immigrants and poor families. Chicago also hosted the 1893 World’s Fair, whose grounds were designed by architect Daniel Burnham. The city was a center of labor activism. At an 1886 gathering supporting workers seeking an eight-hour workday, a bomb exploded as police moved to disperse the crowd. The violence became known as the Haymarket Affair, and a controversial trial led to the execution of August Spies and several other defendants. The Pullman Strike, led by Eugene Debs and the American Railway Union, also took place in Illinois.

Charles Lindbergh was an American aviator, or pilot, who became famous in May 1927 when he flew alone and nonstop from New York to Paris. He was the first person to complete that solo flight, crossing the Atlantic Ocean in a custom-built, single-engine monoplane called the Spirit of St. Louis. The achievement made him an international celebrity and showed how much long-distance aviation had advanced. Five years later, in 1932, Lindbergh’s infant son was abducted from the family’s home in New Jersey. The child was later found dead, and the kidnapping became known as the “Crime of the Century” because it drew enormous public attention. Bruno Hauptmann was convicted of the crime. Lindbergh is remembered both for his historic flight and for the tragedy that followed it.

Gold is a yellow precious metal with the chemical symbol Au and atomic number 79. In the late 1800s, it was central to debates about money in the United States. In 1869, during President Ulysses S. Grant’s administration, speculators Jay Gould and James Fisk tried to “corner” the gold market by buying enough gold to control its price. Their scheme collapsed, causing a financial panic known as Black Friday. Later, Americans argued over the gold standard, which tied the value of money to gold. At the 1896 Democratic National Convention, William Jennings Bryan opposed relying on gold alone and called for “free silver,” which would allow more silver to be used as money. His dramatic address became known as the Cross of Gold speech and helped win him the party’s presidential nomination.

The Iroquois Confederacy, also known as the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, is an alliance of Indigenous nations centered in what is now New York State. Its original five nations were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca; the Tuscarora joined later, making it a six-nation confederacy. Its governing principles come from the Great Law of Peace, a political tradition that helped the nations resolve disputes and make collective decisions while preserving each nation’s identity. In the story of the confederacy’s founding, weapons were buried beneath a white pine to symbolize an end to fighting among the member nations. The alliance remained important during colonial America. At the Boston Tea Party, members of the Sons of Liberty disguised themselves as Mohawks, though they were protesting British policies, not acting on behalf of the confederacy.

William Frederick “Buffalo Bill” Cody was a former bison hunter and Pony Express rider who became one of the most famous showmen of the 1800s. His traveling show, Buffalo Bill’s Wild West, used horseback riding, shooting demonstrations, and staged frontier scenes to entertain audiences across the United States and abroad. Its performers included Sitting Bull, Calamity Jane, and sharpshooter Annie Oakley. Oakley amazed crowds with her accuracy; one famous trick involved shooting a smoking cigar from the mouth of her husband, Frank Butler. Cody’s show helped shape how people around the world imagined the American West, although its theatrical scenes did not always reflect the full reality of frontier life.

Worcester v. Georgia was an 1832 Supreme Court case about whether the state of Georgia could enforce its laws in Cherokee territory. Georgia required white missionaries living there to obtain a state license, and missionary Samuel Worcester was convicted for refusing to do so. Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the Court’s majority opinion, which held that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct political community and that Georgia’s laws had no force within its territory. The decision recognized limits on state power over Native American nations, but it did not stop the later forced removal of the Cherokee people. Marshall had also written the opinion in Marbury v. Madison, the case that established the Supreme Court’s power of judicial review.

William Dudley “Big Bill” Haywood was a former miner who became a leading labor organizer in the American West during the early 1900s. He headed the Western Federation of Miners, a union that fought for better pay, hours, and working conditions, and helped found the Industrial Workers of the World, which sought to unite workers across different industries. Haywood was tried in connection with the assassination of former Idaho governor Frank Steunenberg but was acquitted. The Western Federation of Miners helped lead a major strike in the Cripple Creek mining district of Colorado. Years later, Colorado was also the site of the Ludlow Massacre, when a violent confrontation during a coal miners’ strike killed workers’ family members and others.

Military veterans are people who have served in the armed forces. Some face lasting health problems linked to their service, including mental-health conditions and illnesses caused by toxic exposure. The Brandon Act, sponsored by Senator Mark Kelly, aims to make it easier for service members to seek mental-health evaluations and support. Another law, the 2022 PACT Act, expanded Department of Veterans Affairs healthcare and benefits for veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxic hazards. Burn pits were used to dispose of waste at some military sites, and their smoke could contain harmful chemicals. Comedian and veterans’ advocate Jon Stewart publicly urged Congress to pass the PACT Act. Together, these laws show how the federal government has sought to address health needs connected to military service.

Eugene V. Debs was an Indiana-born labor organizer who became one of the best-known American socialists of the early 1900s. He led the American Railway Union during the Pullman Strike of 1894, a major conflict between railroad workers and their employers. Debs later joined the Socialist Party of America, which argued that workers should have more power in the economy and government. The party nominated him for president five times and elected Victor Berger as its first member of Congress. In 1912, former Milwaukee mayor Emil Seidel was Debs’s running mate. Debs was imprisoned for speaking against U.S. participation in World War I, but he still ran for president in 1920. That campaign, his fifth and last, was conducted from prison.

Joseph Warren was a Boston physician who became a leader of the movement against British rule before the American Revolution. He helped organize colonial resistance in Massachusetts and was appointed a major general in June 1775, shortly before British troops attacked American positions on the Charlestown peninsula overlooking Boston. Rather than direct the fighting from a safer location, Warren took up a musket and fought alongside ordinary colonial soldiers. He was killed during the battle, as British forces finally took the defenders’ position after repeated assaults. The fighting took place mainly on Breed’s Hill, but the battle is conventionally called the Battle of Bunker Hill. Warren’s death made him an early symbol of sacrifice for the American cause.

On April 9, 1865, Confederate general Robert E. Lee surrendered his Army of Northern Virginia to Union general Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox Court House, a Virginia village. The event is known as the Surrender at Appomattox Court House. Grant offered terms that allowed Confederate soldiers to return home on parole, meaning they could go home if they promised not to fight again. He also let them keep their horses for spring planting. Other Confederate forces surrendered later, but Lee’s surrender ended organized resistance by his army and is widely regarded as effectively ending the Civil War. Grant had earlier led the Union campaign that captured Vicksburg, Mississippi, a major victory that gave the Union control of the Mississippi River. He later became president of the United States.

Los Angeles is California’s most populous city and a major center of the film industry. It was also the site of two major episodes of unrest linked to police treatment of Black residents. In 1965, the arrest of Marquette Frye after a traffic stop helped spark the Watts uprising, which lasted several days. In 1991, Los Angeles police officers beat a Black motorist named Rodney King after a traffic stop. Video of the beating was shown around the world. When four officers were acquitted of assault charges in 1992, protests and unrest broke out in Los Angeles and spread to nearby communities. As the violence continued, King publicly appealed for peace, asking, “Can we all get along?”

Michael Cohen is a former New York lawyer who served for years as Donald Trump’s personal attorney. In 2017, he was named a deputy finance chairman of the Republican National Committee. Cohen later became involved in federal investigations connected to Trump and pleaded guilty to several crimes, including lying to Congress. His false statement concerned discussions about a proposed Trump Tower in Moscow, Russia, during the 2016 presidential campaign. Plans for the building included the possibility of a penthouse for Russian president Vladimir Putin. Cohen had told Congress that work on the Moscow project ended earlier than it actually did. He was later disbarred, meaning he lost his license to practice law.

Thomas Gage was a British general and royal governor of Massachusetts whose decisions helped bring on the American Revolution. In April 1775, he ordered British troops to march from Boston to Concord to seize colonial military supplies. The expedition led to fighting at Lexington and Concord, the opening battles of the war. In June, while Gage commanded British forces in Massachusetts, troops led by William Howe repeatedly attacked colonial positions on high ground in Charlestown. The fighting became known as the Battle of Bunker Hill, named for a nearby Boston landmark. The British won the position but suffered heavy casualties. After the battle, Howe replaced Gage as British commander.

Obergefell v. Hodges was a 2015 U.S. Supreme Court decision that established a constitutional right for same-sex couples to marry. Before the ruling, some states allowed these marriages while others refused to issue marriage licenses or recognize marriages performed elsewhere. In a 5–4 decision, the Court held that states must both license marriages between same-sex couples and recognize their lawful marriages from other states. Justice Anthony Kennedy wrote the majority opinion, reasoning that the Constitution’s guarantees of liberty and equal protection apply to same-sex couples. Kennedy had also written the Court’s opinions in three earlier cases involving LGBTQ+ rights: Romer v. Evans, Lawrence v. Texas, and United States v. Windsor. The Obergefell ruling made marriage equality the law throughout the United States.

The United States presidential election of 1824 had four major candidates from the Democratic-Republican Party: Andrew Jackson, John Quincy Adams, William Crawford, and Henry Clay. Jackson won the most popular and electoral votes, but no candidate won more than half the electoral votes, so the House of Representatives had to choose the president. Clay, a Kentucky politician and Speaker of the House, finished fourth in electoral votes and was eliminated from the House decision. He supported Adams, and the House chose Adams over Jackson. When Adams later appointed Clay secretary of state, Jackson’s supporters accused them of making a “corrupt bargain”: they believed Clay had traded his support for the appointment. The accusation helped deepen political divisions in the early republic.

Greg Abbott is a Republican politician and lawyer who has served as governor of Texas since 2015. Before becoming governor, he served on the Texas Supreme Court and as the state’s attorney general. While working in the attorney general’s office, he argued for Texas in the 2005 U.S. Supreme Court case Van Orden v. Perry. The Court ruled that a Ten Commandments monument could remain on the grounds of the Texas Capitol. As governor, Abbott faced criticism after severe ice storms in February 2021 caused widespread power outages, raising questions about oversight of Texas’s electric grid. He also led the state during the aftermath of the 2022 shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, when his Democratic election challenger, Beto O’Rourke, interrupted one of his press conferences.

Chinese Americans are people of Chinese ancestry living in the United States. In the 1860s, thousands of immigrants from Guangdong worked for the Central Pacific Railroad, doing dangerous jobs such as blasting tunnels through the Sierra Nevada. Their labor helped complete the first transcontinental railroad in 1869. Despite this contribution, Chinese workers faced low pay, discrimination, and violence, including an 1885 attack on Chinese coal miners in Rock Springs, Wyoming. Anti-Chinese prejudice also became federal policy. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, signed by President Chester A. Arthur, suspended the immigration of Chinese laborers and barred Chinese immigrants from becoming naturalized U.S. citizens. These restrictions separated families and shaped Chinese American communities for generations.

The Homestead Act was a federal law passed in 1862, during the Civil War, to encourage settlement of public land, especially in the American West. An eligible settler could claim up to 160 acres by living on the land and improving it, often by building a home and farming, for five years. After meeting the requirements, the settler could gain ownership of the claim. This way of life was called homesteading and often involved growing food and doing much of the work needed to support a household. The law helped many families establish farms, but the land made available to settlers was often land that Native Americans had lived on and used for generations.

Reparations are compensation or other measures intended to address serious historical injustices. In the United States, calls for reparations often focus on the enslavement of Black Americans and the discrimination that continued after slavery ended, including laws and practices that restricted where people could live, work, and build wealth. Proposed reparations may include direct payments, investments in affected communities, or other actions meant to repair lasting harm. Supporters argue that these harms still affect families today; debates continue over what form reparations should take and who should provide them. In 2014, journalist Ta-Nehisi Coates published an influential essay in The Atlantic titled “The Case for Reparations.” It helped bring the debate to a wider audience by explaining how slavery and later discrimination contributed to inequalities that persist today.

The Green Mountain Boys were a militia formed in the New Hampshire Grants, a disputed region that later became Vermont. Led by Ethan Allen, they first resisted New York authorities who tried to enforce land claims and remove settlers from the area. After the American Revolution began, the militia turned its attention to British forces. In May 1775, Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys, working with Benedict Arnold, captured Fort Ticonderoga, a British post at the southern end of Lake Champlain. The fort fell with little fighting, giving the Americans a valuable supply of cannons and other weapons. Months later, artillery from Ticonderoga was transported to positions overlooking Boston, helping force British troops to leave the city.

Joseph Brant, known in Mohawk as Thayendanegea, was a Mohawk leader and British military officer during the American Revolution. Educated at Moor’s Indian Charity School, he helped lead warriors from the Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois Confederacy, who allied with Britain. The confederacy’s six nations did not all choose the same side: many Oneida and Tuscarora supported the Americans. After Britain’s defeat, Brant led Mohawk Loyalists to land along the Grand River in what is now Ontario, where they established a new community. Near present-day Brantford, they built an Anglican church in 1785 called the Mohawk Chapel. It later received royal-chapel status. Brant’s life shows how the Revolution divided Indigenous nations and forced many people to rebuild their communities after the war.

Michelle Obama is an American lawyer and author who served as first lady of the United States from 2009 to 2017, while her husband, Barack Obama, was president. As first lady, she promoted healthy eating, education, and support for military families. In 2018, the Smithsonian’s National Portrait Gallery unveiled her official portrait, painted by contemporary American artist Amy Sherald. Sherald is known for painting many of her subjects’ skin in shades of gray rather than using realistic skin colors. In Michelle Obama’s portrait, she sits against a pale blue background wearing a patterned dress. The portrait drew wide attention and helped introduce many visitors to Sherald’s distinctive style. Barack Obama’s portrait, unveiled at the same time, was painted by a different artist, Kehinde Wiley.

Operation Mongoose was a secret U.S. campaign approved by President John F. Kennedy’s administration in 1961 after the failed Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba. The CIA led the effort to weaken and ultimately overthrow Fidel Castro’s communist government, which the United States viewed as a Cold War threat close to home. The campaign used sabotage, propaganda, and intelligence gathering rather than an open military invasion. Kennedy’s administration chose U.S. Air Force officer Edward Lansdale to coordinate the work of several government agencies. Lansdale was known for counterinsurgency work in the Philippines and later became involved in U.S. efforts in Vietnam. Operation Mongoose increased pressure on Cuba before the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, when Kennedy imposed a naval blockade after Soviet nuclear missiles were discovered on the island.

The Combahee River Raid was a Union operation during the American Civil War. On June 2, 1863, Union gunboats traveled up the Combahee River in South Carolina, carrying soldiers who attacked Confederate plantations, destroyed supplies, and helped free more than 700 enslaved people. Harriet Tubman, a formerly enslaved abolitionist, helped plan the raid and used information gathered from local people to guide the mission. Before the war, Tubman had repeatedly risked her life leading enslaved people to freedom through the Underground Railroad, a secret network of helpers and safe places. Her courage earned her the nickname “Moses,” after the biblical leader who led his people out of slavery. The raid weakened the Confederacy while giving hundreds of people a chance to escape enslavement.

In the 2000 United States presidential election, Republican George W. Bush ran against Democrat Al Gore, who had been vice president under Bill Clinton. The result hinged on Florida, where the candidates were separated by a tiny margin. Election officials struggled to count some punch-card ballots because the punched-out paper pieces, called “chads,” had not fully detached. A disputed recount followed, and the U.S. Supreme Court intervened in the case Bush v. Gore. In a 5–4 ruling, the Court halted the recount, finding that inconsistent standards for counting ballots violated the Equal Protection Clause. Bush remained the winner in Florida and therefore won the Electoral College and the presidency, even though Gore received more votes nationwide.

Liliʻuokalani was the last reigning monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaii. She became queen in 1891 and tried to replace the Bayonet Constitution, which had sharply limited the monarch’s power and reduced the voting rights of many Native Hawaiians. In 1893, the Committee of Safety, a group of businessmen and political leaders supported by U.S. forces, overthrew her government. After a later attempt to restore the monarchy, Liliʻuokalani was held under house arrest in an upper-floor room of ʻIolani Palace in Honolulu. King Kalākaua had commissioned the palace, which was completed in 1882 and served as the home of Hawaii’s monarchs. Liliʻuokalani was also a composer who wrote “Aloha ʻOe,” one of Hawaii’s best-known songs.

The Star-Spangled Banner is the enormous American garrison flag that flew over Fort McHenry in Baltimore during the War of 1812. In September 1814, British forces bombarded the fort through the night, but the flag was still flying at dawn, showing that the fort had not surrendered. Francis Scott Key, a Maryland lawyer, saw it from a British ship where he had gone to seek the release of an American prisoner. The sight inspired him to write the poem “Defence of Fort McHenry,” whose words later became the lyrics of the U.S. national anthem, “The Star-Spangled Banner.” The original flag, which measures about 30 by 32 feet, is now preserved at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.

The 2021 Texas power crisis began when a severe cold spell and winter storm struck Texas in February 2021. Freezing temperatures and ice disrupted power plants and natural gas supplies just as demand for heating surged. The state’s electrical grid could not meet that demand, leaving millions of people without electricity for extended periods. Many also lost heat or access to safe water, and the crisis contributed to hundreds of deaths. The grid is managed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, known as ERCOT, and Governor Greg Abbott faced criticism over the state’s oversight of it. Before becoming governor, Abbott was Texas attorney general. In that role, he argued for the state in Van Orden v. Perry, a U.S. Supreme Court case that allowed a Ten Commandments monument to remain on state property.

Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy. It is a medical practice and a subject of debate about health, ethics, bodily autonomy, and the law. In 1973, the U.S. Supreme Court decided Roe v. Wade, holding that constitutional privacy protections extended to abortion and striking down a Texas law that criminalized most abortions. The decision shaped abortion law across the country for nearly 50 years. In 2022, the Supreme Court overturned Roe in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, ending the federal constitutional protection recognized in Roe and leaving states with greater power to regulate or ban abortion. Since then, states have adopted very different laws, including restrictions and measures to protect access to abortion.

Adjusted Service Certificates were documents issued to World War I veterans under a 1924 federal law that promised them a bonus for their military service. Instead of receiving cash right away, each veteran received a certificate showing the amount the government owed them, with payment scheduled for 1945. During the Great Depression, many veterans urgently needed money to support their families. In 1932, thousands traveled to Washington, D.C., and called on Congress to redeem their certificates early. This group became known as the Bonus Army. President Herbert Hoover’s administration ordered the protesters removed by force, an action that drew criticism. Congress did not approve early payment at the time, but it eventually authorized veterans to receive their bonuses in 1936.

The Mexican-American War was fought from 1846 to 1848 between the United States and its southern neighbor, Mexico. It began amid disputes over Texas, which the United States had annexed, and reflected Americans’ growing desire to expand westward. President James K. Polk led the United States during the war. Known as the first “dark horse” president because he was an unexpected presidential nominee, Polk pursued an expansionist agenda. He was also associated with the slogan “Fifty-Four Forty or Fight” during a separate boundary dispute with Britain over Oregon. U.S. forces won the war, which ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. Under the treaty, Mexico gave up a vast area of land that included present-day California and much of the American Southwest.

The Central Park Five case began in 1989, when a woman jogging in Manhattan’s Central Park was brutally attacked and raped. Five Black and Latino teenagers were arrested and convicted in connection with the crime, although they had not committed the attack. The case drew intense public attention and raised questions about how police questioned the teenagers and how race affected the investigation. The five spent years in prison. In 2002, Matias Reyes, who was imprisoned for other crimes, confessed that he had attacked the jogger. DNA evidence corroborated his confession, and the teenagers’ convictions were vacated. The case remains an important example of wrongful conviction in New York City and of the lasting harm that can result when an investigation reaches the wrong conclusion.

Warren E. Burger became Chief Justice of the United States in 1969 after President Richard Nixon nominated him. He led the Supreme Court when it decided Roe v. Wade in 1973. That decision drew on earlier rulings about a right to privacy, including Griswold v. Connecticut, to protect access to abortion. Burger joined the majority in Roe, but his views changed over time. In 1986, while he was still Chief Justice, the Court decided Thornburgh v. American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. The case reviewed Pennsylvania’s Abortion Control Act and struck down several restrictions on abortion. Burger dissented and argued that the Court should reconsider Roe. His career shows how a justice’s position on a major constitutional issue can change.

The Vicksburg Campaign was a Union military campaign during the American Civil War in 1862–1863. Vicksburg, Mississippi, was a Confederate stronghold on high ground overlooking the Mississippi River, making it a major obstacle to Union control of that waterway. Union General Ulysses S. Grant tried several approaches before crossing the Mississippi River south of the city in spring 1863. His army then fought its way toward Vicksburg and surrounded it. After a siege lasting more than six weeks, Confederate General John Pemberton surrendered the city to Grant on July 4, 1863. With Vicksburg captured, the Union gained control of the Mississippi River, dividing the Confederacy and disrupting its supplies. Grant later became the Union’s highest-ranking general and accepted Confederate General Robert E. Lee’s surrender at Appomattox in 1865.

The First Barbary War was fought from 1801 to 1805 between the United States and Tripoli, a North African state on the Barbary Coast. Barbary rulers demanded tribute—payments meant to protect merchant ships from attacks and capture. When Tripoli demanded more money, President Thomas Jefferson refused, and fighting began. U.S. warships blockaded Tripoli, but the USS Philadelphia ran aground and was captured. In 1804, naval officer Stephen Decatur led a raid that burned the ship so Tripoli could not use it. Meanwhile, a U.S.-led force marched across the desert from Egypt and captured the Tripolitan city of Derna in 1805. That victory helped pressure Tripoli’s ruler, called the pasha, to negotiate a peace treaty.

Andrew Johnson became the seventeenth U.S. president after Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in 1865, near the end of the Civil War. During Reconstruction, when the nation was deciding how to bring former Confederate states back into the Union, Johnson favored a more lenient approach than many Republicans in Congress. He attacked his opponents, known as Radical Republicans, during a speaking tour called the “Swing Around the Circle.” The conflict intensified when Johnson tried to dismiss Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, who refused to leave and barricaded himself in his office. Congress argued that Johnson had violated a law limiting the president’s power to remove officials. In 1868, the House of Representatives impeached Johnson, making him the first U.S. president to be impeached. The Senate fell one vote short of removing him from office.

The House Un-American Activities Committee, or HUAC, was a U.S. congressional panel established in 1938 and initially led by Representative Martin Dies Jr. It investigated alleged threats and subversion within the United States, but became especially known for investigating suspected communist influence during the early Cold War. In 1947, HUAC held hearings about the film industry and questioned screenwriters and directors about alleged ties to the Communist Party. Ten witnesses refused to answer these questions. Congress cited them for contempt, and Hollywood studios placed them on a blacklist, making it difficult for them to find work. They became known collectively as the Hollywood Ten. HUAC’s investigations were part of the wider Red Scare, when fear of communism led to accusations that were sometimes unsupported.

Phyllis Schlafly was an American conservative activist who became a leading opponent of the Equal Rights Amendment, or ERA. The proposed constitutional amendment sought to guarantee equal rights regardless of sex. After Congress approved it in 1972, Schlafly organized a national grassroots campaign called STOP ERA, arguing that the amendment would weaken traditional family roles and remove legal protections for women. She used the slogan “I am for Mom and apple pie” to present her views as a defense of family life. In 1972, she also founded Eagle Forum, a conservative organization that mobilized opposition to the ERA and advocated family-centered policies. Her campaign helped make the amendment a major national debate; it did not gain enough state ratifications by its deadline.

On April 20, 2010, the Deepwater Horizon offshore drilling rig exploded in the Gulf of Mexico, killing 11 workers. The explosion was followed by a blowout at the Macondo well, also called BP’s Macondo Prospect 252, deep beneath the gulf. Oil flowed from the damaged well for 87 days before it was capped, making the Deepwater Horizon oil spill the largest marine petroleum release in U.S. history. The oil threatened wildlife, fisheries, and coastal communities along the Gulf of Mexico, including areas near Florida. BP later agreed to a multibillion-dollar settlement over the damage. The name Macondo came from a fictional town in a novel by Gabriel García Márquez, so remember it as the name of the well that released the oil.

The Stono Rebellion was a major uprising by enslaved people in colonial South Carolina in September 1739. It began near the Stono River, which gave the revolt its name. A group of enslaved people seized firearms from a store and marched south, hoping to reach Spanish Florida, where they believed they could gain freedom. One of their leaders is commonly known as Cato, though some accounts also call him Jemmy. More people joined the march before colonial militia forces attacked and defeated the rebels. The uprising showed how fiercely enslaved people resisted slavery and alarmed South Carolina’s plantation owners. In response, colonial leaders passed stricter laws to control enslaved people, including limits on their movement and assembly.

Title IX is a provision of the Education Amendments of 1972 that prohibits sex discrimination in education programs and activities receiving federal financial assistance. It applies to schools and colleges that receive federal funds and is often discussed in connection with equal opportunities in athletics, including access to teams, scholarships, and facilities. Its reach extends beyond sports to other parts of education, such as admissions and responses to sexual harassment. Indiana senator Birch Bayh was Title IX’s principal sponsor in the Senate. A former college football player who later chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee, Bayh argued that the ban on sex discrimination should extend to federally funded education programs. Disputes involving the NCAA, which governs college athletics, have also drawn attention to how Title IX applies to different organizations.

The Black Panther Party was a revolutionary African American political organization founded in Oakland, California, in 1966 by Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale. It called for Black self-determination and community self-defense against police brutality. The party also ran neighborhood programs, including free breakfasts for children and health clinics. Fred Hampton, chairman of the party’s Illinois chapter, helped organize such programs and build alliances among Chicago communities. The FBI targeted the Panthers through its COINTELPRO surveillance and disruption program, and Hampton became one of its targets. In December 1969, Chicago police raided Hampton’s apartment and killed him while he slept. Police initially described the raid as a gunfight, but evidence showed that officers fired nearly all the shots.

Ford’s Theatre is a historic theater in Washington, D.C., that opened in 1863. On April 14, 1865, President Abraham Lincoln and First Lady Mary Todd Lincoln attended a performance there of Our American Cousin, a British comedy by Tom Taylor featuring a character named Asa Trenchard. During the play, actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth entered the presidential box and shot Lincoln. The president died the next morning, making Ford’s Theatre the site of one of the most consequential acts of political violence in U.S. history. The building later became a place to learn about Lincoln’s assassination and continues to host performances, connecting its history as a working theater with its role as a national historic site.

In May 2020, George Floyd, a Black man, died during an arrest in Minneapolis, Minnesota, after police officer Derek Chauvin pressed his knee on Floyd’s neck. Police had been called over an allegation that Floyd used a counterfeit $20 bill at a nearby store, Cup Foods. Seventeen-year-old bystander Darnella Frazier filmed the arrest, and her video helped bring worldwide attention to Floyd’s killing. It sparked protests against racism and police violence and renewed demands for changes in policing. Chauvin was later convicted of murdering Floyd. Protesters and community members created a memorial near Cup Foods at the intersection of 38th Street and Chicago Avenue. That intersection, which became a place for mourning, art, and activism, is commonly called George Floyd Square.

In 1735, printer John Peter Zenger went on trial in the colony of New York for seditious libel after his newspaper published criticism of royal governor William Cosby. At the time, a publisher could be punished for criticizing a government official even if the criticism was true. Zenger’s defense counsel, Philadelphia lawyer Andrew Hamilton, urged the jury to consider whether the accusations against Cosby were true rather than simply whether Zenger had printed them. The jury acquitted Zenger. The verdict did not immediately change the law, but the John Peter Zenger trial later became celebrated as an early landmark in the development of freedom of the press in America.

Roscoe Conkling was a powerful Republican senator from New York during the Gilded Age, when political parties often rewarded loyal supporters with government jobs. He led a Republican faction called the Stalwarts, who defended this practice, known as the spoils system or patronage. Conkling opposed civil-service reform, which aimed to give government jobs to qualified applicants rather than political allies. He mocked the idea as “snivel service reform.” In 1876, Conkling tried but failed to win the Republican presidential nomination; the party instead nominated Rutherford B. Hayes. Hayes became president after a disputed election against Samuel Tilden and a compromise that helped bring Reconstruction to an end. Conkling’s career shows how strongly some Gilded Age politicians resisted changes to the way government jobs were awarded.

The Secretary of War was a U.S. Cabinet official who headed the War Department and helped manage the nation’s military. The office began in 1789 under President George Washington.
