Its first holder, Henry Knox, had commanded the Continental Army’s artillery during the Revolutionary War. In the winter of 1775–76, he organized the difficult transport of cannon from Fort Ticonderoga to Boston, where they helped force British troops to leave. Knox also crossed the Delaware River with Washington before the Battle of Trenton. Much later, Jefferson Davis served as Secretary of War under President Franklin Pierce before becoming the president of the Confederacy during the Civil War. The office lasted until a post–World War II reorganization in 1947 created the Secretary of Defense to oversee the armed forces.

Orval Faubus was the governor of Arkansas during the 1957 Little Rock school integration crisis. After nine Black students, known as the Little Rock Nine, were chosen to attend the previously all-white Little Rock Central High School, Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to block their entrance. His actions defied the Supreme Court’s 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, which ruled that racial segregation in public schools violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. President Dwight D. Eisenhower responded by sending federal troops from the 101st Airborne Division to protect the students and enforce their admission. The confrontation showed that a federal court ruling could face strong resistance from state leaders, and that the federal government could step in to uphold it.

James A. Garfield was a former Union general and longtime Ohio congressman who became the twentieth president of the United States in March 1881. At the time, many federal jobs were awarded through patronage, also called the spoils system: politicians gave positions to supporters and friends rather than choosing workers for their ability. Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office seeker who claimed to support the Republican Party’s pro-patronage Stalwart faction, shot Garfield in July 1881. Garfield died that September, and Vice President Chester A. Arthur became president. The assassination increased public pressure to change how federal employees were hired. In 1883, Arthur signed the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, which introduced competitive examinations for some government jobs and helped establish merit-based federal hiring.

The 1940s brought major changes for workers and immigrant communities in the United States. During World War II, labor shortages led the United States and Mexico to begin the Bracero program in 1942. It brought Mexican workers to the United States on temporary contracts, including for farm work in California, but many faced poor conditions and exploitation. The war also brought the forced removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans. After President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 in 1942, thousands were confined in camps such as Manzanar in California. Documentary photographer Dorothea Lange, working for the War Relocation Authority, photographed Japanese American residents and the conditions they faced. Her images were largely withheld from public view during the war.

On April 3, 1968, Martin Luther King Jr. gave his final public speech, “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop,” at Mason Temple in Memphis, Tennessee. Mason Temple was also the international headquarters of the Church of God in Christ. King had come to support Black sanitation workers who were on strike for better pay, safer working conditions, and dignity. In the speech, he urged people to keep working together for justice through nonviolent action. Drawing on the biblical story of Moses, who saw the Promised Land but did not enter it, King said he had “been to the mountaintop” and had seen the Promised Land. He warned that he might not reach it with his listeners, but expressed confidence that they would get there. King was assassinated in Memphis the next day.

Mississippian Culture was a pre-Columbian Indigenous tradition that flourished across much of the southeastern and midwestern United States from about 800 to 1600 CE. Its communities grew crops intensively, especially the “Three Sisters” of corn, beans, and squash, and built towns with large, flat-topped earthen mounds used for important buildings and ceremonies. One of its greatest settlements was Cahokia, near the Mississippi River in present-day Illinois. Cahokia had plazas, a wooden circle known as Woodhenge, and an enormous platform mound called Monks Mound. Rising about 100 feet and covering roughly 14 acres, Monks Mound is the largest prehistoric earthwork in North America. The culture’s name comes from the Mississippi River, but its communities extended far beyond the river’s banks.

The Pure Food and Drug Act was passed in 1906, during the Progressive Era, when reformers pushed the federal government to protect consumers. It prohibited the sale across state lines of adulterated food and medicines, meaning products made unsafe or impure, and products with false or misleading labels. The law marked an early expansion of federal oversight of goods Americans bought and used. Public concern grew partly because of Upton Sinclair’s 1906 novel The Jungle. The story follows Jurgis Rudkus, a Lithuanian immigrant working in Chicago’s meatpacking industry, and exposes dangerous, unsanitary conditions there. Sinclair hoped readers would focus on workers’ hardships, but many were especially shocked by what the novel suggested about the safety of their food.

Nat Turner’s Rebellion was a slave revolt led by Nat Turner, an enslaved preacher, in August 1831. It took place in Southampton County in southeastern Virginia, with the first attacks near the town then called Jerusalem, now Courtland. Turner believed that signs, including a solar eclipse, called him to act against slavery. He and other enslaved people attacked local households, killing dozens of white people before state forces crushed the uprising. Turner was captured, tried, and executed. In response, Virginia and other Southern states tightened laws restricting enslaved people’s movement, education, and gatherings. The rebellion became one of the best-known slave revolts in U.S. history and intensified arguments over slavery and its future.

McCulloch v. Maryland was an 1819 Supreme Court case about the powers of the federal government and the states. Congress had created the Second Bank of the United States, but Maryland tried to tax its branch in the state. James McCulloch, who worked at the branch, refused to pay, and the dispute reached the Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the Court’s opinion. He explained that the Constitution’s Necessary and Proper Clause, also called the Elastic Clause, gave Congress implied powers: authority not listed word for word in the Constitution but needed to carry out its stated powers. That meant Congress could establish a national bank. The Court also ruled that Maryland could not tax the bank because states cannot use taxes to interfere with a lawful federal institution.

Daniel Webster was a Massachusetts senator and one of the most powerful speakers in the United States during the early 1800s. Along with Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun, he was known as a member of the “Great Triumvirate,” three senators who shaped national debates. Webster strongly defended the Union against arguments that states could reject federal laws. In a famous reply to Senator Robert Y. Hayne, he ended with the words “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable.” He also helped resolve a dispute with Britain over the border between Maine and New Brunswick. As U.S. secretary of state, Webster negotiated with British envoy Lord Ashburton, and their 1842 agreement became known as the Webster–Ashburton Treaty.

The Pony Express was a fast but short-lived mail service that operated from 1860 to 1861, carrying letters between Missouri and California. Riders on horseback passed mail from one to another at relay stations, where they could switch to fresh horses and keep moving. The service aimed to complete the long journey in less than two weeks, an impressive speed before electronic communication reached the West. But maintaining horses, riders, and stations was expensive. When the transcontinental telegraph began carrying messages almost instantly, the Pony Express could not compete and shut down after roughly 18 months. Its assets, including its distinctive logo, were later acquired by the stagecoach company Wells Fargo & Company. Wells Fargo became a major U.S. bank and faced a 2016 scandal involving unauthorized customer accounts and fees.

The 54th Massachusetts Regiment was one of the first Union Army units of Black soldiers raised in the North during the Civil War. Formed in 1863, it gave African American men a chance to fight for the Union and against slavery at a time when many doubted their ability as soldiers. Its commander, Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, came from a prominent Boston abolitionist family. In July 1863, Shaw led the regiment in an assault on Fort Wagner, a heavily defended Confederate position in South Carolina. The attack failed, and Shaw was killed along with many of his soldiers. Confederate forces buried him in a mass grave with his men, intending it as an insult, but his family regarded it as an honor. The regiment’s courage made the 54th Massachusetts a landmark in African American military service.

Police brutality means law-enforcement officers using more force than is necessary or justified. It has been a major issue in African American history because Black communities have often faced both excessive force and a lack of accountability for it. In 1965, the arrest of Marquette Frye after a traffic stop helped ignite the Watts uprising in Los Angeles amid longstanding tensions over policing and inequality. In 1991, Los Angeles police officers beat Black motorist Rodney King after a traffic stop, and someone nearby recorded the beating on video. When four officers were acquitted of most charges in 1992, anger over the verdicts helped spark days of unrest across Los Angeles and nearby communities. King later appealed for peace, asking, “Can we all get along?”

Howard University is a historically Black research university founded in Washington, D.C., in 1867, soon after the Civil War. It was named for Union general Oliver O. Howard, who led the Freedmen’s Bureau, an agency that helped formerly enslaved people gain access to education and other support. Howard has played an important role in educating Black leaders. Kamala Harris earned her undergraduate degree there, and Thurgood Marshall, who later became the first Black U.S. Supreme Court justice, graduated from its law school. Journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones holds Howard’s Knight Chair in Race and Journalism. She won the Pulitzer Prize for Commentary for her work on the 1619 Project, which examines the history and lasting effects of slavery in the United States. She joined Howard after declining a position at the University of North Carolina when it initially refused to grant her tenure.

The Black Sox Scandal was a major baseball controversy involving the Chicago White Sox during the 1919 World Series. Eight players were accused of working with gamblers to deliberately lose games against the Cincinnati Reds in exchange for money. The Reds won the series, and the accusations damaged public trust in professional baseball. The players faced a criminal trial and were acquitted, meaning the court did not find them guilty. Baseball’s new commissioner, federal judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis, nevertheless banned all eight players from professional baseball for life. The scandal showed that a court verdict and a sports league’s disciplinary decision could have different outcomes. Its name, “Black Sox,” refers to the White Sox team at the center of the controversy.

John André was a British Army officer during the American Revolution who served as a secret contact for Benedict Arnold, a senior American general. Arnold had helped win the Battle of Saratoga, but in 1780 he agreed to surrender West Point, a key fortress on the Hudson River, to the British. André met secretly with Arnold to arrange the plan. While traveling through American-held territory, André was captured carrying papers that revealed the scheme. Arnold learned that the plot had been exposed and escaped to the British side, but André was tried as a spy and hanged. Their story is remembered as one of the most famous cases of treason in American history.

The Battle of Bunker Hill was fought on June 17, 1775, in Charlestown, Massachusetts, during the Siege of Boston, early in the American Revolutionary War. Although named for Bunker Hill, most of the fighting took place on nearby Breed’s Hill, where American forces had built defenses overlooking British-held Boston. British troops attacked the position three times. The Americans repelled the first two assaults but, running low on ammunition, were forced to retreat during the third. Britain captured the hill, but its troops suffered heavy casualties. Joseph Warren, a Boston physician and president of the Massachusetts Provincial Congress, chose to fight as a volunteer alongside ordinary soldiers and was killed in the final assault. The battle showed that the American forces could stand up to trained British troops.

The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 was a law passed by the Confederation Congress to govern the Northwest Territory, the U.S. lands north of the Ohio River and west of Pennsylvania. It established a territorial government with an appointed governor and set out a path for the territory to become new states, which would enter the Union on equal footing with the original states. The ordinance also prohibited slavery in the territory, although it allowed the return of people who had escaped slavery in other states. The first governor was Arthur St. Clair, a former Continental Army officer from Pennsylvania. In 1791, St. Clair led U.S. forces against a Native American alliance known as the Western Confederacy and suffered a disastrous defeat at the Battle of the Wabash.

The 369th Infantry Regiment was a predominantly African American U.S. Army unit formed from New York’s 15th National Guard Regiment. Known as the Harlem Hellfighters, it fought on the Western Front during World War I. Because the U.S. Army was segregated and many white commanders resisted assigning Black soldiers to combat, the 369th served under French command. Its soldiers earned a reputation for courage in battle. In May 1918, while on guard duty in the Argonne sector of France, Henry Johnson and fellow soldier Needham Roberts fought off a German raiding party despite being wounded. Johnson’s actions made him one of the regiment’s best-known soldiers, and he was awarded the Medal of Honor decades later for his World War I service.

The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 began when the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad announced another wage cut during an economic downturn. Workers walked off the job in Martinsburg, West Virginia, stopping trains and demanding better treatment. West Virginia governor Henry Mathews asked the federal government for help restoring rail service, and President Rutherford B. Hayes sent federal troops to Martinsburg. The unrest spread to major rail centers across the country, where strikers, police, militias, and soldiers clashed. Although the strike was eventually suppressed, it became the first major nationwide labor uprising in the United States. It showed how important railroads had become to the economy and how far government officials were willing to go to keep trains running.

The Pequot are an Indigenous Algonquian-speaking people whose homeland was in what is now southeastern Connecticut. Before English settlement expanded in the region, they traded with Dutch merchants. In the 1630s, rising tensions over land and trade, along with violent incidents involving colonists and Pequots, led to the Pequot War. The Pequot fought English forces from Massachusetts Bay and Connecticut and their Indigenous allies, including the Mohegan and Narragansett. The war devastated Pequot communities. In 1638, colonial leaders signed the Treaty of Hartford, which formally ended the war and imposed harsh terms on the survivors. Many were forced to live among neighboring peoples, and colonial authorities tried to suppress the Pequot name and identity. Despite this, Pequot people and communities survived.

Elbridge Gerry was a Massachusetts delegate to the Continental Congress and one of the signers of the Declaration of Independence in 1776. He later served as governor of Massachusetts and became the fifth vice president of the United States under President James Madison. Gerry is also remembered for the word “gerrymandering.” During his governorship, Massachusetts lawmakers drew a state senate district with an unusually winding shape that critics said would help Gerry’s political party. An 1812 newspaper cartoon mocked the district by comparing its outline to a salamander, combining “Gerry” and “salamander” to create the new word. Today, gerrymandering means drawing electoral district boundaries to give a political party an advantage in elections.

Mitch McConnell is a Republican senator from Kentucky who was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1984. He served as Senate Majority Leader from 2015 through 2020, a role that gave him major influence over which bills and nominations received votes. In 2017, he used a rule change known as the “nuclear option” to lower the number of votes needed to end debate on Supreme Court nominations, helping confirm Neil Gorsuch. That year, during debate over Jeff Sessions’s nomination, Massachusetts Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren tried to read a letter by civil rights leader Coretta Scott King. After Warren was stopped, McConnell said, “Nevertheless, she persisted.” The phrase became widely associated with Warren, who also faced controversy over her claims of Native American ancestry.

Stephen Decatur was a U.S. naval officer whose victories made him a hero of the early republic. During the First Barbary War, the USS Philadelphia ran aground near Tripoli, was captured, and fell into the hands of a North African state fighting the United States. In 1804, Decatur led a daring night raid into Tripoli Harbor. His men boarded and burned the Philadelphia so it could not be used against American ships. Years later, during the War of 1812, Decatur commanded the frigate USS United States. In October 1812, it defeated the British frigate HMS Macedonian off Madeira, an island in the Atlantic Ocean. The captured Macedonian was brought to the United States and added to the U.S. Navy.

The Bay of Pigs invasion was a failed attempt to overthrow Cuba’s revolutionary government in April 1961. After Fidel Castro overthrew Cuban ruler Fulgencio Batista in 1959, many Cubans who opposed Castro left the country. The U.S. government trained and supported a force of these Cuban exiles, hoping their landing on Cuba’s southern coast would spark an uprising against him. President John F. Kennedy approved the operation, but the invasion force received little support from people in Cuba and was defeated within days by Castro’s forces. Castro went on to serve as Cuba’s longtime prime minister and president. The failure embarrassed the United States, strengthened Castro’s position, and increased Cold War tensions between the United States and Cuba before the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962.

The Connecticut Compromise, also called the Great Compromise, helped delegates at the 1787 Constitutional Convention settle a major disagreement about representation in Congress. Delegates from large states wanted representation based on population, which would give their states more influence. Delegates from small states wanted every state to have an equal voice. The compromise created a bicameral, or two-house, Congress: seats in the House of Representatives would be based on each state’s population, while every state would have equal representation in the Senate, with two senators each. The plan is commonly credited to Roger Sherman, a Connecticut delegate who had represented his state in the Continental Congress. Sherman was also a signer of both the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.

The Radical Republicans were a faction of the Republican Party in Congress during Reconstruction, the period after the Civil War when the United States worked to bring the former Confederate states back into the Union. They argued that formerly enslaved people needed broad civil and political rights, including protection under the law and the right to vote. They opposed President Andrew Johnson, who succeeded Abraham Lincoln, because his lenient policies let former Confederate states regain power without doing enough to protect Black Americans. Radical Republicans pushed for stronger federal action and helped pass the Reconstruction Acts. One of their most prominent leaders was Thaddeus Stevens, a Pennsylvania congressman who championed rights for formerly enslaved people and became a leading House advocate for impeaching Johnson.

The Battle of Fort Sumter began on April 12, 1861, when Confederate forces bombarded a Union-held fort in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina. South Carolina had been the first state to secede from the United States, and the fort had become a point of conflict between the Union and the new Confederacy. Union Major Robert Anderson commanded its small garrison. He had moved his troops there from nearby Fort Moultrie because Fort Sumter was easier to defend. After the bombardment and with supplies running low, Anderson surrendered on April 13. Although no soldiers were killed during the bombardment itself, the attack marked the opening of the American Civil War. It also prompted President Abraham Lincoln to call for troops to put down the rebellion.

The 1990s were a decade of major political change and controversy in the United States. Bill Clinton won the presidency in 1992 and was reelected in 1996, as the country adjusted to the end of the Cold War. In 1991, the Senate considered Clarence Thomas for a seat on the Supreme Court. During his confirmation hearings, law professor Anita Hill testified that Thomas had sexually harassed her when they worked together at the Department of Education. Her testimony sparked a national debate about sexual harassment, although the Senate confirmed Thomas. Later in the decade, Clinton faced an investigation involving his relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. The House of Representatives impeached him in 1998, making him the first U.S. president impeached in more than a century, but the Senate did not remove him from office.

The United States Postmaster General is the official who leads the nation’s postal system. The Continental Congress appointed Benjamin Franklin as the first postmaster general in 1775, before the United States gained independence. Franklin was also a Founding Father and the primary author of Poor Richard’s Almanack. As the federal government developed, the postmaster general became a Cabinet-level official who oversaw mail delivery and postal routes. Amos Kendall held the office under Presidents Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren. Later, John Creswell expanded postal routes in the western United States under President Ulysses S. Grant. The postmaster general is no longer a Cabinet member: since 1971, the position has led the United States Postal Service.

The Italian-American Mafia, also called the Mob or La Cosa Nostra, is an organized-crime network that grew among immigrants from Sicily and their descendants in U.S. cities, especially New York and Chicago. Its roots lie in Sicily, where criminal groups demanded “protection money” from businesses and farmers. In the United States, Mafia groups gained wealth and influence during Prohibition, the nationwide ban on the manufacture, sale, and transportation of alcoholic drinks from 1920 to 1933. They illegally supplied liquor, an activity known as bootlegging. After a violent conflict called the Castellammarese War ended in 1931, five major crime families came to dominate the New York Mafia. Movies such as The Godfather have made the Mafia famous, but its activities involved real violence, extortion, and other crimes.

The United Farm Workers (UFW) is a labor union co-founded by Mexican-American activist César Chávez and labor organizer Dolores Huerta to improve farmworkers’ pay, working conditions, and rights. It became nationally known during the Delano grape strike in California, when grape pickers demanded better treatment from growers. Chávez and Huerta helped lead a march from Delano to Sacramento, while supporters across the country joined a boycott of grapes. In 1968, Chávez undertook a 25-day fast to emphasize nonviolence during the strike. The union’s campaigns showed how farmworkers could use strikes, marches, and consumer boycotts to draw attention to their demands and pressure employers to negotiate.

Roger Brooke Taney was a Maryland-born jurist who served as attorney general and treasury secretary under President Andrew Jackson. In 1836, he succeeded John Marshall as the fifth Chief Justice of the United States, leading the Supreme Court until his death in 1864. Taney is best known for writing the majority opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857). Dred Scott was an enslaved man who argued that living in free territory had made him free. The Court ruled against him, declaring that Black people could not be U.S. citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. The decision struck down the Missouri Compromise, intensified the national conflict over slavery, and became one of the Supreme Court’s most condemned rulings.

The Haymarket affair was a violent turning point in the movement for an eight-hour workday. On May 4, 1886, workers and supporters gathered for a labor rally at Haymarket Square in Chicago, Illinois. As police moved to disperse the crowd, someone threw a bomb, killing and injuring police officers and civilians. The bomber was never identified, but authorities arrested several anarchists, people who opposed government authority and supported radical social change. Their trial was widely criticized as unfair because prosecutors linked the defendants to the bombing largely through their political beliefs and writings. Four were executed in 1887, including August Spies, a German-born anarchist who edited Chicago’s German-language labor newspaper, the Arbeiter-Zeitung. The affair intensified fears of radical labor activism while becoming a lasting symbol of the struggle for workers’ rights.

Joe Biden is an American politician who represented Delaware in the U.S. Senate from 1973 to 2009. He then served as vice president under President Barack Obama from 2009 to 2017 before becoming the 46th president of the United States in 2021. Biden has also appeared on television outside of political news. During the 2010s, he made two guest appearances as himself on Parks and Recreation, a satirical NBC sitcom starring Amy Poehler as Leslie Knope, a local government worker in the fictional town of Pawnee, Indiana. He also appeared on Law and Order: SVU in 2016 to speak about sexual assault. These appearances connected his public role in politics with shows watched by a wider audience.

The Hearst family became one of the most influential families in American publishing. William Randolph Hearst took over the San Francisco Examiner from his father in 1887, later acquired the New York Journal, and built a national empire of newspapers and magazines. His papers competed fiercely with Joseph Pulitzer’s New York World and used sensational stories and headlines to attract readers, a style called yellow journalism. During Cuba’s struggle for independence from Spain, Hearst’s newspapers published dramatic reports about Spanish governor Valeriano Weyler, whom they called “The Butcher.” Decades later, another family member, Patty Hearst, became famous for a very different reason: the Symbionese Liberation Army kidnapped her in 1974, and she later took part in a bank robbery while with the group.

In November 1959, four members of the Clutter family were murdered in their home near Holcomb, Kansas. Herb Clutter was a prosperous farmer; the other victims were his wife, Bonnie, and two of their children, Nancy and Kenyon. The killers, Perry Smith and Richard Hickock, had broken into the house hoping to find a large amount of cash. The crime shocked the small community and drew national attention. Author Truman Capote traveled to Kansas with his childhood friend Harper Lee to interview people connected to the case. His book In Cold Blood reconstructs the Clutter family murders, the investigation, and what happened afterward. Published in 1966, it became a landmark work of nonfiction for using detailed reporting and storytelling techniques often associated with novels.

The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (BCRA) is a 2002 federal law also known as the McCain-Feingold Act, after its Senate sponsors. It changed how money could be used in U.S. elections. The law barred national political party committees from raising or spending “soft money,” funds that had escaped some federal campaign-finance limits. It also restricted certain “electioneering communications,” such as broadcast ads about candidates aired shortly before an election and paid for by corporations or unions. In 2010, a challenge involving a film about Hillary Clinton led to the Supreme Court decision Citizens United v. FEC. The Court ruled that corporations and unions could not be barred from making independent political expenditures—spending not coordinated with a candidate’s campaign. The decision reversed Austin v. Michigan Chamber of Commerce and helped spur the rise of super PACs.

Nikole Hannah-Jones is an American investigative journalist known for reporting on racial inequality and the history of slavery in the United States. She developed The 1619 Project with journalists at The New York Times. The project explores how slavery and its lasting effects have shaped American society, politics, and culture. Hannah-Jones won the Pulitzer Prize for Commentary for her work on it. In 2021, she declined a position at the University of North Carolina after a dispute over whether she would receive tenure, a form of long-term job protection for professors. She instead joined Howard University, a historically Black university in Washington, D.C., where she holds the Knight Chair in Race and Journalism. Vice President Kamala Harris earned her undergraduate degree at Howard, and Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall graduated from its law school.

The Birmingham Campaign was a coordinated civil rights effort in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1963. Led in part by Martin Luther King Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, it used nonviolent marches, sit-ins, and boycotts to challenge the city’s racial segregation. Police responded to some demonstrations with dogs and powerful fire hoses, and televised images of these confrontations shocked viewers across the country. The campaign helped build support for federal civil rights legislation. Later that year, King delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech in Washington, D.C. In 1968, he gave his “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” speech in Memphis the night before he was assassinated.

The Glass–Steagall Act was passed in 1933, during the Great Depression, when many U.S. banks were failing and people had lost confidence in the banking system. It separated commercial banks, which accept deposits and make loans, from investment banks, which underwrite and sell securities such as stocks and bonds. Lawmakers hoped this division would protect depositors and reduce the risks banks could take with their money. For decades, the rules limited whether one banking company could perform both kinds of work. In 1999, President Bill Clinton signed the Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act. That law substantially repealed Glass–Steagall’s key separation provisions, allowing commercial banks, securities firms, and insurance companies to become affiliated under the same corporate organization.

The Battle of Blair Mountain was a week-long armed conflict in 1921 centered on Logan County, West Virginia. Thousands of coal miners marched to demand union recognition and better working conditions, but they met armed resistance from local authorities and forces supporting the coal companies. The fighting became one of the largest labor uprisings in U.S. history. Nearly 100 people, most of them miners, were killed before federal troops arrived and the miners dispersed. The battle took place during the presidency of Warren G. Harding, who had defeated Democrat James M. Cox in the 1920 election after campaigning on a promise of a “return to normalcy.” Blair Mountain showed how fiercely coal companies and their allies resisted union organizing, even as miners risked their lives to seek safer workplaces and a stronger voice on the job.

The Sharps rifle was a mid-19th-century American firearm named for its inventor, Christian Sharps, who received a patent for a breech-loading rifle design in 1848. Unlike a muzzle-loading gun, which had to be loaded from the front of the barrel, a Sharps rifle could be loaded at the breech, near the rear of the barrel. This made it quicker to reload. Sharps rifles became important during “Bleeding Kansas,” a period of violence in the 1850s when antislavery free-staters and proslavery settlers fought over whether Kansas would allow slavery. Antislavery groups sent the rifles to settlers in Kansas. The guns were nicknamed “Beecher’s Bibles” after abolitionist minister Henry Ward Beecher, who supported providing weapons to the antislavery side.

Juan Ponce de León was a Spanish explorer and conquistador who led the first recorded European expedition to Florida in 1513. He named the region La Florida and claimed it for Spain. Although legend says he was searching for the Fountain of Youth, a spring whose water could restore youth, historians have found no reliable evidence that this was the purpose of his voyage. Spanish Florida later covered more land than the modern state, extending north into present-day Georgia. Ponce de León did not found a lasting settlement in Florida, but other Spaniards did decades later. In 1565, they established St. Augustine on Florida’s northeastern coast. It is commonly described as the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded settlement in the continental United States.

Pet banks were state-chartered banks chosen by President Andrew Jackson’s administration to hold federal money. Jackson mistrusted the Second Bank of the United States, a federally chartered institution led by Nicholas Biddle. He believed it gave too much power to wealthy bankers and threatened ordinary citizens. After vetoing a bill to renew the Second Bank’s charter, Jackson ordered federal deposits withdrawn from it in 1833 and placed in selected state banks instead. Critics called these favored institutions “pet banks” because they believed Jackson’s administration chose them for political reasons. The move was part of Jackson’s broader fight against the Second Bank, often called the Bank War. The U.S. Senate later formally censured Jackson for his actions in removing the deposits.

The Cheyenne are an Indigenous people of the Great Plains whose history is closely tied to the westward expansion of the United States. They developed Northern and Southern branches and often allied with the Arapaho. Cheyenne, the capital of Wyoming, bears their name; Fort Laramie is also in Wyoming. As settlers and soldiers moved across the Plains, the Cheyenne faced pressure on their lands and fought to protect their communities. Black Kettle, a Southern Cheyenne peace chief, sought agreements with the U.S. government and signed the 1861 Treaty of Fort Wise. He survived the 1864 Sand Creek Massacre, in which U.S. troops attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho camp. In 1868, Black Kettle was killed when U.S. troops attacked his village at the Washita River.

Purdue Pharma was an American pharmaceutical company that sold OxyContin, a prescription pain medicine containing the opioid oxycodone. Beginning in the 1990s, the company marketed OxyContin aggressively to doctors and encouraged widespread prescribing while downplaying its risk of addiction. In 2007, Purdue Pharma pleaded guilty to misleading the public about that risk. Its marketing and distribution helped make it a major corporate actor in the U.S. opioid epidemic, a nationwide public-health crisis involving addiction and overdose deaths. Opioids are a class of drugs that includes prescription pain medicines as well as heroin and the powerful synthetic drug fentanyl. Although Purdue Pharma did not cause the crisis by itself, its actions helped fuel widespread use of addictive pain medicines and the harm that followed.

Ruth Bader Ginsburg, born in Brooklyn in 1933, was a lawyer and a leading advocate for gender equality. In 1972, she co-founded and began directing the Women’s Rights Project of the American Civil Liberties Union, or ACLU. Through carefully chosen court cases, the project challenged laws that treated people differently because of sex, arguing that such discrimination violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Ginsburg’s legal work helped expand constitutional protections for women and men. President Bill Clinton nominated her to the Supreme Court of the United States in 1993. She became the second woman and the first Jewish woman to serve as a justice on the nation’s highest court. She remained an associate justice until her death in 2020.

The Battles of Lexington and Concord were the first military engagements of the American Revolutionary War. On the night of April 18, 1775, British troops marched out of Boston toward Concord, Massachusetts, to seize colonial military supplies. Paul Revere, a Boston silversmith and member of the Sons of Liberty, rode to warn colonial leaders that the troops were coming. On April 19, British soldiers confronted Massachusetts militiamen on the village green in Lexington. Shots were fired, though it is unclear which side fired first. The British continued to Concord, where they fought more militiamen near the North Bridge. As the troops retreated to Boston, colonial fighters attacked them along the road. Together, these clashes showed that the growing conflict between Britain and its American colonies had become a war.

William Lloyd Garrison was a Massachusetts publisher and radical abolitionist who demanded an immediate end to slavery in the United States. In 1831, he founded the Boston newspaper The Liberator to spread that message. Its first issue declared, “I will not retreat a single inch—and I will be heard.” Garrison used the paper to challenge people who tolerated slavery and to argue that enslaved people should be freed. He believed the United States Constitution allowed slavery to continue. In 1854, he publicly burned a copy of the Constitution, calling it a “Covenant with Death” and an “Agreement with Hell.” His dramatic protest showed how strongly he opposed slavery, though other abolitionists, including Frederick Douglass, disagreed with him about how best to end it.

Geronimo, also known as Goyaałé, was a Chiricahua Apache leader who resisted Mexican and United States expansion in the Southwest. During the Apache Wars, he led a small group that fought to defend its freedom and homeland as settlers and soldiers pushed into Apache territory. After years of resistance, Geronimo surrendered to U.S. forces in 1886. His name later became linked to a very different part of U.S. military history. Near Fort Sill, Oklahoma, paratrooper Aubrey Eberhardt reportedly shouted “Geronimo!” as he leaped from a cliff to prove his nerve. The shout caught on among other paratroopers, who began using it as a cry when jumping from aircraft.

The assassination of a U.S. president is the deliberate killing of someone serving as president. In 1865, actor John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln in the presidential box at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C. Booth then leapt onto the stage and shouted “Sic semper tyrannis,” a Latin phrase meaning “Thus always to tyrants.” Lincoln died the next day. Nearly a century later, President John F. Kennedy was shot while riding in a motorcade through Dallas, Texas, on November 22, 1963. Both attacks are examples of the same historical crime because each targeted and killed a sitting U.S. president. These events shocked the country and led to major investigations and changes in presidential security.

Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission was a 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision about political spending and free speech. The case began when Citizens United, a nonprofit group, challenged restrictions on distributing Hillary: The Movie, a film critical of Hillary Clinton, during an election campaign. The Court ruled that the First Amendment protects independent political spending by corporations and unions, so the government could not limit those expenditures simply because the speakers were organizations. The ruling struck down a restriction in the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002, also called the McCain-Feingold Act after its Senate sponsors, John McCain and Russ Feingold. That law also addressed national-party fundraising of “soft money.” Independent expenditures are spending not coordinated with a candidate’s campaign; the decision helped pave the way for Super PACs, which can raise unlimited contributions for such spending.

The Dakota Access Pipeline is a crude-oil pipeline built to carry oil from the Bakken Formation in North Dakota to a terminal in Patoka, Illinois. Its planned route beneath Lake Oahe, a reservoir on the Missouri River near the Standing Rock Reservation, sparked major Indigenous-led protests in 2016. Members of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe and their allies feared that a leak could contaminate water and objected to the project’s effects on sites important to their history and culture. Protesters called themselves “water protectors.” Their largest gathering site was Oceti Sakowin Camp, near Cannon Ball, North Dakota, where the Cannonball and Missouri rivers meet. The camp became a central place for organizing demonstrations and bringing together Indigenous activists and supporters. Despite the protests, the pipeline began operating in 2017.

The Whiskey Rebellion was an uprising in western Pennsylvania from 1791 to 1794 against a federal excise tax on distilled spirits, especially whiskey. Many farmers turned their grain into whiskey because it was easier to transport and sell, so they felt the tax fell unfairly on them. Alexander Hamilton, the first U.S. secretary of the treasury and a former aide to George Washington, had helped establish the tax to raise money for the new federal government. Resistance grew into threats and violence against tax collectors. In 1794, President Washington assembled thousands of troops, mostly from state militias, and led them toward the region to put down the rebellion. The protesters dispersed with little fighting. The government’s response showed that the new federal government could enforce its laws.

Missouri is a Midwestern state with its capital in Jefferson City. Its city of Independence became a major starting point for settlers traveling west on the Oregon Trail. Missouri also played an important role in debates over slavery before the Civil War. Under the Missouri Compromise of 1820, Congress agreed to admit Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, preserving the balance between them in the Senate. The agreement also banned slavery in much of the remaining Louisiana Purchase north of latitude 36°30′. In 1838, conflict between Missouri residents and Mormon settlers escalated into the Mormon War. Governor Lilburn Boggs issued Executive Order 44, which called for Mormons to be driven from the state or “exterminated.”

The Taft–Hartley Act was a federal labor law passed in 1947, during President Harry S. Truman’s administration. It amended the Wagner Act, which had strengthened workers’ rights to organize and bargain collectively during the New Deal. Taft–Hartley placed new limits on labor unions, including restrictions on some strikes and other union practices. It also allowed states to pass “right-to-work” laws that prohibit union-security agreements, under which workers may be required to join or support a union as a condition of employment. Truman argued that the law went too far in weakening unions and vetoed it, but Congress overrode his veto, making it law. Truman also issued Executive Order 9981 in 1948, ordering the desegregation of the U.S. armed forces.

The Social Security Act was a major New Deal law signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1935, during the Great Depression. Many Americans had lost their jobs or savings, and the law aimed to provide a more reliable financial safety net. It established old-age benefits for retired workers and a system of unemployment insurance to help people who lost their jobs. The law also provided aid to some vulnerable groups, including people with disabilities and children in families with little income. Its design drew on recommendations from the Committee on Economic Security, chaired by Secretary of Labor Frances Perkins. Perkins was the first woman to serve in a U.S. presidential Cabinet and played an important role in drafting the act.

Native American boarding schools were institutions that removed Indigenous children from their families and communities to push them to adopt mainstream American culture. Many students were required to speak English, practice Christianity, and follow rules that restricted their ancestral languages, clothing, and customs. In 1879, Army officer Richard Henry Pratt established the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in former military barracks in Pennsylvania. Carlisle became a model for off-reservation boarding schools, which took children far from their homes to make assimilation easier. Although students also received academic and vocational instruction, many experienced harsh discipline, loneliness, and abuse. These schools disrupted the passing of languages and traditions between generations, and their effects remain important to Indigenous communities today.

The temperance movement was a U.S. social and political campaign to reduce or eliminate alcohol consumption. Supporters argued that drinking contributed to poverty, violence, and family problems. Religious groups and organizations such as the Woman’s Christian Temperance Union encouraged people to give up alcohol and pushed for laws restricting its sale. One of the movement’s most famous activists was Carrie Nation of Kansas, who entered saloons and smashed liquor kegs and bar fixtures with a hatchet to protest drinking. The movement’s efforts helped bring about national Prohibition: the 18th Amendment banned the manufacture, sale, and transportation of alcoholic drinks, and the Volstead Act set out how the ban would be enforced. Prohibition began in 1920, though it did not end alcohol use.

Mike Pence was the 48th vice president of the United States, serving under President Donald Trump from 2017 to 2021. Before becoming vice president, Pence represented Indiana’s 6th congressional district in the U.S. House of Representatives and later served as governor of Indiana. One of his most important duties as vice president was to preside over the counting of electoral votes in Congress after a presidential election. On January 6, 2021, Pence was overseeing the count that would confirm Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election when rioters breached the U.S. Capitol and tried to stop the proceeding. This event is commonly called the January 6 attack. Congress later completed the count and confirmed Biden’s win.

On October 8, 1871, a wind-driven wildfire swept through Peshtigo, Wisconsin, and nearby communities. The area’s lumber industry had left behind dry wood and sawdust, which helped the flames spread rapidly. The Peshtigo Fire killed an estimated 1,200 to 2,500 people, making it the deadliest wildfire in recorded U.S. history. That same night, another major fire began near DeKoven Street in Chicago, Illinois. Known as the Great Chicago Fire, it destroyed thousands of mostly wooden buildings and left many residents homeless. Although the Chicago fire became more famous, the Peshtigo Fire killed far more people. Together, the two disasters show how drought, strong winds, and flammable building materials could turn a fire into a catastrophe.

The Province of Pennsylvania was a British proprietary colony granted by King Charles II in 1681 to William Penn, an English Quaker. Penn envisioned it as a “holy experiment”: a place where Quakers and people of other faiths could worship with greater freedom. He also planned Philadelphia, the colony’s principal city, with a regular street grid. Pennsylvania grew into an important center of trade and ideas, and Philadelphia became home to Benjamin Franklin. Relations with Native Americans were not always peaceful or fair. In the 1737 Walking Purchase, colonial officials used a disputed deed and fast runners to claim far more land than Native Americans expected to give up. The colony’s history thus includes both Penn’s hopes for religious toleration and serious conflicts over land.

The H. L. Hunley was a Confederate submarine used during the American Civil War. Named for its developer, Horace L. Hunley, it was powered by crew members turning a hand crank rather than by an engine. The submarine sank during two test voyages; Hunley himself died in the second accident. After it was raised and put back into service, it attacked the Union sloop-of-war USS Housatonic off Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, in February 1864. Its explosive charge sank the Housatonic, making it the first warship sunk by a submarine in combat. The Hunley also failed to return from the mission and was lost with all eight crew members. Its success showed that underwater vessels could threaten larger warships, even though early submarines were extremely dangerous to operate.

Derek Chauvin was a Minneapolis police officer in Minnesota who was convicted in connection with the death of George Floyd, a 46-year-old Black man. In May 2020, officers arrested Floyd outside a convenience store, and Chauvin pressed his knee against Floyd’s neck for more than nine minutes while Floyd was restrained. Bystanders recorded the arrest, and the video spread widely after Floyd died. His death sparked protests in the United States and around the world against police violence and racial injustice. In April 2021, a jury found Chauvin guilty of second-degree unintentional murder, third-degree murder, and second-degree manslaughter. The case became a major moment in the national discussion about policing, accountability, and the treatment of Black Americans.

The Stonewall Inn was a gay bar in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village neighborhood. In the early hours of June 28, 1969, police raided it, as they had raided other bars where LGBTQ people gathered. Instead of quietly leaving, patrons and neighbors resisted, beginning several nights of protests known as the Stonewall uprising. The events became a landmark in the modern gay rights movement by encouraging more open and forceful activism. In New York City that year, activists formed the Gay Liberation Front, a radical group that demanded equal rights and greater visibility for LGBTQ people. The group later protested at the offices of the Village Voice over its coverage of LGBTQ people. One year after the uprising, the first Pride marches commemorated Stonewall and celebrated the community.

In the early United States, militias were military forces organized by individual states and made up largely of citizens who could be called to serve. They were especially important because the federal Regular Army was small. In 1794, President George Washington called up thousands of militiamen to confront the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania, where people resisted a federal excise tax on whiskey. Alexander Hamilton, the first secretary of the treasury, had proposed the tax and advised Washington during the campaign. The militia also appears in the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791. The Second Amendment begins by describing a “well regulated Militia” as “necessary to the security of a free State” and also protects the right of the people to keep and bear arms.

Hoovervilles were makeshift communities built by people who had lost their homes during the Great Depression, a long economic crisis that began after the 1929 stock market crash. With little money and nowhere else to live, residents put together shelters from salvaged lumber, tin, cardboard, and other materials. The name mocked President Herbert Hoover, who was in office when the Depression began and whom many Americans blamed for the government’s response to it. Hoovervilles appeared in cities across the United States, showing how severely unemployment and poverty affected everyday life. One of the largest and longest-lasting stood on tidal flats near the mouth of the Duwamish River in Seattle, Washington. It remained there until 1941.

COINTELPRO, short for Counterintelligence Program, was a secret FBI program that began in 1956. It used surveillance, informants, and other covert tactics to infiltrate and disrupt political organizations in the United States. Its targets included the American Indian Movement, which advocated for Native American rights, and groups involved in the civil rights movement. The FBI also secretly surveilled Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister who led the Southern Christian Leadership Conference and became a leading voice against racial segregation. In 1964, the Bureau sent King an anonymous letter intended to pressure him to end his activism. COINTELPRO remains controversial because the FBI used its law-enforcement powers to interfere with political activity and civil rights organizing.

George Floyd was a Houston-raised African American man who died on May 25, 2020, during an arrest in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Police officer Derek Chauvin knelt on Floyd’s neck for several minutes while Floyd said he could not breathe. Video of the arrest spread widely, and Floyd’s killing sparked major protests against police brutality and racial injustice across the United States and around the world. Chauvin was later convicted of murder. Minneapolis is Minnesota’s largest city, and St. Paul is the state capital. Floyd’s death also drew renewed attention to earlier police killings in Minnesota, including the 2016 killing of Philando Castile during a traffic stop.

W. E. B. Du Bois was an African American scholar, writer, and civil rights activist who helped found the NAACP in 1909. In his influential 1903 book The Souls of Black Folk, he explored the lives of Black Americans after slavery and the barriers created by racism. Du Bois described a metaphorical “veil” separating Black Americans from a society that refused to see them as equals. He also introduced the idea of “double consciousness”: the divided awareness of seeing oneself through one’s own experiences while also being forced to consider how a racist society sees you. Du Bois challenged Booker T. Washington’s accommodationist approach, which emphasized economic advancement while accepting limits on political rights. Instead, Du Bois urged Black Americans to press for full civil and political equality.

The mayor of New York City is the city’s chief elected executive, responsible for leading its government and overseeing city services. In the 1800s, elections for this office were strongly influenced by Tammany Hall, a Democratic political organization whose leaders were called Grand Sachems. Tammany Hall became a powerful political machine: it organized voters and helped candidates win elections, but it also became notorious for corruption, especially under William “Boss” Tweed. With Tammany Hall’s support, Fernando Wood was elected mayor in 1854 and again in 1856. Decades later, Fiorello La Guardia served as mayor from 1934 to 1945. Wood and La Guardia held the same city office, but Wood’s elections are particularly connected to Tammany Hall’s influence.

The O. J. Simpson murder trial was a nationally televised criminal case in Los Angeles that ended in 1995. Simpson, a former NFL star who had rushed for more than 2,000 yards in a season with the Buffalo Bills, was accused of murdering his former wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend Ronald Goldman. California Superior Court Judge Lance Ito presided over the trial and made rulings about courtroom procedure. Simpson’s defense lawyers, including Johnnie Cochran, challenged the prosecution’s evidence and raised concerns about detective Mark Fuhrman’s alleged racism. One famous moment came when Simpson tried on a leather glove linked to the killings; it appeared not to fit, prompting Cochran’s phrase, “If it doesn’t fit, you must acquit.” The jury found Simpson not guilty of the murders.

Crazy Horse was an Oglala Lakota war leader who resisted U.S. expansion into the northern Great Plains, where settlers and soldiers threatened Indigenous lands. In 1876, he was among the Lakota leaders who fought alongside Northern Cheyenne warriors at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in Montana Territory. The battle took place near the Little Bighorn River and ended in a Native victory over part of George Armstrong Custer’s 7th Cavalry. Sitting Bull was another important Lakota leader associated with the battle. Crazy Horse’s legacy is commemorated by the enormous Crazy Horse Memorial, a mountain sculpture in South Dakota’s Black Hills. Located near Mount Rushmore, the memorial has been under construction since 1948 and remains unfinished.

The United States Declaration of Independence announced that the thirteen American colonies were no longer under British rule. The Second Continental Congress approved it in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776. A five-member committee was assigned to draft the document, but Virginia delegate Thomas Jefferson, who later became the third U.S. president, wrote most of its initial text. The Declaration argued that people have rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments should protect those rights with the consent of the governed. It also listed grievances against King George III to explain why the colonies were separating from Great Britain. Earlier that year, Thomas Paine’s pamphlet Common Sense had urged independence, helping build support for the decision the Declaration formally announced.

Alice Paul was a Quaker suffragist who helped lead the fight for women’s voting rights in the United States. She helped organize the 1913 Woman Suffrage Procession in Washington, D.C., and later founded the National Woman’s Party. Its members picketed outside the White House to pressure President Woodrow Wilson to support a constitutional amendment giving women the vote. After the 19th Amendment was ratified in 1920, Paul continued working for legal equality. She drafted the Equal Rights Amendment, or ERA, a proposed change to the Constitution intended to prohibit discrimination based on sex. First introduced in Congress in 1923 with Crystal Eastman, the ERA was approved by Congress in 1972. By its extended 1982 deadline, however, only 35 states had ratified it—three short of the 38 required.

Colorado’s gold and silver mines drew settlers and workers to the Rocky Mountain region, but mining also led to bitter labor conflicts. In the early 1900s, the Western Federation of Miners led a major strike in Colorado’s Cripple Creek mining district. Its leader, William Dudley “Big Bill” Haywood, helped found the Industrial Workers of the World, a union that sought to organize workers across many industries. Haywood was later tried for the murder of former Idaho governor Frank Steunenberg and was acquitted. Another violent episode in Colorado labor history was the 1914 Ludlow Massacre, when an attack on a striking miners’ camp killed workers and family members. Colorado’s capital, Denver, also became home to a U.S. Mint that processed gold from western gold rushes.

The Oklahoma City bombing was a domestic terrorist attack on April 19, 1995, in Oklahoma City, the state capital of Oklahoma. Timothy McVeigh parked a truck packed with explosives outside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building and detonated it, destroying much of the building and killing 168 people, including children. McVeigh said he wanted to retaliate against the federal government, particularly for its 1993 confrontation with a religious group near Waco, Texas. Terry Nichols, a former U.S. Army serviceman, helped McVeigh plan the attack and obtain materials for the bomb. McVeigh was convicted and executed; Nichols was convicted and sentenced to life in prison without parole. Today, a field of empty chairs at the Oklahoma City National Memorial honors the people who died.

Mary Surratt owned a boardinghouse in Washington, D.C., where John Wilkes Booth and other conspirators met near the end of the American Civil War. On April 14, 1865, Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre during a performance of Our American Cousin. Lincoln died the next morning. Authorities accused Surratt of helping Booth’s circle, including by making her boardinghouse available for their plans. A military commission convicted her of taking part in the conspiracy, though historians still debate how much she knew about the assassination plot. She was hanged in July 1865, becoming the first woman executed by the U.S. federal government. Her case remains notable both for its connection to Lincoln’s assassination and for the controversy over her trial and punishment.

Public schools are government-funded institutions that educate children at the elementary, middle, and high school levels. Because they are run by the government, their policies must respect students’ constitutional rights. For decades, many public schools separated Black and white students under the “separate but equal” doctrine. In 1954, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that racial segregation in public schools violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The case began with a challenge to segregated schools in Topeka, Kansas. Public schools have also been central to student-rights cases: in Tinker v. Des Moines, the Court ruled that students could wear black armbands to protest the Vietnam War unless doing so substantially disrupted school activities.

The Battle of Hampton Roads took place in March 1862 during the American Civil War and marked the first major clash between ironclad warships. Ironclads were steam-powered ships protected by iron armor, which made them much harder to damage than traditional wooden ships. The Confederate CSS Virginia had been built from the hull of the former USS Merrimack and used a ram to attack Union vessels. The Union sent the USS Monitor, designed by Swedish inventor John Ericsson, to confront it. The Monitor had a low-profile hull and a revolving gun turret that could aim without turning the whole ship. Their duel ended without a clear winner, but it showed that ironclads could change naval warfare and make wooden warships obsolete.

On June 20, 2020, President Donald Trump held a campaign rally in Tulsa, Oklahoma, the state’s second-largest city. It was his first in-person campaign appearance in months, after the COVID-19 pandemic had disrupted public events. Supporters gathered at the BOK Center, a downtown arena that opened in 2008 and is named for an Oklahoma-based financial company. The rally drew attention because many seats were empty, despite expectations of a large crowd. Some TikTok users said they had reserved free tickets with no intention of attending, and they were widely credited with helping to reduce the turnout. However, the exact effect of those reservations is uncertain; concerns about COVID-19 and other factors may also have kept people away.

Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer was a 1952 Supreme Court case about the limits of presidential power. During the Korean War, President Harry S. Truman feared that a nationwide steelworkers’ strike would interrupt steel production needed for the war. He ordered the federal government to take control of the steel mills, and the companies challenged his order. The Court ruled that the seizure exceeded Truman’s authority: Congress had not authorized it, and the president’s power as commander in chief did not give him the right to take over private businesses. Justice Hugo Black wrote the Court’s majority opinion. Black had joined the Supreme Court in 1937 after serving as a U.S. senator from Alabama. The decision remains an important example of the Court checking presidential power.

Betsy Ross, born Elizabeth Griscom, was a Philadelphia upholsterer who made household furnishings and flags during the American Revolution. She is best known for a story claiming that George Washington and other members of a committee asked her to sew the first American flag. According to the tradition, that flag had thirteen red and white stripes and thirteen stars arranged in a circle on a blue field, representing the thirteen original states. The story became popular decades after the Revolution, but historians have found no strong evidence that Ross designed or sewed the first flag. She did make flags, so her work was connected to the new nation even if the famous account is uncertain. Today’s American flag has fifty stars and thirteen stripes.

Chris Kyle was a U.S. Navy SEAL who served four deployments in the Iraq War. SEALs are a special operations force trained to work at sea, on land, and in the air. As a sniper, Kyle was credited with the most confirmed sniper kills in U.S. military history, making him widely known for his wartime service. After leaving the military, he wrote the memoir American Sniper with Scott McEwen and Jim DeFelice. The book describes his experiences in Iraq and the effects of war on his life and family. It inspired the 2014 film American Sniper, directed by Clint Eastwood and starring Bradley Cooper as Kyle.

Chisholm v. Georgia was a 1793 U.S. Supreme Court case about whether a state could be sued in federal court without its consent. The executor of Robert Farquhar, a South Carolina merchant, sought payment from Georgia for goods supplied during the Revolutionary War. The Court ruled that a citizen of one state could sue another state in federal court. Many states feared this decision would expose them to costly lawsuits and threaten their independence. In response, the states ratified the Eleventh Amendment to the U.S. Constitution in 1795. It limits federal courts’ authority to hear suits against a state brought by citizens of another state or by citizens or subjects of a foreign nation.

Sir Walter Raleigh was an English explorer and courtier who gained the favor of Queen Elizabeth I. In 1584, she granted him a royal patent to explore and establish English settlements in North America. Raleigh sponsored expeditions to an island off present-day North Carolina, in a region named Virginia in the queen’s honor. The best-known settlement there was Roanoke, governed by John White. In 1587, White’s granddaughter Virginia Dare was born there; she is often described as the first English child born in the Americas. White sailed to England for supplies, but war delayed his return. When he reached Roanoke in 1590, the settlers had vanished. The letters “CRO” were carved at the site, possibly pointing to the nearby Croatoan people. Because their fate remains uncertain, Roanoke is called the “Lost Colony.”

Antonio López de Santa Anna was a Mexican general and political leader who served as president many times. In 1836, he led an army into Texas, where settlers and their allies were fighting for independence from Mexico. His troops besieged the Alamo, a former mission in San Antonio, and killed roughly 200 Texian defenders, including Davy Crockett and James Bowie. Weeks later, Santa Anna ordered the execution of several hundred Texian prisoners in the Goliad Massacre. Texian soldiers rallied with the cries “Remember the Alamo!” and “Remember Goliad!” Santa Anna was defeated and captured at the Battle of San Jacinto, ending the Texas Revolution. He later commanded Mexican forces during the Mexican-American War, which Mexico also lost.

The Chinese Exclusion Act was a U.S. federal law passed by Congress in 1882 and signed by President Chester A. Arthur. It suspended the immigration of Chinese laborers for ten years, while allowing some other Chinese people, including students and merchants, to enter under exceptions. It is often described as the first major federal immigration restriction based on nationality or ethnicity. Chinese workers had helped build the Transcontinental Railroad and worked in mines and other industries, but they faced widespread prejudice and violence. In 1885, for example, a mob attacked Chinese coal miners in Rock Springs, Wyoming. The act reflected this hostility and made it harder for Chinese families and communities to grow in the United States. Its restrictions were later extended and remained in place for decades.

“The switch in time that saved nine” was a humorous nickname, popularized by radio comedian Cal Tinney, for a perceived change in the U.S. Supreme Court in 1937. The Court had struck down some of President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal measures, leading Roosevelt to propose adding justices to the Court. But in West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish, Associate Justice Owen Roberts voted with four justices who supported upholding Washington State’s minimum-wage law, creating a five-justice majority. His vote made the Court seem more willing to accept government regulation and weakened the argument for Roosevelt’s court-expansion plan. The phrase plays on “a stitch in time saves nine”: the “switch” was Roberts’s apparent change in voting alignment, and the “nine” referred to the Court’s nine seats.

Herbert Hoover was the 31st president of the United States, serving from 1929 to 1933. Before entering politics, he worked as a mining engineer and earned a reputation as a humanitarian by organizing food relief during and after World War I. He later served as secretary of commerce under Presidents Warren G. Harding and Calvin Coolidge. The Great Depression began soon after Hoover took office, and many Americans blamed him for the government’s response to widespread unemployment and poverty. In 1932, thousands of World War I veterans, known as the Bonus Army, camped in Washington, D.C., demanding early payment of their government-issued service certificates. Federal troops cleared their encampment, further damaging Hoover’s public standing. That year, he lost his reelection bid to Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Alabama is a southeastern U.S. state that played a central role in the Civil Rights Movement. In Birmingham, Martin Luther King Jr. wrote his “Letter from Birmingham Jail” in 1963, defending nonviolent protest against segregation. That same year, Ku Klux Klan members bombed Birmingham’s 16th Street Baptist Church, killing four Black girls. In 1965, activists in Selma campaigned for voting rights after Black residents faced barriers to registering. On March 7, state troopers attacked marchers, including future congressman John Lewis, as they crossed Selma’s Edmund Pettus Bridge. The violence became known as Bloody Sunday and drew national attention. Later that month, King led a march from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama’s capital, helping build support for the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

The Rock Springs massacre took place on September 2, 1885, in the coal-mining town of Rock Springs, in what was then Wyoming Territory and is now the state of Wyoming. White miners attacked Chinese coal miners, killing at least 28 people, burning homes, and driving many survivors out of town. The violence grew from racism and disputes over mining jobs and wages: some white miners blamed Chinese workers for competition at the mines. It happened during a period of widespread discrimination against Chinese immigrants, including the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, which barred most Chinese laborers from entering the United States. The massacre shows how prejudice and economic tensions could lead to deadly violence against immigrant communities in the American West.

Rutherford B. Hayes was the Republican who became the 19th president of the United States after the disputed election of 1876. He ran against Democrat Samuel J. Tilden, and the result depended on contested electoral votes. A special commission awarded those votes to Hayes, and the political settlement known as the Compromise of 1877 helped secure his presidency. After taking office, Hayes withdrew the remaining federal troops from the South, bringing federal Reconstruction to an end and leaving Black Americans more vulnerable to discrimination and violence. His wife, Lucy Webb Hayes, had graduated from Wesleyan Female College in 1850, making her the first presidential spouse to earn a college degree. She was nicknamed “Lemonade Lucy” because she kept alcohol out of White House events.

The 1838 Mormon War was a conflict in Missouri between members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, often called Mormons, and other residents. As more Latter-day Saints settled in the state, disputes over land, politics, and religion increased. Threats and attacks grew into armed clashes, and both sides feared further violence. Missouri governor Lilburn Boggs responded by issuing Executive Order 44, which declared the Latter-day Saints enemies of the state and directed that they be “exterminated or driven from the State.” Missouri forces and local militias then compelled thousands of Latter-day Saints to leave. The conflict illustrates how prejudice and political tensions could lead to violence against a religious minority in the United States.

Pickett’s Charge was a failed Confederate infantry assault on July 3, 1863, the final day of the Battle of Gettysburg in Pennsylvania. After an artillery bombardment, thousands of Confederate soldiers advanced across open fields from Seminary Ridge toward the Union center on Cemetery Ridge. The attack is named for Confederate general George Pickett, although troops led by other generals took part. Union soldiers fired on the advancing men and repulsed the assault, causing heavy Confederate losses. A key stretch of Cemetery Ridge was defended by the Union II Corps, commanded by Major General Winfield Scott Hancock, who was wounded during the fighting. The failure of Pickett’s Charge helped end Confederate general Robert E. Lee’s invasion of the North and contributed to the Union victory at Gettysburg.

The 1968 United States presidential election took place during the Vietnam War and a year of intense unrest over civil rights, political violence, and the war itself. Antiwar Democrat Eugene McCarthy challenged President Lyndon Johnson for the Democratic nomination, but Vice President Hubert Humphrey ultimately won it without competing in the primaries. At the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, clashes between antiwar protesters and police became a major televised controversy. Republican Richard Nixon promised to restore “law and order” and pursued a Southern strategy to attract white voters in the South. George Wallace, running as a third-party candidate, also appealed to many of those voters and won several Southern states. In the November election, Nixon defeated Humphrey and became president for the first time.

John Smith was an English soldier, explorer, and leader in the early years of Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in Virginia. He helped the struggling colony survive by organizing work and trade, and he explored and mapped much of Chesapeake Bay. His strict approach is often summed up by the rule, “He that will not work shall not eat.” Smith also wrote that Pocahontas, a daughter of the Powhatan leader, intervened when he was in danger, though historians debate whether his account is accurate. Pocahontas later converted to Christianity, took the name Rebecca, and married the English colonist John Rolfe. Their marriage helped bring several years of relative peace between the English settlers and the Powhatan people. She traveled to England as Rebecca Rolfe.

Tobacco is a plant grown for its leaves, which are dried and processed into products such as cigarettes. In early 17th-century Virginia, it became the leading export crop of Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in the Americas. English colonist John Rolfe grew a variety of tobacco that sold well in Europe, making it profitable to ship across the Atlantic in the early 1610s. The crop helped shape Virginia’s economy as planters expanded tobacco farming and needed more land and labor. Rolfe later married Pocahontas, the daughter of Chief Powhatan, who took the name Rebecca after converting to Christianity. Although tobacco brought wealth to some colonists, King James I strongly disliked it and wrote a pamphlet called A Counterblaste to Tobacco.

The Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) was founded in 1957 after the successful Montgomery bus boycott. It brought together Black church leaders across the South to challenge segregation through nonviolent protest, and Martin Luther King Jr. became its first president. The SCLC helped lead major civil rights campaigns in Birmingham, Alabama, and Selma, Alabama, drawing national attention to racial injustice and the fight for voting rights. In 1968, the organization helped organize the Poor People’s Campaign, an effort to demand economic justice for Americans living in poverty. Demonstrators traveled to Washington, D.C., where they built a temporary encampment called Resurrection City on the National Mall. The SCLC continues its civil rights work today.

The Great Recession was a severe economic downturn that began in the United States in late 2007 and spread around the world. Before it began, rising home prices had encouraged risky lending, including subprime mortgages to borrowers who might struggle to repay them. When the housing bubble burst, many homeowners defaulted, and banks suffered major losses. The 2008 bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers became a defining event in the financial crisis. Businesses cut jobs, and governments took steps to prevent further bank failures. Ben Bernanke, then chair of the Federal Reserve, supported a policy called quantitative easing to help stabilize the economy. Under his leadership, the Fed bought hundreds of billions of dollars in mortgage-backed securities, helping banks and making more money available for lending.

The Marshall Plan was a U.S. economic aid program that helped Western European countries rebuild after World War II. It was named for Secretary of State George C. Marshall, who proposed the plan in a 1947 speech at Harvard University. Officially called the European Recovery Program, it provided money and supplies to revive damaged economies. The United States also hoped that a stronger Western Europe would be less likely to turn to communism during the Cold War. West Germany was among the countries that received aid. Its first chancellor, Konrad Adenauer, was a Christian Democratic leader who served from 1949 to 1963. During his time in office, West Germany experienced a rapid recovery known as the “economic miracle,” aided in part by the Marshall Plan.
