The Province of New York was a British colony in North America that included much of today’s New York State, especially the Hudson and Mohawk river valleys. Before the American Revolution, it was the site of John Peter Zenger’s 1735 trial, which became an important example of freedom of the press, and the 1765 Stamp Act Congress in New York City, where colonial representatives protested British taxes. During the Revolution, the Hudson River corridor was strategically important because controlling it could help the British divide the rebellious colonies. In 1777, British general John Burgoyne advanced toward Albany, hoping to gain control of the corridor. American forces stopped his campaign at the Battle of Saratoga, near the upper Hudson River. The victory helped persuade France to ally openly with the Americans.

Sequoyah was a self-taught Cherokee inventor who created a writing system for the Cherokee language. After serving alongside Cherokee warriors in the Creek War, he worked to make it possible to record spoken Cherokee. His system, called the Cherokee syllabary, used 86 characters; each character represented a spoken syllable rather than a single letter sound, as in the English alphabet. This meant Cherokee speakers could learn to read and write in their own language. The syllabary also made Cherokee-language books and newspapers possible, including the Cherokee Phoenix. Sequoyah’s achievement helped his people share news and preserve their language at a time when the Cherokee faced growing pressure to give up their lands.

The Creek War was fought in the southeastern United States from 1813 to 1814. It grew out of divisions among the Muscogee, also called the Creek, over how to respond to U.S. expansion into their lands. A faction known as the Red Sticks resisted that expansion and fought both other Muscogee groups and U.S. forces. General Andrew Jackson led an army that included U.S. soldiers and Indigenous allies against the Red Sticks. In March 1814, his forces attacked a Red Stick stronghold at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend, on a loop of the Tallapoosa River in present-day Alabama. The decisive defeat brought the main fighting to a close. Afterward, the Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the Muscogee to give up millions of acres of land, including land held by groups that had fought alongside the United States.

The Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations was an English colony in New England that later became the U.S. state of Rhode Island, the country’s smallest state. Roger Williams founded Providence in 1636 as a haven for people facing religious persecution, and the colony grew to include settlements on Rhode Island, also called Aquidneck Island. In 1663, King Charles II granted the colony a royal charter that protected religious freedom. During King Philip’s War, a conflict between English colonists and several Indigenous nations, colonial forces attacked a fortified winter village of the Narragansett people in December 1675. This assault, known as the Great Swamp Fight, took place in the colony and caused devastating losses among the Narragansett.

South Carolina is a southeastern state on the Atlantic coast whose history includes major conflicts over federal authority and slavery. In 1832, a state convention declared federal tariff laws null and void within South Carolina. The state argued that the tariffs unfairly harmed its economy, but President Andrew Jackson insisted that federal laws had to be obeyed. During this confrontation, called the Nullification Crisis, Congress passed a compromise tariff to lower duties and a Force Bill authorizing the use of force to enforce federal law. The crisis ended without war, but tensions between states and the federal government continued. In December 1860, South Carolina became the first state to secede from the Union. In April 1861, Confederate forces bombarded Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, beginning the Civil War.

John McCain was a U.S. Navy pilot during the Vietnam War. After his plane was shot down over North Vietnam in 1967, he spent more than five years as a prisoner of war. He later entered politics in Arizona, serving in the U.S. House of Representatives and then for more than 30 years in the Senate. McCain became the Republican nominee for president in 2008. He chose Alaska governor Sarah Palin as his running mate, making her the first woman nominated for vice president by the Republican Party. They lost the election to Democrats Barack Obama and Joe Biden. McCain remained a senator until he died of brain cancer in 2018. His death left a Senate vacancy in Arizona, which Martha McSally was appointed to fill.

Nathan Bedford Forrest was a Confederate cavalry commander during the American Civil War. He rose from private to lieutenant general and became known for his raids, but his legacy is marked by violence against Black Americans. In April 1864, Forrest’s troops attacked Fort Pillow, a Union-held fort on the Mississippi River in Tennessee. After the fort fell, Confederate soldiers killed many Union defenders, including Black soldiers who had surrendered or were trying to surrender. This event is known as the Fort Pillow massacre. After the war, Forrest became the first Grand Wizard of the original Ku Klux Klan, a white supremacist group that used intimidation and violence against Black people during Reconstruction. His role at Fort Pillow and his connection to the Klan make him a deeply controversial figure in U.S. history.

Harvey Milk was an LGBTQ+ rights activist and politician in San Francisco, California. He ran a camera shop on Castro Street, the center of a neighborhood known for its gay community, and became a leading voice for equal rights. In 1977, he won a seat on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors, making him California’s first openly gay elected official. He encouraged LGBTQ+ people to be open about who they were and worked to build support across different communities. On November 27, 1978, former city supervisor Dan White shot and killed Milk and Mayor George Moscone at San Francisco City Hall. At White’s trial, his lawyers argued that his mental state reduced his responsibility for the killings. Milk remains an important figure in the history of LGBTQ+ political representation.

The United States Department of Commerce is a cabinet-level executive department that supports economic growth, trade, and technological innovation. It became a separate department in 1913, when the Department of Commerce and Labor was split into two agencies. Commerce oversees the U.S. Census Bureau, which counts the nation’s population every ten years. Census results help determine how many seats each state receives in the House of Representatives. During the 1920s, Herbert Hoover served as secretary of commerce before becoming president. He encouraged businesses to use common standards for products and practices and helped expand the federal government’s role in aviation and radio. These efforts show how the department has worked to shape the economy as well as collect information about it.

The Iran hostage crisis began in November 1979, when Iranian students seized the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and took American personnel hostage. It followed the Iranian Revolution, which overthrew the U.S.-backed shah and brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power. Many Iranians were angry that the United States had admitted the former shah for medical treatment and feared it might help restore him to power. President Jimmy Carter tried diplomacy, imposed sanctions, and authorized a military rescue mission called Operation Eagle Claw. In April 1980, the mission reached a staging site in Iran known as Desert One, but helicopter problems forced it to be abandoned. A collision there killed eight U.S. servicemen. After 444 days in captivity, the hostages were released on January 20, 1981, the day Ronald Reagan was inaugurated.

Atlanta was an important Confederate railroad and supply hub during the American Civil War. In 1864, Union general William Tecumseh Sherman led a campaign to capture it. After months of fighting, Confederate forces evacuated the city, and Union troops entered Atlanta in September. Its loss weakened the Confederacy and helped boost support for President Abraham Lincoln’s reelection. That November, Sherman’s army left Atlanta, destroying military resources as it began its “March to the Sea” toward Savannah. Union soldiers also damaged railroads by heating and twisting the rails so they could not easily be reused. In 1865, Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 15, which set aside land for some formerly enslaved families and became associated with the phrase “forty acres and a mule.” Atlanta became Georgia’s capital in 1868 and is now its largest city.

The Monroe Doctrine was a U.S. foreign policy announced by President James Monroe in his annual message to Congress in 1823. It warned European powers against establishing new colonies or interfering in the politics of independent countries in North and South America. In return, the United States said it would not interfere in Europe’s affairs or its existing colonies in the Americas. Britain proposed making a joint declaration with the United States, but Secretary of State John Quincy Adams argued that the United States should make its own statement and helped shape the doctrine. Adams also negotiated the 1819 Adams–Onís Treaty, through which Spain agreed to transfer Florida to the United States. He later became the sixth U.S. president.

Victoria Woodhull was an Ohio-born reformer and advocate for women’s suffrage who became the first woman to run for U.S. president. She and her sister, Tennessee Claflin, operated a brokerage firm on Wall Street at a time when few women worked in finance. In 1872, Woodhull was nominated for president by the Equal Rights Party, a third party that supported equal political rights for women. The party named Frederick Douglass, a formerly enslaved abolitionist and writer, as its vice-presidential nominee, though he did not participate in the campaign. Women did not yet have the right to vote nationwide, making Woodhull’s candidacy a bold challenge to the political rules and expectations of her time.

Ida B. Wells was an African American journalist and civil rights activist who investigated lynching, the murder of people by mobs without a trial. In the late 1800s, she used reporting and statistics to challenge claims used to justify violence against Black Americans. Her pamphlets Southern Horrors and The Red Record documented lynchings and called on the public to oppose them. Wells co-owned and edited the Free Speech and Headlight newspaper in Memphis, Tennessee. After she criticized a lynching there, a mob destroyed the newspaper’s office, but she continued her campaign from elsewhere. She later helped found the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, or NAACP. Decades later, Memphis was the site of a 1968 sanitation workers’ strike, during which Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I’ve Been to the Mountaintop” speech.

School desegregation is the process of ending rules and practices that separate public school students by race. For decades, many states, especially in the South, required Black and white children to attend different schools. In 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that state-mandated racial separation in public schools was unconstitutional, rejecting the idea that separate schools could be equal. The case grew from challenges by families in Topeka, Kansas, and other communities. A later Supreme Court order told districts to desegregate “with all deliberate speed,” but progress was often slow. Senator Harry Byrd led a campaign called “Massive Resistance” to obstruct school desegregation. Civil-rights advocates and federal courts continued pressing districts to end segregation and give students equal access to public education.

The Chief Justice of the United States presides over the Supreme Court, the nation’s highest court, and helps lead the federal judicial branch. Like the other justices, the Chief Justice hears cases and votes on decisions, but also has special responsibilities. For example, the Constitution requires the Chief Justice to preside when the Senate tries a president after impeachment. John Marshall, a Virginian, was the longest-serving Chief Justice, leading the Court from 1801 to 1835. His opinion in the 1803 case Marbury v. Madison established judicial review, the power of courts to declare laws unconstitutional. That decision made the Supreme Court a more powerful part of the federal government. Roger Taney succeeded Marshall in 1836 and later wrote the controversial Dred Scott decision.

Edwin McMasters Stanton served as President Abraham Lincoln’s secretary of war, directing the War Department during much of the Civil War. After Lincoln’s assassination, Stanton remained in the cabinet of his successor, Andrew Johnson. During Reconstruction, Johnson clashed with Congress over how to govern the former Confederate states, and Stanton supported Congress’s approach. In 1867, Congress passed the Tenure of Office Act, which restricted a president’s ability to remove certain federal officials without Senate approval. Johnson tried to dismiss Stanton in 1868, but Stanton refused to leave and barricaded himself in his office. The dispute became a test of presidential authority and helped lead the House of Representatives to impeach Johnson, the first U.S. president to be impeached. The Senate did not convict him.

In 1797, Alexander Hamilton published a lengthy public defense known as the Reynolds Pamphlet. Hamilton, who had served as the first U.S. secretary of the treasury, faced accusations that payments he made to James Reynolds were connected to financial misconduct in government. In the pamphlet, Hamilton admitted that he had had an affair with Reynolds’s wife, Maria Reynolds, while she was married. He argued that James had discovered the relationship and blackmailed him: the payments, Hamilton said, were meant to keep the affair secret, not to hide political corruption. By revealing private details to defend his public reputation, Hamilton cleared himself of that particular corruption charge but created a major personal and political scandal. The episode shows how leaders’ private actions can become matters of public debate.

During Andrew Jackson’s presidency (1829–1837), he often sought advice from trusted allies outside his official Cabinet, the appointed heads of executive departments. This informal circle became known as the Kitchen Cabinet, suggesting advisers who could reach the president through a more private route. It grew in importance amid the Petticoat Affair, a dispute in which Washington society, including Vice President John C. Calhoun’s wife Floride, shunned Peggy Eaton, the wife of Jackson’s secretary of war. Two important members were Martin Van Buren and Francis Preston Blair. Blair was a journalist who edited the pro-Jackson Washington Globe, a newspaper that defended Jackson’s policies, and later helped establish the Congressional Globe, which reported debates in Congress. The Kitchen Cabinet shows how a president can rely on unofficial advisers as well as formal officials.

The American Dream is the U.S. ideal that people can improve their lives through opportunity, hard work, and determination, regardless of the circumstances into which they were born. It is often linked to earning a good living, moving up the social ladder, and owning a home. Historian James Truslow Adams gave the idea a famous formulation in his 1931 book The Epic of America. For Adams, the dream meant more than becoming wealthy: it also meant having the chance to develop one’s abilities and lead a fuller life. The ideal has inspired many Americans, but it has also raised questions about whether everyone has equal access to opportunity. Sociologist Robert K. Merton argued that pressure to achieve widely valued goals, when opportunities to do so are blocked, can create “strain.”

Amy Coney Barrett is an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States, the nation’s highest federal court. Before joining the Court, she taught law at the University of Notre Dame and served as a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit. President Donald Trump nominated her in September 2020 to fill the vacancy left by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who had died that month. The Senate confirmed Barrett in October 2020, making her the fifth woman to serve on the Supreme Court. Her confirmation drew debate because it took place shortly before a presidential election, after the Senate had declined to consider President Barack Obama’s Supreme Court nominee Merrick Garland during the 2016 election year.

W. Mark Felt was a senior FBI official who rose to the bureau’s second-highest position. In the early 1970s, he secretly gave information to Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward, who worked with Carl Bernstein to investigate the Watergate scandal. The scandal began with a 1972 break-in at Democratic National Committee headquarters in the Watergate office complex in Washington, D.C. As the reporters investigated, they helped reveal efforts by President Richard Nixon’s administration to cover up its connection to the crime. Felt’s identity was kept secret for decades, and he was known by the codename “Deep Throat.” His family publicly identified him as the source in 2005. The Watergate scandal led Nixon to resign in 1974, making him the first U.S. president to leave office by resignation.

The Powhatan Confederacy was a network of Algonquian-speaking Indigenous communities in Virginia’s Tidewater region, led by a paramount chief. When English settlers founded Jamestown in 1607, the confederacy’s leader was Wahunsenacawh, whom the colonists often called Chief Powhatan. His principal village was Werowocomoco, and his daughter Pocahontas became known for her contacts with the English. The Powhatan communities and the Jamestown settlers traded goods, but they also fought as the colonists sought food and land. The confederacy was not a single village: it brought together many communities under Wahunsenacawh’s leadership. Its history shows that Indigenous peoples were powerful, organized participants in the early history of colonial Virginia.

Robert Mueller is a former federal prosecutor who became director of the FBI in September 2001, just one week before the September 11 terrorist attacks. He led the bureau for 12 years, then was appointed special counsel in 2017 to investigate Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and possible links between Russia and Donald Trump’s campaign. His investigation also examined whether Trump had obstructed justice. Mueller’s findings were presented in a report completed in March 2019. Before the full report became public, U.S. Attorney General William Barr sent Congress a letter summarizing its main conclusions. Critics argued that Barr’s summary gave a misleading impression of the report. The investigation and the debate over its findings became major events in recent U.S. political history.

William Randolph Hearst was an American newspaper publisher who helped make “yellow journalism” famous: reporting that used dramatic headlines, sensational stories, and sometimes unreliable claims to attract readers. In 1887, he took control of the San Francisco Examiner and went on to build a coast-to-coast media empire that included the New York Journal. His newspapers competed fiercely for readers, but their methods could harm the people they covered. In 1903, Hearst’s New York Journal falsely claimed that Annie Oakley had stolen money to support a cocaine addiction. Oakley, born Phoebe Ann Mosey, was a celebrated sharpshooter who performed in Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show. She challenged the false story in court, making her case an example of the real damage sensational reporting could cause.

On September 5, 1975, Lynette “Squeaky” Fromme, a member of the Manson Family, tried to assassinate President Gerald Ford in Sacramento, California. Ford had attended a Host Breakfast and was walking near the California State Capitol, the seat of state government, when Fromme pointed a pistol at him. The gun did not fire, and Secret Service agents quickly restrained her, so Ford was unharmed. Fromme was concerned about environmental damage, particularly threats to California’s redwood trees, and wanted to draw attention to the issue. The incident is known as the attempted assassination of Gerald Ford by Squeaky Fromme. It was one of two attempts on Ford’s life that September, but this one took place in Sacramento.

The Battle of the Little Bighorn took place in June 1876 near the Little Bighorn River in present-day Montana. It was part of a U.S. military campaign against Native peoples who resisted being forced onto reservations. Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors fought under leaders including Crazy Horse, while Sitting Bull helped bring their communities together. George Armstrong Custer, a former Civil War general and then a U.S. Army lieutenant colonel, led part of the 7th Cavalry Regiment in an attack on their large encampment. Native warriors overwhelmed Custer’s force, killing him and the soldiers with him. The Native victory was one of the most significant defeats suffered by the U.S. Army during the Plains Wars, though it led to intensified U.S. efforts to confine Native peoples to reservations.

The White House tapes were secret audio recordings of conversations in President Richard Nixon’s offices. They became crucial evidence during the Watergate scandal, which began with a 1972 break-in at Democratic National Committee headquarters by men connected to Nixon’s re-election campaign. Investigators wanted the recordings to learn what Nixon knew about the break-in and its cover-up, but Nixon refused to hand them over, arguing that executive privilege protected private presidential conversations. In the 1974 Supreme Court case United States v. Nixon, the justices unanimously rejected his broad claim of privilege and ordered him to turn over the subpoenaed tapes. One recording revealed Nixon’s role in the cover-up, severely weakening his support. Facing likely impeachment, he resigned in August 1974.

The Lost Cause of the Confederacy was a post-Civil War interpretation that portrayed the Southern rebellion as a noble defense against Northern aggression. It downplayed slavery’s central role in secession and the war, instead romanticizing Confederate leaders and soldiers. The interpretation spread through memoirs, histories, and monuments, shaping how many Americans remembered the conflict. Lost Cause supporters often cited Sherman’s March to the Sea as evidence of Northern aggression. In 1864, Union general William Tecumseh Sherman led troops across Georgia from Atlanta to Savannah, destroying railroads, supplies, and other resources that could support the Confederacy. After capturing Savannah, Sherman presented the city to President Abraham Lincoln as a “Christmas gift.” Understanding the Lost Cause means distinguishing its claims from the historical importance of slavery to the Confederacy.

The Doolittle Raid was an American air attack on the Japanese home islands on April 18, 1942, during World War II. It was a response to Japan’s surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in Hawaii the previous December, which had brought the United States into the war. Led by Lieutenant Colonel James “Jimmy” Doolittle, sixteen B-25 Mitchell bombers took off from the aircraft carrier USS Hornet, which had sailed from San Francisco carrying the planes and joined Vice Admiral William Halsey’s task force. The bombers struck targets in Japan, including Tokyo. They caused limited physical damage, but the raid raised American morale and showed that Japan’s home islands could be attacked.

H. H. Holmes was an American con artist and serial killer associated with Chicago during the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition. This international fair, also called the Chicago World’s Fair, marked 400 years since Christopher Columbus’s first voyage to the Americas. Its grand, pale buildings earned the fairgrounds the nickname “White City.” Holmes owned a building used as a hotel near the fair, where he could attract visitors looking for a place to stay. The building became known as the “Murder Castle” because of its connection to his crimes. Holmes later confessed to killing 27 people, although historians question parts of his account and the exact number of victims is uncertain. His story became one of the most notorious crime stories of the Gilded Age.

George McGovern was a World War II bomber pilot and a longtime South Dakota Democrat who served in the U.S. Senate. He won the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972 by strongly opposing the Vietnam War and calling for a change in American foreign policy. Choosing a running mate proved difficult. Massachusetts senator Ted Kennedy declined McGovern’s offer; Kennedy’s involvement in the 1969 Chappaquiddick car accident remained a political liability. McGovern then selected Senator Thomas Eagleton, but Eagleton withdrew after news emerged that he had received treatment for depression. McGovern replaced him with Sargent Shriver, who had directed the Peace Corps and served as U.S. ambassador to France. In the general election, President Richard Nixon defeated McGovern in a landslide.

The Chicago Seven trial grew out of protests against the Vietnam War outside the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, where Hubert Humphrey was nominated for president. In 1969, federal prosecutors charged antiwar activists with conspiring to incite riots and crossing state lines to do so. Eight men were originally charged, but the case against one defendant, Bobby Seale, was separated, leaving the group known as the Chicago Seven. The trial became a national spectacle because of clashes between the defendants, their lawyers, and Judge Julius Hoffman. William Kunstler, a prominent defense attorney who represented several defendants, repeatedly challenged the judge’s courtroom rulings and received multiple contempt citations. The case raised questions about the right to protest, freedom of speech, and how fairly the government treated opponents of the war.

John C. Calhoun was a South Carolina statesman who became Vice President under Andrew Jackson in 1829. Their relationship deteriorated over the federal government’s authority and tariff policy. Calhoun argued that a state could reject, or “nullify,” a federal law it considered unconstitutional, while Jackson strongly opposed that idea. The Petticoat Affair added to their tensions: Peggy Eaton, the wife of Jackson’s Secretary of War, was excluded from Washington society by women including Calhoun’s wife, Floride. Jackson supported Peggy Eaton and grew more distant from Calhoun, who resigned the vice presidency in 1832. As Jackson’s trust in some official advisers weakened, he turned to an informal circle that included Francis Preston Blair and Martin Van Buren. This group became known as the Kitchen Cabinet.

Valley Forge was the Pennsylvania encampment where George Washington’s Continental Army spent the winter of 1777–1778 during the American Revolutionary War. After the battles of Brandywine and Germantown, Washington’s troops withdrew to the site, where they faced bitter cold, shortages of food and clothing, and disease. Although Valley Forge was not a battle, it became a turning point in the army’s development. Baron von Steuben, a Prussian-born officer who had served under Frederick the Great, taught the soldiers disciplined drills and how to use bayonets effectively. His training helped turn a struggling collection of troops into a more organized and capable fighting force.

The Lavender Scare was a mid-20th-century campaign in which the U.S. government investigated and dismissed thousands of federal employees suspected of being gay or lesbian. It intensified during President Dwight D. Eisenhower’s administration, especially after he signed Executive Order 10450 in 1953. That order broadened security investigations of federal workers and allowed agencies to dismiss employees they considered security risks. Officials claimed that gay and lesbian workers might be vulnerable to blackmail, even though suspicion alone could cost someone a job. Employees at agencies such as the State Department faced questioning, forced disclosure of their private lives, and dismissal. The campaign was part of the wider Cold War atmosphere of fear and suspicion and shows how government security policies were used to discriminate against LGBT people.

The Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified in 1920, says that citizens cannot be denied the right to vote because of their sex. It was a major victory for the women’s suffrage movement, which had worked for decades to secure women’s voting rights. Activists used speeches, petitions, marches, and protests to press for change. Alice Paul’s National Woman’s Party organized the Silent Sentinels, who picketed the White House to demand action from President Woodrow Wilson. Before the amendment created nationwide constitutional protection, some states and territories had already allowed women to vote. In 1869, the territory that later became Wyoming granted women voting rights. Wyoming is also home to much of Yellowstone, the first U.S. national park.

Michael Dukakis was the governor of Massachusetts and the Democratic nominee for president in 1988. He ran against Republican George H. W. Bush. During the campaign, Dukakis rode in an M1 Abrams tank for a photo opportunity meant to show that he could lead the military. Images of him wearing a large helmet were widely mocked. His campaign was also hurt by attacks on Massachusetts’ prison furlough program, which allowed some prisoners temporary leave. Willie Horton, a convicted murderer, had escaped while on furlough and committed violent crimes in Maryland. Advertisements used Horton’s case to argue that Dukakis was too lenient on crime, although the furlough program had begun before Dukakis became governor. Bush won the election, and the tank photo and Horton ads remain well-known examples of how campaign images and advertising can shape voters’ views.

Georgia is a southeastern U.S. state on the Atlantic coast, with Atlanta as its capital. During the Civil War, Georgia was part of the Confederacy, and Atlanta was an important railroad hub. In 1864, Union general William Tecumseh Sherman captured Atlanta and led his troops across Georgia in a campaign called the March to the Sea. They destroyed railroads and supplies to weaken the Confederate war effort; rails bent into loops became known as “Sherman’s neckties.” The march ended at Savannah, a major port city on Georgia’s coast. Savannah had also been the site of a Revolutionary War siege in 1779, when Casimir Pulaski was mortally wounded while leading a cavalry charge.

The Great Migration was the movement of millions of African Americans from the rural South to cities in the North, Midwest, and West between about 1916 and 1970. Many left to escape Jim Crow laws, racial violence, and limited opportunities, while seeking better-paying jobs and greater freedom. Cities such as Chicago, Detroit, and New York grew as newcomers built communities and influenced American music, literature, politics, and culture. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, or NAACP, was a civil-rights organization that encouraged African Americans to seek opportunity beyond the Jim Crow South. W. E. B. Du Bois was one of its leading figures and edited its magazine, The Crisis. The Great Migration changed both the places migrants left and the cities where they settled.

The Battle of the Overpass was a violent labor confrontation in May 1937 outside Ford Motor Company’s River Rouge Plant near Detroit, Michigan. United Auto Workers organizers and supporters had gathered near an elevated pedestrian crossing to distribute leaflets calling for workers to join the union. Ford security guards attacked them, and photographs of the beating drew national attention to the struggle over workers’ right to organize. The confrontation became known as the Battle of the Overpass because of where it happened. Ford Motor Company was founded by Henry Ford, the industrialist who helped popularize assembly-line production of the Model T and introduced a $5-a-day wage for many of his workers. Despite those innovations, his company strongly resisted union organizing at the time.

The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire occurred on March 25, 1911, in Manhattan’s Asch Building, where the Triangle Shirtwaist Company made women’s blouses on the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors. The fire killed 146 people, most of them young immigrant garment workers. Many workers could not escape because some exit doors were locked, and the building’s fire escapes were inadequate. The tragedy exposed the dangers of crowded factories and weak workplace-safety rules. Public outrage strengthened campaigns for safer working conditions and labor protections. In response, New York state lawmakers created the New York State Factory Investigating Commission. This special body investigated industrial working conditions and recommended protections, helping bring about stronger rules for fire safety and other workplace hazards.

Breonna Taylor was a Black emergency medical worker who was fatally shot by police in her Louisville, Kentucky, apartment in March 2020. Her death became a focus of nationwide protests against police violence and for racial justice. Taylor was 26 years old, and her killing raised questions about how police carry out searches and use force. Contemporary American painter Amy Sherald later created a portrait of Taylor that showed her with grayscale skin tones against an aqua background. Sherald is also known for painting the official portrait of former first lady Michelle Obama. Her portrait of Taylor helped keep Taylor’s name and story in public view.

The White House Correspondents’ Dinner is an annual spring gathering in Washington, D.C., organized by the White House Correspondents’ Association, whose journalist members cover the president and the executive branch. It brings together reporters, political figures, and guests to celebrate journalism and support the association’s work. The program traditionally includes a comedian’s satirical remarks about politics and the news, as well as a routine in which the president jokes about himself. Presidents do not always attend, however. In 2017, when President Donald Trump did not attend, comedian Hasan Minhaj was the featured speaker and delivered a satirical roast of his administration. Minhaj had been a correspondent on The Daily Show under both Jon Stewart and Trevor Noah and later hosted the weekly Netflix series Patriot Act.

The Peggy Eaton Affair was a social and political scandal during President Andrew Jackson’s administration. Peggy Eaton, the wife of Secretary of War John Eaton, was shunned by Washington society women who questioned her reputation. Their refusal to welcome her became a national controversy because the women included Floride Calhoun, the wife of Vice President John C. Calhoun, and the dispute divided Jackson’s cabinet. Jackson defended the Eatons, while Secretary of State Martin Van Buren, a widower, publicly supported them and could avoid the social pressure placed on cabinet wives. The conflict helped weaken Jackson’s relationship with Calhoun. Van Buren later became Jackson’s vice president. Jackson also relied increasingly on informal advisers outside his official cabinet, a group nicknamed the “kitchen cabinet.”

Dred Scott v. Sandford was an 1857 Supreme Court case brought by Dred Scott, an enslaved man who argued that living with his owner in free territory had made him free. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney, who had succeeded John Marshall in 1836, wrote the Court’s majority opinion against Scott. The ruling declared that African Americans, whether enslaved or free, could not be citizens under the U.S. Constitution and therefore could not bring this kind of case in federal court. It also said Congress lacked the power to ban slavery in U.S. territories, invalidating the Missouri Compromise’s restriction on slavery north of a set boundary. The decision intensified conflict over slavery in the years before the Civil War.

Tuskegee University is a historically Black university founded in 1881 in Tuskegee, Alabama, with Booker T. Washington as its first leader. Originally called the Tuskegee Institute, it trained teachers and offered practical education in trades and agriculture. Agricultural scientist George Washington Carver taught there and researched crops such as peanuts and sweet potatoes. He promoted crop rotation, which helped farmers restore soil worn out by years of growing cotton. Carver also shared farming advice with nearby communities through a traveling classroom called the Jesup Wagon. During World War II, the university was associated with the training of the Tuskegee Airmen, a pioneering group of Black military pilots nicknamed the “Red Tails.” The separate, unethical Tuskegee syphilis study took place in the surrounding area, not at the university.

“I Have a Dream” is a speech delivered by Martin Luther King Jr. on August 28, 1963, during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. King, a Baptist minister and leader of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, helped organize the march and spoke from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. He called for an end to racial discrimination and urged the United States to fulfill its promise of equality. In one image, he compared that unfulfilled promise to a “bad check” returned for “insufficient funds.” King described his dream of a future in which his children would be judged not by the color of their skin but by their character. The speech became one of the best-known addresses of the civil rights movement.

Draft cards were documents issued to men who registered with the Selective Service System, the U.S. federal agency responsible for keeping records of men eligible for compulsory military service and administering the draft. During the Vietnam War, the draft could require young men to serve in the armed forces, even if they opposed the war. This made draft cards a powerful symbol of the government’s ability to call people into military service. Some anti-war protesters publicly burned their draft cards to show opposition to both the war and conscription. Burning a card did not erase a person’s registration, but it drew attention to the protesters’ message. Other Vietnam War protests included students wearing black armbands and demonstrators marching at the Pentagon.

Barry Goldwater was a Republican senator from Arizona and a leading voice for American conservatism during the Cold War. He argued for limited federal government, individual liberty, and a strong national defense. In 1964, Goldwater won the Republican presidential nomination after a contest with New York governor Nelson Rockefeller, whose views were more moderate. Goldwater then faced Democratic president Lyndon B. Johnson and lost the general election in a landslide. During the campaign, actor Ronald Reagan delivered a nationally televised speech supporting Goldwater called “A Time for Choosing.” Reagan warned that an expanding federal government threatened individual freedom. Although Goldwater lost, the speech helped make Reagan a national political figure, and Goldwater’s campaign helped strengthen the conservative movement within the Republican Party.

A slave revolt is an organized uprising in which enslaved people resist their enslavers, often seeking freedom and an end to forced labor. One major example was the 1739 Stono Rebellion in South Carolina, near the Stono River, led by an enslaved man sometimes called Cato. Another was Nat Turner’s Rebellion, which began in Southampton County, Virginia, in 1831. Turner, an enslaved preacher, believed a solar eclipse was a sign that he should act. His group killed dozens of white residents before the rebellion was suppressed, and Turner was later captured and executed. Revolts were rare and dangerous because enslavers used armed force and harsh punishments to stop them, but they show that enslaved people actively resisted slavery.

Marcus Garvey was a Jamaican-born activist and Black nationalist who urged people of African descent to take pride in their heritage, build economic independence, and work together across national borders. Born in St. Ann’s Bay, Jamaica, he founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) there in 1914. It grew into a mass-membership organization promoting Black unity and advancement, especially after Garvey moved to the United States. His belief in cooperation among African-descended people worldwide is called Pan-Africanism. Garvey also promoted a “Back to Africa” movement and launched the Black Star Line, a shipping company intended to strengthen Black-owned business and connections with Africa. Encouraging pride in natural Black hair, he advised people not to “remove the kinks from your hair” but to “remove the kinks from your brain.”

Brad Raffensperger is a Georgia Republican who was elected the state’s secretary of state in 2018. That job includes overseeing elections, so he played an important role during the 2020 presidential contest. Joe Biden narrowly won Georgia, and after the election, Donald Trump challenged the result. In a January 2021 phone call, Trump urged Raffensperger to “find” enough votes to change the outcome in Trump’s favor. Raffensperger did not change the certified result. The Washington Post published a recording of the call, bringing the conversation to widespread public attention. The episode became a major example of the pressure election officials faced after the 2020 election.

Regents of the University of California v. Bakke was a 1978 Supreme Court case about affirmative action, a policy intended to expand opportunities for groups that have faced discrimination. The UC Davis School of Medicine, a public medical school, reserved 16 of the 100 seats in each entering class for applicants from disadvantaged groups. Allan Bakke, who had been denied admission, challenged the program. The Court ruled that setting aside a fixed number of seats on the basis of race was unconstitutional and ordered UC Davis to admit Bakke. At the same time, it allowed colleges to consider an applicant’s race as one factor among many in an individualized admissions decision. The case therefore rejected explicit racial quotas without banning all consideration of race in admissions.

The Vietnam War was a Cold War conflict fought from 1955 to 1975 between communist North Vietnam and its allies and U.S.-backed South Vietnam and other anti-communist forces. The United States became deeply involved because its leaders feared that a communist victory in Vietnam would strengthen communist influence across Southeast Asia. American troops fought alongside South Vietnamese forces, while opposition to the war grew at home. In 1971, Daniel Ellsberg leaked the Pentagon Papers, a classified U.S. Defense Department study of American involvement in Vietnam, to The New York Times. The documents showed that U.S. officials had misled the public about the war. Although a ceasefire agreement was reached in 1973, fighting continued. North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon in 1975, ending the war; the city was later renamed Ho Chi Minh City.

The United States Secretary of State is the Cabinet official who heads the Department of State and helps the president direct U.S. diplomacy and foreign policy. The secretary works with other countries, oversees American embassies, and helps negotiate agreements. Hillary Clinton held this position from 2009 to 2013, after Condoleezza Rice. During Clinton’s tenure, the United States helped organize sanctions against Iran to pressure it to limit its nuclear program. In 2012, attackers struck a U.S. diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya, killing U.S. ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. Clinton later ran for president in 2016 and wrote about her election loss in her memoir What Happened.

Fidel Castro was a Cuban revolutionary who led the 26th of July Movement against the government of Fulgencio Batista. The movement was named for a failed July 26, 1953, attack on the Moncada Barracks. After that attack, Castro gave a speech known as “History Will Absolve Me.” During the Cuban Revolution, rebels also attacked the Presidential Palace in Havana, which is still Cuba’s capital. Batista fled in 1959, and Castro took power, later establishing a communist government. He led Cuba for decades, making it a major focus of Cold War tensions with the United States. In 2008, he formally transferred power to his brother Raúl Castro.

The Embargo Act of 1807 was a law signed by Thomas Jefferson, the third U.S. president. At the time, Britain and France were at war and were interfering with American ships and sailors. Jefferson hoped that stopping American trade with foreign nations would keep the United States out of the conflict and pressure both countries to respect American rights at sea. Instead, the embargo badly hurt American merchants, sailors, and farmers who depended on overseas trade, while Britain and France continued their policies. The law became deeply unpopular and was replaced in 1809. Jefferson, a Virginian who drafted the Declaration of Independence, lived at Monticello and had earlier overseen the Louisiana Purchase.

D. C. Stephenson was the Grand Dragon, or state leader, of the Ku Klux Klan in Indiana during the 1920s. The Klan was a white supremacist organization that used intimidation and violence, especially against Black Americans, while also targeting Catholics, Jews, and immigrants. Stephenson recruited members and used their votes to become a powerful political boss with influence over Indiana officials. In 1925, he abducted and assaulted Madge Oberholtzer, an Indianapolis woman. She later died, but before her death she gave a statement describing what had happened. Stephenson was convicted of her murder and sentenced to life in prison. The trial exposed his crimes and damaged the Klan’s reputation, helping bring about a sharp decline in its political power in Indiana.

Daniel Ellsberg was an American military analyst who had worked for the RAND Corporation, a research organization. In 1971, he gave newspapers a classified, multivolume study of U.S. decision-making in the Vietnam War. Defense Secretary Robert McNamara had commissioned the study, which became known as the Pentagon Papers. The documents showed that U.S. leaders had expanded American involvement in Vietnam while often giving the public a misleading picture of the war. The New York Times began publishing stories based on the papers, and the government tried to stop further publication, arguing that it threatened national security. The resulting Supreme Court case became an important test of freedom of the press and the government’s power to keep information secret.

Peter Meijer is a Michigan Republican who represented the state’s 3rd Congressional District, which includes Grand Rapids, from 2021 to 2023. He succeeded Justin Amash in the House of Representatives. On January 6, 2021, supporters of President Donald Trump attacked the U.S. Capitol while Congress was meeting to certify the results of the 2020 presidential election. The House later voted to impeach Trump over his role in the attack, and Meijer was one of ten House Republicans who supported impeachment. That vote drew opposition from some Republican voters. In the 2022 Republican primary, Meijer lost to John Gibbs, ending his time in Congress after one term. Meijer’s surname is also the name of a Midwestern supermarket chain founded by his family.

George III was Britain’s king during the American Revolution. In 1763, he issued a proclamation restricting colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains. The British government hoped to reduce conflict with Native peoples, but many colonists resented the limit on westward expansion. George III remained on the throne as disputes over British taxes and colonial rights grew into war. His reign also saw unrest in Britain. In 1780, the Gordon riots broke out in London in opposition to the Catholic Relief Act, which had eased some restrictions on Catholics. The riots were named for Lord George Gordon, who led the Protestant Association. Crowds attacked buildings across the city, and Newgate Prison was partly destroyed.

Ratified in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights, the First Amendment protects several freedoms: religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and the right to petition the government. It bars Congress from establishing an official religion and protects people’s free exercise of religion. These freedoms are broad, but freedom of speech does not cover every kind of expression. Obscenity, for example, is generally outside First Amendment protection, while pornography in general is not automatically considered obscene. In Roth v. United States, the Supreme Court described obscenity as material that appeals to the “prurient interest,” meaning an unhealthy or excessive interest in sex. The Court later established a three-part test in Miller v. California to decide whether material is legally obscene.

Melania Trump was born in Novo Mesto, Slovenia, and grew up in Sevnica. Before moving to the United States, she worked as a fashion model. She married businessman and television personality Donald Trump in 2005 and became first lady when he took office as U.S. president in 2017. As first lady, she represented the country at official events and focused much of her work on issues affecting children. In 2018, she introduced Be Best, a White House initiative that promoted children’s well-being. Its main areas of concern included online safety, the effects of opioid abuse on families, and the importance of kindness and respectful behavior. She was the first U.S. first lady born in Slovenia.

The International Brotherhood of Teamsters, often called the Teamsters Union, became one of the largest labor unions in the United States. It grew by organizing truck drivers and later represented other transport and delivery workers. Like other unions, it negotiated with employers over pay, benefits, and working conditions. Jimmy Hoffa led the Teamsters during much of its best-known period in the mid-20th century, but the union also faced investigations into corruption and links to organized crime. During Senate hearings on labor racketeering, committee counsel Robert F. Kennedy gained national attention by questioning Hoffa. Kennedy later ran for president and won California’s 1968 Democratic primary, but he was shot at the Ambassador Hotel in Los Angeles that night. Hoffa disappeared in 1975, and his fate remains unknown.

The flag of the United States is a national emblem that represents the country’s history and its states. In 1777, during the American Revolution, the Continental Congress called for a flag with thirteen alternating red and white stripes and thirteen white stars on a blue field. The stripes represent the original thirteen colonies; as new states joined the nation, the number of stars grew. Today’s flag has fifty stars and thirteen stripes. A famous flag flew over Fort McHenry in Baltimore during a British bombardment in 1814. When Francis Scott Key saw that the flag was still visible afterward, he wrote verses first titled “Defence of Fort M’Henry.” Those verses later became the lyrics of “The Star-Spangled Banner,” the national anthem.

Indian reservations are areas of land set aside for federally recognized Native American tribes. Tribal governments exercise authority there alongside the federal government, although the balance of power varies. Reservation boundaries and legal status have been shaped by treaties, federal laws, and government recognition of tribes. Many reservations were created as the United States took control of Native lands during the 19th century. In 1887, the Dawes Act, also called the Dawes Severalty Act, authorized the division of communal tribal lands into individual allotments for Native households. Land left over after allotment could be opened to non-Native settlers. This policy broke up much reservation land and reduced the land held by many tribes. Today, reservations remain important homelands where tribes govern communities and maintain cultural traditions.

Amendments to the United States Constitution are formal changes to the nation’s founding charter. An amendment must be proposed and then ratified by the required number of states before it becomes part of the Constitution. There are 27 ratified amendments; the first ten are known as the Bill of Rights. The Eleventh Amendment addressed a Supreme Court ruling in Chisholm v. Georgia about lawsuits against states. The Twenty-First Amendment repealed national Prohibition in 1933. Gregory Watson helped revive a long-forgotten proposal about congressional pay, which became the Twenty-Seventh Amendment in 1992. Not every proposed amendment succeeds. The Equal Rights Amendment, approved by Congress in 1972, sought to prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex but did not gain ratification from enough states, even after its deadline was extended.

California is a U.S. state on the Pacific Coast, but it was part of Mexico in 1846. That year, amid rising tensions between the United States and Mexico, American settlers in the town of Sonoma declared the short-lived Bear Flag Republic. The Mexican-American War was fought from 1846 to 1848 while James K. Polk was U.S. president. U.S. forces took control of California during the war, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the conflict in 1848. Under that treaty, Mexico ceded California and other western territories to the United States. Soon afterward, the discovery of gold drew many newcomers to California, which became a state in 1850. Today, it is known for its major cities, productive farmland, mountains, deserts, and Pacific coastline.

William Marbury was a Maryland banker whom outgoing President John Adams appointed as a justice of the peace near the end of his presidency. Marbury’s commission, the official document confirming his appointment, was not delivered before Thomas Jefferson took office. Jefferson’s administration withheld it, so Marbury asked the Supreme Court to order Secretary of State James Madison to deliver it. In the 1803 case Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that Marbury was entitled to the commission but that the Court could not issue the order he requested. The justices held that the part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 that would have given them that power was unconstitutional. This decision established judicial review: the Supreme Court’s power to declare laws that conflict with the Constitution invalid.

The Dawes Act was a federal law passed by Congress in 1887 and named for Henry L. Dawes, the Republican senator from Massachusetts who introduced the allotment bill. It changed how many Native American tribes held land. Instead of recognizing land owned communally by a tribe, the government divided it into parcels, or allotments, for individual Native American families. Supporters claimed this would encourage farming and help Native Americans adopt the individual landownership common in U.S. society. Land left over after allotments could be acquired by the government and opened to non-Native settlers. As a result, tribes lost large amounts of land, and the law undermined communal traditions and tribal self-government. The Dawes Act was one part of a broader federal effort to assimilate Native Americans into mainstream American society.

The Nullification Crisis was a confrontation between South Carolina and the federal government in 1832–1833 over tariffs, or taxes on imported goods. Many South Carolinians believed the tariffs hurt their economy and unfairly benefited Northern industries. The state declared that it could “nullify” the federal tariff laws, meaning they would not be enforced within South Carolina. John C. Calhoun, a South Carolina politician and a leading defender of nullification, resigned as U.S. vice president in December 1832 after being elected to the Senate, where he continued to argue for the doctrine. President Andrew Jackson rejected South Carolina’s claim and insisted that federal law must be obeyed. A compromise tariff helped end the immediate crisis, but the dispute revealed a growing conflict over the power of states and the federal government.

In March 1776, as American leaders debated independence and the kind of government the colonies should create, Abigail Adams wrote to her husband, John Adams, urging him to “Remember the Ladies.” John was helping shape the new nation’s political future and would later become the second U.S. president. In the letter, Abigail warned against putting “unlimited power” in husbands’ hands and argued that women’s interests should not be overlooked in the new laws. Her appeal showed how the Revolution’s ideas about liberty raised questions about women’s place in society, even though women were generally excluded from formal politics. The letter, now commonly called the “Remember the Ladies” letter, is one of hundreds Abigail and John exchanged.

The Civil Rights Movement was a mid-20th-century campaign to end Jim Crow segregation and win equal treatment under the law and greater political participation for African Americans. Activists used boycotts, marches, court cases, and other forms of nonviolent protest. Major milestones included the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Freedom Rides, and campaigns to protect Black Americans’ right to vote. Alabama was the site of several important events. In Birmingham, Martin Luther King Jr. wrote his famous “Letter from Birmingham Jail” after being arrested during protests against segregation. In the Selma voting-rights campaign, police attacked marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge, injuring future Congressman John Lewis. King later led a march from Selma to Alabama’s capital, Montgomery, to demand voting rights.

The Populist Party, also called the People’s Party, emerged in the late nineteenth century as farmers struggled with debt, low crop prices, and the power of banks and railroads. It sought reforms that would help farmers and working people, including government regulation of railroads and bimetallism, a monetary system using both gold and silver. Populists hoped that adding silver to the money supply would make debts easier to repay. In the 1892 presidential election, the party nominated James B. Weaver, a former Union general and Iowa congressman. Weaver won 22 electoral votes and carried several western states. Four years later, many Populists supported Democrat William Jennings Bryan, whose “Cross of Gold” speech also argued for silver.

Van Orden v. Perry was a 2005 U.S. Supreme Court case about a Ten Commandments monument on the grounds of the Texas State Capitol. Thomas Van Orden argued that displaying the monument on government property violated the First Amendment’s Establishment Clause, which limits government support for religion. Greg Abbott, then the Texas attorney general, argued before the Court in defense of the monument. The justices ruled that it could remain, considering its historical setting and the other monuments nearby rather than treating it only as a religious display. The decision did not mean every Ten Commandments display on public property is constitutional; the setting matters. Abbott later became governor of Texas and held that office during the state’s February 2021 winter storm and power-grid crisis.

School desegregation in the United States was the civil-rights struggle to end laws and policies that separated Black and white students in public schools. For decades, segregation was defended under the “separate but equal” doctrine, even though schools for Black students often had fewer resources. In 1954, the Supreme Court unanimously decided Brown v. Board of Education, a case that included a challenge from Topeka, Kansas. The Court held that racially segregated public schools violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because separate schools were inherently unequal. The ruling did not end segregation overnight. Some communities resisted, and federal action was sometimes needed to enforce it, as when troops protected the Little Rock Nine while they attended a previously all-white high school in Arkansas.

John J. Pershing, nicknamed “Black Jack,” was a U.S. Army officer who served with the 10th Cavalry, a regiment of Black soldiers known as Buffalo Soldiers. In 1916, after the Mexican revolutionary Pancho Villa and his forces raided Columbus, New Mexico, Pershing led the Punitive Expedition across the border to capture him. The expedition pursued Villa but did not catch him. When the United States entered World War I in 1917, Pershing became commander of the American Expeditionary Forces, the U.S. troops sent to fight in Europe. He helped organize a rapidly growing army and led it during major battles against Germany. His career connected U.S. military campaigns in the American West and Mexico with the nation’s role in World War I.

In November 1775, during the American Revolution, Lord Dunmore, the British royal governor of Virginia, issued Lord Dunmore’s Proclamation. It offered freedom to enslaved people held by colonists rebelling against Britain if they escaped and joined British forces. The offer applied to people enslaved by rebels, not to everyone enslaved in Virginia. Dunmore hoped to weaken the rebellion and gain troops for the British. Some men who responded joined a Black Loyalist unit called the Ethiopian Regiment, which fought in the Virginia campaign. Its soldiers used the motto “Liberty to Slaves” on their uniforms. The proclamation gave some enslaved people a chance to seek freedom, while also revealing a painful contradiction: many colonists demanded liberty from Britain but continued to enslave others.

Francis Scott Key was an American lawyer and poet best known for writing the words to “The Star-Spangled Banner.” During the War of 1812, he watched British ships bombard Fort McHenry in Baltimore in 1814 while he was aboard a truce ship. When he saw the American flag still flying over the fort at dawn, he wrote a poem first published as “Defence of Fort M’Henry.” Set to an existing tune, it became a patriotic song and was later adopted as the U.S. national anthem. Key also practiced law in Washington, D.C. In 1832, he represented Sam Houston before the House of Representatives after Houston beat Ohio congressman William Stanbery with a cane. Houston had attacked Stanbery following accusations that he had defrauded the Cherokee.

On January 28, 1986, NASA’s Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff, killing all seven crew members, including Christa McAuliffe, a teacher who had planned to give lessons from space. The disaster was linked to rubber seals called O-rings in a rocket booster. Unusually cold weather had made them less flexible, allowing hot gases to escape. Engineers at the booster manufacturer, Morton Thiokol, had warned about launching in the cold, but management did not stop the launch. A commission led by William Rogers investigated the disaster. Its members included astronaut Sally Ride and physicist Richard Feynman, who placed a piece of O-ring material in ice water to demonstrate how cold could prevent the seal from working properly.

Independence Day is a U.S. federal holiday celebrated each year on July 4. It commemorates the Continental Congress’s adoption of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. That document announced that the thirteen American colonies were separating from Great Britain and explained their reasons for doing so. Americans often mark the holiday with fireworks, parades, concerts, and other patriotic celebrations. The date also appears in literature: poet William Carlos Williams wrote a poem titled “The 4th of July” that depicts two robins crying. If a question asks for the holiday, the answer is Independence Day; if it asks for the title of Williams’s poem about the robins, the answer is “The 4th of July.”

Roger Williams was a Puritan minister in colonial New England who argued that people should be free to follow their own religious beliefs. He also believed that government should not control religion, an idea known as separation of church and state. These views put him at odds with leaders of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, who banished him. In 1636, Williams established a settlement on Narragansett Bay, on land he obtained from the Narragansett people. He named it Providence because he believed God had guided and protected him. Providence became part of the colony of Rhode Island, which Williams helped found, and later became the state’s capital. Williams also opposed slavery and wrote a book about the language and culture of the Narragansett people.

Ellis Island, in New York Harbor between New York and New Jersey, was the United States’ principal immigration inspection station from 1892 to 1954. During the immigration boom of the late 1800s and early 1900s, millions of people passed through it, many seeking safety or new opportunities after leaving Europe. Officials checked arrivals’ documents and health before allowing them to enter the country. As their ships approached, immigrants could see the nearby Statue of Liberty, a gift from France showing a woman holding a torch and a tablet. On the West Coast, Angel Island in California’s San Francisco Bay served as an immigration station for many arrivals from China and Japan. Because of this similar role, Angel Island is sometimes called the “Ellis Island of the West.”

The Dust Bowl was a drought and environmental disaster that struck the Great Plains in the 1930s. Years of intensive farming had removed much of the native grass that held the soil in place. When rain failed and crops died, strong winds swept up the exposed topsoil, creating huge dust storms known as “black blizzards.” One especially severe storm in 1935 became known as Black Sunday. Farms failed, and many families lost their homes and livelihoods. Some, including migrants called “Okies,” traveled west to California in search of work. The Dust Bowl made the Great Depression worse by adding to the unemployment and hardship already widespread across the United States. The Great Depression was the nationwide economic crisis that began after the 1929 stock market crash.

The Spoils System was a practice in 19th-century U.S. politics in which winning party leaders gave government jobs to campaign workers, friends, and loyal supporters instead of choosing employees for their qualifications. These jobs were a form of political patronage: supporters helped a party win, then received positions as a reward. Critics argued that this could put unqualified people in public offices and encourage corruption. The Stalwarts, a faction of the Republican Party, defended patronage, while reformers wanted hiring based on merit. Opposition to the Spoils System grew after President James A. Garfield was assassinated in 1881 by a disappointed office seeker. In 1883, President Chester A. Arthur signed the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act, which created a commission to oversee federal hiring and introduced competitive examinations for some government positions.

The Iran-Contra affair was a political scandal during President Ronald Reagan’s administration in the 1980s. U.S. officials secretly arranged arms sales to Iran, a Middle Eastern country, despite restrictions on such sales. They then diverted some of the money to the Contras, rebels fighting Nicaragua’s left-wing government, even though Congress had restricted U.S. aid to the group. The scheme became public in 1986 and raised questions about whether administration officials had evaded the law and misled Congress. Oliver North, a Marine lieutenant colonel working on the National Security Council staff, helped organize the arms transfers and the diversion of proceeds. He later became a prominent witness at televised congressional hearings investigating the affair.

A labor strike happens when workers collectively stop working to press an employer or government for changes, such as higher pay, safer conditions, or political reforms. Striking gives employees more bargaining power than negotiating one by one, but it can also lead to conflict. In the 1892 Homestead Strike, steelworkers clashed with Pinkerton agents brought in during a dispute with Carnegie Steel. In 1894, workers at the Pullman railway-car company protested wage reductions. The American Railway Union, led by Eugene V. Debs, supported them by boycotting trains carrying Pullman cars. A federal court ordered the boycott to end, and Debs was imprisoned for contempt of court. He later became a Socialist Party presidential candidate. These events show both the power of organized labor and the resistance strikes could face.

Hunter Biden is an American lawyer and businessman and the son of Joe Biden, the 46th U.S. president. In 2014, Hunter joined the board of Burisma Holdings, a Ukrainian natural-gas producer. His work for Burisma drew criticism and became a recurring issue in debates about U.S.–Ukraine policy and the 2020 presidential election. During that election, news stories about a laptop said to belong to Hunter Biden added to the controversy, although journalists could not verify all the data attributed to it. Twitter’s decision to block links to some of those stories also sparked debate about how social media companies handle political news. Critics raised Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which generally protects websites from legal liability for content posted by their users.

Dorothea Dix was a nineteenth-century American reformer who worked to improve the treatment of people with mental illness. While visiting jails and almshouses, which sheltered people who were poor, she found that many people with mental illness were confined in harsh conditions without proper care. Dix gathered evidence, reported what she saw to lawmakers, and argued that states should pay for facilities devoted to their treatment rather than keep them in prisons. Her campaign helped establish public asylums, including one separate from prisons in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Harrisburg is the state capital and lies along the Susquehanna River. Although care in asylums did not always meet Dix’s hopes, her advocacy changed how many Americans thought about the government’s responsibility to people with mental illness.

The Kent State Massacre occurred on May 4, 1970, at Kent State University in Ohio. Students were protesting the Vietnam War, especially the U.S. expansion of military operations into neighboring Cambodia. President Richard Nixon had announced the Cambodian operation in a televised address on April 30, prompting protests on college campuses across the country. At Kent State, Ohio National Guard troops confronted demonstrators and fired into a crowd, killing four students and wounding nine. The shootings shocked the nation and led to more protests and campus closures. The event became a lasting symbol of the deep divisions in the United States over the Vietnam War and the use of force against protesters.

Aaron Burr was a New York politician who served in the U.S. Senate and became the third vice president of the United States under Thomas Jefferson. In the election of 1800, Jefferson and Burr received the same number of electoral votes, so the House of Representatives chose Jefferson as president and Burr as vice president. Burr was also an early leader of Tammany Hall, a New York political organization that grew from a social club into a powerful Democratic Party machine. His political career is now often overshadowed by a duel in 1804 at Weehawken, New Jersey. Burr fatally wounded Alexander Hamilton, a Founding Father, leading Federalist, and the first U.S. secretary of the Treasury.

Michigan is a Great Lakes state made up of two main land areas: the Lower Peninsula and the Upper Peninsula. The western Upper Peninsula contains Copper Country, a region where copper mining was once a major industry. In July 1913, miners represented by the Western Federation of Miners began a walkout there. They wanted mine owners to recognize their union and shorten their working hours. The conflict, known as the Copper Country Strike of 1913–1914, lasted for months and became especially remembered for the Italian Hall disaster in Calumet. At a Christmas Eve gathering for strikers’ families, a false cry of “fire” caused a rush toward the exits, and more than 70 people, mostly children, died. The strike is an important example of the struggles between workers and mine owners in U.S. labor history.

James Armistead Lafayette was an enslaved Virginian who served as a spy for the Continental Army during the American Revolution. With permission from his enslaver, he posed as a runaway seeking to help the British, which gave him access to their camps. He passed information about British forces commanded by Lord Cornwallis to the Marquis de Lafayette, an American commander. That intelligence helped the Continental and French armies prepare their campaign in Virginia. In 1781, they trapped Cornwallis’s army at the Siege of Yorktown, where he surrendered. The surrender effectively secured American victory in the war. Although Armistead had helped win independence, he remained enslaved afterward. He petitioned the Virginia legislature for freedom, which it granted in 1787. He later added “Lafayette” to his name in honor of the commander he had served.

Lawrence v. Texas was a 2003 U.S. Supreme Court decision that struck down a Texas law criminalizing private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults. The case began after police arrested John Lawrence and another man in Lawrence’s home. Writing for the five-justice majority, Associate Justice Anthony Kennedy explained that the liberty protected by the Fourteenth Amendment includes adults’ freedom to form private, consensual intimate relationships without government punishment. The Court rejected the reasoning of its earlier decision in Bowers v. Hardwick, which had allowed states to criminalize such activity. Lawrence v. Texas was an important victory for LGBTQ+ civil rights, though it did not itself establish a right to same-sex marriage; the Court recognized that right in Obergefell v. Hodges in 2015.

Ted Sorensen was a Nebraska-born lawyer who joined John F. Kennedy’s Senate staff in 1953 and became one of his closest advisers and speechwriters. Kennedy was a Massachusetts Democrat who became president in January 1961. Sorensen helped craft Kennedy’s inaugural address, including its famous appeal: “Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.” The line urged Americans to serve their nation rather than simply expect help from it. Sorensen also worked on Kennedy’s 1962 speech at Rice University, which made the case for sending people to the Moon by asking why Rice played football against Texas. Their long partnership helped Kennedy communicate his goals in memorable language.

Pat Buchanan is an American conservative commentator and former presidential candidate known for his views on national identity, religion, and traditional values. He served as a speechwriter and communications director in President Richard Nixon’s White House. Buchanan later challenged George H. W. Bush for the Republican presidential nomination in 1992 and sought the nomination again in 1996. At the 1992 Republican National Convention, he gave a fiery prime-time speech portraying American politics as a struggle over religious and cultural values, an example of what became known as the “culture wars.” In 2000, he ran for president as the Reform Party nominee. That year, Florida’s confusing “butterfly ballot” in Palm Beach County may have caused some voters who intended to support Al Gore to vote for Buchanan instead.

Rodney King was an African American motorist whose beating by Los Angeles police officers became a major event in U.S. civil rights history. In March 1991, officers stopped King after a high-speed pursuit and repeatedly struck him while a bystander recorded the scene on videotape. The footage was broadcast widely, raising questions about police brutality and racial injustice. Four officers were charged, but their acquittal in April 1992 helped trigger days of riots in Los Angeles. Violence and looting spread from South Central Los Angeles to nearby communities, including Inglewood, Compton, and Long Beach. As the unrest continued, King publicly asked, “Can we all get along?” His case drew national attention to the use of excessive force by police.

The United States House of Representatives is one of the two chambers of Congress, the federal legislature established by the Constitution. The other chamber is the Senate, where every state has two senators. In the House, states receive different numbers of seats based on their populations, though each state has at least one representative. To determine how many seats each state gets, the federal government conducts a nationwide population count called the U.S. decennial census every ten years. Census results are used to reapportion, or redistribute, House seats among the states as populations change. UNIVAC I, an early computer, helped process the 1950 census. In 2020, people could respond to the census online or by phone.

United Airlines Flight 93 was the fourth passenger jet hijacked during the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. It had departed from Newark, New Jersey, bound for San Francisco when al-Qaeda hijackers seized it. After learning through phone calls that other hijacked planes had struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, passengers and crew members decided to fight back and tried to retake the cockpit. The plane crashed in a field in Pennsylvania’s Laurel Highlands before it could reach the hijackers’ intended target. All 44 people aboard died. The crash site is commonly identified with the nearby borough of Shanksville, Pennsylvania, and is now preserved as the Flight 93 National Memorial. Their resistance is remembered as an act of courage during the deadliest terrorist attack in U.S. history.

The Venona Project was a U.S.-led codebreaking program that began during World War II and continued into the Cold War. At Arlington Hall in Virginia, U.S. Army cryptanalysts studied intercepted Soviet intelligence messages. The messages had been encrypted with one-time pads, a method that should be extremely difficult to break when each pad is used only once. Soviet operators sometimes reused pad material, however, giving codebreakers clues that helped them decrypt parts of the traffic. Linguist and cryptanalyst Meredith Gardner joined the Army team in 1946 and made a major breakthrough in reading the messages. Venona’s findings helped reveal Soviet espionage networks in the United States and showed how intercepting and decoding secret communications can produce valuable intelligence.

The Iraq War was a U.S.-led conflict that began in 2003 with an invasion of Iraq to topple the government of Saddam Hussein. President George W.
