Bush ordered the invasion during his first term, arguing that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, although such weapons were not found. After Iraqi forces were defeated, Bush gave a speech aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln in May 2003. A banner behind him read “Mission Accomplished,” but the war was far from over. Fighting continued as U.S. and allied forces faced an insurgency and violence among Iraqi groups. The conflict cost many lives and reshaped Iraq’s government. U.S. forces withdrew from Iraq in 2011.

Ted Kennedy, also known as Edward M. Kennedy, was a Massachusetts Democrat who served in the U.S. Senate for nearly five decades. He was a strong supporter of national health insurance and challenged President Jimmy Carter for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1980. After losing, Kennedy delivered a convention speech remembered for its closing words, “The dream shall never die.” His presidential ambitions were shadowed by the Chappaquiddick incident. In 1969, Kennedy drove off Dike Bridge on Chappaquiddick, a small Massachusetts island. His passenger, Mary Jo Kopechne, died, and Kennedy did not immediately report the crash to police. The incident remained a major political liability for him, even as he continued a long and influential Senate career.

The Second Red Scare was a period of widespread fear of communism in the United States after World War II, especially in the late 1940s and 1950s. As the Cold War began, many Americans worried that supporters of the Soviet Union had entered the U.S. government and other institutions. Federal employees faced loyalty investigations, congressional committees questioned suspected communists, and people in entertainment could be blacklisted, losing work because of their beliefs or associations. Wisconsin senator Joseph McCarthy became famous for accusing people of communist ties, often without solid evidence. His name became closely linked to this era of political fear and repression. Televised hearings in 1954, in which McCarthy’s investigative subcommittee clashed with the U.S. Army, damaged his public standing. The Senate censured him later that year.

Margaret Sanger was an American nurse and birth-control activist who argued that women should have access to information about contraception and family planning. In 1916, she and her sister Ethel Byrne opened the first birth-control clinic in the United States, in the Brownsville neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York. The clinic was soon shut down, and Sanger was arrested because laws at the time restricted the distribution of contraceptive information. She also wrote What Every Girl Should Know and the pamphlet Family Limitation, which brought her into conflict with the Comstock laws governing materials sent through the mail. In 1921, Sanger founded the American Birth Control League, which later became Planned Parenthood, a major provider of reproductive health care. Her legacy is also debated because of her involvement with the eugenics movement.

Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben was a Prussian officer who helped transform George Washington’s Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. After defeats at Brandywine and Germantown, Washington’s troops spent the harsh winter of 1777–78 at Valley Forge, a Pennsylvania encampment west of Philadelphia. There, von Steuben introduced a consistent system of infantry drills, teaching soldiers how to march, move together, handle their weapons, and use bayonets in battle. He began by training a small group of soldiers, who then taught the same methods to others. This made training more efficient and helped turn the army into a more disciplined fighting force. Von Steuben later became a major general in the Continental Army.

Abolitionism was the nineteenth-century movement to end slavery in the United States and free enslaved people. Its supporters included formerly enslaved people, religious reformers, writers, and political campaigners. They used speeches, newspapers, petitions, and antislavery organizations to argue that slavery was morally wrong and should end. One prominent abolitionist was William Lloyd Garrison, a Massachusetts publisher who launched the Boston-based newspaper The Liberator in 1831. In its first issue, he promised, “I will not retreat a single inch—AND I WILL BE HEARD.” Garrison demanded the immediate end of slavery and criticized the United States Constitution for allowing it to continue. Abolitionists did not always agree on methods: Garrison and Frederick Douglass, for example, disagreed about whether the Constitution could be used to fight slavery.

Sandra Day O’Connor made history in 1981 when President Ronald Reagan nominated her as the first woman to serve on the U.S. Supreme Court. Before joining the Court, she had served in the Arizona state legislature and as an appeals-court judge. She often played a key role in closely divided decisions, including Grutter v. Bollinger in 2003. That case began when a white applicant who had been denied admission challenged the University of Michigan Law School’s admissions policy. Writing for the majority, O’Connor said the school could consider an applicant’s race as one factor in a broad, individual review, rather than using a fixed racial quota. She also expressed hope that such affirmative action policies would no longer be needed in 25 years.

“Let’s Go Brandon” became a widely recognized slogan expressing opposition to President Joe Biden after a NASCAR race at Talladega Superspeedway in October 2021. Driver Brandon Brown had just won his first NASCAR Xfinity Series race when reporter Kelli Stavast interviewed him on television. In the background, some spectators appeared to be chanting a profane phrase against Biden. Stavast suggested that they were chanting “Let’s Go Brandon” to celebrate Brown’s victory. The moment spread online, and Biden’s critics began using “Let’s Go Brandon” as a less explicit way to repeat the anti-Biden chant. Understanding the phrase requires knowing both where it came from—the interview after Brown’s win—and how its meaning changed from an apparent cheer for a driver into a political slogan.

Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti were Italian-born immigrants and anarchists accused of taking part in a 1920 payroll robbery in South Braintree, Massachusetts, in which two men were killed. At their 1921 trial, Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Webster Thayer presided. A jury convicted both men of murder, and Thayer later rejected defense motions for a new trial. The case became controversial because critics argued that prejudice against immigrants and anarchists, as well as problems with the evidence, had affected the verdict. Supporters organized protests around the world and called for a new trial, but Sacco and Vanzetti were executed in 1927. Their case remains a well-known example of concerns about whether fear and bias can prevent people from receiving a fair trial.

Louis DeJoy is an American businessman and former logistics executive who became the 75th United States Postmaster General in June 2020. The United States Postal Service’s Board of Governors selected him to lead the agency, which is an independent federal establishment responsible for delivering mail nationwide. Before taking the job, DeJoy was a major Republican fundraiser and had served as a deputy finance chairman of the Republican National Committee. His leadership drew attention before the 2020 election because the Postal Service removed mail-sorting machines and made other operational changes as many Americans prepared to vote by mail. Critics worried that the changes could slow ballot delivery, while DeJoy said they were intended to improve efficiency.

The Battle of Lake Erie was a U.S. naval victory over Britain on September 10, 1813, during the War of 1812. Fought near Put-in-Bay, Ohio, it gave the Americans control of Lake Erie. U.S. commander Oliver Hazard Perry began the fight aboard his flagship, the Lawrence, but when it was badly damaged, he crossed to the Niagara and continued directing the attack. After the British squadron surrendered, Perry reported, “We have met the enemy and they are ours.” Control of the lake let American forces move into the region and retake Detroit. They then defeated British and Native American forces at the Battle of the Thames, where the Shawnee leader Tecumseh was killed. The victory weakened British influence in the Old Northwest.

Joseph Pulitzer was born in Hungary in 1847 and immigrated to the United States, where he served in the Union Army during the Civil War. He later became a newspaper publisher and, in 1883, bought the Manhattan-based New York World. By combining lively stories with investigative campaigns and a prominent Sunday edition, he built it into one of the country’s leading mass-circulation newspapers. Pulitzer competed fiercely for readers with William Randolph Hearst, owner of the New York Journal. Their rivalry helped shape journalism in the late 1800s, when newspapers could influence public opinion as well as report events. Pulitzer’s name lives on through the Pulitzer Prizes, annual awards administered by Columbia University that honor achievements in journalism, books, and other fields.

Utah Territory was a U.S. administrative district created in 1850, decades before Utah became a state in 1896. It included the settlement near the Great Salt Lake founded by members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, often called Mormons. Their leader, Brigham Young, had led them west from Nauvoo, Illinois, after they faced conflict and persecution there. They reached the Great Salt Lake valley in 1847 and began building communities in the region. Before the federal government organized Utah Territory, the settlers proposed a much larger state called Deseret. Young became Utah Territory’s first governor, serving as both a religious and political leader. As more settlers arrived, disagreements between territorial leaders and the federal government shaped Utah’s path to statehood.

Wells Fargo & Company was founded in 1852 to provide express delivery and banking services in the western United States. Its stagecoaches became a familiar way to carry mail, packages, and money across long distances. Another famous mail service of the era was the Pony Express, which used mounted couriers and relay stations to move messages between Missouri and California in about ten days. It operated only from 1860 to 1861: keeping horses and stations running was costly, and the transcontinental telegraph soon made its fast mail route less useful. Wells Fargo later acquired assets associated with the Pony Express and used its name and imagery. Over time, Wells Fargo grew into one of the nation’s largest banks, though it faced criticism in 2016 for opening customer accounts without permission.

United States v. E. C. Knight Co. was an 1895 Supreme Court case about whether the federal government could use the Sherman Antitrust Act to challenge a sugar-refining monopoly. The American Sugar Refining Company had acquired several competing refineries, including E. C. Knight Co., giving it control of most of the nation’s sugar-refining capacity. The Court ruled that refining sugar was manufacturing, not interstate commerce, even though the finished sugar would be sold across state lines. Because the Constitution gives Congress power to regulate interstate commerce, the majority concluded that the federal government could not use that power to stop these acquisitions. The ruling let the company’s dominant position stand and limited federal antitrust enforcement. Justice John Marshall Harlan dissented, arguing that Congress’s commerce power should reach such a powerful monopoly.

James Buchanan, a Pennsylvanian, served as the 15th U.S. president from 1857 to 1861 and was the only president who never married. His presidency was dominated by growing conflict over slavery. In his 1857 inaugural address, he urged Americans to accept an upcoming Supreme Court ruling on slavery in the territories. That ruling, Dred Scott v. Sandford, declared that Congress could not ban slavery in federal territories and that Black people were not U.S. citizens under the Constitution. As Southern states began seceding near the end of Buchanan’s term, his administration tried to reinforce Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor. In January 1861, it sent the steamer Star of the West with supplies and troops, but South Carolina forces fired on the ship and turned it back. The Civil War began shortly after Buchanan left office.

A presidential pardon is a power the U.S. Constitution gives the president to forgive a federal offense and remove its legal penalties. Unlike a commutation, which only reduces a sentence, a pardon can protect someone from prosecution or punishment for the offense. In 1974, President Gerald Ford pardoned former president Richard Nixon for federal offenses he may have committed while in office, shielding him from prosecution connected to Watergate. A pardon does not always take effect simply because the president issues it: in the 1833 case United States v. Wilson, the Supreme Court ruled that George Wilson could refuse a pardon from President Andrew Jackson, making it ineffective without his acceptance. Presidents cannot use this power to pardon state crimes.

Silver is a precious metal that became central to a major U.S. debate about money in the late 1800s. Under a gold-only standard, dollars were tied to gold. Supporters of bimetallism wanted silver recognized alongside gold, hoping that more money in circulation would make it easier for farmers and debtors to repay what they owed. In 1878, Congress passed the Bland–Allison Act over President Rutherford B. Hayes’s veto. It required the Treasury to buy between $2 million and $4 million worth of silver bullion each month and coin it into dollars. The debate continued into the 1896 election, when William Jennings Bryan attacked the gold-only standard in his famous “Cross of Gold” speech at the Democratic National Convention.

The Tuskegee Airmen were the first African American military aviators in the U.S. Army Air Forces. During World War II, they trained in Alabama near Tuskegee Institute, a historically Black school, at a time when the U.S. military was segregated and many people wrongly doubted Black pilots’ abilities. The Airmen included pilots as well as the mechanics and other personnel who kept their aircraft flying. One of their best-known units, the 332nd Fighter Group, escorted bombers over Europe. Its planes had distinctive red tails, earning the pilots the nickname “Red Tails.” The group was commanded by Benjamin O. Davis Jr., a West Point graduate who later became the first African American general in the U.S. Air Force. Their wartime service helped challenge racial barriers in the military.

The Battle of Trenton was a Patriot victory during the American Revolution. On the night of December 25–26, 1776, George Washington led his Continental Army across the icy Delaware River from Pennsylvania into New Jersey. Before dawn on December 26, the day after Christmas, his troops surprised the Hessian garrison at Trenton. The Hessians were German soldiers hired by Britain to fight the Americans. Their commander, Colonel Johann Rall, was mortally wounded during the attack. Washington’s forces captured many Hessian soldiers while suffering relatively few casualties. The victory came after months of difficult defeats for the Continental Army, and it raised American morale by showing that Washington’s army could still win.

The Loyal Nine were a small circle of Boston merchants and artisans who organized protests against the Stamp Act in 1765. That British law required colonists to buy tax stamps for many printed materials, angering people who had no representatives in Parliament. The Loyal Nine arranged demonstrations and used intimidation to pressure officials who would enforce the law. Protesters hung stamp distributor Andrew Oliver in effigy, and a crowd later attacked the home of Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson. The group helped pave the way for the Sons of Liberty, a broader resistance organization whose Boston branch was led by Samuel Adams. Years later, members of the Sons of Liberty organized the Boston Tea Party, destroying taxed tea aboard ships in Boston Harbor in 1773.

Brâncuși v. United States was a customs case about whether an abstract sculpture could count as art under U.S. tariff law. In 1927, customs officials examined Bird in Space, a highly polished, elongated bronze work by Romanian-born modernist sculptor Constantin Brâncuși. Because it did not look like a realistic bird, they classified it as a manufactured metal object and charged an import tax instead of admitting it duty-free as a work of art. Brâncuși argued that the sculpture expressed the essence of flight, not the exact appearance of an animal. In 1928, a customs court ruled that Bird in Space qualified as art despite its nonrepresentational form. The decision showed growing legal recognition that modern art did not have to imitate nature to be considered art.

The Gadsden Purchase was an 1853 agreement in which the United States paid Mexico $10 million for a strip of land that is now part of southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico. U.S. leaders wanted the land partly because its terrain offered a more practical route for a southern transcontinental railroad, connecting the eastern states to the Pacific coast. James Gadsden negotiated the purchase for the United States with the Mexican government while Antonio López de Santa Anna was serving another term as Mexico’s president. Santa Anna had earlier commanded Mexican forces during the Texas Revolution, including at the Alamo and the Battle of San Jacinto. The purchase helped establish the present-day U.S.–Mexico border in that region.

The Fourteenth Amendment was ratified in 1868 during Reconstruction, after the Civil War. It defines national citizenship to include people born or naturalized in the United States and requires states to provide due process of law and equal protection of the laws. Due process means states must follow fair legal procedures before taking away a person’s life, liberty, or property. Equal protection means states cannot unfairly deny people the protection of their laws. In 1954, the Supreme Court applied the Equal Protection Clause in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka. The Court ruled that state-mandated racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional, rejecting the idea that separate schools could be acceptable simply because their facilities were supposedly equal.

Dolores Huerta is a Mexican American labor and civil-rights activist who helped farmworkers fight for better pay and working conditions. Born in Dawson, New Mexico, and raised in Stockton, California, she worked as a teacher before turning to labor organizing. In 1962, she and César Chávez founded the National Farm Workers Association. During a strike by grape pickers, they led a march from Delano to Sacramento to draw attention to farmworkers’ demands. In 1966, their organization merged with a union organized by Filipino American labor leader Larry Itliong. The combined group became known as the United Farm Workers in 1972. Huerta negotiated labor agreements for California farmworkers, while the union’s grape strikes and boycotts helped bring national attention to their struggle.

In February 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, near the Pennsylvania border. Some of its tank cars carried hazardous chemicals, including vinyl chloride, a flammable gas used to make PVC plastic found in pipes and cable insulation. Officials feared that several vinyl chloride cars might rupture, so they released and deliberately burned their contents in a controlled operation. The derailment and burn raised concerns about air, soil, and water pollution, and residents were temporarily evacuated. Norfolk Southern faced class-action lawsuits, while the U.S. Department of Justice sued on behalf of the Environmental Protection Agency over cleanup costs. The incident is widely known as the 2023 East Palestine train derailment; the chemical burned was vinyl chloride.

The Netanyahu family is prominent in Israeli public life. Benjamin “Bibi” Netanyahu is a leader of the Likud party who has served multiple terms as Israel’s prime minister. His older brother, Yonatan “Yoni” Netanyahu, was an officer in the Israeli military. In 1976, hijackers diverted Air France Flight 139 to Entebbe Airport in Uganda, near the capital, Kampala, and held passengers hostage. Yonatan commanded the Israeli commando force sent to rescue them. The mission, commonly called Operation Entebbe, freed more than 100 hostages, but Yonatan was killed during the raid. It is also known as Operation Jonathan in his memory. Remembering the two brothers connects the Netanyahu family to both Israeli politics and one of the best-known hostage-rescue operations in modern history.

The Kingdom of Kongo was a powerful Central African state that emerged before Portuguese visitors arrived in the late 15th century. It maintained diplomatic ties with Portugal, and its ruler Afonso I adopted Christianity and worked to spread Catholicism in his kingdom. Although he valued contact with Portugal, Afonso later objected to Portuguese involvement in the enslavement and sale of people from his realm. Kongo’s royal seat was Mbanza Kongo, a city on a plateau in what is now northern Angola. Portuguese sources later called it São Salvador. The kingdom’s name is related to that of today’s Republic of the Congo and Democratic Republic of the Congo, but the historic kingdom was not the same as either modern country.

Dominic Cummings is a British political strategist best known for directing Vote Leave, the campaign that urged voters to leave the European Union in the UK’s 2016 referendum. He later became chief adviser to Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson, who succeeded Theresa May and entered 10 Downing Street in 2019. Before becoming prime minister, Johnson had served as Mayor of London. Cummings was an influential but controversial figure in Johnson’s government. During the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020, he drew widespread attention for a trip to Barnard Castle, which many people believed broke the restrictions they had been asked to follow. His role in both the Brexit campaign and Johnson’s early premiership made him a prominent figure in recent British politics.

The First Battle of the Marne was fought in September 1914 near the Marne River in France, as German troops advanced toward Paris during World War I. French and British forces launched a counterattack that stopped the advance and forced the Germans to retreat. French taxis famously helped carry thousands of soldiers from Paris toward the fighting. The Allied victory disrupted the Schlieffen Plan, Germany’s strategy for defeating France quickly in the west before shifting its forces east to fight Russia. After the battle, neither side could win a quick victory on the Western Front. Soldiers dug long networks of trenches for protection, and the fighting settled into a costly stalemate.

James Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan, was a British peer and major-general who commanded the Light Brigade during the Crimean War. Britain and its allies fought Russia in this war, much of which took place around the Crimean Peninsula on the Black Sea. In October 1854, at the Battle of Balaclava near Sevastopol, Cardigan led his cavalry in the Charge of the Light Brigade. The soldiers rode into a valley under heavy Russian fire after a misunderstood order sent them toward the wrong guns. The assault failed and caused many casualties, but the riders’ courage became famous through Alfred, Lord Tennyson’s poem “The Charge of the Light Brigade,” with its phrase “the valley of Death.” Cardigan’s name is also associated with the button-front sweater called a cardigan.

The Kingdom of Mercia was a powerful Anglo-Saxon kingdom centered in the English Midlands. It grew into one of the strongest kingdoms in early medieval England and often competed with its southern neighbor, Wessex. Among its best-known rulers were Penda, a seventh-century king, and Offa, who ruled in the eighth century. Offa extended Mercia’s influence over other English kingdoms and is traditionally associated with the building of Offa’s Dyke. This long earthwork, made largely of a bank and ditch, runs along much of the border between England and Wales. It is one of Britain’s most substantial early medieval frontier works, although historians still debate exactly when and why every section was built. Mercia later lost power as Wessex rose to lead the unification of England.

Caligula was the third Roman emperor, ruling from 37 to 41 CE after succeeding Tiberius. His real name was Gaius Julius Caesar Germanicus, but soldiers gave him the nickname Caligula, meaning “little boot,” when he grew up among his father Germanicus’s troops. Early in his reign he was popular, but ancient writers later described him as cruel and extravagant. Some of their stories may be exaggerated, so historians treat them cautiously. One famous account says he gave his favorite horse, Incitatus, a marble stable and an ivory manger and even considered making it a consul, one of Rome’s highest officials. In 41 CE, members of the Praetorian Guard, the emperor’s bodyguards, assassinated Caligula.

Guy Fawkes was an English Catholic who had served with Spanish forces in the Low Countries, where he used the name Guido. In 1605, he joined a group of conspirators who planned to blow up the House of Lords during the state opening of Parliament, killing King James I and many of his officials. They hoped to replace him with his daughter Elizabeth Stuart and restore Catholic rule in England. An anonymous warning letter sent to Lord Monteagle reached the royal court and led authorities to search beneath the House of Lords. On 5 November, they found Fawkes guarding barrels of gunpowder. The failed conspiracy became known as the Gunpowder Plot. In Britain, people still mark 5 November with bonfires and fireworks, sometimes burning an effigy of Fawkes.

The Punti–Hakka Clan Wars were a series of armed conflicts in Guangdong, southern China, mainly from 1855 to 1867. The Punti were long-established local communities, while the Hakka were communities whose ancestors had migrated into the region. Differences in language and customs added to tensions over farmland, resources, and local power. Fighting destroyed villages and forced many people to leave their homes. Some displaced people crossed the sea to Australia, then a collection of British colonies where gold discoveries had attracted migrants from China. Chinese miners there also faced hostility: in 1861, mobs attacked them during the Lambing Flat riots in New South Wales. Australia became a federation in 1901.

A sultan is a Muslim ruler with temporal authority, meaning power to govern people and territory. The title became the customary style of the monarchs of the Ottoman Empire, which was founded by Osman I in Anatolia, a region in present-day Turkey. Ottoman sultans led an empire that expanded into the Balkans and the Middle East. Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453; the city later became known as Istanbul and served as the empire’s capital. Later rulers included Suleiman the Magnificent, under whom the empire conquered much of the Balkan peninsula. Ottoman rulers sometimes acquired memorable nicknames, such as Bayezid the Thunderbolt and Selim the Grim. The Ottoman Empire lasted for centuries before it was dissolved after World War I.

The Roman Republic began in 509 BCE, after Romans overthrew their monarchy. Instead of a king, Rome had annually elected officials called magistrates, including two consuls who led the government and armies. A powerful Senate advised them and shaped policy. The republic fought three Punic Wars against Carthage, a city in North Africa that controlled territory in the Iberian Peninsula. The Second Punic War began in 218 BCE when the Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps with his army to attack Italy. Rome eventually defeated Carthage at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE. Rome went on to conquer much of Iberia, which it called Hispania. The republic later gave way to rule by emperors; the conquest of Hispania was completed under the first emperor, Augustus.

Alexander Nevsky was a 13th-century Russian prince who ruled Novgorod and later Vladimir. He earned the name “Nevsky,” meaning “of the Neva,” after defeating Swedish forces near the Neva River in 1240. Two years later, his forces fought troops of the Livonian and Teutonic Orders, groups involved in the Northern Crusades, on frozen Lake Peipus. This 1242 victory, which helped stop their advance into Novgorodian territory, is commonly called the Battle on the Ice. Alexander also faced a different challenge from the Mongol Golden Horde, which controlled much of Russia. Rather than fight it, he maintained political ties with its rulers and paid tribute. Centuries later, a Soviet film about Alexander used his victory over the western knights to evoke resistance to German invaders.

The African Union (AU) is a 55-member organization that brings African countries together to cooperate on peace, development, and shared political and economic challenges. It was launched in 2002 to replace the Organization of African Unity (OAU), following a process set in motion by the 1999 Sirte Declaration. The AU is headquartered in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia. Addis Ababa was also the site of the 1963 summit at which African leaders established the OAU, making the city important to the history of both organizations. The AU helps coordinate responses to conflicts across the continent; for example, it has led peace talks concerning fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region.

Vasco Núñez de Balboa was a Spanish explorer and colonial leader in the early 1500s. In 1513, he led an expedition across the Isthmus of Panama, the narrow strip of land joining North and South America. With help from Indigenous guides, Balboa reached a viewpoint from which he became the first recorded European to see the Pacific Ocean from the Americas. He called it the “South Sea” and later reached its eastern shore. His discovery showed Spain that another vast ocean lay beyond the lands it was colonizing. Balboa’s success also brought him into conflict with Pedrarias Dávila, the Spanish colonial governor of Darién. Pedrarias accused Balboa of plotting against his authority, had him tried, and ordered his beheading in Panama in 1519.

The Battle of Navarino was a major naval battle fought in 1827 during the Greek War of Independence. Greece was fighting to break free from the Ottoman Empire, which was supported at sea by forces from Egypt. A combined British, French, and Russian fleet entered Navarino Bay, off the coast of Greece, where it defeated the Egyptian-Ottoman fleet. The allied fleet’s senior British commander was Admiral Edward Codrington, who directed the fighting from his flagship, HMS Asia; French admiral Henri de Rigny was another allied commander. Navarino is often described as the last major naval battle fought entirely by sailing ships. The victory greatly weakened Ottoman efforts to stop the Greek independence movement and helped pave the way for an independent Greece, later ruled by King Otto I.

The Weimar Republic was Germany’s democratic government from 1919 to 1933. It took its name from Weimar, the city where an assembly met in 1919 to draft a new constitution after World War I. The republic faced political violence and heavy reparations demanded by the Treaty of Versailles. When Germany fell behind on payments, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, an important industrial region, in 1923. Germany’s response to the occupation worsened an economic crisis, and hyperinflation made its currency nearly worthless. The Dawes Plan of 1924 rescheduled reparations and arranged U.S.-backed loans to help Germany recover. It also helped pave the way for French and Belgian troops to leave the Ruhr. Despite a period of greater stability, the republic ended with the Nazi seizure of power in 1933.

Scott Morrison is an Australian Liberal Party politician who served as prime minister from 2018 to 2022. He took office after a change in leadership within his party and led Australia through major events including the COVID-19 pandemic. In the May 2022 federal election, Morrison’s government lost to the Labor Party, led by Anthony Albanese, who became the new prime minister. The election also saw a “teal wave”: independent candidates, often associated with teal campaign colours, won seats while calling for stronger action on climate change and greater integrity in government. The election produced a crossbench of 16 seats, held by members who belonged to neither major party. Morrison’s defeat therefore ended his time as prime minister of Australia.

The Corn Laws were British rules that placed tariffs and restrictions on imported grain in the early 1800s. They protected British landowners and farmers from cheaper foreign grain, but they also helped keep bread prices high for workers and their families. In 1838, Richard Cobden and John Bright founded the Anti-Corn Law League in Manchester. Through public meetings, petitions, and other mass campaigning, the League built support for free trade and repeal. The issue became more urgent during the Irish Potato Famine, when potato blight destroyed the crop on which many Irish people depended, causing widespread starvation. In 1846, Prime Minister Robert Peel repealed the Corn Laws, allowing grain to be imported more freely. Repeal was a major shift toward free trade, though it did not end the famine.

The Kingdom of Prussia was a powerful German state ruled by the Hohenzollern dynasty. In the 1800s, it led the movement to unite the many German states into one country. Its minister-president, Otto von Bismarck, took office in 1862 and argued that unification would be achieved through “blood and iron,” meaning military strength rather than speeches alone. Under his leadership, Prussia fought wars against Denmark, Austria, and France. Its victory over Austria in the Seven Weeks’ War of 1866 made Prussia the leading German power. After Prussia defeated France in the Franco-Prussian War, the German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871. Prussia’s king, Wilhelm I, became the new empire’s first emperor.

The Punic Wars were three wars between Rome and Carthage, fought from 264 to 146 BCE for control of the western Mediterranean. Carthage was a powerful trading city in North Africa, while Rome was expanding beyond Italy. The First Punic War was fought mainly over Sicily. In the Second Punic War, the Carthaginian general Hannibal Barca led an army that included war elephants across the Alps to invade Italy. Although he won several major battles, he could not defeat Rome. The Roman commander Scipio Africanus then took the war to North Africa and defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE. In the Third Punic War, Rome destroyed Carthage, ending the long struggle and becoming the dominant power in the western Mediterranean.

The Cristero War was an armed conflict in Mexico from 1926 to 1929 between government forces and rebels who were largely Roman Catholic. It grew out of a long struggle over the Catholic Church’s influence in Mexican public life. The 1917 constitution had placed restrictions on the Church, and President Plutarco Elías Calles, who held office from 1924 to 1928, strictly enforced anticlerical laws. These measures limited religious activity and led some Catholics to take up arms. The rebels became known as Cristeros, a name linked to their cry, “Long live Christ the King!” Fighting was especially intense in west-central Mexico. A negotiated agreement ended the main conflict in 1929, though tensions between the Church and government continued.

The Shining Path was a Maoist insurgent organization that waged a violent campaign against Peru’s government during the country’s internal conflict. Founded and led for decades by philosophy professor Abimael Guzmán, who called himself “Presidente Gonzalo,” the group sought to overthrow the government and establish a revolutionary communist state. It began its armed campaign in 1980 and used attacks and intimidation against officials, civilians, and people it considered enemies. In the 1983 Lucanamarca Massacre, Shining Path members killed 69 people in a rural community. In 1992, the group bombed Tarata Street in Peru’s capital, Lima, killing civilians. Later that year, Peruvian authorities captured Guzmán in Lima, a major setback for the organization, although the country’s conflict did not immediately end.

The October Revolution was the Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd, Russia, in 1917. Earlier that year, Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, ending centuries of rule by Russian emperors, and a Provisional Government had taken charge. Many people were frustrated that it continued Russia’s involvement in World War I and had not solved shortages of food and land. Vladimir Lenin, the Bolshevik leader, returned from exile in Switzerland that spring and published the April Theses, calling for “all power to the Soviets,” councils representing workers and soldiers. In October, Bolshevik forces overthrew the Provisional Government in Petrograd. Their victory established a revolutionary government that became Soviet Russia and, later, the Soviet Union.

The Korean Empire was the state proclaimed in 1897 by Gojong, who had ruled Korea as king and now declared himself emperor. His new title asserted Korea’s independence at a time when neighboring powers, especially the Empire of Japan, were competing for influence over the Korean Peninsula. Japan’s power grew after its victories in wars against China and Russia, and in 1905 it forced Korea to become a Japanese protectorate, taking control of its foreign affairs. Gojong tried to resist. In 1907, he secretly sent representatives to the Hague Peace Conference to protest the protectorate and seek international support. Japan blocked their efforts and pressured Gojong to abdicate. His son succeeded him, but Japan continued to tighten its control and formally annexed the Korean Empire in 1910.

Mithridates VI Eupator, also called Mithridates the Great, ruled Pontus, a kingdom near the Black Sea in what is now Turkey. He fought three wars against Rome as he tried to expand his power in Anatolia and the eastern Mediterranean. In 88 BCE, forces allied with him attacked and sacked Delos, an island in the Cyclades. Delos was famous as a sanctuary of Apollo and Artemis and was also a busy commercial port; the attack helped weaken its importance as a trading center. Ancient writers also claimed that Mithridates regularly took small, nonlethal doses of poison to build resistance in case an enemy tried to poison him. This alleged practice became known as mithridatism.

The aedileship was a public office in the Roman Republic and a step in the cursus honorum, the usual sequence of offices for politicians. It came after the quaestorship. Aediles helped manage daily life in Rome by looking after public buildings, streets, and markets, as well as organizing religious festivals and public games. These events could make an aedile popular with voters, so the office was an important way to build a political career. One famous aedile was Cicero, a Roman orator known for his skill in public speaking. In the 70s BCE, he successfully prosecuted Gaius Verres for abuses committed while Verres governed Sicily. The case raised Cicero’s reputation and helped him win election to the aedileship.

Mary I ruled England from 1553 to 1558 after succeeding her half-brother Edward VI. A devout Roman Catholic, she tried to reverse the Protestant changes made under Edward and restore England’s ties with the Catholic Church. She brought Cardinal Reginald Pole back from exile, and he became Archbishop of Canterbury. Her government also executed many Protestants for their religious beliefs, including bishops Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, who were burned at the stake in Oxford. These persecutions earned Mary the nickname “Bloody Mary.” Her proposed marriage to Philip of Spain caused another crisis: many English people feared that Spain would gain influence over their country. In 1554, the Kentish landowner Thomas Wyatt the Younger gathered supporters at Rochester and marched toward London. His failed uprising is known as Wyatt’s Rebellion.

The Glorious Revolution was the upheaval of 1688–1689 that removed the Catholic king James II from the English throne. Worried about his rule and the prospect of a Catholic dynasty, seven influential Englishmen, later called the Immortal Seven, invited the Dutch ruler William of Orange to intervene. William landed in England in 1688, and James fled to France. Parliament then offered the throne jointly to William and his wife Mary, James’s Protestant daughter. The English Bill of Rights of 1689 limited the monarch’s power and strengthened Parliament’s role in government. James did not give up his claim: with French support, he tried to regain his throne in Ireland, but William’s forces defeated his army at the Battle of the Boyne in 1690.

Umkhonto we Sizwe, meaning “Spear of the Nation,” was founded in 1961 as the armed wing of the African National Congress (ANC), which opposed South Africa’s apartheid system of racial segregation and white minority rule. Often called MK, the organization began by sabotaging government facilities and infrastructure, aiming to resist apartheid after years of peaceful protest had failed to bring change. Nelson Mandela was among its early leaders. MK members and other ANC leaders secretly used Liliesleaf Farm, a rural property outside Johannesburg, as a base for meetings and planning. In 1963, police raided the farm and found evidence of their activities. The raid led to the arrest of several leaders and helped bring about the Rivonia Trial, at which Mandela gave his famous “I am prepared to die” speech.

Gavrilo Princip was a Bosnian Serb nationalist associated with Young Bosnia, a movement that opposed Austro-Hungarian rule in Bosnia. On June 28, 1914, he shot and killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and the archduke’s wife, Sophie, during their visit to Sarajevo. Princip was one of several conspirators involved in the assassination, which was supported by members of a secret Serbian nationalist group known as the Black Hand. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and issued it a harsh ultimatum in July 1914. The tense chain of diplomatic events that followed is called the July Crisis. As alliances drew other European powers into the conflict, the crisis led to the outbreak of World War I.

The Fugger family was a merchant-banking dynasty from Augsburg, a city in what is now Germany. During the Renaissance, the family became one of Europe’s wealthiest by trading goods, lending money, and investing in mines that produced valuable metals such as copper and silver. Its most famous member was Jakob Fugger, known as “Jakob the Rich.” He greatly expanded the family’s mining and metal-trading business and lent large sums to the Habsburg rulers. His financial support helped Charles V secure his election as Holy Roman Emperor in 1519. The Fuggers’ wealth also connected them to the religious disputes of the time: part of the money raised through indulgence sales in Germany went toward repaying a debt to the family. Their story shows how bankers could influence both politics and religion in early modern Europe.

Mohammed bin Salman, often called MBS, is the crown prince of Saudi Arabia, a Middle Eastern kingdom whose capital is Riyadh. He became crown prince in 2017 and is widely considered the country’s de facto ruler, meaning he exercises much of its political power even though his father is king. He is closely associated with Saudi Arabia’s military intervention in neighboring Yemen, where a Saudi-led coalition fought Houthi forces. Mohammed bin Salman is also the leading figure behind Vision 2030, a program announced in 2016 to reduce Saudi Arabia’s dependence on oil by developing other parts of its economy, including tourism and entertainment. His rule has combined social and economic changes with authoritarian policies and criticism over human rights, especially after the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi.

Tikal was one of the most powerful ancient Maya cities, located in the rainforest of present-day Guatemala. Its rulers built tall pyramids, temples, and plazas that reflected the city’s wealth and political influence. One important area, the Lost World complex, is centered on a pyramid. Tikal’s long rivalry with the Maya city of Calakmul shaped centuries of warfare and alliances across the region. In 378 CE, a general named Siyaj K’ak’ overthrew Tikal’s king, bringing new political influence from Teotihuacan in central Mexico. Among Tikal’s best-known monuments is a funerary pyramid on the east side of the Great Plaza. Built for the ruler Jasaw Chan K’awiil I, it is conventionally called Temple I and is also known as the Temple of the Great Jaguar.

Shipwrecks are maritime disasters in which ships sink, run aground, or are otherwise lost. They can result from storms, collisions, navigation errors, or other hazards, and their effects may be felt far beyond the people on board. The sinking of the Titanic in 1912 became one of the best-known shipwrecks and inspired poems as well as historical accounts. English poet and novelist Thomas Hardy wrote “The Convergence of the Twain” about the Titanic disaster, imagining the ship and the iceberg moving toward their fatal meeting. Hardy also wrote Far from the Madding Crowd, a novel whose title adapts a line from Thomas Gray’s “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.” Another poet, Gerard Manley Hopkins, wrote “The Wreck of the Deutschland” about a different shipwreck.

Estado Novo, meaning “New State,” was the authoritarian regime established in Portugal in 1933 under António de Oliveira Salazar. Its corporatist system organized the economy through state-controlled groups representing employers and workers, while powerful companies dominated much of Portugal’s economy and its African colonies. The government restricted political opposition, censored the press, and resisted demands for independence in the colonies. After Salazar left office, the regime continued under Marcelo Caetano. On April 25, 1974, the Armed Forces Movement began a largely bloodless military revolt against the government. Crowds joined the soldiers and placed carnations in their gun barrels, giving the uprising its name: the Carnation Revolution. It ended the Estado Novo and opened the way for democracy in Portugal.

The Mandate of Heaven was an idea in early Chinese political thought that explained why an emperor or dynasty had the right to rule. According to this doctrine, Heaven granted its favor to a ruler who governed well but could withdraw that favor from one who was unjust or incompetent. People could then see a dynasty’s overthrow as a sign that it had lost the mandate and that a new ruling house could take its place. The Zhou dynasty used this argument to justify overthrowing the Shang dynasty: it claimed that the Shang ruler’s wrongdoing had cost him Heaven’s support. King Wu founded the Zhou dynasty after defeating the Shang at the Battle of Muye, and the Zhou ruled for centuries.

Pierre Trudeau was a Liberal prime minister of Canada whose popularity helped his party win the 1968 federal election. The excitement surrounding him was nicknamed “Trudeaumania.” He promoted a “Just Society,” aiming to reduce inequality and improve opportunities for minority groups. In 1970, a separatist group kidnapped two officials during the October Crisis, and one of them, Pierre Laporte, was killed. Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act, giving the federal government extraordinary powers to respond. His government also introduced the National Energy Program in 1980. It sought greater Canadian control of the petroleum industry and a larger federal share of oil revenues. Many people in oil-producing Alberta strongly opposed the program, which became a symbol of “western alienation,” or resentment toward the federal government in western Canada.

The Kingdom of Wessex was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in southern England that became the foundation of a unified English state. In the ninth century, its king Alfred the Great defended Wessex against Viking invasions and made a peace treaty with the Viking leader Guthrum. Alfred also gathered laws in a collection known as the Doom Book. His successors expanded Wessex’s control over other Anglo-Saxon lands, helping to form the kingdom of England. Wessex had long competed for power with another Anglo-Saxon kingdom, Mercia, in central England. Mercia’s seventh-century ruler Penda fought many rival kings, while its later ruler Offa is associated with Offa’s Dyke, a great earthwork near the border between England and Wales.

Xi Jinping is a Chinese political leader who became general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party in 2012 and president of the People’s Republic of China in 2013. As general secretary, he leads the party that governs China. His government has promoted ideas known as Xi Jinping Thought, which have been added to school textbooks, while also tightening controls on political criticism and online speech. In 2013, Xi introduced the Belt and Road Initiative, a program to expand trade and infrastructure links between China and other regions. It includes overland economic corridors across Eurasia and maritime routes connecting places such as Africa and Europe. Projects under the initiative include railways, ports, and roads, intended to make it easier to move goods and strengthen China’s international ties.

The Mariel Boatlift was a mass migration from Cuba to the United States in 1980. After Cubans seeking to leave took refuge in the Peruvian embassy in Havana, Fidel Castro’s government allowed people to depart from Mariel, a port west of Havana. Thousands of private boats, many sent by relatives and friends in the United States, crossed the Florida Straits to collect passengers. Many first reached the U.S. at Key West, the southernmost city in Florida. About 125,000 Cubans made the journey over several months. Some were seeking greater freedom or better economic opportunities; the Cuban government also used the departure to remove people it considered “undesirable.” The boatlift created major challenges for U.S. officials, who had to receive and resettle so many arrivals quickly.

Operation Yellow Ribbon was Canada’s emergency air-traffic response to the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks in the United States. After hijackers from al-Qaeda flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, the United States closed its airspace. Many international flights already heading toward North America could not continue to their planned destinations, so Canadian authorities coordinated the landing of hundreds of aircraft at airports across Canada. One of the busiest was the airport in Gander, a town in Newfoundland and Labrador, where dozens of diverted planes landed. Thousands of passengers were stranded there, often for several days. Gander residents welcomed them with food, shelter, and other help. The operation made it possible to bring the planes down safely during an unprecedented crisis.

Khrushchev’s Secret Speech was an address delivered by Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in a closed session of the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in February 1956. Officially titled “On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences,” it became known as the “Secret Speech” because it was not given at a public session. Khrushchev denounced Joseph Stalin, who had died in 1953, for encouraging a cult of personality that treated him as an almost infallible leader. He also condemned the repression carried out under Stalin, including the persecution of Communist Party members. The speech marked a major break with the way Soviet leaders had previously portrayed Stalin and helped weaken hard-line Stalinist leaders in other communist countries, including Hungary.

The Sino-Soviet Split was the breakdown of the alliance between the People’s Republic of China and the Soviet Union during the Cold War. Both countries were communist, but their leaders disagreed about how communism should develop and which country should lead the communist world. In 1956, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev denounced the former Soviet ruler Joseph Stalin and promoted “peaceful coexistence” with Western powers such as the United States. China’s leader, Mao Zedong, opposed these changes, arguing that they weakened the struggle against capitalism. The dispute grew in the late 1950s and 1960s as the countries competed for influence, the Soviet Union withdrew its advisers from China, and border tensions increased. Their split weakened communist unity and later helped open the way for China’s diplomatic contact with the United States.

The Second Council of Nicaea was a meeting of bishops held in the city of Nicaea in 787 to address the Byzantine Iconoclast Controversy, a dispute over religious images called icons. Earlier in the eighth century, Emperor Leo III had banned icons because he believed honoring them was idolatry, or worshipping something other than God. Defenders of icons, including John of Damascus, argued that showing respect to an image was different from worshipping it. The council agreed: Christians could venerate icons, but worship was due to God alone. Irene of Athens, a Byzantine regent who had been empress consort and was the mother of Emperor Constantine VI, supported restoring icon veneration and helped summon the bishops to the council.

The Songhai Empire rose to power in West Africa after the decline of Mali and made Gao, on the Niger River, its capital. In the 1400s and 1500s, its rulers controlled important trade routes across the Sahara Desert. Merchants exchanged gold and other goods, while salt mined at Taghaza brought the empire additional wealth. Salt was especially valuable because people used it to preserve food and add flavor. Askia Muhammad, one of Songhai’s most important rulers, strengthened its government and expanded its influence. In 1591, forces sent by the ruler of Morocco invaded Songhai and defeated its army at the Battle of Tondibi. Moroccan soldiers’ firearms gave them an advantage, and the defeat ended Songhai’s dominance in the region.

Zambia is a landlocked country in southern Africa, and its capital is Lusaka. It became independent from Britain in 1964 and relies heavily on mining, especially copper, which has accounted for about 64% of its export earnings. Because so much of Zambia’s income depends on one metal, changes in copper prices can make it harder for the government to repay loans. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Zambia became the first African country to default on its foreign debt, meaning it could not make required payments to lenders abroad. Its debt crisis prompted debate about loans from China and agreements with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Critics argued that IMF agreements restricted Zambia’s ability to raise taxes on copper mining. Chile, another major mining country, is the world’s largest copper producer.

The Tutsi are a people of Africa’s Great Lakes region, with long histories in Rwanda and Burundi. In 1994, Hutu extremists in Rwanda carried out a genocide that targeted Tutsi people and killed hundreds of thousands. A Tutsi-led force, the Rwandan Patriotic Front, ended the genocide. The violence displaced people across the region, including Tutsi who sought safety in what was then Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Armed Hutu extremists also crossed into eastern Zaire, adding to tensions there. These upheavals helped set the stage for the Congo Wars. The First Congo War began in 1996 and ended with the overthrow of Zaire’s ruler, Mobutu Sese Seko. The Second Congo War drew in numerous African countries.

Charles Trevelyan was a British civil servant who helped oversee government relief during the Irish Potato Famine, also called the Great Hunger, in the late 1840s. Repeated potato blight destroyed the crop on which many poor Irish families depended, causing widespread starvation and disease. Many people left Ireland aboard overcrowded, dangerous vessels known as “coffin ships.” Trevelyan supported limits on government aid and described the famine in terms of divine providence, suggesting that it was part of God’s plan. His approach has been widely criticized because it failed to meet the needs of people facing catastrophe. Prime Minister Robert Peel’s repeal of the Corn Laws lowered barriers to imported grain, but the change alone could not end the suffering.

The Doctors’ Plot was a Soviet campaign in 1952–53, during the final years of Joseph Stalin’s rule. Authorities accused a group of mostly Jewish physicians of conspiring to kill senior Soviet leaders by giving them harmful medical treatment. They claimed the doctors had deliberately caused the 1948 death of Andrey Zhdanov, a powerful Communist Party official, although he had died of heart disease. The accusations were not supported by credible evidence and formed part of a wider climate of Stalinist antisemitism, or hostility toward Jews. Soviet newspapers publicized the charges, spreading fear among doctors and Jewish communities. After Stalin died in March 1953, the government discredited the case, released the accused doctors, and abandoned the campaign.

Operation Orchard was the codename for a covert Israeli airstrike carried out in September 2007 against a facility in eastern Syria. The target was Al-Kibar, a site near the Euphrates River in Syria’s Deir ez-Zor Governorate. Israeli intelligence believed the building was a nuclear reactor under construction, and Israeli aircraft destroyed it before it became operational. Syria initially denied that the site was a reactor, but later investigations found evidence consistent with an undeclared nuclear facility. Israel did not publicly acknowledge its role until 2018. The strike shows how fears about nuclear weapons can shape military decisions: Israel chose to attack a suspected reactor in another country rather than wait to see whether it would be completed.

The Genpei War was a civil war in Japan from 1180 to 1185 between two powerful samurai clans, the Taira and the Minamoto. Both clans sought control of the imperial government, and their fighting spread across much of the country. The war ended at the Battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185, a decisive naval battle in the strait between the islands of Honshu and Kyushu. The Minamoto defeated the Taira there, and the child emperor Antoku drowned during the Taira defeat. Minamoto victory established the clan’s dominance and led to the Kamakura shogunate, a military government headed by a shogun. The war’s stories were later told in The Tale of the Heike, including an episode in which an archer shoots a fan from a ship.

A hacienda was a large agricultural estate in colonial Latin America where a landowner controlled farmland and the labor needed to work it. Haciendas developed in part from the encomienda system, under which Spanish colonists had been granted the right to demand labor or tribute from Indigenous people. Some haciendas grew crops such as sugarcane, which could be turned into molasses or rum. Workers on a hacienda might receive advances of money, food, or supplies from the owner. If these advances were recorded as debts and the workers could not leave until they repaid them, the arrangement was called debt peonage. Because the debts could keep growing, workers might remain tied to the estate for years.

Michael Collins was a leader of Ireland’s struggle for independence from Britain. After the 1916 Easter Rising in Dublin, he became a key figure in the Irish Republican Army (IRA) during the War of Independence, serving as its Director of Intelligence and as Minister for Finance in the revolutionary government. Collins helped negotiate and signed the Anglo-Irish Treaty with British representatives in December 1921. The treaty created the Irish Free State as a self-governing dominion covering twenty-six counties, but it required an oath of allegiance to the British Crown and left Northern Ireland in the United Kingdom. Many Irish nationalists opposed those terms, and the disagreement led to the Irish Civil War. Collins supported the treaty and was killed in an ambush at Béal na Bláth in County Cork in 1922.

Cesare Borgia was an Italian Renaissance nobleman, the son of Pope Alexander VI, who became duke of Valentinois. With his father’s support, he led military campaigns to bring territories in Romagna, a region of northern Italy, under papal control. His rapid rise and forceful methods attracted the attention of Niccolò Machiavelli, who used Borgia’s career as a case study in his political treatise The Prince. Machiavelli examined how rulers could gain and keep power in a dangerous political world. In The Prince, he argues that if a ruler cannot be both loved and feared, it is safer to be feared. He also says a ruler should combine the cunning of a fox with the strength of a lion.

The Twenty-sixth of July Movement was a Cuban revolutionary organization led by Fidel Castro to overthrow the government of Fulgencio Batista. Its name refers to July 26, 1953, when Castro and other rebels attacked the Moncada Barracks. The assault failed, and Castro was arrested, but his courtroom defense, later known as “History Will Absolve Me,” became a statement of the movement’s goals. After his release, Castro organized the movement in exile and returned to Cuba with a small group of fighters. They fought a guerrilla campaign from the Sierra Maestra mountains and gained support against Batista. When Batista fled Cuba in 1959, the revolutionaries took power. Castro later established a communist government and remained Cuba’s leader for decades, handing the presidency to his brother Raúl in 2008.

The National Energy Program was a petroleum policy announced by Canada’s federal government in 1980 under Liberal prime minister Pierre Trudeau. It aimed to increase Canadian ownership of oil companies, give the federal government a larger role in the industry, and secure a greater federal share of oil revenues. The policy was especially controversial in oil-producing Western Canada, where many people believed it would take revenue and decision-making power away from their provinces. This opposition helped fuel a debate about “western alienation,” the feeling that western interests were being overlooked by the federal government. Trudeau had earlier promoted plans for a “Just Society,” including reforms intended to improve opportunities for minority groups. He also invoked the War Measures Act during the 1970 October Crisis.

Lycurgus of Sparta was a semi-legendary lawgiver whom ancient Greeks credited with shaping Sparta’s government and disciplined way of life. Sparta was a city-state in southern Greece known for its two kings and its emphasis on military service. Tradition connects Lycurgus to the Great Rhetra, a foundational statement of Spartan government said to have come from the oracle at Delphi. He was also credited with establishing the agoge, the system of education and training for Spartan boys. Beginning around age seven, boys entered communal groups where they faced demanding physical exercises, strict discipline, and preparation for military service. Historians cannot be certain whether Lycurgus was a real person or whether these changes happened under one leader, but his name became a symbol of Sparta’s institutions.

The Korean War began in June 1950, when communist North Korea invaded South Korea. The peninsula had been divided after World War II, and the fighting became a major Cold War confrontation: the United States and other United Nations forces supported the South, while China fought alongside the North, which also received Soviet support. In September 1950, General Douglas MacArthur led the Inchon Landing, an amphibious attack behind North Korean lines that helped UN forces recapture Seoul. Later, Chinese forces entered the war, and the fighting settled into a costly stalemate. An armistice in 1953 stopped the fighting and established a demilitarized zone between North and South Korea. Because no peace treaty was signed, the peninsula remains divided.

Grigori Rasputin was a Siberian-born religious wanderer and mystic who became close to the family of Nicholas II, the last tsar of Russia. Nicholas and his wife, Empress Alexandra Feodorovna, believed Rasputin could help their son Alexei, who had hemophilia, a disorder that makes bleeding difficult to stop. Alexandra, who was born in Germany as Alix of Hesse and by Rhine, came to rely heavily on his advice. Rasputin’s influence at the Romanov court angered many Russian nobles, who feared he was interfering in government. In 1916, aristocratic conspirators murdered him in Petrograd, before the Russian Revolution led to the overthrow of Nicholas II. Rasputin’s strange reputation and dramatic death later inspired many legends.

The Dauphin of France was the title given to the heir apparent, usually the king’s eldest son, before the French monarchy was abolished during the French Revolution. The title came from Dauphiné, a territory transferred to the French crown in 1349 under an agreement linking it to the king’s eldest son. “Dauphin” is also the French word for “dolphin,” an animal shown on the holder’s coat of arms. Louis XVI held the title when he married Marie Antoinette. Their younger son became dauphin after his elder brother died in 1789. When Louis XVI was executed during the Revolution, royalists recognized the boy as King Louis XVII, although he never ruled.

Sugarcane is a tropical grass that became a major crop in Caribbean plantation economies. Workers cut its stalks and crushed them to extract juice, which was processed into sugar for export; producers could also make molasses from it or distill the molasses into rum. Plantations depended heavily on enslaved labor, and the profits flowed largely to European investors and merchants. Historian Eduardo Galeano argued that returns on Dutch investments in sugarcane helped build European capital. Sugar production also shaped Puerto Rico. The question’s account links the opening of the island’s first sugar mill in 1873 to the rise of colono farmers, who grew cane for mills. Other clues to Puerto Rico are its first governor, Juan Ponce de León, and El Morro, the fort guarding the harbor of its capital, San Juan.

The Battle of Lepanto was a major naval battle fought in 1571 in the Gulf of Patras, near Greece. A Catholic alliance called the Holy League, which included Spain and Venice, defeated the fleet of the Ottoman Empire. The victory was celebrated across Catholic Europe, but it did not end Ottoman naval power. Historian Fernand Braudel argued that Lepanto did not transform control of the Mediterranean Sea as dramatically as some accounts claimed. Braudel studied the Mediterranean during the reign of Philip II of Spain, a monarch who supported the Holy League. Philip II also sent the Spanish Armada to invade England in 1588, though that expedition failed. Lepanto shows how a famous victory can matter greatly without permanently changing the balance of power.

Julius Nyerere was a teacher and nationalist leader who helped Tanganyika gain independence from Britain in 1961. He became its first president and, after Tanganyika united with Zanzibar in 1964, led the new country of Tanzania. Nyerere promoted a form of African socialism based on self-reliance rather than dependence on foreign aid. His central program was ujamaa, a Swahili word meaning “familyhood.” Under ujamaa, the government encouraged people to live and work together in rural villages, sharing resources and building schools and health services. The 1967 Arusha Declaration set out these goals. Although ujamaa expanded access to education and health care, moving people into villages was sometimes forced, and the program struggled to improve agricultural production.

Johann Tetzel was a Dominican friar who traveled through German lands in the early 1500s preaching and selling indulgences. An indulgence was a Catholic grant connected to the punishment for sins; Tetzel claimed that giving money could shorten a soul’s time in purgatory, where believers were thought to be purified before entering heaven. His sales campaign, especially claims that seemed to make payment more important than sincere repentance, became a major target of Martin Luther’s criticism and helped spark the Protestant Reformation. The Catholic Church later addressed abuses involving indulgences at the Council of Trent, an assembly convened by Pope Paul III beginning in 1545. The council reaffirmed the doctrine of purgatory but banned the sale of indulgences.

The Warsaw Ghetto Uprising was an armed revolt by Jewish people imprisoned in a walled district of Warsaw, Poland’s capital, during World War II. The Nazis had confined hundreds of thousands of Jews there, and many had already been deported to the Treblinka extermination camp. When German forces entered the ghetto in April 1943 to resume mass deportations, resistance fighters, including members of the Jewish Combat Organization (ZOB), fought back with limited weapons and supplies. The fighting continued into May. SS and police leader Jürgen Stroop commanded the German operation to crush the uprising; his forces burned buildings and destroyed the ghetto. He later submitted a report titled “The Jewish Quarter of Warsaw Is No More!” Although the fighters could not defeat the Germans, their resistance became a powerful symbol of courage against Nazi persecution.

Ashraf Ghani is an Afghan economist and politician who served as president of Afghanistan from 2014 to 2021. Before entering Afghan politics, he taught at Johns Hopkins University in the United States and worked at the World Bank, an organization that supports economic development. His presidency ended as the Taliban, a movement that had ruled Afghanistan’s capital, Kabul, from 1996 to 2001, rapidly regained control of the country. In August 2021, Ghani left Kabul as Taliban forces entered the city. The 2021 Taliban takeover of Afghanistan marked the movement’s return to national power. As people tried to leave, a large international airlift took place at Kabul’s Hamid Karzai International Airport.

Mobilization is the process of preparing a country’s armed forces for war. Governments call up reservists, gather troops, and move equipment and supplies into position. In the summer of 1914, as Europe moved toward World War I, rapid mobilization alarmed other powers because it could look like preparation for an attack. Even if a government said it wanted peace, its troop movements might lead a rival to mobilize too, making war harder to avoid. Tsar Nicholas II of Russia and his cousin, Kaiser Wilhelm II of Germany, exchanged a series of roughly ten brief messages about their fears that the other country was mobilizing. These messages are commonly called the Willy–Nicky Telegrams, using nicknames for Wilhelm and Nicholas.

Roman warships were combat vessels used to protect the empire’s coasts, transport troops, and fight enemy fleets. Rome’s major fleets included the Classis Misenensis and Classis Ravennas. Its warships ranged from large, oared triremes and quinqueremes to smaller, faster liburnians. During the First Punic War against Carthage, some Roman warships carried a corvus, a hinged boarding bridge with a spike. Sailors dropped it onto an enemy ship so the spike gripped its deck, holding the vessels together while Roman soldiers crossed to fight. Warships also appeared in naumachiae, staged naval battles put on as public spectacles, sometimes in flooded amphitheatres. So the vessels used by Rome’s fleets were Roman warships, and their spiked boarding bridge was called the corvus.

Zheng He, born Ma He, was a eunuch and admiral at the court of China’s Ming dynasty. In the early fifteenth century, he commanded seven state-sponsored treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean. His fleets visited places in Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa, carrying Chinese goods and gifts and bringing back foreign envoys and products. These expeditions helped the Ming court build diplomatic ties and display its power abroad. Zheng He’s voyages were sponsored by the Yongle Emperor, a major Ming ruler who moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing and commissioned the Forbidden City there. Together, the voyages and the new capital showed the emperor’s ambition to strengthen his rule and raise China’s standing in the wider world.

The An Lushan Rebellion was a devastating uprising against China’s Tang dynasty that lasted from 755 to 763. It began when An Lushan, a powerful commander on the northern frontier, turned his armies against the Tang court. Rebel forces captured the capital, Chang’an, and Emperor Xuanzong fled. During his retreat, soldiers blamed his renowned consort Yang Guifei and her family for the crisis and demanded her death at Mawei. Yang Guifei, celebrated for her beauty, later became the subject of Bai Juyi’s poem “The Song of Everlasting Sorrow.” Years of warfare caused enormous destruction and loss of life. Although the Tang eventually defeated the rebels, the conflict left the dynasty much weaker and increased the power of regional military commanders.

The Holy Roman Emperor was the ruler of the Holy Roman Empire, a medieval realm that grew from the East Frankish kingdom and included much of what is now Germany and parts of central Europe and Italy. The title developed from the earlier “Emperor of the Romans,” which Pope Leo III gave to the Frankish king Charlemagne on Christmas Day in 800. Later emperors were traditionally chosen by a group of powerful German rulers called prince-electors. Otto the Great, a Saxon ruler, defeated Berengar II of Italy and was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope John XII in 962. His coronation is commonly treated as the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire. Another famous Holy Roman Emperor was Frederick Barbarossa, who ruled in the 12th century.

Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia was born in 1901, the youngest daughter of Tsar Nicholas II and his wife, Alexandra. A tsar was a ruler of Russia, and Nicholas II was the last to hold that title. After the Russian Revolution, the Bolsheviks took power and held the former imperial family captive. In July 1918, they executed Anastasia, her parents, and her siblings in a basement room of Ipatiev House, a residence in Yekaterinburg named for its former owner. For decades, rumors claimed that Anastasia had escaped, and several women claimed to be her, sometimes hoping to claim a royal fortune. Later DNA evidence confirmed that Anastasia died with her family.

The British women’s suffrage movement campaigned to end laws that prevented women from voting in United Kingdom parliamentary elections. Its supporters used different methods: Millicent Fawcett and other suffragists pursued petitions and lobbying, while some suffragettes used militant protests. Emmeline Pankhurst founded the Women’s Social and Political Union in Manchester in 1903. The group became known for direct action, and Pankhurst was repeatedly imprisoned for campaigning for votes for women. Protesters also joined the peaceful Mud March in 1907, while Mary Richardson later damaged the painting Rokeby Venus to protest the imprisonment of a fellow campaigner. The Representation of the People Act 1918 was a major victory, giving the parliamentary vote to many women aged 30 and over who met property qualifications. Women gained voting rights on the same terms as men in 1928.

Cardinal Richelieu, also known as Armand Jean du Plessis, was a French churchman and chief minister to King Louis XIII in the early 1600s. Nicknamed the “Red Eminence” for his cardinal’s red robes and political influence, he strengthened royal authority by limiting the power of nobles and ending the Huguenots’ ability to act as an independent political force. Under his direction, royal forces besieged the Atlantic port of La Rochelle, a major Huguenot stronghold, and captured it in 1628. Richelieu also directed French policy during much of the Thirty Years’ War. Although he was a Catholic cardinal, he backed Protestant powers against the Catholic Habsburg rulers because he considered Habsburg power a threat to France. His successor, Cardinal Mazarin, continued many of his policies.

The Cycladic civilization flourished during the Bronze Age on the Cyclades, a group of islands in the Aegean Sea that includes Delos and Naxos. Its settlements date mainly to the third and second millennia BCE. Archaeologists have learned about Cycladic life from remains of settlements and objects found in graves, especially sculptures carved from marble. The best-known sculptures are folded-arm figurines: upright, usually nude human figures with elongated bodies and arms folded across the torso, with the hands resting near the abdomen. Their faces are highly simplified, often showing no features except a nose. Although many were buried with the dead, their exact purpose is unknown. These distinctive figures help archaeologists recognize Cycladic art and distinguish it from the art of other ancient Aegean societies.

The Prime Minister of Canada is the head of the country’s federal government, based in Ottawa. The prime minister leads the government and normally holds office while it has the confidence, or support, of the elected House of Commons. Canada’s first prime minister, John A. Macdonald, resigned in 1873 after the Pacific Scandal raised accusations about railway contracts and political donations. Later prime ministers included William Lyon Mackenzie King and Pierre Trudeau. In the 1926 King–Byng affair, Mackenzie King resigned after Governor General Lord Byng refused his request to call an election. Byng then appointed Conservative leader Arthur Meighen as prime minister, but Meighen’s government soon lost a confidence vote. An election followed, and King returned to office.

Matthias Corvinus, also known as Matthias I, was elected king of Hungary in 1458. He was the son of John Hunyadi, a military leader who had helped defend Hungary against the Ottoman Empire. The name Corvinus is linked to the raven shown on Matthias’s coat of arms. As king, Matthias strengthened royal power and became known for his Renaissance court, where he supported scholars, artists, and learning. He also transformed Hungary’s military by maintaining a professional force called the Black Army. Unlike armies made up mainly of soldiers called up for a short time, this force included experienced troops who could serve for longer campaigns. Its disciplined soldiers fought across Central Europe, helping make Matthias one of the region’s most powerful rulers.

The Battle of Austerlitz was fought on December 2, 1805, during the War of the Third Coalition. Napoleon Bonaparte’s French army faced a larger force of Russian and Austrian troops near Austerlitz, in what is now the Czech Republic.
