Napoleon deliberately gave up a strong position on the Pratzen Heights and made his right flank appear weak. Coalition troops advanced from the heights to attack it, leaving their center exposed. At the right moment, French soldiers climbed back onto the Pratzen Heights and struck through that weakened center, splitting the opposing army. This decisive French victory helped bring the war to a close and forced Austria to make peace. Often called the Battle of the Three Emperors, Austerlitz is widely regarded as one of Napoleon’s greatest victories.

The Partitions of Poland were three territorial divisions of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth between 1772 and 1795. Its powerful neighbors—Russia, Prussia, and Austria—seized its lands while the Commonwealth struggled with political weakness and outside interference. In the First Partition, in 1772, all three powers took territory. The Second Partition, in 1793, was carried out by Russia and Prussia without Austria, shrinking the Commonwealth further despite attempts at reform. After an uprising against foreign control, the three powers divided the remaining territory in the Third Partition of 1795. Poland then disappeared as an independent state from the map of Europe. It did not regain independence until 1918, after World War I.

The Tumu Crisis was a major military disaster for China’s Ming dynasty in 1449. Emperor Yingzong personally led a large army north to confront the Oirats, a Mongol group whose forces were commanded by Esen Taishi. The campaign went badly, and as the Ming army retreated toward Beijing, Oirat troops attacked it near Tumu Fortress. Much of the Ming force was destroyed, and Yingzong was captured—an extraordinary humiliation for a reigning emperor. The Ming court chose a new emperor and organized Beijing’s defenses, preventing Esen from turning his victory into the conquest of the capital. Yingzong was later released. The event is commonly called the Tumu Crisis, and it exposed serious weaknesses in Ming military leadership and planning.

African Pygmy peoples is a collective term for several distinct Indigenous communities of Central Africa, including the Mbenga, Mbuti, and Twa. Many have long lived in or near the Congo Basin’s rainforests and traditionally relied on hunting, gathering, and trade with neighboring farmers. The term “Pygmy” refers to the relatively short average height of some groups, but it can be considered offensive or misleading because these communities have different languages, cultures, and preferred names. Their histories were strongly affected by the Bantu expansion, a long-term spread of Bantu-speaking populations that began near the present-day Cameroon–Nigeria border and extended across central, eastern, and southern Africa. These migrations brought farming and, in later phases, ironworking to many areas, changing the populations and societies of the region.

The King of Rome was the title held by each of Rome’s seven traditional rulers before the city became a republic. According to legend, the first king was Romulus, who founded Rome with his twin brother Remus after they had been rescued as infants from the Tiber River. Later kings were credited with shaping Rome’s laws, religious customs, and government, although much of what is known about them comes from stories written long after they lived. The seventh and last king was Tarquinius Superbus, also called Tarquin the Proud. Roman accounts say that Lucius Junius Brutus helped overthrow him around 509 BCE. Afterward, the Romans established a republic instead of choosing another king.

The Roman Forum was the center of public life in ancient Rome. Set in a valley between the Capitoline and Palatine hills, it held government buildings, temples, shops, and open spaces where people gathered. Speakers addressed crowds from a platform called the Rostra, while the Curia Julia housed the Roman Senate and the Temple of Saturn served as a religious site and treasury. The Via Sacra, the Forum’s main road, carried religious processions and triumphal parades. On the Forum’s northwest edge stands the three-bayed Arch of Septimius Severus, dedicated in 203 CE to celebrate Roman campaigns against the Parthian Empire. Its inscription originally honored the emperor and his sons Caracalla and Geta, but Caracalla later had Geta’s name erased.

Nebuchadnezzar II ruled the Neo-Babylonian Empire from 605 to 562 BCE. He captured Jerusalem and deported many of its inhabitants to Babylon, an episode remembered as the Babylonian Captivity. He also expanded and decorated his capital, rebuilding major temples and improving the processional way used for religious ceremonies. One of its most famous monuments was the Ishtar Gate, a ceremonial entrance that Nebuchadnezzar II embellished with blue glazed bricks and reliefs of bulls and mušḫuššu dragons. A reconstructed portion of the gate can be seen at the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. His military campaigns and building projects made him one of Babylon’s best-known rulers.

The Battle of Kursk was a major World War II battle fought between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union on the Eastern Front in July 1943. After its defeat at Stalingrad, Germany hoped to regain the initiative by cutting off a large bulge, or salient, in the Soviet front line around Kursk. The German offensive was codenamed Operation Citadel: Army Group Center attacked from the north while Army Group South attacked from the south, aiming to meet and trap the Soviet forces between them. The Soviets had prepared deep defenses, including minefields and anti-tank positions. The battle involved enormous numbers of soldiers and tanks, including a major armored clash near Prokhorovka. Germany failed to eliminate the salient, and the Soviet Union gained momentum for further offensives.

Cicero was a Roman statesman, philosopher, and master of public speaking. Born in Arpinum, he rose to the consulship even though he lacked patrician ancestry, an unusual achievement in Roman politics. As consul in 63 BCE, he exposed Catiline’s plot against the Roman Republic in a series of powerful speeches. Cicero also wrote about philosophy and rhetoric, the art of effective speaking. His dialogue De Oratore, meaning “On the Orator,” is set in 91 BCE at the villa of Lucius Licinius Crassus. In it, Crassus and Marcus Antonius discuss the knowledge and abilities an ideal orator needs. Cicero later opposed Mark Antony and was proscribed in 43 BCE. After his murder, his head and hands were displayed on the Rostra, the public speaking platform in Rome.

The wives of Henry VIII were six women who married the Tudor king of England during the 1500s. Their fates are often remembered in order with the rhyme “Divorced, beheaded, died; Divorced, beheaded, survived.” Henry’s first wife was Catherine of Aragon, a Spanish-born princess and the mother of his daughter Mary, who later became Queen Mary I. When Catherine did not give Henry a surviving son, he sought to end their marriage. A long dispute over whether it was valid led to its annulment and helped drive Henry’s break with the Roman Catholic Church. His later wives were Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard, and Catherine Parr. “Divorced” in the rhyme is a convenient shorthand: Henry’s marriages to Catherine of Aragon and Anne of Cleves were annulled.

The Good Friday Agreement was signed on 10 April 1998 to help end the Troubles, a decades-long conflict in Northern Ireland involving violence over whether the region should remain part of the United Kingdom or join the Republic of Ireland. Also called the Belfast Agreement, it created a devolved assembly at Stormont, where Northern Irish parties would share power over local government. It also established a North-South Ministerial Council to support cooperation between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland. The negotiations involved parties with sharply different views, so an independent mediator helped them reach a compromise. That mediator was George Mitchell, a former U.S. Senate majority leader from Maine, who chaired the multiparty talks. The agreement became a major step toward peace, though it did not erase all political disagreements.

The Perón family played a major role in Argentine politics. Juan Perón, a former military officer, served as president of Argentina three times and built a political movement that emphasized support for workers. His second wife, Eva Perón, was an actress before becoming first lady. Widely known as Evita, she used her public influence to advocate for workers and women’s suffrage, and she founded the Eva Perón Foundation to help people in need. Eva died in 1952, before Juan returned from exile and won the presidency again in 1973. His third wife, Isabel Perón, later became president after his death. Together, Juan, Eva, and Isabel are the best-known members of the Perón family.

The White Rose of York was a heraldic emblem associated with the House of York, a branch of England’s Plantagenet royal family. It identified the Yorkist side in the Wars of the Roses, a series of struggles for the English throne against another Plantagenet branch, the House of Lancaster. The two sides are traditionally linked with floral symbols: a white rose for York and a red rose for Lancaster. Richard III was the last Yorkist king. In 1485, Henry Tudor defeated him at the Battle of Bosworth Field, a turning point that largely ended the fighting. Henry became King Henry VII, bringing the Tudor dynasty to power. The white rose remains a recognizable symbol of York and its role in this conflict.

The House of Hohenzollern was a German ruling family that produced the kings of Prussia and all three emperors of the German Empire, also called Imperial Germany or the Second Reich. Under Prussian leadership, German states united after the Franco-Prussian War. In 1871, the Prussian king Wilhelm I, who had ruled Prussia since 1861, was proclaimed the first German Emperor at the Palace of Versailles in France. His chancellor, Otto von Bismarck, played a major role in unification. Wilhelm I’s son Frederick III became emperor in 1888 but died after a short reign. Frederick’s son Wilhelm II then ruled until 1918, including during the First World War. Thus, the Hohenzollern dynasty linked the earlier kingdom of Prussia to the newly unified German Empire.

A World’s Fair is a large international exhibition where nations and host cities display achievements in technology, industry, culture, and art. These fairs became especially important during the nineteenth century, when industrialization brought rapid changes in transportation, manufacturing, and everyday life. London’s 1851 World’s Fair took place in the Crystal Palace, a huge glass-and-iron building. The 1893 Chicago World’s Fair featured a new attraction: the Ferris wheel. Standing 264 feet tall, it carried visitors in 36 passenger cars and was designed as a dramatic American response to the Eiffel Tower, which had impressed visitors to Paris’s 1889 fair. Later fairs continued to create landmarks, including the Space Needle built for Seattle’s 1962 World’s Fair.

The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were a legendary complex of lush, irrigated terraces counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Ancient accounts placed them in Babylon, a Mesopotamian city also known for the Ishtar Gate and the law code of Hammurabi. According to tradition, the Neo-Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II had the gardens built in the sixth century BCE for his wife Amytis, who came from Media. The terraces were supposedly meant to remind her of the green, mountainous landscape of her homeland. Keeping plants alive high above the ground would have required a way to lift and distribute water, perhaps from the Euphrates River. Archaeologists have not found conclusive evidence that the gardens existed in Babylon, so their location and even their existence remain debated.

Victoriano Huerta was a Mexican army general who took power during the Mexican Revolution. In February 1913, a period of fighting in Mexico City known as the Ten Tragic Days ended with Huerta’s coup against President Francisco I. Madero. Madero had come to power after opposing the long rule of Porfirio Díaz and campaigning on the slogan “Effective suffrage, no reelection.” Huerta’s takeover ended Madero’s presidency, and Madero was killed soon afterward. Although U.S. ambassador Henry Lane Wilson supported the coup, the United States did not formally recognize Huerta’s government. Huerta ruled as a dictator, but opposition from revolutionary forces weakened his hold on power. He resigned and fled Mexico in 1914.

Austria-Hungary was a large Central European empire ruled by the Habsburg dynasty from 1867 until the end of World War I. It was called a “dual monarchy” because the Ausgleich, or Compromise of 1867, joined the Austrian lands and the Hungarian lands, known as the lands of the Crown of Saint Stephen, under one ruler. Austria and Hungary had separate governments but shared responsibility for matters such as foreign policy and the army. In June 1914, the empire’s heir to the throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, visited Sarajevo with his wife, Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg. A Bosnian Serb nationalist assassinated them there. Austria-Hungary’s response to the killing sparked a crisis that escalated into World War I. Defeat in that war led to the empire’s dissolution in 1918.

Suryavarman II was a king of the Khmer Empire, which ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from its capital at Angkor in present-day Cambodia. During the early twelfth century, he strengthened and expanded the empire through military campaigns. His most famous achievement was commissioning Angkor Wat, a vast temple complex near the Khmer capital. Built as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu, it later became an important Buddhist pilgrimage site. Its towers, galleries, and detailed stone carvings show the skill of Khmer builders and artists. Angkor Wat remains one of the world’s largest religious monuments and a lasting symbol of Cambodia. If asked to name the ruler who commissioned it, the answer is Suryavarman II; if asked to name the complex he commissioned, the answer is Angkor Wat.

Ali Hassan al-Majid was a senior official in Iraq’s Ba’athist government and a cousin of dictator Saddam Hussein. He held powerful posts, including defense minister, but is most notorious for directing the Anfal campaign against Kurdish communities in northern Iraq in 1988. During this military offensive, Iraqi forces destroyed villages, forced people from their homes, and used chemical weapons, killing thousands of Kurds. The attacks earned al-Majid the nickname “Chemical Ali.” After Saddam Hussein’s government fell in 2003, al-Majid was put on trial and convicted of crimes connected to the mass killings and chemical attacks. He was executed in 2010. His role in the Anfal campaign is a major example of the Iraqi government’s violent persecution of the Kurds.

The Second Punic War was fought between Rome and Carthage from 218 to 201 BCE. Carthage’s general Hannibal led his army across the Alps into Italy and defeated Roman forces at Trebia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae. These victories threatened Rome, but they did not end the war. The Roman commander Quintus Fabius Maximus used a cautious delaying strategy, avoiding major battles while wearing down Hannibal’s army. The war also put pressure on Roman finances, prompting the Lex Oppia, a law that restricted women’s public display of wealth through gold jewelry, expensive clothing, and certain carriage use. Rome later drove Carthaginian forces out of Iberia after the Battle of Ilipa. In 201 BCE, the war ended with Rome’s victory over Carthage.

Herculaneum was a wealthy Roman seaside city near modern Naples, Italy. In 79 CE, Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Herculaneum as well as nearby Pompeii. While Pompeii is famous for its ash-covered streets and wall graffiti, Herculaneum was struck by fast-moving, extremely hot clouds of volcanic gas and debris. The material that covered the city preserved details rarely found at ancient sites, including wooden beams, furniture, and parts of buildings’ upper stories. One of Herculaneum’s most remarkable discoveries is the Villa of the Papyri, a lavish Roman residence containing a large collection of papyrus scrolls. The eruption carbonized the scrolls, making them fragile but also helping them survive. Some contain philosophical writings associated with Philodemus, offering evidence of what educated Romans read and studied.

The Knights Templar were a Catholic military order founded in Jerusalem around 1119, during the Crusades. These expeditions by western Christian powers aimed to seize or defend Jerusalem and other holy sites. The Templars’ original mission was to protect Christian pilgrims traveling to the region. They took their name from their headquarters near Jerusalem’s Temple Mount and later fought in Crusader armies. During the Third Crusade, launched after Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187, leaders including Richard I of England and Philip II of France campaigned against him. Donations made the Templars major landholders, and their system for holding and transferring money made them early bankers. After accusations of wrongdoing and pressure from Philip IV of France, Pope Clement V dissolved the order in 1312.

Herodotus was an ancient Greek writer often called the “Father of History” because he investigated the past and brought different accounts together in his book the Histories. Much of it describes the Greco-Persian Wars, in which Greek city-states fought the Persian Empire. Herodotus wrote about the Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BCE, when 300 Spartans, alongside other Greek defenders, fought an invading Persian army at a narrow mountain pass. The Spartans died there, but their stand became famous. Herodotus also recorded stories that modern historians doubt, such as a claim that the Persian army at Thermopylae had more than 1.5 million troops. His work is valuable evidence, but it reminds us to check ancient claims against other sources.

The 1984–1985 United Kingdom miners’ strike was a major labor conflict that lasted from March 1984 to March 1985. It began amid plans to close coal pits, which threatened mining jobs and the communities that depended on them. The National Union of Mineworkers opposed the closures, led by its president, Arthur Scargill, who had held that position since 1982. The union faced the government of Conservative prime minister Margaret Thatcher, which argued that many pits were too costly to keep open. The dispute brought large protests, confrontations between picketers and police, and hardship for mining families. The miners ultimately returned to work without stopping the closures. The strike became one of modern Britain’s defining industrial disputes because it showed how deeply economic change could divide workers, communities, and the government.

The Fall of Constantinople was the Ottoman capture of the Byzantine Empire’s capital in 1453. The Ottoman army was led by 21-year-old Sultan Mehmed II, later known as Mehmed the Conqueror. During the siege, his forces used powerful cannons, including one built by the engineer Orban, against the city’s Theodosian Walls. When the Ottomans entered Constantinople, the Byzantine Empire came to an end. Mehmed made the city an Ottoman capital, and the Hagia Sophia, which had been a Christian church, became a mosque. The fall also had effects beyond the city: Greek-speaking scholars moved west, bringing knowledge of ancient texts to places such as Florence and Venice. In Moscow, the idea grew that it was a “Third Rome,” carrying on the Christian imperial tradition after Byzantium’s defeat.

The Zulu Kingdom was a powerful 19th-century state in southeastern Africa, in what is now South Africa. Its founder, Shaka, built a disciplined army that often used the “buffalo horn” formation to surround enemies. The kingdom’s rise contributed to a period of warfare and migration known as the Mfecane. In 1879, King Cetshwayo’s forces fought Britain in the Anglo-Zulu War. On 22 January, British commander Lord Chelmsford split his column, leaving a camp near Isandlwana, a prominent hill in present-day KwaZulu-Natal. Zulu warriors overran the camp in the Battle of Isandlwana, winning a major victory. Britain sent more troops, however, and defeated the Zulu army at the Battle of Ulundi later that year, ending the kingdom’s independence.

For centuries, Japan’s emperor was the official sovereign, but much of the country’s political and military power belonged to a hereditary ruler called the shogun. A shogun governed formally in the emperor’s name, while the emperor and his court remained in Kyoto, Japan’s imperial capital for nearly a thousand years. The last shogun was Tokugawa Yoshinobu, who relinquished power as the shogunate ended in 1868. This change was part of the Meiji Restoration, which returned governing authority to the emperor. Emperor Meiji then moved the imperial capital from Kyoto to Tokyo. These events marked the end of Japan’s long period of shogun rule and the beginning of major changes in its government and society.

Wilhelm I was a king of Prussia from the Hohenzollern dynasty who became the first emperor, or Kaiser, of a united Germany. He appointed the Prussian statesman Otto von Bismarck minister-president in 1862 and relied on him to strengthen Prussia and pursue German unification. Bismarck used diplomacy and wars against Denmark, Austria, and France to bring German states together under Prussian leadership. During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871, Wilhelm led Prussia against France, whose capital, Paris, endured a Prussian siege. In January 1871, while the war was still underway, Wilhelm was proclaimed German emperor at the Palace of Versailles in France. Bismarck then became the new German Empire’s first chancellor, while Wilhelm remained its emperor until his death in 1888.

The Eighty Years’ War (1568–1648) was a long struggle in which Dutch provinces fought to break away from the Spanish Habsburg monarchy. Philip II of Spain ruled the Netherlands, but many people there opposed Spanish taxes, restrictions on local self-government, and the persecution of Protestants. William the Silent, also known as William of Orange, had earlier served at the Spanish court but became a leading political organizer of the revolt. He helped unite provinces against Philip II before being assassinated at the Prinsenhof in Delft in 1584. The fighting continued for decades after his death. In 1648, the Peace of Münster formally recognized the independence of the Dutch Republic, ending the conflict known as the Eighty Years’ War.

The Edict of Milan was a 313 CE agreement between the Roman emperors Constantine the Great and Licinius that allowed Christians and people of other faiths to worship freely. It ended official persecution of Christians and ordered that property taken from Christian communities be returned. The agreement is named after Milan, the city where the emperors met. Constantine had gained control of the western Roman Empire after winning the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312 CE; according to tradition, he saw a Christian sign before the battle and used the Chi Rho symbol on his soldiers’ shields. He later called the Council of Nicaea, which addressed disputes over Christian beliefs, and founded Constantinople on the site of Byzantium.

Nicholas II became tsar of Russia in 1894 after the death of his father, Alexander III. He was the last sovereign of the Romanov dynasty, which had ruled Russia for more than 300 years. During his reign, Russia faced military defeats, poverty, political unrest, and the hardships of World War I. In 1917, revolution broke out, and Nicholas abdicated, ending the monarchy. As rival groups struggled for power, the Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, took control later that year. Nicholas and his family were held captive and eventually moved to the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, a city in the Ural region. In July 1918, Bolsheviks executed Nicholas, his wife, their five children, and several attendants there.

Ferdinand II of Aragon was a monarch of the Trastámara dynasty who became ruler of Aragon, an eastern Iberian kingdom, in 1479 after the death of his father, John II. His wife, Isabella I of Castile, had begun ruling the western Iberian kingdom of Castile in 1474. Their marriage brought the two kingdoms into a dynastic union, an important step toward the formation of Spain, although Castile and Aragon kept separate laws and institutions. Known together as the Catholic Monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella completed the conquest of Granada in 1492, ending the last Muslim-ruled kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula. That same year, they sponsored Christopher Columbus’s first voyage across the Atlantic, which began lasting contact between Europe and the Americas.

The Golden Stool is a sacred symbol of the Asante people of present-day Ghana. According to Asante tradition, it holds the soul of the nation and represents the unity and authority of its people. Although it is called a stool, no one is meant to sit on it, not even a king. In 1900, British governor Frederick Hodgson demanded to sit on the Golden Stool, showing disregard for its meaning. His demand helped spark the War of the Golden Stool, in which the Asante resisted British colonial rule. Yaa Asantewaa, the queen mother of Ejisu, mobilized fighters and became a leading commander in that resistance. The conflict shows why the stool was far more than a valuable object: to the Asante, it stood for their identity and independence.

The Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor is an enormous burial complex near Xi’an, built for Qin Shi Huang, the ruler who unified China in 221 BCE. Its central tomb remains unopened. An ancient historian described rivers of mercury inside it, and high mercury levels detected around the tomb suggest that the account may have some truth, though its contents are still unknown. In 1974, farmers digging a well nearby discovered pits filled with life-size clay soldiers and horses. This assemblage, called the Terracotta Army, was buried to guard the emperor in the afterlife. The figures were individually modeled, with varied faces, hairstyles, and uniforms. Together, the tomb and its surrounding pits show how much labor and wealth the emperor devoted to his burial.

David Ben-Gurion was a Zionist labor leader and a principal founder of the State of Israel. Born in Płońsk in 1886, he later moved to Ottoman-ruled Palestine and worked to establish a Jewish homeland there. During the final years of the British Mandate, he chaired the Jewish Agency, which represented much of the Jewish community in Palestine. On 14 May 1948, as British rule ended, Ben-Gurion read the declaration establishing Israel at a ceremony in Tel Aviv. He then became the new state’s first prime minister, leading its government through its early years. Israel’s national parliament is called the Knesset. Ben-Gurion’s role in declaring independence and heading the first government made him one of the most important figures in Israel’s history.

Keir Starmer is a British politician who became prime minister of the United Kingdom after the July 2024 general election. Before entering politics, he worked as a barrister, a lawyer who argues cases in court, and served as Director of Public Prosecutions from 2008 to 2013, overseeing prosecutions in England and Wales. He was elected to Parliament in 2015 as a member of the Labour Party, one of Britain’s major political parties. After Labour’s heavy defeat in the 2019 general election, Starmer succeeded Jeremy Corbyn as party leader in April 2020. He then led Labour, which had been the main opposition to the Conservative government, to a large parliamentary majority in 2024. That victory brought Labour back into government and made Starmer prime minister.

The Napoleonic Wars were a series of conflicts from 1803 to 1815 in which France, led by Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte, fought changing coalitions of European powers. Napoleon won major victories on land and gained control over much of Europe, but Britain remained a powerful opponent at sea. In 1805, at the Battle of Trafalgar off the southwestern coast of Spain, a British fleet led by Admiral Horatio Nelson defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets. That defeat ended Napoleon’s plans to invade Britain. After years of fighting and setbacks, Napoleon returned to power briefly in 1815, but forces of the Seventh Coalition, including an army led by the Duke of Wellington, defeated him at the Battle of Waterloo. Waterloo ended the Napoleonic Wars and Napoleon’s rule.

The Edict of Nantes was a royal decree issued in 1598 by Henry IV of France after decades of fighting between Catholics and Huguenots, the country’s Protestants. Henry had been raised Protestant and converted to Catholicism before becoming king. He was the first monarch of the Bourbon dynasty, which followed the Valois dynasty. His edict gave Huguenots defined rights to worship and legal protections, helping to ease the religious conflict that had torn France apart. It did not make all religions equal or end every dispute, but it was an important step toward toleration. If asked to name the 1598 settlement, the answer is the Edict of Nantes; if asked which king issued it, the answer is Henry IV.

The First Crusade was an armed expedition begun after Pope Urban II called on Western Christians at the Council of Clermont in 1095 to aid Eastern Christians and recover the Holy Land. His call followed an appeal for military help from Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who ruled from 1081 to 1118 and faced pressure from the Seljuk Turks. As crusading leaders crossed Byzantine territory, Alexios negotiated with them and sought promises that lands they recovered would be returned to his empire. The crusaders then marched through the Middle East and captured Jerusalem in 1099. They established several Crusader states, including the Kingdom of Jerusalem, which Baldwin I later ruled. The First Crusade was the opening campaign in the Crusades, a series of medieval religious wars.

The War of the Three Henrys was a 1587–1589 conflict within the French Wars of Religion. It was named for its three main rivals: Henry III, the reigning Catholic king of France; Henry I, Duke of Guise, a leader of the Catholic League; and Henry of Navarre, a Protestant claimant to the throne. The struggle centered on who would succeed Henry III. Many French Catholics opposed the possibility of a Protestant king, while Guise and his supporters challenged Henry III’s authority. French Protestants, especially followers of the Reformed or Calvinist tradition, were known as Huguenots. After Guise and Henry III were killed, Henry of Navarre inherited the throne as Henry IV. He later converted to Catholicism to strengthen his rule over a largely Catholic kingdom.

The Alþingi (also called the Althing) is Iceland’s national parliament and is often described as the world’s oldest surviving parliamentary institution. Traditionally founded in 930, it began as an annual outdoor assembly where chieftains gathered to make laws and settle disputes. Those meetings took place at Þingvellir, a rift-valley site in southwestern Iceland. There, a place known as the Law Rock was a focal point for announcing laws and addressing the assembly. The early Alþingi was not a modern elected parliament, but it helped people across Iceland make shared decisions at a time when the island had no king. Today, Iceland’s legislature still bears the name Alþingi, while Þingvellir is protected as a national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Diadochi, a Greek word meaning “successors,” were the commanders and other dynasts who struggled for power after Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE without an adult heir. Alexander had conquered a vast empire stretching from Greece and Egypt to parts of India, but no one person could keep it united. The Diadochi fought a series of wars that divided his lands into Hellenistic kingdoms, where Greek culture mixed with local traditions. One of these successors, the former Macedonian general Ptolemy I Soter, established control of Egypt. He brought Alexander’s body to Alexandria and founded the Ptolemaic dynasty, which ruled Egypt for nearly three centuries. Its last ruler was Cleopatra VII.

The sans-culottes were a radical movement of working people during the French Revolution, especially artisans, shopkeepers, and laborers in Paris. Their name means “without knee-breeches”: instead of the short breeches associated with wealthy men, they wore the long trousers common among working people. The sans-culottes demanded affordable bread, greater political equality, and stronger action against enemies of the revolution. In popular images, they often wore a soft red cap with a tip that pointed forward. Called the Phrygian cap or liberty cap, it became a symbol of revolutionary freedom in France. Its design recalled a cap associated with people freed from slavery in ancient Rome. Clothing helped the sans-culottes show both their ordinary social background and their revolutionary beliefs.

The Honrado Concejo de la Mesta was a powerful association of sheep owners and shepherds in medieval Castile, a kingdom in what is now Spain. Its flocks produced wool, a valuable product sold to cloth makers in other parts of Europe. Many shepherds practiced transhumance: they moved their sheep between summer and winter pastures to find grazing land. In 1273, the Castilian king Alfonso X granted the Mesta formal privileges that helped protect the flocks’ seasonal journeys along established routes. These rights gave sheep owners considerable influence and supported Castile’s wool trade. They could also cause disputes with farmers when migrating sheep crossed land that farmers wanted to cultivate.

Alexis Tsipras is a Greek politician who led Syriza, a left-wing political coalition opposed to austerity, or government spending cuts and tax increases. In January 2015, Syriza won Greece’s parliamentary election, and Tsipras became prime minister during a severe debt crisis. Greece had borrowed heavily and needed international bailout loans, but its creditors demanded further austerity in return. Tsipras promised to challenge those demands, arguing that the cuts had hurt ordinary people and the economy. In July 2015, after Greece missed a payment to the International Monetary Fund, he called a referendum asking voters whether to accept bailout terms proposed by creditors. Voters rejected the terms, although his government later agreed to another bailout. Tsipras’s time in office illustrates the difficult choices governments can face during a financial crisis.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, usually called NATO, is a military alliance founded in 1949 by the United States, Canada, and countries in Western Europe. It was created during the Cold War to help protect its members against possible Soviet aggression. Its best-known rule, Article 5, says that an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all, allowing the other members to respond together. NATO’s creation helped divide Europe into rival blocs. In 1955, the Soviet Union and communist governments in Eastern Europe formed their own military alliance, the Warsaw Pact, named for Warsaw, the capital of Poland. Although the Cold War ended, NATO continued and later took part in military operations, including a controversial 1999 intervention in Yugoslavia.

Thomas Cromwell was a lawyer and royal administrator who became one of the most powerful ministers of England’s Tudor king Henry VIII. Henry wanted to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, but Pope Clement VII refused to annul it. Henry then broke with Rome and claimed authority over the English Church, a major step in the English Reformation. Cromwell helped put this change into law and directed the dissolution of the monasteries, in which religious houses were closed and their property passed to the crown. His work strengthened royal power, but he also made powerful enemies. Henry dismissed Cromwell and had him executed in 1540. Cromwell is remembered both for reshaping England’s government and for his central role in Henry VIII’s religious changes.

In 1588, King Philip II of Spain sent a large fleet, known as the Spanish Armada, toward England. Its plan was to escort a Spanish army stationed in the Netherlands across the English Channel and overthrow England’s Protestant queen, Elizabeth I. English warships attacked and harried the Armada as it approached, and English vice admiral Francis Drake helped lead the defense. A famous story says Drake finished a game of bowls at Plymouth before sailing out, though historians are unsure whether it happened exactly that way. The Spanish fleet failed to join the army and was forced to retreat around Scotland and Ireland. Severe storms scattered its ships and caused further losses. The failed campaign weakened Spain’s attempt to invade England.

The Dutch East Indies was the name for the Netherlands’ colonial possessions across much of the archipelago that is now Indonesia. Dutch merchants first came to the region seeking valuable spices, and the Dutch East India Company established trading posts and took control of territory beginning in the 1600s. Dutch rule later expanded across many islands and lasted, with interruptions, until Indonesia gained independence in the twentieth century. The colony was administered from Batavia, a major port city on the island of Java that served as the center of Dutch colonial government and trade. Batavia is now called Jakarta, the capital of Indonesia. Remembering the two names helps distinguish the colony, the Dutch East Indies, from its colonial-era administrative center, Batavia.

The Cromwell family played important roles in England during two different periods of upheaval. In the 1530s, Thomas Cromwell, a lawyer and Henry VIII’s chief minister, helped the king secure an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. He also helped bring about England’s break with the pope in Rome and directed the dissolution of the monasteries, transferring their wealth and lands to the Crown. About a century later, his distant relative Oliver Cromwell rose to prominence during the English Civil Wars. He helped lead Parliament’s New Model Army against forces loyal to the king. After the monarchy was abolished, Oliver became Lord Protector, governing England, Scotland, and Ireland. Thomas’s work reshaped the English church; Oliver’s military and political career reshaped its government.

The Ezeiza massacre took place on June 20, 1973, near Ezeiza International Airport outside Buenos Aires, Argentina. A huge crowd had gathered to welcome former president Juan Perón home after nearly 18 years in exile. Perón had been overthrown in 1955 and had spent much of his exile in Spain. His political movement, known as Peronism, included both left-wing and right-wing groups, and their rivalry erupted during the welcome rally. Armed right-wing Peronists fired on left-wing supporters in the crowd, killing and injuring many people. Because of the violence, Perón’s plane was diverted to another airport. The episode became known as the Ezeiza massacre and exposed deep divisions within the movement just as Perón returned to Argentina.

“Carthago delenda est” is a Latin phrase meaning “Carthage must be destroyed.” It is traditionally associated with Cato the Elder, a Roman senator and former censor who wanted Rome to go to war with Carthage. According to tradition, Cato ended speech after speech in the Senate with a call for Carthage’s destruction, even when the debate was about something else. Carthage, near modern-day Tunis in Tunisia, had been Rome’s powerful rival in earlier conflicts called the Punic Wars; the Carthaginian general Hannibal had led its forces during the Second Punic War. Cato’s repeated warning helped express Roman fears that Carthage might become a threat again. Rome later defeated Carthage in the Third Punic War and destroyed the city in 146 BCE.

Magna Carta, Latin for “Great Charter,” was issued in 1215 by King John of the Kingdom of England after rebellious barons challenged his taxes and use of royal power. It set out rules the king was expected to obey and protected certain rights, mainly those of nobles and other free people rather than everyone. Clause 61 gave a group of 25 barons the authority to demand that John follow the charter and, if he refused, to take action against him. John soon rejected the agreement, and the conflict continued in the First Barons’ War. Although many of its original provisions were later changed or removed, Magna Carta became an important symbol of the idea that rulers must obey the law. In 1707, the Kingdom of England united with Scotland to form the Kingdom of Great Britain.

The White Australia policy was a system of laws and government practices designed to limit non-European immigration after Australia became a federation in 1901. It grew partly from hostility toward Chinese migrants, who had faced discrimination during nineteenth-century gold rushes, and reflected a wider belief among many white Australians that the country should remain predominantly European. Its main early law was the Immigration Restriction Act 1901. Rather than openly banning every non-European applicant, the act let officials require a prospective migrant to write down a passage dictated in a European language chosen by the officials. They could choose a language the applicant did not know, making the test a powerful way to deny entry. The policy was gradually dismantled during the mid-twentieth century.

Al-Qaeda is a transnational Islamist terrorist organization founded by Osama bin Laden in the late 1980s. It developed from networks formed during the war against Soviet forces in Afghanistan and later carried out attacks in several countries. In 1998, al-Qaeda bombed U.S. embassies in Nairobi, Kenya, and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, killing hundreds of people. The group also claimed responsibility for the 2000 bombing of the USS Cole, a U.S. Navy ship that was refueling in Aden, a port city on Yemen’s southern coast near the entrance to the Red Sea. Bin Laden led al-Qaeda until U.S. Navy SEALs killed him in 2011. Another longtime leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri, helped shape the group’s ideology.

The 1980s, the decade from 1980 through 1989, were a turning point in the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union. Ronald Reagan was U.S. president for most of the decade, from 1981 to 1989. In March 1981, John Hinckley Jr. shot and wounded Reagan outside the Washington Hilton hotel; a copy of The Catcher in the Rye was later found among Hinckley’s belongings. Reagan survived and continued to lead the United States during a period of tension and later diplomacy with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev. In 1987, Reagan publicly urged Gorbachev to tear down the Berlin Wall, which divided East and West Berlin. The wall opened in November 1989 as communist governments across Eastern Europe began to fall, signaling that the Cold War was nearing its end.

Mabo v Queensland (No 2) was a landmark 1992 decision by the High Court of Australia, the country’s highest court. It recognized that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples could hold native title: rights to land based on their traditional laws and customs that existed before British settlement. The case was brought by Eddie Mabo and other Meriam people seeking recognition of their rights to land in the Torres Strait. The court rejected terra nullius, a colonial legal doctrine meaning “land belonging to no one.” That doctrine had treated Australia as legally unowned when Britain acquired it, ignoring Indigenous peoples’ long-standing connections to their lands. The ruling did not automatically return all land, but it allowed Indigenous groups to seek legal recognition of native title.

The Tokugawa Shogunate was the military government that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868, during a period known as the Edo period. Tokugawa Ieyasu founded it after defeating forces led by Ishida Mitsunari at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, and he governed from Edo, now Tokyo. To keep regional lords, called daimyo, under control, the shogunate used a policy called sankin-kōtai, or alternate attendance. Daimyo had to spend alternating periods in their own domains and in Edo, while their families generally stayed in the capital. The travel and expense weakened the lords and made rebellion harder. The shogunate also sharply restricted foreign contact under policies known as sakoku. It ended with the Meiji Restoration in 1868.

The Khmelnytsky Uprising was a revolt that began in 1648 and lasted until 1657. Led by Bohdan Khmelnytsky, it brought Cossacks and other groups in Ukrainian lands into conflict with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The Cossacks were communities known for their military skills, especially as horsemen. Many rebels opposed the Commonwealth’s rule, including limits on Cossack privileges and pressures on Orthodox Christians. Early victories allowed Khmelnytsky to build a Cossack-led government in territory that is now part of Ukraine. This polity was commonly called the Cossack Hetmanate, after the title “hetman” used by its leader. During Khmelnytsky’s leadership, its political center was Chyhyryn. The uprising weakened the Commonwealth and reshaped the balance of power in Eastern Europe.

The Six-Day War was a brief Arab-Israeli conflict fought in June 1967. Israel fought Egypt, Jordan, and Syria and won in six days. During the war, Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. The Sinai Peninsula is a large region of Egypt between the Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea. Israel’s capture of these territories changed the borders and politics of the Middle East and created disputes that continued long after the fighting ended. Egypt later made peace with Israel in a 1979 treaty, under which the Sinai Peninsula was returned to Egypt.

Frederick the Great, also known as Frederick II, ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786. A member of the Hohenzollern dynasty, he built Prussia into a major European power through military victories and government reforms. Early in his reign, he seized the valuable province of Silesia from the Habsburg rulers of Austria. During the Seven Years’ War, Prussia faced a powerful alliance that included Austria, France, and Russia, and at times seemed close to defeat. In 1762, Russia’s Empress Elizabeth died. Her successor, Peter III, admired Frederick and quickly made peace with Prussia, greatly reducing the threat it faced. This unexpected change, which helped Frederick’s kingdom survive, became known as the “Miracle of the House of Brandenburg.”

Anthony Albanese is an Australian Labor Party politician who became prime minister in May 2022 after Labor defeated the government of Scott Morrison. First elected to federal parliament in 1996, Albanese represents Grayndler, an electorate in Sydney. He had COVID-19 during the 2022 election campaign but recovered and continued campaigning. His rise to power came after Australia had faced major disruptions from the pandemic. In March 2020, while Morrison was prime minister, the Australian government introduced JobKeeper, a wage-subsidy program that helped employers keep workers on their payrolls when businesses were struggling. JobKeeper was a pandemic support measure, not a program introduced by Albanese as prime minister.

Louis was a regnal name used by eighteen kings of France. The most famous was Louis XIV, who ruled from 1643 to 1715 and was known as the Sun King. He strengthened royal power and made the Palace of Versailles a center of government and court life. In 1685, he issued the Edict of Fontainebleau, which revoked the earlier Edict of Nantes and took away protections for French Protestants. Another king with the same name, Louis XVI, ruled as France faced a financial crisis and growing demands for political change. He was guillotined during the French Revolution in 1793. Their Roman numerals show which Louis each king was: Louis XIV was Louis the Fourteenth, while Louis XVI was Louis the Sixteenth.

The United Kingdom of Israel was an ancient Israelite realm described in the Hebrew Bible as being ruled from Jerusalem by David and then his son Solomon. Solomon is remembered for asking God for wisdom, receiving a visit from the Queen of Sheba, and overseeing major building projects, including the Temple in Jerusalem. His ally Hiram of Tyre, a Phoenician ruler, supplied cedar timber and skilled workers for construction there. After Solomon’s death, disputes over the rule of his son Rehoboam led the realm to divide into two monarchies: Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Much of what is known about the united kingdom comes from biblical accounts, including the Books of Kings, which were compiled long after the events they describe.

The sinking of the RMS Titanic was one of the deadliest maritime disasters in history. In April 1912, the British passenger liner was making its maiden voyage from Southampton, England, to New York when it struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic. The ship sank on April 15, and more than 1,500 people died. There were too few lifeboats for everyone aboard, which made the loss of life much greater. After receiving Titanic’s distress signal, the Cunard liner RMS Carpathia changed course and rushed to help. It reached the lifeboats several hours after Titanic sank, rescued more than 700 survivors, and carried them to New York. The disaster led to stronger rules requiring ships to carry enough lifeboats and maintain better emergency communications.

Imelda Marcos was the first lady of the Philippines during the presidency and authoritarian rule of her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, from 1965 to 1986. She became known for lavish spending and for sponsoring large, showy buildings meant to present the Philippines as a modern, prosperous country, even as the government borrowed heavily and many Filipinos lived in poverty. Critics called her enthusiasm for grand construction projects an “edifice complex.” One of her best-known projects was the Cultural Center of the Philippines, a performing-arts venue in Manila designed by architect Leandro Locsin. It opened in 1969 as the first major building in an arts complex on Roxas Boulevard. The Marcoses’ rule ended with the 1986 People Power Revolution, after which they fled to the United States.

Attila the Hun ruled a powerful Hunnic empire in the fifth century and led military campaigns against both the Eastern and Western Roman Empires. His attacks earned him the epithet “Scourge of God.” In 451, Attila crossed the Rhine into Roman Gaul, a region roughly corresponding to modern France. He advanced as far as Aurelianorum (Orléans) before a Roman-led alliance stopped him at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains. The next year, Attila invaded Italy. Near the Mincio River, he met a delegation that included Pope Leo I, the bishop of Rome. Later accounts credited Leo with persuading Attila to withdraw, although shortages, disease, and threats to Attila’s forces may also have influenced his decision. Attila died in 453, reportedly after a severe nosebleed on his wedding night.

The Sapa Inca was the supreme ruler of the Inca Empire, which was centered at Cusco in the Andes. This hereditary monarch stood at the top of the empire’s political hierarchy and directed a government that built fortresses such as Sacsayhuamán and a vast road network used by messengers called chasquis. In 1532, Atahualpa became Sapa Inca after a civil war with his half-brother Huáscar. Soon afterward, Spanish forces led by Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca. Hoping to secure his release, Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold. The Spanish took the ransom but executed him in 1533. Later Inca rulers continued to resist Spanish rule, but the office ended after the execution of Túpac Amaru I in 1572.

The Bed-ins for Peace were antiwar protests staged in 1969 by musician John Lennon and performance artist Yoko Ono. Instead of marching, the couple stayed in bed in hotel rooms and invited journalists to interview them about peace and the Vietnam War. Their first bed-in lasted a week at Amsterdam’s Hilton Hotel. They repeated the protest in late May at Montreal’s Queen Elizabeth Hotel, where they recorded the song “Give Peace a Chance” with people gathered in their room. The name “bed-in” echoed the “sit-ins” used by the civil rights movement: both turned an ordinary action into a public demonstration. By attracting media attention, Lennon and Ono hoped to spread their antiwar message around the world.

Marcus Junius Brutus was a Roman senator from a family associated with the founding of the Roman Republic. He feared that Julius Caesar, who had become dictator, held too much power and might end the Republic. Brutus joined Cassius and other senators in a plot to kill Caesar. They stabbed him on the Ides of March, March 15, in 44 BCE, during a Senate meeting at the Theatre of Pompey. Caesar’s death did not restore peace: Mark Antony spoke at his funeral, and rival leaders fought for control of Rome. Brutus and Cassius later led republican forces against Antony and Octavian but were defeated at Philippi. In Shakespeare’s play Julius Caesar, Caesar reacts to Brutus’s betrayal with the famous line “Et tu, Brute?”

The 1918 influenza pandemic was a worldwide outbreak of flu caused by an H1N1 strain of influenza A. It began in 1918, spread through 1920, and killed tens of millions of people—more than died in World War I. It is often called the “Spanish flu,” but that name does not mean the disease began in Spain. During the war, countries fighting in it restricted reports of illness, while newspapers in neutral Spain reported outbreaks more freely, making Spain seem especially hard hit. Troop movements and crowded conditions helped the virus spread. In the United States, one of the first widely reported outbreaks in 1918 occurred among soldiers at Camp Funston, an Army training camp within Fort Riley, Kansas.

The Maurya Empire was one of the first great empires of ancient India. Chandragupta Maurya founded it in the fourth century BCE and, with the guidance of his adviser Chanakya, established a powerful government with its capital at Pataliputra. The empire eventually covered much of the Indian subcontinent. A Greek ambassador named Megasthenes visited the court at Pataliputra and described Indian society in a work called the Indica. The original text has been lost, but parts survive in quotations by later classical writers. Chandragupta’s grandson Ashoka expanded the empire further, then turned toward Buddhism after witnessing the bloodshed of the Kalinga War. Ashoka had his ideas about moral conduct and good government inscribed on rocks and pillars throughout his realm.

Prince Albert was born in the German duchy of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld and married his first cousin, Queen Victoria, in 1840. Victoria ruled Britain from 1837 to 1901, a period known as the Victorian era, and was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876. Although Albert was not king, he became Victoria’s trusted adviser and took an active interest in government, education, science, and the arts. He helped organize the Great Exhibition of 1851, which displayed inventions and products from around the world in London. In 1857, Victoria formally gave him the title Prince Consort, recognizing his role as the monarch’s husband. Albert died in 1861, aged 42, and Victoria mourned him for the rest of her life.

Opium is a narcotic made from the milky sap of the opium poppy, Papaver somniferum. It can relieve pain, but it is also highly addictive. In the nineteenth century, British merchants sold opium grown in India to China, where growing addiction and the outflow of silver alarmed officials. When Chinese authorities tried to stop the trade, Britain went to war with China in the First Opium War (1839–1842). The war ended with the Treaty of Nanking, signed aboard HMS Cornwallis in 1842. Under this treaty, China ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain and opened five ports to foreign trade. Another Opium War followed in the 1850s, making opium a symbol of the unequal power Britain exercised over China.

The Reform War was a Mexican civil war fought from 1858 to 1861 between liberals, who wanted to limit the Catholic Church’s political and economic power, and conservatives, who defended its traditional role. The two sides also disagreed about property ownership and whether Mexico should have a stronger central government or give more authority to its states. One reform that helped lead to the war was the 1856 Lerdo Law. It required religious and civil corporations, including the Catholic Church and Indigenous communities, to sell much of the land they owned collectively. Liberals hoped this would create more individual landowners, but it threatened long-standing institutions and communities. Liberal forces eventually won, and their reforms became an important part of Mexican law.

The Representation of the People Act 1918 was a turning point in British democracy. It gave the vote to nearly all men aged 21 and older, greatly expanding the male electorate. It also allowed women aged 30 and older to vote if they met property qualifications, but women still did not have the same voting age as men. The law was a major victory for the women’s suffrage movement, which had spent decades campaigning for women’s right to vote. Millicent Fawcett was a leading campaigner who used constitutional methods, such as petitions and public meetings, rather than violence. She led the National Union of Women’s Suffrage Societies from 1897 to 1919 and received an honorary degree from Cambridge in 1920. Women gained voting rights on the same terms as men in 1928.

The Toyota War was the final phase of the Chadian–Libyan conflict in 1987. It was named for the Toyota Hilux pickup trucks used by Chadian forces, who mounted weapons on the vehicles and drove them in fast, lightly armed columns across the desert. This mobility helped them surprise and outmaneuver Libyan forces that had occupied parts of northern Chad. A key early victory came in January 1987 at Fada, an oasis town in northern Chad, where Chadian troops under Hassan Djamous surprised and defeated a Libyan garrison. Chad’s forces went on to drive Libyan troops from much of the north. The war showed how speed, local knowledge, and effective tactics could overcome a larger force with heavier equipment.

The emperor of Japan is the country’s hereditary sovereign. In Japanese tradition, the imperial family traces its ancestry to Amaterasu, the Shinto sun goddess. The emperor appears in The Tale of Genji, a novel written by Murasaki Shikibu during Japan’s Heian period. Genji’s father is the fictional Emperor Kiritsubo, named for a residence in the imperial palace. Genji is born to Kiritsubo’s favored consort, but her comparatively low rank makes his position at court insecure. Kiritsubo removes Genji from the line of succession and gives him the surname Minamoto, making him a subject rather than a possible future emperor. Thus, “emperor of Japan” is Kiritsubo’s title, while “Emperor Kiritsubo” is the name by which this particular ruler is known in the story.

The Monarch of the United Kingdom is the country’s sovereign and constitutional head of state. The monarch formally appoints the prime minister, opens Parliament and gives royal assent to laws, but exercises these powers largely according to constitutional convention and the advice of elected ministers. The role is therefore mainly ceremonial and symbolic. The same person is also sovereign of several independent Commonwealth realms, including Canada and Australia. Queen Elizabeth II, a member of the House of Windsor, celebrated her Diamond Jubilee in 2012 and became Britain’s longest-reigning monarch. When she died in September 2022, her eldest son succeeded her as King Charles III. Before becoming king, he had held the title Prince of Wales for more than six decades, longer than anyone else in that role.

The Berlin Conference was a meeting held in Germany from November 1884 to February 1885 during the Scramble for Africa, when European powers were competing for African territory. German chancellor Otto von Bismarck hosted and chaired the conference. Delegates negotiated rules for making colonial claims, including the principle of “effective occupation”: a country could not simply claim territory on a map but had to show that it exercised authority there. The conference did not draw every later colonial border, but its rules helped European empires expand and divide Africa. African leaders were not invited to decide what would happen to their lands. The conference is therefore remembered as a major example of imperial powers making decisions about other peoples without their consent.

The Edict of Worms was a decree issued in 1521 by Holy Roman Emperor Charles V at an imperial assembly in the German city of Worms. It targeted Martin Luther, a theologian whose criticism of Church practices, including the sale of indulgences, helped begin the Protestant Reformation. Church leaders had demanded that Luther withdraw, or recant, his writings, but he refused. The edict declared him a heretic and outlawed him within the Holy Roman Empire, making it illegal to shelter him or distribute his works. Luther avoided arrest because his supporter Frederick III arranged for him to hide at Wartburg Castle. The decree shows how Luther’s religious challenge became a political conflict involving the emperor and the rulers of German territories.

Valeriano Weyler was a Spanish general appointed governor-general of Cuba in 1896, when Cuban rebels were fighting for independence from Spain. To cut off the rebels’ access to food, supplies, and support, he ordered rural civilians to leave their homes and move into guarded, fortified towns. This forced relocation was called the reconcentration policy. Conditions in the settlements were often terrible: overcrowding and shortages of food and clean water contributed to widespread hunger and disease. American newspapers, including those owned by William Randolph Hearst, called Weyler “The Butcher.” Their reports sometimes exaggerated his cruelty, but the suffering caused by reconcentration was real. News about Cuba helped increase public anger toward Spain before the Spanish-American War of 1898.

Megasthenes was a Greek diplomat sent by Seleucus I Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Maurya Empire, around 300 BCE. He spent time at Pataliputra, the empire’s capital in northern India, and wrote an account of what he learned there. Called the Indica, the work described the city, the empire, and the customs of its people. Megasthenes wrote from an outsider’s perspective, so historians compare his claims with other evidence rather than accepting every detail as fact. The original Indica has been lost, but parts of it survive because later Greek and Roman writers quoted or summarized it. These fragments make Megasthenes an important source for studying ancient India and its connections with the Greek-speaking world.

The Paris Commune was a radical government that ruled Paris from March to May 1871, after France’s defeat in the Franco-Prussian War. Parisians had endured a long siege by Prussian forces and were angry with the new French government, based at Versailles. When that government tried to take control of the city’s cannons, members of the National Guard and other residents rebelled. The Communards, as supporters of the Commune were called, sought a more democratic and socially equal society. One of its best-known defenders was Louise Michel, a revolutionary schoolteacher who fought at the barricades. In May, French troops entered Paris and crushed the Commune during the Bloody Week, killing thousands. Michel was captured and later deported to New Caledonia.

The Jacobins were a political club that became one of the most powerful forces in the French Revolution. They met in a former Dominican convent on Rue Saint-Honoré in Paris and built a network of affiliated clubs across France, helping revolutionary ideas spread. Over time, the club became more radical, especially under the leadership of Maximilien Robespierre. In the National Convention, its most radical deputies sat on the chamber’s highest benches, opposite the more moderate Girondins. Because of where they sat, they were called the Mountain, or Montagnards. During the Reign of Terror, Jacobin leaders used harsh measures against people they considered enemies of the Revolution. Their dominance ended after Robespierre’s fall in the Thermidorian Reaction of 1794.

Beheading means killing someone by separating the head from the body. It appears in two biblical stories painted by the Italian artist Artemisia Gentileschi. In one, Judith, a Jewish heroine, and her maidservant kill the Assyrian general Holofernes by beheading him. Gentileschi’s dramatic painting of this scene is commonly titled Judith Beheading Holofernes. In another biblical story, John the Baptist is executed by beheading, and Gentileschi painted the princess Salome holding his severed head. Gentileschi worked in the Baroque period, when artists often used dramatic scenes, strong contrasts, and rich colors to engage viewers. Her paintings show how a violent event from a story could become the subject of a work of art.

Alcuin of York was an English cleric and scholar from Northumbria who became a leading teacher in Charlemagne’s empire. He studied at York’s cathedral school, the principal school in his native region, and later taught there. In 781, he met the Frankish ruler Charlemagne in Parma, Italy, and was invited to join his court. Alcuin became master of the palace school at Aachen, Charlemagne’s principal residence, where he helped improve education and the copying of books. His work was part of the Carolingian Renaissance, a revival of learning under Charlemagne’s dynasty. Alcuin later served as abbot of St Martin’s at Tours. Charlemagne, also known as Charles the Great, was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in Rome in the year 800.

Kamikaze is a Japanese word meaning “divine wind.” It was used to describe the powerful typhoons that helped protect Japan from two invasion fleets sent by Kublai Khan in 1274 and 1281. Kublai Khan was a Mongol ruler who founded China’s Yuan dynasty. After conquering much of the Asian mainland, he tried to bring Japan under his control, sending forces across the sea. Japanese defenders fought the invaders, but severe storms also wrecked many of their ships, especially during the second invasion. The storms came to be seen in Japan as a sign of divine protection. Centuries later, the word kamikaze was used for Japanese pilots who carried out suicide attacks during World War II, but its earlier historical meaning refers to the storms that disrupted Kublai Khan’s invasions.

The Conservative Party, often called the Tories, is one of Britain’s two major political parties alongside the Labour Party. Rooted in the older Tory tradition, it is generally associated with center-right ideas, including support for private business and a cautious approach to political change. Winston Churchill was a Conservative prime minister who led Britain through much of World War II. Another Conservative leader, Margaret Thatcher, became Britain’s first woman prime minister after her party won the 1979 general election. She remained in office until 1990 and introduced policies that reduced the role of the state in parts of the economy. Her government also faced a prolonged confrontation with the National Union of Mineworkers during the 1984–85 miners’ strike.

The War of Saint Sabas was a prolonged medieval conflict that began in 1256 between the Italian maritime powers Genoa and Venice. Both city-states depended on trade across the eastern Mediterranean and competed for commercial privileges, harbor access, and political influence. A major center of the fighting was Acre, a port city in the Kingdom of Jerusalem where Genoese and Venetian merchants had separate quarters. A dispute over control of a religious compound associated with Saint Sabas helped ignite the conflict there. Residents of the rival quarters even fired artillery at one another. Although the fighting spread beyond Acre, the struggle there showed how valuable the port was to both powers: control of its facilities and trading rights could bring wealth and strengthen their wider influence.

Charles Cornwallis was a British general and colonial administrator whose career connected two major parts of British imperial history. In 1781, he surrendered his army to George Washington’s forces at Yorktown, a defeat that helped bring the American Revolutionary War to a close. He later became Governor-General of India, where he introduced the Cornwallis Code, a set of administrative reforms for the British East India Company that gave British officials higher status than Indian inhabitants. Cornwallis also led campaigns against Tipu Sultan, ruler of the South Indian kingdom of Mysore. There, British troops encountered Mysorean rockets: iron-cased weapons that could be launched at enemy forces. William Congreve later studied these rockets and developed a British military rocket system inspired by them.

Operation Vengeance was a U.S. mission during World War II to intercept and kill Japanese admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, the commander in chief of Japan’s Combined Fleet. Yamamoto had planned the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, which brought the United States into the war. In April 1943, U.S. codebreakers decoded Japanese communications that revealed the schedule for Yamamoto’s flight to visit forces in the Solomon Islands. On April 18, Army Air Forces P-38 fighters flew a long distance to intercept his aircraft over Bougainville. They shot it down, killing Yamamoto. The mission showed how intelligence from intercepted messages could guide a precisely timed military attack, even far from an American airbase.

Kievan Rus’ was a medieval East Slavic polity centered on Kyiv that flourished from the late ninth to the thirteenth century. Its princes ruled lands that now include parts of Ukraine, Belarus, and Russia. One of its most important rulers was Vladimir the Great, the son of Sviatoslav I. According to the Primary Chronicle, traditionally associated with the monk Nestor, Vladimir considered several religions. The chronicle says he rejected Islam partly because it forbade alcohol, declaring that drinking was a joy of his people. He embraced Byzantine Christianity and ordered the baptism of his people in 988, a turning point in the region’s religious history. His ties to the Byzantine Empire also included marriage to the princess Anna.

Fridtjof Nansen was a Norwegian explorer and scientist who became known for both Arctic exploration and humanitarian work. In 1893, he led an expedition aboard the Norwegian-built ship Fram. Nansen deliberately let the ship become trapped in Arctic sea ice, hoping the drifting ice would carry it toward the North Pole. Although he did not reach the pole, the expedition gathered valuable scientific information. The Fram later carried another Norwegian explorer, Roald Amundsen, on the expedition that first reached the South Pole in 1911. After World War I, Nansen worked with the League of Nations to help refugees who had lost their citizenship. The League issued internationally recognized travel documents called Nansen passports, which allowed many stateless people to cross borders. Nansen received the Nobel Peace Prize for his humanitarian work.

Operation Barbarossa was Nazi Germany’s code name for its massive invasion of the Soviet Union, launched on June 22, 1941. The attack opened the Eastern Front of World War II, where German and Soviet forces fought some of the war’s largest and deadliest battles. Germany’s leader, Adolf Hitler, hoped to defeat the Soviet Union quickly, but Soviet resistance and the failure to take Moscow prevented a swift victory. The Soviet Union was led by Joseph Stalin, a dictator whose policies had contributed to the devastating Holodomor famine in Ukraine in the early 1930s. Years after the invasion, Stalin also promoted the antisemitic “Doctors’ Plot,” falsely accusing a group of mostly Jewish doctors of sabotage. Operation Barbarossa began a long struggle that helped shape the outcome of the war.

The Khmer are the largest ethnic group in Cambodia, and their language, Khmer, is the country’s official language. Between the 9th and 15th centuries, the Khmer Empire ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from its center at Angkor. One of its most famous achievements is Angkor Wat, a vast temple complex commissioned in the 12th century by Emperor Suryavarman II. It was originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and designed to represent Mount Meru, a sacred mountain in Hindu tradition. Angkor Wat later became a Buddhist site and remains an important symbol of Cambodia; it appears on the national flag. Centuries after the empire, a violent Communist movement called the Khmer Rouge ruled Cambodia under Pol Pot.

The Kingdom of Naples was a medieval kingdom in southern Italy that ruled the mainland territory around the city of Naples, near Mount Vesuvius. It emerged from a struggle over control of Sicily. On Easter Monday in 1282, a revolt against the French Angevin rulers began in Palermo, a city on the island of Sicily. The revolt grew into the War of the Sicilian Vespers, which drove Angevin rule from the island. After the war, the mainland remained under Angevin control and became known as the Kingdom of Naples, while Sicily developed as a separate island kingdom. Remembering the difference between mainland Naples and the island of Sicily helps explain both the kingdom’s name and its origins.

The 2019 United Kingdom general election took place on 12 December after Parliament called an early vote amid deadlock over the agreement for Britain to leave the European Union, known as Brexit. Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s Conservative Party campaigned on a promise to “get Brexit done” and won a decisive victory, gaining an 80-seat majority in the House of Commons. The main opposition party, Labour, was led by Jeremy Corbyn. It won just 202 seats, its lowest total since 1935, after losing many constituencies it had held for decades. The result gave Johnson the parliamentary support needed to move forward with Brexit. It also prompted Corbyn to step down as Labour leader; Keir Starmer succeeded him in 2020.

The Battle of Mogadishu took place in Somalia’s capital in October 1993, during a period of civil war and famine. U.S. forces, operating as part of a wider international effort, launched a raid to capture two senior aides of Somali faction leader Mohamed Farrah Aidid. The raid turned into prolonged street fighting when militia loyal to Aidid attacked the Americans. Two U.S. Black Hawk helicopters were shot down, and troops trying to reach their crews became trapped in the city. After a rescue effort, the U.S. forces withdrew. The battle caused heavy casualties and became a symbol of the dangers of urban warfare. It is often remembered as the “Black Hawk Down” battle.

Partygate was the name given to a political scandal in the United Kingdom over parties and other gatherings at 10 Downing Street and government buildings while COVID-19 lockdown rules restricted social gatherings. The events caused public anger because Boris Johnson’s government had made the rules that others were expected to follow. In 2022, Johnson received a fine for attending a gathering at Downing Street in 2020. The scandal damaged trust in his leadership, although other controversies also contributed to his downfall. In July 2022, Chancellor of the Exchequer Rishi Sunak resigned from Johnson’s cabinet alongside Health Secretary Sajid Javid. Their departures helped set off a wave of ministerial resignations, and Johnson soon announced that he would step down. Sunak later became prime minister after Liz Truss resigned in October 2022.

The Indus Valley Civilization, also called the Harappan Civilization, was a Bronze Age society that flourished across parts of present-day Pakistan and northwestern India. Its major cities included Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. Archaeologists have found evidence of carefully planned streets, drainage systems, standardized weights used in trade, and a writing system that has not yet been deciphered. One of Mohenjo-daro’s most distinctive structures is the Great Bath, a large brick-lined pool with steps at both ends. Its builders used materials and techniques to help keep it watertight. The pool may have been used for ritual bathing or purification, although its exact purpose is uncertain. Finds like the Great Bath help historians understand how this ancient civilization organized its cities and shared spaces.

The Battle of Midway was a major World War II naval battle fought near Midway Atoll in the Pacific in early June 1942. After American codebreakers learned that Japan planned to attack the atoll, U.S. forces prepared an ambush. Aircraft from American carriers sank four Japanese fleet carriers: Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū, and Hiryū. Losing these ships and their experienced crews checked Japan’s expansion and made Midway a turning point in the Pacific War. The United States also suffered losses. Japanese dive-bombers and torpedo aircraft badly damaged the aircraft carrier USS Yorktown, forcing its crew to abandon ship. While Yorktown was being salvaged, the Japanese submarine I-168 torpedoed it and the nearby destroyer USS Hammann; both sank.

The Opium Wars were two 19th-century conflicts between Qing China and Western powers, especially Britain; France joined Britain in the second war. The First Opium War lasted from 1839 to 1842, and the Second from 1856 to 1860. They are named for opium, an addictive drug that Western merchants illegally sold in China and that Chinese officials tried to suppress. Before the wars, the Canton system restricted Western trade to the port of Canton, also called Guangzhou, where approved Chinese merchants handled transactions. Western merchants wanted Chinese goods such as tea and silk, but China accepted mainly silver in payment. Large amounts of silver reached China from Acapulco aboard Manila galleons. After defeating China, Western powers forced it to open more ports to foreign trade and grant other concessions.

Carlos Manuel de Céspedes was a wealthy sugar planter in eastern Cuba when the island was under Spanish rule. On October 10, 1868, at his La Demajagua plantation, he freed his enslaved workers and called on Cubans to fight for independence. This declaration of revolt became known as the Grito de Yara, or “Cry of Yara.” It began the Ten Years’ War, a long struggle against Spanish rule that lasted until 1878. Céspedes later became the first president of the Cuban Republic in Arms, the government formed by the independence fighters. Although the war did not win Cuban independence, his decision to begin the uprising made him a central figure in Cuba’s history. He is often called the father of Cuban independence.

Theodora was a sixth-century Byzantine empress and the wife of Emperor Justinian I. Before becoming empress, she had worked as an actress and, according to some accounts, a sex worker.
