She later supported legal protections for women, including those vulnerable to exploitation. Theodora is especially remembered for her resolve during the Nika Riots, a revolt in Constantinople in 532. The uprising began with clashes between the Blue and Green factions, whose supporters gathered at the Hippodrome for chariot races, and grew into a threat to Justinian’s rule. When Justinian considered fleeing, Theodora urged him to stay and face the crisis. She reportedly said that royal purple made the finest burial shroud, meaning she would rather die as empress than escape.

The Latin Empire was a Catholic state created after Western Christian crusaders captured and sacked Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, in 1204. The city’s capture occurred during the Fourth Crusade, a Venetian-financed expedition that became involved in Byzantine politics instead of reaching the Holy Land. The crusaders set up the Latin Empire to rule Constantinople and other former Byzantine territories. Its first monarch was Baldwin of Flanders, crowned emperor as Baldwin I of Constantinople in the Hagia Sophia, the city’s great church. Although the new rulers controlled the capital, Byzantine leaders continued to rule in other regions. In 1261, Byzantine forces recaptured Constantinople, bringing the Latin Empire to an end.

Jean-François Champollion was a French scholar born in Figeac in 1790 who made a decisive breakthrough in reading ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs. He studied Coptic, a later form of the Egyptian language, and compared it with the matching passages on the Rosetta Stone. This inscribed granodiorite slab records a decree honoring King Ptolemy V in three scripts: hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Ancient Greek. Because scholars could read the Greek text, it offered clues to the other two. French soldiers found the stone near Rashid, also called Rosetta, during Napoleon’s campaign in Egypt in 1799. Building on earlier work by scholars including Thomas Young, Champollion recognized that hieroglyphs could represent sounds. He announced his breakthrough in an 1822 letter to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres.

The Jewel Voice Broadcast was a radio address heard across Japan on August 15, 1945. In it, Emperor Hirohito announced that Japan had accepted the Potsdam Declaration, the Allied powers’ demand for Japan’s surrender in World War II. The announcement came after atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki and the Soviet Union entered the war against Japan. It was the first time the Japanese public had heard a reigning emperor speak on the radio. Hirohito used an unusually formal, classical style of Japanese, so some listeners found the message difficult to understand at first. Hirohito’s reign is known as the Shōwa era, and the broadcast marked a turning point as Japan prepared to end the war.

Pugachev’s Rebellion was a major uprising against the Russian Empire from 1773 to 1775. Its leader, Yemelyan Pugachev, was a Don Cossack who claimed to be Peter III, the former emperor who had been deposed in 1762. The ruler at the time was Peter’s wife, Catherine the Great, who had taken power after his removal. Pugachev’s claim helped him attract people who were unhappy with imperial rule, including Cossacks, peasants, and factory workers. The rebels captured towns, including Kazan, and threatened the government’s control over a large region. Catherine’s forces eventually defeated the uprising, and Pugachev was executed. The rebellion showed how deeply many people resented harsh working conditions, serfdom, and government control.

Stanley Baldwin was a British Conservative politician who served three separate terms as prime minister: 1923–24, 1924–29, and 1935–37. During his final term, he faced a royal crisis involving King Edward VIII, who wanted to marry Wallis Simpson, an American divorcée. Baldwin opposed a proposed arrangement that would have allowed Edward to remain king while marrying her without making her queen. In December 1936, Edward chose to give up the throne rather than abandon the marriage. This constitutional event is known as Edward VIII’s abdication. His younger brother became King George VI, and Edward later married Simpson. Baldwin left office the following year, when Neville Chamberlain became prime minister.

The Rivonia Trial was a 1963–1964 South African court case against Nelson Mandela and other activists who opposed apartheid, a system of laws that enforced racial segregation and denied Black South Africans political rights. The trial was named for the Johannesburg suburb of Rivonia, where police raided Liliesleaf Farm and found plans for armed resistance. Prosecutors charged the activists with sabotage. In a statement from the dock, Mandela defended the goal of a democratic and free society and said it was an ideal for which he was “prepared to die.” He and several other defendants received life sentences. Mandela spent part of his 27 years in prison on Robben Island. After his release, he helped negotiate the end of apartheid, shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk, and became South Africa’s first Black president.

The Columbian Exchange was the movement of crops, animals, people, diseases, and technologies between the Americas and the Old World after Christopher Columbus’s 1492 voyage. Historian Alfred Crosby popularized the term to describe these far-reaching changes. American crops such as potatoes and maize spread to Europe and beyond, while Europeans brought crops and domesticated animals to the Americas. One of these animals was the horse, which Spanish colonizers introduced. Horses later spread among Indigenous peoples of the Great Plains, changing how some communities hunted, traveled, and fought. The exchange also brought devastating diseases to Indigenous populations and involved the forced movement of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Its effects transformed societies and environments on both sides of the ocean.

The Battle of Cannae was fought in 216 BCE during the Second Punic War, near the Aufidus River in southern Italy. A large Roman army commanded by Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro faced a smaller Carthaginian force led by Hannibal Barca. Hannibal placed troops in a center that gradually gave ground as the Romans pushed forward. His stronger infantry then attacked the Roman flanks, while his cavalry defeated the Roman horsemen and came around behind the army. Trapped on all sides, the Romans suffered devastating losses. Cannae became a famous example of encirclement, sometimes called a double envelopment, and showed how careful coordination could overcome a larger force. Rome continued the war, increasingly avoiding direct battles with Hannibal in favor of wearing down his forces.

The Industrial Revolution was a period of rapid economic and technological change that began in Britain in the late eighteenth century and spread to other countries during the nineteenth. New manufacturing tools and machines allowed goods to be made faster and in much larger quantities. Instead of producing most items by hand at home or in small workshops, workers increasingly used machines in factories. Steam engines powered machinery, helped pump water from mines, and later drove trains and ships. In 1769, the Scottish inventor James Watt patented an important improvement to the steam engine: a separate condenser that made it much more efficient. These changes greatly increased economic output, reshaped trade, and drew many people to growing industrial cities, although factory work was often difficult and dangerous.

The Mfecane was a period of warfare, political upheaval, and forced migration across southern Africa in the early 19th century. Its name is often translated as “the crushing.” Fighting and the growth of powerful kingdoms drove many communities from their homes, sometimes setting off further conflicts as people sought new places to live. The rise of the Zulu Kingdom was an important part of this upheaval. Its founder and first ruler, Shaka Zulu, reorganized the army, emphasizing short stabbing spears for close combat and a tactic called the “buffalo horns” formation, which used forces on the sides to surround an enemy. Historians also point to other causes of the Mfecane, including competition for land and resources, rather than attributing the upheaval to Shaka alone.

Sumerian civilization flourished in the fertile alluvial plain of southern Mesopotamia, a region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in what is now Iraq. Beginning around 3500 BCE, the Sumerians built some of the world’s earliest cities. Their society was divided into independent city-states, including Ur and Uruk, each with its own rulers and religious centers. Farmers used river water to irrigate fields, helping support growing populations and specialized workers. The Sumerians also developed cuneiform, one of the earliest known writing systems. To write, a scribe pressed a stylus into soft clay, making wedge-shaped signs. Cuneiform was first used for practical records, such as tracking goods and trade, and later for laws, stories, and other texts.

Simon bar Kokhba was a Jewish leader who commanded rebel forces in Judaea during an uprising against Roman rule from 132 to 135 CE. The conflict is commonly called the Bar Kokhba revolt, or the Second Jewish Revolt. Some of his contemporaries hailed him as the Messiah, a hoped-for leader who would free the Jewish people and restore their independence. The rebels initially gained control of territory, but Rome sent a large army to defeat them. Forces under Emperor Hadrian eventually crushed the revolt in 135 CE. The war caused enormous loss of life and tightened Roman control over the region. Bar Kokhba is remembered both as a symbol of resistance to Roman rule and as a figure whose defeat had lasting consequences for Jewish history.

The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo are an Argentine human-rights organization formed by women whose children vanished during the country’s military dictatorship, which ruled from 1976 to 1983. Beginning in 1977, they gathered every Thursday around the central monument in the Plaza de Mayo, a square in Buenos Aires, to demand information about their children. They wore white headscarves that became a symbol of their protest. During the dictatorship’s “Dirty War,” security forces seized thousands of people suspected of opposing the government. Many were never found, and officials did not account for what had happened to them. These forcibly disappeared people are commonly called desaparecidos, the Spanish plural for “the disappeared.” The mothers’ weekly gatherings made their demand for answers visible in Argentina and around the world.

The House of Stuart was a royal dynasty that first ruled Scotland and later ruled England and Ireland. In 1603, Elizabeth I of England died without an heir, and her cousin, the Scottish king James VI, inherited the English throne. He was known as James VI in Scotland and James I in England, often written James VI and I. Although the kingdoms shared a monarch, they remained separate states for more than a century. During the Stuart era, disputes over royal power and religion helped cause the English Civil War, and the monarchy was briefly abolished. In 1707, Acts of Union joined England and Scotland as Great Britain under the last Stuart monarch, Queen Anne. She died in 1714 without surviving heirs, ending the dynasty’s rule.

The Dawes Plan was a 1924 agreement designed to make Germany’s World War I reparations payments more manageable. Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany owed large sums to the victorious countries, but its Weimar government struggled to pay. In 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied Germany’s industrial Ruhr region after missed payments, while Germany suffered devastating hyperinflation. An international committee of experts chaired by American banker Charles G. Dawes proposed a new payment schedule and loans to help Germany’s economy recover. The plan helped bring the occupation of the Ruhr to an end and eased tensions in Europe, though it did not cancel Germany’s debt. Dawes later served as vice president under U.S. President Calvin Coolidge and shared the 1925 Nobel Peace Prize for his work.

Timur, also known as Tamerlane, was a Turco-Mongol conqueror who founded the Timurid Empire in the late 1300s. From his capital, Samarkand, in Central Asia, he led campaigns that brought lands from India to the Middle East under his control. In 1402, Timur defeated the Ottoman army at the Battle of Ankara and captured its sultan, Bayezid I. The defeat plunged the Ottoman Empire into a struggle for the throne known as the Ottoman Interregnum. Timur died in 1405, but Samarkand remained the political heart of the Timurid Empire under his successors. They made it a center of monumental building, art, and scholarship during a period sometimes called the Timurid Renaissance.

Benazir Bhutto was a former prime minister of Pakistan and a leading opposition politician. On December 27, 2007, she addressed a campaign rally in Rawalpindi as Pakistan prepared for an election. The rally was held at Liaquat Bagh, a public park named for Liaquat Ali Khan, Pakistan’s first prime minister. As Bhutto was leaving the park, an attacker fired a gun and detonated a shrapnel bomb. Bhutto was killed, and the event became known as the assassination of Benazir Bhutto. Her death shocked Pakistan and disrupted the election campaign. Bhutto’s son, Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, later became a leader of her political party, the Pakistan Peoples Party.

The Battle of Kadesh was fought in the early 13th century BCE near the city of Kadesh on the Orontes River, in what is now Syria. Ramesses II led the Egyptian army against Hittite forces commanded by King Muwatalli II. Both sides used large numbers of horse-drawn chariots, making the battle one of the best-known examples of chariot warfare in the ancient world. The Egyptians were nearly overwhelmed by a surprise Hittite attack, but Ramesses rallied his troops, and neither side won a decisive victory. Egyptian accounts celebrated Ramesses as a victor, while the Hittites kept control of Kadesh. Years later, Egypt and the Hittite Empire agreed to one of the oldest surviving written peace treaties.

Empedocles was a Greek philosopher who lived in the fifth century BCE. He taught that everything was made from four basic elements—earth, water, air, and fire—and that two forces, Love and Strife, brought those elements together or pulled them apart. He is also remembered for a dramatic story called Empedocles’ legendary death. According to this account, he leapt into Mount Etna, an active volcano on the island of Sicily. The story says he did this to convince his followers that he was immortal: if he disappeared without a trace, they might believe he had become a god rather than died. It is a legend, however, not a confirmed account of how Empedocles actually died.

José Martí was a Cuban poet, journalist, and revolutionary who helped lead the movement to free Cuba from Spanish rule. Born in Havana in 1853, he spent many years in exile but continued to organize supporters of independence. In 1892, he founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party and began editing its Spanish-language newspaper, Patria, in New York. The paper rallied support for Cuba’s struggle; its name means “homeland.” Martí also wrote poems that remain important in Cuban culture, including verses later adapted for the song “Guantanamera.” He returned to Cuba when the independence war began and was killed fighting Spanish forces at the Battle of Dos Ríos in 1895. Cubans remember him as a national hero for both his writing and his work for independence.

A queen is a royal title that can mean either a woman who rules a country in her own right or the wife of a king. Elizabeth I was Queen of England from 1558 to 1603, and Victoria later held the title as sovereign of the United Kingdom. A king’s wife may be called a queen even if she does not rule independently. Elizabeth I also inspired literature during her reign. The English poet Edmund Spenser portrayed an idealized sovereign named Gloriana in his allegorical epic The Faerie Queene, whose first installment appeared in 1590. Spenser also wrote The Shepheardes Calender. In the poem’s title, “Queene” is an older spelling of “queen.”

The Khmer Empire was a powerful medieval state centered at Angkor in what is now Cambodia. From about the 800s to the 1400s, its rulers built a vast landscape of temples and reservoirs. The reservoirs, called baray, stored water for irrigation, helping farmers grow crops and support a large population. In the early 1100s, King Suryavarman II sponsored the construction of Angkor Wat, an enormous temple complex originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu. Angkor was both a political capital and a religious center, reflecting the rulers’ power and beliefs. Over time, the empire weakened, and attacks by the neighboring Ayutthaya Kingdom contributed to the decline of Angkor as its center of power.

The Armenian genocide was the mass deportation and killing of Armenians by the Ottoman Empire during World War I. Armenians had lived for centuries in a historic homeland spanning eastern Anatolia, in what is now Turkey, and the southern Caucasus, where modern-day Armenia lies. In 1915, Ottoman authorities began forcing Armenians from their homes, often sending them on long marches with little food or water. Many were also killed outright. Approximately 1.5 million Armenians died. The Ottoman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, had once controlled large parts of the Middle East and southeastern Europe. It was defeated in World War I and dissolved soon afterward.

On August 7, 1998, members of al-Qaeda carried out coordinated truck bomb attacks on two U.S. embassies in East Africa: one in Nairobi, Kenya, and the other in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. These attacks are known as the 1998 United States Embassy Bombings. An embassy is a country’s diplomatic office in another country, where diplomats and ambassadors work. The Nairobi explosion caused most of the deaths, while the blast at the U.S. embassy in Dar es Salaam killed 11 people. Hundreds of people died overall, and thousands were injured, many of them local residents rather than embassy staff. The bombings brought worldwide attention to al-Qaeda, the extremist group led by Osama bin Laden, and showed how attacks on diplomatic sites could also devastate surrounding communities.

José Rizal was a Filipino physician, multilingual writer, and nationalist who sought reforms under Spanish colonial rule. His novels Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo exposed abuses by colonial officials and religious authorities, helping Filipinos question Spanish rule. In Manila in 1892, he founded La Liga Filipina, a civic association that promoted unity, education, and peaceful political change. Spanish authorities soon dissolved the organization and exiled Rizal, but its members and ideas helped inspire the Katipunan, a secret society that pursued independence through revolution. Rizal did not lead that armed rebellion; he continued to favor reform. Even so, Spanish authorities accused him of involvement and executed him in Manila in 1896. His writings and death made him a lasting symbol of the Philippine independence movement.

The St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre was a wave of violence against Huguenots, or French Protestants, during the French Wars of Religion. It began in Paris in August 1572 and spread to other French cities. The massacre is named for St. Bartholomew’s Day, a Christian feast day on August 24. Shortly before the wider killings began, Gaspard de Coligny, a prominent Huguenot admiral and military leader, was attacked in Paris. He was later killed during the violence, along with thousands of other Protestants. The massacre grew out of bitter religious and political conflict between Catholics and Protestants in France. Decades later, King Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes, which granted Huguenots limited religious toleration.

The Battle of Watling Street, fought around 60 or 61 CE, ended a major uprising against Roman rule in Britain. Boudica, queen of the Iceni people, led the rebellion after Roman officials mistreated her family and seized Iceni property. Her forces attacked several Roman settlements, including Londinium, before facing an army commanded by Suetonius Paulinus, the Roman governor of Britain. Although Boudica’s rebel army was much larger, the Romans chose a narrow position that limited the rebels’ advantage in numbers. Their disciplined formations and weapons helped them win a decisive victory. The battle takes its name from Watling Street, a Roman road, but its exact location is unknown. Boudica’s defeat brought her revolt to an end and strengthened Roman control of Britain.

The Force Publique was the colonial army and police force established under King Leopold II in the Congo Free State. Despite its name, the Congo Free State was Leopold’s personal possession, not an independent country. During the late 1800s and early 1900s, its government demanded large amounts of rubber from people in the Congo Basin. Force Publique units enforced these quotas through threats and violence. People who failed to collect enough rubber could face severe punishment, including the cutting off of hands. Reports of these abuses helped fuel international criticism of Leopold’s rule. In 1908, Belgium annexed the Congo Free State, ending Leopold’s personal control, but it kept the Force Publique as a colonial military and police force.

The Rosetta Stone is a broken granodiorite slab inscribed with a decree issued in 196 BCE during the reign of Ptolemy V. The decree honors the king and appears in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Ancient Greek. French troops found the stone near Rashid, also called Rosetta, in 1799 during Napoleon’s expedition to Egypt. Because scholars could read Ancient Greek, they could compare its text with the Egyptian versions. Thomas Young made important early discoveries, and Jean-François Champollion later used the stone to help decipher hieroglyphs, opening up many ancient Egyptian texts to study. After French forces surrendered in Egypt in 1801, the stone was taken to London. It has been housed in the British Museum since 1802.

Philip II ruled Macedon, a kingdom north of the main Greek city-states, from 359 to 336 BCE. He strengthened its army by training infantry to fight in a tight formation with the sarissa, a long spear. His victory over Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE brought much of Greece under Macedonian influence. Philip then organized the League of Corinth, a federation whose member states pledged to maintain peace and named him commander of a planned invasion of the Persian Empire. He never led that invasion: in 336 BCE, his bodyguard Pausanias assassinated him at Aegae during celebrations for the wedding of Philip’s daughter Cleopatra. Philip’s son Alexander the Great succeeded him and went on to conquer the Persian Empire.

Erich Honecker was one of the most powerful leaders of East Germany, the Communist state that existed from 1949 to 1990. He led its ruling Socialist Unity Party from 1971 until he was forced from power in 1989, and he chaired the Council of State from 1976 to 1989. His government tightly controlled political life, while the Stasi secret police monitored many citizens. East Germany was closely allied with the Soviet Union. A famous mural on the Berlin Wall shows Honecker sharing a “fraternal kiss,” a ceremonial greeting between Communist leaders, with Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev. The mural was painted after the Wall opened, but it depicts an embrace that took place in 1979. Honecker’s removal in 1989 came shortly before the Berlin Wall fell and East Germany’s Communist government collapsed.

The Battle of Plataea was fought in Boeotia, a region of central Greece, in 479 BCE. It was a decisive victory for a coalition of Greek city-states against the Persian invasion force commanded by Mardonius. Overall command of the Greek forces rested with Pausanias, a Spartan regent who served as guardian to the young Spartan king Pleistarchus. The battle came after the Persians, under King Xerxes I, had won at Thermopylae but suffered a major naval defeat at Salamis. Xerxes had returned to Persia, leaving Mardonius to continue the campaign. At Plataea, the Greeks routed Mardonius’s army, and Mardonius was killed. The victory helped bring Xerxes’s invasion of Greece to an end.

On the Ides of March, March 15, 44 BCE, a group of Roman senators stabbed Julius Caesar during a Senate meeting. Caesar had been named dictator for life, and the conspirators feared that his growing power threatened the Roman Republic. Their attack is commonly called the Assassination of Julius Caesar. The Senate was not meeting in its regular Senate house that day. Instead, it had gathered in the Curia of Pompey, a meeting hall attached to Pompey’s great theater complex on the Campus Martius, an area of Rome. Although the conspirators claimed they were defending the republic, Caesar’s death led to further conflict and civil war. His adopted heir Octavian eventually emerged as Rome’s ruler, helping bring the Roman Republic to an end.

The Battle of Manzikert was fought in 1071 in eastern Anatolia, a region in what is now Turkey. The Byzantine Empire, ruled from Constantinople, sent an army led by Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes against the Seljuk Turks. The Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan commanded the opposing army and won the battle, capturing Romanos IV. The defeat weakened Byzantine control in Anatolia and became a turning point in the region’s history. Although the Byzantines still held some territory there, Turkish groups gained more opportunities to settle and conquer land in the following years. Manzikert is therefore remembered both as a major blow to Byzantine power and as a battle that helped open Anatolia to Turkish conquest.

Alberto Fujimori became president of Peru in 1990 after defeating novelist Mario Vargas Llosa in an election. His presidency unfolded during a violent conflict with the Shining Path, a Maoist guerrilla movement that had carried out attacks across the country. In 1992, Peruvian authorities arrested the movement’s founder and principal leader, Abimael Guzmán, in Lima. His capture was a major blow to the insurgency. Fujimori’s government also committed serious human rights abuses: his administration authorized Grupo Colina, a death squad responsible for killing civilians. In 1992, Fujimori dissolved Peru’s congress and took control of the courts, weakening democracy even as his government fought the Shining Path.

The Terracotta Army is a vast collection of life-size ceramic soldiers, horses, and chariots buried in pits beside the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang, China’s first emperor. After the state of Qin united China and ended the Warring States period in 221 BCE, the emperor had these figures made to guard him in the afterlife. They were shaped from terracotta, a type of fired clay, and arranged in formations like a real army. Although buried for more than two thousand years, the figures came to public attention in 1974, when local farmers digging a well found clay fragments. The excavation site is in Shaanxi Province, east of the historic center of the modern city of Xi’an.

The Yugoslav Wars were a connected series of conflicts that broke out as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia fell apart in the 1990s. Yugoslavia had united several South Slavic peoples under a federal government, but after the death of its longtime leader Josip Broz Tito, political and economic tensions grew. As republics sought independence, fighting erupted in Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nationalist leaders and armed groups fought over borders and control of areas where different ethnic communities lived, forcing many civilians from their homes. The Bosnian War ended with the Dayton Agreement, negotiated in November 1995 at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in the United States. The agreement kept Bosnia and Herzegovina as one country while establishing two main entities within it.

The Russian famine of 1921–1922 was a catastrophic food crisis in Soviet Russia, especially in the Volga region, where millions faced starvation. It followed the Russian Civil War, which had disrupted farming and food supplies, and a severe drought made the crisis worse by destroying crops. The Bolshevik government struggled to feed the population and introduced Vladimir Lenin’s New Economic Policy in 1921, partly to help restore agricultural production. Relief came from both inside and outside Russia. International aid efforts were led in part by Fridtjof Nansen, a Norwegian explorer, diplomat, and humanitarian who organized help for famine victims. His work during the crisis contributed to his receiving the 1922 Nobel Peace Prize.

Hadrian’s Wall was a Roman frontier fortification built across northern Britain under Emperor Hadrian in the second century CE. Stretching roughly 73 miles from the Solway Firth in the west to the River Tyne in the east, it helped Roman soldiers control movement into and out of the province of Britannia. The wall had forts and gates along its route, making it more than a simple barrier. At its eastern end, in modern Wallsend, stood the Roman fort of Segedunum. That name is still used for the archaeological museum and visitor site there, where people can explore evidence of life on the frontier. Hadrian’s Wall later became associated with the boundary between England and Scotland, although the modern border does not follow the wall exactly.

A Roman triumph was a prestigious public procession honoring a general after a major military victory. The general rode through Rome in a decorated chariot, wearing a laurel crown and a purple toga. His soldiers marched with him, while crowds watched displays of captured treasure, weapons, and prisoners. The procession celebrated Rome’s success and showed the general’s achievements to the public, but it could be humiliating or deadly for defeated leaders. In 46 BCE, Julius Caesar held triumphs celebrating his conquests. One prisoner paraded through Rome was Vercingetorix, a Gallic chieftain who had led a major revolt against Roman rule. After the procession, Vercingetorix was executed.

The Kingdom of Benin was a powerful precolonial Edo state in what is now southern Nigeria. Its capital, Benin City, was ruled by an oba, or king, whose court supported highly skilled artists. They made cast-metal plaques and commemorative heads, as well as carvings in ivory. Many of these works recorded rulers, ceremonies, and the kingdom’s history. In 1897, British forces invaded Benin City and removed thousands of artworks, including pieces now known as the Benin Bronzes, which were often made of brass rather than bronze. The reigning oba, Ovonramwen Nogbaisi, was captured after the city fell and later exiled to Calabar. Today, the looted artworks are central to debates about returning cultural treasures to their places of origin.

The Kronstadt Rebellion was an uprising in March 1921 at Kronstadt, a fortified Baltic naval base on Kotlin Island near Petrograd. Sailors, soldiers, and civilians who had once supported the Bolsheviks rebelled against their government, demanding political reforms, greater civil liberties, and more freedom for workers and peasants. Sailor Stepan Petrichenko chaired the rebels’ Provisional Revolutionary Committee. The uprising came after the Russian Civil War had devastated the country and as a severe famine was beginning. Red Army forces crossed the frozen sea to retake Kronstadt and suppressed the rebellion; Petrichenko escaped to Finland. Soon afterward, Vladimir Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy, which eased some economic restrictions, though the Bolsheviks did not grant the rebels’ demands for political freedom.

During World War I, armies on the Western Front dug long, narrow ditches called trenches to protect soldiers from enemy gunfire. These trenches formed the main defensive lines, with opposing armies sometimes separated by a dangerous strip of land called no man’s land. Trenches offered cover, but they could be crowded, muddy, and vulnerable to artillery shells. Rain often left them partly flooded, and soldiers might spend days standing in cold water while wearing wet boots and socks. Prolonged exposure could cause trench foot, a non-freezing injury that made feet numb and swollen and could damage the tissue. Keeping feet dry, changing socks, and improving boots helped reduce the risk, but trench foot remained one of the hardships of trench warfare.

The Greek government-debt crisis was a long financial emergency that shook Greece during the 2010s. In 2009, incoming prime minister George Papandreou revealed that the government had seriously underreported its budget deficit, raising fears that Greece could not repay its debts. Greece received rescue loans, or bailouts, from euro-area countries and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). In return, creditors demanded austerity measures, including spending cuts and tax increases. These measures caused hardship and sparked protests, including marches in Athens. The left-wing party Syriza won Greece’s January 2015 election after campaigning against austerity. Its leader, Alexis Tsipras, became prime minister and held a referendum that July on creditors’ proposed bailout terms. That summer, Greece also missed an IMF loan payment on time.

The Kilwa Sultanate was a medieval Islamic state centered on Kilwa Kisiwani, an island off the coast of present-day Tanzania. It became one of the wealthiest city-states on the Swahili Coast by connecting East Africa with Indian Ocean trade routes. Merchants exchanged goods with traders from Arabia, Persia, India, and other regions, bringing wealth and Islamic influences to Kilwa. The sultanate’s commercial reach extended south to Sofala, a port in present-day Mozambique. Gold from the African interior reached Sofala and was shipped into the wider Indian Ocean trading network. Control over this trade helped make Kilwa a powerful Swahili polity.

Xerxes I was a king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire and the son of Darius I, also called Darius the Great. In 480 BCE, he led a major invasion of Greece. His army defeated the Greek defenders at Thermopylae, where the Spartan king Leonidas and his soldiers made a famous last stand, and Persian forces later captured and damaged Athens. But the Greek fleet defeated Xerxes’ larger navy at the Battle of Salamis. Fighting in the narrow waters near Athens made it difficult for the Persians to use their numerical advantage. According to ancient accounts, Xerxes watched the battle from Mount Aigaleo. The following year, the Greeks won another major victory over Persian forces at Plataea, helping to bring the invasion to an end.

The Acerbo Law was an Italian electoral law passed in 1923, when Benito Mussolini was prime minister. Named after Giacomo Acerbo, the deputy from Abruzzo who introduced the bill and later served as Italy’s minister of agriculture, it changed how seats were awarded in the Chamber of Deputies. Under the law, the electoral list with the most votes received two-thirds of the seats, provided it won at least 25 percent of the vote. This meant a party could gain a large parliamentary majority without winning a majority of voters’ support. The formula helped magnify the Fascists’ victory in the 1924 election and strengthened Mussolini’s hold on the Italian government.

The 1920s were the years from 1920 to 1929. In Europe, the decade was shaped by the aftermath of World War I. Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany’s Weimar Republic owed reparations to the victorious countries, but it struggled to pay them. In 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied Germany’s Ruhr industrial region after Germany fell behind on payments. That year, Germany also suffered severe hyperinflation, which made its money lose value rapidly, while political unrest included Adolf Hitler’s failed Beer Hall Putsch in Munich. The Dawes Plan, adopted in 1924, reorganized Germany’s reparations schedule and encouraged American loans to support its economy. It was also tied to the withdrawal of French and Belgian troops from the Ruhr.

The Schleswig-Holstein Question was a 19th-century dispute over two duchies linked to the Danish crown, just south of Denmark. Holstein belonged to the German Confederation, but Schleswig, immediately to its north, did not. Both had German- and Danish-speaking communities, so growing nationalism made people disagree over whether the duchies should remain connected to Denmark or join a German state. The issue also involved inheritance: different rules raised doubts about who should rule the duchies when the Danish king died. In 1863, Denmark adopted a constitution that tied Schleswig more closely to the kingdom, angering German nationalists and the German Confederation. In 1864, Prussia and Austria jointly invaded Denmark, beginning the Second Schleswig War. Denmark lost, and the two duchies came under Prussian and Austrian control.

Huldrych Zwingli was a Swiss leader of the Protestant Reformation who helped establish the Reformed tradition in Zurich. He argued that Christian practices should be based on scripture, an idea called sola scriptura, and challenged Catholic traditions he believed lacked biblical support. One major dispute concerned the Eucharist, the sharing of bread and wine in memory of Jesus’s Last Supper with his apostles. Zwingli rejected the Catholic doctrine of the Real Presence, which holds that Christ’s body and blood are truly present in the Eucharist; he understood the bread and wine as symbols. At the Marburg Colloquy in 1529, Zwingli debated Martin Luther, who defended Christ’s real presence. Although the two reformers agreed on many other beliefs, they could not settle this disagreement.

After the Qing dynasty fell in 1911, China’s central government struggled to control the country. Regional military commanders built their own armies and ruled large areas, often collecting taxes and fighting one another. These strongmen are known as Chinese warlords, and their struggles gave the period the name Warlord Era. One warlord, Zhang Zongchang, controlled Shandong province. He used armored trains staffed by Russian refugees who had settled in the Chinese city of Harbin after the Russian Civil War. In the 1920s, the Kuomintang, or Chinese Nationalist Party, sent its National Revolutionary Army on the Northern Expedition to defeat warlords and reunify China. Zhang’s forces were crushed during that campaign, and he fled into exile.

Teotihuacan was an ancient city in central Mexico and one of the largest urban centers in the Americas before Europeans arrived. Its name is commonly translated as “the place where the gods were created,” although the people who built the city called it something else that is now unknown. A broad road called the Avenue of the Dead linked its major ceremonial areas and monumental pyramids, including the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon. The Pyramid of the Moon stands at the northern end of the avenue beside a large ceremonial plaza. Built in several stages and once topped by a temple complex, it is Teotihuacan’s second-largest monument. The city’s buildings and artifacts help archaeologists study its history and influence across Mesoamerica.

The Lombards were a Germanic people who entered Italy in 568 under King Alboin. They took control of much of northern and central Italy, and Alboin captured Milan in 569, the year after the invasion began. The Lombards later made Pavia the capital of their kingdom. Their kings included Liutprand, who ruled in the eighth century and strengthened Lombard power. The Lombards did not control all of Italy: other areas remained under Byzantine rule or were governed by the pope. Their kingdom lasted until 774, when Charlemagne, king of the Franks, conquered it. The name Lombardy, the northern Italian region that includes Milan, comes from the Lombards and is a reminder of their rule.

The Jacquerie Rebellion was a major peasant uprising in northern France in 1358, during the Hundred Years’ War between England and France. War had damaged farms and villages, while taxes and demands for money to ransom the captive French king, John II, added to peasants’ hardships. Many peasants also believed that nobles had failed to protect them from soldiers and raiders. Groups of rebels attacked aristocratic estates and challenged noble authority. Guillaume Cale emerged as a leader of the peasant forces, but the revolt was short-lived. In June 1358, an army commanded by Charles II of Navarre decisively defeated Cale’s forces near the town of Mello, close to Beauvais. The defeat helped end the uprising.

Falange Española was a Spanish fascist movement founded in Madrid in 1933 by José Antonio Primo de Rivera, a lawyer and politician from an aristocratic family. Its name means “Spanish Phalanx.” The movement used a yoke-and-arrows emblem and promoted national syndicalism, which called for a powerful, unified nation organized through state-controlled groups of workers and employers rather than competing political parties. During the Spanish Civil War, Republicans imprisoned and executed José Antonio in Alicante in November 1936. His supporters then portrayed him as a martyr. General Francisco Franco, who led the Nationalists to victory, absorbed the Falange into a larger ruling party in 1937. The Falange provided much of that party’s ideology and organization during Franco’s dictatorship.

Operation Solomon was a 1991 Israeli airlift that brought more than 14,000 Ethiopian Jews, known as Beta Israel, from Ethiopia to Israel. The evacuation took place during a period of political upheaval in Ethiopia, when a long civil war was nearing its end. Israeli aircraft departed from the airport in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia’s capital, carrying passengers to Israel in roughly 36 hours. The operation was part of a broader effort to help Beta Israel settle in Israel. Their journey is an example of aliyah, the immigration of Jews to Israel. Operation Solomon is remembered both for the speed and scale of the airlift and for the new lives its passengers began after arriving in Israel.

Ninja, also called shinobi, were covert agents in feudal Japan. They gathered intelligence, slipped into guarded places, and carried out sabotage or, at times, assassination. They are especially associated with the Iga and Kōka regions, where traditions of espionage and stealth were passed down. One important source for what we know about these traditions is the Bansenshūkai, a Japanese compendium completed in 1676. It preserves accounts of ninja training and techniques and is considered one of the most important surviving manuals on the subject. Popular stories often show ninja dressed entirely in black and using remarkable gadgets, but their real work depended heavily on observation, planning, disguise, and avoiding detection.

Sundiata Keita was a 13th-century Mandinka leader remembered as the founder of the Mali Empire in West Africa. At the time, the Sosso ruler Sumanguru controlled much of the region. Sundiata brought together an alliance of groups opposed to Sosso rule and led their forces to victory over Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina, traditionally dated to about 1235. That victory helped establish Mali as a major power. Sundiata’s life and rise to power are celebrated in the Epic of Sundiata, a story preserved and performed by griots, West African storytellers and keepers of oral history. The epic includes legends as well as historical events, so it helps us understand both how Mali began and how later generations remembered its founder.

The Prague Spring was a period of political reform in Czechoslovakia in 1968, centered on Prague, now the capital of the Czech Republic. It began after Alexander Dubček, a Slovak Communist reformer, became first secretary of the country’s Communist Party in January. Dubček promoted “socialism with a human face”: he wanted to keep a socialist system while allowing more freedom of speech, loosening censorship, and making the government more responsive to citizens. Soviet leaders feared that these changes would weaken Communist control and spread to other Eastern European countries. In August 1968, Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia and brought the reforms to an end. Prague Spring remains an important example of an attempt to make Communist rule less repressive during the Cold War.

The Non-Aligned Movement brought together countries that wanted to avoid formal alignment with either the U.S.-led Western bloc or the Soviet-led Eastern bloc during the Cold War. Many members were newly independent nations that wanted to protect their sovereignty and make their own foreign-policy decisions rather than follow a superpower. The 1955 Bandung Conference, where Asian and African countries discussed cooperation and independence, helped inspire the movement. Its first summit was held in 1961 in Belgrade, the capital of Yugoslavia. Yugoslav president Josip Broz Tito was one of the movement’s leading founders and became its first chairman. Although Yugoslavia was a communist country, it had split with the Soviet Union, making an independent path especially important to Tito.

Veliky Novgorod is a historic city on the Volkhov River in northwestern Russia. During the Middle Ages, it was the political center of the Novgorod Republic, a powerful state that remained independent of Moscow for centuries. Merchants made the city a major trading hub with links to the Hanseatic League, a network of northern European trading towns. Novgorod’s public assembly, called the veche, met when a bell summoned citizens to discuss civic matters and choose officials, including the posadnik, a leading city administrator. The republic was one of Moscow’s last major rivals in the Russian lands, but Moscow conquered it in 1478. The name Veliky Novgorod means “Great Novgorod” and distinguishes the city from Nizhny Novgorod, another Russian city.

Edward VIII was born in 1894, the eldest son of King George V, and became king of the United Kingdom in January 1936. He wanted to marry Wallis Simpson, an American woman who had been divorced once and was seeking a second divorce. This caused a constitutional crisis: as king, Edward was also head of the Church of England, whose teachings at the time opposed remarriage after divorce when a former spouse was still alive. Conservative prime minister Stanley Baldwin told Edward that the government would not accept the marriage, even under a proposed arrangement that would deny Simpson the title of queen. Edward abdicated in December 1936, and his younger brother became George VI. Edward later married Simpson and was given the title Duke of Windsor. Baldwin left office in 1937 and was succeeded by Neville Chamberlain.

The Freedom Convoy was a series of Canadian protests in early 2022. It began with truck drivers opposing COVID-19 vaccination requirements for cross-border freight drivers, then grew into a broader movement against vaccine mandates and other public-health restrictions. Protesters drove to Ottawa, Canada’s capital, where trucks occupied streets near Parliament for several weeks. Related protests blocked border crossings, disrupting trade with the United States. Supporters saw the demonstrations as a defense of personal freedom, while critics pointed to the disruption they caused for residents and businesses. In February, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s government invoked the Emergencies Act, giving federal authorities temporary powers to respond to the blockades. This was the first time the act had been used since it replaced the War Measures Act in 1988.

James Cook was an 18th-century British naval officer and explorer who led three major voyages across the Pacific Ocean. On his first voyage, he commanded HMS Endeavour, a converted coal-carrying ship called a collier. The ship reached Tahiti in 1769, where Cook’s expedition observed the transit of Venus across the Sun. Cook then charted New Zealand and sailed along Australia’s eastern coast in 1770, mapping it for Europeans and landing at Botany Bay. Aboriginal peoples had lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years before his arrival, so Cook did not “discover” the continent. His charts helped Britain expand its knowledge of the Pacific and later establish a colony at Sydney, but that colonization had devastating consequences for Indigenous Australians.

The Charter Oath was a declaration issued in 1868 by Emperor Meiji at the start of the Meiji Restoration. That political change ended the rule of Japan’s military leaders, called shoguns, and restored authority to the emperor. The oath set out broad principles for a modern government: it called for public discussion of important decisions, the involvement of people from different social classes, and the pursuit of knowledge from around the world. Although it was not a detailed constitution, it is sometimes described as Japan’s first constitutional document because it stated guiding ideas for how the country should be governed. During this period, Emperor Meiji also moved the imperial capital from Kyoto, which had served as Japan’s capital for nearly a thousand years, to Tokyo.

The Maji Maji Rebellion was an uprising from 1905 to 1907 against German colonial rule in German East Africa, a territory that included much of present-day Tanzania. Many African communities were angered by forced labor, taxes, and German demands that they grow cotton. A spirit medium from Ngarambe named Kinjikitile Ngwale helped inspire the revolt. He taught that consecrated water, called maji, would protect fighters by turning German bullets into water. The belief gave the rebellion its name and helped unite groups that had not always fought together. German forces used superior weapons and a scorched-earth campaign, destroying crops and villages to cut off support for the fighters. The rebellion was defeated, and warfare, forced displacement, and famine caused many deaths.

The Rashidun Caliphate was the first Islamic caliphate, established after the death of the prophet Muhammad in 632. Its name means “rightly guided,” referring to its four successive caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali. Based in Arabia and supported largely by Arab tribes, the caliphate expanded rapidly beyond the Arabian Peninsula. Its armies conquered Egypt and Persia, as well as Syria and the wider Levant. In the Levant, they fought the Byzantine Empire, a Christian state also known as the Eastern Roman Empire. At the time, the Byzantine ruler was Heraclius, who governed from Constantinople. Civil conflict later ended the Rashidun period, and the Umayyad dynasty took control of the caliphate.

Imhotep was an ancient Egyptian royal official who served Djoser, a pharaoh of the Third Dynasty during the Old Kingdom. He is traditionally credited with designing Djoser’s Step Pyramid at Saqqara, a burial monument made of six rising tiers of stone. The pyramid was part of a larger funerary complex built to honor the king after his death and is among Egypt’s earliest monumental stone structures. Although surviving evidence does not tell us everything Imhotep did, his reputation grew long after his lifetime. Centuries later, Egyptians revered him as a deity associated with wisdom and healing. Archaeologists study the pyramid and other remains at Saqqara to learn how ancient Egyptians built monuments and honored their rulers.

The hwacha was a multiple-rocket launcher used by Joseon Korea. It could fire a volley of rocket-propelled arrows at once, sending many projectiles toward an enemy instead of launching them one by one. Arrows are usually shot from a bow, but a hwacha used the thrust of rockets to launch them; some versions could fire other projectiles too. During Japan’s invasions of Korea in the late 1500s, Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s ships used hwachas alongside their cannons. This gave his crews another way to attack enemy forces at a distance. The hwacha is an example of how Korean forces combined traditional weapons, such as arrows, with early rocket technology.

“Paris is well worth a mass” is a remark traditionally attributed to Henry of Navarre, a Protestant who became King Henry IV of France. In the late 1500s, France was divided by wars between Catholics and Protestants, known in France as Huguenots. Henry’s Protestant faith made many Catholics unwilling to accept him as king, even though he had a claim to the throne. In 1593, he converted to Catholicism to strengthen his rule and gain support in Paris, the capital. A mass is a Catholic worship service, so the phrase suggests that winning Paris and securing the crown were worth changing his religion. Historians are not certain Henry actually said it, but the remark captures the political reason often given for his conversion.

The Long March was a vast retreat by the Chinese Communist Red Army in 1934–1935 during its struggle against the Nationalists led by Chiang Kai-shek. After breaking through Nationalist forces surrounding its base in southern China, the Red Army traveled thousands of kilometers across difficult terrain while facing attacks, hunger, and exhaustion. The surviving marchers eventually reached northern Shaanxi province in 1935, where the Communists established a new base. Although the journey cost many lives, it allowed the Communist movement to survive. At the Zunyi Conference, held during the march in 1935, Mao Zedong gained influence over Communist military strategy and leadership. He later led the Communists to victory in China’s civil war and became the founding chairman of the People’s Republic of China in 1949.

The Chinese imperial examinations, also called the civil service examinations or keju, were competitive written tests used to select government officials. Instead of relying only on hereditary appointment, the system gave educated men outside powerful aristocratic families a route into state service. Empress Wu Zetian expanded the examinations during her reign to reduce aristocratic influence and bring more people into government. The system continued to develop under later dynasties. Candidates studied demanding texts, especially Confucian classics, and advanced through several levels of testing. Under the Ming and Qing dynasties, those who passed the final palace examination earned the title jinshi, the highest examination rank. A jinshi could enter the elite ranks of government, though preparing for the exams required years of study and resources that many families could not afford.

The Pilgrimage of Grace was a major uprising in northern England in 1536 against King Henry VIII’s religious changes. Henry had broken with the Catholic Church and begun dissolving monasteries, taking their land and wealth. Many people in the north valued the monasteries as places of worship and sources of help for the poor, and they feared further changes to their faith. The rebels called their movement a “pilgrimage” to show that they saw it as a religious cause. Their leader was Robert Aske, a Yorkshire lawyer who represented them in negotiations with the Crown. Although the rebellion ended after promises from the king’s representatives, Henry later punished its leaders. Aske was executed at York in 1537.

Éamon de Valera was a leading figure in Ireland’s struggle for independence from Britain. During the 1916 Easter Rising, he commanded rebels at the Boland’s Mills garrison in Dublin. After the uprising, he became a leader of Sinn Féin and opposed the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty because it left Ireland divided and required an oath of allegiance to the British monarch. This disagreement helped lead to the Irish Civil War. De Valera later entered parliamentary politics and became the first Taoiseach, or head of government, under a new constitution approved by referendum in 1937. Its Irish-language title is Bunreacht na hÉireann. It replaced the Irish Free State’s 1922 constitution, established the office of president, and named the state Éire. De Valera himself served as president from 1959 to 1973.

The Magyars, also known as Hungarians, moved westward into the Carpathian Basin under the leader Árpád in the late ninth century. There they settled and formed the population from which the medieval Kingdom of Hungary emerged. For decades, Magyar warriors also raided farther west into Europe. Their expansion was checked in 955 at the Battle of Lechfeld by Otto I, a German ruler and the son of Henry the Fowler. Otto was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in 962 and is remembered as Otto the Great. Meanwhile, the Magyars’ kingdom became Christian: Stephen I, later honored as a saint, was crowned its king on Christmas Day in 1000 with the support of Pope Sylvester II.

The Gang of Four was a faction of Chinese Communist Party officials that gained great influence during the Cultural Revolution, a period of political upheaval that began in 1966 under Mao Zedong. Its members were Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Wang Hongwen, and Yao Wenyuan. Jiang Qing, a former actress and Mao’s wife, became a powerful figure who pushed revolutionary ideas in theater, film, and other arts. The group helped enforce radical policies and attack people accused of opposing Mao’s revolution. After Mao died in September 1976, his widow and the other three members lost their strongest source of support. They were arrested in October 1976, ending the Gang of Four’s political power.

The Austro-Prussian War was a short conflict fought in 1866 between Austria’s Habsburg monarchy and the northern German kingdom of Prussia. Also called the Seven Weeks’ War, it grew out of a struggle over which power would lead the German states. On July 3, Prussian forces won a decisive victory over the Austrians at the Battle of Königgrätz in Bohemia, a battle also known as Sadowa. This defeat was the war’s turning point. Prussia’s victory ended Austria’s leadership in German affairs and allowed Prussia to organize the northern German states under its own leadership. It also paved the way for German unification: in 1871, after another Prussian-led victory over France, Prussian king Wilhelm I became emperor of the new German Empire.

Marcus Aurelius ruled the Roman Empire from 161 to 180 CE and is remembered as the last of the Five Good Emperors. He initially shared power with Lucius Verus, who died in 169 CE. Much of Marcus Aurelius’s reign was spent defending the empire’s Danube frontier during the Marcomannic Wars. While on campaign, he wrote personal reflections on how to live wisely, do one’s duty, and face hardship without being ruled by anger or fear. These writings were later collected in twelve books under the title Meditations. They became one of antiquity’s best-known works of Stoic philosophy, which taught people to focus on what they could control and accept what they could not. His death is often seen as marking the end of the Pax Romana, a long period of relative Roman peace.

The Mongols were nomadic peoples from the Central Asian steppe, in the region of present-day Mongolia. Skilled at horseback riding and warfare, they united under Genghis Khan in the early 1200s and built an empire that stretched across much of Asia and into Europe. After Genghis Khan’s death, his descendants continued expanding and divided the empire into several branches. One branch, the Ilkhanate, ruled Persia and nearby parts of the Middle East. It was established by Hulagu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan. Hulagu led the Mongol siege of Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid Caliphate there. The attack devastated the city and its renowned House of Wisdom, a center of scholarship where works from ancient Greece and other cultures had been studied and translated.

The Scots are the people of Scotland, the kingdom north of England. In the late 13th and early 14th centuries, they fought to keep their kingdom independent as English armies invaded. One of their leading figures was William Wallace, who helped defeat an English force at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297. The next year, King Edward I of England defeated Wallace at the Battle of Falkirk. Edward, also known as “Longshanks,” became known as the “Hammer of the Scots” because of his campaigns against them. The struggle continued after Falkirk. Robert the Bruce became king of Scots in 1306 and led further resistance to English rule. These wars are known as the Wars of Scottish Independence.

Frederick I, better known as Frederick Barbarossa, ruled the Holy Roman Empire in the twelfth century. His Italian nickname, Barbarossa, means “red beard.” He tried to strengthen imperial control over the wealthy cities of northern Italy and convened the Diet of Roncaglia in 1158 to assert his authority there. His campaigns brought him into conflict with the Lombard League, an alliance of Italian cities, and with Pope Alexander III, who excommunicated him. Later, Frederick took the cross at Mainz and set out for the Third Crusade, a campaign to the eastern Mediterranean against Saladin. Richard the Lionheart of England and Philip II of France also joined that crusade. Frederick never reached its main battles: he drowned in the Saleph River in 1190 while traveling east with his army.

Jacques Chirac was a French politician who served twice as prime minister before becoming president of France from 1995 to 2007. He also served as mayor of Paris and helped found the UMP, a center-right party, before his second presidential term. In 2002, Chirac survived an assassination attempt during a public celebration of Bastille Day. Held every July 14, this French national holiday commemorates the storming of the Bastille, a Paris prison, in 1789. That event became a powerful symbol of resistance to royal rule and helped launch the French Revolution. Chirac later opposed the 2003 U.S.-led invasion of Iraq, making France’s position an important part of the international debate over the war.

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa was a Roman general, admiral, and statesman who played a crucial role in the rise of his friend Octavian, the future emperor Augustus. Agrippa helped Octavian defeat Sextus Pompey, whose fleet had threatened Rome’s grain supplies. In 31 BCE, Agrippa commanded Octavian’s fleet at the Battle of Actium, fought off the western coast of Greece against the forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Octavian’s victory there secured his path to sole rule of Rome and, eventually, to becoming its first emperor. Agrippa also helped improve Rome through major building projects, including aqueducts and the original Pantheon. His military skill and public works made him one of the most important figures of Augustus’s reign.

Kautilya was an ancient Indian political thinker and strategist closely associated with the rise of Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Mauryan Empire. Tradition describes Kautilya as an adviser who helped Chandragupta defeat the Nanda rulers and take control of their capital, Pataliputra. Kautilya is also traditionally credited with the Arthashastra, a Sanskrit treatise on government and statecraft. It explains how a ruler could govern effectively, covering subjects such as administration, taxation, diplomacy, warfare, and the use of spies and disguises to gather information. The work is an important source for studying ideas about power and government in ancient India, although scholars debate exactly when it was compiled and whether one person wrote all of it.

The Warsaw Pact was a Soviet-led military alliance created in 1955 by the Soviet Union and seven Eastern European communist states. Its full name was the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance. The alliance was formed during the Cold War, after West Germany joined NATO, the Western military alliance led by the United States. Like NATO, the Warsaw Pact promised collective defense: its members agreed to help one another if attacked. It also formalized military cooperation across the Eastern Bloc, though the Soviet Union held the most power within it. The pact took its name from Warsaw, the capital of Poland, where its founding treaty was signed. It remained a major symbol of the division between communist Eastern Europe and the West until it dissolved in 1991.

The Merovingian dynasty ruled the Franks in western Europe from the fifth to the eighth century. Its kings were known for wearing their hair long, a symbol of royal authority. One of its most important rulers was Clovis I, who united many Frankish groups and became the dynasty’s first Christian king. According to the historian Gregory of Tours, Clovis vowed to embrace Christianity during the Battle of Tolbiac. He was later baptized at Reims by Bishop Remigius. His conversion helped create a lasting alliance between the Frankish kingdom and the Roman Church. Over time, power shifted away from the Merovingian kings to officials who governed on their behalf. In 751, Pepin the Short deposed the dynasty’s last king and founded the Carolingian dynasty, which later included his son Charlemagne.

Mawangdui is an archaeological site near Changsha, China, where excavators uncovered three tombs from the Han dynasty. The most famous belonged to a noblewoman commonly known as Lady Dai, whose body was so well preserved that researchers could study details of her health and life. Her tomb also contained a painted silk funerary banner showing her with attendants, along with images linked to the heavens, the world of the living, and the underworld. Objects from the tombs, including silk textiles and manuscripts, reveal much about Han art, beliefs, and daily life. Mawangdui is an important source of historical evidence because its unusually well-preserved burials help historians understand how wealthy people in ancient China lived and honored the dead.

Lester B. Pearson was a Canadian diplomat and prime minister who became known for finding peaceful solutions to international disputes. During the 1956 Suez Crisis, Britain, France, and Israel attacked Egypt after Egypt took control of the Suez Canal. Pearson proposed a United Nations peacekeeping force to help end the fighting, and his work earned him the 1957 Nobel Peace Prize. As prime minister from 1963 to 1968, Pearson also questioned U.S. policy in the Vietnam War, a conflict in Southeast Asia that Canada did not officially fight in. Many Americans who wanted to avoid being drafted into the U.S. military moved to Canada during the war. At home, Pearson’s government helped establish Canadian Medicare, a nationwide public health care system modeled on an earlier program in Saskatchewan.

On July 7, 2021, armed attackers entered the private residence of Haiti’s president, Jovenel Moïse, and killed him. The event is known as the Assassination of Jovenel Moïse. His home was in Pèlerin 5, a neighborhood in the hillside commune of Pétion-Ville, which adjoins Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince. An assassination is the deliberate killing of a prominent person, often for political reasons. Moïse’s death deepened a political crisis in Haiti, where disputes over his presidency had already caused unrest. Investigators arrested several suspects, including former Colombian soldiers, and examined how the attack had been organized. The killing left Haiti without a sitting president and raised urgent questions about who would govern the country.

Leif Erikson was a Norse explorer and the son of Erik the Red, who founded a settlement in Greenland. Around the year 1000, Leif sailed west from Greenland and reached North America, making him traditionally regarded as the first European to do so. His voyage took place centuries before Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic. Norse sagas describe Leif exploring a region with plentiful timber and wild grapes, which he called Vinland. The exact extent of Vinland is uncertain, but archaeological remains of a Norse settlement at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland show that Norse voyagers reached North America. Leif and other Vikings relied on sturdy ships for long sea journeys; he probably traveled in a knarr, a cargo vessel suited to carrying supplies across the Atlantic.

Draco was an Athenian lawgiver traditionally credited with putting the city’s laws into writing near the end of the seventh century BCE. Written laws made rules more publicly known, but Draco’s code became famous for its harsh punishments, including severe penalties for some relatively minor offenses. That reputation gave us the word “draconian,” meaning excessively strict or severe. In the early sixth century BCE, the reformer Solon repealed most of Draco’s laws as he reshaped Athenian government. According to Athenian tradition, however, Draco’s homicide laws remained in force. These laws dealt with cases of killing and distinguished between intentional and unintentional acts. Draco is remembered both for Athens’ early written law code and for the severity associated with his name.

The King–Byng Affair was a 1926 Canadian constitutional crisis about who could decide when a federal election should be held. Prime Minister William Lyon Mackenzie King led a minority government, meaning his party did not hold enough seats to control the House of Commons on its own. Under pressure in Parliament, King asked Governor General Lord Byng, the monarch’s representative in Canada, to dissolve Parliament and call an election. Byng refused and instead invited Conservative leader Arthur Meighen to form a government. King argued that Byng should have followed the prime minister’s advice, while Byng believed another government should first have a chance to govern. Meighen’s ministry soon lost the confidence of the House of Commons, so an election was held. The affair strengthened the expectation that governors general normally follow a prime minister’s advice.

El Alamein is a coastal locality in Egypt, on the Mediterranean route west of Alexandria. Its position made it important in the North African campaign of World War II: Axis forces advancing east across the desert had to pass through a narrow area between the sea and the impassable Qattara Depression. At the First Battle of El Alamein in 1942, Allied forces stopped the Axis advance toward Alexandria and the Nile Delta. The 9th Australian Division helped defend the position and suffered heavy casualties. Later that year, the British Eighth Army, commanded by Bernard Montgomery, attacked Axis positions in the Second Battle of El Alamein. Montgomery directed an offensive called Operation Supercharge, which helped break through the Axis defenses. The Allied victory forced Axis troops to retreat westward across North Africa.

The Red Army was formed by the Bolshevik government in 1918, soon after the Russian Revolution, to defend its new communist state. Its main opponents in the Russian Civil War were the White armies, a loose alliance of groups opposed to Bolshevik rule. Leon Trotsky, the Bolshevik commissar for military and naval affairs, organized the Red Army, recruited experienced officers, and enforced strict discipline. He also traveled by armored train to visit the front, direct operations, and rally troops. The Bolsheviks used policies known as war communism to supply their forces during the war. After defeating the Whites, the Red Army became the armed forces of the Soviet Union. Its name used red because that color was closely associated with socialism and revolution.

The Congo Wars were two connected conflicts fought in and around the Democratic Republic of the Congo from 1996 to 2003. Their roots included the 1994 genocide in neighboring Rwanda, where Hutu extremists targeted Tutsis. Some Tutsis fled persecution, while large numbers of Hutus, including people responsible for the genocide, crossed into eastern Congo. Fighting over refugees, armed groups, and regional security helped draw other countries into the wars. In the First Congo War, rebels backed by Rwanda and Uganda overthrew Congo’s longtime ruler, Mobutu Sese Seko, in 1997 and installed Laurent-Désiré Kabila. A second war began in 1998 after Kabila fell out with his former allies. It involved more than nine countries, earning the conflicts the nickname “African World Wars.” Kabila was assassinated during the second war in 2001.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was an Ottoman general who led the Turkish nationalist movement during the Turkish War of Independence after World War I. His forces rejected the harsh Treaty of Sèvres, which would have divided much of the former Ottoman Empire. The nationalist government abolished the Ottoman sultanate in 1922, and in 1923 Turkey and the Allied powers signed the Treaty of Lausanne. This peace accord replaced the Sèvres settlement and secured international recognition of Turkey’s sovereignty and borders. The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed that year, with Atatürk as its first president and Ankara as its capital. He then introduced reforms aimed at creating a modern, secular state, including changes to education, the legal system, and clothing. His government also abolished the caliphate, though it did not ban Islam.

The May Fourth Movement began on May 4, 1919, when students in Beijing protested the decisions made at the Paris Peace Conference after World War I. During the war, Japan had captured Qingdao and other German holdings in China’s Shandong province. Many Chinese people expected these territories to be returned to China, but the peace settlement gave Germany’s former rights there to Japan instead. Protesters saw this as another example of foreign powers ignoring China’s independence. The demonstrations spread beyond students to workers and merchants, who organized strikes and boycotts of Japanese goods. As public pressure grew, Chinese delegates refused to sign the Treaty of Versailles. The movement became a landmark in modern Chinese nationalism and encouraged calls for political and cultural change.

The Franks were a group of Germanic peoples who established a kingdom in Gaul, a region covering much of modern France and nearby areas, after the Western Roman Empire weakened. Their early kings belonged to the Merovingian dynasty. One of them, Clovis I, defeated the Gallo-Roman leader Syagrius at the Battle of Soissons in 486, helping him expand Frankish control. Clovis later converted to Nicene Christianity, gaining support from the Christian population of Gaul and strengthening his rule. Centuries later, the Carolingian dynasty took power. Its most famous ruler, Charlemagne, began as king of the Franks and expanded their kingdom into a vast empire. Pope Leo III crowned him emperor on Christmas Day in the year 800.

A bronze sword is a bladed weapon made from bronze, an alloy of copper and tin. Copper formed most of the metal, while smiths added a smaller amount of tin to make the blade harder than copper alone. This strength helped them make blades longer than early daggers and knives, giving warriors greater reach in combat. Bronze swords became important weapons in many ancient societies during the Bronze Age. Making one required skill: a smith could cast molten bronze in a mold, then sharpen the blade and attach a handle. Although later iron and steel swords became more common, surviving bronze swords help archaeologists learn about ancient warfare, metalworking, and trade.

The Sejm was the parliament of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, where representatives debated and enacted laws. Its name is still used for the lower house of Poland’s modern parliament. In 1791, the Commonwealth adopted the May 3rd Constitution, which aimed to strengthen its government and was partly inspired by the United States Constitution. Two years later, the Sejm met in Grodno, a city now in Belarus. At this 1793 session, known as the Grodno Sejm, strong Russian pressure and bribery influenced delegates to accept the Second Partition of Poland, in which neighboring powers took more Commonwealth territory. The delegates also nullified the May 3rd Constitution. These events show how interference from powerful neighbors weakened the Commonwealth’s efforts to reform.

The Song dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279, a period of economic growth and remarkable cultural and technological change. Song scholars and craftspeople developed movable-type printing and improved the compass, while gunpowder weapons became more important in warfare. The government also introduced reforms, including Wang Anshi’s baojia system, which organized households for local security. Tea, already known in China, became especially important to refined Song social life. People often ground tea leaves into powder and whisked the powder with hot water, a method that later influenced Japanese tea traditions. The Song faced increasing pressure from the Mongols and fell in 1279. The Mongol ruler Kublai Khan then governed China as emperor of the Yuan dynasty.

The Benalla affair was a political scandal in France that broke in 2018, after video emerged from a May Day demonstration in Paris. It showed Alexandre Benalla, a security aide to President Emmanuel Macron, wearing a police helmet and assaulting a protester even though he was not a police officer. Benalla had been allowed to observe police operations at the protest, but the footage raised questions about why he appeared to act like an officer and use force. The revelations also prompted scrutiny of how Macron’s staff and security team at the Élysée Palace handled the incident. The scandal is named after Benalla, whose actions and position close to the president made the footage a major political issue.

Italy’s Years of Lead was a prolonged period of political violence, especially from the late 1960s through the 1980s. Its name refers to the bullets used in attacks by armed groups on both the far left and far right. These groups carried out bombings, kidnappings, and assassinations amid intense political conflict. One defining attack was the Piazza Fontana bombing: on December 12, 1969, a bomb exploded at the National Agricultural Bank in Milan, killing 17 people. Far-right extremists were linked to the bombing. The far-left Red Brigades later kidnapped and murdered former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978. Together, these events show why the Years of Lead is remembered as a frightening period in modern Italian history.

Roman Britain was the part of the island of Britain ruled by the Roman Empire. Julius Caesar had briefly invaded Britain from Gaul, but lasting Roman rule began after Emperor Claudius’s successful invasion in AD 43. Imperial officials governed the province, while Roman armies built roads, forts, and towns. Many Britons resisted Roman control. During Emperor Nero’s reign, Boudica, queen of the Iceni people, led a major revolt after Roman officials mistreated her family and tribe. Her forces destroyed the Roman towns of Camulodunum, Londinium, and Verulamium. A Roman army defeated the rebellion at the Battle of Watling Street. Roman rule continued for centuries, although Rome never controlled the entire island.

Nubia was an ancient region along the Nile River directly south of Egypt, in what is now mainly northern Sudan. Its position on the river connected it to Egypt through trade, travel, and sometimes war. Nubia was rich in resources such as gold, and its peoples developed their own cultures and states.
