Egyptian rulers campaigned there, but Nubian rulers also became powerful. The best-known Nubian state was the Kingdom of Kush, which had major centers at Napata and later Meroë. Kushite kings conquered Egypt in the eighth century BCE and ruled it as the 25th Dynasty of pharaohs. Nubia is the name of the region; Kush is the name of the kingdom that rose within it.

Nicolae Ceaușescu was the communist ruler of Romania, an Eastern European country whose capital is Bucharest. He became general secretary of the Romanian Communist Party in 1965 and president in 1974. His condemnation of the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 won him attention abroad, but he maintained an authoritarian government at home, supported by the feared secret police, the Securitate. After visiting China and North Korea in 1971, he announced the July Theses, a program calling for tighter ideological control, greater party influence over culture, and renewed political education. His policies also included Decree 770, which sharply restricted abortion and contraception. In December 1989, protests grew into a revolution that ended his rule. Ceaușescu and his wife Elena were executed on Christmas Day.

The Gordon riots were several days of anti-Catholic violence in London in June 1780, during the reign of King George III. They began after the Protestant Association organized a campaign against the Catholic Relief Act of 1778, which had eased some restrictions on Catholics. The association’s leader, the Scottish nobleman Lord George Gordon, presented a petition opposing the act to Parliament. A large crowd gathered in support, but the protest turned into riots that spread across the city. Rioters attacked Catholic homes and chapels, as well as public buildings and prisons; Newgate Prison was partly destroyed. Troops eventually restored order. The disturbances are named the Gordon riots after Lord George Gordon, although he did not control all the violence that followed the petition.

The Republic of Serbia is a Balkan country that was once part of Yugoslavia. During World War II, Nazi Germany and its Axis allies invaded Yugoslavia, and resistance groups fought the occupiers. One group was the Chetniks, Serbian nationalist forces; another was the communist-led Yugoslav Partisans. After the war, Serbia became one of the republics in socialist Yugoslavia. As Yugoslavia broke apart in the 1990s, Slobodan Milošević led Serbia. In Serbia’s southern province of Kosovo, tensions between Serbian authorities and the largely ethnic Albanian population grew into an armed conflict with ethnic Albanian forces. This conflict is called the Kosovo War. NATO launched an air campaign in 1999, and international forces entered Kosovo after Serbian forces withdrew.

The Paris Peace Conference met in 1919 to negotiate the peace settlement after World War I. Delegates from the victorious Allied powers shaped treaties with the defeated countries and planned the League of Nations, an organization intended to help prevent future wars. One disputed decision concerned Shandong province in China, including the port city of Qingdao. Germany had held rights there before the war, but Japan captured Qingdao during the fighting. Although China had supported the Allies and hoped to regain those rights, the conference awarded them to Japan. The decision angered many Chinese people. On May 4, 1919, students demonstrated in Beijing, beginning the May Fourth Movement, which spread into a wider campaign for national independence and reform. China refused to sign the Treaty of Versailles.

The Red Guards were student-led groups that Mao Zedong encouraged during China’s Cultural Revolution, which began in 1966. Wearing red armbands, they gathered at huge rallies in Beijing and pledged loyalty to Mao. He urged them to challenge Communist Party officials and attack the “Four Olds”: old customs, culture, habits, and ideas. Red Guards criticized teachers and other people they considered opponents of the revolution, sometimes using violence. They were also urged to study Quotations from Chairman Mao Zedong, a widely distributed collection of his sayings published in a small red-covered volume. In English, it is commonly called the Little Red Book. As Red Guard factions became increasingly disruptive and violent, Mao’s government eventually moved to curb them and sent many young members to the countryside.

The Wörgl Experiment was a local-currency initiative begun in 1932 in Wörgl, a town in the Austrian region of Tyrol, during the Great Depression. With many people unemployed and ordinary money scarce, the municipality issued notes that residents could use to pay for goods and services. Holders had to buy and attach a stamp each month to keep the notes at full value; otherwise, the notes lost value. This planned loss of value is called demurrage. It encouraged people to spend the notes rather than save them, keeping money circulating through the town. The municipality also used the notes to pay workers on public works projects, such as improving roads. Although the experiment attracted attention for its local economic effects, Austria’s central bank stopped it in 1933.

The Lakota are an Indigenous people of the North American Great Plains. Historically, they have also been called the Teton, and they belong to the larger group often called the Sioux peoples, along with the Dakota. Lakota communities have long shared knowledge and values through stories passed down across generations. One figure in these traditions is Iktomi, a trickster who often takes the form of a spider. Trickster stories can be funny or surprising, but they may also teach listeners to think carefully about choices and their consequences. In one tale, Iktomi is connected with the origin of hoops woven with string nets, often called dreamcatchers, that are used as protective charms for children.

The War of the Austrian Succession was a European conflict fought from 1740 to 1748 over who would inherit the lands of the Habsburg dynasty, which ruled Austria from Vienna. Before his death, Emperor Charles VI had issued the Pragmatic Sanction to secure the succession of his daughter, Maria Theresa. When he died in 1740, several European powers challenged her claim. Frederick the Great of Prussia invaded Silesia, a valuable Habsburg territory, drawing Prussia and Austria into war. Other countries joined the fighting as alliances formed across Europe. The war ended in 1748 with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. The treaty recognized Maria Theresa’s rule over the Habsburg lands, but Prussia was allowed to keep Silesia, which Austria had lost during the war.

Yi Sun-sin was a naval commander of Korea’s Joseon kingdom during Japan’s invasions of the Korean peninsula in the 1590s. Japan’s forces were sent by the ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Yi helped stop them by attacking the ships that carried their troops and supplies. His fleet included “turtle ships,” heavily protected warships with covered decks, and he won a major victory against a Japanese fleet at Hansan Island in 1592. After being removed from command, Yi returned in 1597 to find that Joseon had only a small number of warships left. At the Battle of Myeongnyang, he led just 13 ships against a much larger Japanese fleet. By choosing a narrow strait with powerful tidal currents, he helped his outnumbered force win one of history’s most celebrated naval victories.

The African National Congress (ANC) was founded in South Africa in 1912 to defend the rights of Black South Africans. It became a leading liberation movement against apartheid, the system of laws that enforced racial segregation and denied the Black majority political rights. The government banned the ANC in 1960, forcing many of its leaders to work from exile. Oliver Tambo led the organization from abroad as its president from 1967 to 1991, building international support for the struggle against apartheid. Another ANC leader, Nelson Mandela, spent 27 years in prison for his anti-apartheid activities. After apartheid ended, the ANC won South Africa’s first multiracial national election in 1994, and Mandela became the country’s first Black president.

The Battle of the Red Cliffs, also called the Battle of Chibi, took place along the Yangtze River in 208–209 CE, near the end of China’s Han dynasty. Cao Cao, a powerful northern warlord, led a much larger army south, hoping to bring the region under his control. Sun Quan and Liu Bei joined forces to resist him. Their commanders used a fire attack against Cao Cao’s fleet, helping the smaller allied force win a decisive victory and halt his advance. The battle helped preserve the division between northern and southern powers that later became the Three Kingdoms. It also appears in the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, which adds dramatic stories about the strategist Zhuge Liang and his rivals.

The White Terror was a decades-long period of political repression in Taiwan under the Kuomintang, or Chinese Nationalist Party. After losing the Chinese Civil War to the Communists, Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek relocated the Republic of China government to Taiwan in 1949. His government kept the island under martial law and treated suspected opponents as threats to national security. Many people accused of supporting communism, criticizing the government, or seeking Taiwanese independence were arrested; some were imprisoned or executed. Chiang remained Taiwan’s dominant ruler until his death in 1975. Martial law lasted until 1987, and the White Terror remains a major episode of state repression in Taiwan’s modern history.

A quipu was a recording system used by the Inca Empire in the Andes. It consisted of a main cord with smaller strands hanging from it. The placement and type of knots could represent numbers, while cord colors and other features helped organize information. Inca administrators used quipu to keep track of census totals, storehouse inventories, and the labor people owed to the state. These records helped officials manage an empire spread across mountains and valleys. To move information over long distances, the Inca relied on a network of roads and way stations. Specially trained relay runners called chasqui carried quipu records and delivered verbal messages from one station to the next. Together, quipu and chasqui helped the empire collect, record, and share information.

An ejido is a Mexican system of communal landholding in which the state owns the land while members of a rural community, often farmers or peasants, have rights to use it. Ejidos grew out of demands for land reform during the Mexican Revolution, when leaders such as Emiliano Zapata called for land to be taken from large estates and made available to rural people. Article 27 of Mexico’s 1917 Constitution gave the state authority to redistribute land and provided the legal foundation for the ejido system. This meant families could farm ejido land without owning it as private property. The system aimed to give more people access to farmland and reduce the power of wealthy landowners.

The Spanish Civil War was fought from 1936 to 1939 between Spain’s elected Republican government and Nationalist forces led by General Francisco Franco. Political divisions over land, religion, and the role of the military helped drive the conflict. Nazi Germany under Adolf Hitler and Fascist Italy under Benito Mussolini supplied Franco’s forces with aircraft, weapons, and troops, while volunteers from other countries fought for the Republicans. On April 26, 1937, aircraft from Germany’s Condor Legion and Italian aviation units bombed Guernica, a Basque town in Republican-held territory, during its market day. The destruction of Guernica became a powerful symbol of attacks on civilians and inspired a famous painting by Pablo Picasso. The war ended in a Nationalist victory in 1939, and Franco ruled Spain as a dictator for decades.

The Cuban Revolution was the armed struggle that overthrew Cuban ruler Fulgencio Batista and transformed the country’s government. Batista had taken power in a military coup in 1952 and ruled as a dictator. Fidel Castro became a leading opponent, and his 1953 speech “History Will Absolve Me” helped inspire the Twenty-sixth of July Movement. After an unsuccessful early uprising, Castro and a small group of rebels fought a guerrilla campaign from the Sierra Maestra mountains. As Batista’s forces lost control, he fled Cuba on December 31, 1958. Castro’s rebels took power in 1959. Cuba later became a communist state closely allied with the Soviet Union, making the revolution a defining event of the Cold War. Fidel Castro remained Cuba’s leader for decades before handing the presidency to his brother Raúl in 2008.

Ancient coins were pieces of metal stamped, or minted, with designs to serve as currency. The earliest known examples are associated with Lydia, in what is now western Turkey. They were made from electrum, a naturally occurring mixture of gold and silver. Later, the Lydian king Croesus introduced coins with separate standards for gold and silver, making their value more predictable. Coin-making spread to Greek city-states and empires around the Mediterranean. Athens minted silver tetradrachms worth four drachmas, with the goddess Athena on one side and an owl on the other. Rome used coins such as the silver denarius. Today, ancient coins help archaeologists learn about trade, rulers, beliefs, and the economies of past societies.

The Parliament of England grew out of medieval councils that advised the king. The Magna Carta, agreed to by King John in 1215, placed limits on royal power and helped encourage the idea that rulers should consult others. Parliament developed more fully over the following decades. During the Second Barons’ War, the nobleman Simon de Montfort summoned a parliament in 1265 that included knights from the shires and representatives from towns called boroughs. Over time, Parliament took a two-house form: the House of Lords, made up of nobles and senior clergy, and the House of Commons, whose members represented communities. After England and Scotland united in 1707, the Parliament of England helped shape the new Parliament of Great Britain and, later, the Parliament of the United Kingdom.

János Kádár was a Hungarian communist leader who came to power after the Hungarian Revolution of 1956. The uprising began with demonstrations in Budapest in October, as protesters demanded greater freedom and an end to Soviet control. Soviet troops crushed the revolt in November, and Kádár became head of a new government backed by the Soviet Union. He dominated Hungarian politics for decades. His government first punished many people involved in the revolution, but later allowed more consumer goods and limited private business than were common in other communist countries. This comparatively permissive approach became known as “goulash communism,” after a popular Hungarian stew. Hungary remained under communist rule, but everyday life there was often less restricted than in much of the Soviet bloc.

Juan Guaidó is a Venezuelan opposition politician who became president of the National Assembly, Venezuela’s legislature, in January 2019. That same month, Nicolás Maduro began a second presidential term after an election whose legitimacy was widely disputed. Guaidó argued that the presidency was vacant and invoked constitutional succession procedures to declare himself interim president. The United States and several other countries initially recognized him, but Maduro remained in control of the government and armed forces. In 2019, Guaidó launched a nationwide campaign called Operation Freedom to build support for ending Maduro’s rule. The campaign culminated in an attempted uprising on April 30, but it failed to remove Maduro. Guaidó’s challenge became a major part of Venezuela’s political crisis.

Abel Tasman was a Dutch navigator working for the Dutch East India Company. In 1642, he led an expedition through the southern Pacific Ocean and became the first European recorded to have sighted New Zealand, an island country southeast of Australia whose capital is Wellington. His ships anchored near present-day Golden Bay, where an encounter with Māori, the Indigenous people of New Zealand, turned violent. Tasman did not explore far inland or establish a settlement. On the same voyage, he also charted part of the coast of an island south of Australia. Europeans called it Van Diemen’s Land, but it was later renamed Tasmania in his honor. These voyages added to European maps, though Māori had lived in New Zealand for centuries before Tasman arrived.

The Xiongnu were nomadic peoples of the Eurasian steppe who built a powerful empire north of China. Around 209 BCE, a leader named Modu overthrew his father, Touman, and took the title chanyu, meaning supreme ruler. Chinese histories say Modu trained his warriors to fire whistling arrows at any target he chose, teaching them to follow his commands without hesitation. Under his leadership, the Xiongnu united and became a major power that fought and negotiated with China’s Han dynasty. The Han sometimes used heqin, a policy of arranging marriages and offering gifts to seek peace. Some historians have proposed a linguistic connection between the Xiongnu and the Huns, who appeared in Europe centuries later, but the relationship remains uncertain.

Archduke Franz Ferdinand was the heir presumptive to the throne of Austria-Hungary and the nephew of its emperor, Franz Joseph I. In 1900, he married Sophie Chotek, a Bohemian aristocrat who had served as a lady-in-waiting. Because the imperial family considered her rank too low for an heir’s wife, their marriage was morganatic: Sophie could not become empress, and their children were excluded from succession to the Habsburg throne. On 28 June 1914, while visiting Sarajevo in Bosnia, Franz Ferdinand and Sophie were assassinated by Gavrilo Princip, a member of the revolutionary movement Young Bosnia. Their deaths sparked the July Crisis, in which Austria-Hungary’s confrontation with Serbia drew in other European powers and led to World War I.

Bartolomé de las Casas was a 16th-century Spanish Dominican friar who became Bishop of Chiapas, in what is now Mexico. After seeing the suffering of Indigenous peoples under Spanish colonial rule, he argued that they should be protected rather than enslaved or mistreated. The Spanish crown named him the first “Protector of the Indians,” a role in which he defended Indigenous communities. In 1552, he published A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, a forceful account of violence and other abuses committed by Spanish colonizers in the Americas. His writing made him one of the best-known critics of those abuses, although it did not end them.

The Gallipoli campaign was a failed Allied operation against the Ottoman Empire during World War I. In 1915, the Allies hoped to force their way through the Dardanelles, a narrow waterway, and capture the Gallipoli Peninsula. This could have opened a sea route to their ally Russia. After naval attacks failed, Allied troops landed on the peninsula on April 25, 1915. They included soldiers from the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, known as ANZAC. Ottoman forces resisted fiercely, and the fighting became a costly stalemate. The Allies withdrew by early 1916 without achieving their goal. April 25 is now observed in Australia and New Zealand as Anzac Day, a day of remembrance for people who served and died in war.

The Social War was a revolt by Rome’s Italian allies from 91 to 87 BC. These communities had supplied soldiers for Roman armies but lacked Roman citizenship and a full voice in Roman politics. After efforts to extend their rights failed, many allies rebelled. The name “Social War” comes from socii, the Latin word for allies; the conflict is also called the War of the Allies or the Marsic War. Rome fought the rebels while also offering citizenship to weaken the revolt. One important measure was the Lex Plautia Papiria of 89 BC, named for the two tribunes who proposed it. It allowed residents of allied Italian communities to gain Roman citizenship by registering with a Roman praetor within 60 days.

The Kalmar Union joined the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under one monarch in 1397. It was a personal union, meaning the kingdoms shared a ruler but kept their own laws and institutions. Denmark held the leading role, with Copenhagen as an important center of power. Margaret I, a Danish-born ruler and daughter of King Valdemar IV, brought the three kingdoms together. She arranged for her adopted son, Eric of Pomerania, to be crowned at Kalmar, a town in Sweden, in 1397. Margaret remained a powerful figure even after Eric’s coronation. The union faced repeated struggles over how much control Denmark should have, especially in Sweden. It ended in 1523 when Sweden broke away and chose its own king.

Pericles was a leading statesman of Athens during its fifth-century BCE Golden Age. The son of Xanthippus, he was repeatedly elected strategos, a military commander, and helped guide Athens as it grew powerful. When the Peloponnesian War began between Athens and Sparta, Pericles gave a famous Funeral Oration honoring Athenians killed early in the fighting. In the speech, he praised Athens and its democratic way of life. We know the address from the History of the Peloponnesian War by Thucydides, an Athenian historian who lived through the conflict. Thucydides was later exiled after he failed to prevent Spartan forces from capturing Amphipolis, a strategically important city. His account is a major source for what we know about Pericles and the war.

Self-immolation is the act of deliberately setting oneself on fire. It is sometimes used as an extreme form of political protest intended to draw attention to injustice. In December 2010, Tunisian street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire after authorities confiscated his goods. His death helped spark protests in Tunisia that grew into the Arab Spring. Another widely known case occurred in 1963 during the Buddhist crisis in South Vietnam. At a Saigon intersection, the Buddhist monk Thích Quảng Đức set himself on fire to protest President Ngô Đình Diệm’s government and its repression of Buddhists. Photographs of his protest spread around the world, bringing international attention to the crisis.

Justin Trudeau is a Canadian politician and the son of Pierre Trudeau, who served as prime minister in two separate periods. Justin became prime minister after his Liberal Party won the 2015 federal election and remained in office until 2025. His government led Canada through the COVID-19 pandemic and a diplomatic dispute with China involving the detention of two Canadians known as the “Two Michaels.” In 2022, truckers and other protesters gathered in Ottawa and blocked border crossings in a movement called the Freedom Convoy. Trudeau’s government responded by invoking the Emergencies Act, a federal law passed in 1988, for the first time. It gave the government temporary powers to address the blockades, a decision that sparked debate over public safety and civil liberties.

The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established in April 1992 by Serbia and Montenegro after the breakup of the larger Yugoslav federation. That earlier country had included several Balkan republics and was led for many years by Josip Broz Tito. During the late 1990s, conflict grew in Kosovo, a province of Serbia, between Serbian forces and ethnic Albanian Kosovars. In response to the Kosovo War, NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, launched an air campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The bombing began on March 24, 1999, and ended on June 10, lasting 78 days. NATO said it aimed to stop violence against civilians in Kosovo, but the campaign was also criticized for causing civilian deaths. In 2003, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was renamed Serbia and Montenegro.

The Parliament of the United Kingdom is the country’s bicameral legislature, meaning it has two chambers: the elected House of Commons and the House of Lords. It meets at the Palace of Westminster in London, where its members debate laws and hold the government to account. In 2022, Prime Minister Boris Johnson faced a series of political crises, including criticism over parties held during COVID-19 restrictions. In June, Conservative members of Parliament held a no-confidence vote on his leadership. The following month, several ministers resigned from Johnson’s government, including Rishi Sunak, who had served as Chancellor of the Exchequer, the minister responsible for government finances. Johnson then announced that he would step down. Sunak later became prime minister in October 2022, succeeding Liz Truss.

Louis Philippe I was the only king of France from the House of Orléans. He came to power after the July Revolution of 1830 overthrew Charles X, the last Bourbon king. Called the “Citizen King,” Louis Philippe presented himself as a monarch who would rule under a constitution rather than by absolute authority. The political regime of his reign was called the July Monarchy. Under its revised charter, parliament had an important role, but voting rights depended on property and taxes, so most French people could not vote. His government favored wealthy business owners and faced growing demands for political reform. When another revolution broke out in 1848, Louis Philippe abdicated, ending the July Monarchy and making way for the Second French Republic.

Operation Entebbe was a 1976 Israeli military raid to rescue passengers and crew from Air France Flight 139. Hijackers had forced the plane to land at Entebbe International Airport in Uganda, near the capital, Kampala. Uganda’s ruler, Idi Amin, supported the hostage-takers. After the hijackers released some passengers, they held more than 100 people at the airport. Israeli forces flew to Uganda and carried out a surprise nighttime rescue, bringing most of the hostages to safety. The raid is also called Operation Thunderbolt or Operation Jonathan, after Yonatan Netanyahu, the Israeli commander who was killed during the mission. Air France pilot Michel Bacos chose to stay with the passengers who remained captive. The operation became famous for its long-distance planning and the risks involved in rescuing hostages on foreign soil.

The Golden Law was a Brazilian statute that ended legal slavery throughout the country on May 13, 1888. It was signed by Princess Isabel, the eldest daughter and heir of Emperor Dom Pedro II. Isabel was serving as regent, governing Brazil while her father was abroad. The law was brief but historic: it declared slavery abolished without requiring enslaved people to pay for their freedom. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, after centuries in which enslaved Africans and their descendants had been forced to work, especially on plantations. The Golden Law brought legal freedom, but it did not provide formerly enslaved people with land, money, or other support, leaving many to face poverty and discrimination.

Six British kings have been named George, beginning with George I, a ruler from the German House of Hanover who became king in 1714. Under George I and his son George II, Parliament and government ministers gained influence. Robert Walpole managed the political fallout from the South Sea Bubble, a financial crash, and became the leading minister under both kings. He is widely regarded as Britain’s first prime minister. George II also faced the last major Jacobite rebellion, whose supporters tried to restore the Stuart family to the throne. George III reigned during the American Revolution, when Britain lost its mainland North American colonies; he also experienced periods of serious illness. The sixth and most recent, George VI, reigned during World War II. He worked to overcome a stammer, and his radio broadcasts helped sustain public morale.

Che Guevara, born Ernesto Guevara in Argentina, trained as a physician before becoming a Marxist revolutionary. Travels across Latin America, including a journey with his friend Alberto Granado described in The Motorcycle Diaries, shaped his political views. In the 1950s, he joined Fidel Castro’s movement and became a leading commander in the Cuban Revolution, which overthrew Fulgencio Batista in 1959. After helping govern Cuba, Guevara tried to spread revolution through guerrilla campaigns in Africa and Bolivia. Bolivian forces captured and executed him in 1967. One of the best-known images of Guevara shows him wearing a beret with a star. Cuban photographer Alberto Korda took the photograph in 1960 at a Havana memorial for victims of the La Coubre explosion. Titled Guerrillero Heroico, it became a widely reproduced political portrait.

The Flavian dynasty was a Roman ruling family founded by the military commander Vespasian in 69 CE, after the chaotic Year of the Four Emperors. Its three emperors ruled in succession: Vespasian was followed by his elder son Titus, and then by his younger son Domitian. The family’s rule brought stability after civil war and included major building projects, such as the Colosseum, which Vespasian began and Titus opened. Domitian ruled for 15 years, but his harsh treatment of opponents made him enemies. He was assassinated in 96 CE, ending the dynasty. After his death, the Roman Senate condemned his memory in a practice known as damnatio memoriae, which could involve removing a person’s name or image from public monuments.

Heinrich Schliemann was a nineteenth-century German archaeologist known for excavating places linked to stories from ancient Greece. After earlier work by Frank Calvert, Schliemann dug at Hisarlik, a mound in northwestern Anatolia in modern Turkey. Its layers of settlements are associated with the ancient city of Troy. Schliemann also excavated Mycenae and Tiryns in Greece, important sites connected with the ancient Mycenaean world. At Hisarlik, he found a collection of valuable objects that he called Priam’s Treasure, after a king of Troy in legend. Scholars now know the objects came from a settlement layer much older than the period usually associated with the Trojan War. Schliemann’s removal of the treasure without permission, along with damage caused by his digging methods, remains controversial.

The Battle of the Boyne was fought in Ireland in 1690 during the Williamite War. William III’s army defeated forces loyal to James II, who had lost the English throne after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and was trying to regain it. The armies met at the River Boyne, which William’s troops crossed during the battle. One of William’s commanders, the veteran Huguenot soldier known as the Duke of Schomberg, had advised against the crossing but was killed while leading troops through the river. William’s victory strengthened his hold on the throne, though the war in Ireland continued for another year. The battle is commemorated by the Twelfth of July, a holiday especially associated with Protestant communities in Northern Ireland.

Mehmed II was an Ottoman sultan known as Mehmed the Conqueror because he captured Constantinople in 1453. The city was the capital of the Byzantine Empire and was protected by the massive Theodosian Walls. Before the siege, Mehmed had the fortress Rumeli Hisarı built on the Bosporus, a narrow waterway beside the city, to help control ships entering it. His forces also used powerful cannons to batter the walls. When the Ottoman army broke through, Constantinople fell and the Byzantine Empire came to an end. The conquerors later converted the city’s great church, Hagia Sophia, into a mosque. The victory made Constantinople a major center of the Ottoman Empire and established Mehmed’s reputation as a formidable ruler.

Christina of Sweden became queen as a child after her father, King Gustavus Adolphus, died at the Battle of Lützen in 1632. While she was young, the statesman Axel Oxenstierna helped govern Sweden as regent. Christina grew into an independent ruler with a strong interest in learning, art, and philosophy. She invited the French philosopher and mathematician René Descartes to Stockholm, where he tutored her before dying in 1650. Descartes is known for the phrase “Cogito, ergo sum,” meaning “I think, therefore I am,” and for his book Meditations on First Philosophy. In 1654, Christina abdicated the Swedish throne. She later converted to Catholicism and settled in Rome, where she became associated with the court of Pope Alexander VII.

The Koh-i-Noor is a famous diamond that passed through the hands of several South Asian rulers before becoming part of the British Crown Jewels. Its name is often translated as “Mountain of Light.” Britain took control of Punjab after defeating the Sikh Empire in the Second Anglo-Sikh War in 1849. Under the settlement that followed, the diamond was ceded to Britain by Duleep Singh, the deposed young ruler and last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire. It was presented to Queen Victoria and recut in 1852 to make it sparkle more brightly. Duleep Singh later lived in Britain. Today, the Koh-i-Noor remains a symbol of debates about colonial conquest and whether objects acquired during imperial rule should be returned to their places of origin.

Sabbatai Zevi was a seventeenth-century Jewish mystic born in 1626 in Smyrna, a city in the Ottoman Empire. Many Jews hoped for the arrival of the Messiah, a future leader believed to bring their people redemption. In 1665, Nathan of Gaza became Zevi’s chief prophetic advocate, declaring that Zevi was the Messiah and spreading the claim through letters and proclamations to Jewish communities. The movement gained followers across the Jewish world. But in 1666, after appearing before Ottoman Sultan Mehmed IV, Zevi converted to Islam rather than continuing to claim the messianic role openly. His conversion shocked many followers. Some rejected him, while others tried to explain his actions through their religious beliefs, forming the continuing Sabbatean movement.

Edmund Hillary was a New Zealand mountaineer and explorer best known for reaching the summit of Mount Everest with Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer from Nepal, on 29 May 1953. Theirs was the first documented ascent of Everest, the world’s highest mountain above sea level. Earlier climbers had tried to reach the top, including George Mallory and Andrew “Sandy” Irvine, who disappeared during a 1924 attempt, so it remains uncertain how high they climbed. Hillary later led expeditions to the South Pole. He also spent many years helping communities in Nepal by supporting the construction of schools and hospitals. His achievements made him famous, but his work in Nepal became an important part of his legacy.

The Goths were a Germanic people who became important during the decline of the Western Roman Empire. They developed into two main branches: the Visigoths, often called the western Goths, and the Ostrogoths, or eastern Goths. In 378 CE, Gothic forces defeated a Roman army at the Battle of Adrianople, where Emperor Valens was killed. In 410 CE, the Visigoths, led by their king Alaric I, captured and sacked Rome—the city’s first sack in nearly eight centuries. Later, Visigoths fought alongside Roman forces against the Huns at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451 CE. The Goths went on to establish kingdoms in parts of Europe. Although their name was later given to Gothic architecture, that medieval style developed long after their kingdoms.

The Proto-Indo-Europeans were a hypothetical prehistoric population whose language is thought to be the ancestor of the Indo-European language family. They left no known written records, so linguists infer their language, called Proto-Indo-European, by comparing shared vocabulary and grammar in later languages such as Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, and the Germanic languages. Scholars often place their homeland on the Eurasian steppe, though its exact location remains debated. In the 19th century, the German linguist August Schleicher was among the first to reconstruct Proto-Indo-European using the comparative method. He even wrote a short fable in the reconstructed language to show what it might have sounded like. Researchers also study possible shared traditions, including the importance of horses, but these cultural reconstructions are less certain than the linguistic evidence.

Thomas Müntzer was a radical preacher during the German Reformation who wanted more sweeping religious and social change than Martin Luther. While serving a congregation at Allstedt, he urged ordinary people to challenge rulers he believed were unjust. In 1525, he supported an uprising of German peasants, many of whom sought relief from heavy burdens and greater rights. Their demands were expressed in the Twelve Articles, although Müntzer did not write them. Luther opposed the revolt and condemned the rebels harshly. Müntzer joined the insurgents in Thuringia, where princely troops from Saxony and Brunswick crushed their army at the Battle of Frankenhausen in the Kyffhäuser region. He was captured after the battle and executed later that year.

The Kuomintang, also called the KMT or Chinese Nationalist Party, was founded by Sun Yat-sen in 1912, soon after the revolution that ended China’s Qing Dynasty. At the time, regional military leaders called warlords controlled much of China. To bring the country under one government, the Kuomintang launched the Northern Expedition in 1926. Starting in Guangdong in southern China, its National Revolutionary Army marched north, defeating warlord regimes and extending Nationalist rule. The party later fought the Chinese Communist Party for control of China. After the Communists won the civil war on the mainland, the Kuomintang-led Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan in 1949.

The Maya Long Count calendar was a way for the Maya civilization of Mesoamerica to record dates across thousands of years. Unlike their repeating 260-day and 365-day calendars, the Long Count counted elapsed days from a traditional starting point. It used place-value units: a k’in was one day, a winal was 20 days, a tun was 360 days, a k’atun was 20 tuns, and a b’ak’tun was 20 k’atuns. Maya dates could be written as a series of these units, such as 13.0.0.0.0. That date marked the completion of 13 b’ak’tuns and corresponds to December 21, 2012, on the Gregorian calendar. Some people mistakenly claimed this rollover predicted the end of the world, but it marked a calendar cycle’s completion, not an apocalypse.

Juan Domingo Perón was an Argentine military officer and politician whose movement, Peronism, became a lasting force in Argentina. He first became president in 1946, winning support from many workers through higher wages and social programs, though critics accused him of suppressing opposition. His second wife, Eva Perón, known as Evita, became a popular political figure and advocate for poorer Argentines before her death in 1952. A military coup overthrew Perón in 1955, forcing him into exile. He spent many of those years in Spain, the European country that had colonized Argentina and whose language is spoken there. Perón returned to Argentina and won the presidency again in 1973, but died the following year.

Trench warfare was a way of fighting in which opposing armies dug fortified trenches for shelter from enemy fire. During World War I, British and French forces faced German forces across a strip of exposed ground called no-man’s-land. Crossing it meant facing machine guns, artillery, and barbed wire, so attacks often gained little ground and the Western Front became a prolonged stalemate. This pattern took hold after the First Battle of the Marne in September 1914. At that battle, fought along the Marne River northeast of Paris, Allied forces stopped the German advance toward the French capital. Their victory frustrated Germany’s Schlieffen Plan for a rapid defeat of France. With neither side able to win quickly, both armies dug in, creating the trench lines that shaped much of the war.

A Chinese junk is a traditional sailing ship used for trade and travel. Its distinctive sails were supported by stiff strips called battens, which helped sailors control them, while watertight bulkheads divided the hull into compartments and helped keep the ship afloat if one section leaked. Junks carried merchants and goods between Chinese ports and destinations across the Indian Ocean. During the Ming dynasty, Admiral Zheng He commanded seven major maritime expeditions between 1405 and 1433. His large fleets included junks and sailed from China to South and Southeast Asia, the Arabian Peninsula, and the East African coast. These voyages helped connect distant ports through trade and diplomacy.

The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 began in late October when student demonstrations in Budapest grew into a nationwide revolt against Hungary’s communist government and Soviet control. Protesters demanded political freedom and reform; many carried Hungarian flags with the communist emblem cut from the center, leaving a hole. Imre Nagy, a reform-minded prime minister, announced that Hungary would leave the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact and become neutral. In early November, Soviet troops invaded and crushed the uprising. Thousands of Hungarians were killed, and many more fled the country. Nagy was captured after the invasion and executed in 1958. János Kádár then led a Soviet-backed government. Although the revolution failed, it became a lasting symbol of Hungary’s resistance to Soviet domination.

The Emperor of China was the sovereign ruler at the top of dynastic government. Emperors governed through officials and were traditionally associated with authority over the lands around the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers, although the territory they actually controlled varied across history. The Zhou dynasty developed the Mandate of Heaven to explain why a ruler had the right to govern. According to this doctrine, Heaven granted its approval to a just and capable dynasty, but could withdraw that approval if its rulers became corrupt or governed badly. Rebellion, disorder, or natural disasters could be interpreted as signs that a dynasty had lost the mandate. A new dynasty could then claim the Mandate of Heaven to justify replacing it.

The encomienda was a system used in Spain’s American colonies after the conquest. The Spanish crown granted a colonist, called an encomendero, the right to demand labor or tribute, such as goods or payments, from an assigned Indigenous community. In principle, encomenderos were supposed to protect the people under their control and teach them Christianity. In practice, many Indigenous people faced harsh labor, exploitation, and abuse. To curb these abuses, Charles V, who ruled Spain as Charles I and was also Holy Roman Emperor, issued the New Laws in 1542. His son Philip II later succeeded him on the Spanish throne. As colonial economies shifted toward large-scale agriculture, the encomienda gradually gave way to the hacienda system, based on large estates.

José de San Martín was an Argentine general who helped win independence from Spanish rule for Argentina, Chile, and Peru. In 1817, he led the Army of the Andes on a difficult crossing of the mountains from Argentina into Chile. His forces helped defeat a Spanish army at the Battle of Chacabuco, opening the way for Chilean independence. San Martín then turned toward Peru, a major Spanish stronghold, and proclaimed its independence in Lima in 1821. The fight was not yet over, so in 1822 he met privately in Guayaquil with Simón Bolívar, another leading South American independence leader. Their meeting is commonly called the Guayaquil Conference. They discussed the remaining campaign to free Peru and who would lead it; afterward, San Martín stepped aside, leaving Bolívar to continue the struggle.

The Trudeau family is a prominent Canadian political family that includes Pierre Trudeau and his son Justin, both of whom served as prime minister. Pierre led Canada for much of the period from 1968 to 1984, while Justin became prime minister in 2015. One of the greatest challenges of Pierre’s time in office was the October Crisis of 1970. Members of the Front de libération du Québec (FLQ), a group seeking independence for the mostly French-speaking province of Quebec, kidnapped British diplomat James Cross and Quebec cabinet minister Pierre Laporte. Laporte was murdered, though Cross was later freed. Pierre Trudeau’s federal government invoked the War Measures Act, giving authorities extraordinary powers to respond. The crisis remains a major event in Canadian history.

The Crimean War (1853–1856) was fought mainly on the Crimean Peninsula, which extends into the Black Sea. Russia faced an alliance of the Ottoman Empire, Britain, France, and Sardinia as the powers competed for influence in the Black Sea region and Ottoman territories. The war is remembered for the long siege of the Russian port of Sevastopol and for Florence Nightingale’s care of wounded soldiers. One famous event was the Charge of the Light Brigade at the 1854 Battle of Balaclava. Because of a mistaken order, British cavalry rode directly toward Russian artillery and suffered heavy losses. Alfred, Lord Tennyson commemorated their courage in a poem about roughly 600 soldiers riding into the “valley of Death.”

The Gunpowder Plot was a failed conspiracy in 1605 by English Catholics who hoped to end the Protestant rule of King James I and put a Catholic-friendly monarch on the throne. The plotters planned to blow up the House of Lords during the state opening of Parliament, killing the king and many political leaders. Before the opening, an anonymous letter warning of danger was delivered to William Parker, 4th Baron Monteagle, a Catholic peer. He passed it to the royal government, helping prompt a search of Westminster. On 5 November, Guy Fawkes was arrested while guarding barrels of gunpowder stored beneath the chamber. The discovery stopped the attack, and the plot’s failure is still remembered in Britain on 5 November.

The 2018 North Korea–United States Singapore Summit took place on June 12, 2018, at the Capella Singapore hotel on Sentosa Island. It was the first meeting between a sitting U.S. president, Donald Trump, and a North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un. The meeting followed years of tension over North Korea’s nuclear weapons and missile tests, including tests of intercontinental ballistic missiles. Trump and Kim issued a joint statement promising to work toward better relations between their countries and the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. The summit was historic because the two leaders met face to face, but their statement did not set out detailed steps or a timetable for North Korea to give up its nuclear weapons.

In 1685, King Louis XIV of France issued the Edict of Fontainebleau, named for the royal palace where it was proclaimed. It revoked the Edict of Nantes, a 1598 settlement made by King Henry IV that had given limited religious protections to French Protestants. These Protestants, many of whom followed the teachings of John Calvin, were called Huguenots. Louis XIV wanted religious unity under the Catholic Church, so the new edict ended official toleration of Protestant worship and increased pressure on Huguenots to convert. Despite restrictions on leaving France, many fled persecution and settled in Protestant areas, including the Dutch Republic and Brandenburg-Prussia. The edict was a major turning point in French religious history because it drove a large Protestant community out of the country.

Aldo Moro was a leading Italian politician in the Christian Democratic Party and served several terms as prime minister. During the Cold War, he supported the Historic Compromise, an effort to bring his party and the Italian Communist Party into closer cooperation and make Italy’s government more stable. This approach was controversial at a time when many feared communist influence. Italy was also living through the Years of Lead, a period of political violence involving extremist groups. In March 1978, a far-left militant group called the Red Brigades kidnapped Moro and killed five members of his escort. After holding him captive for 55 days, the group murdered him. Moro’s death shocked Italy and became one of the best-known events of the Years of Lead.

World War I soldiers fought in the armies of the 1914–1918 conflict, often facing trench warfare, artillery fire, and poison gas. The English poet Wilfred Owen served in the British Army and wrote about the suffering of ordinary soldiers rather than celebrating battle. In “Dulce et Decorum Est,” weary men scramble to put on gas masks during an attack, but one soldier fails and appears in the speaker’s recurring nightmare, “guttering, choking, drowning.” The poem challenges the idea that dying for one’s country is glorious. In “Anthem for Doomed Youth,” Owen asks what funeral bells can honor soldiers killed in war and mourns the young lives lost. Owen himself was killed in action on 4 November 1918, one week before the Armistice ended the fighting.

Winnie Madikizela-Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid activist and politician who became a highly visible leader while her husband, Nelson Mandela, was imprisoned on Robben Island. Apartheid was a system of racial segregation that denied Black South Africans political rights and freedom of movement. Winnie spoke out against it and helped organize resistance despite repeated arrests and government surveillance. In 1977, the apartheid government banished her from Soweto to Brandfort, a remote town in the Orange Free State. She remained there under severe restrictions until 1985, but continued her political organizing. Her determination made her a symbol of resistance, although her later association with violent actions by her supporters made her legacy controversial.

Vespasian was a Roman general who became emperor in AD 69, after Nero’s death sparked a struggle for power known as the Year of the Four Emperors. Vespasian’s forces defeated those of rival claimants, and he founded the Flavian dynasty. Before becoming emperor, he had led a campaign against the Great Jewish Revolt alongside his son Titus. Vespasian left the campaign to claim the throne, and Titus later completed the conquest of Jerusalem. In Rome, Vespasian began building the Colosseum, also called the Flavian Amphitheater, on the site of an artificial lake in Nero’s palace complex. Titus inaugurated the huge arena after his father’s death. It became famous for gladiator fights and other public spectacles, including staged naval battles.

Whaling is the hunting of whales and the processing of their bodies into useful products. For centuries, whale blubber was rendered into oil that fueled lamps, especially before kerosene became common in the 1800s. Whaling voyages could last months or years, with sailors working together to sail the ship, launch smaller boats, and bring in their catch. They sometimes sang sea shanties to coordinate tasks such as hoisting sails. During the early U.S. whaling trade, Nantucket, an island off Massachusetts, was a leading center. As ships grew larger and the trade changed, the industry shifted toward mainland ports such as New Bedford. Nantucket’s whaling history is commemorated at the Nantucket Whaling Museum.

Klemens von Metternich was a conservative Austrian statesman and diplomat who played a leading role in European politics after the Napoleonic Wars. He chaired the Congress of Vienna, a diplomatic gathering held in 1814–15 to redraw Europe’s borders after Napoleon’s defeat. Metternich wanted a balance of power among the major countries so that none could dominate the others, and he opposed revolutionary movements that threatened Europe’s monarchies. He famously called Italy a “geographic expression” because the Italian peninsula was then divided among separate states rather than united as one country. Later in the 19th century, Charles Albert, king of Piedmont-Sardinia, tried to unify Italy. When revolutions swept Europe in 1848, Metternich was forced to resign.

The Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, dominated Mexican politics for much of the twentieth century. Founded in 1929 as the National Revolutionary Party (PNR), it later became the Party of the Mexican Revolution (PRM) before adopting its final name in 1946. Its candidates held Mexico’s presidency continuously from 1929 to 2000. During this period, the outgoing president usually chose the party’s next presidential nominee through a practice called the Dedazo, giving him great influence over who would succeed him. One PRI president, Lázaro Cárdenas, nationalized Mexico’s oil industry in 1938 and created the state-owned company Pemex. The PRI’s 71-year hold on the presidency ended in the 2000 election, when Vicente Fox of the National Action Party defeated PRI candidate Francisco Labastida. Fox took office that December.

Cato the Elder was a Roman soldier, statesman, and writer who lived from 234 to 149 BCE. He fought in the Second Punic War, one of the wars between Rome and Carthage for power in the Mediterranean. He later served as consul in 195 BCE and censor in 184 BCE, a role that included overseeing public morals and the list of Roman citizens. Cato valued traditional Roman habits, especially hard work and simple living. After visiting Carthage in his old age, he came to see the city as a threat to Rome. He became famous for ending speeches with the demand that “Carthage must be destroyed.” Cato also wrote De agri cultura, a practical guide to farming and estate management that is often considered the oldest surviving complete work of Latin prose.

The RMS Lusitania was a British Cunard ocean liner that carried passengers across the Atlantic. During World War I, it left New York for Liverpool, England, but never reached its destination. On May 7, 1915, the German submarine U-20 torpedoed it off the southern coast of Ireland. The submarine’s commander was German naval officer Walther Schwieger. The Lusitania sank quickly, killing nearly 1,200 people, including Americans. Germany called its submarines U-boats and used them to attack ships traveling to Britain. The sinking shocked people around the world and heightened tensions between Germany and the United States. Although the United States did not enter the war immediately, the attack helped turn American public opinion against Germany.

The Janissaries were an elite infantry corps of the Ottoman Empire, an Islamic empire centered on what is now Turkey. For centuries, many recruits came through the devşirme levy, which took Christian boys from parts of the empire, converted them to Islam, and trained them for imperial service. Janissaries became highly skilled soldiers and an important part of the Ottoman army, especially as the empire expanded. Over time, however, they gained political power and resisted changes to their privileges and military practices. In 1826, Sultan Mahmud II ordered Ottoman forces to suppress the Janissaries after they opposed his plans for a reformed army. The destruction of the corps is known as the Auspicious Incident, and it cleared the way for a new Ottoman army.

Belisarius was a leading Byzantine general under Emperor Justinian I, who sought to restore lands once ruled by the Roman Empire. In 533, Belisarius led an army into North Africa and defeated the Vandals at the Battle of Ad Decimum, helping the Byzantines regain the region. He then fought the Ostrogoths in the Gothic War, a campaign to recover Italy. In 540, the Ostrogoths surrendered Ravenna to Belisarius. Ravenna had been an Ostrogothic capital and became a key center of Byzantine rule in Italy. Belisarius’s victories made him one of the most successful commanders of Justinian’s reign, although holding the reconquered territories proved difficult.

Pemex, short for Petróleos Mexicanos, is Mexico’s state-owned oil company. It was created in 1938 after President Lázaro Cárdenas nationalized the country’s oil industry, bringing oil production under Mexican government control instead of leaving it largely in the hands of foreign companies. The decision made oil a symbol of national independence and gave the government a major role in Mexico’s economy. Pemex became responsible for finding, producing, refining, and selling petroleum, an important source of fuel and public revenue. Its history also shows the risks of oil production: in 1979, a blowout at its Ixtoc I well in the Gulf of Mexico caused one of the world’s largest oil spills.

Swiss banks are financial institutions in Switzerland, a country known for its neutrality during World War II. A 1934 Swiss banking law strengthened client privacy: Article 47 made it a crime for bank employees to reveal confidential customer information. During the war, some Swiss banks held gold that Nazi Germany had looted from occupied territories. Decades later, questions arose about whether the banks had properly accounted for assets belonging to Holocaust victims and their families. In 1997, Christoph Meili, a Swiss security guard, found documents at UBS that were marked for destruction and appeared relevant to Holocaust-era assets. He took the documents rather than letting them be destroyed, drawing international attention to the controversy over Swiss banking secrecy and the fate of wartime assets.

In classical Athens, ostracism was a democratic procedure used to send a citizen into exile, usually for ten years, without taking away their property. Citizens scratched the name of the person they wanted removed onto a shard of broken pottery, called an ostrakon; the plural, ostraka, gives ostracism its name. The vote could be used against someone thought to be gaining too much power or threatening the city. One person affected was Xanthippus, who was recalled from exile during the Second Persian invasion of Greece. His son Pericles later became a leading statesman during Athens’s Golden Age. Pericles also delivered a famous funeral oration for Athenians who died in the Peloponnesian War, recorded by the historian Thucydides.

Burisma is a Ukrainian natural-gas company founded in 2002 that grew into one of the country’s largest private gas producers. It became internationally known for its connection to U.S. politics. In 2014, Hunter Biden joined Burisma’s board of directors, where he served until 2019. Hunter is a Yale-trained lawyer and co-founder of the investment firm Rosemont Seneca Partners. His appointment drew scrutiny because his father, Joe Biden, was then vice president of the United States and was involved in U.S. policy toward Ukraine. Critics questioned whether Burisma hoped to gain influence or improve its reputation by appointing him. The controversy made the company a frequent subject of political debate, but questions about the appointment do not, by themselves, establish wrongdoing by either Biden.

Anne Boleyn was the second of King Henry VIII’s six wives and the mother of the future Queen Elizabeth I. Henry wanted to end his marriage to his first wife, Catherine of Aragon, so he could marry Anne, but the pope would not grant him an annulment. Henry therefore broke with the Roman Catholic Church and established royal authority over the Church of England. Anne became queen in 1533. During her queenship, Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy in 1534, declaring Henry the supreme head of the Church of England and rejecting the pope’s authority in England. Anne later lost Henry’s favor after she did not give birth to a surviving son. Accused of treason, she was executed at the Tower of London in 1536.

Hernán Cortés was a Spanish conquistador who led an expedition into Mexico in 1519. There he encountered the Aztec Empire, whose capital was Tenochtitlan, on the site of modern-day Mexico City. Cortés and his forces took the Aztec ruler, Moctezuma II (also called Montezuma II), captive, but resistance to the Spaniards grew. After an uprising in 1520, the Spaniards tried to flee Tenochtitlan at night. Many died during the retreat, which became known as La Noche Triste, or “the Sad Night.” Cortés later returned with Indigenous allies, and their forces captured Tenochtitlan in 1521, bringing down the Aztec Empire. His conquest was a turning point in Spanish colonization of the Americas, though it caused enormous suffering for Indigenous peoples.

Pope Alexander III reigned from 1159 to 1181, when popes and Holy Roman emperors were competing for power in Europe. His main imperial opponent was Frederick I, known as Frederick Barbarossa, or “Red Beard.” Alexander’s election was disputed, and Frederick supported a rival claimant to the papal throne, known as an antipope. Alexander resisted the emperor and excommunicated him, while Frederick tried to strengthen imperial control in northern Italy. After subduing Milan, Frederick convened the Diet of Roncaglia to assert his authority over Italian cities. Their conflict eventually ended in a settlement that recognized Alexander as pope. Years later, Frederick joined the Third Crusade, in which Richard the Lionheart fought against Saladin, but drowned in the Saleph River on the journey.

In 1888, a series of murders in Whitechapel, a crowded and poor district of London, frightened the public and drew intense newspaper attention. At least five women, often called the “canonical five,” are widely believed to have been killed by the same unidentified person. The name Jack the Ripper became attached to the killer, but no one was ever proved to be responsible. Some victims’ organs were removed, prompting speculation that the murderer had medical training, though this remains uncertain. One theory claimed that Jack the Ripper was a physician serving Queen Victoria, the British monarch who reigned in 1888. Victoria ruled from 1837 to 1901, making her Britain’s longest-reigning monarch until Elizabeth II surpassed her reign in 2015.

Ashurbanipal was the last great king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, which dominated much of the ancient Near East in the seventh century BCE. He ruled from Nineveh, the Assyrian capital and his seat of government, in what is now northern Iraq. Ashurbanipal expanded the empire through military campaigns, but he is also remembered for learning. At Nineveh, he assembled a royal library containing thousands of clay tablets inscribed with cuneiform writing. They preserved literature, religious works, and records, including a version of the Epic of Gilgamesh. The library’s surviving tablets have helped historians understand ancient Mesopotamian cultures. Although Ashurbanipal’s reign was a high point for Assyria, the empire weakened after his death, and Nineveh fell to enemy forces in 612 BCE.

Gustavo Petro is a Colombian left-wing politician who became president in August 2022. Earlier in his life, he belonged to the M-19 movement, which began as an armed rebel group and later entered democratic politics. He also served as mayor of Bogotá, Colombia’s capital. Petro won the 2022 presidential runoff as the candidate of the Historic Pact, a coalition of left-wing parties and movements. His campaign focused on reducing inequality and addressing climate change. One of his pledges was to stop issuing new contracts for oil exploration, a significant proposal for an oil-producing country. This climate goal relates to the 2015 Paris Agreement, an international treaty in which countries agreed to keep global warming well below 2°C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

Tomás de Torquemada was a Dominican friar from Valladolid who became the first Grand Inquisitor, or chief official, of the Spanish Inquisition in 1483. This royal tribunal was established under Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile to investigate alleged heresy and enforce Catholic religious orthodoxy. Torquemada directed its early expansion across their kingdoms. The Inquisition paid particular attention to conversos, Jews who had converted to Christianity, and later to moriscos, Muslims who had converted. People accused of heresy could face questioning, punishment, and public ceremonies known as autos-da-fé, at which some had to wear garments called sanbenitos. Torquemada is also associated with the 1492 Alhambra Decree, which ordered Jews who did not convert to leave Spain.

Unit 731 was a secret Imperial Japanese Army organization that developed biological weapons during World War II. Its main complex was near Harbin in Japanese-occupied Manchuria, in northeastern China. Led by army physician and microbiologist Shiro Ishii, the unit tested diseases such as plague on prisoners, often killing them, to study how infections spread and how they might be used in warfare. Its victims included Chinese civilians and prisoners of war. After Japan’s defeat, U.S. officials sought Unit 731’s experimental data and granted Ishii and other members immunity from prosecution in exchange. Today, Unit 731 is remembered as an example of wartime atrocities and the abuse of medical research.

Sophia Alekseyevna was a daughter of Tsar Alexis and the half-sister of Peter the Great. When Alexis’s successor died in 1682, a dispute broke out over whether Sophia’s younger half-brother Ivan or the even younger Peter should rule. The Streltsy, a corps of Russian infantrymen, revolted in Moscow and intervened in the succession struggle. After the uprising, Ivan V and Peter I shared the throne, while Sophia governed as regent because both were young and Ivan was in poor health. She remained in power until 1689, when Peter’s supporters removed her from the regency. Peter later became Russia’s sole ruler and carried out major reforms. Sophia’s story shows how soldiers and rival royal families could influence who held power in early modern Russia.

Sinn Féin is an Irish political party founded in 1905 by the journalist and nationalist Arthur Griffith. Its name means “Ourselves,” reflecting the idea that Irish people should govern themselves rather than be ruled from London. The party became closely associated with the campaign for Irish independence and later with Irish republicanism, which seeks a united, independent Ireland. After winning seats in the British Parliament in 1918, Sinn Féin representatives refused to take them and instead formed an Irish assembly called Dáil Éireann. This practice of not taking seats in the British Parliament, known as abstentionism, has continued among the party’s elected members. Griffith served as president of Dáil Éireann in 1922. He died that year, during the Irish Civil War.

An embassy is a country’s permanent diplomatic mission in another country, usually located in the host country’s capital. It is led by an ambassador and staffed by diplomats who manage official relations with the host government, assist citizens abroad, and help resolve disputes. Embassies can also become targets during international conflicts. In 1979, after a revolution brought Ayatollah Khomeini to power in Iran, militant students seized the U.S. embassy in Tehran and held American hostages for 444 days. In August 1998, the jihadist organization al-Qaeda carried out coordinated bombings of the U.S. embassies in Nairobi, Kenya, and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, killing more than 200 people. These events show both the importance of embassies and the risks diplomats and embassy staff can face.

The Canadian fur trade was a colonial-era exchange in which European traders offered manufactured goods, such as metal tools and cloth, to Indigenous communities for animal pelts, especially beaver fur used to make fashionable hats in Europe. Indigenous peoples were skilled hunters, traders, and guides whose partnerships helped shape trade routes and alliances across what is now Canada. The trade also changed local economies and contributed to the emergence of Métis communities, whose ancestors included Indigenous people and European fur traders. In 1670, the English Hudson’s Bay Company received a royal charter granting it exclusive trading rights in Rupert’s Land, a vast region whose rivers drained into Hudson Bay. Competition between trading companies helped drive European expansion into the continent’s interior.

The Red Brigades were a far-left armed organization active in Italy during the Years of Lead, a period from the late 1960s to the 1980s marked by political violence and terrorism. They wanted to overthrow Italy’s government and replace it with a revolutionary socialist system. Their most notorious crime was the 1978 kidnapping of Aldo Moro, a former prime minister and leading member of the Christian Democrats. Moro had helped pursue the Historic Compromise, an effort to bring his party and the Italian Communist Party into political cooperation. The Red Brigades seized him as he traveled to parliament, held him captive for 55 days, and then killed him. His murder shocked Italy and became one of the defining events of the Years of Lead.

The Assad family ruled Syria for decades after Hafez al-Assad seized power in 1970. Hafez, a military officer and leading member of Syria’s Ba’ath Party, ousted his rival Salah Jadid in a takeover he called the Corrective Revolution. The name suggested that he was correcting the policies of the previous government. Hafez became president in 1971 and built a tightly controlled state in which the Ba’ath Party, the military, and security forces held great power. After his death in 2000, his son Bashar al-Assad became president, continuing the family’s rule. The dynasty remained in power through years of civil war but ended when Bashar’s government fell in 2024.

Aurangzeb was the sixth emperor of the Mughal Empire, which ruled much of the Indian subcontinent. When his father, Shah Jahan, became seriously ill in 1657, Aurangzeb and his brothers fought over who would succeed him. In 1658, Aurangzeb defeated his elder brother Dara Shikoh at the Battle of Samugarh, near Agra. This victory was a turning point in the struggle for the throne, and Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 to 1707. Through lengthy military campaigns, he expanded Mughal rule across much of the subcontinent. He also fought the British East India Company in Child’s War. The company failed to defeat his forces and had to pay a large fine before it could resume trading.

The Revolutions of 1848 were a wave of uprisings across Europe, often called the “Springtime of the Peoples.” Beginning in France, they spread through the German states, the Habsburg Empire, and parts of Italy. Protesters demanded constitutional government, greater political rights, social reform, and national self-determination—the right of peoples to govern themselves. In the German states, elected delegates met in the Frankfurt Parliament to draft a liberal constitution and consider uniting Germany. They offered the crown of a united Germany to Prussian King Friedrich Wilhelm IV, but he refused it, and the effort failed. The revolutions did not achieve most of their immediate goals, but they shaped later debates about German unification. In 1862, Otto von Bismarck criticized the failures of 1848 in his “Blood and Iron” speech.

The Grand Principality of Hungary was an early Hungarian state that emerged after the Magyars conquered and settled the Pannonian, or Carpathian, Basin in the late ninth century. Tradition credits Árpád, the son of Álmos, with leading the Magyars into the region. His descendants formed the Árpád dynasty, the ruling house of the principality. At first, the Magyars followed their own traditions and were led by princes rather than Christian kings. Around the year 1000, Árpád’s descendant Stephen I became Hungary’s first Christian king, marking the transition from the grand principality to the Kingdom of Hungary. The Árpád dynasty continued to supply Hungary’s monarchs until its male line ended in 1301.

The Global Silver Trade was the early modern movement of silver bullion—silver in bars or coins—across oceans, especially into China. Spanish colonies in the Americas produced enormous amounts of silver. Potosí, a mining city in present-day Bolivia, became famous for Cerro Rico, a mountain that yielded vast quantities of the metal. Silver from New Spain also crossed the Pacific: ships carried it from Acapulco to Manila in the Philippines, where merchants exchanged it for Chinese silk, porcelain, and other goods. China was a major destination because silver was widely used there as money and to pay taxes. Later, Western merchants trading at Canton, also called Guangzhou, paid for Chinese products with silver before turning to the illegal opium trade.

Oskar Schindler was a German businessman who ran an enamelware factory in Kraków, Poland, during World War II. At first, he profited from the forced labor of Jewish workers, but as Nazi persecution intensified, he used his money and connections to protect them. In 1944, he arranged for more than a thousand Jewish workers to be transferred to a factory in Brünnlitz, where they survived the Holocaust. Their names became known as “Schindler’s list.” His actions inspired Steven Spielberg’s 1993 film Schindler’s List. The film is largely black and white, but a girl in a red coat stands out during its portrayal of the Nazi liquidation of the Kraków ghetto.

The Sri Lankan Civil War was fought from 1983 to 2009 between Sri Lanka’s government, dominated by the Sinhalese ethnic majority, and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, also known as the Tamil Tigers. The Tigers sought an independent homeland called Eelam for the country’s Tamil minority, mainly in the north and east. Velupillai Prabhakaran founded and led the Tamil Tigers throughout the war. The conflict grew out of long-standing tensions over political power, language, and discrimination against Tamils. It involved guerrilla warfare, bombings, and major military offensives, causing tens of thousands of deaths and forcing many civilians from their homes. In May 2009, government forces defeated the Tigers in a final offensive, killing Prabhakaran and ending the war.

Konrad Adenauer was the first chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany, commonly called West Germany. A leader of the Christian Democratic Union, he took office when West Germany was founded in 1949 and served until 1963. After World War II, Germany was divided and its economy badly damaged. At the 1945 Potsdam Conference, an Allied meeting at a palace near Berlin, the victorious powers agreed on arrangements for administering defeated Germany; West Germany’s coal and steel industries faced restrictions in the following years. Adenauer helped rebuild the country, including through American Marshall Plan aid, during a period of rapid growth known as the “economic miracle.” He also strengthened West Germany’s ties with the United States and Western Europe during the Cold War.

Rollo was a Viking leader whose followers raided and settled in what is now northern France. In 911, he reached an agreement with Charles the Simple, the Carolingian king who ruled West Francia from 898 to 922. Under the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, Charles granted Rollo land around the lower Seine River in exchange for his allegiance and a promise to help defend the region from other Viking attacks. Rollo was baptized as Robert, but his Norse name was Rollo. His territory became the foundation of Normandy, named for the “Northmen” who settled there. Rollo is often described as Normandy’s first duke, although rulers of the region did not use that title at first. His son William Longsword succeeded him.

The Communist Party of Germany, or KPD, was founded in late 1918 by revolutionaries including Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. It grew out of the Spartacist movement, which sought a socialist revolution after Germany’s defeat in World War I. Ernst Thälmann led the party during the 1932 elections, when it competed with Adolf Hitler’s far-right Nazi Party. After Hitler became chancellor, a fire broke out on 27 February 1933 at the Reichstag, Germany’s parliament building in Berlin. The Nazis blamed a Dutch communist for the Reichstag fire and used it as a pretext for an emergency decree that suspended civil liberties. Communist politicians were arrested, helping Hitler weaken his opponents and consolidate power.

Mansa is a Mandinka royal title meaning “king” or “emperor.” It was used by rulers of the Mali Empire, a powerful medieval state in West Africa founded by Sundiata Keita. One of its best-known rulers was Mansa Musa, also called Musa I. During his reign, Mali grew wealthy through trade, especially in gold and salt, and the city of Timbuktu became an important center of commerce and Islamic learning. Scholars studied and taught at Timbuktu’s Sankore mosque and university. Centuries later, Europeans often described Timbuktu as a mysterious, hard-to-reach place. Remember the distinction: Mansa was the ruler’s title, while Timbuktu was a famous city within the empire.

The Huguenots were French Protestants who followed the teachings of John Calvin. In the 1500s, religious tensions between Catholics and Protestants helped spark the French Wars of Religion, in which Huguenots fought against the Catholic-led French crown. Thousands of Huguenots were killed in the 1572 St. Bartholomew’s Day massacre. After decades of conflict, King Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, granting Huguenots limited freedom to worship and some civil rights, though France remained a Catholic kingdom. In 1685, King Louis XIV revoked the edict, renewing persecution. Many Huguenots then fled France, including to Brandenburg-Prussia, where rulers offered incentives for them to settle.
